At daybreak the cheeks of the main topgallant crosstrees were found broken; the crosstrees were at once lashed under the cap with a stout seizing. The rigging was set up. At noon in 30° 31' 47" of latitude observed and in 54° 44' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 47' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 21' 30" of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 56° 15' E.

1801-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light variable air from SE. At 4.30 made all sail and trimmed close-hauled.
1801-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the sixteenth the weather continued fine and the winds remained at south-east, but so light that there was every appearance of a calm coming on. The sea was extremely smooth, and yet a long south-easterly swell made us roll a great deal. There is every appearance that some gales from that quarter must have passed through these waters, and that they must have been violent.
At noon our observed latitude was 29° 44' south and the longitude by dead reckoning 51° 35'. That given by our timekeepers placed us in 53° 28' 50" according to No. 38, and in 53° 57' 58" according to No. 38 (sic). From the Naturaliste they signalled 54° 30' to us, which made a difference all the more considerable as our timekeepers had always placed us further east than those of that ship, which was then ahead.
In the forenoon we took more than thirty distances of the sun from the moon to check the previous day's observations, and their result, taking a mean, gave for the observed longitude 55° 28' 48", and consequently a difference to the east of 1° 59' 58" from the mean of our timekeepers. The agreement of this observation with the preceding one, which had given 2° 7' 40", confirmed to us that our timekeepers were behind by that amount, and tomorrow, if the weather permits, we shall check by fresh observations this error, which we had not even suspected.
During the evening the winds varied from south-east to south-south-east, the sky still very fine and the winds light. Taking advantage of the fine weather, we caught various kinds of molluscs, and above all a small chambered nautilus with its creature, which gave us all the more more (sic) pleasure as there is every reason to believe that the animal is not known, although its shell is found almost everywhere.
In the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth the weather was very fine and the sky clear, but the winds drew nearer to the east, and at times we had them at east-south-east, very light. We continued to steer north-east with all sail set.
1801-03-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE and SSE. At noon in 29° 43' 12" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 27' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 10' of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 45° E. At 6 the Naturaliste asked to pass under our stern, which we granted. At 7 we spoke, and Captain Hamelin gave us the result of his lunar observations.

1801-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, the wind SE to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth the winds came back to south-east and south-east by south, almost calm. The sky was cloudy and fine. At various times squalls formed in several points of the horizon, but none came near us, and the heat of the sun seemed to have absorbed them before they had risen to any height above the horizon.
In the forenoon we multiplied our observations by distances, and their result placed us in 56° 8' 45". The mean longitude of the timekeepers at the same time was 53° 59' 19", so that we found, to within a few minutes, the same difference as on the preceding days, which seems to establish quite positively that our timekeepers were running slow.
In the forenoon we saw, for only the second time since our departure from Tenerife, three or four tropicbirds, which came and played above the ship's vane. But they kept too high to be shot at with a musket. Since the thirty-second degree we had lost sight of the albatrosses.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 41' and the longitude by dead reckoning 51° 59'. Timekeeper No. 31 then placed us in 53° 46' 56" and No. 38 in 54° 11' 42", which gave us, for the run made, a difference to the north of 4' 43" and another to the east of 6' 42".
During the evening the weather was fine, but there was little wind, and although we had all sail set we made little way.
The mean result of several azimuths and amplitudes gave a north-west variation of 18° 27' 30".
The night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth was fine, and although the sky was at times covered with clouds coming from the south, they passed over our heads without bringing us any wind. They moved, however, fast enough to give us reason to believe that in a more southerly latitude it must be blowing a stiff breeze from that quarter. Although all our observations of longitude placed us in that of the Isle of France [Mauritius], I would not alter course and continued to steer north-east, not believing myself certain enough that our timekeepers, whose rate had been so regular as far as the Cape of Good Hope, could have undergone, between the Cape and the spot where we (now) are, so considerable a difference as the one we have noticed these three days past.
1801-03-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from SE to SW. At noon in 28° 40' 40" of latitude observed and in 55° 52' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 58' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 38' of longitude. Light rain during the night.

1801-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SW, WSW, NW and SW. The sea smooth. At 10 we had a squall which brought the winds round to SSW.
1801-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the eighteenth the winds remained at south-west and the calm continued until eight o'clock. In the forenoon there were squalls in almost every point of the horizon, each driven by a different wind. Several of them passed over us on board, bringing abundant rain and no wind. In the intervals we repeated our observations by distances, the result of which again gave 2° 27' 42" east of the timekeepers, but the weather had not been very favourable and we set little store by these latest results.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 3' 32" and the longitude by dead reckoning 52° 15' 5". That then given by our timekeepers was, for No. 31, 54° 4' 54" and by No. 38, 54° 34' 12". We found in the 24 hours a difference to the east of 1° 16' and one to the north of 7' 7 seconds.
Scarcely was it noon when we had a squall that brought the winds round to south-south-east, and it blew a pleasant breeze. We thought that once the squall had passed we should again have a calm, but this time we were mistaken to our advantage, for the winds, having settled in the south, went on steadily increasing. We were even afraid that the weather might turn bad during the night, so heavy was the sky with dark clouds and so ugly its look. The barometer seemed inclined to fall, and we accordingly took our precautions for the night by furling our mainsail and our topgallant sails, which we did not need in order to keep company with the Naturaliste, though she had all sail set.
In the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth we did not have the bad weather that appearances had foretold. Quite the contrary: it blew a very good breeze from south to south-south-east, and we made good way steering north-east. For although our observed distances placed us much further east than the timekeepers, I found it hard to believe that their rate had suffered the retardation we thought we had perceived. During the night the weather was very cloudy and a few good gusts passed over, yet we lowered, at times, of (sic) our topsails only to wait for the Naturaliste, which was crowding sail to follow us.
1801-03-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At noon in 28° 3' 32" of latitude observed and in 56° 49' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 18° 8' NW. The lunar distances gave 56° 2' of longitude.

1801-03-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy and the winds a strong breeze from SSW to south. The mizzen topsail sheet having parted, we clewed the sail up to leeward to repair it.
1801-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth we had very fine weather and a pleasant breeze, variable in the forenoon from south to south-south-east, and we made good way. The winds continued so in the afternoon and during the night, so that the twenty-four hours gave the longest run we had made since rounding the Cape of Good Hope. It was beyond dispute the finest day of our voyage, since the fair wind we had was accompanied by a fine sky.
At noon the observed latitude was 25° 2' south and the longitude by dead reckoning 53° 54' 51". That given by the timekeepers was, for No. 31, 55° 31' 9" and by No. 38, 56° 8', which gave us, in the twenty-four hours, a difference to the north of 9' 30" and one to the west of 17' 18".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, and at four o'clock I signalled to the Naturaliste that at midnight we should steer north-north-east, as I found myself far enough to the east not to fear making the land to leeward of the Isle of France [Mauritius]; I feared, on the contrary, finding myself too far to windward of it if our longitudes observed by distances were better than those given by our timekeepers.
On board the Naturaliste the timekeepers gave 30' more to the east than ours, which seems to us all the more astonishing as they had always shown a more westerly longitude, and it will only be on our arrival at the Isle of France that we shall truly be able to know which have kept the most regular rate. I am inclined to believe, as I have already remarked, that the great damp we long experienced may have somewhat altered their daily motion, although very little difference has been observed in the comparisons.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the weather continued fine and the winds shifted to south-east; the breeze was less strong. Nevertheless we made tolerably good way, carrying only as much sail as was needed to keep pace with the Naturaliste, which had all she could carry.
1801-03-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 25° 2' 50" of latitude observed and in 57° 29' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 14° 17' NW. At noon the course was signalled and given N 33° 45' E. At 4 signalled the course N 22° 30' E for midnight.

1801-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea and the wind light from south, SE and SSE. At noon the course was signalled us NE by N until midnight, when we were to steer NNE.
1801-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth the weather continued fine, but the breeze was much lighter than the day before, and these twenty-four hours gave us no more than a very ordinary day. In the morning the winds came round to south-east by south; in the afternoon they went back to south-south-east, and towards evening to the south.
After sunrise we were visited by a fair number of tropicbirds, which stayed about us for some time and then disappeared.
In the morning we began caulking those of our boats that needed it, and made ready the capstans, which were encumbered by our plant boxes; I had had these lashed round them, as the place best suited to their safety.
At noon the observed latitude was 22° 50' and the longitude by dead reckoning 54° 34' 51". That by No. 31 was then 55° 54' 12" and that by No. 38 56° 20' 54". In these twenty-four hours there was a difference of 56 seconds to the north and 17' 8 seconds to the east.
In the afternoon the breeze was very light. The Naturaliste, which was at half cannon-shot, asked to pass under our stern, and we spoke each other. It was agreed to continue on a north-north-east course until noon the next day, and that during the twenty-first the anchors would be got ready for anchoring. The longitude shown by her timekeepers was 30' further east than ours, and that from six lunar distance observations 36° 58' (sic), which gave her a small difference from ours, placing us a little further to the east.
The mean result of two amplitudes and two azimuths gave a variation of 13° 30' north-west; on board the Naturaliste they had 14° 30'.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first the sky was very cloudy and the wind almost calm; for some hours it was then in the south and even south-south-west. There were a few clouds that gave a little rain, but only in small quantity. The sea was fairly smooth, and yet the ship rolled a great deal, running before the wind.
1801-03-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 2 a.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the second time, in 58° 6' of longitude. The rigging was set up. At noon in 22° 48' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 9' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 55' NW. At 5.30 we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander told Captain Hamelin to bend his sheet cables without waiting for the signal.

1801-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind light from SE, south, SSW and south. We asked the commander whether we should bend the cables without waiting for a signal; he answered no.
1801-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first we had very light weather and the winds singularly variable from south-south-west to south-east by way of the south. As there was little wind, we rolled a great deal. The sea, though smooth, had a heavy and very high (swell) from the south. In the morning we saw a great many tropicbirds, but we remarked that they never showed themselves in the afternoon, which seemed to us all the more singular since from early morning, at sunrise, they were already hovering above the masthead vane.
In the morning the cables were bent on, and the anchors were made ready to be let go when the time came.
At noon we observed the latitude as 21° 49' 54", and the longitude by dead reckoning was 54° 59' 58". That by No. 31, reduced to noon, was 56° 13' 48", and by No. 38 56° 42' 0. We found that in the twenty-four hours we had a difference to the north of 7 minutes 47 seconds and one to the east of 5 minutes 54 seconds.
In the afternoon the winds were southerly, a light breeze, and I signalled the course north by east, finding myself, by the rate of the timekeepers, far enough to windward not to miss the Isle of France [Mauritius], and much too far advanced if our observations of longitude are good, since they place us nearly two degrees east of the timekeepers.
The mean result of two amplitudes at rising and setting, combined with that of two azimuths, gave a north-west variation of 12° 30' for the evening and 12° 45' for the morning, which seemed to confirm that we were well to the east of our timekeepers, since this variation is very nearly the one now observed at Rodrigues.
At the beginning of the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second there was a pretty breeze from the south-south-east, but during the night the wind fell away a great deal. We continued on a course of north by east with all sail set, in order to make ground to the north and get into the latitude of Round Island, which M. d'Après places in 19° 50' south latitude.
1801-03-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SSE. We bent our cables and got the anchors ready to let go. At noon in 21° 29' 40" of latitude observed and in 58° 14' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 49' NW. At 1.30 the course was signalled and given N 11° 15' E.

1801-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from south, SSE and SSW. At 3 the winds shifted all at once to WSW. At sunrise land was thought to be seen in the WNW; the wind fell light. Saw a great number of tropic birds.
1801-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, we had fine weather and the winds variable from south-south-west to south-south-east, a light breeze. At six o'clock I made the signal to steer north-west and to crowd all possible sail, so as to try to sight land before nightfall should a good breeze spring up during the day. But we lost that hope, for there was little wind all morning, during which we saw a great many tropicbirds. The calm of the morning proved very fortunate for us, since we caught two small fish of so bizarre a shape that I hope no one will ever have seen the like. These fish were lodged under tufts of fucus which seamen call grapes. They were the first we had met with since our departure from Europe. It appears that the season in which we passed through the general winds and the trade winds was not the time when this plant breaks away from the bottom of the sea, which is usually found covered with it in fine weather.
At noon the observed south latitude was 20° 20' 19" and the longitude by dead reckoning 54° 33' 51". By the rate of the timekeepers we found ourselves in 55° 56' 54" by No. 31. Citizen Bissy having made no observation that day, I did not have that of No. 38. In the 24 hours there was a difference of 10' 24 seconds to the south and 2' 30" to the east.
During the evening there was a pretty breeze, and we crowded sail until nightfall to try to sight the land, since by the rate of the timekeepers we ought to sight it before night.
At sunset the weather turned squally and at times we had rain. I made the signal to the Naturaliste to pass under our stern, and when she was within hail I told her that during the night we would trim our sails so as to make only three knots, and that I would heave to if the horizon was not clear enough to see some distance.
At eleven o'clock, the sky being very cloudy and overcast, we reefed the topsails and stood out to sea until four in the morning, when we headed for the land with all sail set.
1801-03-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to ESE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and given N 45° W. Saw a great deal of weed. At noon in 20° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 1' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 35' NW. At 3 the weather turned overcast, with light rain. At 4.45 signalled the Naturaliste to pass under our stern; at 6, being within hail, the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to steer N 67° 30' W, that at 8 he would regulate his canvas so as to run only 3.5 knots, and that if the weather turned bad he would heave to on the starboard tack, of which he would warn him by two lights. After speaking the Naturaliste we bore up N 67° 30' W. At 11 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under close-reefed topsails; the breeze light, with lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SE, N, NE, east and SE. At 5 passed under the commander's stern; he gave us verbal orders to run no more than three and a half knots to the WNW, and that if the weather turned bad we should heave to. At a quarter past eleven the commander hove to on the starboard tack. We did the same. At 4 a.m., the wind having shifted to the north, we went onto the port tack.
1801-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the winds suddenly shifted to north-east, a pretty breeze. As we had put our head on course, we crowded sail towards the land so as to sight it during the day, not doubting that we should have it in view before nightfall unless the rate of the timekeepers had gone amiss. Throughout the morning we saw a great number of birds of different species, which told us that we were not very far from it. Nevertheless, at noon we had not sighted it. The latitude observed at that time was 19° 54' and the longitude by dead reckoning 53° 6'. That shown by the timekeepers was then 54° 47' 17" by No. 38 and 54° 15' 19" by No. 31. In the 24 hours there was a difference of 54" to the north and 8' 38" to the west.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a pretty breeze, and we crowded sail until sunset.
At five o'clock the lookouts at the mastheads sang out land, and it was not long before we made it out from the deck. After sunset we took the following bearings.
Bearings of the land at six in the evening:
The northernmost land west 22° north!
The southernmost land west 19° 31 south!
Round Island west: 2° south! all by compass.
At seven o'clock we furled our topgallant sails and all the light sails, and at eight we trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack.
The Naturaliste, having passed under our stern, asked me what my intentions were for the night. I replied that we would keep our present position, making various boards, so as to stand early tomorrow into the passage between Round Island and Gunner's Quoin. It was also agreed that we would carry a light at the stern all night and that changes of tack would be indicated by the usual signals. During the night we had several squalls of rain with a little wind and a great deal of lightning, though without hearing the thunder roll.
1801-03-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to SE. At 5 a.m. shaped our course west, crowding sail. At noon in 19° 54' 0" of latitude observed and in 56° 34' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 53' NW. At 5 p.m. the land was sighted in the S 75° W. At 6 took the bearing of Round Island N 68° W, the southernmost point of Mauritius in sight S 70° W, and the most conspicuous peak S 88° W. At 8.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 9.30 the Naturaliste passed under our stern; Captain Hamelin asked the commander his intentions for the night, and he told him he would stand off and on until daybreak. During the night overcast and squally weather, with rain and lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.30 we made the land, and a moment later the commander signalled us the course WSW. At 1 a.m. went about, the weather stormy and squally. At daybreak we sighted the land WNW, distant about 6 leagues. The commander hailed us to steer for Round Island and to keep in his wake as close as possible. He asked whether we had anyone on board who knew the passage; we answered that we had Citizen Piquet, ensign.
1801-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at four in the morning, I made the signal to the Naturaliste to go onto the larboard tack, and we stood in towards the land. At daybreak we were much astonished to see that the current had carried us a considerable way to the south; but as there was no help for it and the lost ground had to be made up, we crowded sail to close with Round Island, which we had great difficulty in weathering because of the strength of the current and the little wind there was. The weather, however, was squally with rain, and some of the squalls gave us a little wind while they lasted.
Bearings at noon
Round Island north-east )
The highest part of Flat Island north-west by north ) all by compass
Pointe aux Canonniers west by south-west )
The land farthest to windward south )
To pass between Round Island and Gunner's Quoin we followed the Neptune Oriental, and we ranged along the latter at a cannon-shot and a half. In passing we met a race of current which threw us almost broadside on to starboard, although we then had all sail set and a good breeze.
After clearing Gunner's Quoin we steered for Pointe aux Canonniers, abreast of which we hoisted our colours, confirming them with a gun fired with powder only. The fort there did the same, but as we rounded it they lowered their flag, fired a blank gun and hoisted it again. Not knowing what this manoeuvre meant, we did the same on the off chance, and continued on our way to reach the anchorage of the Deux Frères.
At four o'clock we made out, over Île aux Tonneliers, the vessels lying in the harbour, and we expected to reach the anchorage in less than half an hour; but the winds, coming round to south-south-west, headed us and obliged us to stand out to sea. From four o'clock until eight they were very variable from S. SW to S. SE. We beat up in short boards to reach the anchorage but could not succeed, and as the calm overtook us we let go one of our bower anchors in nineteen fathoms, coral bottom, off Tombeau Bay.
As soon as we were at anchor I made the signal of it to the Naturaliste, but she did not answer, not having seen it because she had stood too far out.
During the night the weather was dead calm and the ship rode very quietly at her anchor. Until daybreak we kept a light at each of our mastheads so that the Naturaliste might see them when she came back in towards the land. That vessel anchored at eleven o'clock, half a league from us.

Citizen Péron observes in his note that the variations of the barometer have fairly generally corresponded to those of the atmosphere, especially in the first days of the decade, during which the weather was very unsettled and the state of the sky changeable. He concludes from this, and no doubt rightly, that the hygrometric state of the air has a marked influence on the fall of the mercury in the tube of the barometer. It is almost certain that the barometer would always stand at a great height if the sky, free of vapours and moisture, were always clear; and as it is only when the sky is overloaded with vapours that bad weather occurs, it is quite natural that the weight of the air should make the barometer fall all the lower as the atmosphere is more or less charged with these same vapours, which are the first and principal cause of its variations.
General observations. Thermometer
From Citizen Péron's continued observations it appears that this decade is one of those that have given us the most heat since our departure, and above all that the heat was sustained in a constant and uniform manner. From the slight difference between the results of each noon and midnight of the same day, he maintains that it is its very uniformity that is the reason we noticed it less than at other times when, although weaker, it sometimes seemed to us quite unbearable. This reasoning is perhaps not without foundation.
General observations. Hygrometer
From Citizen Péron's Remarks it appears certain that we always found a greater quantity of moisture in the atmosphere when the winds blew from the eastern quarter, varying to the north, than when we had them from the east, varying to the south. The explanation of this phenomenon will perhaps not be difficult if one considers the great extent of land to the north and its nearness to us compared with any land we might have had to the south. It seems to me quite simple to believe that the vapours drawn from the land by the sun must be in far greater quantity than those it can draw from the sea, and it is no doubt in consequence of this principle that the north winds constantly gave us a higher degree of humidity than the south winds, which, having much less land to cross to reach us, meet on their way only the vapours that the sun has been able to draw from the sea.

General observations on the temperature of the sea water
The very numerous experiments made by Citizen Péron seem, according to his report, to have fully convinced him that the temperature of the sea water at the surface is generally warmer than that of the atmosphere, at least in the waters we have crossed. He proposes to set out the cause of this phenomenon in a detailed memoir, not finding satisfactory enough what has been said of it by those who have so far concerned themselves with seeking its true cause. He does not believe, moreover, that the observations made before this voyage were numerous enough, and it is for this reason that he never failed to make them every day that we kept the sea, and in all the different variations in which we found that element, during four consecutive months at sea.
This work will no doubt be interesting and new, and natural philosophers will find in Citizen Péron's account all the information they could wish for.
State of the atmosphere during the month of Ventôse.
In the first decade the weather was generally hot, rainy and damp. Northerly winds prevailed at times, but more often they came to us from the east towards the south, moderate.
In this decade there was no electrical phenomenon nor meteors of any kind. Although we fairly often had rain and many thick black clouds in the sky, we did not hear the thunder roll, and the weather turned fine without any shift of wind.
2nd decade Up to the 25th of Ventôse
During these fifteen days the sky was fairly generally fine, with little moisture in the air, but very hot. The winds were very variable in the first days, and we then had an overcast and apparently stormy sky. Once we had reached the general south-east winds, the sky cleared and fine weather followed. Nevertheless we sometimes had rain, but it never lasted long.
It was remarked that as soon as we had the south-east winds the gusts were very frequent, and it was for this reason that the crews, who were enjoying the best of health, were forbidden to sleep in the open air, although it was very hot below decks.
On the morning of the thirteenth we saw a double rainbow, perfectly formed, but on the 23rd, following (a) heavy squall of rain, we had a triple one. It was the first time such a phenomenon had struck our eyes, and we much regretted that it did not last longer than it did.
1801-03-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.15 a.m. shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7 the commander gave verbal orders to Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at a cable's length. At 8 took the bearing of Serpent Island N 24° W, Mauritius from N 75° W to S 50° W; signalled the Naturaliste to make ready to let go a bower anchor. At noon Round Island N 45° E, Flat Island N 34° W, Pointe aux Canonniers S 79° W. At 1.30 we hoisted our colours and confirmed them with a gun. The fort of Pointe aux Canonniers hoisted the national flag and confirmed it. At 2, being abreast of it, it saluted us with the flag; we returned the salute. At 3 the breeze drew round to SSW, variable to W. We stood on whichever tack served us best, firing guns to call the pilot. At 4 took the bearing of Pointe aux Canonniers N 75° E and Pointe aux Tonneliers S 24° W. At 8, being almost becalmed, we anchored under the coast in 20 fathoms, coral bottom, the light of Île aux Tonneliers bearing south and that of Fort Diane S 22° 30' W. The shore under which we lay anchored sent up two rockets every two hours.

1801-03-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and a fresh breeze from ESE. After doubling Coin de Mire the commander signalled us to follow his movements; he was lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 3, the commander having fallen calm under the land, he went onto the starboard tack. A moment later the winds shifted to SSW; we stood on on our tack and went about a moment afterwards to run in for the land. We struggled all along against the fickleness of the winds to reach the anchorage under Île aux Tonneliers, but their weakness did not let us come near enough to the land to let go the anchor. At nightfall we fired a gun and hoisted our ensign at half mast to call a pilot. At 8.30 p.m. we stood off to seaward, the currents setting us WSW. At 10.30 p.m. we went onto the starboard tack. The winds having shifted, we ran in for the land and sounded without finding bottom; it was not until 10.35 that we found 26 and 17 fathoms. We let go the anchor in 14 fathoms, coral bottom, and veered 36 fathoms of cable. We sent a boat to sound all round the ship, Port Louis bearing from us S by E at a short distance, the commander in the NE by E at a great distance; the weather fine, a flat calm. At daybreak we showed our colours and our ensign at the stern half mast. At 6.45 we sighted a boat coming off from the shore towards us, approaching only with caution; when within hail she called to us, and on our answer she came aboard. The captain of the port, who was in her, left us a pilot and gave us a signal to identify ourselves from the shore. We were visited by the health officers and by the colonial assembly; the said captain of the port went aboard the Géographe. At 7.30 hove up, broke the anchor out and catted it. We got under way, casting to port. Favoured by a breeze off the sea, we shaped our course for Port Louis, doubled the Deux Frères at 9, leaving them to port, and doubled Île aux Tonneliers. At 10 we anchored in five fathoms and a half; shortly afterwards the Géographe came and anchored ahead of us.
1801-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
(the month of Pluviôse is here an error, and so on until the 30th: read Ventôse)
Entry into the north-west harbour of the Isle of France [Mauritius]
On the 25th, after sunrise, seeing no boat coming off from the shore, we got under sail to make for the entrance of the harbour, which we would have reached without meeting a single canoe had the breeze not failed us. However, at about seven o'clock, being some one league from the Deux Frères, we sighted a boat which we judged to be the pilot's. It went first to the Naturaliste, which was ahead of us, and shortly afterwards it came to meet us. When the officer in command of it had come on board and the first compliments were over, I asked him why he had not come out the day before in answer to the various signals that had been made. He excused himself by saying that the lookouts had signalled us as enemy vessels, and he added that our appearance had so alarmed the island that all the troops and national guards had been ordered to their respective posts, where they had spent the night, in order to oppose the landing we were supposed to have had in view. I could not help laughing at the fright that vessels as peaceable as ours had caused. And I merely observed to this officer that our conduct ought to have made us all the less suspect, since throughout the night, at the anchorage we occupied, we had had lights at all our mastheads, which is not what vessels intending hostilities usually do, since they must at least conceal their position so as not to be troubled by the artillery of the forts beneath which they lie.
However that may be, the port officer and the pilot settled the course to be steered to reach the Pavillons. But before manoeuvring accordingly, we had to make an agreed signal to the shore to make known that the vessels came from France.
(in a note at the foot of the page: Port officers and pilots are expressly forbidden to bring vessels coming from France inside the Deux Frères before the Commission I have just mentioned has been on board and has seized all the letters and public papers found there. This measure extends even to letters addressed to the administrators, and it was seen with displeasure that I handed to the aide-de-camp of the General-in-Chief those that were directed to him).
When it had been made, we steered under easy sail on the point of the compass indicated, so as to give the Intermediate Commission, representing the colony, time to come on board, seeing that no vessel coming from France may enter the passes before the members of this Commission have come on board to learn what news she brings and the reasons for her putting in.
At half past nine a harbour boat flying a flag at her stern came into view. We were at once informed that it was that of the Intermediate Commission, and preparations were made to receive it. The Naturaliste received its first visit, and half an hour later we saw four persons arrive, two of whom wore the tricolour sash.
The officer of the watch having received them in the customary manner, I then invited them into my cabin, where I was informed of the purpose of their visit. The conversation turned at first on the situation of France, but soon more particular enquiries were made about the intentions of the Government towards the Colony, &c. I was above all questioned about the nature of the expedition I was about to make, and finally whether there was not on board some secret agent charged with carrying out the decree on the freedom of the blacks. Having answered all these questions as best I could, they demanded of me the general surrender of all letters that might be on board.
I was assured on their word of honour that they would be duly delivered to their addresses. I made no difficulty about those I was carrying myself, but, not content with this particular deference, they asked me to have the pipe sounded so that the officers and the crew should comply with this measure, which they called a measure of security for the safety of the Colony. I thought I ought not to refuse this request, and the order was given as they wished. After the surrender of the letters came that of the public papers, and at last we made our way into the harbour.
As soon as the vessels were at anchor there, the members of the Intermediate Commission proposed that I should go ashore with them, which I accepted. At eleven o'clock we landed, and I was taken to Government House, which I reached only with difficulty, so crowded was the way by the number of people whom curiosity or the desire to learn the news had gathered. They all questioned me at once, and I had no other means of satisfying them than to announce that, having handed over to the Commission the public papers I had brought, they must apply to it for political news; but as for news particular to France, I assured them that everything was in the best possible order and that they would soon learn that a glorious peace would secure the stability and prosperity of the Republic.
My interview with M. Magallon, Governor General, was unremarkable. The gathering, besides, was too large for him to speak to me of business. This first meeting was confined to acquainting him with the reason for my arrival and the mission I had to fulfil. He invited me to dinner, together with M. Hamelin, and we parted.
On leaving the Governor General's I was taken to the place where the Intermediate Commission holds its sittings. There I found several of its members assembled, who were no doubt counting on my visit. After the first compliments on my safe arrival, all the letters I had handed over were inspected in my presence. I noticed that several were set aside when the others were sent to the post. Having asked why they were being held back, I was told that the tranquillity of the Colony depended on it, and that those to whom they were addressed would receive them as soon as their contents were known.
After answering the various questions put to me, I went to the municipality, where I found the hall filled with people waiting impatiently to be told the news I brought. I was seated beside the mayor, who, having announced aloud the reasons for my putting in at the Colony and the short stay I intended to make there, then read out a letter written to him by the brother of General Villaret (de) Joyeuse.
This letter stated, in substance, that General Villaret would soon arrive in the Colony as Governor-in-Chief, that he would bring with him a considerable sum for the payment of those in the Government's pay, and that he himself would go to Lima to fetch a further supply of funds, which would soon restore to the Colony the splendour it had once enjoyed. His arrival was to take place six or eight months after that of the General, et cetera, et cetera.
From the municipality I went to the Intendance, and in the Administrator who resides there I did not find the courteous and gracious welcome I had met with everywhere else. I have since learnt that he had taken it amiss that, on leaving the Governor's, I had gone to the Intermediate Commission before going to pay my respects to him. I do not know whether the order I followed compromised the dignity of the Intendant, but as I was accompanied throughout these rounds by a member of the Commission and a municipal officer, it seemed to me quite natural to follow the order they indicated.
Besides, the Ordonnateur ought rather to have blamed my guides than me, if I committed this blunder, and not to have taken his revenge in the way he did.
The rest of the day passed without incident. M. Hamelin and I dined with the General, where nothing happened worth mentioning.
1801-03-16.journal_breton_geographe: The wind a light breeze from SE. At 5 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7.30 an officer of the port and a pilot came out to us; they did not come aboard until they had asked whether there was any contagious sickness. At 10 we anchored in the North West Port in 4 fathoms, black mud mixed with grey sand, the flagstaff of Île aux Tonneliers bearing N 18° W, that of the Discovery Hill S 30° W, Le Pouce S 15° E and Pieter Both S 40° E. Several members of the colonial assembly and of the municipality came aboard. Orders were given to hand over all letters for the colony. The commander and Captain Hamelin went ashore shortly afterwards; leave to communicate with the shore was brought out to us, and many boats loaded with people, who had been waiting only for that leave, came alongside. The port's longboats helped us to moor; the boats were put in the water. Continuation. At 9 p.m., being charged with the duty of the roads as commanding ship, Citizen Ronsard, officer of the guard, went the rounds; Citizen Le Bas, frigate captain, went with him, knowing the usage of the service at Mauritius. He hailed a Danish ship that had a fire burning; a man who was on deck answered him rudely, and, having said he was a petty officer, Citizen Le Bas had him put into his boat. On reaching the ship he wanted to make him go first. The stranger then told him he was an officer like himself; in spite of which he pushed him by the shoulder. The gunner's mate tried to do the same; the unfortunate man's feet caught in the lashings that were on the gangway and he fell into the hold and was badly bruised on the shoulder. He was dressed and sent back to his ship. The 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1801]. The brig L'Utile got under way for Réunion. An officer from La Cayenne came to tell us that we should no longer be charged with the duty of the roads. A water lighter came out to us. The topgallant masts were got down.

1801-03-17.journal_anonyme: During the day, the pilot being on board, we weighed to warp further in; by nightfall we were moored in six fathoms with 70 fathoms of cable out to starboard and the port cable made fast to a mooring buoy. On the morning of the 26th we laid a third anchor astern. Stay at Mauritius, Germinal to the 5th Floréal [Year 9, 25 April 1801]. During our stay at Mauritius we were busy overhauling the rigging and caulking the ship, and fresh provisions were embarked. The nights were cool enough and the days calm. By day the winds were fairly regularly from SE to SSE, and by night from NW to WNW. We had many deserters, and several officers and scientists of the two corvettes stayed behind at Mauritius. To prevent desertion the commander made us get under way to lie at the outer anchorage. On the morning of the 28th [Germinal, Year 9, 18 April 1801] the officers of the Naturaliste were assembled aboard the Géographe by the commander's order. They all went with the captain to the appointed place. The commander said he had held a council to determine what measures it would be best to take to bring back our deserters; and at the same time he read out the petition addressed to the constituted authorities of the colony to reclaim them. The commander having asked each man's opinion, all were of the view not to sign this petition; and by unanimous agreement among the officers of both ships the following declarations were entered in the Géographe's log: The officers forming the wardrooms of the two corvettes Géographe and Naturaliste, convened in council by the commander-in-chief of the expedition of discovery to deliberate on the most effective means of bringing back the deserting seamen of both ships, have declared that the commander alone had the right to take whatever measures should appear most fitting. All the officers signed this declaration, but Citizen Hamelin stated that he would not sign it, and the commander said he ought not to do so. Captain Baudin having announced that the purpose of the meeting was fulfilled, we took leave of him and all our officers returned on board; we hoisted in our longboat and our large boat. At 6 a.m. on the 2nd Floréal [Year 9, 22 April 1801] a naval gendarme brought us ten men by order of the fitting-out office. On the 3rd Floréal [Year 9, 23 April 1801] a boat sent by the fitting-out office brought clothing and money for various seamen shipped the day before. At 3.30 p.m. on the 5th [Year 9, 25 April 1801] the commander gave the order to unmoor; we at once sent a longboat to weigh our kedge anchor. At 5 a.m. on the 5th the winds ESE, a light breeze; at a quarter to seven the commander made us the signal to get under way. We at once hove short and hoisted our topsails to the mastheads, and as soon as the anchor was aweigh we filled and stood on. Bearings at eight in the morning: Coin de Mire NE by E; Île aux Tonneliers E by S 5° S. The winds variable from east to ESE and to west. Noon bearings: Coin de Mire N 60° E; the discovery hill of the port E by S; Morne Brabant SSW 5° S.
1801-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe: On the twenty-sixth most of the naturalists landed their effects and took lodgings in different quarters of the town. On board we were busy mooring the ship with four moorings, as is the custom of the port. The few means given us for this work made it last the whole day, so that it was entirely lost for the particular tasks we had to do on board. Nevertheless I had a statement drawn up of the replacements of sea provisions I needed, having decided to make the request for them to the Administrators General the next day.

1801-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh I sent the Ordonnateur General a statement of my requirements and wrote him the letter which is to be found in the correspondence I had occasion to carry on with the Administrators during my stay in port.
On board we were busy unrigging the ship, and as it was right to give a little rest to these men, who had been at sea for seven months six months, it was arranged that each day twelve should have leave to go ashore and that the others should go only when the first had returned.

1801-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth the victualling clerk took to the Ordonnateur the statement of our daily provisions, but the request was refused. In the morning I went myself to the Intendant to urge him to grant us some refreshments in bread and fresh meat. But I was no more fortunate nor better received than the victualling clerk had been. In vain did I represent to the Ordonnateur the drawbacks of his refusal and the discontent the crew would feel at it; all was useless and I obtained nothing, on the pretext that there was no money in the treasury to pay the butcher and the baker.
The consumption of our sea provisions was too precious to me not to make him feel that it would cost him less to feed us on fresh meat than to replace the biscuit and salt meat he wished to make us consume. (In the margin: his reply) was that we could consume as much as we pleased, but that he would replace nothing for us. I then invited him to answer the letter I had had the honour of writing to him concerning our needs, since I would make up my mind once he had officially made known his intentions to me. And I withdrew, very ill pleased in truth, seeing clearly that there was more ill humour in his refusals than any impossibility of granting my requests.
On leaving the Ordonnateur's I went to the General-in-Chief, to whom I related what had just happened. He promised me to see the Intendant during the day, and assured me that he would do all he could to spare us the unpleasantness I was already beginning to foresee, and which I did not conceal from him.
In the evening, on my way back on board, I learnt of a placard that had been posted at the corners of some streets, on which was written in large letters: "VOYAGE OF DISCOVERY FAILED". I do not know what motive can have given rise to this ill-natured joke, and I like to believe that it will not come true.

1801-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth I handed to the Swedish Captain commanding the ship Kent a letter announcing to the Minister of Marine our arrival in the Colony. The copy of this letter will be found in my correspondence with the Administrators of the Colony, following the one I addressed to him at the time of my departure for New Holland.
In the morning I received from the port twenty-six caulkers, whom I had asked for the day before, to go over the ship's seams down to her waterline. We had all the more need of this work because the ship, being new, had suffered so much from the heat that all the oakum had come out of the seams, which made us take in a fair amount of water whenever the sea was at all rough.
In the course of the day no one went ashore, since we had been obliged to lend the longboats of both vessels to the ship Kent, which was leaving for Europe. We spent our time on board housing the topmasts and unbending our sails.

1801-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, as no one had gone ashore the day before, half the crew were allowed to land, some to wash their linen and the others to stroll about. As it was, besides, a décadi and consequently a day of rest, no work was done on board. In the morning three Arab vessels left the harbour, and one of them ran onto the rocks that lie to larboard of the passage going out. She would no doubt have stayed there had I not, as soon as I noticed it, sent her my longboat and that of the Naturaliste, each with a cable and an anchor, to get her out of trouble. For in the port no move was made to bring her help.
At half past three in the afternoon, seeing that she was not yet out of danger, I wrote to the Ordonnateur, the General being absent, to express to him how surprised I was at the indifference with which a vessel was watched going to her loss, and I urged him to send her fresh help before nightfall.
At four o'clock, and before the port had made any move, this vessel got herself off the reefs on which she had struck. By the return of my longboat I received a letter of thanks from the Captain who commands her. But it cost me a cable and an anchor. The anchor, let go among the rocks, was broken in weighing it, and the cable badly damaged. I informed the Administrators of this, asking them to replace these two articles for me, since they had been used to perform the duties of the port. I am awaiting the answer to my letter.
The rest of the day passed without incident.

1801-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 1st of Germinal the topmasts were housed and at once stripped so that their rigging could be examined. The slings of our lower yards were found to be broken in two places, and their ties were so damaged that they had to be changed.
The caulkers continued their work, and I made ready to have put into a storehouse, which the Intendant had had the kindness to lend me, the articles for barter and even the provisions that were on board, so as to make it easier to take in our water.
In the course of the day I received from the Intendant the letter, a copy of which is in my correspondence with that Administrator, concerning the requests I had made to him for the replacement of our provisions. On reading them one will see his good disposition towards us, and I do not doubt that the Government will thank him in the manner he deserves for the interest he has taken in the health of my crew and in the success of the expedition.
At ten o'clock I went to see the captain of the port to ask him to lend us the place called "La Tour" to set up our observatory there. He lent himself with the best grace in the world to our
requests; it was agreed that the next day we would have our instruments carried there in order to determine accurately the rate of our timekeepers.
During the day the longboat the port had lent me, manned by fifteen blacks to lighten the labour of the crews, made two trips in the harbour, and we deposited in the storehouse lent to me the articles mentioned in the officers' journal. It was at this time that several of the scientists asked the ship's chief surgeon for hospital tickets so as to go and recruit their health there. One of the officers of the Géographe named Baudin had two days earlier taken lodgings in the town, and I learnt of it only through his absence at the moment he was due to take the watch. This conduct seemed to me somewhat extraordinary, and I put off expressing my surprise to him until I should next meet him.

1801-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second we continued landing our stores, while the caulkers, carpenters and seamen were each busy in their own line to hasten our work and put us promptly in a state to sail. The same work went on aboard the Naturaliste, which happened to have greater needs than ourselves, having one of her catheads to change and part of her head to repair. She received the same number of caulkers as we did, and the carpenters she needed for her other work.
In the morning the crew complained to me of the way they were being fed in the roads. I carried their representation to the Intendant, whom I found quite as unaccommodating as on the previous days. In vain did I point out to him that so unsuitable a measure would not fail to serve as a pretext for desertion, and that if once it took hold among my crew it would be difficult to check its consequences; nothing could make him change the resolution he had taken to give me nothing. At last, having driven him to the end of his patience, he told me that the Minister of Marine, in announcing my arrival to him, had also informed him that we needed nothing, and that consequently he would give us nothing.
I thought it right to point out to him that needing nothing referred only to what was required for the rigging of the vessels, but that the same could not be understood of the customary ration after long voyages. This argument had no more success than the others, and I was obliged to turn about in some other way to obtain a few refreshments.
That day eight men went into hospital, complaining of severe colic with fever. The ship's surgeon attributed the cause to the quality of the water, and from that very moment I ordered that a drink composed of rum, sugar and water mixed together should be prepared for the daily ration, so as to prevent the illnesses the raw water might cause.

1801-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, seeing that I must expect nothing from the Administration either for the replacement of the sea provisions I so essentially needed or for the daily ration, I thought it proper to put an end to the murmurs of the crew, at least as regards part of their complaints. Accordingly I went to find the butcher whom the Government employs to supply the hospital. I explained my position to him, and the way I went about it led him to promise to give us butcher's meat three times a décade, and he agreed to receive payment only when the Administrators should be in funds. It seemed to me that I had won a great victory, and I went at once to the Intendant to announce to him the success of my efforts. But what was my surprise to see him on the spot issue a written prohibition to the contractor against supplying us with anything except for ready money, declaring to him that no
account would be taken of any advances he might make us. I confess that this conduct on the part of the Intendant put me all the more out of humour because I saw in it a very marked design to do us harm, so much so that I asked him whether it was he who had had "Voyage of Discovery Failed" posted up, and whether he really persuaded himself that he would succeed in it. However, to put an end to all argument, as the conversation was becoming too serious, I withdrew and went again to find the butcher, with whom I entered into a formal engagement to pay him before my departure. And by this means I procured fresh meat for the crew three times a décade. On the other days I obtained a little fish and some vegetables at the bazaar. Nevertheless I had the vexation of seeing many of my people go into hospital, where, in treating them as sick men, they cost the Government three times as much as it would have cost to keep them in the good health they had brought into the Colony.
After what had just happened, I made it my duty no longer to call on the Ordonnateur, and I intend only, whenever circumstances require it, to make my requests to him in writing, so as better to establish his conduct towards us.
During the day we continued on board with the work we had to do and with the survey of our rigging. Our instruments were also taken ashore and the astronomers took possession of the place that had been lent to us. We also landed the sails that needed mending, and for greater safety and convenience they were deposited in the workshops of the Republic, which could not on any pretext be refused us, since no one was working there on the Government's account, the sailmakers attached to that establishment being in the town working on the account of the Administrators of finance.

1801-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the hope of being more fortunate by applying to the Intermediate Commission representing the Colony, I sent it a statement of requirements which I cut down as far as I possibly could. Several persons had already urged me to take this step, but I had always declined, so that the Administration should have no cause to complain of it. However, as this was the only means left to me and as I was truly beginning to perceive that there was a wish to force my crew to give up the rest of the expedition, I hesitated no longer and sent to the members of this Commission the letter which is attached to my correspondence.
I was very impatient to know what success it would have, when one of the members, and one of my old acquaintances in the country, came to tell me that I must expect nothing from it, since the fear of seeing the English appear from one moment to the next made them wish that I should remain longer in the Colony, so as to lay hands on my men should the English appear. This news, which was the outcome of a secret deliberation, became known to me, and while appearing to know nothing of it, I judged it proper to take a decisive course as soon as the answer to my letter reached me. Supposing, as I had every reason to expect, that I was given nothing, I had resolved within myself at least to take the vessels out of the harbour, and as soon as they were ready I would have made sail for Batavia or Manila, where I was quite sure of not meeting with the same difficulties.
The conduct of the Intendant towards the crews had led several of them, persuaded that I would be unable to sail, to begin to misbehave and even to grow insolent. Several were put in irons on board to serve as an example, but they made little of this punishment.

1801-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth the administrative assembly of the Colony, in answering my letter, gave me to understand that I must no more expect help from it than I had obtained from the administration on behalf of the Government, and from then on I began to see that it would be difficult for me to get away from the Isle of France [Mauritius], where I very sincerely regretted, but too late, having put in.
During the day I handed over to the Government the Chinese A-Son, in accordance with the instructions the Minister of Marine had given me concerning him. I also saw with regret that several officers of the staffs of the two vessels were taking rooms ashore and having their effects carried there, contenting themselves with appearing on board only once or twice a décade to perform there what they call their watch duty, to which alone they believe themselves bound while the vessels are in port. I complained of this conduct to several of them; they answered that the care of their health was their first duty and that the chief physician of the hospital had so judged it. The truth is that these gentlemen were in much better health than I, for at that time I had caught a chill which made me suffer a great deal.
However that may be, given over to my anxieties about the outcome of my voyage, I prepared to leave the Isle of France as soon as possible with the only means left to me, and I gave orders to press on more vigorously than ever with our work of every kind; but I could not obtain from the administrators any additional workmen, whether caulkers or day labourers. Yet the Government has two thousand workmen and more at its disposal for the service of its Navy and its workshops. But they are more often employed on the account of private persons than on any other. My intention was, on leaving the Isle of France, to make for New Holland in the latitude of Eendracht Land, and to put in at one of the Molucca Islands, so as to be able, next summer, to visit the south coast of Van Diemen's Land and the strait that separates it from New Holland.
Being at dinner the same day with the Danish Consul, Pelgrom, my friend of long standing, I confided my troubles to him and my regret at having come into this Colony. After a few moments' reflection he asked me what sum the replacements I needed for the two vessels might amount to.
As I had the statement of them on me, I showed it to him. By the estimate I had made, it came to twelve thousand Spanish hard dollars. When he had read it, he told me that he hoped to procure them for me, and to that end he invited to dinner the next day all the Danish captains who were in the Colony, assuring me that he was quite certain they would make up this sum for me among them all, the more so as several had remittances to make to Europe and could find no better opportunity. This idea so pleased me that, forgetting all my troubles, I already looked upon my business as settled and the continuation of my voyage as assured.
The rest of the day passed without incident, and I awaited the outcome of the next with much impatience.
During the night of the fifth to the sixth the weather was very bad. Heavy rain mingled with loud claps of thunder troubled us greatly in the roads, and the changeableness of the winds made us fear we might meet with some squall. All the vessels' moorings were doubled for greater safety.

1801-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, in the morning, the weather cleared again and sunrise brought back the land winds. The swell running in the harbour told us that it had blown a fresh gale outside, from north to north-north-west.
When the caulkers and day labourers had come on board, we went on with our work aboard. Four men were missing that day, the third master among them.
At eleven o'clock I went ashore and paid a visit to the hospital to see the officers and naturalists who, according to the note that had been handed to me, were supposed to be there. The errand proved quite useless, for I found nobody there. The Sisters of Charity who serve the hospital assured me that these gentlemen came in sometimes in the evening, and even rather late, but that as a rule they spent the day in town, where no doubt their amusements were more varied than they would have been had they stayed in such a place.
At one o'clock I went to Consul Pelgrom's house, and there found assembled twelve Danish captains and three Swedish ones. The Consul told me that he had not yet said anything to them and that he was keeping back until the dessert the reason for the invitation he had sent them. At two o'clock we sat down to table, and although the dinner was of great magnificence, I longed for nothing but to see the moment of the dessert arrive. It came at last. The first toast was to the success and complete accomplishment of the voyage I was about to undertake, in which all the nations of Europe had taken the keenest interest. This toast was proposed by the Consul. The second toast was to the health of all those who would help to give us all the assistance we might need and without which the voyage could not take place. The Consul then explained that, having applied to the Administrators for the Government and to the Intermediate Commission for the Colony, I had been unable to obtain any assistance from them, on the pretext that, the Colony being threatened with an early attack by the English, the Government needed all its resources and that, moreover, they had no funds at their disposal. He then proposed to several of them who had remittances to make to Europe that they should give me a sum of ten thousand piastres at the ordinary exchange of the Colony, pointing out to them that such remittances would be more agreeable and profitable to their principals than making them in any other way.
All the Danish captains thought this sum so trifling that every one of them wished to make it up in equal shares; but one of them, having more need than any other to send funds to Europe, asked to be given preference for all that I might need, and it was not without great discussion that the others agreed to grant him this preference.
I confess that I had not expected so complete and so prompt a success. I expressed my gratitude to each of them individually. But I could not see without pain that the French, and above all the merchant capitalists, were about to cover themselves with shame in the eyes of all Europe for having refused me so trifling a sum.
On rising from table, the Consul withdrew into his study with the Danish captain who had obtained the preference, and there the captain signed a formal undertaking to give us whatever money we should need for the purchase of our replacements; and the Consul for his part bound himself to give him bills of exchange drawn by me at four months, at an exchange of thirty-three and a third per cent profit, the rate of the Colony, even in time of peace. I thought it proper to inform the Administrators of the change in my situation and addressed to them the letter which is to be found in my general correspondence with them.

1801-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh of Germinal the fine weather continued. On board we were busy landing our stores, and the casks in the hold were partly emptied. The four men who had not come back the day before did not appear that day either, and I put off declaring them deserters until the following day.
The caulkers went on paying the upper works of the ship, which were entirely bare of oakum. The same work was going on aboard the Naturaliste.
During the day I handed to Consul Pelgrom's chancellor the list of provisions I needed to replace those consumed during the campaign, and it was he who was charged with seeking them out and collecting them.
During the night of the seventh the weather was very rainy and we often had strong gusts, without thunder.

1801-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth the rainy weather continued and the wind was east-south-east in strong puffs. As it was not possible to caulk outside, the caulkers were employed inside on the second deck. The ship's carpenters repaired our topgallant crosstrees, which were broken, and work went on stowing the hold. During the day I had twelve double casks landed, which were intended to hold the arrack I meant to take on board.
The four seamen who were missing were declared deserters at the office of the maritime register, and I gave their descriptions to the police.
The rain we had had during the day continued for part of the night, and the wind at south-east blew in strong gusts mingled with a few claps of thunder.

1801-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth the weather was fine and work went on outside the ship with the caulking. Part of the crew was employed in overhauling the rigging, while the rest worked at stowing the hold and emptying our water casks.
I have until now forgotten to make mention of Citizen Gutte. This individual was found on board two days after our departure. When I questioned him on the reasons that had led him to take this course, he answered that, having been deported from the Isle of France [Mauritius], where he had a wife and children, he had arrived in Europe without resources and that, having found no opportunity of returning to his family, he had thought fit to take advantage of this one in order to escape from the poverty in which he had been living for six months. When the Intermediate Commission came on board, I informed it of the declaration this man, very well known in the Colony, had made to me. I was asked to keep him on board, confined, until the Assembly had deliberated on what it should do about him. All the steps that Citizen Gutte's friends and acquaintances were able to take could not get him admitted into the Colony. All he was able to obtain was permission to go ashore on condition that he be confined to his quarter, and I know that it is proposed to send him to the Seychelles by the first opportunity. It was on this day that an invitation was received on board from the Municipality to let him go ashore. His wife and children had often come to see him on board during the time he was confined there. For the rest, he behaved very well while he was with us and seemed to us, in every respect, incapable of being a dangerous man to any party.

1801-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, half the crew had leave to go ashore for the day of the décade, with orders not to fail to come back and sleep on board. In spite of the rain in the morning, most of the officers supposedly in hospital on account of sickness and to recruit their health went off walking to various plantations, and when I went to make my visit to the sick I found nobody, as had happened to me every time I had presented myself there.
In the morning a brigantine from Bourbon [Réunion] entered the port
In the evening, at gunfire, only four men were missing from the part of the crew that had gone ashore; they came back during the night.

1801-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, after the caulkers and carpenters had set to work, we began to take in our water, the hold having been made ready for it. We had been obliged to shift part of our stowage to clear our spare anchors, which lay right at the bottom, at the bottom. We placed two of them at the cathead by the opening of the main hatchway and a third abaft, so as to have them ready in case of need.
The rest of the day passed without incident and the night was very fine.

1801-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, everyone being at work, I went ashore to see whether they were seriously engaged in collecting the sea provisions of which I had given the list. On arriving in the port I was pleased to see that our salt meat was being delivered aboard a lighter intended for us, together with the beer I was shipping in place of wine, the price of wine being too high for me to take the quantity I needed.
When half the goods in the lighter had been taken on board, the rest was sent to the Naturaliste, which shipped them likewise.
In the afternoon we did not have the ship's caulkers, and I do not know why. During the night the water tank was sent ashore to be filled, having been emptied during the day.

1801-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth we were busy swaying up the topmasts and the lower yards, and we shipped the rest of our liquor in wine and country arrack. I took only forty hogsheads of wine for the two ships, in case we should have sick men during the campaign, for my intention is not to issue it as a ration but only at one meal each décade. As I shall be the first to submit to this rule, I like to think that everyone will conform to it willingly and with good grace.
During the day a foreign ship under Prussian colours came in from Bordeaux. This ship, having left France eighteen days before us, brought nothing new. She had on board forty-four passengers who had not lived on very good terms during the passage.
A rather singular adventure befell this ship, and it deserves to be mentioned. On her way to the Isle of France [Mauritius], she came to make Rodrigues Island in the part, the part (sic), to the south. The Frenchmen on board at first took this island for the Isle of France, but on approaching it more closely they recognised from its appearance that it was not. Nevertheless, nobody recognised Rodrigues, and all maintained that it was surely São João de Lisboa, which a great many seamen have long sought in vain. In this conviction,
they closed the land as much as possible, and at last, as the weather was fine, they let go the anchor on a coral bottom in forty fathoms. The boats were at once sent ashore with fifteen armed men, in case the island should be inhabited by some nation hitherto unknown.
The boats landed in a cove where they met nobody, and the party then advanced about a league into the interior of the country. But as the day was drawing to a close, they thought of re-embarking, putting off a more extensive visit until the morrow. Before leaving the island, however, they took possession of it in the name of the French Republic, and placed a duplicate of the act of possession in a bottle, which was hung from a tree, so that if any ship should later touch at this part of the island, she would learn that she was not the first to have come there.
When the boats had returned on board, the Captain was told that the island did not appear to be inhabited and that possession of it had been taken in due form in the name of the Republic, and he was handed a copy of the deed of ownership. A great dispute then arose on board, and the Prussian Captain maintained, with reason, that the island, having been discovered by a Prussian ship, ought to belong to the King of Prussia and not to the French Republic. But as this right was contested, he decided to spend the night at anchor, and the next day he again sent one of his boats ashore, which planted a Prussian flag on a height, and he enclosed in a well-sealed bottle a second act of possession in the name of the King his master, reserving the right to assert his claims on his arrival at the Isle of France. The ship then made sail and continued on her way to this port, where she arrived three days later, still not quite persuaded that she had seen only Rodrigues instead of São João de Lisboa.
The stir caused by this new discovery gave rise to inquiries, and after the ship's journal had been examined, together with the variation she had observed, the latitude of the place and the distance run since the time of her discovery, it was demonstrated to her captain that the land she had visited was nothing other than Rodrigues Island, which quite truly belongs to the French Republic.

1801-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth we took in part of our firewood and whatever of our sea provisions was ready. The crew was entirely employed in rigging the ship, and we swayed up our topgallant masts. The weather was very fine all day, but we suffered greatly from the heat, the breeze having failed.
Ashore, great preparations were being made to receive the English, who were expected to appear at any moment, word having come that a considerable armament was being fitted out in India, whose destination was unknown.

1801-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, all our water casks being full, we began to take back on board the various things we had put ashore for our greater convenience while breaking out the hold, which had had to be done to get at our spare anchors and several other things that it was necessary to have ready to hand for the rest of the campaign.
During the day our caulking was at last finished, outside and in, and we were glad to be rid of 28 men who had greatly hindered the other work we had to do. I am persuaded that ten Europeans would have done in eight days what twenty-six blacks had difficulty doing in twenty.

1801-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth we began to clean the ship, which the caulkers had left in a pitiful state. Most of the blacks on labour duty were employed in scraping inside, while the crew worked at the rigging and reeving the running rigging.
We shipped few items of our sea provisions that day, because we had to stow in the hold those that had come in the preceding days, so as not to be too much encumbered.
On my visit to the hospital I was no more fortunate than I had been every time I had presented myself there; that is to say, I found nobody.
In the afternoon I went to the observatory, which is under the direction of Citizen Bernier, our chief astronomer having appeared there only once or twice since our arrival. But as Citizen Bernier is far more capable of this work than the other, I am glad of his absences.

1801-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth a large part of our sea provisions was shipped and stowed about the ship in various places until such time as they could be put in their proper place, our stowage not yet being finished.
At noon I went ashore to attend a grand dinner given me by my old acquaintances in this Colony. We drank freely to the success of the voyage, and everyone congratulated me on having been able to obtain, through Consul Pelgrom, the replacements I needed; but I was warned to be on my guard with regard to the crews, and was assured that several persons had already made approaches to induce them to desert, and that perhaps they would fail me at the moment I least expected it. This fear on the part of my friends seemed to me ill-founded, inasmuch as up to that time the men had in general strayed little from their duty.

1801-04-08.journal_baudin_autographe: On the eighteenth we shipped fifteen thousand pounds of wheat, and the Naturaliste as much. As we have convenient mills on board for grinding it into flour, I preferred to take it in this form because I am persuaded that it will keep very well. Besides, it would have been very difficult to have it ground ashore at the Republic's mill. I had asked leave of the Intendant to do so, and he answered me that the mill was not working, that is to say for us, for having gone there myself, I found it in full activity for the public, who pay the Administration for it.

1801-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth little work was done on board, the weather having been rainy almost all day. However, in the intervals between the squalls, the longboat made several trips ashore to fetch from the storehouse where our effects lay those that would take no harm from the rain, and we shipped the pitch, the tar, the vinegar and various other less considerable items. I had resolved not to lose a moment in trying at least to get out of the port, for I had just been informed that the Intermediate Commission had resolved to detain the ships there, should the English appear, in order to distribute their crews among various posts. Although such conduct would have been contrary to the law of nations, I have no doubt whatever that it would take this course if the case should arise before I was out of the port.
