In the evening I told the general-in-chief what I had learned; he answered that nothing of the kind would happen and that he did not suppose anyone would go (to) such an extremity.

1801-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, two thirds of the crew had leave to spend the décade ashore. They had behaved too well up to then to give me any uneasiness about their future conduct.
Nothing new happened during the day, and among the various ships that entered the port was a large English prize from India laden with masts and spars. This ship, of which the owners of the privateer that took her made little account, was a real loss to the English.
At gunfire, all those who had been ashore had come back on board, with the exception of three persons.

1801-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first we continued our preparations for departure, and during the day we shipped most of the things that were ashore.
The three men who had not come back the day before arrived on board in the morning. Two small brigantines came into the port from Madagascar, with a cargo of rice and black slaves.

1801-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second we took on board our sails that had been in store and under repair in the Republic's workshops. We also stowed our spare spars which, (for) greater convenience, were placed differently from the way they had been on leaving Le Havre.
The stowage of the hold was well advanced, so that I saw the moment of departure approaching with a satisfaction that would be hard to express.
As I had ceased keeping a table for the officers and naturalists since the tenth of Germinal, I began shipping my own provisions. It was a great mistake on the part of those in France to insist that I should be charged with this.

1801-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third the sails were bent to the yards, and the spare ones put in the places intended for them.
During the day I was warned that eight persons were planning to desert. As I had no well-established certainty of this plot, I did not think it proper to take any other measure than to double the watch on the gangways during the night and to put the boats in the charge of the sentries. Nevertheless, six of the eight men who had been pointed out to me deserted by swimming. Their shipmates told us that they had gone out by the head.

1801-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the corvettes were swung, and in the afternoon, to my great satisfaction, they were moved out to the roadstead beyond the Pavillons. I was then in safety and had nothing more to fear from the intentions of the Intermediate Assembly should the English appear.
It only remained for me to get back the men who were in hospital and the deserters, whom it seemed to me easy to find. I had a list of their descriptions drawn up and sent it to the office of the maritime register and to the police.
In the outer roadstead the ships were moored with a bower anchor and a strong hawser to a kedge, in 18 fathoms, muddy sand bottom.
Bearings from the anchorage:
Pointe des Canonniers NE ¼ N
The Coin de Mire NE 5° N
The Pouce SE ¼ S 4° south
The Montagne du Port south 5° east
The land to the west SW ¼ W, all by compass.
At seven o'clock I went ashore in the boat of the port officer who had come to take the ship out to the roadstead.
As the Naturaliste had not got under sail, although I had made her the signal to do so, I supposed that her anchors had fouled. But on passing close to that ship, I was informed that the guard hulk or pontoon commanded by Citizen Mangin had prevented her from getting under way, on the pretext that no ship was permitted to leave at sunset.
I was much displeased with M. Hamelin for having paid heed to such an order and for not having obeyed the signal I had made, since he was to take orders from no one but me.

1801-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth we began to paint the ship, not having had time to do this work in the port. At seven o'clock the Naturaliste got under sail with a pleasant breeze from the south-east and came to anchor beside us.
I was informed that during the night, in spite of all the precautions her captain had been able to take, three of her men had deserted by swimming. I complained to the General of the conduct of the officer commanding on board the guard hulk the day before, and held him responsible for the desertion of the three men who had gone off the day before, inasmuch as it would not have happened had he not prevented that ship from moving out to the Pavillons. The General, without much approving the conduct of the officer of the pontoon, did not seem to me to pay much attention to my representations.
In the morning I went to the hospital to make a thorough inspection of our sick and their condition. I was not surprised to find neither the officers nor the naturalists there, for they went there only when they were not on a pleasure party or did not know where to go for dinner. But I was very much surprised to learn that during the night eight of my best seamen had deserted by climbing over the walls. I pretended to believe this statement, but after more exact inquiries I learned with certainty that, far from having climbed over the walls, they had gone out by the main gate with their baggage, on a pass from the Commissary in charge of that branch of the service.
This conduct showed me clearly the regret that was felt at seeing us outside the port, and the intention of delaying our departure, which it was supposed could not take place for want of men. It was believed, moreover, that I could not do without the officers who were staying ashore, and people still persisted in believing that the voyage had failed, since they did not know the means I intended to use to procure men if those I should claim were not returned to me.
At sunset I went on board to consider the means of having our deserters arrested.

1801-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe: On the twenty-sixth we were busy on board setting up our shrouds fore and aft. Several boats from the port brought us the rest of our effects, and I sent to ask the Ordonnateur to be so good as to have the accounts prepared, few as they were, that I had to sign.

1801-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh the preparations for departure went on briskly, and as it was known ashore that I was short of men, people began to be uneasy about thirty blacks on labour duty whom I kept aboard the two ships for the daily service of the boats, which were continually going and coming from the roadstead to the port and from the port to the roadstead.
In consequence of these fears, the Intendant sent me a port officer to ask for them, but I refused to send them back to him, for the reasons set out in the letter I wrote to him on the subject.
At ten o'clock I hoisted the pennant for orders, having decided to assemble the officers of the two corvettes in council to communicate to them my intention regarding the letter I intended to address to the General-in-chief, to the Administrator and to the other constituted authorities of the Colony. The council, once assembled, having left me the choice of the means to be employed, I addressed to them the letter that is to be found in my correspondence, persuaded that it could not fail to have a good effect.
The rest of the day passed without incident, but at eight o'clock the port officer who had come in the morning arrived for the second time, with twelve men from the guard hulk, six of whom were for the Naturaliste. When handing them over, he gave me a letter from the Intendant who, claiming that I no longer had any reason to keep the blacks on labour duty, was persuaded that I would make no difficulty about returning them. I kept the six men intended for me and sent those for the Naturaliste on board her. But I kept the blacks none the less, writing once more to the Intendant the reasons on which I based my acting thus.

1801-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, at four in the morning, I sent my longboat, manned by ten blacks, to the port to fetch the things that might still remain to us ashore. She came back at ten o'clock, fully laden with all sorts of things.
By the same opportunity I sent word to the astronomer Bernier to pack up all his instruments and dismantle the observatory, my intention being that everything should be on board by the next day.
During the day I received from the General-in-chief a reply to the letter I had written him the day before about our deserters and our situation. It seemed to me, from one paragraph of his letter, that he was not overly pleased with the measures I asked him to have carried out. However, I do not think my letter contained anything offensive to him in particular, and I wrote him a second one on the subject.
The rest of the day passed without incident, and I put off going ashore until the next day to sign the accounts and to learn what would at last be the result of my requests to all the administrations of the Colony.

1801-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth I went ashore at daybreak, and on leaving the ship gave orders to send the longboat ashore at about nine o'clock with the master gunner to fetch our powder.
On my arrival ashore I was informed by my friends that my letter to the Intermediate Commission had not been received there with pleasure. I was all the less surprised at this as I had been persuaded beforehand that they would not be pleased with the course I was taking, which was
to place under their responsibility, and even under that of the whole Colony, the safety of the ships and the continuation of the expedition. It is certain that if our deserters were not given a hidden refuge, they could not fail to be found very quickly. In a rather heated interview I had occasion to have with some members of this assembly, I did not conceal from them that it depended on them alone to have the men I was missing returned to me. And although they excused themselves on the grounds of the difficulty of finding them, I did not leave them unaware that I knew on good authority that when they had had someone to deport, they had very well found the means to have him arrested, even in the middle of the woods, and that it was easier to find forty men and more whom we were missing than a single individual.
After this conversation I went to the police, and by means of some rewards that I promised the constables, they assured me that they would set out on the track of my people.
In the afternoon two blacks were executed. The nature of their punishment drew a great many onlookers, and having no doubt that some of our seamen would be among them, I asked the chief of police to take measures accordingly.
What I had foreseen did indeed happen, and twenty-two were arrested. But as the guard to whom they were entrusted to be taken to the port prison was composed only of tavern-keepers and canteen-keepers, they let fourteen escape on the way and brought only eight to the port. It appears that those they let escape were their debtors, for among those they brought in, not one owed them anything.
While I was at the General-in-chief's, I received a letter from the Intermediate Assembly in reply to the one I had addressed to them, together with a copy of the deliberations to which it had given rise.

1801-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, all the offices being closed, we could do nothing ashore. At about ten o'clock the General sent to ask me to call on him, and in the interview we had together he told me of the administration's uneasiness about the thirty blacks who were still aboard the corvettes. The Intendant had persuaded him that my intention was to carry them off, which would have greatly displeased certain persons of his suite, or perhaps himself, for they know very well how to make a considerable income out of them. I assured the General that this idea had never occurred to me, but that I was quite determined to keep them on board until I had a crew sufficient to set sail. I added that if the Ordonnateur was in such haste to have the Government's blacks back, it depended on him to procure me men, and that he had the means at his disposal, by having handed over to me from the guard hulk the men who were being kept there to man a privateer in which he was not uninterested and which was only waiting for my departure to fit out for a cruise with some of my deserters.
The General promised me to make to the Head of the administration such representations as he thought proper, and we parted.
The rest of the day passed without incident. Nobody went ashore from the ship, not even the blacks, although it was the day of the décade.

1801-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Floréal, early in the morning, we hoisted in the large longboat and three of our boats. During the night of the thirtieth to the first, two men, taking advantage of the darkness, took to the water in the hope of reaching the shore, although we were more than a league from it. The sentry having noticed it, the jolly boat was at once manned to give chase. One was caught, but the second got away.
The one who was overtaken was quite exhausted and would no doubt have drowned before he could reach the shore. In all likelihood his companion will have met that fate.
At ten in the morning I was informed of the hiding place of sixteen of our deserters by a Spanish seaman, who promised to deliver them to us if I would give him twenty piastres. I accepted his proposal and even offered him thirty if he told me the truth. Having gone at once to the police, I asked there for a sufficient guard, and had the Spaniard, who acted as guide, accompanied by the master gunner of the Naturaliste, who happened to be ashore. The guard I had obtained set off at once for the district called Grande Rivière and came back towards evening with twelve, whom I had put in prison until the next day. All but three belonged to the Naturaliste. Having had them questioned, in the presence of the officer of the guard at the port gate, on the motive for their desertion, they declared that crimps for the privateer I have mentioned had offered them one hundred and fifty piastres in advance and that they had been unable to resist so handsome an offer.
I told the General of this discovery and urged him to put an end to the abuses that have hitherto resulted from it for the ships of the Republic. He promised me to take measures accordingly, but as he is not master to do as he pleases, there is every reason to believe that things will remain as they are until further orders.
He informed me that, as a result of the Intendant's efforts, I would receive the next day twelve men from the guard hulk whom the Intendant had told him were seamen.

1801-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second I applied to the Intendant, or rather I addressed to him the letter of which a copy is to be found in my correspondence, to obtain a few head of livestock in order to leave them at some place I intend to visit. I do not know whether this request will be as fruitless as those I have made to him before, but I have reason to believe that he will grant it, inasmuch as I have managed to engage his self-esteem in not refusing it. Besides, it is too small a matter.
During the morning I settled most of the business still outstanding ashore, and I was informed by a boat from the ship that the twelve men, six of whom were for the Naturaliste, had been taken on board.
During the night two of these same men deserted by swimming, but they were overtaken by our boats, which I sent after them.

1801-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third I received from the Intendant a most satisfactory reply to the request I had made him the day before.
During the day I returned to him all the black day labourers and men on labour duty who were aboard the two ships, and he was all the better pleased as those who drew the income from them had persuaded him that my intention was to carry them off, which would truly have done them great harm, since their income would have fallen by about twenty-five to thirty piastres a day.
As I had announced to the General-in-chief that I had decided to get under sail on the morning of the fifth, he sent an invitation to me, and likewise to M. Hamelin, to take a farewell dinner at his house on the fourth, which we both accepted.
In the course of the day we were entirely taken up with the arrangements for our departure, and everything was put in its place and in order aboard the corvettes.
In the afternoon all the boats were hoisted in, with the exception of one, which was kept for the daily service of the ship.
The two men who had deserted the day before made me redouble my precautions during the night, and the watch on the gangways and the head was doubled, with orders to fire on anyone who tried to escape.

1801-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the morning, Captain Hamelin and I went ashore and called on the Governor, to whom I gave a nominal list of the number of people who are (sic) aboard the two ships. The Géographe was fifteen persons short, not counting the scientists, of the number I had with me on my arrival. But I pointed out to him that I found myself sufficiently provided and asked him only to have each of us given three of the Malays who were in the guard hulk and were to be sent back to Batavia; this he granted us, and the order was given on the spot to send them on board. By this means I had a hundred men all told, and the Naturaliste eighty-five. We were thus in a position to put to sea with an easy mind.
On leaving the General's house we went to the offices for the signatures we had to give, but as the accounts were not entirely finished, we had to go back at four in the afternoon.
At one o'clock we went to the General's, who gave us a very good dinner; the Intendant was there, as well as several other officials. Everything passed off as well as could be, and there was no question at all of the little difficulties I had met with during my stay in the Colony; I was merely congratulated on having had the good fortune to find the resources to be able to leave it, the Intendant still protesting his regret at not having been able to help us for want of means.
After dinner I handed the General the packets, in duplicate, that I was addressing to the Minister of Marine. My dispatches contain: 1) an extract from my navigation journal since France, 2) the account of our expenses in the Colony, 3) a copy of my correspondence with the Administration, 4) a private letter to the Minister of Marine. The whole under cover.
All these papers are in duplicate, and the General promised me to take advantage of the first favourable opportunities that might offer to have them forwarded to their destination.
Having taken leave of the General at about four o'clock, we parted, and I went to the Danish Consul's, to whom I handed the 3rd and 4th duplicates of the letters with which the General had charged himself.
At seven o'clock, having nothing more to do ashore, I returned on board, fully resolved not to come back until my return voyage. On my arrival I found the ship riding at single anchor, and had it not been calm we should have got under sail at once, having shipped that same day the herd the Intendant had given us.
Navigation Journal. Departure from the Isle of France.

1801-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth of Floréal, Year 9, at six in the morning, we hove short so as to take advantage of the land winds as soon as they came. At seven o'clock we had the breeze from them, and although it was still light we weighed at once, to my great satisfaction, for until that moment I had always been uneasy, not only for the safety of the crews but also about the manner in which I should leave a Colony where I had met with so many different vexations. I had indeed managed to replace most of the deserters with men who were, to be sure, unwilling, but I had at least enough of them to work the ships, and I was little grieved by the officers and scientists who had abandoned the expedition.
At ten o'clock we were becalmed, and it was only after noon that we were able to gain an offing from the coast with the help of a light breeze from the south-east, which lasted long enough to take us out to sea, so that by sunset we had nothing to fear from the currents should it fall calm during the night, as seemed likely.
Bearings at six in the evening:
Le Morne Brabant south 3° east
The peak of the Ravière Nord east 16° north
The northernmost point of the island N 44° E, all by compass.
During the evening we were busy drawing up the watch bill for the service, and we also held a sale of several items belonging to the deserters we were leaving in the Colony. The crew, once under sail, seemed to me fairly content, and I have no doubt that they will all perform their duty well.
The greater part of the night of the fifth to the sixth was calm. However, at midnight we were able to stand to the south, Le Morne Brabant bearing east 5° north, at an estimated distance of four leagues. We then had a rather pleasant breeze from the east, varying to east by south, but we found a very heavy swell from the south.
The rest of the night passed without incident; we trimmed our sails to keep station with the Naturaliste, which, despite the change she had made in her stowage during our stay at the Isle of France, proved to sail no better than usual.
1801-04-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. At 6 a.m. made the signal to get under way. At 7 got under way and shaped our course west. At noon Coin de Mire bore from us N 55° E and Le Pouce S 70° E; shaped the course S 45° W, running along the land at 4 miles' distance. At 4, Le Pouce N 67° 30' E, the Piton of Rivière Noire N 80° E and Morne Brabant S 10° E. At midnight, Morne Brabant N 85° E, 12 miles off. The 6th [Floréal, 26 April 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ESE. At 8 took the bearing of Morne Brabant N 5° E, 24 miles off, from which I took my point of departure in 21° 8' of latitude and 55° 7' of longitude. The anchors were secured in their stowage and the mizzen topgallant mast struck. At noon in 21° 19' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 12' of longitude by account. Variation 13° 26' NW. At 2.30 took the bearing of Réunion S 67° 30' W, at the limit of sight.

1801-04-26.journal_anonyme: The winds from the WNW, light. Bearings taken at 5.30 p.m.: Morne Brabant south 5° E, estimated distance 3 leagues and a half; the signal hill of the NW port NE by E. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze.
1801-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the sixth, in the morning, we took our departure from the bearings of Le Morne Brabant, which at six o'clock bore north 5° east of us, at an estimated distance of eight leagues.
I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south by east, observing that on close-hauled courses we would always keep a point free in the sails, as much to make less leeway as to go faster.
At half past seven we had a squall which brought us a little rain and a good deal of wind. We were obliged to bear away several points and to furl the mizzen topsail until it had passed. It lasted about half an hour.
In the morning I had the mizzen topgallant mast unrigged so as to ease the head of the mizzen topmast, which is too weak for its great height. We had been obliged to do the same on the passage from France, but as the mast and its sail were of very little use to us, this in no way slowed our sailing and served, on the contrary, only to make the handling of the after sails quicker and easier.
At noon the longitude by dead reckoning from the morning's point of departure was 54° 43' 48"; there was no observation of latitude, nor any hour angle for the rate of the timekeepers.
In the afternoon we were busy getting the cables below and stowing the anchors. The gun deck, being somewhat encumbered by the departure, was cleaned and put in order.
Our livestock were put in convenient pens so as to preserve them in case of bad weather, and everything was arranged for the best.
During the evening the weather was fine. There was a pleasant enough breeze from the east, varying to east-south-east, and had we been alone we should have made fair progress.
The night of the sixth to the seventh was fine, the wind in the same quarter, and we found the sea a little easier than the day before.
Note. In the arrangements made for the service at sea, it was settled that Commander Ste Croix le Bas would command the first watch, Ensign Freycinet the second, Ensign Picquet, from the Naturaliste, the third, Ronsard and the chief quartermaster the fourth, and Bonnefoy with Maurouard the fifth. By this means nobody had any cause for complaint but myself, since I found I had two of them to supervise.
Citizen Bernier, astronomer of the Naturaliste, transferred aboard the Géographe in place of M. Bissy, who had stayed ashore and in hospital, either for form's sake or until he had gathered a sufficient number of pupils, as he proposed to teach drawing.
Citizen Bernier wished to have with him the two timekeepers whose rate he had followed aboard the Naturaliste, and we handed over to Citizen Faure those which had served us on board.
M. Le Villain, assistant zoologist, transferred aboard the Naturaliste, on which only two scientists remained, and on the Géographe I had the places uselessly occupied by MM. Milbert and Garnier filled by Citizens Petit and Le Sueur. It will be judged from the work of these two young men whether the choice I made of them was good or bad.

1801-04-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the wind a strong breeze from east to ESE, the sea running from the south.
1801-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the seventh the weather continued fine, and we pressed south (as) far as we possibly could, always trimming our sails to keep station with the Naturaliste. During the morning the weather was somewhat variable and at times we had some rather heavy puffs of wind; nevertheless, we found the sea much smoother than we had had it until then, and the ship was steadier.
I settled with the steward the manner in which I wished the provisions we had on board to be issued, and so that the articles of which we had only a small quantity might last longer, we agreed that the issues should be made in the following manner, namely:
Two rations of arrack a day and one ration of beer at noon,
On meat days, one meal of rice,
On vegetable days, one meal of peas at noon and one of rice in the evening,
Coffee twice each décade, on the 5th and the 10th,
Fresh bread once each décade, to the officers as to the crew,
Six bottles of cased wine to the officers on the 5th & 3 on the 10th of each décade.
As, after what had happened on the passage from France, I had given up keeping a table, I arranged to invite two persons each day, an officer and a naturalist, so that with my secretary I always had four persons at my table and at my expense. I had clearly foreseen, from the time of leaving France, that there would be malcontents and that, however good my fare, there would always be someone who was not satisfied with it. Nevertheless, I must admit that the scientists never complained of it, and whatever discontent this arrangement caused me, it was only ever M. Bissy and the officers who complained. And so I am very glad that they were pleased to stay ashore.
At noon the observed latitude was 22° 44' 49" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 55° 12'. That given by No. 27 was 55° 25' 18" and that of No. 35, 55° 21' 9". We found in the 48 hours a difference to the north of 8 seconds and one to the east of 9' 13".
During the evening the weather was the same as in the morning; the breeze was not very steady, but in general the wind was from the east to east-south-east, moderate and often even light. The course was the same.
At sunset we closed with the Naturaliste, which was well to leeward, and during the night we sailed a quarter of a league apart, that ship having all sail set. The night passed without incident. From time to time a few small squalls passed with rain, but they were of little consequence and short duration.
Note: according to the report of the chief surgeon, there was only one man sick on board, of a tertian fever, and I learned with pleasure that no one had yet been found to have venereal disease. In this I am much more fortunate than on my departure from Tenerife, for on the day after we sailed I had more than ten cases aboard the Géographe.
1801-04-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At noon in 22° 40' 30" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 29' NW.

1801-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from ESE. The sea smooth enough. The weather fine and the sky serene. At 10 a.m. we found the third forward shroud of the mainmast had parted above the futtock shrouds; the damage was repaired at once.
1801-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the eighth, during the day, the weather was fairly fine, although the horizon was very limited and the sky laden with damp vapours which produced a dull, whitish haze that was not at all agreeable to the eye. The wind, which had been for some time in the east, varied a little towards the south, and we continued to stand on close-hauled. The ship laboured a little during the day, as there was a rather heavy swell from east-south-east to south-east which made us roll a great deal.
At noon we observed the latitude 23° 59' 50" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was 55° 18' 42". That given by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was for No. 27, 55° 36' 57", and for No. 31, 55° 30' 27". We had in the 24 hours 1' 4" of difference to the north and 12' to the east.
During the evening the sky became clearer than it had been in the morning, and we had the promise of a fine night. The wind varied a little from east towards north, but not for long.
At four o'clock the Naturaliste, which was about three quarters of a league to leeward of us, made us the signal of damage to one of her main shrouds; we bore away towards her to learn more exactly what it was, and after I had spoken to M. Hamelin, he told us that one of his mainmast shrouds had parted, but that the damage had been repaired.
He also informed us that he was pleased with his crew, which numbered eighty-seven men all told, all in good health. After we had parted company, I signalled to him that we would steer south-east by compass, if the wind allowed, before leaving the region of the trade winds.
The night of the eighth to the ninth was very fine, as it had promised to be at sunset. As it was the day of the full moon, the night was so bright that our horizon was wider than it had been during the day. Throughout the night the wind kept close to the east and the breeze was light.
1801-04-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 23° 58' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 53' NW. At 2 the course was signalled S 45° E should the wind draw aft. At 3.45 the Naturaliste signalled us damage to her main shrouds; we bore down on her and spoke.

1801-04-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 the course was signalled SE, and we signalled the commander the damage to our lower shrouds.
1801-04-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the ninth, in the morning, we had the wind from the east, varying to east-south-east, a pretty breeze, but the sea remained heavy with swell and the ship laboured a little. After breakfast the crew were employed in setting up our fore lower shrouds and our topmast shrouds fore and aft, which stood in great need of it, the rigging at the mastheads not having been hauled taut enough in the way it had been set up on the day before we left port.
At noon the observed latitude was 25° 4' 50" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 56° 2', which gave a difference north of 8' 24 seconds and one east of 5' 30 seconds. The longitude shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 56° 7' 32", and for No. 35, 55° 59' 16".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the wind shifted a little from the east towards the north. We had a pretty breeze until sunset, when it varied and dropped a little, and for a short while only.
By two azimuths taken in the evening and the morning we found the variation of the compass needle to be 13° 32' 30" north-west. At four o'clock the Naturaliste signalled to us a fresh damage in her fore shrouds, which was soon repaired. And we continued to steer south, making as much easting as we possibly could.
During the night of the 9th to the 10th the weather was fairly fine, but the wind was very variable and obliged us to perform various manoeuvres until daybreak.
Note. On the morning of the ninth, while the holders were drawing water for the day's ration, a plaintive voice was heard in the hold which caught their attention. They having come to report it to the officer of the watch, a search was made with a light in the fore part of the hold, whence the groans that had been heard had come. After a quarter of an hour's search without discovering anything, the same voice that had been heard a few moments before was heard again, and at last a young black was found lying there almost unconscious.
The surgeon was at once sent below, and he, having judged from the weakness of the pulse that want of food was the sole cause of the state in which the man was found, ordered that he be brought into the air by degrees, and afterwards had him take something light.
When this black had recovered his senses and a little strength, he was questioned as to when he had come on board and to whom he belonged in the Isle of France [Mauritius].
His answer to the first question was that he had been on board for five days and had taken no food whatever during all that time. His master, according to his statement, is M. Gloux, a resident of the Isle of France.
1801-04-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SE. At 6 a.m. a young Black man was found in the hold, where he had hidden himself at Mauritius. Want of food had left him so weak that he could not stand; he said he belonged to M. Gluaux, an inhabitant of Mauritius. At 9.45 the Naturaliste made us a signal that could not be understood. At noon in 25° 6' of latitude observed and in 56° 2' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 0' NW. At 5 we spoke the Naturaliste; she told us that at 9.45 she had signalled us the height of her masts, 106 feet 8 inches from the truck to the gun deck.

1801-04-30.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from east; the sky cloudy. At 1 bore away to close the commander. By three we were near enough to him. The commander having worn ship, we went onto the starboard tack. At 5 p.m. the mist having kept us from seeing the commander, we shortened sail to wait for him; and at 7.30 we went about, supposing he had gone onto the port tack.
1801-04-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the tenth, before daybreak, the shifting of the wind, which had come round for a moment to the south, nearly caused us to lose the Naturaliste. The officer of the watch, having been taken aback, brought the ship onto the larboard tack, and the Naturaliste, which was close to us, having seen this manoeuvre, did the same. But at five o'clock, the wind having come back to the south-east, we at once went back onto the other tack. Being persuaded that the other ship would do likewise, we made her no signal. At daybreak we clearly made out the Naturaliste in our wake, at a great distance. Persuaded that she was standing on the southern board, I contented myself with having the mainsail clewed up and the mizzen topsail laid to the mast, to give her time to come up with us. The sky, which was fine at that time, became covered with mist, and all the rest of the day the weather was squally and rainy.
At eight o'clock, not seeing the Naturaliste, which we had last taken bearing on to the north-east, I went about to go and meet her. But it was not until about ten o'clock that we sighted her in a clear spell, standing, as I had supposed, on the south-south-west board. She was then nearly three leagues to windward of us. As I was persuaded that she must have seen us just as well as we had seen her, I went about again and hove to to wait for her.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, having come up with us, she hoisted her private signal, to which we answered. During the mist I had fired several guns, which no doubt she did not hear, since she did not answer them, or if she did answer, we did not hear her guns.
I was all the more pleased that she had closed with us, as the weather became so bad and so thick in the evening that in all likelihood we should not have met again until we reached the coasts of New Holland, had she failed to sight us in the clear spell which occurred in the morning, when I was standing to the north to look for her.
At noon there was no observation for latitude, and the estimated longitude was 56° 6' 12" east.
At four in the afternoon, the weather having a very threatening look for the night, I had the topgallant sails unbent. The sea, moreover, was already high and the ship was pitching a great deal. I likewise signalled the Naturaliste to do the same (and) to show a light every hour during the night if the ships should not keep within plain sight of each other. At the same time a second reef was taken in the topsails.
During the night of the tenth to the eleventh the weather was rather bad until about ten in the evening, but then, the moon having gathered strength, the squalls and mist dispersed. The sky became clear and we (had) fine weather for the rest of the night. The wind was in the eastern quarter, varying to east-south-east, a strong breeze, and we found the sea fairly high and rough.
1801-04-30.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, a very thick fog, with rain. The wind light and then a strong breeze from SE to E. Lay to from 8.45 until half past noon on account of the fog. Fired several guns, as did our consort. At noon in 25° 50' of latitude by account and in 55° 27' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-01.journal_anonyme: The wind very variable and in gusts. At noon a thick mist came up and we lost sight of the commander. We fired two guns to which he did not answer. At 1.30 we sighted him and fired a third gun, and he at once answered our signals. We at once trimmed close-hauled on the port tack.
1801-05-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the eleventh, in the morning, the weather was fine; only the sea was a little higher and rougher from the very strong breeze of the day before. Nevertheless we shook out a reef from our topsails and dried our other sails. In the forenoon the backstays which I had had prepared were put in place, to strengthen our lower masts, which I did not think well enough supported, and I am persuaded that it is necessary to give them one more shroud abaft.
At noon we observed the latitude of 27° 28' 30" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was then 56° 12'. That of the timekeepers placed us, by No. 27, in 55° 57' 10", and by No. 35 in 55° 51' 15". So that in the two days we had a difference north-south of 1' 12" and one second, and west of 12' 50".
In the evening the weather became overcast, without however any sign of turning bad. The sea, on the contrary, had become much smoother, so that we shook out a reef from our topsails and the topgallant sails were rigged. The wind was in the eastern quarter, varying to east-south-east, a light breeze.
After the crew's dinner a distribution of roll and plug tobacco was made to those who needed it. Woollen clothing was likewise issued to the men we had taken on at the Isle of France [Mauritius] to replace our deserters, the clothes they had beginning to be too light for the temperature we were experiencing.
At sunset the weather was very overcast but without threatening appearance; we continued close-hauled under all sail, except the topgallant sails, which were furled so as not to leave the Naturaliste too far behind.
During the day we saw an albatross, which told us that we were approaching the variable winds, for these birds are seldom found further north than 28° of south latitude.
In the night of the eleventh to the twelfth the weather set in altogether fine, and although there was much moisture in the air and a sort of haze, everything cleared away as the moon rose above the horizon.
1801-05-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At noon in 27° 29' 18" of latitude observed and in 55° 53' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 18° 1' NW.

1801-05-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south. The sea smooth, the sky rather dark. At half past five the commander signalled the course ESE.
1801-05-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twelfth, in the morning, we had the finest weather in the world and a breeze from the north-north-east. As soon as it was light I signalled the Naturaliste, which was a little to windward of us and at a short distance, to steer east-south-east, and I put my own ship on that course. The sea having become very smooth, we made good way until noon.
In the forenoon the people on board were busied in preparing two preventer shrouds for the mizzen mast, which was not firmly secured, as had been done on the previous days for the mainmast. And by means of this precaution I believe I have made our masts as sound as they can be and fit to withstand a few gales, should we happen to meet with any.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 37' 15" south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 58° 14'. That shown by the timekeepers placed us, by No. 27, in 57° 51' 57", and by No. 35 in 57° 46' 0". We found that in the twenty-four hours we had a difference south of 1' 21" and one west of 22' 3".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the breeze was a little less strong than it had been in the morning. The Naturaliste made as much sail as she possibly could to profit by it, and we kept her company under our courses, with a reef in the topsails, and the staysails, which from time to time we were obliged to haul down so as not to leave her too far astern.
In the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth the weather continued fine, but we found much moisture in the air. The wind having gone round to north-north-west and north-west, a pretty breeze, we judged that we had left the south-east trade winds.
1801-05-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NW. At 6 the course was signalled and given S 67° 30' E. At noon in 28° 35' of latitude observed and in 57° 51' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 17° 0' NW.

1801-05-03.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from NNE to NNW and north. The commander very close in the SE 5° E.
1801-05-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the thirteenth the fine weather continued, and during the day we pushed on as far to the east as we possibly could, making the Naturaliste crowd sail so as to profit by it.
In the forenoon I had our mill for grinding wheat set up, and it was placed under the quarterdeck in a convenient spot, sheltered from any accident. I hope we shall make good use of it, and I am putting off its trial until tomorrow. In arranging the parts we have followed everything laid down in the instructions given us, and it seems to us already that it will work very well.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 53' 17" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 60° 58' 30" east. According to the rate of our timekeepers, that of No. 27 was 60° 36' 43" and that of No. 35 60° 30' 40", which gave us a difference of 0° 21' 50" to the east, and by the observed latitude there was a second one, to the south, of 0° 0' 55".
During the evening it continued to blow a pretty breeze, and we were obliged to shorten sail a great deal to wait for the Naturaliste, who was nevertheless under a press of canvas.
At sunset we observed 16° 34' 20" of north-west variation, the mean result of amplitudes taken with three different compasses.
After sunset the sky became covered, in several quarters of the horizon, with dark and misty clouds which seemed to foretell a change of weather. But after the moon rose everything cleared away and it was very clear. In the night the breeze was light and the wind went round to west-north-west. The Naturaliste not having closed with us until about nine in the evening, we began to make more sail so that she need not shorten hers, the weather being very fine and the sea smooth.
1801-05-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to WNW. The hand mill was rigged and we ground wheat. At noon in 28° 53' 42" of latitude observed and in 60° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 30' NW.

1801-05-04.journal_anonyme: Winds from N to NNW. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8.45 the captain signalled the commander the longitude by lunar distances.
1801-05-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the fourteenth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the wind varied from west-north-west to south-south-west, a pretty breeze. We continued to steer east-south-east, regulating our sail to the sailing of the Naturaliste, which had caused us to lose a great deal of way over the past two days. In the forenoon we met a heavy swell from south to south-east which made the sea somewhat high and rough, but as it blew a good breeze the ship was not at all troubled by it.
At noon the observed latitude was 29° 14' 21" and the longitude by dead reckoning 63° 44'. That shown by the timekeepers at the same hour was, for No. 27, 62° 17' 58", and for No. 35, 62° 11' 42". In the 24 hours we had a difference south of 0° 2' 19" and one to (neither figure nor direction).
In the afternoon the breeze died away a good deal and the wind went round from south-south-west to south and seemed inclined to settle at south by west. The sky became overcast and damp and there was every appearance of a change of weather.
In the course of the day we saw an albatross and three or four water-skimmers, with the belly and the underside of the wings a fine white and the upper part of the body and wings a light grey.
At sunset the sky remained overcast and there was much moisture in the air; the wind stayed at south by west.
In the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth the wind fell still lighter. At moonrise, or at least shortly afterwards, the gloom which had hidden the stars from our view cleared away entirely and the sky became very clear. The sea was running a heavy swell from south to south-south-east and was tossed by cross seas. The ship laboured all the more because there was little wind and she was (not) steadied by her sails.
1801-05-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to south. At noon in 29° 11' 20" of latitude observed and in 62° 12' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 19' NW.

1801-05-05.journal_anonyme: Winds NNW, very light, the weather very unsettled, a swell running from SW to SSW. Saw many birds.
1801-05-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the fifteenth, in the forenoon, the wind was variable from south to south-west and it was almost calm. The ship laboured a great deal from the agitation of the sea, and above all from the heavy swell from south to south-south-east, which, taking us on the beam, made her roll heavily. The sky was very fine all day, and no sign on the horizon told us from what quarter the wind would come when it made up its mind to blow.
In the forenoon we took advantage of the calm to fumigate the ship in every part, and for that purpose a general clearing of the decks was made.
We also took a great number of distances of the sun from the moon, the mean result of which gave 64° 6' 15" for the east longitude, which produced a difference of 0° 17' 36" by which the timekeepers were further to the east.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 59' 51" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 65° 14'. In the 24 hours we had a difference of 12' 8" to the south and one to the east of 32' 5". No. 35 placed us in 64° 30' 3" and No. 27 in 64° 23' 51".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, the breeze still very light and the sea swelling and high. Towards evening the wind varied from south to south-east; it then began to blow a little and the ship laboured much less.
In the night of the fifteenth the sky clouded over and the wind seemed to settle in the southern quarter towards the east, (which) made us make a little way to the north. I did not wish to change tack until the wind had settled, and as I was gaining a little to the east, I continued to keep close-hauled on the same tack. Although the sky was laden with clouds during the night, and they even looked rather threatening, we had but very little wind and much moisture, without rain or mist.
1801-05-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 28° 57' 20" of latitude observed and in 64° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 48' NW.

1801-05-06.journal_anonyme: Winds SE, variable to ESE. The weather fine, a swell running. At 9.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-05-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the wind was extremely variable from south towards east and the sky had a threatening look; for nearly the whole forenoon we had squalls, mist and sometimes rain.
At ten o'clock, the board we were on being no longer of any use, I signalled to the Naturaliste that we were going onto the other tack, and at the same time we went (?) about and trimmed our sails on the larboard tack, heading south.
At noon the observed latitude was 28° 37' 2" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 66° 22'. That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 63° 23' 9", and for No. 35, 63° 17' 2", so that the dead reckoning already placed us 58' 51" further to the east.
In the afternoon the weather continued squally and the breeze freshened considerably. However, as it seemed inclined to turn fine towards evening, I put off having a second reef taken in, in the hope that after sunset the breeze would moderate. But at seven o'clock, although the sky had become clear and fine, the breeze, which was then from east by south to east-south-east, increased so much that we had to resolve to take the second reef in the topsails and to furl the main staysail. The Naturaliste, which was close to us, did the same.
In the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth it continued to blow a gale from the east-south-east quarter and the sea became high. Nevertheless the sky was fine and clear, with no sign of bad weather, which led us to believe that so stiff a breeze could not last long and that it would surely soon be over, perhaps with the rising of the moon. This conjecture was not borne out, for it blew all night, and blew in earnest. We were obliged several times to let fly our mainsail to wait for the Naturaliste, which was dropping too far astern.
1801-05-06.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 28° 35' 36" of latitude observed and in 65° 17' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-07.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea high and with a little swell. Wind ESE in gusts.
1801-05-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the seventeenth, in the morning, the wind the wind (sic) was almost as strong as the day before, only it sometimes varied a little towards the east. The sea was beginning to rise and from time to time we felt heavy pitching. The sky was cloudy and fine, with no sign of bad weather.
In the forenoon we were visited by a fairly large number of albatrosses of both kinds, that is to say those that are all grey and those that are almost white. We particularly noticed the Cape pigeon, because it was the first we had seen since leaving France, having met none east of the Cape of Good Hope after rounding it, although we had been in a more southerly latitude than the one we are now in. We also saw several alerions, or storm birds, which seemed to us much smaller than those commonly met with.
At noon the observed latitude was 30° 28' 31" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 65° 28' 42". That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 65° 14' 6", and for No. 35, 65° 8' 9".
In the afternoon the sea seemed to us a little calmer and the breeze had also fallen, although it was still blowing a gale.
At sunset we saw with pleasure that the wind was hauling a little from the east by way of the north, and we hoped soon to have it at north-east.
During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth the wind came in gusts and the sky was sometimes cloudy and fine and sometimes misty. It blew a strong breeze from east to east-south-east, and we continued to keep close to the wind with two reefs in each topsail.
At ten o'clock the Naturaliste, having closed with us, hailed us, but the force of the wind prevented us from hearing what was said. The rest of the night passed without incident. Only we remarked that the sea was not high in proportion to the force of the wind.
1801-05-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. Saw albatrosses and pintado petrels. At noon in 30° 29' 10" of latitude observed and in 65° 8' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-08.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ENE, the sky cloudy, a high sea.
1801-05-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the eighteenth the weather was fine and the sea became smooth. Nevertheless we changed nothing, or at least very little, in our sail, because we had enough to outsail the Naturaliste, even though she had shaken out a reef from her topsails and set her topgallant sails and staysails. The wind having shifted towards the north, we were able to steer east-south-east, which is the course I intended to make and which I signalled to the Naturaliste.
At noon the observed latitude was 31° 37' south and the longitude by dead reckoning 67° 40'. That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 66° 20' 34", and by No. 35, 66° 14' 51". We found that in the twenty-four hours we had a difference north of 0° 4' 47" and one west of 0° 16' 32", according to the reckoning of the distance run and the courses steered by the ship.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and at times a pretty breeze blew from the north-east. We much regretted being unable to take full advantage of it by making sail, but as I did not wish to part from the Naturaliste, I confined myself, as usual, to regulating my progress by her poor sailing.
All day long we had the company of several Cape pigeons and other petrels, which came to play about the ship. We tried to catch some with a line, and often they took the bait we offered them while avoiding the snare we had set for them. The naturalists were much amused by this game.
The night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth was fine and the breeze fairly steady; the sea was no longer swelling and we hoped that the north-east winds would not forsake us so soon. The atmosphere was very damp all night and the horizon had a dull whitish colour that was not pleasant to the eye.
1801-05-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. At noon in 31° 39' 30" of latitude observed and in 65° 15' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 27' NW.

1801-05-09.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NE by E. The sea smooth, the weather fine and the sky very clear. Sailing a short distance from the commander. At two in the morning the sea was covered with luminous molluscs.
1801-05-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the nineteenth, in the morning, the fine weather of the day before was gone. We had a sky heavily laden with vapours and overcast, with a rather threatening look in every quarter of the horizon. However, the breeze was moderate throughout the forenoon, and we had the wind in the north-east quarter, varying to north-north-east.
A heavy north-west swell, which began to make itself felt in the course of the previous night, seemed to tell us that we should soon have winds from that quarter, or that they had already blown hard from that point of the horizon.
At noon we saw the sun show itself for a moment through the misty clouds overhead. The latitude we observed, though doubtful, placed us in 32° 9' 29" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was 69° 41' 30" east. There was was (sic) no hour angle that day to find the longitude shown by the timekeepers.
In the forenoon the barometer fell suddenly to 28. 3 from 28. 4,5, the height at which it had stood for two days. This sudden fall seemed to foretell some squalls, and the state of the atmosphere seemed likewise to confirm it.
However, in the afternoon the wind increased but little, but it drew more towards the north, and (we) even had it at north-north-west, where it stayed only a short while.
At eight in the evening, the wind being at north-east, the sky became more laden with vapours and mist and the rain began to fall. We then furled all our light sails, and did well to do so, for at nine o'clock it began to blow a gale. And during the rest of the night the squalls followed one another so rapidly that scarcely had one passed before we began to feel the effect of the next. At midnight we furled our mizzen topsail, and the topsails were lowered right down so as not to leave the Naturaliste too far astern, to whom we showed a light every hour to indicate our position.
1801-05-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with mist and squalls. The wind a strong breeze and blowing hard from NE to N. At noon in 32° 10' of latitude by account and in 67° 19' of longitude by account.

1801-05-10.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from NE by N in gusts, attended with rain.
1801-05-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twentieth, in the morning, the weather grew worse and worse. We had such an abundance of rain that we could very easily have filled all our empty casks if if (sic)) we had had occasion to need it, but we contented ourselves with collecting some for the livestock and for washing the crew's linen when the fine weather should return. In the forenoon the wind seemed fairly steady at north-north-east, and we remained under the foresail and the two topsails with all reefs in, the Naturaliste under her courses and only two reefs in her topsails, so as to make more way, the sea moreover not being very bad.
At noon the longitude, by the reckoning of the course run, was 71° 21' 30", and we reckoned ourselves in 32° 51' 18" of south latitude.
In the afternoon the behaviour of the barometer told us that the bad weather would not end with the day, for it was falling continually, though not as fast as it had done when the bad weather began. At eight o'clock it stood at 27 inches eleven lines, and in the night it was not below 27. 9. Before nightfall I had the storm staysail bent, and I signalled to the Naturaliste that both ships would carry a light all night so as better to keep watch on each other. That ship furled her mainsail at five o'clock and took a third reef in her topsails. This manoeuvre caused her to drop far astern, so that, to give her time to come up with us, I hove to at eight o'clock, all the more since I could not see the light we had agreed upon; accordingly the topsails were furled and I brought to, head to wind, under the foresail and the mizzen staysail.
At half past nine, the weather having cleared a little, we saw to my great astonishment the Naturaliste within pistol shot of us, trying to pass us to windward. I at once had that ship hailed to bear away, and she passed to leeward. This manoeuvre surprised me all the more because I cannot see for what reason M. Hamelin sought not to let us know his position, by showing at least from time to time the light he had been ordered to carry all night.
When that ship had passed us, I bore away and steered the course signalled, with only the main topsail drawing.
It blew a gale from north by east to north-north-east all the rest of the night, but the rain stopped and the sky became a little less dark, the sea beginning to be bad and the waves high.
1801-05-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from NNE. At noon in 32° 46' 30" of latitude by account and in 70° 2' of longitude by account. We signalled the Naturaliste to keep a light all night; she did so, as did we. The 21st [Floréal, 11 May 1801]. Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from NNE to NW and SW. At noon in 33° 32' 20" of latitude by account and in 73° 37' of longitude by account. At 6 p.m. we lost sight of the Naturaliste.

1801-05-11.journal_anonyme: The same winds and squally. Continual rain; by the commander's order we kept a light burning all night. But no longer seeing the commander, we sent up a rocket; at 6 he was sighted in the SE by E. The ship labouring a great deal from the violence of her pitching and rolling. The wind NNE, a strong breeze.
1801-05-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-first, in the morning, the weather was much the same as the day before, except that we found the sea much worse and the gusts stronger. However, we had only very little rain, but the sky was full of dark and misty clouds, driven by the wind with a speed the eye could scarcely follow.
At daybreak the Naturaliste was very far from us, which led us to think that that ship had carried very little sail during the night. She could barely be seen from the deck. Nevertheless I continued on my course under the same sail, persuaded that if she increased hers a little she would soon have come up with us. Besides, the weather did not allow me to shorten sail, since the sea would have troubled me greatly. Nevertheless, at eleven o'clock, seeing that she was not drawing any nearer, I decided to heave to, and by this means she soon closed with us.
In the forenoon we saw the sun at times, but only for very short intervals.
In the evening the wind varied from west-north-west to south-west, still in gusts and squalls. The barometer still standing below 27 inches (sic), there was no sign that the bad weather was at an end.
Although the ship was violently tossed about by the agitation of the sea, I saw with pleasure that our masts ran no risk, and I rejoiced greatly at having set about securing them in good time.
At noon our estimated longitude was 74° 52' 30" east and the latitude, likewise estimated, was 34° 18' 38" south.
In the night of the 21st to the 22nd the barometer began to rise and we had hopes of a change.
Nevertheless I dreaded this change, because if the wind were to drop too quickly, we should be tormented in a far more disagreeable way than we had been by the bad weather, the sea being very high. All night we kept the stern lantern lit to let the Naturaliste know our position, but (we) could not make out that ship's light, although at times our horizon was fairly wide, the sky having cleared from time to time; but as we had changed nothing in our sail, I was persuaded that she could not be very far off. The ship laboured a great deal during the night from the violent motion the heavy sea gave her.

1801-05-12.journal_anonyme: A heavy wind from SSW and SW, blowing hard. We struck our topgallant masts and the jib boom and lowered the mizzen gaff. On the morning of the 22nd, the weather having cleared, we swayed up our topgallant masts, ran out the jib boom and hoisted the gaff.
1801-05-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the twenty-second the weather turned fine again from the morning onwards, and it was the south-west winds that brought us this change. The Naturaliste was a long way off, in our wake, and as we had laboured a great deal the previous night, I feared that some damage might have befallen her masts if she had not, like us, taken the precaution of fitting her masts with backstays. Nevertheless, it could be made out very well with the spyglass that she had all her masts standing, which made me continue on my course, persuaded that by making such sail as the weather then allowed she would soon have come up with us.
The barometer, which in less than twelve hours had risen from 27 inches ten lines to 28 inches four, told us that the bad weather was over, and the sky had also cleared of all those thick misty clouds which had brought us such violent squalls and gusts.
However, seeing that the Naturaliste was not drawing nearer and remained at the same distance, I hove to to wait for her. When she had closed with us near enough for her signals to be clearly made out, she signalled to us some damage to her main shrouds, which was being repaired. At two o'clock she was abeam of us, and I signalled to her that we were going to steer east by south. We both trimmed our sails to that point of the compass.
Having had the sun clear at noon, we observed the latitude of 33° 42' 27" south, and the estimated longitude was 77° 54' 30". That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 77° 17' 13", and for No. 35, 77° 11' 42", so that in three days we found a difference from the dead reckoning of only 4' 19" to the south and 21' 19" further to the east by the result of the timekeepers.
In the afternoon the weather set in altogether fine, but the sea being very high and the wind almost astern, the ship laboured a great deal. We then had our courses set and two reefs in each topsail, and the Naturaliste was carrying her topsails with a single reef, and her studding sails.
In the night of the 22nd to the 23rd the weather continued fine, but we were none the less troubled by the agitation of the sea, which caused the ship to roll so violently that our masts could not have withstood it without the precautions we had taken to secure them.
1801-05-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to WSW. At daybreak the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake at a great distance; at 11.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack to wait for her. At 1 she had closed; we signalled her the course S 78° 45' E and shaped it. At noon in 33° 39' 40" of latitude observed and in 77° 12' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW. The 23rd [Floréal, 13 May 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze and light from SW to WNW. At noon in 33° 34' 0" of latitude observed and in 79° 50' of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, being almost becalmed with a heavy swell from the SW, our masts were labouring greatly from the rolling; we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and signalled the Naturaliste to follow our movement. At 5 we spoke her; the commander informed Captain Hamelin that if it freshened we should shape the course S 78° 45' E.

1801-05-13.journal_anonyme: Wind SSW to SW. The wind a strong breeze, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, a very high sea and the ship rolling extremely. The course was signalled E by S.
1801-05-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-third the fine weather and a fine sky continued, but we saw with regret that the wind, which was at south-west varying towards west, was gradually dying away, and that we were going to be much troubled by the swell, which was extremely long and high. The seas were so high that the two ships, though within half a cannon shot of each other, lost sight of one another when they were in the trough, and although it was still blowing a pretty breeze, our sails were entirely becalmed between the waves.
In the forenoon we saw several albatrosses and Cape pigeons, and among others a small gouelle, the upper part of whose body was a fine light flax-grey and the underside of the belly a very fine white, with a black ring round the eye, which made this bird very pretty to look at. It was the first of this species we had met with, and we judged it to be an inhabitant of the islands of Amsterdam and St Paul, which were, for us, the nearest known lands.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 41' 49" south and the longitude by dead reckoning was 79° 16' 30". That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 79° 54' 54", and for No. 35, 79° 49' 16". In the twenty-four hours we had a difference of 4' 38" to the north and a second one of 7' 29" to the west.
In the afternoon the wind fell so light that we could not keep on our course for fear of losing our masts. We were rolling so violently that I was in continual anxiety, which did not cease until I decided to take the sea ahead, heading south by west. I signalled to the Naturaliste, which was rolling at least as much as we were, to do the same, and we both steered on that point of the compass until the breeze was strong enough to counterbalance the effect of the swell.
At sunset we caught a Cape pigeon on a line, which greatly amused the naturalists; it was handed over to Maugé to be stuffed.
In the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth the calm lasted until one o'clock, when the wind, having gone round to the north, began to freshen. Both ships then resumed their course and we steered east by south by compass, the Naturaliste with all sail set and ourselves under our four courses, with two reefs in each topsail.

1801-05-14.journal_anonyme: Winds light from SW to north. A heavy swell running. The course signalled south.
1801-05-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the wind varied from north to north-north-west, a pretty breeze, and the heavy south-west swell troubled us no longer, so that we continued to steer east by south by compass, the Naturaliste making as much sail as possible to profit by the fair wind.
In the forenoon the sky, although cloudy and very heavy in several quarters of the horizon, was fairly fine, and at times we had sight of the sun.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 31' 21" south and the longitude by dead reckoning 82° 22' 50". That shown by the timekeepers, reduced to the same hour, was, for No. 27, 81° 11' 30", and for No. 35, 81° 7' 1", which gave us, in the twenty-four hours, a difference to the west of 30' 44" and one to the north of 6' 45".
During the evening it continued to blow a good breeze and the wind at times varied as far as west-north-west.
The sea was beginning to grow smooth, and the heavy south-west swell which had tossed us about so much became much lower.
All day we had the company of a great number of albatrosses and various kinds of petrels, but we caught only one on a line, and even that one was lost to us, for as we were hauling it on board the line broke.
At the beginning of the night the weather had a threatening look and the sky became laden with vapours and very thick clouds in every quarter of the horizon, and although it was blowing a strong breeze they shifted little. The Naturaliste took in all her studding sails, and we our staysails.
The night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth was finer than appearances had led us to expect, and we observed a rather singular phenomenon. The sky was at times clear and without a single cloud, while two or three minutes later it would suddenly be darkened. This happened to us three or four times during the watch from eight o'clock to midnight, which I kept in its entirety for fear of bad weather and because of the too slight experience of the officer in charge of it. During the night the wind sometimes varied as far as north, but stayed there only a little while and always came back to west-north-west, a fine breeze.
1801-05-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At midnight we shaped our course. Saw several albatrosses and many pintado petrels. One of the latter was taken with a line. At noon in 33° 35' of latitude observed and in 81° 7' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-15.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NW, variable to SSW.
1801-05-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the wind was at north-west, a good breeze, until about five o'clock, when it suddenly shifted to south-south-west without losing any of its strength. We at once trimmed our sails on the starboard tack and continued on our course east by south by compass.
In the forenoon the weather was fairly fine, though under a very cloudy and misty sky. From time to time we had sight of the sun, and at noon we observed the latitude of 33° 18' 47" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was 86° 16' 50". That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 85° 18' 28", and for No. 35, 85° 14' 16". In the twenty-four hours we had a difference north of 4' 16" and a difference east of 12' 58".
In the afternoon we again met with a very heavy south-west swell, and it seemed to us that it must have blown with great force in these waters before our arrival. As on the preceding days, we had a fairly large number of petrels and albatrosses as travelling companions. We caught another of the former on a line, but the hook having broken as we were hauling it on board, it was lost to us.
In the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth the weather continued fine, but the wind fell a great deal and ended by settling at south-east, and at times even at east-south-east. However, I did not change tack, and chose to wait on the same board to see in what quarter of the horizon it would settle. It seemed, moreover, that it would not be long in coming back to the north-west, the clouds being driven from that point with some speed.
Since the wind had fallen the ship laboured a great deal, but not, however, as much as the swell had made me fear.
1801-05-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to south. At noon in 33° 22' 50" of latitude observed and in 85° 14' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW.

1801-05-16.journal_anonyme: The winds south, variable to SSE and ESE. At 7 a.m. on the 26th we sent a boat aboard the commander with an officer to set the marine timekeeper, which had not been wound the day before.
1801-05-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the twenty-sixth we spent the greater part of the day becalmed, and the ship, like all of us, was much tormented by a very heavy south-west (swell), which made her roll very violently.
At eight o'clock the Naturaliste asked by signal to send a boat on board. We accordingly hove to to receive it. The officer she sent me having arrived, I was informed by him, and by the letter M. Hamelin wrote to me, that his two timekeepers had stopped, (because) the day before they had forgotten to wind them. We set going again the No. (no figures) which he had sent me, and I sent him a note with the difference of time from our No. 27. When everything (was) settled the boat returned on board, and in my reply I urged M. Hamelin not to leave both timekeepers in the charge of the same person, to prevent their both being forgotten at once in future.
At noon we observed the latitude of 32° 54' 1" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was 87° 32' 50".
That shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 86° 47' 14", and for No. 35, 86° 43' 35". We found that in the twenty-four hours we had a difference south of 6' 12" and one east of 12' 46".
During the evening the sky became covered with rather dark and thick clouds, and there was no likelihood of the calm lasting long. However, at the beginning of the night we did not get the wind that appearances had promised us.
The night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh passed almost in a calm, and it was not until about two o'clock on the morning of the 27th that (we) had the wind from the north-east quarter, rather light, yet sufficient for us to be no longer so roughly tormented as we had been all the while it was calm. As soon as the breeze had come we steered close-hauled on the larboard tack.
1801-05-16.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the breeze light from SE to NE. At 7.15 the Naturaliste asked to send a boat aboard; we at once hove to. At 8 Citizen Saint-Cricq brought one of the Naturaliste's marine watches; they had stopped, Citizen Faure, who had charge of them, having forgotten to wind them. At 9, the boat having left, we filled and stood on. At noon in 32° 51' of latitude observed and in 86° 44' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-17.journal_anonyme: Winds NE to NNE in gusts. A swell running. At 7 a.m. the course signalled ESE.
1801-05-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-seventh the breeze was very fine throughout the day and we had very fine weather, although the sky was so overcast that the sun could not be seen. The Naturaliste being ahead of us at daybreak, we shook out one of the reefs of our topsails and set all our staysails to join her more quickly.
In the forenoon we saw a great number of Cape pigeons, albatrosses and other sea birds. We were lucky enough to catch four of the former on a line, not counting all those we missed, but the others did not come near the bait offered them.
We observed in the Cape pigeons we caught a thing which is perhaps not without interest. The first one caught having been handed over to Citizen Maugé to be stuffed, he smothered it as he had done the first. But on being taken, this bird brought up a fairly large quantity of oily matter which congealed at once and looked to us exactly like melted yellow wax poured out on paper or on a vessel, which made our gentlemen say that this bird yielded wax. The three others offered us the same spectacle, which the first had (not) done. We collected a fairly large quantity of this matter, which I am keeping for anatomical examination. It would no doubt be rather interesting to know what the principal food of these birds is, that it should turn into as much oil as they brought up, for I think it is nothing else.
At noon, not having had the sun, our estimated latitude was 33° 30' 1" south and the longitude 88° 33' 45" east.
In the afternoon the birds which had kept us such good company in the morning, though at their own expense, forsook us, and towards evening we saw none at all. It continued to blow a pretty breeze from north to north-east and the sky remained overcast. The hygrometer, however, showed much moisture in the air, but as the barometer was very high we had no fear of bad weather for the night, which indeed was fine, although the sky remained very dark and overcast throughout.
1801-05-17.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NNE. At 7.15 signalled the course S 67° 30' E, which had been given since 4 o'clock. Saw albatrosses, petrels and many pintado petrels; several were taken. At noon in 33° 20' 10" of latitude by account and in 87° 43' of longitude by account.

1801-05-18.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts. Laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the commander, who was astern.
1801-05-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
