On the twenty-eighth the weather remained overcast all day, but a pleasant breeze blew from north-north-east to north-north-west and we made good way. The heavy south-westerly swell which had been with us for so long was beginning to subside considerably, and the sea was very fine.
The Naturaliste, carrying all sail and her studding sails, obliged us to rig our topgallant sails, but they did not serve us long, and we soon had to furl them in order to wait for her. That day we had none of the company of the Cape pigeons on which we had nevertheless counted the day before, so as to make up the dozen that I intended to keep for the collection of the Muséum. Among the birds we met with there was one species new to us, but we do not know to what genus to refer it. It was a bird the size of a sea snipe, with exactly its manner of flight. Its body above was a light grey, and the underside of the belly very white, as was the lower part of the wings. The tail was likewise grey above and white below, with a black border at the tip.
At noon we had no altitude of the sun, but the latitude by our dead reckoning was (no figures) south and the longitude by dead reckoning (no figures).
In the evening the sky became a little less overcast than it had been in the morning; now and then we saw the sun appear through the clouds, but for so short a time that one might say we had not seen it at all. The (winds) shifted to north-north-west and the breeze was moderate and fairly steady.
During the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth the winds were the same; from time to time we saw a few stars shining, and there was every appearance of a fine day on the morrow. We continued to steer east-south-east, keeping our sail in accordance with the Naturaliste's.
1801-05-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh and then a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At noon in 33° 55' 50" of latitude by account and in 91° 28' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-19.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts, the commander far ahead of us. We sent up a rocket, and at 3 he answered with a light at the masthead. We took his bearing SE. Saw whales.
1801-05-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the winds were variable from north-north-west to north-west, a fine breeze, but the sky had a very ugly look: the whole horizon, both to windward and to leeward, being heavily laden with great, thick black clouds which at times gave us strong gusts. The sea too was beginning to rise somewhat, so that we sent down our topgallant sails and took a second reef in the topsails.
In the course of the morning the barometer fell suddenly to 28p 2l 6 from 28.5,6, at which it had stood for some time, which led us to think that we should again have some squalls. Nevertheless the weather seemed inclined to set fair, and we had sight of the sun, which had not happened to us for three days.
At noon the observed latitude was 34° 29' 38", and the longitude by dead reckoning was 95° 26' 50", whereas that given by our No. 27 was only 94° 31' 33" and by No. 35, 94° 30' 40". We found that since the last observations we had a difference of 13' 25" to the south and one of 9' 51" to the west.
During the evening the weather seemed inclined to set fair. Most of the low, misty clouds that had hidden the sky from us dispersed, and we were able to contemplate it at our leisure, which had not happened to us for a long time.
At sunset we took an amplitude, the result of which gave the variation of the needle as (no figures) north-west.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth the sky again clouded over with dark, misty clouds. After the moon had set, a good breeze continued to blow from north-north-west and we made good way, with the Naturaliste a short distance from us and crowding sail to follow us. As there was no appearance of squalls and the wind was fairly steady, I let her carry her main topgallant sail.
1801-05-19.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 30' 40" of latitude observed and in 94° 31' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 11' NW.

1801-05-20.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, the sea rather high, the wind a strong breeze from ESE. Saw many albatrosses.
1801-05-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the thirtieth the winds were much the same as the day before and a pleasant breeze continued to blow. Although the sea was beginning to run high, the ship behaved none the worse for it and we made good way.
At eight o'clock I signalled to the Naturaliste the course east by south, and myself steered on that point of the compass.
In the course of the morning the weather seemed inclined to set entirely fair, although the barometer had fallen a good deal and the hygrometer showed a considerable quantity of moisture in the air. For almost the whole morning we had a fine sun and a fine sky, though cloudy. At noon, however, we were unable to observe its meridian altitude, because at that moment it was wrapped in a cloud which hid it from our sight until about three o'clock in the afternoon.
By our dead reckoning our latitude should have been 35° 5' south and the longitude 99° 54 50". The distance run in the twenty-four hours was the greatest we had made since our departure from France.
In the afternoon the weather did not look well. At times we had a few small squalls with rain, but they were not of long duration, nor was the wind they brought us too strong.
At four o'clock, not wishing to go too far to the south, I had her steered east and signalled that point of the compass to the Naturaliste. In the course of the day we saw only a very few Cape petrels and a single albatross. But we quite often observed the bird of which I spoke yesterday, whose flight perfectly imitates that of the snipe. It seemed to us that this bird has the same habits on the sea, when it is rough, as the alerion or storm bird, that is to say, it beats the water with its feet and, at first glance, seems to walk upon it.
At nightfall the sky was covered by a very thick mist, and shortly afterwards it came on to rain. At nine o'clock the wind shifted suddenly to the south-west and took us aback. The yards were at once trimmed on the larboard tack and we continued on our course. During the night several signals were made to the Naturaliste, which appeared to us to have shortened sail a good deal. She answered some and not others, which obliged us to haul up our courses for some time in order to wait for her.
For the greater part of the night the weather was very rainy and the winds light. The sea had something of a swell, and we began to perceive that we should soon see a fine sky, the horizon clearing a great deal in the quarter from west to south-west.
Meteorological observations made on board the corvette the Géographe

General remarks: Barometer.
Citizen Péron observes that the results he has obtained from his observations are much the same as those he had previously. He believes, however, that the northerly winds which prevailed during the fortnight have had an influence on the means he obtained, which he thinks ought to be greater on account of the change of latitude.
In the last decade he likewise found the extreme of the variations of the barometer much greater than he had expected, and he attributes the cause to our having followed the same parallel for a long time without any kind of bad weather.
General remarks: Thermometer.
According to Citizen Péron, the northerly winds which brought us warmth likewise influenced the extreme of the variations of the barometer thermometer, since, despite a change of 13° in latitude, the results gave him only 7° in sixteen days, four of which were very bad.
During the last decade the mean temperature of the atmosphere was lower still than that of the preceding decade: he explains the cause by the character of the winds that prevailed, as well as by two strong gales we had experienced in the last days of the last days of the decade.
General remarks: hygrometer.
The mean of the hygrometer having been fairly high, the squalls and frequent rains we have had are truly the cause of it.
The disproportion Citizen Péron found in the results of the third decade seems to him explicable only by the nature of the winds, which did not allow the moisture in the air to descend to a lower region, for it is a fact that there was a great deal of it.

General remarks on the temperature of the sea water.
Citizen Péron, who at the time of his departure from Europe could not imagine that the temperature of the sea water was higher than that of the atmosphere, is at last beginning to believe it, all his observations and experiments having almost constantly given him results contrary to his opinion.
Electricity, meteors.
There were none of any kind during the first fifteen days, although we had rain at times and a stormy sky. It was the same in the third decade.
1801-05-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NNW. At 8 the course was signalled and given S 78° 45' E. At noon in 35° 10' 20" of latitude by account and in 98° 42' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 31' NW. At 4 the course was signalled and given east. During the night sent up rockets.

1801-05-21.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, fresh enough. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8 shortened sail to wait for the commander, who had fallen to leeward. At 8.30 p.m. went about and signalled our tack to the commander.
1801-05-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the first of Prairial the day was extremely fine and exactly resembled a fine summer's day in Europe. The sea, however, though calm, had a very heavy swell from west-north-west, but as we took the seas almost from astern we were only slightly troubled by it. The lightness of the wind prevented us from making much way, and at times the ship would hardly answer her helm.
During the day we saw several large birds, much resembling albatrosses in their flight and even in their plumage, and at a distance we took them for such. But when they came nearer to us and we could easily observe them well, we saw distinctly that they were a new species, in that their bill, head and the tip of the tail were black. We much regretted having had no opportunity of procuring one of them, but perhaps we shall be more fortunate later on.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 34° 47' 52" south and the longitude by our dead reckoning was 102° 32' 50". That given by our timekeepers at the same time was, for No. 27, 101° 29' 59" and for No. 35, 101° 30' 57". In consequence of this observation we found that since the last meridian altitude we had a difference of 2' 26" to the north and one of 15' 34" to the west.
In the evening the weather continued fine and we took several observations of lunar distances from the sun, which gave as their result 102 degrees 37 minutes of east longitude, which put us 57 minutes farther east than the timekeepers. But as the weather was not favourable, the observation is doubtful.
At sunset the wind shifted to the east. Nevertheless we held on the northerly board until eight o'clock, to give the wind time to settle. At that time it began to freshen from the north-east, and we brought our tacks aboard to larboard, making a signal to the Naturaliste to do the same. That ship was then well ahead of us and she went about.
During the night of the first to the second the weather was fairly fine and the breeze increased gradually until daybreak. After the moon had set the sky became clouded and dark, but the breeze remained no less steady and moderate.
1801-05-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW, SW, SE, E and NE. At noon in 34° 47' 0" of latitude observed and in 101° 20' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 53' NW.

1801-05-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind a light breeze from NNW. Saw many birds and fish of various kinds.
1801-05-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks
On the second, in the morning, the winds varied from north-north-east to north, and we continued our course east by compass to bring ourselves into forty-four degrees of south latitude. The sky, though very cloudy, was tolerably fine, and a pleasant breeze blew all morning. But for the heavy west-north-westerly swell that stirred the sea, it would have been very fine.
In the course of the morning we saw several times some of those grey and white birds whose flight so closely imitates that of the snipe. They were even in a fairly numerous flock, but we drew no conclusion from this as to the nearness of land, since we had already met with a good many of them more than two hundred leagues west of the position we were in when we saw these last. It nevertheless seemed to us rather astonishing that a bird, so feeble in appearance, should venture so far from land.
At noon the observed south latitude was 34° 37' 28", and the longitude by our dead reckoning was 104° 15'. That given by the timekeepers put us, by No. 27, in 103° 12' 17", and by No. 35 in 103° 14' 10". In the twenty-four hours there was a difference to the south of 5' 3 seconds and one to the east of 18 seconds.
During the evening the weather was fine. The winds drew a little to the northward by way of the west, and we made tolerably good way, still steering east by compass. The result of the amplitudes and azimuths gave (no figures) of north-west variation.
After sunset the sky clouded over with misty clouds, but the night was none the less fine, and even fairly clear until the moon set. We carried sail all night to take advantage of the fine weather; the winds shifted to north-west and to west, where they seemed inclined to settle.
1801-05-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 103° 12' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 9° 20' NW.

1801-05-23.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, a light breeze, heading east. At 7 the commander made us the signal to bend our cables. At 7.30 p.m. we sounded without finding bottom.
1801-05-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the third, in the morning, the weather was fairly fine, and the winds shifted from west-north-west to west, gradually dying away; we continued our course to the east with all sail set.
In the course of the morning we had points (sic) of so many different kinds, caused by the clouds spread around the horizon, that we could not help remarking on them several times. We had indeed noticed, for the past three or four days, that they presented an aspect quite different from what we had seen in other climates, but they had been very far from showing us such strange and picturesque shapes as those they have offered for some time now. This is no doubt an effect of mirage and of the position in which they stand with regard to the sun.
At ten o'clock I made a signal to the Naturaliste to bend her cables, and we did the same on board.
At noon we observed the latitude to be 34° 13' 37" south, and the longitude arrived at by our dead reckoning was 107° 9' east. That of the timekeepers was then, for No. 27, 105° 44' 54" and, for No. 35, 105° 47' 31".
In the twenty-four hours there was a difference to the north of 3' 45" and one to the west of 14' 23".
In the evening the weather continued fine, but the breeze kept dropping, so that we made very little way. As the Naturaliste was ahead, I had the topgallant sails and studding sails set. It was the first time since our departure that we had happened to carry so much sail.
At about four o'clock the Naturaliste, having brought to, lowered a boat, no doubt to pick up some birds or some other object of natural history she had sighted on the water.
At sunset the weather was fine, but the horizon, in the quarter from west to south, was heavily laden with dark, thick clouds, which seemed to tell us that the wind would soon come to us from that quarter.
At seven o'clock it did indeed shift to south-south-west and brought us a squall which in a moment enveloped the whole horizon. It lasted until eight o'clock and brought us a fair amount of rain but little wind. The weather then set fair again and the sky became very clear. We then lay becalmed until ten o'clock, when a light breeze came to us from the south which enabled us to continue our course under all sail for the rest of the night. The sky was fine, apart from a few small squalls, which gave only a little rain and still less wind.
1801-05-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW, SW, SE and south. We signalled the Naturaliste to bend her cables, and bent ours. At noon in 34° 13' 30" of latitude observed and in 105° 45' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 31' NW. In the evening the Naturaliste signalled 105° 57' of longitude and asked leave to shorten sail.

1801-05-24.journal_anonyme: The winds WNW, variable to south and SW. We hove to to wait for our boat, which was aboard the commander. At 4.30 we filled and stood on under all sail, the weather misty and rainy.
1801-05-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the fourth, in the morning, we had the wind from the south, a light breeze, variable to south-south-east and to south-east by south. The sky was fine in the morning, and as the sun rose above the horizon the breeze increased, so that at nine o'clock we had to furl our topgallant sails, less, however, because of the strength of the wind than in order to wait for the Naturaliste, which was dropping well astern.
At ten o'clock that ship made me a signal to let me know her longitude by dead reckoning, which put her in 106° 50', and at the same time she asked my leave to shorten sail at seven o'clock in the evening. I answered her signal with the attention flag, but not at all her request to shorten sail, which I even found very odd. In the course of the morning we made as much way to the east as possible.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 45' 38" south, and the longitude by our dead reckoning 109° 18'. That given by the timekeepers at the same time was, for No. 27, 107° 51' 1" and for No. 35, 107° 54' 14", so that this timekeeper, which had always been behind No. 27, had for several days been gaining on it and had at last ended by passing it.
In the afternoon a pleasant breeze continued to blow from south-south-east. The sky was fine until sunset, but the horizon, in the quarter from south-east to north-east, was heavily laden with clouds, and everything told us that we should soon have the wind from that quarter.
At four o'clock, the Naturaliste being a little ahead of us, I made her the signal to close, general and absolute, and, having passed within hail of her, I ordered her to keep during the night two miles from us, in our wake, and, beginning at eight o'clock, to sound every two hours until four o'clock in the morning. Although we had had no sign during the day of the approach of land, this precaution seemed to me all the more necessary because, according to some of our charts, in the latitude we were in, bottom (was) found nearly fifty leagues from the coast.
After sunset the sky clouded over with mist, and at eight o'clock it came on to rain, so that our horizon was very limited. At that time we sounded, but a line of two hundred and fifty fathoms gave us no bottom, which we ought nevertheless to have found according to the chart of M. Bellin, who places the westernmost point of New Holland, in our latitude, in 110 degrees 30' of east longitude, whereas the other charts place the same point in 113° 20'.
At ten o'clock, the wind having shifted to south-east, variable to south-south-east, with a very overcast and misty sky, I made a signal to the Naturaliste to stand on the southerly board, and having carried out the same manoeuvre myself, we both lay to on the larboard tack and remained so until the following morning.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth the weather was very changeable; at times we had a fairly wide horizon, but for most of the time it was dark and misty; the winds shifted from south-east to east, so that we lost little by making no way.
1801-05-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 33° 42' 40" of latitude observed and in 107° 51' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 4' NW. At 12.15 the course was signalled S 78° 45' E. At 4.30 made the signal to close. Shortly afterwards we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander ordered Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at half a league and to sound every two hours, and to warn us by two vertical lights should he find bottom, adding that we should warn him in the same way if we found bottom. At 8 hove to and sounded without finding bottom at 265 fathoms. At 8.30 filled and stood on. At 10.30 lay to on the port tack under the mizzen topsail, the mizzen and its staysail, the main staysail and the fore staysail.

1801-05-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind SSE. At 3 the course signalled E by S. At 4 we shortened sail to wait for him; being within hail he ordered us to keep in his wake at half a league's distance and to sound every half hour. Hove to at 7, 8 and 10 and ran out 120 fathoms of line without finding bottom. The commander having gone onto the port tack, we did the same. At midnight, two and four o'clock ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the fifth, in the morning, the wind being east, a light breeze, we stood close-hauled on the southerly board. In the course of the morning the sky set entirely fair and we had a fairly wide horizon, and all we lacked was a fair wind. The breeze increased a little as the sun gained strength, but on the whole it was very moderate.
In the course of the morning we saw several flights of birds, but all were of the same species we had been meeting for several days and at a great distance from the coast, so that nothing had yet told us that we were near the lands of New Holland.
At noon we observed the latitude to be 33° 51' 16" south, and the longitude for the same hour was, by No. 27, 108° 27' 33" and by No. 35, 108° 33' 20", so that, according to the chart that seems to me most deserving of confidence, we still have 4° 47' to run to the east before reaching land.
By our dead reckoning the longitude arrived at was 110° 1' east, and we found that in the 24 hours we had a difference to the south of 2' 15" and one to the west of 3' 54", which differed very little from the reckoning of our course.
Having observed the meridian altitude, and not wishing to go any farther south, I made a signal to the Naturaliste to go about, and we both stood on the north-north-east board. The sky in the evening was so fine that it could be compared to that usually met with in the tropics, and we were ourselves astonished to find it so clear at this season of the year.
From the azimuth observations and the ortive amplitudes taken during the day, the mean of all the observations gave (no figures), and as the weather was very favourable, there is every reason to believe that it differs little from the true variation of the needle in the waters we are crossing.
The night of the fifth to the sixth was one of the finest and clearest we had had since our departure from Europe. The moon, which was nearly full, gave us light without the slightest interruption.
At ten o'clock in the evening, the wind having shifted to east-north-east, a signal was made to the Naturaliste to go about and keep close-hauled until the wind allowed us to steer east by south. We carried out the same manoeuvre ourselves, and we kept on our course all night, taking advantage of the wind, which drew more and more into the north-east.
1801-05-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to NE. At 5 filled and stood on. At noon in 33° 51' 40" of latitude observed and in 108° 29' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 8' NW.

1801-05-26.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind variable from NE to NNE. At 1 p.m. wore onto the starboard tack, and at 10 p.m. went about. At 1 a.m. ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks
On the sixth we had the wind from the east-north-east quarter, a pleasant breeze and a smooth sea. After sunrise I signalled to the Naturaliste the course east by south, and then set all sail to press on ahead, so as to make the land before nightfall, in case the longitude of New Holland, in the part where I intended to fall in with it, did not differ much from that given it by the chart of M. Bellin. But it was labour lost, for at nightfall, although the weather was fine and the horizon fairly wide, we sighted nothing, nor even any sign that might lead us to suspect that (we) were at a short distance from it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 50' 49" south, and the longitude by our dead reckoning, from the distance shown by the log, was 111° 15'. That of the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was, for No. 27, only 110° 1', and for No. 35, 110° 6' 31". We found that in the twenty-four hours we had a difference to the south of 5' 49" and one to the east of 1° 5' 29" (?), which was very considerable.
In the afternoon, the weather continuing fine, we left the Naturaliste astern in order to crowd sail towards the land, but as the sea was becoming a little rough and we were taking it head on, at about three o'clock we furled our topgallant sails, whose masts seemed to me poorly stayed.
At sunset, having no sign of the approach of the coast, I should have continued to crowd sail, but as the Naturaliste was too far off, since she could scarcely be made out from the maintop, I had sail shortened to wait for her.
During the night of the sixth to the seventh the weather was fine and the sky fairly clear. We had, however, constant lightning in the quarter from south-south-west to south-east, which, following without interruption, seemed to foretell winds from that quarter. Our expectation was disappointed, for the winds stayed constantly in the north-east, varying at times towards north-east by east, which made them unfavourable to our course by carrying us too far to the south of the one I should have wished to hold.
At midnight we brought to in order to sound, but a line of two hundred fathoms gave us no bottom. After the lead had been brought back on board, two rockets were sent up to show the Naturaliste our position. As I thought that ship would have continued to carry sail, I supposed, from the little we had carried ourselves, that she could not be very far from us. No answer was made to this signal, however, and I then kept under the topsails, almost shivering in the wind, so as to make less way.
At two o'clock, sweeping the horizon with my night glass, I perceived that ship astern of us and to windward. I had a light hoisted at the mizzen gaff, and when she had closed with us, sail was increased.
1801-05-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. At 7 signalled and shaped the course S 78° 45' E. At noon in 33° 49' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 44' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. The Naturaliste, far astern, was lost sight of at nightfall. Sent up rockets and showed a light at the gaff to give her our position. At midnight we sounded and ran out 200 fathoms without finding bottom.

1801-05-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NNE. The commander standing in for the land. At 5 it bore from us east 9° S, distant about 5 leagues, the commander out of sight. At 3.30 a.m. we had closed him within hail. At 7 he signalled us land without giving the bearing. At 7.30 we took its bearing in the SSE, with two detached points. At 10 took the bearing of the northernmost land ESE. Noon bearings: the furthest point to leeward that could be seen, east 25° 30' N; the point at which the land seemed no longer to continue, east 33° 10' N; the middle of the land which to windward appeared separate from the first, east 37° 45' N. None of these corrected for 6° 30' of NW variation.
1801-05-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & remarks. View of New Holland
On the seventh, from four o'clock in the morning, we began to set all sail except the topgallant sails, and at half past seven, as the topmen were loosing them, they announced the land bearing east by north. As the wind was then north-north-east, variable to north-east by east, we had great difficulty in closing with it, and it was only at about half past ten that it began to be made out from the deck.
The first view we had of it corresponds exactly to the coloured drawing of it that I give, and any ship making the land in the same latitude as we did will easily recognise it. The southern part of Cape Leeuwin, seen in the distance, presents a fairly even coast and, at a distance of nine to ten leagues, seems to form several islands or at least inlets whose depth cannot be seen. The middle of the most prominent land is fairly high and ends in two low points, after which come the other lands shown in figure No. 1. In fine weather it can easily be seen at a distance of ten leagues. At the moment we sighted it, our latitude by dead reckoning was 34° 25' 55" south and the longitude arrived at 112° 51'. We put off determining the error of the timekeepers until we should be nearer the land, as they seemed to us from that moment to be giving a westerly difference.
At noon the observed latitude put us in 34° 35' 58", and the longitude by dead reckoning, reduced to noon, was 112° 57' 42" east.
That given by the timekeepers at the same time was, for No. 27, 111° 42' 7" and for No. 35, 111° 47' 19".
Bearings of the land at noon:
The easternmost point of the land in sight east 22° north)
The point of the land farthest north east 47° north) all by compass
A point to the north of the preceding one east 35° north)
A point of the same land east 43° north)
After taking the bearings I had a sounding made, and we found bottom in a hundred and four fathoms, a bottom of broken and jointed coral. The Naturaliste, which had sounded at the same moment, signalled to us 117 fathoms, a bottom of fine white sand. That ship was then about two miles astern of us and a little to windward.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but we were almost becalmed until four o'clock in the afternoon, when the wind shifted to south-east, variable to south-south-east. We at once trimmed the yards on the starboard tack and closed with the land, which, from the bearings taken at sunset, appeared to us in the form shown in drawing No. 3.
Bearings of the land at sunset:
The most prominent land to the north north 5° east) all by compass
The middle of the same land N. NE 4° east)
The easternmost point NE 5° east)
After sunset we continued our course N. NE to close with the land and work to the north, sounding frequently, and at eight o'clock I hove to, to pass the night in that position if the weather continued fine. We could then make out the land very clearly, and our dead reckoning put us five leagues from it.
Throughout the night the weather was fine and the wind south-east, variable to east, a light breeze. Soundings were taken every two hours, and they sometimes showed several irregularities of the bottom. As every cast gave us a good bottom of sand, sometimes mixed with small points of coral, I resolved, to make the night seem less long and to satisfy my curiosity, to have one of our dredges put over, being persuaded that, despite the great depth of the water, I might come upon some fine shells or other curious objects. Accordingly we set about
dredging. We then had a fine bottom of seventy-two fathoms, pure greyish-white sand. At ten o'clock the dredge was put over and we paid out a hundred and fifty fathoms of line. Half an hour later it was hauled in, and to our great satisfaction it was found to be quite full of various objects that we were most impatient to examine. A tub having been made ready beforehand, everything was emptied into it, and it was not without astonishment that we saw in it a great variety of things new to us.
When it had been emptied, it was put over again, and we then set about reviewing what we had just brought up from the bottom. Most of the objects consisted of sponges and pieces of soft coral, several fine marine plants and a great quantity of small sponges that resembled potatoes in shape.
Of living animals we found only two species of worms, which were at once put into spirits.
The marine plants and the different kinds of coral seemed to us the most valuable, and we made an ample collection of them, as well as of small branches of coral, but apart from two small white nerites and a limpet we took no shells.
At half past ten we hauled in our dredge, which was found to be even fuller than the first time, and with much the same objects. We much regretted that various lithophytes which we had had the good fortune to come upon were broken. But this harm seemed to us beyond remedy, owing to the pressure caused by the water and the heaping together of the various objects taken in the dredge.
However that may be, this first trial at so great a depth seemed to us so satisfactory that I promised myself, whenever the occasion should present itself, to make good use of the time we should lose in not making way.
Nature of the soundings and of the bottom during the night.
At six o'clock in the evening 87, clean grey sand
At eight o'clock in the evening 97, sand and some points of coral
At ten o'clock 72, grey sand, points of coral and fragments of shells
At midnight 100, grey sand and small coral
At two o'clock in the morning 102, grey sand and small coral
At four o'clock in the morning 105, grey sand and small coral
At six o'clock 110, grey sand and small coral.
At eight o'clock in the evening, the Naturaliste having passed within hail, I called to her that my intention was to lie to during the night if the weather remained fine; she asked my leave to send on board to compare her timekeepers, which she had been unable to use since the last time she had come on board to compare them.
At nine o'clock M. de St Criq arrived, and he again settled their rate with M. Bernier, our astronomer, who in every respect is worth a hundred thousand times more than the one who, fortunately for us, stayed behind at the Isle of France [Mauritius].
I took the same opportunity to send M. Hamelin the table of our agreed signals for the boats, to which I added an instruction on the conduct to be followed by the officer to whom he should entrust his longboat, should we at times be obliged to send it off for several days on discovery.
Nota: at eleven o'clock in the evening a spirit thermometer, enclosed in a wooden case which was then filled with tallow, was let down into the water. This thermometer remained at a depth of about fifty fathoms until five o'clock the next morning. After it had been taken out of its case it was found to stand at 17°9, the air of the atmosphere then being at 17°, which gave 0°9 more for the temperature of the sea water at that depth. We had noticed earlier that the objects brought up in the dredge gave off a very perceptible warmth, but our eagerness to examine them prevented us from thinking of placing the thermometer among them.
View of New Holland. Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, in the morning, we were much astonished not to see the land, of which we had still had a perfect view at four o'clock. It could now be seen only from the maintop, and we concluded, rightly, that a strong and violent current, or at the least a change of tide, must have carried us to the south-east, since the bearings we then took gave us:
The land farthest north N ¼ NE ) all by compass
The middle of the same land N. NE )
and the easternmost point NE 6° N )
Having fixed our position, we made sail, but as the wind was then E. SE and very light, the course we were obliged to hold brought us little nearer the land.
In the course of the morning we saw several whales of ordinary size, much like those met with south of Madagascar. They passed close enough to the ship to give our gentlemen a spectacle quite new to them in their manner of spouting the sea water.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 34° 46' north south, whereas that by dead reckoning gave us 34° 9' south, so that between the reckoning and the observation we had 35' of difference to the south.
The longitude given by the timekeepers was then 111° 45' 59" for No. 27 & 111° 41' 55" by No. 35, which gave 4' 6" of way to the east in the 24 (hours), so that the current or the tide carried us directly south 6° east. This small mishap was a lesson to us, and I hope that the currents in this direction will not play us such a trick again.
After the observation of the sun, the land, of which we then had a perfect view from the deck, lay according to the following bearings:
The land farthest north: north 16° east ) all by compass
A low point on which could be made out )
two small peaks north 22° east, north 30° east ) The easternmost land in sight, N E. )
The lead at the same moment showed 104 fathoms, a bottom of sand and fine coral.
Figure No. 5 gives an exact view of the aspect the land then presented to us, which in this part is, as I have already observed, of moderate height and apt to be seen at 10 or 12 leagues in fine weather.
During the evening, the wind having shifted to east-south-east, a pleasant breeze, we crowded sail towards the land, from which at sunset we were no more than two leagues at most. We then shortened sail to wait for the Naturaliste, which was well astern, and took the following bearings while drawing the view shown in figure No. 6.
Bearings of the land at sunset.
The northernmost point N1/4 NW )
The low point of a fairly high land NE 5° east ) all by
The extremity of this same land east 15° N ) compass.
The southernmost land E. SE. )
At the same hour the bottom was 87 fathoms, sand and rotten shells.
At half past seven we hove to with the main topsail to the mast and waited for the Naturaliste, which joined us shortly afterwards and hove to on the same tack as ourselves.
So as not to pass our time doing nothing, I had the dredge put over to see whether we should be as fortunate as the day before, or more so. We took some madrepores, sponges of various colours and even some curious pieces of soft coral on which were various plants and lithophytes. This first trial encouraged us to make a second, although I was not (without) anxiety for the fate of my dredge, seeing that the nature of the bottom
shown by the lead, which I had cast every half hour, declared it to be bad. We nevertheless hauled it in without mishap, but whether it had been badly directed or from some other cause, we took nothing that time.
At about ten o'clock the Naturaliste, which was farther inshore than we were, went about and came to inform me that she had found a strong current setting, according to her reckoning, to the east-south-east, which had brought her so close to the coast that she had got into as little as twenty-five fathoms, rocky bottom, and had clearly made out the breakers on shore.
Like the Naturaliste, we had taken our marks on the land at the beginning of the night. One bore east 22° north and the other east 5° north, and at the moment the Naturaliste was speaking to us, one bore east 11° north and the other N 10° west, which led me to believe that the currents were carrying us rather to the NW than to the south-east.
However that may be, we both filled away and ran for about an hour to the N. W under our topsails, after which we hove to again on the starboard tack.
Throughout the night the weather was very fine, and by the light of the moon we could make out perfectly the land and all the white patches with which it (is) marked in this part. Our dead reckoning put us about two leagues from it.

1801-05-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE and light from SSE to E. At 1.30 the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake. At 7.30 the land was sighted; it stretched from S 78° 45' E to N 67° 30' E and appeared to be divided in two parts. We signalled it to the Naturaliste. At noon the land from N 43° E to N 68° E, being in 34° 35' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 42' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 15' NW. At half past noon the lead gave 104 fathoms, coral and sand. At 7.30 hove to on the starboard tack; the Naturaliste passed under our stern and the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to lie to all night; he gave him leave to send aboard to compare his watches. At 8.30 Citizen Saint-Cricq arrived with the marine watches and left at 9. At 10.30 the boat came back to bring us hay. The dredge was put over and brought up marine specimens; the lead gave from 92 to 100 fathoms, coral, sand and shell. At midnight the land N 15° E.

1801-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind varying from SE, SSE and ESE. At half past noon hove to to sound. The lead brought up 93 fathoms, white sand mixed with broken shell. We thought we noticed that the winds set to the south. Bearings taken at sunset: the southern end of a stretch of land we judged to be an island, east 47° N; the furthest part to the north bore N 23° 40' E. At 7.30 passed under the commander's stern and asked his leave to communicate in order to set our marine timekeepers; he granted it and warned us that if the weather stayed fine we should lie to heading north. Soundings: at 9 p.m., 89 fathoms, reddish sand and broken shell; at 10, 11 and 12, 90 fathoms, the same. We lay to on the starboard tack until four o'clock, when we filled and stood on. At daybreak took the bearing of the land east 27° N. At 10, east 38° 10' N.
1801-05-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ENE. Shortly after midnight the land was lost sight of. At 7 we filled and stood on, and the land was seen from aloft. From midnight to noon the lead gave from 100 to 105 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon the land bore from us N 33° E to N 38° E, being in 34° 45' 0" of latitude observed and in 111° 46' of longitude by No. 27. The variation 6° 90' NW [sic]. By the reckoning we had made way to the north and west, and by the observation we had made it to the south and east, which can only be put down to the violence of the currents, which set south and SSE. At 5 took the bearing of the north point in sight N 11° E, the south point in sight N 67° 30' E, and an islet lying near the latter N 78° 45' E. From 5 until midnight the lead gave from 45 to 33 fathoms, sand and coral. During the night we lay to, in sight of land.

1801-05-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ESE. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 took the bearing of the easternmost part of the land in sight N 23° 20' E, the westernmost part N 45° E, estimated distance 16 miles. Passed under the commander's stern; he ordered us to heave to. At 8.25 sounded and found 25 fathoms, sand and broken shell. At five in the morning the commander having filled, we did the same. At noon sounded and found 28 fathoms, rock and coral. At the same hour took the bearing of the southernmost point of the land east 38° 30' S and the northernmost N 21° 30' E.
1801-05-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, at daybreak, we crowded sail to close with the land, from which our dead reckoning then put us four leagues distant. The weather was very fine, and the sunrise promised us a fine day. Our only regret was that the wind was from the east quarter, variable to east-north-east, and very light. But as on the preceding days it had veered from east towards south when the sun gained strength, we hoped that the same would happen to us in the course of the day.
At sunrise the following bearings were taken:
The land farthest north relative to our position, N ¼ NE)
A cape in front of which there is a large white patch NE ) all by compass
The land farthest south of us east ¼ SE )
From the bearings and the dead reckoning of the reduction of the various courses since noon yesterday, our latitude by dead reckoning was 34° 3' 46", which brought us very close to that which almost all the charts, old as well as modern, give for the latitude of this cape.
From early morning the aspect the coast presented to me had led me to suspect that the point we had in sight might well be it, but to settle my opinion on this matter with greater certainty, I put off the verification of this conjecture until the observation of the sun's altitude at noon.
The breeze having increased a little and the wind drawing towards the east, we stood somewhat closer in to the land, towards which the tide also seemed to be carrying us, so that by eight o'clock noon we were at most three leagues from it. The observed latitude was then 34° 10' 35" by most of the instruments, and those whose observation put us farthest south differed by only 2' 15 seconds. So that the mean of our observations gave 34° 7' 6" 3"' for the latitude observed at noon. The sky was then very fine and the horizon so clear that no doubt can remain as to the result of the observations.
From this latitude and the position assigned to Cape Leeuwin by most of the charts we have of it, it would therefore appear certain that the projecting point abreast of which we were, and which then bore east 17° south, 3 leagues distant at most, must truly be that cape, which is moreover very easy to recognise by the large white patch that lies near it and a little to the south. Mean longitude of the timekeepers at noon 111° 37' 57".
Having then joined the Naturaliste, which was about a quarter of a league ahead of us and to windward, I asked her observed latitude. It was (no figures), and consequently differed from ours by only (no figures). I then questioned him to learn which of the points we had in sight he believed to be Cape Leeuwin. His answer was that he presumed it to be the point bearing SE 5° south. He based his reasoning on the fact that, the evening before, we had sighted this same point, at the extremity of which it was believed that the small islet placed on the charts had been seen.
I had seen, as had M. Hamelin, this small islet the day before, which, by the report of all those who went up to the mastheads, is no islet at all, but rather a low land joined to another coast which stretched out of sight to the south-south-east. Besides, if the cape bearing south-east 5° south, which we had in sight, were truly Cape Leeuwin, it would follow that its latitude would be thirty-four degrees thirty-three minutes six seconds, which I am very far from believing.
It seems to me demonstrated, by the extent of coast we have run along to the south of Cape Leeuwin, that the place where M. St Aloüarn may have anchored cannot be in the latitude by dead reckoning that he gives in his journal, for, supposing we had not seen his islet, we should at least have sighted one of those he speaks of, since we made the land in 34° 35' 58". Thus, in running along the south coast of New (Holland), we made twenty-eight minutes fifty-two seconds of latitude to the north, to arrive at 34° 7 6, always near enough to the land
to be able to make out islands, islets and reefs of rock, had there been any. The whole coast we have run along since 34° 35' 58" is clear of dangers, even very clear. It is far from being low and flooded as far as (no figures); on the contrary it is full of heights which follow one another fairly closely, and it can only be at eight or ten leagues' distance, when the lower lands that join them together cannot be seen, that these heights could be taken for islets. It was no doubt from a great distance that M. St Aloüarn saw the coast and the islets he reports.
In the evening we had the wind at south-east and south-south-east, as we had expected, which brought us in to within four miles of the coast, and until after sunset we continued to run along it, following all the windings presented by the various inlets it might offer us. We saw with regret that it offered neither shelter nor anchorage for ships. And, except for two small sandy coves where the sea appeared somewhat quiet, it broke with a great noise all along the coast, which is extremely sheer and steep.
While we were running along the coast, the astronomers and geographers were constantly occupied in taking angles and bearings in order to draw up the chart of it, and I think this work will be well done, judging by the assiduity with which they pursued it and by our short distance from the land.
All the country we explored seemed to us barren, as regards the land nearest to us, which faces the sea shore. The heights most remarkable to us were (for) the most part covered with a kind of heath that seemed to us of little height, and here and there one could make out some clumps of trees of a fairly fine green, which served only to make the places that were bare of them the more unpleasing to the eye. One of the things that struck me most was that, in the fairly considerable extent of land we examined at such close quarters, we saw no ravine that appeared to have an outlet to the sea for the waters.
The mountains, for there are many which are not so high and which bear that name, stood little inland and ended at the sea in a slope that seemed to us fairly gentle, but at the water's edge the coast was, as I have already said, sheer and difficult of access.
These lands will be easy to recognise in future by navigators who frequent these waters. The various white patches, larger or smaller, that are found on them are arranged with enough symmetry for there to be no mistaking them. They are shown in the view that I have had drawn (and) coloured expressly for this purpose. The wooded parts and those that are not will likewise be seen in it.
For a long time we believed that this coast was not inhabited, but we soon had proof to the contrary, for at nightfall we saw fires in various places which showed us that it was not without inhabitants.
If during the day I had seen any places suitable for bringing the ships into, I should not have failed to return there the next day, but apart from there being no anchorage, the bottom is bad, as we found almost everywhere only sand mixed with large coral, or a hard bottom of pure coral and rocks.
As I had gone on ahead of the Naturaliste, I found at sunset that I had explored a much greater extent of coast than she had, and so that she might know the course the night would oblige me to steer, I kept my stern lantern lit until she had joined me.
I do not know whether the coast we have just examined can offer anything of interest to natural history, since we did not land on it, but at least what
struck me as rather extraordinary is that we had a visit from no land bird, and two Cape pigeons are the only sea birds we met with, which is an almost sufficient indication to establish the barrenness of the land and the few resources that the sea can offer to the others.
Another thing, likewise rather singular, and in which I have put no faith, is that the lookouts at the mastheads firmly maintained that they had seen several large quadrupeds come out of a small, fairly tall grove of trees which we then had in sight, which they said were oxen, or at least appeared so to him. They appeared to him, at different times, to go into and come out of the grove I have just spoken of.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth the weather continued fine. We spent it partly hove to and partly under sail, about four leagues from the coast. 1801-05-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SE. At 5 we filled and stood on, running along the coast at about 6 miles. It seemed to me to offer no safe anchorage: it is fringed with reefs on which the sea broke with force; the dunes are covered with heath and a few bushes are to be seen here and there. The lead giving from 30 to 40 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon, being in 34° 11' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 44' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 4' NW. The northernmost point in sight bore from us N 20° E, the southernmost S 45° E, and a white cape (taken for Cape Leeuwin) S 78° 45' E. At 5 we saw a fire on the shore, which convinced us that the coast is inhabited. At 7.30 we hove to. The Naturaliste passed under our stern and spoke us. The trend of the coast is roughly north and south. Note: Cape Leeuwin lies further south than this white cape.

1801-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; we ran along the coast to the north. At 4 p.m. took the bearing of Cape Leeuwin south 15° 30' E, distant about six leagues. Running along the coast we saw a fire ashore and then several more. We hoisted a lantern at the gaff to make ourselves known to the inhabitants. Soundings: at 8 and 9, 30 fathoms, rock and coral; at 10, 38 fathoms, fine sand; at 11 and 12 the same, mixed with broken shell. At 1 the commander having altered course we did the same. At 2 filled and made all sail. At 6.25 a.m. went about to close the commander, who was far to leeward. At 6.40 sounded in 28 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon we saw that the land stretched away all along to starboard and formed a bight, of which several points could be seen at noon from the quarterdeck. Noon bearings: Point P ahead of us S 2° E; Point N furthest astern S 3° 30' E; Point O which we had doubled S 27° W. These points are so named after the surveying engineer's work.
1801-05-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, at four in the morning, the weather being very fine and the sea smooth, we trimmed our sails close-hauled on the larboard tack, the wind being then at south-east by east, varying to east-south-east, and at daybreak we made all sail. The Naturaliste did the same, and we closed with the land, from which we were three leagues distant.
Bearings of the land at sunrise
The northernmost land in sight east 18° north)
The southernmost land in sight south 5° east ) all by compass.
The middle of the land formed by these two points south-east )
At eight o'clock we went about and stood well in towards the land, which we ran along at a league's distance as far as its northernmost part relative to our position, a part made very remarkable by a reef that stretches a good quarter of a league out to sea and on which the sea was breaking with great force.
When we had rounded this cape, the easternmost lands began to show themselves, and, holding on the tack that carried us to the north-east, we sighted a great bay, of which the cape we had just rounded formed the southern point, while the northern one extended as far as west by north-west. And even then one could scarcely make out, from the mastheads, the end of the inlet it forms towards the east, so that this expanse presented us with an immense bay which, by our reckoning, measured more than fifteen leagues from one cape to the other. After rounding the southern point I have just mentioned, the wind being south-east, we had no other tack to hold but that to the north-east. And as it was carrying us away from the coast, I supposed that we were over very deep water, which led me to sound often so as not to stand off too far; but I was much astonished to find that, instead of approaching the soundings we had which it put at the usual depths, the water was shoaling gradually, and that from the thirty-five fathoms we had had on rounding the point, it was no more than 33 when we were six or seven leagues from it. The Naturaliste, which was then to leeward of us, had much the same ground, fine clean sand.
At noon the latitude by dead reckoning was 33° 32' 42" south and the observed latitude 33° 23' 49", which gave us, as the difference in the dead reckoning of our courses over the twenty-four hours, 8' 53" of northing. The longitude given by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was for No. 27, 112° 13' 38" and for No. 35, 112° 20' 29", our great cape then bearing south 38° west.
Shortly after the observation, the Naturaliste signalled to us that it did not think the course we were steering a good one to follow, since it could see a danger to the north-north-west. I answered with the attention flag, but continued on the same tack so that it might make more certain of it, being persuaded that the danger was surely like those so often reported to us, and was nothing other than whales playing on the surface and throwing the water up to a great height.
At two o'clock, so as not to stand too far from our great cape, which bore south 38° west, I went about to approach the land. We sounded every half hour on board, and for a long while the lead brought up a bottom of fine sand, sometimes very clean and sometimes coarse yellow sand. We even had one, in 28 fathoms, exactly like that commonly found at the mouths of rivers, and we all thought, from the appearance the land presented to us, that we should find one. Several persons who went up to the mastheads even believed they could see it, and in consequence of their
report I resolved to anchor off the open coast in twenty to twenty-one fathoms, if the ground continued good.
On approaching the land we saw two sandy coves on which the sea seemed fairly quiet, and it was off the easternmost of them that I came to anchor in 23 fathoms, fine sand mixed with a little mud, four miles at most from the shore. The Naturaliste being far to leeward, and having been well able to make out our manoeuvre since it was still daylight, I was in no anxiety about the one she would make to join us, and indeed at eight o'clock she came to anchor abreast of us.
As soon as I was at anchor I sent my boat to sound all round the ship, and even to a fair distance. All the soundings it took gave excellent holding ground, and I was without anxiety for my anchor. This done, and not wishing to spend a night doing nothing, I had the dredge run out by my boat to a distance of two hundred and fifty fathoms from the ship. We were not very fortunate, though we got some rather curious things in the way of sea urchins, starfish and plants.
During the night a boat was made ready to set off the next day before daybreak to go and examine the country. I gave the command of it to Citizen Freycinet; all the scientists wished to go with him, but as the boat could hold only eight men in all, there were some malcontents, and there will often be more on such occasions. The gardener Riedelé and the mineralogist Depuche were the only ones chosen to go ashore: the one to give us an idea of the country, and the other to learn the nature of the soil, which offered us a more agreeable prospect than the parts we had examined until then.
During the night of the tenth to the eleventh the weather was fine and the winds moderate from south-south-east to south-east. About eleven o'clock, however, we had a rather heavy gust which made us drag our anchor and very nearly caused us to fall aboard the Naturaliste, which we nevertheless did not touch, though it was a very near thing.

Anchorage on the coast of New Holland in 33° 30' 55 seconds of south latitude & 111° 56' 56" of east longitude. From the 11th Prairial, Year 9, &c. (31 May 1801)
On the eleventh, an hour before daylight, my small boat set off for the shore under the command of Citizen Freycinet, and the persons chosen the day before went with him. This officer had been furnished with the orders relating to the mission he had to carry out, and I am pleased to believe that he will acquit himself of it with exactness.
At daybreak preparations were made to hoist the longboat out, one (sic) that I wished to send it (sic) to examine the lands around us, and above all the cape that forms the southern entrance of the bay, whose position I wished to fix with exactness. For this reason the astronomer Bernier and the geographer Boulanger were ordered to embark for the purpose. The command of this longboat was entrusted to Citizen Picquet, to whom I gave a written order as to what he had to do. At ten o'clock the longboat, well manned and armed and furnished with everything it needed, set off.
Citizen Hamelin having come on board, we agreed upon the work we were to undertake with our boats. But before he sent a boat ashore, I wished to await the return of mine so as to know where I stood regarding the places that seemed to offer us an easy landing.
At noon we observed the latitude of the anchorage where we lay: 33° 30' 55", and the longitude given by the timekeepers put us in (no figures).
Shortly afterwards my boat returned, and the persons who had accompanied M. Freycinet, as well as he himself, made me the following reports:
Report of Citizen Freycinet, commanding the boat, on our first landing on the west coast of New Holland.
"In accordance with the instructions that you that you (sic) transmitted to me yesterday evening, the 10th instant, I set out in the
morning in the small boat with Citizens Depuche and Riedelé to examine the part of the coast of New Holland lying to the south of our present anchorage.
"At seven o'clock I arrived in a small cove bounded by two fairly prominent points, which bear from each other roughly north-north-west and south-south-east. They are about a league and a quarter apart. The head of this cove is a beach of white sand, and although landing there at first seemed easy, I found a considerable surf. For this reason I forbade the boat's crew to leave their boat for a single moment, and when the naturalists and I had been landed, I had the boat hauled off, where she remained riding to her grapnel.
"My first care (was) to range over the country a little so as to gain a general knowledge of it, and of its inhabitants if there were any. I was soon certain that there were none, and found no trace of human industry. The quantity of timber I could see on the heights made me hope to discover some springs of fresh water, but my searches in this respect were fruitless. The land, despite a great quantity of vegetable productions, seems too sandy to be fertile, and this region seems to me to offer navigators no other resource than firewood; the commonest tree is a species of eucalyptus. It grows only to a moderate height. There is also found in quantity a shrub which grows in clumps and which the shape and smell of its leaves would lead one to take for laurel, but Citizen Riedelé told me it was a species of (no name)
"Another tree, whose leaves, rather like those of vetiver, form a tuft rising above a fairly thick, charcoal-coloured trunk, furnished me with a kind of pod, a specimen of which I hand you.
"On the heights overlooking the cove where I landed there are several very large blocks of granite.
"I also saw several large black birds, but too far off to be able to say anything of them. Our boat was followed by a flock of gulls whose tameness surprised us. I thought I could make out on the sand the tracks of quadrupeds, and chiefly those of a cloven-footed animal.
"After a walk of about an hour I returned to the boat to take the soundings of the little cove, as you had directed me. My plan was to fix each of them by bearings taken on the north-north-west point and on one of the corvettes, these two points being known with great precision. The wind having freshened and the sea growing more choppy, the motion of my small boat prevented me from continuing bearings that were already somewhat uncertain, since I was obliged to take them with a boat compass.
"At ½ a cable's length and at two cables' lengths from the shore, the soundings gave me the depths whose results you will find below:
" distances from the water's edge
" at ½ a cable, from a fathom and a half to three fathoms, fine sand and rocks
" at 1 cable, from three to seven fathoms, fine sand mixed with coral
" at 2 cables, from ten to fifteen fathoms, fine sand and clean ground.
"I was unable to sound the cove from one point to the other; that work would have required more time than you had allowed me. Besides, with the wind still freshening, I had reason to fear that I might be unable to reach the ship if I let myself be set down upon the coast. A quarter of the way from the north-north-west point to the south-south-east point there is a rise whose point ends in a small shoal. It would be dangerous for boats to land at this little spot, as also a cable's length from there, to the south by south-east. All along the coast, at half a cable's length, small rocks lie scattered under water; they are quite visible and easy to avoid.
"I think that, if the breeze is at all strong, large boats cannot land on this beach without being put at risk. But the anchorage at half a cable's length is fairly good. Along the whole part of the coast in sight, the sea seemed to me to break with violence.
"At ten o'clock the naturalists Depuche and Riedelé came down to the boat. I at once made for the ship, sounding from 7 minutes to 7 minutes. The depth increased gradually until about five cables' lengths from the coast. From then on I constantly found twenty fathoms on a bottom of fine sand.
Report of Citizen Picquet, commanding the longboat.
"In accordance with the orders you gave me on the 11th instant, at a quarter past ten in the (a blank), I took command of the longboat, armed for war, in which embarked Citizens Bernier, astronomer, and Boulanger, geographer, whom I was to put ashore as near as possible to the western point of our present anchorage. But the coast, which I ran along at a very short distance from west-south-west round to west, offered me no place to land, being lined with reefs and sandy beaches on which the sea breaks with violence.
"At the request of the astronomer and the geographer, I placed myself half a cable's length west of the point they wished to determine. But the cloudy sky did not allow any observations to be made. I then resolved to regain the corvettes' anchorage. The winds from east-south-east to south-east forced me to beat to windward, and the currents set me to the south. As I found it impossible to make headway, the sea being high, and finding no shelter on the coast because of the surf that the swell from the open sea brings in upon it, I beat about all night.
"For the rest, the coast seems to me clear at a mile's distance. The various soundings I took a league to the east of the western point were as in the following table:
"at 10 toises from the shore: two fathoms, bottom of fine sand and rocks,
"at 50 toises: five fathoms, same bottom,
"at 100 toises, fifteen fathoms, sand,
"at 200 toises, above fifteen fathoms, sand.
"The currents off this point are very violent. I believe them caused by the tides, and I observed that the ebb set to the south-west and the flood to the north-east. The trend of the land, at a league to the east-north-east of this point, is east-south-east and to the south-south (sic) by south-west, as nearly as can be observed with a boat compass.
"The land seemed to me sandy, covered with trees along much of the shore, and bare towards the summits. A quarter of a league to the east of the western point I noticed a bar which breaks heavily, at the moment one least expects it, on a bottom of 7 to 8 fathoms of water."
Report of the mineralogist Depuche.
"The land where we went ashore, which lies south-west by south of the corvettes, forms a small half-elliptical cove. The two points that form it seemed to me unapproachable because of the rocks running out from them and the breakers these produce. Throughout its extent it offers a beach of very fine white sand. The uniformity of this beach is broken at intervals by large greyish or reddish rocks which stand out of the sand, in which they seem as it were planted. The sea breaks against all these projections, but with much less violence than against the two points. The bottom is strewn with rocks which seemed to me of the same nature and similarly placed. They are very visible, although covered by 6, 8, 10, 12 & 15 fathoms of water and more as one goes farther out. What makes them especially noticeable is the contrast between their dark colour and the white sand that forms the bottom everywhere else. This contrast so affects the colour of the sea that from the neighbouring heights it would be easy not only to count the number of these rocks but also to show exactly their shape and the space they occupy. For the rest, none of them seemed dangerous to us, and at two cables' lengths from the shore they lie in at least eight or ten fathoms.
"The sea breaks upon the beach in such a way that, despite the fine weather we enjoyed, we had to wade in up to the waist to reach the shore. Here, in a few words, is the aspect of the country that lay before us from the point where we landed, that is to say from the middle of the cove. First one found a very level, sandy beach extending some fifty paces from the limit of ordinary tides, as far as I could judge. It is bordered by a small cliff, if I may give that name to a terrace five to eight feet high, likewise composed of very fine white sand. This cliff seemed to me to extend through the whole cove and everywhere to bound its shore. It is just above it that the vegetation begins. At first it is not very vigorous, but it becomes more so after two or three hundred paces, as one advances over ground less sandy and higher. This terrace does in fact rise in
a gentle slope and ends at the foot of a hillside which forms what might be called the first plane of the ground. The hills that form the second are much more extensive and much more barren. The first contain a fair number of trees of middling size; shrubs and parasitic plants are numerous there. The latter, on the contrary, offered us only a short heath, or plants which from a distance had its appearance, broken at intervals by a few stunted trees.
"The hills of the first plane end in a gentle, lengthened slope towards the middle of the cove, whence there results a small valley which opens on to the beach and runs into the interior of the country, forming several windings. This valley communicates with the shore in the same way as those you observed all along the coast we were following on the ninth of Prairial, that is to say by a very low sandy beach. This beach contains no trickle of water, nor any trace of the passing streams that ravines and valleys often produce. Yet the vegetation is more vigorous along the sides of this valley than anywhere else; the trees, standing closer together, seemed to me covered with fine foliage and, above all, taller and better nourished.
"Before concluding this topographical account, I would observe to you, Commandant, that the cove in question seemed to me to be the third in the bay we were entering, counting from the point we rounded on the tenth, and that these three coves and another farther to the east together form a fourth cove which takes in the whole coast before our eyes.
"The place where we landed seemed to me remarkable for the fine granite I saw on every side. That which forms the rocks at the water's edge is of a very fine but perceptible grain. These rocks are divided into layers of greater or lesser breadth, each regular in its thickness. They even go so far as to contain between them plates of a black and shining substance, which I recognised as black mica sprinkled with very fine grains of quartz. One also sees plates of transparent quartz (rock crystal in the mass); they may be half an inch or an inch thick. The outer surface of this granite has been rounded and polished by the perpetual action of the waves. Several of the rocks are topped by a more or less thick crust of a calcareous substance, all partitioned and filled with shells, pulverised and petrified or merely expatés. These crusts or deposits come away easily from the granite, which served them, so to speak, as a matrix (illegible), and this without their surface being in any way altered. The rounded form that the granite presents, at the very place where the matter rested, proves in the most evident manner that the existence of this matter is much later than the first lands where the waves break upon these shores. I believe it due to the animals (a blank) so abundant in these parts.
"On most of the neighbouring heights the rock shows bare. I visited several of these points and everywhere found granite in which feldspar, quartz and mica plainly predominated. Feldspar is sometimes present in such quantity that the other two substances can scarcely be distinguished. I also came upon several pieces in which quartz was plainly abundant.
"Here, as at the water's edge, the granite is composed of almost straight and very distinct layers. I have said that the former were separated by plates of black mica. This mica is pulverised and forms, with the grains of quartz, a particular granite of black colour. Others are mixed with transparent quartz. These are most often separated by plates of crystallised feldspar, so that it is very common to find the whole surface of a large block of granite covered with pretty crystals of that substance. All of them take the primitive form peculiar to it. On one of the slopes that form the little valley, I observed several layers of granite jutting sharply out of the ground. Their inclination might be roughly 30 to 70 degrees; they had a breadth almost equal to their thickness, and I can compare them to nothing better than quadrangular prisms of basalt, or the profile of a wall built of large blocks. The fissures that divided them into large sections were so regular and so evenly spaced, the layers so distinct and so numerous, that it is impossible not to be convinced here of the truth, first recognised by M. de Saussure and still disputed by several naturalists, that granites are capable of forming layers, and that granitic terrains may, like secondary terrains, be composed of a greater or lesser number of superimposed beds, et cetera.
"In spite of the efforts I made to determine the direction towards which all these granite layers incline, I was unable to do so in any general way. Most seemed to me to dip towards the north-west. Others seemed to have quite the contrary inclination. This was no doubt owing to the fissures perpendicular to the layers, which it was easy to confuse with the outer layers. The solution of this sort of problem would have required more time than I had at my disposal.
"Over the whole brow of the hillside we walked over, I also found pieces of bog iron ore. All are of irregular shape. They are half an inch in size at most. They are abundantly scattered over the surface of the soil, which itself seemed to me very ferruginous.
"Finally, if I sum up the various geological observations I have just set out for you, I should be led to the following remarks:
"1) the ground where we went ashore offered me none of the products belonging to the domain of fire; the soil is therefore not volcanic.
"2) nor did it offer me any of the substances called of second formation; it therefore does not belong to the sedimentary terrains.
"3) the primordial substances show themselves everywhere; it is therefore of first formation.
"4) sand abounds there, and bog iron ore and ferruginous vegetable earth are found there; it has therefore been modified by alluvial deposits. Judging by analogy from the neighbouring points that could be seen from the cove and above all from the anchorage, particularly the two points that bound the land before our eyes, we shall conclude that primitive rock and alluvial ground make up the whole of this part of the great bay we are entering.
Particular remarks
"I saw black birds with large heads and long tails, white underneath; they had a hooked beak like that of parrots, and the same cry as those birds. I came upon a small grey bird the size of our robin redbreasts in France. Like the latter, it seemed to delight in the brushwood; I was unable to get very close to it. I killed a lizard of ordinary size, prettily variegated on the back; it made its home in a cleft of the rock.
"The country abounds in ants; they did not seem to me formed otherwise than those of Europe. One also often finds there masses of earth that must have been the work of some animals.
"Many whitish seabirds flew by hundreds above our boat and watched us with attentive curiosity. The tail of these birds is forked, and the two parts composing it are plainly separated.
"In several places I noticed burrows like those of our rabbits. Several seemed to me freshly dug; I looked carefully to see whether I could find any hole, but the loose earth showed none. The seashore, however, offered us the prints of a cloven foot. Everywhere, and in quantity, one finds droppings more or less fresh. They have the consistency and shape of horse dung. In their largest dimension they are hardly more than an inch, or even three quarters of an inch.
"A kind of tree which I can compare to nothing better than the vacoa of the Isle of France [Mauritius], although its leaves are infinitely less broad, bears a resin of a very pleasing reddish-yellow colour. It gives off a bad smell when burning. This tree, and several other tall resinous forest trees, seem to have undergone the action of a fairly violent fire. Was it the natives, or the heat of summer, that kindled it?
"Finally, Commandant, I saw nothing that could make me suspect that the district was inhabited by any living beings other than animals.
