1801-05-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and ESE. At midnight we were losing the land appreciably and the lead gave no bottom at 60 fathoms; we filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails. At 8 crowded sail to close the land, which bore from us S 5° E to N 72° E; Cape Leeuwin S 9° E. At 10.30 saw a thick smoke in the S 27° E. We ran along the coast until noon at 3 miles, when it appeared to take an ESE trend and form a gulf. At noon, being in 33° 22' 20" of latitude observed and in 112° 3' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 25' NW. We took the bearing of the southernmost land in sight S 38° W, and of the cape forming the SW entrance of the gulf S 85° E; the lead having given since 2 o'clock from 54 fathoms to 30, sand, rock and coral. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack; at 1 went onto the port tack and stood in for the land; the Naturaliste signalled us a danger in the N 22° 30' W. At 5 anchored in 23 fathoms, muddy sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 78° 45' W and a point S 14° E. At 7 the Naturaliste anchored near us. At 11 we dragged two thirds of a cable's length; the mizzen topsail, which had been kept on the mast, was furled and we brought up. The gulf in which we anchored was named Geographe Bay, and the SW point of the gulf, Cape Géographe.

1801-05-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At a quarter to one we took the bearing of a reef NW by W by compass, distant 2 leagues and a half. At the same moment Cape B S 25° W. At 7.30 we went about and stood to windward of Point O. At 4.30 sounded in 25 fathoms, sand and coral. At 4.30 went onto the starboard tack. At 5.15 the commander let us know by three lights that he was at anchor; he then bore from us S 14° E. We went about and stood on on the port tack. At six we went about again; at a quarter to seven, the commander bearing from us SW by W, we went onto the port tack and, steering for the Géographe, passed under her stern; he ordered us to anchor. At 7 [a figure struck out, illegible] we were anchored in 20 fathoms, muddy sand mixed with blackish gravel, and veered 100 fathoms of cable. Saw several fires on the coast. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 3° S; Point O WSW 2° 30' S; Point P south 7° 30' [one word illegible]. From 4 to 8 we struck the main topgallant mast and stopped the topsails with rope yarns. At 8 a.m. the Géographe had sent her boat ashore, and as ours was about to shove off the commander hailed us to send it only when his was back.

The most prominent land in the south-eastern quarter south by south-east 3° east

1801-05-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At 5 a.m. Citizen Freycinet left in the small boat to survey the country abreast of the anchorage; the gardener and the mineralogist went with him. The longboat and the large boat were put in the water. The first was sent off under the orders of Citizen Piquet to survey the coast and determine the position of Cape Géographe; the astronomer and the surveyor went in her. At noon Cape Géographe bore from us N 86° 15' W. The latitude observed 33° 28' 30" and the longitude by No. 27, 112° 1' 30". At 12.15 Citizen Freycinet was back; he had had great difficulty in landing and had not found a drop of drinkable water. In the evening the boats were hoisted in, and a light was kept at the masthead during the night to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea choppy and the wind in gusts. We sent a boat ashore which did not return until 5. At 7 p.m. the captain was back from his visit to the end of Point P, lying S 37° E. At 7 a.m. we received the order to get under way; at 9.30 we filled with the winds ESE, a fresh breeze. Bearings: Point N S 43° W; Point O S 2° W; Point P S 2° E; and the easternmost land east 2° S.
1801-06-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, we sighted our longboat, which, for a reason I cannot guess, had spent the whole night out, although I had expressly ordered the officer commanding it to be back before nightfall. As soon as it was a short distance from us, we prepared to get under way, and I warned the Naturaliste to do the same, which she did.
When Citizen Picquet had come on board, he informed me of the cause of his delay, and as I have transcribed in full the written report he made me of this excursion, which met with no great success, I shall say nothing of it here.
Having got under sail, we stood on the north-north-east tack, the wind being east, a light breeze, and the sea very smooth.
When our anchor was up, we found on the bill that had taken the ground a kind of black clayey mud mixed with a great deal of fine sand and above all of mica. Our cables suffered no chafe of any kind, and even the service was quite intact, a proof of the goodness of the ground. It seemed to us, however, that although good, it must be somewhat hard. But once the anchors have dragged a little, I think it unlikely that they will come home a second time. From the matter brought up from the bottom we made several balls, which we are preparing to dry so as to take them to France.
While we were under sail, standing on the north-north-east tack, the lookouts at the mastheads reported to us several times that they could see a chain of breakers stretching very far out to sea. I myself thought I could make them out from below, and it even seemed to me that they were very low islands on which trees could be distinguished with the naked eye. Several of the officers went up to the topgallant crosstrees at different times, and all declared that they were breakers on which the swell was even breaking heavily. For my part, I maintained that I could see trees there, and that quite distinctly.
However that may be, we held on our course, lead in hand, so as to see what it might be. I intended to send my longboat, which was in tow, ahead to examine them, but I put it off until we should be nearer.
As we held on our course, a succession of these same breakers showed themselves all round the horizon, so that to reach the anchorage we had occupied two days before we must necessarily have passed over them.
This circumstance alone undeceived us, and I saw clearly that what we were seeing was nothing other than the effect of mirage, and no doubt of the position of the sun and of the tide. Nevertheless there were many unbelievers on board, and several remain persuaded that it is a chain of breakers. But the truth is that they exist only in their imagination.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 18' 41", and the longitude, deduced from the rate of our timekeepers, was for No. 35, by 111° 56' 56" and for No. 27, 111° 56' 56".
After noon we went about to stand in towards the land; the wind was then very light and we were heading no higher than north. Supposing the wind did not change, we had a good board towards the land. But it was so variable that we had little hope of getting beyond our first anchorage.
In the afternoon, standing in towards the land and consequently to the south, the succession of breakers we had seen in the morning to the north showed itself, and the lookouts reported them in the same way. The passage seemed to us completely closed, and many
people could hardly conceive how we had entered so large a bay without noticing the dangers that surrounded it. But as I too had observed the dangers like the others, and the illusion had ceased for me, I held on my course without turning aside and without paying heed to anything that was said, so that about four in the afternoon we passed under all sail through the midst of the reported reefs, on which we had twenty-eight fathoms of water, bottom of very fine, clean grey sand. The wind then began to die away, and we were still far from the coast, which, at the place we were heading for, is much lower than any we had seen until then.
At six o'clock, being in a flat calm and the current setting us to the south-west, we came to anchor about three leagues from the coast in twenty-three fathoms, bottom of very fine grey sand.
When we were at anchor, all our sails furled, I had the dredge cast, and we took up some curious objects which I keep with great care, so strongly do I believe they will prove new and valuable.
About an hour after we had let go the anchor, the wind shifted to the south and blew a pleasant breeze. We much regretted that this breeze had not come sooner, but we consoled ourselves with the hope of having an interview with the inhabitants of the country the next day, for the fires we saw on the coast left us no doubt that some were to be found very near the place of our anchorage.
At seven o'clock the Naturaliste came to join us and anchored abreast of us. During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth the weather was fine and the breeze moderate.

1801-06-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E, very variable. At 6.30 a.m. hoisted the topsails and hove short; hailed the Naturaliste to get under way at once. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet arrived; he had not been able to land at Cape Géographe nor anywhere near it; the currents had carried him offshore and he had beaten to windward all night without gaining. At 8 we got under way and lay to until 9, when we shaped our course N and N 22° E, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At noon in 33° 19' of latitude observed and in 112° 1' 30" of longitude by No. 27; Cape Géographe then bore from us S 45° W. At half past noon went close-hauled on the port tack, steering S 11° E. At 6 anchored in 23 fathoms, grey sand; saw a very large fire in the S 56° W which lasted 2 hours. The dredge brought up many objects of natural history. Est. lat. 33° 30' and est. long. 112° 13' at the anchorage.

1801-06-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. At 1.10 we went about, as did the commander, and we sounded in 25 fathoms, gravelly sand; at 4, 23 fathoms, the same bottom. Bearings taken at sunset: Point N W 21° 30' S; Point O W 44° 30' S; Point P south 5° 30' W; the end of the land to windward of us east 1° 30' N. At 6.30 saw a fire ashore which we took bearing SW by W. At 6.45 we were at anchor. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 18° 15' N; Point O W 28° 15' N; Point P W 61° 15' N; the easternmost end of the land E 18° 15' N. At 8.30 a.m. filled under all sail. At 10 a.m. went about and sounded in 18 fathoms, sand and shell; at 11, 20 fathoms; at 11.30 went onto the port tack, the same bottom and the same depth as at 11.

On the thirteenth, at daybreak, I sent my longboat, well manned and armed, under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy, to examine a spot to leeward of us where the configuration of the land led me to believe that there might be some gully or small stream running out into the sea. This midshipman, who was then acting as an officer on board, was also ordered to go round the bay in which we lay and to take soundings in it. When the longboat had left, we got under sail and followed it fairly closely, always keeping the lead going, with a very good bottom of fine sand mixed with shells and some fragments of coral.
In the forenoon the wind was extremely variable, from east to south-east and from east to north-east, which made the board we were standing on as bad on one tack as on the other. However, at about ten o'clock it held until noon at east by north, and by this means we worked into the south-south-east part of the bay to within a short distance of the land. The longboat constantly signalled to us an easy coast to land on and good anchorage in from ten to twenty fathoms.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 33' 26", and the longitude deduced from the rate of the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 111° 55' 5", and for No. 35, 112° 4' 31". Since our landfall I no longer made use of the run estimated by the log.
At one o'clock we went about to stand out to sea, having no more than fifteen fathoms, good bottom. The coast then showed us a beach of fine white sand on which the sea broke very little. This cove was about two leagues wide at the entrance and still a league deep from the spot where we were. The whole coast in this part is low and even, covered with fine green trees and easy of approach, as are all those we have run along so far. Having cast the dredge several times in this cove, we took several rather fine shells of the scallop kind and above all some starfish of a new species.
In the evening we continued to beat to windward, tack upon tack, to get as far to the east as possible, but the wind was so light that we made very little way. However, at about six o'clock we had, until eight, a rather pretty breeze from the south-south-east, with the help of which we advanced two leagues to the east. Then, the calm having returned, we anchored in eighteen fathoms, sandy bottom, but less fine than that we had had before.
In the night the weather was fine and the wind went round to the east
Report of Midshipman Bonnefoy, commanding the longboat.
"The Commander having ordered me to go and sound near the land in the longboat, I left the "ship at seven in the morning and ran for a point which lay south by west of our "anchorage.
"At about a cannon shot from the ship I found 20 fathoms, very fine reddish sand, and at 9 "o'clock, a league from the coast, 19 fathoms, fine sand and black mud mixed with a great many small flakes of "talc, or at least what seemed to me to be such.
"At half past 9, heading south-west, we had before us a bay very easy to "land in, the sea not breaking at all on the rocks that lie in it, nor on the sandy beach by which "it is surrounded.
"At 10 o'clock we found 16 & 17 fathoms, still the same sandy bottom, and at half past "ten,
"we had nine fathoms, same bottom, a cable's length from the coast.
"At noon, being at the head of the bay, in two fathoms, almost ashore, we "manoeuvred to get out of it, and in half an hour the depth increased to 5 fathoms, white sand.
"I observed that the lead can be seen even in ten fathoms, so clear and pure is the water.
"The coast, near the sea, is low and wooded. I saw nothing that might lead one to suspect "that fresh water could be found there.
"At one o'clock, being near the south-east point of the bay, I took my departure from there "to return on board, sounding at intervals of 10 and 10 minutes.
"From one o'clock until two the depth increased regularly from five fathoms to ten, "sandy bottom mixed with mud, and from two o'clock until half past two from 10 to 12 f., "very fine gravel, the soundings afterwards increasing gradually. At three o'clock I was in 15 "fathoms, bottom of sand and black mud. At half past three I had 16 & 17 fathoms, same bottom.
"In the bay we saw a very large turtle, which the noise of our oars made dive.
"Note: of the various bearings taken from the longboat.
"At eight o'clock, two miles from the Géographe's anchorage, the westernmost land of the coast to the "west of our first anchorage bore west 7° 15 south.
"At nine o'clock, at a distance of four miles from the first point, that is to say from the corvette, the same "point bore west 11° 15 north.
"At half past 9, 5 miles from the corvettes, the same point west 22° 30' north.
"At eleven o'clock, a rock lying about a mile off the coast and a cable's length from the longboat "bore north 39° 45 west,
"a rock whitened by the droppings of sea birds, on which there was a great number of them, "at a distance of half a cable's length, bore north 67° 30 west,
"the rock which marks the beginning of the bay south 5° west
"The sea, at that hour, seemed to me to have fallen two feet on the rocks.
"At half past eleven, being abreast of the rock which lies to the south and half a cable's length off,
"it bore south-west of me.
"At noon the detached rock bore north-north-west
"The south point of the large bay south-east, distant 4 and a half to 5 miles.
"the middle of the same bay south-west, distant a mile and ½.
"The Géographe north-east, four to five miles distant.
Throughout the day we saw clearly and distinctly three large fires at a short distance, roughly in the direction of the first anchorage we had occupied. These fires were, or at least seemed to me, too large and extensive for one to believe that the natives of the country were near them. I am persuaded, moreover, that had there been any, they would not have failed to come and show themselves on the shore, and at the short distance we were from it, it would have been difficult not to see them. I think, therefore, that these fires may well have been lit by them, but I doubt that they were gathered there as we passed.

1801-06-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from ENE to south. At 6.45 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the longboat to survey part of the gulf. At 8 got under way and shaped our course SSW and SSE, close-hauled on the port tack. At 10 saw a very thick smoke in a wood near the shore. Our longboat made us signals of good anchorage near the land. At noon, being in 33° 33' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 55' of longitude by No. 27. Cape Géographe bore from us N 66° W and another point N 57° E. At noon went onto the starboard tack, heading north. At 2.30 went onto the port tack, heading S 22° 30' E. At 3.30 went onto the starboard tack, heading east. At 4 Citizen Bonnefoi arrived with the longboat. At 5, Cape Géographe N 82° W. At 8 anchored in 18 fathoms, coarse sand, in 33° 27' 40" of latitude by account and 112° 24' of longitude by account. The day's soundings were from 22 to 15 fathoms, grey muddy sand and red sand.

1801-06-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. We sounded every half hour in 18, 16, 16, 18, 19, 19 and 20 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. At 8.10 p.m. we let go the port anchor in 20 fathoms and veered 65 fathoms of cable; the lead brought up, alongside and all about, 20 fathoms of reddish sand mixed with gravel. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 4° 45' S, estimated distance 5 leagues; the end of the opposite land, which we shall call J, E 43° 30' N, estimated distance 10 leagues. At 9.15 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack.
1801-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, in the morning, we got under way in very fine weather with a breeze from the east varying towards the north. As I did not wish to leave this bay without knowing its depth, we beat to windward for the greater part of the day, trying to work as far to the east as possible.
From time to time in the course of the morning we saw great clouds of smoke rising on the coast, which by then was beginning to be much higher than the one we had coasted the day before. All the soundings taken in the morning showed a uniform and regular change of depth, whether we were standing in towards the land or out to sea, and so far this coast is very clear and easy of approach throughout the whole extent we have run along.
At noon, standing on the northern tack, the latitude was observed to be 33° 15' 55", and the longitude deduced from the timekeepers was for No. 27, 111° 56' 24" and 112° 6' 27" for No. 35. I cannot conceive how this easting shown by the timekeepers was so small, since the sight of the land told us perfectly well that we had advanced on that point of the compass more than they indicated. However, as the rate of our timekeepers had not varied, and as we could not doubt that the observations were behindhand, they were multiplied more than ever; and supposing, then, that those of the evening gave more easting than those made in the morning, it appears that the mirage which had so often (made) us see breakers where there were none was the true cause of the error, which we perceived too plainly to doubt it, and from then on we sought to guard against its effects.
At one in the afternoon we went about towards the land, and after sunset we anchored in 12 fathoms about two leagues from the coast.

Captain Hamelin, having come on board, remarked to me that he had noticed, as we had, that the astronomical observations made in the evening had (given) them more easting than those of the morning, and we agreed that the cause must be ascribed to the quality of the atmosphere in these waters

1801-06-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to NE. At 8.15 a.m. got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, heading N 11° E. At noon in 33° 15' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 20" of longitude by No. 27, Cape Géographe bearing S 56° W and another point N 56° E (a). At 1 went onto the port tack, heading S 45° E. At 5.30 anchored in 12 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing S 79° W and point (a) N 45° E. Latitude observed 33° 27' 30", longitude by No. 27, 112° 7' 30" at the anchorage. The day's soundings were from 25 to 18 fathoms, coarse red sand. During the night several fires were seen in the bay.

1801-06-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. At 1.45 sounded in 23 fathoms, reddish sand mixed with glittering gravel; at 4, the same bottom and the same depth. Bearings taken at 4 on the 14th Prairial: Point N, forming the starboard end of the gulf, south 73° W; the port end of the same bight N 65° E, at 10 miles' distance; the end of the land stretching north, called the Paps, N 48° E. At 4.45 the lead brought up 16 fathoms, fine sand. At 6, 14 fathoms, and it kept shoaling from 13 to 14, the same bottom. At the same hour went onto the starboard tack, and shortly afterwards onto the port tack, standing in for the anchorage. At 6.30 we let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, fine sand mixed with broken shell; the soundings were the same all round the corvette from 6 until midnight. The currents setting us onto our cable, we laid the mizzen topsail aback. At midnight we saw a fire on the hill bearing from us S 6° W. Fine weather, smooth sea, and a light breeze.
1801-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the wind being very light from the east to east-north-east, I resolved, at the request of Citizens Bernier and Boulanger, to remain at anchor so as to send them both ashore to take hour angles and (some) distances of the sun from the moon. The weather was very fine and there was not a cloud. I therefore decided to go with them, and had the large boat made ready accordingly.
As on the previous day my intention had been not to remain at the anchorage, I had given orders that my longboat, the command of which I had entrusted to young Bougainville, should set off at four in the morning and make as far as it could to the north-east, visiting all the coves and creeks that might lie on its way.
At nine o'clock we left the ship to go ashore. All the scientists, as may well be imagined, wished to be of the party, so that besides the astronomer and the geographer I had as travelling companions Citizens Maugé, Riedelé and Depuche, and we set off. The small boat had left at five in the morning, taking with it Péron and Leschenault. They were to be back by nine o'clock. But the midshipman in charge of it, having fallen far to leeward through bad handling, had not yet landed them when we left.
On our way ashore we met a strong current setting to the south-west, and it then seemed to us that it must be the ebb. We had to row, and hard at that, for three full hours, and at last we reached the shore in the middle of the cove that lay abreast of the ships. Until then we had seen none of the natives of the country, but at the moment we landed we saw one who was half in the water, busy fishing by darting at the fish with a spear. At first he seemed to pay little attention to us and to be occupied solely with his fishing. But when we had landed, about a musket shot from him, he came out of the water and, without too much haste, made for a sand dune opposite him. I noticed only that, although his step was firm, he often looked in our direction, no doubt to see whether he was being followed.
We were indeed going after him, and he was approached fairly closely on the rise where he had halted. Citizen Depuche, who was ahead of everyone, showed him some strings of glass beads with which I had provided myself. But as he kept advancing, the man began to shout with terrible force, making signs for us to go back, and as he directed them all towards the ships, we had no doubt of what he meant to tell us. Nevertheless, as we still advanced, he threw himself into all sorts of attitudes while continuing his howls, and at last he picked up three kinds of lances or spears and went off in haste, without having made any hostile gesture towards us.
This man was of a very black colour, and naked from head to foot except for a skin or piece of bark covering his back. To judge by the colour of his beard, which was very long and grey, he must be a man well advanced in years. Although he had taken flight, we followed him; but when we reached the top of the dune to which he had first withdrawn, he had already got well ahead of us and was at the far end of a plain that ended at the edge of a wood. Besides the three spears he carried, he had a firebrand in his hand, which leads me to believe that as soon as they catch anything, by fishing or otherwise, they cook it and eat it at once.
Having no further hope of overtaking him at the great distance he had already put between us, I gave up the pursuit. But Citizen Depuche wished to go farther, accompanied by two men from the boat. He followed the path the man had taken for about half a league and came back without having caught sight of him again.
From the moment we gave up the pursuit of this man, whom we had no hope of overtaking, we busied ourselves in examining the place where we were, and the astronomer and geographer began their observations.
The whole coast, as far as the eye could reach, is lined with sand dunes, among which there are some that, not being covered with brushwood, show those large white patches seen from the sea when one coasts along at a certain distance. All of them end at the sea in a fairly steep slope. But the side facing the land is much less abrupt and everywhere covered with brushwood and shrubs of different kinds. Beyond lies a plain a short quarter of a league across, ending at the edge of an immense forest that offers a very pleasing prospect. Our gardener found its soil, though sandy, of very good quality and even very fit for cultivation. Crossing the plain I have just spoken of, over which are scattered here and there several tall forest trees whose leaves rather resemble those of firs, we came upon several well-trodden paths and followed them. They led us to large circular clearings where fires had quite recently been made, which proved that the natives sometimes stop there, no doubt to feast on the fruits of their fishing or hunting.
The traces of fire are so numerous everywhere, and the paths so well trodden, that it seemed to me this place is much frequented. The large trees that form the beginning of the (in the margin: forest seemed to us to be of the species (no name), but none of those we had in view were in flower. In crossing the plain we came upon a fair number of quail, and we (did not) have the skill to kill a single one. Our gardener made an ample collection of plants, and Maugé and I shot various kinds of very curious birds.
In the course of this excursion we thought we recognised the tracks of several quadrupeds, without quite knowing what they might be. We picked up some of their droppings, which seem to me very close to those of the dog, and certain signs noticed on the sand lead me to believe that the natives make use of them, for we saw very distinctly on the beach the footprints of men and of an animal following them, which we believe to be a dog.
After a walk of about three hours we returned to our boat, and the coxswain and those who had stayed behind to guard it told us that six savages had appeared on the point and that, after watching them for about a quarter of an hour, they had gone off into the dunes, and our men had lost sight of them.
On the seaward face of the dune I noticed three distinct lines of seaweed and broken shells, which enabled me to judge the height to which the sea must rise in different circumstances. As it was then the ebb, the first layer of seaweed, still fresh, showed clearly that the sea had not risen higher, and it was the time of neap tides. A second layer of seaweed and broken shells, like the first, could be seen six feet away, and as the seaweed was dry, I think it marked how far the sea reaches at the spring tides of the new and full moons. The third layer, lastly, much higher and almost at the foot of the dunes, seemed to me the place to which the sea rises in gales, when they blow from the north round by the west to the south-west.
All the dunes seemed to me the work of the sea, which brings the sand, and of the wind, which heaps it up and carries it some distance in the course of time. The flat ground one comes to after passing the dunes did not seem to me any higher than the surface of the sea. The tide, by my reckoning, must rise four feet at neaps, eight or nine at springs, and at least fifteen in gales. On the shore are found fragments of fine shells, which made us much regret not having them whole.
While we were ranging a little into the interior of the country, I had sown in the plain we crossed, which is well sheltered from the sea winds, some maize, and pips of pear, apple, peach and apricot, and various other kinds of vegetables. If all these things thrive, they will in time provide an additional means of subsistence for the people living in this part of New Holland, whose existence seemed to me very wretched.
Among the plants we found, two occur in the neighbourhood of Paris: a kind of wild sorrel and (no name).
We brought back on board a few roots of celery, which we found very good in soup, as well as another plant called (no name).
Before re-embarking, persuaded that the natives would not fail to come and see what we had done at our landing place, I had a stick planted in the ground, to which I tied an empty bottle, a string of glass beads, a little biscuit, a nail and a few other trifles. May these things not give rise to quarrels among them, and may whoever finds them first remain their owner.
At six o'clock the boat was back on board, and I had it hoisted in at once so as to set sail the next day at daybreak.
About half past seven, while we were at dinner, M. Hamelin came on board with several of his officers who had been ashore. One of them, M. Hérisson, told me that having landed to the south of the ships, about three leagues to leeward, he had gone inland, and that chance had led him to the banks of a great river, or at least a lake, which he had followed for more than two leagues without seeing its end. On (the) lake he had come upon a great number of birds of different kinds unknown to him, but which he had been unable to shoot, not being a sportsman. M. Hérisson could not tell whether this lake or river, for he believes it to be one, opens into the sea, since he was too far from his boat to look for its mouth; but at least he is certain that it runs very far into the interior of the country.
M. Hérisson's report seemed to me too interesting for me not to order a fresh visit, so as to have more certain information on the nature and usefulness of this lake, or river if such it be; and although he had told me that its water was brackish, and that in the neighbourhood he had found a kind of well dug by the natives, in which the water was very good. I resolved to remain at anchor and ordered M. Hamelin to send off the same officer during the night, telling him that I would also send my longboat, the command of which I gave to M. Le Bas. M. Hamelin having asked to go himself on this search, I gave him permission.
During the night of the 15th to the 16th the weather was very fine and there was little wind, from the east to north-east.
Report of Citizen Bougainville, Midshipman, commanding the longboat.
"On leaving here I steered, according to your orders, north-east by north as soon as I was two cables' lengths from the ships. I then began to sound, and from that moment until 7 hours 10 minutes, when I was already about six miles from the Géographe, the lead constantly gave me 15, 14 & 13 fathoms, sometimes a bottom of white sand, sometimes of small red and grey gravel. At half past seven I went about and headed for the land. The northernmost point in sight bore bore (sic) north-east 5° east. The easternmost, and the nearest to me, south-south-west. I held on this tack until about a mile from the coast, and the depth decreased steadily from 15 fathoms to 11 f. ½, always a bottom of white or grey sand. At eight forty-five I again headed out to sea, and the depth increased gradually in the same proportion as it had followed in decreasing on the previous tack.
"From that hour until one forty-five I continued to beat to and fro in the hope of reaching the point that bore to the east of me, which, from the trend of the land, I take to be the northernmost point of the great bay. One then discovers another bay, much less considerable, but which seemed to me to run far inland, just as though the waters of a great river discharged into it.
"All this time I continued to sound, and the lead gave me as before 14, 13, 12, 10 & 8 fathoms of water so long as I was at some distance from the land. But about three cables' lengths from the shore the nature of the bottom varied greatly. Here are the principal changes it underwent: 6, 5, 4, & 3, sometimes a bottom of red and grey sand, sometimes of rock and coral, and coral and broken shells.
"At half past 11 I saw to the south-west, two miles off, a very thick smoke. The ships then bore west of me, and the point of land nearest to me north-north-east 5° east.
"The land then had the shape of an island, of which the point formed one extremity and the point from which the smoke rose the southern extremity. All the rest of the bay was below my horizon. One could see only, near the ships, which my reckoning put five leagues off, a small stretch of coast lying west by south-west.
"At a quarter past noon I thought I noticed that the tide was rising, and the current was then setting to the north-east by north.
"At two o'clock, despairing of being able to round the eastern point before nightfall, although I was then no more than a mile and a half from it, I bore away to run along the coast and draw nearer to the ships. From my reckoning of my run, I think this point is five and a half leagues from the ships. Taking a bearing of it and of the ships, I found that it lay north-east by east.
"I continued to follow the coast about two cables' lengths from the shore, sounding from 10 minutes to 10 minutes, and always found five and four fathoms, a bottom of grey sand mixed with coral and sometimes small rocks, which besides was easy to see through the clearness of the water.
"The whole of this part of the coast offers an easy landing; it is lined with low sand dunes covered with a kind of very dry heath. Above them could be seen the tops of the tall trees standing behind. Except for a black bird whose cry is rather like the croaking of the crow, and a few others of the booby kind, I saw nothing along the shore. Only I made out a great number of burrows of an animal smaller than the rabbit. I also thought I could tell, from the lines of seaweed the sea leaves as it retreats, that it must rise there about ten feet. "Towards three o'clock we were obliged to stand a little off the shore because of a shoal covered with rocks in several places, on which the sea was breaking with some force. This shoal may be (a mile in breadth) by (a mile in length) (in the margin: to be corrected: this reef is 2 miles in length and 80 metres, or half a cable's length, in breadth) and lies three cables' lengths from the shore. When I made it out, I was nearly four leagues from the ships, which then bore west-north-west of me; I had the easternmost point north-east and the southernmost point south-west.
"At half past 3, the wind heading us a great deal, I feared letting myself be set too far to leeward and worked my way back to the ships.
"From the moment I left the land until I arrived on board I did not I did not (sic) cease sounding, and the lead gave me successively 5, 5 ½, 6, 7, 9 10, 11, 11 ½, 12, 12 and a half fathoms, a bottom of grey sand mixed with small red gravel.
Stay at the anchorage, latitude observed at noon: 33° 26' 49" south
Longitude by the timekeepers 112° 21' 15, mean of 4 sets of observations taken before and after noon. 112° 29' 4" by distances taken ashore. Latitude of the place of observation, 33° 30' 0"
1801-06-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from E. At 4 a.m. Citizen Bougainville left in the longboat to sound along the coast, and I in the small boat to have grass cut for our livestock; the zoologist and the botanist came with me. At 8.30 the commander and all the scientists went ashore in the large boat. At 4 p.m. I came aboard, Citizen Bougainville at 5.30 and the commander at 6. The latter had seen Aboriginal people, who would not communicate; I had seen no inhabitants but had seen their tracks, and those of a dog's paws. No one had found drinkable water.

1801-06-05.journal_anonyme: At 6 a.m. we sent off two boats to go ashore, one under the orders of Citizen Heirisson and the other under those of Citizen Freycinet. They found bare footprints, which makes us believe there are Aboriginal people here; they also found kangaroo tracks and celery like that of France. The weather fine, the sea smooth and the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. On the 16th at 4 a.m. our two boats were sent off in company with the longboat, which by the commander's order took four days' provisions.
1801-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth (5 June 1801), at three o'clock in the morning, I dispatched my longboat, well armed and furnished with everything needful, under the command of Citizen Ste Croix, my flag captain. M. Hamelin went off himself in his boat, accompanied by M. Hérisson, to visit the lake or river of which he had spoken to me the day before, so as to gain more exact knowledge of the places he had pointed out to us. I had asked this officer to make me an exact and very detailed report of what he had seen and observed the day before. I expected to receive it before his departure, and as he has not yet sent it to me, I suppose he cannot have had the time to write it.
Be that as it may, my longboat and two boats from the Naturaliste set off at the appointed hour. The wind was then north-east, a pleasant breeze. And as they were to steer to the south of our anchorage, they must have reached the place intended in good time.
In the course of the morning the breeze blew strong from the north-north-east and the sea rose high, which left me not without anxiety for the fate of my boats, since the swell must have been breaking on the coast. All the scientists who were on board, with the exception of the astronomer, the geographer and Maugé, who all had a great deal of work each in his own line, embarked in the longboat, and I gave M. Le Bas, as his second, Citizen Ronsard, acting as ensign on board.
I await their return with all the more impatience because, the weather being unfit for keeping boats along the coast, I fear that their eagerness to discover the place they are going to visit may lead them into some imprudence. I did not fail, however, before their departure, to impress upon them all everything that the strictest foresight ought to make them consider.
At noon we observed on board a latitude of 33° 26' 43" south, which differed by only six seconds from the latitude observed the day before. One may therefore conclude that that of our anchorage is fairly well determined. The longitude taken ashore the day before by distances of the sun from the moon was 112° 29' 4", and that of the timekeepers being 112° 8' 29", there was a difference to the east of 20' 35" from the timekeepers.
Hour angles were taken on board, morning and evening, the result of which was found to be 112° 16' 9" for the morning and 112° 9' 20" for the evening (in the margin: Bernier). This difference between the two observations served to show that the effects of mirage had caused those we had met with on the preceding days, and that the altitudes observed must have been affected in the same manner.
In the afternoon the breeze moderated a little and the wind shifted to the north. The sea was very rough and the ship pitched heavily, which did nothing to lessen my anxiety about the situation in which the boats I had ashore might find themselves, and whose return I awaited with the greatest impatience. A little before sunset, having sighted two of our boats running along the coast to work to windward, I judged that they were returning on board, but I saw nothing of my longboat, which is easy to make out by its sails. A light was kept all night at the mizzen masthead to show the boats the position of the ships. But it was labour lost; nothing came to us. However, at about two o'clock in the night, the Naturaliste having put out her light, we judged that her boats had returned.
During the night the sea continued high and the wind was moderate from north to north-north-east, though from time to time there came some good gusts.
At anchor. Observed latitude at noon 33° 26' 38" south.
Longitude by the timekeepers.
Nota.
The longboat set off at four o'clock in the morning under the command of Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas to go and examine the mouth of a river which was believed to have been discovered to the south-south-east of our anchorage. All the naturalists accompanied it, as did Citizen Ronsard, acting as ensign. This boat was furnished with everything necessary for its safety and that of the persons in it. It also carried three days' provisions, although it was to return the same day!
1801-06-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 3 a.m. the longboat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Le Bas; with several of the scientists he was to survey the country and try to communicate with the Aboriginal people. Struck the topgallant masts. During the night kept a light at the gaff to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-06.journal_anonyme: The winds having fallen light, we put the dinghy in the water to send the commander a letter the captain had left on board. In the afternoon the wind blew lightly from the east, the sea still with a heavy swell. At 7 p.m. the large boat was back; Citizen Saint-Cricq had seen many Aboriginal people who took flight at his approach. The day before, the commander had seen six Aboriginal men, five of whom fled at his approach; the sixth, an older man, came towards the commander with threatening gestures, pointing to his ship and giving him to understand that he was not looking for him and that he should withdraw from this land, which belonged to him. The commander, seeing that he could learn nothing from this man, took the opposite direction and went off into the woods with all those accompanying him.
1801-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth (6 June 1801), in the morning, we saw nothing of our boats; we did, however, perceive that one of the Naturaliste's boats had returned to that ship during the night. The wind being then too strong and the sea too high to send and learn what news it might have brought, we had to wait for a more favourable moment.
In the course of the morning, although the sky was very fine, the breeze from north-north-east to north became so strong that at every gust I expected to be obliged to get under sail. But as the holding ground seemed very good, since we were not dragging our anchor although I had only seventy fathoms of cable out, I continued to keep my position. I merely had the topgallant masts struck. It was then impossible for our boats to return, but I was none the less displeased that they had not come back on board the day before, having had the time needed to clear up the doubt as to whether or not a river ran into the sea in our neighbourhood.
Yesterday's breeze having been less strong, we had observed that at about two o'clock it had begun to moderate, and I hope it will be the same with today's, for if it were to continue until evening, I presume the sea would be too high for us to ride at anchor.
At noon the latitude was again observed at 33° 26' 28", and the longitude by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, (no figures) and for No. 35 (no figures) by the morning observation, while that of the evening was (no figures) by the first and (no figures) by the second. The difference which for some time past the morning and evening observations had produced was a problem rather hard to solve. We remained convinced, however, that the state of the atmosphere could, and indeed must, be its cause, being in all likelihood more charged with vapour before the sun had passed the meridian than after it had passed it.
In the evening the breeze moderated, as I had expected, and the sea became smooth. I had the peremptory signal for the boats to return on board hoisted at the mainmast, and accompanied it with a gun, which was repeated every two hours. At sunset, however, I saw no sign that they were on their way back to the ship, although the horizon was very clear and I could make out the shores of the coast perfectly over an extent of six leagues, from south-west to north-east.
At about four o'clock in the afternoon, the Naturaliste's boat that had returned to her during the previous night came to the Géographe, and the mineralogist who was in it, and who had gone ashore the day before, reported to me that what had been taken for a river was nothing but an inconsiderable lagoon into which the sea water flowed. He assured me that he had been to its mouth, which is barred by a kind of wooden stakes that the natives of the country plant across its opening to catch the fish that the rising tide carries in. He had judged the spot of so little consequence that he had not even cared to wait there for the return of his fellow travellers. He added that some of those who were ashore had communicated with the natives of the country, and above all with a woman who was pregnant and about forty years of age. From his report it appears that our people caused her no fright and that she waited for them very patiently at the spot where she had stopped. It was not so with a man who was with her, and who took to flight. Various presents were made to this woman, which seemed very agreeable to her, and it was noticed that she set more store by a small mirror than by all the other things that were offered to her.
After the report the Naturaliste's mineralogist had just made to me, I could hardly conceive what could have caused my longboat's delay. The only reason that seemed to me likely was that M. Ste Croix Le Bas, to whom I had entrusted its command, had let himself be won over by the fine speeches of the naturalists who were with him, and that, without regard for the insecure situation in which the ship lay, he had, without foreseeing the consequences, allowed himself to be persuaded and granted them more time than he ought. Being so persuaded, I firmly resolved that such a thing should not happen again, and that henceforth, whether these gentlemen are pleased or not, it matters little to me, they shall go ashore only when the ship no longer runs the risk of being driven from her anchorage and they of being (stranded) on a deserted and unknown coast.
After sunset, having seen nothing on the horizon to announce their return, I gave orders to light fires at all the mastheads and to continue firing a gun every two hours; my short distance from the land leads me to believe that they will be aware of this order to come on board at once. And if the officer commanding the longboat has judged from the sunset what weather there is to be tomorrow, I have no doubt that all will be on board by ten o'clock at the latest.
Dampier, in his Voyage to New Holland, observes that when the sun rises and sets a very bright red, the breeze the next day is usually very strong. From nine o'clock in the morning until three o'clock in the afternoon, et cetera. Although we are not in the same latitude as Dampier was when he made this observation, his remark is none the less just, and I have found up to now that every time the sun has risen or set as he describes, the wind has been very strong the next day.
At half past nine at night, although the wind had greatly moderated, M. Hamelin came on board. He had been about twenty-two hours at sea in his small boat with four men. During the height of the wind, which lasted from eight o'clock in the morning until four o'clock in the afternoon, he had spent all (that) time riding to his grapnel at the risk of being swamped a thousand times. The sea broke with such force that he did nothing but bail out continually the water that came in. He told me that my longboat was aground on the sand, without knowing precisely how this accident had come about. This news struck me like a thunderbolt, because of the situation of those who had embarked in it. Before leaving his fellow travellers, M. Hamelin gave them all the arms and ammunition he had, so that they might be better able to defend themselves. They still had two days' provisions left. We agreed together that at four o'clock in the morning his large boat and mine should set off to carry to the place he pointed out to me whatever might be needed to get the longboat afloat again, and at least to bring back those who were ashore if it had to be abandoned. From ten o'clock the wind had gone round to the east and the sky was fairly fine, but in the middle of the night it shifted to the south-west and the north, and began once more to blow a strong breeze. It would be hard to convey all that I suffered meanwhile, seeing that the next day I should be unable to give any help to the men who were in my longboat and perhaps already at the mercy of the natives of the country, who, seeing their distress, seemed to me likely to grow bold.
Bearings of the land.
At four o'clock, the point forming the southern entrance of the bay west 6 south
Another point, the nearest to us, north 56° east
The northernmost land in sight north 30° east
Bearings at the anchorage.
The westernmost point west by south
The northernmost point north 45° east
A large white patch to the right of the ship south 45° east
Nota.
The longboat did not return on board. But at sunset I saw it under sail, as well as the Naturaliste's large boat. I do not know what either of them was doing or looking for, but I was inclined to believe that they were beating up to reach the ship during the night.
1801-06-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE, a high sea. At 9 a.m. struck the topgallant masts. At 2 p.m. the wind fell. At 3 fired a gun and made the signal to recall the longboat. At 4.30 and at 6 fired a gun and showed a light at the gaff. At 7.45 Captain Hamelin came to tell the commander that our longboat had been cast on the shore, but that no one was lost. He himself, in his boat, had been obliged to pass the previous night at anchor offshore and had only reached his ship at nightfall.

1801-06-07.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from the east. At 7 p.m. the captain's boat was back and brought us the unhappy news that the Géographe's longboat was cast away on the coast. The captain wrote at once to the commander, who was in mortal anxiety; a boat was sent off with the letter. The commander, judging that the captain had not given him enough detail, decided to send for him aboard; the captain embarked at once in his boat and returned shortly afterwards.
1801-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
In view of the weather during the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth, I changed my mind as to the manner in which I should send help to our people ashore, and after having the master carpenter and six good oarsmen embarked in my large boat, I sent it at once to M. Hamelin's ship, addressing to him the following letter:
The Commander of the expedition &c. to Captain Hamelin
"At four o'clock in the morning my boat will be alongside your ship, and yours, which I invite you to hold ready for the same hour, will, if the wind is manageable and moderate, show it the place where it is to land.
"At daybreak you will yourself get under sail and go in search of an anchorage abreast of the spot where you know our people are, so as to ensure their return. You will accordingly stand in as close to the land as you can without, however, endangering the safety of your ship. Only take care, should the tack you are on carry you to leeward of the anchorage you are to take up, not to stand too far from it. By this precaution it will always be easy for our boats to rejoin you.
"As soon as you are in position, I shall follow you."
Having then given Citizen Bonnefoy, acting as ensign, orders concerning the command of my boat and the course he was to steer, I sent him to the Naturaliste to set off in company with that ship's boat, and I wrote to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas, to whom I had entrusted the command of my longboat two days before, the following letter:
The Commander of the expedition to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas. 11 o'clock at night, 17 Preirial.
"I have just learnt, Citizen, from the arrival of M. Hamelin, of the unfortunate accident that has befallen the longboat whose command I had entrusted to you. It seems to me that you had every means of preventing or avoiding it, had prudence and foresight guided your conduct before and after landing.
"Be that as it may, as this is not the moment to make you the reproaches you appear to deserve, I hope at least that you will not endanger the fresh help you are about to receive from the two ships, and that you will watch with a more active foresight over the safety of the boats that are coming to fetch you, as well as of all those who accompanied you. I order you, if there is no means of saving my longboat without running fresh risks, to abandon it and to distribute all those who are ashore between the Naturaliste's boat and mine, and to repair as soon as possible on board whichever ship it will be (most) easy for you to reach, having regard to your position.
"You will receive provisions and munitions of war. I hope that the former reach you in time and that you may not be obliged to make use of the latter. For the rest, our boats are furnished with everything you may need to get the longboat afloat again, if that is possible, which, however, I am far from believing, since the critical position in which you find yourself has not enabled you to find the resources you needed. Greetings, N. B.
The boat, as I said above, went to the Naturaliste at four o'clock in the morning, but the wind increased so much and the sea became so high that he did not think fit to dispatch them.
Following this mishap, I at once made the signal to Captain Hamelin to carry out the order I had given him. He answered that he was about to do so. At seven o'clock, that ship being still not under sail, I repeated the signal to execute, and he then answered me
that it was impossible for the moment, because the messenger he had used, and afterwards a threefold purchase, had both parted.
This mishap having decided me to get under way myself and run along the whole coast, not knowing the place where the landing was to be made, I had a reef taken in each topsail, that is to say a second, for one was already in. And at nine o'clock I was under sail. The wind being then from north to north-north-east, a strong breeze, I set only my topsails and, having put the ship on the larboard tack, I closed the coast to a distance of three miles and ran along it thus, watching with the greatest attention for any signals or for anyone walking on the shore. At eleven o'clock, being two leagues from the point I had started from, there was a small sandbank on which the sea rises a little. I skirted it in six fathoms of water at a mile's distance; it may be of about the same length, and seemed to me to run north-north-east and south-south-west. Having passed it, I continued on my course, with the lead going constantly and six fathoms of water, sometimes very fine sand, sometimes very coarse. I could make out, as perfectly as if I had been ashore, every object lying on the sand. But I saw no one who could make me suspect that our people were anywhere near. At half past eleven several very thick columns of smoke rose from behind the dunes, which seemed to announce that someone was there. I hardly knew which to steer for, since several were already to be seen to leeward of me. Nevertheless, I held on my course and made for one that seemed to rise directly from the shore. At noon, having made three leagues of way, I sighted two persons on the shore, but as they at once withdrew into the dunes, I judged that they were natives of the country. It had, however, seemed to me from their gait that they were some of our people. Shortly afterwards, still running along the coast in six and seven fathoms, I saw four or five other persons walking ahead along the shore and stooping from time to time to pick something up. The smoke I had steered for having cleared away, I again imagined that these must be natives who did not wish to make their position known, and the the (sic) men I had seen likewise made for the dunes and disappeared.
My anxiety for the fate of those ashore then growing more and more, I resolved to anchor at that very spot in order to send and examine it. And yet it seemed to me that those I was seeking were not there, since, instead of waiting for us and making us some signals of recognition, they fled at our approach and did not reappear.
Having let go an anchor at noon in seven fathoms, sandy bottom, I at once dispatched my large boat, whose charge I entrusted to Citizen Bonnefoy, with a most express prohibition against landing if the landing were difficult, as indeed it seemed to me it must be in the weather then prevailing. He had orders, after examining that spot, if he saw there no wreckage of our longboat, to run along the coast until sunset and then to return on board at once. It seemed to me only natural to think that if our gentlemen were anywhere near, they would come to the boat, if not all of them, at least some, and that at the very least they would show themselves.
My boat having left, I kept my eyes continually on the coast to see whether I could make out anyone, and I had the pain, bitter indeed, of seeing it let go its grapnel without anyone having shown himself. Thinking then that it had surely sighted my longboat or some of its wreckage, I could not hold back my tears and withdrew to my cabin to reflect on the further steps I should have to take. It seemed to me then beyond doubt that the natives of the country, having perceived the distress in which those ashore had found themselves, had attacked them and overpowered them. It will be better imagined than I could describe all (that) was painful in the mere idea by which I was affected, and which so many
circumstances together served to confirm. For I could not conceive that no signals had been made to us and that no one had shown himself on the coast. Given over to these sad reflections, my heart filled with pain and grief, I knew not what course to take, when, at about half past three, I was told that several persons could be seen on the edge of the shore who seemed to be talking with the men in the boat. It was even added that several of them were thought to be recognised, and that there was no doubt they were some of those we were seeking. Having at once looked at the shore myself, I saw, like the others, several persons who seemed to me to be talking with the men in the boat. But I was so convinced that these could not be those who were ashore, since they had made us no signals to make themselves known, that I persuaded myself they were natives trying to prevent our men from landing, and that no doubt they were busy breaking up our longboat, which several persons believed they had recognised.
From that moment I watched until nightfall, with the most scrupulous attention, every movement of my boat and of those who were ashore. It seemed to me that an easy landing place was being pointed out to it and even that it was making for it. At four o'clock I thought I saw it send ashore a hawser with which I had furnished it, as well as various articles suitable for getting the longboat afloat again, if that could be done. All these manoeuvres calmed me a little, and I then put down to the carelessness and apathy of all those ashore the conduct they had shown in not making themselves known. Nevertheless, I was still far from free of anxiety, and I awaited nightfall with the greatest impatience, because I had agreed with the officer commanding the boat that he would send up one or two rockets to let me know that he had found our people. At six o'clock, although it was very dark, no rocket had yet been sent up. Fearing that this might be an oversight on the officer's part, I then had several port-fires burnt, and at last, at half past seven, I was answered by a rocket, which calmed my anxiety and delivered me from the painful existence I had been living for three whole days, unable to find, even in sleep, the rest I so greatly needed.
At nine o'clock in the evening my boat, having returned on board, brought back only Citizen Péron, who was more dead than alive, having been obliged to go into the water to embark, since the boat had been unable to reach the beach. Citizen Le Bas would not allow the other naturalists to embark, on the pretext that he needed them to help him get the longboat afloat again, but I think it was rather so as to be more numerous and to overawe the natives of the country the more, should they become bold.
According to the report of Citizen Bonnefoy, who commanded my boat, he had reached the shore and made out the longboat embedded in the sand before seeing anyone. No doubt they were all keeping on the far side of the dunes to be better sheltered from the wind. It appears that it will be very difficult to save the longboat, which is so deeply embedded in the sand that the sea covers it entirely. I intend tomorrow to make a last effort, and to abandon it if I cannot get it off.
At about three o'clock in the afternoon the Naturaliste made sail and came to anchor near us at a short distance. M. Hamelin told me that after doing all he could during the morning to get under sail, he had not been able to manage it, and that in the afternoon, having made fresh efforts, he had been able to weigh his anchor only because the arms had parted from the shank and remained at the bottom, as had his buoy rope and buoy. He intends, if the weather permits, to send for it tomorrow.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth the weather was fairly fine, although in the evening it had had a very bad look. The wind was moderate from east to east-north-east, but the swell was so strong and so high that the ship rolled at her anchorage as in a heavy sea in a calm.
Change of anchorage. Observed latitude south (no figures). Longitude by the timekeepers (no figures).
1801-06-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 4.15 the large boat was sent aboard the Naturaliste. At 7.30 took the second reef in the topsails, which were stopped with rope yarns, and signalled the Naturaliste to carry out the order received; she asked leave to slip her cable. We hailed her to send our boat back; an officer came to explain to the commander what prevented him from getting under way: in heaving round, his stoppers had parted several times and he had a man hurt. At 8.30 got under way; at 9 shaped our course and steered successively S 78° 45' E, S 67° 30' E, S 45° E, S 22° 30' E and south, the lead giving 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 and 8 fathoms, fine sand. At 11 several people were seen on the shore. At 11.30 we anchored in 8 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 85° W and another point N 34° E. Latitude observed 33° 33' 0", longitude by No. 27, 112° 13' 50" at the anchorage. At noon the wind and sea fell; the large boat was sent off with a hawser, provisions and stores for the longboat's crew. Fired two guns. At 3.30 the Naturaliste got under way and came and anchored near us. Captain Hamelin came aboard and informed the commander that after much effort to weigh his anchor it had come up with a fluke broken. At nightfall showed a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour. At 8 the large boat came back and brought Citizen Péron, one of the shipwrecked naturalists. During the night the longboat's crew made a fire on the shore.

1801-06-08.journal_anonyme: Blowing hard from NE, a very high sea. The Géographe's boat came aboard at 4 a.m. with orders to man our large boat and put into it all the gear needed to repair the stranded longboat; the bad weather prevented the two boats from shoving off. At 7 o'clock the commander gave written orders to get under way and anchor within the bay. We at once hove round at the capstan, but the heavy sea tried us greatly and the cable came in only with difficulty; at half past eight all the stoppers parted and the little cable we had got in ran out again, wounding one of our quartermasters severely. At 9 the Géographe was under sail and recalled her boat; one of our officers went aboard her for orders. At 2 p.m. we rigged a voyol to heave with more power at the capstan. At 3 we found the flukes had parted from the shank; we finished getting in the rest of the cable and catted the stump of the anchor. At 3.30 we shaped our course NW by N and anchored at 5 in 5 fathoms of water, fine sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable, the commander bearing from us SSE. The captain went aboard the Géographe. At 5.30 saw two fires in the SW. A fresh breeze from ENE. On the 19th at 4 a.m. our large boat left with the commander's boat to carry help to the stranded longboat.
1801-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth (8 June 1801), in the morning, the weather being fairly fine, although the sea was still high and swelling. Despite the east-north-east wind that had risen again during the night, and the north-east wind then blowing, I sent off my boat, giving the command of it to Bougainville with a most express prohibition against leaving it or exposing it to the slightest risk. I likewise ordered the Naturaliste to dispatch hers with eight men. And my master carpenter was to make an exact examination of the longboat and of its situation, so as to decide whether we should persist in trying to save it.
By the same opportunity I wrote to M. Ste Croix Le Bas the following letter:
"The Commander of the expedition &c. to Citizen Ste Croix Le Bas,
"By the letter I addressed to you yesterday, which I had little hope of getting to you, not knowing where to find you, I ordered you to return on board, or at least to send back part of those who are with you and who are assuredly of no use to you. I hold you personally responsible for this disobedience, which makes me prolong my stay at an insecure anchorage that I should not keep if I cared less for your personal safety and for that of all those who are with you.
"You ought to have judged from the look of the weather that it would probably soon turn bad, and the barometer announces it only too plainly, since it fell six lines in the course of yesterday.
"I am sending you, for the last time, my boat and the Naturaliste's to carry you all on board. I am pleased to believe that you will no longer oppose anyone's embarking. The safety of the ships and of those in them must not be sacrificed to the very uncertain salvage of a longboat which will be out of service for a long time, according to the reports made to me of its present situation. For the rest, I am sending you the master carpenter, who will judge of it better than anyone.
"Greetings, N. B."
From the moment my boat left until its return on board, I was in continual anxiety for fear that some damage might befall it such as would prevent it from getting back. I could see through my telescope how heavy the surf was on the shore, and the persons I was waiting for could not embark there without going into the water up to their backsides. At last, at about
noon, I saw the Naturaliste's boat make sail and head back. It came alongside at about two o'clock with all the naturalists. All were soaked to the skin and chilled through.
The officer commanding it told me that the longboat was so deeply embedded in the sand, and the sea so heavy on the shore, that we must absolutely give up, at least for the moment, any idea of saving it. As soon as I was informed of the accident that had befallen it and of the manner in which the sea had thrown it on the shore, I had considered it entirely lost, but as MM. Le Bas and Ronsard, perhaps to excuse their negligence, persisted in sending me word that they would save it if I sent them everything they asked for, I reluctantly sent them, in men and gear, everything that was asked of me.
During the evening the ship laboured so heavily in the roadstead that I feared at every moment some damage to my masts and rigging, although the topgallant masts were struck. I fired a gun every hour to bring back as quickly as possible my boat and the Naturaliste's, which I had sent off again,
fearing that mine could not hold all those who were ashore.
At last, at about four o'clock, it came on board with all my people, but to embark them all it had been necessary to abandon all the other gear. So that, besides my longboat, fully armed and rigged, I also lost all the supplies that had been asked of me in the hope of getting it afloat again.
Almost all the objects the naturalists had collected and gathered during their stay ashore met the same fate, and in this respect Riedelé fared worse than the others, for, besides the boxes he had left ashore, the sea, having passed over his head as he was embarking in the Naturaliste's boat, carried off the most precious things he had shut up in a tin box.
As soon as M. Ste Croix Le Bas had come on board, he did not fail to come and excuse himself for what had happened to him, still persisting in saying that no one was at fault and that, had the sea not been so bad, he would have saved the longboat. I listened to his excuses without answering them, the state he was in not being suitable for making him the reproaches he deserves.
As soon as the boat was empty I had it hoisted in, but my anxieties were not yet at an end, since the Naturaliste still had two boats ashore: her large boat, which I had sent off so that mine might be less crowded, and her small one, which I had seen go ashore in the morning with one of her officers, no doubt for his amusement, since it went and landed very far from the spot where our people were. At nightfall both were still ashore, and all the guns fired to bring them back on board could not make them hasten their return.
At sunset the weather had the worst possible look. Great black and hideous clouds encircled our whole horizon from north to west, and there was no doubt that the wind would come from that quarter during the night. I was quite resolved to get under sail, even if it meant returning to this same spot the next day, should the weather be fine, to send ashore for the tackles, grapnels, blocks, cordage, spars, planking, crowbars, jack &c. that had been left there and whose loss I greatly regretted. But on the other hand I did not wish to leave until the Naturaliste's boats had returned. At eight o'clock they had still not appeared, although we were burning on board, every quarter of an hour, very brilliant port-fires to show them the position of the ship, and the Naturaliste sent up rockets from time to time.
At last, between half past eight and nine o'clock, they both arrived. M. Millius, who was in the small boat, told me that, having gone to the place where the longboat was to see whether he could be of any use, he had found no one there, but that, seeing a great many of our effects on the beach, he had tried to save some of them, and that this attempt had cost the life of one of his boatmen, who was drowned, carried away by a wave. Fear of endangering his other oarsmen made him give up any further attempts. But for this misfortune, I should at least have had the consolation, in my ill fortune, that no one had fallen victim to the imprudence of two officers; but happiness was not made for me, and by a quite particular fatality, he who had least deserved to suffer from it must needs become its victim.
As soon as M. Millius and his men had rested a little, I sent them back to their ship and had M. Hamelin informed that, in view of the fall of the barometer, which now stood at only twenty-eight inches, and of the look of the weather, I was going to get under sail at once, and I invited him to do likewise.
Hardly had the Naturaliste's boats shoved off than I bitterly repented having sent them away, fearing yet some fresh misfortune, for there suddenly came upon us a very strong squall from the north, which
could only make these boats drift to leeward of their ship, or at the very least greatly delay their arrival on board and increase its difficulties. The squall we had did not, happily, last long, for it ceased after a quarter of an hour. But it was nevertheless strong enough to make the Naturaliste drag her anchor, and she was driven a quarter of a league to leeward of us. This accident could not have come more opportunely to let her boats reach her with greater ease.
At half past ten I was under sail, and the Naturaliste too. The wind was then almost calm and from the north-north-east quarter. We stood on the north-west tack to work up into the middle of the bay, where I intended to beat to and fro until the wind had settled and the sky cleared. From the time we got under sail until midnight the wind was very light and we often had rain. But from then until daybreak we had it north-north-east, blowing so fresh that we were obliged to take the third reef in the topsails and even to furl them. As the part of the bay in which we were was perfectly known to us, having crossed it sounding in every direction and knowing the nature of the soundings and their distances from the coast, I lay to under the main topsail, the fore-topmast staysail and the mizzen staysail, a sail under which the ship behaved very well, and thus we passed the rest of the night, the Naturaliste at a short distance from us.
Report of the master carpenter concerning the longboat.
"I regard your longboat," the master told me on his return, "as lost, because it is impossible to work on it, the sea being too rough, and, short of a calm lasting some days, the sea will not be quiet at the spot where it lies.
"This longboat is entirely sunk and the sea covers it by more than two feet. It is, moreover, entirely full of sand and so embedded all round that it forms a shoal more than five feet in circumference, on which one can walk as on a platform. I do not think the longboat is damaged. But short of a spring tide, when the sea will fall enough to leave it uncovered, it is useless to try to dig it out of the sand. If, before having all the articles sent ashore that were asked for, and which are lost to us, I had been able to see for myself, I should have spared you the additional loss of all the articles I left behind, having been unable to re-embark them in the boat that was intended to carry everyone on board."
Bearings of the land.
At noon, the point forming the southern entrance of the bay west 5° north
The most prominent land to the north north-east by north
Nota. I got under way to go and lie opposite the spot where Captain Hamelin had told me my longboat was ashore.
Nota.
My large boat, entrusted to Citizen Bonnefoy, set off as soon as we were at anchor to see whether, along the coast, he could discover the wreckage of my longboat or anything else that might show him the spot to which all those who had been in it had withdrawn. He returned on board at half past seven and brought me news of everyone.
1801-06-08.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to ESE. At 4 a.m. our large boat and the Naturaliste's were sent off with express orders to bring back all the men who were ashore and to abandon the longboat and the gear that had been sent to get her off. The barometer falling fast made us fear bad weather. In the afternoon the two large boats brought back all our people. The longboat was abandoned with a kedge anchor, hawser, tackles, arms and stores. At 8 a boat from the Naturaliste came aboard. Citizen Milius, who commanded her, told us that he came from the shore and had lost one of his boat's crew named Vasse: the sea being very high and breaking with force on the shore, the boat had been obliged to keep at some distance so as not to be swamped; each man had taken to the water to embark, hauling himself along by the boat's grapnel line; all succeeded except Vasse, who, being drunk, was carried away by a sea. At 9 got under way, as did the Naturaliste. The wind at noon; at 11 almost calm, with rain. The barometer still falling.

1801-06-09.journal_anonyme: The wind NE freshening a great deal; our large boat went aboard the Géographe carrying part of the people who had been ashore, and was sent off again to fetch the rest. Seeing that we could not get the longboat off, we abandoned her with all the gear we had landed, and sent up several rockets to mark our position for our two boats, being in great anxiety on their account. At 8 our small boat was back, telling us that the large one was following. At the same moment the ship dragged in a squall and we veered cable; but still driving fast towards the land, the captain decided to get under way. We hove round at once at the capstan, but the ship still casting towards the land, and the capstan meeting little resistance from the cable, we supposed the latter had parted or the anchor been damaged — which we verified at 10.30 p.m., for having then finished hauling the warp aboard we saw that the anchor had only one fluke left. As soon as it was catted we made sail with the winds SSE, variable and very light. Citizen Milius, first lieutenant, took charge of the working of the ship. At 7.30 a.m. a strong breeze, a high sea and the sky overcast.
1801-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, in the morning, it continued to blow fresh from north-north-east to north, the sky overcast and hazy, with rain. It then became necessary to decide to make sail, and accordingly I had the courses and the main topsail set, with all reefs in. The Naturaliste, which we sighted during a clear spell, was a long way to leeward of us. And as she was crowding sail, I presumed that she was near the coast, which the haze hid from our view, but from which, judging by the lead, we reckoned ourselves three leagues distant at its nearest part.
During the morning some heavy gusts passed over, and we beat to windward with fair success, although the tacks were not long and we lost a great deal by wearing. Nevertheless, we worked far enough to windward to get out of the bay, and I should have done so at once had the Naturaliste not seemed to me (to have) fallen too far to leeward.
At noon we had a short clear spell, and the weather seemed inclined to turn fine, although the barometer, which stood below twenty-eight, warned us that it would grow worse.
