Our hope of fine weather did not last long, for at two o'clock the sky had a worse look than it had yet had, and the gusts were much stronger than in the morning.
At about four o'clock the Naturaliste had almost closed with us, and I had furled my mainsail, finding myself far enough to windward to stand out to sea if the weather grew worse, which seemed to me hardly possible, for it was already very bad. The evening had passed like the morning, beating to and fro without having lost or gained much, but always in a position where we had nothing to fear.
At eight o'clock, seeing no sign of change, I resolved to stand out to sea and leave the bay, for fear that if the wind shifted to the north-west and the bad weather continued, I should find it difficult to get to the south, since the north-north-east tack could not be long. The sea had become very high, and although the ship must have been well steadied by the sail I was carrying, she nevertheless laboured with very hard and violent motions. At ten o'clock the Naturaliste was near enough to us for us to make her out clearly; it would appear, however, that she did not see us, since she twice sent up rockets, no doubt to show us her position. As we saw her perfectly well, I answered her only with a light which I had hung at the mizzen gaff.
At midnight, perceiving from the lead and the nature of the bottom that the current or the tide was setting me towards the land, I stood off on the offshore tack and left the bay, for my own peace of mind and for the ship's safety. I made the signal for this to the Naturaliste, but I do not know whether she saw it, having seen nothing that might lead me to suppose so.
During the rest of the night it continued to blow fresh. The squalls followed one another in rapid succession, and it was beyond dispute the worst weather we had had since our departure from France.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From ten o'clock to midnight: eight and ten fathoms, sandy bottom.
From midnight to four o'clock: 12 & 16, same bottom
From four o'clock to eight: 23 & 25, bottom of fine gravel
From eight o'clock to noon: 15 to 20, fine sand.
The haze and the rain did not permit any bearings to be taken.
Nota. All the persons who had been ashore in the longboat were back on board by six o'clock in the evening; there remained ashore only two of the Naturaliste's boats, which I awaited with great impatience in order to get under sail. They arrived at nine o'clock, and the officer who was in them told me that one of his boatmen had been drowned, having been carried away by a wave at the moment when (he) was embarking.
1801-06-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, almost calm. At midnight it began to freshen, and the wind blew hard in gusts, with a high sea and rain. At 3.30 lay to; at 5 filled and stood on. At noon, in a clear interval, took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 85° W, about 18 miles off. The Naturaliste to leeward, beating like ourselves to get out of the gulf; the wind from NE to north. At noon in 33° 25' 20" of latitude by account and in 112° 5' 50" of longitude. At 4, Cape Géographe S 82° W, about 12 miles off. At 7.30 the Naturaliste was in sight to leeward; at midnight she bore from us SSW at a short distance.

1801-06-10.journal_anonyme: At 1.30 p.m. we wore ship. At 2.30 we sighted the Géographe ahead and to windward of us standing on the opposite tack; at 3.30 wore ship. At 4.30 the commander bearing from us north. At 5.30, at 8 and at midnight wore ship. Bearings taken at 2.30 p.m.: the starboard point of the gulf on entering N 78° W, distant 10 miles. At 3.30 the same point N 86° W, distant 8 miles. Thick weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts.
1801-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, at daybreak, we found ourselves outside the bay, the wind and weather being still the same. We found the sea somewhat less swelling, however, but the current or tide, which was setting us to the south-east, seemed to be running much faster.
Although at times our horizon was fairly wide, we saw nothing of the Naturaliste, which, to all appearance, had not left the bay or had stood less far out to sea. Nevertheless, I was not uneasy, being persuaded that on standing in again towards the land I could not fail to find her.
At ten o'clock, the wind still increasing, I furled the mainsail and the fore topsail and carried only the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed and the mizzen staysail. Then I went about again towards the land, persuaded that I was about to fall in with the Naturaliste. But at noon we had still not sighted her. We saw only, during the morning, several whales sporting on the water, and one among others with which a swordfish was waging a furious battle, which amused us greatly despite the bad weather. At noon, not having had the sun, we got no meridian altitude, but by our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 33° 30' south latitude.
In the afternoon the wind shifted to north-north-west, from which it blew just as hard as it had done while it was north-north-east, and with no sign of any change. I held the inshore tack until three o'clock, when, being no more than three leagues from the land, I wore round with her head to seaward, having no hope now of finding the Naturaliste except at the Swan River, which I have appointed as the first rendezvous in case of separation.
During the evening of the twentieth the squalls were heavier and stronger than they had been, and the wind was warm. The weather was very bad and the barometer at 27. 10 lines. In the evening we made ready to pass a bad night, but as the course I was steering was carrying me out to sea, I did not think I had much to fear.
At six o'clock we had 50 fathoms and the lead showed rocks. At seven o'clock we had no more than forty-six, same bottom. So sudden a decrease made me uneasy, since on the course I was steering I must necessarily be drawing away from the coast. I had reason, therefore, to be astonished at seeing the depth decrease when it ought to have increased. At last, at half past seven, having no more than thirty-five fathoms, rocky bottom, my anxiety redoubled for fear of meeting some reef in the offing, and I went about towards the land, sounding continually. On this tack, which I held for an hour, I went from 35 to 27, grey sand (in the margin: récif du Naturaliste). And then, recognising the soundings of the place where I was, I went about once more and put the ship to the test, for I made her carry her four principal sails, with three reefs in the topsails, and the mizzen topsail with the storm staysail. A quarter of an hour after the sails were trimmed we had 28 fathoms, then 35 and then 45, grey sand, and at midnight no bottom at 70 fathoms. I then had the mainsail, the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail furled, and kept to the sail I had carried before.
I do not know to what to attribute this sudden change in the depth, although it seems to me more fitting to think that it comes from the trend of the land than from any other cause, and that the tides, the leeway and the heavy sea must have brought us closer in than our dead reckoning allowed. For the rest, as we are being carried violently to the south-south-east and shall have to work back to the north as soon as the wind becomes manageable and allows it, we shall be in a position to clear up this uncertainty. Nothing leads us to believe that there is a shoal in this part off the coast, and although that was at first my opinion, I prefer to believe I prefer to believe (sic) that we had more leeway and a stronger tide than we supposed by our dead reckoning.
During the rest of the night we sounded often without finding bottom at 70 fathoms, and this was because the coast, then changing its direction and trending more to the south-south-east, we were drawing further away from it. The weather continued very bad. The barometer, which at the beginning of the night had risen two lines, consequently to 28, fell again to 27. 10 and seemed to us not likely to stop at that point. The sky having too threatening a look.
If, as I suspect, the Naturaliste has kept within the bay, I fear she may have suffered damage there, being obliged to carry sail continually to hold her own against the sea and the tides that set her towards the coast; and as all that we have seen of it offers no shelter when the wind is from north-north-east round by west to south, it is a very bad place when the wind blows hard from any of the points of that quarter.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From noon to four o'clock 20 to 21 fathoms, fine sand.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock 22, 25 & 26, fine grey sand.
From eight o'clock to midnight, 28, 23, 16 & 17, grey sand.
From midnight to four o'clock in the morning, 20, 21 & 25, grey sand and fine red gravel.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock from 25 to 28, grey sand.
From eight o'clock to noon from 28 to 33, fine sand.
Bearings of the land at noon
The cap des Mécontents north 5° east
At four o'clock in the afternoon, the point forming the southern entrance of the bay west 8° south four leagues
At midnight, the point forming the southern entrance of the bay south-west
At three o'clock, the same point south-south-west
Nota: at ten o'clock the Naturaliste bore south-south-west of us at a short distance. From that time she was not seen again for the rest of the night.
1801-06-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard and variable from NE to NW in gusts, a high sea, with rain. At 1 we lost sight of the Naturaliste. At 3 the southern shores of the gulf bore from us S 45° W, and at 4, S 22° 30' W. At 10, being clear of the gulf, lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the storm staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon in 33° 46' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 40' of longitude by account. At 1 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 50° E and the point of the islet (seen on the 8th) S 41° E. At 9 filled and stood on under courses. From midnight to 8 a.m. the lead gave from 20 to 33 fathoms, grey sand; from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. no bottom at 80 fathoms; from 6 p.m. to midnight from 50 to 28 fathoms, rocky bottom.

1801-06-11.journal_anonyme: During the night the kedge anchor was carried away by a sea which parted both lashings. A very high sea, the wind still blowing hard. Given the weakness of our crew, both watches were kept on deck. At 8 a.m. Point N bore from us west. But the winds having headed us 2 points in a squall, we wore ship.
1801-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second the weather was worse still than the day before. We spent the day beating to and fro, tack upon tack, to hold our own against the sea, the wind and the currents. But in spite of all our efforts we were being swiftly carried to the south-east or, at the very least, to the south-south-east. In the course of the morning the winds shifted to north-west and varied as far as west-north-west, attended by heavy rain and by gusts so violent that I expected from one moment to the next to lose some of our sails. The barometer then stood at 27 inches eight lines, and we had never seen it so low, so that the bad weather seemed to us to be drawing to its end. The sea ran so high that as the ship rolled the water came in over the lee gangways, and we had all the trouble in the world to save ourselves from the falls that the quickness of the ship's motion brought upon us. For my own part I took one of which I fear I shall long feel the effects.
At noon we were, by our dead reckoning, in 34° 10', (in the margin: Cape Leeuwin) lying east and west of the point that we had earlier taken for Cape Leeuwin, which is easily recognised by the great white patch shown by the hill forming the extremity of that point. We then thought we could see that Cape Leeuwin must lie further to the south, since we had in sight a fairly long stretch of coast extending to the south-east, which we ought not to have seen had the point we first took for the westernmost land truly been so, for all the other land to the east would then have been shut in from us.
It follows from this that the westernmost point of Leeuwin's Land lies a good deal further south than the 34 degrees 10 minutes that most of our charts assign to it for its latitude. I put off making sure of this fact until a more favourable time.
During the evening the winds remained at west-north-west, still in gusts, and we often had very heavy rain. My intention was, if they did not change, to stand on the southerly tack until midnight and then to take the one that would bring me back towards the land. At the beginning of the night the weather seemed inclined to clear. The barometer rose about a line and a half, but only to fall again afterwards to 27 inches 8 lines, where it had stood for almost the whole day.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third we stood on the southerly tack until midnight and then went back to the northerly one until four in the morning, when, the lead having given forty fathoms, rocky bottom, we took the southerly tack again. During the night we had a great deal of lightning, rain and frequent thunder.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From noon to six o'clock, veered 80 fathoms, no bottom.
From six o'clock to eight, 50, 48, 46, rocky bottom.
From eight o'clock to midnight, 35, 27, 28, rocky bottom.
From midnight to four in the morning, 28, 35, 45, grey sand.
From four o'clock to eight, 70 fathoms, no bottom.
From eight o'clock to noon, 70 fathoms, no bottom.
Bearings of the land at noon
The Cap des Mécontents north 5° east
At noon the land in sight to the north, north-east 5° east
The land to the south, south-east 4° east
At eight in the morning the land was seen from south-east to north-north-east
and at noon Point Leeuwin lay west, 3 leagues off.
(words struck out, afterwards (?))
1801-06-11.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from NNW to W; a high sea and rain. At midnight lay to again under the same canvas. At 8 the land stretched from N 22° 30' E to S 45° E. At noon in 34° 5' 20" of latitude by account and in 111° 44' 10" of longitude by account, Cape Géographe bearing from us N 15° E and Cape Leeuwin east, about 9 miles off. At 4, Cape Géographe N 11° E, Cape Leeuwin N 25° E and the point of the islet S 68° E. We have had no sight of the Naturaliste since the 21st at 1 a.m.

1801-06-12.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a very high sea, blowing a strong breeze from the WNW in gusts. Bearings at 2 p.m.: the middle of the two headlands E 5° S. At 4.30 took the bearing of the end of the land NNE 1° E, distant 10 leagues. Sent up rockets and showed a light every half hour to mark our position for the commander, whom we had lost.
1801-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, although the weather was much the same, the squalls and gusts nevertheless began to come less often and less heavily. The sky was at times cloudy and fine, and we sighted the land, though without being able to make anything out, because it was too thick with haze. I was then standing on the southerly tack, being fully resolved to close with the land (only) when the weather cleared or the winds allowed me to steer directly north-west.
Throughout the morning the sky was fairly fine, and at noon we at last had a meridian altitude, which placed us in 34° 39' 49" south latitude, so that since leaving the bay we (found ourselves) carried more than twenty leagues to the south, although by the various tacks I had made I had always tried to reduce the loss of ground as far as possible.
During the evening the hope of seeing the weather clear away vanished. The sky was once more overcast with dark, thick clouds, and the gusts began again with all all (sic) the same force and violence as on the previous days, which decided me to hold on the southerly tack, although the winds were settling in the western quarter.
At sunset our conjectures about the portion of land that we had judged the day before to be the westernmost of what is known as Leeuwin's Land were confirmed, and we had a full view of the islet where M. St Aloüarn must have come to anchor; but it is no doubt very far from lying, as he says, in 34° 17'. I believe on the contrary that it is very close to 35°, since it is nearly ten leagues by dead reckoning from the point where we observed 34° 10', and directly south-south-east of it. If the weather is fine tomorrow, it will be a good opportunity to verify this fact.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth the winds shifted to west and varied to west-south-west, which obliged me to take the north-westerly tack. We had no lack of rain, thunder or lightning during the night. But although the squalls were heavy, they were nothing (in) comparison with those we had endured on the previous days. Besides, they followed one another far less rapidly, and the fineness of the sky once they had passed seemed to foretell the end of the bad weather, which the barometer refused to announce to us, standing constantly between 27. 8 and 27. 10.
While we ran on the north-westerly tack we sounded every hour, but we never found bottom with 70 & 80 fathoms of line.
Soundings and nature of the bottom. Astronomical time.
From noon to three o'clock, 45 & 35 fathoms, rocky bottom.
From three o'clock to five, 37 & 50 fathoms, sand & coral.
From five o'clock to midnight, veered 60 fathoms, no bottom.
From midnight to four in the morning, veered 70 fathoms, no bottom
At five o'clock, 55 fathoms, rotten shells.
At six o'clock, 40 fathoms, rocky bottom.
At seven o'clock, 36 fathoms, sand and coral
From eight o'clock to noon, 36, 35, 35, 40, sand and coral.
Nota: there is an error in what I said on this day about the position of Point Leeuwin.
Bearings of the land
At four o'clock the southernmost land south 67°30' east
The more northerly land north 11°15' east
At eight in the morning Point Leeuwin north by east
The islet east by south
The land in sight to the north, north 5° east.
1801-06-12.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from WNW to WSW. A high sea, with light rain at intervals. At 8 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight, north; Cape Leeuwin N 11° E; the point of the islet N 79° E; and the islet S 79° E. At noon the land could no longer be seen. We were in 34° 37' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' of longitude by account. At nightfall the wind fell away a great deal.

1801-06-13.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from WNW. At 6 p.m. wore ship. A very high sea, the wind still blowing hard and in gusts, with much lightning from SSW round to NW.
1801-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth the weather cleared and we had a fine day. We took advantage of it to close with the land, from which our course and the tides had carried us a considerable distance. Although the sky had cleared, we nevertheless had some fairly strong gusts in the morning, but that did not prevent me from making sail and shaking out a reef in the topsails.
When we had drawn somewhat nearer the land, we had a perfect view of the westernmost part of what is known as Leeuwin's Land, and we likewise recognised the islet where M. St Aloüarn must have anchored; but we did not see, and indeed there does not exist, the chain of islets which he claims extends to the south-east or south-south-east, nor the reefs he says he took bearings of to the north-west of the anchorage where he then lay. We ranged along this part of the coast close enough to be able to affirm that he was mistaken.
The land lying to the south-east and east-south-east of the western point of Leeuwin's Land may well, at a distance of seven or eight leagues, appear to the eye as islets, and this is not the only part of the coast that gives the same effect. But if one approaches them, as we did, to within two or three leagues, one sees perfectly well that everything one took to be islands belongs to the mainland, to which they are joined by lower ground that can be made out only at a short distance.
For the rest, the westernmost part of Leeuwin's Land is of a good height and can easily be seen ten leagues out to sea. But the islet, which is separated from it by about two leagues, is much lower and can be seen only at a moderate distance.
As we could get no observation at noon, the sun being wrapped in cloud, it has not been very easy for us to determine exactly either the latitude or the longitude of this point. But going by the later observations we made, referred to those taken on our arrival on this coast, (it) cannot give an error of more than three minutes in the latitude of this point, which we fix at 34° 17 and 111° 54' 0" east longitude.
Moreover, as I intend to see this cape again when I make for Van Diemen's Land next summer, I hope to determine its latitude and longitude exactly.
In the afternoon, having closed with the land, we coasted along it once more and took fresh bearings of the various points we had already seen, the better to confirm the first ones.
In the evening the weather was fairly fine and the barometer rose to 28 inches, which was very welcome to us, for during four days the bad weather had greatly distressed us and, still more, our livestock, which we lost almost entirely. This loss was all the more keenly felt as we had tried every means of sheltering the animals from the bad weather.
During the night the weather was fairly fine and the winds moderate from the west. I stood on the north-westerly tack so as to be in a position to re-enter the next day the bay from which the bad weather had driven me, in order to finish surveying it.
Running up from Point Leeuwin to the c, we remarked for the second time, and it is perhaps a rather singular thing, that this whole stretch of coast, which offers no shelter even for a boat, is everywhere fringed with rocks
of granite on which the sea breaks with a great noise, whereas in the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay] they are seen only on the first point, which forms its entrance, all the rest being nothing but sand dunes.
It is also to be remarked that from the western point of Leeuwin's Land to the one forming the entrance of the bay I have just spoken of, the bottom is consistently foul, whether near the coast or out at sea, whereas in the bay one finds everywhere a clean, good bottom on which one may anchor at whatever distance one pleases from the shore.

1801-06-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze, variable from W to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted; at 7 filled and stood on, lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 8 the point of the islet N 15° E and another point N 22° 30' W. At noon in 34° 26' of latitude by account and in 111° 55' of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 3° W, Cape Leeuwin N 7° E, the point of the islet N 56° E and the islet N 68° E. At 4.45 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 28° E, 23 miles off; the White Mountain, which had at first been taken for Cape Leeuwin, east, 10 miles off; Cape Leeuwin S 50° E, 22 miles off. During the night carried little sail so as not to run past Cape Géographe. The topgallant masts were swayed up.

1801-06-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from WNW. At 3.30 went about, being only 5 or 6 leagues from the land, and steered close-hauled. At 5.30 hove to, being 15 to 18 miles from the coast, and sounded in 25 fathoms, fine sand. At 5.50 stood on again. At 7.15 the wind having hauled in a squall, went onto the port tack; at 7.45 the lead brought up 45 fathoms, fine sand. At 10.30 a.m. we passed over a weedy bottom in separate patches, easy to make out, which seemed to rise above the bottom from 14, 12, 13, 11 to 10 fathoms. At 10.30 we let go the anchor in 9 fathoms, clean grey sand. Bearings of the anchorage: the western point of Rottnest Island W half N; the SW point W 27° S; the west end of the island lying off the end of Rottnest S 9° E; an islet or rock lying east of that one S 25° E; the southernmost visible end of the mainland S 33° E.
1801-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, at daybreak, the weather being fine and the winds westerly, a pleasant breeze, we first put the ship's head to the north; but having found that the currents during the night had carried us well out to sea, as had the course we had held, we steered for some time north-east and finally east, to re-enter our great bay, from which we were about six leagues distant.
In the morning a second reef was shaken out of the topsails and I had the main topgallant sail rigged. I was rather vexed at entering the bay with westerly winds, because of the difficulty I should have in getting out again should they remain in that quarter and the weather turn bad. But the hope that I might have the land breeze during the night, as had always been the case the first time I put in there, made me go on regardless.
At noon, being north and south of the point that forms its entrance, we observed the latitude of 33° 30' 32" south, and the longitude given by the timekeepers was then 111° 27' 13". I expected to find the Naturaliste there, but having had no sight of her, I think she will have made for Rottnest Island, which I appointed as her first rendezvous in case of separation.
At four o'clock we were abreast of the place to which I had advanced, and we continued our bearings from that point, which is easy to recognise from the notes we had taken while we lay at anchor there.
At sunset the weather was fine and the barometer at 28 inches 2 lines, which set our minds somewhat at rest. Nevertheless I kept at some distance from the coast and trimmed the sails close-hauled on the larboard tack, as I was to spend the night beating about, the winds not being suitable for anchoring.
At eight o'clock, having no more than eighteen fathoms of water, I went about and steered south-west and south-west by west under the topsails and the foresail. I found the same bottom until about ten o'clock, when it began to deepen, and at eleven I was in twenty fathoms, clean sandy bottom.
At the beginning of the night we had several squalls with wind and rain, but they did not last long. However, towards half past ten it began to blow a strong breeze, although the sky was fairly fine and clear, and everything seemed to warn us that the night would be neither fine nor easy to get through, having the land under our lee and at a very short distance.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth the weather did indeed turn bad, and we had gusts so strong that a second reef had to be taken in the topsails. At midnight we took the northerly tack, which we held until daylight, with the lead going, and it never gave less than nineteen to twenty fathoms of water, with various kinds of bottom.

1801-06-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to NW. At 7, having doubled Cape Géographe, we bore away east into the gulf to see whether the Naturaliste might be there. At noon in 33° 31' of latitude observed and in 111° 27' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 50' NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Géographe S 73° W and a NE point of the gulf N 55° E. At 5, having seen nothing in the gulf, we hauled to the wind on the port tack; at 6.30 went onto the starboard tack. During the night overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts, with squalls.

1801-06-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from WNW. We sent our large boat to survey Rottnest Island; she was back at 8 p.m. A national flag was planted on a high hill nearest the shore, in case he should pass that way when we were no longer at the anchorage. The winds variable from W to WNW.
1801-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, at the break of day, we had so heavy a squall, with rain, that we had to reef our topsails and even lower them right down. This blast lasted about half an hour, after which the weather cleared and the sky became very bright, though cloudy. The winds still held in the west and blew so hard that we could not shake out the second reef of our topsails. However, as we had the land under our lee and at a short distance, we sent up our mainsail, which had been changed the day before, the one on the yard being no longer fit to stand further blasts, if, as there was every appearance, we should have more of them.
At eight o'clock, the fog that hid the greater part of the coast from us having cleared a little, we saw it distinctly stretching away astern of us to the south-east and ahead of us to the north-east.
This coast appeared to us much less even than that of the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], but behind the dunes forming its shore one could clearly make out two ranges of mountains, far higher than anything we had seen until then, and we reckoned that the range lying furthest inland might be fifteen leagues from us.
Throughout the whole day we could take no bearings of the coast, along which we ran sometimes at three leagues' distance and often more when we found ourselves abreast of some inlet. The wind was so unmanageable all day that we sought only to work a little way off the land rather than to approach it.
At noon we observed the latitude of 32° 38' 41", and the longitude given by the timekeepers for the same hour was, for No. 27, 111° 45' 20" and for No. 35, 111° 48' 30".
From the dead reckoning of the courses run, we found that the currents or tides had changed direction, since we had a difference of ten minutes to the north.
In the afternoon the weather was no finer than it had been in the morning; on the contrary, the wind increased considerably and the squalls followed one another more rapidly than ever, an almost certain presage of a bad night. At four o'clock we were obliged to furl our mizzen topsail and carry nothing but our courses, with two reefs in the topsails.
Running along the coast in the evening, we found ourselves abreast of a large bay whose northern extremity no doubt ends at the point that must form the entrance of the Swan River, or Rivière des Cygnes, from which we were now no more than five or six leagues distant, according to the reckoning of the distance run since noon and the latitude observed at that time. But
we had no hope of seeing it so soon, since we had to retrace our steps as soon as the weather allowed, to examine the coast we had just passed without having been able to determine its trend and windings.
At six in the evening we went about, although the breeze was very strong. As we were heading south-west by south, I think this tack will carry us fairly well off the coast, and we shall always be able to judge by the lead how near we are to it.
At half past seven the weather sheet of our main topsail gave way. But the sail was quickly gathered in and was not damaged by the force of the wind.
For the rest of the night the weather was continually squally and rainy, with very strong gusts from west-north-west to west-south-west. During the night we made two boards, the lead telling us when it was time to go about.

1801-06-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to W in gusts. At midnight went onto the port tack. At 8 we were about 18 miles from the land; it appeared to stretch away in the N 22° 30' E and to form a bight. At 11 a very conspicuous point bore from us east, about 12 miles off. At noon in 32° 36' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 45' 20" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. At 6 the land stretched from N 11° E to S 67° 30' E. Went onto the starboard tack. Squally weather, with rain.

1801-06-16.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze in gusts from W to W by N, blowing hard. Our large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq. At 8.30 p.m., the corvette dragging, we let go our sheet anchor with a range of 30 fathoms. At 9 a.m. the boat was back, not having been able to land because of the bad weather.
1801-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, the winds the winds (sic) were west-south-west, often varying to south-west. The sky, though very cloudy and overcast, was less rainy than the day before, and in the course of the morning it even became fairly fine. However, the weather not being fit for standing in to the land, we held on close-hauled on the southerly tack until ten o'clock, when we took the north-westerly tack to stand further off the coast until the weather should allow us to come back and examine it with more safety. When we went about, our distance from the land might have been four leagues at most, and we then had from 18 to 15 fathoms of water, sandy bottom, sometimes coral and even rocks.
The fog covering the greater part of the land made it too indistinct for us to take bearings that were reliable or could be recognised on our return to the same spot; for that reason we confined ourselves to taking bearings of the two extremities in sight, to the north as well as to the south, and of the middle of the land abeam of us.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 32° 42' 57", and that by dead reckoning placed us in 32° 37' 47", which gave us a difference to the south of 10' 10" for the various courses made during the twenty-four hours. The longitude given by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, was 111° 46' 14" for No. 27 and 112° 57' for No. 35, whose daily rate was gaining more and more on that of No. 27.
In the afternoon the winds shifted to west and it fell almost calm, which made us hope for a change in our favour, for since the new moon the weather had almost always been bad, and the winds, if not altogether contrary, at least hard to manage. The barometer, besides, had already risen to 28 inches 2 lines.
As the weather was then fine and we were making little way, we amused ourselves with dredging, the bottom being sandy and the depth not great, since we had only 18 to 20 fathoms of water. Among the various objects of natural history that we took with the dredge, there was nothing very remarkable but a few sponges and several medusae. Among these last we took one of extreme beauty, and no doubt quite new to collectors. The dredge brought up several starfish new to us, which will be new to many others as well, several holothurians like those of which I give the drawing, and lastly a prodigious quantity of shells of the species known as the swallow. But they were all so small that we are convinced this is a variety of the known species and that this one grows no larger, for it would be very surprising if, among the thousands we drew up from the bottom of the sea, and at different times, there had not been some larger ones.
The variety of colours of the sponges would make them very interesting if they kept the fine colours they had on coming out of the water; but as they lose a great deal, they will not offer those who receive them the same interest as the pleasure they gave us in taking them.
During the night of the 27th to the 28th the weather was fine. We made a few boards with the winds at north and north-north-east so as not to draw away from the coast, in order to resume our work early the next day.

1801-06-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze and light from WSW to SW. At midnight went onto the port tack; at 4 onto the starboard. At 8 the land stretched from N 56° E to S 34° E. At 10.45 went onto the port tack, being about 4 miles from the coast, which appears to trend NNE and SSW. It is very low near the shore; inland, fairly high and well wooded mountains could be seen. At noon the northernmost land in sight bore N 34° E, 10 miles off, and the southernmost S 22° E, 21 miles off. At noon in 32° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 22' NW. The dredge was put over several times and brought up many objects of natural history. At 10, the breeze being from the north, went onto the starboard tack.

1801-06-17.journal_anonyme: Grey weather, the sky cloudy, blowing a strong breeze and in heavy gusts from WNW. At 6.30 a.m. the small boat was sent off to Rottnest with two days' provisions; the large boat took six days' provisions to go and examine the Swan River. At 8.30 a.m. the longboat was sent off with 2 days' provisions.
1801-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the weather being fine, the winds north-north-east, a pleasant breeze and the sea smooth, I had the ship stand to the east from daybreak to close with the land, from which the lead then put me about four leagues distant. The sky was so clear and serene at sunrise that we already looked upon this day as one of the finest we had yet had since our arrival in these waters. We were then very far from foreseeing the almost sudden change that came about in the course of the morning.
Be that as it may, at eight o'clock, being now only a short distance from it, a league at most, with no more than eight fathoms of water, sometimes good sandy bottom, sometimes sand and coral and even at times hard coral without sand, we bore away to the south-south-east to run along it through its whole extent, determine all its points and, in short, finish our work in this quarter.
By half past nine we had already run nearly four leagues of coast at the distance I have just mentioned. Many azimuths, angles and bearings had been taken, and everything until then was going as well as could be. We had only about four leagues left to run to reach the point forming the northern entrance of the fine, large Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], when the men on the forecastle called out breakers ahead of us. As I was always on deck, I saw them at once myself and promptly had the ship bear away, bringing her to the starboard tack. We passed at a mile and a half at most from these breakers, on which the sea rolled with great force, which made them all the more conspicuous.
We had scarcely drawn half a league away from them when a most violent squall came upon us from the north-north-east, without our having been able to see where it had come from. I had the ship steered west for some time to get a little further from the coast, which I intended to close with again as soon as this squall had passed. But little by little, the sky having darkened, mist, rain and a strong wind took the place of the pleasant breeze we had had for part of the morning, and we had to keep close-hauled on the larboard tack.
At noon, having been unable to observe the latitude, all our morning's work became useless; our hour angles, our azimuths &c. were a pure loss, and nothing remains of all we had done but an exact knowledge of the coast and some remarks on the various views presented to us by the unbroken chain of sand dunes that everywhere borders it.
When we sighted the reef I have just spoken of, we were steering south by south-west and had it right ahead of us. After drawing a little away from it, we had it bearing south 10° east. The position we assign to it on the chart, though somewhat doubtful, cannot be out by more than a mile or a mile & a half, either to the north or to the south; and as it is comparable to a dune made wholly of sand, with no other greenery than what grows on its summit, it will be all the easier to recognise when we come back to look for it, since it is the most remarkable one to be seen along this whole part of the coast.
So far as I could judge of this reef from the short distance at which we passed it, it does not appear to me to be more than a cable's length long by half a cable wide, and to all appearance there would be a passage between it and the land; at least the calmness of the sea in that place gives reason to suppose so. As it is the only known danger (in the margin: see the Naturaliste's reef) that we have yet met with on Leeuwin's Land, I have named it L'Unique.
In the afternoon the weather became so bad, and the winds, which had shifted first to north, then to north-north-west and north-west, so strong, that we had to take in the three reefs in the topsails one after another, furl our mainsail, the mizzen topsail and finally the fore topsail, and even with what
sail remained to us, the ship had quite as much as she could carry.
The rain was almost continual all the morning evening, so that, having no further hope of closing with the land that day, I continued to stand out to sea until six in the evening, when I went about again to the north, the winds being then west-south-west and the sea very high. We had at that time thirty fathoms of water, sandy bottom, which should have put us seven or eight leagues from the nearest coast.
During the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth the weather continued squally and often rainy. The gusts, however, were less strong than they had been during the day, but the sea was no less heavy and troubled. During the night we continued to sound every half hour, as had been the rule since we had been on the coast. The lead never gave less than 23 fathoms and often more.

1801-06-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather until 10.30, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NE; afterwards overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from N to W. At 3 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 bore away east for the land. At 8 took the bearing of a very high mountain inland, S 35° E; we then bore away south and S 11° W and ran along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It runs roughly north and south and is very low; it is not so well wooded as in the gulf. I thought I could see that it was fringed with coral. The sea broke there violently. The lead gave from 8 to 13 fathoms, coral bottom. At 10.15 breakers were seen ahead in the S 10° E at a short distance; we at once hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. The wind freshened by degrees. At noon the land stretched from N 68° E to S 40° E. At noon in 32° 43' 57" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 26' NW. At 1 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail; at 6 lay to with the port side to the wind.

1801-06-18.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sky cloudy and a very high sea. We kept a light at the gaff all night to mark our position for the boats. At 10 a.m. the dinghy brought the news that the small boat was cast on the shore and could not be got off without the help of a large boat, her crew being short of water and having very little food. The sea being very high and the wind too strong for the dinghy to do the work of a large boat, we had to wait for the longboat's return — and she too, unknown to us, was then on shore and short of every kind of provision.
1801-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the weather was at least as bad as it had been the day before, and in the course of the morning we had no lack of either wind or rain. The sun, however, showed itself from time to time, and when the squalls and gusts had passed, the sky stayed fairly fine for a few moments.
As the winds had held fairly steadily between west and west-north-west, we (kept) always on the northerly tack, hauling as far to the west as we could, sounding every half hour without ever having less than twenty-three fathoms of water, and very often 25 and 28, sandy bottom and sometimes coarse gravel.
The ship's canvas was not well suited to working her to windward, since we carried only the foresail, the main topsail and the mizzen staysail; but that was all the ship could bear, and even then in the gusts she sometimes had too much.
For the greater part of the morning we had no sight of the land, but at noon it showed very distinctly, and the part nearest to us bore north-east by east, four or five leagues off and perhaps less, for one one (sic) could clearly make out the white patch of the dunes bordering the coast, which, it is true, seemed to me higher in this part than in any other.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 32° 16' 28" south, and that of our reckoned course was 32° 16' 23", so that the small difference we found was attributed to the tides, which, having acted on our course in opposite directions during the twenty-four hours, had had no net effect on us. This reasoning is perhaps not certain, but at least it is probable, since on the preceding days, when the course had not been on the same tack, there had always been fairly considerable differences, either to the north or to the south.
Judging by the latitude observed at noon, we were not very far from Rottnest Island, and I even think we had a good sight of it, because towards two o'clock we discovered a land which seemed detached from any other, bearing north-east of us at a distance of six to seven leagues. This land seemed to us higher than any we had seen until then; but the weather being too uncertain to approach it more closely, I went about on the other tack so as to be able to weather easily, before nightfall, the point of a fairly deep bay which lay abeam of us, and whose northern extremity no doubt ends near Rottnest Island and perhaps forms the entrance of the Swan River.
Although we were then fairly close to the coast abeam of us, the depth kept increasing from 25 to thirty fathoms, bottom of greyish and sometimes red sand.
The sea in these waters was extremely heavy and high, which was one more reason for me not to run any further north in weather that had the worst of appearances.
In the afternoon the winds varied from west to west-south-west, and the rain, squalls and strong gusts began all over again. Nevertheless, as I wished to weather before nightfall the point nearest to us, of which I have spoken above, I had the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail set, both close-reefed. But at five o'clock I was obliged to furl the former because of the violence of the squalls we had at that time.
A little before nightfall we took bearings of the land nearest to us to the east, and of that which lay to the north of us, north-east; the estimated distance of the first was four leagues and of the other, eight.
After sunset the weather was thoroughly bad, and in the strong gusts the winds sometimes went round as far as south-west, which made the tack I was then on a rather poor one. Nevertheless the lead constantly gave 25 fathoms, sandy bottom.
I decided to hold on until I should find no more than twenty.
At eight o'clock the squalls became so frequent that one did not wait for the other. Most of them were very heavy, and all foretold a very bad night. The barometer, which during the day, although the weather was not fine, had risen to 28. 1 line, fell in the evening to 27. 11 and seemed to confirm what the state of the atmosphere had already made only too plain to us. For all that, however, the sea was less heavy and high than we had had it all day.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth the weather was extremely bad. It blew fit to carry everything away until midnight, when, the winds having gone round to south-east, the rain began to fall in torrents, accompanied by thunder and lightning, and it seemed as though the elements were in convulsion.
Besides all the discomfort such weather caused us, an event of another kind, and far more unpleasant than the rain, the thunder and the lightning, came to add to our anxieties. At the change of watch at eight o'clock, the lead was regularly giving from 25 to 24 fathoms, clean grey sandy bottom, the same as we had found when running north; but at half past eight it gave no more than 21 fathoms, rocky bottom. At nine o'clock we likewise had 20 and one fathoms, same bottom, but at half past nine we suddenly found ourselves in twelve, still rocky bottom, so that we had at once to wear round and take the northerly tack, hauling as far to the west as we possibly could. We drew away very quickly from a spot that might have proved very fatal to us had I not been continually on deck, with the lead always going.
Half an hour at most after we had trimmed the sails on the larboard tack, the depth increased by three fathoms, another half hour later by three fathoms more, and finally at one o'clock we were once more in 25 fathoms, clean sand.
As we wore round, the bell was rung and the whole crew was promptly on its feet; although it was in the height of a squall, the manoeuvre was swiftly carried out, and I took pleasure in doing the crew the justice due to it on this occasion.
At eleven o'clock, the winds having gone round to south-south-east, they abated greatly, and we had nothing more to suffer than the rain and the storms.

1801-06-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with thunder, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to south. At noon in 32° 16' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 39' 30" of longitude by No. 27. The land bore from us N 79° E at a great distance. At 2 filled and stood on, starboard tack, under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the storm staysail, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. (The Naturaliste, at anchor off Rottnest Island, sighted us at 2 in the S 22° 30' W, 24 miles off.) At 5 the north point in sight N 45° E and the south point N 79° E. At 9.30, having found ourselves on a shoal of reddish sand, we went onto the port tack and gave the course N 45° W, and at 10, N 67° 30' W. At 9.30 the lead had given 12 fathoms, and a quarter of an hour before, 25 to 21 fathoms, grey sand.

1801-06-19.journal_anonyme: The dinghy was sent off under the orders of Citizen Couture to join the large boat. At 2 p.m. the Géographe was sighted in the SSW under her topsails, 24 miles off; we lost sight of her 2 hours later. The winds from east to ESE.
1801-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, in the morning, the winds having come back to south-west, it went on blowing hard, but at least the sky was cloudy and fine, and the squalls of the day before had passed, if not entirely, at least they no longer followed one another with the same rapidity. Only the sea was extremely heavy, and the rolling it caused the ship strained her greatly, as it did all of us.
At eight o'clock, seeing no sign of a change in the weather, I decided to steer north-west by north to reach a latitude better suited to navigation and to our work, reserving to myself the option of coming back from north to south to resume the work I was abandoning, should the weather become manageable.
On the seventh we had sighted the land, and on the eighth we began to take bearings of it, sometimes from afar, sometimes from close in, until the evening of the twenty-ninth. The bad weather, however, had allowed us to do very little of any value up to that time. And except for the coast from the western point of Leeuwin's Land to the one forming the entrance of the fine bay which I have named after the Géographe, all the rest was no more than detached and rough-sketched pieces, which the least spell of fine weather would have enabled us to finish in two days, had we had the good fortune to get it. It was this expectation, and the little that remained to be done, that had until then decided me to stay exposed to all the bad weather we have met with, which twice drove us out of the bay and made us drift as far as south of Point Leeuwin. So that for twenty-three days we (had done nothing but) beat to and fro, tack upon tack, to claw off the coast onto which the winds kept driving us every time we came near enough to examine it properly.
The four anchorages we made in the bay furnished us with fairly interesting details about the quality of the soil, the trend of part of the coasts, the population it can hold and the resources navigators might find there in wood, fishing and hunting. But they must not expect to find water there in any way, and what they might obtain by filtration by digging into the ground would be but a very meagre resource. For the rest, the anchorage in the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay] is good and secure everywhere from thirty to ten fathoms. The quality of the bottom, though very changeable, is none the less good, and the few madrepores that are sometimes met with there are too soft to damage the cables.
The regularity of the bottom throughout this bay is such that one can tell, very nearly, how far one is from the coast during the night. As a rule one has ten fathoms at a short league from the land, and that is where the anchorage is least good. But by keeping two leagues from the coast, in fourteen to fifteen fathoms, one is in complete safety there and the holding ground is firm. League by league, going out to sea, the depth increases gradually, and at ten leagues from the innermost part of the bay one finds 27 and 28 fathoms, very fine sand.
It is with regret that I leave a place which must be one of the most pleasant in the fine season, and in which, while busy with our geographical work, we collected by means of our dredge many objects of natural history, some of them entirely new to science. But as I am quite resolved to retrace my steps at some time or other to finish the exploration of this coast completely, I shall always be in a position to make the best use of it I can.
In my fair-copy journal will be found the various reports made to me by all those who have been ashore several times. There will perhaps be little agreement in the way each of them sees things in particular, but nevertheless all are in sufficient accord on the main points, such as the nature of the soil, its productions, its resources, its population and above all its constitution, about which there appears to be no doubt.
In the morning of the thirtieth, having decided, as I have said, to go back up to the north, I had the ship steered north-east by north, the wind being south-west, a strong breeze, such that I did not venture to set the mizzen topsail or shake out a reef of my topsails, in which all three had long been taken in. Nevertheless we were making good way, and the ship, with the little sail she carried, was still running her two leagues and two leagues and a half an hour.
We could get no hour angle in the morning, but at noon, the sun having shown itself, we observed the latitude of thirty-one degrees fifty-seven minutes south, which placed us, according to some of our charts, due east and west of Rottnest Island or the Swan River, which I left with great reluctance, though it was only put off to another time.
During the evening the breeze continued to blow hard, and the sea was so high and heavy that we had not seen it so high in all the passage we had made up to then. We sounded several times in the morning and the evening without finding bottom at fifty or at seventy fathoms.
After sunset the wind abated greatly, and at times we had small squalls with rain but without the violent wind of the previous days. At eight o'clock the storm staysail and the mizzen topsail were set, with all reefs in. The rest of the night passed without incident and the weather was fairly fine. Only the sea was constantly rough and strained us greatly. During the day the barometer rose again to 28 inches three lines, which led us to judge that the bad weather was drawing to its end.

At five o'clock the land appeared from east 11° north to north 45° east, at an estimated distance of 6 to 7 leagues, the sky overcast and looking very bad.
Particular remarks
Our landfall at the cape or point of Leeuwin's Land was made in the finest weather in the world, both by night and by day. The land and sea breezes seemed at first to follow a steady and regular course. In the morning we usually had them from the eastern quarter, varying to north, and in the afternoon they almost never failed to come to us from south-east towards south, and remained there for the greater part of the night. The breezes were then moderate and very pleasant. The sky was almost always fine and the night lit by the moon. The fine weather stayed with us right into the Baie du Géographe, where we still kept it for some days. But at the last quarter of the moon it changed entirely, and from the time when we were forced to leave that bay it was bad for longer than we had had it fine, and we had scarcely one fine day from the sixteenth of the month of Prairial to the first of Messidor, when I resolved to move north.
The currents, while we were on this coast, twice changed direction. From Point Leeuwin to the Cap des Mécontents they set us strongly to the south towards the west, and sometimes also towards the east. But from that cape northwards they seemed to us to run more usually to the north towards the west than in any other direction.
The tides on the coast and inside the coves are not very strong there, and at neap tides rise little above six feet, and at new and full moon above eight or nine. When they rise higher, it must be from some accidental cause or from the force of the winds from north to south by way of west
All the coast we have seen is free of reefs or dangers running out to sea, and those lying close in to the land are too visible not to be avoided. The whole seashore is nothing but an unbroken succession of sand dunes of greater or lesser height, some of which serve as good landmarks.
From Point Leeuwin to the Cap des Mécontents (word struck out with a cross), the coast, or the hillocks lying a little back from it, are not as well wooded as in the Baie du Géographe. Nowhere can one anchor there without running the risk of having one's cable at least badly damaged, if not cut, whereas inside the Cap du Géographe the anchorage is clean throughout the whole extent of the bay.
The variation of the compass needle was from (no figures) to (no figures) NW
During our stay in the Baie du Géographe we found few resources there. Fish was very scarce, but whales on the other hand very common. Nor did we see more than one or two sea turtles. The land does not appear to furnish much for the food of the natives, who seemed to me to draw it chiefly from the sea. Wherever we went inland, we came across no tree bearing edible fruit, nor any leguminous plant. The only refreshment we found there was wild celery and a kind of purslane, but the latter was not as good as the former.
Shells, and especially those of the scallop class, are not rare there. The timber appeared to be of poor quality and little suited to working. Several kinds yield a resin, of which we have several specimens and which could no doubt be turned to account. Nor was the quality of the soil judged suitable for regular cultivation.
1801-06-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to SW. At 8 the land was seen at the limit of sight. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At noon in 31° 59' 10" of latitude observed and in 111° 6' 30" of longitude by account. The variation in Geographe Bay was 5° 25', the mean of a great number of observations I made there, all of which agreed within 5 minutes. The Naturaliste, which during the gale in the gulf had doubled the north point, had shaped her course for Rottnest Island, the first place of rendezvous, and had anchored there on the morning of the 25th.

1801-06-20.journal_anonyme: The winds from E to SSE freshened. The corvette dragging fast, we veered 90 fathoms of cable. At 4 p.m. let go the starboard anchor, allowing it to take up the range of 30 fathoms that had been made. Squally weather, the wind in gusts.
1801-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Messidor, in the morning, although the sky was very cloudy and our horizon rather dark, we nevertheless had a pretty breeze from the south-west, varying to south-south-west. The mizzen topsail, which had been furled during the night, was trimmed once more and at eight o'clock, although the sea was still very high and running with a heavy swell, I had one of the three reefs let out of the topsails. I likewise shaped our course north by west, finding myself far enough to the west to have nothing to fear from the Abrolhos, which I meant to pass at a good offing.
During the morning the weather seemed about to set in entirely fair. We did indeed still have a few small squalls with rain and a little wind, but they were of short duration. The barometer, moreover, was rising considerably and already stood at 28 inches 5 lines. As it had never once deceived us up to that time, I had great confidence in it. I was surprised, however, to see the sea continually heavy and foul, which led me to believe that further south of our latitude the weather could not be very fine.
At noon we observed 30° 32' 28" of latitude, and the longitude shown by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 109° 52' 6" and for No. 35, 110° 7' 36". According to the dead reckoning of the distance run in the 24 hours, there was a difference to the (no direction) of (no figures) and one to the (no direction) of (no figures). This difference is perhaps the effect of the heavy sea rather than that of the currents or the tides.
In the afternoon the weather was fine and the horizon very clear. But for the heavy swell, which strained the ship and her masts exceedingly, we should have made tolerable way to the north by west, and perhaps during the night we should have reached the latitude of the Abrolhos, which our charts place very differently from one another. According to the one used on M. d'Entrecasteaux's voyage, the southernmost part of this danger lies in 29° 30' south latitude, and according to a Dutch chart which seems to have been drawn with some care it is fixed at 27° 58'. So that, not knowing well to which of the two charts to give the preference, one must keep a careful look-out and be continually on one's guard.
At sunset we took an amplitude at setting, which gave 5° 8 NW for the variation of the compass, but the motions of the vessel were so violent and so rapid that it must be regarded as very doubtful.
At the change of watch at eight o'clock, I gave orders that soundings should be taken every two hours and that at least 70 fathoms of line should be veered, so that we might become aware in good time of the Abrolhos Shoals, if indeed they should lie in our track, a thing I am far from believing, since if it blows no harder than it does at present, we shall hardly be, by noon tomorrow, in the latitude assigned to them by the chart that places them furthest south.
During the night of the first to the second, the sky, though very cloudy, was fair enough. We sounded at 10 o'clock, at midnight, at two o'clock and at four in the morning, but found no bottom with a hundred and ten fathoms straight up and down, which enabled us to continue on our course without altering it and without anxiety.
1801-06-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSW. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' W. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 52' 6" of longitude by No. 27. At 10 and at midnight sounded without finding bottom at 110 fathoms. Water was put on an allowance of 1 bottle a day.

1801-06-21.journal_anonyme: At 8 a.m. the corvette Naturaliste got under way, and at the same moment one of the dinghies was sent off to Rottnest Island. The dinghy sent off the day before to Rottnest came aboard at 10 a.m. She brought the news that the longboat had been cast ashore on the 29th at 8.30 a.m.; a dinghy was sent off at once with six days' provisions and the tools needed to repair her. The sky overcast, a swell running, the winds blowing at intervals from the ENE.
1801-06-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second of Messidor, in the morning, the sky was fair and clear enough. The winds shifted to the south, varying to south-south-east, a light breeze. We then let out a second reef in our topsails and set our mainsail and our staysails, although the sea was still very high and running with a heavy swell.
In the course of the morning, the sky, which had been fair and clear enough at sunrise, suddenly became overcast, and immediately afterwards we had a light, gentle rain and a great deal of mist. At eight o'clock I had given orders to steer north by east and we were making our way on that point of the compass, the breeze being then from south-east to east-south-east, rather light and dying away all the while.
At noon we had no observation for the latitude, and that by dead reckoning placed us only in 28° 58' south, that is to say still to the south of the Abrolhos Shoals according to the chart of the Dépôt, and precisely in the latitude of the southernmost part of this danger according to a Dutch chart which, as I have already remarked, seems to me to have been drawn with some care and in which, for that reason, I had some confidence. Besides, as our dead reckoning put us a good way to the west of this danger, I had no need to fear falling in with it while steering north by east.
In the afternoon the mist cleared away, but as a calm followed it, we made very little way until sunset, when the winds, having shifted to east-south-east, freshened a little. Our horizon, from the east round by the north to the north-west, became very clear and extended very far, so that everything promised us fine weather. The barometer, in the morning, notwithstanding the rain and the fog, had risen to 28 inches seven lines, which had very seldom happened since our departure, but in the afternoon it fell to 28. 5 and 28. 6, where it seemed inclined to settle.
At nightfall I gave orders to sound once more every two hours, and I shall continue to take this precaution until we have weathered the shoals I have just spoken of, because of the uncertainty as to their true position.
During the night of the second to the third, the weather was very fine and clear, with the winds from about east-south-east, a pretty breeze and even a little strong, since it obliged us to take a second reef in the mizzen topsail. We sounded several times in the night without finding bottom at 70 & 80 fathoms. We continued to steer north by east although at midnight I reckoned that I had passed the Abrolhos Shoals; the sea having become very smooth, we were no longer tormented, as we had been on the preceding days, by the motions of the vessel.
1801-06-21.journal_breton_geographe: Misty weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW, SSW, S, SE, ESE and E, with light rain. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude by account and corrected, and in 109° 30' of longitude by account. Variation 5° 1' NW. At 10 sounded without finding bottom at 70 fathoms.

1801-06-22.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from the east. Everything Citizen Milius, lieutenant, asked for to repair the longboat was sent to him.
1801-06-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the sky was not darkened by a single cloud. The winds were east-south-east, varying a little towards the east, but during the morning they were so light that we made little progress.
As soon as it was daylight I had the ship steered north-east by north, and at sunrise the land was sighted from the mastheads, which leads me to believe that we passed much closer to the Abrolhos Shoals than the dead reckoning of the course I had made indicated.
At ten o'clock we had a perfect view of the land from the deck. It presented itself to us in a very regular form, and we were even rather astonished to see so great a stretch of coast offer us no point that could be remarked in preference to another. Only, the coast seemed to us higher than any we had seen until then, and the mountains that give it its height much nearer to the sea shore than on the Leeuwin coast, where they really lie rather far inland.
At noon the latitude was observed as 27° 24' 16" south and the longitude by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 109° 48' 54" and for No. 35, 110° 4' 53".
Reckoning from the latitude observed on the first of Messidor, we found a difference to the south of 35 miles, caused no doubt by the currents, supposing the course estimated in the ordinary way to be correct.
In the afternoon it continued calm until two o'clock, but then a light breeze sprang up from the south which, afterwards shifting to south-south-east, increased as the sun sank towards the horizon. We took advantage of this breeze to close with the land, from which, a little before sunset, we were two and a half leagues, or three leagues at the most. We could then make out the whole coast perfectly, from east-south-east to north. But its aspect, far from being fine and pleasant like that of the Leeuwin coast, offered us on every side nothing but a fairly considerable elevation, on which not a tree was to be seen, but only a kind of grass or moss of a very dark and often blackish colour. Everywhere on the slope facing the sea could be made out a kind of gully, caused no doubt by the running off of rainwater. In several places the ground was bare, and we judged from its colour that it must be sand.
The sea shore likewise appeared to us cut sheer and so steep-to that there must be water, and plenty of it, right up to the land.
For the rest, I do not remember having seen any country that presented so disagreeable a prospect as this part of Eendracht Land. Seven or eight leagues of coast, which we had time to examine well before nightfall, have no other merit than that of being very clear of dangers and easy for navigation, although they offer no shelter, were it even for a longboat. What remains for us to see as far as Dampier's Shark Bay will perhaps be more interesting. But it is only too likely that this whole coast is alike, and the Leeuwin's Land part is infinitely better, although its soil is sand, as is the case with this one.
After sunset and at nightfall I shaped my course so as to range along the coast at a distance of three or four leagues. The winds were still south-south-east, a pretty breeze, and the sea smooth. We steered successively north, north by west, north-north-west, north-west by north and finally north-west. At seven o'clock we sounded and found no bottom at fifty fathoms. As this coast seems to be of no interest for navigation, and still less for natural history, I thought I ought not to stop there, the more so since the survey the Dutch made of it seemed to me
quite well done. I have merely taken views of the coast which will give an idea of what it may be like.
At eight o'clock I gave orders to keep on the north-west course until midnight, and said that I would continue it until daylight if, before that time, a line of fifty fathoms brought up no bottom.
During the night of the third to the fourth, we had no bottom at fifty fathoms up to that time, but from nine o'clock until eleven we found it, fine sand, at 55 and 53 fathoms, and at one o'clock after midnight we had it at seventy-five, rocky bottom. During the rest of the night they forgot to sound, and from the reason the officer gave me for it, it appears that it was my fault for not not (sic) having told him that it had to be done every hour, as had been the practice until then whenever we were in the neighbourhood of the coast or did not wish to go too far from it.
It is well to say, however, that having kept the watch myself until midnight, I said to the officer who relieved me: "You are in fifty-two fathoms of water; you will continue on the same course, and at one o'clock, when you sound, if the depth increases you will come up a point to windward, and if on the contrary it decreases, you will bear away a point." It seems to me that this order did not mean that he was to sound only at one o'clock, which was contrary to our usual practice, established long since.
For the rest, the night passed without incident; the weather was fine and the winds south-south-east, a pretty breeze and a smooth sea.

1801-06-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to south. At 7 the land was sighted; it stretched from N 45° E to east. The course was given N 33° 45' E. The sea was covered with weed. At noon in 27° 23' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 48' 54" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 27' 20" NW. The land from N 19° E to S 80° E. At 4 it stretched from N 11° E to S 34° E. We bore up N 45° W to run along the coast, which lies roughly NNW and SSE. It does not offer the same appearance as the Leeuwin land: it is very high and sheer. Not a tree is to be made out. At 9.30 shaped the course N 67° 30' W and carried little sail. At 9 the lead gave 55 fathoms and at 11, 52 fathoms, sandy bottom.

1801-06-23.journal_anonyme: At two in the afternoon the hand mill was set up aft on the port side. At 4 p.m. the large boat was back from her expedition; Citizen Heirisson brought a bottle of fresh water which he had got in the upper part of the Swan River. At 11 p.m. we put the repaired longboat in the water. The wind a fresh breeze from the east.
1801-06-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, at daybreak, we did not sight the land, because we had continued until that time to run NW ¼ W, the ship going 7 to 8 knots. At four o'clock in the morning, however, having asked the helmsman how much water had been found at that sounding, it was he who informed me that the lead had not been cast since one o'clock. I then set the course NW ¼ N, and at daylight we hauled close to the wind, with all sail set.
When I came on deck I asked the officer, who was very far from being at his post, why he had not informed me that the land was not in sight. His answer was that he had received no order to do so. It was, moreover, given with such ill grace that I turned my back on him and went to tell the boatswain to have the topgallant sails rigged. When they were in place, the topmen asked several times whether they should be let fall; I told them yes. Thereupon the officer of the watch, Citizen Picquet, for I must needs name him, told me that since I was giving the orders myself he would leave the watch. "You are quite at liberty to do so," I replied, "and even for the whole voyage if it pleases you." He withdrew and I kept his watch in his stead.
At ten o'clock the look-outs sighted the land, and shortly afterwards we saw it ourselves from the deck. We continued to stand in towards it, and at noon we were still about three leagues from it. From the latitude observed at the same time, we recognized that it was the southern point of Dirk Hartog Island. It then bore SE ¼ E from us. And we had observed 26° 1' 15" south latitude; the longitude by the timekeepers, for the same moment, was 109° 2' 48" for No. 27 and 109° 18' 29" for No. 35. The dead reckoning of the distance run in the twenty-four hours gave a difference of 17 minutes to the south.
In the evening we ranged, at a league's distance, along the western coast of Dirk Hartog Island, which in its whole extent offered us nothing but an arid, disagreeable and dismal aspect, worse indeed than the part of Eendracht Land we had seen the day before. The sea broke with great force all along the coast, and we often saw it rise to the height of the cliffs, which are cut sheer and straight as a wall, without any slope perceptible to the eye. The lead was cast from time to time, but we never had bottom at 25 fathoms. It is true that the vessel was making a good deal of way, or at least appeared to be by the log. But the time we took to pass from one point to another and the frequent tide-rips we met with made us only too well aware that the current was extremely strong in that quarter and that it set to the south-south-west.
All the vegetation we perceived on the island came down to some sort of heath and a grass of a very dark colour. Even this variety appeared rather seldom. The coast was made up of horizontal layers of sand and no doubt of granite, which we shall be better able to verify when we are in Dampier's Shark Bay.
At sunset we were abreast of the north-west point of this island. The land makes an elbow to the north-east and then seems to extend to the north, just as my Dutch chart represents it very well. Shortly afterwards we sighted the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], which we approached as closely as we could with what daylight still remained to us.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth the weather was very fine and a pretty breeze blew from south-south-east. According to the bearings taken at sunset and at four seven o'clock in the evening, I shaped my course to the north, sounding every hour. At ten o'clock, the depth having decreased by six fathoms, I had her kept away north-north-west, and at one o'clock, the depth having increased by five fathoms, I resumed the course to the north until two o'clock, when I decided to stand off on a short board to the south-west, and at four o'clock, until daylight, on another to the east-north-east. As at two leagues, or three leagues at the most, from the îles Stériles we had fairly steadily found 52 fathoms
of water, it seemed to me quite simple to keep on that same depth while steering north, convinced that at daylight the next day I should find myself within sight of them and roughly at the part that forms the entrance of the bay. What we see tomorrow morning will show whether this reasoning is sound, and whether the currents, against which I have so far been unable to guard myself, will still keep working against us, contrary to our expectation.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth the weather was fine; the atmosphere, however, was laden with damp vapours, although there were few clouds, and these at times described a ring round the moon which was not at all pleasant to see.

At noon the same land extended from NE to SE, five leagues' estimated distance. It was the last of the îles Stériles, or the one that forms the entrance of Shark Bay.
Nota: on the morning of the 4th, Citizen Picquet, who had withdrawn from his watch in the morning, came to find me in my cabin, where he set forth how much he had been offended that I had had various manoeuvres carried out without informing him, and asked my permission to resume his duty. I took this opportunity to inform him that any officer who left his watch showed very ill grace, and that besides I found him little fitted for a voyage such as the one I was making. This officer, full of self-conceit, believes himself, moreover, far better informed than he really is, at least in practice. Although it was not my intention that he should resume his duty on board, I nevertheless consented to his request, and I hope that no other occasion will arise to deprive him of every kind of command on board.
Eendracht Land, Bearings
