1801-06-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to south. At 1 shaped the course N 56° 15' W; at 5 shaped the course N 33° 45' W and crowded sail. At 7 the commander gave orders directly to the helmsman to steer N 22° 30' E, and had the yards trimmed, taking no notice of Citizen Piquet, the officer of the watch, who observed to him that he was useless on deck and that he would leave the watch if the commander wished; and on his orders he left it. At 9 the land was sighted; at noon it bore from us N 11° E to S 56° E. At noon in 26° 1' 35" of latitude observed and in 109° 2' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 20' NW. Bore up north and ran along the west coast of Dirk Hartog Island. We passed through tide rips whose direction was north and south and whose strength may have been 3 to 4 knots, for despite our apparent speed of 6 to 7 knots we doubled the land only very slowly. At 4 bore up N 22° 30' E, at 5 N 33° 45' E. At 5.15 took the bearing of the west point of Dirk Hartog S 22° 30' W and the north point S 78° E; the southernmost of the Dorre islands from N 30° E to N 40° E. At 6 set topsails, heading N 11° 15' E. At 7, Dorre Island from N 50° E to N 8° [E]. Bore up north and N 22° 30' W to draw off from it.

1801-06-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from ENE to NE and NNE. The longboat was put on her chocks. The large boat was sent off to help Citizen Saint-Cricq, to go to the island lying south of the anchorage.
1801-06-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, in the morning, we did indeed sight the land to the south-east 5° east, but it could be seen only from the mastheads. The winds were then south-east, a pretty breeze, and we were close-hauled with her head east-north-east, which ought to have brought us up with it promptly; but although we had all sail set and the vessel was making, by the log, four and three knots, we could never get close enough to see it from the deck, so strongly did the current prevent us from making headway.
During the morning the breeze fell away considerably and at noon the ship would scarcely answer her helm. At that time we observed the latitude, which was 24° 18' 33", placing us off the north point of the outermost of the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], and consequently at the mouth of Shark Bay, which I wished to enter. What little wind there was then shifted to the north-east, and we at once brought our tacks to larboard.
During the evening the calm continued and we made very little progress. At five o'clock, however, the land began to be visible from the deck, bearing from east-north-east to east. I continued until eight o'clock close-hauled on the larboard tack, the winds varying from east to south-east, very light. At eight o'clock we went on the northern board, making very little way because of the calm that then prevailed. The bottom was 40 fathoms, fine grey sand.
During the night I gave orders to sound every hour, according to custom, and as I had spent the previous night on deck, the officer of the watch was ordered to warn me if the depth began to decrease, my intention being to let go a kedge anchor should it fall calm while we were in no more than thirty or thirty-five fathoms.
From eight o'clock until midnight the weather was fair enough and the moon lit up the horizon very pleasantly. But at that time it clouded over, and until morning the moon was continually surrounded by a halo which made its appearance disagreeable and seemed to foretell a change in the weather and even in the winds, which I feared to see shift to the north-west, because the sea, although still smooth, was heaved up by a considerable swell which came to us from that quarter of the horizon, extremely laden with dark, thick clouds.
At two o'clock, having perceived the land to the east-north-east, I had her head put to the north. We were then in 40 fathoms, very fine grey sand. The winds being variable from east-south-east to east-north-east and very light, sail was likewise shortened so as not to work up to the north, in order to keep at the entrance of the bay, where I intended to come to anchor.

1801-06-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from south to NE. At 2 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 4 went onto the starboard tack and crowded sail to close the land. At 8 the northernmost Dorre island S 50° E. At noon in 24° 18' of latitude observed and in 109° 3' 26" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 23' NW. At noon went onto the port tack; at 5 the land from N 68° E to N 85° E; at 8 went onto the starboard tack. Saw very large sharks.

1801-06-25.journal_anonyme: At 2 p.m. the dinghy was back; she was sent off again under the orders of the second petty officers. A strong breeze from NE to NNE.
1801-06-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth of Messidor, at break of day, we stood close-hauled on the north-east board as far as the winds would allow, to close with the coast and come and reconnoitre it. By my reckoning, and after allowing for the distance the currents might have carried us during the calm of the day before, I placed myself off the northern extremity of the last of the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], and consequently at the mouth of Shark Bay, which I expected to enter the same day. But the weather had so foul an appearance that I retained little hope of reaching it.
The whole horizon, from south-west to north-west, was so dark and so laden with great black, thick clouds that I had never yet seen a sky of such ugly appearance. The sun was likewise obscured by many clouds heaped one upon another, which made the atmosphere very disagreeable to look upon. The barometer, however, which I consulted often, was falling slowly and seemed to be holding at 28 inches 2 lines, from 28. 3 and 5, which had been its height the day before. As it had never yet deceived us, I liked to believe that the weather would presently set in fair and that the easterly winds would soon drive away the masses of cloud, which did not fail to cause me some uneasiness.
In spite of the foul appearance of the weather, I resolved to close with the land, and for that purpose I went about at nine o'clock, carrying all sail.
At a quarter to ten the breeze at first increased a little, and then the weather turned squally with strong gusts and rain, so that it seemed to me that the bad weather had set in and was about to break, although the winds were still in the quarter from north-east to north-east by east. In consequence of this fear, which seemed to me only too well founded, I wore round again and stood out to sea, so as to weather it more easily should it come on.
After changing tack, the wind and the gusts still increasing, I had the mainsail furled and all the reefs taken in the topsails.
At eleven o'clock the rain, the wind and the gusts ceased. The sky, without being any clearer, nevertheless had a better appearance, and I flattered myself that a fine sky would soon replace the one we had had in the morning.
At one o'clock we stood in again towards the land and kept on that board until five o'clock in the evening, when we had to stand out to sea once more. The wind was then very uncertain, and the sea, although it was almost calm for us, was driven by two very heavy swells, one coming from the north-west and the other from the north-east. The sky again became covered with clouds and mist. Although we were fairly close to the land when we went about, the bearings that were taken were very unsatisfactory, and we were all the less certain of our position because we had been unable to observe the sun at noon, and so to learn whether the currents had carried us in the direction they had had until then.
Towards six o'clock we perceived two great columns of smoke on shore, and at nightfall we saw quite clearly the fires that caused them. As the îles Stériles are not inhabited, it seemed to me that these fires were a little to the north of the point of the mainland which forms the entrance of the bay and which then bore east 18° south of us.
During the night the winds were almost calm and the sky cloudy and dark. We made little way, sounding every half hour in order to learn whether the currents were setting us towards the land or whether we were going off to sea, as the course we were making ought to have carried us, and the current too, for at that time, according to my earlier observations, it should have been ebb. Besides, whether the tides were carrying us towards the land or out to sea, we were far enough from the coast to have nothing to fear from the effect they might have.

1801-06-25.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to NE. At 2 a.m., having sighted the land in the N 68° E, headed north under topsails. At daybreak it stretched from S 45° E to S 79° E. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under all sail. At 9 went onto the port tack; the wind freshened. At 10, the wind a strong breeze, lay to on the starboard tack under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon the land S 67° 30' E, being in 23° 56' 40" of latitude by account and in 109° 15' 32" of longitude by account. At 1 lay to on the port tack. At 4.30 the land in sight from S 45° E to S 68° E, about 24 miles off. A very thick column of smoke in the S 72° E. At 5.30 filled and stood on on the starboard tack under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail.

1801-06-26.journal_anonyme: At 3.30 p.m. the large boat was back from her mission. At 10 a.m. fired three swivel guns and hoisted a flag at the masthead to recall the dinghy, which was ashore. A light breeze from W.
1801-06-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, in the morning, the weather set in fair although the sky remained overcast. The great clouds heaped one upon another that we had had the day before had disappeared, and we had hopes of being able to observe the meridian altitude at noon. The heavy sea from the NW had likewise gone down, so that we stood in towards the land to close with it and reconnoitre it properly. Accordingly we let the reefs out of our topsails and set all sail.
At sunrise we had sighted the coast, which extended, relative to our position, from north-east to east-south-east.
At noon the latitude was observed as 23° 50' 45", which, as I suspected, put me to the north of the entrance of the bay. As we were unable to take an hour angle either in the morning or in the evening, the sun having appeared only around noon, we could not fix the longitude of the cape or point towards which we were then steering. At four o'clock, however, an hour angle was taken which, though somewhat doubtful, then placed us in 109° 23' 32" by No. 27 and 109° 38' 30" by No. 35.
In the afternoon we continued to stand in towards the land, with all sail set, the weather being very fine and the sea calm. We coasted fairly close along a great stretch of the coast to the north of the entrance of the bay, and we could make out perfectly a long chain of reefs which, although lying right against the shore, offers no landing place for a longboat. The view I give of this coast will show how arid and disagreeable to the eye it is.
At sunset the wind fell away considerably, and so as not to be carried out to sea by the current or set too far in, I resolved to anchor as soon as I had a good bottom of thirty to thirty-five fathoms, which kept me under sail until a quarter to eight, when, having then thirty-four fathoms at a league and a half from the land at the most, I let go a bower anchor, intending to remain in the position I then had until daylight the next morning. Eighty fathoms of cable were veered and I believed myself quite safe.
At half past nine, however, we were obliged to weigh our anchor, the vessel, in spite of the little wind there was, dragging continually to the north-west. As I could not persuade myself that the anchor had been badly let go, it seemed quite natural to me to believe that the bottom was hard and that it had been unable to take hold; but when it was up we found that the cable had taken a turn round the stock of the anchor, and we recognized the cause that had made us drag. It is rather difficult to conceive how this turn was made in anchoring, for according to the
boatswain's report the anchor and the cable were quite clear. It seems to me, however, that there must have been too much of the latter at the hawse-hole, and the anchor, in falling, must surely have fouled itself in the slack of the cable.
During the night of the seventh to the eighth the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate. We spent it beating to windward, tack upon tack, so that at daylight we found ourselves in much the same place where we had anchored the day before.

Nota: the northern entrance of Shark Bay is very easy to recognize. The lands that form the opening of the bay on that side are high and steep. The Dutch plan gives a very exact and very well made view of it. Of all the charts we have, it is the most exact and the best made. It appears that the Dutch took great pains in surveying the whole of this coast, on which they may well have designs for the whale fishery, which is the only resource it can offer.
These creatures are there in such great numbers that one is often troubled by them, and the boats sometimes run some risk, so close do they come to them.
On the other hand, when one is beating about in the bay, they cause continual uneasiness by the enormous masses of water they throw up, which look like reefs on which the sea is breaking furiously.
Eendracht Land, Bearings.
On the sixth at sunrise, the land extended from E ¼ SE to south-east.
At noon the same land bore E.SE, three leagues distant.
At four o'clock in the evening the land of the continent appeared east 22° south
A very thick smoke was seen east 18° south.
1801-06-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to SE. At daybreak the land was sighted from the topgallant crosstrees; crowded sail to close it. At 9 went onto the port tack. At noon in 23° 47' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 30" of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 80° E and the southernmost S 12° E. We ran along the land to the north of the bay. At 5 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight N 40° E; a large cape, the nearest, forming the entrance to Shark Bay, S 57° E; the land in sight as far as south. At 7.45 anchored abreast of a cove in 34 fathoms, sandy bottom, the large cape bearing N 33° 45' E and the entrance of the cove from N 55° E to S 45° E. At 10 got under way, because we were dragging and the current was setting us onto the coast; our anchor had fouled its stock. Shaped our course N 11° 15' W, running along the coast at a short distance.

1801-06-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from W to WSW. The dinghy came aboard at 3 p.m. and brought back a sea snake. At 7.30 on the 8th the captain embarked in the large boat. The winds from the south drew round to the east.
1801-06-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, in the morning, we crowded sail to run into the bay. The weather was very fine and the sea easy. We ranged at a very small distance along the whole coast, which is high in that part, so as to keep well to windward of the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], which I expected to see from one moment to the next. From eight o'clock until noon it blew a fresh breeze from the eastward, and we were obliged to shorten sail in order to sound more at our ease.
Towards eleven o'clock the lands to the north were already far from us, and nothing could be seen of them any longer but the summits of the highest hillocks, which looked like a chain of islands. It is no doubt the appearance this whole coast presents that has led many navigators, who did not approach it closely enough, to believe that there were many islands lying off the mainland. But it is none the less true that from Cape Leeuwin to the north of Dirk Hartog Island there are none except Rottnest Island and the islets that neighbour it. And all the land that lies between the former and Dirk Hartog Island is a continent which may be ranged very close along its whole extent.
After Dirk Hartog Island come the îles Stériles, of which it no doubt forms part itself, for its only advantage over those lying to the north of it is that it is a little higher. But the eye rests with no more pleasure on the one than on the others.
At noon we observed the latitude of 24° 38' 1", and the longitude was found, by good observations, to be 109° 23' 32" for No. 25 (sic) and 109° 38' 30" for No. 25 (sic)
At the same moment the southernmost point of the îles Stériles bore south 51° west of us, the northernmost land of the mainland north 25° east, and the easternmost land in sight south 7° east.
At one o'clock the breeze began to die away, and at two we came to anchor in 16 fathoms of water, bottom of black, muddy sand. 70 fathoms of cable were veered.
As soon as we were at anchor, I sent a boat ashore on the first of the îles Stériles to reconnoitre the coast and see whether landing was easy there. Citizen Riedelé embarked in her, and they steered he steered their course for a sandy cove that lay abeam of us.
During the evening the weather continued fine and it was almost a flat calm, so that the vessel could never swing head to wind, the current being stronger and running at a speed of one mile by the log. It set to the north-west on the ebb.
When the boat had gone, I sent to sound at one and two cables' lengths around the vessel. Astern 19 fathoms were found, on the larboard side 18, on the starboard side 17 and ahead 17 fathoms, black, muddy sand, such as we had had in 20 fathoms.
The rest of the evening passed without incident. I merely informed the gentlemen naturalists that if the report made on the boat's return were favourable, I should go ashore the next day, and that those who wished to accompany me might make their preparations beforehand.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth the winds were almost calm and variable from east to north-west. We continually heard the blowing of the whales, and by the fine moonlight we could easily make out the places where they were disporting themselves.
At ten minutes past eight it was slack water, and shortly afterwards the flood began.
Towards two o'clock in the night the large boat returned on board, but as I had not rested for a long time and had retired to my cabin, I was not told of her return.
Bearings of the anchorage.
The southernmost land of the îles Stériles in sight west 43° south.
The northernmost point of the first of the îles Stériles west 16° north
The northernmost point of the mainland in sight north 56° east.
1801-06-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SSE. At midnight steered north, running along the coast. At 4 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack; the large cape then bore from us N 45° E, 9 miles off. At 8 bore away south, S 11° 15' W and S 22° 30' W to enter Shark Bay. At 7 the large cape bore from us N 65° E. At 10 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the south. At noon in 24° 38' of latitude observed and in 109° 23' of longitude by No. 27. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island S 51° W, and the mainland from N 25° E to S 7° E. At 2.30 anchored in Shark Bay in 16 fathoms, muddy sand, the northern Dorre island bearing from N 74° W to S 47° W and the northernmost mainland N 56° E. The large boat, under the orders of Bonnefoi, was sent off to Dorre Island. At 4 the current ran 1 knot, the ebb making, its direction NW. At 8 a fire was seen on Dorre Island, lit by our boat's crew. At 8.15 the tide turned, the flood beginning. During the night a light was kept at the gaff.

1801-06-28.journal_anonyme: We made ready to get under way. On the 9th at 7 a.m. we got under way with the winds NE, a fresh breeze. At noon we sounded in 26 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. The weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky without cloud.
1801-06-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Stay at anchor in Dampier's Shark Bay.
On the ninth, in the morning, Citizen Bonnefoy, to whom I had given the command of my boat to go and reconnoitre the coast, having told me that he had landed with great ease in two convenient coves, I at once had the large and small boats manned, and all the naturalists embarked in them. The gardener, who had accompanied Bonnefoy the day before, had brought back two bundles of various plants which he had gathered by moonlight and which had all seemed new to him. So that, although he had spent the greater part of the night, he wanted to go back again.
At eight o'clock the two boats shoved off; I embarked in one and the other was entrusted to Citizen Picquet. We took with us a seine and everything needful for fishing and shooting. And we set out so convinced that we should catch a great quantity of fish that we neglected every kind of provision except biscuit and water.
When we set out the sky was fair and the wind calm. We took two hours to reach the shore, because all the boats' oarsmen, who had not been picked, did not know how to row.
Towards eleven o'clock the sky clouded over, without, for all that, having a bad appearance. I was all the more vexed at it because it would prevent me from observing the latitude on shore and taking hour angles there. But the others were glad of it, since this weather seemed to them better suited to the fishing, the shooting and the excursions each of them meant to make.
Our first care, when the large boat had been emptied, was to put her on her grapnel in a safe place, and the small one was made ready for running out the seine.
The first two hauls we made were not lucky, for we caught nothing at all. We then began to regret not having brought something to go with our biscuit, but it was too late.
The gardener and the other naturalists went inland on the island to examine its productions. Maugé and I went after the birds, and everyone was ordered to be back on the shore by five o'clock at the latest, to dine there and then return on board.
Our various excursions into the interior of the island yielded us twelve or fifteen species of new plants, two very fine lizards and seven birds, two of which are particularly remarkable for the beauty of their plumage. We also saw a few kangaroos. I even fired at one, but in all likelihood I did no more than frighten it, for after receiving the shot it made off as briskly as ever.
The ground forming the island we were on is of sand, mixed here and there with a few tables of rock of a fairly hard grain. Most of the shrubs growing on this barren land were in flower or about to flower. The tallest we met with in all our excursions were no more than ten feet high. One only, on the top of the hillock, might have been from fifteen to eighteen, but nature, to punish it for having grown so high, had condemned it to death, for we found it in that state. The thickest trunk of all the shrubs we met with might have been from seven to eight inches in diameter. But such a size is seldom seen there.
Chance had brought us to land at the place on the island where the vegetation was most vigorous, for those who crossed it from north to south were rather sorry to have taken that trouble, since everywhere they met with nothing but arid sands and many tables of rock on which there was not even any moss. What had led them to undertake this excursion was that they believed they had recognized many tracks of a fairly large cloven-footed animal, which they hoped to see by covering a great deal of ground; but they met with nothing, and only saw a few black snakes, some of them quite large.
Back on the shore, we saw with pleasure that the boats' crews had
caught about a hundred fish, among which there were some very pretty ones for the variety of their colours. But in general they were all of a small kind, coming very close to the sardine, and that was indeed the name we gave them. The largest closely resembled the European whiting in shape and taste. We thought we observed, however, that this one had a longer head.
When the share-out had been made, we cooked our portion for dinner and everything was found very good. As there was little of it, I confined myself to eating oysters and crabs, of which a good supply had been gathered.
At low tide we found on the reefs that border the beach in various places some very fine turban shells, a few ordinary ears (?) and a fine crown of Ethiopia with its animal, which no doubt is not as in Europe and of which I give a drawing. We also gathered some rather fine mussels and several other ordinary shells, and above all limpets, on which the sailors made a good feast.
At five o'clock everyone was back except Citizen Péron who, having no doubt given way to his ardour, had gone too far to be back at the appointed hour. While waiting for him we sat down to dinner, and we dined without him, for he did not come back.
At six o'clock, the men I had sent to meet him having returned without catching sight of him, I went back on board in the large boat and left Citizen Picquet ashore with the small one to wait for him, ordering him to return on board as soon as the moon had risen, the sky not looking too promising.
At half past nine we arrived on board in very calm and very dark weather, and as two great fires could be made out on shore, one in particular very high up on the dunes, we concluded from them that Citizen Péron had not yet come back and that he had in all likelihood lost his way on the island, which, so I was told, he had intended to cross.
On my return on board I was informed that during the day more than six hundred pounds of good fish had been caught with the line, besides two or three dogfish, which everyone found very good eating. This news gave me all the more pleasure because it made me forget my regret at not having caught fish for everyone with the seine.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth the sky cleared again, and towards two o'clock we had the winds from the south-east, a strong breeze, which was not favourable to the return of the boat, which had no water and very few other provisions.
Bearings of the anchorage.
The southernmost land of the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands] in sight south 47° west
The northernmost point of the first of these two islands west 16° north
The northernmost land of the mainland in sight north 56° east
1801-06-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SSE. At midnight Bonnefoi came back with the large boat. At 7.30 a.m. the commander and all the naturalists went to Dorre Island in the two boats. Saw a great number of whales; fish were taken in abundance and some were salted. At nightfall our people lit a fire ashore; we showed a light at each masthead and burnt flares every half hour. At 9.30 the commander and the naturalists arrived in the large boat. The small one had stayed ashore under the orders of Citizen Piquet, to wait for the zoologist Péron, who had not appeared at the hour fixed for departure.

1801-06-29.journal_anonyme: The weather hazy and squally, with lightning in the west. At 2 p.m. the lead brought up 27 fathoms, grey sand, coral and gravel. The wind ESE, variable to SE. At 11.30 a current was observed setting from NNW to SSE.
1801-06-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, in the morning, it blew a strong breeze from south-south-east, and at sunrise the boat was still not seen coming back, a proof that Citizen Péron had not rejoined during the night and that he had spent it somewhere on the island without knowing where he was.
At last, by dint of looking, the boat was made out towards ten o'clock under sail, beating back towards the ship, where she arrived with some difficulty at one o'clock in the afternoon. Fortunately Citizen Péron was in her. After coming on board he presented himself to me in the most pitiful state, having eaten nothing for twenty-four hours and being worn out with fatigue, having wandered almost the whole night, until, falling with weariness, he fell sound asleep at the foot of a bush, until daylight, when, having got his bearings, he came back to the shore, where he found the men who were searching for him.
As he is to make me a report of his adventure, I shall confine what I might say of it to this, but I have fully promised him that when he goes ashore again I shall have him accompanied by someone who, never losing sight of him, will answer to me for his being back at the place of departure by the hour that will be appointed.
As it was too late to get under sail, we spent the rest of the day and the whole night, which was fine, at anchor. The winds almost calm.
1801-06-29.journal_breton_geographe: Latitude observed at the anchorage 24° 46' 20"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 20' 40". Variation, the mean of 7 observations at the anchorage, 6° 1' 7" NW. The tides set NW and SE, and the sea rises 7½ feet. At half past noon the small boat arrived, bringing back Citizen Péron, who, having gone too far into the island, had lost himself there and passed the night in the scrub; at daybreak he had found our people. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S and SSE.

1801-06-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSE, variable to ENE and N. At eight in the evening the lead brought up 24 fathoms, sand and rock [several words illegible] every half hour. At midnight we hove to with the port side to the wind. At 7.45 went about onto the starboard tack. Bearings taken at noon: the northernmost peak NE by N; the one to the NE, NE 1° N; the southernmost NE 1° E.
1801-06-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, at sunrise, we got under sail to go and examine the mainland coast to the east of the anchorage we were leaving. The winds were then south-south-east and very light, variable to south-east. We stood on close-hauled on the starboard tack with every sail set, sounding continually. In the course of the morning we had from sixteen fathoms, sandy bottom, down to thirteen, the same bottom.
All the morning we saw a great number of whales all around us, which afforded much amusement on board. They are so little wild in these waters that they came always right up to the ships, and it would have been easy for us to shoot them with a musket if a ball could have killed them.
At noon the observed latitude was 24° 40' 5", and the longitude given by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 109° 21' 23" and for No. 35, 109° 31' 47". The northernmost land in sight then bore north 5° east, and the easternmost, also in sight, east 5° north. We then had thirteen fathoms of water, bottom of grey sand. But perceiving very white water ahead of us at about a league, I had a boat hoisted out, which I sent to sound ahead of the ship, with orders to stop when it was over good anchorage in between nine and ten fathoms. I gave the command of it to Citizen Bonnefoy, who carried out this task with great intelligence.
At one o'clock, being in a flat calm and with the ebb beginning, I had the anchor let go in ten fathoms, bottom of grey sand, and recalled the boat on board.
As soon as we were at anchor and our sails furled, I sent it off again with Citizen Bougainville to examine the coast and look for a place fit for landing, so that it might be sent to be explored. I very earnestly enjoined M. Bougainville not to venture in at night, and to return on board without going ashore if he had not time to find, before sunset, a place fit for landing.
At two o'clock the boat shoved off, and MM. Depuche and Riedelé Bernier, having wished to go in her, accompanied Citizen Bougainville.
During the night of the eleventh to the twelfth the weather was very fine and the winds south-east, variable towards south, almost calm. At one o'clock in the morning my boat returned, and the officer commanding her reported to me that he had reached the land in four fathoms of water and had been unable to get any closer, because everywhere he had found the coast fringed with a reef on which the sea broke with a great roar, although it was calm. This reef, according to Citizen Bougainville and those who went with him, runs out nearly a league to sea, and it would be useless to try to land there, at least at the place where they approached it and along the league and a half of coast that he ran along before nightfall and his return on board.
Bearings of the land at our second anchorage in Shark Bay.
The northernmost land in sight of the first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], west 11° 15' north.
The easternmost land of the mainland in sight, east 22° 30' south.
The view I give of the mainland coast renders as faithfully as could be the appearance the coast then presented to us, and the prospect is not a pleasant one.
Soundings from the first to the second anchorage.
Having started from 16 fathoms, bottom of sand and mud, the depth kept decreasing gradually down to 10 fathoms, the same bottom. At eleven o'clock I sent off the small boat to sound ahead of the ship at about a league's distance from the place where we anchored; as she signalled only eight fathoms, I stopped, the winds being almost calm and the ebb against us.
Bearings at the anchorage. Shark Bay
The northernmost land of the first Île Stérile, west 15°15' north
The easternmost (land) of the mainland in sight, east 22°30' south
The land of the mainland in sight in the northern quarter, from east to north-east by east
1801-06-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SW. At 7.30 got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, N 67° 30' E, east and S 67° 30' E, the small boat sounding ahead. Saw a turtle. At noon in 24° 44' 4" of latitude observed and in 109° 26' 8" of longitude by No. 27. At 1 anchored in 9 fathoms, fine sand, the north point of the northern Dorre island bearing N 79° W, the mainland S 67° 30' E about 12 miles off. At 2.15 the small boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Bougainville to survey the mainland. During the night a light was kept and a flare burnt every half hour to mark our position for the boat. Variation 5° 22' at the anchorage. At midnight she was back; it had been impossible for Citizen Bougainville to land because of the bar, which broke with force all along the coast and two cables from the shore.

1801-07-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds varying from N to NNW and W. At noon and at four o'clock went about. At 5 p.m. sounded every half hour in 27, 24, 23, 23, 24 and 25 fathoms, rock and coral bottom. We had a great deal of rain during the night. At 4 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Noon bearings: the end of the great southern cliff E 25° 15' S; the north end of the next great cliff E 7° 15' S, estimated distance 11 miles.
1801-07-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the twelfth, being informed by the reports of the day before that there was no possibility of landing at the place where I had anchored the previous day, I weighed at daybreak to go and examine the island that lies in the middle of the bay, which I flattered myself I should sight in the course of the morning if the wind kept blowing as it did at the moment we got under sail. But towards ten o'clock the breeze, which was then easterly, variable to east-south-east, began to die away, and at noon the ship was moved only by the current, which at that time was still in our favour.
All the morning we had the spectacle of several whales sporting on the water, and although it was no longer new to us, everyone still watched it with as much pleasure as if it had been the first time.
At noon we observed the latitude of 25° 0' 21", and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us at the same time in 109° 29' 50" by No. 27 and in 109° 43' 54" by No. 35.
From several sets of distances of the sun from the moon taken during the morning, the mean gave 109° 25' 43", so that our timekeepers seemed to differ by only 11' 9" to the west, which calls for a longer series of observations to confirm it.
In the afternoon, although we were in a flat calm, we remained under sail until four o'clock in the hope that the sea breeze might come to us. But the ebb being then against us, and the ship drifting a good deal to the north-east, we furled our sails and anchored in 13 fathoms, a fine bottom of grey sand.
At sunset we sighted part of the second of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], which then bore west 5° north. At the limit of sight we also saw a continuation of the same island bearing south-west. It is by mistake, or for want of knowing the place, that the officer then on watch marked in his sunset bearing, or that of half past four, when we anchored, an islet, for there is none in that quarter.
During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth the wind was calm until about ten in the evening, when a light air came to us from the south-east and lasted for the rest of the night, during which the weather was very fine.
Soundings while we were under sail.
Weighing in 10 fathoms of water, we decreased increased our depth until noon, when we were in 13 fathoms, sand and weed in long, narrow leaves.
From noon to the moment we anchored we kept the depth of 13 fathoms, in which we let go a bower anchor.
Note: while we were under sail in the calm, the dredge was cast several times and brought up, in objects of natural history, several fine starfish of a new species, a great many of the shells called strombs, and a few scallops which were nothing very brilliant in their colours and which are nevertheless thought to be a new species.
Soundings & nature of the bottom during the 24 hours.
During the evening, 11 ½ fathoms, white sand mixed with broken shells.
Bearings of the land
At noon the mainland stretched away from us from north 70° east to south 45° east.
Undated, a log table, meteorology filled in between 1 and 4 o'clock
(according to the dated entry of the next table, this is the beginning of the log table for 12 to 13 Messidor).
1801-07-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from NE to SE. At 6 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course S 11° 15' E, south, S 11° 15' W and S 67° 30' W, the lead giving from 10 to 13 fathoms, grey sand. At noon in 25° 0' of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 35" of longitude by No. 27. The mainland in sight N 70° E. At 4.15 we anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand, the southern Dorre island bearing from S 45° W to N 85° W. The mean variation of three observations was 4° 13' 42" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds a light breeze at WNW. At 1 the lookout reported breakers inshore and offshore; 20 minutes later they seemed to stretch a long way out to sea, and at the same moment we hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack. From noon to 4 the soundings varied from 21 to 27 fathoms, coral and white gravel mixed with broken shell. From 4.30 to 8 sounded every half hour in 28 fathoms, coral and gravel; 26, 26, 26, 25, rock and gravel bottom. At 4.30 a.m. went about and stood in on the shore tack; at 6 went about again.
1801-07-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth of Messidor, at daybreak, we again got under sail to go in search of the island in the middle of the bay of which Dampier speaks. And as he says he feared he would not find water enough to pass to the east of it, I sent my boat on ahead to sound in advance, with orders to drop her grapnel as soon as she found less than eight fathoms of water, steering directly south, which was the course I intended to follow.
As soon as the boat had gone we followed her under our fore topsail and mizzen topsail, so as to keep her always ahead of us. Until noon she signalled to us more than ten fathoms of water throughout, good anchorage, and as we were also sounding continually on board, we sailed a long while before the depth decreased by a fathom. At noon, however, we had no more than eleven and a half.
At ten o'clock we sighted from the deck that island in the middle of the bay which I had expected to see the day before, according to the Dutch chart, in which I had a fair degree of confidence, although I had already satisfied myself that the first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], that is to say the northernmost, was placed on it 19' further north than it really is, as we had occasion to observe. I fully supposed that the placing of this first island must affect that of the one I was seeking, and I likewise expected to find it too far north, as indeed it is, since at noon, having observed 25° 18' 37", this put us abreast of the middle of the island, while at the same moment it still bore from us it still bore from us east 19° south at its southernmost part.
I reserve for a more particular examination of this bay the task of making known the errors to which this chart seems to me to be liable.
For the greater part of the morning there had been a pleasant easterly breeze, but towards noon the calm overtook us, and at half past one we had to anchor so as not to fall too far to leeward, what little air there was being then from the south-east.
I had ordered my boat, if we anchored in sight of the island, to push on to the shore to examine it well and see whether she could find a place fit for landing, my intention being to stop there to determine the rate of our timekeepers and set up our observatory. As we were anchored nearly three leagues from the coast, the boat did not return before nightfall.
In the afternoon a light north-westerly breeze sprang up towards three o'clock, but I did not think it prudent to draw nearer the land and chose to wait for the boat's report.
During the night of the 13th to the 14th the weather was fine; it continued to blow a light breeze from the north-west until about nine o'clock, when the winds went round to the north. In the night I had two guns fired in the hope that they might be heard by the Naturaliste, if she were anywhere near the place where we lay at anchor. Rockets were also sent up, but all to no purpose: none of these signals was answered from any quarter. At nine o'clock the boat returned on board, having found no place fit for landing.

1801-07-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to E. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course south, the lead giving from 12 to 11 fathoms. At noon in 25° 19' 26" of latitude observed and in 109° 23' 5" of longitude by No. 27, the east point of the middle peninsula bearing S 71° E and the westernmost point in sight S 13° E. The small boat sounding ahead of us. At 1.30, being in a flat calm, we anchored in 11 fathoms, white sand, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 50° E and the westernmost point in sight S 5° E. At 7 and at 7.15 fired a gun to warn the Naturaliste should she be in the bay; showed a light at the gaff, burnt flares every quarter of an hour and sent up a rocket every half hour to give our position to the small boat, which arrived at 9. The mean variation of three observations was 3° 59' 20" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-03.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sea rather high, the winds varying from NW to N in strong gusts. At 6 p.m. went about onto the port tack. The wind still very violent, with lightning from every point of the horizon. At 10.30 wore onto the starboard tack. About six in the morning we lay to. Continual rain.
1801-07-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, at daybreak, we got under sail with a pleasant breeze from north-north-west, variable to north. As the distance we had to run was small, we set only our topsails. We had besides the small boat going ahead and sounding, although we were doing the same thing continually on board.
At nine o'clock, being in nine fathoms, bottom of white sand mixed with broken shells, we anchored again about a league and a half from the land. On our way to the anchorage we ran along, for about a league, the edge of a large sandbank on which the sea was running very high. The boat, which had examined it the day before, had found 7, 6 & 5 fathoms at the place where she crossed it, but to judge by the swell of the sea, it appears that there is much less water on it nearer the island. I intend, during our stay at the anchorage, to have it better examined. According to the report of Bonnefoy, who commanded the small boat, this bank runs directly to the east and may extend a league and a half in that direction.
As soon as we were at anchor the topgallant yards were sent down, and my intention was to moor for greater safety. But in the course of the morning the weather changed and took on an ugly look, and I put off this operation so as to be better able to get under sail should it turn bad.
Meanwhile I sent my boat ashore to examine the coast and look for an easy landing. She came back towards eleven o'clock with the bad news that she had been unable to land in any of the coves she had entered, the whole coast being fringed with a shelf of rocks on which the sea broke heavily, the winds being north-north-west and fairly strong.
At noon we observed the latitude of 25° 30' 44" south, and shortly afterwards we perceived, to the south of our anchorage, two more sandbanks which we had not noticed on our way in, so that we found ourselves in a very bad position, from which I sought to extricate myself at once by getting under sail. As it was then ebb tide, the current made the ship cast on the opposite tack to the one that would have suited us best, and we were obliged to wear round when the anchor was aweigh. This forced manoeuvre carried us very close to the bank we were trying to avoid, and when the ship had finished her turn we had no more than six fathoms of water and a very heavy swell. We at once crowded sail to claw off, and stood on towards the bank that bore east of us and which we had seen in the morning. We closed it as far as eight fathoms, and then the helm was put down to go about, but the ship missed stays. The sails were trimmed again, and after running a cable's length we tried a second time to go about, and succeeded.
From two o'clock until sunset we were constantly busy beating to windward between the banks, which seemed to stretch further as we worked up into the wind. We always stood in towards them as far as eight and seven fathoms, and then we went about.
At sunset the weather turned squally, with rain. The winds, which had been north-west, went round to the west, blowing fresh, and it was not until nine o'clock that we at last found ourselves out of danger. The tack then carrying us to the north, we soon had 11 and 12 fathoms, and I spent the rest of the night keeping in that depth while waiting for daylight. Everyone kept watch, except the naturalists, the midshipmen and the naval officers, who spent a very good night in their cabins and appeared only when their watch called them on deck, where they were of little use. Although the barometer had fallen to 28 inches 1 line, the weather was not very bad, and in the night, indeed, when the moon was somewhat high above the horizon, the rain ceased and the sky grew clearer.

1801-07-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to N. At 7.30 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course south under topsails, the small boat sounding ahead. At 9.30 we anchored in 9 fathoms, sand and shell, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 83° E, a fairly conspicuous hill S 25° E, the westernmost point in sight S 3° W. The topgallant masts were struck. Citizen Bonnefoi, who was sounding in the small boat, found off the east point of the peninsula a sandbank with only 2 fathoms on it; at the edge of the bank he found 6 fathoms, and the Géographe then bore from him S 22° 30' E, 9 miles off; the east point of the peninsula S 33° 45' E and the westernmost point in sight S 33° 45' W. The small boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey the coast and look for a place fit to set up our observatory. Latitude observed at the anchorage 25° 30' 27"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 25' 37". The wind freshening, at 1 o'clock Citizen Bonnefoi came back; he had not been able to land on the peninsula because the sea broke there with force. At 2 we got under way, casting to starboard towards the land although we had meant to cast to port. We at once bore away and went onto the starboard tack. This manoeuvre had brought us very close to the east point. At 2.30 went about onto the port tack. The wind a strong breeze from NNW to W; overcast and squally weather, the sea rather high. At 3, being very near the east point and the bank, we put the helm down and missed stays; we had only time to gather way and put about again, and fortunately we came round onto the starboard tack. Several people maintained that we had touched at the moment when the ship, being in stays, had gathered sternway. At 4 went onto the port tack; at 5.30 onto the starboard; at 6.30 onto the port; at 11.30 onto the starboard. During the night the wind blowing hard, the sea not very high, with rain. The soundings since getting under way have been from 6 to 11 fathoms.

1801-07-04.journal_anonyme: The wind showing no sign of changing, we kept under the same canvas throughout; squally weather, a high sea and continual rain, the wind WNW in strong gusts.
1801-07-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, during the morning, the weather cleared, yet the sea was running very high, and a heavy swell from the north gave us to understand plainly enough that it must have blown hard from that quarter of the horizon. We were then running along the land that trends south-south-east on the mainland coast, where it forms a very large bight. The colour of the water, which was extremely white, told us that the depth was not very great, and at times we had only nine and eight fathoms.
Having no longer any hope of being able to set up our observatory to fix the rate of our timekeepers anywhere but on the northernmost of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], I resolved to go and seek a good anchorage there, as sheltered as possible from the north and north-west winds, which are the worst on this thankless and barren coast.
At noon we sighted the northernmost of these islands, bearing west 23° south. The north point of the mainland then bore north 22° east, and this point appeared to us to be the one that must form the entrance of the bay.
In the afternoon, the winds being west-south-west, variable to south-west, we were standing close-hauled on the westerly tack towards the north when, at one o'clock, we dropped from 15 fathoms to six, although we were in the middle of the channel. We bore away at once, and at two o'clock, having ten fathoms of water, we sought to close with the land on which I meant to set up the astronomers and the naturalists.
During the evening the winds went round to the south, so that, having no hope of reaching the anchorage before nightfall, I went about at six in the evening and spent the rest of the night, which was fairly fine, beating to and fro.
At eleven o'clock the officer of the watch, having noticed a considerable whiteness on the water on the lee bow, at once brought the ship onto the larboard tack; but as he did not have me informed, I can say nothing for or against what he believes he
saw. But supposing he had seen something, we were then in twenty-five fathoms of water, bottom of grey sand. The rest of the night passed without incident, except that the winds, which we had had in the southern quarter, went round to the south-east, very light, and the sky was fine.
