1801-07-04.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from W to SW. At 2 a.m. lay to with the port side to the wind under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At daybreak the wind fell. During the day the weather was fine and the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. At 6.45 filled and stood on, the course N 33° 45' E. At 7.15 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the west. At 8 shaped the course N 11° 15' E. At 9.30 the mainland was sighted to the east. At 10 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 10.30 little Koks Island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At noon in 24° 44' 43" of latitude observed and in 109° 25' 32" of longitude by No. 27. The north point of Koks Island S 67° 0' W and the mainland north (the northernmost point in sight). At 1, the bottom having shoaled from 15 fathoms to 6, we bore away N 11° 15' W; the depth increased gradually, and at 2.30 we lay close-hauled again on the port tack. At 6 went onto the starboard tack. At 11, the sea being thought to break on the lee bow, we went onto the port tack.

1801-07-05.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, blowing hard from the west. From 8 to midnight and from midnight to 4 a.m. we sounded every hour without being able to find bottom, running out 87 and 100 fathoms of line. The wind having drawn round to NNW and then to NNW, we trimmed the sails and bore away NE. The weather fine, a swell running.
1801-07-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the sixteenth, the winds being south-east, variable to east, we steered for the northernmost of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], which then bore west-south-west, and at eight o'clock we anchored in 13 fathoms of water, grey sand, having veered out 35 fathoms of cable.
As soon as we were at anchor and the sails furled, I at once had the longboat and the small boat hoisted out to carry our instruments and tents ashore. I went myself in one of the two, and we came to settle in a cove about a league from our first anchorage.
Before leaving I gave orders for the ship to be moored south-east and north-west, for the topgallant yards to be sent down, and even for the topgallant masts to be struck should it come on to blow at all. I also directed Citizen Le Bas, to whom I left the command of the ship, to have a sheet cable bent to a third anchor and to keep it ready for letting go should it come on to blow.
All the shipboard duties having been arranged, I went ashore and at once had our tents pitched, two in number, in which all the scientists and I lodged. The astronomical circle and the telescope were placed in spots suited to observation, but we could do nothing that same day, having had only the time needed to make ready for the next.
On leaving the ship I informed M. Freycinet that the next day he would set out in the longboat with the chief helmsman to go to the south point of the second of the Îles Stériles, to determine its latitude and take hour angles and bearings there. I told him to have the longboat fitted out so that she should lack nothing, and to provide himself with victuals in keeping with the mission he would have to carry out, which I was to explain to him the next day, as he was to come to our tents before setting out.
The weather was very fine all day; nevertheless we found the sea somewhat swelling and the landing none too easy in the cove we had chosen, which seemed to us well sheltered, its two entrances being closed (by) two large rocks about a hundred paces long, a musket-shot from the shore and fifty paces wide, forming two islands.
When the winds are anywhere from north round by west to south-east, this cove is very convenient, but when they are from north to south-east by way of east and the breeze is somewhat strong, one has to go into the water so as not to endanger
the boats, the sea breaking too heavily on the shore, which is nonetheless only a fine sandy beach.
During the night the weather was calm, and we had a cloudless sky which promised us good observations for the next day.
1801-07-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to E. At 3.30, the soundings having shoaled appreciably, we went onto the starboard tack; at 5.30 onto the port tack. The northern Dorre island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At 7 shaped our course S 45° W to stand in for the anchorage. At 8 anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand. At 9.30 the commander and all the naturalists landed on the northern Dorre island to camp there. The tents, the astronomical instruments and provisions were sent ashore. At 10.30 we moored NE and SW with a bower anchor, having 60 fathoms to starboard to the NE and 50 fathoms to port to the SW, Koks Island bearing N 30° W, the north point of the northern Dorre island N 50° W 10 miles off, the tents N 60° W 8 miles off, a large headland of Dorre Island S 22° 30' W. The topgallant masts were struck, the sheet anchor got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The two boats came back from the shore and were sent off again to the camp with effects for the commander; they came aboard during the night.

1801-07-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW. The amplitude at setting gave us 7° 15' of NW variation. At 8.30 p.m. went onto the port tack. Ran out 100 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 1 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 3 hove to on the other tack. Noon bearings: the white cliff E 4° 30' N, estimated distance 23 miles; the nearest peak E 5° 30' S, estimated distance 25 miles; the furthest E 10° 30' S, distance 28 miles.
1801-07-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth we were not disappointed in our expectation: the weather was very fine, and we made various observations with our astronomical circle to make quite sure of the rate of our timekeepers, about which we had some doubts.
Towards eight o'clock M. Freycinet and the chief helmsman came in the longboat to take my orders and carry out the mission of which I had informed him the day before, before coming ashore. But as he had taken victuals for only two days, and he needed them for four to carry out his mission properly, I put off his departure until the next day, though not without some ill humour at his lack of foresight and at whoever had sent him off with so scanty a supply of victuals.
Be that as it may, I employed the boat's crew in cutting wood, which had to be fetched from more than three quarters of a league inland, through scrub in which walking and carrying were very laborious. Nevertheless, by dint of hard work and toil, we managed to make up her full load.
The lovers of pleasure, and I have a great many of them, went off hunting kangaroos and killed some twenty of them. Part of them was sent on board and the rest was kept for our own consumption ashore.
In the afternoon we made several hauls of the seine, but without success, for we caught nothing at all. The shellfish gathering was more fortunate: a great many crabs were collected, quite good (sic) to eat, nerites of (burgis ?) of different species, and above all a great many oysters, but small and very hard to open. They had much the shape and taste of those eaten in the colonies, whether of America or of the Isle of France [Mauritius] and Bourbon [Réunion]
Among the sea birds killed on the first day there was a pretty species. Some are known by the name of sea-pie, half their body being black and white, and their bill and feet a fine red. Maugé considers that two eagles that were killed must be a new species, since they appeared to live only on the fish and shellfish of which a good store was found inside them. For that reason we named it the fishing eagle.
The land birds were the same as those we had seen at our first anchorage on this coast.
Towards evening I sent the two boats that were ashore back to the ship, and I urged upon M. Freycinet the utmost exactness in the mission he had to carry out, and told him to take victuals for six days. This mission was not very complicated: it was confined to going to the south point of the second, and at the same time the largest, of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], to determine its latitude precisely and take various hour angles there so as afterwards to calculate the longitude. For this purpose I gave him my timekeeper, on which he could rely.
We spent the night ashore very merrily, and we were not troubled by the dew or by the cold, although the former was very abundant and the latter rather sharp during the night. The sky was cloudless, the winds south-east, almost calm. The thermometer nevertheless fell to ten degrees from the 19 at which it had stood during the day, in the shade.
1801-07-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to SSW. At 5 a.m. the boats were sent off to the tents with bread and water. We worked on the rigging and the sails. At nightfall the boats came back loaded with firewood.

1801-07-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather with rain, the winds varying from NW by N to NW and WNW. At 2.45 went about. At 9 a.m. a very violent squall passed over with rain; sounded every half hour and ran out 60 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-07-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth the weather continued fine, and we repeated the previous day's observations with success. I shall give the data results when they have been calculated.
From the shore we saw the longboat set off on the mission she had to carry out. I had given M. Freycinet the chief helmsman as his companion, a well-informed man on whom he could rely. This travelling companion did not seem to me very agreeable to him, and he would much rather have taken his protégé, the midshipman Breton, one of the most useless of all those on board.
In the course of the day our gardener made an ample harvest of plants, all fine and new. On our departure from this island I shall make known the various species and the numbers of them he will have found there.
The other naturalists busied themselves with fishing and shooting. Citizen Péron, whose extreme ardour leads him to undertake everything without a thought for the dangers to which he exposes himself, went to explore the western part of the island, and went there, as is his custom, alone. He found nothing of interest on his excursion, and so as not to have undertaken it in vain, he made for the seashore to gather shells there.
He amused himself first at the expense of the crabs, and having taken off his shirt, he shut up some fifty of them in it. This obligingness on his part deserved a happier fate than the one in store for it. For, having tried to get onto some rock where the sea seemed to him to break only moderately, he was knocked over by a wave which threw him down and carried off most of the fine shells he claims to have found. His fall caused him several injuries in different parts of his body, which made him (take) the course of turning back. But instead of taking his bearings so as to head from west to east, he went from north to south, so that for the second time he lost his way completely and did not rejoin us until about nine in the evening, overcome with fatigue and weariness, having been obliged to abandon on the way his tin box, his shirt and his crabs.
Our hunters during the day waged a war to the death on the kangaroos and killed nearly thirty of them.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth the sky was very fine and the winds almost calm, between south and south-south-east.
1801-07-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE and calm. At 5 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp with water and provisions, and the large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to the southern Dorre island. At nightfall the small boat arrived loaded with wood.

1801-07-08.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sky overcast, a swell running. A light breeze from WSW to SW by W. The land in sight at a great distance. At midnight hove to and sounded several times without finding bottom. At 6 a.m. filled and stood on.
1801-07-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the nineteenth Citizens Boulanger and Maurouard set out to examine, overland, the south point of the first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], on which we had established ourselves. They left at daybreak, and their intention was to go right round it. They made their preparations accordingly.
Citizens Bernier, astronomer, Depuche, mineralogist, and I likewise set out to take hour angles and altitudes of the sun at the northern one, so as to fix its position in a certain and precise manner, for the one given to them by the Dutch chart I am using is very faulty and differs, according to our previous observations, by nearly 20' in latitude. We had very fine weather during this excursion, which took only two hours to reach the most northerly point of land of this island. After resting a little, at half past ten we took an hour angle, and several angles from the point where we were to the ship.
Before and after the sun's passage across the meridian we obtained good altitudes, so that our journey was a success and (we) shall be able to determine accurately and
precisely the entrance of the bay.
Our work being finished, and to our satisfaction, we explored the surroundings of this point, at the tip of which lies a small islet, separated from the island by about a musket-shot and yet joined to it by a reef which does not uncover entirely but on which the sea breaks with a great roar. This islet lies north 5° east of the point on which we made our observations.
Before setting off to return to our tents, we placed in a well-stoppered bottle, set in a spot sheltered from the ravages of the weather, the following note:
"On the nineteenth of Messidor, Citizens Bernier, astronomer,
"Depuche, mineralogist, and the commander-in-chief of
"the expedition came to this north point of the island
"to determine its its (sic) latitude and longitude, in order to
"fix precisely the entrance of Shark
"Bay, discovered by Dampier to the north of the Îles Stériles".
Signed Baudin, commander, Depuche mineralogist, Bernier astronomer.
On our way back we followed the seashore and amused ourselves gathering shells. This gathering was not fortunate, and we found only three or four species that we had already met with.
Towards evening the weather looked very threatening in the quarter from south to south-south-east. The whole horizon was laden with great thick clouds, and it seemed to us that it must be raining fairly heavily four or five leagues from our encampment.
In the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the weather cleared again; the winds went round to the north-west and then to the west, almost calm ashore.
I had ordered the coxswain of the small boat, whom I met, to cut wood in a cove (and) to return on board before the bad weather that seemed likely to come on during the night. Although he had faithfully promised me to leave at once, he did not set off until after sunset. The south-easterly breeze blowing in the offing no longer allowing him to reach the ship, he was obliged to spend the night riding to his grapnel and to throw overboard all the wood he had gathered in the evening, which would not have happened had he left at the moment I gave him the order.
1801-07-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW. At 4 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp; she came back at 11 loaded with wood and left again at noon for the camp. At 4 the weather turned overcast, the breeze freshened and drew round to SSE, blowing strong, with a high sea. During the night kept a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour.

1801-07-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSW and SW. At 1 we sighted the Abrolhos at a middling distance. At 4.45 hove to; at the same hour the lead brought up 34 fathoms, fine sand; the depth and the bottom did not vary until 8. We filled for 10 minutes and then hove to again. At 4 the winds having drawn round to ESE we hove to on the starboard tack. At 6 filled and stood on.
1801-07-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, at sunrise, the sky being fairly fine although it seemed to us that a good breeze was blowing from the south-east in the offing, we saw our longboat and small boat under sail making for the ship. The haste of M. Freycinet's return at first gave me a poor opinion of the success of his mission, because it did not seem possible to me that he could have carried it out properly in so short a time. However, I shall await the report he makes to me before judging it.
During the day no boat came to us from the ship, and we were forced to cut down our ration of water for fear the weather might not be fine the next day. Observations with the astronomical circle were continued ashore, and these were the last. My intention was to return on board, for fear of a change of weather at the new moon, which was to fall the next day.
MM. Boulanger and Maurouard came back towards four in the afternoon from their excursion to the south of the island, the end of which they were unable to reach, the distance by their reckoning being much greater than the one it is given, from which it follows that this excursion was useless.
Our gardener continued his excursions into the interior of the island and, despite its barrenness, brought back from it every day new plants and very curious specimens. Maugé, for his part, did not lack work: he was supplied with fine birds, and the insects and shells occupied him when he could no longer see to work.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first the weather turned fine. The breeze died away a good deal, and we had hopes of seeing our boats arrive early the next day with our supply of water, which was beginning to run very short.
1801-07-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 10.30 Citizen Freycinet arrived in the large boat from the southern Dorre island, which he had left the day before at 4 o'clock at the beginning of the bad weather; he had spent the whole night lying to and at daybreak had shaped his course for the ship. At noon the small boat was seen anchored astern of us with a red flag at her mast; the large boat was at once sent off to carry her a line from the ship. At 2, suspecting that the large boat had let go the line, one of the yawls was sent to carry her the end; at 5 all three boats were aboard. The small boat had left the camp the day before loaded with wood; she had spent the night beating without being able to fetch the ship, and had been obliged to throw her wood overboard. At daybreak she had gained a little at the oars, but had been forced to anchor, her crew, who had neither drunk nor eaten, having no strength left.

1801-07-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light from SE to ESE. From 4 to 8 p.m. the lead brought up 29 to 30 fathoms, blackish sand. At 8 hove to with the port side to the wind, heading SW. At 2 we hove to on the other tack, and at 5.30 a.m. we filled and stood on.
1801-07-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, the weather being fine, we at last saw one of our boats arrive, which had left the ship towards seven o'clock, the time by which she ought to have reached the shore. At eight o'clock the longboat likewise arrived, that is to say left the ship; she arrived towards nine o'clock. M. Freycinet came to give me the report of his excursion, which, as I had foreseen from the haste of his return, amounts to next to nothing. Instead of bringing us back good observations, he brought back a great quantity of kangaroos for his table. Although I had not told him to take his protégé Le Breton, he took him along, if not to help him, at least to give him the pleasure of hunting, which he acquitted himself of very well.
In the first boat that reached us there were a number of hunters and several persons who are sick when it is a matter of doing duty on board, but who found strength to run about hunting all day in the full heat of the sun. Among them was young Bougainville, who will soon end by being quite worn out.
As soon as the longboat arrived I sent her to cut wood, and the small boat returned to the ship laden with part of our baggage, for I was seriously thinking of striking camp. I thought she could make two trips in the course of the day, but as on the second she had to take off all the useless people who had been sent to us and who were counting on staying the night ashore, this prevented her from doing the service for which I intended her. Citizen Péron was also sent off to the ship to have his injuries dressed. The astronomer Bernier returned there too.
In the night the weather continued fine, and we spent part of it preparing for the embarkation of all our effects the next day.
1801-07-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE. At 5 a.m. the two boats were sent off to the camp with provisions and water. Our fishermen, who had taken nothing since we anchored, made a very good haul today. In the evening the two boats came back from the camp. Twelve lashes with a rope's end were given to the seaman Gimes for having threatened to throw Citizen Bougainville, midshipman in charge of the party in the large boat, into the sea.

1801-07-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from E to SSE and SE. At 8 p.m. hove to with the port side to the wind. From 4 to 8 the lead brought up 30 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell; 28, 28, 32 and 33, grey sand and gravel. At 2 a.m. filled and hove to again at 4. At 5 a.m. filled and stood on; at 7 a.m. and at 11 went about.
1801-07-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the twenty-second, the weather being very fine and the winds almost calm between north-east and east, our two boats arrived. The longboat was at once sent off to fetch wood, of which we were beginning to run short, because no one had taken care to warn me of it when we were in Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], where there was every facility for cutting it. As it was known that we were to proceed shortly to Shark Bay, it appears that it was judged we had enough, which indeed turned out to be so, but we then no longer had the same facility for procuring it, the wood produced by the islands being of poor quality and little fit for the use of ships.
As soon as our boats arrived we struck one of our tents, which was at once carried on board together with several others of our effects. When the longboat had made one trip with wood, she was employed in carrying us and all our baggage, so that by sunset we were all on board, together with our effects.
I was all the more anxious to get there because the barometer and the hygrometer seemed to foretell the end of the bad fine weather. In the night the sky did indeed become covered with clouds in every quarter of the horizon, and the winds, though still light, settled in the west, variable to north-west. The sea soon became swelling and rough, and the breakers could be heard distinctly on the western side of the island.
1801-07-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW. At daybreak the two boats were sent off to the camp. At 10 they came back loaded with effects and left again at once. At 2 the small boat arrived loaded with effects from the camp and went back at once. The topgallant masts were swayed up, the rigging set up and the repair of the sails continued. At 5 the commander and all the naturalists came back aboard in the two boats, which brought the tents, the astronomical instruments and the rest of the effects that were at the camp. The boats were hoisted in. On board 24° 50' 30" was observed at the anchorage, and 109° 12' 46" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 4° 33' NW, the mean of 5 observations. The tides set NNW and SSE and run at one knot and a half. At the camp 24° 47' 30" of latitude and 109° 2' 9" of longitude were observed. At the north point of the northern Dorre island 24° 45' 30" of latitude and 108° 59' 12" of longitude were observed.

1801-07-12.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, the sea smooth, a light breeze variable from N by NW to N and NNE. At 1 the lead brought up 27 fathoms, reddish sand and fine gravel. At 8.30 p.m., being 2 leagues and a half from the coast and standing in for it, we changed tacks.
1801-07-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the twenty-third, the weather looking threatening, I had the sheet cable unbent and its anchor stowed. Then we unmoored, and at half past eleven we were under sail. The winds being north-north-east, a pleasant breeze, I expected to be able to get out of the bay before nightfall, or at least to put myself in a position to pass through the middle of the channel; but as in the afternoon they came to us from the north, variable to north-north-west, we spent the evening beating about the bay, lead in hand.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth we were not without anxiety, caused not only by the bad weather we had but still more by the irregularity of the bottom. My intention was, given the weather and winds prevailing, to keep between twelve and eighteen fathoms of water so as to hold roughly to the middle of the bay, but we often happened to drop to drop (sic) all of a sudden from eighteen and twenty fathoms to twelve and even less, so that at any moment we might run upon some high low shoals which would have served us a very nasty turn.
It seems to me that the depths and soundings marked on the Dutch chart I am using are placed at random, and that the only good thing about this chart is the outline and trend of the land, which, with the exception of the Île du Milieu in the bay, appeared to us very accurate and well drawn. It seems to me proven that in the middle of the northern entrance of Shark Bay there is a fairly extensive bank, on which we advanced as far as six fathoms of water. Had the sea been less heavy at the time, I would have had it examined by the boat, but when I found myself there on returning from the Île du Milieu it was impossible to hoist out a boat, and I could barely see the land of the mainland coast, which is not nearly so low in that part as it appears on the chart.
Afterwards, standing to the west to reach the second of the islands first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], on which I meant to set up our observatory, I suddenly passed from 15 fathoms to eight, and it was only on closing with the island that I found by the lead a regular depth of 15, 14, 13 and twelve fathoms, a bottom in which I anchored, the land bearing from me as given in the bearings I recorded on the day of our anchoring.
Thus, from what befell us, I believe I passed over the two ends of this bank, and as no breakers appeared in the middle, perhaps the passage across it is practicable, but I do not guarantee it.
There are few parts of this bay that we did not cover at various times, as may be judged from the tracks laid down on the plan of it I give, and our only regret was that we could not find a place to land on the mainland coast. Every time we were there the winds were either north or north-west or west, so that the sea broke everywhere with great violence. The coast, though lined with sandy beaches which from afar promise an easy landing, is fringed with a shelf of rocks which often runs out nearly half a league to sea.
1801-07-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At 6 a.m. the sheet anchor's cable was unbent and the anchor stowed. At 9 we unmoored; at 11.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W, the south point of the same island S 50° W, the large headland of Dorre Island S 33° W. At noon overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze. Beating to get out of Shark Bay. At 4.45 the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W. Continual rain during the night.

1801-07-13.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from N to NNE and NNW, squally weather, the sea rather high. At 4 wore onto the port tack. At 1.30 a.m. the lead brought up 50 fathoms, reddish sand. Calm about four o'clock, the sky dark with a great deal of rain falling; about 9 it freshened from the NNE.
1801-07-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the twenty-fourth we were awaiting daylight with great impatience, thinking that we should have sight of both coasts, or at least of one of the two, to fix our position and the course we must steer to get out to sea. The weather looked threatening and the sea was rising. The barometer, which had fallen to 28 during the night, boded nothing good, and it was becoming both prudent and urgent to make for the open sea in order to be safe.
At daybreak a great cloud came spreading over us and gave us so
great a quantity of rain that it would have been easy to catch several casks of it, but we were so taken up with the lead and the working of the ship that the sailors barely had time to collect enough to wash their linen. The winds, which during the night had been fairly steady at north-north-east, became very variable and finally settled in the south-west towards seven in the morning. Our horizon was so (narrowed) (in the margin: here because) by day that it scarcely stretched a cannon-shot, and we were quite as uncertain of the course to steer to get out as if we had been in the dead of night. (in the margin: here because)
However, as a decision had to be made, I had the ship steered west when the winds allowed, to close with the first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], whose soundings I knew. A lead was cast every five minutes. When I put her head to the west I had fifteen fathoms, and I followed that course until thirteen; then I steered north to regain the middle of the bay. At eight o'clock I was again in fifteen fathoms. The weather, still rainy, gave no range to our horizon, which remained very narrow. From north I went over, until ten o'clock, to a north-north-west course, still in 15 fathoms. From ten o'clock to noon I had her steered north-west, convinced that I was in the middle of the bay. And indeed the depth increased gradually to eighteen fathoms, and at noon we had thirty-two, which placed us entirely outside, without our having had any sight of the land.
I then went to take some rest, for I had been on deck for twenty-six hours without resting a single time. I again observed on this occasion that none of the officers except the one on watch came up on deck, and the frequent tacks we made no more prevented them from sleeping soundly than (if) we had been in the most agreeable situation. Before retiring I ordered the north-west course to be continued so as to get out to sea, and soundings to be taken only once an hour.
Throughout the evening the sky was dark, overcast and rainy. The rain, however, though continual, was much less heavy.
In the afternoon, the winds having gone round to the south, we lay in a flat calm until four o'clock, when they came to us from the north-east, a pleasant breeze. We stood on the northerly tack, edging towards the west, under the foresail and the three topsails, with two reefs in each. My intention (was) to get far enough out to sea to weather a gale if, as the signs seemed to announce, one came on. But before leaving this coast I wished to go and take the latitude of the point that forms the entrance of the bay on the north side, so as to know exactly its distance from the first of the Îles Stériles, which the Dutch chart seems to me to have placed too close.
A little before sunset of sunset (sic), we had a clear spell which let us see for a moment the mainland coast, which then bore from south to east over a considerable extent, at about three leagues' distance from us.
During the night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth the weather was hardly finer than it had been during the day. I set the course north for the night, with orders to sound every hour and to go about at three in the morning if there were signs of fine weather. But the weather was very unsettled and the winds variable, which obliged us to make various manoeuvres until the next day.
***(this is actually page 264)
Bearings of the land.
At four in the afternoon,
the northernmost point of the first of the Îles Stériles bore north 40° west.
1801-07-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a flat calm, a light breeze from NNE, and from S to SSW at 7 a.m. At noon in 24° 31' 32" of latitude by account and in 108° 59' 46" of longitude by account. At 8 squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE. At 10.30 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail and the mizzen staysail. At 11.45 the wind shifted to W and hauled to NW and NNW.

1801-07-14.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, continual rain, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a light breeze variable from NNE, NNW to south. At 7.30 p.m. the lead brought up 37 fathoms, reddish sand. At the same hour the wind shifted to SSW. At 4 a.m. we hoisted a flag at the gaff in honour of the 14th of July. At 11 we sighted the land at a distance of 30 miles.
1801-07-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the twenty-fifth, the weather seeming inclined to clear, I sought to close with the land so as to find myself, towards noon, due east and west of the cape that forms the northern entrance of the bay, since that point had become important to us for determining the width of the opening, the entrance by the first of the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands] being well established from our observations made ashore.
At half past ten we had reached the point I was seeking, and we then hove to to wait for the sun's passage across the meridian.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 24° 18' 58" south, and the longitude deduced from the rate of our timekeepers was, for No. 27, 109° 9' 3" and for No. 35, 109° 18' 58". The great cape that forms the northern entrance of the bay then bore east 17° north, at a distance of two to three leagues. I did not approach it any closer, since the winds were west-north-west and the sky had no very fine look. Besides, we had already run along the whole of this coast so closely that there was no possibility of being mistaken, given the knowledge we had of it.
After the observation of the meridian altitude, having nothing more to do on this coast, I shaped a course to go and examine, as promptly as possible, the north-west point of this same land, and steered north with a fine, strong breeze from west-north-west, the sea fairly smooth and the sky seeming inclined to rid itself of the clouds that made its aspect far from pleasant.
During the evening the weather continued to clear, and at sunset the winds went round to the west, variable to west-south-west, which made us run a good distance during the night. On the strength of Dampier's observation and of the difference to the east he had experienced in these same waters, I had her steered north by west during the night, which was fine.
We sounded every hour but found no bottom at 60 fathoms.
Remarks during our last stay at the Îles Stériles.
From the observations made ashore, the north point of this island the first of these islands lies in 24° 45' 30" south latitude, and its longitude, taking the mean of the results given by our timekeepers, would be 109° 34' 44" east. The dip of the magnetic needle was observed there to be 49° with needle No. 2 and 54° with No. 4, on 16 Messidor. These observations, repeated on the 18th, gave, with needle No. 2, 50° and with No. 4, 52° 15, so that the mean would be 51° 18' 45".
The variation observed on board was found to be, at the place where the ship was anchored, 7° 8' 18"; the same observations made ashore gave only 5° 45' 15".
Although the sky was fine during the first days of our encampment ashore, it was not possible to make any observation, either by night or by day, to determine by that means the true longitude of this island. The moon was then too close to the sun, and there was no eclipse of Jupiter's satellites
For the rest, our head gardener Riedelé, to whom every moment is precious, found on this small island seventy species of plants, most of which will no doubt be unknown to botanists. The zoologist Maugé, wholly taken up with natural history and anxious to fulfil his duties well, collected there ten species of birds which he believes to be new. The others hunted kangaroos and a few lizards. Among the latter we caught two which are no doubt the same that Dampier speaks of under the name of guanos, and which is truly very hideous. But we caught two of another species, very pretty in colour and very large. See the figure drawn from life in the fair-copy journal.
One remark I have made, which is perhaps not without interest, is that none of the animals we met with seemed to us vicious. These lizards, hideous as they are, let themselves be taken in the hand without trying to flee or defend themselves. Two black snakes, which were not taken for fear of them, gave those who were looking at them all the time they cared to spend examining them, and did not hide until they were approached very closely. The wounded kangaroos that were taken still alive made no attempt to bite, and a young one that was caught without being harmed at once began to lick the hand of the man who had caught it.
Among the shells we found only four or five fairly handsome species, and only two that seemed to us unknown. Citizen Maugé collected ten sorts of insects, most of which belong to the class of dung beetles. We found only two species of butterflies, one diurnal and the other nocturnal. And several caterpillars were taken of the first, which is quite handsome seen from beneath and, seen from above, bears a close resemblance to the cabbage butterfly of Europe.
The fish caught on the line are in general of the perch kind, and only one sort was taken in any great quantity, which the sailors call Cap and say is common and alike in the colonies. The fish known by the name of parrotfish are exactly the same as those seen between the tropics. For the rest, I have had drawn in colour those that seemed to me the rarest and most curious.
During our stay ashore we lived constantly on crabs, oysters, nerites of (burgis), crayfish, fish and kangaroos. The shark, when it is young and small, seemed to me very good, and I preferred it to the kangaroo, which was everyone's delight.
The boats going to and fro sometimes saw very large green turtles on their trips, but we had not the skill to catch any. We came upon two dead ones on the shore whose heads were the size of a sheep's. Although I have seen very large ones at Ascension Island, they came nowhere near the bulk the two whose remains we found must have had. One also sees on the coast some bones of whales, but they are small and offer nothing remarkable.
Most of the wood we gathered on the coast had no doubt (been) carried there by the tides from the mainland, for we found a good deal of it that had begun to burn. And besides, the island does not produce wood of that quality. For the rest, this bay offers few resources to navigators: not a drop of water, very little wood and that very hard to cut. Fishing alone, or the need to repair considerable damage, can induce anyone to go there. One lies well there so long as the winds are west east and south-east, even as far as south if they are moderate, but from every other point of the horizon, if it blows at all, the sea runs very high there and landing is no longer practicable.
When I went to anchor off the mainland coast, the weather had been very fine for two days and the winds very moderate from north-east and east, coming directly over the land. I had reason to think that landing would be easy, and yet the boats could not approach the coast nearer than half a league, the sea breaking everywhere with a great roar.
During our stay in Shark Bay, the chief helmsman, whom I had specially charged with observing the tides, made me the following report:
"On the 8th of Messidor at eight o'clock the flood began. The same day at 20 hours, return of the flood.
"On the 9th at noon 45 minutes, beginning of the ebb. The same day at 13 hours, return of the ebb
"On the 9th at 8 hours 30 minutes, beginning of the flood. The same day at 19 h 15', return of the flood.
"On the 10th at noon 45 minutes, beginning of the ebb. On the 10th at 13 h 10', return of the ebb.
"On the 10th at 9 h 20 minutes, beginning of the flood. The same day at 20 h, return of the flood.
"I observe that during the observations, which lasted two and a half days, the waters "remained sensibly at the same height, although one can be certain, from the rocks on the shore, that the sea "rises and falls there more than eight feet vertically.
"The intervals between tides are not equal because it is extremely difficult to "know precisely the moment of slack water. The true interval between tides "should be 12 h 24'; here it is only 11 h 43', which gives a difference of 41', but it seems "that the number of observations is not great enough to remove this inequality".

Bearings of the land.
Towards the end of the noon-to-four watch we sighted the mainland in a clear spell. It bore from south to east.
On the 25th at noon, the great cape that forms the northern entrance of Shark Bay bore east 17° north, at two or three leagues at most.
The other land, running up to the north, could be seen from east to north-east.
1801-07-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 6.30 filled and stood on, and at 6.45 shaped the course S 45° E, and at 8 east. At 9.30 the land was sighted in the N 79° E and we steered for it. At 10.30, being abreast of the large cape at the entrance to Shark Bay, we hove to with the port side to the wind. At noon in 24° 17' 16" of latitude observed and in 109° 9' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 3° 35'. The large cape bore from us N 73° E, and the land in sight as far as N 44° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course north. At 4 took the bearing of the large cape S 78° E, the southernmost land S 35° E. At 5.30 the course was given N 11° 15' W. The large cape then bore from us S 43° E, and the land in sight from S 32° E to S 64° E. At 10 p.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the fourth time, in 109° 10' of longitude.

1801-07-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, continual rain, a light breeze from NNW to SW. At 4 p.m. fired 21 guns in memory of the 14th of July, whose anniversary was celebrated. At 6.45 a squall got up in the SW with lightning and a little thunder; we steered NNW. At daybreak we sighted the land and made all sail to close it. At noon the lead brought up 47 fathoms, rocky bottom.
1801-07-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth the weather was fine and the wind west-south-west, a pleasant breeze. We stood to the north, edging towards the east, until noon, and having observed the latitude of 22° 17' 3", I had her steered north-east to close with the land, which we sighted at two o'clock in the afternoon, bearing from east to south-east of us at a distance of eight leagues.
The longitude given by the timekeepers put us at noon, according to No. 27, in 109° 6' 18", and according to No. 35 in 108° 57' 59".
In the evening we continued to steer north-east under all sail until eight o'clock, and then we lay to until midnight with her head to the east, and from midnight to four in the morning on the other tack with her head to the west. We sounded every hour during the night, which was very fine, but found no bottom at 120 fathoms. I might well have stood in for the land, but I feared to fall in unexpectedly with the banks of which Dampier speaks, being very nearly in the latitude he gives them; besides, I could not count on a good watch being kept, I was myself in need of rest, and I was suffering cruelly from a colic of the lower belly. One day more or less did not seem to me a great loss, and I had no need to add to my anxieties.
***(this is in fact page 266)
Bearings of the land.
On the twenty-fifth at sunset, the northernmost land in sight bore east 26° south
The southernmost east 58° south
The middle of this coast east 47 south.
1801-07-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SE. At 6.30 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 22° 17' 3" of latitude observed and in 109° 6' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 42' NW. The course was given N 45° E. At 4 the land was sighted from N 79° E to S 67° 30' E, as far as the eye could reach. At 8 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at midnight hove to on the port tack.

1801-07-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A light breeze from SW to SW by W. At 8 p.m. the lead brought up 58 fathoms, fine sand. From 9 to 10 and 11 ran out 70 fathoms without finding bottom. At daybreak sighted the land, which I take to be the entrance to Shark Bay.
1801-07-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at four in the morning, the weather being fine and the wind south-east, a pleasant breeze, we steered from south to east-north-east, hauling as close to the wind as possible, in order to make the land, which by my dead reckoning I expected to see at sunrise. Indeed, we thought we could make it out, and we held on the same course because the lookouts claimed to see it on that point of the compass. But after running until noon without discovering anything, and having observed 21° 6' 27" of south latitude, I went about and stood to the south until four o'clock, when the wind failed us and we could neither steer the ship nor give her any way at all.
The longitude given by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, put us according to No. 27 in 110° 16' 18", and according to No. 35 in 110° 4' 21".
Throughout the day, as throughout the night, the lead was cast every hour, and we found no bottom at a depth of 120 fathoms.
Towards nine o'clock we had a light air from the west-south-west, shifting a little towards the south, but in general it was almost calm all through the night, which was very fine in spite of the fickleness of the wind. This calm was all the more unwelcome because we had every reason to fear that the currents would carry us much farther out to sea than I wished, since at noon we were 19' 21" beyond what the dead reckoning of our courses over the 24 hours indicated.
***(this is in fact page 267)
Bearings of the land.
On the twenty-seventh at four in the afternoon,
the land showed from east by north to east-south-east.
The distance was too great for us to make it out properly.
1801-07-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE. At 4 filled and stood on, the course N 45° E; at 6.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 110° 18' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 33' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 13' 0" of longitude. At noon went onto the port tack; at 6 a flat calm. At 8, a light breeze from WSW, shaped the course S 25° E.

1801-07-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to SSW. We ran along Dirk Hartog Island and sounded in 45 fathoms, reddish sand. At 7.45 a.m. we let go the port anchor in 18 fathoms, fine muddy sand, and veered 60 fathoms of cable. At 8 a.m. we sent the small boat away to sound. At 9 it was back and we fired two guns. From 10 until midnight a current setting ESE held the ship almost broadside on.
1801-07-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 28th, in the morning, the wind went round to the south, and at sunrise it freshened and held all morning at south-south-east. We steered east under all sail without sighting any land or finding bottom at 120 fathoms.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 21° 4' 50", whereas by dead reckoning it should have been 21° 20'; so we again had a difference of 15' 10" to the north, although by dead reckoning our whole course had carried us south. The longitude given by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 110 50 48, and for No. 35, 110° 35' 22". Two sets of distances put us in 112° 54' 4", which gave us so great a difference to the east that we judged them very doubtful, although the weather was fine and suited to such observations. Still, a difference of 2° 10' 59" to the east did not allow us to place any confidence in them.
However that may be, I continued to stand east until four in the afternoon. A a (sic) very light breeze from south-south-east did not allow us to make much way; at that time, the wind having gone round to the south-west, still very light, I took the tack standing south towards the east.
At sunset, having no sight of land and no bottom, I held the same course until nine o'clock, when, having found thirty fathoms, coarse gravel, I went about and stood out to sea.
During the night of the twenty-eighth to the 29th the wind was very light, and we spent the night keeping ourselves in 30 and fifty fathoms, the weather being very fine and the sea calm.
***(this is in fact page 268)
1801-07-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to SW. At daybreak shaped the course east and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 4' 58" of latitude observed and in 110° 54' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 46' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 47' 6" of longitude.

1801-07-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind very light from the south. On the 29th the weather was unsettled and calm; a breath from N by NE gave us hopes of getting under way, but the calm returned. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq to go to Dorre Island, and the dinghy to Dirk Hartog.
1801-07-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, at daybreak, we saw the land in the south-east, stretching a little towards south-east by south. The sky was then dark and overcast and did not look promising. It cleared, however, in the course of the morning, and at nine o'clock we made out that the land we had in sight, then at a distance of four leagues, was an islet about a league and a half in extent, bearing east 12° north of us.
According to our charts, and above all the Dutch one, which is more detailed than the others, this should be one of those placed to the east of the north-west point of Eendracht Land, and we ourselves judged it to be so.
At ten o'clock we sighted another island extending from east 53° south to east 21° south, and shortly afterwards a third bearing south 10° west. We stood on to range along these islands, seeking to close with the north-west point of the mainland, which I flattered myself we should soon sight, the distance at which the Dutch chart places it not being great. The second of these islets appeared to us larger than the other two and, by our estimate, three leagues in extent, which is entirely contrary to the shape the chart gives it. Moreover, the ground of the first two appeared to us very sandy and barren; only the third had a little verdure, produced by plants of very low growth. In doubling the first, we saw at its eastern point a reef on which the sea was breaking heavily, although it was calm. The second also had one, but of less extent.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 21° 19' 27" south. Thus, according to the Dutch chart, we were still 15 minutes from the north-west point of Eendracht Land and should have sighted it, the weather being then very fine. But a calm having come on, we lost hope of making it before nightfall. From sunrise until noon we had had soundings running from 51 fathoms to 27, grey sand.
The longitude given by the timekeepers, reduced to noon, gave for No. 27, 111° 1' 34", and for No. 35, 110° 42' 59". By further sets of distances between the sun and the moon, the difference found the day before appeared once again, and we had doubts about the results given by the timekeepers. Distances 112° 26' 57".
In the afternoon the calm continued, or at least the breeze was so light that we made very little way. At three o'clock the wind, which some time before had gone round to the north-east, shifted to west-south-west, which made us take the tack to the north-west.
During the night of the 29th to the thirtieth we beat to and fro to keep our position, putting off until the next day the reconnoitring of the mainland coast. During the night we had from 46 to 75 fathoms, muddy sand.
***(this is in fact page 269)
Bearings of the land.
On the twenty-ninth at daybreak, we sighted the land extending from south-east to south-east by south, at a distance of five leagues. We supposed it to be an island.
At half past nine this island bore east 12° north of us.
At noon we took the bearings of two others, one north 66° east and the other south 10° west; these are the islands shown on the Dutch chart.
1801-07-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WNW to WSW, from SE to NE and from WSW to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E. At 9 took the bearing of an islet N 78° E, 12 miles off. At noon it bore from us N 66° E, another from S 37° E to S 19° E, and another S 40° W. At noon in 21° 19' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 1' 32" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 53' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 26' 57" of longitude. At 3 the last islet bore from us S 67° 30' W.

1801-07-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to NNW, running under the fore topsail, mizzen topsail and jibs. At 1.30 let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, sand and fine gravel, and veered 35 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the NW point of Dirk Hartog Island W 13° N; the southernmost visible end of the same island S 9° E; the middle of Dorre Island N 17° W. While running in we sounded and found 15 and 13 fathoms, sand and gravel. At 9.30 p.m. the large boat was back. The dinghy returned at 10.30 a.m.
1801-07-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, at sunrise, we again sighted the islands seen the day before, but they could only be made out from the mastheads. The easternmost then bore from south to south-east of us. The calm having continued until eight o'clock, the wind went round to the east, a pleasant breeze. We took
advantage of it both to close with the land and (to) ascertain properly the position of the islands we had in sight.
At eight o'clock the first of the three seen the day before bore east 25° south, the second south 62° east, the third west 43° south. A land ahead of us, which we judged to be the mainland, west 22° 30' south.
During the morning we continued to stand towards the most prominent land in sight, which was indeed the mainland. But in running along the islands at a distance of two leagues to two and a half, we were surprised to see a far greater number of them than the Dutch chart shows. This leads me to believe that those who surveyed the mainland in this part, together with the islands lying off it, had not gone as far to the east as we had. We were likewise surprised to find no bottom, at so small a distance from the land, at 50 and 60 fathoms, whereas, when we were farther to the east, it was found at 30 up to nearly six leagues from the coast.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 21° 31' 30" south, which agrees fairly well with the latitude the Dutch chart gives to the north-west point of New Holland. And I think it is placed there with far greater accuracy than on any of the other charts. The islets and islands also seemed to us better placed on it than on Robertson's chart and on the French chart drawn up at the Dépôt, which place them, I believe, too far to the east, as may be judged from the following bearings:
Bearings at noon after observing the meridian altitude.
The land taken for the mainland, or the north-west point of the coast, west 37° south.
The most prominent land to the west on the same coast, west 43° south
Three sandy islets from east 71° south to east 28° south
A small island on which there appeared to be very little vegetation, east 25° south
Another island where the vegetation was more lively, east 6° south
(Sketch of which it would be well to take a copy)
The three other islands sighted in the morning were then out of sight.
After noon, the weather still being fine although the sky already looked very threatening, we continued to run along the mainland coast, whose north-west point bore east 77° south of us at one o'clock, and the westernmost land south 13° west. We could then make out very clearly the reef the reef (sic) marked on our charts at the north-west point. My intention was to come to anchor at the spot where the English and Dutch charts show a good anchorage, and I was about to stand in accordingly when the wind shifted suddenly and violently to the west and then to west-north-west, which obliged me to stand out to sea.
At five o'clock the weather turned bad, and the barometer, which had fallen to 28 inches two lines since noon, obliged me to take precautions for the night and against the bad weather. We therefore took another reef in each topsail and sent down our topgallant sails. As our foresail was in poor condition and unable to withstand a squall, I had it changed, and we bent a new one at once. While we were busy with this work the weather turned bad, the sky clouded over at every point of the horizon, and we had heavy rain until six o'clock. The wind was then west-north-west and I was making south 43 west.
Unable to bring myself to leave this coast without having examined it and cleared up a doubt that had arisen, I decided to stand off from the coast only far enough to ride out the bad weather without fear, should it come. I spent the night going about from tack to tack seven or eight leagues offshore, finding no bottom at one hundred and twenty fathoms.
During the night of the thirtieth to the first the weather was not fine, and we quite often had strong gusts from the west-south-west, some of them heavy enough to make us furl the mizzen topsail and, shortly afterwards, reef our topsails, in which, however, two reefs had already been taken taken in.
When, before the bad weather, we were running along the part of the mainland coast which in that place runs east and west, we lost sight of the land at the which, once arrived at the western point, and further off another land could be seen trending from the west towards the south, which no doubt goes on to join another stretch of very high land that bore south-west of us and is shown on the Dutch chart as the highest land of the continent. Several people maintained that the land we had just passed was an island and that it was wrongly taken for the mainland. In spite of appearances, I did not share this opinion. But, without pronouncing on the question, I put off clearing up the matter until the weather should be manageable. Besides, it seems to me impossible that the Dutch, who followed the whole of this coast very closely, should not have noticed this island, if indeed it is one, which I am very far from believing. I think that what we saw is only the opening of some deep bay, or perhaps even the entrance of what they call Willem's River. At all events, I hope that this conjecture will soon be verified.
***(this is in fact page 270)
Bearings of the land.
On the morning of the thirtieth, the land was seen again from the mastheads from south-south-east to south
At noon, one of the islands seen the day before bore east 25° south.
A second south 62° east
The stretch of land taken for the mainland extended only from west 37° south
to west 45° south. But we were still too far from this
part to make sure that it was not a third island.
1801-07-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather in the forenoon and overcast in the afternoon. The wind from WSW, SW, ESE, E, ENE, N, NE, NNE and WSW. At noon in 21° 32' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 30' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 9' NW. An island S 65° E, another S 62° E, another from S 47° W to S 53° W; it is this last that the commander took for the entrance to the Willem River, and off which he hove to on the 3rd Thermidor [22 July 1801] in the afternoon. The wind a strong breeze, with rain, squalls and gusts.

1801-07-20.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from SW to W. The sky cloudy with light rain at intervals. At 7 p.m. the corvette dragging, we veered to 80 fathoms of cable; the tide set NW, as observed at 8.30 and at 9. At noon the currents had the same set.
1801-07-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Thermidor, at four in the morning, we had been standing since midnight on the tack heading north 65° west, the weather still threatening and very ill suited to approaching the land. We nevertheless sighted it at daybreak, bearing south 45° west of us, but it could only be seen from the mastheads. We held on the same tack until eight o'clock, and then we took the and then we took the (sic) tack heading south 22° 30' west, keeping the same sail, that is to say under our topsails and foresail. The sea was beginning to run high, with a hollow swell, which gave no promise of the return of fine weather. The barometer, however, seemed to promise it, since it had already risen above 28 inches.
At ten o'clock we sighted the land, and at noon it bore as follows:
The part of the coast taken for the mainland south-west, at a distance of 15 miles
Some of the islands seen the day before from south to south-east 5° east
We had no observation of latitude that day, and at noon we went about. We sounded at the same moment; there there (sic) was no bottom at 120 fathoms.
In the afternoon we steered west, hauling up towards the north as much as we could, but the wind being variable from south-west to west-south-west, the course took as much of the north as of the south, so that on this tack it made good scarcely more than west. The sky remained very cloudy and threatening. There were, however, several clear spells which seemed to herald the return of fine weather, and the barometer too was beginning to rise.
At four in the afternoon the land was again sighted from the mastheads, bearing then somewhere to the south, but the distance was too great to make out what it might be.
At eight o'clock we put her on the starboard tack, and at midnight we went about again until four o'clock, so as to keep ourselves, if possible, in the position we had been in at sunset.
During the night of the first to the second the sky was fairly fine, and we had the wind from south-south-east to south-east, a strong breeze. The sea had become very heavy. We sounded every hour during the night without finding bottom at one hundred fathoms.
The sunset, according to Dampier's remarks, foretold a strong breeze for the next day, and I earnestly hoped it would not come, so that I might draw nearer to the coast.
*** (this is in fact page 271)
Bearings of the land.
On the first of Thermidor at noon, the land of the mainland bore south 50° west at 15 miles
one of the islands of the day before south-east
1801-07-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SE. At noon in 21° 26' 22" of latitude by account and in 109° 55' of longitude by account. Variation 2° 53' NW. An island south, another from S 34° E to S 50° E. The mainland S 50° W, about 15 miles off. At 4 the land could be seen from aloft to the south.

1801-07-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. We observed a current setting strongly ESE. At 7 a.m. we weighed the starboard anchor, and when it was up we found the shank broken 2½ feet above the flukes. Let go the starboard anchor. At 9 a.m. sent off a boat under the orders of the chief quartermaster to go to Dirk Hartog and observe the tides.
1801-07-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, in the morning, it continued to blow a strong breeze from south-east by east to south-east, and at sunrise it freshened further. At the same moment we saw the land, which (we) judged to be still that forming the north-west part of Eendracht Land. We were then a fair way offshore, and it seemed to us that it would be difficult to get near it if the if the (sic) breeze continued from the same quarter and with the same strength.
At four in the morning we did not go about, the lead having found no bottom at one hundred fathoms. As the land extended from south-east to south by west, the tack we were on was the best for closing with it, and indeed we had a perfect view of it from the deck at seven o'clock. Only, from the point of the compass on which it bore, it appeared to us that for the past two days the currents or tides had carried us a good way to the north-west.
At eight o'clock we went about and stood east by north, so as to draw nearer to the point we wished to reconnoitre when we should go onto the other tack, which I intended to do as soon as the meridian altitude had been observed.
At noon the latitude was found to be 21° 28' 28", exactly the same as the Dutch chart gives to that much-desired point. The mean longitude of the timekeepers was 110° 20' 48", and we were about six leagues to leeward of the point, which then bore south 5° east of us. From this bearing it appears that the land we had in sight was not the point we were seeking to close with, for it could not bear south of us if its latitude is correctly determined. The most prominent land to the westward bore south 15° west of us.
After the observation, the wind being south-south-east, variable to the east, a strong breeze, we changed tacks and stood close-hauled on the tack heading south towards the west until six in the evening.
This tack brought us a little nearer the coast, from which, at four o'clock, our estimate put us five leagues off. The coast then showed from south 34° east to south 8° west. The land was extremely high and lofty, as may be seen in the drawing I give of it, and in the aspect it presented we in no way recognised the north-west point we had passed so close to two days before, although our latitude was very nearly the same.
At sunset fresh bearings were taken, and the land in sight bore on the following points of the compass:
The land to the east, trending south, east 27° south
The highest part of the same land, which was in its middle, south 22° east
The farthest visible point of the southernmost land, south.
In view of these bearings and the ship's position, we held on the same tack until six o'clock, when we went about. The wind was then south-south-east, variable towards the east, and the sea somewhat heavy. In the soundings taken during the night, from sixty to one hundred and twenty fathoms, we found no bottom.
The course for the night was set close-hauled on each tack, the tacks being changed at midnight and at four o'clock. During the night the weather was fine and clear, and the breeze fairly fresh from south-south-east.
***(this is in fact page 272)
Bearings of the land
On the second at sunset, the easternmost land, trending south, bore south 67° east.
The highest part of the same land, which was also its middle, south 22° east
The rest of the land in sight lay due south.
[2V p. 270***]

Bearings of the western point of Eendracht Land.
On the third at noon, the point forming the north-west extremity of Eendracht Land east 56°30' south
The reef joining this point east 55° south
The east north point forming the entrance of Willem's River east 87°30' south
The south point of the same river south 1° west
The land extending to the south of Willem's River south 18 west
To the north and east of the north-west point, one of the islets reconnoitred a few days
before could be seen bearing east 55° south, a second east 15° south.

1801-07-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At daybreak the mainland was sighted from S 11° 15' W to S 33° 45' E; at 8 it could be seen from S 10° E to S 65° E. At noon in 21° 28' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 20' 48" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 47' NW. The land from S 5° E to S 15° W.

1801-07-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NE to ESE. On the morning of the 3rd we laid out the port anchor, the currents setting ESE.
1801-07-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third of Thermidor, in the morning, we closed with the land, the wind being south-south-east, a pleasant breeze, and we came in search of that north-west point of the mainland after which we had been running for several days. At half past nine it was nearly abeam of us at a distance of a league and a half, and at ten o'clock we hove to to await the sun's passage across the meridian and observe the latitude. Meanwhile several angles and azimuths were taken, and at noon we observed the ship's latitude to be 21° 33' 5" south, the point then bearing east 56° 30' south of us, which would fix its latitude at 21° 36'. That is to say, little different from the latitude the Dutch chart gives it, reckoning from the reef of the mainland and not from the reef that stretches a little out to sea off this point, on which the sea could be seen breaking in an extraordinary manner, from the height to which it rose as it spread over the rocks there.
I should very much have liked to reach the anchorage the charts show, but as I was to leeward of it and the current and the leeway were carrying me to the north-west, there was no likelihood of reaching it by beating to windward, all the more so as the breeze had freshened a great deal and we should have had to reef the topsails. Besides, the coast seemed to me hard to land on, and although the wind was blowing off the land, the sea broke all along the shore with enough force to prevent a longboat from coming alongside it.
At noon we took the bearings of all the most remarkable points, and they bore as follows. The longitude of the timekeepers was 110° 35' 1" for No. 27 and 110° 2' 5" for No. 35.
The point forming the north-west extremity of Eendracht Land east 56° 30' south
The reef joining this point east 55° south
The east point, forming the entrance of Willem's River, east 87° 30' south
The west point of the same river south 1° west
The land extending to the south of Willem's River south 18° west.
To the north and east of the north-west point,
one of the islets sighted a few days before could be seen, bearing east 55° south
and another east 15° south
These two islets could only be seen from the mastheads, and they belong to those we had coasted along a few days before, whose position relative to the point of the mainland I have given.
From the observed latitude, our bearings and the ship's position, it seems certain that the English and French charts place this point too far north.
The French chart puts it in 21° 30' south
Arrowsmith's chart in 21° 20'
Robertson's chart in 21° 5'
And the Dutch chart in 21° 35'
Everything leads us to believe that the Dutch chart, which we have often found at fault in its latitudes, is accurate for that of this part. The configuration of the land is also very well detailed on it, and when one compares it with that of the land itself, there is no mistaking it.
I also think that the islands to the east of this point are placed too far to the east, not excepting the Dutch chart. Having completed all our observations, we stood north-east under all sail
, all sail set, and we soon lost sight of the land as well as of the bottom.
When we came to heave to north and south of the point I have just spoken of, we had at first found bottom at 35 fathoms, sand and rock. Then we had it at 40, brown sand. The leeway while we were hove to having carried us to the north-west, at noon we found it at 55 fathoms, muddy sand.
From the north-west point to the entrance of Willem's River, the land presents itself in the form of an island whose two extremities can be perfectly distinguished, and it is for this reason that those who do not know there is a river there still think it an island, joined, it is true, to the other point by a reef on which we saw the sea breaking with quite as much force as on the north-west reef, and I believe that even in the calmest weather a boat could not pass over it.
One sees from the bearings of the two points of land forming this entrance how narrow the opening is, since at the short distance we were from it, it is only 3° 30' by the compass.
I think that our observations on the lie and the placing of this point on the chart, and of our track since our landfall on the Leeuwin coast, will prove satisfactory and will serve hereafter as a basis for the lie of the whole of this coast, which the Dutch seem to have visited with care and on which they would no doubt have settled had it offered them the resources they hoped to find there. But a country that has neither fresh water nor a harbour for the safety of ships could not suit them. Nor, in time to come, will it suit anyone to seek to settle there, at least in this part.
1801-07-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. At 5.45 the high land of the mainland from S 5° W to S 34° W; the island taken for the entrance to the Willem River from S 27° E to S 57° E and from S 62° E to S 78° E. At 10 hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At noon in 21° 33' 5" of latitude observed and in 110° 35' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 16' NW. The high land of the mainland S 48° W. Willem Island from S 18° W to S 1° W and from S 2° E to S 33° E. The east point, which bore from us S 33° E at 6 miles, is surrounded by reefs stretching as far as S 35° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course N 45° E. At 8 Citizen Le Bas was to take the watch, but the commander, who had had some difficulty with him that morning, forbade Bonnefoi to have him woken and took his watch himself. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. The commander hove to at noon under the lee of an island which he took for the entrance to the Willem River. From the deck two islands could be seen, one from S 33° E to S 2° E and the other from S 1° W to S 18° W; and the space between these two islands, from S 2° E to S 1° W, is what he took for the river's mouth. But from the topgallant crosstrees I saw, as did several other people, the two islands joined by a chain of reefs awash, on which the sea broke. I saw land as far as the eye could reach to the south, an islet in the S 35° E and another in the S 75° E.

1801-07-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. In the afternoon weighed the starboard anchor and let go the port one, veering a range of 80 fathoms. At 11.15 p.m. the current turned back towards the ESE.
1801-07-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Having taken a new point of departure on leaving the north-west point of Eendracht Land, I set the course north-east, and we held to that point of the compass with a pleasant breeze from south-south-east, variable to south-east.
On the third, at sunset, we shortened sail, although we had lost the bottom at sixty fathoms and had sighted no land on the horizon.
During the night of the third to the fourth the weather was fine, the wind in the same quarter, and we kept the same course. But at that time, the lead having brought up 56 fathoms, coarse sand, I had her hove to until daylight while we went on sounding, so as to learn in which direction the leeway of the ship, or the currents if they were stronger, would carry us.
Judging from the soundings up to six o'clock on the morning of the fourth, it appears that they carried us to the east, since the depth decreased, whereas the ship's leeway should have set her to the north-west; we then had fifty fathoms, fine grey sand.
On the fourth, at daybreak, we resumed our course to the north-east, the wind being east-south-east, a pleasant breeze. And at sunrise a land was sighted to the south-east from the mastheads, which at eight o'clock seemed to extend to east by south; I presumed, from the course we had made, that it must be the continuation of New Holland and not the Rosemary Islands, which, according to the latitude Dampier gives them, and even our charts, although it is not the same, could not bear on that point of the compass from us. I thought, too, that if, as Dampier says, there is a chain of islands stretching as far as the mainland, I could not fail to fall in with one of them by keeping to the north-east and before passing 20° of latitude. That is why I did not alter it. Besides, the wind would have carried us away from them rather than brought us nearer.
At eight o'clock the lead gave no more than 37 fathoms, and I expected to see the land at any moment. But at nine o'clock it was 46 and at ten o'clock 50, which made us lose hope of falling in with it as promptly as I should have wished.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 20° 6' 47", which put us very nearly in that which the charts give to the Rosemary Islands. The longitude given by the timekeepers put us in 111° 29' 45" by No. 27 and in 110° 53' 39" by No. 35.
From the course we have made since leaving the north-west point of the mainland, I believe I have grounds for thinking that the chain of islands of which Dampier speaks does not extend, as he says, so far to the east and south of these Rosemary Islands, and that the openings that may occur in it, if indeed there are islands to the south of the Rosemary Islands, are much wider than he states, since one could pass through the channels they form without sighting the lands that may lie to the north as well as to the south.
On the evening of the fourth we found the sea heavy and were even obliged to furl our topgallant sails to ease the masts. The course was still on the tack heading north, edging east as much as the wind allowed.
At sunset we had no bottom at 76 fathoms, but at eight o'clock we found it at 82, grey sand.
During the night the weather was fine and we lost the bottom. The wind was much the same.
1801-07-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E as far as the eye could reach. At 6.30 filled and stood on under all sail, the course N 45° E. At noon in 20° 6' 8" of latitude observed and in 119° 29' 4" of longitude by No. 27. At 5 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. Variation 2° 21' NW.

1801-07-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and bright. A light breeze from WSW to N and NE. At 4.30 p.m. slack water; at 5 it set east.
1801-07-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, in the morning, the weather continued fine, and towards six o'clock the wind went round to east-south-east, varying towards the south. We held on the tack heading north by east until ten o'clock, and I then took the tack to the south, under all sail.
Some time after sunrise we were visited by several tropicbirds with red bills and tails. It was the first time since our arrival on this coast that we had met with this kind of bird. Although a few are sometimes seen when making the Isle of France [Mauritius] and Bourbon [Réunion], we had not met with any like them since our departure.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 19° 8' 48", and the longitude of our timekeepers, reduced to the same hour, was for No. 27, 112° 21' 12", and for No. 37 (sic), 111° 41' 48". The daily loss this timekeeper had been showing for some time gave us serious doubts as to the soundness of its results.
On the evening of the fifth we held on the tack to the south until half past five, when, the course taking us too far to the west, we put her on the starboard tack.
