The breeze had by then had (sic) greatly diminished, and there was every appearance of a calm for the night. We were mistaken, however, for we had a pleasant land breeze from south-south-east to south-east which carried us on to the east.
At eight o'clock the lead was cast and we had bottom at 90 fathoms, grey sand. At ten o'clock none was found at one hundred fathoms, nor during the rest of the night, which was very fine and clear, with not a cloud to hide the light of the moon from us.
1801-07-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. Saw tropic birds. At noon in 19° 8' 35" of latitude observed and in 112° 21' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 59' NW.

1801-07-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from WSW to SE by way of south. The chief quartermaster, coming to report to the captain on his observations of the tides, brought back a pewter plate found on Dirk Hartog Island bearing a Dutch inscription; the captain had another placed beside it and planted a national flag. Shortly afterwards he embarked in his boat.
1801-07-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth the weather continued fine through the morning, and the wind went round from south-east to east-north-east, a light breeze. I expected it to freshen as the sun rose above the horizon, but my conjecture was not borne out, for there was little wind, and at noon we were almost in a flat calm.
At half past seven we went about and took the tack to the south, under all sail, seeking to approach the land.
At noon the observed latitude was 19° 14' 7" south, and the longitude by the timekeepers put us in 112° 49' 4" by No. 27 and in 112° 4' 47" by No. 35. That observed by five sets of distances between the sun and the moon gave 1° 40' more to the east.
Shortly after the meridian altitude had been observed, the wind went round to south-west and south-south-west, which made us take the starboard tack, standing south towards the east. The breeze was very light at first, so we made little way, but at sunset it freshened and we advanced a little, the lead in hand.
At eight o'clock, finding no bottom at 60 fathoms, we held on our course. At midnight we had it at eighty fathoms, mud, and we were then almost becalmed, the wind at south, variable to south by west.
At one o'clock the bottom was found to be mud at 72 fathoms. It was the first time we had found bottom of that kind. At three o'clock it was the same but at 80 fathoms, and at five o'clock we found 87.
For the rest, the night was very fine and the sea calm. We had nothing to complain of but the calm, because I supposed that the currents would carry us to the north-west.
1801-07-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine, warm weather, the wind a light breeze from E to south. At noon in 19° 14' 10" of latitude observed and in 112° 49' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 31' NW.

1801-07-26.journal_anonyme: A hazy sky, a choppy sea, a fresh breeze from SW to W. Burnt priming to show our position to the small boat. At 2 a.m. it was back.
1801-07-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh the calm lasted until nine in the morning, but the wind then went round to the south-west, and all day we had a pleasant breeze from that quarter of the horizon. We took advantage of it to close with the land, which I hoped to sight before nightfall, and so as not to lose way I did not have soundings taken during the day.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 19° 30' 17", and the longitude of the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 113° 46' 40", and for No. 35, 112° 57' 35". The dead reckoning of the distance run in the 24 hours gave six minutes more to the south than the observation.
During the evening the wind went round from south-west to west-south-west, and we were still standing to the south.
After sunset, not having sighted the land, I had soundings taken, and we had, at 32 fathoms, a bottom of grey and red sand mixed with small broken shells. The mainsail was then furled, and at seven o'clock, having no more than 29 fathoms, the same was done with the topgallant sails and the staysails. At eight o'clock the bottom was at 28 fathoms, although we had made little way in that last hour.
As my intention was to come to anchor in twenty fathoms if I found good holding ground, I continued to stand south and even south-south-west, the wind having gone round to the west. But at midnight we still had twenty-five fathoms, the calm having prevented us from making headway. Nevertheless, I had the foresail brailed up and (we) continued on our way under the topsails. The soundings from midnight to four o'clock were between 24 and 23 fathoms, still good bottom.
Towards evening, shortly before sunset, we had seen a great number of whales, which appeared to us much larger than those we had seen off Eendracht Land. This was a warning that we were in moderate depths of water, for it has not seemed to us usual to meet with them in 50 and 60 fathoms, and according to our observations they keep more generally in twenty fathoms and under than above.
All night the sky was very fine and cloudless. The light of the moon gave us a horizon of at least three leagues' extent, yet we did (not) make out the land in spite of the shallowness of the water.
1801-07-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light and a fresh breeze from south to W. From 10 until noon we crossed several tide rips whose direction seemed to be NNE and SSW. At noon in 19° 30' 0" of latitude observed and in 113° 51' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 54' NW.

1801-07-27.journal_anonyme: Squally weather with rain, a light air from NNE to north.
1801-07-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, a little before five in the morning, being in 21 fathoms, we sighted the land on the larboard bow. We put her head to the north to wait for daylight, and as soon as it began to dawn we made the land out much better.
At six o'clock we resumed the tack to the south, and at sunrise the land we had in sight appeared to us in the form of an island whose south-western part was much higher than its south-eastern. From the mastheads other lands could be seen in the distance, stretching as far as the eye could reach, which were judged to be the mainland, although we could not yet make out the lower lands that seem to join together all the heights we could see on the land, and which at first glance looked like as many islands as there were hillocks.
However that may be, we continued our course to the south, but the depth decreased so rapidly that before we had made more than a league there were only fifteen fathoms. We did not alter course for all that, but at nine o'clock, having no more than nine to nine and 1/2 fathoms, I anchored on a good bottom of red and grey sand, because opinions were divided about the land we had in sight, which was at least four leagues from us. Some maintained that it was an island, and others that it was the land of the mainland.
As, of all our charts, only that of the Dépôt shows an island on the coast where we found ourselves, in the latitude of our dead reckoning, which put us in 20° 17' south, I thought it proper to verify the fact. I accordingly had my longboat hoisted out and gave the command of it to Citizen Ronsard, to go and reconnoitre the land and take soundings along the course he would follow to reach the part that appeared to us the easternmost.
The boat, well manned, left the ship at nine o'clock and stood to the south with a pleasant breeze from the west. After it had gone, I also sent the small boat to take soundings to the east, and I remained at anchor to await the return of these two boats.
At noon the observed latitude was 20° 20' 0" south, and the longitude of the timekeepers put us in 114° 5' 31" by No. 27 and in 113° 15' 24" by No. 35, because this timekeeper was losing daily on the lead it (had) gained over the other.
After the meridian altitude had been observed, the small boat I had sent to take soundings to the east of the ship, not noticing that the wind and the current were in its favour, went off without realising it much farther from the ship than the limit I had set for it, which was a league at most, so that it was obliged to drop its grapnel, but made distress signals to us, and as I did not know what not knowing what it might be, I got under way at once to go and meet it. On the way we made to join it we never had less than 9 and 10 fathoms, sand mixed with red gravel.
At two o'clock we anchored again, having joined and hoisted in our small boat, which I feared would not arrive which would not have arrived that day, nor even during the night, the breeze having freshened considerably and being really too strong for it, had I not gone to meet it.
Shortly before sunset we saw to the north 55° east a very considerable eddy which several people believed to be nothing but a tide-race. But I do not share this opinion, and I am persuaded, on the contrary, that it is a shoal with little water over it at low tide. I am all the more inclined to believe what I put forward as certain because every time the sea has shown us the same effect and we have held on the same course, lead in hand it is true, the depth has suddenly decreased, and in less than ten minutes we went from 14 and 15 fathoms to 9 ½ and 10, which obliged us to change course at once.
After sunset, having had no sight of my longboat and the breeze continuing strong, I no longer expected its return before the next day, hoping only that the wind would drop in the night.
However, as the wind was fair and they had provisions for only one day, it might be that he would try to return on board, and in order to show him the new position of the ship, whose getting under way he had perhaps not noticed, I gave orders for rockets to be fired every hour. During the night of the eighth to the ninth the weather was very fine and clear, but the breeze was still very strong from the west and the sea heavy. As we were on a good bottom with sixty fathoms of cable out, the ship held firm on her anchor and we were not obliged to veer out a longer scope. Towards two o'clock it began to fall calm and the sea became smooth. At the turn of the tide the sailors set about fishing, but their attempts were not successful, for they caught nothing.
Bearings of our first anchorage on the north-west coast
of New Holland.
The west point of a land having the appearance of an island south 38° west
The east point of the same land south 20° west
The lands presumed to be those of the mainland extending from south 5° west to south 30° east
This land presented to us the aspect given in the drawing I had made of it, and the anchorage where we lay in 9 fathoms of water put us five leagues from the nearest coast.
On the lands we are inclined to believe are those of the mainland, several fairly high hillocks could be made out in the distance, but not the low lands joining them to one another.
1801-07-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 4.45 a.m., having sighted land to the south, we bore up for it and made it out to be an island. At 8 its east point bore from us south and the west point S 10° W, 15 miles off; the mainland could be seen as far as S 45° E. At 8.45 we anchored in 10 fathoms, red sand, the west point of the island bearing S 11° 30' W and the east point S 7° 30'. The mainland being very low, only its highest points could be seen from the deck, and they looked like so many islands. The nearest to the east point of the island bore from us S 6° E, the second S 16° E, the third S 24° E and the fourth S 29° E. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Ronsard to survey the island; the small boat, although deep with water, left at 9.30 to sound 3 miles to the east. The current was then running 1.3 knots. At noon 20° 19' 59" of latitude and 114° 5' 53" of longitude by No. 27 were observed. The small boat was seen anchored 6 miles to the east with a signal at her mast, which made us think she needed help; and having no boat to send her, we went to her with the ship. We got under way at 1 and bore up for the boat; at 2 we anchored very near her and she came aboard (variation 1° 21' NW at the anchorage). Citizen Baudin, midshipman, who was in charge of her, told us that after sounding 3 miles to the east of the ship (as ordered) he had tried to come back aboard, but that the current had carried him away and he had been obliged to anchor and set all his crew to baling out the boat, which they could never get free of water. We lay anchored in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, the west point of the island bearing S 21° W and the east point S 17° W; a rise of the mainland south, another S 9° E, another S 20° E. In the N 51° E the sea formed an eddy that seemed caused by a shoal. During the night a rocket was sent up every hour.

1801-07-28.journal_anonyme: Misty and squally weather, light rain at intervals. A fresh breeze from SW. At noon the tide began to turn to the westward.
1801-07-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, in the morning, the weather was fine and the breeze light, though still from the west to south-west quarter. The sea was calm as well, and at sunrise I expected to see my longboat on its way back to the ship. But having no sight of it, I feared it had allowed itself to run aground and that this was the cause of its delay.
However, at seven o'clock it was seen from the mastheads, and it turned out to be it was a long way to the west of the spot where we lay at anchor. At nine o'clock it was on board, and Citizen Ronsard, who commanded it, not having noticed our change of anchorage, had left the shore at moonrise, flattering himself that with the breeze then blowing he would be on board before midnight. But having searched for us in vain by the bearing he had taken of our first position, and finding himself in deeper water than that of the anchorage where we had been at his departure, he decided to beat about during the night so as to find us more easily at daylight. He had seen nothing of all the rockets we had fired during the night.
As soon as he had arrived we got under sail and ran along the coast until seven in the evening, keeping in ten, eleven and sometimes twelve fathoms of water, but in general the bottom proved proved very uneven.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 20° 20' 13", and the longitude of the timekeepers put us by No. 27 in 114° 8' 51 and by No. 35 in 113° 14' 21". The weather was then very fine and the wind almost calm. In the morning we had had it from south-south-east to south, but in the afternoon it came back to the west, a pleasant breeze, and we made a little way, heading for the land, which then bore east-south-east of us.
At about five o'clock I saw ahead of us an eddy like those we had met with before. I at once gave orders to steer two points to windward so as to leave it to starboard, but on approaching it, lead in hand, the depth, which had been twelve fathoms, suddenly fell to eight and a half. I at once stood north-east, and the depth increased as quickly as it had decreased. We passed within a mile of this shoal, and the sea broke on it as on a reef.
At sunset I had a view taken of the lands in sight, and it will be seen in the drawing I give of them how low they are in this part. We then had no more than ten fathoms of water, and yet they could scarcely be seen
from the deck. The effect the sight of this coast produced on me truly showed me what ought to be called low and drowned lands. And although Dampier says they are of middling height at low water, I believe that had he seen those we are running along, he would have expressed himself differently. For the rest, as I hope soon to be at the place where he made his landfall, we shall be able to verify whether what remains for us to see is more pleasing than what we have just passed.
During the evening we saw four or five great clouds of smoke at various places along the coast, so there is no doubt that this part is inhabited. But the fires that produced them seemed to us to be somewhat inland.
At seven in the evening, the weather being fine and the breeze moderate, I decided to anchor until daylight. I preferred this course to that of remaining under sail a little offshore to pass the night, which would have taken me too far from the land and which the winds from east-south-east, or at least from south-east, that I had to expect, would not have allowed me to close with easily. The bottom was then nine and a half fathoms, coarse sand mixed with very small red, brown and black stones, with a few fragments of small broken shells.
Bearings of our second anchorage on the north-west coast of New Holland
The easternmost point of the land in sight east 30° south
The southernmost land to the west, also in sight, south 22° 30' west
The middle of the land abeam of us east 74° south
The bottom was nine and a half fathoms, coarse gravel and sand.
As soundings were taken every hour during the night to find out whether the tide rose and fell at the anchorage we occupied, it was observed that it fell by two fathoms and rose by as much.
Report of Citizen Ronsard, acting Ensign,
commanding the longboat for the reconnaissance of the land
"Citizen Commander,
"Setting out the day before yesterday, in accordance with your orders, to reconnoitre the land nearest the anchorage, I steered south by west, sounding at every mile run by my reckoning. I constantly found a bottom of sand or gravel in eleven and a half fathoms of water, up to three leagues from the ship. Then the depth decreased gradually, and at four leagues I had no more than ten fathoms. I found the same water over the space of a league. The bottom was also of the same nature, except for one sounding that brought up black mud. At noon I reckoned myself more than five leagues from the ship and a league and a half from the land. I then had eight fathoms of water, fine sand. The west point of the land I was steering for bore south 20° west of me, and the lands of the mainland towards the east, at a great distance, stretched away to the south.
"As we advanced, low lands were discovered to the east which seemed to form islets, and this is all the more certain because, when we were farther in, the lands of the mainland could be seen at a great distance to the south and south-south-east. From then on the depth decreased, and I found no more than three fathoms. The sea being calm, and finding myself abreast of a small sandy cove, I made for that spot all the more willingly as landing there seemed to me easy and even convenient. Although my wish was to push farther south in order to make sure,
"as you had recommended to me, whether the land off which the ship was anchored was an island or joined to the mainland by some lower land, I nevertheless decided to drop the grapnel in this cove, which seemed to me which seemed to me (sic) so well suited to the safety of the boat. Once I had entered it, it seemed to me from the marks the tide had left that it might have fallen eight feet, and I beached the boat on a very smooth sandy shore where (it) lay in complete safety. The care of it was entrusted to two men, and I disposed of the rest so as to turn them to the best account and at the same time to the greatest use. Two were assigned to walk along the seashore to collect shells, if any were to be found, and two others were ordered to go some distance inland to gather plants, and I told them always to choose, among those they might come across, the ones that had flowers or at least fruit.
"As for myself, accompanied by Mr Fortin, I attended more particularly to the nautical observations with which you were good enough to charge me, and accordingly I set off overland to the east-south-east, taking with me a man to carry any natural history specimens that circumstances might put in my way. On my way I came upon two springs of running water which, by my estimate, might yield about three casks a day and perhaps more. Thus water and wood can be taken in on this land, although the vegetation there is not abundant.
"Having reached the summit of the highest rocks in the eastern part, I became convinced that this land is an island separated from the mainland by an arm of the sea of about seven or eight miles, and as the tide was almost at low water when I was at that spot, I could distinctly see in the middle of the channel the banks that lie in the stretch of sea which (sic) lies there makes it an island. If there is water near these banks, this place might offer a good anchorage.
"The low lands to the east, which form the second of the islands, are separated from this (sic) where I was, which is some four or five miles (sic) high. But it forms a striking contrast with the one where I landed, in that (nothing) is to be seen on it but sand covered with scant vegetation, whereas the one where I was is high, steep and full of rocks. At the west point of this island there is a bank that extends a good way out to sea in the same direction.
"I reckon that high water took place ashore at noon. At the end of the ebb the tide appeared to me to have fallen 20 feet, and at the top of the flood it had risen only to within four feet of the mark of the highest tides.
"The currents inshore seemed to us to set from east to west, but they did not seem to have much strength as we approached the coast.
"The soil of the island is for the most part a mass of basalt prisms piled one upon another. Often, and particularly on the summits of the peaks, they rest on one of their smallest faces. Some of these rocks tower so high above the others that from a distance they might be taken for tree trunks; elsewhere they look like sloping walls. In the valleys they are heaped up without order and seem to have fallen there from the neighbouring slopes. For the rest, all these lavas have very sharp edges, except for those beaten by the sea and those found in a kind of barcanes (barances?) or gullies where it seems that the rainwater has rushed down in torrents. Their outer surfaces are covered with an oxide of iron that gives the whole island a reddish-brown colour, so that the parts which are
"washed away from them by the waters seem to supply nourishment to vegetation, being then mixed with a little sand which the winds have no doubt carried there. Each of these deposits among the rocks forms a kind of garden very pleasing to the eye and gives off a most agreeable scent. It is in such places that I collected the plants I have brought back, having taken care to choose what seemed to me likely to be of interest to botany (sic).
"I saw no trace of inhabitants on this land; one might nevertheless be inclined to think that the natives of the mainland sometimes go there, since I came across some tree trunks at the foot of which fires must have been made. Another observation may also confirm this conjecture, in that I found in various places fragments of lava freshly broken, without its appearing that they had been shattered by the impact of other masses that time or the wind might have brought down. These breaks had the colour of undecomposed basalt.
"The only living creatures we met with were a kangaroo of the large species and another quadruped the size of a large dog, fawn in colour, with a long, bushy, hanging tail. I saw it from too far off to be able to give a more exact idea of it, and when I gave chase it was not possible (for me) to cut off its retreat or force it to pass closer to me. An eagle, a crow and several gulls, as well as two kinds of small land birds, showed themselves to us.
"We also came upon a snake as thick as one's arm, more than five feet long, grey and covered with scales, a multitude of very large grasshoppers, flies like those of France, ants of the large and small kinds, and several black butterflies with white spots.
"The seashore yielded various kinds of shells, of which I have brought back a sample.
"At nightfall, having cleared up the point of geography for which I had been sent, I prepared to return on board as soon as the boat should be afloat, and at ten o'clock we embarked. On getting under way I steered north by west. Inshore the sea was calm, but when we were in the offing it became high and heavy. After standing on for about five hours and finding myself in eighteen fathoms of water, which put me well to seaward of the ship, I went about so as to keep myself in shallower water until daylight. But at sunrise, not seeing the ship, I stood back towards the anchorage I had left, and it was while returning towards the land that we sighted her; I at once took the shortest course to rejoin her."
Report of the chief helmsman, Fortin, employed on the same
expedition as Mr Ronsard.
(no written or figured entry)
1801-07-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW to WNW. At 10.30 Citizen Ronsard arrived in the large boat; he had walked over the island and found very good water there. It is well wooded and landing is easy; he brought back many shells, among them two of the kind called the admiral, which led the commander to name this island, and another small sandy one 2 miles from it which we cannot see from the ship because it is awash, the Admiral Islands. At 10.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon in 20° 20' 13" of latitude observed and in 114° 10' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 50' NW. At 1 bore away S 67° 30' E towards a very thick column of smoke. At 4 took the bearing of the Admiral Islands from S 33° W to S 67° 30' W, the mainland stretching from S 15° W to S 67° 30' E. Several columns of smoke could be seen at different points of the mainland, the most conspicuous being the one we were steering for. At 4.45, the water having shoaled, we bore up gradually as far as N 56° 15' E. At 5 an eddy formed by a shoal was seen abeam at two cables. At 5.30 took the bearing of the Admiral Island S 34° W, the sandy Admiral island S 5° W, the mainland in sight from south to S 50° E. At 7.30 we anchored in 10 fathoms, grey sand, the mainland bearing from S 24° W to S 57° E (this bearing was taken the next day at daybreak). At the anchorage the currents set east and west and run 1.5 [knots].

1801-07-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from SE to SSE falling away a great deal. Two men were sent to Dirk Hartog with 15 days' provisions to make signals to the Géographe should she appear on the coast. About 8 in the evening the captain held a council on what course to take in the separation we found ourselves in; it was decided that we should wait as long as the quantity of water we had on board would allow, which was down to 70 casks.
1801-07-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, as soon as we had properly made out the land and taken its bearings from the mastheads, for it could scarcely be distinguished from the deck, we got under way with the intention of running along the coast. But at sunrise the wind shifted from south-south-east to south-east, and we lost sight of the land all the more quickly because, in my opinion, it could not be made out at a distance of more than three leagues.
At nine o'clock, the breeze having freshened to a stiff gale, we were forced to take a second reef in the topsails, and then continued on our course, lead in hand, keeping close-hauled. Throughout the morning the soundings were fairly regular, from 10 to 15 fathoms, over a bottom of sand and coarse gravel mixed with small broken shells.
At noon we observed the latitude as 20° 0' 33", and the longitude by our timekeepers was 115° 6' 0" by No. 27 and 114° 7' 57" by No. 35. It is difficult to account for the daily loss this timekeeper has shown since we left Shark Bay, unless one supposes that one of the two received some severe shock when they were taken ashore, which, however, is not likely, given the precautions that were taken to protect them from such an accident.
In the afternoon the wind veered as far as east, and the breeze having abated, we shook out the reefs it had obliged us to take in the morning.
At sunset we could see nothing of the land, which is all the less surprising since we then had 23 fathoms of water.
During the night of the 10th to the 11th the wind came back to south-south-east, and we continued to keep close to the wind in order to close with the land. But as the breeze was very light, we made very little progress. The bottom over which we passed during the night was 25 to 30 fathoms, grey sand, sometimes mixed with coarse gravel and small flat stones of various colours.
1801-07-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SSE. At 6.30 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 11.30 took the bearing of a column of smoke S 5° E, no land being in sight. At noon in 20° 0' 30" of latitude observed and in 114° 46' 0" of longitude by No. 27.

1801-07-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene. Winds from ENE to NW, almost calm. Saw several meteors in the NE.
1801-07-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, at eight o'clock, we had the sea breeze, and it was much more moderate than on the previous day. We went about onto the southerly tack, having then 35 fathoms of water, wishing to close with the land, from which the direction of the wind that had blown the day before had carried me rather too far out to sea.
At noon we were already in 21 fathoms, but without sight of any land. The latitude had been observed as 19° 40' 52".
In the afternoon the wind varied from east towards north, and for two hours the soundings were very irregular, between twenty and eleven fathoms, which made me fear that we were in the neighbourhood of some shoal. However, as I wished to make the land, which could not be very far off, since for half an hour past several columns of smoke had been seen at different points of the horizon.
At two o'clock the lookouts, who for half an hour had been reporting land to windward of us, and which we could by then see from the deck, informed us that there lay before it, at a considerable distance, a shoal on which the sea was breaking heavily. Several persons went up to the mastheads to examine it, and as their report confirmed what the lookouts had announced, I at once had every man sent to his station, so as to be ready to go about promptly should the case require it. And I held on my course as if there had been no danger at all, merely taking the precaution of sounding often. But as the bottom still kept between eleven and fourteen fathoms, I wished to push on further. However, I was told several
times that we were drawing very near to the breakers that lay to windward of us, which made me decide to go about onto the other tack.
We then took bearings of the land in sight, which appeared to us in the form of an isolated point touching the mainland, which we could not see, although several persons, especially among those who see nothing but islands, declared that it was one. If that be so, it must lie a fair distance from the continent and have its inhabitants, for several fires could be clearly distinguished upon it.
The northerly tack took us away from the land, and although there was very little wind, at sunset it could scarcely be seen from the mastheads, bearing then south-east by east.
During the night of the eleventh to the twelfth the wind was very variable until eleven o'clock, and almost calm. It then shifted to west-north-west, and we steered on the northerly tack towards the east, keeping between twenty and twenty-five fathoms. At midnight we steered north-east over the same depths. We then had a moment of anxiety about the weather we might have on the following day. The sky had clouded over and the barometer had suddenly fallen a line and a half. The hygrometer, however, varied little, and Citizen Péron remarked that if there were to be bad weather, it would be stormy rather than rainy.
1801-07-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to N. At noon in 19° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 115° 10' 27" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 1° 39' NW. At noon a very low land was sighted in the S 75° E, having the look of a sandy island. The sea broke on it with force, especially at its southern part, where a chain of breakers began and stretched away to the south. This islet cannot be far from the mainland, for from the topgallant crosstrees I saw a smoke in the distance. At 5 the sandy islet (seen from the crosstrees) bore S 56° E. At 8 calm; at 9 a fresh breeze from WNW, the course was given N 22° 30' E and at 10, N 33° 45' E.

1801-07-31.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW in strong gusts. At 4.30 the tide began to turn.
1801-07-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, at daybreak, the sky had a rather ugly look, the whole horizon from west to north being laden with heavy, thick clouds. However, as the horizon from west to south was very clear, and the wind lay in that quarter, it seemed to us that we should have fine weather, which indeed proved to be the case, for the wind, freshening from south to south-south-west and south-west, drove away the clouds, and by ten o'clock the sky was perfectly fine.
At sunrise, although we were in 31 fathoms, we nevertheless sighted the land from the maintop. It appeared in the form of a fairly high hillock, bearing south 5° west. I have no doubt that this land is some rise in the interior of the continent, despite its resemblance to an island, for we have so often been deceived by a similar appearance that one cannot be too wary of it.
At six o'clock I had the ship steered east-north-east, but as we were sounding every half hour and saw the depth increase instead of diminishing as I had expected, we steered east, and I held this course until noon, still surprised to see the depth increasing when I expected to see it diminish very rapidly, as it had done on the preceding days.
During the morning there was a pleasant breeze from south to south-south-west, and we made good way to the east.
At noon the latitude was observed as 19° 18' 41", and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us, by No. 27, in 116° 12' 18", and by No. 35 in 115° 14' 7".
As this latitude put us at a considerable distance from the land, and the lead confirmed it, I had the ship kept close-hauled on a south-south-easterly heading, the wind being then south-west, in order to make the land before nightfall and see whether this part of the coast was more approachable than those we had seen before.
At half past two we began to see several columns of smoke rising from different points of the coast, but even so the land itself could not be seen from the topgallant crosstrees. We continued under all sail until sunset without sighting it from the deck, but it could be made out fairly well from the mastheads. We then had eleven and twelve fathoms
(of water), and the two extremities of the land in sight bore, the first east 55° south, the second south 33° west, and the middle of this land south. It was not possible to take a view of it, since it appeared to lie absolutely level with the sea, without any rise that could be noticed.
However, as I had resolved to approach the land as closely as possible, I continued to stand to the south, but at six o'clock, having suddenly passed from eleven fathoms to eight and a half, I went about and stood out to sea, this course having seemed to me the most prudent.
During the night of the 12th to the 13th the wind was at first south-west and fairly moderate, but it shifted successively to south-west, and at midnight we had it at south-south-east, a strong breeze, which obliged us to take a second reef in the topsails. At that time the lead gave 32 fathoms, which made me decide, so as not to stand too far from the coast, to heave to on the larboard tack until daylight, sounding every hour, in order to learn whether the current was setting us towards the land, or the leeway carrying us out to sea, as I supposed.
For the rest, it blew a strong breeze at moonrise, and this was a bad omen for the weather we might have on the following day.
1801-07-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to south. At midnight the course was given N 45° E, and at 4, N 56° 15' E. At 6 took the bearing of the sandy islet S 5° W. The course was given east. At noon in 19° 17' 51" of latitude observed and in 116° 8' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 56' NW. At half past noon lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 3.30 a column of smoke was seen in the S 45° E, no land being in sight. At 5.30 it was seen stretching from S 35° E to S 33° W, and a large column of smoke S 57° W. At 6, having only 9 fathoms, went onto the port tack. At midnight hove to with the port side to the wind; a strong breeze.

1801-08-01.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a fresh breeze from S by E, SSE and ESE. At noon we got under way under topsails. We sounded and found from 6 to 9 fathoms, sand, coral and broken shell. At 3 let go the starboard anchor in 9 fathoms. Bearings of the anchorage: the visible NW end of Dirk Hartog W 6° S; the SE end of the same island W 39° S; the middle of the island within the bay E 12° S.
1801-08-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth, in the morning, it continued to blow a very strong breeze, as I had expected. At daybreak we found ourselves rather far from the coast, since the depth was 36 fathoms, and I therefore had the ship steered close-hauled to close with it, the wind being south-east, varying to south-south-east. After sunrise it grew so strong that we had to take the third reef in the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail, but at about eleven o'clock it began to slacken. The sea had become heavy, and although our course ought to have brought us nearer the land, the soundings, which at noon were 39 fathoms, made it plain enough that the currents and the ship's leeway were carrying us away from it, setting us to the north and perhaps even to the north-west.
At noon the latitude was observed as 19° 10' 12", and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us, according to No. 27, in 116° 24' 31", and according to No. 35 in 115° 22' 16". In the course of the morning several distances of the sun from the moon were taken, the results of which gave (no figures), whence there resulted a difference from the timekeepers of (no figures) " " " "
" " " " " "
" " " " " "
In the afternoon we continued close-hauled, crowding sail as the wind then allowed. The breeze had already begun to moderate, but it was not until sunset that we were able to shake out a reef from our topsails, and this did us little good, for shortly afterwards the calm became so complete that the ship would scarcely answer her helm. The sea, however, was still running high, and it was only at eight in the evening that we found it calmer; the depth was then 45 fathoms.
From the observations made on the previous day and on this same day to determine the variation of the compass, we found it to be (no figures) north-east, which did not agree, given our longitude, with the observations of the navigators who preceded us. But this remark is not surprising, since its change since those times must necessarily have brought about one in the variation.
During the night of the thirteenth to the fourteenth the calm lasted until ten o'clock,
and then we had the land breeze, which, light at first, became fairly strong when it shifted to south-south-west. Nevertheless we continued to stand to the east, lead in hand and under little sail, in the hope of not being far from the land on the following day. However, as the lead gave constantly between thirty-eight and forty fathoms, it seemed to me that we could not be as near the coast as we supposed, even though at sunset several columns of smoke had been seen rising from the land without the land itself being sighted.
1801-08-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course given east. At noon in 19° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 116° 22' 9" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 15' NW.

1801-08-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a clear sky. A light breeze S, SE, SSE and ESE. At 10 the tide turned to the SE.
1801-08-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, after sunrise, the wind varied from south-south-east to south-east by south, and the breeze was strong enough during the morning not to allow us to shake out a reef from our topsails, which had two reefs in. The sea was even rather heavy, and we had forty-two fathoms of water, which showed us clearly that our track had carried us further north than our dead reckoning allowed.
All morning we stood to the east as far as the wind permitted, and it was not without astonishment that we saw the depth increase, whereas it seemed to us, from the trend the charts give to the land, that it ought to diminish. The quarter in which the wind held did not allow us to go about onto the other tack, so we continued to run east, edging a little to the north.
At noon the latitude was observed as 18° 48' 29", and the longitude by the timekeepers, reduced to the same time, placed us, by No. 27, in 117° 7' 45", and by No. 35 in 115° 55' 29". The distances of the sun from the moon taken the previous day having been found faulty, owing to the difficulty met with in taking them, they were taken again during the morning, and the result was that we were in 119° 7' 36", which gave an enormous difference from the timekeepers, since by No. 27 there was a difference of 1° 59' 34" west, and by No. 35 3° 11' 53", likewise west. What can be the cause of so great a difference in timekeepers whose rate had varied so little before we left Shark Bay, the astronomer Bernier persisting in saying that they suffered absolutely no shock or jolt, either when they were put ashore or when they were brought back on board?
At about two in the afternoon the breeze began to abate a little, but much less than it had done on the preceding days, which made me keep the reefs in the topsails.
At four o'clock we had bottom in 34 fathoms, but at sunset we had no sight of land, which led me to hold the same course. At eight o'clock the depth was thirty fathoms, and as some of our charts show this same depth, in the latitude where we reckoned ourselves to be, almost right against the land, it seemed to me that it would not be prudent to hold the same course for long, so that at half past eight I brought to, the leeway being bound to carry me to the north and consequently away from the coast.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth the wind was south-south-east and at times variable to south, a strong breeze, the sea nevertheless fairly smooth. At midnight the breeze, far from diminishing as it usually did, only increased, so that we had to take the second reef in the fore topsail. During the rest of the night the wind blew with the same force, and everything foretold a stiff gale for the following day. The lead, which at eight o'clock gave 29 fathoms, increased during the night and until daybreak by 6 fathoms, so that at sunrise we found (ourselves) in 35.
1801-08-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to south. At noon in 18° 44' 17" of latitude observed and in 117° 8' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 42' NW. The lunar distances gave 118° 35' of longitude. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds SSE to SE, almost calm. At 2 p.m. the large boat took 15 days' provisions to go and survey Shark Bay.
1801-08-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, having only thirty-five fathoms of water at sunrise, we made as much sail as the wind, which was blowing very hard from the south-east to south-south-east, allowed us to carry, and I still kept the hope of soon seeing the land.
At ten o'clock the depth passed suddenly from 35 fathoms to 39, which led me to believe that we were drawing away from the land instead of approaching it. But at noon, having again found thirty-five, I changed my opinion. It was vexing that the wind did not allow us to make a little way to the south in order to approach it more quickly. Nevertheless I still kept the hope of sighting it before nightfall, if, that is, the direction our charts give it was correct.
At noon the latitude was observed as 18° 6' 34", and the longitude by our timekeepers, whose results, since the last observation by distances of the sun from the moon had given us a difference of 2 and 3 degrees, seemed to us very uncertain. However, as we could not give them up entirely, we found ourselves according to No. 27 in 118° 5' 34", and according to No. 35 in 116° 79' 54".
In the afternoon we continued to stand to the east, making as little northing as possible. The lead gave 35 fathoms fairly constantly, and it was only at sunset that the depth began to diminish a little. At that time we had no sight of the land, nor even any sign that could lead us to suspect we were near it. We did indeed see a few black and white boobies which, at sunset, were heading south, no doubt to make for the land, but it was not possible for us to reckon how far they might have to go to reach it.
After sunset the breeze began to diminish, and the wind having drawn a little more towards the south, we were able to steer east by south-east. At eight o'clock the depth was 30 fathoms, and I held the same course until we should come into 25 fathoms, giving orders that I should be told as soon as we had reached it.
At half past eight, although we had not sighted the land by nightfall, I noticed a glow on the horizon to leeward of the ship which seemed to me could only be caused by a fire on land. I at once sent a man aloft as lookout in the maintop, and without climbing any higher he saw the fire perfectly well at the spot where I had told him to look. However, as the depth was still great enough for us to have nothing to fear, I held the same course until nine o'clock, but then, seeing the fire on land perfectly clearly from the quarterdeck, and having only 23 fathoms of water, I had the ship put about, and we steered south until one o'clock in the morning, when, the breeze having shifted to east-south-east and blowing very hard, I hove to on the starboard tack so that the leeway would carry us to the north.
During the rest of the night the sky was very fine and clear, but from time to time we met with very violent gusts from south-east to east-south-east, the direction the wind took. The depth increased gradually, and from one o'clock in the morning until five o'clock the next day we passed from 28 to 35 fathoms, fine sand mixed with small broken shells.
1801-08-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course east. At noon in 18° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 118° 3' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 2' NW. At 8.30, having sighted a fire ahead, we went onto the port tack. At 9 the fire bore from us N 50° E; it could no longer be seen at 10.30. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky a little cloudy. A light breeze from ESE to SSE and south. At 2.15 p.m. the corvette made sail until 6 p.m., when we anchored in 8 fathoms, sandy bottom. On the 16th at 11 a.m. a thick smoke was seen on the mainland which had risen all at once. The captain, wondering what could have caused this kind of eruption, sent off the small boat under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq.
1801-08-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, in the morning, it continued to blow a very strong breeze from the south-east to east-south-east. At sunrise the lookouts did not see the land, and I do not know why, for at a quarter past seven we sighted it perfectly, and the way we had made from sunrise until that time was not great enough for for (sic) us not to have seen it earlier.
However that may be, when we saw the land from the mastheads, it bore east 36° south. From south to south by south-east a very thick smoke could also be seen, which no doubt came from the fires we had noticed the day before. The depth was then 35 fathoms.
At nine o'clock we saw the land perfectly from the deck, and it appeared to us much higher than any we had seen until then, that is to say, since we had been running along the north-west coast. I flattered myself that this character of the land would allow us to approach it closely enough to examine it well, since I presumed that the water would be deeper than we had found it in the places where the land is low and drowned, and which had not allowed us to come near it. However, at noon we had no more than fourteen fathoms, whereas an hour before we had found twenty.
The meridian altitude at the same time placed us in 17° 28' 26", and the longitude by our timekeepers was, by No. 27, 118° 26' 13", and by No. 28 (sic) 117° 5' 54".
During the morning we made every effort to take a few series of distances of the sun from the moon, but the breeze was so fresh that we could not manage it, because of the motion our instruments suffered from it despite all our precautions to steady them. According to the bearing taken at noon, the land extended from north 57° east to south 52° east.
As the land then lay to leeward of the rhumb on which we were steering, I had the ship steered north-east, and we soon perceived land trending still further towards the north. From noon until four o'clock the lead gave fairly constantly from 15 to 12 fathoms, a fine bottom of sand and small broken shells, but then it passed to ten fathoms and even to 9, which made us bear away by two points in succession so as to keep in ten fathoms. The breeze had greatly abated, and we were carrying our topgallant sails, though with two reefs in the topsails.
The land we coasted along in the afternoon, at a distance of four leagues at most, is very recognisable and of a far less wild aspect than any we had seen since we had been on this part of the coast. Behind the seashore two fairly considerable rises could be made out, covered with verdure; the first, that is to say the top of the dunes, was likewise covered with plants or shrubs, which made the prospect pleasant. The ground running down to the seashore was of two quite distinct colours: in some places it was a fairly bright red, and in others a very white sand, which seemed to promise an easy landing. My intention at first was not to anchor, but calm having set in after sunset, I anchored in nine and a half fathoms, good holding ground, though with the fear of being obliged to get under way during the night if the breeze should come to blow as hard as it had on the preceding days.
During the evening we saw a great number of fires all along the coast, but several were so large that they did not seem to us likely to be the places where the natives stayed. It was probably a conflagration in some parts of the woods, for the smoke was so great that the air was darkened by it.
During the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth the weather was fine and the breeze almost calm until about two o'clock in the morning, when it began to freshen from the south-east, but it was moderate. Although we were at anchor, I had given orders that soundings be taken exactly every hour, so as to learn whether the flood or ebb of the tide was noticeable at the spot where we lay. We were surprised not only to perceive none, but also to find that the current had little strength, since despite the little wind there was, we constantly lay head to wind, a thing we had not experienced at our other anchorages, although the breeze there was much stronger.
Bearings from the anchorage.
The northernmost land in sight, north 57° east
The southernmost land, likewise in sight, south 5° east
The middle of the land, that is to say that which lay abeam of us, south 68 east.
The soundings from noon until the time we anchored were fairly regular, from 15 fathoms to nine and a half.
1801-08-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 1.30 the previous day's fire was sighted in the N 33° E. It disappeared at 4. At 6 filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 7.15 the land was sighted from the crosstrees from east to N 68° E. At 10 it could be seen from the deck; it appeared fairly high, in the S 56° E. At noon in 17° 28' 16" of latitude observed and in 118° 26' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 14' NW. The land from S 64° E to N 68° E, with several columns of smoke at different points of the coast. At 1 bore away N 45° E and ran along the coast, on which we saw a countless number of fires and smokes. At 4 bore away N 22° 30' E. The northernmost land in sight N 54° E; low, wooded land which appeared to form a bight S 85° E; a great white cliff S 53° E; a white headland S 22° E. At 6 anchored in 9 fathoms, coarse sand and broken shell, the land bearing from S 5° E to N 57° E. An immense fire burned all night in the N 68° E.

1801-08-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from SW to W and N. At 2 p.m. got under way under topsails and staysails. At 5 anchored in 5 fathoms, fine sand. At 9 p.m. the small boat was back and reported that the smoke we had seen came from the fires of the Aboriginal people, gathered to the number of 9, men and women together.
1801-08-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, in the morning, I intended to send a boat ashore to examine the coast and visit the country, but before dispatching it I wished to make sure of the weather we should have after sunrise, for the way the sun had set the evening before, and the look it had at its rising in the morning, seemed to foretell a strong breeze for the day.
This forecast proved no false one, for scarcely had the sun risen five or six degrees above the horizon when it began to freshen to a strong breeze, which decided me to get under way at once. As soon as we were under sail I shaped my course to approach the land a little more, wishing to run along it in eight or nine fathoms so as to examine properly a sheer-cut point which had the appearance of a cape, from which the land was likely to take another direction. But after an hour's sailing, having passed all at once from nine and a half and even eleven fathoms to seven, I had the ship steered north in the hope of finding more water, and it was not without astonishment that I saw it diminish to six and even five fathoms, although we were perceptibly drawing away from the land. From eight o'clock until nine we bore away by degrees from north round to west, still still (sic) over a bottom of six fathoms and six and a half fathoms, and it was only then that the depth began to increase.
At half past nine, being in fifteen fathoms, I again put the ship's head to the north, having, on that point of the compass, several pieces of land to windward of us which looked like a number of islands. We stood towards them until ten o'clock, but finding no more than eight fathoms, we had to bear away again to north-west to get into deeper water. We were then certain that the land in sight was a chain of islands which are probably joined to one another by reefs or sandbanks with very little water over them, since in several places the sea could be seen rising to a great height upon them. The first two islets, that is to say those we had doubled, are of small extent and can hardly be seen at more than three leagues' distance. Two others, to the north of these, are larger and may be two leagues in extent from north to south, but off the northern point of the first there is a reef which stretches far to the north and on which the sea breaks. We were then steering north-west, and the depth was from eight to fifteen fathoms. When we had doubled these two islands and the reef off the
last, we saw no more land except to the north-east and at a great distance, and I then resumed a north-north-easterly course, keeping close-hauled. But the depth having passed suddenly from 15 to 9 fathoms, it seemed to me that we were on the edge of a bank. This was all the better confirmed when the lookouts I sent up to the mastheads reported that they could see (it) perfectly by the change in the colour of the water, and that it extended as far as to leeward of us. However, as we were at a great distance from the land, since it could scarcely be seen, I held the same course, lead in hand. But not for long, for a quarter of an hour later we found no more than six and a half fathoms, which obliged me once more to bear away as far as north-west by west to find deeper water. We held this course until noon without the depth increasing very rapidly. By then, however, we had eleven fathoms and sometimes twelve.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 53' 30", and the longitude by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 118° 28' 3", and by No. 35, 116° 47' 54".
After noon, being in fifteen fathoms, I steered from north-west by west to north, coming up into the wind a little every quarter of an hour, so as to round at my ease the northern part of the bank we had discovered. At two o'clock the depth began to diminish again, and we fell once more into seven and a half fathoms, although we were then steering north-north-west. We had to bear away again and steer north-west. This same depth of seven to eight fathoms lasted nearly half an hour, and at last it passed to 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 between half past two and three o'clock. From three o'clock until half past three, steering north-north-west, we passed suddenly from 15 to 18 fathoms and from 18 to 20. Although there was very little wind, the sea was somewhat agitated, and I concluded from this that we were entirely clear of that bank, on which, with a fairly strong breeze, the sea had been very calm and smooth.
At four o'clock we trimmed our sails close-hauled with all sail set, in an effort not to stand too far from the continent. The depth was then 22 fathoms.
At sunset there was no sign of land, and we had the ship steered north towards the east as far as possible.
During the night of the 17th to the 18th the breeze was very light, or, to put it better, we lay almost becalmed until eleven in the evening, when a light breath of wind came from south-south-east. The depth was then 27 fathoms. At midnight it was 23, and we were steering north-east by north. This shoaling made me think that we were not very far from the coast. But at one o'clock the lead gave 30 fathoms, and at two o'clock 35. We then steered north-east, and I held this same course until daylight under all sail, finding no bottom at 35 fathoms. The breeze had by then increased, and we were making fairly good way, with the wind at south-east.
Note: At half past seven in the morning M. Picquet, who was on watch and entirely taken up with badgering the helmsmen because he thought the clock was not going fast enough for his impatience, vexed me all the more because the noise he was making prevented me from working in my cabin, where I was busy at the time. As we were standing in towards the land with the lead going, the helmsman charged with that duty called out to him several times: M. Picquet, 9 fathoms ½, M. Picquet, 9 fathoms ½, M. Picquet, 9 fathoms ½, without his paying the slightest attention. I then raised my voice and said to him in my turn: M. Picquet, it is the lead you must attend to and not the clock. His vanity, no doubt offended by my remark, made him come forward, with a very reprehensible show of temper, as far as the door of my cabin, which I take care to keep open both day and night when he is on watch, and he said to me in so many words: Upon my word, Sir, you are
very ridiculous to object to my watching the clock. My answer was that the only impertinent and ridiculous person on board was himself, and so that he should have no further occasion to put me in the position of punishing him as he would have deserved, I removed him from the command of a watch until such time as I could be rid of him altogether.
The verbal order I gave him not having seemed sufficient to him, he asked me for one in writing, and I accordingly sent him the following letter:
"The Commander of the expedition to Citizen Picquet,
"Your repeated impertinence, your conduct in the service and your uncivil replies, every "time I have reminded you of your duties, having at last exhausted my patience, I inform you that "you will no longer command a watch on board.
"The safety of the ship and of all the persons on board requires this precaution of me. "I only regret not having taken it sooner" . N.B.
So as not to disturb the order of the service, I took over his watch, which I kept until our arrival at Timor. The midshipman who stood it with him was placed with M. Freycinet, and I kept with me the one who stood it with him.
1801-08-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At 6 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet, officer of the watch, having the glass set and asking the chief quartermaster whether note had been taken of the time elapsed since getting under way, the commander, who was in bed, called out to him from his cabin that he was tiresome, that it was a question of the lead and not of the glass, and that if the watch wearied him he might leave it, and that he would take it himself; and he did take it. At noon in 16° 53' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 36' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 42' NW. Took the bearing of a sandy islet S 89° E and the north point of the land in sight N 74° E; at a short distance from that point a bank could be seen stretching far away to the N 22° 30' W, on which the sea broke. Since 8 a.m. the bottom has been very uneven. We were no doubt on the edge of a bank whose direction is at first N by NW, then runs NW, and then takes a northerly direction again. We tried to keep near the course N 45° E but were always obliged to bear away. At 1 we lost sight of the land; at 7 calm. From 8 to 11 the course made good was N by NW; from 11 to noon NW; from noon to 3.30 NW by N; and from 3.30 to midnight N and NE by N. Commander Baudin gave me orders to take the watch in Citizen Piquet's place, and I kept it until Timor.

1801-08-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to SSW and south.
1801-08-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, at sunrise, we had no sight of the land, from which, nevertheless, we could not be very far, judging by the course steered during the night, supposing, however, that the trend our charts give it is correct, which seems very doubtful, since having steered east-north-east for almost the whole morning with a pleasant breeze from south-east to south-south-east, we did not sight it at noon, nor for the rest of the day.
The observed latitude was 16° 1' 27", and the longitude deduced from the timekeepers placed us, by No. 27, in 118° 59' 0", and by No. 35 in 117° 26' 29".
In the evening there was little wind, and we had observed for several days past that as soon as the sun had passed the meridian the wind died away by degrees, and by the time it set there was so little that the ship could hardly keep steerage way.
All day we had the company of a great number of birds, such as boobies, gulls and frigate birds. Particular notice was taken, however, of a flight of ducks which circled the ship two or three times. Whales appeared only in small numbers, but much larger than any we had seen until then.
From sunrise until sunset the lead varied from 40 fathoms to 30, with various bottoms suitable for anchoring.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth the weather was fine and the wind calm until midnight. As I was then on watch, having taken over M. Picquet's, I had the dredge cast several times; besides bringing up several fine objects of natural history, it also served to show us the direction of the currents, which were then setting us to the north-west. Although we were heading east during the calm, the tide ran so strongly that the dredge acted on the ship like a kedge anchor and came straight from ahead, and it was from that direction that we hauled it back on board.
At midnight the wind shifted to south and then to south-south-west, a pleasant breeze. We spent the rest of the night standing on under our topsails, still with the lead in hand, so as not to be taken by surprise by too sudden a shoaling of the water.
1801-08-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to E. At 2 a.m. the course was given N 45° E and at 5.30 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 16° 0' 14" of latitude observed and in 118° 59' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 29' NW. At 7 calm; the dredge was put over and brought up many objects of natural history.

1801-08-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south to SSE. At 4 a.m. the longboat was put in the water together with the small boat and the dinghy, and most of the gear was embarked in them for the camp set up ashore to repair the longboat.
1801-08-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, in the morning, it continued to blow a pleasant breeze from the south-south-east. We stood to the east under all sail without sighting land, which could not fail to surprise me, for I believed myself much nearer to it, although the lead was still at 50 fathoms. We therefore had to crowd sail in order to come and make it, and this we did, holding on our course to the east.
At noon the latitude was observed as 15° 40' 57", and the longitude by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 119° 46' 7", and for No. 35, 118° 13' 59".
Shortly afterwards the lookouts reported land a little to leeward of us, and we ourselves soon saw it from the deck. It appeared at first in the form of an island of moderate and very even height, but we soon saw the low land that accompanied it at both ends, and we were convinced, by the extent we could see, that it was the continent. As I intended to anchor on this coast, I continued to stand towards an inlet that lay before us, in the middle of which we met a very strong current which prevented us from advancing and made us drift towards the part of the land that bore north of us, a little towards the west. The lead then gave 20 to 25 fathoms, but the bottom was so bad that there was too much risk in anchoring there. I therefore decided to retrace my steps, but I had to steer west and even west-south-west in order to clear several banks which we sighted and of which we had until then known nothing. The breeze was very light, but the current was setting us to the north-west. Very fortunately we drew away from the land, drifting past abeam of a bank of considerable extent on which, despite the calm, the sea was breaking heavily.
A little before sunset we saw, awash, several sandbanks from which the sea had just withdrawn, and it is no doubt these that M. Saint Aloüarn meant to indicate on his chart by the great number of dots which appear there and seem to form so many islands. It is possible that between these banks and the mainland there is a channel through which one could pass, but I think it is not for ships such as ours to go looking for them. This supposition may be all the better founded since, between the mainland and the banks that had just been uncovered, a fairly large stretch of water could be clearly seen where the sea appeared calm.
At sunset we were already a little way out to sea, and the lead gave 25 to thirty fathoms, but the bottom was so bad that we had to give up anchoring for the night, unless forced to it by some unforeseen circumstances. It was then calm, and the current seemed to be setting south with considerable speed.
From six o'clock until ten we made very little way with the help of our sails, and the depth was diminishing enough to make us uneasy about where the turn of the tide might carry us. I therefore had a chain bent to the second anchor so that we could use it if need be. This precaution proved unnecessary on this occasion, for the breeze having come to us a little earlier than usual, we drew away with the help of our sails. During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the sky was very fine and the wind south. We kept close-hauled on the larboard tack under little sail, sounding continually. We were surprised to see that, as we stood out to sea, the bottom was always coral and rock, all the more so as it was the first time we had met with a bottom of this kind on the coast. _____________________________________________________________________________________
1801-08-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At midnight the course was given east. At noon in 15° 40' 41" of latitude observed and in 119° 46' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 36' NW. Land was sighted to the north; at 3 went onto the port tack. At 4 it bore from us from north to N 45° E, and at 5.30 from N 22° W to N 52° E. Calm at 5, the current setting us in the N 45° W; at 9.30 a light breeze. We could not anchor at nightfall, the bottom being coral.

1801-08-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds almost calm, the horizon loaded.
1801-08-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, in the morning, having been hove to since four o'clock, we ran north-east until eight o'clock, and then I had the ship steered east-north-east to close with the land, which we had sighted at sunrise and which bore from east 16° south to east 26° south. As we drew nearer to it, we became convinced that it was the same part of the coast we had examined the day before.
From eight o'clock until noon we had a fairly pleasant breeze from the south, and we were steering east-north-east when the lookouts at the mastheads reported a sandbank on which the sea was breaking heavily. Nevertheless, as we had no bottom at 30 fathoms, I did not alter course until we could clearly see from the deck the bank and the breakers that had been reported to us. To clear this danger we were obliged to bear away as far as north, and we passed about a league from it without finding bottom at 25 fathoms. Having cleared it, we came up into the wind by degrees to resume the course that was to bring us back to the coast. The danger we had just passed appears in the form of a small islet of very white sand, high enough in its middle to be seen by day at two leagues' distance, but it is covered by the sea at its northern and southern ends by shoals on which the sea rolls with force and which extend half a league in the same direction.
To the east of this bank could be seen land which we judged to be that of the continent, at a distance of about five leagues, appearing chiefly to extend from the east, trending towards the north. At ten o'clock, losing sight of it, we hauled a little closer to the wind to bring it nearer, but at half past ten we sighted a second sandbank covered by the sea, which we passed at three-quarters of a league without finding bottom at 45 fathoms. A third, bearing on our starboard bow, obliged us to bear away once more, and at half past eleven, the sea appearing clear to us, we again put the ship's head north-east by east and east-north-east.
From what had happened to us from yesterday noon until the same hour today, it appears that the coast is hardly approachable from 16° forty minutes of latitude to 15° 17', which is the latitude we observed at noon.
By the longitude of our timekeepers we were, by No. 27, in 119° 46' 7", and according to No. 35 in 118° 13' 59". The depth was 45 fathoms, sand and coral.
In the afternoon the breeze died away as it had done on the preceding days, so that, making very little way, we did not sight the land at sunset. Despite the little wind there was, we shortened sail at eight o'clock and held the same course under our topsails only until five o'clock the next morning, sounding every hour.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st the weather was fine and the sky damp. For several days past the hygrometer had stood at 95° and sometimes above, while the barometer remained fairly constantly at 28 inches 2 lines. The behaviour of the hygrometer seemed to foretell a change of weather at the new moon, and I expected it all the more because, since we had been on the coasts of New Holland, each new moon had brought about some changes.
The wind was very light and variable during the night, from west to south-west, and the lead gave between 35 and 40 fathoms, sand and coral, which made the bottom unsuitable for anchoring. During the day and part of the night the dredge was cast several times, and besides a few branches of coral, it also brought up fragments of pieces of the same kind and several fine fan-shaped sponges, as well as fine jellyfish, very difficult to preserve whole despite all the various methods we have tried in order to do so.
1801-08-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 4 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E, crowding sail. At 7 the same land as the day before was sighted from aloft, from S 64° E to S 74° E. At 8.30, having sighted ahead at a short distance a sandbank awash, we bore up north. Having cleared it we resumed our course, and then saw in the S 45° E low land on which the sea broke furiously; at 10 we lost sight of it. At 10.30 a sandbank was seen abeam to windward (S 22° 30' E) 2 miles off. At noon in 15° 17' 40" of latitude observed and in 119° 56' 35" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 34' NW. At 1 the course was given N 78° 45' E. We passed close to a shoal of fish over which there was a very great number of birds; from a distance it might have been taken for a sandbank with the sea breaking on it. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty, a light breeze from SSE, SSW and SE. At 1 a.m. the tide turned to the NW.
1801-08-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, at half past five in the morning, the weather being very fine and the sea calm, we made all sail, having a light breeze from the south varying to south-south-east, and steered east by north-east until sunrise, and at seven o'clock I had the ship's head put to the east to come and make the land, which we sighted at ten minutes to eight. It then bore from east 22° south to east 50° south.
During the morning the breeze increased a little, but it was so light that the current carried us further than the wind
At noon the latitude was observed as 15° 8' 30", and the longitude by the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 120° 49' 40", and for No. 35, 119° 9' 39".
The most north-easterly land in sight then bore, as taken from the deck, south 75 east, an island south 50° east, and the southernmost land south 22° 30' east.
During the morning the nature of the bottom changed entirely, and instead of finding it sand and coral, as we had had it for some time, it was a fine grey marl into which the lead sank entirely. Over this bottom, the first of this kind we had found, we cast the dredge. But it brought up only mud, of which we made a few balls as samples. Once dried in the sun, they soon became very firm. The mineralogist Depuche thinks that, for the fineness of its grain, it is far superior to what is used in the pottery made in France.
In the afternoon the breeze died away entirely, and the currents, according to our dead reckoning, seemed to be setting us to the north-west at one mile an hour. All evening we had in view a great number of birds of the booby and gull kind. We also crossed several tide rips which seemed to us very swift, and which made us cast the lead several times for fear of finding ourselves on some bank.
At sunset we had in sight a long chain of islands, behind which the continent could be seen, but it lay at too great a distance to give a reliable bearing of it. All the islands in sight seemed to offer some openings where shelter might perhaps be found, and for this reason I decided not to stand away from them during the night, so as to be able to visit them the next day. The breeze having freshened a little after sunset, we continued to run along the land until eight o'clock, and then we put the ship's head out to sea under our topsails.
Bearings at sunset.
The chain of islands and islets we had in sight extended from east 3° north to east 60° south
A stretch of fairly high land, which we judged must form part of the continent, bore from east 87° south to east 42° south to east 87° south.
During the night of the 21st to the 22nd we had either calm or very unsteady winds for as long as it lasted. At midnight a fire was thought to be seen at east 33° 15' south, but without being certain of it, it was judged to be one from a fairly bright glow that was thought to be seen on the horizon.
The lead, which was cast every hour, was very regular, and we never had less than 35 fathoms, always a bottom of marl into which the lead sank up to the upper end of its height, which was 15 inches.
At about two o'clock, the officer of the watch having informed me that it was beginning to freshen from the south, I had the ship hove to with the larboard side to the wind to wait for daylight, continuing to sound.
1801-08-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm and a light breeze from W to SSW. At 5.45 filled and stood on N 78° 45' E under all sail. At 7 the course was given east; at 8 the mainland was sighted from S 40° to S 68° E. At 10 a flat calm; until noon the current set us S 67° 30' E. At noon in 15° 8' 10" of latitude observed and in 120° 44' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 44' NW, the mainland bearing from S 22° E to S 75° E and an island S 50° E. From noon to 3 the current set us N 45° W. At 3, a light breeze, shaped the course east. At 5.45 took the bearing of the northernmost part of the mainland in sight N 87° E; a sandy islet A S 85° E; the nearest land (of the mainland) S 63° E; an islet S 30° E; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 3° E. At 7.30 a dull roar was heard, caused by a tide rip which we crossed. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack.

1801-08-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy and the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE.
1801-08-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, at daybreak, we found ourselves only about a league from the coast, and it was not without astonishment that I saw myself so near the land with 35 to 36 fathoms of water, for my dead reckoning put me nearly four leagues off. I can only attribute this to the rapidity of the current, which must have carried us to the south-east at great speed. But since we were sounding every hour, the shoaling of the water ought to have made it known to me; at least that was how I had thought I could guard against such effects.
The islet abeam of which we found ourselves was a rock about half a league in extent, very high in its middle, its two ends terminating, to the south, in a low point which stretched a good league out to sea, and to the north in low land which joined it to another, larger island. All these parts could be seen very well at sunrise, but as the tide was then flooding, they were soon covered by the sea, so that all round the island nothing could be seen but a very extensive line of breakers, on which the sea, despite the calm, was breaking heavily.
