Had the flood not carried us to the north, and fairly briskly too, we should have been obliged to anchor so as not to fall upon them, and to wait in that position until the wind allowed us to double it. We passed a short league off this danger, having 36 fathoms, good bottom of marl Bearings at sunrise:
The islet most in view, east
A chain of islets, some larger, some smaller, from east 10° south to east 63° south.
A stretch of land presumed to form part of the continent, from east 29° south to south 5° west.
All the islands and rocks that fringe the continent in this part lie very far from it and do not appear to offer passages for small boats except at high water, although several present wide openings. It is, moreover, easy to judge from the colour of the water, which is very white, that there must be very little of it in most of the channels these islands form.
In view of our observations, we therefore had to give up stopping on this part of the coast. Accordingly, with the help of the currents, for it was almost calm all morning, we drew away a little from the coast and ran along the land that lay to the east of us, edging a little to the north.
At noon the latitude was observed as 14° 59' 43", and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us, by No. 27, in 121° 6' 42", and by No. 35 in 119° 25' 5". Our position laid down on Robertson's chart, which I use because its scale is larger than that of the others, was again at fault, in that it places the land much further west than it is, always according to the rate of the timekeepers as well as by the observations of distances.
The islet abeam of which we found ourselves at sunrise is particularly remarkable for its white colour in its highest parts and brown towards the sea; when seen from two or three (leagues) away, being then level with the water, it appears as a shoal on which the sea breaks with violence.
In the afternoon we had very variable winds, of little use for making progress, and one may say that it was calm rather than wind. The light airs they gave us at times came sometimes from the south, from the south-west, and even from the north-west.
At sunset a large rock which we had doubled presented so singular a shape that I made a separate drawing of it, which will allow it to be recognised by all those who may later have occasion to see it. Whether one comes from the south or from the north, it appears in the form of a very regular barn, but as one doubles it, it takes on exactly that of an
upturned bowl and shows all its regularity to the eye
Bearings at sunset.
A chain of the islets seen earlier bore from east to south
And the one so singular in shape was the southernmost, looking like a barn, while when (we) drew it in the form of an upturned bowl it bore south 20° east.
After sunset we had a light breeze from west to west-north-west until about eight or nine in the evening. As we had seen no land to the north, trending towards the east, at sunset I had the ship steered north-east by east until then, and at eight o'clock we put her head north-east by north to stand away from the coast and have sea room for drifting during the night. The calm having overtaken us again between nine and ten o'clock, we made very little way. I ordered the officer who took the watch at eight o'clock to sound every hour while the depth was over 30 fathoms, and every half hour when it was under, as I did not wish to go any closer to the land than 25 fathoms.
At nine o'clock, having found the depth I had prescribed to him, we went about at once and steered west-north-west, a course that could not fail to carry us out to sea. However, before the calm overtook us, we were still only (in) 28 fathoms, and at midnight in 26. As I was taking the watch at that time, I had a kedge anchor let go and veered out 40 fathoms, the bottom having appeared to us very good and clean.
While the sails were being furled, the land was clearly seen from the yards, and when I had been told that it bore south-east, I soon sighted it from the deck. Although we had no certain knowledge of the time of the tides in these waters, I thought that the ebb was beginning, and in order to learn whether the water rose and fell at our anchorage, I had a sounding lead cast regularly every hour.
At midnight we had 26 fathoms, the depth in which I had had us anchor.
At one o'clock we had 25, and successively until six o'clock the depth diminished, so that by then we had no more than 20, and barely that, so that we recognised that the sea had fallen by six fathoms where we lay, and no doubt more inshore.
The log, which was also hove every hour, gave three knots of speed. For the first two hours it was a knot and a quarter, for the next two nearly two knots, and for the last two a little over a knot. The ship lay head to the current, swinging from south-south-west to south-south-east.
1801-08-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm, and a light and very variable breeze. At midnight a fire was sighted in the S 57° E. At 2 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 5.30 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E. Islet A then bore from us S 5° E; at 8 it bore south, and off its west point there were breakers stretching as far as S 12° W; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 34° W; a fairly conspicuous point of the mainland S 11° E; the northernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 50° E; an islet S 85° E; another east. From 8 until noon a flat calm, the currents setting us S 67° 30' E about 4 miles. At noon in 14° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 121° 5' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 20' NE. Islet A bore from us S 35° W, a second S 40° E, a third S 44° E, a fourth S 46° E, a fifth S 80° E and a sixth S 88° E. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack (heading NE by N). At 8.30 went onto the starboard tack (heading SW by W). At 10.30 onto the port tack (heading NW). At midnight, being in a flat calm, we let go a kedge anchor in 24 fathoms, soft mud. Bearings taken at the anchorage (on the 23rd at sunrise): we were near a chain of islands stretching from S 36° W to S 71° E; island B, the nearest, bore from us S 51° E, 4 miles off. Latitude observed at the anchorage 14° 47' 40"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 121° 25' 0"; the variation NE at the anchorage 0° 7' 20".

1801-08-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze in gusts from S, SSE and SE.
1801-08-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, having ascertained our position, we found ourselves at anchor abreast of a great number of islands, the nearest of which was a good league off. The others extended from east 42° north to south. Most of them appeared to leave fairly considerable openings, so that the hope of finding, among so many islands, a good shelter for ships decided me to send to examine them, particularly in the part that seemed to me best to answer my purpose.
I therefore had the boat hoisted out at once and gave the command of it to Citizen Bonnefoy The naturalists Depuche, Riedelé and Maugé embarked with him, and at seven o'clock they set off. They first steered for the nearest land we had in sight had abeam, and on coming within cannon-shot of the shore they still had twenty fathoms, the bottom of the same nature as that on which we are anchored; but it was impossible for them to land, the whole coast being fringed with reefs on which the swell rises to a great height. They then altered course to run into the inlet I had pointed out to them, but scarcely had they rounded the south point of the first island when they saw it joined to the second by a chain of rocks
awash, over which the tide was already beginning to rise. Nevertheless, they coasted along it as far as its middle, in the hope of finding some gap through which they might pass. But their search was fruitless and they returned on board, some much vexed at not having been able to get ashore, and the others at having searched in vain, to no purpose and in the fiercest heat of the sun, for a place fit for landing.
At noon we observed the latitude of 14° 47' 50", and the longitude by the timekeepers put us, by No. 27, in 121° 24' 54" and, by No. 38, in 119° 34' 59".
This position, laid down on Robertson's chart, had put me over part of the land that he places in this latitude on his chart, so that it was once more demonstrated to us either that our longitude, deduced from the timekeepers and the lunar observations, was wrong, or that he places them much further to the east than the west than they really lie.
From this anchorage we took several bearings, and supposing the rate of the timekeepers passable, or the observations by distances good, it will be possible to correct the chart for this part, whose latitude, moreover, is exact, since it is the result of a great number of observations made in fine weather and at our ease.
The boat having by then returned and been hoisted in, we got under sail to look for a place more favourable for landing. During the evening we coasted a long succession of islands and islets of greater or lesser size. But the largest of all these islands did not appear to us to be more than two leagues from one end to the other. They are generally of fairly considerable height and seem to be joined beneath the water by shoals, on most of which the sea rolls very high, which is no doubt caused by the violence of the currents, for the winds were so light that, in a place where there were none, these shoals would be very dangerous even to boats seeking (to) get into the openings they leave visible between them.
In the afternoon the breeze was very light and we were steering north towards the east, running along the islands we had sighted at two leagues' distance, when the look-out at the masthead reported a breaker ahead of us. We approached it, sounding as we went, until we could make it out from the deck, and we found that it lay roughly north-east and south-west. The depth was then 30 fathoms. Nevertheless we steered north for some time, but seeing that the depth increased, we gradually luffed up and resumed our course north-east by north. We passed four or five miles from this reef.
At sunset, the land bearing from east 3° south to east 21° north, this last part seemed to us to be the mainland, as it appeared behind the islands; see the drawing I give of it.
After sunset I continued to steer east, edging towards the north, in a very light breeze until ten o'clock, and then I dropped a kedge anchor in 38 fathoms, clay and sand bottom.
During the night the speed of the current was measured every hour with the log. At half past ten it was running half a knot and a half and setting south-south-east. At midnight it was running only one knot half a knot in the same direction. The depth was then 24 and a half fathoms, so that it had fallen by 3 and a half fathoms in two hours, the ship having anchored up and down on this depth, taken up and down after she had swung to her anchor.
For the rest of the night the men were busy fishing, but apart from a few mâchoirons, or rather barbels, nothing else was caught. This poor success was put down to the strength of the current, which fouled the fishing lines.
1801-08-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to WNW. At 2 a.m. the current set N by NE and ran 1.5 knots. At 7.15 the tide turned. At 7.30 the large boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey island B, the nearest. At 9.30 he came back without having been able to land, the sea breaking on every part of the island. At noon we got under way, the course N 33° 45' E. At 4 the course was given N 22° 30' E. At 4.30, having sighted in the N 56° E and N 68° E a breaker lying roughly NW and SE and 5 miles off, we steered north; but the water deepening, we resumed N 22° 30' E. At 5 took the bearing of an islet S 87° E, a second S 88° E, an island N 85° E to east, a third islet N 83° E, a fourth N 80° E, a fifth N 78° E, a sixth N 77° E, a large island from N 74° E to N 69° E. At 8 saw a fire in the S 22° 30' E. At 10, being becalmed, we let go a kedge anchor in 38 fathoms, muddy sand. At 10.30 the current ran 5.5 knots setting S 22° 30' E [sic]. At midnight it ran 0.5 in the same direction.

1801-08-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE.
1801-08-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, we were still at anchor off a chain of islands, of which I counted seven, running from east 10° south to east 69° south. The middle of the island nearest to us bore east 45° 30' south, at a distance of about two leagues. This island, like those in its neighbourhood, is high and steep, but surrounded by reefs which make landing impossible and which we could make out perfectly from the deck. I do indeed think, as Dampier remarks, that one could land on some parts of these islands when the tide is high, running one's boat aground on the sand and waiting for the tide to return in order to come off again. The naturalists would dearly have liked me to do so. But quite apart from the fact that I have no boat to put at risk, this land, like all the land we had passed for several days, did not seem to me suited to research in natural history, and above all in botany, for nothing could be seen on it but a few trees scattered here and there, of middling height and of still poorer growth.
At seven o'clock we got under sail with a very light breeze from the south-west, which I hoped would freshen in the course of the morning. We steered first north-east and then took a course more to the east to examine a large tract of land which showed itself to the east by north and then extended as far as east-north-east. The land, at the distance we then were from it, had the appearance of three islands with a fairly wide opening between each of them
At noon we observed the latitude of 14° 16' 58 and the longitude of the timekeepers put us in 121° 50' 32" by No. 27 and in 119° 58' 13" by No. 35. This position, like the previous one, laid down on Robertson's chart, (in the margin: again puts us) over the extremity of the land he marks as the northernmost in this part of the chart. We then saw perfectly well that the lands on which we were heading were truly three islands, with the mainland behind. It seems to me that these three islands are not badly placed on M. St Aloüarn's poor chart, and I believe that he did indeed sight them, though from afar, for had he come within three leagues of them he could not have failed to notice all the dangers that lie more than a league off the coast, on which the sea breaks and rolls enough to make one shudder, were one to be caught among them. The first of these three islands then lay at a distance of three and a half to four leagues at most, bore from us east 23° south.
At half past two in the afternoon we found that we had cleared the reef which guards the approach to these islands. It extended from south 16° east to west 60° south. There is every reason to believe that part of the rocks forming its bar must uncover at spring tides; but in any case, as the sea breaks heavily on it even in calms, it will always be easy for vessels navigating these waters to sight it.
Having cleared the danger I have just spoken of, we hauled up to the wind again, but not for long, for the look-outs at the masthead soon reported another breaker to the east-north-east. Shortly afterwards we sighted it from the deck, and to clear it we were obliged to bear away to the north-east. This one being of much smaller extent than the one we had just passed, and at the distance at which we cleared it, which was no more than three-quarters of a league, there were, as at the other, 35 fathoms of water, sand and clay bottom.
From eight four o'clock until eight we continued on our course, sounding as we went, but as the depth of water gave no warning of the approach of the dangers that may be met at every step along these islands, I had the ship brought to anchor on good ground in 35 fathoms.
During the night of the 24th to the 25th we had a flat calm. The log was hove every hour,
in order to learn, if possible, the strength and direction of the currents. From half past eight until eleven o'clock its speed was one and one-third knots an hour by the log, but much greater judging by the dead reckoning. It set to the south-south-west, and the ship lay constantly swung with her head north-north-east. At half past eleven it was slack water, and at midnight the ship swung her head to the north N south-south-west, the current then setting north-north-east, at the moment of the tide's return on the coast.
The tide rose and fell much less at this last anchorage than at the others, which no doubt comes from the greater depth of the ground on which we lay. The difference in the soundings was no more, for the flood as for the ebb, than two and a half fathoms. Consequently much less considerable than in the places where we had found it to be five fathoms and even five & a half.
1801-08-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SW to NW. At half past midnight the tide turned and set NNE, its speed increasing to 1.5 knots. At 5 it was 0.9, to the north. At 7 it was slack water; we got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, and at 8 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 14° 15' 12" of latitude observed and in 121° 50' 32" of longitude by No. 27. At noon a reef was sighted between the land and us, stretching NW and SE. At 3.30, having sighted from aloft breakers ahead (N 67° 30' E), the course was given N 45° E. At 4.15, having sighted breakers from N 67° 30' E to N 85° E, we steered N 33° 45' E. At 5.30 resumed the course N 45° E. At 5.45 took the bearing of the land [illegible] of the mainland east; an islet S 19° E; the offshore breaker of that islet S 22° 30' E; the west end of a second islet S 11° E and the west end of a third S 5° W. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings at the anchorage: the breakers from N 87° E to S 75° E; the land [illegible] of the mainland S 79° E; the three islets taken at 5.45 appeared to form only one, whose ends bore from us, one S 9° E and the other S 11° W. Calm during the night. From 8 to 9 the current set S 22° 30' W and ran 1 knot; from 9 until midnight it set south.

1801-08-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and serene, a fresh breeze from ESE to south.
1801-08-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, having ascertained the position of the anchorage where we had brought up the day before, at eight in the evening, we took its bearings as follows:
The easternmost land relative to the ship's position, east 11° south
A long chain of breakers from north 57° east to east 15° south
A high land in the form of an island, east 32° south
Another island, to all appearance, east 38° south
A third, very high island, east 81° south
A fairly extensive breaker, south 5° west
And a fourth, very high island, south 5° west.
As soon as the sun rose we prepared to get under sail with a light breeze from the south, varying to south-south-east. Once our anchor was up we steered east thirty-two degrees north, to examine a land which the look-outs at the masthead reported to be ahead of us. In the morning we had very fine weather, but the breeze was light.
At noon the latitude was observed as 14° 2' 6", and the longitude of the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 122° 12' 4" and, for No. 35, 120° 15' 37".
The position laid down on Robertson's chart had put us over all the northernmost lands shown by the charts of and yet we were quite certain that we had not yet reached the latitude of those which the look-outs reported to be ahead of us.
The little way we had made in the morning had changed our position but little relative to the trend of the land. Those furthest ahead of us, however, bore from east 5° north to south 57° west. Within this range there were several islands and islets and a stretch of coast which we judged to be that of the mainland, until we should have proof to the contrary.
It will no doubt be difficult for anyone who sees the ship's log book to make anything of all the bearings entered in it. From the very beginning I used every sort of means and remonstrance to get the officers to pay attention to this work, but all I could say was useless, and as they all thought themselves very learned, I was unable to persuade them to take them in the way I should have wished. It is for this reason that I have trained in my own way one of the quartermasters, in whom I recognised much intelligence, to take them directly for me, and I hope that one will (not) find in them the confusion found in all those of the others.
In the afternoon we continued to advance eastward, edging a little to the north as far as the wind would allow, but its want of strength did not let us make much way until eight o'clock, when I anchored in 35 fathoms, sand and clay bottom. I then reckoned myself abreast of the land which must be the northernmost on this part of the coast. But at the distance I was from it at sunset I had not been able to make out whether it was the mainland or an island, although it presented itself in the latter aspect. But as it was much lower than all those we had passed until then, it is possible that it was joined to the continent by some still lower land, which I put off verifying until the next day.
During the night of the 25th to the 26th the log was hove every hour, as usual, to learn the speed and direction of the currents. As we anchored at the beginning of the ebb, the ship rode head to the current, heading NNE, and its speed until midnight was one and one-third knots; then it fell off noticeably until 9/10 of a knot, when she came broadside on and swung her head to south-south-west, gradually gaining the same speed. On the flood as on the ebb, the sea fell and rose where we lay at anchor by two fathoms only.
During the night it was a flat calm, but the atmosphere was very damp and the hygrometer rose to 98°; the barometer stood between 28 in. 2 l. and 28 in. 5.
In the morning we had seen several sea snakes, much longer and thicker than those we had met with until then, though they were spotted in the same way. The whales had deserted us entirely, and indeed long since, and we saw only a few birds of the booby and gull kind.
1801-08-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to NW. At 7.45 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° 15' E; a breaker was sighted between the land and us. At noon took the bearing of the east point of a land supposed to be the mainland S 73° E; the middle of an island S 68° E; the breaker seen in the morning S 34° E; an islet S 6° W; an island from S 15° W to S 8° E; a second islet S 26° W. In the distance two hummocks could be seen, one S 45° E and the other S 48°, supposed to belong to the mainland. At noon in 14° 2' 6" of latitude observed and in 122° 12' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 14' NE. Shaped the course N 73° E at 4. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy sand. Calm during the night. From 8 to 11 the current set SSW and ran 1.3 knots; from 11 until midnight it ran only 0.9 knots.

1801-08-14.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon the currents set to the SE.
1801-08-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, at sunrise, we took a bearing and a view of our anchorage astern, recognising that the land which we had expected to terminate the mainland to the north-west in this part was yet another island, four or five leagues in extent, but indeed the northernmost land we had yet met with. The following bearing gave us the direction of the land as follows:
The easternmost point of a long, flat island, east 19° south
An isolated peak, east 40° south
A high land having the appearance of an island, east 45° south
Another island, east 47° south
Two isolated peaks which are perhaps on the mainland, east 55° south
A very high land in the distance, with the appearance of an island, east 64° south
The southernmost land in sight, east 69° south
As our horizon was very wide and we had no land in sight from the east round to the north, I thought that the island abreast of which we were anchored must terminate it in this part. So, as soon as we were under sail, I had the ship steered east by south. But as soon as we had rounded the west point of the island I have just mentioned, we perceived ahead of us a very extensive reef on which the sea broke heavily, and which, to clear it at a short league's distance, obliged us to steer more to the north and even for some time north-east. As soon as we had passed it, I resumed the course east, convinced that I would not be long in sighting the mainland, which must lie in that direction. We did indeed sight it at about ten in the morning, and the depth was still the same as that found when we cleared the reef I have spoken of, that is to say thirty-three fathoms. Shortly afterwards there were only
thirty, and we continued on the same course, convinced that we would soon come upon the mainland, as I considered myself clear of all those long chains of islands, islets and reefs which had prevented me from approaching it. I was much deceived in my expectation, for at eleven o'clock the look-outs reported that they could see ahead of us, and even to leeward, a long line of breakers stretching as far as the eye could reach. Nevertheless, we continued to run east to examine the land we had seen, but we soon came upon the reef that had been reported to us, so that we had to bear away to the north to east-north-east to run along it to the east-north-east. We were forced to steer north-east without yet being able to clear it. From north-east we came to north-north-east and finally to north. We would no doubt have got clear of it on this course had the wind not failed us, but the calm having overtaken us at about two o'clock, and the flood carrying us at great speed towards the reefs which were then abeam, we were obliged to drop a kedge anchor in thirty-two fathoms, sand and clay bottom. As it was a flat calm, we merely let our sails hang loose without furling them, so as to be the readier to profit by the breeze should it spring up in the rest of the evening.
At noon we observed the latitude of 13° 52' 16" south, and the longitude of our timekeepers put us, according to No. 27, (in) 122° 36' 55" and, according to No. 35, in 120° 21' 33". A set of distances taken by the astronomer Bernier gave 123° 19', which put him east of No. 27, in which we had more confidence than in No. 35, by 0° 42' 5". I had also taken that day a sextuple distance, the result of which put me in 121° 12' 41", so that I found myself differing from Citizen Bernier by 1° 16' 19" to the west, and from No. 27 by 0° 34' 16".
At four in the afternoon, the time at which we anchored, we took the following bearing:
The visible end of the reef, which seemed to extend to the north-east, east 28° north
An islet apparently attached to the reef, east 5° south The continuation of the same reef extending southward, east 45° south
A fairly high land presumed to belong to the mainland, east 75° south All these points, and the latitude and longitude of the ship, being impossible to reconcile or square with any of the charts with which I am provided, I am provided that New Holland is laid down on them only by conjecture. It was easy, however, to see that that of the Dépôt, though imperfect, was the least bad, in that it gives fairly well the configuration of the land, whose north-west point in this part is indeed formed by a long flat island having on its eastern side a great reef on which the sea breaks heavily, and which we had examined and cleared that morning. It was on the indication of this same chart that I steered east, edging to the south as much as I could with the winds then blowing, when I sighted the second reef it shows, part of which I coasted until the calm obliged me to anchor. I merely thought I could see for the moment that it was not placed far enough north, but I put off verifying its position exactly until the next day.
During the night of the 26th to the 27th the weather was fine and the wind calm. The speed of the current was found to be one and ½ knots from four o'clock until six, setting (to the) N. NE. It then set to the south-west at the same speed. The water stood at the same height on the flood as on the ebb, or at least we noticed no appreciable fall, since during the time we were at anchor.
1801-08-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze and calm, from S to SW. At midnight it was slack water; from midnight to 2 the current ran 0.5 knots and from 2 to 4, 1.5 knots to the NNE. At 6.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 78° 45' E. At 8 took the bearing of an islet D south; several hummocks supposed to belong to the mainland from S 7° E to S 24° E; an island C, off whose east point there is a reef, from S 29° E to S 40° E. At 8.30, having sighted a shoal ahead, we steered N 56° 15' E. At 10 the course was given east. At 11 a chain of breakers was sighted stretching from south to east; we bore up N 67° 30' E and then N 56° 15' E. At noon took the bearing of island C from S 47° W to S 38° W; islet D S 31° W; the hummocks of the mainland from S 23° W to S 3° W; the mainland in sight from S 57° E to S 68° E; the chain of breakers stretched from S 8° E to N 58° E, with a sandy islet in the middle of the breakers N 85° E. At noon in 13° 52' 16" of latitude observed and in 122° 36' 52" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 5' NE. The lunar distances gave 123° 19' of longitude. Shortly after noon the chain of breakers was seen to stretch as far as ahead of us (N 56° 15' E); we steered N 22° 30' E and then N 22° 30' W. At 2.30, being in a flat calm with the tide setting us onto the breakers, we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom, island C bearing from S 25° W to S 22° W and the sandy islet of the breakers S 62° E. At 6 the current ran 1.1 knots to the NNE. At 7.30 it was slack water; it turned shortly afterwards and set SSW. At 10 the current ran 1 knot, and at midnight 0.3 knots.

1801-08-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At 2 p.m. the large boat was back from her mission.
1801-08-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at daybreak, we prepared to get under sail, and at sunrise we were much astonished to see abeam of us a great sandbank, awash, occupying the whole extent we had taken bearings of the day before, on which the sea broke with such force (in the margin: that it rose to a prodigious height). We could make out perfectly several elevations on this bank, formed by rocks of different shapes, which at high water serve to make the danger known from further off, as had happened to us.
As soon as our anchor was up, we set all sail, steering NE ¼ north to run along the bank we had sighted. From north-east by north we came gradually to NE ¼ east, taking care to keep a sharp look-out and to sound every half hour. The depth was constantly 29 and 30 fathoms until half past eight, when we found ourselves in a very considerable tide-rip. At first I paid little attention to it because, ten minutes before we met it, we had had 30 fathoms of water. Nevertheless, I had the lead cast, and it was not without astonishment that I (in the margin: found) myself in 20 fathoms. Five minutes later there were only 15. And at eight fifty there were only eleven. I at once brought the ship onto the larboard tack, and I believe it was high time, for perhaps, had we run on ten minutes longer, we would have been aground, though at a very great distance from the land, since it could hardly be made out from the masthead. Be that as it may, steering north-west, we soon found 15 fathoms and shortly afterwards 20 and 25. As soon as we were in deep water and entirely out of (in the margin: this danger), as the colour of the water showed us as well as the lead, we coasted along its edges (in the margin: of the bank), which were perfectly well defined. We were then steering north, believing we had no further danger to fear. As I was constantly engaged in looking round the ship with my glass, I perceived dead ahead of us, at half a musket-shot's distance, a very white patch on the surface of the water. I immediately had the ship's head put to the NE, not doubting that it was a danger I had seen. The lead was at once cast and brought up 23 fathoms, whereas before there had been no bottom at 35. I sent the quartermaster up to the topsail yard to examine what it might be. As soon as he was there, he told us that it was two small hillocks of sand, which we very fortunately passed within pistol-shot without any further decrease in depth. Having passed them, we lost bottom at 35 fathoms. This danger lies in latitude 13° 28' south and, by our timekeepers, in 122° 35' of longitude. Its extent is no more than 15 to 20 feet in circumference, and it is consequently all the more dangerous if one comes upon it.
Continuing to steer north a little towards the east, we soon sighted the continuation of the bank we had got out of in the morning. But at this point it was breaking heavily and described so great an arc that, to be able to clear it, we had once more to stand on the larboard tack and steer west-north-west until eleven o'clock, when its most visible part bore on our starboard bow. This then made us steer north-west. Part of the bank was dry, and in its south-eastern part, relative to us, it seemed to offer a passage which I wished to go and examine when, for the third time, fresh breakers were reported to larboard of us, so that we had once again to resume the course west-north-west. Nevertheless, we still had upwards of 30 fathoms two cannon-shots from the reefs.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 34' 59", and the longitude of our timekeepers put us, by No. 27, in 122° 35' 18" and, by No. 35, in 120° 30' 45". The mean result of three sets of
distances of the moon from the sun taken by the astronomer Bernier gave 123° 31' 58" for the ship's longitude, which, referred to No. 27, in which, as I have already observed, (in the margin: I had more confidence), put her 0° 56' 40" further east than that timekeeper indicated.
It did not seem to me doubtful that the bank shown on the chart of the Dépôt de la Marine is the one along a great part of which we had already coasted, but it seems equally certain that its northern extremity is placed much too far south, since according to the latitude observed at noon of 13° 34' 59" put us with a point of it still in sight to the north-north-east at a league and a half's distance, without our being able to affirm whether it was its extremity or not. The calm which came on before we could clear it left us in doubt on this point, and the ebb, which caught us soon afterwards, carried us so far from it that it was not possible for the moment to gain a more exact knowledge of it. The winds, having likewise gone round to the north-east in the evening, obliged us to steer no higher than NNW, and at five o'clock we went about to take up an anchorage along the edge of this bank, the depth having reached 44 fathoms on the NNW board.
At seven in the evening, finding ourselves in 32 fathoms and becalmed, we dropped a kedge anchor for the night on a bottom of a different nature from those we have found for several days, being of mud and coarse sand of various colours and small shells, whole and broken.
During the night's tides the strongest current was one and a half knots, and the sea, on the flood as on the ebb, rose and fell about two fathoms at the anchorage. For the rest, the sky was very damp and the wind almost a flat calm, except for a few little momentary puffs from the south or south-south-west.
1801-08-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from S to SSE. At 1.15 the tide turned, the currents then setting NNE and running more than 1.2 knots. At 6.30 we got under way and steered N 56° 15' E and N 45° E. At 8.30 the colour of the sea showed a shoal; we had 29 fathoms, and a moment later only 20. We bore away and the bottom shoaled to 15 fathoms and then, at 11, to 11; we then hauled to the wind on the port tack. The water deepened and we came round to the north. At 9.30 two white patches like two small banks were sighted ahead (to the north). We steered N 11° 15' E to pass between them and the great bank. At 10.30 breakers were sighted stretching from N 33° 45' E to N 78° 45' E; we steered N 56° 15' W to weather them. At noon a point of the great bank bore from us N 50° E, 6 miles off, being in 13° 34' 18" of latitude observed and in 122° 35' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 26' NE. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At half past noon the point of the bank supposed to be the northernmost bore from us N 22° 30' E. At 7 we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 8.30 we swung to the flood, which set SW and ran 1.4 knots.

1801-08-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SE.
1801-08-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, from half past four in the morning, we prepared to get under sail in the hope that the breeze would rise with the sun. But as the flat calm continued, we were forced to remain at anchor to wait for the breeze, so that the currents should not carry us on a course opposite to the one I wished to follow.
At about ten o'clock a light air sprang up from SSE to east-south-east, which I judged to be the beginning of the breeze. We therefore weighed our anchor and got under sail, but without making much way, for it continued calm. From the time we weighed until noon the depth held between 33 and thirty-five fathoms, sand and coarse gravel mixed with a little fine coral which the dredge brought up.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 25' 1", and the longitude of the timekeepers put us, by No. 27, in 122° 39' 28" and, by No. 35, in 120° 30' 39".
Three sets of distances taken by the astronomer Bernier, reduced to noon, gave as the mean for the ship's longitude 123° 22' 1". So the observations by distances had drawn one degree closer to the rate of the timekeepers since those made at the previous moon, which had differed from it by one degree forty-two minutes. The astronomer Bernier thinks that this great convergence may be caused by the computation of the tables, which he does not believe to be exact, having observed no change in the rate of the timekeepers.
In the afternoon the weather was very fine, but it continued calm. As the current was then carrying us to the south-south-west, we thought we saw the sea breaking on our starboard side, and we accordingly put the ship's head to the north-east to get away from that spot. From noon until six o'clock the depth went from 35 fathoms to 50, no bottom, which made me believe that we were clear of all the banks among which we had been entangled for two or three days. At seven o'clock the light air
having gone round to the north-east, varying towards the east, we steered north 28° west. At eight o'clock the lead was cast, although we had made little way, and we were much astonished to find ourselves in 29 fathoms, sand and gravel bottom. I then had the ship steered west-north-west, but the depth having suddenly decreased, successively and in a very short time, until it was no more than nineteen fathoms, sand and coarse gravel. I anchored to wait for daylight. I had by then stood on the south-south-east board and the depth had increased by four fathoms.
During the night, although it was blowing a pleasant breeze, the ship having swung head to the current with her head to the north-east, at the turn of the tide she lay with her head to the south-west, which makes me think that all the banks and shoals we had met with had changed the direction of the tides, which before had been NNE and SSW. The speed of the current was one and a half knots at its strongest, and the sea rose and fell nearly four fathoms where we lay at anchor.
During the night the weather was fine, but the air so damp that the men of the watch were much troubled by it
1801-08-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSE to NE. At 1 we swung to the ebb, setting NE and running 0.7; at 4 it ran 1.3 knots. At 8 it was slack water; at 9.30 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° E. At noon in 13° 24' 49" of latitude observed and in 122° 39' 28" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 36' NE. At 1 a flat calm; at 5.30 the breeze freshened from NE and we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack, the lead giving no bottom at 50 fathoms. At 8, having found 29 fathoms, we bore away N 67° 30' W and N 78° 45' W. The water shoaling further, we hauled to the wind on the port tack, and at 9.30 we anchored in 24 fathoms, sandy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 10 the current set SW and ran 0.7 knots. At 2 slack water; the current then set NE and ran 1.3 knots.

1801-08-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, the sunrise promised us a strong breeze for the morning, and for that reason we made haste to get under sail. When our anchor was up I had the ship steered north-east, persuaded that we would find the water deepening, since the day before it had shoaled as we steered north-north-west, north-west, west, west-south-west, and south-west and south, whereas it had deepened whenever the course took in the least easting. This conjecture proved correct, for scarcely had we run half a league to the north-east when we found thirty fathoms, and soon afterwards forty. There is reason to believe that our last anchorage was at the eastern extremity of the part of the bank examined on the previous days, which I have since found marked and shown on the English chart published in 1787 by Robertson, the only one that mentions it and gives it the extent it may have.
On weighing our anchor we lost our buoy and part of its buoy-rope; it seems that it became caught on some coral rock, which cut it in two as cleanly as if it had been done with an axe. Nevertheless, our cable had suffered not at all while we were at anchor.
In the morning the breeze which the sunrise had foretold duly came, and we were obliged to take two reefs in the topsails so as not to endanger our course. The sea quickly became heavy and the ship laboured a good deal in it. Most of the scientists were seasick.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 1' 31", but there was no hour angle for the rate of the timekeepers.
I expected the breeze to slacken after the sun had passed the meridian, but it did nothing of the kind. It continued with the same strength until sunset. Until eight in the evening I held the northern board, edging east as much as possible, and so as not to go too far from the coast, I took the southern board towards the east until three in the morning, when I went about again onto the northern one.
During the night of the 29th to the 30th the weather was fine and clear, only it continued to blow a strong breeze from east-south-east to south-south-east. At midnight we lost bottom at 54 fathoms.
1801-08-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to E. At 6 a.m., the wind having freshened a great deal, we began to heave round, the ship dragging. At 6.45 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack; we lost our buoy and buoy rope. At noon in 13° 0' 54" of latitude observed and in 122° 47' 40" of longitude by account. At 8 went onto the port tack. At noon no bottom at 40 fathoms. From noon until midnight we had from 45 to 55 fathoms.

1801-08-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky. Wind SE, a light breeze. At 3.45 p.m. sent off [the boat] under the orders of Citizen Ransonnet with 2 days' provisions to fetch the 2 men who had been stationed on Dirk Hartog.
1801-08-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, in the morning, it continued to blow a fresh gale from the quarter of the quarter (sic) of east-south-east. We were close-hauled on the northern board towards the east under the foresail and our topsails, two reefs in, and the ship had as much as she could carry. During the morning we suffered some damage to our sails, which the wind split in several places.
The latitude observed at noon was 12° 20' 34". There was no hour angle that day for the rate of the timekeepers, the wind and the heavy sea not allowing one to be taken.
In the afternoon the breeze, though a little less strong, did not allow us to make more sail, and I was surprised to find the sea as heavy and agitated as we met with it. The cause must no doubt be put down to the ebb of the tides which, acting against the wind, must have raised the heavy swell by which we were more than once drenched.
During the night of the 30th to the first it blew in gusts; yet we found the sea a little less heavy than it had been during the day.
From eight o'clock to midnight the lead brought up from 50 to 45 fathoms, muddy sand, and from midnight to four o'clock the next morning, from 46 to 42, coarse gravel. At eight o'clock the next morning we had 45, muddy sand. All night long we were surrounded by boobies, gulls and other sea birds, whose repeated and ceaseless cries made me fear that we were still in the neighbourhood of some dangers, which made me redouble my attention that a good look-out be kept, but we saw nothing.
1801-08-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to E. At 3 went onto the starboard tack under the foresail, both topsails double-reefed, the fore staysail, the mizzen and its staysail. At noon in 12° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 123° 2' 46" of longitude by account. The lead gave from 40 to 43 fathoms.

1801-08-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth, the winds a light breeze from ESE to north. The large boat was back on the 30th. She was sent off again to fetch the rest of the gear.
1801-08-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first, the winds were steadily from south-east by east to east-south-east, a strong breeze, and the sea a little less heavy than on the preceding days. I was informed in the morning by the Capitaine de frégate, or rather he told me once again, that we had only three or four days' wood left and at most twenty days' water at the ordinary ration. The naturalists, for their part, who had been without fresh provisions for more than a month, were sighing for the port of call of Timor, and though they said nothing of it to me, they talked of it among themselves in such a way that their conversation reached me. I myself felt the necessity of not persisting, in the state I was in, in going to examine the north cape of Van Diemen's Land. The want of a longboat or of any other craft capable of going ahead of the ship was becoming more and more indispensable to me, whether to examine the coast closely or to send it to explore, so that, seeing I could do nothing, I decided to steer north-west to reach the anchorage that everyone longed for with the greatest impatience.
This news had such an effect on several of the sick on board that a number of them found strength enough to come up on deck to make sure whether it (was) true.
At ten o'clock, then, I gave the course north-west, which was followed until noon. The observed latitude then being 10° 59' 53", I had the ship's head put to the north-west. According to the longitude indicated by the timekeepers, reduced to the same hour, No. 27 put us in 123° 44' 40" and No. 35 in 121° 23' 47". The distances were, as I observed at the time they were taken, 42' further east.
In the afternoon we found it very disagreeable that it continued to blow a good
breeze, and although the sea was still swelling and heavy, we nonetheless shook a reef out of our topsails, and towards evening we set the topgallant sails.
All day the sky had an ugly look and was darkened by heavy clouds which foretold, if not bad weather, at least rain.
After sunset the weather looked no better. However, we continued on the same course until eight in the evening, when, reckoning myself by the distance run by the log to be in 10° 25' south latitude, I had sail shortened for the night, giving the course west-north-west.
At two in the morning, the sky being very dark and overcast, I had the ship hove to to wait for daylight.
1801-08-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to ESE. At 10 a.m. the commander decided to shape our course for Timor; we headed north, making sail. At noon in 10° 59' 57" of latitude observed and in 123° 37' 52" of longitude by account. During the night overcast weather; we sounded several times without finding bottom at 120 fathoms. At noon the course was given N 45° W and at 9, N 67° 30' W.

1801-08-20.journal_anonyme: Throughout the 24 hours fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NW, W and SW. Calm at the close of the day.
1801-08-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, at five in the morning, we crowded on all sail, even our studding sails, to make the land, which I hoped to sight before noon if the longitude indicated by our No. 27, in which I had fair confidence, proved good. But I was disappointed in my expectation, for we saw nothing of it. It is true that the horizon was very limited and that the sky looked even worse than the day before.
At noon the latitude was observed as 10° 21' 53", and the longitude of the timekeepers was, for No. 27, 121° 34' 31" and, for No. 35, 119° 13' 56", so that this position, added to Robertson's chart, which I was using because its scale is larger than that of the others, put me over the south-west point of Timor. The same position laid down on the other charts that were given to me put me so short a distance from it that, if the longitude of this island was correctly placed, I ought to have sighted it. But as nothing could be seen, there is every appearance that No. 27 goes hardly better than No. 35. We shall see in the course of the evening, if the breeze holds, whether the distances will be more accurate and agree with the position that the Connaissance des temps gives this island.
In the afternoon the weather was very dark and hazy, so that our horizon was very limited. However, at about three o'clock, through the fog that hid the land from view, we made out the high mountains of the island of Timor.
A little before sunset, the horizon having cleared further, we had a very pleasant view of it, and until six o'clock we stood in towards the coast to within about a league and a half, or two leagues at most. As none of us knew this coast, we were uncertain whether a low point which bore three leagues to the west of us was the south-west point of the island. Had we been able to see the island of Roti, our doubts would have ceased. But the horizon was too limited in that direction, and we did (not) reckon it at more than four leagues. I therefore resolved to beat about all night within sight of the island of Timor, so as not to fall to leeward of the Semau Strait, through which I intended to pass in order to gain an exact knowledge of it.
During the night of the second to the third the weather was very changeable and the winds moderate, from east to east-north-east.
Bearings of the land at sunset:
The westernmost land in sight, west 10° north
The farthest land in sight to the east, north 56° east
The land abeam, north 42° west, distance about 2 leagues.
1801-08-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the port tack; at 5 filled and stood on, the course S 78° 45' W; at 10 it was given west. At noon in 10° 21' 42" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 31" of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, in a clear interval, the high land of Timor was sighted from N 11° E to N 68° W. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack, the land stretching from N 36° E to N 80° W, 6 miles off. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.

1801-08-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NE, SW, south and SE. Calm from 8 until noon.
1801-08-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, in the morning, as soon as day began to break, I stood in to within a mile and a half of the coast, so as not to miss the entrance of the Semau Strait, which it seems to me can only be made out from a short distance off the coast of Timor. As the longitude of the timekeepers, and even that of the distances, was faulty, supposing that of the south-west point of this island to be correctly placed on the charts, I thought it right to make sure of the depth of every cove, and for this reason we often had to bear away to west-south-west and south-west to round all the points we met with before reaching that last one. The whole coast, which we often ran along at less than the distance I have just mentioned, is not equally clear everywhere, and one even meets shoals quite often, easy, it is true, to make out by the colour of the water. So they are not dangerous, and within cannon-shot of these dangers there is no bottom at 30 fathoms.
Several points likewise have a small chain of breakers which sometimes extend more than a mile offshore and on which the sea breaks heavily. But in general, the fifteen leagues of coast we ran to reach the south-west point of the island of Timor is very clear and easy to recognise once it has been sighted. See the various views of it in the journal.
It was not until ten o'clock that we sighted the island of Roti, whose most visible extremity then bore south-west by west. We continued on our course with a very strong easterly breeze and at last, at about half past eleven, reached the western extremity of Timor. As we rounded the point and the reef that fringes it a good mile offshore, I had the sails trimmed close-hauled, and the winds served us to perfection, for a moment later they went round to the south-east, which greatly eased our entry into this strait. The breeze was then so fresh that we could not carry the topgallant sails.
At the entrance of the strait the following bearing was taken:
The south-west point of Timor, east 66° south
The south point of the island of Semau, west 22° south
The middle of the north side of the island of Roti, south 2° east
As soon as we were in the strait, I sought to close with the coast of Timor in the hope of finding, abreast of the sandy coves met with there, some places fit for anchoring, although the plans we have of this part show very great depths everywhere. At first we found no bottom at 50 fathoms in mid-strait, but as we approached the coast of Timor we got it first at forty and, two or three casts later, at 28, the nature of the bottom differing at every cast of the lead. Some brought up coarse gravel, and these were the first, others fine black sand and mud, and others sand mixed with a few small fragments of madrepore. I then decided to anchor in these waters in order to send to examine what distance we still had to run to round the point which I believe to be that of Kupang, from which I reckoned myself still two leagues off. At the same moment the wind suddenly failed us, and so as not to be carried by the current onto a sandbank that lay abreast of us a mile off, we let go a bower anchor in 28 fathoms, fine sand bottom mixed, as I said above, with a few broken fragments of madrepore, but too weak to give any concern for the cable.
As soon as our sails were furled, I at once had the large boat hoisted out and gave the command of it to M. Freycinet, so that he might go and examine Kupang point and the course to be held, after rounding it, to enter the bay of that name.
He was also ordered to push on as far as the Dutch settlement, that is to say Fort Concordia, if he did not find himself too far from it; accordingly I gave him the following letter for the Governor of this settlement:
"Governor,
"I have the honour to inform you that, having been dispatched by the French Government on a voyage of "discovery and public utility, I have found myself obliged to abandon the coasts of New Holland, where "I have been unable to procure the water and other refreshments necessary for its continuation.
"I hope that, by virtue of the passports of your nation which I carry, and which I reserve the right to "communicate to you at our first meeting, you will be good enough to help us in everything that lies in "your power.
"The officer bearing my letter is instructed to ask you to send us a pilot, none of "us knowing the anchorage in Kupang roads. I am &c. …".
At two o'clock the boat left the ship, well manned, and Midshipman Bougainville accompanied M. Freycinet. I had a Malay and a Dutchman embarked in the boat to act as interpreters.
The anchorage we occupied on the north south-west coast of the island of Timor was extremely pleasing to the eye. We were surrounded by land and as if enclosed in a circle of which the island of Roti formed the end, though at a fairly considerable distance. The lands all round, except however at the point which I presume to be that of Kupang, are of good height and covered with trees from the water's edge to the very top. To larboard of us, the island of Semau offered the same prospect, and to the east we had the island which lies abreast of the bay that is marked there.
Yet, for all the beauty of the place, we saw there only one wretched hut and two or three inhabitants busy fishing at low water.
Although Dampier, who passed through this strait, says that the tides there are not strong, we nevertheless found a fairly rapid current, the flood setting north-east and the ebb south-west. When we entered this strait it was still flood, and judging by the tide-mark on shore, the sea must rise to a good height. We were much astonished at four in the afternoon to see ahead of us, and a little to starboard, a sandbank uncovering, of which we had had no knowledge before, the calm no doubt preventing the sea from breaking on it. Its extent seemed to us small, and I put off sending to sound it until the next day.
In the afternoon we took a great many cross-bearings to obtain a plan of this part, and I give a separate drawing of the spot where we are at anchor, so particularly pleasing did it seem to me.
After sunset we had a light breeze from the north which lasted about two hours; then the winds went round to the south-east and fell calm. The night was very damp and without the least wind.
Bearings from the anchorage
1801-08-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to ESE. At 2 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 we bore away west and ran along the southern side of Timor at a short distance. At 10 Roti Island was sighted in the S 56° W. At 11.30, being off the mouth of Semau Strait, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and ran in; Roti then bore from us south. At noon took the bearing of the south point of Semau S 70° W, the northern part of Roti S 2° E, the south point of Timor with its reefs S 24° E. At 12.45, the breeze having fallen and the tide setting us out (to the south), we anchored in 28 fathoms, muddy sand, the south point of Timor bearing S 15° W, the end of the reefs off that point S 25° W, the south point of Semau S 49° W, a small island off Semau from N 45° W to N 29° W. At 1 the large boat was sent off to Kupang, the Dutch settlement on Timor; we did not know whether the settlement might be in English hands, and the boat carried an Anglo-French flag of truce. Citizen Freycinet, who commanded her, was to inform the governor of our arrival in the strait and of the stay we meant to make at Kupang.

1801-08-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty. A light breeze variable from SE to south, SSE and SSW. A fresh breeze. At 7 p.m. Citizen Ransonnet, acting ensign, went to take charge of the camp; and the next morning at 5 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, and I embarked in the large boat to go and survey the north of the bay. Our starboard anchor being foul, we weighed it, after which we let it go in 6 fathoms, sand and weed. Bearings of the anchorage: the north point E 19° N; the south point S 10° E; the camp S 23° 30' S.
1801-08-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the morning, I flattered myself that my boat would be on board before daybreak and that at sunrise we might weigh anchor to reach the anchorage in the bay of Kupang, where I intended to make my way with the help of my longboat and my small boat, supposing that the pilot I had asked for was not sent to us.
Towards seven o'clock, seeing no sign of my boat, I decided to send one of my smallest craft ashore with the geographer Boulanger to take fresh bearings from the land and to sound the bank I spoke of yesterday. As we were only a quarter of a league from the spot where this boat was ordered to land, I could protect it if need be with the ship's guns, which I had made ready for that purpose. But this precaution proved needless, for we had no call for it whatever, and the boat's crew landed without the least difficulty, although they met a few Indians with whom we saw them in conference. As soon as Citizens Boulanger and Maurouard had taken their bearings, they followed the Indians into the interior of the country and we lost sight of them.
On their return on board, about noon, we were told that they had been well received by the natives of the country and had gone about half a league inland, where they had found some thirty men gathered in various huts, all armed with muskets, who declared themselves to be in the service of the Dutch Company.
The soundings, at musket-shot from the shore, were two to three fathoms; then, over the same distance again, they increased to five to eleven, bad bottom. From there to the ship the depth increased suddenly from twenty to thirty, and the bottom was not found to be very good. At the edge of the bank I spoke of there were four and five fathoms of water, and then great depth. A ship at anchor with a chain would seem to me reasonably safe in the place where we lay.
At half past ten we sighted our boat crowding sail to join us, but as there was little wind and the tide was against her, she did not reach the ship until about two o'clock in the afternoon, bringing us a pilot sent by the Governor.
Monsieur Freycinet, who had command of her, reported to me that the flag of truce he carried at first caused a good deal of alarm, but that he lowered it as soon as the fortress had hoisted Dutch colours. He also told us that the English had made themselves masters of the fortress last year, but had been forced to evacuate it in a single night, not having (known how to) win the friendship of the people of the country, whose refuge and rights they had violated in the most shameful manner; this brought upon them a war with those people in which they lost many men without having reaped any fruit from this conquest. One may well expect that they laid waste the country as far as they could. And indeed the town is for the most part destroyed, and what the sword could not reach has fallen prey to the flames. They did not fail to blow up the fortress, which, however, has been entirely restored through the energy of the Dutch and the help given them by the various sovereigns with whom they live on good terms.
As soon as the pilot arrived, who turned out to be a Frenchman and a native of Bayonne, we got under sail and worked in towards the coast of Semau so as to keep clear of a danger that lies off the point of Kupang and runs out nearly a quarter of a league to sea. We had been anchored a short league inside this point, and after rounding it we still had three leagues to go to reach the anchorage in the bay.
The best course to follow, when the wind allows, is to keep to the middle of the channel. But if one has to beat to windward, the greatest care must be taken not to go too near the projecting points of the land, whether on the side of Timor or on the side of Semau, since all of them have reefs that run out a good way to seaward and that can be made out from some distance by day through the change in the colour of the water. For the rest, the channel seemed to me very convenient, and although the depth is considerable, one may, in a calm, drop a kedge anchor in fifty or sixty fathoms while waiting for the breeze; but if one lets go a bower anchor in less depth, it is well to have chains, otherwise one runs the risk of having one's cable damaged, as happened to us.
Another drawback, which keeps the Dutch from using this channel, is that the winds there are very variable and for that reason one sometimes finds oneself in difficulty. This too happened to us, for less than a mile from the coast we were once taken aback all of a sudden and obliged to go onto the other tack, keeping all sail aback so as not to forge ahead. But when there is wind one runs no risk and there is good working room; the narrowest part of the channel seemed to me to be three quarters of a league across at most.
As soon as we were off the opening of the bay of Kupang, the wind having shifted to the east, a pleasant breeze, we beat up tack upon tack to reach the anchorage, and as there was fine moonlight and our pilot seemed to me a fairly good one, we kept on making sail, taking care not to go too near a small island in the middle of the bay which the Dutch call Turtle Island. In passing the fort at sunset we affirmed our colours with a blank shot, and the fort answered in the same way. At last, at nine o'clock, we anchored in 28 fathoms, good muddy bottom, within musket-shot of a Dutch brigantine lying in the roadstead. After we had affirmed our colours, the Governor sent a boat on board to ask me not to salute, sending word that not only had he very little powder left, but also that it would lead to certain inconveniences, since the natives of the interior had orders to come into the town under arms whenever they heard more than three guns fired. In this matter I did what seemed to me would be agreeable to the Governor, and no salute was fired.
Bearings of the anchorage in the bay of Kupang:
The westernmost point in sight of the island of Timor, west 28° south
Fort Concordia, west 81° south
The north point of Timor, east 88° north
The northern extremity in sight of the island of Semau, north 71° west
The two extremities of the small Turtle Island, from north 10° 30' west to north 16° 30' west. Distance from the land about a mile and a half.
1801-08-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. At 8 the surveyor landed on Timor with his instruments, abreast of the anchorage; he came back at half past noon. He had been very well received by fishermen living on the strait, who told him that Kupang was in Dutch hands. At 1 Citizen Freycinet arrived from Kupang; he had been very well received by the governor, who was sending us a pilot, a Frenchman in the Company's service, to take us to Kupang. We got under way at once; the cable was found chafed. At 6, after doubling the last point of the strait, the wind shifted to the east; we missed stays, boxed her round to the south and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. We fired a gun, to which Fort Concordia answered with one. We made several boards to gain the anchorage, where at 9.30 we let go the anchor in 24 fathoms, muddy bottom; the topgallant masts were struck at once. Bearings at the anchorage, being moored: Turtle Island from N 11° W to N 17° W; the north end of Semau N 71° W; the west point of Timor S 62° W; Fort Concordia S 9° W; the northernmost point of Timor in sight N 2° E.

1801-08-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from S, NE, SW and SSW.
1801-08-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the (fifth), at eight o'clock in the morning, I made ready to pay a visit to the Governor, and at nine I went ashore, not only to pay him my compliments but also to learn what the country could supply and to find lodging there for our scurvy patients, two of whom had it in the highest degree. Before leaving the ship I wrote to Citizen Picquet, whose duties had been suspended since the time I recorded in its place. This officer, who does not even deserve the name, has never ceased to behave badly on board, and anyone else, less patient and less fond of peace and quiet, would have treated him very differently from me.
"To Citizen Picquet,
"I give you notice, citizen, that you are to see, with the least possible delay, to "finding lodging ashore, where you will await the arrival of the Naturaliste, being no longer a member of "my staff.
"At that time, if it still suits Capt. Hamelin to receive you, he will employ you "as he shall judge fitting to your personal merit and your talents.
"Moreover, I request you to conduct yourself ashore so as not to give the inhabitants of the country "as many grounds for displeasure as you have given me since the moment when I had the "kindness to receive you on board the Géographe.
"You will be given the ship's ration, in accordance with the issue that will be made of it during the "ship's stay in this roadstead." NB
As soon as Citizen Picquet had received this letter he presented himself like a madman, and on entering my cabin, foaming with rage, he began thus: "Damn it, Monsieur, you have a fine nerve writing to me in this fashion." This opening and the state he was in made such an impression on me that I at once ordered him, without uttering another word, to leave my presence immediately, and I shut my door as soon as he had passed it. Such an instance of insubordination could not go unpunished, and from that moment I resolved to have him placed in the Dutch fortress, contenting myself with keeping him on board until I had made arrangements accordingly with the Governor.
This unseemly scene having kept me on board longer than I had intended, it was ten o'clock when I went ashore, accompanied by Citizen Bonnefoy, midshipman, acting as ensign. As the pilot was in the boat and the tide was high, we entered the river and landed near the fortress. The Governor and his secretary came to receive us with great courtesy and then led us to his house.
After the first compliments, I presented to him the Company's passports and the letter accompanying them. He read them at once and asked me to entrust them to him for a day or two so that he might take a copy, which he told me he was obliged to send to Batavia for his own personal responsibility. I did not think I ought to refuse his request, and I entrusted them to him.
We then spoke of our particular needs, of the house in which to put our sick and of another, separate one to lodge the naturalists, which were found very promptly. The Governor had the civility to tell me that as soon as my boat had left he had provided lodging for me and that he
would take me there after dinner. The conversation then becoming general, I inquired about the resources of the country, which, from the account the Governor gave me, cannot be considerable, whereas the pilot he sent on board had spoken of them to us in quite another way.
When I represented to him the necessity I was under of building a launch to replace the one I had lost, he remarked to me that the thing would be possible, but that there would nevertheless be some difficulty in procuring timber fit for the purpose, since it had to be chosen and felled about three leagues from the bay. Nevertheless, he promised to give me guides and even men to help us in this work.
At one o'clock we sat down to table. The dinner was good, cleanly served and even with elegance. The Governor had no doubt invited the principal personages of his settlement, since there were three more persons present, namely his secretary and the physician, both Dutchmen, and the commandant of the burghers, or of the Malay natives of the country.
After dinner we had, as the custom is, to smoke a pipe and wait until the sun was less fierce before going out, and at that time he showed me the various lodgings he intended for us. First he accompanied me to a superb house which, set down in a European colony, would make a graceful figure there. It belonged to the widow of a Governor who had died in the country, who was good enough to withdraw to her estate so as to let me have it for the length of our port of call. The second was less elegant but quite as convenient; it was rented for eight piastres a month and set aside for the naturalists. The third, which was to serve as a hospital, was spacious, well aired and the property of the Company. The English had damaged it badly, as they had the church beside it, but work was in hand to prepare the part our people were to occupy.
We then took a walk until sunset, and I took leave of the Governor and his company to return on board, not intending to settle ashore until the next day.
During the day the Governor sent on board as a present a small ox, a pig, a sheep and various fruits of the country, apologising for not having been able to do better, and he even added that they lacked the most necessary things for want of communication with Batavia. In the course of conversation he told me what I already knew of the conduct of the English after the surrender of the fortress, and the only news he gave me was the capture by that nation of all their other settlements in the Moluccas.
At eight o'clock I returned on board and found the ship moored in the manner I had ordered. The night passed without incident; the sky was very fine, and the wind, which had been northerly, a fresh breeze, during the day, fell calm as soon as the sun had set.
In my conversation with the Governor I forgot to inform him of my intention of placing Citizen Picquet under arrest in the fortress until the arrival of the Naturaliste.
1801-08-23.journal_breton_geographe: At 9.30 a.m. the commander landed, accompanied by Citizen Bonnefoi. His boat came back with lemons, limes and oranges sent by the governor; we were given leave to communicate with the shore. Several canoes brought poultry and fruit to sell. In the afternoon we moored east and west with a bower anchor; a prau brought us a buffalo, two sheep and firewood, of which we were short. In the evening the commander came back aboard.

1801-08-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the air thick. A fresh breeze variable from SSW, SSE and south. At 5.15 a.m. the camp's dinghy came to fetch the caulkers to work on the longboat.
1801-08-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, in the morning, all the naturalists who wished to go ashore were ordered to be ready by eight o'clock and to embark their belongings in the ship's boats.
As I was preparing to leave, M. Picquet came to me again to ask leave to go ashore and look for lodging for himself in accordance with the letter I had sent him the day before. I answered that he need not take that trouble, that I would see to it myself, and that I would have him informed when it was ready. He withdrew making very expressive gestures, to which, however, I appeared to pay no attention, so as to avoid coming to unfortunate extremities.
As soon as we had landed, I took those of the naturalists who were in the boat with me to their lodging, of which they took possession, and I went to my own to do the same, having my belongings carried there. We were such close neighbours that we could easily talk to one another through the window without having the trouble of leaving our houses.
The sick were likewise settled ashore in the course of the morning, and before noon everything was in order at the hospital.
As I had no kitchen set up, I went without ceremony to ask the Governor for dinner, and I took with me M. Boulanger, our geographer. The Governor received us as well as the day before and gave us a very good dinner.
The rest of the day passed without incident, and we spent it putting our affairs in order and settling ourselves so as to inconvenience no one any longer.
In the evening at eight o'clock the Governor sent me word that he had just been informed that a three-masted ship had appeared at the entrance of Semau Strait, that this ship had made a signal which was judged to be a request for a pilot, but that her colours could not be made out. He added that he had given orders for one to be sent to her the next day, and that he was accordingly sending back at once the man who had brought him this news. We were all the more pleased at this report because we thought it could only be the Naturaliste, about whose fate I had been greatly concerned.
1801-08-24.journal_breton_geographe: In the morning he landed with all the naturalists, to live ashore. The sails were unbent, the topgallant masts got down and the running rigging unrove. A hospital was set up in the town, where the surgeon-major and all the sick went. All our empty casks were sent ashore.

1801-08-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and SSW.
1801-08-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, towards eight o'clock in the morning, I received a visit from the Governor and his clerk. I handed him the list of the fresh provisions we needed for each décade, as well as of those I intended to take on board at our departure. I also let him know how anxious we were to begin our launch without delay, and he at once ordered a Frenchman who had been settled in this country for thirty years to take us to the place where suitable timber was to be found, so as to mark the trees and afterwards fell them. Citizen Ronsard, engineer, and the master carpenter were charged with this task, in which our head gardener Riedelé asked to be included so as to learn the productions of the district to which they were to go. His request was granted, and it was settled that they would set out the next day at daybreak.
After breakfast the Governor withdrew to his house, assuring us again that he would do everything in his power to procure us the things we might need.
At the moment he withdrew I was very far from foreseeing the new scene that was about to take place; but scarcely a quarter of an hour after he had gone out, M. Picquet presented himself, asking to speak to me in private. He was in uniform, with his sword at his side. Being unable to suspect his intentions, I went with him into the hall, for at the moment he arrived I was under the gallery, busy with Citizen Boulanger copying a detailed plan of the island of Timor which the Governor had lent us.
When we were in the hall, M. Picquet came up to me and said: "Monsieur, since we are no longer on board here, I hope you will be so good as to give me satisfaction
for the manner in which you have treated me, and I have come ashore expressly for that purpose." Until then he had held his hat in his hand, but having finished his speech he put it on his head to await my answer.
I looked at him sternly for more than two minutes without answering him a word, and I confess I did not think myself capable of so much patience. My silence, which he took for a fresh affront, made him furious, and he asked me why I did not answer him, adding that he was well worth the trouble. I then replied, with all possible moderation, that if I had not yet answered him in the manner I ought, it was for fear of having misunderstood what he had said to me, and that to remove my doubts on this point I begged him to be so good as to repeat himself. There is doubtless no one who, after such treatment, would not have recognised the crime of which he was making himself guilty and would not have withdrawn, covered with shame and with contempt for himself. But M.
