Picquet, far from feeling any remorse, then replied: "Damn it, if you have not understood me, follow me, and," putting his hand on his sword, "if you dare come near me, you will see what use I make of it." His words did not prevent me from moving, but it was to go into the gallery, and I ordered the first man I came upon to fetch me four musketeers from the castle to have him taken to prison. This order, which he doubtless did not expect, made him quiver with rage and drove him for two or three minutes to give vent to all manner of invective, and then he vanished like a flash. Monsieur Ronsard, whom he met, tried to stop him and speak to him, but he merely told him he was going on board. As Monsieur Ronsard knew nothing of what had happened, he came to the house and I told him of M. Picquet's conduct. It was then that he told me he had met him and that from his wild look he had judged there must have been a rather violent scene.
Knowing that M. Picquet was back on board, I then wrote the following letter to M. le Bas:
"I am pleased to believe, citizen, that M. Picquet's intentions were not known to you when "you allowed him to go ashore, and in order to inform you of them I am glad to let you "know that he presented himself at my house, not to make me any apology for his past conduct, but "only to pour out invective and finally to propose that I draw my sword against him. &c. &c..
"When the French Government learns this news it will no doubt blame me for not having had him "shot on the spot as an example, but I resign myself to bearing the reproach, not on "his account, for he deserves no consideration, but for his family, which I know to be respectable.
"For the rest, for fear of being obliged, after having suffered so much, to go to extremities that "are repugnant to my character, you will have him confined on board until further orders from me, and if "he behaves badly there in the least, you will confine him to his cabin with a sentry at his door and "inform me of it at once.
"I believe the Naturaliste has been signalled in Semau Strait." NB
As it was then nearly noon, I countermanded the guard I had sent for and put off until the evening telling the Dutch Governor what I had to say to him about this officer and the course I had decided to hold to.
M. Picquet's scandalous scene soon spread through the town, and it was even reported on board before my letter reached it. About two o'clock in the afternoon I received the following answer from M. Le Bas:
"Commander,
"There was talk of a visit to be paid to the Governor by M. Picquet when this officer "asked me for leave to go ashore.
"You will do me justice in believing that the intentions he displayed at your house were not "known to me. I am too firm a supporter of subordination and discipline to suffer any departure from them, and "no one on board, I swear to you, has applauded his conduct. I have conveyed your orders to him and he "will comply with them.
In the afternoon I paid the Governor a visit, accompanied by a person of the country who acted as interpreter. In my conversation with him I begged him to be so good as to receive into the fortress the officer whose conduct I had made known to him, so that I should not be obliged to inflict on him the penalty laid down by the general law of all nations against one who behaves as the said Picquet has done. He made no difficulty about granting my request; he only asked me to make it in writing so that he might make a formal report of it to the Council at Batavia.
As this Commandant intended to send off to Batavia, in 25 to 30 days, a brigantine that was in the roadstead, I also proposed to him to send him over to that colony, from where I would make suitable arrangements with the Governor of Batavia for his passage back to Europe, where he must go to give an account of his conduct. All my requests were granted, with the sole remark that they be made in writing.
Having agreed on our business, we settled that I would send him my letter the next day, but that he would meanwhile have the lodging he intended for him in the fortress made ready, where he would be confined until the departure of the ship for Batavia.
The rest of the day passed without incident. The morning's scene was the sole news of the whole day and a great cause of astonishment to the Dutch.
1801-08-25.journal_breton_geographe: The topmasts were struck and the lower yards lowered; the sheet anchor was got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The crew had fresh meat and fish.

1801-08-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the sky cloudless. A fresh breeze from SW and SSW.
1801-08-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, in the morning, I did not fail to write the Governor the following letter, as we had agreed the day before. It was couched in these terms:
"Monsieur le Gouverneur,
"It is in the name of the French Republic that I address myself to you, asking you to have the "kindness to receive into the fortress one of the officers who was a member of my staff, although he "was not on the corvette I commanded on leaving France. But it is no longer possible for me to "keep him on board any longer, in view of his bad conduct. As it seems to me needless to go into "details on this subject, I have only to beg you to have him confined in the fort until the departure of the "vessel which you intend shortly to dispatch to Batavia. I shall meet all the "expenses that his detention and his departure may occasion, upon your request.
"The letter which I beg you to forward to the Governor General at Batavia will enable you "to judge of the means I am employing to have his return to Europe made easier for him, where he must appear to "give an account of his conduct.
"This officer holds the rank of ensign, which I leave him, and his name is Picquet. He is "about 22 or 23 years of age, and mad or violent by temperament. He will be taken to the fort tomorrow, or sooner if it is "possible." Signed N. B.
The same day I gave a dinner for the Governor, his secretary and the surgeon, who are the three first persons of the settlement. All the scientists and
naturalists were there, in such a way that not all of them were content, because I had not presented them in a body at the time of my arrival.
In the middle of dinner we heard a very pleasant piece of news: an orderly came to tell the Governor that a large ship had been sighted at the entrance of Semau Strait and had made some signals, as is the practice when asking for a pilot. We had no doubt that it was the Naturaliste, and we accordingly urged him to send one, which he promised us to do. This was the second time we had had this report, and as one always flatters oneself that what one desires will come to pass, we thought that this ship, which had not appeared the day before as we had expected, had met with winds that had kept her from reaching the entrance of this strait, but that she would no doubt be more fortunate this time.
As it was agreed, when we parted in the evening, that M. Picquet should be put in the fortress the next day, I wrote the following letter to Citizen Le Bas:
"The Commander &c.:
"I give you notice that tomorrow morning M. Picquet will go ashore with all his belongings to occupy "the apartment I have had prepared for him.
"I have likewise provided for his food and for his departure for Batavia, as well as for his return to "Europe, where he will arrive long before us.
"You will be good enough to warn him on my behalf to be ready for the moment when I come on board, which "will be about eight o'clock if you will have the kindness to send me the boat. You will order the "master gunner to have the marines in uniform and their arms loaded with ball."
Signed N. B.
About eight o'clock in the evening, a further message from the Governor informed me that several guns had been heard fired to the north of the island of Semau, and that it seemed likely the ship which had appeared to be making for the strait had changed her mind and preferred to come by the usual passage. I at once ordered Citizen Le Bas to send off the longboat the next day at daybreak, giving the command of her to Citizen Bonnefoy, to go and reconnoitre in that quarter.
During the night nothing out of the ordinary took place. The weather was very fine and the winds almost calm, from east to east-south-east.
1801-08-26.journal_breton_geographe: Work was interrupted, the crew being unwell, which was put down to the water. The carpenters were sent ashore with their tools and planking to build us a longboat there under Citizen Ronsard's direction. A canoe brought us firewood. Some of the local people reported that a three-masted ship had anchored at the entrance to Semau Strait, from which she had got under way, and that they had heard gunfire to the west of Semau.

1801-08-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A fresh breeze from SSW.
1801-08-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, as early as four o'clock in the morning, the longboat commanded by Citizen Bonnefoy left the ship and shaped her course according to the directions I had given.
At eight o'clock I went on board and found everything prepared as I had ordered the day before. After speaking with M. Le Bas, I sent word to M. Picquet to have his belongings put in the boat and that the guard was about to take him to the Dutch fortress, where he would be confined until the departure of the ship the Governor intended to dispatch to Batavia as soon as possible. At the request of the other officers, I left this officer, who does not deserve the name, his rank of ensign, warning him nevertheless that if he abused it to behave badly towards the people of the country, the Governor of this settlement would be authorised by a writing from me to take it from him. He had the fortress for his prison for as long as he behaved well there. He was not taken to the fort by the guard, as I had planned, and I gave my officers this further mark of indulgence. At nine o'clock he left the ship.
Shortly afterwards I went ashore myself to attend to my affairs and to arrange the departure of those who were to go and fetch the timber the carpenters had chosen for building our launch, which I was most impatient to see begun.
In the afternoon Citizen Bonnefoy came to report to me on the cruise he had made in the boat. After rounding the north point of the island of Semau, he had coasted along its western side as far as its southern extremity, looking into the various coves he came upon, but he sighted no ship either at anchor or under sail, so that it appears the ship seen the day before was a vessel passing by with no intention of putting in at this settlement. I informed the Governor of the report that had just been made to me. And that of the people of the strait, which he received at almost the same time, turned out to agree with what I sent him word of.
He also informed me that Citizen Piquet had been received into the fort and that he had asked him for his sword, to return (it) to him when he came out.
1801-08-27.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the large boat to try to discover whether this ship might be the Naturaliste. At 9 the commander came aboard; the detachment took up arms (loaded and with bayonets fixed) and he gave orders to take Citizen Piquet, ensign, to Fort Concordia with his effects, and to send him his provisions. Citizen Freycinet obtained leave to take him there alone. He was received ashore by the Dutch guard and taken to the fort, where the sergeant commanding the fort asked him for his sword. After this business the commander went back ashore. At 2.30 Citizen Bonnefoi came back in the large boat; he had coasted the western side of Semau without discovering anything.

1801-08-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW. At 5.30 a.m. a Malay named Sodomson, shipped at Mauritius, died of putrid fever.
1801-08-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
The tenth was without remarkable event. As it was the décade holiday, no work was done on board, and half the crew had leave to go ashore on condition of not wandering off into the countryside.
During the day I handed the Commandant of the fort a list of all the articles of barter we had on board, informing him that I had no other money to give him for our expenses during our stay at Timor.
Our sick ashore were already beginning to feel the good effects of the change of diet, and I neglected nothing for their speedy recovery.
On board, almost the whole crew was upset by the water. I think the cause must be put down to its having been drawn at high tide, and to the men, in order to spare themselves trouble, not having gone far enough up the river. To avoid the unfortunate consequences that might follow, and also to relieve the crew of this work, which is always laborious in hot countries, I decided to have it done by the people of the country.
1801-08-28.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; a large part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-08-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to SW. At 3 the longboat came loaded with wood and went back ashore at once.
1801-08-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh we began to put our water casks ashore and to empty those in the hold that were filled with sea water. The men of the crew who took them down to the bank of the river had also brought some twenty breakers for the daily use of the ship, but after filling them, not having taken care to leave someone to guard them, they went further on under pretext of bathing, so that during their absence seven of them were stolen. I complained of it to the Governor, who promised me to do his best to discover the thieves. He warned me that in future we must put our casks at the fortress, that he would have them filled and would answer to me for them, and that if we went about it otherwise we ran the risk of losing them.
On board, the topmasts were housed and the topgallant masts sent down. Part of the crew was employed with the seine, and the fishing was not bad. Besides various kinds of fish, we took two turtles.
The Governor, who is the only one who carries on any trade with strangers, procured us every other day a wild buffalo weighing about two hundred pounds, so that on board as well as ashore we fared very well. But we were short of vegetables and other refreshments, which are much better than meat. All foodstuffs went up in price for us, and although witnesses of what he made the people of the country pay, we were obliged to give double.
1801-08-29.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. A working party was set up ashore to fill our casks; at low water we watered in the Kupang river.

1801-08-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE.
1801-08-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, work continued on board to make the ship ready to take in the water, the wood and the other things we might need.
Once again I gave a dinner for the Governor, his secretary and the commandant of the militia of the country, who is an important personage here.
Since our arrival the Dutch Governor had treated us very well, and not a day had passed without his making us some present of pork, venison, vegetables and mutton; the original breed of these sheep seemed to me to come from the Cape of India, or at least closely to resemble those of that country.
In the afternoon we went to pay a visit to the lady who had let me have the fine house in which I was lodged and who, for that purpose, had withdrawn to one of her estates, about three quarters of a league from the town.
I was far from expecting the reception we were given, which was truly such as to astonish strangers. More than a hundred slaves of both sexes, very well dressed, formed two groups at the ends of the verandah under which we were received. And the lady of the house, a Timorese by birth, came forward as far as the steps to receive us civilly and invite us in. Her bearing was noble and her manners easy.
After the first compliments, I had my interpreter thank her for the kindness she had shown in letting us have her house, for which she would accept no payment. And when I told her how sorry I was for the trouble her removal must have caused her, she answered obligingly that she was always flattered when an occasion arose of being useful to strangers, and above all to Frenchmen.
Tea and coffee were then served to those who wished to take them, and these drinks were accompanied by a multitude of sweetmeats made in her house and handed round in turn by some twenty young girls, very neatly dressed and most of them pretty. Those who tasted these delicacies declared that they could not be made better in Paris. It appears that the Governor had announced our coming and that this lady wished to appear before us in all her splendour. All the dishes were of silver, very finely worked, and the luxury yielded nothing to the elegance.
The sight the whole presented was truly beautiful, and had I been able to foresee it I would have brought with me the draughtsman, who would no doubt have made a fine picture of it. We stayed with this lady about an hour and a half, and as night was coming on I told the Governor, who had accompanied us, that I was at his orders and that we would leave whenever he thought fit. He answered that the approach of night need not trouble me, since we would see as clearly as in broad daylight on our way back. So we stayed another half hour, and at sunset, at half past six, we made ready to leave. Seeing our preparations for departure, this lady sent me word that, knowing we collected shells, she had a few which she begged me to accept, much regretting that they were not finer. Then she had one of her women present me with a basket in which were a very fine helmet, two tuns and a spindle of a very pretty in colour, and a spindle. I thanked her warmly for this gallantry, and we took our leave of her, asking her permission to come and see her now and then during our stay on the island.
The Governor was quite right in telling me that we would see as clearly as in broad daylight, for a great number of torches were at once.
lit. Some were great wax torches and the others were made of the wood called candlewood and smeared with a kind of resin, so that the whole gave out a great deal of light, even to a great distance. The slaves carrying the wax torches went ahead fifteen paces in front of us, and the others at the same distance behind.
Our departure from this house was no less brilliant than our arrival had been, and the whole looked exactly like a stage set at the Opéra in Paris. The road we took on our way back was different from the one we had taken to get there, and we returned along the seashore.
On the way I was informed that this lady had been the wife of a Dutch Governor who, on his death, had left her all his property, although he had had no children by her. Her name is (a blank) and she may be about fifty years of age. She is said to have an income of thirty thousand rix-dollars and a thousand slaves at her disposal, distributed distributed (sic) over three fine estates, well built and well kept. The four finest houses in the town belong to her, and although she lost a great deal when the English took the fortress, she still passes for the richest person in the country.
On our way to her house through the interior, we met a herd of more than two hundred head of horned cattle, very well kept. But the oxen, like the heifers, are of a very small breed and seem to me to be of Manila stock. She also has numerous flocks of sheep and kids and a great deal of poultry. In short, it appears that this estate lacks nothing, since it has some very fine ponds in which a great number of carp and many other freshwater fish may be seen swimming about.
The Governor took us to see a spring whose volume is very considerable, and it is from this same spot that various channels have been cut to carry it to the estate we had just left.
On our arrival in the town the Governor saw us back to our house, and we bade one another good night, thanking him warmly for the agreeable pleasure he had given us.

1801-08-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE.
1801-08-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth we carried on our work as usual. Two persons from the ship went into hospital, one stricken with dysentery and the other with a fever whose character is not yet known.
Our carpenters, who had gone to fetch timber fit for building our launch, returned. They were away longer than I had supposed because they were obliged not only to cut it themselves but also to carry it to the boat, the people the Governor had provided having refused to help them in anything. However that may be, I had it taken at once to the yard we had chosen, and this work will at last be pressed forward without interruption.
At dinner I was much surprised to learn that several of the naturalists had taken it amiss that I had not taken them all with me to visit the lady at whose house I had been the day before. I had taken only Citizen Ronsard, whom I happened to meet, and Messieurs Bernier and Maugé. The account these gentlemen will have given the others of the manner in which we were received will no doubt have made some jealous and given rise to talk. I do not in the least consider myself obliged to have eight or ten persons in my train whenever it pleases me to pay someone a visit, but it is true that, had I been able to foresee what befell us, I would gladly have given them that satisfaction, without,
however, believing it to be any obligation on my part.
In the evening the boats landed a good number of water casks, and I had them taken to the fortress, or at least placed under the eye of the castle guard, so as to prevent their being stolen or damaged, for in this country people are very fond of the iron hoops on them and make no scruple of carrying them off when they find the chance.

1801-09-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and east. The large boat came in from her mission to the north of the bay. She brought eight enormous turtles, which gave us great pleasure.
1801-09-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, an imprudence committed by someone from the ship gave rise to complaints from the Governor. Some persons whom M. Le Bas had allowed, without my orders, to go ashore to shoot, scattered over the countryside, and their excursions having been unsuccessful, they no doubt wished to make up for it by firing at tame pigeons. I do not know whether they killed any, but several grains of shot wounded a girl who happened to be nearby. Her parents did not fail to bring her to the Dutch Governor to have the fact established, and this very nearly set us at odds with the people of the country. However, I got off with making a few presents and promising that it would not happen again.
Accordingly, I wrote a letter to Citizen Le Bas forbidding anyone from the ship to come ashore with firearms without a written permission from me, signed by my hand. This prohibition gave rise to grumbling and even to talk. But I paid little heed to it.
We spent the day busy with our affairs, and on board the anchors were weighed to examine the cables, for we had been warned that this precaution was necessary although we lay on a muddy bottom, since experience had shown that coral rocks are sometimes met with which cut them.
1801-09-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fish were taken with the seine and distributed to the crew; the watering continues.

1801-09-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW. During the night the winds drew round from south to WSW, almost calm.
1801-09-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth I suffered a rather violent bout of fever, which came on me all of a sudden and obliged me to keep to my room. I do not know to what to attribute its cause, for having risen in the morning between half past four and five o'clock, as is my habit, I was in very good health.
Nothing new happened during the day. But towards eight o'clock in the evening, I was told that sixteen hoops had been taken from our water casks, which I had nevertheless had placed under the eye of the castle guard. I at once had complaints made of it to the Governor, who replied that he had already warned us this might happen to us and that we had been wrong not to take them into the fortress as he had told us. He added, however, that he would make every effort to recover them if it were possible.
The fever, which had come on me in the morning towards seven o'clock, left me in the afternoon, and I passed the night fairly well.
1801-09-02.journal_breton_geographe: Part of the crew went ashore to walk about. Fish and a small turtle were taken with the seine.

1801-09-03.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky overcast, the winds very light and variable from WSW, SW and W. We set up our shrouds, stowed our anchors and hoisted in the longboat and the other boats.
1801-09-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth I felt as well as usual, and the fever did not appear all day, nor during the night. It was not so with the steward, who appeared to the medical men likely to have a serious illness and who, to prevent or cure it, was placed in their hands.
In the morning I received a visit from the Governor, to whom I gave breakfast, as well as to his secretary. He then asked to speak to me in private, and having sent for an interpreter, we went into my room. He then informed me that five men of my crew had presented themselves at his house the day before to ask to be discharged, wishing to go on to Batavia. These five men came from a Prussian ship that was at the Isle of France [Mauritius], whose Captain had had them put in prison for reasons unknown to me. These men were sent on board the corvette the day before our departure
by order of the two administrations of the Isle of France and at their own request, made in writing, no doubt rather to get themselves out of prison than with any intention of making the voyage. However that may be, not wishing to discharge these five men, who were very necessary to me, I merely told the Governor that they might nevertheless obtain their discharge if they managed to find five other Europeans, good seamen like themselves, to replace them. From the Governor's insistence on obtaining their discharge, I am inclined to think that he was the most interested party and that he wished to have them for employment on his brigantine, which was shortly to leave for Batavia.
During the day we took on board several cords of wood. The keel, the keel (sic), the stem and the sternpost of the launch were set up; her length and other dimensions were somewhat greater than those of the one we had lost.
1801-09-03.journal_breton_geographe: The coopers went to repair our casks and put on hoops that had been stolen. Fish and a small turtle were taken.

1801-09-04.journal_anonyme: A high sea, misty and squally weather and a cloudy sky. A fresh breeze from W to SW in strong gusts. At 10.20 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course W by N.
1801-09-04.journal_baudin_autographe: On the seventeenth work went on both on board and ashore, but it went slowly because I could obtain no relief for the crew in carrying the things that had either to be taken on board or landed. I could never persuade the people of the country to help us, whether by paying them by the day or by giving them some of our articles of barter. Idleness and sloth are their greatest delight, and as they have few wants they scarcely think of procuring themselves some comforts by work when the opportunity offers. Only the slaves are forced by their masters to work, but that does not extend to hiring them out to strangers.
1801-09-04.journal_breton_geographe: A prau brought us 2 cords of wood.

1801-09-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to south. Soundings from midnight to 4: from 1 to 2, 65 and 66 fathoms, fine reddish sand; at 3 and at 4, 80 and 85 fathoms. At noon on the 18th we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn.
1801-09-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth our occupations were much the same as the day before; however, we took on board some forty casks of water, and this was the heaviest part of our work. The Governor had them brought to the ship by his slaves or those belonging to the Company, but they would never lend us a hand to hoist them on board, nor even wait until they were empty to take them back.
Pages 49 to 77 are blank
DEPARTURE FROM KUPANG, BAY OF TIMOR, FOR VAN DIEMEN'S LAND, SOUTH OF NEW HOLLAND
1801-09-05.journal_breton_geographe: In the evening Citizen Le Bas, who until now had borne the whole duty alone, entered in the ship's log that, all the midshipmen except one (Bonnefoi) reporting themselves sick, Citizens Freycinet, Bonnefoi and myself were left with the duty.

1801-09-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea and the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom; from 2 to 4 the same.
1801-09-06.journal_breton_geographe: I went to the hospital ashore for the itch. At 9 p.m. a canoe brought a letter from the commander to Citizen Le Bas, telling him that there were two English frigates and three small vessels anchored in Semau Strait, which was causing much alarm ashore; he ordered him to send Citizen Freycinet at daybreak to reconnoitre them.

1801-09-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea with a little swell, a fresh breeze from ESE to SE. From 10 until midnight sounded without finding bottom. At 10 set the studdingsails and staysails.
1801-09-07.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Freycinet, carrying our passports and a letter from the commander to the English commodore, left for Semau Strait; he was back at 2 and had seen no ship at all. Work was suspended, but no one went ashore; we rested on board. Canoes brought us water.

1801-09-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE. At 3.30 a.m. ran out 87 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 4 a.m. the breeze got up from the SE.
1801-09-08.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. 95 sacks of wheat were sent to the hospital to be dried and winnowed by the convalescents.

1801-09-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south; we sounded without finding bottom. At sunrise we set the studdingsails.
1801-09-09.journal_breton_geographe: Having tasted the water the canoes were bringing us, we found it brackish and sent it back.

1801-09-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds very light and variable from SSE to SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-09-10.journal_breton_geographe: The two topmasts were swayed up and the lower yards hoisted. Our boats and some canoes continue to water for us.

1801-09-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SSE to SE. Ran out 90 fathoms of line without finding bottom.

1801-09-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE, south and ESE. Sounded all night without finding bottom.
1801-09-12.journal_breton_geographe: The mizzen topgallant mast was swayed up.

1801-09-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. The sky cloudy and dark. A strong breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught a tern.

1801-09-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSE, ESE and east. Sounded without finding bottom.
1801-09-14.journal_breton_geographe: The topgallant masts were got up.

1801-09-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught two boobies. At 9.15 a.m. sighted land N 5° E. Noon bearings: the westernmost visible end N 18° E; a remarkable peak N 22° E, distance 8 miles; the northernmost visible end N 32° E.

1801-09-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from east to SE and ESE. At 3.10 lost sight of the land. At 9 a.m. bore away for Savu Island; running along the southern side of this island, we saw on the shore several local people and a few huts. Noon bearings: the south point of Savu S 5° W; the visible end of this island N 70° E; the middle of this part of the island S 36° W.

1801-09-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE, south and SE. Sounded all night without finding bottom. From the 30th [Fructidor] to the 1st complementary day [Year 9, 17-18 September 1801]. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light and variable from S by W, S by E, SE and E by S. Saw several fires on the coast.
1801-09-17.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-09-18.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order.

1801-09-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky, a light breeze variable from E to NW, south and SE. At 3 went about onto the port tack.

1801-09-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3.15 p.m. the breeze got up from the SSE. At 8 it drew round to SE by E, making us run 7 knots. At 2 took a reef in the mizzen topsail. Bearings at 10: the visible south point of the land east 30° S, about 30 miles off; the north point east, estimated distance from the furthest land [sentence incomplete].

1801-09-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind variable from WNW, SE, SW, NW. During the night we sounded without finding bottom. Lay to from 4 until 5.15, when we filled and stood on. At 6.15 hove to to put the large boat in the water. She left under the orders of Citizen Freycinet, carrying the national flag and pendant; we hoisted our colours and put a signal flag at the foremast head. Shortly afterwards we sighted a boat ahead of us which seemed to have come from the ship in sight, which we recognised to our satisfaction as the Géographe.
1801-09-21.journal_breton_geographe: At daybreak a three-masted ship was sighted beating in towards Kupang; bets were at once laid that it was the Naturaliste. The commander sent orders to make the private signal, and shortly afterwards we recognised the Naturaliste, which also made the private signal. Our boat was sent off to her with some refreshments. At 1 she anchored near us to the NW, two cables off. She saluted us with 5 guns, which we returned, and at once dressed ship. We sent her fresh water and our boat to help her moor.

1801-09-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from SSW to SE and to east and south. At 1 we anchored in 28 fathoms forward and 26 fathoms aft. In the afternoon the two skiffs and the longboat were put in the water to moor us. At 9 a.m. on the 5th we were moored, the western anchor with a range of 50 fathoms to port, the eastern anchor with a range of 100 fathoms to starboard. Bearings of the anchorage: the middle of the fort of Kupang south, distance 1 mile; the south point of Timor S 65° W, 5 miles; the north point N 7° E, 21 miles; the middle of Sandy Island N 11° W, 5 miles.
1801-09-22.journal_breton_geographe: The ship's outside, the masts and the yards were painted. A little fish was taken with the seine.

1801-11-12.journal_anonyme: Hardly had we arrived at Kupang than we set about overhauling the rigging; the orlop deck was taken up, we watered and fresh provisions were embarked. The town of Kupang is defended by a poor fort, and more surely by the courage of the Malays. The English took Kupang during this war, but the men left to garrison the fort were massacred by the Malays and Timor returned into Dutch hands. During our stay the nights and mornings were calm; about 11 the breeze often got up very strong, the winds being then NW and NNW. They fell away at the close of the day and drew round to east and SE. On the 1st Brumaire [Year 10, 23 October 1801] we sighted a frigate standing in for Kupang Bay. Commander Baudin sent a boat aboard her under the orders of a midshipman carrying our passports; on our boat's return we learnt that the frigate sighted was the Virginie, which had come to attack us. As soon as the English frigate's captain had seen our passports, he filled and beat out of the bay. During our stay we lost two men from dysentery. The Géographe lost 5, among them Citizen Riedlé, the gardener-botanist, a man full of zeal for his calling; he was given the same funeral honours as would have been paid to the head of the expedition. He was buried beside Mr Nelson, Captain Bligh's gardener-botanist, who also died at Timor. We lost 9 men by desertion.
1801-11-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the evening we unmoored; the cable was found chafed about 20 fathoms from the bend. The second anchor was weighed and let go again at once. The small boat and the yawl were hoisted in.

1801-11-13.journal_anonyme: At five in the morning we got under way with a light breeze from SE. At noon we took the compass bearing of the NW point of Semau W 29° S, 5 miles off, and the NW end of Sandy Island E 11° N, distance 8 [miles].
1801-11-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, from four o'clock in the morning, we made ready to get under way, although it was my day of fever. I was too impatient to leave a country where sickness had used us so ill to put off my departure until the next day; I therefore made the signal to the Naturaliste to get under sail and did the same myself. The winds were then from east to south-east, very light. But I flattered myself that the land breeze would make itself felt at sunrise and that, by this means, we might round the small Turtle Island and its great reef before the sea breeze came in. This hope was not fulfilled, for towards eight o'clock we were becalmed. But as the ebb was then running, it did much to carry us out through the passage to the north of Semau.
From the information I obtained during my stay at Timor, it appears that large and small vessels alike should prefer this passage to any other, since it is much more convenient than the one lying to the north of Turtle Island and the southern part of the bay of Kupang. There is more room to beat, and the banks are fewer.
Towards eleven o'clock, the wind having shifted to the north-west, a pleasant breeze, we stood towards the coast of Semau, which we could not weather, so that we were obliged to beat about for some time; but in the afternoon it shifted to west-south-west and we got out to sea, passing about three leagues from Turtle Island, whose reef, which lies to the west of that land, runs out nearly two leagues to seaward. Bearings of the land at noon:
Fort Concordia, south 45° east
Turtle Island, west 18° south
The north coast of Semau, west 36° south
In the afternoon, the winds having held fairly steadily in the south-west quarter, varying towards the west, we were obliged to stand on the tack heading west towards the north, and we kept on it until the middle of the night, when we went onto the southerly tack.
At sunset the land lay from us according to the following bearings:
A part of the north coast of the island of Roti, south 5° east
The land of the same island most in sight, south 10° east
The north coast of Semau, south 16° east
A part of the north coast of Timor in sight, north 25° west.
During the night of the 22nd to the 23rd the winds were light and very unsteady. We had a fairly fine sky, though very damp, and a calm sea. According to our observations, the current appeared to set us to the north-west during the flood as well as during the ebb.
At midnight the signal to go about was made to the Naturaliste, and we likewise changed our tack to stand to the south, my intention being to pass out between the island of Roti and that of Savu, if the winds were not too contrary.
1801-11-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE, SE, E, NE, NNW, WNW, W, WSW and SW. At 4 a.m. the topgallant masts were rigged and the topsails hoisted, stopped with rope yarns. At 5 got under way with the Géographe and shaped our course N 33° 45' W, N 56° 15' W and N 67° 30' W to leave the bay. At 11, the wind having hauled to the NW, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At noon, the commander having gone onto the port tack, we followed his movement. The NW point of Semau then bore from us S 61° W, 5 miles off, and the NW point of Turtle Island N 79° E, 8 miles off. At 4, Roti Island from S 84° W to S 88° W, and Batu Island N 45° E. The captain cancelled the distribution of hens made on the 20th; he gave 100 to the officers, 50 to the chief petty officers, 30 to the second petty officers, 20 to the petty officers, and the rest to the sick.

1801-11-14.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WNW to SW, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, the course NNW. At 4 a.m. we steered S by E, with a great deal of thunder and lightning. At noon took the bearing of the island of Roti S 46° 30' W.
1801-11-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, in the morning, after making out the land and taking bearings of it, we were rather surprised to find ourselves scarcely further on than the evening before; and although there had been little wind during the night, I had nevertheless expected the current to have carried us a fair way to the westward.
Bearings in the morning at sunrise.
A part of the north coast of Semau east 27° north
The most prominent land of the same island east 10° south
The northern part of Roti south 30° east.
During the morning the wind was very variable from south to east and often calm. We kept as near as we could to a westerly course, making all the southing that was possible. At about eight o'clock, the Naturaliste having closed with us, we spoke her, and I was informed that most of her sick were becoming convalescent, but that two were in danger. Our own situation was much the same. Those suffering from dysentery were a great deal better, but I was in continual anxiety for our second gardener, whom a malignant fever had reduced to such a state of weakness and torpor that his recovery was very doubtful.
As this was not my bad day, I was fairly well; nevertheless I often felt a numbness in my legs which made me know only too well that I was not yet out of danger.
At noon we observed the latitude of 9° 58' south, and the longitude by dead reckoning, according to the courses run since our departure, was 121° 13' east.
At the same time, the most prominent land of the island of Roti stretched away to the south-south-east, at a great distance.
In the afternoon the calm continued until about three o'clock, when the wind, having shifted to west-south-west, variable towards the south, freshened a little. We then lost sight of the land and shaped our course as close to the wind as possible, but we saw with regret that we were being carried strongly to the north-west by violent tide-rips which came upon us from south to south-east.
(Reproduce the sketch which is in the margin)
During the night of the 23rd to the 24th the sky was once more cloudy and very damp. I do not know whether this state of the atmosphere contributed to the discomfort that all our sick felt, but the fact is that they were less well than usual. I myself felt it, and passed rather a bad night, in the course of which we were often becalmed, although a cool air came to us at times from the east, which would have been very welcome had there been any wind.
Nota: During the day I had the consumption of water regulated, so that we should not suffer what we had so nearly suffered during our last passage. The allowances of tea and coffee were likewise fixed, as was that of sugar, for had the ordinary course been followed, we should have had nothing left at the end of three months, although we have on board as much as we need for nine.
1801-11-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8 took the bearing of the SW end of Semau S 78° E, the part of Timor in sight N 69° E. At 9 we passed under the commander's stern; he gave us the course south. Variation 0° 58' NW. At noon, being in 10° 3' 30" of latitude, we took the bearing of Dorr Island S 46° E, 18 miles off by the observed latitude and the bearing. The longitude was 120° 45'. It is from there that I took my point of departure. Savary, boatswain's mate, died of dysentery. It was signalled to the commander.

1801-11-15.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WSW to SW, the weather fine, the sky clear and the sea smooth. At noon a man named Savary died, which was announced to the commander by the agreed signal.
1801-11-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
[3V p. 79 ter] Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, the wind continued extremely variable and the sky became stormy in several quarters of the horizon. A little before sunrise we had several fairly heavy squalls of rain, but without wind. At daybreak the sky became very overcast, and we saw several waterspouts form; and although the currents of air in the atmosphere were different, at least to judge by the opposite motion of the clouds, all of them had the same inclination. These phenomena occurred at different times and lasted no more than three or four minutes, after which they dispersed.
At the doctor's visit, all our sick were found to be fairly well, with the exception of our gardener's boy Riedelé Sautier, who was in his death agony, having been seized with tetanus during the night. All the remedies usual in such a case were administered to him at once, but they were of no avail, and at about noon he died. Apart from the regret his loss causes me on account of his personal qualities, I saw with much sorrow that the botanical part of our voyage would be very incomplete, since I had had the misfortune to lose the two persons who attended to it with zeal and assiduity.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 9° 39' 9" south, which gave us a large difference to the north from our dead reckoning. From an hour angle taken in the afternoon, the longitude of the ship was found to be 120° 38', taking 121° 47' as that of Timor. Although we took some two hundred distances during our stay at Kupang in order to determine its longitude exactly, we did not yet know the results, as they have not been calculated.
In the afternoon the weather turned fine, and the horizon, which had been thick and hazy all morning, became clear. The wind likewise shifted to south-south-east, and we kept as close as possible to a course south by west.
During the night of the 24th to the 25th it held in the same quarter, but was so light that we made little progress. The tide-rips we passed through during these twenty-four hours seemed to us stronger than those we had met with in the preceding days, and they had the same direction.
1801-11-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to ESE. At noon in 9° 38' 32" of latitude observed and in 120° 15' 46" of longitude by the watches. The variation 1° 5' 40" NW. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-11-16.journal_anonyme: The winds from south to SSE and ESE, the course SW and SSW, fine weather, smooth sea, the air rather thick and the winds light. At noon we sighted the land of Savu; we took the bearing of a very conspicuous headland SSE.
1801-11-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the sky was very overcast and almost constantly charged with stormy vapours which gave us reason to fear some squalls. The wind, however, was very light from the south towards the east, which enabled us to make a little progress to the southward.
At noon the observed latitude was 10° 0' 44' south, and the longitude by the rate of No. 35 was 119° 50'. That by dead reckoning was 120° 18'.
While the meridian altitude was being observed, we sighted land to the south, stretching 12° to the eastward. This land was the island of Savu, to which the Dutch sent a sergeant during our stay at Timor. The duties this man performs in the country during the six months he spends there come down to making the inhabitants pay the Company the tribute it has imposed upon them in the alliance it has made with them. This consists of rice, raw wax, honey and a few slaves, as well as a little sandalwood. In exchange for these articles the Company gives some handkerchiefs and cloths made in Java.
The private trade between this island and Timor, though of little consequence in itself, is nonetheless fairly brisk. As the inhabitants of Savu are seafarers, while those of Timor seldom leave home, they bring them painted cloths of various colours for the dress of men and women, which are generally preferred, for the elegance of their design and their fineness, to those made on Timor. Fish oil, coconuts, mats made from fan palms, and dried fish make up the greater part of their cargo, on the value of which the Company levies a duty of ten per cent, and reserves for itself, at whatever price it pleases, whatever may suit it.
In the afternoon, the wind having drawn closer to the east, we were able to stand in a little towards the land, and we ran along the south-west part of Savu at a fair distance. At about four o'clock we had a perfectly clear view of the island which lies off the south-west point and abreast of it. This island is high and well wooded, and seemed to us likely to be inhabited. The channel between it and Savu may be four or five leagues wide, and probably offers a good passage to vessels that would keep fairly close to the coast of Savu in order to take advantage of it.
Bearings at sunset:
The most prominent point of the eastern part of Savu east 54° south
A low point belonging to the small island I have mentioned south 10° east A rather remarkable hillock on the same land west 88° south The southernmost and westernmost part of the land in sight west 75° south.
From these bearings I signalled to the Naturaliste the course for the night, south-south-west, supposing that the wind would allow us to steer it.
During the night of the 25th to the 26th the wind was very variable and unsteady, and the sky cloudy and threatening storm. We had a few light squalls, but of short duration, and the wind held fairly steadily in the quarter from east to south-east, at times a pleasant breeze, at times light.
During the night several fires were seen on the small island to the south-west of Savu, so there is no doubt that it is inhabited; and indeed, by its pleasant aspect, it seemed to us to deserve to be
1801-11-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. The commander signalled the death of a man (Sautier, gardener). At noon sighted Savu Island in the S 22° 30' E, being in 10° 4' 13" of latitude observed and in 119° 53' 3" of longitude by the watches. At 8.30 observed 1° 5' 30" of NW variation. At 1 the course was signalled S 11° 15' W. At 6 took the bearing of Savu from S 17° E to S 67° E and Benjuar Island from south to S 9° W. At midnight Benjuar Island bore from us S 22° 30' E. There was a fire on it.

1801-11-17.journal_anonyme: The wind varying from SE by E to south, a light breeze. At 1 the commander signalled the course S by W. At 4 took the bearing of the NW end of Savu S 10° E; the SE end E 41° S; Benjuar Island S 7° W.
1801-11-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, as soon as the moon had set, the weather turned fine and we had the beginning of a pleasant breeze from the south-east, which seemed likely to freshen at sunrise.
Bearings of the land at the same hour:
The land in sight of the island of Savu east 16° north
The north point of the small island near Savu east 12° north
The south point of the same island south 89° east
An islet ahead of us south 28° west.
The above bearings, when laid down on all our charts, gave only poor results, and it seems to me beyond doubt that most of the land, with the exception of Savu, is wrongly placed on them.
On Robertson Arrowsmith's chart, the island lying to the south-west of Savu bears the name of Île Bonjour, and this is the only chart that gives it one. His Île Nouvelle, which comes next, is placed much too far to the west and south.
On Robertson's, the island off the south-west point of Savu is placed well enough, but the other is laid down a good deal further to the west-south-west than it actually is, and one would fall victim to the error of his chart, especially at night, for the width he gives for the channel is less than half of what he states.
The same is true of the French chart published in 1791. The manuscript chart of M. d'Entrecasteaux's voyage is the most accurate of all as regards the subject of which I speak.
A reflection which the sight and the lie of the land suggested to me is perhaps not without foundation. It seems to me that the island Arrowsmith named Île Bonjour is Little Savu. Its nearness to the large island of the same name, its inhabitants, its extent and its pleasant aspect seem to confirm this opinion. The other island, marked on the charts as New Savu, is no more than eight or nine leagues at most from the one I have just spoken of. It is a barren rock rather than anything else, some two leagues in extent. We coasted along the northern side of this island at a distance of three-quarters of a league. Everywhere we found nothing but rocks heaped one upon another, which looked as though they must be the work of some convulsion of nature. A few clumps of trees are its only ornament. The coast, apart from a few coves of very white sand, is formed of sheer rocks, and the sea was breaking furiously upon it everywhere, although we were to leeward of it.
At eight o'clock we had doubled this rock, and at noon it bore north 30° east of us.
The latitude then observed was 11° 2' 23" south, and the longitude by No. 35 was 119° 14' 27"; dead reckoning placed us in 119° 50'.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the breeze was light. We steered as near south as we could, regulating our speed by the sailing of the Naturaliste, which made us lose a great deal of ground.
At sunset I had the vexation of learning of the death of one Corroyer, one of our best seamen and a helmsman. We all regretted him, for he was very steady and most active. He had fallen ill with dysentery only a few days before our departure, and although the doctors treated him from the very beginning, they could not save him.
The night of the 26th to the 27th passed without incident. The weather was fine, but the wind shifted to the south, drawing westerly, which made it very unfavourable for the course we had to make
1801-11-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 4, Benjuar Island from S 68° E to S 85° E, 5 miles off. At 6.30 New Savu was sighted in the S 30° W. At noon it bore from us N 30° E, 15 miles off, being in 11° 2' 10" of latitude observed and in 119° 18' 39" of longitude by account.

1801-11-18.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from SE, south and SSW. Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light air. The commander signalled us the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, having passed, since the day before, all the known islands lying to the south and west of Timor, I signalled to the Naturaliste that we would steer south-south-west by compass if the wind allowed.
During the morning the breeze was very light from the south. We had, on the other hand, very fine weather and a calm sea, though it was driven by a heavy south-westerly swell of which we could not guess the cause.
At noon we observed the latitude of 11° 34' 28" south, and the longitude deduced from the rate of No. 35 was 118° 13' 39", while dead reckoning placed us in 119° 33' 12", which gave for the timekeeper a difference to the west of 1° 19' 33" since leaving Timor. It seems likely that so great a difference, in so short a time, must be attributed to a strong current which carried us west by north, as we had observed in the tide-rips we met with in doubling the islands, whose direction ran from south-east to north-west.
In the afternoon the wind varied from south to south-south-east and made our course a little better, but not for long, for at sunset it went back to the south.
During the night of the 27th to the 28th we found the sea heavier than it had been during the day, and the ship pitched a great deal. The damp was considerable during the night, and our sick, although under shelter, were troubled by it. I myself, though convalescent, suffered much from it, and felt such weakness in the backs of my knees that I could not stand on my legs. I also had some gripes, but they did not last long
1801-11-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to SSW. At 1 hove to to wait for the Géographe. At 1.45 she had closed; we filled and stood on. At 8, 0° 49' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 36' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 29' 3" of longitude by account. The cables were unbent and the anchors secured in their stowage.

1801-11-19.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from S, SSE to SW, almost calm, the weather fine, the sea smooth. The commander signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth the weather continued fine, but the wind was so variable that we made little progress on our proper course. The sea, still running with a swell from south to south-west, gave no sign of an early change in the wind. I flattered myself, however, that at the full moon we should experience one that would improve our course, being persuaded that the wind, if it did not come from the south towards the east, would at least come from the west towards the south. What follows will show whether this conjecture was right.
In the morning our sick felt much relief from what they had suffered during the night. Nevertheless, two were in great danger, and the doctors were of the opinion that they could not recover. Citizen Maugé, who was also suffering from dysentery, did not look well, and I was not without anxiety on his account, all the more because I feared that the men we had lost to the same disease might make some impression on him which could only delay his recovery.
At noon we observed the latitude of 11° 30' 51", and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 116° 59' 36". That by dead reckoning was only 118° 45', which increased still further the timekeeper's difference to the west.
In the afternoon the wind varied from south to south-south-east, and the sea, though fair, still ran with a swell. We continued on the tack to the west by south, hauling as close to the wind as possible, but the Naturaliste's poor sailing and that vessel's leeway when close-hauled prevented us from profiting by what little advantage we might have drawn from it.
During the night of the 28th to the 29th the wind went back to the south, drawing westerly; the breeze was very light, or rather we were almost becalmed for the greater part of the night. The ship was long surrounded by fish; we managed to harpoon only one porpoise, and even that we lost just as it was being hauled on board, the harpoon having broken.
1801-11-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. The commander signalled us the death of a man (Corroyer). At 7.45, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 33' 12" of latitude observed and in 117° 29' 15" of longitude by account.

1801-11-20.journal_anonyme: Winds from S, SW and WSW. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, a fresh breeze.
1801-11-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the wind having shifted to south-west, variable towards the west, we brought our tacks to starboard on the tack to the south by east. The breeze was light and the sea still ran with a swell.
During the morning all hammocks were stowed and the decks cleared. The ship was cleaned and fumigated throughout, and our carpenters, once this first task was done, were ordered to finish the work that remained to be done on the longboat.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 11° 34' 22 and the longitude by No. 35 was found to be 116° 17' 48". That by dead reckoning placed us in 118° 5', which consistently gave less distance run to the west than the timekeeper showed.
During the evening the breeze was very variable and light, and we continued on the same course in order to work to the westward. It was by an oversight that I said above that in the morning we took the course to the south by east.
At about four o'clock in the afternoon we lost one Poussin, a good seaman, attached to the service of the hold. It is only too likely that all those attacked by dysentery will meet the same fate; and the symptoms of this terrible disease are so frightening that at the slightest touch of it a man believes himself already dead, which does not a little to aggravate the illness of those who have it. The fevers, though bad, are not so fatal to us, and since our departure from Timor we have lost only one man to that sickness.
During the night of the 29th to the 30th the weather was fine and the sky less damp than usual. Nevertheless, I passed a very bad night. My sleeplessness was complete, and the weakness in the backs of my knees greater than on the preceding days. My condition seemed to herald a fresh relapse. We continued to sail close-hauled, gaining to the westward as much as was possible
1801-11-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. At noon in 11° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 116° 47' 51" of longitude by account.

1801-11-21.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from W to SW, the sea and the weather fine, the breeze pleasant.
1801-11-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, the wind having at last shifted to south-west, varying at times towards the west, we went about to stand south, edging east, in order to make latitude. The Naturaliste was ordered to do the same, and we continued to hug the wind the wind (sic) close-hauled, until it should allow us to steer south-south-west, which is the course I intend to hold if the winds become favourable before we are carried too far to the south.
At noon we observed 12° 19' 0" of latitude, and the longitude by our No. 35 placed us in 117° 11' 28". That by dead reckoning was 118° 33' 12", which gave a difference of 0° 24' 34 to the east by the timekeeper beyond the estimated course. What can be the cause of this great difference in these twenty-four hours, so entirely opposite to those we had observed until then?
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, the breeze light and variable as usual.
During this day, finding myself fairly well despite the indisposition I had felt the day before, I went with the doctor to pay a visit to our sick. It was only the second of its kind since our departure, as my health had not allowed me to make more.
I found Citizens Maugé and Depuche fairly well, but not entirely out of danger; the sailmaker much troubled by a pain in the liver, but showing the outward symptoms of poor health. All the fever cases were well into convalescence and will soon be out of danger. But our gunner Masson was dying from the effects of dysentery, with no hope of recovery. I ordered some changes in the sick berth for their greater comfort, and saw that we would soon cease to lose men.
The night of the 30th to the 1st of Frimaire brought nothing new; the wind was light and variable as usual, and we made very little way
1801-11-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from SSW to W. At noon in 12° 20' 50" of latitude observed and in 117° 22' 45" of longitude by account. At 4, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation.

1801-11-22.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from W to WSW and WNW, the weather fine, a swell running from the SW and a fresh breeze.
1801-11-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Frimaire, in the morning, the wind was extremely light after sunrise. It drew, however, more to the west than it had yet done, which gave us hope that it might vary from west towards north as we drew nearer to the coasts of New Holland.
In the course of the morning one Mantel, a gunner and a mason by trade, died from the effects of a dysentery which had kept him languishing for a long time. Three days before his death he had tried to throw himself into the sea, and he would have perished then and there but for the promptness with which he was rescued. When he had been brought back on board, he said to us with great composure: "You are doing me a very poor service, for I know well that I cannot recover from my illness; so you are only prolonging my sufferings by a few more days."
At noon the latitude was observed to be 13° 00' 41", and the longitude by No. 35 gave 117° 6' 22". We were surprised to see by the timekeeper a few minutes' distance to the west, whereas, compared with the dead reckoning of our course, it gave us 14' 8" to the east. This difference seemed to point to an approaching change in the direction of the currents, which until then had carried us to the eastward, according to the results of the same timekeeper. The longitude by dead reckoning was 118° 48' 18".
In the afternoon the wind was much the same as we had had during the morning, only the breeze was a little fresher. We continued to steer south, making as much westing as was possible. As several flocks of birds of the gull kind had been (seen) during the day, I presumed that we might be in the neighbourhood of the rocks and sandbanks of which Dampier speaks. Accordingly I had a good lookout kept, but we saw nothing that could confirm my conjecture; and if they exist in these waters, it seems likely that we were to windward of them, for the swell we had had from the south-west for several days had lost none of its strength. At eight o'clock in the evening, being by our reckoning in 13° 22' south latitude, we were beginning to approach the latitude that Dampier gives for the banks and rocks of which he speaks in his first voyage to the southern lands. But as the weather was very clear and fine, and our night horizon extended at least two leagues, our (sic) continued our course, taking the precaution of keeping a good lookout. All night, the sky remaining fine, we sailed without anxiety, making, nevertheless, only as much way as was needed so as not to be in 13° 50' before daylight
1801-11-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 8, 1° 46' 20" of NW variation. Saw a tropic bird. At noon in 13° 5' 10" of latitude observed and in 117° 42' 51" of longitude by account. We shifted our suit of sails.

1801-11-23.journal_anonyme: The winds from W to WSW, a fresh breeze. The commander signalled the course SW by S; he also signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second the fine weather continued, and it would be hard to meet with finer than we have had since our departure from Kupang, except, however, for the wind, which was often light and contrary to the course I intended to hold in order to double the westernmost point of New Holland.
At sunrise the wind varied a little from west towards north, and the breeze was stronger than usual. We then reckoned ourselves at no great distance from the latitude of the rocks seen by Dampier, which he places in 13° 50' south latitude. But we saw no sign that could lead us to suspect that these dangers lie in the waters we crossed. According to our longitude, we must have passed about thirty-five leagues from them, going by the position Robertson gives them on his chart of 1791.
At eight o'clock we spoke the Naturaliste. Captain Hamelin gave me news of his sick, twelve in number, but all well into convalescence. That vessel was much more fortunate than we, in that she had lost only one man since leaving Timor, whereas we have lost four. We agreed to steer south-west by south, if the wind allowed, so as to get a little further to the westward and be able to double the western point of New Holland, as I remarked above.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 56' 57" south, and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 117° 16' 13". That by dead reckoning was much greater and placed us in 118° 58' 42". The distance we reckoned we had made to the south in the 24 hours proved less than we had thought, and the course worked out gave 0° 17' 17" more to the south than the observation. This difference can only be attributed to some current that must have set us to the north, for since the morning we had no longer felt the heavy south-westerly swell we had met with on the preceding days.
In the afternoon the breeze was fairly good, though less strong than in the morning, and the wind drew further round towards the west by way of the south. At sunset we were almost becalmed, the ship barely answering her helm.
During the night of the 2nd to the 3rd the sky was extremely fine and pleasant, but the calm lasted a long time, and it was only in the middle of the night that the breeze rose a little from the west, varying now towards the south and now towards the north.
1801-11-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. We spoke the commander, who gave us the course S 33° 45' should the wind draw aft. He signalled us the death of a man (Mantel). At noon in 14° 2' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 55' 33" of longitude by account, and in 117° 35' 0" of longitude by the watches. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds. At 5.45, 2° 3' 20" of NW variation.

1801-11-24.journal_anonyme: The winds varied from NW, W and WSW. At 9 we began to lie our course. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-11-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, although the barometer had begun to fall from daybreak, the weather remained very fine and clear, and during the morning we had a pleasant breeze from the west-south-west until about the time the sun crossed the meridian, when it veered more to the south. The Naturaliste having fallen far to leeward, we bore down on her and closed with her. That vessel seemed to us to make much more leeway on this passage than on the previous one, which perhaps comes from the change she made in her stowage during our stay at Kupang.
At noon we observed the latitude of 14° 52' 54" south, and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 117° 42' 52", while dead reckoning put us in 119° 20' 48". The difference between observation and dead reckoning continued to be northerly, and we had 10' 48" more to the south by dead reckoning.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine. That day I felt better than I had since our departure, and I stood fairly firmly on my legs, which until then had served only to give me proof of my great weakness. Our other sick were also much better, especially Citizens Maugé and Depuche, who were suffering from dysentery. Among the crew, two men left the sick berth, but two others entered it who had caught the fever, I hardly know how.
The barometer, which for a great part of the day had stood at 28 and sometimes even below, made us fear bad weather. Nothing, however, seemed to herald it, the sky being very fine and almost cloudless. The calmness of the sea was likewise proof that no squalls had passed in the vicinity, for it would have been rougher than we found it.
During the night of the third to the fourth the sky remained fine and clear. The hygrometer, however, stood at 98°, which indicated great humidity in the air, the effects of which were felt particularly by the men on watch. After the moon rose, which was at about half past ten, the damp became less considerable and everyone felt the better for it. During the night the wind veered from the west towards the north and our course improved; at times we were able to head south-west by south and make a little way on that point of the compass.
1801-11-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to SSW. At noon in 14° 55' 35" of latitude observed and in 117° 46' 0" of longitude by the watches. At 5, 1° 48' 0" of NW variation. Saw a shark. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 45° W.

1801-11-25.journal_anonyme: Winds SW, WSW and SSW, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky serene throughout the twenty-four hours. At 8 a.m. a topman named Fanfan died of dysentery.
1801-11-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 118° 03' 55"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 14' 8" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 12' 53 to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, after sunrise, the breeze, which for part of the night had been from the west towards the north, continued in the same direction and freshened a little as the sun rose towards the meridian. As we were already well advanced to the south, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south-west, and we steered on that point of the compass whenever we could lay it.
During the morning several distances of the sun from the moon were taken, the mean result of which placed us in 118° 3' 55", reduced to noon. The longitude shown by No. 35 differed at the same time by 14' 8" to the west, and dead reckoning placed us 1° 12' 53" further east than the distances. The meridian altitude was 15° 37' 19", which likewise gave a difference from the course run of 8' 47" less to the south. As the differences had been more or less considerable since leaving Kupang, there is no doubt that the currents were then setting to the north. A greater number of observations by distances, if the weather stays fine, will enable us to judge whether they set easterly or westerly.
At about ten o'clock in the morning the Naturaliste, by a signal agreed between her and me, informed me that she had just lost a man who had died of dysentery. All our sick on board were much better, and I hope I shall have no more losses to regret, above all not Citizens Maugé and Depuche, who are suffering from this fatal disease.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the breeze fell off a good deal and the wind varied once more from west towards south. The calmness of the sea foretold a calm, and we did indeed have one after sunset. At the same time the sky, which all day had been perfectly clear and fine, suddenly clouded over. In the north-west it had an ugly look. We were persuaded that the wind was about to come to us from that quarter of the horizon, and perhaps even the bad weather that seemed to be foretold by the barometer, which was still tending to fall; but nothing of the kind happened. Little by little the clouds dispersed, despite the dead calm that then prevailed, and at moonrise the sky became as clear as it had been during the day. At about midnight we had a light cool air from the west, which was strong enough to give the ship steerage way. It freshened a little as the moon rose above the horizon
1801-11-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SSW. At 7.30, 0° 57' 26" of NW variation. Hubert, known as Fanfan, died of a disease of the liver. At noon in 15° 38' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 58' of longitude by the watches.

1801-11-26.journal_anonyme: Winds W to SW and SSW, a light breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The winds varied from W to WNW and WSW. At 8 a.m. a man named Ivan died of dysentery.
1801-11-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 118° 14' 27"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 9' 17" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 18' 21" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, after spending part of the night becalmed, we had a light breeze from south-west towards west which little by little veered from west towards north. At sunrise I had the ship bear away square before the wind towards the Naturaliste in order to speak Captain Hamelin. That vessel was nearly two leagues to leeward and was sailing large, so that I could make nothing of the course she was steering. Having come up with her, I asked why she was not keeping close-hauled, as I had signalled. Captain Hamelin sent me word that his ship was steering very badly and that, although he kept the helm constantly a-lee, she did not answer it at all. As this vessel had never seemed to us to have (such) bad qualities, I represented to him that it was absolutely necessary to change something in her stowage and to trim her more by the head or by the stern, as he should see fit. He promised me that he would see to it, which he must of necessity do, for it is not possible for us to sail in company unless he remedies it. I reckon that since our departure from Timor she has made us fall more than forty leagues to leeward. For three times a day, and often twice in the night, we are obliged to bear down on her to avoid a separation which might prove fatal to one or the other of us.
At noon we observed the latitude of 16° 9' 15" south, and the longitude shown by No. 35 placed us in 118° 5' 10". A set of several distances of the sun from the moon taken during the morning gave us 118° 14' 27", which differed by only 0° 9' 17" further to the east than by the timekeeper. The difference in the dead reckoning was much more considerable, since we found (ourselves) carried 1° 18' 21" to the east. By the observation of the meridian altitude, the currents were still setting north by east, but they seemed to us to have less strength, the differences growing ever smaller as we advanced to the south. That of this day was 0° 11' 27".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the wind fell off a good deal and drew round from west towards south. At four o'clock the Naturaliste signal(led) to us that she had lost a man, which brought the total since our departure from Timor to eight men in the two ships, seven of them from dysentery.
At sunset, or at least shortly afterwards, the wind having shifted to south-south-west, very light, we changed tacks and took the course west by north. The night of the 5th to the 6th was very fine and the wind variable from south-south-west to south-west, very light. The sky was fine and the damp heavy enough to be troublesome. As the Naturaliste was still a long way to leeward, several signals were made to her with lights, and we closed with her.
1801-11-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SW. Le Bouru died of dysentery. At 8.30, 0° 32' 20" of NW variation. We spoke the commander, who urged the captain to use every means to keep the ship from making so much leeway, having been told that she was always very slack; he answered that this was not surprising, as she was too much by the head. At noon in 16° 14' 24" of latitude observed and in 118° 6' 0" of longitude by the watches, and in 118° 11' 0" of longitude by lunar distances.

1801-11-27.journal_anonyme: Winds WSW to SW, very light throughout the 24 hours.
1801-11-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 117° 29' 8"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 4' 4" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 2° 0' 20" to the east
