Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth the wind continued south-west, varying a little towards the south. The breeze was very light until sunrise, when it freshened a little. But at about nine o'clock it fell calm again and we made very little way.
During the morning we saw several fairly large flights of birds of the gull kind. They settled in great flocks on the water, which made us think they were busy feasting. Despite all our attention to discover what might be drawing them to the spot where they were, we saw nothing.
Before noon we set about making an inventory of the articles and effects belonging to Citizen Riedelé, our gardener who died at Kupang. Among his papers was found a kind of will containing his last wishes as regards his own affairs, with which he charged me personally. I had all his collections and papers gathered up, to be handed over to the Muséum, which, on learning the news of his death, will regret him no less than I do.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 58' 57", and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 117° 27' 8", which now differed from the timekeeper by only 0° 4' 4". It would be difficult, from the distance run by dead reckoning or from the weather we have had, to explain how we could have advanced 0° 45' 19" to the westward, and this difficulty can be resolved only by supposing a very violent current setting roughly in that direction, since the difference to the north is not great enough for it to depart much from it, which tomorrow's observation may verify.
In the afternoon the weather remained very fine and the sky perfectly clear until sunset. The wind held steadily in the same direction it had kept for a long time, but it was very light. Towards the end of the day we caught a very fine dorado, which pleased us all the more as it was the first delicate fish taken at sea since our departure from France.
The night of the 6th to the 7th was fine, with light airs from the SW. We continued to steer close-hauled on the tack to the west by north.
1801-11-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.30, 1° 47' 10" of NW variation. At noon in 15° 59' 51" of latitude observed and in 117° 49' 30" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 1° 54' 50" of NW variation.

1801-11-28.journal_anonyme: Winds SW and S by W; at 9 they drew round to NW and held there all night. Fine weather. A light breeze.
1801-11-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 116° 53' 7"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 11' 19" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 39' 17" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, we had a pleasant breeze, but the wind was constantly in the south-west quarter, varying a little to the south, which made it no better for the course we had to make. From all that has been published on the monsoons and the trade winds, we had reason to be surprised at finding it so different from (what) it ought to have been; for, supposing we were still in the waters proper to the monsoons, we ought to have found westerly winds variable towards the north, and if we had passed the line assigned to them, we should have had them from the south-east. There is no doubt that we were in one or other of these two regions, and yet we had none of the winds that are held out to us as certain. It is therefore true that the seasons are not as certain as is believed, at least out at sea away from the coasts, and what happened to us is the proof of it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 24' 3" south, and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 116° 41' 48". Three sets of distances taken during the morning gave, reduced to noon, 116° 53' 7", from which there resulted a difference of 0° 11' 19" further to the east than the timekeeper.
In these 24 hours we met with a rather remarkable peculiarity. The day before, when the ship made little way, the results of the timekeeper as well as of the distances gave us a difference of 40 minutes to the west, and the dead reckoning of the distance run gave no more than 10. Today, the rate of the same timekeeper and the distances observed gave us 31' 57" of distance to the west, whereas by the course we made the difference was 60 minutes, or one degree. These two differences in opposite directions present no small problem, one hard to solve, which the rest of our voyage may clear up.
During the evening the weather continued fine and the breeze fell off as the sun drew near the horizon. The wind also veered further to the south, and even drew a little easterly, which gave us hope of soon having it from the south-east, as we ought to have found it long since.
All our sick, with the exception of the sailmaker, were doing very well, and the doctor considers them out of danger. As for myself, although sound in body for several days, there still remains in my legs a great weak(ness) which wearies me.
Part of the night of the seventh to the eighth passed in calm, or at least with very little wind, and when it gathered a little strength, it came to us once more from the south-west quarter.
1801-11-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At noon in 15° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 116° 55' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-11-29.journal_anonyme: The winds S by W to south; during the night they were SSW, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-11-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 115° 52' 51"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 9' 51" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 25' 33" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth the wind followed its usual pattern, that is to say that in the morning it varied from south-west towards west, while at noon it began to vary from south-west towards south. I confess that I could make nothing of the direction of these winds, which ran so contrary to what we are told about the regularity of their changes in the waters subject to the monsoons, and about their constancy from the south-east in the region of the trade winds. If the winds we are meeting were produced by some accidental cause, it seems to me that their pattern would not have been so regular nor lasted so long, for the cause that produced them ought not to have remained so long in the same state.
At noon we observed the latitude of 14° 43' 45", and the longitude by our No. 35, the only one we have left, placed us in 115° 43' 30". The distances taken in the morning gave 115° 52' 51", which changed the difference shown by the timekeeper, which until then had been to the east and which today is found to be 9' 51" to the east.
After what had happened to us on the two preceding days, we expected a large difference, either to the east or to the west, from the course run by dead reckoning; to our great surprise, however, it was slight, for we found only 13' more than the observation. So what judgement can reasonably be passed on the differences in opposite directions that we met with on the 6th and 7th?
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the wind, as I have already observed, veered towards the south as the sun drew near the horizon. Its strength likewise diminished in proportion, and after sunset we were almost becalmed until the middle of the night, when a somewhat stronger breeze began to make itself felt, drawing from the south towards the west.
During the night of the 8th to the 9th nothing new occurred. We were often obliged to bear down on the Naturaliste, which was always falling far to leeward. That ship sails much worse than she did before.
All our sick are much better, even the sailmaker, who is the worst of them all. I consider Maugé out of danger and M. Depuche well advanced in his convalescence. It is high time, moreover, that all these dysenteries came to an end, for they have used us very ill
1801-11-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 7.45, 1° 42' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 14° 46' 24" of latitude observed and in 115° 54' 24" of longitude by account.

1801-11-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Observations by distances of the sun from the moon reduced to noon 115° 15' 4"
Difference from No. 35: 0° 0' 38" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning: 1° 31' 20" to the east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth the breeze was very light before sunrise, and it was only at about eight o'clock that it began to freshen. The wind having shifted to south-west and even to west-south-west, we changed tacks to take the course south by east, and we held it until one o'clock in the afternoon, when the wind's fickleness obliged us to go back to the larboard tack.
During the morning there was a pleasant breeze, and at times we were obliged to reef the topgallant sails. The sky was then cloudy though fair, and the sea smooth.
At noon the observed latitude was found to be 14° 56' 22" south and the longitude by No. 35 115° 15' 42", which gave a difference of 0° 0' 38" to the east for the timekeeper. It seemed to us that the estimated course for the 24 hours had been less affected by the currents than usual, since the differences resulting from the observations were less considerable. That from the meridian altitude was, however, 15' 17" further south, but that in longitude was only 5' 24" to the west.
During the evening the weather cleared again, that is to say all the clouds the sun had brought us before crossing the meridian dispersed and the sky became very clear. The wind then shifted to south-south-west and even to south by west, and fell off until sunset, when it gathered a little more strength. At that time we were obliged to run for a while with the wind well on the quarter to close with the Naturaliste. Since our departure from Timor it had rarely happened that we were not obliged to make this manoeuvre three or four times in twenty-four hours.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth the wind held south and south by south-south-west. The breeze was fairly pleasant, and had we been alone we should have made good use of it.
From eight o'clock in the evening until four o'clock on the morning of the tenth, the sky, although very clear and brilliant with starlight, brought us a great deal of damp. The decks and forecastle and quarterdeck of the ship were as wet with it as if water had been thrown over them, and the moist vapours clinging to the rigging could be plainly made out.
The sick, except for the sailmaker, go on improving steadily, and I flatter myself that in the course of the next décade most of them will be out of the hospital
1801-11-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.15, 2° 40' 40" of NW variation. Saw tropic birds and flying fish. At noon in 14° 53' 38" of latitude observed and in 115° 17' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-12-01.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, a fresh breeze; at 11 they drew round to SE and we lay our course SW. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-12-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth the wind continued from south by west to south, and during the morning even came round as far as south by east. But this did not last long, for before the end of the day it resumed its usual pattern. The breeze was nevertheless pleasant, and at times accompanied by strong gusts. The sky, very clear at sunrise, gradually became covered with white clouds which could be seen forming on the horizon, and as the sun rose they increased in number, so that by ten o'clock the sky was very cloudy, though fair. The phenomenon had been occurring for only two or three days. Until now it has not lasted long, for by five o'clock in the evening at the latest all the clouds had vanished in the same way as they had formed in the morning.
At about seven o'clock Captain Hamelin made me a signal asking leave to send a boat on board. The weather being fine at the time and the breeze still moderate, his request was granted and we bore down on him to close with him. When I hove to within musket shot of that vessel, the boat was sent off, and M. Freycinet the Younger handed me two letters, one from M. Hamelin and the other from MM. Millius and Saint Criq.
By M. Hamelin's letter I was informed that since our departure he had lost three men, dead of dysentery; that he still had ten sick, among them Citizen Le Villain of Le Havre, who was having great difficulty in recovering and about whom there was even some anxiety. The other nine were less ill and out of danger. By a great number of distances observed on board that vessel, the longitude was 115° 18' 28", reduced to noon on the ninth, and that of their timekeeper 115° 28' 6", which gave them 0° 10' 12" to the east for its rate. Thus their longitude observed by distances differed from ours by only 0° 3' 24" east, and that of the timekeepers by 12' 24".
In that of MM. Millius and Saint Criq, these two officers begged me to accept, to share with the officers, half of a calf which the Governor had presented to them at Timor and which they had kept until that day. By the return of the boat, which I sent back at once, I informed Captain Hamelin of the result of our observations and of the condition of our sick. To MM. Millius and Saint Criq (I sent) (in the margin: my thanks).
After the boat had left, we continued on our course under easy sail until the Naturaliste was in a position to follow us, which was not long.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 14° 53' 13", and we were surprised to have made no distance to the south, since the course of the twenty-four hours seemed to indicate some; indeed, after working it out, we found that we only 3' to the south.
In the afternoon the sky, as I have already observed, cleared of the clouds that had come up in the morning, and the wind fell off. The sea, which the breeze had made choppy, became smooth, and the wind went back to the south, drawing westerly. Before nightfall we closed with the Naturaliste. During the night we had fine weather, a smooth sea, little wind and a great deal of damp.
1801-12-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 8, 1° 22' 30" of NW variation. At 6 we asked the commander leave to communicate; he having granted it, we lay under topsails to wait for the Géographe, which was to windward at a great distance and was bearing down on us. At 7 hove to; our boat carried half a bullock, which Citizens Milius and Saint-Cricq were sending to the commander and the officers of the Géographe. At 8.30 we filled and stood on. At noon in 15° 0' 24" of latitude observed and in 114° 16' 12" of longitude by account. Saw tropic birds. At 4, 2° 8' 50" of NW variation. On the evening of the 10th I received orders to take Citizen Milius's watch, he having been ill for several days.

1801-12-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SSE and south; during the day they drew round to S, SSW and SW. Fine weather, a swell running.
1801-12-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, after sunrise, and as the sun rose higher above the horizon, we did not have the clouds that we had observed in its course on the two preceding days. The sky was fine all day, but the breeze light. The winds, however, varied from south towards east, which gave us reason to hope that we should soon have them at south-east, although the swell still came to us from the south-west, fairly strong and high.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 3' 3" south, and the longitude deduced from the rate of No. 35 was 113° 21' 5". In these 24 hours the currents had set us only 0° 5' to the north, so that the difference was far less considerable than we had had it until then.
In the afternoon the winds were in much the same quarter as in the morning, but we observed at sunset that they did not follow their usual course by veering from south to south-west, which was infinitely agreeable to us.
As we were all on the quarterdeck, between five and six in the evening, making conversation, it fell upon the great humidity there was at night. I then asked Citizen Péron, who was in charge of that part of our observations, whether he continued to make them in his bed, since he spoke of them as though he had observed on deck or in some other part of the ship. From the moment of our arrival at Timor this savant had thrown himself headlong, and even with fury, into shells, although he had no knowledge whatever in that line. A snail, a nerite, etc., was a treasure to him, so that in order to gather them in profusion he spent all his time on it, and by this means neglected other work which he would have performed much better than the one he has just taken up and which, according to his principles, he will no doubt pursue.
However that may be with the future, since we are concerned here only with what happened yesterday, he saw plainly that I meant to tease him, but to get himself out of the matter he told me that, as his mother was bearing no more children and he was the sole hope of the family, he had no wish to kill himself making observations at night, and that besides he had made enough of them on that subject on our way to Timor. I pointed out to him that, however good his observations were, the sun was not in this part of the hemisphere when we ran along the coasts of New Holland, and that consequently it was well to have observations made at different seasons. His answers, full of excuses and hardly befitting a savant, astonished me, and so that the conversation should go no further I confined myself to saying to him: "You are quite free to work or not, but at least you will not take it amiss that I have others carry on the work which formerly you would not have let them do." I therefore asked him to hand over to me the hygrometer of which I had made him the keeper.
The night of the 11th to the 12th passed without incident. It blew in gusts from south-south-west to south-south-east, and we found the swell somewhat strong & high
1801-12-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 7.30, 1° 9' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 8' 49" of latitude observed and in 113° 16' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-03.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE to south, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The currents appeared to set strongly to the north.
1801-12-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth we had fine weather, a pleasant breeze and winds from the south varying towards the east, but the sea was rather rough, driven by a fairly high swell from the south which made us make a great deal of leeway to the north.
During the morning the carpenters worked on the masts and spars of our longboat, which they had finished putting in order in the past few days; for, as I have already remarked, we had taken it on board at Timor in a very unfinished state, the sickness of our carpenters having singularly delayed the work.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 00' 55" south, and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 112° 5' 42". We were astonished to have gained nothing to the south by the course of the twenty-four hours, which by the reduction gave us 15° 16' 57".
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and there was a pleasant breeze, even after sunset, which was not usual. At six o'clock we steered for the Naturaliste to close with her. At half past seven she was abeam of us at half a mile's distance. Despite the changes Captain Hamelin has made in her stowage, this ship still sails very badly and makes a great deal of leeway. Judging by the course she makes each day, it appears that in order to steer tolerably and make some headway she must keep her sails two points full.
During the night of the 12th to the 13th the sky was very fine until midnight, but then it became very cloudy. The breeze also fell light and the winds shifted from south towards west. The sea was then very rough and heaving with a great swell. The humidity was considerable and troublesome.
During the evening I had gone with the doctor to visit all our sick. It seemed to me that, with the exception of the sailmaker, who is suffering from a disease of the liver, all the others were doing fairly well. Citizens Maugé and Depuche continue to improve, and although they are not yet entirely cured, they are nevertheless regarded as altogether out of danger. Our hydrographer Boulanger is also beginning to recover, and the fever he brought, like me, from Timor has not appeared for six days.
As for myself, I am well and my strength is beginning to return.
1801-12-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 1' 46" of latitude observed and in 112° 9' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-04.journal_anonyme: Throughout the twenty-four hours the winds varied from south to SSE. A strong breeze, a high sea, the weather clear enough.
1801-12-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the thirteenth there were signs of a change of weather and perhaps of wind too, which we greatly desired so as not to be carried too far out to sea from the western point of New Holland. Had the winds allowed us, as at the beginning of our passage, to stand to the south, my intention was to look for the Rosemary Islands of which Dampier speaks, and which I believe lie much further to the east than they are placed on our charts. But to all appearances this plan must be given up, at least for the present.
During the morning the winds, which in the night had been fairly steadily at south-south-east, came back to south at sunrise and varied now towards the east, now towards the west. We found the sea heaving with a heavy swell all day.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 12' 24", that by dead reckoning for the course run being 15° 14' 59". This apparently gave us little difference to the west, and we could not check the fact by the rate of our timekeeper, since it was not possible to get an hour angle, so cloudy was the sky both morning and evening. By our longitude by dead reckoning we were only in 112° 28' 0", but we knew from the last observations that we were much too far to the east.
In the course of the evening the sky was not fine, and I even feared bad weather for the night, which the barometer also seemed to foretell. We had none, however. The night was dark and damp and the breeze moderate from south-south-east. The heavy swell that had prevailed for some time made the Naturaliste drift considerably to leeward, so that in order not to lose her we had almost always to keep the sheets eased and often to bear away.
1801-12-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 15° 15' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 4' 0" of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze in gusts.

1801-12-05.journal_anonyme: Winds S by E to south, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a heavy swell running. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-12-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the fourteenth, although the sky was still very cloudy, the weather nevertheless looked less threatening than the day before, but the sea was even more swollen than usual, and I should not be surprised if some violent gales had passed over the southern part of New Holland.
In the morning we had the winds at south, varying to south by east, moderate. The effects of Citizen Riedelé, who died at Timor on 29 Vendémiaire, were sold on board. The impossibility of keeping them on board during the time we have yet to remain at sea decided me to take this course, which is moreover in keeping with the ordinances and with his wishes, according to the paper he addressed to me.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 44' 6", and the longitude indicated by our No. 35, reduced to the same hour, placed us in 109° 11' 23", which gave a run to the west in forty-eight hours of 2° 54' 42", whereas by dead reckoning we found only 2° 34' 18". We therefore had a difference to the west of 20 (sic for 20') beyond our dead reckoning.
During the evening the weather seemed inclined to set fair and most of the clouds dispersed. The sale of the belongings and effects of Citizen Riedelé was continued, and everything fetched a very high price. I bought on my own account part of his books, which I shall treasure in memory of him.
According to the doctor's report, it appears that Citizen Depuche is not yet entirely out of danger and that his dysentery might have grave consequences. Citizen Maugé, without being entirely rid of his, is doing very well and will undoubtedly soon recover. The master sailmaker's illness is turning into dropsy and leaves little hope of saving him. All the others are infinitely better.
During the night of the 14th to the 15th the weather was fairly fine though cloudy. The winds kept close to south and the breeze was moderate.
1801-12-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 41' 21" of latitude observed and in 109° 51' 54" of longitude by account.

1801-12-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the fifteenth the weather seemed inclined to set fair. Most of the clouds dispersed and the sky became clear.
In the morning there was a fairly pleasant breeze, but in gusts, and the winds were in the quarter of south by
east, varying to south. The heavy swell we had had for several days began to go down.
At noon the observed latitude was 16° 4' 2" south, and for the first time since our departure from Timor we had a small difference to the south of about two minutes. By timekeeper No. 35 our longitude was 107° 39' 20", which gave us a difference of 21' to the west beyond the distance run by dead reckoning.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine. We closed with the Naturaliste, which was more than two leagues to leeward, and at four o'clock, having come within hail of her, I asked for news of her sick, and whether he had made to his ship the changes he had told me of.
To the first of these questions he answered that all his sick were doing very well, and especially M. Le Villain, who had long been in danger from the effects of a dysentery.
To the second he let me know that he had indeed altered the stowage of his hold, but that his ship held no better to the wind. Only he found an advantage in her sailing, for he recognised that she had more speed than before.
During the night of the fifteenth to the sixteenth the winds were much the same as we had had them in the course of the day, and the breeze was moderate. We did not, however, have a fine sky, and every point of the horizon became laden with clouds. In spite of this there was little variation in the barometer, which stood steadily at 28 inches one line. The humidity was also less considerable than on the previous days.
1801-12-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At 8.30, 3° 19' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 16° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-07.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, a fresh breeze in gusts, fine weather, a swell running. Saw tropic birds.
1801-12-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the sky, though cloudy, was nevertheless fairly fine, and we had a pleasant breeze from south by east to south, and sometimes to south by west. We kept on our course close-hauled, under sail matched to that of the Naturaliste, or at least to her speed. That ship had lost a good deal to windward in the night and we had to bear away down to her to close with her. At eleven o'clock she furled her topgallant sails and unrigged them. There was then a good breeze and the sea was beginning to rise, although it was still tolerably smooth, but the sky looked threatening for the evening and the night.
At noon we observed the latitude of 16° 24' 9" south, and the longitude deduced from No. 35 placed us in 106° 10' 57", which gave for the 24 hours a run of 1° 28' 23" to the west. By dead reckoning of the course run we found a difference of only 0° 3' 53" to the east and 0° 2' 40" to the south.
In the evening it blew a strong breeze and the sea became rough. At two o'clock we took a second reef in the topsails and furled our staysails.
Citizen Depuche was more troubled that day by his dysentery than he had been before, and I fear some grievous turn for him, since the remedies seem to have no effect on him, at least in appearance, for he is extremely weak and languid.
Citizen Maugé continues to improve, and although he still passes a little blood, he feels well and has a good appetite.
The other sick, with the exception of the sailmaker, will not be long now in leaving the sick-berth.
On this day the sale was completed of all the effects belonging to those we had lost, whether at Kupang or elsewhere, that is to say at sea since our departure from Timor.
During the night of the 16th to the 17th the weather was not bad, as it had threatened to be, but the sky remained laden with a great many clouds. Before sunset the winds had gone round to south-east. I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south-south-west, but that ship, being unable to lie so close to the wind, steered south-west, and being obliged to follow her we lost all the advantage the change offered us
1801-12-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SE. At noon in 16° 28' 43" of latitude observed and in 106° 59' 30" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-12-08.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, SE and SE by S, a strong breeze, a high sea, the sky cloudy. The commander signalled the course SSW.
1801-12-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventeenth the south-east winds seemed settled, and we hoped to see them continue on that point, and even to have them more towards the east should they come to vary. As it had blown a strong breeze the day before, the sea was rather rough and swollen, and it grew more so for the rest of the day, the breeze having again become very strong once the sun had risen above the horizon.
The sky, which we had had cloudy for several days, was so again on this one. Our horizon was of little extent and dull, of a whitish colour like that commonly met with between the coast of Africa and the Cape Verde Islands.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 17° 24' 52" south, and the longitude deduced from dead reckoning was 107° 12' 20". Having had no hour angle, we did not have the one our No. 35 might have indicated. The difference between the reduced course and the meridian observation gave 0° 3' 16" to the south.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze. The heavy swell then running strained the masts somewhat, and I had the topgallant sails unrigged.
At five o'clock we bore away for the Naturaliste to close with her; although she was very far to leeward, we rejoined her before nightfall.
During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth the winds were the same and the breeze abated little, but as the Naturaliste had furled her main topgallant sail and her staysails, we furled the mainsail.
The humidity shown by the hygrometer during the night was less considerable than appearances suggested, for, to judge by how low the clouds were, there seemed to be more of it. The barometer also rose to 28 inches two lines, which it had not done for a long time
1801-12-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 17° 27' 0" of latitude observed and in 105° 47' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-09.journal_anonyme: The winds SE, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a high sea, the ship pitching heavily. Saw several petrels and some flying fish.
1801-12-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth the winds continued at south-east, a strong breeze. The Naturaliste, however, was carrying her main topgallant sail, which gave me no great pleasure. I made her no signal to take in sail, because we had agreed together that she was never to carry enough to endanger her masts on the pretext of wishing to keep up with me, and that I much preferred to wait for her. At the same time as she had every sail set except her fore topgallant sail, I had for all my canvas the foresail, two reefs in all the topsails, and the mizzen. Even so, with so little canvas spread, I heeled over a good deal. He, on the contrary, did not appear troubled by it. It is true that this was not the first time he had let us see that his ship did not heel readily.
At noon we observed the latitude of 18° 34' 6" south, and the longitude deduced from dead reckoning of the course placed us in 106° 15' 44". The small extent of the horizon, morning and evening alike, did not allow us to take an hour angle.
In the afternoon the winds were the same as we had had them in the morning. At two o'clock we began to close with the Naturaliste, the weather looking threatening. For all her canvas, that ship had nonetheless fallen nearly two leagues to leeward. At five we had her abeam at half cannon-shot.
According to our previous observations, we were beginning to approach the spot on the chart where the Triades are placed, and perhaps tomorrow morning we shall sight them, if they have been correctly laid down by the Dutch, though I doubt it. Besides, we saw nothing in the evening, nor at sunset, that could lead us to believe we should see them the next day.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth the breeze was a little less strong than it had been during the day, but it was hardly until after the moon had set that it began to fall light. The sky grew no finer for it; on the contrary it became cloudier, and one could scarcely make out a few stars from time to time, and even these were of a rather pale colour
1801-12-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 18° 37' 18" of latitude observed and in 104° 44' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-10.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SE by S, a strong breeze and in gusts, the weather overcast and misty. At 6.30 a.m. the main jib split.
1801-12-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the nineteenth the weather was, as on the preceding days, very cloudy and threatening, the sea still rather rough and swollen. The winds held at south-east, a strong breeze, varying at times to south-east by south.
At daybreak our latitude by dead reckoning placed us, within very little, in that at which the Dutch chart places the Triades, and according to the observed longitude we should have passed close enough to see them. Nevertheless we sighted nothing that could make us suspect we had passed as near as the position marked on the charts indicates.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 19° 46' 18", and the longitude by No. 35 was found to be 102° 5' 2". Our difference from the course by dead reckoning was 0° 6' 24" to the south and 0° 7' 15" to the west.
In the afternoon the sky seemed inclined to clear, becoming brighter at several points of the horizon. But this clearing did not last long, for at sunset it was cloudier than ever. The air was then very cold and we were obliged to put on woollen clothing, at least most of us.
The sick who remained to us did not fare too well from it either, and despite the care taken to close the ports early, several complained of pains they were not accustomed to feel. Citizens Maugé and Depuche are recovering day by day; the latter, however, is still weak and languid.
During the night of the 19th to the 20th the weather was tolerable though very cloudy; the winds kept in the south-east quarter, moderate; the night was nevertheless cold without being very damp.
1801-12-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 8, 3° 56' 20" of NW variation. The flying jib boom was rigged in. At noon in 19° 46' 40" of latitude observed and in 103° 37' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-11.journal_anonyme: The winds SE to ESE, a strong breeze, the weather fine, a high sea and the sky cloudy.
1801-12-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the twentieth the weather seemed inclined to set altogether fair. The clouds with which the sky had been laden for several days dispersed for the most part as the south-east winds freshened and the sun rose above the horizon. The sea too became calmer, and everything seemed to promise us fine weather to come. We changed nothing in our sail, however, and even so the Naturaliste, with every sail set, had difficulty in keeping up with us.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 21° 7' 49", which gave us a large difference to the south from our dead reckoning, which placed us only in 20° 49' 41", so that we hardly knew to what cause to attribute this difference. The most general opinion, however, was that, having necessarily passed fairly near the Triades, whether they are placed according to the observations of the Dutch or of the Danes, we might have met a current between these islands or rocks which set more to the south than if we had passed well clear of them. This reasoning, questionable as it seems to me, is perhaps not without foundation. But however that may be, we had nonetheless 0° 28' 8" of difference to the south. The longitude indicated by No. 35 placed us in 101° 10' 26".
In the afternoon several distances of the sun from the moon were taken, but the results were so different from what was expected that no account was taken of them.
On board the Naturaliste they observed 100° 3'.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the breeze at south-east, little variable and fairly pleasant. The sky became very fine, the clouds having for the most part disappeared.
After sunset we likewise had fine weather, but the breeze fell a little. I signalled to the Naturaliste that we would steer south, if the winds allowed.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st the heavy sea we had had on the previous days diminished and the sea became smooth. The sky remained fine during the night, and although there was little wind, the air was cold
1801-12-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. Spoiled coconuts were served out to the crew. At noon in 21° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 102° 49' 24" of longitude by account, and in 100° 52' 40" of longitude by lunar distances. The commander signalled the course S 11° 15' W.

1801-12-12.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SE, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. At noon the commander signalled the course S by W.
1801-12-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first the weather continued fine, with a pleasant breeze from south-east by east to east-south-east. We could have steered directly south but for the Naturaliste. As that ship was running with the wind free, however, we likewise kept our sails full, but she made no less leeway for it and went hardly any faster, although the sea was smooth and she had set all the sail she could carry.
At noon we observed the latitude of 22° 31' 10", and the longitude by No. 35 was 100° 28' 10", which gave us a difference to the west of 14' from the distance by dead reckoning, although the two latitudes compared with each other gave a difference of only 3' 3".
In the afternoon we meant to take distances of the sun from the moon, but clouds which rose at that time did not allow us to do so. Apart from this drawback, however, the weather was fine.
During the evening the winds were fairly steadily at east-south-east, a pleasant breeze, and we much regretted not making better use of it than we were doing, for the reasons I have mentioned above.
At sunset, seeing no great likelihood of breeze for the night, we shook a reef out of our main topsail so as to encourage our travelling companion not to shorten sail.
At about midnight our master sailmaker died. He had fallen ill a few days before our departure from Timor, but not of the dysentery. He complained only of some pains in the belly and the liver. At first it was thought that his illness would be nothing and that he would soon be well again, but instead he went steadily from bad to worse from the time we put to sea, and some time afterwards it was recognised that the seat of the disease was indeed in the liver. The remedies judged suitable for him were accordingly administered, but they were without effect. He gradually became dropsical, and there was no longer any hope of saving him.
The sky, though cloudy, was fine during the night of the 21st to the 22nd, and the winds held at SE ¼ E, a light breeze.
1801-12-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to E. At 7.15, 4° 0' 0" of NW variation. Saw a pintado petrel. At noon in 22° 12' 34" of latitude by account and in 100° 26' 46" of longitude by account. At 4.15, 3° 33' 30" of NW variation.

1801-12-13.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to E by S, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, and cloudy during the night.
1801-12-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude observed by distances of the sun from the moon 99° 27' 28"
Difference from the timekeeper 0° 22' 7" to the east
Difference from dead reckoning 3° 52' 16" to the east
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-second the breeze was light in the morning and the winds the same as the day before. But the sky was very fine, with few clouds on the horizon. We noticed that for the last two or three days, as we were beginning to approach the sun, the air was infinitely more agreeable and less damp, but that at night the cold was sharp and penetrating. The men of the watch were obliged to change their clothing and put on winter garments so as not to suffer from it.
At noon the observed latitude was 24° 3' south, but somewhat doubtful because we were beneath the sun. Nevertheless the error could not be very considerable. That by dead reckoning placed us in 23° 52' 7".
The longitude indicated by No. 35 was found to be 99° 49' 35", and that by distances of the sun from the moon 99° 27' 28", so that the result was that the observations, compared with each other, gave between them a difference of 22' 7", by which the timekeeper was to the east. The same observations compared with the dead reckoning gave 3° 52' 16", by which we found ourselves to the east.
From the Naturaliste they signalled to us 99° 42' for the longitude observed by distances. In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the winds drew a little nearer to the south and came even to south-south-east. The breeze was also stronger and unsteady.
An inventory and sale were made of the effects that had belonged to our master sailmaker, so that they should not be taken or lost and his family might have the proceeds. The loss of this man grieved me all the more because he was extremely sober, hard-working and orderly, understood his trade very well, and I was well pleased with him. Apart from the qualities peculiar to him, he was a good seaman and always the first aloft on the yards when it was needed.
During the night of the 22nd to the 23rd we had a very cloudy sky and strong gusts from the south-east, yet fairly fine weather. We changed nothing in our sail, unless it were to wait for the Naturaliste, which happened often
1801-12-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 8.15, 4° 33' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 24° 3' 37" of latitude observed and in 100° 1' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-14.journal_anonyme: The winds SE by E to SSE and SE, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy.
1801-12-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third there were signs of a change of weather, in that the sky, which we had had fine and very clear for several days, was heavily overcast and laden with thick clouds which, for the most part, prevented us from seeing the sun. The sea was also less smooth, and we met a heavy swell from the south which seemed to come a little from the west.
Yet although the sky was so laden with clouds, the barometer, which we consulted often, varied very little in its course and foretold nothing bad.
During the morning part of our spare rigging was brought up on deck to be examined and given a little air. The day before, a leak had been noticed that ran from the second deck down into the boatswain's store, which made us fear that some piece might be damaged. But we were pleased to see that the rigging of the mainmast, which was brought up first as being the most doubtful, had come to no harm. I noted only that what we were doing that day would not have been done when the sky was very fine and the sun very hot.
At noon we were able to observe the latitude, which was found to be 25° 30' 30" south. The longitude by No. 35 placed us in 98° 39' 2", which again gave a fairly considerable difference to the west, since we found we had made 11' 33" more than the dead reckoning gave us. The difference between the two latitudes was also 11' 52".
During the evening the sky became still more overcast and thick than it had been in the morning. Nevertheless the clouds were of a fine light grey and offered nothing disagreeable to the eye, nor anything alarming for the night. But the southerly swell had increased considerably, and as we were taking it almost ahead, the ship pitched a great deal and laboured a fair amount. We then had for all our canvas our courses, one reef in the main topsail, two in the fore topsail and two in the mizzen topsail. It pained me to see the Naturaliste carrying her topgallant sails, for fear of seeing her masts come down.
During the night of the 23rd to the 24th the sky remained as it had been at sunset, heavily overcast. We saw neither the moon nor the stars, but neither did we have bad weather. The winds were fairly steadily at south-east, moderate.
1801-12-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 7.15, 5° 18' 20" of NW variation. Saw a petrel. At noon in 25° 36' 38" of latitude observed and in 99° 5' 10" of longitude by account. At 4.30, 6° 45' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-15.journal_anonyme: A light breeze SE to SE by S. Overcast weather, the sea smooth, the night damp. At noon the winds varied from SE by S to E by S.
1801-12-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the morning of the twenty-fourth the sky remained dark and overcast as it had been the day before, and even more so, for we scarcely saw the sun all day. The heavy swell we had had the day before was, however, less strong, and the sea became fairly smooth. The winds, which in the morning had varied now towards the south, now towards the east, came round as far as east-south-east, but they held there only unsteadily and changed often.
We had no hour angle during the morning, but a few minutes before noon the sun showed itself for an instant and we observed the latitude, which was found to be 26° 37' 18", giving, with that by dead reckoning, a difference to the south of 11' 8". The run to the west appeared to us to have been 0° 46' 18".
At about one o'clock in the afternoon the Naturaliste made us a signal asking us to send our doctor on board her. We then shortened sail to let that ship come closer, and when she was abeam of us at a short distance we both hove to. I did not have a boat put in the water, which decided him to send me his. But when it had put off, it made so much water that it barely had time to return on board.
Captain Hamelin then asked me to send him mine, but it was in the same state and could not stay afloat either. I then decided to pass astern of that ship, and I hove to so close under her lee that we were almost yardarm to yardarm. His boat then came on board without danger, and the officer in it handed me a letter from that captain in which he asked me to be so good as to send him our doctor, and even Citizen Péron, who is one also, for a consultation on the medicines to be given to M. Le Villain, assistant naturalist, who was very ill and even in danger from the effects of a dysentery, to which had been added an intermittent fever of the most violent kind.
Our two doctors set off at once and went on board. According to the report they made me on their return, it is to be feared that Citizen Le Villain will succumb to the force of his illness, and it seemed to me that they have little hope that he can be pulled through.
At four o'clock we put our head back on our course with our usual sail, and the Naturaliste, after taking her boat up on her gangways to caulk it, did the same. I intend to make the same repair to mine as soon as the weather permits.
During the night of the 24th to the 25th the weather was still very overcast. The moon, though well advanced, could not disperse the clouds, but we had no strong winds, only a few light gusts that passed from time to time.
1801-12-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 26° 34' 12" of latitude observed and in 98° 19' 28" of longitude by account. At 2, at the request of the ship's surgeon, the captain asked the commander to send us his surgeon; the commander having consented, we hove to and sent a boat aboard the Géographe. She brought Citizens L'Haridon and Péron, who consulted with our surgeons on the illness of Citizen Levillain, the zoologist. At 4 they returned to their ship, and at 4.15 we filled and stood on.

1801-12-16.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SSE, a fresh breeze, misty weather, the sky overcast. At 2 a boat was sent to the Géographe to fetch the surgeon-major.
1801-12-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth the winds were extremely variable, and in the whole day they scarcely stayed an hour together on the same point of the compass, although they strayed little from south-east, whether their inconstancy turned towards the east or towards the south. The sea, though smooth, was still driven by a strong swell from south to south-south-west, which seemed to tell us that we should have the winds from that quarter. The sky was overcast as on the other past days, but the clouds were no longer so thick nor of so dark a colour. The sun even showed itself quite clearly at different times in the morning, and we were able to observe it.
At noon the latitude was found to be 27° 41' 50", which gave little difference from the dead reckoning, but it was not the same with the distance made to the west, for the timekeeper placed us in 96° 43' 50", which gave 1° 55' 12" in forty-eight hours, whereas by our dead reckoning we had only 1° 24' 18".
In the afternoon the sky cleared, and at sunset there remained very few clouds in the air. But the breeze had fallen off a great deal. Six of our sick came out of the hospital that day and were put back to work, but I still excused them for some time from keeping the night watch.
Citizen Maugé is entirely recovered and is now in very good health. M. Depuche, our mineralogist, is still languid and has great difficulty in regaining his strength. Our doctor maintains that he does not have the dysentery and that his illness is the same one from which Dampier suffered so long on his first voyage.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth the sky was very fine and clear, but the winds very slack and, within a little, as variable as they had been during the day. We steered close-hauled under our ordinary sail, with the Naturaliste a short distance to leeward, hoping soon to reach the region of the variable winds, which will allow us quickly to make up the distance lost which the trade winds have forced us to make to the west.
1801-12-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 27° 38' 16" of latitude observed and in 97° 41' 58" of longitude by account.

1801-12-17.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SSE and ESE. A light breeze, the sky overcast, the weather misty.
1801-12-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth the sky continued fine in the morning and the winds still unsteady and light. From south-east they went round to south-south-east, and even further to the south as the sun approached the meridian. The sea was then fairly smooth, although driven for several days past by a strong swell from south to south-south-west. The barometer, which in the preceding night had risen to 28 inches five lines, foretold nothing but fine weather, but we lacked a fair wind.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 28° 25' 24", and that by dead reckoning gave us 28° 33' 11". This was the first time it had given us a difference to the south, for until then the observation had been greater than the dead reckoning. This no doubt comes from the distance run having been badly estimated.
According to the rate of our No. 35, the longitude reduced to noon was 96° 27' 6", which gave in the twenty-four hours 0° 16' 44" of distance to the west, while the reduction of the course by dead reckoning, according to custom, gave 0° 35' 16". Thus the dead reckoning was over by 0° 18' 42".
After the observation of the meridian altitude, the wind being at south, we trimmed our sails and brought our tacks to starboard so as to stand as far to the east as we could, and thereby shorten our passage, which the distance made to the west could not fail to render long if we did not soon meet some good breezes from that quarter.
Throughout the evening the breeze was very light, but the winds went round to south by west, which led us to believe that we were not far from being in the variable winds. Towards the end of the day the sky became very fine and clear, all the clouds having disappeared shortly after sunset.
I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south-east by east, until the winds should allow us to make good way by standing further to the south.
During the night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh the sky remained fine until about two in the morning, but then it clouded over and turned squally. The winds were then at south-south (sic), varying at times to south-west by south. During the squalls we had some strong gusts, which did not, however, force the Naturaliste, which was a short distance from us, to furl her topgallant sails, for she kept them set all night.
1801-12-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. At 8.15, 6° 46' 0" of NW variation; 7° 51' 40" at 5.15 in the evening. At noon in 28° 22' 53" of latitude observed and in 97° 1' 16" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E. At 1.30 he cancelled the previous signal and signalled the course S 67° 30' E; at 3.15 he made the signal to steer a point to windward of the course signalled.

1801-12-18.journal_anonyme: Winds south, a fresh breeze. At half past noon went about and headed ESE. In the afternoon the winds varied from SSW to SW and we steered SE by E. In the forenoon the winds freshened and the topgallant masts were struck.
1801-12-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the twenty-seventh the sky looked very threatening. The squalls, which had begun in the past night, became more frequent and heavier. The sea too was beginning to rise. The winds were at south-south-west, varying to south-west by south, a strong breeze, and the ship was making good way south-east by east under her courses, with one reef in each topsail. The barometer, which until daybreak had stood at 28 inches four lines, fell all at once, or at least in a very short time, to 28 inches 1.5 lines, which did not promise us fine weather.
The Naturaliste having furled and unrigged her topgallant sails, we took a second reef in our topsails and furled our staysails so that she could follow us. But we were spared sending down our topgallant masts, for they had been down ever since our departure from Timor.
Although the sky kept its threatening look for the greater part of the morning, it nevertheless seemed inclined to clear. At about eleven o'clock the misty clouds covering the sun, which had not yet appeared, parted, and at noon we were able to observe the latitude, which was found to be 29° 1' south. That by dead reckoning gave 29° 3' 59". This placed us exactly on the parallel of the vigia marked on our charts as a bank of rocks awash. It is that it lay about thirty leagues from us to the east. But whether it exists or not, we saw nothing during the day that could make us suspect we might have it in our neighbourhood. As, on the course we are steering, we must pass fairly close to it, perhaps tomorrow we shall have some sign of its existence.
From an hour angle taken in the afternoon, the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 98° 40' 12", which gave as the run to the west for the 24 hours, the course being reduced to noon, 2° 13' 6". The dead reckoning gave 2° 22' 2", and a difference of 10' 56" too far to the east by the dead reckoning.
At sunset the sky was fairly fine and did not look threatening for the night, but the breeze had fallen off a great deal and we had reason to fear that the winds would come to us from the south. The sea was heavy with swell all night and the ship laboured a great deal. The winds were indeed the same, but very light.
1801-12-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to south. At noon in 29° 10' 35" of latitude by account and in 99° 20' 46" of longitude by account.

1801-12-19.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, blowing hard. Dark weather, the sky cloudy. In the forenoon the winds varied from S by W to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-12-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the morning of the twenty-eighth the fair wind of the day before fell away a great deal, and we found the sea extremely heavy with swell and unpleasant. The motion of the ship was so violent throughout the day that I feared some damage to my masts. The Naturaliste suffered some to her sails and signalled it to us at about ten o'clock. As we were a short distance from each other and she was ahead of us, she was taken aback and came round, so that to avoid her we were obliged to lay all our after sails aback against the mast.
On the course we were steering, as I remarked yesterday, we must have passed fairly close to the vigia shown on our charts, but we sighted absolutely nothing that announced its vicinity. Throughout the day two birds were seen of the kind called shearwaters, and it is to be believed that in the neighbourhood of this danger there must be a fairly large number of them.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 29° 26' 46" south, and the longitude by dead reckoning was 104° 12' 38". We had no hour angle to obtain that of our timekeeper.
In the afternoon the calm continued and the winds were from south by west to south. The ship laboured even more than she had in the morning, and I could hardly conceive how the Naturaliste could carry her topgallant sails aloft. It is true that the low height of her masts made her better able to bear the shaking caused them by the flapping of her sails as she rolled, and it was for quite the opposite reason that I was anxious for my own when the same thing happened.
Two men who had been well cured of the dysentery and out of the sick-berth for several days went back into it, having been attacked afresh. The doctor's opinion is that not only must they have eaten too much, but that they have also indulged in some debauch with their shipmates to make up for the diet to which they had been held during their illness
During the night of the 28th to the 29th the sky was fairly fine, though covered with misty clouds which greatly shortened our horizon. Despite the brightness of the moon. The winds did come back to south-west and even to south-west, but so light that the ship laboured no less, the sea still running very hollow and long.
1801-12-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. The topmast backstays were set up. At noon in 29° 20' 41" of latitude observed and in 101° 3' 52" of longitude by account.

1801-12-20.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE, a light breeze. The weather fine, the sea smooth. During the night the winds varied from SSW to SW by S. The course SE by E.
1801-12-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth the sea was still very heavy with swell and unpleasant for a great part of the morning, but we had a light breeze from the south-west which made the motions of the corvette less abrupt. We preferred, however, to rig our studding sails to keep up with the Naturaliste, which was carrying all the sail she could set, rather than to rig our topgallant sails.
The sky, though very cloudy, was fairly fine all day, and there was every sign of a good breeze for the evening.
At noon we observed the latitude of 29° 54' 22" south. That by dead reckoning was only 29° 48' 40", which gave us 0° 5' 42" more to the south than we had reckoned from the distance by dead reckoning.
The longitude by No. 35 was 101° 2' 8" for the run of two days, which carried us to the east by 2° 21' 56"; the dead reckoning gave 0° 20' 40" more.
In the evening the sea nevertheless began to be heavy with swell, but calmer. The different seas by which it had been tossed the day before merged into a single one, and we rigged our main topgallant sail. Until after sunset the winds had been favourable to us and the breeze pleasant, but at about eight o'clock they went round to south-south-west, varying to south, and obliged us to keep close-hauled.
The night of the 29th to the 30th, though dark and the sky very cloudy, passed without incident. The winds remained much as they were and we continued on the same course.
At about eight in the evening a smell of burning and a fairly thick smoke spread about the quarterdeck, without anyone knowing where it could come from or what its cause was. I at once had Citizen Freycinet called (in margin: and told him) to go forward and see what it might be. His answer was that he had given the order to the master gunner. Ill pleased with such unconcern in a case of this kind, I went there myself at once and made a general inspection of the galleys, the oven and the forge, which had been in use during the day. I found everything in order, without the least sign that the smoke which had spread came from that part of the ship. Having then gone down into the gunroom to see whether anything might be discovered, I saw nothing there either, but I smelt a smell of burning which I could not define.
Having given orders that all the lights in the officers' and the naturalists' cabins be put out at once, which displeased most of them infinitely, the smell gradually dispersed, without our having discovered where it came from. Until then I had granted, to please everyone, that lights might be kept until ten o'clock. The pretext put forward to obtain this was always work, reflection, and the habit they had formed of doing what they had to do and write up much better at night than by day. I ought no doubt, at that time, not to have permitted (in margin: having any) what was permitted, for the general safety, for from that moment the fear that someone might set fire to his cabin was not the least of my anxieties, having been only too often a witness of how few precautions each of them took to guard against such an accident.
1801-12-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 29° 34' 29" of latitude by account and in 102° 12' 16" of longitude by account. All night the Géographe was astern at a great distance. At 5.45, 8° 0' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-21.journal_anonyme: The winds SW to WSW, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, heading SE by E.
1801-12-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth the sky looked very threatening and seemed to announce some gales. In the morning the winds were very variable from south by west to south-west by west, but this time we got off with a fright, for at about eight o'clock the sky began to clear and became brighter. The breeze also increased a little, and we rigged our topgallant sails to take advantage of the wind, which was fair, and to give chase to the Naturaliste, which by chance happened to be a fair way ahead of us. The sea was then fairly smooth and had very little left of the heavy sea that had made itself felt on the previous days and had greatly wearied us.
At noon we observed the latitude of 30° 16' 7" south, and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 102° 23' 10". We could not conceive how, after making the whole of the distance estimated by the log on a south-east by east course, and even a few degrees more towards the south, we found ourselves so little advanced in latitude. The difference we had in these twenty-four hours is the most considerable there has been so far, since by the dead reckoning of the courses and the distance run we placed ourselves in 30° 51' 44" south latitude and 103° 4' 8" longitude, whereas by the observations we found only 30° 16' 7" for the latitude and 102° 23' 10" for the longitude, so that the difference between the observations and the dead reckoning was 0° 35' 34" to the north and 41' 58" to the west. We are all the more ignorant of the cause that may have given rise to this difference as we noticed nothing to which it can be attributed.
As soon as the observation of the sun for its meridian altitude was finished, I signalled to the Naturaliste the course south-east, if the wind allowed.
For the greater part of the evening the sky was fairly fine and the breeze pleasant, but at about six o'clock it became overcast and cloudy, with strong squalls from time to time. We furled our topgallant sails, having closed with and passed the Naturaliste.
After sunset the wind freshened a great deal, and so that our companion should not be obliged to make too much sail to follow us during the night, I had a second reef taken in the topsails and remained under the courses. The night, without being fine, was not however very bad; strong gusts passed over, but they were not of long duration. The sea, nevertheless, was beginning to grow rough and uncomfortable.

1801-12-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 2 a.m., having lost sight of the Géographe, we shortened sail to wait for her. At daybreak she closed and we crowded sail. At noon in 30° 18' 37" of latitude observed and in 104° 9' 52" of longitude by account. At noon the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 4.15, 6° 55' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-22.journal_anonyme: The winds SW by S until midnight, when they drew round to south and SSE, a strong breeze. The commander signalled the course SE.
1801-12-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Nivôse the sky was scarcely finer than it had been during the previous night, but the winds, though stronger, were also a great deal more disagreeable to us. Their shifts from south towards east were not suited to our course either, so that we had to steer close to the wind, as close-hauled as possible. As the sea was already running somewhat high and I feared some squalls, I had the topgallant sails unrigged and the preventer shrouds of our lower masts set up a little, for, through the straining they had undergone on the 28th and 29th of Frimaire, they had come to have some slack in them.
The Naturaliste was falling off to leeward as usual, for as soon as the sea gets up this vessel sails very badly close-hauled.
At noon we did not see the sun, and the latitude by the dead reckoning of our courses came to 30° 22' 50". The distance made to the east, applied to the last result of our timekeeper No. 35, put us in 104° 26' 10", on the supposition that the difference found the day before had not been appreciable for that day.
We learned with regret, in the course of the morning, that Citizen Maugé, who had been entirely recovered for more than ten days, was about to be attacked again by an illness of which he believed himself wholly rid. When he came to my cabin to dine, as I had not seen him during the morning, the change I noticed in his face led me to ask him whether he was not as well as usual. To which he replied that he was not, having suffered greatly all night from pains in the lower belly. He put this down to stewed prunes, which he had for some time been in the habit of taking. He ate little on this occasion and withdrew early to his cabin, finding the cold rather too sharp.
During the evening the weather remained as it had been in the morning, and the winds still variable in the same quarter. But the breeze was steadier and the gusts followed one another less closely. Only the sea was rougher.
At sunset we closed with the Naturaliste, about two leagues to leeward, so as not to lose her during the night, which, despite unpromising appearances, was fine, with a sky as cloudy as ours was. We had nothing to complain of but the cold, to which most of us were very sensitive, as is usual when one passes suddenly from a very hot climate to a decidedly temperate one.
1801-12-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 30° 31' 1" of latitude by account and in 106° 14' 22" of longitude by account. At 8 a main topmast backstay parted and was replaced for the time being by a lee backstay. At 9 Citizen Levillain died.

1801-12-23.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from south to SSW. At 8 the main topmast backstay parted close to the crosstrees. Citizen Levillain, the zoologist, died of a bloody flux.
1801-12-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second the winds continued very contrary to us, since they came from the south and south by east and we needed to make ground to the south. The heavy sea and the leeway of the ship caused our course to bear somewhat to the north, but even so it suited us better to keep on the eastern tack, because there at least we gained on one side while losing on the other, whereas on the western tack we should have lost on both.
At about six in the morning, Captain Hamelin informed me by a private signal that Citizen Le Villain, embarked as assistant naturalist, was no more. During his stay at Timor he had been attacked by a dysentery of which he had been successfully cured. But as soon as he found himself in good health on board, where he had withdrawn early, he paid no further heed to the diet he was urged to keep, and ate everything indiscriminately and to excess. He soon suffered pains in the belly and colics which, having turned into diarrhoea, brought on shortly afterwards a relapse and a second dysentery, much harder to cure than the first, of which, despite all the resources of medicine and every other care, he died.
This young man, who had already made a voyage with me for natural history, had talents and would no doubt in time have become accomplished in that field, had not a premature death taken him from us. He was, moreover, of a gentle and affable disposition and good company. His comrades will no doubt mourn him on all these counts when they learn of the end of his career, which I am not making known to them at present, because Citizens Depuche and Maugé are not well. Citizen Maugé in particular gives me much anxiety, since he had been perfectly recovered, and it seems that having eaten too much will be the cause of a second relapse.
At noon we observed the latitude of 30° 3' 58" south, which put us about 13 minutes to the north of our last observation. The longitude given by No. 35 put us in 107° 4' 23", so that in forty-eight hours we had advanced 4° 31' 13" to the east, whereas by dead reckoning we found only 3° 53' 0", which gave the timekeeper 0° 48' 13" more, a difference roughly equal to that found on the 30th of Frimaire by the observation of the sun at noon.
During the evening the winds were no better than they had been in the morning. But the sky was less overcast and seemed inclined to clear, especially in the north-west quarter, the horizon being very clear. We hoped the winds might shift there at sunset, but in this we were greatly mistaken, for they veered further to the south and blew so fresh a breeze that, so as not to strain our masts and not to oblige the Naturaliste to carry too much sail, we took a third reef in the main topsail and furled the mainsail.
The breeze blew very hard during the night from south to south-south-east, but the weather was fine and the sky fairly clear. We kept on the eastern tack, reckoning ourselves still eighty leagues from the nearest lands of New Holland.
1801-12-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSW to SSE. At daybreak the main topmast backstay was set up again. At noon in 30° 1' 38" of latitude observed and in 107° 58' 16" of longitude by account.

1801-12-24.journal_anonyme: A high sea, the weather overcast, the wind a strong breeze from south to SE and SSE. At 8 a.m. wore ship.
1801-12-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, after sunrise, the winds continuing to blow fresh from the south-south-east and seeming inclined to settle there, we held on the eastern tack until eight o'clock, when we wore round, the sea being too rough and heavy to attempt to go about. The Naturaliste did likewise and we stood to the south-west. Hardly had we trimmed our sails on the new tack than the winds shifted from south-east towards east, which made our course all the better, as we were making little ground to the west, at least according to our dead reckoning.
During the morning the sky was fairly fine and the weather clear, but the sea remained heavy and rough, as though it had been raised by several different winds.
At noon we observed the latitude of 30° 8' 26", which surprised us greatly, for by our dead reckoning we expected to find we had made ground to the north. The difference between the estimated and the observed latitude was considerable, since by our dead reckoning we put ourselves in 29° 40' 42", which gave 0° 27' 44" to the south that we had not been expecting.
The longitude given by No. 35 put us in 108° 4' 57" and gave only 7' 54" of difference in the estimated distance to the west.
In the evening the winds were in the same quarter and the sky remained fine, though more overcast. The breeze was also more moderate and the sea began to go down. After sunset we let out a reef in our main topsail and followed the Naturaliste under our courses and topsails, with two reefs in each.
During the night of the third to the fourth we had the same wind as during the day, only it was moderate and the sky much more overcast. We kept the same course under the same sail. The sea became smooth and we were no longer troubled by the heavy swell of the past days.
Citizen Maugé, who had suffered the relapse I spoke of yesterday, did not spend the day very well and complained of very sharp pains in the lower belly. His face had grown dejected and my fears for the course of his illness only increased.
Citizen Depuche, for his part, was a little better and seemed to be entering upon full convalescence. The other sick men were also changing for the better.
1801-12-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 30° 9' 28" of latitude observed and in 109° 0' 28" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 6° 57' 0" of NW variation. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.

1801-12-25.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a strong breeze from SE. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.
1801-12-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, at daybreak, the Naturaliste being about two leagues to leeward of us, we were obliged to bear away towards her in order to close with her. I can hardly conceive on what point of the compass this vessel can have steered during the night. For, having lost sight of her at midnight, we sailed a good full until three o'clock without sighting her. We then resumed a close-hauled course, so as not to find ourselves too far ahead of her, while waiting for daylight to join her. In the morning we had the winds from south-east, variable to south by east, a light breeze, the sea having become very smooth. The sky remained overcast and damp as it had been during the night, and we seldom saw the sun. At noon, however, the latitude could be observed and was found to be 31° 28' 58" south; that by dead reckoning gave 31° 36' 52".
As we had no hour angle, we were obliged to fall back on the dead reckoning for the distance made to the west, which came to (no figures).
In the afternoon the winds were extremely variable from south by east to south by west, and the sky did not look well. At sunset especially it seemed to warn us of bad weather, and the barometer too was beginning to fall. Very dark and widely spread clouds seemed as though fixed on the horizon from the south round to the south-west, and did not begin to rise until about ten o'clock. The whole atmosphere then became very dark and bad weather seemed unavoidable. But we were ready to meet it, having only our courses and topsails set, with two reefs in our topsails. The Naturaliste, which was a little astern, was still carrying her topgallant sails. Nevertheless the sea was smooth and no swell or ground-sea was to be felt, which gave us hope that it would all dissolve into fog, as had already happened several times.
During the night of the fourth to the fifth, although every appearance promised us heavy weather and the fall of the barometer seemed to confirm it, we had none. The sky was extremely dark and overcast, with the winds from south by east to south, very moderate. I stayed on deck until ten o'clock, but then the clouds that had alarmed us spread out and, instead of wind, brought us only a great deal of damp. The rising of the moon, which was entering its last quarter, changed nothing, and the damp continued for the rest of the night.
1801-12-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At noon in 31° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 108° 4' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-26.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 5 went about. At 9.30 a.m. the course was signalled S 45° E.
1801-12-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, the sky remained dark, overcast and laden with thick clouds at every point of the horizon. I do not remember ever having met, in the climates where I have spent the winter, an atmosphere so long laden with vapours of so disagreeable an aspect as the one we are passing through at this moment. Since leaving the trade winds we have had it almost always the same. At first, little accustomed to sailing under so cloudy a sky, we expected some squall at every moment from the look of it, for in any other climate such clouds would not spread out without bringing on a few.
The winds having shifted from south to south-south-west, we went about at four in the morning and stood on the south-east tack. During the morning the breeze was good, with now and then a few gusts and some fog, but all of it short-lived. Nevertheless the sea was beginning to get up.
