At noon, having no altitude of the sun by observation, the latitude given by dead reckoning put us in 32° 2' 28". The longitude given by the timekeeper since the last observation put us in 106° 40' 41".
In the evening the weather was a little clearer and less overcast than in the morning. The sun even showed itself several times, but of a pale colour and in the guise in which one sees it in Europe on the dismal days of winter. At its setting the sky clouded over, as usual, and the winds drew nearer to the south. The sea was beginning to grow hollow and rough. Before nightfall we closed with the Naturaliste, which had fallen far to leeward, and I signalled to her that I would steer south-south-east if the winds became favourable.
During the day Citizen Maugé, who had been attacked again by a dysenteric flux, had an indigestion which exhausted him greatly, and he found relief from the remedies given him only towards the end of the day.
The night of the fifth to the sixth passed without incident and was exactly like the preceding ones; that is to say, the sky was constantly overcast, laden with damp, cold vapours, without bad weather. The winds kept for the most part to the south, moderate, without the sea becoming any rougher than it had been at sunset; only the waves were longer and less frequent.
1801-12-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSW. At 9.30 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 11 we had a squall in which the middle staysail was split; in hauling it down it was shifted. At noon in 31° 55' 2" of latitude by account and in 107° 42' 10" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E.

1801-12-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE. At 5.30 p.m. the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E in case the winds should draw aft.
1801-12-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth the winds were the same as on the preceding days, and it was (not) without vexation that we found them so contrary to our course, for since leaving the trade winds they had been favourable to us on only two days. Well, with patience and a resignation forced upon us, we must hope that they will change, if not before the end of this moon, at least at the beginning of the next. And perhaps we shall then have a sky that lets us perceive that we are in the summer of this hemisphere.
During the morning we saw the sun now and then, but at such short intervals that no hour angle could be taken. Nevertheless at noon we observed the latitude, which was found to be 31° 42' 15", whereas that by dead reckoning put us in 32° 5' 16", so that we found we had a difference to the north in forty-eight hours of 23 minutes one second, caused no doubt by a change in the direction of the currents, which until then had given us differences to the south.
In the afternoon the sky, though overcast and dark, looked better than usual, but not for long, for at sunset it clouded over again with great dark, thick clouds. The winds, which had at times varied from south to south by west, shifted to south-south-east, a light breeze, and seemed inclined to settle there for the night. At eight o'clock, having closed with the Naturaliste, which was to leeward, I signalled her to go about and we stood on the south-west tack, to try to regain to the south what we had lost in the two previous days and put ourselves in a position to double the western point of Leeuwin's Land.
The night of the sixth to the seventh was (not) fine. As for the clearness of the sky, we could barely make out now and then a few stars, and even the moon once it had risen above the horizon. But otherwise we had no bad weather, although it seemed to be heralded by an extremely long and hollow swell from the southern quarter.
Citizen Maugé was much better on this day than the day before and found great relief from the pains he felt in the lower belly after passing, through the effect of a purge, a great quantity of foul water, which was no doubt the principal cause of his illness. At least the doctors judged it so.
Citizen Depuche is in much the same state, without any very noticeable change, and our geographer still has fever and severe colics. The other sick men are well on the way to a speedy recovery.
1801-12-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 39' 10" of latitude observed and in 109° 13' 4" of longitude by account. Saw albatrosses and petrels.

1801-12-28.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from south to SSE. At 8.15 the commander, after closing us, went about, and we did the same.
1801-12-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh we held on the tack from south towards west as far as the winds would allow, but their shifts and fickleness gained us so little ground to the south that this day counted for almost nothing in our navigation.
In the course of the morning the weather seemed inclined to clear, and although the sky was still very cloudy, we had sight of the sun for part of the day. It was the first time such a thing had happened to us since we had left the region of the trade winds.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 31° 50' 22" and the longitude given by No. 35 was found to be 108° 19'. On board the Naturaliste they reckoned 108° 48'. The rate of the timekeeper, compared with the dead reckoning of our course over forty-eight hours, gave us a distance made to the east of 1° 38' 19", whereas the other gave us 2° 18' 24", which made a difference of 0° 40' 5" in the estimated distance. From the differences in the latitudes, the currents seemed to set to the north towards the east.
During the evening the weather continued fairly fine until nightfall, but about an hour before sunset the sky became dark and very cloudy as usual, and the clouds were even of a deeper colour than ordinary, which did not bode too well for the night. It was not a bad one, however, and there was even very little wind, which no doubt helped to bring down the heavy swell we had had from the south, for it diminished greatly and strained us less.
Citizens Depuche and Maugé spent the day fairly well. The latter especially no longer felt the pains he had suffered on the preceding days. And his dysenteric flux seems to have stopped.
At the request of the officers of the staff, the tea remaining on board, amounting to ten pounds, was divided up during the evening. Four were first set aside for the sick, present or to come; the remainder was divided into two equal portions, one of which was allotted to the crew and the other to them.
I can hardly conceive how those who spare no expense where pleasures or fancies are concerned should not have provided themselves with a box of tea, rather than have recourse to that shipped for the use of the seamen.
1801-12-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 49' 38" of latitude observed and in 108° 57' 40" of longitude by account.

1801-12-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south to SE. At 9 squally weather with fairly violent gusts; the dinghy was put on the gratings to be repaired. At 7.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-12-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth the winds were almost calm for the greater part of the day and the sky cloudy, with a little very fine rain, or rather at times a thick mist. Every point of the horizon presented to view great dark clouds driven by a high wind in different directions. When any of these clouds passed our way, they seemed to bring us thunder and wind, and yet they gave us only light catspaws accompanied by a soft drizzle or a thick fog.
The whole morning was spent shifting our sails from one side to the other while making almost no way. But we were compensated for this by the capture of a dozen of those beautiful blue snails we had met with in doubling the Cape of Good Hope, of which I have given a drawing in my fair-copy journal. The sea, though swelling, was calm, which made it easier for us to spot them. We also took advantage of the little wind there was to set up our topmast and topgallant shrouds, which needed it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 32° 0' 39" south, but we judged it faulty because the horizon was too dark and of little extent.
In the afternoon the sky became fine and, at about four o'clock, a light breeze sprang up from south towards west, which allowed us to steer for some time south-east and south-east by east. But after sunset the winds went back to south and south by west, very faint. We then let out a reef in our topsails to close with the Naturaliste, which I had allowed to pass ahead.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth the sky was overcast but fine; we had a light breeze from the south-east and kept on the south-east tack, drawing more to the south whenever the shifting of the wind made it possible. At ten o'clock we passed the Naturaliste, which was a little to windward of us.
On this same day there were some small displeasing difficulties at the table of the staff and the naturalists, which gave rise to complaints. Those who had caused them came to my cabin and I made them, in a friendly way, such representations as I judged fitting to stifle early these petty dissensions, which usually end with people falling out seriously with one another. From the account given me by both parties, it seemed to me that both were in the wrong. However that may be, I hope that it will not happen again and that I shall not be obliged to take the course I have announced if they will not agree and live on good terms.
1801-12-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. Saw albatrosses. At noon in 31° 59' 56" of latitude observed and in 108° 23' 58" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW.

1801-12-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, calm until 3, when the breeze got up from the south, variable to SW and SSE by way of south. Obs. lat. 32° 12' 22".
1801-12-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, the winds varied from south towards east and the breeze was light. The sky, though very cloudy at sunrise, became fine, contrary to its habit, which made us hope that the winds might perhaps veer into the quarter from east towards north and that we could make up for lost time by making a good course, but nothing of the kind happened and (they) settled at south-south-east.
At daybreak, the Naturaliste being very far from us, we were obliged to haul up our mainsail and staysails to wait for her. This would not have happened if, during the night, the officers who kept watch on board that vessel had answered the signals we made to learn her position.
As it was calm in the morning, we took a few more snails like those I spoke of yesterday, but we found them less handsome.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 32° 11' 7". We had no hour angle, or to put it better, none was taken, and I do not know why, for the sky was fine enough for it.
After the observation of the meridian altitude, the winds seeming settled at south-south-east, I made the signal to go about and we changed tacks. In this way the Naturaliste found herself ahead of us and at a considerable distance, but we soon came up with her, being to windward of her.
During the evening a good breeze blew and we made fair progress to the south-west. The winds shifted a point further south at times, but only in catspaws that did not last long.
The night passed without incident, except that the sky clouded over with clouds that did not look threatening and that brought a little wind when their direction carried them over us.
At nine in the evening, the Naturaliste beginning to drop astern, we furled all our staysails and took a second reef in the fore topsail.
1801-12-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SE. At noon in 32° 12' 23" of latitude observed and in 109° 20' 46" of longitude by account. At 6, 6° 47' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to east. At half past noon went onto the port tack and made all sail.
1801-12-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, we experienced some favourable changes in the shifting of the winds, in that they went round from south-east to east-south-east and even to east by south. It was the first time since we (had) left the trade winds that they had drawn so far to the east. We continued to steer as far to the south as possible in order to gain latitude, since we could not make a direct course. The sky was very overcast during the morning and showed itself only at very short intervals.
At about ten o'clock M. Freycinet, head of the staff mess, came to tell me that it was impossible for them to live on the ordinary ration, such as the regulations allow to everyone. According to the account he showed me, they had consumed in the décade all that was due to them for a month. I pointed out to M. Freycinet the difficulty he would put us in if things went on at this rate, telling him that in six months the staff table would by itself have consumed all the provisions on board, and that my duty imperatively required me to take as much care of the seamen, who were men of toil and hardship, as of officers who appear on deck only four hours a day. As they had very little fresh meat left, I took this opportunity to show him the waste that had been made of what had been shipped at Timor, and that the fresh provisions would have been enough for six months had they been used with moderation.
I pointed out to him, moreover, that instead of there being twelve persons at their table, including the naturalists, there were only seven, since three who had been ill since our departure had been fed constantly at my table, and that, apart from this, I (was accustomed) to invite two other persons when my dinner was passable. That I was thus equal in number to them, that I had shipped far fewer provisions, and that what remained to me would still last a long time thanks to the order I had established, and that he ought to do the same. The various observations he made to me in the name of all decided me to grant them a third over and above what was due to them, to satisfy them. But it is none the less true that seven persons are consuming the entire ration of twelve, and I do not know whether the supplement they are to be given will even be enough.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 13' 32" south and the longitude by the timekeeper gave 107° 43' 26" east of Paris. From which it follows that, in order to advance a little to the south, we have lost in three times 24 hours on different tacks 0° 35' 34" of distance to the east. By the dead reckoning of the courses we had run, it came to 0° 41' 48", which gave over the three days a difference of only 0° 6' 14" from the observations.
During the evening the winds, which at about eleven in the morning had shifted to east by south, soon came back to south-east, and after sunset they drew a little further to the south and were very variable all night. The breeze was likewise unsteady and the wind came in light catspaws. This night was the darkest we had yet had, though without any sign of bad weather. We did not see a single star shining, although the clouds were not very thick.
At about four in the afternoon, having come alongside the Naturaliste, Captain Hamelin asked me whether he might hold the sale of the dead men's effects. I answered that he might. M. Hamelin also told me that his convalescents were having great difficulty in recovering and that their recovery was dragging on. The longitude of his his (sic) timekeepers differed little from ours.
1801-12-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 33° 15' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-01.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze. The effects of the late Le Bourgeois and Savary were sold.
1802-01-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, we had, contrary to custom, a fine sky and the promise of a fine day, but the winds were no more favourable to us than on the preceding days and kept as usual from south-east to south or south-south-east. When they came from that part of the horizon, or from south-west to south when they changed direction. The weather was cold during the morning and, although the breeze was light, the air gave us more coolness than the sun gave warmth. We were, however, at the height of summer.
At noon the observed latitude was 34° 8' 7" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 106° 50' 43". The difference we found between the dead reckoning and the observation over these twenty-four hours was 0° 17' 28" to the west and 0° 3' 57" to the north.
In the afternoon the sky continued fine and the sea calm, without being disturbed by any wave to herald an approaching change. However, from noon until two o'clock the winds went round successively to the south and from there to the south-west, and for a moment we even had them at west-south-west. At the first shift we went about to head east, and as they became favourable to us we drew round from east towards south. The Naturaliste made the same manoeuvre and I signalled to her the direct course south-east by compass. That vessel apparently did not see our signal, although she was not very far off, and we kept it hoisted until after sunset without her having answered it.
At about seven in the evening the winds began to draw towards the south. The sky became cloudy and dark; nevertheless the night was fine and there was little wind.
During the day we saw various species of petrels, about the size of a duck, with grey backs and white bellies, and the neck and head a dark brown verging on black, which made the white patch on the neck very recognisable. It was the first time we had seen such birds
1802-01-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. The effects of the late Bourgeois and Savary were sold. At noon in 34° 0' 0" of latitude observed and in 107° 50' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south. At 1.30 changed tacks. The effects of Citizen Levillain were sold.
1802-01-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth the winds (were) all day in the quarter from south towards east. There was little wind and the weather was very fine. However, the little coolness there was seemed to us colder than the heat of the sun was hot. We took advantage of this fine day to air part of our spare rigging, which the boatswain thought needed it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 34° 4' 58" south and the longitude given by our timekeeper was 107° 40' 15". The difference between the estimated course and the observation gave a difference of 7' 44" to the north and 11' 58" to the west.
During the evening the wind fell away a great deal, and the sky, which was very fine at sunset, gave (no) promise of wind for the night, which did indeed pass almost in a calm. Despite the fineness of the sky, we were much surprised at the behaviour of the barometer: from 28 inches three lines, to which it had risen the day before, it stood at noon at only 28 in. 1. 5, and we had never had such fine weather. At sunset ………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………..
According to the doctor's report, our sick were much better, and Citizens Maugé and Depuche were once more entering upon convalescence. Yet this improvement announced by the doctor did not show in their faces, for both of them had them singularly drawn and livid, which seemed to me no good omen. Citizen Maugé especially gave me great anxiety, and although his dysentery had stopped for the second time, he is far from seeming to me out of danger.
Two men of the crew likewise left the sick bay, and the others did not look as though they would stay there long.
1802-01-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. The mizzen topgallant mast was wedged and its shrouds and backstays set up. The effects of the late Levillain were sold. At noon in 34° 4' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 51' 10" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30 he was to leeward at a great distance. We supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flags giving the course; so we bore away S 67° 30' E, and east, and closed him.

1802-01-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from south to SSW and W. At 1.45 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30, being far to leeward, we supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flag that gave the course; we at once bore away S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth we had at sunrise every appearance of a fine day, the sky being clear and entirely rid of those thick, dark clouds that had accompanied us for so long. But the fine sky that was so pleasant to see brought us a calm until about eight o'clock, when, the winds having shifted from south by west to west, a light breeze sprang up which allowed us to steer south-east, so as to put ourselves early in the latitude of the western lands of Leeuwin's Land, which I intended to sight if the weather stayed fine.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 34° 7' 31" south, and that by dead reckoning put us in 34° 11' 4", so that the difference to the north was slight, since it came to only 3' 33". The longitude by the timekeeper put us in 108° 29' 29", and by the estimated distance to the east we found 7' 9" of difference.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to north-west and west, it began to blow a pleasant breeze and we crowded sail to make the most of it. During the evening the sky was fine, but little by little it clouded over and grew dark. The barometer, which had of its own accord fallen to 28 inches despite the fine weather, seemed to warn us of some squalls, which in any case we were to expect at the change of the moon. The sea, however, was fairly smooth, and as we felt none of those heavy swells that herald bad weather to come, or even bad weather that has passed through the waters where one is, it seemed to us that we need have no fear from the present state of the sky, which nevertheless was not fine at about eight in the evening, and by that time the sea was already beginning to be a little rough.
During the night of the thirteenth to the fourteenth the winds varied from west to west by north. It blew a strong gale, in gusts. We even had a little rain, but more usually misty clouds which brought us fairly strong catspaws. At ten o'clock we took a second reef in our topsails and furled all our light sails, to be better prepared in case of need. I also had the stern lantern lit for the rest of the night, so that the Naturaliste, which was astern, might regulate her sail accordingly. The sea was beginning to get up and we had to expect some squalls, but as the wind seemed likely to be favourable to us, we were not sorry to see it gathering, provided, however, that it did not do so to excess.
1802-01-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 6 a flat calm; at 8 the breeze got up from WNW and blew from WNW to W, a fresh breeze. At noon in 34° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 109° 54' 46" of longitude by account. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E for 8 o'clock. At 11 we had a slight squall with rain; the fore studdingsail boom broke as the studdingsails were taken in.

1802-01-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from W to WNW; set the studdingsails and royals. The commander signalled the course for 8 o'clock as S 33° 45' E. At 4 a.m. overcast weather, a strong breeze and a high sea.
1802-01-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
[3V p. 185 Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth the winds were variable from west to west-north-west and it blew a strong gale. At four in the morning, reckoning myself in thirty-five degrees of south latitude and at no great distance from the western lands of New Holland, I had her steered east by south in the hope of sighting them during the day if the breeze, or to put it better the high wind we had, continued. Although the sea was beginning to run very high, we changed nothing in our sail, which, however, seemed to strain our upper masts in the heavy rolling that the seas caused the ship.
During the morning we saw many petrels with white bellies and dark grey backs, as well as several albatrosses of middling size. The little petrels known as storm birds also kept us good company and stayed in great numbers in the eddy made by the ship's wake. Despite every means we employed, we could not manage to catch any; they did not even try to find out what the bait we offered them was.
At noon we observed the latitude of 35° 14' 54", which put us a little to the south of Leeuwin's Land, and if the longitude by our timekeeper had been exact, we ought to have sighted the land, since it put us in 111° 30' 57". It is true that the horizon did not extend beyond five or six leagues, the sky, though fine, being laden with vapours.
By the dead reckoning of the course run, our latitude came to 35° 39' 43, so that we had a considerable difference to the north by the observation. As it came to 24' 49", and we had never found one so large, it seemed to us that a strong current had carried us violently to the north, and this conjecture seemed all the better founded because, in the reduction of the estimated distance to the east, there was only seven minutes' difference from that given us by the timekeeper for the twenty-four hours.
During the evening it went on blowing a strong gale from west-north-west to north-west. The sky was fairly fine until about three o'clock, but then it clouded over, and at times we had strong gusts. The barometer, below 28 inches, did not promise us a fine night. We made our dispositions accordingly, and at six o'clock, having no further hope of seeing the land, given the state of the horizon, I had her steered south-east.
From the signs we observed, there is every likelihood that we should have seen it had the weather been finer. I am even persuaded that we were on soundings, on soundings (sic), since several whales showed themselves near the ship, and in these waters we have noticed that they seldom keep far out from the coasts. As the weather was not convenient for sounding, I continued on my course.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth we had continual squalls and strong gusts, sometimes with rain, sometimes without. As the wind was very good for letting us make up a little of the time lost, we all bore the discomfort that goes with it, but we were less troubled by it than by the heavy sea, which wearied us greatly and the ship still more.
1802-01-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to WSW. A high sea. Two large pieces of wood passed alongside. At noon in 35° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 112° 44' 16" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. Saw a whale. During the night the wind in gusts, with rain and frequent squalls.

1802-01-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to WSW. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. In the forenoon the weather cleared.
1802-01-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather was much the same as the day before, but the winds shifted to west by south, which made us fear we should soon see them veer into the southern quarter and fall calm. For that is fairly commonly their behaviour, in this meridian at least. They behave so around the meridian of Madagascar. They had, however, lost none of their strength at west-south-west, and on the contrary obliged us to take the third reef in the fore topsail, which I congratulated myself on having changed the day before, for fear of seeing it carried away by some gust. The sea was then very high, and we perceived from the seams of our gangways (?), from which the oakum had worked out, that the ship had strained a great deal more than we had judged.
At noon the latitude was observed, though doubtful because of the great height of the sea, which made the horizon difficult, as 36° 31' 27". That by the dead reckoning of the course run in the twenty-four hours gave us 36° 54' 39". So that the same difference found the day before recurred, and we had one to the north of 0° 23' 12". That of the distance made to the east, compared with the one given by the timekeeper, was only 59 seconds, proof that the difference does not come from the dead reckoning of the course and that a strong current setting to the north is met with in these waters.
In the afternoon the winds followed the course we had presumed they would take, and shifted to the south-west without falling calm. But the sky looked worse than when they had been from west towards north. The clouds were darker and thicker, and the rain, when it fell, very cold. We bent our storm staysail in case of need. The barometer, keeping steadily at 27 inches 10 lines, promised nothing good, and the state of the atmosphere seemed to confirm it.
However, at about six o'clock the sky became fairly fine and the horizon clear in the quarter from south-west to north-west; the winds even drew nearer to the west and the sea seemed less rough to us. We even set our mainsail. The weather was squally until midnight, and a little before that time we were struck by a squall that obliged us to haul up the mainsail and ease off its sheet so as to run two or three points freer until it had passed. Then the winds shifted to west-south-west by west and came round to south-south-west and fell calm, which troubled us greatly, the sea tossing us every which way, so as to make us fear damage to the masts or the sails from the jerks the scant wind gave them in the heavy rolling
1802-01-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea. The wind a strong breeze from W to SW, with rain. At noon in 36° 28' 23" of latitude observed and in 115° 56' 58" of longitude by account.

1802-01-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze and in gusts. At 1 lowered and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. As soon as it was repaired we took the 2 reefs and sheeted home. At daybreak the weather turned fine; we rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail.
1802-01-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, we had the winds from west-south-west round to north-west by north and the breeze moderate, but as the sea was high and the waves hollow, the ship and her masts strained a great deal. However, following the Naturaliste, which was carrying every sail and her studding sails, forced me to make more sail than I should have wished, for fear of suffering some damage. Nevertheless, as the weather was then fine, I had a reef let out in each topsail and the studding sails rigged, as well as the topgallant sails. The sea seemed to be calming, though still very rough.
At noon we observed the latitude of 37° 38' 40" south, and that by dead reckoning gave us 37° 57' 37", consequently a difference to the north of 18' 57". The longitude given by the timekeeper was 117° 25' 53" and the distance to the east by dead reckoning 2° 45', which gave a difference from that given by the timekeeper of only 3' 27". Thus there seems scarcely any doubt that the currents set to the north with a fairly great speed, which will perhaps continue to diminish as we proceed to the south of Nuyts' Land.
In the afternoon the prospect of the fine weather continuing vanished; the sky clouded over with great black, thick clouds and became very dark. The winds shifted to the west, where they held fairly steadily, and a good breeze blew. As the ship was straining too much under all her sail and, besides, the weather looked very bad, I had the studding sails and topgallant sails furled so that the Naturaliste, which contrary to her habit was ahead, might do the same, which she did.
Throughout the day we had the company of a fairly large number of albatrosses of the great species and of the two two (sic) varieties known in this kind of bird. We also saw several petrels of middling size.
The night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth was very dark and without bad weather. Very thick, damp clouds often passed overhead, giving us a little rain of short duration, without much wind or squalls. The sea went down a great deal, but there was always a hollow, swelling sea which caused us rolling motions all the more disagreeable because we were running before the wind.
1802-01-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to NW. Saw albatrosses, petrels, bonito and weed. At noon in 37° 40' 15" of latitude observed and in 118° 41' 40" of longitude by account. At 4 the Géographe was far astern and was not crowding sail; we shortened ours. At 7.15 hove to on the port tack, and at 8 filled and stood on.

1802-01-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from NW to W. At 7.15 hove to to wait. At 8, having closed, we filled and stood on.
1802-01-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, in the morning, the winds, which had been at north-west for the greater part of the night, shifted after a heavy squall of rain to west by south and then to south-west, continuing to blow a good breeze.
For most of the morning we had no lack of rain, but at about eleven o'clock the sky cleared from west to north and we soon had sight of the sun, whose warmth was very welcome to us, as the cold was keenly felt. The hygrometer, despite the rain, stood at 90°, and it had seldom happened since our departure that it showed this degree of saturation.
All morning we had the company of many petrels of the species that seamen do not like to have about, since most of them are persuaded that its presence is an ill omen. As they were in great numbers in the ship's wake, it seems likely that this species is more abundant in these seas than in others, where one meets with it only rarely and only when the weather is bad.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 39° 20' 46" and that by dead reckoning came to 39° 28' 29", which gave a difference to the north of only 7' 43", a much smaller amount than those of the past days. The longitude given by the timekeeper was 120 22' 30", and the distance made to the east by dead reckoning was 3° 0' " and that by the timekeeper 2° 56' 27".
In the afternoon the sky was fairly fine and the winds backed from south-west towards west, without the breeze losing any of its strength. I kept on the south-east course, not only to get to the south of Bass Strait in order to find weaker currents, but also to have a longer board should the winds later shift to the south, which seemed to me fairly probable.
I do not know whether the state of the atmosphere, laden for several days with a great deal of vapour, should be blamed for the malaise that all our sick generally felt, but it is none the less true that for three or four days their convalescence, far from becoming firmer, seemed on the contrary likely to be longer.
During the night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth the weather, without being very fine, was not bad, and the squalls that came to us brought more fog than rain and wind.
1802-01-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W. At 2.30 the main topsail tie and lift parted; all was repaired by 3.30. At noon in 39° 18' 41" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 34" of longitude by account. At 5.30, 5° 40' 40" of NW variation. Rain during the night.

1802-01-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from NW; all sail set, studdingsails and royals.
1802-01-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, in the morning, we had the winds from the western quarter, at times variable to west-south-west, and a continued good breeze, but the sky, which had been fairly fine, clouded over and we had abundant rain, hail and strong gusts for nearly two hours on end. The sea was likewise beginning to run very high and swelling, but as we were running almost before the wind we set our topgallant sails, the Naturaliste carrying every sail and her studding sails.
During the day we saw many birds of different species, most of them unknown to us. The one that attracted most notice was a kind of sea snipe, with a flight every bit as quick and darting as that of the land snipe, but without its long bill. On our first arrival on the coast of New Holland we had indeed made out birds like these in size and flight, but those we had in view on this day had not the same colour of plumage, and the tail seemed to us less tapering than that of the one I spoke of at the time. The whole upper part of the body of these was a dark brown and the underside of the belly very white. The head and neck were an ash grey that caught the eye. The albatrosses also seemed to us smaller than those met with in the waters of the Cape of Good Hope.
We also saw several clumps of seaweed of the species known by the name of fucus giganteus.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 41° 9' 32" south. That by dead reckoning was 41° 17' 40", which again gave a difference to the north of 8' 8". The longitude given by the timekeeper was 123° 42' 7", which gave a distance made to the east over the twenty-four hours of 3° 19' 37"; the dead reckoning gave 3° 24' 0".
In the afternoon the winds continued to keep in the quarter from west to west-south-west and the sky took on a very bad look for the night. The barometer, which stood constantly at 27 inches 8 & 9 lines, did not promise either that it would be fine, so that we made our preparations accordingly. Before sunset the topgallant sails were unrigged and I had two reefs taken in each topsail. The Naturaliste also furled her studding sails and her other light sails.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth it blew a strong gale with strong gusts; we furled our mainsail and ran under our topsails and foresail, continuing to steer east-south-east, the course I had taken and signalled immediately after the observation of the sun's altitude at noon.
1802-01-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW, with rain. At 2.30, in a squall, the main topsail sheet parted; by 3.30 the damage was repaired. At noon in 41° 8' 14" of latitude observed and in 124° 16' 40" of longitude by account. The commander signalled the course S 67° 30' E.

1802-01-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from W to WSW. At noon the course was signalled S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth we had the wind west-south-west, a fresh breeze, until about eight o'clock, when it came back to the west. The sky was heavily overcast in the morning and the horizon hazy. From time to time we had fairly strong gusts accompanied by a little rain, but they did not last long. The birds that had accompanied us the day before appeared once more, though in smaller numbers.
During the morning we saw almost nothing of the sun, but around noon it showed itself for a moment and we were able to observe its altitude, which, although doubtful, put us in 42° 0' 10". That found by dead reckoning of the course run gave 42° 0' 8", which leads me to believe that the observation was not a good one, given how little difference resulted from it. The distance made to the east, applied to the previous day's longitude, put us in (no figures).
In the afternoon the sky remained as dark as it had been in the morning, and the horizon continued to be very limited. Nevertheless the winds were steadier and less variable. The sea, still heavy, wearied us greatly by the rolling it caused the ship, and the discomfort was offset only (by) the good progress we were making, which enabled us to make up the time lost before we had been able to get to the south and east of Leeuwin's Land.
Our sick were much troubled by this weather, which was nonetheless very much to our advantage.
Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, was the one who felt its effects most, for it brought on a continual vomiting which forced him to keep to his cot for several days on end. It was the same with Citizen Maugé, who, unable to keep his feet against the rolling, remained shut up in his cabin the whole time.
The night of the nineteenth to the twentieth passed without incident. The winds were much the same. Although it was darker than any we had yet had, there was no bad weather and very few of those strong gusts that had almost always followed us. The sea also seemed less agitated, and the waves were longer, without breaking over one another as they usually did.
One of our foreign sailors, taken on at the Isle of France [Mauritius], was punished in the middle of the night and received twenty-five strokes of a rope's end for having drawn his knife on the second boatswain, who was sending him back to his post.
1802-01-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to WNW. Saw a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 42° 7' 2" of latitude by account and in 128° 5' 28" of longitude by account. During the night the wind blowing hard in gusts, with rain; kept the topsails reefed. In the night of the 9th [Nivôse, 30 December 1801] I had a high fever which forced me to keep my bed all through the 10th [Nivôse, 31 December 1801]; on the 11th [Nivôse, 1 January 1802] I was a little better, and a purge and an emetic set me up. It was not until the 14th [Nivôse, 4 January 1802] that the surgeon-major allowed me to resume my watch. I was still weak, but within 4 days I was in as good health as before my illness.

1802-01-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast and fresh weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from W to WNW and SW. Saw a whale and some seaweed.
1802-01-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth the winds continued very favourable to us and the sky was fairly fine all day, but we found the sea so rough and the swell so heavy, high and hollow, that it was not possible for us to make more sail. The rolling was indeed so violent and so frequent that I feared at every moment some damage to the masts or rigging. Yet the Naturaliste, in order to keep up with us, was carrying her studding sails and topgallant sails without seeming in any way troubled by it.
As on the preceding days, we had the company of several birds of the kind I have already mentioned, but far fewer in number. Two whales were also seen a short distance from the ship, and they followed us for more than two hours. It was a diversion for us to watch them try their speed against ours. Sometimes we outran them, but when they took it into their heads to give chase, they soon caught up with us.
At noon the observed latitude was 43° 2' 32". That by dead reckoning was 43° 0' 16", so that the small difference found for the past two or three days between dead reckoning and observation showed us that we no longer had the strong current which had at times given us large differences to the north.
The longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 132° 14' 16", which, since the last hour angle observed, gave 8° 32' 48" of easting in forty-eight hours. By dead reckoning we found we had made 8° 52' 0", which gave a difference of 17' 51" in excess. Thus the dead reckoning of the course run was tolerably good.
In the afternoon the sky seemed inclined to clear and became fairly bright. We did all we could to take azimuths in order to learn the variation of the needle, but the ship's motion was so incessant that we found it very hard to place any confidence in the results the calculation of these observations gave us. It appeared to us, however, that the variation must have changed and now be north-east instead of north-west, which nevertheless must not be regarded as certain, after what I have just said of the difficulty of obtaining well-established results by the compass.
During the night of the twentieth to the twenty-first we had very fine weather until the moon set. Towards the end of the day the winds had gone round to west-north-west, and during the night they seemed inclined to settle in the north-west. This change was very welcome to us, for it put an end to the great rolling that had tormented us all day. But the sky, for its part, became dark and misty, which gave us a very limited horizon. For the rest, it blew a pleasant breeze and we continued to steer east by south, the course I had signalled to the Naturaliste after the observation of the meridian altitude.
1802-01-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to WNW. Saw a whale and a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 40° 57' 53" of latitude observed and in 132° 8' 16" of longitude by account. At 2 the commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E. In the course of the day the five courses and topsails were shifted. Variation 2° 38' NE.

1802-01-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NW. We shifted the foresail and the main topsail. The commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E.
1802-01-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first the winds remained in the north-west, a strong breeze. This was very fine weather for us, and so we made full use of it to approach Van Diemen's Land, which we were all most eager to see. The sky, however, did not look good during the morning, being almost constantly laden with vapours and fogs which at times brought us a fine, gentle rain. Nevertheless we saw the sun now and then, and at noon we were able to take its altitude, which was found to be forty-three degrees fifty minutes, so that our course turned out to have made more southing than I had thought.
Although the weather was very misty and the clouds were driving along at great speed, the sea did not seem to herald bad weather, whereas the barometer and the hygrometer warned us of the contrary. The former had fallen to 27. 8.5, with every appearance of falling further, and the latter had risen to 96° of humidity, which had not happened for a long time.
We could not take any hour angle during the day to know exactly the distance made to the east in these twenty-four hours, but our dead reckoning gave us 4° 37' 0", which put us in 136° 51' 16". Consequently, we were about one hundred and ten leagues from the South West Cape of Van Diemen's Land.
After the observation of the meridian altitude, I had the ship steered east by north so as to gain a little to the north, and for the rest of the day we continued to steer on that point, making good way. But at about two o'clock the wind freshened so much as to oblige the Naturaliste to take in her topgallant sails, and ourselves, so as not to leave her too far astern, to take a third reef in our topsails. The sea was still tolerably smooth, but if the wind continues with the same strength it will not be long in becoming very heavy. All evening the sky was dark and laden with a thick mist which greatly limited our horizon.
At half past six we were struck by a very violent squall, accompanied by much rain, which brought the wind round to the west. Shortly afterwards the sky seemed disposed to clear for the night, as indeed it did, for the night was tolerably fine and even fairly clear. We made no change in our course and passed it under our ordinary sail, still making good way.
1802-01-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW, with rain. The sails unbent were examined and condemned, except the foresail. At noon in 43° 38' 29" of latitude by account and in 136° 36' 16" of longitude by account.

1802-01-12.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, rain at intervals, a high sea and a strong breeze from NW to W. At 6.30 the commander made the signal to bend our cables.
1802-01-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, the weather was fairly fine and the wind in the west, a pleasant breeze. The sea being still rather heavy and swelling, we rolled a great deal, the ship having no wind on her side to steady her.
At about eight o'clock I made the signal to the Naturaliste to bend her cables, and we did the same during the morning. At ten o'clock we were struck by a heavy squall of wind, rain and hail. It lasted more than half an hour and made me fear a change in the weather. But as it passed over, the sky became fine again, and indeed clearer than it had been until then.
In the course of the morning we saw several companies of birds flying in flocks, but they kept too far from the ship for us to judge whether they were known to us or not.
At noon the observed latitude was 43° 33' 14" and that by dead reckoning 43° 32', which gave little difference. The longitude indicated by the timekeeper put us in 140° 51' 25", which gave 8° 37' 16" of easting since the last observation, whereas dead reckoning gave us 9° 50'. The difference in forty-eight hours was very considerable, since we found ourselves 1° 12' 41" further west than we had reckoned.
In the afternoon the weather remained fine. During the evening several schools of porpoises were seen, which came to play around the ship but did not stay long. We harpooned none, because the ship had too much way on.
At sunset Captain Hamelin asked me whether I intended to carry sail all night. I replied that it would depend on the weather we had, but that when I hove to, if that should happen, I would make him the signal by lighting my stern lantern, and that he was to govern himself accordingly.
At eight o'clock, having no sight of the land, from which I reckoned myself still twelve or fifteen leagues off, we continued to steer east by north until about ten o'clock. But the weather then became so bad that I decided to heave to, with the ship's head south, towards the west.
During the rest of the night the weather was very bad; we had rain, hail and very strong gusts continually. One may even say that, for the state of the atmosphere, it was the worst night we had had up to that time.
1802-01-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to W, with rain. At 6.30 the commander signalled us to bend our cables, which we did, and got the anchors ready to let go. In a squall the fore studdingsail boom broke; it was at once replaced by one from the main yard. At noon in 43° 31' 30" of latitude observed and in 141° 2' 40" of longitude by account. At 5, 6° 22' 30" of NE variation. At 10 the commander having hove to on the starboard tack, we did the same, after lowering the topsails on the caps.

1802-01-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW to W and SW. During the night the commander having hove to, we did the same. At 3.45 we sighted the land in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander. We closed the coast and ran along it. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30', distance 9.5 miles; the Mewstone S 85° E, distance 5 miles; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 46° E, distance 4 miles.
1802-01-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of Van Diemen's Land:
At eight o'clock in the morning, the South West Cape north 10° west, 2 ½ leagues
The Maatsuiker Islands E. NE, 3 leagues
The Mewstone east
At noon the Mewstone south 68° west
The land nearest to us north 61° west
South Cape north 49° 45' east
The northernmost land in sight from north to 54° to the east
The Scully Islands east 45° south
Historical events & Remarks.
VIEW OF THE WESTERN COAST OF VAN DIEMEN'S ISLAND
On the twenty-third, at daybreak, we sighted the land, which bore from north-north-east to east-north-east of us. But it was so shrouded in mist that its shape could be made out only with some difficulty. Our reckoning put us about eight leagues from it. The part of the coast we had in view was high and would no doubt have presented a pleasant aspect had the weather been clearer. Nevertheless we crowded sail to approach it more closely, and at eight o'clock, having closed it, we took a bearing of the South West Cape of the lands of Van Diemen's Island, north ten degrees west, at a distance of about two and a half to three leagues. Tasman's Maatsuiker Islands then bore east-north-east of us, three leagues by our reckoning, & Furneaux's Mewstone east.
Our position being well determined, we made for the latter rock in order to round it, passing very close to it on its south side, and then steered more to the north to close with the land. The weather, though squally, was fairly fine during the morning, and as it blew a good breeze we reached, about noon, the southernmost cape of the land I have just spoken of. As we coasted fairly close along the whole stretch of coast lying between these two capes, I had views taken of all of it, and I hope they will not be without interest.
At noon the Mewstone, which was still in sight, bore south 68° west
The land nearest to us north 61° west, and South Cape north 49° 45' east.
The most north-easterly land in sight extended from north to 54° east.
My intention being to run straight into the Baie de la Recherche [Recherche Bay] so as to shelter there from the bad weather that threatened us, I closed with the Naturaliste and ordered her to go ahead under easy sail, the weather not allowing us to put boats out to guide us to the anchorage. But as the plan of it given in M. d'Entrecasteaux's Voyage seemed to us to have been made with the greatest care, we we (sic) placed complete confidence in it and followed it.
However, as the Naturaliste had orders to sound continually while under way, and was at about at (sic) a mile and a half from us, who were steering in her wake and also sounding without finding bottom at fifteen fathoms, we were very surprised to see her suddenly bear away and all at once come close-hauled on the starboard tack. We then had the Îles Stériles in sight at a short distance. We at once imitated the Naturaliste's manoeuvre and, like her, took the starboard tack so as to weather the Îles Vertes. The weather then looked as bad as it could, and the gusts were so strong that, although we had only the topsails and the foresail set, the ship had as much sail as she could carry.
After working up to windward of the Îles Stériles and rounding them, the Naturaliste bore away before the wind to double into the channel. For my part, I had a second reef taken in the topsails and was still undecided whether I would run in, giving up the Recherche anchorage, which it was no longer possible to reach. The weather was still bad and the land so hidden by rain that it could scarcely be made out. But at about two o'clock, the squalls and the rain which hid it from our view, as well as the Naturaliste, I found myself in the middle of the channel and nearer to the Île d'Entrecasteaux [Bruny Island] than to the mainland. I then decided to run into the channel, the Naturaliste being about two leagues ahead. We therefore threaded the channel strait to reach the anchorage of the Grande Anse, which I had named to the Naturaliste as the rendezvous in case of separation.
Coasting along the Île d'Entrecasteaux, we saw at its northern end a band of fifteen to twenty natives who came down to the water's edge to watch us pass. They remained standing for some time, all gathered together, apparently making signs that we could not well understand. But as we were making good way, we soon lost sight of them. Until then the lead had found no bottom at twenty fathoms. After rounding the Île aux Perdrix [Partridge Island], we saw the Naturaliste at anchor and came to take up our berth near her, at the spot marked on the plan of the Grande Anse with twenty-three fathoms, muddy bottom.
It would doubtless be difficult to see anything better done than the plan of it given by Citizen Beaupré, engineer-geographer of that expedition, and one may be assured that he has left nothing to be done by those who may come after him to survey this part of the strait.
As soon as we were settled at our anchor, Captain Hamelin came on board and told me the reasons that had prevented him from entering the Baie de la Recherche. A bank of rocks lying ahead of him, in five fathoms of water, had made him fear running aground if he tried to pass on one side or the other. He had therefore preferred to steer to windward of the Îles Vertes or Stériles, so as then to bear away and run into the channel.
We agreed together that, the very next day, his longboat would go to the Port de l'Espérance [Port Esperance] and examine it, to make sure that the English had made no settlement there and to see whether any convenient places were to be found there for taking in water. Mine was to go and examine the Rivière Huon [Huon River] and the Port des Cygnes [Port Cygnet].
Towards the end of the day we saw several fires in different parts of this Grande Anse, in which one lies as in a basin, although it was blowing a strong breeze from south to south-west. The sea there was calm, and it can never be rough there, from whatever quarter the winds may blow. The prospect from this anchorage is extremely pleasant, as may be judged from the view of it that I give.
M. Hamelin and I also decided that the next day we would go and visit the coast and the natives, if indeed they would let themselves be approached. It was also of great interest to us to see whether there were any good places in this anchorage for hauling the seine.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth the weather was constantly bad and rainy. Very strong gusts passed over us, but we did not drag our anchor, having only the force of the wind to hold against and no swell. We had sixty fathoms of cable out
1802-01-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 3.45 the land was sighted in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander at once. At 4 we signalled it again. At 4.30 filled and stood on and closed the land, which we made out to be the SW cape of Van Diemen's Land. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30' W, 10 miles off; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 56° E, 4 miles off; and the Mewstone S 85° E, 5 miles off. At noon took the bearing of the South Cape N 48° E, 4 miles off, and the Mewstone S 67° 30' W. Latitude by account 43° 33' 6", the same by the bearing 43° 44' 0"; longitude by account 143° 50' 22", the same by the bearing 144° 30' 0". Running very close along Van Diemen's Land and shaping our course to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel. At half past noon we spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. Several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 breakers were sighted ahead at a short distance (these breakers are marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart and lie between the south point of Anse des Ormiers and the Sterile Islands). The captain, who took them for canoes of the Aboriginal people coming aboard, said "let her come to port"; and I, who had the watch, repeated his order and had it carried out by the helmsman, who kept hauling his tiller to port. But a few minutes later, being already almost in the wash of the breakers, everyone having cried out that we were on the breakers, we hauled smartly to the wind on the starboard tack and weathered the Sterile Islands handsomely. The commander, who was keeping astern at some distance, followed our movement. At 3.15, being a little offshore, we bore away for Cape Bruny. The commander, who at that moment was taking in reefs, held his wind a while longer and at last shaped his course as we had. Having reached the mouth of the channel, we ran in; and after doubling Pointe Labillardière and the NE point of Partridge Island, we hauled to the wind to gain the anchorage of the Grande Anse in Bruny Island. At 4.15 we let go the anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud, under Partridge Island, Huon Island bearing S 88° E, Lahaye Island N 51° W, and the north point of Partridge Island N 82° W. At 4.45 the commander anchored S 30° E of us, two cables off. We asked his leave to put the boats in the water and to send one aboard him, which he granted. The boats were put in the water and we sent for the Géographe's doctors to see Citizen Milius, who was still ill. I went with the captain aboard the Géographe and had the pleasure of embracing my friends. The dinghy went fishing under Partridge Island and came back without having taken anything.

1802-01-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, standing in to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel and running very close along the land. At noon spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. We crowded sail; several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 we sighted several lines of breakers ahead. We at once hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack to weather the Sterile Islands; the Géographe followed our movement. At 3.45 we bore away for Cape Bruny; having reached the mouth of the channel we ran in and made for the anchorage of Grande Anse. At 4.15 we let go the starboard anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud. Bearings of the anchorage: the point of Partridge Island S 82° W; Lahaye Island N 54° W; Huon Island S 88° E. At 5 a.m. the longboat was sent off to look for a watering place.
1802-01-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, early in the morning, our boats set off as we had agreed the day before, and I gave M. Freycinet the following instructions in writing:
At the anchorage of the Grande Anse, Canal d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel].
To Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant,
"I entrust to you, Citizen, the command of my longboat, to go and visit several places which, although already well determined in the survey made of them by General d'Entrecasteaux, may offer us various objects of curiosity and of natural history.
"In consequence of this resolution, Citizens Péron and Guichenot will
accompany you on this excursion, as will Messrs Barbe and Lesueur. I therefore ask you to afford them every means of making the task they are about to undertake with you as useful as possible.
"On leaving the ship you will steer for the Rivière de Huon [Huon River], and after entering its mouth you will put in at the Port des Cygnes [Port Cygnet], where you will remain some time in order to procure us some birds of that species.
"I think two days will suffice for the excursion you are about to make. You will therefore take provisions for that length of time only.
"I have no need to urge upon you an unremitting vigilance for the safety of the longboat and of all who accompany you. But if you meet natives, which is very probable, you are absolutely forbidden to commit any hostility towards them, unless the safety of some individual in particular or of all in general depends upon it. The inhabitants of this country are reputed, from what is known of their character, not to be ill-natured unless they are provoked. It is therefore by kindnesses and presents that you must dispose them in our favour.
"You will not forget to see whether there is any convenient place for taking in water, and to take the soundings and bearings of the places where you land." Signed N. B.
On M. Freycinet's departure I had him issued with mirrors, glass beads, snuffboxes, axes, knives etc. etc. etc., and recommended to him economy and impartiality in any distribution he might make of them.
At about eight o'clock I embarked in my large boat, accompanied by Citizens Laridon, physician, (and) Bernier, astronomer, to go ashore. The small boat, carrying Messrs Ronsard, Bougainville and Petit, draughtsman, also joined the party. As we passed under the Naturaliste's stern, Captain Hamelin joined us.
It was not without difficulty that we managed to reach the shore, for it was blowing a strong breeze from the south-west and a strong current was setting us considerably to the south-east. However, after pulling hard for about an hour and a half, we landed on the Île aux Perdrix [Partridge Island], which lay only a mile from where the ships were anchored. Having landed, we wished to cross the island in its breadth, but we were soon obliged to make our way back to the seashore, so difficult did we find the way, and so choked with grass and brushwood. The trees on this island are well grown and tall. Most are of the eucalyptus kind, but we met with few plants in flower. When we had managed to regain the seashore, we followed it, walking continually over rocks of a granitic nature against the foot of which the sea was breaking. We found a ball of granite rather curious for its shape, having exactly the shape and size of a twelve-pounder shot. Shortly afterwards we caught sight of three persons from the Naturaliste: it was M. Leschenault and two men of that ship's crew, who had landed before us. They were in the midst of four natives, and all were walking along together. Although they were coming towards us, we quickened our pace to meet them sooner. The natives, who had followed them until then, intimidated no doubt by our great number, withdrew into the wood and we lost sight of them.
M. Leschenault told us that, having been to the end of the island, they had forded the little channel that separates it from the Île d'Entrecasteaux [Bruny Island], and that they had
come straight up to him, making many gestures that showed confidence and no intention whatever of doing harm, and that, moreover, they were without arms of any kind. As soon as they had come near, M. Leschenault took them by the hand, caressed them and gave them some presents. Confidence was promptly established in them, and from then on they accompanied this naturalist wherever he went, now talking among themselves, now singing. One of them, who wore a necklace of rather well polished shell beads, made him a present of it.
Leaving M. Leschenault to pursue his excursion, we continued ours in order to examine a sandy beach that looked suitable for hauling the seine. The natives who had kept to the wood then reappeared (and) came up to us without the least mistrust. We took them by the hand and caressed them as M. Leschenault had done, and also gave them a few trifles as presents. There were only three of them; the others had taken another way, but they were not long in rejoining their companions and making us great signs of friendship. Some of us who were eating biscuit gave (a) piece to each of those around us, but they thought little of it, nor of bread either.
We could understand nothing of the long speeches they made us, but their signs were much more intelligible, and we understood perfectly that they were telling us to follow them and join their companions, who were on the other side of the water. We therefore walked on together to the end of the island, but we did not think fit to accompany them further, since one had to go into the water up to the waist to cross the channel that separates this island from the large one. Most of the things we had seemed to tempt them greatly, and they would have been very pleased to see us give them our clothes. These men were naked from head to foot. One alone had a piece of skin covering part of his shoulders and loins. Their colour is much less dark than that of the negroes of Africa. And perhaps it is because they do not find themselves black enough that they paint different parts of the face with charcoal. All were tattooed from the shoulder down to about six inches below it. The lines were circular, and some ran lengthwise. For the rest, there was nothing disagreeable in their faces. Their expression was cheerful, even merry, the eye lively, the nose somewhat flat, the mouth large, with fine white teeth, well set and without any defect, unless indeed their great width be one. Their height did not seem to us below five feet two inches nor above five feet six. The body was well proportioned, but the legs weak and spindly, with little calf. They might have been from twenty-five to forty years of age.
After they had left us to join their companions, we retraced our steps, having found that the seine could conveniently be hauled at this spot, and perhaps even to advantage, the water not being deep and the bottom fine sand. A second band of six or seven natives, who had also communicated with our men left to guard the boats, were going back with the presents that had been given them, which they wore round their necks. One had put there a jacket a sailor had given him, a piece of bunting etc. etc.
Among those who made up this last band, two were remarkable for the elegance of their costume. One, who wore the skin of a
kangaroo or some other animal, had his shoulders and chest covered down to the navel. His head seemed to us covered with a kind of cap in the shape of a wig, which for a long time we believed to be made of seaweed. But having examined it more closely, we recognised that it was his hair, which, divided into little strands five or six lines wide and about an inch long, and held together with grease and a reddish-brown earth, formed a skullcap around his head that was tossed about in different ways by every movement he made. The other, who was quite naked, merely had his head shaved, with a ring of hair running round it.
We brought back from this excursion many mussels, different in shape from ours, a few limpets of little interest and several sea-ears, as well as different kinds of nerites. Three or four shells unknown to us were picked up, but of very small size.
As we had brought nothing ashore for dinner, we all re-embarked at four o'clock to return on board.
I forgot to mention that when we tried to cross to the other side of the island through the woods, we came upon trees of prodigious girth, most of them burnt out to a height of seven or eight feet; the fire had been directed with symmetry, and the space hollowed out by means of the fire could easily hold eight to ten people. All the openings, without exception, were sheltered from the winds from south to north by way of west. One also meets in the wood several of these great trees that the winds have thrown down, and they always lay with the head of the tree to the north, incontestable proof that the south-west, west and north-west winds are more violent in this quarter than those from any other point of the compass.
Birds seemed to gather there in great numbers, and several had a very pleasant song. Parakeets and parrots, however, seem to be the dominant kind. I do not know why this island was named the Île aux Perdrix, for we saw no partridges there. Although we covered a fairly considerable extent of ground, we killed only a thrush and a parrot.
Judging the height of the tide by the high-water mark, it must rise four or five feet when it is at its greatest height.
The night of the twenty-fourth to the twenty-fifth was like the preceding ones. It blew a strong breeze from south to south-south-west, in strong gusts mingled with rain.
1802-01-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to WSW, with squalls and rain. At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat to water in Port Espérance or in the Huon River; Citizens Freycinet, lieutenant, Faure, surveyor, and Bailly, mineralogist, took the opportunity to come along. At 8 the captain and some of the officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island and communicated with the Aboriginal people. The dinghy went fishing and took nothing. In the evening all the boats (except the longboat) came back aboard. An inclination of 68° 36' 0" was observed in the Grande Anse.

At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat, manned with 7 men and provisioned for 2 days, to water in Port Espérance; and should I be unable to water there, I was to go to the Huon River. Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly came with me. The weather was overcast and squally with rain; a good breeze from the south carried me to Port Espérance in very little time. I closed the south point and ran along the coast within a boathook's length. I went into the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream; the longboat touched, and having got off without difficulty, I landed on the starboard point with Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly. We made for the stream; it was dry, with only brackish water in a few holes. Having re-embarked, I crossed the harbour to look for another stream marked on the chart abreast of the first. I tried to land thereabouts, but it was impossible (the shore being foul, and the longboat touching on a muddy sand bottom at some distance from the beach). I ran along the shore and saw a trickle of water running over the sand; seeing no convenience for watering there, I decided to go to the Huon River. The wind was a strong breeze in puffs and very variable; I beat for 3 hours between Lahaye Island and the north point. At last I put the men to the oars, and having doubled the north point with great difficulty, I made sail and shaped my course for the Huon River. I closed and ran along the right bank. At sunset, finding myself abreast of Port des Cygnes, I went in after doubling the second point to starboard. I sighted the Géographe's longboat in a cove; I bore up for her and landed beside her. I learnt that when the longboat had come alongside the shore, several Aboriginal people had run up with cries of joy, that the eldest (probably the head of the family) had thrown his arms round the neck of Citizen Freycinet the elder, commanding the longboat, and that they had taken him to their huts.

After searching the cove without finding water, I came back to the boats, where I found Freycinet the elder and 6 Aboriginal people: 2 men, a young woman and 3 little boys. The elder of the men had a short, curly beard; their hair was woolly and smeared with a kind of red grease. The two men and the woman, who must have had hair on their private parts, had shaved it. The woman had her face smeared with black; and to show us how she blackened it she rubbed both hands on a burnt tree, puffed out her cheeks and drew her hands over them from her ears to her nose and eyes. She then wanted to do as much to each of us. They each had a kangaroo skin which covered their shoulders only. The men did not appear to us jealous; they let us caress the young woman, who seemed to take some pleasure in it. We loaded them with presents; they took everything eagerly and, without examining it, handed it to the woman, who stowed it in her kangaroo skin. Several times I tried to make them look in a mirror and held it before their eyes, but they at once turned away sharply. I also tried to show them the use of knives by cutting wood in front of them; they paid no attention and threw themselves on the knife to get it, and as soon as they had it they gave it to the woman. The only thing that held their attention was a tricolour plume I had on my hat; I gave it to the younger of the men, who at once put it in his hair, and the elder seemed vexed that I had not given it to him. Before we arrived they had stolen a bottle of brandy from the Géographe's longboat and hidden it in a hollow tree, where the boat's crew, who had seen them do it, recovered it. When we re-embarked, all of them (except the eldest) got into my longboat; but we had scarcely shoved off when the eldest called them, and they took to the water. They made signs to us as long as we could see them.

I passed the night, with the Géographe's longboat, in a very fine cove next to the last. At daybreak the Freycinets and I went round it on foot, hoping to find fresh water there. We found several streams, which we went up; the water was drinkable only too far from their mouths for the ships to water there, though we filled a few breakers. After our round we re-embarked. Freycinet the elder sounded the cove, and I shaped my course for the head of the harbour, running along the land within a boathook's length. Having reached it, I ran along the shore to port, and seeing no stream I resolved to return aboard, having only two meals' provisions left. I gave the order to steer out of the harbour. A short distance from where we had passed the night I met the Géographe's longboat standing for the head of the harbour. Freycinet the elder hailed me and asked what I was about; I answered that I was going back aboard. He told me he was going to dine at the head of the harbour on a swan he had just shot. Whereupon Freycinet the younger, without warning me, gave the coxswain orders to steer for the head of the harbour; we set our sails and chased swans. Right at the head of the harbour the water shoaled suddenly and we grounded on soft mud. We rowed, poled, got off, and grounded again. Citizen Freycinet had taken the tiller and I had taken an oar. We had been rowing some minutes when I gave the order to pole; Citizen Freycinet appeared displeased and spoke harshly to me. The boat's crew did not know which of the two to obey. I observed to Citizen Freycinet that the captain, having entrusted the longboat to me, had thought me capable of handling her and that I answered for her. He said no more; I repeated the order I had given, and shortly afterwards the longboat was afloat. I had her anchored to give the crew a moment's rest and let them dine. I then had it out with Citizen Freycinet, and the longboat being out of all danger, I offered to hand over the command of her to him. He took it. We landed near the Géographe's people and dined there. In the evening we left in company with the Géographe's boat, and on the 26th [Nivôse, 16 January 1802] at 5 a.m. we arrived aboard. I reported to the captain what had passed. He blamed Citizen Freycinet's conduct and told me I had been wrong to give up the command of the longboat to him.

1802-01-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and a strong breeze from S to SSW. All the boats were back except the longboat.
1802-01-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, although the breeze was still very strong and the wind southerly, varying to south-west, the large and small boats, commanded by Citizens Bonnefoy and Ransonnet, set off to fish, with orders to go to the place assigned to them. As I was quite convinced that the natives in the neighbourhood would not fail to go and find them, I had a few trifles handed to them to maintain a good understanding. This being the only means to employ in such circumstances, I even recommended each of these officers to give them a little of our catch if it was plentiful, and yet to be always on their guard.
Citizen Maugé, although still very ill, wished to go ashore, and in fact went, despite all the representations I made to him about his condition and the dangers to which he would be exposed from the inclemency of the air and the state of the atmosphere, laden with damp vapours unhealthy even for persons in good health.
