None of these considerations, however, could hold him back. Without regard for the consequences that might follow, he set off. The astronomer Bernier
also set off to observe the latitude of this cove, and the variation and dip of the magnetic needle. From the way the natives had behaved the day before, I contented myself with putting two marines, with their arms, in the large boat, this means of defence seeming to me sufficient for the safety of all who were going.
After the departure of my two boats, Captain Hamelin went ashore at the place where the seine was to be hauled; I had agreed the day before to be there too, but the weather, which was rainy, looked so bad that I preferred to remain on board to put in order various things I had to do.
At one o'clock one of the boats returned with very few fish, of the plaice and ray kind, and the fishing was very poor. The small boat could not come back at the same time because she had let herself go aground. The large one had met with the same fate through the carelessness of the officer commanding her. While the fishing was going on, the natives of the country gathered in great numbers at the place our men had chosen for hauling the seine ashore. Men, women and children and Europeans were all mingled together, without mistrust of one another and without fear. The boat that had remained aground being the only one ashore, there were only six of our men there, and the natives, all told, numbered more than fifty. A large fire was lit, and all having gathered round it, they were asked to sit down, which they did at once, and the best understanding reigned between them and the boat's crew. The opportunity was taken to draw several of them, whose portraits will be found in the journal. But it was not possible to obtain those of the women and children, for the women could not stay a moment in the same place, nor could the children; as for the men, they were more docile, and the character of their faces was easily captured.
At three o'clock, the small boat having returned, I strongly reproved Citizen Bonnefoy for having let her go aground; he laid the blame on the boat-keepers, which is always the custom, for officers never wish to be in the wrong. This imprudence, however, was the cause of Midshipman First Class Maurouard, whom I had attached to the astronomer, receiving a spear-thrust at the very moment they were preparing to embark. He was struck on the right side of the neck, and the spear passed right through it horizontally, apparently running only under the skin. This spear was no doubt vigorously thrown, for it went through a double woollen waistcoat, and no one knows where it came from. The wound did not seem dangerous to the doctors, and they hope he will soon be cured of it. It seemed to me, however, serious enough for me not to share that opinion.
It is rather difficult to guess what could have started the hostility, for according to the report each has made to me individually, it appears that the best understanding reigned constantly between the two parties. A quarter of an hour before embarking, all the natives had, it is true, disappeared, but as they had gone off loaded with presents and very merry, no one had the least mistrust of them.
As soon as the spear was thrown, Citizens Bonnefoy and Maurouard, who were armed with muskets, climbed a rise to see whether they could discover anything, and did indeed see seven or eight of the natives armed with spears, who made no movement on catching sight of them. Everyone was ordered to get into the boat, which was then afloat, and they themselves then came to embark without having been (pursued) in any way.
The more I have reflected on this unexpected accident to find its cause, the less
easy I have found it to discover, and unless the detail I am about to relate gave rise to it, it must no doubt be attributed to treachery and to the little fear inspired in them by those who were still ashore.
While everyone was gathered round the fire, waiting for the tide to come back, Citizen Maurouard, a strong and vigorous man, wished to try his strength against the native he judged the strongest of the band. He began by taking him by the wrist, in the way young men do in Europe, making signs to his adversary to offer him as much resistance as possible, which he understood very well, but he could not hold out against that offered by Maurouard. After this first success the two athletes grappled with each other to see which would throw the other. Maurouard was again the victor and threw the other down. As this scene took place on the sand, the fall could not be dangerous for either. Besides, it all passed off with laughter, and the vanquished seemed more pleased with his fall than the victor with his triumph.
It seems probable to me, however, that the natives, seeing their companion beaten by strength, may afterwards have sought to show that they were not beaten in skill and cunning, and that this is perhaps what led to the spear being thrown, since it is the only one that was. It is not to be supposed, however, that they wished to be answered with a musket shot, for they are very much afraid of that weapon, even when someone merely touches it.
If several are to be taken at their word, the women tried various ways and means to draw some of them aside, and the signs they made to them were too expressive for their intentions to be mistaken. Some of the Naturaliste's boatmen even asserted that, having followed some of them, the women had of their own accord fully satisfied their curiosity, but not their desires.
It was remarked for the second time that the natives would neither eat nor drink anything our men took ashore with them; but those who, at the very beginning of their arrival, were in the Naturaliste's boat stole everything they could lay their hands on, down to the thwart pins. A boy of about fifteen to eighteen had had, as his share, a marlinspike, which he had fastened round his body by means of the lanyard attached to it. Although he had taken the precaution of hiding the iron under his kangaroo skin, he was found out by the lanyard. The marlinspike was taken from him, which made him cry a great deal. Then one of the elders of the band struck him rather roughly, speaking to him very fast, and he stopped his lamentations. As what was being said to him could not be understood, we could not tell whether he was reprimanding him for the theft he had committed or blaming him for not having been more adroit, which is only too likely, given the desire they show to take possession of everything we had. They took an empty bottle from our boat, which was left to them.
One of our sailors having exchanged his jacket with one of them for a kangaroo skin, the native at once put it round his neck and went off by himself. His first care was to cut off all the buttons, and then he abandoned the jacket, which the sailor recovered on embarking. Another, who had been put into a pair of long canvas trousers, was so hampered by them that he had all the trouble in the world reaching a tree about twenty-five paces away. There he quickly rid himself of this irksome garment and would not even take its buttons, of which they seemed very fond.
Citizen Bonnefoy exchanged a small mirror with a woman for her necklace. The medallion of this necklace was an English sou and a metal button. But it could not be
learned at what time she had received it. On looking at herself in the mirror she had just been given, she made all sorts of grimaces, the repetition of which seemed greatly to amuse her, and then she withdrew apart with a child she was nursing to daub herself with charcoal, and afterwards came back to show herself off in her new finery, so true is it that in every country of the world women neglect no means of pleasing or seducing.
At sunset, the sky having cleared a good deal, the winds died down and there was every appearance of a change. Only we had to fear seeing the wind go round to the north by way of the east. For I had decided to shift our position as soon as my boats returned, which I expected, at the latest, during the night. M. Hamelin, who came on board in the evening, was informed of this intention.
During the night the winds went round to the north, as the signs had led us to expect, and the breeze was very light. The longboat arrived at about two in the morning, and as I had given orders that I should be told when she came in sight, I received these gentlemen and saw with regret that their excursion had not had the success I had expected of it.
1802-01-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to W. The captain and the officers landed on Bruny Island and came back aboard at noon.

1802-01-16.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the wind fell away a great deal. In the afternoon the breeze varied from SSW to W, N and NNE. At 6.30 a.m. the longboat was back, not having been able to find a convenient place to water.
1802-01-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, in the morning, the winds being north, varying to north-north-east, there was no way of getting under sail. So that this day should not be entirely lost, I sent the carpenters ashore to cut wood and make up whatever we might need in that line.
As there had been little order the day before among the men who had gone fishing, and as, the moment anyone was ashore, he went off wherever he pleased without permission and at his own whim, I thought fit to remedy this abuse and, in order to prevent it in future, I gave M. Ronsard, who was charged with this task, the following instructions:
"The Commander etc.,
"To Citizen Ronsard, lieutenant on board the Géographe.
"You will take command of the longboat, Citizen, and proceed to the same place where we landed together the day before yesterday. The object of your mission is to have her filled with firewood and to return on board at once. The ease you will find in this work means that it should be neither long nor difficult, and so that it may be finished the more quickly you will employ everyone on it. While the carpenters cut it, the others will carry it on board, and under no pretext, whether of fishing, shooting or otherwise, will you allow anyone to stray out of your sight.
"Midshipman Baudin, who accompanies you, will supervise the sailors in carrying the wood, while you and the two gunners I am giving you will protect the workers, should the natives try to trouble you. The purpose of the task you are going to perform is therefore to occupy yourself solely with this work and to return on board as soon as it is finished, or even earlier if I make you the signal.
"I trust you will place the longboat in such a position that there is no fear of her going aground."
Signed N. B.
After the longboat had left, I asked M. Hamelin, who was on board, to send his own to the same place for the same purpose, and I then invited him to take Citizen Faure, geographer, in his boat to go and sound
in every direction the cove of our anchorage, which does not appear to have been sounded when General d'Entrecasteaux had it surveyed.
Several of the naturalists also went ashore to make researches in their respective fields, but as I had visited that place the day before, it seemed to me that they would not find much there.
In the afternoon we had a very heavy squall with abundant rain and thunder in plenty. This storm lasted a good hour, and our workers ashore must have been greatly inconvenienced by it. I learned with regret that M. Depuche, who is only just beginning to convalesce, was there, having gone ashore in one of the Naturaliste's boats. This mineralogist, not very reasonable on this occasion, has doubtless not reflected on the unfortunate consequences that may follow from his imprudence. His conduct, which he is pleased to call zealous and which seems to me to deserve quite another name, has decided me to let him do in future whatever may please him according to his way of reasoning. The little account he takes of our advice in what concerns his life relieves me of continuing to give it.
A little before sunset all the boats were back aboard their respective ships, and I informed Captain Hamelin that we would get under sail the next day if the weather at all permitted, in order to advance as far as possible up the channel and reach the Port du Nord-Ouest, where I intended to stay to replenish my water.
The night of the 27th to the 28th (sic) passed without incident; the winds were still between west and north-west, in strong gusts and often with rain.
It had been noticed during the day that the natives were no longer in our neighbourhood, for no one was seen, nor even any of their fires. Captain Hamelin, who had gone to the northern end of this cove to sound round it, came upon about thirty of them, who, seeing his boat approach the shore, no doubt thought that he meant to land there and seemed disposed to oppose it. All were armed with spears, and so that they should not run short of this weapon, several could be seen carrying great bundles of them. One of them, walking in front, had in his hand a burning brand with which he set fire to everything wherever they passed. This, I believe, is rather their custom when they wish to forestall or begin war among themselves.
1802-01-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW. At 5 a.m. I came back aboard with the longboat without having been able to water, either in Port Espérance or in Port des Cygnes. In the latter I had a dispute with Citizen Freycinet and handed over the command of the longboat to him (see my report to the captain). At 8 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, was sent off in the large boat to sound the inner part of the Grande Anse. Our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went for firewood on Partridge Island; the sick were sent there to walk about a little. I took the opportunity to go shooting on the island. At 4 p.m. the weather turned overcast and stormy and the wind freshened from the WNW. Our longboat being loaded, we made haste to leave so as to reach the ship before the storm broke; but we were scarcely halfway when the wind came on to blow hard, with a high sea, thunder, lightning and pouring rain. We did not take in an inch of sail; two cables from the ship the foremast broke off level with the collar, and before the grapnel and its rope could be got ready we drove and anchored in the ship's wake. At 6, the breeze having fallen a great deal, we came aboard. Citizen Faure came back in the large boat at nightfall. The draught was taken: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 10 feet 10 inches, difference 1 foot 1 inch. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman of the Géographe, in charge of a party in a boat, received a spear wound in the shoulder on Bruny Island.

1802-01-17.journal_anonyme: The weather, fine enough at first, turned overcast; the wind freshened from the WNW and the storm broke at 4.30 with a great deal of rain. At 5 a.m. the commander made the signal to get under way; at 8.30 we were under sail, and at 10 and at noon we were abreast of Pointe Riche, forming the southern entrance to Isthmus Bay.
1802-01-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at five in the morning, the wind being west, a pleasant breeze, we prepared to weigh. I made the same signal to the Naturaliste, and we hove short after sheeting home and hoisting our topsails. We expected to be under sail shortly, but we did not manage it until about half past seven, the holding ground of our anchorage being so good that we had infinite trouble breaking out our anchor. Indeed, we managed it only after having already broken the great purchase that had to be clapped on the cable. When our anchor was quite up and out of the water, there was more than a thousand pounds' weight of black, firm mud on it, which the flow of the water had neither washed away nor loosened from the anchor.
The Naturaliste had the same difficulty. It appears that with good cables one would be in complete safety in this roadstead, even in very strong winds.
As soon as we were under sail, we closed with the land to larboard so as to keep the wind and run as far up the channel as possible. Despite the confidence we were bound to have in Citizen Beaupré's plan, we kept the lead going constantly and everywhere found the soundings he gives. It is, as I have already observed, difficult to produce a work more exact and more detailed than his plan of this strait, and with such a plan one could pass through it by day or by night, if the winds allowed a direct course.
When we had crossed the large and the small cove, as well as part of the Baie de l'Isthme [Isthmus Bay], we came to examine the small island that lies a short distance from Cap Legrand. We were obliged to beat to windward to round it, but it was impossible for us to pass Cap Legrand, so that we came to anchor a short distance from that cape, in nine fathoms of water, bottom of sand and very black mud, about a mile from a point of the cove which lay a little ahead of us and which seemed fairly deep. In the northern part of this bay there was a small island, much smaller than the Île Verte and entirely covered with trees, which the chart does not mention, doubtless because of its slight importance.
On the passage we made to reach the anchorage we now occupy, the winds were very inconstant and seemed to follow the direction of the mountains. Wherever there were gaps through which they could escape, very strong puffs came through, and the moment after we would be in a flat calm.
The view is extremely pleasant all along the channel. The mountains are wooded from the water's edge to their summits, and the different shades of green make the landscape very pretty. One may judge of it from the view given of it.
At about three in the afternoon I went ashore accompanied by Citizens Bonnefoy and Guichenot. During the three and a half hours we stayed there, we made a fairly long excursion into the country without meeting any of the natives. We found several traces of their stays and a single hut, if indeed that name can be given to the shelters they are accustomed to put up to protect themselves from wind or rain. We brought back from this short excursion a few plants for drying, a very pretty little quadruped that no one knows, and four different species of birds. We saw some quail, two or three wood pigeons and many parrots and parakeets, which it was not possible to approach, any more than two kangaroos.
The seashore offered us nothing of interest in shells or marine plants. The species found there were not plentiful and were similar to those we had collected in the Grande Anse.
The night passed without incident, and the winds went round to the north-west, which (made) them entirely contrary to the course we had to steer the next day. We had rain at times, but the squalls did not last long.
1802-01-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to N. At 5 the commander made the signal to get under way. At 9.30 got under way and shaped our course up the channel. We had great difficulty weighing our anchor; we broke a messenger and then rigged a voyol. At noon, being abreast of Isthmus Bay, the wind headed us; we beat until 2.30 without being able to weather Green Island. The commander then having anchored east of Green Island, we anchored in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand, Pointe Legrand bearing N 3° W, the Géographe and the middle of Green Island N 22° E, Pointe Riche S 33° E, and Satellite Island from S 15° W to S 22° W. Citizen Faure went to sound the channel; he saw a seal on Green Island. Several officers and naturalists landed on Van Diemen's Land abreast of the anchorage.

1802-01-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze with strong gusts at intervals from W to NW. Being near Green Island, we anchored on the opposite side of the channel in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand. Satellite Island bore from us S 15° W to S 22° W; Pointe Riche S 33° E; the middle of Green Island N 22° E; Pointe Legrand N 3° W. Pointe Legrand bore from us N 22° E, past Green Island.
1802-01-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, there was no way of getting under sail, the winds being north-west and very variable. During the forenoon we had some rather violent squalls. Nevertheless, I had Citizen Bernier put ashore on Cap Legrand so that he might take its latitude by means of an artificial horizon and observe the dip of the needle there. After his departure the yawl likewise carried ashore Citizen Péron and M. Freycinet, one of my officers. During the night we had seen no fire to tell us where the natives might be.
In the afternoon the (sky was) very cloudy and looked most unpromising. (Heavy) gusts from north-west to west were felt, one of them more more (sic) particularly than the others, since it set us adrift even though our anchor was on good holding ground and we had seventy fathoms of cable out. Being unable to bring the ship up by veering more cable, we were obliged to let go a second anchor with sixty fathoms, and we held fast. But in drifting we had lost more than half a league, which made our getting under way rather difficult if the winds did not shift.
Towards four in the afternoon the sky, which until then had been very rainy, seemed about to clear. The Naturaliste, which was at anchor off the southern part of Île Verte and which, like us, had been set adrift by the squalls that had passed, took advantage of the winds, which had come round to the west and were blowing fresh, to get under way, and easily doubled Pointe Legrand; but our position not being as favourable as hers, we could not do the same, and we had to resign ourselves to spending the night where we were.
According to the observations of Citizen Bernier, taken before and after noon, Cap Legrand would lie in latitude (no figures)
The dip of the needle was observed to be (no figures)
Before nightfall, which promised to be tolerable, I had the anchor weighed that the gusts had obliged me to let go in the evening. We also rove our top-ropes in case it should be necessary to strike the topmasts.
Citizen Péron brought back little from his excursion, and I knew beforehand that the shore yielded little in the way of shells or marine animals. The vegetable productions were the same as those we had already met with, but our hunters were more fortunate and supplied us with five or six species of birds.
The night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth passed without incident; the sky was fairly fine and the wind calm, apart from a few cat's-paws. No fire was seen anywhere on our horizon.
1802-01-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to NW in gusts, with rain. Despite the bad weather we ran out a warp towards Pointe Legrand and hauled in on it, being obliged to let go the bower anchor in heavy gusts. At 5 the wind hauled to the W and drew round to WSW. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port; at 7 doubled Pointe Legrand and at 7.45 Pointe Gicquel. At 8 we anchored at the entrance of the North West Port, Pointe Legrand bearing S 12° W, Pointe Gicquel S 25° W, Pointe Pierson N 36° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.

1802-01-19.journal_anonyme: In the roads of the North West Port, Van Diemen's Land. We warped in towards the anchorage; at 3.30 the breeze got up and we hoisted our topsails, but having dragged our kedge anchor we let go a bower. At 6 p.m. we got under way and anchored at the entrance to the North West Port. Bearings: Pointe Legrand S 12° W; Pointe Gicquel S 25° W; Pointe Pierson N 36° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.
1802-01-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth we had the winds northerly and very light. Although they were contrary to the course we had to steer to reach Port du Nord-Ouest [North West Bay], where I intended to stop, I had sail made from four in the morning in order to take up a better position than the one we were in. By tacking back and forth we succeeded in doubling Cap Legrand, and we would have continued to advance a little way into the channel had the winds not failed us. At ten o'clock, being in a flat calm with the current against us, we anchored on the larboard shore in eleven fathoms, muddy bottom. The Naturaliste was in much the same position, but about a league ahead of us. After anchoring we veered twenty-five fathoms of cable and kept our topsails hoisted so as to get under way should the wind allow it in the course of the day.
The sky was very fine all morning and the sun very hot. It was truly summer weather, and this day became for us the most agreeable we had had for a long while.
At one in the afternoon, a light breeze from the north-west springing up, we made sail again. Although the current was against us, I hoped to be able to approach the entrance of the port before nightfall. We accordingly beat to windward, but with little success. We were even carried by the current into the bight of the bay that lies on the western side of Île d'Entrecasteaux [Bruny Island], and we came near enough to the land to fear being obliged to anchor there, which would have been unavoidable had the direction of the current not changed towards four in the evening. We were then able to work out of that bight, and towards six o'clock we succeeded in reaching the Naturaliste, near which we anchored. Shortly afterwards Captain Hamelin, who had arrived at the entrance of this port the day before, informed me that he had had it examined by his boats, that the plan of it was very exact, but that the rivers marked on it had not been found in the ravines. This news was all the more unwelcome to me because I had chosen this place solely from the certainty I had that fresh water, and even in abundance, was to be found there.
As we had great need to replace what we had consumed since leaving Timor, and not knowing whether, in the other parts of the coast we had to explore, we should find it easy to water, I decided to send to reconnoitre the Rivière du Nord [Derwent River]. The various streams shown on the plan seemed to us likely to supply it. The longboat of the Naturaliste, the best of all our boats, was charged with this duty, which is to take two days, and M. Breton received orders to leave the next day at daybreak.
The place where we found ourselves was very well inhabited. Fires could be seen at every point of the coast, and in great numbers. However, several boats from the Naturaliste that approached it could not communicate with the natives. They fled at their approach, and it was never possible to come up with them. Several were also seen crossing by canoe from the mainland to Île d'Entrecasteaux. One of these canoes, in which there were four men, came within musket-shot of the Naturaliste without being willing to come any closer, despite all the invitations made to them by holding out various objects to induce them to come alongside. It could not be clearly made out whether their oars were paddles or poles, but they pulled in the same manner as if they had been paddles.
During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth the sky was fairly fine; nevertheless some rather strong gusts from the north-west passed over. We were at anchor in thirteen fathoms on a good muddy bottom.
Bearings from our fourth anchorage in the Canal d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]:
(no mention of bearings)
1802-01-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW. A dog was heard barking ashore. The Aboriginal people lit many fires at different points of the coast. Officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island to try to communicate with them, but they fled at their approach. The longboat, with a working party, went for firewood to Pointe Gicquel. Two catamarans were seen crossing the channel from Pointe Pierson to Pointe de la Sortie, in one of them four Aboriginal people and in the other six. The captain dredged all the afternoon and took a considerable quantity of scallops. The longboat came back at nightfall loaded with wood. At 6 the Géographe anchored near us.

1802-01-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, winds from N to NNW, a light breeze. The longboat went for wood. The large boat was sent off to the North River.
1802-01-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth our boats left the day before at daybreak, as I had agreed with Captain Hamelin the day before. His boat went to the Rivière du Nord [Derwent River] as we did, and I gave the command of mine to Citizen Ronsard with the following instructions:
"The Commander &c., to Citizen Ronsard, lieutenant de vaisseau,
"At daybreak you will have the longboat manned, take command of it, and proceed "to the head of Port du Nord-Ouest [North West Bay], surveyed by M. d'Entrecasteaux.
"As M. Hamelin has had the whole circuit of this port examined, he has satisfied himself that there is "no water there at this season. You will therefore have no search to make in that quarter. But "you will do everything in your power to procure swans, and that is the sole object of your mission. The "plan of this port that was given to us is, moreover, so exact that it leaves nothing to be desired as to geographical "detail.
"You will take with you Citizen Barbe and Midshipman Baudin, and you will embark two "days' provisions, although I do not think you will need them for so long. You "will not forget to provide yourself with some beads and other trifles to make presents of to the "natives, should you meet any. Remember above all that you are forbidden to commit any "hostility towards them, unless the safety of the persons accompanying you is endangered". Signed N. B.
When the boats left, the weather was very fine, the sky clear and the winds
north-west, a pleasant breeze. But in the course of the morning they shifted to the south-west, accompanied by rain and very strong gusts. The Naturaliste was set adrift, and so that the Géographe should not be, I had a second anchor laid out, as much to check the swinging of the ship, which the current turned in every direction, as to hold better against the force of the wind.
A small tent was also set up ashore for the astronomer, so that he might observe the eclipse if possible.
When all this was finished, I sent the seine to be hauled in a pretty little sandy cove about a mile from the ship, which seemed to me very convenient for the purpose. It lay on the starboard shore, that is to say on the northern part of Île Bruny [Bruny Island].
Throughout the day we saw fires at various points of the coast, but at a fairly great distance from us. The natives did not show themselves on either of the two stretches of coast we visited. Yet our people went a good way into the interior of the country, especially on the land to larboard.
In the afternoon the weather, though not very favourable, was finer than it had been in the morning. Our gardener brought back several species of trees and shrubs, which were potted to add to those we had collected elsewhere, and in exchange for what he had just taken he left all sorts of stone-fruit and vegetable seeds, which were set in the places most suitable for their rapid growth.
The fishing was not plentiful, but the few fish obtained were of very good quality, as were the lobsters. The birds brought back were like those we already had. It was only remarked that the crows, which we had not yet obtained, were like those of Europe in plumage, in their cawing and even in their habits. Among the fish there is a small one, rather peculiar in its fore fins, in that they bear a perfect resemblance to hands and it uses them to fasten itself to the rocks when it is out of the water.
During the night of the thirtieth to the first of Ventôse (sic), the sky cleared and the winds went back to the north-west, varying towards the west. Only a few gusts passed, and of little consequence.
At about midnight I heard a boat hailed; I thought it was my boat returning from the mission I had entrusted to it, but I was mistaken: it was merely some of the ship's officers who, having spent part of the day aboard the Naturaliste, were returning at so unseemly an hour.
Citizen Maugé, who since his relapse had gone steadily from bad to worse and who, despite his condition and my remonstrances, had insisted on going ashore as if he were in good health, found himself this day much worse than usual, and I began to fear that his illness would become most serious and that he might not even recover from it. The report the surgeon has just made to me at this moment is unhappily only too consistent with my opinion and my fears.
Citizen Depuche, who likewise regards his excursions as zeal when they are nothing but imprudence, is less well than usual, and perhaps he will end by sharing the fate of the others if he continues to pay as little heed as he has done hitherto to the advice that friendship and duty have led me to give him, and which he treats as whim and a wish to thwart him.
The other sick are fairly well, with the exception of one of our seamen, who is still very weak and languishing.
1802-01-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW, with heavy gusts and rain. At 5 the longboat, with a working party, went for wood. At 6 I was sent off in the large boat to go up the North River to look for a watering place for the ships; I was armed with two blunderbusses and four muskets and had 4 days' provisions. At 2 p.m. the ship dragged, veered cable and then let go a second anchor. The yards were sent down and the topgallant masts struck. The longboat came back loaded with wood.

1802-01-21.journal_anonyme: Squally weather. A fresh breeze from WNW with strong gusts and rain. At 2 we dragged and veered 12 fathoms of cable; shortly afterwards let go the port anchor.
1802-01-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first, in the morning, I again dispatched my launch under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy to go round Port du Nord-Ouest [North West Bay] a second time and look for the freshwater stream marked on the plan I had before me. I could not persuade myself that none existed, as Citizen Hérisson, who had been the first charged with this survey, had declared to me.
Captain Hamelin, for his part, likewise set out in his launch to examine very closely the whole of the larboard shore as far as abreast of Île Verte, in order to make sure whether or not any of the rivers exist that the English have marked in that part on the poor plan that Arrowsmith has published of the channel discovered by M. d'Entrecasteaux.
After these two boats had left, the astronomer made ready for his observation of the following day, which was to take place between half past nine in the morning, (sic) Jupiter being due to pass over the sun.
The other people on board were busy pumping the water out of the hold and getting our stowage casks ready, for I was still convinced that we should find a place suitable for filling them in the neighbourhood of our anchorage.
In the forenoon the sky was fairly fine, and we took advantage of it to send some of our sick ashore for a change of air. As on the preceding days, we saw many places where fires were lit, but we saw none of the natives appear on the shore.
In the afternoon the sky was (finer) than it had been in the morning. The winds shifted to west-north-west, varying to north-west, in strong gusts, followed by a flat calm.
Towards three o'clock my launch returned on board with the bad news that she had found nothing but dry ravines wherever she had gone in. Shortly afterwards the boat that had gone to haul the seine also came back, bringing enough fish to give some to the whole crew. There were in particular many small rays, very pleasingly mottled.
At six o'clock Citizen Ronsard likewise returned from the swan hunt on which he had been since the day before. He brought back two birds of that species, four small ducks or teal, and some land birds like those we already had. But he had at last found the freshwater stream that the others had searched for so long and to no purpose. This officer reported to me that it would not, in truth, be very easy to take in there the quantity of water each ship needed, but that by clearing somewhat the mouth of the river, which is choked by trees carried down into it by the torrents that must occur during the winter or the rainy season. This news was extremely welcome to me on that account, but it served only to show me how little one should rely on the vigilance and thoroughness of a search often entrusted to an officer who thinks only of his speedy return on board when he is charged with a mission that is not to his liking.
Captain Hamelin, back from his excursion, also reported to me that he had found a small freshwater stream at no great distance from where we were anchored, but it was only a small trickle and hardly suitable as a watering place for two ships such as ours. He recognised from the signs he met with that some European ships had stopped there and taken in water, since he saw that several large trees which prevented boats from approaching the banks had been sawn through, and others cut down with an axe.
After consulting together on what remained for us to do, we
agreed to go further into Port du Nord-Ouest and to choose, in preference, the place found by M. Ronsard and marked on the plan we had of this port. Accordingly we unmoored at once, intending to get under way the next day or to warp ourselves in if the wind was calm.
The place found by Captain Hamelin must be the one the English have named, on Arrowsmith's plan, Annas River, a most unsuitable name for so insignificant a stream.
During the night of the first to the second the sky was fairly fine after moonrise, and the cat's-paws that passed from time to time were not strong.
1802-01-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW in gusts, with light rain at intervals. At daybreak the captain left in the longboat to look for a watering place. The two anchors were weighed and one let go in 30 fathoms, mud and shell, Pointe Legrand bearing S 13° W, Pointe Gicquel S 61° W, and Pointe de la Sortie N 45° E. At 9 p.m. the captain came back with the longboat; he had not found a watering place, but he brought back a great quantity of oysters, which were distributed to the crew.

1802-01-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WNW to W in strong gusts. The wind having fallen, the commander gave us orders to warp in. At 10 the large boat came back from her mission to the North River; she found there a very convenient watering place.
1802-01-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, at four in the morning, I again sent off Citizen Ronsard to make a more exact survey of the place he had told me of. As he had sounded the channel at various points and there were several banks in it that dry a good way out at low water, he was ordered to wait until the tide had gone out and then set up beacons on them, so that our launches should not run aground on their way there.
As soon as the boat had left, the wind being completely calm, I had a warp of five to six hundred fathoms laid out, and we hove ourselves along it after weighing our bower anchor. During this work we had a few short-lived cat's-paws, but our hawsers held fast.
The astronomers had been put ashore at four in the morning, and I hoped that they would easily be able to observe the passage of Jupiter over the sun, the weather being fine at the hour when it was to take place.
Having hove ourselves up to the length of our warp, we let go a bower anchor in order to lay out another. But the winds having shifted to the north-east, we at once took advantage of them to make sail, and by means of our fore and aft staysails we entered this port, though not as far as I should have wished, since the calm and the ebb that had just set in obliged us to anchor where we were, which was a good league from the place we had just left.
The Naturaliste, which was not under way when the wind came to us, was obliged to lay out a second warp; but towards five in the evening, a second cat's-paw from the north-east making itself felt, she had it taken up by her launch and made use of her sails. As it lasted longer than the one we had had towards two in the afternoon, she went nearly half a league further in than we did.
Captain Hamelin having come on board in the evening, we agreed to send out our two longboats the next morning on an excursion to make the survey of which I shall give the details in tomorrow's entry.
On his return Citizen Ronsard informed me that he had beaconed the whole channel at low water, but that he had noticed the tide had risen much less than the day before. It appeared, from what he told me, that the launches would not be able to float at low water at the mouth of the river, although there were five to six feet of water at the place where they could land. I put off until the next day ascertaining for myself how matters stood, intending to go ashore as soon as the boats I meant to send out on an excursion of eight or ten days had left. Citizen Ronsard brought back a pelican of great beauty in the length of its bill and the arrangement of its plumage. Its size seemed to us greater than that of those known to us, and we did not doubt that it would be a superb specimen for the natural history cabinet.
When the astronomers returned, I learned with regret that they had not been able to observe the eclipse,
which had made me stay two days at the anchorage I had just left. They attributed the cause not to the weather, since the sun was very clear, but to their telescopes, which they did not find powerful enough. It is a fine opportunity missed for the accuracy of the lunar tables.
The night of the second to the third passed without incident. We distinctly saw several fires round about us, and we hoped that the next day it might perhaps be possible to communicate with the natives.
On the excursion Captain Hamelin had made, he had met two of them crossing in their wretched canoe from the large island to Île d'Entrecasteaux [Bruny Island]. As soon as they were ashore they drew the canoe up into the wood and, according to their custom, set fire all along the shore where they passed. This was no doubt for fear that the path they had taken might be seen in the grass.
1802-01-22.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNE. By the commander's order we warped into the head of the port. At 5.30 p.m. we got under way with a light breeze from NE and stood into the port. At 6.15 we anchored in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom [corner torn], Pointe Gicquel bearing S 22° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 84° E.

At 10 a.m. I came in from my errand; before coming alongside, the captain ordered me to go and report my mission to the commander. I informed him that I had found a very convenient watering place; he told me that for the present it was of no use to us, because Citizen Ronsard had found a river at the head of the port where we should water. I came back aboard and gave him the following report:

By your orders I left the ship on the 30th Nivôse [20 January 1802] at 6 a.m. in the large boat, armed and provisioned for four days. I was to go up the North River to see what facility there might be for watering the corvettes, and to be back aboard on the morning of the 2nd Pluviôse [22 January 1802]. The weather was fine enough and the wind a fresh breeze from the north; I was obliged to beat at the river's mouth. The weather turned squally and the wind blew hard in gusts from the north with rain. I was reduced to carrying only the foresail and mainsail, both reefed; yet by taking advantage of the wind's small shifts (and probably helped by the tide) I reached by nightfall the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream (on the left bank at the foot of the plateau). I made the boat fast in a little creek to starboard and went with three armed men towards the stream, where I found very good water. The tide was then low; I came back to the boat, and having embarked, I went in with the first of the flood to the head of the cove, hugging the land to starboard close enough to touch the oars on shore, finding 3 fathoms, 2½, 2, 1½ and 1 fathom, where I landed 200 paces from the watering place, afloat; and there I had my breakers filled, and a tierce I had with me. I sounded the cove: I had 5 fathoms in the middle and on the starboard side; the port side is low and muddy. This watering place is very convenient; there is anchorage for the corvettes abreast of the cove in 10 and 15 fathoms, and even in the cove in 5 fathoms. The longboats can come alongside the bank at low water and load there. The only labour would be to roll the casks from the watering place to the boats, over 200 paces of dry, level ground.

I passed the night in this cove, and on the 1st Pluviôse [21 January 1802] at daybreak I left it to go up the river. I had to beat the whole way with a fresh breeze. Having got about 3 miles beyond the place where D'Entrecasteaux's boats had been, and having found from that point 5 fathoms down to 2½, I met a very violent current at a point which hid the river's course from me. Yet the tide was low, for several branches partly sunk in the mud, with shells on them, showed how far the tide rose. I rowed in the middle of the river, along the right bank, along the left bank, without being able to stem the current. I landed on the left bank near the point I had not been able to double, and after walking some time along the river I saw that beyond the point it ran NW and then appeared to divide into two arms, one running N and the other WSW. However much I wished to find the river's source, I thought I ought to stop my survey there: you had fixed the 2nd for my return, and besides my mission was fulfilled, since I had found a watering place. I went down the river and passed the night at the same place as the night before (the Watering Cove). I shot several swans there, and sounded the cove more carefully. At daybreak I left it and reached the ship at 10 a.m. Going down the river I sounded it and found from 10 to 20 fathoms.

On the strength of the report I had made to him, the commander sent off his large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to go up the river. He was favoured by the wind, which he had aft the whole way; the first evening he slept 3 miles above the place where I had been stopped, and met no violent current. He examined the arms I had seen: the WSW one was the river's course, the other only a very large inlet. He went up the river as far as it was navigable by boat and on foot, about 9 miles, without seeing its source.

During our stay in the North West Port the sick were put ashore every fine day; they were given 2 armed men to guard them, and these two men cut firewood for us.

1802-01-23.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from N to NW and NE. At 5.30, being at the end of the warp and the breeze freshening, we got under way under fore-and-aft sails and let go the anchor in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 22° E; Cape de la Sortie E 6° N. We moored east and west.
1802-01-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth (sic) (third), in the morning, the weather being very fine and the winds almost calm, I dispatched my longboat, giving command of it to Citizen Freycinet, lieutenant de vaisseau, with the following instructions:
"Port du Nord-Ouest [North West Bay], Canal d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel],
"The Commander &c., to Citizen Freycinet, lieutenant de vaisseau
"Tomorrow, at daybreak, you will take command of the longboat and go to "survey the Rivière du Nord [Derwent River] in circumstantial detail.
"According to the report made to me, this river, which divides into two branches at no great distance from "the place where the boats of the Recherche and the Espérance stopped, deserves to be "seriously examined, and it is for this reason that I entrust this work to you. You will accordingly "ascend it as far as it is possible to advance, and if, as Midshipman "Le Breton, who was sent there by Captain Hamelin, declares to me, it divides into two branches, you will choose the one "that appears to you the more advantageous or the more navigable, and you will even examine both of them if "you can manage it.
"You will doubtless find a strong current at the place where the division occurs that has been "reported to me and of which I have just spoken to you, but this must not make you abandon this "survey unless want of water obliges you to. This current, which is rapid in the middle, will "surely be much less so along one of the two banks.
"You will take with you Citizen Péron and a midshipman of your own choosing. You "will take provisions for your men for eight to ten days, and a studding sail to make a tent for yourself if you should "have occasion to stay ashore or in any part of the coast.
"Although the boat of the Naturaliste did not communicate with any of the natives, perhaps you will be "more fortunate, and in that hope you must provide yourself with some trifles to make them presents. I "shall not repeat what I have already told you about the manner in which you are to conduct yourself towards "them, being persuaded that you have not forgotten it". Signed N. B.
After this boat had left, I invited Captain Hamelin to come on board, and when he had arrived I agreed with him that his boat should make a somewhat longer excursion and that he should send it, well manned, to examine Tasman's Frederick Hendrick Bay and to see whether, in the communication it appears to have with that of Marion, there was a passage practicable for our corvettes. Had Citizen Boulanger been further advanced in his convalescence, I should have asked him to make this excursion, but not being
yet strong enough, Citizen Faure, engineer of the Géographe, went alone. The mineralogist Bailly, who was invited to be of this party, preferred to stay behind, finding it too long or too arduous.
The Naturaliste's boat left at six in the morning. Ours had shoved off at four. In this way I hope they will not fall in with each other, which will be no bad thing, for their meeting could only hinder or delay the mission each has to accomplish, as had already happened.
Our launches had likewise been dispatched early in the morning to carry our casks ashore and fill them. And on leaving the ship at eight o'clock in my small boat, I expected to find everyone at work when I arrived. But in this I was much mistaken, for having doubled a point that hid her from view, I found her busy chasing swans instead of being at the place to which she had been ordered. It was not without annoyance that I watched what she was about, the more so since she no longer had time to arrive with the high tide as I had calculated. Citizen FreyciRansonet, the ensign to whom I had given the command of her, did not suppose, no doubt, that I was watching him so closely. However that may be, I went straight ashore to the appointed place, and I had plenty of time to examine the river and its surroundings before she arrived. As the tide had already fallen a good deal, she could not get through the channel I had had beaconed; she grounded, but not for long, for she floated off again, the bottom being very soft mud, and reached the larboard shore, where Captain Hamelin's launch lay. When she had let go her grapnel, I went aboard her and gave orders that all the casks be made into a raft and hauled onto a small island lying opposite the mouth of the river, so that they could be filled at low tide. M. Ransonnet was very surprised to see me, and no doubt far from pleased at what I said to him about his conduct in this expedition. Captain Hamelin gave the same order to his men, and within an hour all our casks were ready to be filled as soon as the moment was favourable.
The small island I have just mentioned seemed to me very suitable for setting up our observatory, and I decided that the next day all our instruments should be taken over to it, that is to say those we might need.
When I examined the country bordering the stream, we found that the low ground surrounding it is a fairly extensive plain intersected by various channels into which the sea rises at every tide, the water in them being as salt as that in the middle of the bay. This plain, if cultivated after the waters had been drained off, would be very fertile, for the soil is excellent. That of the hills bordering it, at about a cannon-shot's distance, is equally good, and this place seemed to me convenient for a settlement.
On the excursion we made into the interior of the country, we followed for nearly four leagues the freshwater stream where we are to take in our water. Its bed is very winding and of a fairly considerable width. It appeared to us to have its source on the Montagne du Plateau [Mount Wellington]. On this excursion we saw a kangaroo of the large species, and Citizen fired a ball at it at a good distance but did it no harm. As he had seen it close to, he assured us that it was the size of a mill. Land birds seemed to us very scarce; we saw only a few parakeets and a partridge or quail of ordinary size. We were more fortunate in the way of botanising: the gardener gathered several plants for planting, and I a fairly considerable number for the herbarium.
This place was formerly inhabited by a family of the natives, and we came upon eight of their ajoupas, which had not been abandoned long, for the eucalyptus bark of which they are made was still fresh. In them we found a cord of tree-bark fibre and a poor vessel of very hard wood which in all likelihood serves them for drinking. Almost all the large trees we saw were badly damaged by fire, and most of them
ready to fall at the slightest north-westerly squall that may blow.
On returning to our boats I killed a snake about two feet long. It did not seem to me to have anything remarkable about it. The markings on its skin were ash-grey, flecked with white spots, and the underside was all white. It made no movement that could lead me to suspect it was dangerous. When I killed it, half its body was in a hole and it was trying to get entirely inside. When I tried to pull it out after it was dead, it broke in two.
At three o'clock we re-embarked to return on board, leaving our launches busy taking in water. We had the winds southerly and very light, and the flood against us, which delayed us a great deal. I followed the whole of the starboard shore and saw nothing out of the ordinary.
The night of the third to the fourth passed in a calm and was fairly fine; one of our boats, which had gone line-fishing, saw several natives on the seashore at no great distance, also fishing by torchlight.
1802-01-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: The weather was fine and the wind a light breeze from N to NW. At 6 a.m. the large boat, with 15 days' provisions, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey the North Bay and the passage marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island. At 7 our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went to water at the head of the port. We moored east and west with a kedge anchor. Draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 2 inches, difference 0 feet 9 inches. The observatory was set up on a small islet at the head of the port, at the mouth of the river.

1802-01-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds east, variable to SE, almost calm. During the night a very thick fog kept us from making out the coast; during the night the winds went right round the compass and varied from [one word illegible] WNW, W and WSW, a strong breeze. Citizen Saint-Cricq embarked in the dinghy with his instruments to go to the observatory set up at the head of the North West Port.
1802-01-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the forenoon, we had so strong a breeze from west-south-west to west that we were set adrift three or four times by the force of the gusts. We could not even hold with two anchors and were forced to put out a third to bring ourselves up. This blow lasted until three in the afternoon, the weather cloudy and fine, after which calm set in and lasted all night.
Nothing happened on board this day that deserves any particular Remarks. Only, the observatory was set up ashore and the instruments were carried there.
Our launch, which I expected on the evening tide, did not come, no doubt through the negligence of the officer commanding her, who was perhaps out shooting at the moment when he should have left, as he was at the moment when he should have arrived.
On board, the men were busy putting the inside of the ship in order and inspecting our sails, some of which were found to be damaged, even though they were stowed away and hung up in their covers. Some leaks had opened through the seams of the deck, which would not have been noticed so soon but for this inspection.
The boat that went fishing from four in the afternoon until nine in the evening brought back enough fish to give some to the whole crew. The largest were of the ray and dogfish kinds, the others plaice, perch and a kind of mullet which, from experience, we judged the best of all.
1802-01-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SW in gusts; it fell away at nightfall.

1802-01-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze in gusts from WSW, south, SW and W. At 7.30 a working party of 6 men was sent ashore to stay there and fill the casks.
1802-01-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, towards five in the morning, we at last saw our launches returning; perhaps they would still be ashore had they had provisions, for I had had only two days' worth put aboard them. They brought fifteen or eighteen casks, which were at once emptied into our stowage casks. I sent it off again towards eight o'clock under the command of Citizen Ronsard, who had been charged with beaconing the narrow and difficult channel leading to the river, or rather to the stream, and who even claimed he could take the launches right up to its mouth at the sea.
I likewise embarked in my small boat to go to the observatory and see how they had established themselves there. I saw with regret, and even with displeasure, that this place was about to become the tavern of the two ships and a continual resort from the ships, for five boats came there while I was present, or at least the people they carried, as well as those who manned them. On an island no more than twenty-five to thirty feet long by fifteen at its greatest breadth, there were seven or eight different cooking fires, and I was told that the day before they had narrowly missed
being all burnt there, together with the tents and the instruments, because the various fires, spreading from one cooking place to the next, had set the grass alight. Fortunately the wind was off the land, for otherwise all would have been lost.
Everything I saw made me leave in great haste a place that will serve only to delay our operations and prolong our stay in this roadstead.
Citizen Depuche, whom until that time I had cared for and treated as though he belonged to me, left the ship (with) bag and baggage to go and settle ashore. The surgeon informed me of the remonstrances he had made to him to dissuade him from so ill-considered and thoughtless a step, but all was in vain, and he grew so obstinate as to lose his temper with the surgeon as with those who tried to make him see the unfortunate consequences that might result from this folly, his health not being firmly enough restored for him to follow the whims of his head.
Fear of seeing me disapprove of his conduct no doubt prevented him from telling me of his resolution, for he left without saying anything to me.
While I remained ashore, I made a long excursion with the surgeon and the gardener along the banks of the river and into the interior of the country. We saw very little that was new and brought back little in the way of plants, seeds or objects of natural history, this part of the coast not being very rich in variety of species.
Both going and returning on board, we saw no swan or pelican, which I attributed to the great number of musket shots that had been fired over the last three days. The men whose duty was to protect the launches in case of need, imitating the conduct of the officer who commanded them, scattered into the woods as soon as they got ashore and came back only when driven by hunger or when they had no more ammunition. As I witnessed what happened on the launch's second trip, I decided that in future I would no longer give firearms to the men in her, and would limit their means of defence to a sabre, a course Captain Hamelin has already adopted.
During this day the weather was fine and the breeze light. At night we had a flat calm and a fine sky, the winds or the cool air coming from the north-east quarter.
1802-01-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from W to NW. At 6 a.m. the longboat came in loaded with water. She left again at 7.15 with a working party of 7 men commanded by a midshipman, who are to stay at the watering place to fill the casks, roll them down and raft them, so that the longboat may find them ready and have only to take them in.

1802-01-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind east, a fresh breeze. Calm all the afternoon. From 4 to 10 the breeze got up from NE to ENE, freshening a great deal; at noon it was blowing hard from that quarter.
1802-01-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth our launches did not appear at the turn of the tide, which made me fear that they were still aground, at least mine, for she was in that situation the day before when I embarked to return on board. Citizen Ronsard, having declined to follow the Naturaliste's launch out of fondness for the channel he had beaconed, ran aground in it, whereas the other stayed afloat at the same place they had been able to reach the first time, which is within swivel-gun range of the mouth of the freshwater stream at the sea.
In the course of the morning I had the tubs of living plants that we had collected and planted since entering the channel surrounded. Their number up to that moment was not large, since it amounted to only some forty shrubs. It is certainly not for want of searches and excursions into the interior of the country that it is no higher than the figure I have just given, and it must be attributed only to the small variety to be found there.
One of our boats was also sent out fishing, and her trip was not a lucky one, for she came back at sunset without having caught anything. At the same time we sighted our longboat, absent for three days, returning from the mission I had entrusted to Citizen Freycinet. I was much surprised to see her return so soon, and I began to fear that he had carried it out badly. I make no mention here of what Citizen Freycinet reported to me, since
I shall give in writing the report he is engaged in making to me of what he saw and met with. Citizen Péron, who accompanied him, was not fortunate in his search for objects of natural history and brought back so little that it is not worth speaking of.
From ten in the morning until sunset the winds were from east to north-east in gusts and a strong breeze, the sky fine though very hazy and laden with vapours. At night we had calm and fine weather. Our watering launches not having appeared, we hoped they would come during the night, the more so since it had been remarked that the tide rose much higher at this period than at any other.
1802-01-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE to ENE. At 9 p.m. a musket shot was thought to have been heard ashore to the NE; the yawl was at once sent away armed, and found no one.

1802-01-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A strong breeze from ENE to NNE. The longboat went watering.
1802-01-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, at daybreak, we saw our launches returning on board with their cargo. The wind was completely calm and the ebb helped their return. At half past six they were alongside and were unloaded at once. My intention was that they should leave again immediately. But just as they were about to shove off, so strong a gust came upon us from north to north-north-west that they had to be held back, and they could not set out until towards eight o'clock.
During the forenoon the sky was very overcast and misty. We saw the sun only at very short intervals, and the clouds were so low and so thick that there was every appearance that we were going to have some strong squalls. I was all the more vexed that our launches had left because the barometer, by its sudden fall, confirmed the state of the atmosphere. Both were obliged to put in for shelter because of the force of the wind. Mine clumsily made for the starboard shore, where she was not sheltered from the winds, which had gone round to the north-west, whereas the Naturaliste's came and took shelter on the larboard shore.
Nevertheless, towards noon, although it was still blowing in strong gusts, the sky grew clearer and seemed about to turn fine. We saw our boats get under way to go to the head of the port, where they would be sheltered for the night should the weather turn bad again.
During the forenoon we also cleared our cables, which had taken a turn round each other with the shifting of the wind, so as to have them ready to give a longer scope if the occasion required; the top-ropes of the topmasts were also rove so as to be quite ready to strike them if we were forced to.
After noon the winds shifted to the west; it continued to blow a strong breeze, but it was, however, much less strong than it had been in the morning. The carpenters were sent ashore to cut trees suitable for making us planks, of which we were beginning to be in very great need. The petty officers also asked for one of the small boats to go fishing. It was granted them, in the belief I hold that we shall have calm during the night and even from sunset, as has almost always happened to us since we have been in this port.
From sunset until ten o'clock it continued to blow in strong gusts, but at that time calm followed, and we had very fine weather for the rest of the night.
The boat I had sent fishing took advantage of it to return on board. A fair quantity of fish had been caught.
1802-01-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 4.15 a.m. the longboat came in. She weighed the kedge anchor and carried it SW of the bower, so that we are now moored NE and SW. Overcast weather; the breeze freshened and blew strong in gusts from NW to W. At 6.30 (on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802]) the mooring hawser parted; we veered cable to 150 fathoms. The longboat weighed the kedge anchor; not being able to get the end of the hawser, which was foul of the flukes of the bower anchor, we unbent it and put a buoy on the end. The longboat left for the watering place. At 9 a second anchor was let go.

1802-01-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from WNW to NW in heavy gusts. It fell away about four o'clock. The longboat came aboard with her load of water. She left again at once for the watering place.
1802-01-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, at four in the morning, I was rather surprised to learn that our launch had returned on board with her full load of water. The diligence Citizen Bonnefoy showed on this occasion served only to demonstrate to me that those who, until then, had been charged with this duty had been more occupied with their pleasure than with their duty, and I did not fail to let them know it by pointing out to them the difference that resulted.
If there was ever an occasion to excuse the late return of the launch, it was, no doubt, the one in which Citizen Bonnefoy found himself, for the strong wind and even the bad weather had lasted all day and part of the night. Nevertheless, in four hours of calm he did what the others had not been able to do in forty-eight hours of fine weather.
As soon as she was unloaded, she left again under the command of the first-class midshipman Maurouard.
The weather was fine in the morning, and at sunrise the winds shifted to the north-west, a light breeze. I went ashore with our carpenters to examine the trees they were to have felled the day before and which I intended for making us planks, of which, as I have already remarked, we were beginning to be in great need.
Scarcely had we arrived when it began to blow with the utmost violence from the west to west-north-west quarter. As, when I left, no officer was up, although it was past seven o'clock, I gave the quartermaster of the watch the orders necessary for the safety of the ship should the weather turn bad.
During the morning I inspected the trees that had been felled the day before. They were handsome on the outside and of fine appearance, but all had their heart damaged. Several more were cut which, having no defect visible to the eye, seemed to me likely to be sounder. But I was mistaken, for they were even more rotten than those the carpenters had chosen. As it had become useless to fell any more, we stopped there, confining ourselves to taking those that were best and most suited to the use we intended to make of them. After sawing them into lengths of ten to twelve feet, we got them down to the water's edge by rolling them from the top of the hill, which was very steep. Several, however, became lodged in holes from which we had considerable (trouble) getting them out.
At three in the afternoon we came back down to the shore to return on board, but the breeze was so strong that we had to wait wait (sic) for a lull, which came towards four o'clock and of which we took advantage at once, for the sky looked very threatening for the night. We had intended to bring back some of our trees in tow, but we had to give it up for fear of being set adrift. Before embarking we had noticed that it had blown no less on board than ashore, since the lower yards had been lowered and the topgallant masts sent down. Nevertheless, the ship did not appear to us to have dragged her anchors.
At five o'clock I was back on board, well soaked by the seas that the roughness of the water had sent into our boat. It was high time to arrive, for scarcely had we got there when it blew with the utmost violence. I brought back from this excursion some flowering plants that no one had yet found and several kinds of seeds, among which there are some of indigo, which seemed singular to us in such a latitude; moreover, this plant is fairly common here.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth the winds were westerly, in puffs and strong gusts, but less violent than during the day.
1802-01-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NW. At 3.30 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once. A little rain.

1802-01-29.journal_anonyme: Rainy weather, the sea smooth, a strong breeze in [one word illegible] puffs from NW, WSW, WNW and W. The longboat came in with her load of water. She was sent off again at once.
1802-01-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth our launch arrived on board at the same hour as she had done the day before. But she did not bring back, as usual, her full load.
The midshipman commanding her reported to me that the tide having risen extremely high that day, the water had been found to be of poor quality, and that he had preferred to return on board with the tide rather than wait until it was low to complete it.
She went back for the same purpose as soon as she was unloaded. By the same occasion I received a letter from the astronomer Bernier, who complained that he and his companions had no provisions, although he had several times asked those who had gone ashore and come back on board to send them some. I sent his letter to the officer in charge of the mess so that this inconvenience might be remedied.
Shortly after the launch had left, the wind increased considerably and we had squalls almost as strong as the day before. She beat to windward for a long time with little success, but at last, having reached the larboard shore, she decided to ship her oars and made her way there by rowing. The Naturaliste's did just the same
During the forenoon the gusts were often accompanied by rain, and at times we had it quite heavily. Nevertheless, I sent the small boat to haul the seine, having nothing better to do and the strong wind not allowing us to go and fetch our lengths of spars.
In the afternoon the weather was more agreeable than it had been in the morning, and the breeze abated a good deal towards three o'clock. At six our boat returned from fishing. The second boatswain, to whom I had given the command of her, reported to me that they had had a meeting with the natives, who, seven in number, had gathered round them. At the moment they became aware of them, they were dining in the shelter of a rock, and it was by bursts of laughter that the natives announced their presence, long before they were seen or their arrival suspected. All were armed with a spear, and one of them carried a fairly (large) bundle of them, in which, according to the estimate made, judging by their usual thickness, there might have been about a hundred. As our men were not armed nor in a state of defence, they thought at first of re-embarking so as to avoid any surprise; but as the natives had stopped at some distance from them to watch their movements, one of our fishermen, who had two bottles, in one of which there was still a little rum, showed them to them, making signs to induce them to come and take them. At once they laid down their weapons, which they entrusted to the keeping of the one who was already carrying the bundle I have just mentioned, and came up to them cheerfully, showing by gestures and cries of joy that they had no ill intentions.
Our fishermen, seeing them so happily disposed, all went back to the place where they had lit their fire, and the natives followed them there without the least mistrust. They then went on with their meal, which consisted of fish they had caught and what, by way of precaution, they had brought from the ship. The natives, who had mingled with them, were offered a share of what remained, but they would take nothing, nor even taste the liquor left in the bottles; they showed, however, a great desire to have them. They were duly given them, with a little rum, which they made no use of and even poured out on the ground, delighted to possess the vessels.
After this first present, the familiarity between them and our men became so great, and confidence was so well established on both sides, that they all began to dance together. But this exercise tiring them too much or not amusing them greatly, they
soon grew weary of it and preferred to occupy themselves with things more to their taste. Everyone having sat down again, their attention fixed on the pockets and the metal buttons on some of our men's waistcoats. Several did not wait to be asked to search in them for whatever might suit them, while others made known by unmistakable signs the pleasure the pleasure (sic) they would have in receiving buttons. Several were cut off and distributed to them, and they showed great satisfaction at it.
After about two hours spent together, our men thought of re-embarking to look for a more convenient place for fishing, and they parted the best friends in the world. The embarkation was in no way disturbed, and the natives continued to give them great signs of joy and contentment. No women or children showed themselves during this meeting, but as a fairly thick smoke was seen two-thirds of the way up the hill at the foot of which they were, it was not doubted that they were in that place.
The boat was at that time in the last cove at the northern end of the island of Bruny d'Entrecasteaux [Bruny Island], and our men even thought they recognised among the seven natives who came and mingled with them two of those with whom we had communicated during our stay at the Grande Anse.
The fishing, without being very plentiful, was enough to give some to everyone. The fish caught were, with the exception of one, of the same kinds as those I have already spoken of. The strange and extraordinary shape of this last may be seen in the journal containing the objects of curiosity and natural history.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth it blew in strong gusts accompanied by heavy rain which, in general, was of short duration.
1802-01-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW. At 4 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at 6. The carpenters went to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-01-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, blowing hard in heavy gusts from W to WSW and WNW. In the forenoon they drew round to SE and SSE, almost calm. We were busy stowing the sheet anchor.
1802-01-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, in the morning, our longboat not having returned as usual, I took advantage of the calm then prevailing to send for the plank trees we had felled, together with the spars for our own use.
I had prepared, the day before, the answer I was making to Citizen Bernier to the letter he had addressed to me, of which I here enclose the copy:
"The Commander &c.
"To Citizen Bernier, astronomer,
"It was not possible for me, citizen, to take advantage of the departure of the longboat yesterday to answer the "letter which you did me the honour of writing to me on the seventh of this month. Not that it did not "reach me in time, but those who could give me information on its contents having, "according to the custom on board, risen only between eight and nine o'clock in the morning, I was afraid of interrupting the sleep, "free of care and anxiety, which they were enjoying, although the weather and the circumstances were little "suited to warrant it.
"However that may be, from the information I have obtained, it appears that, with the exception "of oil, and perhaps also of vinegar, you ought to have wanted for nothing. Yet your letter "tells me quite the contrary, since you appear to be in want of everything. I therefore beg you, in future, to "let me know what you need so that I may have it sent to you. I only recommend you "not to wait until the last moment to have the list of it sent to me the list.
"No one has been able to tell me what you mean by ordinary shipboard rations, and you may, "moreover, rest assured that no one whatever has extraordinary ones, not even of water, given the difficulty "of obtaining it as easily as I should have wished,
"obliged to tell M. de St Criq that I earnestly beg him, when he kills any rare and valuable "birds, to send them to us. We shall keep only the plumage and the wing tips. The "remainder, that is to say the body, will be scrupulously delivered to whatever destination he may have named. We do "indeed have a wood pigeon like the one he sent yesterday on board the Naturaliste. And as it is a "bird as rare as it is valuable for natural history, it would have been of the utmost importance to preserve part "of its skin in order to repair the one of the same kind which we have had the good fortune to procure.
"My regards to all those who are with you". Signed N. B".
At nine o'clock our large boat returned with the trees and spars she had gone to fetch. While they were being taken on board, M.
