Hamelin came aboard, and shortly afterwards I set off in his boat to go (ourselves) to the place where the natives whom our people had seen the day before were staying. The care they had taken to keep several fires burning all night left us in no doubt that they were in that spot. I took with me the draughtsman and the surgeon.
Towards ten o'clock we saw a canoe with four or five men in it, who set out from the north point of Île d'Entrecasteaux to cross to that of Pierson. They stood up to paddle and seemed to us to go very fast, for we soon lost sight of them. Shortly afterwards we reached the shore. Seven of the natives, among whom was a child of twelve to fifteen years, showed themselves on the slope of the hill facing our landing place. They were unarmed, but very watchful of all our movements. As we drew near them, we made them several signs of friendship to induce them to wait for us, for they kept moving on ahead as we approached. It seemed to us rather surprising to see them so distrustful, whereas the day before they had not made the slightest difficulty about mingling with our people.
As I had provided myself with a few presents, I dangled before their eyes one or two strings of glass beads, which caught their attention. One of them having made me a sign to give them to him, I made him one to come and take them. Before making up his mind to do so, he consulted the others, who, to all appearance, approved his resolution, and he came forward with an air of assurance which proved to us that he was without distrust, although he had a stone in his hand. As soon as we had joined him, we loaded him with caresses which entirely reassured him, and I gave him some glass beads, which he examined with pleasure. His companions, having witnessed what had just taken place, were not long in coming up and were just as well received. We then had six of them with us, but the youngest always kept apart and nothing could tempt him. After we had walked about together, they addressed several speeches to us, accompanied by gestures, and we could not doubt that they looked on us with no pleasure, since they were inviting us to re-embark. Among the various words they uttered, that of kaoué kaoué was repeated often, very often, and even in a tone of command. In the language of the negroes of Mozambique, on the coast of Africa, it means go away, but I cannot say whether it has the same meaning among those of Van Diemen's Land.
However that may be, we paid little heed to their kaoué and their signs, and we went on into the interior of the country to botanise. They followed us for some time, but as we were making towards a spot from which rose a fairly thick smoke, they raised such an uproar that we judged it must be the place where their women and children were staying
whom they did not want us to approach. As I happened to be furthest ahead of all, the native who was near us, unarmed, turned me about, showing me plainly that we must not go that way. As I wished to preserve the good understanding that reigned between us, I changed direction, telling the others to do likewise, and they appeared very well pleased at this. Then they left us and seemed to make for our boat, which lay some distance from the shore and which they could not reach by wading.
During the excursion we made through the woods we we (sic) found little in the way of plants, and I brought back only one new species of the heath class and some indigo seed. We saw only a single kangaroo of the small species and very few birds. Most of the trees were burnt, as everywhere else, and the ground was sandier than any we had met with until then.
At about two o'clock, judging by the height of the sun, we retraced our steps to return on board. As we drew near the shore, we met three of the natives to whom we had given presents in the morning. It appeared to us that they had followed us at a fair distance, and we were surprised to see them armed with two or three spears apiece. Nevertheless, we approached them, going forward to meet them. Their kaoué began again as we advanced towards them, and they kept all the while at a fair distance. Weary of being unable to come up with them, we decided to sit down, all of us, on a tree lying across our path, and wait to see what course they would take. Seeing us in this position, they too halted to look us over, talking among themselves. They were then fifty paces from us. The gestures we made them to come nearer were well understood, and whether to obtain the new objects we were holding out to them or for some other motive, they went and laid down their spears behind some trees and joined us, having only one or two stones in their hands. When we were all together, they made signs to us to put aside my musket, which a seaman seated beside me was holding. For our part, we gave them to understand that they should throw away their stones, which they did at once. Having invited them to sit down, they did not need to be asked twice, and soon they became as familiar as if we had been well accustomed to being together. Everything we had in our hands or about us seemed to take their fancy, and they made an inspection of our pockets, but with our consent. Having left nothing in them after searching the pockets, they went on to our clothes, and to humour them in everything we showed them our chests, about which they seemed very curious. However, they showed astonishment only at that of the surgeon, which, having no hair on it, drew from them loud exclamations and still louder bursts of laughter. Having satisfied themselves on this part, they went on to our legs, and several of us were obliging enough to lend ourselves to this whim of theirs. They would gladly have seen something else, but we did not think it proper to show them. Of the three natives seated beside us, two had on their legs two rather large wounds, still fresh. The third had a dislocation of one of the fingers of the right hand. All three were between forty and forty-five years of age and rather ill-made, especially in the lower part of the body. Their faces, painted with pounded charcoal, over which they had applied the red ochre we had given them, had nothing disagreeable about them. On the contrary, they were well marked and full of character. The forehead, being very prominent, made their eyes appear deeply sunk and even small at a certain distance. The cheekbones were very high, the mouth large, the teeth broad, fine, white and even. The eyes
lively, but the look uneasy and always on the watch. At the slightest movement we made they were on their feet at once, and above all if anyone touched the musket, whose effect they certainly knew and of which they are very much afraid. It seems to me beyond doubt that, in other circumstances, some of them have had have had a sad experience of it.
During the nearly two hours that our interview with these three natives lasted, we had ample time to observe them at our leisure. We pronounced various words to them, which they repeated very distinctly, and I was even surprised at how little trouble it gave them. However, those containing "r" or "s" did not come to them so easily.
Captain Hamelin, wishing to exchange some other things for their spears, put the proposal to them by signs which were well understood, and it was agreed that they would give a spear for a uniform button. The bargain being struck, one of them went to fetch one and handed it over on receiving the agreed price. The other two did likewise and handed theirs over in the same way, taking care not to let go of them until they had been paid in advance. As one of them had brought two, we wished to see whether, by paying him only after receiving the spear, he would consent to give it, but he took good care not to, and even wanted to keep it after being paid for it. But as, according to the custom that had been established, one held (the) spear by one end while handing over the button, he was obliged to let go of it, and this did not seem to please him.
The bargaining being over, the natives kept some distance from us, as if they were afraid we might use against them the weapons they had just sold us. However, seeing that we were making our way back to our boats, they followed us again. Citizen Petit, who had drawn one of them, had the drawing he had made of him snatched from his hand. But, as nimble as the man who had snatched it from him, he took it back, and we went on towards the seashore. We had scarcely got there when the three natives with whom we had been on such good terms, and whom we had loaded with presents, began to pick up stones and soon hurled them at us; several reached our boats, although at a great distance, and happily wounded no one. I was not so fortunate as the others, for a rather large one, striking me at the moment when I was stooping to examine the valve of a shell, wounded me slightly in the hip. I at once levelled my musket at the man who had thrown it, and this movement so frightened him that he ducked down and ran off as fast as his legs would carry him, although he was well out of range of my musket.
Fearing that they might return to the attack at the moment of our embarking, I decided to advance towards them again while everyone was getting into the boats. Captain Hamelin followed me. We saw the natives again at a considerable distance, calling to one another with very loud cries, which were answered from far off. We then went back to embark, convinced that they would soon appear in fairly large numbers. This did in fact happen, for shortly afterwards we saw twelve or fifteen of them show themselves at the water's edge, from which we were far enough away not to be able to make out what they were carrying. They were heading south-west. As the wind was fair, we steered towards them, closing the coast. Then, seeing that we were gaining on them much faster than they were walking, although they had quickened their pace, they split into several bands and went into the woods, where we soon lost sight of them.
On our way back on board, we tried to account for their hostile conduct at the moment of our parting. We could find no cause for it but regret at having exchanged their spears with us, which perhaps they thought they would obtain by this means.
Captain Hamelin dined on board and spent the rest of the evening there. Our longboats did not appear, to our great surprise, which made us fear that the water had not risen enough to float our raft of full casks.
Throughout this day the weather was very fine and the wind light, from the east to south-east. It was the same during the night, which passed in a calm.
1802-01-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from WSW to SE. The carpenters went back to cut wood. The commander and the captain communicated with the Aboriginal people on Bruny Island and handed out trinkets to them; at the moment they were embarking they received a volley of stones, which wounded no one. The commander alone had the misfortune to take one on the back, which did him no harm. It was the same group that had wounded Citizen Maurouard with a spear.

1802-01-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SE to east and SSE. The captain communicated with the Aboriginal people of Bruny Island. The winds drew round to SW, NW, NNE and ENE, a light breeze. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-01-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, in the morning, we still saw no sign of our longboats returning, and I gave orders for a boat to be manned to go and find out the cause of their delay.
As the crews had provisions for one day only, it seemed to me rather hard to explain why they had not come back, even empty.
Several persons on board, always ingenious in tormenting themselves or pestering others, came to share with me their fears for the fate of those on shore, on the ground that they were poorly armed. They would not take the trouble to reflect that there were more than forty people in the same spot, and that by their numbers alone they had no need of arms. So natural an observation could not, however, set their minds at rest, and their fears, on seeing the longboats come in sight, which we sighted towards half past seven, did not cease until they were on board and they had looked over and counted everyone in them. I could not help laughing at so ridiculous a weakness in those who had put themselves forward to make these representations. And I took the opportunity to point out to them all the danger to which they exposed themselves by using up on shooting parties the ammunition I gave them for their own defence, and which their wastefulness had led me to withdraw.
Something far more disagreeable to me than all I had been told about the fate of the men employed in watering came to crown the ill humour into which the delay of our longboats had put me. This was the quality of the water that had been brought, which had to be thrown into the sea. The coxswain of the longboat declared to me that the fault lay with Midshipman Le Brun, who was in command of that boat, in that he had not been willing to wait until the tide was low enough to have the casks filled. In proof of what he said, he had me taste a barrel of water drawn an hour and a half after our casks were filled, which turned out to be very good. The result of this conduct is that we have just lost two days for nothing. The only excuse the midshipman gave me was that the Naturaliste, in whose longboat there was an officer, had done just the same, and that he had regulated his conduct by hers. I think, from this, that had that officer taken it into his head to set fire to his longboat, he would have done just the same in imitation of him.
What had just happened had also occurred on the previous trip, so that, to see whether matters would go better by entrusting the longboat to the coxswain alone, I decided to send him by himself as soon as we had examined our cables, which it was indispensable to weigh for fear that the anchors, all three of which lay ahead, might damage our cables as we swung. During the morning we were busy with this work, which was not finished until one o'clock in the afternoon.
Towards three o'clock the longboat left for her destination, and I gave the coxswain in command of her such orders as I judged proper for him to carry out his errand well, flattering his self-esteem, and by this means I hope we shall not be obliged to throw away the water he sends us.
Having little to do on board, I sent the small boat out to fish with lines
with seven men. This method had served us fairly well whenever it had been tried. Besides, the weather was very fine and suited to procuring us something. As the stretch of coast they had chosen as the best was in the very place where we had been attacked with stones the day before, and several columns of smoke told us of the presence of the natives, they were expressly forbidden to land anywhere, and ordered to return on board before nine o'clock.
They did in fact return at that time, and our fishermen told us that they had seen a great number of natives, whom they reckoned at forty persons, including the women and children. The latter were fairly numerous. All of them, having come down to the seashore opposite the boat, never stopped inviting our people by signs to come ashore, and having failed in this, they began to dance and to play all manner of antics. From the boat an empty bottle was shown to them; it was known that this vessel pleased them greatly, from the value they had set on those given them previously. They invited our people by very expressive signs to give it to them, which they did by throwing it into the water a short distance from the boat. One of the women of the band, and according to the fishermen not the oldest, at once stripped off the kangaroo skin that covered her back and, having started to swim, came and took it, with great demonstrations of joy when she was back on the shore. The dancing and the invitations to our people to come and join in began again, but they did not go. On leaving for the ship, they gave them to understand that they would come back the next day, and they seemed very well pleased at this.
Throughout the day the weather was very fine and the winds from the east to south-east, a light breeze. At sunset they shifted to the west, where they remained all night, during which there were a few strong gusts, but of short duration.
1802-01-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNE, S and WSW. The carpenters went to cut wood. At 7 the longboat came in from the watering place and went back there at 11.

1802-02-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the winds very light from ENE, east, NW and SW. At noon squally weather and the winds a strong breeze from SW to NW. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-02-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, in the morning, the sky was very fine, though with winds variable from west to west-south-west, which was not usual. I sent word to Captain Hamelin to send me one of his boats with five or six men, and that I would furnish as many, to go fishing with the seine.
Meanwhile our longboats arrived with their full load of good water. Not only did they make greater despatch than usual, but the water they brought us was of the best possible quality, which confirmed me in the opinion that it was useless to put in them any of those who, by their duty, ought to have been present.
At nine o'clock we left the ship for the fishing, as I wished to see for myself how the natives would behave, especially after the report that had been made to me the day before. At our departure the weather was very fine and the breeze from the west not strong. On our arrival on shore we met no one. But we had scarcely had time to make one haul of the seine when the natives appeared, with loud exclamations that showed their pleasure at seeing us. There were sixteen of them, but only four men. The rest consisted of two women and children of various ages; the oldest did not appear to be more than twelve and the youngest five, except for an infant at the breast of about three months.
The men did not need to be asked twice to come to us. But the children were not so trusting at first. None had either weapons or stones in their hands. I gave each of them some large glass beads, which seemed to give them great pleasure. Then, when I gave them to understand that I wished to give (some) to the children as well, they called them and they came up to us, though not without fear. One of the youngest, who had not dared to follow the others, was called several times in vain by his father, who therefore decided to go and fetch him, and he brought him
to us almost by force. We soon reassured him, as well as his companions, with our caresses accompanied by small presents, so that at the end of half an hour they were as much at home with us as if we had been old acquaintances.
As I wished to have portraits of the women and of some of the children, I told them to sit down, which they did most obligingly. But as the men were preparing to haul in the seine, it was no longer possible to keep them from running to it, whether because of the novelty to them of this way of fishing or for some other reason that I cannot explain.
The joy of the children, and even of the grown men, knew no bounds when they saw the fish caught in the seine. Their exclamations and capers showed us plainly how pleased they were. We offered to share our catch with them, but they would accept nothing, giving us to understand that they did not eat fish, but only shellfish and crustaceans.
The seine was laid out for the third time, and while the boat carried it offshore to give it the necessary sweep, we went and sat down again at the foot of the slope of the mountain facing which we found ourselves. The natives followed us there, and we all sat down together on the grass. I always had beside me two men who watched all my movements, because I was the only one with a firearm. If I happened to shift it from right to right left, their uneasiness showed at once, and one had only to move it to see how much they dread the effect of a musket.
The children, growing more and more familiar, played with our people with the best grace in the world. They had a most engaging gaiety. Their faces too were very pleasing, not being disfigured by dirt or by the black and red colours which the men and women use to adorn themselves. Our people tried running races with them, turning somersaults and various other games, which greatly amused the natives. We took advantage of this moment of merriment to finish the drawings that had been sketched at the time of their arrival.
When the seine was hauled in, they all ran to it as on the first occasion, and above all the children, who hauled heartily on the ropes, imitating and repeating very intelligibly everything our people said. I was truly astonished that children who at first had seemed so fearful and so timid should have been tamed in so short a time to the point they had reached. When our people would not dance, play or run with them, they plagued them until they had done what they wished. Another circumstance, no less extraordinary and not easy to explain, is that the men who were with us were the same who, a day earlier, had assailed us with stones at the moment of our departure. They recognised us perfectly, giving us to understand that they had seen us before. Yet they were in our midst and at our mercy. Someone wished to remind them of what they had done to us on that occasion, but I opposed it, so that they should not believe we bore them any resentment.
The fishing we did during our stay on shore was not plentiful, and we caught little more than was needed for one day's consumption on board each vessel. When it was finished, preparations were made to cook in the kettle for our men's dinner. As soon as it was ready and the rations had been served out, we invited the natives to share it, but none would take anything, and they seemed much astonished to see fish being eaten.
We were expecting at any moment three of our party who had gone on to the north of the cove where (we) were. They were not long in returning, it having been announced when landing that
I would go back on board at three o'clock. When we saw them rejoining us, they were accompanied by a dozen natives whom, as they drew nearer to us, we recognised to be women. They soon told us how they had come upon them as they were returning from fishing, laden with a great quantity of lobsters and abalone, which they had doubtless taken among the rocks at the extremity of the north point of this island. These women at first showed some fear at this encounter and at once fled into the woods, where they went to put down and hide the fruits of their fishing. Our people followed them, making signs of friendship and showing them the presents they wished to give them. It seems that the hope of obtaining a bottle decided them to stop and wait for our gentlemen, who soon joined them. When they saw that no attempt was being made to seize their catch, confidence was soon established. They began by sitting down, and the fair ones, doubtless wishing to please the new company by which they found themselves surrounded, daubed their faces with charcoal black moistened with their saliva, and then pressed their admirers so hard that they let the same be done to them, so that when they came back they could be known only by their clothes. One of the women, having withdrawn into the woods with M. Hérisson, may perhaps have fully satisfied her curiosity, for they were very curious to see not only the chests of our officers and scientists, but also whether they resembled the men of the country in their make or their faculties.
This addition to our company made us stay an hour and a half longer on shore to observe them better. But the women kept more apart, and as soon as anyone tried to approach them, they drew back. I think that the presence of the men, who were doubtless their husbands, was the chief cause of their reserve, for they had shown much less of it when they were at a distance from them. There seems no doubt that they are all of the same family. Among the women were two girls who were not yet of marriageable age. They were entirely naked, but each woman wore on her shoulders a kangaroo skin, which served only to cover their shoulders and a small part of the breasts.
At the moment when I announced that we were about to leave, two of the men climbed up the slope of the mountain, where the children and the women followed them. They each took up a bundle of spears, whether to be on their guard or to attack us. A third soon followed them, so that we were accompanied to our boats only by one man and a child of about nine. Both of them followed Captain Hamelin and tried, at the moment he was getting into the boat, to snatch his sword from him. We had no doubt that those who had armed themselves with spears had done so only to cover his retreat had he succeeded in his aim and been pursued. This (is), however, only a conjecture, for Captain Hamelin, who suspected the attempt, had taken his precautions to forestall it.
Our embarkation was thus in no way disturbed, and we all arrived on board at half past five.
The surgeon informed me, as soon as I arrived, that Citizen Maugé had been very unwell during the day and that he was beginning to fear he could not pull him through, his illness having the most ominous symptoms. This news grieved me greatly and made me fear that what I had long foreseen was about to come to pass.
During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth the weather was very fine and the winds shifted to the north, almost calm. Our longboat did not return from her errand on this tide, having perhaps been sent off from the ship too late to take advantage of it.
1802-02-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SW to W. At 7.15 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place. She went to fetch firewood cut by the two men guarding the sick; at 1 she brought in her load and left at 3 for the watering place. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 10 feet 8 inches, difference 1 foot 0 inches.

1802-02-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze variable from WNW to W. The longboat left for the watering place. The forenoon was almost calm; the carpenters worked on the starboard hawse bolsters.
1802-02-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we had the finest weather in the world; the sea and the wind were absolutely calm. As we had little to do, the small boat was sent out with the seine and made for the same place where we ourselves had been the day before. I gave the command of her to the boatswain.
At nine o'clock M. Freycinet wished to go ashore, to the same place, with Citizen Péron. I pointed out to them that, by rising earlier than usual on pleasure days, they could have taken advantage of the boat that had left between seven and eight o'clock, which would have been much more convenient. However, I had a boat manned for these two gentlemen, asking them to send it back to me as soon as they had landed. Some officers of the Naturaliste, who were to be of the party, were summoned by a signal agreed upon the day before, and at last, at half past ten, they set off.
Captain Hamelin, who had been out dredging for oysters since the morning, returned towards five in the evening with a good supply of that shellfish and a few other species for natural history. Citizens Depuche and Bailly, mineralogists, had gone with him. By a most extraordinary chance, M. Bailly, having gone ashore to examine some stones that had caught his attention, started a kangaroo the size of a strong lamb. He had no musket to shoot it, but, suddenly recovering from the fright it had given him, he threw his hammer at it and had the good fortune to break one of its thighs, and caught it.
This animal walks entirely on its hind feet, making no use whatever of the fore feet, which seem to serve it only for scratching the ground and making the hole in which it lodges. The one Citizen Bailly caught, and which has been painted from life, is perhaps a variety of those we have seen, for it does not resemble them at all in the colour of its fur, any more than it does those I saw in the Muséum in Paris. It was a female.
In the afternoon we sighted the Naturaliste's boat returning from the excursion I had had her make in order to ascertain positively whether there is a passage from Frederick Henry Bay to Marion Bay, as our charts seem to indicate, since they show us the island of Abel Tasman as separated from the great land of Diemen by a narrow channel.
According to the report of the geographer Faure, whom I sent there expressly, it appears that it is by mistake that the land of Abel Tasman is made an island. It is joined to the land of Diemen by an isthmus which the sea can at no time cover, and which is about ninety paces in length and about as much in breadth. Citizen Faure went over the whole of it in every direction. In the plan he made of it one may see not only that of Frederick Henry Bay, but also the isthmus that joins the so-called island of Tasman to that of Diemen, from which it is certainly not separated by any channnel (sic).
This excursion was not without use to geography, since it corrects an error, but it was of little advantage to natural history. However, some fine whelks were brought back, only one of them whole and with its animal.
Our boat also returned from fishing at sunset and brought us a fairly large quantity of fish. Part of it was taken on board the Naturaliste.
As I was waiting only for the return of Captain Hamelin's boat to sail from this port, I gave (orders) that the next day, at daybreak, the lower yards and our topgallant masts, which the strength of the south-west wind had obliged us to send down, should be hoisted. During the night the weather was fine though hazy; our longboats did not appear.
[3V p. 233 A] Copy of the original documents that may serve to throw some light on the conduct of Citizen Millius, Commander, under the orders of Citizen Hamelin, commanding the Naturaliste. (documents inserted here, but written in another hand. The reason why they are in this place is not explicit, nor explained)
1st document,
Letter from Citizen Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Citizen Commander,
Lieutenant P. Millius is an excellent officer, a good seaman, a good observer, and deserves the rank of Commander (sic); I expect it for him from your justice.
Be so good, I beg you, in your letters to the Minister of Marine, as to bring all my officers to his notice, and in particular Captain Millius, an officer of the highest merit.
Greetings and high consideration.
Signed, Citizen Hamelin.
This letter is dated from the Isle of France [Mauritius], 27 Vendémiaire.
[3V p. 233 B] 2nd document,
Letter from Citizen Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Citizen Commander,
I request for Lieutenant P. Millius the rank of commander. This officer, favourably known at Brest and at Rochefort, ports in which he has served, has long held his present rank.
He was first lieutenant of the frigate La Fraternité, which I commanded in the Year 5. He had already served at sea as lieutenant in the Révolution. Since that time he has never ceased going to sea, and all the chiefs who have known him agree in granting him eminent talents (particularly in seamanship, which only his zeal equals).
To recommend to you the advancement of Citizen Millius is to call upon you for an act of justice.
Greetings and high consideration.
Signed Citizen Hamelin
This letter is written at Kupang, island of Timor, on the 5th complementary day of the Year 9.
[3V p. 233 C] 3rd document,
Letter from Captain Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition at the moment of his sailing from Port Jackson on the west coast of New Holland.
Citizen Commander
I leave Citizen Millius here, too ill to be able to re-embark.
(Note) this letter contains many other matters unconnected with this affair
Signed Commander Hamelin.
It must be observed that Citizen Millius's illness was so serious that the physicians had met several times to pronounce on his condition, which was regarded as hopeless. The certificates Citizen Millius holds bear witness to this.
Thus with the unfavourable sequel that M. Baudin has laid to this officer's account is a piece of malice
[3V p. 233 D] Another letter from Captain Hamelin which clearly proves that Citizen Millius, although still very ill, wished to resume his duty on board the Naturaliste at the time of the second call at Port Jackson.
Captain Hamelin to the Commander of the expedition.
Citizen Commander,
The present state of Citizen Millius's health is, in my eyes, too unsatisfactory for me to be able to believe him recovered. (He) asks that he resume and continue his service at sea for a long time.
His bilious temperament and his severe relapses are too well known to me for me to expose myself again to continual anxiety on board about his welfare.
Signed Citizen Hamelin
[3V p. 233 E] 5th document.
Letter from Captain Hamelin
to Citizen Millius, commander.
Citizen,
In accordance with the reports of the English physicians Thomson, Harris and Milchalon, informed by Citizen Bellefin, our chief medical officer, of the poor health you have suffered for a very long time, and particularly of your present state of illness, and in accordance with your wish, I agree to your leaving the corvette the Naturaliste.
I wish you a speedy recovery and a happy voyage.
Friendly greetings.
Signed Citizen Hamelin.
1802-02-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. The carpenters worked at shifting the hawse bolsters. Fish were taken and distributed to the crew. Citizen Faure came in at 4.30 in the large boat. He had surveyed the North Bay and had found no passage between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island, which is joined to the land by a spit of sand; he had found fresh water in many places. The captain brought back many fish and oysters, which were distributed.

1802-02-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE to NE and WNW. At 4 the large boat came back from her duty; she found that Marion Bay does not communicate with Frederick Hendrik Bay, only a narrow spit of sand separating them, so that Abel Tasman Island is no more than a peninsula; and she was unable to communicate with the Aboriginal people.
1802-02-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, in the morning, it was a flat calm and the air so hazy that we could scarcely make out the nearest land, although (we) were no more than one mile from it. Nevertheless our longboats arrived towards eight o'clock, and the coxswain told me that the cause of his delay was that, the tide having risen very little the day before, they had been unable to fill their casks, not having had enough water to take them in to the shore.
As soon as they were unloaded, I sent them off again at once to fetch some twenty casks that were still there. And shortly afterwards I despatched the large boat to take in the tents and astronomical instruments that had been landed. By the same opportunity I sent M. Bernier, our astronomer, the following note:
"I am sending you, citizen, the large boat to take off all the effects that are on shore, as well as the "astronomical instruments you took there. As you must have been informed of this measure early this "morning by the Naturaliste's boat, you will no doubt cause no delay to the return "of the one I am sending you, which I expect this evening, as well as yourself. Signed N. B".
"P. S. Although it is not necessary to tell you that M. de Criq is to take advantage of this "same opportunity, I beg you nevertheless to let him know".
During the morning the haze cleared a little and we had a light breeze from the north-east. Captain Hamelin came on board and left shortly afterwards with Citizen Ronsard, a keen sportsman. Having little to do on board, I sent part of the crew fishing with the seine.
In the afternoon the air remained thick with haze and the winds still in the north-east, very light. The carpenters were employed in squaring and sawing into planks the lengths of tree trunk we had cut on shore.
When my boat returned from fishing, we found the catch fairly plentiful, even larger than any we had made until then; we took enough for two full days for both vessels.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth the large boat returned on board with all the astronomical instruments and the remainder of everything that had been carried ashore. The winds were absolutely calm and the sky very hazy.
The natives witnessed the fishing we had done and behaved in a very peaceable and friendly manner towards our people. Of all that was given them, nothing seemed more welcome to them than a few empty bottles.
1802-02-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At daybreak swayed up the topgallant masts. The longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once, empty, to fetch the remaining casks and bring back the party stationed at the watering place. We sent to fetch from the shore the pieces of timber the carpenters had cut. The astronomical instruments came back aboard.

1802-02-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE, NE, NNE, N and NW. The observatory was struck, as was the camp set up ashore for watering.
1802-02-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, towards nine o'clock in the morning, our longboats returned on board with the rest of the water casks that were on shore, which completed the stowage of our hold. There was no way of getting under sail that day, what little breeze there was having been from the north-east, variable to the east. The air, moreover, was so thick with haze that one could hardly make out the nearest land.
I had not thought it proper until now to speak of what was going on aboard the Naturaliste between Captain Hamelin and Citizen Millius, his first officer, the more so as I had never heard anything but good of the latter from his captain. Yet I had been informed in a most exact and circumstantial manner that the two of them lived on very bad terms. Citizen Millius, who had been granted a great deal more authority than was proper, had grown so accustomed to it that he had several times taken it upon himself to inflict exemplary punishments on members of the crew, convinced that he need not even account for them to his captain. The latter, having wrongly tolerated this at the outset, wished to put a stop to innovations
that might occur in future, and made his intentions on this subject known to him. They were ill received and afterwards became the source of all the unpleasantness that both of them have suffered from the discord that has long reigned between them. Had Captain Hamelin informed me during our stay at Timor of what was going on, I would eagerly have taken advantage of the letter Citizen Millius then addressed to me to grant him the discharge he was requesting on grounds of illness, and he truly was ill at that time. But, as I still knew nothing, I was the first to urge Citizen Millius to continue the voyage, pointing out to him that his advancement depended on it and that he should not entertain chimerical fears about his condition, given that I found his illness much less serious than my own. In short, I went to such lengths, and on several occasions, for he often came to see me on the same matter, that I succeeded in persuading him to carry on with the voyage. Perhaps he made up his mind to it only in the hope that I would give him M. Le Bas's place. This was far from my intention, as I did not wish to have an officer who thought himself more capable than I, although perhaps he was less so.
From our departure from Timor until our arrival at Port Nord Ouest, Citizen Millius was treated as sick throughout and did no duty, apart from a few high-handed acts of authority. Captain Hamelin took this amiss and reproached him in a friendly way, inviting him not to put him in the position of having to make known to him that he alone commanded on board &c.
I shall not relate the two unseemly scenes this officer publicly made to his captain, being persuaded that M. Hamelin will have recorded them in his journal, and that I would have punished them severely had he complained to me. But when Citizen Millius came to see me to urge me to receive him on board in his capacity of commander, a rank he had obtained only at the insistence of M. Hamelin, I avoided giving him a positive answer, confining myself to telling him that I would see whether the thing could be done without upsetting the order of duty I had established. I hoped by my silence, which was easy enough to interpret, to let him know that the thing was not possible. But as I was informed that he had packed his trunks and was only waiting for his order of discharge, even complaining a good deal that I had not already given him an answer, I addressed the following letter to him:
"The Commander &c. to Citizen Millius, Commander on board the Naturaliste, under the orders "of Captain Hamelin,
"Citizen, in reply to the request you made to me these past days to be placed on the "Géographe, I regret to inform you that the matter is more difficult than I should have imagined. I "could receive you there only by acting with authority, which would make a great many malcontents and would thereby disturb "the tranquillity that still reigns on board.
"I hope to have hereafter a more favourable opportunity of showing you how much pleasure I should "take in doing whatever may be agreeable to you". Signed N. B".
Captain Hamelin having come to dine on board, I showed him the letter I had addressed to M. Millius and took the opportunity to let him know how wrong he had been not to have informed me of M. Millius's conduct towards him. He excused himself on various pretexts which did not seem to me to clear him of this want of confidence.
Moreover, all I had already learned indirectly of M. Millius's character and pretensions was, for me, a very powerful reason for persisting in not receiving him on board, and, of two evils, I would rather leave things as they are than bring trouble and disorder on board by receiving him.
In the afternoon, as the weather continued hazy and the winds light from the east to south-east, we saw no likelihood of being able to sail before nightfall. All our boats, except (the) longboat, which I wished to keep in tow, were hoisted in, but I did not judge it proper to unmoor.
The night of the fifteenth to the sixteenth passed in a calm, with the sky still very hazy.
Citizen Bernier reported to me that some twenty natives, men as well as women and children, had come to visit them on the island where they were established, which could be reached by wading at low water. Two of them were allowed into the tent to examine what it contained. Only the beds seemed to catch their attention. During their stay with our gentlemen, the two goats and a sheep we had put ashore to recover a little amused them more than all the rest. They often spoke to them and several times invited them to eat.
Although they had behaved peaceably, the seamen of the boats nevertheless had cause to complain of them, in that they stole three bottles from them containing arrack. This was much less to drink the liquor than to obtain the vessel, as we knew from our own experience.
These natives were likewise among those we had had with us during our stay at the Grande Anse; at least, several of them were thought to be recognised. When they left the tents, they went into the water above the waist to cross to the mainland. One alone, however, got into one of our punts without the least distrust and had himself taken across by our people. It was not observed that any of them seemed to have any authority over the others. The men were entirely naked, holding their foreskin in their hand, according to a fairly common custom. Only the women had a kangaroo skin over the shoulder.
1802-02-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. The starboard anchor was weighed and 100 fathoms of the port cable hauled in. At noon the longboat came in from the watering place with the rest of the casks full, the working party and the effects from the camp. She was hoisted in, as was the large boat.

1802-02-05.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from east to south and SSE. At half past noon the longboat was back. On the 16th at 4 a.m. hove short, sheeted home and hoisted the topsails; the misty and almost calm weather prevented us from getting under way, and we lowered and furled the topsails and veered 6 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, at daybreak, we unmoored so as to get under sail as soon as the weather should clear. What little breeze there was then came from the west. We hoped that at sunrise the haze would lift and the breeze freshen. Accordingly, we rode apeak on a kedge anchor.
It was not without difficulty that we managed to weigh our bower anchors. They were so deeply sunk in the mud that, after breaking our messenger, we were obliged to clap a heavy purchase on the starboard cable, and even then we had considerable trouble making it break out.
During the morning, the winds having gone round to the east, a light breeze, and afterwards to the north-east, we gave up hope of being able to sail. The sky, moreover, was so hazy that it would have been difficult to get under sail even had they been fair. Having nothing better to do, I had the inspection and examination of the objects of curiosity and natural history collected or gathered by M. Le Villain up to the time of his death continued in my presence, Captain Hamelin having had them brought on board. The things handed over to us were of so little merit that I found myself obliged to write the following letter to the commander of the Naturaliste:
"The Commander to Captain Hamelin
"Citizen,
"I inform you that, after making an inventory and a general inspection of the objects of "curiosity and natural history collected and gathered by M. Le Villain, we were greatly astonished to "find among them only things of little value, very common and without merit. We knew him to have,
"however, a fair number of shells which Citizen Maugé, chief zoologist, "had taken the trouble to prepare and which he had placed in a separate box enclosed in the "cases where the things of little value that were left there were, and still are.
"As the cases were properly closed, and at once, it seems to us beyond doubt that since his "death someone on board has taken the liberty, without your knowledge, of opening them and removing objects which "indisputably belonged to the Government.
"I therefore invite you to make a scrupulous search to recover what is missing and to inform me "of the authors of such an offence.
"I have likewise just been informed that when the various objects belonging to him were sold, "several of those which they had obtained by purchase or by gift were included. This proceeding is "entirely contrary to the ordinances, which authorise only the sale of linen or of whatever is liable "to spoil. If these articles are not among them, you will be good enough to reclaim them from those who "bought them, draw up an inventory of them, of which you will send me a copy signed by you, and hold them at the "disposal of his family, to be dealt with as it sees fit. It is said that there were some articles "of gold which also went into the sale.
"Among the birds, no trace has been found of those stuffed at the Isle of France [Mauritius], and it is asserted "that they were publicly sold. They fall into the category of objects belonging to the Government".
"Your fellow citizen. . Signed N. B".
In the course of the day, the winds never ceasing to vary from south-east to north-east, it was not possible for us to sail. At sunset we could not help remarking the brilliant colour of its disc, which was of the most vivid red one could imagine. In fifteen to eighteen degrees north, and sometimes even in a more southerly latitude, I had on occasion seen a similar phenomenon on the coast of New Holland, but on those occasions the sky was usually clear and serene, whereas on this one the whole atmosphere was laden with a haze as damp as it was thick. This appearance was almost always the presage, and even the announcement, of some squalls for the following day, and perhaps we shall feel its effect.
At the beginning of the night, Captain Hamelin sent me in his boat several small cases and deal boxes containing various objects of natural history which had been sold as his effects. These objects being the property of the Government, since we knew beyond all possible doubt that they had been collected by different persons during the ports of call we made up to the death of this assistant zoologist, I claimed them in its name in order to hand them over to it. All were carefully examined on their arrival on board and are now deposited in cases made expressly for them, with a mark certifying that they were gathered and collected during the voyage.
The sky having been fairly fine and the wind calm for the greater part of the night, I remained on our kedge anchor. But at about three o'clock in the morning a gust of north wind came upon us, bringing with it a stifling heat. As this wind came to us from the head of the bay, it seemed to me that the cause of this sudden heat must be attributed to the burning of the mountains there, which, since our arrival, have been continually on fire. The first squall we received set us adrift, and being unable to bring up with a hundred fathoms of hawser out, we were obliged to let go a bower anchor while waiting for daylight, to see what would become of the weather, which from then on had a very bad look.
The barometer had suddenly fallen to 27 inches 7 lines from 28 in. 1, at which it had stood a short while before the squall. The thermometer, which I had exposed to the open air after feeling for myself the sudden heat that had come on, rose to 18 degrees in less than a quarter of an hour. When taken out of my cabin, it stood at twelve and a half.
1802-02-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. At 4.15 a.m., having a light air from the south, we hove short, hoisted and sheeted home the topsails; but a flat calm coming on, we furled the topsails and lay at long stay. We had caught the end of the hawser that parted on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802] and kept it aboard.

1802-02-06.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sea smooth, a flat calm. The breeze got up from the NNE and drew round, freshening, to NW, W and SW. The corvette dragging fast towards the land, we struck our topgallant masts. The Aboriginal people lit fires round the shores of the port.
1802-02-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, at daylight, the weather, instead of setting fair, grew worse, and what the sunset had foretold the evening before came true during the morning. The gusts from north-west to west became so strong that we were obliged to veer a hundred and twenty fathoms of our cable so as not to drift too far towards the starboard shore, from which we were now no more than a mile distant.
After sunrise, the winds went round to the west and increased still further in strength. The sky grew dark and laden with vapours, and we had rain cold enough to make itself felt. Having little room left to drift, so short was our distance from the land, I had a second bower anchor let go to port as a precaution and thirty-five fathoms of cable veered. It served not only to hold us more securely but also to check the swinging of the ship. The kedge anchor was weighed with the longboat.
Towards eight o'clock, seeing no sign of change in the state of the sky, I had the topgallant masts unrigged and put on deck, for they were of very little use to us and had served very little during the campaign. We put up stump masts in their place, which served us just as well without our topmasts being burdened with a useless weight in these circumstances. This country, moreover, seems to me ill suited to topgallant masts, for since we have been here we have sometimes had two days of fine weather, but never three.
However that may be, from ten o'clock until noon the sky became quite fine and clear. The heavy clouds that had alarmed us in the morning dispersed, and the gusts, though very frequent, were less strong and shorter. I wished to take advantage of this lull to get under sail. We accordingly hove in our port anchor, but something having given way under the force of the wind, I had the work stopped and decided to wait until the wind became more manageable. My position, moreover, was not of the most favourable, so that it seemed to me far more prudent to put off sailing for a day or two, if need be, than to run the risk of being cast on the shore.
Towards noon, the winds went round to the south, a strong breeze, and in the course of the day and evening varied to south-south-east. I was then all the less sorry not to have sailed, as it had seemed to me from the direction of the clouds that they would not stay long in the west or south-west, as we had had them in the morning.
Throughout the day we saw great fires at a short distance from the coast. They grew so much with the violence of the wind that by noon the whole of the port side was ablaze. The starboard side, though the fires there were fairly considerable, was less so. There is no doubt that it is the natives who are the cause of these great conflagrations, for the direction of the wind would not have given the fire the direction we successively saw it take. It is perhaps not for the mere pleasure of destruction that they thus set fire to their forests, and it is reasonable to suppose that they have some useful purpose in it. Following this reasoning, it might perhaps be kindled only with the aim of destroying the grass and other brushwood that make their progress laborious and difficult, or for the hunting of certain quadrupeds known to be in the neighbourhood.
After sunset, the breeze abated a good deal; the winds went first to the east and then to the north, dead calm. The sky, though damp, was fairly fine during the night, and we constantly had in view all the havoc the fire was wreaking at the head and in the surroundings of Port Nord-Ouest [North West Bay]. The little wind there was when they went round to the north was probably the reason we did not feel, as on the previous night, the heat of the burning land.
1802-02-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm; the heat was stifling. At 2.30 a.m. a light breeze got up from NNE, drew round to NW and W, freshening, and at last to SW, a strong breeze with violent gusts. At 5 we had dragged and veered cable, and slipped the hawser with a buoy whose lashing gave way. At 6 the topgallant masts were got down. At 7.30 we dragged and let go a second anchor, the wind blowing hard from WSW to SSW. The Aboriginal people lit many fires round the shores of the port; we saw five of them on the nearest shore, each with a brand in his hand, setting fire everywhere. At nightfall the wind fell away, and it was calm during the night.

1802-02-07.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze in gusts from SW, SSE and south; it fell away in the afternoon. We made attempts to get under way, but a calm coming on we let go a bower anchor.
1802-02-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, at half past three in the morning, I was told that the winds were north-west, a light breeze, and the sky fine. I gave orders for the bell to be rung at once and for work to begin without delay on weighing our port anchor, for we still had two down. As soon as it was stowed, the starboard one was hove in. The weather was still fine and the winds from the same quarter. But about an hour before sunrise a very thick fog, which did not allow us to see the coast, though we were only a mile from it, came to darken the air. As I thought it would soon be dispersed by the sun, we hove apeak and held ourselves ready to get under sail as soon as it cleared, although the wind, which was north-west, was very slack. The Naturaliste did the same and sheeted home her topsails.
At seven o'clock the crew were given their breakfast, still in the hope that the sky would clear, and we saw with regret that the fog was growing thicker and thicker.
Towards eight o'clock we were in a dead calm, without the least sign of a breeze in any quarter of the horizon. However, towards ten o'clock we had a little wind from the south-east, variable to the east. There was then no longer any means of sailing, and we were forced to lower our topsails and veer thirty fathoms of cable so as not to drag. M. Hamelin's boat having come on board, he asked me for leave to send it fishing, since there was no likelihood of the winds changing for the rest of the day. I likewise sent a boat with the seine, and we went ashore on the starboard coast.
The excursion we made into the interior of the country, though of fair length, yielded nothing of interest. I brought back from it only one new and rather pretty bird, as well as a plant with ripe seeds which no one had yet come across until then.
Citizens Depuche and Péron having asked to be put ashore to go and converse with the natives of the country in order to enlarge the vocabulary they had begun, I gave orders for them to be given one of our light boats, and they set off. I pointed out to them, nevertheless, that their hopes would be disappointed and that they would meet no one, being persuaded that the natives had changed their abode, as no smoke had been seen at the place where they had settled on their arrival. Although they were persuaded of the contrary, the event proved to them that my remark was not as ill-judged as they thought, since on their return they reported to me that they had found no one.
The fishing done by our boat was fair. Among the fish caught were three of those which Anderson calls the elephant fish. This name was no doubt given to it by that naturalist only on account of the trunk that hangs from the end of its snout. The description he gives of it did not seem accurate to our naturalists. One of these three fish carried under its belly two most extraordinary things, the substance of which I shall do my utmost to preserve, as it seems solid enough to warrant that hope: it is thought to be a casing in which the offspring of this fish is enclosed. This conjecture is all the more likely as it was a female, which dragged them behind her, having them attached by a ligament to the opening of the womb. Two fine shells of the whelk kind were also taken with the seine.
During the night of the eighteenth to the nineteenth, the winds were a dead calm and the sky very overcast, with little sign of fine weather for the following day.
1802-02-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather. At 4.15 a.m., a breeze from NNW, we weighed both anchors in turn and got under way under topsails. We hauled in 50 fathoms of the hawser, which had stayed foul of the anchor's flukes, and took the draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 7 inches, difference 4 inches. At 7.30 a flat calm; anchored and lay at long stay with the topsails hoisted. The breeze got up from the south and veered as far as east. At nightfall the commander signalled us to follow his movements; accordingly we lowered the topsails and veered cable.

1802-02-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather; throughout the twenty-four hours a very light breeze variable from south to ESE and SE. In the forenoon the commander having squared his yards, we did the same.
1802-02-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, we remained in a dead calm until about nine o'clock in the morning. The sky, though very dark, was fairly fine. At that time a light breeze came to us from the south-east, which veered little by little towards the east, and towards noon the winds, having freshened a little, settled in that quarter of the horizon.
Seeing no prospect whatever of sailing during the evening, I sent two boats fishing, one with the seine and the other with lines. The latter was far more fortunate than the small boat, for it caught enough fish to distribute some to the crew. What the other brought back is hardly worth mentioning.
During the evening, the winds stayed in the east, a pleasant breeze, but at the beginning of the night the sky had so bad a look that we veered twenty fathoms more cable than we had had out during the day, so as to ride more safely at our anchor. However, despite the look of the sky, there was no bad weather, and the greater part of the night passed in calm.
Citizen Maugé was very ill during this day, and it is only too probable that we shall have the misfortune to lose him soon, for he is visibly wasting away every day and his belly swells more and more. Towards four o'clock in the afternoon he sent for me and spoke to me of his situation. I did all I could to persuade him to be patient, the more so as for several days he had become very anxious and even difficult. He begged me to assemble the two surgeons of the Naturaliste for the following day, if we did not sail, so that they might consult together on the continuation of his treatment for the further course of his illness. I promised him to do all he wished in this respect and did not even want the meeting he asked for to be put off until the next day, but he insisted that it be deferred until then.
1802-02-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to NE. Fish were taken and distributed.

1802-02-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a little misty; shipped the winter spar. A fresh breeze from E by S to NE. The dinghy brought back fish and went straight back to the fishing.
1802-02-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, the weather was so hazy that at daylight we could scarcely make out the land, or even the Naturaliste, which was quite close to us. We hoped that the sun, at its rising or as it climbed above the horizon, might perhaps disperse the haze and that the winds would become fair. Accordingly, we hove short so as to take advantage of them at once if they were favourable to us.
At nine o'clock, the haze being as thick as at daybreak and the wind a complete calm, I informed our chief physician of Citizen Maugé's wish that he should consult with the others on his situation and the best means to be employed to pull him through. M. Laridon confirmed to me what he had already told me concerning the little hope he had of seeing this naturalist recover, and wrote to Citizens Bellefin and Colas to come on board as soon as possible.
The letter was carried at once, and at eleven o'clock both of them arrived on board. According to the consultation they held together, Citizen Maugé's illness was judged to be mortal and incurable by the resources of medicine, so that if he recovers from it, the cause will have to be attributed to the unknown workings of nature rather than to the remedies the faculty will employ.
Towards noon I went ashore with Captain Hamelin, and we stayed there about three hours. My intention was to obtain a few butterflies of the country. But this excursion was not a fortunate one; all those I caught were of the same
species and not very pleasing to the eye.
Three of our boats were employed in fishing, and all three were fortunate; enough fish was caught for two days, besides a fairly large quantity that was given for the Naturaliste.
In the course of the evening, the winds were very light from the east to east-south-east, and we had rain. The sky remained so overcast and hazy during the day that we saw the sun appear only at two very short intervals.
The night of the twentieth to the twenty-first passed in calm, the sky still very dark and hazy.
1802-02-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. At 4 p.m. the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. She was back at 8.15 and was hoisted in, together with a catamaran she had found adrift in the channel.

1802-02-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 4 the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. At 8 p.m. she was back; she was hoisted in, together with a catamaran belonging to the Aboriginal people which they had found adrift in the middle of the channel. From the 21st to the 22nd [Pluviôse, Year 10, 10-11 February 1802]. Overcast, misty weather, fine rain throughout the twenty-four hours, a flat calm.
1802-02-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, there was no more prospect of being able to sail than on the preceding days. The sky was extremely overcast, the wind calm in the east-north-east quarter, and the atmosphere very thick. Before deciding to allow the boats to go fishing, I waited until about eleven o'clock in the hope that, if the winds settled, they might go round into the south by way of the west. But it was in vain, for when the breeze began to freshen a little, they held in the east with no hope of seeing them change.
During the evening, the winds were south-south-east, a light breeze, and at the beginning of the night we had the vexation of seeing no sign of change in the state of the atmosphere, which became covered with thick haze. The wind fell entirely calm.
Captain Hamelin's boat, returning from fishing, brought on board a canoe, the only mark of ingenuity we have so far observed among the inhabitants of this part of the coast. I believe the term raft or floating buoy would suit far better than that of canoe the assemblage of bundles of tree bark which they lash together and use to cross from one shore to another. The sticks they use to set it in motion likewise bear no resemblance to the paddles used in canoes; see the drawing I give of it. These buoys, pointed at both ends, may be two or three inches hollow on the inside, and have the advantage over canoes of being unable to capsize, their displacement being considerable. The rowers stand in them or sit on their heels.
1802-02-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a flat calm. Fish were distributed to the crew. Rain during the night.

1802-02-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, the haze continued all day and the wind was a complete calm; what little breeze made itself felt from time to time came to us from the south-south-east. The sky was so dark all day and the air so thick that the shores of the coast could scarcely be made out. We saw with regret that this day too was lost to us, having no means of employing it usefully. The surroundings of the harbour and other parts of the strait had been so thoroughly explored by the naturalists that it seemed they could find there only things already in their possession. On the other hand, the hope that the wind might change from one moment to the next did not allow me to send boats too far off. For had we been able to foresee at the outset what befell us, I would not have failed to send someone to visit the place where M. La Hay's garden was established; it is the only part of the strait we have not visited.
In the evening, the weather being still the same, boats were sent fishing, and the catch was fairly good and plentiful, although it was done with lines.
The night passed in calm, the sky even hazier than usual.

1802-02-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, the sky continued extremely hazy and thick, the winds from the south to south-south-east almost calm. We were still apeak in the hope that they would go round to the south towards the west, but this expectation was disappointed, for towards ten o'clock what little breeze there was fell entirely calm and did not come back to us, from the south towards the east, until the afternoon.
I then decided to send one boat fishing with the seine and another with lines. The catch was fairly plentiful, and besides the fish we took some hundred crabs of the spider-crab kind.
Towards evening the sky seemed inclined to clear, the haze lifted a a (sic) little, and the night, which passed in calm, was fairly fine. We took it as an omen of a change in our favour for the next day.

1802-02-13.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather. A light breeze from south and SE, with fine rain until four in the morning. The dinghy left for the fishing.
1802-02-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, we were disappointed in our expectation. The sky, it is true, was finer than usual, and at times we saw the sun, which had not happened to us for a long while. But what little wind there was came from the south, variable to the south-east. Despite the slight prospect there was of sailing during the day, I would not put any boat out to go fishing, but I sent my longboat, which had not been hoisted in and which I intended to keep in tow, out dredging.with the dredge
At noon it returned and brought us only a single fine shell, which, though dead, compensated us a little for our (stay) at anchor, so beautiful and precious did it seem to us. None of us knows it, nor anything that comes near it.
During the day, Citizen Maugé seemed to me worse than usual. As I went to see him every two hours, I found him in such a drowsiness and so great a weakness that he could hardly stir, and truly I despaired of his recovery, although the physicians had long assured me that they regarded it as impossible. It seemed to me that the patient himself was affected by it, for he spoke to me of nothing but his approaching death the whole time I was with him, and of (the) regrets of his friends, whose advice he had scorned in undertaking this voyage against their wishes. I at once called the physician of the Naturaliste, and a fresh consultation was held. The results were the same as the first time they had met, that is to say that the illness was mortal and that he could recover from it only through some extraordinary cause. This new opinion made such an impression on me that I passed the day very badly. I had always kept some hope until that moment, and it was Citizen Maugé's condition alone that made me lose it, rather than all that the physicians told me, for all their learning.
At sunset the calm came on and lasted the greater part of the night. The sky, nevertheless, was fairly fine until two o'clock in the morning, when, the winds having gone round to the north, variable towards the east, it became cloudy and overcast.
1802-02-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to ESE. Latitude of the observatory, North West Port: 43° 1' 1"; longitude 145° 5' 0"; variation NE 10° 25' 0".

1802-02-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from east to ESE. At 4.30, the breeze being from the NW, we hove round on the cables, and at 5 hoisted the topsails; at 5.30 got under way and made all sail, ranging along Van Diemen's Land. After doubling the east point of the North West Port the winds headed us; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter, and on the 10th board we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 44° E; Pointe Pierson N 15° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E.
1802-02-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, at daylight, the winds varied from north to north-north-west. Our eagerness to be gone made us get under sail at once. The breeze, though very light, allowed us with the help of the ebb to make about a league, but at that point the winds went round to the north-east and even to the east, which
was directly contrary to our course. We then began to beat to windward, tack upon tack, and this manoeuvre lasted until ten o'clock with very little success. The winds were so inconstant that we had (them) now in the north, now in the east, and sometimes even in the south-west, but every cat's-paw lasted only an instant and a dead calm followed at once; at ten o'clock the flood was strong enough to set us drifting at great speed towards the coast of Île Bruny [Bruny Island], and we were obliged to come to anchor at a musket-shot at most from the land. The Naturaliste, at the same time, was fortunately on the mainland side and anchored two-thirds of the way across the channel.
As the position in which I found myself was not a good one to keep, I had a warp run out to the north-north-east, but the current having set our longboat to the south-west, it was of little advantage to us; still, it enabled us to get a little farther from the coast.
In the afternoon, the winds being east, variable towards the north, we ran out a second, which brought us to about the middle of the channel. And we remained on a kedge anchor in twenty fathoms of water, good holding ground.
At sunset, the sky, which had been fine during the day, grew dark and the wind fell calm. I sent two boats fishing at four o'clock in the afternoon, having nothing better to do.
According to the surgeon's report, Citizen Maugé was much worse than usual, and I had no difficulty in satisfying myself of it in the several visits I paid him during the day.
The night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth passed in calm, the sky fairly fine.
1802-02-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from NNW. At 5.30 we got under way and shaped our course to leave the port, hugging the eastern shore of the port, after doubling its east point. The wind headed us, drawing round to NE and ENE; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter. At 9, on the tenth board, we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, Pointe Gicquel bearing S 44° W, Pointe Pierson N 15° E, and Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E. The breeze varied from east to west by way of north.

1802-02-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to east. During the night the wind drew round to W, a fresh breeze; stopped the topsails with rope yarns. The winds hauled to the SW and drew round to south; the topsails were lowered.
1802-02-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, the sky was hazy and overcast until sunrise. From daybreak we hove apeak and hoisted our topsails, the winds being then north-north-west and very light. We were waiting, before sailing, for them to gather a little strength to stem the current, which was against us. But they soon went round to the south, and when the sun dispersed the haze towards seven o'clock, they came to the south-east and the east.
We were then obliged to veer cable and lower our topsails. For the rest of the day it blew a good breeze from the east. The astronomer went to take the latitude (of) the point that forms the entrance of the harbour on Île Bruny [Bruny Island]. The small boat and another went off fishing, and the longboat dredging. None of these boats had any luck. During the day there was communication with the natives, who behaved very peaceably. It is true that they were few in number.
During the night it was calm, as usual.
1802-02-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to NE by way of east; a little rain.

1802-02-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from ENE to NE. At 5 a.m. loosed the topsails and got under way on the starboard tack, the winds a light breeze from NNW to NE. Being under Van Diemen's Land we were taken aback and went onto the port tack; at 6.30 we let go the anchor.
1802-02-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at three o'clock in the morning, a light breeze sprang up from the north, which decided me to have the bell rung at once so as to be ready to get under sail at daybreak. The weather was fine and the sky clear, which made me think the winds might be favourable to us. As soon as we were under way we made sail on our course, but scarcely had we gone half a league when the wind fell entirely calm and the ship no longer answered her helm. We were obliged to let go the anchor with all sail set.
At seven o'clock the breeze sprang up from north-north-east to north-east. The sails had to be furled and cable veered. The weather was fine for the rest of the day; the astronomers were put ashore to make observations, and two boats were ordered to go fishing.
Towards seven o'clock a light breeze sprang up from the south-west, and we at once got under
sail, so impatient was I to be out of the strait, which I believe it is not prudent to enter when one has no time to lose, because of the difficulty of getting out of it. As soon as we were apeak, the calm came on, and we had to hold on and wait, against our will, for a more favourable moment. At last it came, and during the night we managed to double Pointe Pierson [Pierson Point]. The ships anchored about a league outside the points. By this means we had less to fear from the changeableness of the winds, since, unless we had them directly from the south-east, we could hope to get out by beating to windward. During the night, the weather and the sky being fine, a boat was sent to sound for half a league round the ship; the bottom was found at 12 to 14 fathoms, mud. Towards two o'clock the breeze sprang up from the south-east quarter, and the winds came in fairly strong gusts. Towards the end of the night, calm replaced it.
1802-02-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze from NE to NNW. At 5 a.m. we got under way on the starboard tack; being close in with Van Diemen's Land, we were taken aback and went onto the port tack. At 6.30, the commander having anchored, we did the same. The rigging was set up. The wind, a fresh breeze from NNW, hauled to N, NNW, NW, W and SW. At 6 a flat calm. At 6.15 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander signalled us to get under way at once. At 7.15 we were under sail, shaping our course to leave the channel. At 8, after doubling Pointe de la Sortie, we anchored in 14 fathoms, the south end of Willaumez Island bearing east, Pointe de la Sortie S 22° W and Pointe Pierson S 50° W. Calm during the night.

1802-02-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE, N, NNW, NW, W and SW. It fell calm; at 6 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander made the signal to get under way; at 7 we were under sail and shaped our course to leave the channel. After doubling Pointe de la Sortie we let go the anchor; at 10.30, the breeze having settled in the SE, we got under way under our fore-and-aft sails; shortly afterwards we sheeted home the topsails and took in the courses, a fresh breeze from SE. At noon took the bearing of Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W; Pointe de la Direction N 4° 30' E; and Cape Trobriand S 1° E.
1802-02-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, towards eight o'clock in the morning, the breeze having sprung up from the east, variable to east-south-east, we got under sail in fine weather, with the current in our favour and the hope of doubling Cap de Direction and even Île Villiaume before the return of the flood, which was due at one o'clock or half past one in the afternoon. We made several boards between the cape and Île Bruny [Bruny Island], lead in hand, and at noon we doubled, at a quarter of a league's distance, the rocks off the point of the latter island, getting no bottom at fifteen fathoms.
During the evening we continued to beat to windward, tack upon tack, between Cap Raoul [Cape Raoul] on the Presqu'île de Tasman [Tasman Peninsula] and Cap Trobriant on Île Bruny.
