The boards were then long, yet we gained little, the current being against us. The winds were then south-east and the sky very damp. After sunset the breeze abated a good deal and the flood had us much at its mercy, carrying us rapidly towards one or the other of the two coasts according to the tack we were on. At the beginning of the night, Cap Raoul bore south 85° east of us, and Cap Trobriant south 16° west.
From sunset until about two o'clock in the morning, what little wind there was amounted almost to a calm and was very variable; we made a little way only with the help of the tide, which was then in our favour. The sky became so covered with clouds and haze that we often lost sight of the land, although we were not very far from it, sounding in between twenty-eight and thirty-six fathoms.
At one o'clock, the winds having gone round to west-south-west and then to south-south-west, a pleasant breeze, we made sail to double Cap Raoul, leaving the Naturaliste far astern.
1802-02-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At 9.15 a.m. we got under way and beat between Bruny Island and the northern peninsula to weather the Tasman Peninsula and reach Maria Island. At noon Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W, Pointe de la Direction N 5° E, Cape Trobriand S 1° E. At 4, Pointe de la Sortie N 73° W, Pointe de la Direction N 59° W, Cape Trobriand S 9° W, Cape Cannelé S 6° W. At 11.30 a flat calm.

1802-02-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. During the night sounded every half hour and found from 28 to 40 fathoms. We rigged the topgallant masts after cutting off their poles. A fresh breeze from SE, south and SSW.
1802-02-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, before daybreak, we had doubled Cap Raoul [Cape Raoul] in hazy though fairly fine weather. The winds were then south-west, a pleasant breeze, and the sea was also troubled by a heavy swell from north-south. At seven o'clock we doubled Cap Trobriant Pillar and little Tasman Island, then directing our course to pass between the Rochers d'Hyppolite [Hippolyte Rocks] and the mainland. Running along this whole coast at three-quarters of a league at most, and often less, we took bearings and views of it everywhere. This part of the coast is thinly wooded compared with that of the strait, but on the other hand it offers a great number of sites of the greatest interest.
As the whole stretch of coast between Cape Pillar and Cape Frederick Hendrick bears no name, we gave one to each of the points or capes at which our bearings began and ended.
The high lands that form Cape Pillar are, on the whole, fairly barren and thinly
wooded, but a little to the north of this cape the vegetation shows itself in a pleasing aspect, varied by the shading of its colours. I named Pointe des Organistes the first point to the north of Cape Pillar, abreast of the Rochers d'Hyppolite.
In crossing the channel that separates them from the mainland, we got no bottom at 30 fathoms, and the current set to the north with some speed. The Dépôt chart shows only two of them; there are, however, three, quite distinct and separate from one another. The largest of the three lies farther to the east than the other two, and I believe that, by beating to windward, one could pass between the first and the second, although the opening is not large. This first rock is high, and coming from the south it presents the shape of a gunner's quoin.
After doubling them, we continued to run along the mainland at half a league and three-quarters of a league distance. We named Pointe Petit the point forming the northern entrance of the first bay-shaped inlet marked on the Dépôt chart. The view of this whole part is very pleasing. The lands are high, lofty and well wooded. The inlet offers a very remarkable beach of white sand, and the sea there seemed to us fairly calm. This cove could offer shelter only to small boats; at least, that is how I judged it, from its lack of shelter from north to south by way of east. This point is low and level.
From Pointe Petit to Cap des Pitons, the lands are high and of fine appearance. The summits and slopes of the mountains are extremely steep on the seaward side and offer no place fit for landing, except in the large cove found in this part. There, as in the other, one sees a fine beach of white sand and the sea smooth right up to the shore.
From Cap des Pitons to Cape Frederick Hendrick, the lands are higher than anywhere else and well wooded. The former cape is very remarkable for the projecting steeple-shaped peaks found on it, which give it a very peculiar aspect. The interval separating it from Cape Frederick Hendrick offers neither anchorage nor shelter, and the sea breaks everywhere with force.
From the course we held after leaving Cape Pillar (in the margin: as far as Cape Frederick Hendrick), it seems to me that the coast does not trend enough to the west, and the two capes must be different from the one that was given to it. It will be possible to judge better from the plan we are going to draw up of this part of the coast.
As Cape Frederick Hendrick forms the entrance of the bay which has been given the name of Baie de Marion [Marion Bay], we crossed it without visiting it, intending to have it scrupulously examined during the stay I meant to make at Île Marion [Maria Island]. For I am persuaded that there is an error in the Dépôt charts in this placing of the bay that Tasman named Frederick Hendrick Bay.
Towards four o'clock in the afternoon, we anchored in nine fathoms, sandy bottom, roughly east and west of Oyster Bay. The Naturaliste, which had stayed astern, having been unable to double Cap Raoul, arrived towards five o'clock. That ship passed outside the Rochers d'Hyppolite.
Citizen Maugé, during this day, was much worse than usual, and according to the physician's report there was no likelihood that he would last the night. Although I had to expect this sad news from one moment to the next, it made such an impression on me that I was ill from it.
Bearing of our anchorage at Maria Island. The southernmost point of this island in sight, south 28° east. Two rocks a little offshore on which the sea breaks, south 24°30' (26° 30'). The entrance of Oyster Bay north 60° east & north 7° east.
(No Thirtieth Pluviôse)
1802-02-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N, SW, S, SSE. At midnight the course was given S 45° E. Cape Trobriand then bore from us S 34° W, 3 miles off. At 4 it bore S 68° W; the wind having headed us, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 8 the course was given S 78° 45' E. Cape Raoul bore from us N 8° E, Cape Pillar N 58° E and Little Tasman Island N 70° E. We bore up by degrees to N 11° 15' W. At 10.15 doubled Tasman Island. At 11.15 doubled the great Hippolyte Rock. At noon, in 43° 8' 30" of latitude observed, it bore from us S 8° W. The topgallant masts were rigged, their poles having been cut off, and the topgallant sails bent. At 3.30 we ran into the channel separating Maria Island from Van Diemen's Land. At 4.15 anchored near the Géographe in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, an islet in the channel bearing N 19° W, the northernmost point of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 6° W, the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 4° E, the SW point of the same island S 29° E, the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 9° E, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E, Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W. During the night the wind a strong breeze from E to NNE. A little fish was taken.

1802-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 3 we ran into the channel that separates Van Diemen's Land from Maria Island; at 4.15 we anchored in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the westernmost visible end of Maria Island N 4° E; Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E; the south end of the same island S 29° E; Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W; the southernmost visible cape of the Tasman Peninsula S 9° E.
1802-02-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNW. At 3.30 the large boat, provisioned for 10 days, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure to survey the Schouten Islands. At 6 the captain left for Frederick Hendrik Bay. I landed on Maria Island abreast of the anchorage with our botanist and the second surgeon, and, shooting as we went, reached the head of Oyster Bay. I looked there for the watering place marked on Cox's chart and found none; I saw only a pool of brackish water and the bed of a stream where there might be fresh water in the rainy season. At spring tides the sea rose into the pool, for there was a channel traced in the sand and marine plants round its edges. In the evening, coming back, we found a grave near a hut of the Aboriginal people; we turned over the earth and our surgeon recognised among the ashes and charcoal human bones that were partly burnt. The grave was covered with grass and small pieces of bark held down by two spears whose ends were driven into the ground, the whole covered with large sheets of bark that we had difficulty in moving. We put everything back as we had found it and came back aboard. In our walk we saw no Aboriginal people; we found several huts, in one of which they had slept not long before, for the grass was still fresh and there were crayfish shells recently grilled. We found fresh water in several holes. At 5 p.m. the weather turned overcast and it freshened. The topgallant masts were struck and a light shown at the gaff for the captain's boat. At 11 the wind drew round to SE, a strong breeze.

1802-02-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind light from NNW. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened from the north; veered 30 fathoms of cable and struck the topgallant masts. The dinghy went fishing; the longboat was sent off with 3 days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Freycinet. From the 1st to the 2nd [Ventôse, Year 10, 20-21 February 1802]. Overcast and misty weather, the wind ESE, a fresh breeze. The dinghy came back from the fishing with a great many fish and crayfish. At 6 a.m. the commander cockbilled his yards and put his pendant and his ensign at half mast on account of the death of the zoologist Maugé; we did the same. At 9 the body of the deceased was carried ashore and buried; all the officers of both ships attended his funeral.
1802-02-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Ventôse, early in the morning, I ordered Captain Hamelin to send off his large boat to examine Schouten Island and the others to the north of it, to which Tasman gave various names. The officer placed in command of it was ordered to visit the channel separating them from the mainland, and Citizen Faure to draw up an exact plan of it as well as of the whole coast. Eight days' provisions for everyone were put on board, this time seeming to me sufficient for this expedition.
For my part, I sent off Citizen Boulanger to go round Maria Island and survey a plan of it. Citizen Péron was employed on this excursion.
After the departure of these two boats, I went myself to examine Oyster Bay; despite all my searching, I did not find the place pointed out by Cox as the one where water and wood could be taken in. The circuit of this bay, which I made on foot, only acquainted me with two places around its circumference that had the appearance of a watering place in the rainy season, or winter season. But we came upon two fairly wide though shallow channels into which the sea rises at high tide. We went all the way round them, and all the water we found in various holes was salt and even foul, having no outlet and being renewed only at the spring tides or in bad weather.
The first channel may be a hundred and fifty to two hundred paces long, following its various windings. We saw in it remains of wood cut with the saw and the axe, which leaves no doubt that it is the place Cox meant to speak of. This channel lies about a quarter of the way round the bay on the southern side
The second channel is about three-quarters of the way round, on the northern side. Its mouth to the sea is extremely narrow and can be seen only when one has reached it. Then it widens little by little as one advances inland. Following its various windings, it looks exactly like a small river of a range width (sic). There is no doubt that the channel was hollowed out by rainwater and that in the wet season it is swollen by the waters running down from the neighbouring mountains. But at present it is full only of seawater, just as salt at its inland end as at its mouth to the sea. As it was late when we made this discovery, we (decided) to go as far as its end, and we retraced our steps after following it for more than a quarter of a league, putting off till the next day seeing how far it extended. The ground forming the two banks is flat and full of samphire. Between these two arms of the sea there is very little width to cross the island. The narrowest place is no more than a hundred paces and the widest two hundred in a straight line. From there one sees a large part of the eastern coast of this island and a second bay, in which there is a bar on which the sea breaks to a great height, and the noise made by four waves rolling one over another makes the sight very pleasing, but landing impossible, except at the extremities of the points that form it.
On our way to the north point of Oyster Bay, we saw some twenty natives on the edge of the beach, men, women and children. Most of them were armed with a spear made like those of the Canal d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. They made no hostile gesture at our landing; they merely drew back a little from the shore. The signs of friendship we made to them after landing seemed to reassure them, and the presents that closely followed these demonstrations established confidence between them and us.
Having all sat down together pell-mell, we examined them attentively, and they did just the same with us. The women and children, however, kept a little apart and did not seem to us as merry as those of Île Bruny [Bruny Island], which no doubt comes from their having had fewer occasions to see ships and the strangers aboard them. The children above all seemed very timid and fearful. Despite the urging of their fathers and mothers to come and take what we offered them, they dared not approach us, and we were obliged to throw the things to them, and after picking them up they withdrew very quickly.
The grown men, like the women, were entirely naked. The latter, like those of the Canal Bruny, wore a kangaroo skin over the shoulder. The men were better made than those we had already met. Though tattooed like the others, the bands on their arms were more numerous, except that they seemed to us a little less wide; they had spindly legs and rather large bellies. The women's features are not pleasing. They are generally ill made and of middling height. Some of the men had their faces daubed with charcoal. Their habits and manner of living seemed to us similar to those of the people of the strait. Before parting at sunset, we exchanged a few trifles with them for their spears. This exchange was made in a very friendly manner on both sides. We took leave of them, giving them to understand that we would return the next day.
Captain Hamelin went to visit Baie de Marion [Marion Bay], and I am awaiting his return to know what remains for us to do in this quarter.
(two lines struck out)
1802-02-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 1 a.m. the captain came in in his boat. At 10 a.m., on the commander's signal, the longboat was put in the water. At 11 she was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to survey the coast from Cape des Sarcelles to the northernmost point in sight from the anchorage. Many crayfish were taken and a meal of them distributed to the crew. At 2 the carpenters went to Maria Island to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-02-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, following the report of M. Hamelin, who believed he had fully identified Frederick Hendrick Bay, I had my longboat fitted out and gave the command of it to M. Freycinet with the following order:
"The Commander to Citizen Freycinet, lieutenant de vaisseau
"According to the report Captain Hamelin has just made to me, there is no doubt that "Frederick Hendrick Bay lies in the southern part of the one the new charts call "Baie de Marion [Marion Bay], and that it is on the eastern side of the Presqu'île de Tasman [Tasman Peninsula] and not on the "western side, as the Dépôt chart shows it.
"In order to settle the doubtful opinion this point of geography has presented, you will take "command of the longboat and proceed directly to the cape we have just named "Cap des Sarcelles. There you will observe the latitude and endeavour to determine its longitude by hour "angles.
"From this cape you will make your way directly along the whole of the mainland coast, as close inshore "as you can. All the coves you come upon must be scrupulously visited, so as to "make sure there is no opening in them. On your arrival at the entrance of Frederick Hendrick "Bay, you will proceed with caution, in that the sandbanks marked on the plan of it given us by "Valentin exist and dry out at low water. Should there not be enough water to go round "this bay in the longboat, you will do so by land, but in either case it must be completed in its "entirety. You must bring the greatest exactness to all your bearings and multiply them as much "as you possibly can, for the perfection
of the plan of this bay and of its depth.
"If during your absence bad weather should force me to sail, you will find me again off "Cape Frederick Hendrick. Citizens Bernier, Depuche and Barbe are appointed to accompany you.
"You will not allow the munitions of war intended to ensure your defence and the safety of the longboat "to be disposed of in any manner or on any pretext whatever". Signed N. B".
Immediately after the departure of this boat, Captain Hamelin's longboat was ordered to proceed to Cap des Sarcelles, which forms the entrance of the channel between Maria Island and the mainland, and to follow the whole coast northwards so as to obtain a plan of it and of the coves along it.
The other boats were sent fishing and into Oyster Bay. But none had any luck. Those of the scientists who went ashore communicated with the natives and brought us back nothing new.
Citizen Maugé was in his death agony all day and ended his career towards eleven o'clock at night.

1802-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from NE to SE. The dinghy carried the sick ashore. At 3 squared our yards, following the commander's example. The dinghy came back from the fishing and brought a great quantity of crayfish.
1802-02-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, at daybreak, I gave orders for the yards to be topped a-cockbill on board and the flag hoisted at half-mast, so as to announce to Captain Hamelin the loss we had just suffered. I also sent him a note inviting him to ask those of his officers and naturalists who wished to attend the burial of our unfortunate fellow voyager to leave the ship when our boat set off.
At nine o'clock I embarked for the burial of a man whose death and last words filled me with grief, for a few moments before dying he said to me, "It is for having been too attached to you that I am dying and that I scorned the advice of my friends, but at least remember me in return for the sacrifice I have made for you".
As we left the ship, a discharge of all our guns was fired; when we were halfway from the ship to the land, a second took place, and on our landing on the shore, the third. The body of this naturalist was buried between two casuarinas and two eucalyptus trees, and on one of the former the following inscription, engraved on a lead plate, was placed:
Here was buried Citizen René Maugé, zoologist in the expedition of Discovery
under the command of Captain Baudin,
The expedition suffers an irreparable loss in the death of Citizen Maugé. This naturalist did not bear the title of scientist, but he did more on his own than all the scientists together. Wholly occupied with his work, he thought only of doing his duty well, and never did I have occasion to remonstrate with him on that score.
It is very painful for me to see that Citizen Riedelé and he, the only two true friends I had on board, should have become the victims of the friendship they bore me, the sole motive that led either of them to undertake this campaign, which proved so fatal to them.
After completing the burial of Citizen Maugé, at which I was accompanied by Captain Hamelin, several of his officers and some of the scientists, I went to examine a ravine discovered by the carpenters of the Naturaliste, in which
it was asserted there was no lack of fresh water. A beaten path, worn by the natives, soon led us to it, but we were astonished, after what we had been told of it, to find in a hole only a little stagnant water with an extremely insipid taste. All that could be drawn from it in the course of the day was three galley casks, besides what was consumed by those on shore. This torrent must nevertheless be considerable in the season of heavy rains.
Several natives had gathered round our people and had even put the carpenters to rout after pestering them a great deal. They even made a few attempts to take their axe from them. One of them, and it was the youngest, was led off by force into the wood. They contented themselves with examining him from head to foot without, moreover, doing him any harm; they did not even take his axe from him when the ceremony was over. When we arrived, the natives withdrew, and we had great difficulty in gathering them round us. However, we managed it with time and signs of friendship. All carried a spear and a kind of club, very roughly made and hardly capable of doing much harm when thrown from a short distance.
When we had succeeded in bringing them together, we recognised them as the same ones we had met the day before and on the day of our arrival. Confidence was soon restored, and the rest of the day was spent with them quite peaceably.
Citizen Ronsard, who had been ordered to ascertain whether the arm of the sea which the failing daylight had not allowed us to follow to its end was considerable, or whether it did not communicate with some reservoir of fresh water, declared that he had gone all round it and that the water was salt from one end to the other.
The natives of Île Marion [Maria Island] know the effect of our firearms just as well as those of the Détroit d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel], but they were not so much afraid of them, and the noise produced (by) the explosion made little impression on them. They asked M. Ronsard to shoot a few birds, which they went and picked up themselves and which were given to them. They lost no time in plucking them, and having grilled them a little at our people's fire, they ate them with a hearty appetite without wasting any of them, that is to say, guts and all.
At four o'clock I returned on board with Captain Hamelin, leaving everyone ashore and two boats to bring them back when they saw fit. The large boat came back the same day, and the geographer Boulanger is going to set about drawing up the plan of the island he has just been round.
Citizen Péron, having discovered a tomb, brought back from it several human bones and even some portions of flesh that the fire had not consumed. Citizen Leschenault likewise found another one, so that he seems not to doubt that the custom of burning the dead is practised by the inhabitants of this island and of the mainland. The tomb of which I give a detailed drawing, and (from) what we have seen, made with the greatest order and care, they are infinitely superior to all that is known of them, and one may say that they are more anxious to preserve and hand down the memory of their dead relatives or friends than to think of their own preservation.
Citizen Péron, who examined a tomb at his leisure, will give us a more exact description of it than what I could say from the report made to me, and the drawings of Citizen Petit will make up for whatever may be lacking.
During the night the sky was hazy and rainy. The winds south-east in strong gusts. The warp of fifty fathoms, which had been shortened to thirty during the day, which was fine, was veered out again.
1802-02-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW to SE and to N. Many crayfish were taken and given to the crew. At 5 p.m. Citizen Freycinet came in with the longboat; as she was making a great deal of water she was hoisted in at once to be repaired. Light rain during the night.

1802-02-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SE to N. At 5 the longboat came in from her expedition; she had surveyed from Cape des Sarcelles as far as the northernmost point of the Van Diemen's Land anchorage. She was making a great deal of water; she was hoisted in and put on the gratings to be repaired.
1802-02-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, in the morning, Captain Hamelin having come to see me, we went off in my boat to visit a small island to the north of our anchorage, which lies roughly in mid-channel between the mainland and Maria Island. We reached it at nine o'clock. As it is ringed all round with large rocks awash and a great many pebbles, landing there is not easy. We nevertheless went ashore and explored the whole of it. Not a tree nor a shrub is to be found on it; yet the soil covering the core of granite rocks of which it is formed is good and fit for vegetation. Everywhere we saw a kind of long, very fine grass which would doubtless make good pasture for cattle. The whole surface of this island, which is shaped like an O, is flat and may measure three hundred paces from east to west and one hundred and eighty from north to south. Everywhere one sees fragments of burnt oyster shells, ear shells, etc., which show that the natives stop there when crossing from one shore to the other. It was for (this) reason that I named this island Île du Repos.
From its middle we took the bearings of the land as follows:
The most prominent point to the north of Van Diemen's Land, north 3° east
The middle of a small islet in Oyster Bay, north south 65° east
The south-west point of Maria Island, south 35° east
Cape Frederick Hendrick, south 18° east
The land at the head of the bay
Cap des Sarcelles, south 3° west
A rock awash on the western side of Île du Repos, two cables offshore, north 65° west
Neither this island nor the shores of the coast yielding anything for natural history, we crossed the channel, made our way into Oyster Bay and landed on a low point in that part of it. There we saw three canoes of the natives, exactly like the one seen in the channel as to their shape. But they were made of bundles of rushes, arranged in the same way as those made of tree bark, and were smaller. We found there several large spears, which we took and which, from their great length, seemed to us better suited to fishing than to any other use.
While we were ashore we saw no natives, because they were in the other part of the bay with several of our people who happened to be there. At four o'clock we returned on board.
The boats that had been sent out fishing in the morning brought back few fish, but lobsters enough for every man to have one. This whole coast is in general poorly stocked with fish, at least to judge by our fruitless attempts to catch any.
During the day the sky was heavily overcast and the winds from east to south-east, a light breeze. In the night they shifted to the north and brought us rain.
1802-02-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a flat calm and continual rain. The dinghy went to Oyster Bay for oysters and brought back a full load.

1802-02-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm, continual rain. The dinghy came in loaded with oysters. At 7.45, having dragged in a squall, we veered 80 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, Captain Hamelin let me know that his longboat had returned, telling me that he would hand over to me for examination the plan that the officer who had had the
command of it had surveyed, and which he was busy writing up. A small river of fresh salt water had been discovered on that part of the coast, but the boats could not get into it.
Throughout the morning the weather was rainy and misty and the wind northerly, a light breeze. Three boats were nevertheless sent out fishing.
The evening was no finer than the morning had been, and the scientists who had gone ashore in the hope of seeing the natives came back without having met them. Our boats' fishing, too, was plentiful only in lobster and oysters, and the dredge brought up nothing of value for natural history.
In the night we had the wind southerly in gusts and, most of the time, calm. The rain was continual and heavy.
(in another hand)
1802-02-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 5 the dinghy left for Oyster Bay. At 7 the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 7.45 we dragged and veered cable. At noon the wind blowing hard from SSW, a high sea. At nightfall the wind and sea went down a great deal. A light was kept at the gaff on account of the dinghy.

1802-02-25.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from WSW. At sunset the wind and sea went down a great deal. Kept a light at the gaff all night to show our position to the dinghy. At 6.30 a.m. the captain embarked in his boat to go and meet her. At 10.30 a.m. the dinghy came in loaded with oysters.
1802-02-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, the wind held in the south and the sky looked very threatening. At about eight o'clock we had a heavy squall and much rain. The force of the wind made us drag our anchor; we veered 70 fathoms of cable without bringing the ship up, which obliged us to let go a second anchor. At ten o'clock the sky cleared and the sun appeared for a few moments, but not for long. The rain began again, and the rest of the morning was far from fine.
In the afternoon the rain was continual and heavy, the wind varied from south to south-south-west, and the sea grew rough. Since the morning the barometer had fallen to 27 in. 8 l., and everything foretold some squalls. However, a little before nightfall it rose again to 28 in. and the rain stopped. Nevertheless, as a precaution, we veered a hundred fathoms of our main cable and seventy of the other.
During the night the wind died away entirely and the sky became clear and fine.
1802-02-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 10.30 the dinghy came back loaded with oysters. The breeze from N to NNW.

1802-02-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to NNW. At 2 furled all sail. The dinghy went fishing. In the forenoon weighed the port anchor to inspect it; as soon as it was up we let it go again in 13 fathoms, fine sand. Obs. lat. taken ashore while at anchor 42° 42' 10"; long. 145° 54' 0".
1802-02-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, in the morning, we had the finest weather in the world and a calm. At daybreak we weighed our anchors and let go the starboard one which, as I had thought, was found not to be fouled. After this manoeuvre the boats were sent off to fish, and the scientists went ashore, as did the gardener.
During the morning we dried our sails, and the crew's clothes were put out to air.
We had no sight of our longboat, and I could not conceive the cause of her delay.
The weather continued fine in the evening, and we had a light breeze from the north-east. The swell raised by the strong wind of the day before had not yet entirely gone down, and the ship rolled a great deal.
At noon the latitude of the anchorage was observed to be 42° 42' 30". In the evening the weather continued fine, and so it remained during the night. At sunset we sighted our longboat returning from her mission, which gave me infinite pleasure. I think the work she was to carry out will be accurate, the time spent on it having been sufficient to do it to full satisfaction.
Our scientists, on their excursions, did not see the natives.
1802-02-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNW. The anchor was weighed and another let go in 13 fathoms, fine sand. The sick went ashore. At 11.30 Citizen Faure came in in the large boat. He had examined the supposed Schouten Islands and found only one and several small islets; what was taken for the Schouten Islands is only a very high peninsula joined to the land by a very low neck. The masts were swayed up and the topgallant sails bent. On the commander's signal the large boat was hoisted in. At nightfall the sick came back aboard. During the night the breeze from SW. Latitude of the anchorage 42° 38' 30"; longitude 145° 17' 17"; variation on Maria Island 11° 37' 0" NE.

1802-02-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNW. Swayed up the topgallant masts and squared the yards. On the commander's signal, hoisted in the large boat. At 9 got under way, a light breeze from NNE, standing SSE to weather the rocks off the SW point of Maria Island; at 10.30 went onto the port tack. Bearings taken at noon: the easternmost visible point of Maria Island N 38° E; an islet taken from the anchorage N 20° W; Cape Frederick Hendrik S 6° W; the southernmost visible cape of the Tasman Peninsula S 6° E. Obs. lat. at noon 42° 44' 4" south.
1802-02-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, at daybreak, the longboat came on board. From the verbal report made to me by the officer (In the margin this note: Citizen Freycinet of the Naturaliste: it is the only place offering any resources and the only port of call in bad weather, but the channel leading to it needs to be better known.) who had commanded her, I was entirely convinced that Frederick Henry Bay was wrongly placed on the Dépôt chart, as it was on the newly drawn English chart. And I could not conceive how it had been placed on the eastern side of the Tasman Peninsula. Unless that peninsula were really an island; but as we are now quite certain of the contrary, the plan given of it by Valentin, though inaccurate in detail, leaves no doubt that the bay which has been named Baie de Marion [Marion Bay] is the very one in which Tasman anchored on coming out of Storm Bay, and that he visited the inlet shown on his plan.
For the rest, I refer to M. Freycinet's report and his plan for fuller details.
No natives were seen during this excursion, but everywhere signs were found of the stays they sometimes make there.
At about eight o'clock I went ashore in Captain Hamelin's boat, and we returned on board at one in the afternoon, having sighted his large boat coming back from visiting the islands mentioned by Tasman, Furneaux and others, which lie on the chart to the north of Maria Island.
This boat, in which I had embarked Citizen Faure, geographical engineer, had orders to work up along the islands as far as 42° of latitude and to come back through the channels which they must form between themselves and Van Diemen's Land.
Citizen Faure took eight days to carry out this mission. He did indeed work up as far as the 42nd degree, always expecting to find some openings that would let him round these islands, and it was not without astonishment that he saw that only two exist, of little size: Schouten Island, and a rock forming a second, about a mile in extent.
On his way back he passed between Schouten Island and the rock I have just mentioned, and entered a large channel lying between the two lands, of which the eastern part presents islands. On reaching its northern end he found a deep bay and several coves offering shelter for a good anchorage, but no opening to the sea, any more than to the north; see his plan and his track.
It appears, from the detailed particulars given by M. Faure, that Tasman and Furneaux passed too far from the land to make it out properly, and that, seeing isolated hills, they took them for islands, being unable to see the low land joining them one to another. This error is often repeated at sea at any considerable distance, but the boat coasted along the whole of this shore too closely to have been deceived.
Having nothing more to do at Maria Island or in its neighbourhood, I ordered Captain Hamelin to be ready to get under sail the next morning, so as to make for the strait that separates Van Diemen's Land from New Holland.
During this stay we had cause to regret that we could find no place suitable for watering. Not that fresh water is lacking there; on the contrary, it is found in various parts of the main coast and even on Maria Island, except at the place indicated by the English; but it is impossible to take it in with boats.
The whole coast, from Cape Frederick Hendrick to the one we have named Cape (no name), is high and well wooded, and can easily be seen from ten to twelve leagues off when the horizon is not hazy, which is not usual in these waters. See the views of it that I have had taken.
In the afternoon the longboat was hoisted in and everything was made ready to get under sail the next morning, with the intention of making for the south point of Schouten Island by threading the Maria Island channel, if the winds allowed, for it has too little width and depth for a large ship to beat through it.
During the night the wind was calm and the sky very fine.
Particular remarks made during our stay in the Canal
de Bruny d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel], southern part of Van Diemen's Land,
and on our port of call at Maria Island.
The channel discovered and surveyed during the voyage of Rear-Admiral d'Entrecasteaux is unquestionably of great use to navigation, since it offers countless ports and resources, whether for ships with damage to repair or for those seeking only refreshments and a little rest. The only drawback it presents is the difficulty of taking in water there to replace what one would have consumed in getting there. Nevertheless we found several streams which it would be easy to lead down to the sea, if one were provided with everything needed to give them an outflow.
The place named Port des Cygnes [Port Cygnet], which I had carefully examined, is of the whole channel the one that seems most suitable for establishing a colony of Europeans.
The natives with whom we communicated in that port, and those of the Grande Anse where we lay at anchor, seemed to us of a gentle and peaceable character. They are generally of a good height, but not very well made. Their features have a particular character, and all bear an air of likeness which seems to indicate that the population is not large, at least on Île Bruny [Bruny Island], where we saw the greatest number of them together. Once we counted fifty-five of them, men, women and children all included. Although nearly all have thin legs and weak arms, they nevertheless appear strong and vigorous. All of them without exception have very wide mouths, with broad teeth, complete and regular. These seemed to the scientists to have been filed, but I believe that is a mistake, because the upper jaw closes squarely on the lower, so that they look like molars rather than cutting teeth. Their (eyes), though deep-set, are lively and their look uneasy, which may be caused by the difference that men so unlike themselves must have inspired in them. Their bellies are large, their hair woolly, but much less thick than that of Africans and not so long. The arms, shoulders and the part above the navel are tattooed in a fairly regular manner. This tattooing is done in a way rather hard to conceive, for the marks stand up above the skin. I leave it to our scientists to give the reason for it, but it seems to me that they use neither fire nor any cutting instrument to produce it, since the scars would then be sunk into the skin instead of standing well above it. Among these peoples tattooing seems to be practised only at a set age, for the children, even those of twelve to fifteen, bore no mark of it. Although their noses are flattened, they in no way resemble those of the negroes of Africa. Some, indeed, have long and well-proportioned noses. Among the children we noticed one who might well have had some European for a father; his skin was light brown, whereas the usual colour of these
islanders' skin comes much closer to that of the Caribs of America than to that of the Africans of the Guinea coast.
Although we saw several of them with their shoulders and chest covered with a kangaroo skin, they generally go naked, as far as the men are concerned. But all the women we saw wore skins which seem intended rather to form a kind of bag, in which they put what they are given or what they pick up as they walk.
The men have a rather singular habit, which greatly amused our sailors: that of almost always holding the end of their foreskin in their hand, and it is accordingly much elongated. These peoples, though savage and wandering, did not seem to me given to making war among themselves; or at least they bear no scars on their bodies that might lead one to suspect that they do so often. The only scars we saw on them were caused by fire. They also seem subject to a kind of yaws, for several had ulcers on their legs. We saw no mark of smallpox on their faces or bodies. Perhaps they are also fortunate enough not to know the great pox.
Their huts are the most wretched that could be imagined. A piece of wood bent in an arc forms the whole framework, which is covered with a few pieces of bark that they strip from the eucalyptus trees. All the signs of industry we saw among them consist of their spears and a club which is not very dangerous. The vessels they use for drinking is (sic) made of a kind of seaweed whose frond is very broad and thick. They also use it as a shoe when their feet are sore. The baskets which the women use for fishing is not without merit, for the long labour it must cost them. They accordingly set great store by them and part with them only reluctantly. The canoes they use to go from one place to another are rather a kind of float than anything else, and resemble those craft only in their shape, which is pointed at both ends and more raised than the rest. The one we found on the shore was 14 feet long from the tip of one point to the other. It was formed of three bundles of eucalyptus bark rolled one upon another and shaped like a yard, that is to say thicker in the middle than at the ends. These three bundles were joined together by ties of the same bark, which makes them fairly easy to assemble, but little to the use that can be made of it. The inside length of this frail craft was nine feet and one inch, its outside breadth two feet nine inches and its depth two feet two inches. We had several times seen them cross from one shore to the other in the channel, three and four persons at a time. They were not seen to use paddles, but long poles which they make serve instead. They usually crouch when propelling this sort of skiff, and we saw them venture out in it only in very calm, fine weather.
These peoples appear to draw their chief subsistence from the sea bottom and to live more particularly on shellfish than on anything else. They did not seem to us to think much of fish, and we could not get them to accept any, whether the fish taken alive in the seine or that which our people cooked for their dinner and which they saw them eat with good appetite. They likewise thought very little of our biscuit and of fresh bread. At first they accepted it and, imitating us, pretended to eat some, but as soon as we moved a little away from them they threw it aside. Some drank a little arrack, but in small quantity. The bottle that held it seemed to give them more pleasure than what was in it.
Among the various things we distributed to them, beads, hardware, etc., the buttons of our clothes seemed to please them more than all the rest.
Several got into our boats, perhaps with the design of taking whatever might be there to their liking, and did indeed lay hands on several things; but we met with no resistance from them when we made them give back what we did not wish to let them carry off. Some of the boatmen having stripped off their jackets to make them presents of them, they accepted them without allowing us to put them on their bodies. To show the use they meant to make of them, the jackets were afterwards found at the foot of a tree. Only, they had removed the buttons, which were of mother-of-pearl and not of metal.
At our first meeting, the natives of Île Bruny whom we met came to us upon mere demonstrations of friendship, or in the hope of obtaining some presents from us. They came forward unarmed, received our caresses with pleasure and what we gave them with great demonstrations of joy. They imitated readily and with gestures, repeated several French words distinctly, and followed us in our excursion over the country and along the shore. Although we were armed with muskets and sabres, they have a perfect knowledge of both these weapons and seem to dread their effects, of which, no doubt, one of their own will have been the victim.
The day before we left the Grande Anse, Citizen Maurouard, midshipman first class since our departure from Timor, received, at the moment when he least expected it, a spear thrust which went through him a little above the shoulder and gave him a fairly deep wound. It is rather difficult to say why it was thrown at him, for the whole morning had been spent with them, their wives and their children, on the best of terms.
On leaving the Grande Anse I went to Port Nord-Ouest [North West Bay], where I expected to take in water more easily than anywhere else, given the difficulty of carrying our casks to the places where it was to be found and which were known to us. We anchored a little inside the entrance of that port, and even made a rather long stay there only to fill a hundred casks with water that was unpleasant though drinkable. The stream that supplies it runs into the sea, but the number of banks and the shallowness of the water there prevent longboats and other boats from getting near it. One is obliged to make the empty casks into a raft to take them to the watering place and to bring them back full in the same way, which makes this work long and laborious for the crews and causes a considerable loss of time. It was on an island opposite the mouth of this stream that our observatory was set up. On our arrival in this port we saw many fires and much smoke, which showed us that it was fairly well inhabited. Yet for several days we saw none of the natives. However, on the third day after our arrival, some were seen on the cove of Île Bruny facing Pointe Gicquel. I went ashore at once to observe them and to give them some presents if we could communicate with them. As the boat approached they withdrew into the woods. But, appearing to pay no attention to them, I amused myself along the shore picking up a few shells. Soon they showed themselves again and little by little came near enough for us to speak to one another. By signs, and by showing a few glass beads, I urged them to join me. There were four of them, each with a spear in his hand, and I had my musket. We spent a good while inviting one another to come over, and seeing that they did not stir, I went to them. They waited for me very quietly, received my presents with pleasure,
and we began a conversation in gestures and a few words. Captain Hamelin, in whose boat I had come ashore, having joined me with two of his men, we all sat down on the grass. We had plenty of time to examine at our ease the natives, who differ in no way from those of the Grande Anse. On parting to return on board, at about three in the afternoon, we gave them to understand that we would come back the next day to the same place, promising them fresh presents if they would be there. But whether our return was not agreeable to them, or for some other reason, they assailed us with a hail of stones thrown very skilfully and even from a great distance. As we were embarking, several passed over the boat still travelling fast, and one struck me rather hard on the left hip. Although they were out of range of my musket, I took aim at them, and this movement having been enough to scatter them all, I was not obliged to let them hear its report. Before we parted, Captain Hamelin and I had taken the precaution of trading in exchange for Navy buttons, which they valued highly. A button stamped with an anchor was the price of a spear. This exchange was made in good faith and without cheating.
In spite of what had happened to us, we went ashore the next day, but in greater numbers. We found the natives again at the very spot we had pointed out to them. Only, the company was larger, for their wives and children were there. I gave them all glass beads, some buttons and other trifles. We were astonished to see the same men who had thrown stones at us the day before put themselves in our hands without the slightest sign of distrust, and that alone proves to me either that they are not wicked by nature or that they judged us incapable of doing them harm. As soon as we were all together, they were told to sit down, which they did at once, inviting us to do the same. Our people were mingled pell-mell with their wives and children, but I had beside me two men wholly taken up with watching all my movements and above all my musket. If I happened to shift it from left to right or from right to left, they at once looked uneasy and were ready to get up and go. Nevertheless it was not hard to reassure them, and confidence was soon restored. The children, who at our approach had seemed very fearful and timid, soon grew familiar and played all sorts of games with our people. They tried running and jumping against some of them, but they did not shine in any of these exercises. The women were not beautiful, and their kangaroo skins did nothing to lessen the impression their faces made on us.
During this meeting several hauls of the seine were made and we took a fair quantity of fish. The men and the children, with great demonstrations of joy, lent a hand in hauling the seine ashore, but they steadily refused to share with us the fish that was caught in it, making signs to us that they did not eat it. These fish were chiefly of the ray and plaice kinds and very good to eat. None of us shared the opinion of Mr Anderson on the one he named the elephant fish, better known as the Antarctic chimaera, and which he says was one of the best of those caught during his stay in Adventure Bay. On the contrary, in our view it is the worst of all those we took at the mouth of the channel and in the bay. We all dined ashore, seated among the natives, without being able to persuade them to take anything, but they received with great pleasure the empty bottles we gave them. I do not know whether they feared we would take them back at the moment of departure, but as soon as one was given them they passed it to their wives, who went and hid it in the wood and then came back to take their places among us.
I made one of them a present of a small mirror, which did not produce the effect I expected of it,
for after looking at herself in it for a moment she passed (it) to another, who made no use of it. The fair ones, like the men, had their faces daubed in various ways, either with crushed charcoal or with a kind of dark red ochre. They likewise painted several of our scientists, who lent themselves with good grace to this whim of theirs. This ceremony greatly amused the onlookers and drew great bursts of laughter from the natives.
During that day a fairly large number of words were collected which are not found in La Billardière's vocabulary.
Our parting, before sunset, passed without incident and was much friendlier than that of the day before.
Every day that we remained in the channel, waiting for the wind to let us get out of it, we saw them and talked with them on the shore or a little way inland, but they never offered to take us to see their camp, and when we asked them to lead us there they answered: I do not understand you.
In my journal I give several drawings of the faces and dress of these peoples, as well as a model of their huts and their canoes.
The quality of the soil in this southern part of the great island of Van Diemen is everywhere fit for cultivation, and its goodness would guarantee the success of the harvests if active and industrious people applied themselves to it. The eucalyptus and the casuarina are the dominant trees there. As several persons have already described them, I shall not speak of them. The plants in general show little variety, insects are very rare, and kangaroos uncommon and hard to hunt. The woods are full of three or four sorts of parakeets and of two species of crows, of which we have a good supply for the natural history cabinet. The mosquitoes are not so numerous nor so troublesome as in America, but there is a large, very annoying fly, extremely abundant, whose bite is painful. Small birds are not plentiful and, with the exception of a kind of swallow that perches on the trees, the others are seen only here and there.
Sea birds are more plentiful there, but harder to approach than land birds. Of the latter we could procure only two swans and a superb black and white pelican.

Note: the thermometer varied, in the morning from 7° 8 to 14°, at noon from 14° to 22° and in the evening from 12° to 15°. At noon the hygrometer almost always stood between 65 & 80, but morning and evening it often went up to 97°.
During our stay at Port NO we had some fine days, but in general the sky was overcast and often very misty. The winds blew more from the quarter
from north to south by the east than from north to south by the west, but we sometimes had gusts and squalls from this latter quarter so strong that two bower anchors and more than a hundred fathoms of cable could hardly hold us. The sea, however, is never very rough and the holding ground is very good. The winds from east to south are light and bring much mist. Those from the south-west often bring rain, and those from west to north fine weather.
Of Maria Island and of the bay called Baie de Marion [Marion Bay].
On leaving the Canal d'Entrecasteaux, we were obliged to weather Cap Raoul [Cape Raoul] close-hauled, the winds having been constantly south-east, varying to east; having shifted during the night to south-west and south, we found ourselves in the neighbourhood of Cape Pillar and in the morning rounded the little Tasman Island. Then steering north, a little towards the west, we ranged very close along the eastern side of the great island of Van Diemen, passing through the middle of the channel between it and the Rochers d'Hyppolite [Hippolyte Rocks]. This whole coast, of which I give views from point to point, presents a very pleasing aspect and one of the most picturesque that can be met with.
Cape Pillar is sparsely wooded and consists only of granite rocks heaped one upon another in very irregular shapes. The same is true of little Tasman Island.
From Cap des Organistes to Cape Frederick Hendrick the coast is generally high and very steep-to; with a good wind one may range along it within short cannon-shot without any fear. The large rocks sometimes seen off the points are in no way dangerous; there is plenty of water everywhere. This part is as well wooded as that of the Canal d'Entrecasteaux, and its greenery seemed to us more pleasing. This is perhaps because the natives, frequenting it less, the trees there are not half burnt as they are everywhere else. The eucalyptus and the casuarina seemed to predominate everywhere.
The channel between Cape Frederick Hendrick and Maria Island is fine and deep. Bottom is first found in 30 and 25 fathoms only when one has rounded the south-west cape of that island. Then it shoals quickly, and there are no more than eight and nine fathoms at the entrance of Oyster Bay. It was abreast of this bay that we anchored, on the second day after leaving the Canal d'Entrecasteaux.
From the very first day that we went ashore, we communicated with the natives who inhabit this island. There were twenty-three of them, men, women and children. They received us in a friendly way and without the slightest distrust. Each of them nevertheless had a spear and was on the defensive, but the presents I gave them soon reassured them, and mutual confidence was soon established between them and us.
The natives seemed to us much stronger and more robust than those of the Canal d'Entrecasteaux or of Île Bruny. They are in general taller and better made. Perhaps they have more means of subsistence, or less trouble in procuring it. But their women are no more agreeable than the others, and their children more fearful and less trusting than those of Île Bruny. There is no doubt that they are the same people, as much from their language as from their habits. The same way of covering themselves with kangaroo skins, of building their huts and of feeding themselves is common to them, except that these ate the birds we gave them, whereas the others would not accept any. They thought no more than their fellows of our biscuit, bread and arrack, but they had the same desire for our bottles, for glass beads and the khaki buttons; they hesitated for a long time, however, before trading their spears.
Their canoes, though of the same shape, are not made of bundles of tree bark; rushes take its place, arranged in the same way.
One of the most remarkable things we discovered, by a happy chance, is the manner in which they bury their dead. I give a drawing of their tombs, but there is no doubt that they burn the dead and keep the ashes and the bones that the fire has not destroyed, preserving them with care. The two that we found and which were dug open presented a sight that greatly surprised us. First a kind of hut in the shape of a sugar loaf had to be taken apart. The eucalyptus bark forming it rested on four tree branches bent into a semicircle and stuck into the ground by their ends. Above these four hoops, which formed roughly the bottom of a basket, were found two or three layers of fine grass, of a kind very common on this island and which must be good pasture for cattle. On lifting this grass we found a heap of ashes, among which were several bones of a human body and even some portions of flesh that the fire had not yet consumed. At the end of the heap of ashes was a small channel, which is in all likelihood the one in which they place the corpse to which they pay the honours of burial. We were all the more delighted with this find because no traveller has told us anything on the subject, at least nothing that has come to my knowledge.
Citizen Péron, in his capacity as Observer of Man, will doubtless give a very detailed account of the form of this tomb, as well as his ideas on the cause of this custom among these peoples, a custom very different from that practised in the islands of the South Sea.
During our stay on this island we added a good many new words, carefully collected, to our little vocabulary. The natives of this country did not seem to us to have been often visited by Europeans, and we found among them, unlike those of Île Bruny, no object received from them. We (in the margin: again on M. Freycinet's plan) managed to learn from them the place where they go for fresh water, and it is certainly not the spot indicated by Mr Cox on the plan he drew of this island. The two streams they showed us run into the sea in the Baie de l'Est, across the middle of which there is a fearful bar whenever the winds are at all from north to south by the east. Our firearms did not make as much impression on the natives as on those of Île Bruny. The noise of the report caused them only a moment's surprise, and they showed astonishment only on seeing the blood flow from the birds they begged us to kill for them, which they ate at once without gutting them, merely leaving them in the fire until the feathers were well burnt, which did not take long.
During our stay at Maria Island, Captain Hamelin's boat had orders to work up as far as the 42nd degree of latitude to survey the islands drawn on Mr Flinders's chart after Furneaux. It found only the one named Schouten Island by Tasman, and another smaller one which might be named Île des Veaux marins, since it is covered with seals. The channel separating these two islands is narrow but deep. The land to the north is joined to the great island of Van Diemen and forms a deep bay, on each side of which are various coves offering good shelter.
The Naturaliste's longboat was likewise sent to examine the whole coast the coast (sic) from Cap des Sarcelles to the south point of Schouten Island, where the boat's work was to begin.
I sent my own to survey and examine with the most scrupulous attention Baie de Marion. For, from what I knew of Tasman's voyage, it seemed impossible to me to believe that the bay he named Frederick Henry was the one placed on the Dépôt chart, being already quite sure that the land which has been named Tasman's Island is a peninsula joined to the mainland by an isthmus, of no great size, it is true, but fairly high and rather well wooded. The report of the officer who had
command of her confirmed this conjecture, which is fully demonstrated by the plan I have had drawn of this part of the coast, beginning from Cap des Sarcelles as far as the cape of Frederick Henry Bay.
My large boat was employed in going round Maria Island to check Mr Cox's survey of it.
We had no luck with fishing at this port of call. The fish we took there was very good, it is true, but not plentiful. It was not the same with oysters and a kind of lobster, for every day more were taken than the crew could eat. The oysters were of good quality, but the lobsters far superior to those eaten in Europe for the delicacy and lightness of their flesh. It appears that the natives make these two things their chief resource for food, for everywhere one comes upon heaps of remains which show how great a quantity of them they consume.
We bought from the natives of this island some very large spears, such as we had not seen until then. They gave us to understand that they used them for hunting the kangaroo. They gave no great proof of skill in throwing those they commonly use. Only one hit the mark aimed at, once, at a distance of fifteen to twenty paces.
They also showed us how they sharpen them. It is first with a stone, which they use as we would a piece of glass, and to give them a polish they use an oyster shell that they have made sharp.
Our gardener gave one of them a pruning knife, showing him how he should use it. He made the same use of it as of his stone, and gave it back to him when he took up his oyster shell to finish his work.
These peoples appear to have no knowledge of iron or of its usefulness. They paid not the slightest attention to the nails we tried to give them, and returned them to us as a useless thing.
The son of the Naturaliste's master carpenter having been led off by force into the wood, they contented themselves with examining him from head to foot, without doing him any harm. And after satisfying their curiosity, they let him go free to rejoin his companions. This young man was carrying a large axe, which did not tempt them in the least, although they had watched with great attention the way he used it.
One of the Géographe's ship's boys was likewise examined by these peoples, in the presence of Citizen Péron. The natives found him so happily endowed that they showed great joy and satisfaction.
Results of the astronomical observations etc. made at Maria Island
(neither text nor figures)
SEA JOURNAL
of NICOLAS BAUDIN
Volume 4
ARCHIVES NATIONALES, SÉRIE MARINE, 5 JJ 39
DEPARTURE FROM MARIA ISLAND FOR BANKS STRAIT
On the eighth, at about eight in the morning, we got under sail to leave the Maria Island channel by the south, with a very faint light breeze from the north. I should much have liked the winds to allow me to pass to the north of the island and go out by the channel between it and Schouten Island, but it was not possible.
We had scarcely made half a league when we found (ourselves) in a flat calm, but as the ebb was still running we let ourselves drift to the south, hoping that the flood would bring us a little wind. Nevertheless a kedge anchor was got ready for anchoring, in case it should be needed.
At eleven o'clock a faint breeze from the south-east began to be felt and, as we rounded the south-west point of Maria Island, it gathered strength and drew more to the east. The tack we were then on was taking us into Baie de Marion, but we did not go in, because as soon as the south point of Maria Island had been rounded the winds varied from north-east to north-north-east, a pleasant breeze, so that we passed at a fair distance from Cape Frederick Hendrick. We held on the tack to the north towards the east until midnight in very fine weather, but with the winds dead against the course we needed to make to reach the forty-second degree of latitude, where the survey of this part of the coast carried out by Citizen Faure, geographer on board the Naturaliste, came to an end.
When one enters the Maria Island channel to come and anchor abreast of Oyster Bay, bottom is first found in 28 or 30 fathoms only when one is inside the south-west point of that island. The land in this part is high, lofty, well wooded and pleasant to look upon.
The bight of Oyster Bay is fairly deep and offers a fine beach of white sand, but there is very little water in it, and ships of our draught would not be safe in this bay if they happened to drag their anchors in west or south-west winds, and it would be extremely difficult to beat out of it. Opposite the north point of this bay there is a small island shaped like an A, as I have already observed. It is through the channel it forms with Maria Island that one must pass to go out by the north. This route can be attempted only with winds that allow one to keep the middle of the channel. Otherwise one would run the risk of becoming embayed and perhaps even of running aground. Should one have to beat and the ship miss stays, the distance from one shore to the other is three quarters of a league, or a league at most.
The land opposite Maria Island is high and well wooded; there are various fairly deep coves there, but they are ill suited to offer shelter, for the winds from north to east blow straight into them and make the sea very rough, especially when they are opposed to the set of the current. The port found by (in the left margin: Citizen Freycinet of the Naturaliste is the only place offering some resources and a place of refuge in bad weather, but the channel leading to it needs to be better known).
During our stay at this anchorage we saw no smoke along the whole stretch of this coast, a proof that it is inhabited only at certain times.
1802-02-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from SSW which hauled to south and east and settled at NNE. At 9 got under way and shaped our course S 22° 30' E to double the SW point of Maria Island. At 10.30 the air drew round to SSE; we were taken aback and lay close-hauled on the port tack, standing for Cape des Sarcelles. The breeze freshened, drawing aft as far as north. At noon, being in 42° 44' 4" of latitude, we took the bearing of the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 38° E, the islet in the channel N 20° W, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 6° W, and the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 6° E. At 4, Schouten Island N 6° W, Maria Island from N 27° W to N 61° W, Tasman Island S 20° W. At 6, the NE point of Maria Island N 45° W, Tasman Island S 43°, Cape Pillar S 47° W. At 10, not seeing the Géographe, we showed a light at the foremast head; it stayed there until 11.45 without her answering.

1802-02-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NNE to N and NW. Took the bearing of the middle of Schouten Island N 6° W; the visible north part of Maria Island N 27° W; the south point of the same island N 61° W; Little Tasman Island S 20° E. At 9 p.m. sounded without finding bottom at 80 fathoms.
1802-02-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six in the evening, the nearest land to the south of Cape Pillar, south 43° west
The easternmost point of Maria Island, north 42° west
The most prominent land to the north, north 22° 30' east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, we stood on the northern board from the west from midnight until eight in the morning, in order to close with the land and follow it closely should the fair wind set in. But nothing came of it, and after sunrise the winds settled between north and north-west, falling off in strength as the sun rose above the horizon.
At daybreak we sighted the land, and from the position of Maria Island relative to us we recognised that the currents had carried us a long way to the south since our departure. At eight o'clock we went about and stood out to sea, hauling as close to the wind as possible on a course east towards the north.
During the morning the sky, though fine, was laden with damp vapours which at times brought us mist and calm.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 43° 4' 31", which confirmed that the currents had carried us much farther to the south than the dead reckoning of our run indicated. The longitude given by the timekeeper placed us in 146° 14' 37". Although the land was perfectly visible, we were too far off to take any useful bearings of it.
In the afternoon we continued to steer east towards the north. The wind, which had fallen off a good deal, freshened again into a fine breeze, but it was from the north and too contrary to the course we had to make for us to be pleased with it. The sea became swelling, and at sunset the sky was covered by a rather thick mist.
From several azimuths taken on board in the morning, the variation of the needle was found to be 11° 30' north-east. But this observation seems doubtful to me, as I do not believe it to be so great.
During the night of the ninth to the tenth, the weather was not fine. We were struck by several strong gusts which made us lower the topsails, and we took in another reef. At times the rain was heavy, and the mist continual. We did not alter course during the night; the winds made it no better on one tack than on the other.
1802-02-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to NW. At midnight the Géographe was sighted. At noon in 42° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 146° 33' 0" of longitude by the watches. Took the bearing of the NE point of Maria Island N 41° W and Tasman Island S 47° W. At 5.15, 10° 58' 40" of NE variation; at 6.30, 11° 19' 10" the same. Fine rain and thick mist during the night.

1802-03-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from north. At 10.30 p.m. we lost sight of the commander; kept a light all night. At 1.45 a.m. we sighted him ahead and at very little distance; crowded sail to close him. At 8 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, the winds were constantly between north and north-east throughout the morning, and the sky extremely damp and hazy. The sea, which had been rather heavy during the night, was now stirred only by a slight swell from the north-east. The breeze too had fallen off a good deal.
At eight o'clock we stood on the north-west tack to close with the land, although the weather was better suited to taking us away from it than to coming in to make it. But on the other hand, I did not wish to find myself too far out to sea when the wind turned fair, which might happen at any moment.
At noon we had no observation; on the contrary, the sky grew hazier than it had yet been, and we had a fair amount of rain.
By dead reckoning of the courses run, we were in 42° 54' south latitude and in the 147th degree of longitude east of Paris.
In the afternoon the weather seemed inclined to clear. The rain stopped towards four in the evening, and the haze lifted at sunset. Although our horizon was then fairly wide, we saw nothing of the land, which made me fear that the currents had carried us much further to the south-east than we supposed, all the more since this had happened to us on the first day after our departure.
At eight o'clock we went about to spend the night in the offing. The Naturaliste did likewise. The sky was then fine, but the rapid movement of the hygrometer towards very great humidity soon showed us that the fine weather would not last long. The barometer, however, stood high enough for us to have nothing to fear from heavy weather, which did not seem to be as close upon us as the hygrometer announced.
At midnight, the wind being north, variable N by NW, a strong breeze and in gusts, the sky was covered with so thick a fog that we could scarcely see one another. This heavy fog lasted about half an hour and then grew less dense. But our horizon extended hardly more than a quarter of a league. From time to time we caught sight of the Naturaliste, a little to leeward and near enough not to part company.
1802-03-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Misty and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW and NNE. At noon in 42° 39' 38" of latitude observed and in 147° 49' 54" of longitude by account. At 5, 10° 11' 0" of NE variation.

1802-03-02.journal_anonyme: Misty and rainy weather, a fresh breeze from north. At 8.15, after missing stays twice, wore onto the port tack. At 6.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Variation by azimuths 12° 33' 10 NE
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, the winds were the same as on the preceding days, that is to say, dead against our course. At six o'clock we went about to stand in towards the land. The sea was beginning to grow swelly and the breeze uneven. The damp and the haze of the night had cleared somewhat. The state of the sky promised us good observations in the morning and at noon. But none of these fine hopes came to anything. The haze returned towards ten o'clock and did not let us see the sun again for the rest of the day.
At noon, by our dead reckoning, we were in 41° 58' south latitude and 146° 39' east longitude. The hygrometer then stood at 98° 30 and did not seem likely to stop there. The barometer had also fallen a little, though not so as to announce bad weather.
In the afternoon we continued to run in towards the land until six in the evening. Our horizon extended about a league, and that seemed to me sufficient to have no fear of coming upon it unexpectedly. We saw nothing of it on this tack. Although the Naturaliste was fairly close to us, it often happened that we could not see each other, which decided me to make her the signal to go about by firing swivel guns.
During the evening a great quantity of large molluscs had been seen drifting past the ship, like those we had often seen stranded along the shore. We also met with many clumps of seaweed. All these signs led us to believe that we were not very far from the coast, and that on the next day's run I should be able to sight it, if the weather allowed us to approach it.
During the night the sky was fairly fine, though a thick haze ringed the horizon; the winds varied from north to north by west, moderate, and we stood on the eastern tack under little sail, the Naturaliste in our wake at a short distance. The sea had become smooth, though a heavy swell from the north-east was still felt.
During the day, the decks and 'tween decks had been fumigated throughout the ship to renew the foul air which the great humidity must have brought into them.
1802-03-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Very misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NNE. At noon in 42° 17' 41" of latitude observed and in 147° 36' 30" of longitude by account. In the afternoon the bell was rung every quarter of an hour and swivel guns fired. The 12th [Ventôse, 3 March 1802]. Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 8.15, 9° 28' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 41° 50' 20" of latitude observed and in 147° 33' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 a flat calm; at 3.15 the breeze got up from the SE. We lay under topsails with the yards square, making short boards to starboard and port to wait for the commander, who had signalled no course. At 7.15, being within hail, he ordered us to lie close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails until midnight; from midnight to 4 to steer S 22° 30' W; and that then, if the weather allowed, we should bear away west to close the land. Should he lie to, he was to warn us by a swivel gun. From 8 until midnight the commander showed us a light every half hour.

1802-03-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from north. A smooth sea, a very thick fog; rang the bell to make ourselves heard by the commander. At 6.30 changed tacks on the commander's signal.
1802-03-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, there was no sign of any change in the wind, which still held between north-east and north-west, and the sky was extremely hazy. At four o'clock we had stood on the north-west tack to close with the land during the day, should the sky clear a little. The breeze was very light in the morning, and we often lost sight of the Naturaliste although she was only a very short distance from us.
At noon we had a flat calm, the ship scarcely answering her helm. By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 41° 47' 58" south latitude and 146° 34' east longitude.
In the afternoon the winds shifted to the south-east, a pleasant breeze, but the sky grew no clearer for it. We steered north by compass and made fairly good way until eight o'clock. The Naturaliste, which I had spoken at about half past seven, was informed that at eight o'clock we would come to the starboard tack until midnight and would stand close-hauled under the topsails; that at midnight we would go on the larboard tack under the same canvas until daybreak, and that we would then bear west to come and make the land, if the weather was clear and suitable for approaching it. I also warned her that should we heave to or lie to, this manoeuvre would be signalled to her by two swivel-gun shots.
That ship's estimated latitude was the same for her as for us, but she placed herself much further to the east.
At eight o'clock we trimmed the sails on the larboard tack as had been agreed. We kept that ship in sight until eleven o'clock by means of the lights we showed each other every hour, but then we lost sight of her entirely, the haze having become too thick.
A little before midnight the winds shifted to the east, a pleasant breeze. We were taken aback and came round on the same tack until the hour appointed for changing it. At midnight we trimmed on the larboard tack and steered south-south-east. The winds varied little for the rest of the night, but the sky was so hazy and damp that one could scarcely see from the bow to the stern of the ship. The winds were light and we made little way during the four hours.

1802-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south and SSW.
