At 4 went onto the starboard tack to close the commander; he ordered us to keep close-hauled on the starboard tack until midnight, and from midnight to 4 to steer SSW. Overcast weather during the night and the wind a strong breeze in puffs. At 6.30 we lost sight of the commander.
1802-03-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Eclipse of the sun at 2 h 13' 49" for the beginning. Its end was not visible to us, the sky being too overcast with clouds.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the thirteenth, the winds were in the east and still very variable, or rather, we had almost a calm in the morning and a constantly hazy sky. Nothing was seen of the Naturaliste in the morning, nor during the various clear spells that occurred in the course of the day. I was beginning to fear that Captain Hamelin, whom I had told the day before that we would steer south-south-west, had taken this notice too literally and had not observed that the winds were then in the south-east. But as I could not fail to meet him on the coast, which we were to close with as soon as the weather turned fine and clear, I was not uneasy about it.
At noon the sun showed itself a little. We observed its altitude, which gave 41° 30' 30". This result, though very doubtful, agreed tolerably well with our dead reckoning, which placed us in 41° 28' 40".
In the afternoon we had good reason to regret that the state of the sky did not allow us to observe completely the beginning and the end of an eclipse of the sun which took place. It began at two hours thirteen minutes forty-nine seconds and was very long. We watched this eclipse until nearly half past three, but the sky having become entirely overcast, we could not learn the time at which it ended. This eclipse was not central for us, in that we were too far advanced to the east. While it lasted, the sky grew rather dark. On a fine day this spectacle would have been most pleasing.
Towards evening the weather seemed inclined to clear, and the horizon was fairly wide. As it was thought that the Naturaliste had been sighted, two rockets were sent up at nightfall, which were not seen, supposing she had indeed been sighted, for no answer was made.
During the night we made two boards. The sky became cloudy, and finer for us than we had had it since our departure from Maria Island. The breeze was very uneven and the winds variable from south-east towards east.
1802-03-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a light breeze from ESE to SSE. At midnight went onto the port tack, the course S 22° 30' W. The commander, on the same tack, then bore from us N 11° W; at 12.15 we lost sight of him to the north. We sent up several rockets without his answering. At 4 shaped the course west. At 6.15 the Géographe was sighted in the S 45° E, and at 6.30 further south. We then shaped the course S 22° 30' W; having lost sight of her again, we resumed the course west. The mist very thick; we fired several swivel guns without answer. At noon in 41° 29' 52" of latitude observed and in 147° 11' 0" of longitude by account. At 3, in a clear interval, we saw an eclipse of the sun for about 2 minutes. At 6.15 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack under topsails. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, almost calm from the SSW. At 1 the breeze got up from the ESE and freshened steadily. At 6 sighted the land in the west, and at 6.30 sighted the commander in the ENE. We fired three swivel guns to make ourselves seen.
1802-03-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the fourteenth, in the morning, the horizon was fairly good although the weather was overcast and squally. At seven o'clock it became clearer and we sighted the land to the west. Shortly afterwards the Naturaliste was seen, and we closed with her. We continued to steer for the land, hugging the wind as closely as possible, my intention being to begin an exact survey of it from the 42nd degree of latitude, the point at which the geographer Faure had stopped when I sent him to find out whether the channel marked on the charts was navigable.
At noon the observed latitude was 41° 33' 36", but we had no hour angle to learn the longitude given by the timekeepers.
During the evening we beat to windward, tack upon tack, to work up to the south, and I hoped that with whatever wind there might be during the night we could expect to reach, by the next day, the latitude at which I intended to begin our work. This hope was not fulfilled. A little before sunset we fell calm, and it lasted for the greater part of the night, which was fine with a clear sky. We were about a league and a half from the coast when the calm set in, but as there was always a little breath of air from time to time, we steered south-east whenever the ship gathered a little way.
At seven o'clock the bottom was forty-eight fathoms, sand, broken shells and small fragments of coral, nevertheless very suitable for anchoring in case of need. At eight o'clock the bottom was the same.
In the watch from eight to midnight it decreased by five fathoms, and we never had more than that until daybreak. We sounded every hour, for fear of being set on the coast by the currents or the tide.
All the land we saw during the day, both south and north of St Patrick's Head, is very high, well wooded and of a pleasant aspect. I (took) no views of it at that time, preferring to make them when coming back up from south to north. The whole coast in this part appears very clear of dangers, and no doubt, when there is a wind, one may approach it more closely than we were, although we could distinguish perfectly the shore, which appears to be of sheer rocks.
1802-03-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to E. At 2 went onto the port tack, the course S 67° 30' W. At daybreak crowded sail and shaped the course N 56° 15' W. At 6 land was sighted to the west, and at 6.30 the Géographe in the ENE; we fired swivel guns so that she might see us. At noon in 41° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' of longitude by account. The land in sight from S 4° W to N 33° W. At 7 a flat calm; the Géographe, out of sight, did not answer the lights we showed.

1802-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE to east and NE. At 4 took the bearing of the southernmost visible end S 8° E; the northernmost visible end N 16° W. At 4 went about onto the starboard tack. At 9 a.m. we came up with the commander, who told us he was going to send a boat to the coast; he ordered us to keep close-hauled. At 10.15 the commander hove to and put his boat in the water. We then lay close-hauled on the port tack.
1802-03-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ when it had passed, and a swivel gun was fired when every half hour. In spite of all these precautions, it was not seen coming back during the night.
At nine o'clock, Captain Hamelin having passed under our stern, I had him asked to repeat the signals we made, so that a greater number might be better seen or heard. It was all to no purpose.
It would be hard to explain why that ship fell aboard us and broke our spritsail yard. She had passed to leeward with every sail set, carrying a great deal of way. Apparently the officer of the watch meant to weather us by a clever manoeuvre of his own devising, and, having misjudged the distance, ran her head into our fore shrouds. Fortunately we bore away in time to keep from smashing against each other.
From the Fourteenth to the Fifteenth
On the fifteenth, in the morning, we had the winds north-east, a light breeze, and almost calm. At daybreak we found ourselves about two short leagues from the land, in 43 fathoms, bottom of sand and broken shells. We steered south-south-west east and south-east to run along the coast until daylight allowed us to make it out clearly.
At sunrise we stood closer in to ascertain its direction and the outline it may have in this part. The land here is very high and presents to the eye several ranges of well-wooded mountains of pleasant aspect. As by our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in the 42nd degree of latitude, I wished to make sure whether or not the islands seen by Captain Furneaux existed. I was well (in the margin: persuaded) by what he himself says of this land that he had seen it only from a great distance, since he describes it as low land, but that was not enough to settle the existence of these islands. Notwithstanding the report of Citizen Faure, geographer on board the Naturaliste, whom I had sent expressly to visit them, I continued south as far as 42° 12' without meeting any. It is true that, although I ran along this coast much closer than any navigator has done, I was for a moment deceived by appearances; but I soon saw, as I advanced southwards, that what I had taken for an island was nothing other than a very lofty mountain which juts out towards the sea and ends there in a sudden fall on its southern side. On the northern side, however, it joins the mainland, or rather another mountain, by a very low neck of land, although one wholly covered with trees. Given this, it is not surprising that it should have appeared as an island to Captain Furneaux, if he passed only two leagues off it, since we, who were much closer to the coast than he was, were for a moment in doubt as to what it might be.
In the morning, the weather being very fine and clear and the breeze moderate, I had my longboat hoisted out and gave the command of it to Maurouard, midshipman of the first class. Our geographer, Citizen Boulanger, who unfortunately is very short-sighted and can take bearings and angles only when he has his nose right up against the land, embarked in it in order to get nearer to the coast than can be done with a large ship. I charged him most expressly, before he left, to return on board before nightfall and to keep such a position relative to us as not to lose sight of us. All these precautions were in vain. At noon he could no longer be seen. No doubt he ran in so far towards the land that he did not stop until he had no means of getting any closer to it.
At noon the observed latitude was 42° 10' 44", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us (in) 146° 9' 21". We then went about to close with our boat and stood in towards the land until we were too close to approach it further, without catching sight of the boat. At four o'clock we went about to gain a little offing, and at five we stood in again towards the land. The breeze was then rather strong, and I was very vexed that my boat was absent, having no sight of it. From six o'clock to eight we made two more boards and had no better luck. It was not seen.
As it had been agreed that it would be back before nightfall, I decided to heave to under the topsails. The breeze was then less strong and the sky fine. Lights were lit to show it our position, and every hour a rocket was sent up $$$ (see page 14)
1802-03-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to N. At 3.30 the commander was sighted in the S by SE. At 5, 7° 10' 42" of NE variation; at 8, 7° 35' 0" the same. At 9.45 we spoke the commander; he told us he was going to send his large boat to the coast and that meanwhile we should stand off and on. At noon in 42° 10' 9" of latitude observed and in 146° 49' 36" of longitude by account. The north end of Maria Island S 20° W, the north end of Schouten Island S 38° W, the Schouten isthmus S 81° W. At 5 p.m., in going about, when the after sails were shifted, the main topgallant brace not having been let go, the yard broke in the middle. At 8 the Géographe showed a light at her masthead; she then bore from us N 56° E on the port bow. At 8.15 she sent up a rocket; we were to windward of her and very close; she still had her light and was lying to. We bore away before the wind and hauled to the wind to leeward of her under all sail. She was ordering us to repeat the signals she would make for her boat, which had not yet returned. As we ran alongside her — fortunately she got off with her spritsail yard and we with our crossjack yard, both of which broke. At 11 our damage was repaired. We sent up rockets and fired a swivel gun to imitate the commander, whom we lost sight of at 10 in the S 56° W.

1802-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, the sea smooth, keeping the same tack as the commander. At 8.15 he sent up a rocket; we were ahead of him. He was then lying to; we bore away to pass under his lee. The commander ordered us to repeat what they should do at the same instant; his spritsail yard fouled our main shrouds, and his jib boom caught our crossjack yard and broke it. We set about repairing the damage.
1802-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, having kept all night a short distance off the coast in the hope of seeing my boat come back, and making signals to it, as I have already said, every half hour to show it my position, I closed with the land to a mile and a half at most, and often less, in order to find it. To do so the more surely, I began a close search at the very point where it had landed, then working back up to the north. I thought that the fair wind it had had the day before might have led Citizen Boulanger to break the explicit order I had given him the day before to be back before nightfall. The fine weather that had passed, and the happy prospect of its lasting all this day as well, did not, however, lessen my anxiety, for I feared that in trying to land to spend the night his boat might have suffered some damage.
After reaching the great cape which I have named cap Pelé, because it is utterly bare of greenery, I came to examine at very close range the one the English have named St Patrick's Head, running along the coast at the distance I have just mentioned, and we saw absolutely nothing that could make us suspect that it was in this part.
At noon we observed 42° 4' 45" of latitude, and the longitude given by our timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 146° 4' 28". The weather being still fine and the sea smooth, with winds from north to north-north-west and north-west, I did not go about until it was no longer possible to approach the coast any further, taking care to make the offshore boards very short, so that the boat could never lose sight of the ship if it was in these waters. On the inshore board, which was longer in the evening than in the morning because the winds shifted to west by north-west, guns were fired every quarter of an hour, and the mountains echoed them so that they must have been heard almost to the extremities of the island. Nevertheless, I had the sorrow of seeing the sun set without anything being sighted. I then placed myself halfway between St Helens Point and St Patrick's Head. Towards eight o'clock, having seen a fire which appeared to me to be very close to the shore, I did not doubt that it was our people showing us their position by this means, the more so as it was very well kept up all night. Accordingly I gave orders that it should not be lost sight of, which made us heave to under our topsails, now on one tack, now on the other. It appears, however, that the currents set us to the east, for the soundings, which were 55 fathoms at eight in the evening, had gone to 75, sand and broken shells mixed with some madrepores.
For a while we feared we were in for bad weather, for a very dark cloud from the south brought us so heavy a gust that we were obliged to furl our topsails and lie to under the fore topmast staysail and the mizzen staysail. As this squall came to us over the land, I was not uneasy about the boat on its account, not supposing it to be at sea then. The strong wind lasted until midnight, after which it moderated, and the sea, which was beginning to run high, soon became smooth again, as did the sky, which remained very clear for the rest of the night.
I was very unwell during the day, and the anxiety that the absence of my boat gave me was not likely to restore me
1802-03-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNW to NNE. At daybreak the commander was sighted. At 8 the Schouten isthmus S 64° W. At noon in 42° 3' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 42" of longitude by account. At 5.30 the commander fired several guns; he then bore from us N 40° W at a great distance. At 5.45 the Schouten isthmus S 57° W and Maria Island S 24°. At 7 a flat calm, the weather overcast in the S 45° E with the look of wind. At 8 it blew hard from the SE; shaped our course north. At 10 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the wind blowing hard with a high sea. During the night we fired a swivel gun and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. Changed tacks several times. At 9.15 fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the commander. At 5 the land in the west; at 7 p.m. the commander was not to be seen. Took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 5° E; Eddystone Rock W; the northern end of Van Diemen's Land N 28° W; the southernmost of the Furneaux Islands N 11° E.
1802-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, the winds were variable from south-west to south, moderate at first and very light in the morning. As soon as it was daylight we sought to draw nearer to the coast and to come and examine the fire we had seen the day before, which, as we had judged, turned out to be very close to the water's edge. Had the winds not been suitable and very favourable for our boat's return, I should have thought, as everyone on board believed, that it was indeed our people's fire. But not seeing them come back, I took quite the contrary view, refusing even to credit the reasons put forward to account for their delay; for everyone was then saying that in all likelihood the boat was lost, but that at least the men were ashore, since they made it so well known by the way their fire was kept up. However plausible all these arguments might be, they changed nothing in my way of thinking.
At last, between noon and one o'clock, being no more than a short league from this fire, which held everyone's attention, I hove to in order to have the launch hoisted out. I gave the command of it to Citizen Bonnefoy, with orders to go and examine this fire and find out what it might be. The launch was provided with eight days' provisions and with whatever might be needed to set the boat afloat or repair it if necessary. Citizen Bonnefoy had orders, if he met no one and found no sign of our people having passed, to proceed to visit a large sandy cove which I had not ventured to enter the day before, although I had approached it closely enough to make out anyone ashore had there been people on the beach.
As soon as Citizen Bonnefoy had left, all our eyes were turned on him and we followed his every movement. He was seen to approach the coast, examine the fire and then head south, a very clear proof that he had found nothing. When he was abeam of us we filled our sails and followed him with the ship. He went round the whole of the cove I have just mentioned, found everywhere a fine sandy beach and an easy landing, and no sign that could lead him to think that our boat was in this inlet. From this cove he rounded cap Blanc within pistol shot and returned on board at seven (struck through with a cross) and a half with the sad news that he had seen nothing. The launch was hoisted in at once, and it was (time), for the wind increased considerably and the sea rose.
During the night it blew a fresh gale from north to south-west. We kept a little off the coast and put off until the next day the continuation of our search, working back up to the north. The soundings at half past ten were 70 fathoms, and at midnight 75, coral bottom.
I was confined to bed almost the whole of this day with colic in the lower belly, which made me suffer so much that I found no relief in any of the remedies I was given.
Before nightfall the signal to close had been made to the Naturaliste, but whether she did not see it or feared to fall aboard us a second time, we soon lost sight of her, as she was steering a course opposite to ours. I hardly know how to interpret this manoeuvre.
1802-03-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to W by way of S, E and N. At midnight shaped the course north. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze. We had no sight of the Géographe. At 8.45, 7° 46' 30" of NE variation, shaping our course for Banks Strait and running along the coast. At noon in 41° 11' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 29' 6" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands N 11° W, Eddystone Rock west, and Van Diemen's Land from S 5° E to N 28° W. At 3.45 a ship was sighted in the S 68° E which was thought to be the Géographe. We bore away for her and were not long in making her out to be an English schooner lying to. At 6.15 we hove to to windward of her and showed our colours; she at once filled and crowded sail. We did the same and steered for her. Having soon come up with her, we hailed her that we were a ship of discovery and a friend. She then hove to again, and so did we. I went aboard her with Citizen Milius and we came back aboard at 7.30. We filled and stood on and the schooner held her course. She was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before, bound for Maria Island to fish and to hunt seals and kangaroos. She was manned with 14 men and a boy. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. At noon fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the Géographe, which was thought to be in sight to the south. At 3.45 we sighted a ship in the ESE which we took for the Géographe; we bore away for her and were not long in recognising her for a schooner. We hoisted our colours and Citizen Milius went aboard; she was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before; she was fur sealing.
1802-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ (continued from page 21) that some further search should be made. We all presume that it could only be in the south that it would be possible to find some trace of it. The present declaration is signed by all.
Although I was of an opinion quite opposite to everyone else's, being unable to persuade myself that the boat was south of cap Pelé, since it was expressly to proceed north, I complied with the wish everyone expressed that we should return to the south, and I manoeuvred accordingly during the night.
Historical events & Remarks.
The whole of the eighteenth was spent solely in searching for our boat. For the third time we ran along the whole of the coast we had already visited, but we went further north of the island than we had yet done, convinced that our boat, favoured by the winds and the fine weather of the past three days, had wished to take advantage of them and push on ahead. We kept within two miles of the coast all day, and in spite of that nothing was sighted. I myself did not know what to think of the fate of my boat and of those in it. Yet the weather we had had could not make me believe that the boat had been swamped, unless it had been well out to sea on the night of the 16th to the seventeenth, when a squall of four hours' duration obliged us to lie to.
At noon the sky, though fine, was too hazy to allow us to take the sun's altitude, but from the knowledge of the coast our earlier runs had given us, we placed ourselves at sunset between Eddystone Point and St Helens Point, that is to say in about 41° 25' south latitude.
Not wishing to take anything upon myself regarding the further search for our people and the boat, I addressed the following order to Citizen Freycinet, who is the senior officer on board:
"Citizen, this evening at eight o'clock, and earlier if possible, you will assemble the officers and the "naturalists in the great cabin in order to learn whether, in spite of all the searches, unhappily "fruitless, that we have made for three days to find our boat, sent out on geographical "operations, there is anyone who still holds the hope that it might be found by "returning to the south.
"A formal record shall be drawn up of the opinions and answers, which each shall sign".
The chief petty officers were ordered to do likewise, and here is the result of this step.
"This day, the eighteenth of Ventôse, Year 10 of the French Republic, at half past seven in the evening, "by order of the Commander of the expedition of discovery, Citizen Henri Freycinet, lieutenant de "vaisseau on board the corvette the Géographe, assembled the officers and the naturalists embarked in this "ship, to learn whether, in view of the searches made to find the longboat lost for three "days on a geographical expedition, it is more advisable to continue looking for it to the north of "St Helens Point or to return to the southern part where the boat parted from the ship &c. Citizen "Freycinet laid before them the facts entered in the ship's log table concerning the winds "that have prevailed since the boat's departure and the manoeuvres made to facilitate the return of this "boat. After a serious examination of all these circumstances, the officers and naturalists have "concluded that they all retain some hope of finding the boat in the fairly "considerable inlet (in the left margin: which forms) the northern point of Schouten Island. They further declare that they do not think it necessary to "make further searches from cap Pelé to St Helens Point, the whole of this part having "been scrupulously visited by our launch and the corvette. The officers and naturalists have signed the "present declaration".
Opinion of the Chief Petty Officers.
The petty officers, having consulted together regarding the boat, although holding no great hope for it, would think it rather urgent, if the winds permit $$$ (continued on page 20)
1802-03-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SW. At noon in 40° 22' 39" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' 54" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 68° W to S 68° W. At 4.30 the wind shifted from W to SE and veered to ESE and SSW; the sea driven from the west and breaking against the SE wind made us appear ringed with breakers. At 5.45 we saw a waterspout. At 6 the Furneaux Islands bore from N 33° W to N 66° W, and Van Diemen's Land from S 22° W to S 66° W.

1802-03-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW, south and SE. At 4 took the bearing of the northern end of the Furneaux Islands N 40° W, the southern end N 55° W. At 4.30 the winds having shifted to SE we went onto the port tack. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 15° E; the northern end N 70° [illegible]; the southern end of the Furneaux Islands N 18° W, the northern end N 14° E. At 9 we sighted a ship at anchor between Swan Island and the land of the Furneaux Islands. At 10 hove to and put the large boat in the water to go aboard the ship sighted.
1802-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, at daybreak, we were preparing to close with the land to continue the search for our boat. A sail was sighted ahead of us, which at first was taken for the Naturaliste, but we soon perceived that we had been mistaken: the vessel in question was schooner-rigged. As I presumed she must be some craft from Port Jackson, and perhaps employed in surveying this coast, I bore down on her, and at seven o'clock, having come up with her within half pistol shot, I hailed her.
I was then informed that she was indeed an English schooner bound for Maria Island or its neighbourhood for sealing. Being very glad to take this opportunity to have help given to my boat, should anyone chance to come across it, I had a boat hoisted out and sent an officer on board to ask the master to be good enough to come and speak with me. At a quarter past seven he arrived, accompanied, no doubt, by his mate. I told him of the misfortune that had befallen me and proposed to him, paying him whatever he wished, to stay with me for two or three days, so as to leave no cove, however small, without examining it thoroughly. I could not bring him to accept my proposals, and he excused himself on the ground that the sealing season was too far advanced, but said that I might rest assured he would not fail to search on his own part, in case events had decided our people to go back to that place.
The master of this schooner also gave us some information about various good anchorages to be found in the Furneaux Islands, and especially at the one the English have named Preservation Island, where, according to them, it is easy to take in water and wood. They also told us that between Eddystone Point and Swan Island there is a very extensive reef running out more than four or five miles to sea, which is (not) marked on Mr Flinders's new chart and which they assert exists. When asked whether they were in need of anything, they begged me to give them a chart of the strait and a half-hour glass, having broken their own.
The Naturaliste had also met this craft and had told her that we would probably speak her. Captain Hamelin informed me that he was going to anchor in the strait, and it is probably this quite private notion that led him to part company with us without informing me. At eight o'clock I had these two men taken back to their ship, promising them a handsome reward if they brought my people back to Port Jackson.
We then closed with the land, but the winds being south by south-west and south-south-west, we made little progress towards the south.
At noon the observed latitude was 41° 36' 29", and the longitude given by the timekeeper placed us in 146° 57' 10".
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to south and south-south-east, we stood in fairly close to the land, so as to be able the next day to run along it at a very short distance. The night was fine and we spent it hove to.
1802-03-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to NE. At 8 took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 15° E to N 76° W, Swan Island N 56° W, and the Furneaux Islands from N 18° W to N 14° E, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. A ship was sighted at anchor under Swan Island; shortly afterwards we made her out to be an English brig. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Milius to go aboard her. At noon in 40° 44' 58" of latitude observed and in 146° 14' 12" of longitude, the north point of Swan Island bearing N 75° W. At 12.15 a boat we had taken for the brig's came aboard. What was our astonishment! It was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th [Ventôse, 6 March 1802] at 10.15 a.m. abreast of the Schouten Peninsula. This boat had tried to come back aboard the Géographe on the evening of the 15th, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land and run along it as far as Swan Island, where very fortunately she had found the English brig, who gave them provisions of which they were short. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman commanding the boat, had at once made for Banks Strait, knowing that the ships were to pass that way. At 1.45 we anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, the north point of Swan Island bearing S 61° E, the SW point of the same island (past Hunting Islet) S 35° E, the westernmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight S 48° W, the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 38° W, their east end N 27° W. At 3.30 Citizen Milius came back from the brig, which was the Harrington, Captain Campbell, of Port Jackson, bound on a sealing and fishing voyage. At 7.30 the Harrington passed alongside; Captain Campbell promised ours to come and dine with him the next day.

1802-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm, a light air from NE to NNE. At 12.15 the boat we had taken for the brig's boat came aboard; it was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th at 10.30 a.m. This boat had tried to close us, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land. They had run along it as far as Swan Island, where they found the English brig, who gave them the provisions they lacked. At 10.45 anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, and veered 150 fathoms of cable. Bearings: the northern end of Swan Island S 61° E; its SW end (past a hunting islet) S 35° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 48° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 38° W; their eastern end N 27° W. At 3 Mr Milius was back in the large boat; she was the Harrington of Port Jackson, Captain Campbell.
1802-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
$$$ (continued from page 25) In accordance with the statement of the officers, naturalists and petty officers, I changed course to work back up to the north, standing out to the east as far as the winds allowed.
The weather was fairly fine in the evening, but we found the sea very swelly and driven by a sea from the north which did not promise us the early return of a fair wind.
In the night the sky was fairly fine, but the winds came in squalls and strong gusts.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, the weather was fine, and the winds being north by west, we had weather to our heart's desire for running along the coast, keeping often less than a mile from it, and without seeing anything but a few columns of smoke on the tops of the mountains. From cap Pelé as far as cap Blanc the ground is extremely barren and thinly wooded. The mountains in all this part are nothing but heaps of rock on which very little vegetation appears. They end abruptly at the sea, and passing as close as we did, one sees several large rocks detached from them, at the foot of which there appears to be deep water. The searches we made in this part gave us no light on what we wished to know.
At noon the observed latitude was 42° 16' 26" and the longitude 146° 3' 55". Schouten Island then bore south 2° west, and Maria Island could be seen in the distance further south.
Having again assembled the officers, the naturalists and the petty officers to learn whether they wished us to go still further south, they sent me the formal records of which the following is a copy:
"This day, 20 Ventôse, Year 10 of the French Republic, at noon, by order of the Commander of "the expedition of discovery, Citizen Freycinet, lieutenant de vaisseau on board the corvette the "Géographe, convened the officers and the naturalists to determine how far to the south "the search for our longboat should be pushed.
"The officers and naturalists declare that it would be useless at the very least to run further south than the "southern point of Schouten Island, abreast of which the Géographe now lies. The manner "in which our launch and the corvette have visited the coast from St Helens Point to here, together with the "consideration of the facts entered in the ship's log table, leaves every moral certainty that the boat "could not have passed the two points between which our searches have extended, and that it has only too "unhappily perished at sea.
"At sea, off the east coast of the island of Anthony van Diemen, the same day and year as above. "Here follow the names of the officers and naturalists.
"The chief petty officers having assembled for the second time, with the Commander's authorisation, "in order to consider, should there be occasion, fresh means likely to help us discover traces or signs "of the course our boat may have taken. Considering the rigorous searches that have been made for it both with the "ship and with the launch. Considering the number of days that have elapsed since it went missing and the very "close distance to which we have approached the land in covering a stretch of more than 25 leagues, both "on this side of and beyond the point the boat was to reach. Considering, finally, the impossibility of the boat's having reached "the limit where we now find (ourselves). We have unanimously considered that a longer "search would henceforth be useless in these waters and that a further loss of time would be prejudicial to "the expedition, being persuaded that our hope, if it is still permissible to hold any, can only be fulfilled by "working back up to the north. &c". Signed by the petty officers &c.
1802-03-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NNW. At daybreak the large boat was sent off to Point Portland under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, who was to make observations there. At 8 the brig Harrington, which lay anchored 2 miles west of us, got under way and shaped her course S 67° 30' W. At 7 p.m. the large boat came in from Point Portland.

1802-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW and NNE. Began painting the ship's outside. The large boat came back from Cape Portland. The Géographe's boat was put in the water to go and survey from Eddystone Rock as far as Swan Island.
1802-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, the winds were very unsettled throughout the day, but always between north and west, and unfavourable to the course I wished to take in order to come and make St Helens Point and then run up the coast to the entrance of Bass Strait. At eight o'clock we stood on the western tack with the wind north by west. The breeze was then light and the sea very swelly, under an overcast sky. Nevertheless, at noon we observed the latitude, which was found to be 42° 11' 11". The longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 147° 7' 49", much further Sst than our dead reckoning did.
In the afternoon we continued on the western tack, heading northward. The sky grew dark and even hazy, the breeze fairly strong and the sea still rough and swelly.
We had already noticed several times that, however little strength the breeze had, the sea quickly rose, but also that it quickly went down as soon as the breeze dropped. We attributed the cause to the currents which, running counter to the direction of the winds, produced this effect.
For four days I had been very unwell and found little relief in the remedies the doctors made me take. My illness was caused by colic in the lower belly, which tormented me continually and which the unhappy event that had befallen our boat was not likely to relieve. The more I reflected on this event, the less I could convince myself that any mishap had befallen it if it kept to the coast, and I still hope to find it somewhere at the entrance of the strait. It is true that the men in it will not have been spared hardship from want of provisions and perhaps of water, but after all, if their courage has not failed them, they will still be alive.
At eight o'clock, the winds being north-west, we stood for the night on the northern tack, heading eastward, with every reef in the topsails, the breeze coming in gusts and the sea rough. The sky, however, was fairly fine and even clear at times.
1802-03-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 8 a.m. the Géographe's boat was sent off with Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger to survey the coast from Eddystone Rock to Swan Island; she had 5 days' provisions. The dinghy went fishing to the Furneaux Islands. The corvette was painted. At 9 Citizen Saint-Cricq went to make observations on Swan Island; I landed there with my gun, as did several officers and naturalists. We sent the boat back, and she carried Citizen Milius to Hunting Islet. At nightfall she came to fetch us from Swan Island and took us to the islet; we killed a seal there, which we left. We loaded the boat with geese, penguins and other birds that we took in burrows under the grass; we came back aboard at 2 a.m. (on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802]).

1802-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 6 the large boat was back from Swan Island; we went on painting the ship's outside. At 2 everyone came in in the large boat with a very good bag. At 4.45 slack water; at 5.15 the ebb, and at 11.30 the flood.
1802-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, the weather was fine during the morning, the breeze fell off a great deal and the sea became smooth. The winds seemed inclined to settle in the north-west, and as we were making little way, I kept on the northern tack, heading eastward.
At noon the observed latitude was 41° 34' 7" and the longitude 147° 21' 27". By dead reckoning I certainly did not place myself so far to the east. Nevertheless, I did not alter course in the evening and stood on the same tack until eight at night. The sky, which had been fine all morning, began to grow hazy after the sun passed the meridian, and became so much so towards the end of the day that our horizon extended half a league at most. As every time the weather had turned hazy we had had it for several days on end, I began to fear the same would happen to us this time. But at nightfall we had the pleasure of seeing the haze lift, and it was only after moonset that it came on again. The hygrometer had forewarned us of this change, for it was moving rapidly towards humidity. The barometer had also fallen a good deal. Since the day before we had had it below 28 inches, and that was not a good sign, for we had always had some squalls when it went below 28.
In the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third, the winds, after being light and very variable from north-north-east to west-south-west by way of north, suddenly jumped to south-south-west (and) took us aback. It was then two in the morning, so that we stood on the southern tack, heading eastward, which we held until daybreak. The sky was very hazy and the damp so heavy that all those on watch were as much troubled by it as if there had been heavy and continual rain. It seems that hazy weather is very common in these waters, for it has very often happened to us to have it several days on end since our entry into the canal d'Entrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel] until now. But I do not think it unhealthy, or at least no one has yet felt any ill effects from it.
1802-03-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a flat calm. The dinghy came in from the Furneaux Islands with a little fish and loaded with young seals. I was put ashore on Hunting Islet with three men and two days' provisions to kill seals; I had my gun and was well supplied with powder and shot. It was a pleasure party for me. At 8.30 p.m. the large boat was sent off to Port Kent (in the Furneaux Islands) with Citizen Faure, surveyor, and several naturalists. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 38' 50"; longitude 145° 51' 0". NE variation on the 19th [Ventôse, 10 March 1802] at 4.15 p.m., 10° 6' 0"; on the 20th [Ventôse, 11 March 1802] at 8.45 a.m., 9° 12' 0"; the same day at 5.30 p.m., 10° 4' 30"; at 6.30 p.m., 10° 35' 0"; on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 23' 20". The flood sets west and the ebb east. The greatest rate of the current is 2.8 knots. Citizen Milius proposed that I should go to Hunting Islet to kill seals. I accepted with pleasure, took 3 men with me and 2 days' provisions, and had myself landed on the west side of the islet. The weather was superb and I promised myself much amusement from the trip.

1802-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. The dinghy came back from the fishing with few fish. The large boat landed Citizen Breton with three men. At 8.30 she left for Port King in the Furneaux Islands with Mr Faure, the surveyor, and Bailly, the mineralogist.
1802-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the winds, which during the night had jumped to south-south-west, shifted to south at about daybreak and from south to east-south-east, but they soon came back to south-south-east and seemed inclined to settle there. We then steered west to draw nearer the coast, although the sky was still very hazy.
At eight o'clock the weather looked so threatening that, not judging it prudent to continue on this course, I preferred to lie to while awaiting a more favourable change. The breeze was very strong all morning. The sky also grew a little clearer. We saw the sun now and then, but not at the moment when it would have been most needful to us for observing its meridian altitude.
At noon, by our dead reckoning, we placed ourselves in 41° 22' 19" south latitude, and the estimated longitude put us in 147° 5', about 15 or 16 leagues from the coast.
We continued to lie to until 4 o'clock in the afternoon, when, seeing the barometer rise to 28 inches 2 lines despite the look of bad weather, we filled the topsails and the foresail and steered west again. Our horizon might extend three leagues.
From noon until five o'clock the weather was tolerably fine, the breeze moderate and the sea high. We continued to steer west until six o'clock, when, having made the land clearly, we stood on the north-east tack to keep a little off the coast, from which our dead reckoning placed us about six leagues.
During the night the winds were from east by south-east to east-south-east and often came in gusts followed by calm, especially towards the end of the night. The weather also turned to rain, and we had a fair amount of it until morning. We sounded several times during the night without finding bottom at 70 and eighty fathoms. We carried little sail, in the hope that the weather would turn fine for the next day, so that we might enter the strait if there were occasion.
1802-03-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
At 1 a.m. the wind blew a strong breeze from ESE. The topgallant masts were struck; the weather overcast at noon. The cable, having to bear the force of the wind and the flood tide, chafed badly; at 3.30 it parted. Another anchor was let go at once and the parted cable hauled in. We dragged until 5, when the cable held. The wind blowing hard in gusts; at 6.15 the cable parted. We at once lay to under the fore staysail, the storm staysail, the mizzen and its staysail, and hauled in the parted cable. At 9 took the bearing of a fire in the S 22° 30' E. During the night squally weather, with thunder, lightning and pouring rain.

At daybreak, each of us having armed himself with a handspike, we went hunting. We killed several enormous seals which we found asleep on the grass. We skinned them for the hides and took only the livers and kidneys, which we ate and which I found excellent. In the forenoon we took birds in their burrows, and this, with the kidneys, gave us a passable dinner. The weather had turned overcast and seemed likely to grow bad; the sea broke terribly on the east side of the islet. In landing I had taken the ship's bearing past a point at noon; I saw her much further west. I supposed she had dragged; shortly afterwards the mist hid her and I saw her no more. The wind blew hard from the east. At the close of day, being at the south part of the islet, I saw a boat doubling the south point of Swan Island and landing on its SW side; I had no doubt it was the Géographe's boat, which had left the ship on the 21st to survey from Eddystone to Swan Island. The night was horrible, with pouring rain and thunder, the sky on fire; and having no shelter we were soaked through. The bad weather, with the anxiety our situation caused me, made me pass a dreadful night.

1802-03-15.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from east to ESE, a swell running. The cable chafing extremely, at 3.45 it parted; the starboard cable was at once bent round the mast and at 4 the anchor was let go. We had doubled the turn round the bitts and clapped on breaking stoppers at intervals. The turns came off the bitts and the cable ran out to the end with 4 or 5 fathoms lashed to it; we let go the bend at the foot of the mast and took a turn round the bitts, having first bent a spare brace to serve as a buoy rope on the buoy. We hauled in the port cable, which had parted near the bend; we dragged until 5, when the cable [one word illegible] end on, the wind still blowing hard. At 6.15 the starboard cable parted and we lay to on the starboard tack.
1802-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, we saw the land again, and I found myself much closer to it than my dead reckoning made me. As it was heavily shrouded in haze and the weather was far from fine, it seemed to me that I was four leagues from it at most. The winds being east, variable to east-south-east, I went back on the north-east tack to gain an offing, crowding sail.
Throughout the morning we had rain continually on our backs and often thunder over our heads. Everything seemed to herald the approach of some violent squalls, and yet the barometer stood steadily at 28 3.5, so that it appeared to us from its behaviour that (the) present weather was only a storm which would not last long. But however that might be for the future, as I was much too close to the land for strong Sst winds, I sought to get away from it.
At noon, the winds having shifted to east-north-east, we stood on the south-east tack under our courses, with every reef in the topsails.
By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 41° 1' 19" south latitude.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a strong breeze from east-north-east. The rain, though continual, was less heavy, and the sky, still dark, less laden with vapours; the barometer, steady at 28 3, underwent no change.
At eight o'clock we stood on the north-east tack, which we held until the next day. During the night the winds varied from east-north-east to east-south-east. The sky was again covered with dark, thick clouds. The rain and the squalls began again and the weather was fairly bad.
For five days I had been much troubled by the colic I have spoken of, and it was only from this moment that I began to feel some relief from the remedies that were administered to me. The doctors feared that I might be taking some serious illness, and I myself was of the same opinion. But from the state in which I find myself today, it appears that I shall soon be entirely recovered.
1802-03-15.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea. At 6 a.m. the Furneaux Islands were sighted in the N 45° E. A cable and an iron chain were bent to the mooring anchor. At noon in 40° 27' 26" of latitude by account and in 145° 29' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 land was sighted in the N 22° 30' E. At 6 rain, mist and thunder; the wind fell a little and the sea went down a great deal. We sounded exactly every half hour and found from 21 to 39 fathoms, coral bottom.

At daybreak we went hunting again and killed several more seals, which did us good, for we had no provisions left. I had the meat taken and smoked, not knowing to what we might be reduced. The rain was useful to us: every hollow in the rocks was filled with water, which I found drinkable. I had a breaker I had with me filled, and several bottles that had held brandy and vinegar, and urged my three men not to touch them but to go and drink from the hollows as I did. In a clear interval I saw the Furneaux Islands and did not see the ship. I no longer doubted that the bad weather had forced her to get under way. I went at once to the south part of the islet, and having seen the boat in the same place as the day before, I put my handkerchief on the end of an English oar (a) that was on the beach and planted it in the rocks. Shortly afterwards I saw several people run from the boat behind some rocks, almost certain that my signal had been seen. I left it there and went to reassure my men. About 4 o'clock Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger came in the Géographe's boat to fetch us and took us to Swan Island. We shared the little provisions they had left; they had dug a well which gave us very good water; I had my gun, which gave us game. There was a great quantity of geese, which were our chief food while we waited for the Naturaliste.

On the morning of the 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1802] a boat was seen coming from the Furneaux Islands and standing for Hunting Islet; we made her a signal with a handkerchief and a musket shot, and she came and joined us. It was our large boat, which had left the ship on the evening of the 22nd for Port King, where she had ridden out the bad weather. Captain Hamelin had told midshipman Brèvedent that should he not find the ship at the same anchorage, he was to come and fetch me from Hunting Islet and then make for Waterhouse, where we should wait for him, or he for us. Accordingly we left Swan Island, 25 people in the two boats, and shaped our course for Waterhouse, where we arrived at nightfall and slept.

1802-03-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard [illegible] from the ESE [illegible], a high sea. At 2 sighted the land in the N 22° 30' E; at [illegible] the wind fell away. Rain, mist and thunder; the weather having turned [illegible] we set our courses. On the [illegible] tack.
1802-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the winds were east-south-east, more moderate than on the preceding days. The sky also grew clearer during the day, and the rain came only at intervals and not heavily. At four o'clock we had stood on the southern tack and held it until noon, when, having observed the latitude, though doubtfully, we found ourselves in 41° 20' 42". The estimated longitude placed us in 147° 27', but it was all the less reliable because in the morning we had had a good sight of the land, although the horizon was of only middling extent and not very clear in that quarter. When we saw the land, it bore west of us, stretching away to the north and south.
As the observed latitude placed us well to the south of the entrance of the strait, I had the ship steered north-north-east until four o'clock. The weather still looked too threatening to take a westerly course, and for this reason I preferred to keep in the offing until it turned fine.
Towards four in the afternoon the breeze freshened a great deal. The sky became laden with vapours, the rain began again and squalls were frequent; the winds also shifted to the east.
Despite the small likelihood of an early change in the weather, the barometer was determined to reassure us by rising to fair. At noon we had it at 28 in. 4.8, which had not happened for a long time. When the rain and wind came back before sunset, it held at the same height, and I thought it very much at fault. The same was not true of the hygrometer, which was moving by great strides towards great humidity, having passed successively from 95 to 98.
During the night the weather was very unsettled. At times we had it fine, but more often overcast, damp and rainy. The squalls, though frequent, were nevertheless much less heavy than those we had had on the preceding days. Towards the end of the night it seemed inclined to turn quite fine. We made two boards, one to the south and the other to the north-east, under the foresail and our topsails with every reef taken in.
My health began to improve during this day, and I was able to leave my cabin, suffering much less than I had until then.
1802-03-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 2.30 a.m. we had a heavy squall, after which the wind fell away by degrees. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE; land was sighted to windward and the topgallant masts swayed up. At 9 filled and stood on. At noon the land from S 22° W to S 45° E, being in 40° 40' 22" of latitude observed and in 145° 0' 30" of longitude by account. At 4, Flat Island S 55° E. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened; during the night the wind a strong breeze.

1802-03-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from east to ESE. [Illegible.] At 2.30 went about; took the bearing then of the westernmost visible end of the land S 35° W; the easternmost visible end S 68° E; Flat Island S 79° E.
1802-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
at noon, in 40° 48' 6"
The southern point of the land of Van Diemen in sight bore south 10° west
The northernmost point in sight south 25° west
The southernmost of the Furneaux Islands north 56° west
The northernmost point in sight of the same islands north 45 west
At four o'clock
The western extremity of the Furneaux Islands in sight north 60° west
The easternmost extremity north 14° east
An isolated rock followed by breakers north 10° west
A part of the land of Van Diemen south 12° east
The land of the same island north-west 33° 45' south
(in the margin) At five o'clock we had
Cape Portland south 38° west
Little Swan Island south 9° east
Preservation Island north 36° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, in the morning, the sky being fine and the winds east by north, a pleasant breeze, I decided to bear away to enter Banks Strait. The barometer, which still stood very high, seemed to promise us a continuation of the fine weather; accordingly I set the course west-north-west by compass, convinced that we were less far north than our dead reckoning made us, not having seen the sun for several days.
At six o'clock the land had been sighted to the west-south-west, but it was too hazy to make out what it might be. From the moment I decided to bear away, we continued on the west-north-west course, and at noon we observed the latitude as 40° 48' 6", which placed us exactly in that which the English chart gives for the entrance of the strait. We then had a perfect view of the Furneaux Islands, which close its opening on the north. The longitude given by the timekeeper was 146° 20' 42", differing little from the distance at which we placed ourselves from the land by our estimate by eye.
In the afternoon the course was brought gradually a little more to the west, and we passed no more than a league off the various rocks lying south of the first island, on which the sea breaks heavily, which makes them easy to avoid.
At four o'clock the sky began to thicken. Once again the whole horizon was covered with dark, thick clouds and already looked most threatening. As we were well advanced, there was nothing to be gained by turning back. And so we held on our course as if the weather had been very fine.
The westernmost extremity in sight of the Furneaux Islands bore north 60° west
And the easternmost extremity north 14° east
An isolated rock on which the sea broke heavily north 10° west
The southernmost land of the island of Van Diemen bore south 12° east
And the northernmost relative to to (sic) our position west 35° 45' south. The Furneaux Islands, at the entrance of the strait, appear to be bare of trees and even of greenery; at least very little is to be seen. But further in they are well wooded and of a pleasant aspect. Their height is considerable, and in fine weather they must be easily seen at 12 & 15 leagues. The land along the seashore of the island of Van Diemen is low in this part, and the mountains one sees lie far inland.
At five o'clock we sighted Cape Portland, which bore south 36° west, Little Swan Island south 9°30' east, and the island we judged to be Preservation Island north 36° west.
At six o'clock we put the ship's head to the west, and at eight to west by south-west, to keep in mid-channel during the night, my intention being to stop at the island the English have named Waterhouse. The bottom we had in crossing the channel is 30 to 35 fathoms, unsuitable for anchoring. At eight o'clock it was no more than 24, a mixture of sand, madrepores and small flat stones. The sky then looked so threatening that we took a second reef in the topsails and let fall our foresail, standing on until eleven o'clock. The bottom had increased by 4 fathoms and was hardly any better. Nevertheless, one could anchor there in case of need. We found the current very strong in passing through the strait.
(In the left margin, written vertically) and its direction seemed to us parallel to our course, that is to say, setting to the west. From midnight until daybreak the weather was so bad, with the rain and the violent squalls we met with, that I decided to lie to, two hours on each tack. The bottom went from 28 to 34 fathoms while lying to on the northern tack, and from 34 to 30 on the southern.
1802-03-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 10.30 the Furneaux Islands were sighted N 50° E. At noon in 40° 41' 40" of latitude observed and in 145° 28' 6" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from us N 60° E, Rocky Islet S 10° E, the land from S 7° W to S 65° E.

1802-03-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from east. At 6.30 took the bearing of Waterhouse Island from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7 we [illegible] the large boat, which was standing towards us; at 7.15 went about and bore down on her; at 7.45 hove to with the lee side to the wind. At 8 the large boat came in with everyone aboard.
1802-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At eight in the morning, the land forming the bight of Cape Portland, for its extremity could not be seen, lay east 12° north
The south-west point of Water House east 6° north
And the little islet I have mentioned south 7 west
The land of Van Diemen's Land in sight south 10° west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, the weather became less foul than it had been during the night. The rain ceased at the setting of the moon, but the sky remained dark and overcast. At daybreak, the haze that had hidden the land from us having cleared, we saw it distinctly and found ourselves opposite a small, flat and very level island, which is no doubt the one the English have marked on their chart with a dot. It nevertheless seemed to us large enough to have deserved a different shape. By my reckoning, it may be at the very least half a league from east to west. It offers no particular point by which it might be distinguished and is extremely level over its whole surface. It appeared to us steep-to and free of danger, at least on its northern side. At about a league's distance, the bottom was 36 fathoms, and ill suited to anchoring.
From the bearing of this island and that of Water House, which lies four away from it, we recognised our position and saw with regret that we were a long way to leeward of it.
At eight o'clock, we went onto the tack towards the north and east. There was a pleasant breeze and the weather was manageable, though the sky still had an ugly look. Until noon the depth kept increasing, and by then it was 38 fathoms. In the course of the morning, we took advantage of what little wind there was to change our foresail and main topsail, which were unfit to withstand the first gales that might come upon us.
At noon, the sun having appeared at the moment we least expected it, we observed 40° 37' 44"; this observation is nevertheless doubtful, the haze making the horizon as indistinct as it was limited. Immediately after noon the sky clouded over again, and we lost sight of the land entirely until six o'clock, when we took bearings of the easternmost land, in the south-east, the westernmost, south 30 west, and the islet seen in the morning, south 11° 15 west.
At four o'clock, we had stood on the tack towards the south and east, and at seven o'clock, being in 35 fathoms two leagues to windward of our islet, we went onto the tack towards the north and east, which we held until eleven o'clock
From eight o'clock until eleven, the breeze from east to east-south-east was very strong. We had gusts so heavy that we had to take the third reef in the topsails. But towards two o'clock the weather turned fine and cleared. The breeze became very light and the current seemed to carry us westward with some speed.
1802-03-18.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 6.30, Waterhouse from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7.15, standing on the north board, a boat was seen making for the ship; we at once went about and bore up for her. At 7.45 we hove to to wait for her. At 8 I came aboard in our large boat with Citizen Leschenault, midshipman Brèvedent in charge of the party, and 2 of the boat's crew. The Géographe's boat and a large part of our people had stayed at Waterhouse, thinking the ship was going to anchor there. The boat was hoisted in at once and we put the ensign at half mast and fired a swivel gun to call the Géographe's boat. At 8 Waterhouse bore from us S 16° E to S 44° E. At 9 filled and stood on. At 9.30 hove to; the Géographe's boat came in, having again left several people behind — among others Bailly the mineralogist, who wanted to stay at Waterhouse because, he said, the ship was to anchor there. The captain sent the boat off at once to bring back the rest of the people, sending word to the obstinate mineralogist that if he did not come back at once he would leave him ashore. Filled and stood on. At noon in 40° 48' 30" of latitude observed and in 145° 52' 48" of longitude by account. At 2.15 hove to; the boat came back with the rest of the people and was hoisted in at once. At 3 filled and stood on. At 4, Waterhouse from S 2° E to S 14° E. During the night squally weather with light rain, the wind a strong breeze, with lightning.

At daybreak the Naturaliste was seen standing for the island. I proposed going aboard at once, but everyone said she was going to come to the anchorage and that we must wait for her. At 6 she took the north board. I embarked in our boat with 4 men and reached the ship at 8.

1802-03-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to [illegible]. At noon took the bearing of the northern end of Swan Island S 62° E; its southern end S 49° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 46° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 45° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 20° W.
1802-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six in the morning,
The easternmost land south-east
The westernmost land south-west by south
The middle of the little île Stérile south by south-west
At eight o'clock
The land in sight to the west south 40° west
The most prominent land to the east south 75° east
The little île Stérile south 15° west
At noon
The northernmost land in sight of the Furneaux Islands north 54° east
Cape Portland north 88 east
The north point of Water House south 59° east
The little île Stérile south 59° 30' west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, the weather was very fine in the morning, but at sunrise we were becalmed and made very little way until ten o'clock, when a light breeze came to us from north-west by west. We likewise found ourselves very little advanced to the eastward by the two boards we had made during the night, since at daybreak the little île Stérile lay only a little to leeward of us, at about a league and a half at the most.
As it was my intention to visit the island the English have named Water House, I made use of what little breeze we then had and closed with the coast in order to identify it by sight of the channel it must form with the mainland. For otherwise it would not be possible to distinguish it from the rest of the coast, with which it must merge if one is at any distance from it. At eleven o'clock, having made it out, we steered west. I ran along the whole of its western side in the hope of meeting the Naturaliste there, to which I had named it as a rendezvous in case of separation before our entry into the strait. The more I have reflected on the motives that may have led Captain Hamelin to leave me on the east coast of Van Diemen's Land, the less I have been able to conceive the reason, and I am still more astonished not to have met him at the appointed place. For having sailed almost round that last island, I have had no sight of him. Perhaps I shall be more fortunate at Port Dalrymple, since he sent me word by the master of the English schooner, to whom I spoke myself, that he was making for the strait and would anchor wherever he could, so that it will perhaps be very difficult to meet with him.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 40° 44' 11", and the longitude by the timekeepers placed us in 145° 5' 12", about 0° 19' 0" farther west than the position of Water House, which then lay south 59' east of us at a distance of one league. This island is of a good height in its northern part and much lower in its southern. It is, in general, thinly wooded, and the trees growing on it are of no great height and only on the eastern side. The whole of the western part is dry and barren. Several large black rocks can be made out there, which contrast sharply with the colour of the ground, which is yellowish. This island did not seem to me to deserve the name it bears, for it seems to offer no likelihood of finding water there, and I am persuaded that it was named Water House only because the English who visited it must have had a great deal of rain there, which is not rare with easterly and south-easterly winds, for every time we have had them from that quarter we have not been short of it. The bottom, when we left it, was 16 fathoms, sand.
However that may be, not finding the Naturaliste there, I did not stop and brought the ship onto the larboard tack as soon as I had made sure either that she had not been there or at least that she had left. The winds were then variable from west to west-south-west and the breeze somewhat strong; it continued so until sunset. The sea was already beginning to rise, the sky grew more and more cloudy and the barometer kept falling, so that I was very glad to stand out to sea.
During the evening, although it was blowing a strong breeze, we carried all sail in order to make out, before nightfall, the islands of the northern part that form the continuation of the little Furneaux archipelago; but at sunset, the sea having become very heavy and the wind gusty, we took a second reef in the topsails. The islands then lay in the position given by the bearing.
(In the left margin, written vertically) As the weather was fine and the strong breeze had cleared away all the clouds, we were not sorry to have it blowing so hard, inasmuch as it left us free to observe at our ease the beginning and the end of an eclipse of the moon visible to us, which we observed with precision. I shall give its results in tomorrow's entry, when the calculations are finished.
1802-03-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At 10.30, being roughly at the place where the two anchors had been lost, we hove to and filled several times to try to make out their buoys. At noon took the bearing of the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 20° W, their east end N 54° E, the north end of Swan Island S 62° E and its south-west end S 49° E. (a) This oar was found by us when we landed on the islet for the first time (on the 21st [Ventôse, 12 March 1802]); it had been picked up to be carried aboard and was fortunately forgotten, for there was not a piece of wood on the islet but what the sea brought. At 2, having been unable to make out our buoys, the captain decided to go and look for the Géographe to the south; we made sail to leave the strait. At 4 Swan Island bore from us N 57° W to N 61° W. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly 5 digits; it ended about 10.30. During the night overcast weather, with rain.

1802-03-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, lying to on the starboard tack, a fresh breeze from W to south and SE. At 2 we were at the place where we had lost our two anchors; we hoped to make out the buoys, and not seeing them we bore away to go in search of the Géographe. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly five digits; it ended at 10.30.
1802-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At six o'clock:
The northern extremity in sight of the Furneaux Islands north 30° west
At ten o'clock, at night:
One of the Furneaux Islands in sight north 56° east
At midnight:
The same island north 28° east,
Other land was thought to be seen to the north of this island.
At five in the morning,
The northernmost Furneaux island in sight north 7° east
From this point to south 17° west could be seen a long succession of high land divided into several hummocks which appeared to form so many separate islands.
At noon,
The same land extended (in the left margin: from north) 42° 30' east to south 20° west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, the winds having greatly abated, we began to beat to windward under all sail, abreast of the Furneaux Islands, whose land our dead reckoning placed abeam of us at about six leagues. At eight o'clock, we took a general set of bearings of the land in sight.
This group of islands appeared to us much larger than the number shown in this latitude on the English chart would suggest, which no doubt comes from the fact that the distance at which we were from them prevented us from seeing the low land that joins most of them to one another. I give, moreover, a very exact view of the appearance the land presents in the latitude of 40° 21 minutes and the longitude 144° 57' 48" according to our timekeepers.
From the eclipse of the moon observed the day before, our No. 35 was found to differ by only 0° 1' 28" 5''' to the west from the longitude given by the Nautical Almanac, which gave 11h 6m 0s for the time of the middle of the eclipse, and which for us was at 1h 48m 46s 9 thirds.
The time has been reduced to the meridian of Greenwich because, in the Connaissance des temps published in Paris, the times of the phases of the moon were through an oversight copied out without being reduced to the meridian of Paris.
The shadow entered between Heraclides and Aristarchus; at the greatest phase it went out opposite Aristotle. At the greatest phase, it extended from Grimaldi to the Sea of Crises.
As there was very little wind in the morning, we held the tack to the north with west-south-west winds, variable at times to south-west. But at noon they shifted to the west, and we took the tack to the south in order to come and make Port Dalrymple. We saw that day many porpoises, some grampuses and two whales of middling size. The birds showed themselves in such small numbers that one is inclined to believe that none of these islands is very rich in fish, at least to judge by that conjecture.
In the evening, the winds continued very light and the smoothness of the sea foretold a calm. The bottom was 42 fathoms, sand and shells. This was the greatest depth we had had in the strait up to that moment, but it is far from being of the same nature everywhere. The tack to the south that we had taken at noon was not a long one, for the calm and the want of breeze obliged me to put the ship's head to the north-west, the winds being at west-south-west.
From eight o'clock until midnight, the weather was fine and the winds suitable for working to the westward, which we did. But from midnight until daybreak it clouded over, became rainy and took on the worst possible appearance for the day. We lay to from midnight until four o'clock so as not to run too far to the westward, wishing to make Port Dalrymple. We then had two reefs in the topsails, and the wind, which was at north, kept on increasing. The barometer, however, still stood at 27 inches 10 lines and the hygrometer between 94 & 95.
1802-03-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to W by way of NE. At noon in 41° 29' 33" of latitude observed and in 146° 37' 30" of longitude by account. Van Diemen's Land still in sight. At 10.30 the weather turned overcast. At midnight hove to. During the night we burnt priming and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-21.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the wind a light breeze from NE to W and NW. The sea smooth. At 4 the land in sight from N 24° W to S 5° E. We hove to during the night. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of Maria Island from S 54° W to S 41° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 25° W; the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon took the bearing of the south end of Schouten Island N 68° W, 8 miles off.
1802-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Nota + Bearings of the land.
At six in the morning
The land, though very hazy, showed itself from SSE to north-east.
At seven o'clock, we sighted the rock the English have named the Pyramid
At eight o'clock we had it to the west at ¾ of a league's distance
The Kent Group N by NW
And the largest of the Furneaux Islands E by NE
At noon, the easternmost point of the Kent Group lay, to our great satisfaction, ESE.
(in the margin) Furneaux Islands
At four in the afternoon
The northernmost islet in sight north 10° east
Cape Franklin north 60° east
The southernmost land in sight south 19° 30 east
At the close of day, the land could be seen from north 29° east to south 10° east.
That which was nearest the corvette lay north 87° east.
Nota: All the bearings are to be carried to the log table of 30 Ventôse to the first of Germinal.
Historical events & Remarks
On the thirtieth, we had very foul weather throughout the morning. The sky was constantly dark, laden with clouds and full of vapours which gave us continual rain, strong squalls and a heavy sea. The breeze, which was still at north, became so strong that we had to take the third reef in our topsails and even to furl our mizzen topsail, which was carried away through a bad handling of the sails by the officer of the watch. As soon as the pieces had been gathered up, I had the fore topsail furled, for fear the same should happen to it, and the foresail too, setting the fore staysail in its place. So that we remained almost as if lying to under the fore-topmast staysail, the fore staysail, the main topsail close-reefed and the mizzen staysail. The ship behaved very well under this canvas, but although she was making two and a half knots and sometimes three knots, the helm had to be kept hard a-starboard, otherwise she fell off a great deal if it was righted.
In the course of the morning the winds varied from north to west-north-west without this bringing any change in the weather, but I was very glad to see them take that direction, because it made it easier for us to work off the coast of Van Diemen's Land, on which we found ourselves rather too far embayed for such unmanageable weather.
At eight o'clock, we wore round and then kept close-hauled under the same canvas, the ship's head to the north. When we wore, the bottom was 45 fathoms, and at noon, although we had made about three leagues to the north by our dead reckoning, it had not yet increased. By our dead reckoning we were, at that time, in 40° 34' 15" of latitude and 145° 27' 18" of longitude.
During the evening the weather was less rainy than it had been in the morning, but wind succeeded the rain, for it was much stronger. We saw the sun now and then and had some hope that at its setting the sky might become fine. At two o'clock the lead brought up forty-six fathoms, and at four o'clock, 45. By then the wind had increased considerably. As nothing in the air foretold a change for the night, I prepared to weather the equinoctial gale, which there was no means of avoiding. We began by running in the jib-boom and lowering the mizzen gaff.
