Next, we took a reef in our courses, in case the nearness of the land, onto which the leeway and the current were setting us, should oblige us to have recourse to them, (in another hand, the following interjections: hé! hé! hô! hô!).
At eight o'clock, the bottom being still 45 fathoms but the wind more violent, it seemed to me that we had as yet lost nothing, or at least little, so that I remained under the same canvas until there should be a noticeable decrease, being unable to go about onto the other tack inasmuch as it had become too bad.
From eight o'clock until midnight the sea was extremely bad; we shipped several seas, which in truth troubled us little. But a more pressing danger made itself felt. The bottom decreased steadily from 45 to 41 fathoms, and from midnight to one o'clock we passed from 41 to 35. As there was no more time to lose, I had the bell rung so that everyone should be on deck, and we set our courses, not without difficulty. But at last it was done. The corvette certainly had as much as she could carry, and more than once we had the gunwale in the water. The winds were then at south-west and we were heading north 57 west, which, with the leeway and the variation of the needle, did not prevent our (course) from making a great deal of easting. When we had trimmed the sails, we doubled
(In the left margin, written vertically) and trebled all the sheets and tacks, but this did not prevent our fore-topmast staysail from being carried away, as well as the storm staysail, which fortunately came to no harm, being in the lee of the mainsail. During the watch from midnight to four o'clock, I would not have the lead cast, for everyone's greater peace of mind. For had the bottom been found still decreasing, most of them would perhaps have believed themselves lost beyond help.
1802-03-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from N to WNW, a high sea. At 5 lay to. At 8 Maria Island from S 41° W to S 54° W and the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon in 42° 18' 45" of latitude by account and in 146° 33' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-03-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze in gusts from NW to W and SW. A high sea; the middle of Schouten Island bore from us N 84° W. At 10 blowing hard in gusts, a very high sea, the weather overcast.
1802-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Nota +:
(in the left margin): + the bearing is to be carried to the log table of the first to the second of Germinal.
Bearings of the land.
At four in the afternoon:
The northern extremity of the largest of the Furneaux Islands south
At six o'clock:
The land extended from south 70° west to south 30° west
At nine in the evening, land was thought to be seen in the south-west, but whether it was seen or not, the bottom being no more than twenty fathoms and the sea still heavy, we steered east-north-east to stand off from the coast.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Germinal, as soon as it was light, we perceived the land to leeward of us, lying lying (sic) from south-east to north-east by north. It was with much pleasure that I found myself at a reasonable distance from it, that is to say about four leagues by my reckoning. We continued to keep close-hauled under our courses and, at sunrise, I had the topsails set, with all (reefs) taken in, the better to work up to windward, the wind being still violent and in gusts. The sky, however, was fine, though very cloudy.
At seven o'clock, having made out the rock the English have named the Pyramid clearly, we rounded it at about three quarters of a league's distance, and when we had it to the west, the Kent Group lay N by NW of us. Our position then being well determined, I decided to shape a course out of the strait in order to put myself somewhat under shelter from the wind and sea on the eastern side of the Furneaux Islands, as I saw no sign of any change in the weather.
After rounding the Pyramid, we were not long in perceiving the second rock that the English chart shows to the south and west of the Kent Group. We rounded it at the same distance as the first, in order to pass through the channel it forms with the islands. The passage is a fine one, but the sea there was extremely heavy and the current rapid, for we were running eleven and twelve knots by the log. Had the weather been more manageable, I should have sounded the whole of this channel, but there was no means of attending to it in the weather we had. I should likewise have passed through the one that separates the islands of the Kent Group from one another, where there may perhaps be some good anchorages, despite the little promise of them they offer to the eye, and we ranged along them closely enough, both on the west and on the east, to perceive most of the coves they contain.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 39° 22' 44", which corresponds very nearly to that which the plan gives to these islands, from which we may have been three minutes to the north. As there was no hour angle, we do not know whether their longitude corresponds to that which we might have observed.
All the islands seemed to me to offer few resources to navigators. They seem, indeed, to be no more than mountain tops with very little vegetation on them, though here and there a few trees can be seen, standing apart from one another. The Pyramid is nothing but a barren rock, and the little island facing the Kent Group is of no other nature. But at the northern extremity of the latter there are two rocks which stand out a fair way to seaward and which look like two little haycocks. The English chart makes no mention of them.
As soon as we had passed the Kent Group, we shaped a course to make the northern point of the Furneaux Islands, and at four o'clock we had sight of the two islets that lie there. At six o'clock they lay south 70° west of us.
From this bearing, we shaped a course to run along the land on its eastern side, having 40 fathoms of water, but whether the current was setting us more towards the shore than we thought, or whether there is little water in that part, at eight o'clock there were no more than 32 fathoms. At the same hour, we had gone onto the north-west tack so as not to go too far to the south. But at nine o'clock, having no more than twenty fathoms and still heavy winds, I had her bear away to east-north-east in order
(In the left margin, written vertically) to stand off from the coast, which we had in sight. We quickly lost soundings, and at midnight we lay to, the ship's head to the north-west. During the night it continued to blow a strong gale with very violent squalls. The sky, however, was fine, and the clouds, though numerous, gave us no warning of anything like what we experienced. The sea, though under the lee of the islands, was almost as heavy as that we had had before.
1802-03-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from W to SW, a high sea and rain. At 8 the land in sight from S 45° W to S 68° W, 30 miles off. At noon in 41° 51' 0" of latitude observed and in 147° 15' 24" of longitude by account.

1802-03-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze W to SW in gusts, light rain at intervals. At 7.15 a.m. went about.
1802-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, the weather was fine, but the sea was still very heavy and swelling and the wind in strong gusts. We continued to lie to on the same tack, waiting for it to become manageable, which the barometer seemed to promise us, inasmuch as at four in the morning it stood at 27 inches 7 lines and seemed likely to rise further during the day, which in fact took place, for at noon it was already at 28 in. 1 l. 5 l., and the gusts were beginning to become much less strong and frequent.
The latitude was observed as 39° 6' 34", and the longitude by our timekeeper placed us in 146° 50' 47", so that we found ourselves much farther east than we had thought.
As there was every appearance that the weather was about to set fair, we put our lower yards back in their places and the reefs that had been taken in their sails, which had served us so well in working off the coast, were shaken out. Despite my regret at the absence of the Naturaliste, I was very glad that in these circumstances she was far from us, presuming her to be in a better position than ours had been when the bad weather began.
The equinox, as it appears from the weather we have just had, is no less to be feared in these seas than in those of Europe. And ships which at that season find themselves to the west of the Furneaux Islands would do very well to keep out to sea until it is past, for if they are not good weatherly sailers they run the risk of being set onto these islands by the currents, which are very rapid there, so as to find themselves in great difficulty, as happened to us ourselves.
In the afternoon, the weather became altogether fine, the sky cleared and the wind gradually abated. At five o'clock, we set our main topsail so as not to be too much troubled by the motion of the ship caused by the seas, which were still very heavy. At eight o'clock, we set the foresail and the fore topsail and the ship was steered on the tack towards the north and west. This same course was held during the night, with winds from the west variable to west-south-west. The weather was fine and the breeze very moderate, at times even light. We sounded several times without finding bottom at 110 fathoms.
1802-03-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SSW to WNW in gusts, a high sea and rain. At noon in 42° 1' 3" of latitude observed and in 148° 3' 34" of longitude by account. The weather cleared and the wind and sea went down. At 1.30 we filled and stood on under courses. At 4 fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze.

1802-03-24.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, blowing hard from SW. At 1 the wind and sea went down; our main topsail having split, a new one was bent. About 8 p.m. the winds drew round to NW and freshened.
1802-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, the sky was extremely fine and clear and the sea smooth. There remained neither in the air nor on the water any trace of the weather we had had for three days. During the morning we repaired the little damage we had suffered in some of our standing rigging, and the mizzen gaff was put back in its place. At six o'clock, a reef was shaken out of the topsails, and at eight o'clock we made all sail, with the exception of the mainsail, in which there were some repairs to be done.
From sunrise until eight in the morning, we were surrounded by an immense number of grampuses, which came to play about and amuse us with their movements and their leaps. Then they disappeared, heading westward, half a league from the ship. They churned up the sea in such a way that, had we not known what it was, one might have believed there was a shoal awash in the place they occupied.
All the sailors' clothes and hammocks were aired to draw out the damp they had taken up over several days. The ship was likewise cleaned and fumigated in every part.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 38° 26' 41" and our longitude placed us in 146° 9' 1", about six or seven leagues from the coast of New Holland, of which we nevertheless had no sight, no doubt because the land in that part is low, as the English chart we are using indicates.
During the evening the weather continued fine, and the winds were very slight from north-north-west, but then they shifted suddenly from west-north-north-west to west and to south-west. We went about to change our tacks and continued to stand to the north until eight in the evening, when, being in quat seventy-five fathoms of water, fine grey sand, we steered south a little easterly.
From six in the evening, the sea could be seen rising visibly and becoming exceedingly swelling, which was no good omen for the weather we might have during the night; we took precautions against it in advance by taking a second reef in the topsails. Nor was this labour lost lost (sic), for after eight o'clock the wind became very violent and the sea very heavy. At moonrise the squalls were so frequent and the gusts so strong that we were obliged to furl the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail in turn. At ten o'clock the same was done with the foresail, and we lay to under the main topsail after taking in all its reefs.
During the rest of the night it continued to blow a very strong gale, and at times we met with extremely heavy gusts. They were usually accompanied by heavy, cold rain, which made them more disagreeable still. The sea had become very heavy and was beginning to be as bad as on the preceding days. We hoped, however, that this would not last, the barometer holding at 28 inches 2 lines. At midnight, the bottom was eighty fathoms, and at two o'clock it was no longer found at a hundred and ten.
1802-03-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind freshening and blowing strong in gusts at 3 a.m. from NNW to WSW. At noon in 42° 14' 26" of latitude observed and in 147° 7' 0" of longitude by account. At 1.45 land was sighted to the west; at 6 Maria Island bore from us from S 58° W to S 65° W and the south end of Schouten Island S 88° W.

1802-03-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, blowing hard from NW to W and SW in heavy gusts, a high sea. At 1 the land sighted in the west stretched from N 45° W to S 55° W. Saw a fire on Schouten Island. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 58° W to S 65° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 45° W.
1802-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, the wind increased more and more, and the flaws, or rather the gusts, were so strong that more than once I feared losing my main topsail, which I was nevertheless obliged to keep set because of the force of the wind, so that the ship should be less laboured by the sea, which had become very heavy. This second gale seemed to me to be the continuation of the equinoctial one, despite the short interval between the two.
We continued to lie to during the morning, the ship's head to the south, which did not fail to throw us a good deal to the eastward. But I nevertheless preferred this course to the northerly one, which would have carried me about as far.
At noon, the latitude was observed as 38° 56' 17" and the longitude was 146° 43' 31". Towards two o'clock the gusts began to become less strong and less frequent. The barometer likewise seemed to promise us the speedy return of fine weather, having risen to 28 inches 4 lines, which did not often happen to it, as I have observed several times. But on the other hand the sea remained heavy and swelling, which made me decide to keep on the southerly tack rather than make a little sail to stand on the northerly one. However, at six o'clock, the weather having set fair with every appearance of a moderate breeze for the night, we went about and the foresail was set, which did not prevent the leeway, which was still very considerable owing to the great agitation of the sea.
During the night the sky became cloudy and fine. The north-west tack was continued under the same canvas, that is to say with the foresail, the main topsail, the fore-topmast staysail and the mizzen staysail. At midnight, 70 fathoms of line were run out without finding bottom, and from midnight to four o'clock it was not found either at 110. This confirmed me in the opinion I held, that we were farther east than our dead reckoning made us, and even than the longitude given by the timekeeper, the hour angle not having been taken in weather suitable for such observations.
1802-03-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW. At 4 a.m. Maria Island bore from us S 75° W. At 8, Schouten Island from N 87° W to S 86° W and Maria Island from S 60° W to S 49° W. At noon in 42° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 55' 13" of longitude by account. At 6, Maria Island from S 56° W to S 61° W and the islet south of Schouten Island N 89° W. During the night squally weather, with rain.

1802-03-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a strong breeze from SW. A high sea; during the night overcast and squally weather and we reefed the topsails several times. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 78° W to W; Schouten Island from N 67° W to N 64° W.
1802-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, the sky was not as fine as it had been in the night, but the wind had dropped a great deal and the sea was tolerably smooth. We made all sail to re-enter the strait before nightfall, if it were possible, or at least to close with the land if we could not manage it.
In the course of the morning the winds became more favourable to us, allowing us to steer west by compass. And had they not been as light as they were until noon, we might have hoped to see the land before nightfall. That day a sale was held of part of the effects of Citizen Maugé, who died during our stay at Maria Island. These articles consisted of wine, arrack, gherkins and other provisions for the table, taken on board by him both on leaving Europe and during our stay at the Isle of France.
At noon the estimated latitude was 38° 35' 1" and the longitude 146° 24' 27"; although the weather was then very fine, the sun was wrapped in clouds which did not allow us to bring it down to the horizon.
In the afternoon, we had the winds from the east to north-east, a pleasant breeze. We steered west and southerly so as not to get too far to the north, hoping it might be possible to see the land before sunset, though our dead reckoning placed us at a fairly considerable distance from it. But we had no sight of it. After sunset the winds varied from east towards south, and during the night from east towards north. The weather was fine and clear and the breeze fairly fresh.
At a quarter to eight, I ordered the officer of the watch to have a sounding taken, which he did. And at eight o'clock he reported to me that, having run out 90 fathoms straight up and down, he had not found bottom at that depth. I was astonished, for I expected to have it at a much smaller depth. The course west and southerly was continued until nine o'clock, and at that time I came on deck myself to have a sounding taken. We then found ourselves in 43 fathoms. Surprised at not having had bottom at 90 an hour before, I made inquiries into the manner in which the lead had been cast, and I was informed that, to get it done the sooner, they had been content to luff the ship up a little into the wind, but that she was making at least three knots when the line was thrown. I expressed my displeasure to the officer who had been on watch when this happened, at his handling of the ship, making him understand the danger to which it exposed us, above all at night.
I then settled the canvas under the topsails, in which I had a second reef taken, and during the rest of the night boards of about three leagues were made, now to the north, now to the south. As we sounded every hour, we never found less than 41 fathoms nor more than 47, a sandy bottom fit for anchoring.
1802-03-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to SSE, with light rain at intervals. At 10.30, 9° 50' of NW variation. At noon in 42° 39' 2" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 25" of longitude by the watches; by account 146° 58' 24" of longitude. At 6, Schouten Island from N 37° W to N 41° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 78° W. At 11 calm, the weather overcast.

1802-03-27.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a light breeze from SSW to south, with light rain at intervals. About 3 a.m. the winds hauled to the east and freshened. In the forenoon saw whales. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W; Schouten Island from N 26° W to N 39° W; Tasman Island S 30° W.
1802-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At five in the morning the land of the continent of New Holland was perceived, extending from north to NE by north
At ten o'clock, other land was seen in the south-west, presumed to be the Kent Group
At noon, the same land lay south 24° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, at break of day, we sighted the coast of New Holland, and I was surprised to see land of a fair height, though not as high and mountainous as that of Van Diemen's Land or of the Furneaux Islands. The ground appeared to us level and broken in several places, as if it were separate islands. The English chart does not seem to suggest that this land can be seen at the distance at which we reckoned ourselves to be, which by my reckoning might be six or seven leagues.
From the beginning of the day, when the land was taken in bearing from north to north-east by east, we continued to steer north and somewhat west in order to run along it and make it out better. But in all likelihood it forms a considerable bight in the place where we found (it), for at eight o'clock it could no longer be seen except from the mastheads.
Persuaded that I was much farther north than the entrance of the strait, since I had no sight of the Furneaux Islands, although the horizon was clear and extensive in that quarter, I had the ship's head put to the south-west so as to be in 39° of south latitude at noon if the good breeze continued. No soundings were taken in the morning so as not to lose time, as I wished to re-enter the strait before nightfall, if it were possible.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 39° 9' 2" and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 145° 19' 56". At the same moment, we took the bearing of a high land which lay south 24° west of us. We were for some time uncertain whether it was not the Kent Group, but this uncertainty was not of long duration, inasmuch as, having steered south to make them out properly, we passed through the channel they form with the Furneaux Islands. This channel has not yet been examined, or if it has been attended to since the chart the English have given of the great strait that separates Van Diemen's Land from the Furneaux Islands and from the southern part of New Holland, there will be several changes to make in it. Several islands and islets lying halfway along the channel to the south of the Kent Group are not placed on it.
A rock which at first presents itself in the shape of the Pyramid may lead navigators into error with a limited horizon, which is not rare in these waters. But as one approaches it, it takes on quite a different shape, after the manner of a brioche. It is entirely bare of verdure at its base, and its summit is white. When the two extremities of the Kent Group lie one north 6° east and the other north 16° 30' east, the rock is north 51° east and very nearly in the middle of the channel, though a little nearer the Kent Group than the Furneaux Islands. Another, larger rock is seen north 59° east, and the Pyramid south 10° east;
To the west of the Kent Group is the rock mentioned on the chart, but then one sees, north 66° west, a high islet of which it gives no indication and which cannot be one of those placed to the south of Wilson's Promontory, because of the small distance at which it lies from the little island I have just spoken of.
The Kent Group and the land round about appeared to us to be placed too far to the east, at least according to our observations and the courses we followed in rounding the islands on their southern sides.
(In the left margin, written vertically) After the bearing, we continued the course west and southerly until midnight, at which time a second reef was taken in the topsails and we hove to to wait for daylight. We sounded often in the night. The first sounding gave 47 fathoms and the last 52, fine and grey sand mixed. The weather was fine and there was a good breeze from east-north-east to north-east by east. The sea, though smooth, had a slight swell.
1802-03-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NE. At noon in 42° 45' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 39' 7" of longitude by account, Schouten Island bearing from us N 26° W to N 39° W, Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W and Tasman Island S 30° W. Saw a whale. At 6 took the bearing of the high land (the supposed Schouten Islands) forming Schouten Island and the Schouten Peninsula, from N 18° W to N 38°; Maria Island from N 73° W to S 80° W; and the southernmost end of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 30° W.

1802-03-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N and NE, the sea smooth. At 6.30 a.m. the winds drew round to NW. Having been taken aback, we boxed her round. At noon took the bearing of the NE end of Maria Island N 46° W.
1802-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At four o'clock,
the easternmost land of the Kent Group lay west 31° north,
An isolated islet lying almost in the middle of the channel to the south of the group, east 15° south,
And the islet lying at the western part of the group, west 16° south.,
The Pyramid was also in sight, and on the horizon could be seen a high land of small extent which lay west 4° south.
At six o'clock,
The rock in the middle of the channel between the Kent Group and the Furneaux Islands lay north 51° west,
Another, larger rock, nearer the Furneaux Islands than the group, north 59° east,
The Pyramid south 10° east,
The extremities of the Kent Group, one north 6° east, the other north 16° 30' east,
The islet to the west of the group north 37° west,
(In the left margin, written vertically)
A second islet to the west of this one, which does not appear to be marked on the chart, was seen north 66° west,
The opening of the channel of the Kent Group north 2° east.
At six in the evening,
The second islet I have just spoken of north 73° west,
And the Pyramid south 63° east.
At eight in the morning, part of those shown to the south of the Promontory were seen from north 25° east to north 27 east.
At noon, these islets were taken in bearing on the following points of the compass:
The middle of a large rock south 85° 30' east,
Two others, less large than the first, south 28° east and south 76° east,
Three rocks or islets to the north of the first rock, north 25° east, north 36° east and north 45° 35' east,
The land of the Promontory north 21° 50' west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, at daybreak, we again saw the islet which the evening before had been taken in bearing north 73° west, but we had no sight of the Kent Group or of the Pyramid, which made me think that the islet we had in view was rather one of those lying to the south of the Promontory than that of the evening before, despite its perfect resemblance.
We continued to steer north to come and make out the (in the left margin: land) of the mainland and, above all, the Promontory, in order to ascertain whether its position was correctly determined.
At noon, we had the sun over the land; nevertheless, the result of the observations made both by fore and by back observation to obtain its meridian passage gave the ship's latitude as 39° 30' 5". Thus the error produced by some instruments must be compensated by those the others may have had. The longitude given by the timekeeper placed us in 143° 56' 58".
It would follow from the observations, and from our short distance from the land, that the Promontory would be farther north than it ought to be and too far to the east. This confirmed our conjectures about the Kent Group, whose latitude, however, appeared to us well determined.
At the same time of noon, we took the following bearings, namely:
The middle of a large islet, or rather of a very high rock, lay south 55° 30' east of us
Two other rocks, smaller than this one, south 78° 15' east and south 74° 20' east.
Three others to the north of the first were taken in bearing, one north 27° east, another north 36° 10' east and the third north 46° 35' east.
The summit of an islet forming the eastern extremity of the land lay north 17° 50' east.
Other islets could be seen from north 5° 15' west to north 16° west, and the westernmost land in sight was north 21° 50' west.
It was difficult, amid so many islets or rocks of greater or lesser size, to make out with certainty the land at the end of the Promontory, although the whole of the land that must form it could be seen very well
From noon until three in the afternoon, we continued to steer north 22° 30' west, and then we had a perfect view of the southern extremity of the Promontory, having passed at a very short distance all the land and islands that had hidden it from us. We then took a second set of bearings, which gave us:
Wilson's Promontory east 7° north
The west point of the most prominent land north 29° 30' west
The islets then extended from north 67° west to south 71° east. Among them are included the islets lying to the west and north of the Promontory. There were fifteen in sight at that moment. This leads me to think that the chart does not show as many as there must be, since we had so great a number in sight at that moment that it is to be believed the distance run since the morning must have put several of them out of sight.
The land of the Promontory is very high and mountainous, forming two and sometimes three ranges of mountains rising one behind the other. Those nearest the seashore end there in a steep slope, which denotes much water in the channels they form with the islands. Their appearance is pleasing only from a distance, for most of them are barren, and the rock of which they are formed shows bare in several places. The interior, or the second and third range, is better wooded. In short, this coast presents no dangers but those that are visible. The depth of water at a league at most from the islets is above 30 fathoms.
(In the left margin, written vertically) At six in the evening, the west point forming the bay shown to the north-west of the Promontory lay north 33° west. At this extremity the sea could be seen breaking, but not far out. During the night the weather was fine and the breeze moderate. We kept at a reasonable distance from the land in order to run along it the next day.
1802-03-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8 Tasman Island bore from us S 30° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 65° W. At noon in 42° 55' 8" of latitude observed and in 146° 38' 25" of longitude by account. The wind having drawn aft, we steered N 33° 45' W and N 11° 15' W. Saw many tuna and porpoises. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Pillar S 18° W, Maria Island from west to N 51° W. At 9.30 hove to abreast of Schouten Island. Light fine rain.

1802-03-29.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind a light breeze from SW, south and SSE. Saw a considerable quantity of tuna and porpoises. At 9.30 p.m. hove to under the main topsail. At midnight, being very near Schouten Island, we filled and stood on; at 1 hove to again until 5, when we filled and ran along the coast at a distance of 2 miles. It is clear and well wooded but offers no shelter from the winds off the sea. At noon took the bearing of the middle of a low stretch of land having the look of an island S 19° W; the land from S 10° E to N 19° W.
1802-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six in the evening,
The western extremity forming the first bay to the north-west of the Promontory, north 33° west,
One of the islets to the south-east of the Promontory, east 18° 30' south.
At eight in the morning,
The islet to the south-east of the Promontory, east 21° 40' south,
The western extremity of the previous day's bay, west,
The westernmost land in sight, north 29° west,
That of the Promontory, east 12° 45' north.
At noon,
The easternmost point of land in sight, south 68° east,
The land north 74° 45' west,
A land that was thought to be the island forming Western Port, and was not, north 38° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, at daybreak, we shaped a course to come and make out the second bay to the north-west of the Promontory, with a light wind from south-east to east. The land of the Promontory could be seen in the east, and the bay point forming the entrance the western extremity of the second bay lay to the west of us. This bay appeared to us to form a much deeper bight than the English chart seems to indicate. It contains, moreover, a great many coves, larger or smaller, formed by projecting points which might deserve the name of capes, from the way in which they are placed. The land of this second bay is of a good height at the two extremities of each point. But most of the ground forming its shore is low and broken here and there by rises that look like islands. The seashore is formed of sand dunes which present to the eye several white patches. In the interior, at a fairly considerable distance, a long chain of mountains of middling height can be seen, at least relative to the distance at which we were from them. They nevertheless appeared to us well wooded. Their direction ran from north-east to south-west.
At noon, we observed the latitude of 38° 47' 19", and the longitude by our No. 35 placed us in 142° 58' 4". There is no doubt either that this latitude, and even that of the day before, are faulty, or that that (sic) the chart the English give of it has neither the position nor the configuration the coast must have in this part. Without having ranged the land as closely as the course they appear to have followed indicates, we coasted along its shores at a league at most and often less, which enabled us to see several reefs and islets of which their plan makes no mention. Some of these rocks even obliged us to haul our wind in order to weather them.
In the afternoon we continued to run along the land; we passed very close to a large projecting point which some maintained was the island forming Western Port, because its eastern side forms a bight that seemed to indicate a channel. But after rounding it, we could no longer doubt that there was neither island nor port in that place, having run along the whole of its western side at three quarters of a league. After making sure that Western Port could not be in these parts, we steered north and westerly to make out the land of this bay, which is generally low and sandy. Seeing nothing that might lead us to suspect that Western Port was in this part, it was believed that we had passed it, going by the longitude of the timekeeper, which indeed placed it to the north and east of us. However, I could not hold to this idea, because since Wilson's Promontory we had ranged the land closely enough that we could not have failed to see it had it been on the course we had followed.
Continuing to steer north and westerly, we saw ahead of us high land, which was no doubt some mountains of the interior of the country, as we were still too far off to make out the edges of the shore. But as night was coming on, we confined our work for the day to the position in which the ship then found herself. At sunset, the most prominent land to the west lay west 2° south and the easternmost south 20° east.
During the night, we held the tack to the south and west under little sail. The lead, which was cast every hour, never brought up more than 49 fathoms nor less than 47.
1802-03-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At midnight, being too near Schouten Island, we filled to draw off and hove to again at 1. We sent up a rocket every hour. At 5 filled and stood on, running along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It is clear and well wooded. At 8.45, 8° 31' of NE variation. At noon in 41° 44' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 49" of longitude by account. At 3 we were abreast of a small well-wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 50" of latitude. It is the only place on the coast we have run along where a ship can shelter from the winds off the sea. According to Citizen Maurouard there is good anchorage between the land and the island, and it can be entered by either the north or the south passage. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack.

1802-03-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to SSE and south. At 3 we took the bearing, to the west of us, of a small and fairly well wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 51" of south latitude. It is the only place on the east coast of Van Diemen's Land where a ship can take refuge. It lies a short distance from the land, and one may run in by either the south or the north passage. At noon took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 18° W to S 86° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 54° W to N 18° W.
1802-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At daybreak the land extended, relative to our position, from south 20° east to west 2° south. Within this interval a large inlet could be seen in which no land appeared, and which we went to examine.
At eleven o'clock, having reached the inlet above, the entrance of Western Port bore east 6° north of us and the western extremity of the land west 30° south.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, at daybreak, we had a pleasant breeze from the east, variable to east-north-east. We took advantage of it to make way under all sail, steering north-north-east to go and examine a large inlet which lay on that point of the compass and in which no land could be seen. Although our last bearing, taken the evening before at sunset, was well known to us, I was unwilling to run for the land we had in sight to leeward of us without first ascertaining what the part in which no land could be seen might be.
The course from north to north-north-east which we held until eleven in the morning, making great way, at length brought us into the large inlet of which I have just spoken. As the land is extremely low throughout this part, we did not have a clear view of the shore until we were at most a league and a half from it. While we were following the coast round, we saw an opening which seemed to us must undoubtedly be the place the English have named Western Port (Western in another hand). The bearings I had taken at that time, when laid down on the chart, agreed well with the dead reckoning of our course and the distance run the day before. I therefore remain persuaded that this place is truly Western Port. But I persist in saying that the whole of the coast placed to the east in the plan has been badly observed as far as the western point of the first bay.
At noon we observed the latitude of 38° 32' 13" and the longitude indicated by the timekeeper put us in (no figures)
To get out of the inlet we had entered, we had to steer south-west by west and south-west. In this way we ran along a long chain of high mountains whose foremost range ends abruptly at the sea. The change we noticed in the colour of the water made us cast the lead several times. But as we found no bottom at thirty fathoms, we put it down to the effects of the sun.
At eleven o'clock, when I took the bearing of the place I am persuaded is Western Port, the most prominent land to the west bore west 30° south, and the middle of the channel, which may be a league wide, was east 56° south.
At three in the afternoon, continuing to run along the coast, steering south-west and south-west by west, we reached the cape that had seemed to us to form the extremity of the land in sight to the west. And when we had it on that point of the compass, the lands we saw farther to the west extended bore , then, west 22° 30' south, so that it would follow that the cape lies in 38° 48' south latitude and the distance to be run is 30 miles and a third. All this part of the coast is high, well wooded and pleasant in appearance. Small coves of white sand, of little consequence, are to be seen there where, and sometimes the sea breaks, but close inshore. The cape which appeared to me to be the most southerly since Wilson's Promontory I named Cap des Représentations, on account of (the) differences that were (put) to me by the officers at that very moment.
For the rest of the day we held on to the south-west, running along the coast at a short distance. It was pleasant in appearance and without any danger that was not visible. The bearings were carried as far forward as possible and we stopped at the point I named Pointe de la Plateforme, so as to begin again the next day at the same place. At eight o'clock we took the southerly tack to stand a little off the coast.
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) During the night the weather was fine and the sea smooth. At eight o'clock we had bottom at 45 fathoms, of poor quality. At midnight it was 54, of the same nature. From midnight to 3 o'clock it ran from 54 to 51, and at four o'clock we had no more than 30, which made us go back on the southerly tack until daybreak. When we had bottom at 30 fathoms, the land could be seen to the north-east.
1802-03-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to NW by way of east. At 2 a.m. hove to; at 5 filled and stood in to close the land. At 8.30, 9° 54' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 49' 17" of latitude observed and in 146° 50' 25" of longitude by account, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. At 5.30 the air having come from the west, we steered offshore; shortly afterwards it came back to ESE. We hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 6 Swan Island S 81° W. At midnight calm; lay to.

1802-03-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds east, almost calm. At 1 a.m. hove to under the main topsail. At 3 filled and stood on, and at 4 hove to again in the same way. We got a kedge anchor ready to let go. At noon took the bearing of the middle of Swan Island S 75° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 65° W to north.
1802-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At four o'clock,
the easternmost point of the land in sight bore north 16° east,
Cap des Représentations north 89° west,
The land stretched as far as the eye could reach to the west of this cape.
At eight in the evening,
a point which in the course of the evening had seemed to us to form the southern extremity of the land
bore west of us at about a league and a half.
At noon,
a cape which I named Cap du Maréchal bore east
and the land ahead of us stretched as far as west by north-west, forming a coast full of cliffs falling sheer to the sea.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, at daybreak, we closed with the land to come up with Pointe de la Plateforme, to the south of which we lay at most four leagues off. At seven o'clock, being well assured of our position of the day before, we resumed our work in the hope of a good day, for there was a pleasant breeze from east to east-north-east and we steered north under all sail. The coast we ran along from seven o'clock until noon is high and mountainous, and to the eye just as varied and pleasant in appearance as that of the day before, being almost entirely wooded down to the water's edge, with the exception, however, of some large white patches seen in various places, which might serve as landmarks. The direction of the coast, from Cap de la Plateforme to the one we doubled at noon, was (no figures).
I named this last cape Cap du Maréchal because on an eminence at the water's edge upon it two hollows are to be seen which have exactly the shape of a horseshoe.
At ten o'clock we were becalmed for a moment. The winds, or at least a light breeze which came to us from the westward, made us take the south-westerly tack, but not for long, for at eleven o'clock the easterly breeze returned and it blew quite fresh.
At noon the latitude was observed as 38° 52' 15" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 140° 38' 4".
During the evening we continued to run along the coast, which here changes in nature and appearance. Although the ground at the water's edge is high and steep, it looks barren as far as the range of mountains to be seen in the interior, which are well wooded. In the morning a smoke had been seen to the west of this land, which told us that it was inhabited in that part, for it was the first we had seen since leaving the Promontory. We saw this same fire again in the afternoon, on the top of a height at the water's edge, but it was not very large.
The whole of the coast we ran along appeared to me unapproachable and not even to offer shelter for a boat. Although it is divided into several coves, some larger than others, which would seem to promise an easy landing, the sea breaks all along the shore. Of this we made positively sure from the short distance we were off it.
I gave the name Cap des Falaises to the first cape one meets after doubling Cap du Maréchal, from which it lies eight leagues ½ distant. The course to reach it is north 23° west. Very nearly the same as that from Pointe de la Plateforme to this first cape. But the distance is not as great, being only 19 miles ½. After passing Pointe des Falaises one comes upon a large inlet which offers nothing of interest to the eye and is of a very dreary aspect. We coasted it along its whole extent, and to get out of it we had to make way to the south, after which the coast stretches to the west and west by south-west as far as the eye can reach. It was at this last point that we ended our bearings after sunset.
At seven o'clock we trimmed our sails close-hauled, heading south, to stand off the coast for the night, and at eight o'clock the lead gave 29 fathoms, being by our dead reckoning a good two leagues off at that time.. During the night the weather was fine and the breeze light. We ran about four leagues on the southerly tack and then hove to, drifting to the north-west. The soundings increased steadily to 46 fathoms, coarse gravel and rotten shells.
1802-03-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm with very variable light airs. At 5 filled and stood west with a light breeze from SE. At 8 the north point of Swan Island bore from us S 69° W. At 9.30, 10° 6' 40" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 26" of latitude observed and in 146° 41' 31" of longitude by account, Swan Island (its middle) bearing from us S 75° W. At 2.30, the breeze from the west, we made several boards until 6.30, when we fell into a flat calm. At 7.15 we let go a kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage taken at daybreak: Swan Island (its middle) S 19° E, and the Furneaux Islands from N 42° E to N 28° W.

1802-04-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NW to west. A calm coming on, at 7.15 we let go the kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, and veered 50 fathoms of hawser. At 6.30 a.m. got under way under topsails and made all sail. At noon took the bearing of the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 5° W; the eastern end N 50° E; the north end of Swan Island N 88° E; Waterhouse Island from S 48° W to S 59° W.
1802-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six in the evening,
The most prominent land to the east bore south 71° east.,
The westernmost land in sight north 65° west,
And that nearest the ship north 48° east, this last at a distance of one league.
At six in the morning,
The easternmost land in sight was north 45° east,
The westernmost, north 22° 30' west,
In the interior a lofty peak could be seen, bearing north 56° 15' east
At noon,
Île aux Alouettes [Lady Julia Percy Island] bore, at its northern part, north 41° west,
and at its southern part, north 69° west,
From this point land could be seen to the west as far as the eye could reach.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, we found ourselves rather too far from the coast, which obliged us to trim our sails on the starboard tack to draw closer to it, the wind being then north-east, a good breeze. After identifying the point where we had stopped the day before, we ran along the coast to examine a fairly high land which lay a little to leeward of us and which appeared to me to jut far out in relation to a cape showing to the west-north-west of our position. As it was blowing a good breeze, we came up with this land easily and quickly and found it to be an island a good league or so from the mainland, offering an easy passage between itself and the shore. This island, which is very flat and level, was the first we had met since leaving the Promontory that lay at such a distance from the mainland. As I intended to pass through the channel it offered, we hauled our wind as much as was needed to stand into it. But just as we were about to double it, the wind suddenly failed us and we were carried much closer than I should have wished to a long line of breakers by which the whole of its eastern side is girt. Our position was then all the more disagreeable because the bottom, which was still at 27 fathoms although we were barely a league from the coast, was not at all fit for anchoring.
At noon we observed the latitude 38° 27' 32" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 139° 39' 54". Shortly afterwards a light air came to us from the south-east, of which we very quickly took advantage to get away from this island coast, which we doubled at its southern part at a distance of one league. This island is entirely without trees and seems to be covered only with a kind of very low heath, and did not appear (to me) to offer the slightest resource. It is easy to recognise and its latitude well determined, since it bore east of us at the moment when we observed 38° 27' 32" of latitude. Its southern extremity is higher than the northern, and the sea breaks there with even greater force than on its eastern side. The coast of the mainland opposite it is formed of dunes broken by large white patches, and the edge of the shore is sandy.
In the afternoon the wind shifted to the east, a pleasant breeze, and we continued on our course to learn the depth (in another hand: the extent) of a large inlet which lay to the north of us. Before leaving this island I named it Île aux Alouettes, because we caught a lark which came to rest on board when we were abreast of it.
While making our way north into the inlet before us, we saw a second island, likewise lying a little off the mainland, whose channel also appeared easy; but not wishing to give up the examination we intended to make of this great bay, we continued to steer north-west until we had assured ourselves that it offered nothing of interest. Then we changed tacks and hauled close-hauled on the south-south-west board to double, before nightfall, which was beginning to draw on, the second island of which I have just spoken. This second island is no more than a barren rock followed by two others which appear separate at a certain distance but are all joined together by a reef awash. This island was named Île du Dragon, from the perfect resemblance it bears, from the east as from the west, to the fabulous animal to which that name has been given. The lands of the mainland are high, falling sheer to the sea and somewhat wooded, but approaching them is made difficult by a long line of breakers whose noise can be heard from quite a distance.
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) At seven o'clock our bearings ended at the point of a bold cape easy to recognise the next day. Although we were at most a league and a half from the land, the bottom was at 45 fathoms and very poor for anchoring. From eight o'clock to midnight, on the tack to the south towards the east, it went to 85, and on the tack to the west towards the north, from 85 to 55, the same quality. For the rest, the weather was fine and the sea calm. The (winds) varied from east towards south as well as from east towards north. (Fires were seen) in various parts of the coast.
1802-04-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to ENE. At 6.30 a.m. got under way and shaped our course for Waterhouse. At 8, the Furneaux Islands from N 32° W to N 56° E, Swan Island from S 64° E to S 51° E and Cape Portland S 19° W. At 8.15, 9° 54' of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 42" of latitude observed and in 146° 15' 49" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands from N 5° W to N 50° E, the north end of Swan Island N 88° E, Waterhouse from S 48° W to S 59° W. At 1 both large boats were sent off under the orders of Citizens Heirisson and Maurouard to go round Waterhouse and look for any orders the commander might have left there. At 5.45 we let go a kedge anchor in 23 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 16° E to N 56° E, the easternmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 78° E, the north point of Waterhouse S 87° E, its SW point S 23° E, Flat Island S 66° W.

1802-04-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE. Our large boat and the Géographe's boat were put in the water to go round Waterhouse and look for any instructions the commander might have left there. At 5.45 let go a kedge anchor in 20 fathoms, grey sand mixed with broken shell, and veered 60 fathoms of hawser. Bearings of the anchorage: the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 16° E; the eastern end N 56° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 78° E; the westernmost end S 52° W; the north end of Waterhouse S 87° E; the south end S 23° E; Flat Island S 66° E. At 10 a.m. both large boats came back without having found anything to show that the commander had been there.
1802-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At half past 5 in the evening, a second islet off the coast, which I have named Îlot du Dragon, bore north 3° west, distance one league.
At seven o'clock, the most prominent land ahead of us bore west 20° north
At six in the morning, Îlot du Dragon was east 28° north
At noon, the most prominent land to the east bore south 70° east
The westernmost, north 45° west
A large white patch formed by a sand dune, a good league from us, bore north 75° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we found ourselves in a very favourable position for beginning our bearings from sunrise. The pleasant breeze then blowing from north-east to north-north-east even gave us hope of carrying them fairly far in the course of the day. But we were disappointed in our expectation by the calm and by light breezes from north to north-west, which did not allow us to get very far and which even carried us away which carries us away from the land, from which we were at most a league when it came to us. The coast we had in sight in the morning was high and fairly well wooded in the interior of the country. After it came a sandy, barren tract, ending at the water's edge in dunes which everywhere showed large white patches and offered few landmarks. There was also, abreast of us, a large inlet whose western extremity, to the eye, appeared to end in the north-west.
For several days it had been noticed that in the morning the wind came to us fairly regularly from north-north-east to north-east, that it blew a good breeze until about nine or ten o'clock, and that it then fell off markedly, so that at noon we found ourselves becalmed. Between noon and two o'clock the wind shifted from east to south-east and blew a pleasant breeze. If this pattern were regular for them in this season, it would be a great advantage to us, but a longer series of observations on this point is needed to say how things stand.
At noon the latitude was observed as 38° 17' 57".
In the evening we continued to run along the coast, which here is quite level except for a few mountain tops to be seen in the interior of the country. The shores are unbroken dunes at whose foot the sea breaks with such force that it would be impossible to land there. About half past three, steering north-west with a pleasant breeze from the south-east, and having entered an inlet no less considerable than that of the day before, though its mouth was not so wide, we saw, at the very moment when we were sailing in the greatest security, a breaker right ahead of us which the sun had hidden from our sight. We were then no more than two miles from it, so that we had only just the time needed to trim our sails on the larboard tack, standing south-south-west and south-west to double it. Perhaps the channel between this danger and the mainland is navigable, but I do not vouch for it, having left it to starboard as we doubled it. Its extent is not considerable, being no more than a mile in its greatest length. After passing it, we steered west by south-west and west to come up with the westernmost land we then had in sight. When abreast of the danger I have just spoken of, I did not have soundings taken, so as not to dishearten anyone if the depth proved small. A gratuity of one louis was granted to the man named Ciré, topman, who first sighted it and gave us warning.
As we drew near the land again, we saw a third islet lying a short distance from it, which we afterwards found to be joined to it by a reef on which the sea rose to a great height. I gave this islet the name Îlot du Chameau because it had roughly the shape of that animal. It is easy to recognise by a lofty peak leaning to the north-west. Our bearings for the day ended at a point projecting a little farther, which we had ahead of this islet. Other land could also be seen west 22° 30' north.
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) At eight o'clock we took, as usual, the southerly tack, which was held until midnight in fine weather. At that same time we sounded, to regulate our southerly course, and found bottom at 23 fathoms, not very suitable for anchoring. To our great astonishment no bottom was found at nine o'clock at 45, and at ten o'clock it was eighty-two, at midnight ninety, when we took the northerly tack.
1802-04-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SE. At 10 both boats came in from Waterhouse, where they had found nothing to show that the commander had been there. The sick were sent to Waterhouse; the seamen known as shooters were sent there to shoot for the crew. At half past noon the large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to Port Dalrymple. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 11 feet 5 inches, difference 3 inches. At 11 p.m. the sick and the shooters came back aboard; the shooting was not as good as might have been expected.

1802-04-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze varying from NNE to ESE. Our large boat was sent off to Port Dalrymple.
1802-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At four o'clock,
took the bearing of the eastern extremity of the land, south 72° 30' east,
The middle of the breakers seen at the head of the bay, N 11° 30' west
The western extremity of the land north 85 west
At daybreak the land could be seen from north to north-east, but at too great a distance to make out its shape. During the morning none of the points identified the day before could be seen on this land.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we found ourselves in a position quite different from the one I expected to be in. This circumstance was no doubt produced by two causes, but entirely different from each other. The first was through the fault or carelessness of the officer who had the watch from midnight to four o'clock, in not informing me that at one o'clock he had found no bottom at 115 fathoms. And the second must be attributed to the strength of the currents which, in all likelihood, carried us to the west at greater speed than usual, since we found we had passed far beyond the point of bearing which was to serve as our landmark for our work that day.
However that may be, we sighted the land clearly at daybreak, but it presented itself to us in a form so different from what we had seen until then that we recognised absolutely nothing of what we had observed the day before. As the wind was then variable from north to north-west, and remained so all the morning, I did not go about until the afternoon, so as to have a horizon wide enough not to have the sun above the land, which, where we were, is very low and ends at the sea in sand dunes of moderate height, full of white patches lit up at times by the sun, which makes them visible from quite far off.
At noon the latitude was observed as 37° 52' 20" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 137° 37' 40". Consequently much farther west than the dead reckoning of the courses run up to this day, in spite of their small difference from the altitudes observed since leaving the Promontory.
Throughout the evening we ran along a very low and quite level coast, on which (no) elevation was to be seen other than sand dunes, some higher than others. Although we were four and five leagues from the coast, the depth of water was considerable and we had fifty fathoms at that distance. The bottom was of rather coarse, reddish sand, and seemed to us good for anchoring. It was the first of this kind we had yet met with on the coast. We continued to steer east, making some southing, to come and identify the last bearing we had taken, not wishing, as far as possible, to leave any gap along the whole of this coast.
About four in the afternoon the sky became very cloudy and there was every appearance of a change in the weather. However, the wind, which had been from the west for the greater part of the day, shifted to the north-east, but the breeze was very light and we made little progress. A heavy swell from the south-west was also making itself felt, and I greatly feared some squalls from that quarter of the horizon, all the more so as the thermo-barometer was beginning to fall and the hygrometer to move towards damp.
At eight o'clock we made the course more southerly and spent the night beating to and fro in the hope of identifying the next day the point we were trying to regain. The wind, which was very light and variable, nevertheless gave us little hope of succeeding.
During the night the noise made by the swell breaking back on the coast was heard so plainly that, had the lead not shown us that we were well off it, we would have reckoned ourselves no more than a league away.
1802-04-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from ESE to north. At 10.30 I went with Citizen Milius and several others to shoot on Van Diemen's Land. The dinghy, which had been fishing at Waterhouse, brought back a little fish. At nightfall a light was shown at the gaff and priming burnt every half hour.

1802-04-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze variable from east to north. We kept a light at the gaff until the arrival of our boat, which was back at 1 a.m.
1802-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At six in the evening,
the two extremities of the land in sight bore, the one north
68° east, and the other north 25° east.
At eight in the morning,
the land could be seen from north to east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, the wind during the morning was north, variable towards the east, and so light that the ship could scarcely steer. We were about four leagues from the coast, which we continued to run along to reach a bold point which, at the distance we were from it, we judged must be the one we had been looking for since yesterday. The weather was very fine all the morning, and the clouds that had piled up one upon another had vanished. But the swell was still the same. The barometer, which the day before had stood constantly at 28 inches 5 lines, was rising a little, and we then had it at 28 inches 6 lines.
All through the morning the noise made by the sea on the shore, or on the reefs lying a little off it, could be heard. We could make them out perfectly from the deck, and the sea could be seen rising to a very great height. At nine o'clock, being becalmed, I had the lead cast. Bottom was found at 23 fathoms, of a kind of white mud or decomposed marl of the same colour, and very hard to the lead.
At noon the latitude was observed as 37° 56' 15" and the longitude indicated by the timekeeper was 138° 5' 49".
We then had very fine weather, but the wind so slack that the ship barely steered. It was a great regret to us not to be able, for want of wind, to profit from the fine weather we had had for five or six days, all the more so as the bad season was advancing apace.
About two o'clock, having clearly identified the points fixed by our last bearings, we made sail to continue our work, following the coast at so short a distance that we often had no more than fifteen fathoms, being less than a league off. The land in this part was the lowest we had yet had. Some peaks of moderate height could indeed be seen in the interior of the country, but they were few in number. The whole of the shore is a succession of sand dunes, for the most part barren and without greenery. In front of the beach could be made out an unbroken line of rocks running a short way out to sea, on which the waves break with extraordinary force. This was the cause of the continual noise we heard.
At sunset we sighted a fairly extensive sandbank lying at the extremity of the land most in view to the west. When it was first taken in bearing it lay west-north-west by compass, and as daylight began to fail it was thought to extend as far as west-south-west. As we were then somewhat farther from the land, which here forms a fairly large cove, the depth had increased by six fathoms in the space of an hour and a half. Having taken the south-south-westerly tack to stand off from the coast and from any dangers that may lie there, we put off the examination of this bank until the next day, weather permitting. During the day several smokes were seen in the interior of the country, but none on the seashore.
During the night it was calm most of the time. Nevertheless, although the ship seemed to make no headway, the depth increased continually and rapidly, since at eleven o'clock no bottom was found at 110 fathoms. On the northerly tack, which was held from midnight until daybreak, none was found at that depth either.
1802-04-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to WNW. At 1.15 we came in from Van Diemen's Land, where we had spent the 13th [Germinal, 3 April 1802]. We saw many kangaroos there; we were able to fire at only one, which we missed. We found good water and a watering place on the shore where it would be very easy to water in fine weather, because the boat could come alongside the rocks and fill the casks with a hose. Geese and other birds were killed and distributed. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 45' 34"; longitude 145° 37' 00". NE variation on the 12th [Germinal, 2 April 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 22' 00"; the same day at 4.30 p.m., 10° 08' 40"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 12' 30"; on the 14th [Germinal, 4 April 1802] at 4 p.m., 10° 48' 20"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 13' 30"; on the 15th [Germinal, 5 April 1802] at 6.15 a.m., 9° 30' 40". The tides were scarcely perceptible; the flood sets SW and the ebb NE. The greatest rate of the current was 1.0 knot.

1802-04-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from north to WNW. Calm for the rest of the day. At 7.30 the breeze got up from the ENE. We fired a gun to call the dinghy and hoisted our topsails; at 11 the dinghy being back, she was hoisted in.
1802-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
At six in the evening
the easternmost land in sight bore east-south-east
The westernmost land north-west
At half past six
we thought we saw a fairly extensive breaker stretching from west-north-west to west-south-west
At daybreak the land could be seen, though very hazy, from east-north-east to north.
Nota: the calm and the haze did not allow bearings to be taken along the coast during this day.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, after spending the greater part of the night becalmed, without seeming to have made much way, we nevertheless found ourselves four or five leagues from the land, with no bottom at 120 fathoms. With what little wind there was we steered north-east to draw nearer to it, and at nine o'clock we were in 60 fathoms, very bad bottom. What little wind there was then came from the west to north-west. But it suddenly shifted to north-north-east and, having taken us aback, we changed tacks. Our distance from the land may have been two and a half to three leagues. At the time we were obliged to change course, nothing could be seen of the sandbank which we believed we had sighted the evening before at sunset.
It is quite possible that what had been taken for a sandbank was something like what we saw in the morning, which the lookouts likewise reported as a bank on which the sea was breaking heavily, but which, as we advanced, we found to be nothing but a very large school of porpoises which, by their leaps and their various evolutions, so stirred up the sea that at a distance the eddies they caused had all the appearance of a shoal on which the swell was breaking.
Throughout the morning the sky was very overcast, dark and often hazy, so that our horizon was very limited. Nevertheless, from time to time we saw the sand dunes which border the coast and some fairly high mountains in the interior. They are very low at the water's edge and similar in appearance to those we had run close along the day before.
At noon the latitude was observed as 37° 42, but very doubtful, the weather being ill suited to such observations. That by dead reckoning put us in 37° 46' 5", which would give little difference.
In the evening the weather continued overcast, very dark and hazy, with a limited horizon. Nevertheless, from time to time we saw the land, whose two extremities as far as we could see extended from north by north-east to east. Several soundings were taken during the evening without finding bottom at 90 and 110 fathoms. At four o'clock, so as not to stray too far from the coast, we went about to stand to the north-east, in the hope of seeing the weather clear up, despite little sign of any early change. For we had continual and even fairly heavy rain. My intention was to hold this course until we had fifty or sixty fathoms, so as to keep far enough from the land to have nothing to fear from winds from south to south-west if the weather turned bad.
At eight o'clock, having found bottom at 60 fathoms, we went about to stand off and made two boards during the night, always keeping on soundings. There was little wind, and it was very light and variable. On the other hand we had a great deal of rain and a sky constantly damp, very dark and hazy whenever the rain ceased. We did not stand in towards the land beyond 60 fathoms, and on the offshore boards we changed course at 85 and 90. The decrease or increase in the depth of water was very rapid according to whether we stood off or in towards the coast.
1802-04-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to south. The boats were hoisted in. At 10.30 hoisted the topsails and fired a swivel gun to call the yawl, which was fishing; at noon she came in and was hoisted in. At 1.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 67° 30' W for Port Dalrymple, where we were to pick up our large boat. At 6 the middle of Waterhouse bore from us N 76° E, 5 miles off, and Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. At 8 a flat calm. During the night overcast weather with continual light rain.

1802-04-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to ESE. At 1.30 got under way and made all sail, studdingsails to port. It fell calm all at once. At 6.30 took the bearing of the middle of Waterhouse Island N 76° E, about 5 miles off; Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. The breeze having freshened, made all sail. At 2, being very close to Flat Island, within a mile, and unable to weather it, we wore ship and made sail to work to windward.
1802-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four in the afternoon,
In a clear spell that lasted only a moment, the land was seen from north to north-east.
At noon,
The westernmost land in sight bore north 22° 30' west,
The southernmost south 63° 30' east,
The eastern point of an islet on the coast (nearest) the ship was seen north 77° 30' east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the wind continued very light and variable from south towards west, but the rain stopped and the sky seemed inclined to clear. At daybreak we sighted the land, but at too great a distance to make out clearly where we were and the point where our bearings had ended. We steered north towards the east to close with the land, in order to make positively sure of the place where we had stopped, which we identified about eight in the morning. Having made quite sure of our position, we resumed our course north towards the west, running along the coast at a league at most. In this place it is made up entirely of barren sand dunes, unpleasing to the eye. In the interior of the country fairly high, well-wooded ground can be seen.
In the morning we coasted a very large cove forming a fairly considerable inlet in its north-eastern part. This inlet ends in a projecting cape, at the extremity of which lies a small island running out to sea about half a league. Its south-eastern part is low and very narrow, but the northern part is higher and can be seen from quite far off. This island is surrounded by breakers all round, and consequently hardly approachable. The same is true of the whole coast, which is guarded by a reef and a line of rocks of varying height which do not allow a landing.
After doubling this island, the course took much more northing than it had until then, and to continue along the coast we steered for a good while north-north-west, changing course only to keep clear of some breakers which at times extend out to sea.
At noon we did not see the sun, although the weather was fairly fine. By our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves in 37° 27'.
About three o'clock we sighted a sunken reef lying nearly half a league from the coast. We saw it rather late, for it was already abeam of us when it was sighted from the deck. We at once brought our larboard tacks aboard, the wind being south-south-east, to stand a little away from it. Nevertheless, we passed no more than a mile from it, in ten fathoms, hard, rocky bottom.
Having gradually come back to our north-north-west course, we came to examine another cape which lay north by north-west of us and seemed to end the coast on that point of the compass. This cape is formed by a salient point falling sheer to the sea. Off it lie three small rocks, one of which is particularly remarkable when coming from the east, in that it is cleft in two and forms an embrasure such as that of a fortress might be. Here again the coast forms a large inlet and appears to run north by north-west. The land is no longer so low, nor formed of sand dunes, as we had had it for more than half the day.
Our bearings ended after sunset at a line of islets and rocks which do not touch the coast, though they lie at no great distance from it. Towards evening the south-south-easterly breeze freshened, and we were very sorry to see it come at a moment when we could not profit by it, being obliged to stand out to sea for the night.
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) During the night a pleasant breeze blew from south-east to south-east by south. Under easy sail we held the south-south-westerly tack until midnight, and then we took that of east-north (sic) and north-east, the wind having become variable and very light. The various soundings taken gave 30 fathoms at two leagues from the land and 64 when we went about. This figure was the greatest we reached and, by our dead reckoning, must have put us at most five leagues from the coast. In general the soundings were very irregular on the first board.
1802-04-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze and calm. At 8 a.m. Flat Island bore from us S 19° W, 4 miles off. At 11.30 the breeze allowed us to shape our course S 45° W. At noon in 40° 49' 34" of latitude by account and in 145° 15' 36" of longitude by account, Flat Island bearing from us S 81° E to S 88° E, 3 miles off. At 6 it bore N 56° E and Rocky Islet S 55° W.

1802-04-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light air from N to south by way of east. At 5 a light breeze got up from the WSW. We lay close-hauled on the port tack. During the night a fresh breeze from south to SSE and SE. At midnight hove to with the main topsail to the mast; at 2 filled and set the courses. At 9.30 a.m., being abreast of Port Dalrymple and seeing our boat, we clewed up our courses and fired a swivel gun. At 10 wore onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail. The large boat came in and was hoisted in at once; at 11 filled and made all sail, studdingsails to starboard.
1802-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four in the afternoon,
the middle of an islet I have mentioned bore north 5° east
and the two extremities of the land in sight extended from north 3° west to south 56° east.
At daybreak,
the land was seen from north to north-north-east
At noon,
the rocks and shoals which had made us change course bore east 21° 30' north
and the land in sight east 10° north.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth we closed with the land in light easterly airs, and at eight o'clock we identified perfectly all our points of bearing of the day before. But we found ourselves somewhat farther from the coast than we had reckoned, although during the night we had kept between 64 and 45 fathoms. In the morning the sky was dark and overcast and the horizon hazy, which made the stretch of coast in sight look as though divided into a multitude of small islands. But when the haze cleared, the whole coast, from north-north-west to east, showed itself in its full extent. Here, as I observed yesterday, it is high, covered with trees and falling sheer at the water's edge, where the shore is not a succession of barren and sterile sand dunes like the one we had coasted for the greater part of the day. About the middle of the cove the coast forms here there are two islets or rocks, longer than they are high, which make it recognisable by their shapes, being divided by openings resembling those of a fortress on which guns had been mounted. The sea breaks around these rocks and at each of the points, but these breakers do not extend out to sea.
At half past nine, running along the coast at a distance of one league, I had soundings taken. I thought we might have fifteen fathoms at that distance, but only ten were found; we would have continued the course we were then making had the bottom not dropped to 8 and even to six fathoms, without any sign warning us of so sudden a decrease. But on bearing away to stand a little farther out, we were much astonished to see a rock awash of which no one had until then had any knowledge, and which even the lookouts had not seen. To double it we were obliged to steer south-west without the depth increasing appreciably. This rock, on which the sea breaks heavily, is surrounded by reefs and seems to be joined to the mainland by a chain of breakers which leaves no hope of a passage, although the channel between it and the land is more than a league wide. To the north of this rock two smaller ones are to be seen, and a breaker which extends to the north-north-west.
