We passed about a league and a half from this danger in 15 fathoms, rounding it on its western side. It will be prudent for the navigators who come after us to beware of it, on account of its distance from the mainland. As soon as we were a little to the north of it, we sought to close with the land, and the depth decreased quickly, for in half an hour we went from 15 fathoms to twelve. Nevertheless, we were much astonished from the east-north-east to push into a great bay in which no end to the land could be seen on that point of the compass. We ran into it as far as eight and nine fathoms before sighting it, and we followed it round at that same depth. The land in this part is very low and forms several inconsiderable coves ending at the sea in sand dunes of moderate height or, to put it better, very low.
At noon the latitude was observed as 37° 1' 47" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 136° 59' 12", which gave us a difference of 3° from that by dead reckoning since leaving the Promontory.
After sunset, our bearings for the day being finished, we took the tack from south-south-west to south-west in a strong breeze from south-south-east to south-east. During the night it blew a strong breeze. We carried little sail so as not to
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) stray too far from the coast, keeping between twenty-five and thirty-five fathoms over a fine sandy bottom. It would have been possible to anchor there had the breeze been less strong. From midnight until four o'clock we lay hove to, but the drift and the current set us a good deal to the west, the depth continually increasing, which decided me to take the north-easterly tack to regain soundings of between twenty and 25 fathoms before daybreak.
1802-04-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to E. At 1, Rocky Islet S 11° E, 1 mile off. At 8 it bore from us S 85° E. At 9, being abreast of Port Dalrymple, we fired a swivel gun to call our boat, which was sighted at 9.30 under the land. At 10 hove to; she came in and was hoisted in. At 11 filled and stood on, the course north. At noon in 40° 56' 16" of latitude by account and in 144° 42' 6" of longitude by account. At 6 hove to with the port side to the wind.

1802-04-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, light rain, a fresh breeze from SE to east and ESE, freshening. At 7 sighted the land in the N 10° E. At noon took the bearing of island (A) S 66° E; a low island (G) N 70° E; another, a sugarloaf, N 58° E; (M) N 50° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a very conspicuous white rock, pierced in its western part, N 7° E. Wilson's Promontory, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations, lies in 39° 10' 54" of south latitude and 147° 37' 31" of east longitude. Islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of east longitude.
1802-04-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
the two extremities of the land in sight bore, the one south 46° east,
and the other north 23° west.
At daybreak the land was seen from east-north-east to north.
At noon it stretched away to the north-west as far as the eye could reach.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, at daybreak, we closed with the coast to continue our work, but it was only about ten o'clock that we were able to begin it, since we found ourselves farther off than the soundings we had had during the night seemed to indicate. We steered north-east to approach it within a short league, which brought us once more into a large, deep cove of as little interest as those we had visited until then. To get out of it we had to pass successively from north-east to north-west by west. The whole of the coast we have been running along since yesterday is made up of nothing but sand dunes, which inspire nothing but gloom and regret. Quite apart from the poor and disagreeable aspect it presents to the eye, the sea breaks all along the shore with extraordinary force, and the two or three swells it forms before reaching it show that there is in this part a shoal which must extend at least half a mile out to sea.
The lookouts at the mastheads, and the curious who chose to go up there, reported that the interior of the country, as far as their sight could penetrate, was nothing but barren sands on which there was no vegetation whatever.
The coast we explored that day had, however, one advantage which we had by no means found in that of the day before, namely that the water was deeper and the bottom regular. Although within a short league of the land, we never had less than 16 fathoms when doubling the points of the small coves met with there, and 19 to 20 when they were passed or even before reaching them.
At noon the latitude was observed as 36° 1' 10", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 137° 9' 40".
In the afternoon we continued to run along a coast that was all sand and formed of dunes of the same nature. But about three o'clock we began to make out high land which seemed to us likely to be pleasant in appearance. Shortly afterwards a ship was sighted which at first we thought must be the Naturaliste, for we were far from believing that any other Europeans were to be found in these waters, and in the season in which we were there. However, we were much mistaken, for as we drew nearer we recognised by her masts and her size that it was not she. At length, at five o'clock, when we could make each other out perfectly, this ship made us a signal which we did not understand and consequently did not answer. Then she hoisted English colours and shortened sail. For our part we hoisted our national colours and I hauled close-hauled to come up with her. As she hailed us first, we were asked what ship it was. My answer was: French. I was then asked whether it was Captain Baudin who commanded. I was very surprised, not only by the question but also at hearing myself named. When I had answered yes, the English ship hove to. Seeing her preparing to send a boat on board, I too hove to to wait for it. The English captain, Mr Flinders, the very man who (in the left margin: discovered the strait which ought to bear his name and which), most wrongly, has been named Banks Strait, came on board, expressed great satisfaction at the agreeable meeting, but was very reserved on everything else. As soon as I learned his name, I paid him my compliments on the pleasure I felt in making his acquaintance. &c.
I communicated to him all that
(In the left margin, written perpendicularly) all that we had set in order up to that moment concerning our geographical work. As it was already late, Mr Flinders told me that if I would stand off on one board during the night and back towards the land on a second to wait for daylight, he would return on board the next day and give me various particulars of the stretch of coast he had visited from Cape Leeuwin to this place. I was much flattered by his proposal and we agreed to keep company during the night, which was very fine.
1802-04-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 5 a.m. we filled and stood on, the course N 11° 15' W. At 7.15 a very high islet (A) was sighted in the N 10° E. At 10.25 it bore from us east (true); a neighbouring islet D N 86° E; another S 85° E (B). At noon in 39° 16' 28" of latitude observed and in 144° 32' 0" of longitude. Took the bearing of a very conspicuous white rock, pierced on its west side, N 7° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a rock M N 50° E; a very high islet P N 58° E; another, C, low, N 70° E; islet A S 66° E. From this bearing and that of 10.25, islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of longitude. At 12.45 we hove to and put the Géographe's boat in the water; she was provisioned for 15 days and left at 1.30 under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, accompanied by Citizen Boulanger, surveyor, to fix the promontory and survey the coast as far as Western Port. At 1.45 we filled and stood in for the promontory. At 3.15, being very near it, we bore away N 65° 15' W and ran along the islets at its end. At 4.30, 8° 45' 30" of NE variation; at 5.45, 8° 29' 0" the same. At 6 took the bearing of a very conspicuous cape N 45° E and another, A, N 33° W, half a mile off. Between these two capes there is a large bight. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 50" of longitude. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; the wind a strong breeze, the weather overcast, with light rain. At midnight filled on the port tack, the land in sight to the NE.

1802-04-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to SE and NE. The Géographe's boat was put in the water with fifteen days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, lieutenant, and Boulanger, the surveyor, to determine the position of the promontory. At 9 p.m. went onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail; the lead brought up 40 fathoms, rocky bottom. At 6 filled and made sail. At noon took the bearing of cape (B) N 41° E; Western Island N 46° W, about 10 miles off.
1802-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
The land stretched from south-east 85° east to west.
At noon,
It extended from north 72° east to south 72° west.
An islet quite close to us then bore north 25° west
Historical events and Remarks.
On the nineteenth, in the morning, Mr Flinders making ready to come back on board, as he had told me the day before, I hove to again to wait for him. At half past six he arrived, accompanied by the same person who had come the day before. As he was much less reserved on this second visit than he had been the day before, he told me that his ship was called the Investigator and that he had left Europe about eight months after me. He also told me that he had begun his survey of the coasts of New Holland at Cape Leeuwin, had visited the islands of St Peter and St Francis, as well as the whole coast as far as the place where we met. He also showed me the plan of a harbour he had discovered in an island from which we were only fifteen to twenty leagues distant, and which he had named Kangaroo Island, from the great number of them he found in that place. This island, according to his account, is long, high and extensive, and offers a good passage between itself and the mainland. He stayed there six weeks, and consequently had time to examine it well.
Before we parted, Mr Flinders gave me several charts published by Arrowsmith since our departure. When I told him of the accident that had befallen my boat, and asked him to give it such help as lay in his power should he chance to meet it, he told me that a similar misfortune had befallen him at his Kangaroo Island, where he had lost eight men and a boat. The second ship which accompanied him had also been separated from him in the equinoctial gale, and which I weathered partly in Bass Strait and the end of it outside. Mr Flinders told me on leaving that he was going to make for the strait and try to examine a land said to exist between the Hunter Islands and the harbour they have named Western Port. At eight in the morning we parted, wishing each other a good voyage.
For the rest of the day there was little wind. At times we were even becalmed, at the mercy of the current, which was setting us onto the coast, from which we were then only a league distant. After identifying my points of the day before, we coasted the high land we had seen a little before sunset. The coast in this place was, if not very pleasing to the eye, at least preferable to the sand dunes we had just left.
At noon the latitude was observed as 35° 36', but very doubtful, and at three o'clock we sighted the island & the islets of which Mr Flinders had spoken to me. I steered to enter the channel which separates this island from the mainland, but as the little wind there was did not allow me to enter it before nightfall, I went about at five o'clock to stand out to sea.
While running along the mainland during the day, we sighted three islets or rocks which lie so short a distance from it that, to have seen them, one had to hug the coast as closely as we did. In case of calm one could anchor there in 24 or 21 fathoms, the bottom being sand and good for anchoring, a thing rare enough from the Promontory to this place.
At sunset Mr Flinders's ship could still be seen standing on the south-westerly tack.
During the night the wind was fairly fresh from south to south-south-east until midnight, but then it fell calm, and shortly afterwards we took the tack towards the land.
1802-04-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from N to S by way of east. At 3.30 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on. At 7.30 Cape A bore from us east, 11 miles off. At noon in 38° 46' 0" of latitude observed and in 143° 55' 6" of longitude by account, a cape B bearing N 41° E and Western Island N 46° W, 10 miles off. At noon the large boat and the small boat were put in the water and provisioned for 10 days. At 1.45 they left under the orders of Citizen Milius, accompanied by Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey Western Port. At 4.15, 9° 16' 0" of NE variation; at 5.15, 9° 14' 30" of variation; at 5.45, 38° 48' 19" of latitude observed. At 4 the promontory S 70° E, cape B N 55° E, Western Island from N 27° W to N 32° W, the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 61° W. At 5.30 the promontory S 75° E, Western Island N 14° W.

1802-04-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE. The large boat and the small boat were put in the water, one under the orders of Citizen Milius, frigate captain, and the other under those of Citizen Brèvedent, midshipman; they left to survey Western Port. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 48" of east longitude.
1802-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
two islets or rocks, from which we were a short distance off, bore one south 50° west, and the other south 57° west.
The westernmost land of the mainland in sight bore north 71° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, in the morning, having identified all our points of the day before, we steered for two islets lying to the east of Kangaroo Island. The first is nothing more than a heap of rocks high enough to be seen from five or six leagues out at sea. It appears clear of danger, and we never had less than 16 fathoms at a league's distance. The same cannot be said of the second rock, which has on its south-east side a long reef on which the sea breaks heavily and rises to a great height. As I am drawing a view of these two islets, I shall say no more on the subject. The latitude of the first seemed to me to be 35° 42'. As the one lying to the south-east of it is at no great distance, navigators cannot fail to sight both of them together.
The channel which separates the two islets from the mainland is fine, deep and convenient. The same is true of the one they form with the eastern coast of Kangaroo Island.
We were much hindered in the afternoon by the dying away of the wind, which fell almost calm. But the current served us fairly well, although it set us towards the mainland as it ran to the north-west. We passed at a short league from it, in 18 fathoms of water, off a projecting point from which the coast appears to run away to the north-north-west. The land here is of a good height and most varied to the eye, but it leaves one regretting that it is impossible to land, since the shore falls sheer into the sea. Now and then, however, one comes upon little sandy coves where the sea also breaks along the edge of the beach.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 39' 51" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 135° 42' 10".
In the evening, we stood on to close the eastern part of Kangaroo Island, which we had in sight and about which Mr Flinders had given me some particulars. At sunset we had a light breeze from the east which, though very faint, enabled us to do so. The bottom was very irregular along the track we made to get there, and the lightness of the breeze decided me to come to anchor at about nine in the evening, in twenty-six fathoms, sandy bottom. But whether it was too hard or for some other reason, our anchor did not hold and we were obliged to get under sail again. While our anchor was down, we observed that the current was very strong and that it truly set to the north-west, since we were dragging our anchor to windward. The rest of the night was spent beating to and fro, waiting for daylight, so as to continue taking bearings of the principal points which may fix the position of this island relative to the mainland. The channel it forms with the cap de l'Etoile is about four and a half leagues, or five leagues at most.
During the night, the weather looked very threatening for the following day. The sky clouded over in the north and at times we had rain without wind.
1802-04-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from WNW to S, and calm. At 8.45, 8° 34' 50" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 58' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 43' 12" of longitude by account. At 4 Western Island N 8° W, 14 miles off. At 4.30, 9° 54' 20" of NE variation. At 6, Western Island from N 6° W to N 15° W, 8 miles off.

1802-04-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south and to the west. At 4 took the bearing of Western Island N 8° W, about 14 miles off. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the other tack; at 7 a.m. filled and stood on. At noon Western Island N 47° W; Cape Bon N 75° W.
1802-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four in the afternoon,
The two extremities of the mainland bore one north 70° east and the other north 56° west.
The most prominent land of Kangaroo Island from south 29° west to south 78° west.
The middle of the two double islets in the evening was (south) 46° east for the one, and south 36° east for the other.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, in the morning, as we were standing in towards the mainland in the channel it forms with Kangaroo Island, we suddenly saw on the shore, from which we were then no great distance, a very bright light, such as is commonly carried by those who go fishing along the seashore at night. At daybreak we saw it much more clearly, and someone even thought he had plainly made out the person carrying it. This may well have been so, for it could be seen moving in different directions and it was not a fixed fire, since we had it now ahead of and now astern of the first bearing we had taken of it. When day came, it disappeared.
Until sunrise the winds were very light and unsettled, but then they settled in the north and it blew a good breeze until noon. We ran along a fair stretch of the eastern part of Kangaroo Island and looked into several rather deep coves, where in the fine season, that is to say in summer, there are good anchorages and shelter from winds from north-west round by west to south. But from any other point of the horizon the sea must be rough there, since we found it so with moderate northerly winds. The soundings all along the coast are fairly regular. They are ten fathoms at a league and a half from the coast, and seven and six at a short distance. The interior of the country presents a rather pleasant aspect, and although most of the trees had lost their leaves, enough green ones still remained to make the view agreeable. I ran along the land very close, not only to obtain exact bearings of it but also in the hope of finding the harbour which they (in the left margin: which the English) say they found there, and in which Mr Flinders told me he had stayed six weeks to survey this part of the coast. It seems, up to this moment, that I misunderstood or misheard the latitude he gave me for it, for the land does not appear to us, so far, to extend as far north as I believe I heard him tell me.
In the course of the morning we were obliged to go about in order to weather a projecting point which the winds did not allow us to weather without standing off a little.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 40'. There was no hour angle.
During the evening we continued to run along the coast at a short distance with a pleasant breeze, and after sunset we stood to the north and by east to close with the mainland. During the night the winds were light and unsettled. We tried to keep in 20 fathoms and had succeeded, when at midnight we suddenly dropped into 15 and shortly afterwards into 12. A low, level land was then seen, on which the sea was breaking heavily enough to be clearly heard. We did not know what land it could be, which led us to bear away by degrees as far as south-east, when we found 20 fathoms again. The rest of the night was spent beating in short tacks so as not to stand too far from the land we had seen during the night, in order to identify it the next day. When it was seen, we were steering north-east and its two extremities in sight bore one north 15° east and the other south 85° west.
1802-04-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to W. At half past midnight hove to; at 7 filled and stood on. At 7.30, 8° 6' 20" of NE variation. At 8, Western Island N 48° W. At noon in 38° 55' 26" of latitude observed and in 143° 50' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island N 27° W, cape B N 75° E. At 6, the middle of Western Island N 10° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to SSW and NW. At 6 took the bearing of the middle of Western Island N 10° W, about 9 miles off. At noon we had it bearing from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off.
1802-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
the extremities of the mainland in sight bore one south 70° east, and the other and the other (sic) north 25° east
Those of Kangaroo Island extended from south 33° east to south 68° west.
At two in the morning,
a land was sighted; it was taken from north 15° east to south 85° west.
At eight in the morning,
the middle of the land seen in the night bore north 15° west
and the mainland extended from south 67° east to south 33° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, we saw again the land we had sighted during the night. It appeared very low to us, just as we had judged it, but much more extensive. Its two extremities stretched from south 67° 30' east to south 63° 30' west. It seemed to us that it must be an island, the middle of which bore north 45° west from us. (In the left margin: it is the southern part of the land which separates the two gulfs).
We also sighted a part of Kangaroo Island, whose two extremities in sight stretched from south 33° 30' west to south 67° 30' east. As we also had in sight the high land of the mainland at a distance of five or six leagues, I preferred to steer for it on our last bearings rather than stop at this island, being convinced moreover that I should see it again as I followed the mainland coast, which here forms a very large indentation.
During the morning there was a pleasant breeze, but from the north, which was not very favourable to the course we should have to make after closing the coast near enough to survey it properly.
A calm having come on at about eleven, and the currents setting us rapidly into a large bay abreast of us, we were obliged to wear round so as to stand a little out to sea as soon as the breeze should spring up.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 27' 0" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 135° 33' 6".
During the evening we had a light air from north to north-north-west, by means of which we stood a little out to sea, but it was very faint and did not last long. Nevertheless, we had drawn off nearly a league and a half from the coast; the bottom was then 20 fathoms, good for anchoring. The short stretch of coast we covered in the course of this day is high and very mountainous. We saw no danger there that was not visible. Most of the mountains were bare of trees, others had trees that had lost their leaves, and the greater part offered only arid ground covered with dried grass the colour of straw.
At sunset the wind, or rather the light air, went round to the south-west; we steered north-north-east for the land which bore from us on that point of the compass, reckoning ourselves eight leagues from it, so as to approach it during the night and lose no time the next day. The land trending well to the north in this quarter, we hoped to find some harbour in the gulf it seems to indicate, for it is most surprising that we have not yet found one along the whole extent of coast we have visited.
During the night the weather was fairly fine until about two o'clock. But then it came on to rain, with heavy squalls, which obliged us to take a second reef in our topsails. During the night we made various boards so as to keep in sight of the coast which, from the way we had seen it meet the sea, seems to offer no danger.
1802-04-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8, Western Island N 4° W, 9 miles off. At 10.30, 7° 24' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 143° 35' 30" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off. At 4, cape B N 83° E, and Western Island from N 16° W to N 25° W. The Géographe's boat was sighted standing towards us; at 4.30 hove to. Citizen Saint-Cricq came in from his errand; the boat was hoisted in and at 5 we filled and stood on. At 6, Western Island from N 30° W to N 38° W and cape B N 86° E. During the night overcast and stormy weather.

1802-04-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At half past noon hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 3 filled with the winds south to SSE and SSW. The Géographe's boat was sighted; we hove to and at 4 she was hoisted in. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4 hove to on the other tack. At noon Western Island N 35° W, about 8 miles off.
1802-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock, the westernmost point of the mainland in sight bore south 12° west,
The westernmost point of Kangaroo Island south 29° west,
The easternmost point of the same island north 25° east.
At noon the two extremities of Kangaroo Island extended, relative to our position, from south 78°30 east to south 26 west,
The land nearest the ship north 24° 30' east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, we had the wind at east-south-east, blowing fresh and squally. The sky, however, did not look threatening and seemed likely to clear during the day, which indeed it did as soon as the wind had gone round to the south. We took advantage of this to push on to the north along a stretch of the mainland which trended that way. As it went on blowing a strong breeze through the morning, we made good way and explored the coast at a short league from the land and sometimes less. Along the coast the bottom was found to be from 16 to 20 fathoms, good for anchoring, being sand, though somewhat hard. This part of the same coast had very few trees and yet offered several rather picturesque views. We discovered no shelter there for vessels, and only one fairly large cove whose beach appeared to be of very white sand. The other coves fell sheer into the sea and seemed to offer no landing place; although they were sheltered from the wind, the sea broke on the shore as if the swell had passed over a sandbar.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 12' 0" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 135° 47' 22".
In the afternoon, after passing the chain of mountains of which this coast is formed, we sighted a very low land which began at the end of a point running out into the sea with a very gentle slope. At first we thought it was only a tongue of land that could not be of any great extent. But as we drew nearer, this tongue of land, which we had judged beforehand to be of little consequence, stretched further and further to the north, trending somewhat to the east. We followed it all along its shore until four in the afternoon, when, the depth continually decreasing, we thought we had reached the head of the gulf. The lead then gave 7 and eight fathoms, sandy bottom. As we also had land in sight to the west, we no longer doubted that we (were) deep inside a gulf whose breadth was unknown to us. At about five o'clock we began to bring our course round somewhat to the west. We sounded continually, always having seven and eight fathoms. But at sunset we suddenly dropped into five fathoms and even less. We bore away at once, keeping close-hauled on the southerly tack towards the west. But it was nearly half an hour before we saw the depth increase by half a fathom. At last we passed successively from 5 to 6, 7, 8 and 16 fathoms. But it was not long before it decreased again, which decided me to beat to and fro in order to try, if possible, to keep between fifteen and twenty fathoms, being at eight in the evening in 18. The crew were forbidden to turn in before ten o'clock, the hour by which I expected to be free of all anxiety for the night if the depth went on increasing. At nine o'clock, having found eighteen fathoms of water, those who were not on watch were allowed to go below. But not for long, for at half past nine we suddenly dropped into eleven, and they were called up again at once so as to go about more readily. For the rest of the night everyone was on watch. We made various boards, taking as our turning points the soundings as they fell off from the greatest depth we had found, on the one tack as on the other. By this means we kept between 15 and twenty fathoms, having had the good fortune to enjoy fine weather; otherwise we might perhaps have found ourselves in serious difficulty.
(In the left margin, written vertically) I gave this gulf the name golfe de la Mauvaise [Gulf St Vincent] on account of the fatigue it caused the whole crew. The winds were very variable during the night. We reckoned that the south-south-west tack, which we took several times, would carry us out to sea, but it did (nothing of the kind) and served only to show us the land to leeward of us, and the depth decreased as rapidly as on the easterly tack.
1802-04-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SW. At 2 hove to; at 7.30 filled and stood on. At 8, Western Island from N 38° W to N 47° W and cape B S 88° E; hove to. At 10.15 filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 37' 20" of latitude by account and in 143° 37' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 35° W, 8 miles off. At 4 it bore N 45° W, 15 miles off, and at 6.15 N 38° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a strong breeze from SSW to south and SW. We beat all night abreast of Western Port. At 4 hove to; at 6 filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off; Cape de la Roche N 89° E.
1802-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the land which seemed to us to form the southern extremity of the second part of the gulf bore west by south. And we had in sight a part of Kangaroo Island extending extending (sic) from south-south-east to south-west by west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, we found ourselves surrounded by land except in the south-west, which appeared clear and to offer a good passage. We had in sight both coasts forming the gulf, not having seen the larboard one the day before, owing to the closeness with which we had run along the starboard coast. The two coasts are very different from each other. The starboard one, as I have already observed, is formed by a chain of high mountains without much verdure, whereas the one opposite is a flat, level coast on which there are only two or three rises, formed by sandhills, that can serve as landmarks. These sandhills, which begin at the water's edge, are well wooded, and before the land itself can be seen they are made out on the horizon, just above the water, rising little by little until one has come near enough to make out the land that bears them.
As we had examined the whole starboard coast of this gulf, I wished to become acquainted with the larboard one as well. This made me steer south-west with the wind at south-east, a pleasant breeze. As we approached it, we first discovered a very extensive shoal sweeping round in a great curve, which runs out at least a league and a half into the sea. We went partly round it in a depth of water that left us nothing to fear. This danger is easy to recognise by the colour of the water over it, which is a very light green. After weathering it, we closed with the coast. The depth then decreased from 24 fathoms to seven and a half, which prevented me from approaching any nearer, not wishing to run the same risks as the day before. I had the ship go about, steering east-north-east, but we had scarcely made two miles when the depth, which had increased a little, suddenly fell to five fathoms. I bore away to the north-east, having steered south-west to reach the spot where I had been. We quickly regained 7 and eight fathoms, and the lookouts then reported that they could see in the south-west a sandbank half uncovered, whose northern end, to judge by the colour of the water, extended as far as the larboard bow and bore north-north-east from us. The course we made to the north-east seems to confirm what they reported, for we were nearly an hour in 8 & 10 fathoms, and as long in 11 & 12. Although the breeze was light, we made fair headway. The depth having then gone from 12 to 25 fathoms in a short time, we hoped once again that we were out of difficulty and steered to close with the mountainous starboard coast, whose depths were known to us. The weather in the morning, though cloudy and with light squalls, was fine, but the winds very variable.
At noon we had no observation of latitude, the sky having clouded over. I was sorry to give up the larboard coast of this gulf, which, besides, offers no advantage to navigators, but I cannot say for certain whether this coast is not formed of several islands, which I suspect to be very likely, although I am not sure of it.
In the afternoon, the wind having gone round to the south-east, a pleasant breeze, we sought to close with the coast that was known to us in order to examine Mr Flinders's Kangaroo Island. At five o'clock, being at the mouth of the gulf we were leaving, we hauled close to the wind on the southerly tack towards the west so as to close the island during the night, which was fine, with a moderate breeze. The soundings were very regular, between 26 and 20 fathoms. The bottom was sometimes good for anchoring, being sand and coarse gravel, and sometimes foul, of coral or hard.
1802-04-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SW. At 4 hove to and at 6 filled and stood on. At 8, 8° 8' 50" of NE variation. Cape B N 38° E and Western Island N 37° W, 12 miles off. At noon in 38° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 143° 31' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off, and cape B N 89° E; the breeze light. At 4 a flat calm, Western Island from N 38° W to N 43° W.

1802-04-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to SE by way of south. At 11.30 hove to on the port tack, Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off.
1802-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
(no entry)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, having closed during the night with the northern part of the coast of Kangaroo Island, which we had left on the evening of the 21st to stand over to the mainland, we came to identify our last bearings on this island and, having made them out clearly at a short distance from the coast, we ran along it, steering west, until about ten in the morning, when it then seemed to us to trend a little towards the south. The weather was fine all morning and a pleasant breeze blew from the east.
The lookouts at the mastheads kept reporting that we had on our starboard hand a very low land, which opened out as we advanced to the west, but we did not sight it from the deck. We did, however, see several smokes in the north, which assured us of the truth of what they reported.
As I did not expect to meet, off the mainland, an island of such extent from east to west as the one we had in sight appeared to be, I was surprised not to see its end come into view, for as we doubled one point, another immediately appeared to take its place. The whole coast we ran along, in the morning as in the afternoon, was high and steep. At intervals along the water's edge little shallow coves could be seen, but without any shelter on the west side from north to south-east. The bottom varied little and we never had less than twenty fathoms, and often twenty-five, at a short league from the coast. The aspect of this island is pleasant and very varied. Although it is not entirely wooded, it had the merit of cheering us far more than anything we had seen until then.
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 30' 35" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 134° 46' 34".
In the afternoon, several islands were reported to leeward of us. I thought they might be some considerable heights on the mainland whose low extremities could not be made out. But at three o'clock we passed a small, very high island about which we had no doubt. But I do not think that the other lands reported as islands, which we could see from the deck, are in fact islands, although they looked like them.
We continued during the evening to run along the northern part of Kangaroo Island and did not see its end until sunset. Although it blew a good breeze, we made slow progress, and a strong current, which appeared to us to run east and west, seemed greatly to retard our way.
During the night we made several boards between the small island seen in the evening and Kangaroo Island, and at two o'clock we ran to the north to draw nearer the mainland, which I wished to be close to so as to examine it the next day. The weather was very fine all night and the breeze moderate, from east to east-north-east and from east to south-east.
1802-04-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to ENE. At 8, Western Island N 16° W, 9 miles off. At 9, 6° 19' of NE variation. At 11.30 hove to and at noon filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 34' 34" of latitude by account and in 143° 24' 42" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off. At 4 the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 57° W, Western Island N 31° E, and cape B N 55° E. During the night the wind a strong breeze. Wilson's Promontory lies in 39° 10' 54" of latitude and 144° 37' 31" of longitude. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude.

1802-04-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to east and to NE by way of north. At noon filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off; the western end of the mainland N 62° W.
1802-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land.
On the 26th at noon, the group of islands we had identified in the morning extended from north 30° east to west 35° south. The eastern one, forming the channel by which we had entered to draw nearer the mainland, was south 48° east, and the western one south 78° west.
The mainland could be seen from south 68° east to north 74° 45' east.
At six o'clock, the eastern islet forming the channel through which we had passed was south 42° east, the western one west 24° north. The mainland could be seen from north 69° east to to (sic) south 58° east. To be checked.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, at daybreak, we saw land at several points of the horizon, and at sunrise we found that most of it consisted of islets and rocks, separated from one another by channels which, judging from a distance, appeared fairly convenient. Four of these islets and rocks bore north of us, trending east, and five trending from north towards west. Another stretch of land, which from its extent we judged to be part of the mainland, bore north-west. As I wished to draw nearer the mainland, I had the ship steered into the middle of a channel about three leagues wide, the water there appearing deeper than anywhere else, and so we found it, for the lead never gave less than 26 fathoms and sometimes a great deal more. The view I give of this channel and of the islets and rocks forming it will make them easy to recognise.
During the morning the winds were very light and variable. As the current was in our favour, we crossed the channel, drawing nearer the mainland, which here has a very dismal appearance. Two high points, easily made out, were formed of brown rocks of a very dismal colour, and the land between them consisted of white sandhills, most of them bare of any kind of vegetation. Setting out from the eastern point of the mainland I have just mentioned, a reef awash was discovered, lying about the middle of the channel between the mainland and the islet which, to the east of the channel, forms the one through which we had passed. As it was very extensive, it may be presumed that it leaves no passage between itself and the mainland. We could also see the sea breaking on the stretch of coast we judged to be part of the mainland, and several smokes rising from the interior of the country. The calm, and the little air that could be felt, having come to us from north to north-north-west, we were obliged to go about and retrace our course through the same channel by which we had entered, (in the left margin: waiting until the wind should allow us to decide on the course we should have to make).
At noon, the observed latitude was 35° 15' 6" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 134° 11' 29".
The southernmost land of the mainland, from which we were then only about a league and a half at most, bore south 68° east and extended to north 74° 45' east.
The islet forming, to the east, the channel through which we had passed was south 48° east. For the greater part of the evening we lay becalmed, heading west towards the south. But at about four o'clock, a light breeze having come to us from south to south-south-west, we resumed our course north towards the west so as to draw nearer the mainland.
By the bearing taken at six o'clock, the southernmost point of the mainland relative to our position bore south 59° east, and the land could be seen extending to north-north-east. The eastern islet forming the channel through which we had passed was south 42° east, and the western one west 25° north.
During the night, which was very fine, we carried little sail, steering north towards the east. We never lost sight of the land and the depth held steadily at 32 fathoms.
1802-04-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to NE. At 8, Western Island N 6° E, 9 miles off. At 8.45, 6° 28' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 44' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 33' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off, and the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 62° W. At 4, Western Island from N 11° W to N 24° W. At 4.30, 8° 1' 40" of NE variation.

1802-04-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and the wind a strong breeze from east to NE and to NW by way of north. At 3 p.m. bore away for Western Island; at 5 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. From the bearing of the promontory, which lay a mile north of us, I concluded its latitude to be 39° 10' 26".
1802-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land
At six in the morning evening, the mainland extended from north-east by north to south-south-east.
At noon, it could be seen from east 23° south to east 78° north. The middle of what was in sight formed a large bay of low land bearing east 20° north.
At sunset, the northernmost land in sight was north 22° 30' east, and the southernmost, also in sight, bore east 75° south. The two extremities of the island we had just rounded were one east 61° south and the other north-east 12° south. The middle of the islet I have mentioned east 3° south.
At noon, the mainland extended from north 45° east to south 40° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, having stood on all night north towards the east under little sail and without losing sight of the land, we found ourselves abreast of a very large and no less deep bay. From the deck the continuation of the land into several inlets could scarcely be made out, but from the tops it could be seen very well.
As the winds were then southerly and very variable, we kept close-hauled, steering steering east and even more to the south. But the breeze was so light throughout the morning that we made little progress. From the direction the land seemed to take, there was every appearance that, if we were not in a new gulf, we were at least in a very deep indentation towards the east, since we could not see the land come to an end in that quarter.
At daybreak we had no sight of the islands seen the day before. Despite the little way we made during the day, the depth nonetheless decreased considerably and even rapidly. At ten o'clock we were in thirty fathoms and half an hour later we had no more than 25. From twenty-five it went to 17, at which moment, the ship having been taken aback, we found 21 by the time the manoeuvre to bring her back onto the same tack was completed. The wind being then at east-north-east obliged us to stand to the north, which by noon had brought us back into 25 fathoms, having made no more than a league since the moment we had found 17.
At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 42' 46 and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 134° 37' 40".
As we still had a great deal to do on the coast of New Holland and had no more than two months' water left, I judged it proper to begin reducing it early, that is to say that instead of issuing two and a half bottles a man, only two were issued. This was no doubt not a very considerable reduction, since more was still being issued than the regulations prescribe for long voyages. Nevertheless it caused discontent, not among the seamen, but in another quarter. Be that as it may, it changed nothing in the decision I have taken on this matter, being convinced that one can very well do without taking tea and coffee twice a day. Thus, pleased or not, I was the first to comply with it with good grace.
During the evening, the wind having gone back from east towards south, we closed with the coast, but the breeze was so light that we made little progress. All the land we had in sight during this day is low and offers few remarkable points. The shore is formed sometimes of sandhills and sometimes of sheer cliffs in which (nothing) is to be seen but crevices between the windings they form.
At five in the afternoon we saw two islands lying close to the mainland. The first, that is to say the southernmost, may be a league and a half long from south-south-west to north-north-east, and the second is only a rock of about half a league, having, like the first, a reef at each end on which the sea breaks heavily. We passed at a league from these two islands in 9, 10, 11 & 12 fathoms, and three leagues from the mainland.
(In the left margin, written vertically) During the night the weather was very fine. We stood north towards the east until eight o'clock, when, having shortened sail, we ran one board out to sea until midnight, when we hove to in 17 fathoms. The drift or the current having carried us into 20 fathoms, we resumed our course north towards the east to draw nearer the coast, which could not then be far off.
1802-04-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SW by way of north. At 8.30, 6° 26' of NE variation. At noon in 38° 42' 17" of latitude observed and in 143° 51' 24" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. At 3.30, having sighted our two boats, we hove to; at 4 the large one, with Citizen Milius, came in and was hoisted in at once. At 4, Western Island N 34° W, 9 miles off. At 5.15 the small boat came in and was hoisted in. At 6, Western Island N 43° W. At 8 we filled and stood on, the course S 45° E. The weather turned overcast with light rain; at midnight we hove to.

1802-04-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW. The two boats came in at 5.15 and were hoisted in at once. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4.30 filled and wore onto the starboard tack, and shaped our course to leave the strait.
1802-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
The mainland extended from north 50° east to south 37 east,
A land to leeward could be seen from north 38° west to north 46° west
At two o'clock,
A reef was sighted ahead of us.
At three o'clock,
It bore north 71° east from us at a distance of a league at most.
At sunset, being a short distance from the head of the gulf, the western land bore from west 20° north to west 80° north, and the eastern land extended, for us, from south 34° east to north 64° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, we found ourselves about four leagues from the land, in 17 fathoms, sandy bottom. At eight o'clock we had closed with it in 15 fathoms, same bottom. And for the rest of the morning we coasted along it at a distance of two leagues. The winds, which were almost calm at that time, did not allow us to approach any nearer.
The whole coast we had in sight during the morning was generally of moderate height. At intervals, however, there were rises higher than most of the coast, to which they were joined by lower land, well wooded, at least to judge by eye, for the tops of the trees could be made out without the shoreline being visible.
The soundings were fairly uniform from daybreak until noon, remaining almost always between twenty and sixteen fathoms.
At noon we observed the latitude 34° 11' 38" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 134° 47' 27".
In the morning we had sighted a fairly high land to leeward of us, which bore north-west. The sight of this land, which was quite extensive, gave rise to several conjectures on board. Some maintained, without quite knowing why, that it must be the beginning of the Isles of St Peter and St Francis, although their latitude was very different. Others thought they saw in this isolated land a very extensive island of which no one before us had had any knowledge, etc.
My opinion, which I kept to myself, was that we might well be in a second gulf reaching much further north than the one we had just passed. However, as the swell seemed to me too heavy for a place so deep within the land, I did not quite know what to make of it.
Be that as it may, we continued to steer north, edging to the east, running along the coast, which opened out in the direction of north by east, and as we advanced the depth decreased proportionately. But between one and two in the afternoon it suddenly went from 15 to 12 fathoms and, within half an hour, from 12 to 9. Then the lookouts at the mastheads reported breakers ahead of us and a little on the larboard side of the ship. We soon made them out clearly from the deck, which led me to bring the ship onto the larboard tack, convinced that I should find no passage between them and the mainland coast on the eastern side.
Having trimmed the sails close-hauled, heading west-north-west, we continued to steer on that point of the compass, coasting in eight fathoms of water along the reef I have just mentioned, which appeared to us to be the top of a sandbank awash. For no rock could be seen rising above the level of the sea. But the sea broke heavily. The extent of this danger is not great and it seemed to us to be no more than half a league where the surf was breaking.
At three o'clock, as we began to draw away from it, I had a bearing taken, and it then bore north 71° east from us, which, from the distance estimated since noon, would fix its latitude (at) 34° 8' 54" and the longitude at (no figures)
The little wind there was having gone round to the south, we steered west until four and, the depth being then 13 fathoms, we resumed our course north-north-west to see whether the land we had on the larboard hand joined that to the east, as I suspected. At sunset, being still too far from the western coast to examine it properly, we resumed our course north towards the east until eight o'clock, when we changed tacks to spend the night beating to windward.
(In the left margin, written vertically) From eight in the evening until midnight the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate, but at that time, the wind having gone round to west-north-west, it became so strong that we could carry only the foresail and our topsails with all reefs taken in. The rest of the night was anything but pleasant, and the movement of the barometer was (not) such as to reassure us, embayed as we were in the supposed gulf, should the weather turn bad and the wind shift to south-west.
1802-04-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from SW to SSW. At 4 we filled and stood on, the land from N 22° E to S 79° E. At 8, cape A N 28° W, the promontory S 84° E, islet P S 70° E. At noon, cape A N 34° W, the promontory S 77°, 6 miles off, islet P S 68° E. By this bearing we were in 39° 8' 45" of latitude and 144° 30' 18" of longitude. At 6, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 71° E, the 2 islets C S 86° E, islet P S 81° E, islet A S 57° E. At midnight the promontory N 85° E, 15 miles off.

1802-04-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a flat calm. At 1.30 the breeze got up from the SW. Made all sail. At 7 p.m. clewed up and furled the topgallant sails and struck the main topgallant mast to repair it. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the north, the promontory bearing N 85° E, 5 leagues off; we wore onto the port tack and passed between the islets and rocks of the promontory. At noon took the bearing of two rocks, one N 42° E, the other N 78° W, half a mile off; the promontory N [illegible], 9 miles off; the sugarloaf N 88° W; islet A S 25° E; rock D S 57° E; an island H N 70° E.
1802-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
On the twenty-ninth at daybreak, the eastern land could be seen from east-north-east to east-south-east at a distance of six leagues. The horizon in the west was too hazy to make out the coast in that quarter.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, I expected the weather to clear and that during the day we should be able to explore the part of the coast we had seen the day before. But instead, the sky, which had been fairly fine during the night, became damp and misty, looking very threatening for the rest of the day.
At seven o'clock, land was seen from the mastheads from east-north-east to north-north-west, which proved only too well that we were in a gulf, as I had always thought from the shallowness of the water and its steady decrease whenever we stood to the west or to the east, crossing from east to west the breadth it forms from one coast to the other.
As the weather looked too threatening to think of examining the western part of this gulf, I sought to stand as far to the south as possible, so as to be in a more advantageous position. The winds, in the morning, varied from north-west to west-south-west and were frequently accompanied by squalls and strong gusts.
At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 42' 31", but doubtful. There was no hour angle. At the same time, a land was seen from the mastheads in the south-east by south, which we recognised in the evening as one we had already seen on entering the gulf.
At one in the afternoon, the wind still increasing and accompanied by strong gusts, we wore round and steered north-west towards the west so as to stand off from the coast for greater safety during the night, which promised to be a rather trying one for us. At two o'clock, the wind still rising and the sea growing heavier and heavier, the mizzen topsail had to be furled and, shortly afterwards, the fore topsail. Although we had no more sail set than the foresail, the main topsail with all reefs taken in, and the mizzen staysail, the ship in the gusts had quite as much as she could carry. We continued on the north-west towards west tack until eight in the evening, when, having 23 fathoms of water, we took that as our point of departure for beating during the night, in which the weather was very bad and the squalls even heavier than we had had them during the day. Several times we were obliged to lower our main topsail on the reefs, despite the little canvas left to it. The boards were of four hours, and we managed to keep between twenty and 24 fathoms of water, beating over a bottom which never exceeded 30 fathoms, decreasing to the west as to the east once one had reached it.
This night was very trying for the crew and for me, since (we) spent it constantly on deck. All the officers, except those who changed watch, spent it as peacefully in their beds as if the ship had been in the greatest safety. As this was not the first time this had happened with them, even in a more critical position than the one we were in, I was not at all surprised and left them quite undisturbed, a course I have decided to take whenever such an occasion arises.
The stay and the halyard of our fore-topmast staysail gave way twice during the night, but the sail was only slightly damaged. The squalls, which brought us rain, were very cold, and sometimes the water was like half-melted snow, which led us to conclude that winter cannot be very pleasant in these climes.
The scientists, however, are of the contrary opinion, because they have seen parakeets in D'Entrecasteaux Channel.
1802-04-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NE. At 1.30 we hove to, and at 3 filled and stood on. At 4 the promontory N 68° E. At 5 shaped our course to double the promontory, hauling to the wind on the port tack. At 8, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 78° E 1 mile off, the 2 islets C S 82°, islet P S 75° E and islet A S 56° E. At 8.55 the white rock bore abeam, true north, 3 cables off. At 9.50 the promontory bore abeam, true north, 1 mile off. We passed among the islets and rocks of the promontory, leaving to port the white rock, the islets C and rock M, and to starboard islet A, islet D, islet P and so on. At noon in 39° 14' 20" of latitude observed and in 144° 58' 0" of longitude by account, the promontory bearing N 63° W, the islets C one N 42° W and the other N 78° W, half a mile off, islet P N 88° W, islet A S 25° E, islet D S 75° E, and an island H N 70° E. At 4 took the bearing of the northernmost end of the mainland in sight N 76° W, the promontory N 76° W, islet P S 85° W and islet D S 16° E. At 4.30, 7° 26' 20" of NE variation. At 5.30 the promontory N 80° W, the middle of island H N 66° E, another island S 68° E. At 8 the wind drew round to the west, freshening; we shaped the course N 56° 15' E. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, a high sea, with rain.

1802-04-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NE to W, SW and NW. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, the weather overcast and squally, a high sea, a great deal of rain. At 6 a.m. land was sighted to windward; at 8 it stretched from N 23° E to N 45° W. The wind still a strong breeze. At noon the land from N 22° W to N 70° E.
1802-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak, the land of the eastern coast of the gulf could be seen in the east-north-east
At noon, being nearer the coast, it extended from north 22° east to south 45° east. We thought we made out an islet at south 12 west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, we experienced very little change in the weather. It went on blowing hard throughout the day. Most of the squalls brought rain and came in gusts. They were, however, less heavy than the day before, since we were able to set the fore topsail, the mizzen topsail and the storm staysail.
As I wished to ascertain exactly our distance from the eastern coast of the gulf, which I shall call it until I have proof to the contrary, we went about at four in the morning to steer south-east, for the wind was then at south-south-west and seemed inclined to settle there.
At daybreak the land showed itself to the lookouts at the mastheads in the east-north-east, but it was not visible to us until about ten o'clock. It was recognised as a portion of the coast seen the day before.
From four o'clock until half past eleven we were over a bottom of from 24 to 17 fathoms, and we kept this last depth for more than three hours without any appreciable decrease. But then we went from 17 to ten while still three leagues from the land, which made us go about and stand to the west, still with a heavy sea and strong winds, with rain and short-lived squalls, now heavier, now lighter.
At noon, the observed latitude was 34° 38' 30". There was no hour angle.
From noon until eight in the evening we kept on the tack west towards south, my intention being to draw nearer the western coast of the gulf, so as to leave it the next day by that side if the weather were manageable and the winds fair. As the squalls had become less frequent, we had for a moment the hope of soon seeing it clear, and the barometer seemed to announce it, since it was rising a little. But after sunset our hopes vanished. The gusts and squalls began again and ceased only for short moments.
The night was generally bad. We always had a regular bottom on both the tacks we
ran and were almost always between 22 and 24 fathoms, hard, rocky bottom.
From eight o'clock until midnight we ran on the tack east towards south, and from midnight until daybreak on that west towards south. The sky was constantly thick, laden with dark clouds, most often rainy and followed by strong gusts. We kept the same sail as during the day without adding to it, the position I was in not leading me to think it necessary to strain the ship's masts.
1802-04-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At 6 the land was sighted; at 8 it stretched from N 22° E to N 45° E, and at noon from N 22° W to N 70° E. At noon in 37° 57' 40" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 12" of longitude by account. At 4, Cape Howe N 32° E and the southernmost end of the mainland in sight S 76° E. At 5.30, Cape Howe N 20° E; the land in sight during the night.

1802-04-21.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze from NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Howe N 32° E; the visible end of the land S 76° W. At 4.30 the weather cleared. At noon land in sight from N 45° W to S 61° W. At noon we found the same latitude, the same longitude and the same variation that Cook found. We were also at the same distance from the land and in the same month.
1802-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak, the land extended from east to south, forming a curve whose middle bore south-east. The part lying between south-east and south appeared broken by higher land, which we judged to be the islets we had seen on entering the gulf.
At half past five in the evening, the western land extended from west by north (to) south-west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Floréal, the weather was hardly finer than on the preceding days. All morning we had rain, squalls and wind. Nevertheless it was less violent than it had been until then, and the squalls it brought us were also less heavy and sooner over than they usually were, but on the other hand they followed one another more rapidly. In the morning we found the sea more swelling than usual, but the waves less high. The lead always gave a regular bottom on the one tack as on the other, and the bottom was sometimes (sic) of coarse sand and rubble mixed with coral and madrepores.
At six o'clock, having been on the tack west towards south since midnight, we sighted land ahead of us. To windward and to leeward it extended from south 50° west to north 5° west. Several of the portions lying within the above interval looked as though they formed several islands, which may very likely be so. But the land to the north of west was recognised as that of the mainland and consequently as the other side of the gulf, of which we had had but little knowledge, owing to the contrary winds and the bad weather we had had for several days.
At half past six in the morning, we took the tack east towards south so as not to fall too far to leeward of the islets we had thought we saw in the morning, which are very likely those that bore west of us when we entered the gulf by way of the channel I have mentioned. We continued on this tack until noon, having in sight the eastern land and the islet forming the channel by which we had entered. From the mastheads we thought we recognised this islet by its shape and height. As my intention was to leave the gulf by a different route from the one that had brought me into it, I went back onto the westerly tack so as to be better placed to take advantage of the first fine weather that might offer.
At noon we saw the sun for a moment and observed its altitude, 34° 40' 27". This latitude, though I suspect it to be doubtful, still seems to me preferable to that by dead reckoning in a place where the currents are strong and changeable in direction.
During the evening we had for a moment (the hope) of seeing the weather clear, but it was short-lived, for after sunset it became worse than it had been until then. During the night the gusts were so frequent and so strong that they several times forced us to lower our topsails on the cap, although they were close-reefed. In any other position than the one I was in, I should certainly not have carried them. At six o'clock, when we went about, we had the land in sight from west-south-west to north-west, at a distance of three leagues at most, the bottom being 19 fathoms, much mixed with sand, coral and rubble. Two boards were made during the night so as to keep roughly in the middle of the channel.
1802-04-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather with frequent squalls, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W, a high sea. At noon in 36° 18' 4" of latitude observed and in 148° 48' 42" of longitude by account. At 4, the Pigeon House N 18° W and Mount Dromedary S 54° W. During the night the wind blew hard. At 4.30 p.m., 9° 50' 50" of NE variation.

1802-04-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from SW to W and NW. At 4 a.m. Mount Dromedary bore from us S 54° W, the Pigeon House N 18° W. At 5.30 blowing hard from the west, a high sea. At 3.15 a.m. the wind having fallen a little, set the mizzen topsail. At daybreak the land as far as the eye could see in the west (from aloft); at 5 it stretched from W to N 45° W. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
On the second, at seven o'clock in the morning, the eastern land could be seen, though hazy, from south-south-east to east, at a distance of four leagues.
The haze did (not) allow an exact bearing to be taken at sunset; we could only see land to the south 5° west and more to the south 50° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, standing on the eastward board towards the south, towards seven o'clock we sighted the same eastern land that we had seen the day before. But as it lay further to the south of us than it had been set, we were convinced that we had drifted a fair way to the north, which did nothing to improve our position.
The weather still continuing to look ill, with no hope of a change, I had us take the westward board towards the north, the wind being then south-south-west, and when we had trimmed close-hauled on the larboard tack, the reef was taken in the foresail and the mainsail, which we set again as soon as this was done, so that we stood on under our four principal sails with all their reefs taken in. The ship seemed to behave well under this canvas and fell off far less than before. The squalls and gusts we met with made her heel no more than usual, but in truth they were less violent than during the night.
At noon the observed latitude was 34° 38' 27", and the longitude by the timekeeper, which we had not been able to obtain for three days, put us in 134° 6' 26".
From the observation of the latitude we found ourselves further north than the day before, which confirmed us in the belief that the course, or rather the wearing round, had thrown us to the north.
At one o'clock in the afternoon, the wind seeming inclined to shift to the south-west, we took advantage of the interval that usually came between the squalls to go about on the southward course towards the east. In spite of the heavy sea, the ship came round very well under the canvas she was carrying, the only precaution taken being to let fly the fore sheet in good time and to ease off the bowlines forward, a manoeuvre which greatly displeased the learned naval officers who accompany me and who, no doubt, would have missed stays had they gone about it otherwise. When we went about, the western land could be seen and the depth was 23 fathoms. I reckoned myself to be three and a half to four leagues from it.
In the evening the wind became moderate, the squalls less heavy and the sea grew smooth. We took this as a sign of an approaching change in our favour, although the barometer had as yet told us nothing of it.
At six o'clock in the evening, having run all evening on the eastward board towards the south, we (sic) went about and stood off at two leagues from the eastern coast, which we clearly recognised to be the southern extremity of the gulf we had entered. During the night the sky was fine and the squalls moderate. Those that brought rain or wind did not last long, and on the whole the weather was tolerably fine, and even very fine if one compared it with what we had had for the past three days.
The soundings during the night differed little from those we were accustomed to have, except that the depth was noticed to be a little greater and the bottom of fine grey sand, whereas it had almost always been unsuitable for anchoring, or very bad.
1802-04-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW. At daybreak the land was sighted as far as the eye could reach to the west. At 8.15, 10° 6' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 28' 38" of latitude observed and in 149° 44' 0" of longitude by account. At 5.45, Cape St George S 80° W.

1802-04-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from NW to NNW. At 5 p.m. Cape St George S 82° W. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. Furled the main topgallant sail and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. At noon the land in sight from S 15° W to N 45° W.
1802-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, the wind and (the) weather became more moderate, and we took advantage of this to try to work up to the west in order to examine the land in that part of the gulf, but we could not manage it.
At ten o'clock, steering west a little southerly, we were obliged to go about all of a sudden to avoid a shoal, on the edge of which we found ourselves in 20 fathoms of water. The lookouts the lookouts had long since reported a tongue of breakers which barred our passage to the west, extending from west-north-west to south-south-west. When we went about, we could indeed make out this danger from the deck, but we were still more than a league from it and the depth was 28 and 29 fathoms. As the sea did not break on the shoal that lay in front of this chain of rocks, we came within very little of running upon it. Happily the ship did not miss stays, and we should very probably have been in great difficulty had she failed to come round. We also had in sight at that time a great part of the land forming the opposite side of the eastern coast of the gulf, as well as the five islets and rocks we had seen on 26 Germinal, but we had to give up looking for a passage through the channels they form, some of which appeared to me navigable. The current, the wind and their positions did not allow us even to approach them except at a great distance. Although I had already lost four days in trying to examine them, I resolved to leave this group of islands by the same channel that had brought me into it, so as to be in a position to withstand the bad weather should it come on again.
At noon we observed the latitude as 34° 50' 28", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 133° 58' 28".
In the afternoon the weather seemed inclined to set fair. The squalls, the rain and the gusts disappeared entirely, and the sky was fairly fine all evening. The reef we had met with in the morning, and the shoal lying in front of it, appeared to us to extend from the mainland to an island some three leagues in extent, which bore west 22° 30' south of us. None of the boards we made between the eastern land of the gulf and this danger could be longer than two hours, or than two and a half to three leagues at most.
Throughout the night we carried out the same manoeuvre, keeping as close as possible to the island forming the channel by which we had entered and by which I also meant to leave the next day. We had very fine weather all night and a moderate breeze, the moonlight allowing us to keep the coast well in sight at all times.
The whole crew was on watch so as to be the readier for going about.
1802-04-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to W. At noon in 35° 11' 26" of latitude observed and in 148° 41' 42" of longitude by account. The land from N 34° W to S 45° W. At 8 a.m., 10° 40' 10" of NE variation. At 3.15 we had a heavy squall from the west. During the night squally weather, the wind a strong breeze. The land has been in sight throughout.

1802-04-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; went about onto the starboard tack. A strong breeze from SW to W and SSW. At 4.30 the middle of the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W. At 5 p.m. we heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we supposed it was in honour of St George's day. At 7.30 p.m. the weather turned overcast and the wind blew hard; we stayed under our courses. At 6.30 hove to and put the large boat in the water; Mr Milius was about to embark in her to go up to Port Jackson, but rain came on and the boat was veered astern. At 8 a.m., having seen a boat standing towards us, we hove to; the pilot came aboard and we at once beat to windward. At 11.45, under North Head, having missed stays, we wore ship; in this last movement our large boat, which was in tow, capsized and the painter parted. Our small boat, together with the English boat, was sent to save the boat's crew and to take the swamped boat in tow to carry her ashore.
1802-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, in the morning, having spent the whole night beating to windward, we found ourselves exactly at the mouth of the channel by which we had entered the gulf. As there was then a pleasant breeze from south-south-east, variable to south-east, we took advantage of it to get clear of the group of islands and rocks by which we had been surrounded for several days. We passed at a short distance from the island that lay to leeward of us, whose eastern and southern end is much higher than the northern and western. As I have already spoken of this island and its shape, and as I give a view of it, as well as of the two rocks off its southern part, I shall not dwell any longer on the subject.
When we had rounded it, we sought to close with the western coast of the great Kangaroo Island, which we were beginning to make out, but the wind having failed us, we made little way.
In the course of the morning fresh bearings were taken of the islands and islets lying off this part of the coast, which offered us no anchorage so long as we were engaged in examining it.
At noon the observed latitude was 35° 23' 40", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 133° 49' 31".
During the evening the breeze was very light and the sky fine, though the horizon was not very extensive. We swayed up our lower yards and shook out all the reefs in our sails, convinced that the weather was going to set fair. Should it turn bad, we were at least in a position where we had nothing to fear, and very different from the one we had been in during the three days of bad weather we had just come through.
At sunset we furled our mainsail, and at eight o'clock we shifted our tacks and stood on close-hauled on the starboard tack until midnight, when we took the southward board towards the east until daylight.
During the night the sky was fine and the breeze moderate. We also found the sea smooth, since we were not far from Kangaroo Island, whose extremities in sight after sunset bore from south 40° east to south 83° east of us. The land, or rather the islands, lying in the quarter from north towards west, bore from north-west to west-south-west of us.
During the two boards we made in the night, we had soundings in 50, 60 & 78 fathoms.
1802-04-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 11 we showed our colours and the flag of truce. At noon in 33° 47' 23" of latitude observed and in 148° 50' 36" of longitude by account. Signals were seen on the south point of the entrance to Port Jackson, which bore from us S 65° W to S 68° W, and the land from N 26° W to S 56° W. At 4 the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W, and at 5.30 N 62° W. We heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we thought it was in honour of King George's birthday. At nightfall a fire was lit at the entrance to Port Jackson; at 6 it bore from us S 59° W, at 8 S 54° W, at 10 S 85° W, at midnight N 79° W. During the night the wind blew hard, the weather overcast, with rain and thunder.

1802-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, having in sight a small archipelago of islands and islets, the first was set at north 23° west, the 2nd at north 12° west, the 3rd at north 17° east, 2 rocks belonging to it at north 18° 15' east, the 4th at north 78° east, the 5th at east 7° south and the 6th at east 7° south.
At sunset other islands were seen, whose extremities extended from west by north to north-west by north.
Those passed during the day lying one behind another, their northern extremity was set at north 6° west, 18 miles distant, and the easternmost part at east, 25 miles.
(in the margin: Two small islands near the land could be seen to the north-west, and the one furthest out to sea at north 10° west.).
Historical events & Remarks.
