On the fifth, in the morning, we steered north, making some westing, to close with the land lying on that point of the compass in order to examine it, giving up, on account of the advanced season and the direction of the wind, any visit to the southern part of the great Kangaroo Island, whose land in sight bore from north 60° east to south 66° east of us.
Although the sky did not look well in the morning, we nonetheless had fine weather and a pleasant breeze from east-south-east, variable to east-north-east, but we found the sea somewhat swelling and a good deal agitated, which we put down to the speed of the currents, which appeared to us to run against the direction of the wind.
In the course of the morning we sighted the five islands to the east of the channel by which we had entered the gulf, and whose northern part we had visited. Three of these islands are fringed with reefs on their southern side, and the sea broke heavily there at a considerable distance from the shore. All are arid and barren, showing no sign of vegetation, and they can hardly be regarded as anything but rocks set at some distance from the mainland, whose land can be made out in the distance. We passed at a short distance from this group of islands and islets, whose position can be well determined from all the various bearings that were taken of them. They all differ in extent, although the largest did not appear to me to be more than two leagues from east to west.
At noon we observed the latitude as 35° 19' 3", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 133° 20' 34".
In the evening the weather continued fine and the breeze held. We coasted now along the mainland and now along islands lying a short distance off it. I do not know whether a good passage would be found between these islands and the mainland, but the channels they form, whether among themselves or with the mainland, did not seem to me wide enough to venture into, above all in the season we are in. These last islands are larger than those passed in the morning, and almost all have reefs off their ends which run a good way out to sea. The one in particular which we rounded at sunset has one on which the sea broke extraordinarily, and we made it out at more than two leagues' distance. To weather it we were obliged to steer west-south-west for some time, having previously been heading north-west.
At sunset we saw several lands which still had the appearance of islands, although I believe they are not. The westernmost land in sight bore west by south of us, forming a large bight as far as north-north-west, in which no land could be seen. We put off until the next day finding out what this might be, and at six o'clock the southward board was taken, to beat to windward during the night.
1802-04-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SSE. At 6.15 we hove to and put the large boat in the water. Citizen Milius and I were to embark in her to go to Sydney and inform the English governor of our arrival and the object of our voyage; but the weather appeared so bad to Citizen Milius that the boat was veered astern. At 8, having sighted a boat standing towards us, we hove to to wait for her. At 8.15 she came aboard and brought us an English pilot; he at once made sail to gain the port. At 9 a swivel gun was fired to confirm our colours. At 11.45, under North Head, we missed stays and wore ship. In this last movement the large boat (which was in tow and under sail) capsized and her tow rope parted. The pilot's boat and our small boat at once went to save the boat's crew and to take the boat in tow and beach her. At 3.30 we anchored at the entrance to the port in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, North Head bearing N 67° E, South Head S 52° E, Camp Cove S 16° E, Bradleys Head S 36° W and Middle Head N 65° W. At 4.45 Citizen Milius and I left in the Géographe's boat for Sydney. Squally and very overcast weather, with pouring rain, the wind from WSW to SW.

1802-04-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SW to SSE. At 1.45, the wind having drawn aft, we bore away for the entrance to the port and shortened sail by degrees. At 3.30, having doubled South Head very close, we let go the anchor at the mouth of the channel in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, and veered 60 fathoms of cable, South Head bearing S 52° E; Camp Cove S 16° E; Bradleys Head S 36° W; Georges Head S 48° W; Middle Head N 65° W; North Head N 67° E by compass. As soon as the sails were furled, the Géographe's large boat was put in the water and left for Sydney Town; the wind a strong breeze, squally weather and rain. At anchor at the entrance to Port Jackson.
1802-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, in the morning, we found ourselves at about the same place where we had left off our survey of the coast visited on the fifth. But we recognised that all the heights of land we had made out the evening before, at sunset, were nothing but a small archipelago of islets and rocks of greater or lesser size. As they seemed to have navigable channels, above all with the wind we had, I resolved to pass between them and the mainland, and we were fortunate enough to have hit by chance upon the best passage. For in passing through the one I had preferred to the others, we saw several reefs which seem to show that they are not convenient.
As I give a detailed view of these rocks and islets, it will be easy to recognise the channel that should be taken in preference to the others. All these islets and rocks are entirely bare of vegetation, or at least one sees on them (nothing) but a few withered bushes. But the water around them is deep, and we never had less than twenty-four fathoms in the channel we entered.
The mainland, as may be seen from the views that have been made of it, is hardly more pleasing in aspect than the islands. The edge of the coast is, as everywhere else, sheer to the sea, and a reef guards the approach to the shore, which in several places is formed of nothing but a mass of rocks piled one upon another. And the sand dunes, without verdure, extend as far as the eye can reach into the interior, the land being now high and now low, but in general of a good height. Several lofty mountains can also be seen in the interior of the country, forming a chain of no great extent.
At noon our position was such that we had the sun over the land to the north as well as to the south, which prevented us from observing its passage across the meridian. We were then almost becalmed, but a breeze from south to south-west having sprung up, we got out of this archipelago, where it would not have been convenient to spend the night with contrary winds.
In the evening we rounded a point of the mainland at the end of which the land suddenly turns north-north-east for about three leagues, and forms a very deep cove, which we visited as far as the wind would allow us, having it then from east to east-south-east. As this cove lies within a chain of mountains, I expected to find good shelter there for the night, but the wind did not allow us to reach its innermost part. For the rest, it offers nothing remarkable; its shores are nothing but barren sands, and the mountains forming its extremities are nothing but enormous masses of rock piled one upon another. What struck us as most remarkable in this place was the direction of an isolated mountain running from east to west, while all the others ran from south-east to north-west.
At sunset we took the board out to sea, having seen nothing to the west that might give us any concern during the night. As we had land on all sides, I stood a little off the mainland and spent the night hove to, on one tack and the other.
1802-04-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW. A meal of provisions was sent to the crews of the large and small boats by a fishing boat. The governor sent vegetables. I came back aboard with an English officer to invite the captain to dine with Colonel Paterson, the lieutenant-governor (Governor King was at Parramatta); he excused himself on account of the bad weather, and I went back to Sydney with the officer. The topgallant masts were got down. An orderly brought the captain a letter announcing the governor's arrival at Sydney. At nightfall a small fishing boat brought Citizen Moreau, who had been in the small boat. He had been obliged to have the small boat in which he came carried by hand from the beach where the boats lay to the inside of the harbour. He asked the captain to send provisions to the boats' crews, who were without; and this contemptible man, who counts every mouthful of his crew's food and would feed them on grass if he could, ordered that only one meal be sent them, saying that if more were sent the rogues would not come back aboard and would rather stay ashore idling. Citizen Moreau observed to him that it was impossible for the boats to come back with him in them, that they had tried several times to return aboard and had always been forced to put back on account of the sea and the wind; that the wretched boats' crews, who had had only one meal since the morning before, would have died of hunger had not one of the English boatmen lent him money to buy them a little fish; that they were soaked and had neither shelter nor a change of clothes; that one of them was injured; and that they would therefore be better aboard if they could get there. None of these truths made any impression on this hard and barbarous man: only one meal of provisions was sent to the boats' crews.

1802-04-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the winds a strong breeze from south to SSW. Almost continual rain. At 3 a [boat] came aboard to invite the captain, on Colonel Paterson's behalf, to dine with him; but the bad weather prevented him from accepting the invitation. The topgallant masts were struck and the topmasts got down. An orderly brought packets to the captain to announce the governor's arrival at Sydney Town (he was in the country when we arrived at Port Jackson). A fishing boat brought me back on board.
1802-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, we found ourselves a long way to leeward of the land set and examined the evening before. I put this down to the currents, which had carried us to the north-west, for the little way we made during the night must have cancelled out, since we must have drifted as much on one tack as on the other, given the fixed hours at which the tacks were shifted.
But however that may be, as soon as it was daylight we trimmed close-(hauled) to a light easterly breeze, which held only until about ten o'clock in the morning, when it gave way to a calm which prevented us from making as good a day's run as I had hoped.
In the course of the morning the lookouts at the mastheads reported that we had several islands and islets on our larboard side to leeward, and they counted as many as nine. Before noon we made out three of them from the deck, but we did not see the others. The weather was very fine during the morning, and in spite of the lightness of the wind we succeeded in closing the coast to within two leagues. The land in this part is not uniform, either in height or in aspect, but all of it ends sheer to the sea and the water there is deep. We had 40 fathoms at a league and a half's distance. In these waters there are two or three fairly deep coves, and the shore at their head is very low and bare of vegetation.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 55' 20", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 132° 15' 17".
From noon until two o'clock we were in a flat calm, and the ship could hardly keep her head on her course. But then a light breeze came to us from the south-west, variable to the south, with which we closed to within a league of the coast, and so ran along it until sunset. Its direction was from north towards west, which gave us reason to think that we should soon sight the islands of St Francis and St Peter. Perhaps all those we have passed in the last two days form part of that archipelago. The four or five leagues of coast we ran along in the afternoon are of a good height but of a most peculiar aspect. The shore is formed of a long succession of sheer cliffs where the rock shows bare, yellow in colour where lit by the sun, and a very dark brown in the parts not facing it. The interior of the country appears every bit as barren as the seashore. We (saw), however, a fire at a considerable distance from the coast.
At sunset we sighted all the islands the lookouts had reported in the morning; several were of a most peculiar shape, as may be seen from the drawing I give of them.
Ahead of us we also made out two islands larger than those lying to leeward of us, which seemed to offer a good channel between them and the mainland. As night was coming on and it was not prudent to venture further in than we already were, we trimmed on the larboard tack to beat to windward during the night. But towards seven o'clock, the wind
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) being almost calm, with little likelihood of any during the night, I resolved to let go a bower anchor in 33 fathoms, the bottom being very fine, clean sand, without any mixture of coral or madrepore. It had not often been our lot to meet with such a bottom. By this means we passed the night quietly, the weather being fine and the breeze moderate.
1802-04-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south, with continual rain. The longboat was put in the water. Citizen Milius and I came back aboard. A warp was run out.

1802-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south to SSW and SW, continual rain. At 3 our boat left for Sydney Town. We ran out a warp and hove round on the cable, but the wind having freshened we left off the work with 45 fathoms of cable out. At 5 a.m. weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser; being at long stay we let go the bower anchor. The captain embarked in his boat with the officers and scientists to go and pay a visit to the governor. At 11.30 our large and small boats came aboard undamaged; only a seaman named Happeday had his shoulder crushed in the wreck of the large boat.
1802-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, at daybreak, we weighed with the wind in the quarter from north towards west, which obliged us to spend the day, or at least a great part of it, beating to windward in the channel lying between the mainland and the islands near which we had come to anchor. As it was full night (when) we anchored, we had only made out the islet nearest to us, which is also the highest. Its middle bore west 22° north of us.
At sunrise we made out the islands that surrounded us, which were five in number, lying at greater or lesser distances from one another, but all had a barren look and seem to offer neither shelter nor resources to the navigators who may frequent these waters.
Among these five islands there is one, very flat and fairly long, forming a fairly deep cove ending in a sandy beach. But I do not know whether the channels separating it from the others are navigable, not having entered them. As for the one between the mainland and these islands, it is about four leagues wide and the water in it is deep, for we found no less than 28 fathoms, and that only for a moment, since we generally had between 33 & 30.
In the course of the morning Citizen Freycinet came to point out to me that most of our helmsmen were sick and unfit for duty, and that it was absolutely necessary to choose men from the rest of the crew who could take their place. He added that, to remedy this difficulty, he asked to be authorised to have the master carpenter and the second caulker take the helm. I pointed out to him that in such a case what was needed was not so much orders as a simple request, and one made with good grace, since the two men's trade was so different from the one for which he wished to employ them. My answer, no doubt, was not to his liking, for he replied that such a step towards people so far beneath him could not be taken by an officer such as himself, et cetera, et cetera.
I then decided to give a written order, which is entered in the log book kept by the officers, that all the midshipmen, of the first as well as of the second class, should take an hour and a half at the helm during their watch, which was certainly no hard labour for them and could only contribute to their instruction. It produced, however, quite the contrary effect to the one I had expected, for all these gentlemen, regarding it as a dishonour, intrigued together to be excused from it. M. Bougainville, whose turn came first, flatly refused to go and, to cover his disobedience, made use of the pretext that he was sick; M. Brun claimed that by the regulations he was exempt from it as of right. Midshipman Baudin was the only one to show goodwill, which brought him a great deal of teasing from his comrades. They all expected me to punish them in some other fashion, but they were much mistaken, and I merely forbade them all duty of any kind aboard, telling them that I would do without them for steering just as well as I had done without them for everything else.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 47' 35", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 132° 10' 54".
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) We had in sight the five islands of the morning and the tops of some rocks seen the day before. In the afternoon, the wind having suddenly dropped, it came to us from the north-west. We sought to close with the mainland but, having made little way by nightfall, we could not clearly make out the contours it appears (to have). We made out only an island and a rock far out to sea, which we passed during the night, hugging the island off which we had anchored the day before.
1802-04-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The governor sent us vegetables. At 7 the captain, accompanied by the officers and naturalists, went to pay a visit to the governor; they were back at 2. At 11.30 a.m. our two boats came in. Only one man, Happedey, had a dislocated shoulder. From 5 a.m. until 4 p.m. we warped.

1802-04-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW, SW and WSW, with light rain until 4. At 1 weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser. At 2 the captain and all those with him came back from Sydney Town. At 4 weighed the kedge anchor and let go the bower, which proved to be foul, and hove round on the hawser. When we were at long stay on the hawser we ran out a warp and catted the bower anchor. At 9.15 weighed the kedge anchor, on which we were up and down, and hove round on the warp. A sloop bound for Tahiti sailed from Port Jackson.
1802-04-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, having made a little way to the north and west during the night without losing sight of the land, we continued to run along it and to take the bearings that may fix its position. The sky, though cloudy during the morning, was fairly fine, but the wind was not favourable to us, being variable from north-north-north-east (sic) to north-north-west.
The land we had in sight was for the most part of a good height and divided by other, lower land. But all of it presented only a dreary and disagreeable aspect, being for the most part barren and without vegetation, or at least having at that time no kind of verdure that might lead us to believe that in the fine season it is any different from what we saw of it.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 36' 54", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 131° 10' 57". Supposing it to be correct, we had only to work up to the north to sight the islands of St Peter and St Francis, but the wind did not allow us to do so.
After the observation of the sun we went about so as not to stand away from the coast. The wind, moreover, which died away as it shifted into the quarter from north towards west, brought us a little nearer to it, although for the rest of the day it was light and very unsteady.
Before sunset the sky clouded over and looked very ill. The movement of the barometer likewise seemed to warn us of some gales, for it was falling very rapidly and stood at no more than 28 inches 2 lines, from the 28 6 at which it had stood the day before. The hygrometer followed much the same course.
The winds from the northern quarter, whether towards east or towards west, were warm and kept the thermometer much higher than when we had them from the south, by east as well as by west.
During the night the wind, after going round several points of the compass, shifted to the south and at last settled in the south-east. The breeze was very light until midnight, when it began to freshen. We steered north to close with the coast, from which we then found ourselves a fair way off, taking care to sound every hour. The depth it gave us was never below 35 fathoms nor more more (sic) than 46, which was the depth from which we had started at eight o'clock in the evening. For the rest, the night passed without incident; we had now and then a little rain of short duration, and the sky, though dark and very heavy in the south-west, did not for the moment bring the bad weather I was expecting, which, I believe, will not fail to come with the new moon.
1802-04-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. We warped from 4 a.m. until 9.30. The Nautilus, a private vessel fitted out as a letter of marque and bound for Tahiti, left the port. At noon Captain Scott of the sloop Porpoise came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the sloop Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern. We saluted her with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". The governor and the civil and military officers of Sydney came aboard, where they stayed until 2. The captain, the officers and the naturalists went to Sydney to the dinner given by the governor. We warped as soon as they had left. At 3.15, being under Bradleys Point, we got under way with a light breeze from NNW. At 5 we anchored in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and at once moored NNW and SSE with a kedge anchor, in Neutral Bay, near Rock Island.

1802-04-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm at noon. Captain Scott, commanding the sloop Porpoise, came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the brig Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern; he was greeted with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". He came aboard at once with the civil and military officers of Sydney Town. He left at 2 and was followed by the captain and his officers. At 2.30 ran out a warp; the kedge anchor was weighed at once and, the tide carrying us in, towed by the longboat and the large boat, a light air came on and we set our fore-and-aft sails. At 5 we let go the anchor in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and veered 40 fathoms of cable. The longboat carried out a kedge anchor and we moored NNW and SSE with 90 fathoms of cable out.
1802-04-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, having closed with the mainland during the night, we hove to under the topsails from five o'clock until the day was far enough advanced to make out the coast and our position. The noise of the surf breaking on the shore told us that we were not very far from it, although the lead gave 35 fathoms.
At sunrise we found ourselves off a fairly deep bight. The land, however, could be clearly made out; it is of moderate height, but the points forming its extremities are much higher, to the north as well as to the south.
From the point forming the northern entrance of this cove runs a reef, which extends a long way in a south-easterly direction and on which the sea breaks heavily. Although it appeared to us to close the passage into this bight, it is possible that it may be practicable. The wind, which was then from east to east-north-east, did not allow us to make sure of it. We passed a good league from the reef I have just mentioned, having found no less than 35 fathoms.
At seven o'clock the lookouts at the mastheads reported an island to leeward of us, which we soon made out from the deck. It appeared to us to be of a good height and to offer an easy channel between it and the mainland. On its southern side could be seen a reef of some extent, where the sea rose to a great height. As it seemed to lie well out to sea, it was judged not to be connected with this island.
In the course of the morning the wind was very light and variable. As it shifted to the north-east, we lost all hope of entering the channel this island forms with the mainland. Here we found the sea running very high, with a long swell from south-south-west which leads us to believe that we no longer had any land on that point of the horizon.
At noon we had no latitude by observation, the sky being dark and overcast. That by dead reckoning put us in 32° 51' 36".
After rounding the small island I spoke of above and the reefs off both its ends, we drew near the mainland, which here is very low. It seems to me that, had we passed through the channel formed by the island and the projecting point opposite it, we should not have found it easy to pass between it and the mainland, so close did it seem to us to lie. The land of the continent is so low on this part of the coast that it can scarcely be seen from the deck at two leagues, and long before, we had seen several columns of smoke rising from different parts, without the lookouts at the mastheads having any sight of the coast.
A little before sunset we were greatly surprised to see that we still had land to leeward of us, as far as south-west by west. For we had not expected, from our estimated latitude and our position on the chart, to see it trend so far to the south as it did. The barometer standing at no more than 28 inches, and believing the bad weather to be about to make itself felt, I spent the night lying to, so as not to become entangled among
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) unknown lands or islands should it come on. During the night the sky was very dark and the breeze light until about three o'clock, but then it increased by degrees and became fresh, without gusts. Soundings were taken regularly every hour and we constantly had from 35 to 38 fathoms of water.
1802-04-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At 2.30 a.m. the captain, the officers and the naturalists came aboard. The mainsail and main topsail, which needed repair, were unbent. The longboat made one trip for water. A large English three-master came in, loaded with whale oil.

1802-05-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm; hoisted in our large boat. At 4 a three-master came into the port from the whale fishery. The longboat went watering.
1802-05-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
( $$ continued from page 127) even more closely than we had done when working up to the north. At six o'clock the rock I have mentioned and the westernmost island came into view again, and we took our departure from them for the course to be held during the night. The number of islands in this group is much greater than the charts indicate, and as I intend to go round them on their western side, I hope that I shall be able to determine it.
During the night the wind was very unsteady and the breeze moderate. We held a course from west towards south as far as the wind allowed; the soundings were regular, from 35 to 43 fathoms.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, a little before daylight, lying hove to in 37 fathoms, we suddenly passed into 30, and that within the space of half an hour. This unexpected change surprised us all the more because during the night the depth had been very regular, increasing fathom by fathom only at intervals of time fixed by the clock. Half an hour later, having found forty fathoms, we remained hove to until daylight. At that time we sighted the land to windward of us at about four leagues' distance. It appeared in the form of a small island of little extent, but I remained convinced that it was a point of the mainland, and the same one that had been set the day before at south-west and south-west by west.
However that may be, the wind being north-north-east, variable to north, a strong breeze, we stood on the starboard tack, hugging the wind as close as we could, but we could not approach the land near enough to see that of the day before, which, as I have observed, is very low. As we rounded the land we had in sight, the lookouts reported another, further to the north, which likewise seemed to them to be an island, since they could see nothing in the bight lying in its direction relative to the one we were leaving. They could only make out a reef, which seemed to lie midway between these two lands. The wind not allowing us, for the moment, to go and find out what this part might be, we continued on the westward board towards the north until ten o'clock, when, the wind having shifted to north-north-west, we took the north-eastward board.
All morning the sky was dark and overcast, the breeze fresh and the sea somewhat swelling. The long swell from south-south-west to south-west that we had met with the day before had almost entirely disappeared.
At noon the observed latitude was 32° 47' 16". There was no hour angle for the longitude by the timekeeper. At the time of the observation the land bore from west 76° 15' north to north 3° 45 east of us. Another could also be seen further to the west in the form of an islet, and in the space separating these two lands several rocks awash, on which the sea broke heavily, seemed to show that the channel they form with the land is not convenient. As we were then standing on the northward board towards the east, with a pleasant breeze from the north-west, we soon closed with the land we had had in sight since the morning, which, from its difference from that seen the day before, did not seem to me to belong to the mainland. This conjecture was soon borne out for, as we advanced to the north, it was recognised that it could only be the beginning of the group of islands and islets known by the name of St Francis. Running along their eastern side, we counted eleven of them in sight, from the one that appeared to us the westernmost to the one seen furthest to the north. We entered the channel which separates this group of islands from those called St Peter, which we also sighted, but too far to the east to be properly examined. The islands of St Francis are generally of little extent. The largest of those we saw during the evening is no more than three leagues from north to south, and the others much less. All are barren, bare of vegetation, and seem to offer no resources to navigators. Most of the channels which
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) separate them from one another are obstructed by reefs, which must make passage through them difficult, supposing they are practicable at all. Only two seemed to us to offer a good one, and I should have attempted it had the wind not been against us. As we ran along seven of these islands at a short distance, it was easy for us to judge them well. At three o'clock, being unable to weather the one ahead of us, we went about and retraced our course, coasting along them ($$ see end, page 126)
1802-05-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The sick were sent to the hospital at Sydney. The longboat made two trips for water. A notice was read to the crew by which Captain Hamelin warns the inhabitants of the colony that he will not be answerable for debts contracted by his crew. During the night the wind a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The establishment of the port at Sydney Cove is 8 o'clock; the tide rises there 7 feet 6 English inches.

1802-05-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm. The longboat went for water and wood; the sick were carried to the hospital; the cables were got out of the hold to come at the bar iron. During our stay at Port Jackson we watered, fresh provisions were embarked and we got wood. On the 13th [Floréal, Year 10, 3 May 1802] tents were set up ashore for the observatory. A Frenchman authorised by the governor was shipped aboard and came on board. At 5.30 p.m. on the 19th [Floréal, Year 10, 9 May 1802] the ship Investigator came into the port, having left England 10 months before and coming from the SW coast, where she had met the Géographe in 35° 41' south and 126° 49' east longitude. On the 20th [Floréal, Year 10, 10 May 1802] at 5 an English longboat brought us an anchor. At 7 a.m. on the 21st [Floréal, Year 10, 11 May 1802] an English ship brought the news of the preliminaries of peace. The winds were constantly from WNW to WSW and sometimes from the east. We embarked as provisions [one word illegible], potatoes, [one word illegible] and wheat [two words illegible]. At 7 we made ready to get under way. At 10.15 we were under sail.
1802-05-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we steered north to close with the group of the islands of St Francis, which it was my intention to go round on its western side in order to examine the mainland from the point where General d'Entrecasteaux had stopped. But towards eight o'clock, the lookouts having reported land to the west, we saw shortly afterwards, and not without astonishment, that it was the same we had left the day before, and that we were more than six leagues to leeward of it, whereas the course held during the night ought, if not to have put us to the east of it, at least not to have carried us as far from it as we found ourselves.
There seems to be no doubt that during the previous night we experienced a strong current which carried us to the east much further than (we) could have supposed.
All morning we steered north to explore the land ahead of us, which was not known to us. These are, no doubt, the two islands mentioned on the chart of the Dépôt, which places them to the east of the islands of St Francis. These two islands, which we approached very closely, are well marked on that chart, but their latitude did not seem to us correct. For at the moment when we observed the passage of the sun across the meridian, the latitude of the ship being 32° 31' 3", we were no more than a league from the southernmost, which is placed in 32° on the chart. The longitude by the timekeeper, reduced to the same time, put us in 130° 58' 14". A similar error had appeared to us the day before in the placing of the southernmost of the islands of St Francis.
At noon, being unable to weather the northern point of the island off which we found ourselves, we went about. It then bore north by east of us, and the second island was at north-east by north. The channel separating them from each other is narrow, but and I do not know whether the passage through it is easy. Throughout the day we were surprised to find the sea running very high and as agitated as if it had been blowing a gale. Although there was little wind and the long swell we met came to us directly from under the lee of the land that bore from south-west by west to north of us, we could put it down only to the strength of the currents. The two islands I have just spoken of are of a good height and every bit as barren and sterile as those seen before; so (no one) will be surprised that they were given the names of two saints who had taken vows of poverty.
I greatly regretted not being able to enter the channel these two islands form with the group of St Francis, so as to examine the mainland in this part. At two o'clock we tried to get into it by going about, but the sea was so agitated that we could not manage it. Although a pleasant breeze was then blowing, we could never keep the ship close-hauled, even with the helm hard a-lee. I then decided to continue on the south-westward board so as to work up to windward of the islands, the westerly winds and the currents leaving me no hope of getting into their channels from the east. During the night the wind was very variable, from north-west to west-south-west, where it settled. We had rain at times and a great deal of damp; the soundings gave between 38 & 42 fathoms.
1802-05-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The longboat made one trip for water. An observatory was set up on Green Point.

1802-05-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, having steered all night from south towards west as far as the wind allowed us, we again sighted the islands of St Francis, the southernmost of those in view bearing north-north-east of us, but they could be seen only from the masthead. As it was my intention, as I have already stated, to go round these islands by the west, the wind not allowing me to attempt it by the east, we steered a (little) more to the west towards north than to the north. All morning we had an extraordinarily strong and high swell, which led us to believe either that it had been blowing very hard from that south-westerly quarter, or that we should shortly have some gales from that point of the horizon. However, as the barometer, which in the past days had fallen as low as 27 inches 5 lines, was beginning to rise again, and as we had it that day at 27 8, we hoped to get off with a fright, the sky, moreover, being tolerably fine.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 1' 39", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 130° 40' 19". This latitude put us further south than I had expected. We steered north-north-west until eight o'clock in the evening.
Citizen Chle Baudin was that day made Midshipman of the first class, and I addressed the following letters to him:
"It is with great pleasure, Citizen, that I have seen you, since our departure from Timor, exercise yourself in all the tasks that go to make a good naval officer, and without the practical knowledge of which no one deserves to be one.
I hope that, in making you Midshipman of the first class by virtue of the powers the Government has granted me for the purpose, you will continue to merit, by modest, laborious and active conduct, the advancement it allows me to give to those who behave well. And that, far from believing, as your comrades think, that it is an exemption from personal duty and from particular instruction, you will make yourself useful aboard in whatever way I may judge fit or proper to employ you." Signed N. B.
To this letter I added the following:
"You will find enclosed with this letter, Citizen, the one appointing you Midshipman of the first class, a rank I did not think fit to grant you at Timor, but which your conduct since our departure from that port of call now earns you. You cannot doubt how agreeable it is to me to be able to advance you, and you must be convinced that the pleasure I feel in doing so is equal to the pain I feel at having done so for those who have abused it. I therefore urge you always to conduct yourself in an exemplary manner and to take no heed of the indiscreet and thoughtless remarks your comrades have made or may yet make. Think of yourself alone and earn your advancement. Reflect on the satisfaction it will give your family and those who solicited your embarkation on this expedition. You and Citizen Bonnefoy will probably be the only Midshipmen who will not have disappointed the expectations of the Government, so let this be one more reason for the conduct you are to keep until the end of the campaign. The likeness of your name to mine makes me speak to you as if you were my son, but be well assured that this consideration, if it existed, could not bring me to grant you what I believed you had not deserved. Your advancement therefore depends on you alone, and if, being Midshipman of
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) the first class, you were, like so many others, to persuade yourself that there is nothing left for you to learn, you would in that case put me in the position not only of repenting of what I had done for you, but also of asking the Government that the rank you now obtain and the one that awaits you be regarded as unearned." Signed N. B.
1802-05-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to SW. The mainsail was bent and the turns of the cables taken off. We sent for 124 lb of bread from Mr Palmer's house. The longboat made two trips for water.

1802-05-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, at daybreak, the flat calm that had prevailed during the night having made us fall far to leeward of the islands of St Francis, which we had been fairly close to the evening before at sunset, we sought to close with them by standing north as far as the wind allowed us. But although it had shifted from north towards east by eight o'clock in the morning, the breeze was so light that we saw them only at a very great distance. We nonetheless had a perfect view of the rocks and breakers and breakers (sic) to the east the west of these islands, as well as of the island lying furthest out in that direction, which I have already spoken of when mentioning the others. During the morning we had the same depth as the previous night, 40 fathoms, but at noon we got no bottom at 50 fathoms.
At the same time the observed latitude was 32° 46' 12", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 130° 21' 8". The land in sight of the group of the islands of St Francis then bore north 23° 45' east of us, and the westernmost island of the group, marked on the chart, lay to the north. We could no longer see the reef lying about halfway along the channel, nor the southernmost island of the group.
The heavy swell we had had the day before began to be less trying for us, and the sky having turned fine, we hoped that the fine weather was about to return, although the rise of the barometer was not as rapid as the state of the atmosphere seemed to promise.
In the afternoon, the wind having shifted to north-east and even further to the east, we steered north to draw near the mainland in order to go round the islands on their western side, but we made little progress owing to the lightness of the wind. At eight o'clock, the lead, the depth being 38 fathoms and the wind very light, we hove to and so passed the night, during which the wind was very variable and unsteady. There were squalls at times, which brought us more rain than wind. The sea, though agitated by a very heavy south-westerly swell, gave no warning of bad weather and seemed rather to be the aftermath of a past gale than the herald of a coming one
1802-05-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to W. Sent for bread. The cables that had been got out of the hold were found gnawed by rats in several places.

1802-05-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, reckoning myself far enough to the west to weather the islands of St Francis comfortably, we shaped our course under a press of sail to close with the mainland in that part, so as afterwards to go round the islands on our way back to the east, convinced that I should find some good passages in the channels separating them from the mainland.
At eight o'clock we sighted land to the north, and at ten o'clock we found ourselves in a deep bay whose two extremities could be seen from west round by north to south-east.
We stood into the bight lying directly ahead of us, hugging the wind close-hauled, with a rather strong breeze. On entering this large cove we did not make out the islands that lay to leeward of us.
I was astonished to find this part of the mainland much further south than the chart of General d'Entrecasteaux's voyage shows it, for when we went about, the estimated latitude was only 32° 12' 28" and our distance from the coast three leagues. There lay ahead of us at that moment a small islet of little consequence for its size, on which the sea broke heavily.
At ten o'clock, being fairly close to the coast, we went about to come and examine the entrance of this cove on its western side. And while we were coming round, so strong a gust suddenly fell upon us that our topmasts were for a moment endangered. After filling the sails again, we were obliged to furl our topsails and the mizzen topsail, so violent was the wind. But as we were in a bight and it came to us over the land, the sea was smooth. At first I persuaded myself that this very strong gust would be only momentary, the more so as the sky was fine, but as we opened the western point of this cove, we found the sea so heavy and agitated that there could be no doubt that it came from afar and that we were very likely about to meet with some gales. The barometer, for its part, had fallen to 28 inches.
At noon the observed latitude was 32° 21' 57". There was no hour angle.
In the afternoon, steering south towards west to get out to sea clear of the islands, from which we could not be far, the wind did nothing but increase and ended by becoming so violent that, had I not been obliged to make way in order to claw off the coast, I should have lain to. Although we carried no more canvas than the foresail and the mainsail, the ship was labouring under it and often heeled over very heavily.
At four o'clock we sighted the westernmost island of the group of St Francis. We passed no more than a league and a half from it. The sea broke frightfully all along its shore. The other islands soon came into view. We carried as much sail as possible to get to the southward. The heavy sea, the wind, the leeway and the ship's canvas were (not) favourable to the course we had to (make); nevertheless we weathered them during the night, never having less than 43 to 45 fathoms, fine sand.
As I feared a sudden shift of wind more than the land, I spent the whole night on deck, none of the officers aboard knowing what it is to
(In the left margin, perpendicularly) find oneself in such circumstances, in which the ablest seamen are often at a loss. I had, as usual, the officer who happened to be on watch for company. The others passed the night very quietly in their cabins. The shift of wind I feared did not come, but the night was none the less bad and the gales violent.
1802-05-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to NW. Sent for bread. An Englishman came to fetch a gallon of brandy in payment for the notices printed at Sydney.

1802-05-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events and Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, the winds, though still in the quarter from west to west-south-west, were less violent than during the night. Towards eight o'clock they shifted to the south-west, and we were able to set our topsails with all their reefs in. Although the sea was still extremely heavy and swelling, we held on the southerly tack, heading a little to the east, until noon, when we took the westerly one, heading a little to the north, so as not to stand too far from the coast.
In the course of the morning the look-outs at the mastheads told us that they could see land to the north-east, and believed they recognised some of the islets we had seen on the preceding days.
At noon the latitude was 32° 23' 44", which gave us nearly a degree to the south in the past 24 hours. There was no hour angle that day. The depth was then 42 fathoms.
During the evening the sky was very dark, though without looking threatening. The strength of the wind fell off by degrees, and at sunset it was very moderate.
At eight o'clock, the soundings having come down to no more than 35 fathoms, we wore round and steered south, a little to the east, until four o'clock, when we resumed our course west, a little to the north.
In the night we had a few (squalls), but of as little duration as consequence. The sky, though overcast, was very dry, and as the barometer was rising I was pleased to believe that fine weather was about to return and that we should be able to finish what remained for us to do on this coast.
Everyone was longing for a port of call, and in truth we all stood in need of one. There was no more wood for daily use; we were reduced to shifts to procure any, and our supply of water could not last long. I felt these privations like everyone else, but the desire to carry out the intentions of the Government made them more bearable to me than to the others. The scurvy, which was beginning to make headway among several of the crew, was what grieved me most; nevertheless I held to my resolution of rounding the St Peter Islands by the west, a thing that was neither long nor difficult, provided the weather set fair.
One of our scientists, whom I do not name, was seized with a most peculiar malady: the fear of dying took hold of him, and he persuaded himself that his career was at an end.
1802-05-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to WSW. Sent for bread; took the turns off the cables. The longboat carried 128 bars of iron to Sydney and brought back 60 sacks of wheat.

1802-05-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth we made our way to the westward, in order to come and examine the point where General d'Entrecasteaux had stopped, and afterwards to return eastward to examine the part of the mainland lying between that point and the one where we had stopped, to the west of the islands of St Francis and St Peter. The winds, which for eight days had been constantly variable from north-west to south-west, in gusts or very violent, had not allowed us to finish our work in the same manner as we had begun it.
During the day the breeze was very light, the sky overcast and the sea less bad than on the preceding days, though disturbed by a long swell from west to south-west. We had soundings fairly steadily between 36 and 40 fathoms, but in the evening the depth increased and we passed successively from 40 to 45 and even 50, afterwards falling back to 45. These irregularities we found in the soundings during the evening were the first of the kind we had met with at so great a depth of water.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 11' 42"; there was no hour angle for the longitude by the timekeeper.
In the afternoon the sky remained overcast, and even very heavy in the quarter from south-west to west, so that we again feared we might have to weather some gale from that point of the horizon. But we got off with a fright, for the night was fairly fine and the breeze very light. We continued to steer west under easy sail, my intention being to stand north the next day, if the winds remained the same and the weather was favourable for coming in to examine the land.
In the morning I received complaints from the crew about the poor quality of the salt meat that had just been served out, and which was indeed not good. It had nevertheless come from an intact and well-conditioned cask. I gave orders for it to be set aside and another opened, which turned out to be even worse than the first. We therefore had recourse to a third, which at last proved very good. As we had only one more of that kind left, the examination of the state it might be in was put off until the next day.
The biscuit we were using was not very excellent either, and had long been crumbling to dust, being all riddled with worms and eaten by moths.
1802-05-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW. Sent for bread. The longboat brought from Sydney 40 sacks of wheat, pumpkins and potatoes. The topgallant masts were got up.

1802-05-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, in the morning, we steered north, a little to the west, to close with the mainland, as I found myself far enough to the west to take up the coast again at the point where General d'Entrecasteaux appears to have left it. Although the weather did not look fine, we at least had the winds favourable for returning south should it turn bad. In the course of the morning the look-outs at the mastheads reported land, and some breakers a good distance out to sea, bearing north-east by east from us. As the wind came to us directly from that point of the horizon, we could not make them out from the deck, and the mainland only became visible from there towards noon. The sky was then so overcast and dark that that one (sic) could scarcely see to work or read in one's cabin. The barometer nevertheless stood at 28 inches 4 lines, which did not announce any fresh gales.
In the evening we continued to stand in towards the coast, and we did not have long to wait to make it out properly. It first appeared to us of a fairly regular shape and of middling height, but as we drew nearer we saw that it was like most of those we had seen before, that is to say sheer at the water's edge, forming various coves, more or less deep, but all of little consequence. We also made out two islets and a rock lying at a good distance from the coast, far enough to suggest that one could easily pass between them and the mainland, although the sea breaks heavily round about. The two islets and the rock are rather remarkable, which is why I think that General d'Entrecasteaux did not advance far enough to the east to have sighted them, or, if he did reach the point where we now are, which I believe to be the one where he stopped, that other circumstances must have hidden them from his view.
Be that as it may, we took various bearings of this part of the coast, which will link up with those we shall take on returning eastward as soon as the wind allows. At six o'clock we put the ship's head to the south to stand a little off the coast, and I meant to spend the night there hove to, but the weather began to turn very bad and the wind to blow in gusts. As the barometer had fallen three lines in less than four hours, I no longer doubted that some gale was very close at hand, nor was I mistaken in my expectation, for the night was extremely bad. Serious reflection on the position in which I found myself — the weakness of my crew, who were now no more than 30 men for working the ship, the pressing need we had of firewood, the shortness of the days and an infinity of other particular reasons — decided me to abandon the coast and make first for the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, where the anchorage is good, and from there for Port Jackson, where I have always kept the hope that the boat believed to be lost may have arrived. The change of course was not long in spreading, and everyone showed his satisfaction at it; and truly we all stood in great need
(Perpendicular in the left margin) of a little rest.
1802-05-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SSE. Sent ashore for bread and vegetables. The main topsail was bent.

1802-05-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth we continued our course to the south with strong northerly winds, which would not have failed to drive us well out to sea had I persisted any longer in staying on the thankless coast of New Holland. Three gales that I had already weathered in the space of ten days had constantly thwarted my wish to visit the islands of St Francis and St Peter in their whole extent, which, to judge by what we have seen of them, are scarcely worth the trouble we have taken to succeed in it. Nevertheless, I remain convinced that, on a careful examination, some shelter must be found there for navigators who come to frequent those parts. But to carry out this work with any likelihood of success, it is absolutely necessary to be there in midsummer, when the days are long and the weather manageable. That, too, is what I intend to do next season. The southern part of the great Kangaroo Island may also be of much interest, and although Mr Flinders told me he had stayed there six weeks, it seems to me, from the sketch he drew of it in my cabin, that he did not visit the whole of it.
During the day of the nineteenth the weather was, if not very bad, since we always had the wind aft or on the quarter, at least rainy and damp. Our sick, and above all the scurvy cases, who already numbered 14, were sorely troubled by it, and on several of them sores broke out that had not yet appeared. The physicians found this effect of dampness quite remarkable among seafaring men.
Throughout the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the whole horizon was ablaze; the flashes of lightning were so frequent that the eye was dazzled and often even pained by them. We hardly knew what the weather was going to do, but we were agreeably surprised to find that it would be no worse than it was, and that the rain would prevail over the wind.
1802-05-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from W to WSW. The longboat made one trip for water. Sent ashore for vegetables and 106 lb of bread. At 5.30 p.m. the English ship Investigator came in, Captain Flinders, 10 months out from England and bound on a voyage of discovery. He had met and spoken the Géographe on the SW coast in 35° 41' of latitude and 126° 49' of longitude.

1802-05-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Longitude by two sets of distances of the sun from the moon 129° 42' 41"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 35 129° 15' 51"
Difference west of the timekeeper from the observation 0° 26' 50"
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twentieth the weather continued dark and laden with vapours. The damp was even greater than the day before, and the whole morning passed in rain that soaked us to the skin. Several claps of thunder were heard in the distance, but did not reach us. The wind, falling off by degrees, told us of an approaching change, and although the barometer was still very low we hoped it would be in our favour. The sea, however, was still swelling and driven by a south-westerly sea that laboured us a great deal.
Towards ten o'clock we caught a very pretty land bird that came to rest on board. It would be rather hard to explain how it came to be so far out to sea, for we do not suppose there is any land in our neighbourhood, judging by the course and the distance we have made to the south since leaving the mainland.
At noon there was no observation, but we stood south by east, as I found myself far enough south not to fear running during the night upon any of the islets which we knew to lie in that quarter of the horizon, and which we had taken bearings of when coming from the east.
During the evening the weather seemed inclined to set fair. The whole horizon from north round by east to south-east became clear, and the view extended a good way. The winds, however, though very variable, stayed in the northern quarter towards the west; only the breeze was very light, so that the heavy south-westerly swell laboured us a great deal through the great rolling it gave the ship.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st the weather was tolerably fine, and towards the end of it the winds shifted from the north towards the east without increasing in strength. We continued on our course south by east under the same sail I had ordered for the night, which was the mainsail furled and two reefs in each topsail.
1802-05-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. Sent for 105 lb of bread. A great many articles of trade were carried to the captain's lodging, and pumpkins and cabbages brought back. An English longboat brought us an anchor and 162 gallons of brandy. At 7 an English ship came in bringing news of the general peace.

1802-05-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first the sky, which had been tolerably fine during the night, again became laden with damp vapours, and from time to time we had squalls followed by little gusts, but of short duration; this did not prevent us from shaking a reef out of our topsails, the more so as the sea was calmer. The winds, which were then very variable from the north round towards the east, seemed inclined to settle in the north-east, but only for a moment, for they soon came back to north-north-west, variable to west-north-west, and almost calm. The sky, which had been dark and overcast for the greater part of the morning, cleared, and at noon we observed the latitude of (no figures); the longitude shown by the timekeeper put us in (no figures)
In the afternoon the weather continued fine. We steered south-east by south, but the breeze was so light that we made very little way.
According to the report the physician made to me, our sick were worse than usual, and he could only attribute this unfortunate turn, above all in those who were attacked by scurvy, to the great dampness that had prevailed for several days. Care and attention to them were redoubled, and I hope that if we soon reach the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, rest and good food will bring them through.
At sunset the weather was perfectly fine and the horizon clear on every side, so that we had hopes of a fine night lit by the moon, which was already fairly well advanced; but it was almost calm and we were making only very little way.
During the night of the twenty-first to the 22nd the breeze continued very light and the weather fine. The winds varied from north by west to north-west, but but (sic) they were not strong enough to steady the ship and protect her against the tossing given her by the heavy swell, which never left us.
1802-05-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to NNE. An English boat brought us 296 pumpkins and 2800 lb of potatoes. The anchor received yesterday was stocked. Rain during the night. The 22nd [Floréal, 12 May 1802]. Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from E. Sent for 400 lb of bread and took the turns off the cables. A great many articles of trade were carried to the captain's lodging. At 8.30 p.m. an English ship came in from the whale fishery on the coast of New Zealand.

1802-05-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, during the day, the weather was fairly fine and it blew a pleasant breeze from north-north-west, variable to west-north-west, but we still found the sea heavy, swelling and very rough; nevertheless we crowded sail, continuing to steer south-east by south, for I was convinced that it would not be long before we had the winds from the quarter between south and south-west.
In the course of the morning we saw a good many birds, among which was the pintado petrel, which we had long since lost sight of. The others were albatrosses and a species of small ash-grey and white petrel of which I have already spoken.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 38° 26' 3" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 131° 5' 56".
In the evening the sky, though tolerably fine, clouded over at several points of the horizon, and seemed to announce wind and rain for the night.
At sunset it became misty and damp. Our sick felt it keenly, and several of them said they were suffering unbearable pains, though their illness did not appear to have grown worse, according to the physicians' report.
During the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third it blew a good breeze, but we had a heavy sea, a constantly overcast sky and now and then some small squalls, though of little consequence. We saw no sign that day of any approaching change in the weather, and it seemed to us that the end of autumn in these climates is not very pleasant.

1802-05-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
[3V p. 233 F] 6th document.
Reply of Cit. Hamelin to the request of Cit. Millius, who asked him to resume his duties on board the Naturaliste.
Citizen,
I am forwarding to Commander Baudin your request of today's date to resume your duties on board on the grounds of your recovery.
I have the honour to point out to you that you have often experienced similar improvements, which have always been followed by relapses that, by interrupting your service, have cost me several months of anxiety.
Greetings
Signed: the Capt. de frégate
C. Hamelin
[3V p. 233 G] All the original documents, with the physicians' certificates, are in the hands of Capitaine de frégate Millius.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, the weather, though still overcast and damp, was all the more bearable for those who were in good health as the wind was fair and the breeze fresh. We continued to steer south-east by south, so as to get early into the latitude of South West Cape, which I meant to come and examine just as I had done on my first entry into the strait. As I expected to see the winds shift at any moment from the north-west to the south and south-west, I was glad to make them favourable for the course that remained for me to make to reach the strait.
During the morning the sky remained constantly the same, that is to say almost always overcast and laden with damp vapours, which were no good omen for what was to come. At noon, however, we had a latitude, somewhat doubtful to be sure, but which at any rate gave us 40° 37' 16", and the longitude by the timekeeper was found to be 133° 4' 14".
In the afternoon the weather was the same as we had found it in the morning, and the winds remained steadily at north-north-west, a good breeze, which was exceedingly agreeable to us, although we could not take full advantage of it by making a great deal of sail, because the sea was too swelling and rough and the motion it gave the ship quick and violent.
During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth we found the sea so bad that we were obliged to furl our mainsail, which, being often becalmed by the height of the seas, was jerking so violently that we feared it would split. The same was done with the spanker. For the rest, the remainder of the night passed without incident and the weather was not bad.
1802-05-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to NE, with rain. An Englishman with an order from the captain came to fetch 90 bottles of arrack. Sent for pumpkins at the captain's lodging. The three Black men, Charlot, Jean and Jasmin, were discharged by the captain's order.

1802-05-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, a heavy squall accompanied by gusts brought the winds round to west-south-west, and from that moment they became very variable and died away by degrees. Shortly afterwards they came back to the north round by the east without gaining strength, but they brought us rain so heavy that it was continual throughout the morning, with no sign of ending as soon as we could have wished.
At noon there was no observation, and the dead reckoning of the distance run in the twenty-four hours put us in latitude 41° 49' 2". The longitude, likewise by reckoning, was 134° 54' 16". We then steered south-east, having only very little way still to make to the south in proportion to what we had yet to run in longitude.
In the afternoon the rain continued, and though it was less heavy than it had been in the morning, it was no less continual and troublesome, above all for our sick, who at that time numbered twenty, for the sick-bay was growing every day and a speedy port of call was becoming more and more indispensable.
I had expected that the heavy rain which had fallen all day would have changed the state of the sea, the more so as the breeze was very moderate, but the sea remained constantly swelling and high, so that the ship and her masts laboured all the more, the wind not being strong enough to steady her.
Towards the end of the day we saw little sign of a change in the weather for the night. The rain, however, seemed likely to stop soon, inasmuch as several points of the horizon were no longer so laden with vapours. We had fairly fine weather until midnight, and even an almost dead calm, but from midnight, the winds having gone round to the south-east, the breeze became so strong that we were obliged to furl most of our sails, keeping only the foresail and the main topsail until we should know what would become of a wind which, from its very beginning, announced itself with so much force and violence.
1802-05-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to ENE. The longboat made one trip for water and one for wood. At daybreak a working party of fifteen men had been sent to cut wood.

1802-05-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, although the winds had changed entirely during the night, the rain went on for some time longer, but at length it stopped towards eight o'clock in the morning, and the sky became tolerably fine, though cloudy. The winds, which were at south-east, varied little, and the breeze was no less strong than it had been during the night. In the course of the morning we experienced a sudden change in the temperature of the atmosphere. The air became dry and even cold. The thermometer suddenly dropped to eight degrees, which had not happened to it even at our departure from Le Havre, where it stood at 9°. This change, which we had not expected so soon, was keenly felt by most of those on board, and everyone began to put on his winter clothes. I was not the last to do so.
At noon we had no observed latitude. That by dead reckoning put us in 42° 45' 17", and our longitude proved to be 134° 32' 16", as we had made some way to the west during these twenty-four hours.
As the wind was dead against our course, I had nothing changed in the sail and continued on the southerly tack, falling off to the west as little as possible. In the course of the day we saw again the same birds, as to species, that we had met with two days before, but in much greater numbers. We had the good fortune to take on a line a variety of albatross that was unknown to us and which we found very handsome. This bird, it seems, is very voracious, and more than a score of them were caught on the baits thrown out to them. But as their strength was considerable, we could not haul them on board before they had broken our lines, and more often still the hooks by which they were held, so that we got only one.
During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth the wind fell away a great deal from the outset, and we even spent part of it becalmed, without the ship answering her helm. This gave us hope of a change of wind, and so indeed it came, for the winds went round to south-south-east and made our course a tolerable one.
The heavy swell and the long, high sea we had constantly had since leaving the coasts of New Holland ceased to be felt from the time we met with the winds at south-east.
1802-05-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to N. Sent a working party of 15 men to cut wood. The draught was taken: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 11 feet 7 inches, difference 1 inch. The longboat made one trip for wood.

1802-05-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth the weather was fairly fine in the morning, but the winds were very variable and light compared with the preceding days. We found the sea no (less) disturbed by a heavy swell from the south and south-east, which made it uncomfortable although it appeared fairly calm.
At noon we observed the latitude of 43° 21' 38"; the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 134° 26' 17".
During the evening the weather differed little from what we had had in the morning, and was indeed much more pleasant than we had found it for several days, though cold enough to make us blow on our hands. Our sick found great relief in it, and the pains they had felt until then much less sharp. I hope that the fresh provisions I shall be able to procure for them in the channel or elsewhere will restore them entirely, provided the weather there is at all fine.
During the night of the 26th to the 27th the sky clouded over several times, but on the whole the night was fine and the winds very variable from the south towards the east. We even had them at north-east, but only for a moment.
During the day, and even during the night, we had the company of a good number of birds of the petrel class, which the moonlight helped to see the ship, which they seemed to follow.
1802-05-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. Sent the working party of 15 men for wood; sent ashore for cabbages. The longboat made one trip for wood. At 10 p.m. the rain stopped, the weather cleared, the wind fell and drew round to the west. Citizen Milius stayed at Port Jackson on account of illness. Three Black men were discharged; a seaman named Horsfall (the one who escaped from the Virginie at Timor and came aboard by swimming) deserted. Two Frenchmen, convicts, were shipped.

1802-05-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
The day of the twenty-seventh passed without incident, and as the weather was fine our sick felt even better than the day before, a quite incontestable proof that great dampness, if it is not the cause of scurvy, at least greatly hastens whatever predisposition one may have to that disease
Although we were extremely pinched for firewood, since we were reduced to burning everything that was worthless in the way of planks, casks, etc., etc. A little fire was made in their quarters to draw out as much of the damp as possible, but what could be given them was so slight that it can have been of no great use to them.
At noon, although the weather was then tolerably fine, we could not observe the sun's passage over the meridian, the (sky) being covered with clouds. By our dead reckoning the latitude proved to be 43° 11' 40".
During the evening the weather continued fine and the sea became tolerably (no mention). The swell, though it still persisted, had lost so much of its force that we were little troubled by it.
From the morning, the winds having gone round to the south towards the west, we took advantage of them to make our way eastward, so as to reach the D'Entrecasteaux Channel as soon as possible and there supply ourselves with whatever we might lack. During the evening we had them at south-west, a fresh breeze, and made good use of them.
The night of the 27th to the twenty-eighth brought a few squalls and even rain, but the wind, which was fair for us, kept us from paying much attention to it, and we carried all sail.
1802-05-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to WNW. The longboat made one trip for water and wood. The observatory was struck. It was verified that our mill could give 9 lb of flour in 1½ hours from 15 lb of wheat. At 8 a cooper named Bouteiller was brought aboard in the large boat, wounded by a dagger thrust given him by midshipman Desgouhières, who was in charge of the party. Bouteiller and the other boat's crew were drinking in a tavern at Sydney; the midshipman went there and ordered them aboard the boat. Bouteiller, drunk, answered him insolently and came at him to strike him; he drew his dagger and Bouteiller took a thrust in the lower belly which the surgeon judged mortal.

1802-05-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth the weather was much less pleasant than on the two preceding days, and our scurvy cases had foretold this change the evening before by the return of their pains. The barometer and the hygrometer indicated it likewise, for the first was falling rapidly and the second moving towards damp.
During the morning the sky was rainy and covered by a thick mist, which penetrated so deeply into the interior of the ship that no part of her was spared.
We had no observation for the latitude at noon, and one might even say that we had been without one for a long time, for those we had obtained before seemed to me very doubtful as to their accuracy. When the sun was out, the horizon was so shortened or so laden with vapours that they have always seemed uncertain to me, although not everyone is of the same opinion. That by dead reckoning put us in 43° 43'. I continued to hold an easterly course, edging a little to the south, so that some unexpected error should not expose us to any danger.
During the day we found the sea rough and a little (no adjective), but that was unavoidable in the weather we were having; nevertheless we continued to to (sic) crowd sail, so as to lose as little time as possible and reach a port of call, of which we stood in absolute need.
In the afternoon I had the ship steered east so as not to go too far south, and this course was kept up during the night, although our short distance from the land, according to our reckoning and even the results of the timekeeper, called for greater prudence. But as the night had some fine spells, and at times our horizon was fairly wide by favour of the moon, we continued on our course with the same confidence as if I had found myself far out to sea.
1802-05-18.journal_breton_naturaliste:
At midnight the weather turned overcast and the wind freshened. At 1 it was blowing hard in gusts, with thunder and rain; at 3 the weather cleared and the rain stopped. Cries were heard which were at first thought to come from Garden Island; but then believing them to be those of a drowning man, a boat was at once sent, which found about half a cable off a man trying to reach the ship by swimming. Questioned as to who he was and what he wanted, he said he was a soldier and had deserted to come aboard. He was taken at once aboard the Lady Nelson, which lay anchored near us. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW. At 5 the pilot came to take us out; the longboat went to weigh the kedge anchor, but the buoy rope having parted she came back aboard and was hoisted in, as were the other boats. At 8 the bower anchor was weighed, and at 10.15 we got under way from the kedge and shaped our course out of the port. At 11.30, after doubling North and South Head, we hove to and sent back the pilot, then filled and stood on; the anchors were secured in their stowage. Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from WSW to south, with rain; lay to under the foresail, both topsails close-reefed, the storm staysail, the fore staysail, the mizzen and its staysail.

During our stay at Port Jackson Captain Hamelin behaved in a manner unworthy of a French officer. Mr Palmer, the colony's commissary, had offered to supply him with everything he might need; he took only bread for the stay and wheat for the voyage. The governor supplied him with 162 gallons of brandy from the government stores and an anchor, which he paid for with bar iron. He had a great many articles of trade carried to his lodging at Sydney, and there he bartered them himself for potatoes and pumpkins that the inhabitants brought. This traffic, shameful in an officer — and above all in an officer commanding a ship and representing the French government — gave rise to difficulties between Captain Hamelin and the wretched convicts who were bartering their vegetables for tools, and Harris the justice of the peace had to restore peace between them.
