Captain Hamelin had so good a reputation at Sydney that one day, dining in town, a lady asked me whether he sold women's shoes.

1802-05-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from WSW, SSW and south; the wind came on to blow hard. At daybreak a man not belonging to the crew was found; he said he was an English soldier and had come aboard by swimming during the night of the 27th to the 28th [Floréal, Year 10, 17-18 May 1802].
1802-05-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the sky continued overcast, misty and rainy, and for our part we continued on our course as though it had been the finest weather in the world, without changing anything in our sail.
At eight o'clock we sighted the land in a clear spell, and I recognised that we were a little north of the South West Cape of Van Diemen's Land, finding myself in much the same position as when I had first sighted it. As these lands were well known to me, I set accordingly the course that remained for me to make in order to enter the channel. Only I feared that the shortness of the day would not be enough for us to get there, as I had not been able to see the rock called Mewstone to the east until noon.
The breeze was then blowing hard from the west-north-west quarter and we were making great way. I nevertheless continued to carry as much sail as could be carried without endangering the masts. But in the evening it became so strong that, despite my wish to arrive before nightfall, I found myself obliged to have a second reef taken in the topsails.
At four o'clock we sighted Tasman's Pedra Branca rocks, but we were still to the west of them, as also of the entrance of the strait, which took away my hope of being able to enter it before nightfall, and the night did not look fine,
At sunset, which came soon. which came soon after that time, we suddenly fell, if not into a flat calm, at least into an air so variable that we were scarcely trimmed on one tack before we had to go on to another. This fickleness of the winds, caused no doubt by the different positions of the long and numerous range of mountains that form this part of the coast, kept us in continual activity for two hours and was not pleasant for us, the more so as the depth of the water, though at a short distance from the coast, was considerable and the bottom foul. But at last, towards eight o'clock, the wind settled in the west towards the south, very strong breezes, and obliged us to take in the third reef in the topsails and to furl our our (sic) mainsail.
We took advantage of the first gusts that came to make a little way to the east, edging to the north, so as to spend the night under Bruny Island, of which we had taken good bearings. By this means I got clear of the Pedra Branca rocks, on to which the current or other circumstances might have set us had the calm and the light, fitful airs lasted longer.
After moonrise, which took place towards half past ten, the winds increased still further, considerably; the sea was very heavy and rough, and despite the violent squalls we met with, I reached Bruny Island, where I lay to until midnight, when, finding myself too near the land, I ran a little to the south and then to the east, where I stopped until daylight.
1802-05-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SSW to S. At 3 a.m. Bouteiller died of his wound. At daybreak a stranger was discovered; he said he was an English soldier and had come aboard on the 28th about 3 a.m. The topgallant masts were got down. The weather cleared, the wind fell and was a light breeze from S to ESE. At noon in 34° 20' 23" of latitude observed and in 149° 36' 24" of longitude by account. At 2 we filled and stood on; at 4 the land from N 12° W to S 29° W.

1802-05-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a strong breeze from south, SE, W and NW. At noon the land from N 28° W to S 48° W.
1802-05-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings from the anchorage, Adventure Bay:
The south point of the entrance of the bay, or Fluted Cape, south 33° east
Cape Trop Billant north 10° east
The middle of the isthmus north 30° west
The south point of Tasman Island north 64 east
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth. On the thirtieth, in the morning, being under Bruny Island at a distance of about three leagues, we could scarcely see the land, so wrapped was it in mist and covered with vapours. As we found ourselves somewhat to the east of it, I gave up hope of being able to enter the strait. Not only were the winds too violent for us to regain the ground we had lost, but the weather was so unsuitable that it would have been the height of imprudence to attempt it. Necessity and the want of firewood then made me resolve to try to reach the anchorage of Adventure Bay, and I was fortunate enough to get there by running along the coast from the Boreel Islands [The Friars] to that bay almost within musket shot, seeing at times the tops of the mountains but not the edges of the coast. Inside the Boreel Islands I was surprised to find the sea as heavy as we met it, which made me suspect that easterly or south-easterly winds had prevailed a good deal on this coast.
Towards eight o'clock, the weather having cleared a little, it was then easy for me to recognise Adventure Bay from the plan of it given by the geographers of General d'Entrecasteaux's expedition, so that we were already very close to it when the weather gave me hope of being able to anchor there, which indeed took place at half past eight. I do not remember ever having seen a more picturesque sight than that presented by Fluted Cape, a name that (is) very well suited to it.
As soon as we were at anchor, the longboat and every man on board able to wield an axe were sent ashore to cut wood for us.
Two other boats were likewise dispatched there, one to carry the scientists and others, and the third for fishing. Our sick, who had a great interest in it, awaited the return of the latter with great impatience, and their hope of feasting during the day was not realised, for it did not return until very late, but at least with a catch plentiful enough for everyone to have a share, although there were only four people with lines.
Our longboat and our scientists brought back (sic) about four cords of wood; the scientists, few new things, but the names of several people from the Recherche carved on the bark of the trees.
Everything was arranged for a second trip for wood to be made during the night if the weather set fair.
Citizen + (in the left margin: + Péron), who makes, or always believes he makes, new discoveries, claimed to have found a river that no one had seen before him, since none of the voyagers who have visited this part better than we have mention it. But be that as it may, water was plentiful there and none of the ravines lacked it. It appears that it had already rained abundantly in this part of the coast. The vegetation was so vigorous that all the trees were covered with foliage of a fine green
infinitely more pleasing to the eye than when we entered the strait (in the left margin: the first time), in the middle of the fine season.
The fish we caught were of the same species as those we already knew. The gardener, who is not one of the scientists, nevertheless managed to find four new plants that we had not met with elsewhere.
The physician Laridon believed he had settled the question of the quadrupeds, and brought back some fire-blackened bones which, in my view, belonged to some seals or other marine animal that must have served as food for the natives. If they are from a land animal, which is not likely, it must be bigger than an elephant.
At midnight the longboat left the ship under the command of Citizen Ronsard, both to cut wood and to see whether the water, which by everyone's account was very plentiful in various places, was also convenient to take on board by means of our longboat.
During the night the weather set fair and the winds went round to north-north-west, a light breeze.
1802-05-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NW, SW to SE. At 10, 10° 19' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 25' 24" of latitude observed and in 149° 17' 36" of longitude by account. The land from N 28° W to N 48° W.

1802-05-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from W to S and SE. At daybreak sighted the land; at noon it stretched from N 29° W to S 51° W.
1802-05-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Prairial the weather was extremely fine throughout the day. We did not, however, draw every possible advantage from it, despite the precaution I had taken that not a moment should be lost. My longboat, which I had sent off in the middle of the previous night, did not return until about three o'clock in the afternoon, whereas she should have been on board at ten in the morning. The small boat, which was to have arrived before her, did not come alongside either until after the longboat, and might perhaps still be ashore had I not recalled her with a shot from a swivel gun.
All these setbacks, and the course of the barometer, which was falling continually and at noon stood at 28 inches, made me change my mind and resolve to get under sail as soon as we were ready for it. As soon as the longboat was unloaded, therefore, we set about hoisting her on board, together with all the other boats. This work was long, and we had barely finished it at six in the evening, in a season when night fell at five o'clock and even earlier.
I should have liked to weigh at once, but the excessive fatigue of my crew made me, whatever might happen, put it off until the next day. And as the sky did not look threatening, I even excused them from keeping watch.
Midshipman Le Brun, whom at the request of Captain Hamelin I had made Midshipman first class, and whose insubordinate conduct, following the counsels of the son of M. Bougainville, who behaves as badly as can be, was put in the lions' den for the night for having treated with the utmost indecency the master gunner, who remonstrated with him about the dangers to which he was exposing us
all by lighting his pipe at the bitt lantern with a paper spill which, without further thought, he threw on the deck after using it.
As the young man, though full of strength and vigour, had done no duty on board for a month, I reduced him to Midshipman second class, the rank in which he had been embarked at the Isle of France [Mauritius].
Citizen Bougainville, who had done no more duty than he since the same time, kept his, but I hope that my observations to the Minister of Marine will make known to him how little fitted he is to make a good officer, and still less to serve in that capacity.
The night of the first to the second was much finer than the course of the barometer had led us to expect. I was all the more delighted as the rest of the crew, who truly needed it, was not interrupted. The winds varied from north to north-west and even to west, but the breeze was moderate and without gusts, which I believe is not usual in these waters at this season.
1802-05-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to south. At daybreak the land was sighted; at noon it bore from us N 29° W to S 51° W, being in 34° 56' 40" of latitude observed and in 149° 9' 30" of longitude by account.

1802-05-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to S by E. At 12.15 went onto the starboard tack. At 10 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-05-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, little Tasman Island bore north 55° east
Cape Pillar north 40° east
Cape Batral (Balsah, Baltra?) north 33° west
Fluted Cape south 76° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, from five o'clock in the morning, the weather being very fine and the winds at west, variable towards north, we made ready to get under sail. We began by stowing our second bower anchor, which as a precaution had been kept clear for letting go in case of need. This work finished, we weighed the one that was on the bottom and got under way, which did not happen until about seven o'clock, although we had set about it early enough to have been ready before that time.
During the morning we had a pleasant breeze and fine weather. It continued so in the afternoon, so that by nightfall we had doubled Cape Pillar and had a clear sight of the Hippolyte Rocks, as well as of Cape Frederick Hendrick and Maria Island. But as the winds began to fall calm, we had all the more reason to fear having them from the north, since we were beginning to have a fairly heavy swell from that point of the horizon, which, moreover, was very clear and wide.
During the night we were not mistaken in our expectation, for the winds were constantly at north-west, varying at times towards north. We tried in vain to close with the land so as to begin the next day the geographical work on this part of the coast. We could not manage it, although we hauled our wind as close as we possibly could.
Had I not been very unwell and obliged to keep to my cabin when we ran along this coast in every direction trying to find our boat again, this work would not have remained to be done, and despite the unhappy event that had just befallen us, I should have taken advantage of it for bearings which perhaps we shall not be able to take from so close, if the wind does not favour us as much in the present circumstance as it did then.
During the night the sky was tolerably fine and the sea, though swelling, troubled us little.
1802-05-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a pleasant breeze from SSE to E. At noon in 35° 25' 4" of latitude by account and in 149° 12' 6" of longitude by account.

1802-05-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from SE. The sea smooth. At 6 p.m. went onto the starboard tack; at 6 a.m. onto the port tack.
1802-05-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the afternoon
Cape Pillar bore east 23° north,
and Cape Frederick Hendrick east 69° 44' 5 north
At noon,
the middle of Maria Island south 89° west,
Cap Pelé south 87° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, in the morning, the sky, though very cloudy and overcast, was fairly fine. The lands seen the day before bore from us at daybreak on the points of the compass given below, or rather they extended from north 76° 15' west to south 62° west. We were too far off to give each of them, with any certainty, the various names indicated in the log.
As the winds were still from the north towards the west, we continued on the easterly tack, heading a little to the north, hauling our wind as close as possible. The sky having cleared during the morning, we had the sun at noon and the latitude was observed to be 42° 43' 0". The longitude by the timekeeper put us, at the moment of the observation, in 146° 17' 6".
The heavy northerly swell having gone down a great deal, we hoped soon to have the winds from another quarter of the horizon.
Throughout the evening, however, they remained the same and varied very little. But during the night they shifted they began to become very variable, though still from the north, veering towards the west. Only their strength was diminishing gradually.
I was informed during the day by the physician that several of our sick were worse than usual, although the weather was mild and not very damp. I was all the more surprised at it as it had seemed to me that the circumstances ought to hasten their cure rather than increase their illness. Following the warning I had just received, I sought to learn the cause, and I succeeded in discovering the reason, which is that, like gluttons, they had eaten so much fish that most of them had given themselves indigestion. Those who had not been attacked by dysentery before got off with suffering a little from the stomach pains they had. But those who had already had it and were not cured of it were attacked by it again, and it is very doubtful whether they will recover.
My cook, without being in the latter case, but who had been ill for three months and consequently on a diet, indulged himself so freely that he had an attack of indigestion which ended his career on the very day of our departure.
1802-05-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a pleasant breeze from ESE to south. At noon in 35° 32' 58" of latitude by account and in 149° 23' 0" of longitude by account. At 8 the wind freshened by degrees.

1802-05-24.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, the sea smooth enough, a fresh breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. The wind freshened steadily and blew hard, with a high sea. At midnight took all the reefs in the main topsail; the fore topsail split while we were taking in the reefs. During the night the port cathead was carried away by a sea. The fore topsail was repaired and the port cathead was made good.
1802-05-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
The southernmost point in sight of Van Diemen's Land south 21° west
Cap Pelé south 38° 30' west
The northernmost land in sight north 37° 30' west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, towards the end of the night of the third, the winds having gone round to the south-west, we steered north until daybreak. At that time we had a good sight of the land, but at too great a distance to establish the true position of the ship, which, according to the dead reckoning of the distance run, should have been abreast of Schouten Island or a little north of it.
To settle the question we steered west, edging a little to the north, thinking that I should recognise the coast perfectly as we drew nearer to it, and above all when we were only a short distance from it. As the sky was very overcast there was little likelihood of having the sun's passage over the meridian at noon, and indeed we did not have it. Everyone, however, and the scientists above all, claimed to recognise quite well the cape I had named Cap Pelé, and I was the only one who recognised neither that cape nor the appearance of the neighbouring lands lying to the north and south of it. This surprised me all the more as I believed, and still believe, that I have a memory quite as good as theirs, without having their wit.
Be that as it may, I steered for a high land which seemed to me to be the cape I was looking for, but after approaching it I went about to stand to the south, being fully convinced that it was not. It would have been easy to begin the bearings at the spot where I was and in that way to take advantage of the wind, which was very favourable to us, but I preferred to come and identify the cape I had seen the first time, which by its position proves the non-existence of the islands shown by Captain Furneaux, rather than leave it behind.
This mistake on my part pleased more than one person on board, and did no little to persuade each of them that they were more capable of handling the ship than I.
As I had entirely forgotten that I was in my bed, ill, at the time when we were on this part of the coast, I no longer found it hard to understand why I did not recognise lands I had never seen.
During the evening the breeze fell away a great deal and became variable. We made two boards until nightfall, which met with little success, and we gained little to windward, finding that I had passed Cap Pelé, which I hope to reach during the night, so as to begin at daybreak taking bearings of the whole of this coast as far as the entrance of Banks Strait.
During the night the winds were entirely calm and the ship lay for several hours on end without steerage way; at least we were at most three leagues off.
1802-05-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind blowing hard from S to SSW. At midnight, the fore topsail having been split while reefing it, we lay to. The port cathead was carried away by a sea. At 6, the wind having fallen, we filled and stood on. The cathead and the fore topsail were repaired. At noon in 36° 8' 40" of latitude by account and in 150° 9' 54" of longitude by account.

1802-05-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. A high sea. Continual rain. At 6 wore onto the port tack; at 9.45 wore onto the starboard tack; at 11 set the mizzen topsail.
1802-05-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
(end of page 175) from us, I had not been able to receive it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 42° 9' 4" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us in 145° 21' 44".
In the evening we continued to steer south, and at three o'clock in the afternoon, having finished our work south of Schouten Island, we came close-hauled on the larboard tack to work up to the east and north as far as possible.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, in the morning, the calm we had had during the night continued until about seven o'clock. But then a light breeze sprang up from the north-west which, having gone round by degrees to the north, gained a little strength as the sun rose above the horizon. We took advantage of it to close with the coast, which we approached to within a league, and from then on began our geographical work, running from north to south.
According to our bearings of the day before and the observations taken ashore, the current had carried us two leagues north beyond our reckoning. As I was ill at the time when we ran along this coast for the first time, I saw not without astonishment that not even its most remarkable points had been fixed, and that no more account had been taken of it than if we had been far out to sea. And yet they boasted of having passed much closer to it than I did, and even without precaution, since they did (not) even take the trouble to have soundings made.
Be that as it may, having very favourable winds for going south, I took advantage of them and had Citizen Ronsard and the astronomer Bernier do all the work on this part, which extended as far as the southernmost point of Schouten Island and of the rocks and islets belonging to it.
I find it hard to understand how Captain Furneaux could have placed on the outline of this coast the three fairly large islands mentioned on his chart. Unless he meant some large rocks lying close in to the shore, to which the name of islands, however small one may suppose them, cannot apply. From what he says, that they are low lands, I am therefore justified in believing that he saw this coast only from afar, and even from very far. For assuredly it is high, and very high. I am therefore all the less surprised that he saw islands in the latitude he gives, as it is precisely one of the highest parts of the coast, so that he took for islands the summits of mountains whose low lands joining them to one another he could not see.
We, who this last time have run along the whole of this coast from latitude 42° 8' to 42° 30', were at first deceived as he was, but the error was only momentary, for we made quite sure that what appeared to be islands were nothing other than mountains separated from one another by low lands which then form bays of greater or lesser depth.
Between Schouten Island and the mainland there is a channel which appears navigable and may offer, in case of need, some places of refuge. But neither the weather nor the season was suitable for venturing into it, which moreover prevented me from examining it. The longboat, which during our stay at Maria Island was sent there expressly with the hydrographer Faure, will no doubt make known the resources it may offer to navigators. According to the verbal report he made to me, he did not, any more than we, come across the islands placed on Captain Furneaux's chart. But he did find a deep inlet running a considerable way to the north. As his plan was not finished at the moment when the Naturaliste parted company (see end of preceding page)
1802-05-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 36° 9' 16" of latitude by account and in 149° 29' 48" of longitude by account.

1802-05-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW. Shook out the reefs of the topsails. At 10 a light breeze got up from N by E; rigged out the studdingsails to starboard.
1802-05-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the sixth, in the morning, having worked a little to the east during the night, we sought to close with the coast by going about, in order to continue our bearings; but as the winds still held in the quarter from north round to west, with an overcast sky and squally weather, this day was entirely lost. We did indeed sight the coast, but we found ourselves too far off to be able to make out which part of it we were on; all the more so as at noon we had no observation of the sun's passage across the meridian.
In the course of the morning, one of the helmsmen, who had been suspected of stealing fish-hooks, took such offence at the suspicion that he raised a devilish uproar. I could not manage to silence him, despite the repeated orders I gave him to that effect, and as soon as I had gone back into my cabin he would start again. Wearied by all this din, I gave orders that he be given twelve strokes with a rope's end, and this was about to be carried out when, to escape it, he threw himself into the sea. Although the weather was none too manageable, we at once laid all our sails aback and put the small boat out. As he was a very good swimmer, it was not difficult to pick him up. My intention was to have him given twenty lashes when he came aboard, but the surgeons having found him unfit to receive them, the matter was put off.
In the evening we continued to stand in towards the land, which was very hazy, and at six o'clock, reckoning ourselves no more than three leagues from it, we went about and stood out to sea under little sail, so as not to draw too far away from it, the winds being still variable from west to north and the sea high and swelling. During the night the wind was light, which mattered little to us, provided we had it fair on the morrow.
1802-05-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. At noon in 36° 40' 29" of latitude observed and in 150° 3' 54" of longitude by account. The wind a light breeze from N to WNW. The topmast studdingsail booms were rigged in.

1802-05-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, a light breeze from NW, from south to SW.
1802-05-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the seventh, the winds being the same as the day before, or very nearly so, we gave up hope of closing with the coast in such a way as to examine it properly for the continuation of the geographical work that still remained for us to do.
As the weather was still squally, with a very threatening look, and we sometimes had very strong gusts, we held on upon the northern tack so as to get far enough far enough (sic) up in that direction to range along the land on returning south, the winds showing no sign of changing as soon as we should have wished. We had no observation at noon for the latitude, but we did not fail to perceive that the currents had carried us to the east beyond our dead reckoning, since we had no sight of the land although our horizon was at times very extensive.
In the course of the morning, someone, though I do not know who, having reproached the surgeon Laridon with being the reason why I kept the sea so long, in that he did not inform me of the condition of our sick nor of their number, he brought me a long list on the subject, of which I certainly had no need, knowing the number as well as he did. Had it been in my power to lessen the ills they suffered, I should no doubt have done so; but being unable to bring myself to abandon a coast whose bearings had been neglected while we were searching for our boat, and which had at that time been run over in every direction, I invited him to tell those who had put him forward to make representations to me that our stay at sea was the consequence of their own negligence, and that they had only themselves to blame if it came to pass.
I do not know whether the surgeon carried out his errand, but I none the less continued to beat about until it should please the winds to become favourable to us. Besides, so little remained to be done that we needed only one or two days of fine, fair weather to finish this work. It is true, however, that these two circumstances seem rare in this season.
During the night the winds were the same, and nothing gave notice of an early change.
1802-05-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to SSW. At noon in 37° 37' 80" of latitude observed and in 150° 2' 0" of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze in gusts. At 11.30 the wind was blowing in heavy gusts; I had the watch and woke the captain to ask leave to take the second reef in the topsails, which I had just lowered to half mast. He refused at first, telling me it was not blowing (he was in his bed, well covered, the curtains drawn). I then proposed shaking out the reef; and he told me to take the second reef.

1802-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. The wind having freshened, we took all the reefs in the topsails. At 4 a.m. the weather cleared; at 10 overcast weather, a fresh breeze in gusts.
1802-05-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth, the winds shifted to the south-west, and our position was none the better for it. During the morning they came in gusts and squalls so strong that they obliged us to furl our mainsail and keep every reef in our topsails.
As everyone knew that my intention was to put in at Port Jackson, although I had communicated it to no one, the officers, like the naturalists and scientists, were vexed that I did not take advantage of the fair wind then blowing to shape a course for it. This was a matter of near indifference to me, since I had made up my mind and wished to wait some time longer before abandoning this coast, rather than return to it a third time.
Throughout the day we stood on the inshore tack, and we had no sight of the land at sunset, although the view was then very extensive.
By an observation we had at noon, though somewhat doubtful, we found ourselves north of the 41st degree, which decided me to take the southern tack; this I held all night, which was fine and even pleasant for the season we were in. But the sea, which was swelling and high, tired us considerably.
From the distance we had run during the day in trying to close with the land, which our dead reckoning placed much nearer than we really were, I no longer doubted that the set of the currents was carrying us fairly briskly to the east. But as we had to get to the south, I was forced to shape that course and consequently to draw further away from the coast, since, by the direction of the wind, it trended to the east.
The weather, which had become very dry, made me fear on the other hand that we should meet with fresh setbacks if the winds happened to shift to the north when we were in the south, as had already occurred since we had begun the work on this part of the coast.
1802-05-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather with frequent squalls, the wind blowing hard from W to SSW. At midnight, in taking in reefs in the main topsail, it was torn from its bolt-rope; we unbent it at once. At noon in 39° 17' 15" of latitude observed and in 150° 43' 42" of longitude by account. The repaired main topsail was bent. At 8 p.m., when Citizen Freycinet went for the captain's orders, he charged him not to shorten sail, and not to do as I had done, who, being drunk the evening before, had asked leave to take in reefs.

1802-05-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from SW. At daybreak the port cathead was found carried away and was repaired at once. At 10 the wind a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea rather high.
1802-05-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the ninth, the winds being still south-west and varying little, we held on upon the southern tack. The state of the atmosphere, though tolerably fine, seemed to foretell an early change. The part of the horizon between south and east became heavy with clouds, and the south-westerly breeze grew very light. I expected from one moment to the next to have the winds from the south, but this hope was not fulfilled and the day passed in fruitless waiting.
At noon we had a good observation of latitude, and in the morning several hour angles had been taken. By the sun's passage across the meridian we found ourselves in 41° 15' 20" of latitude, and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 147° 11' 8". Not being far enough advanced to the south to change course, we continued on the south-south-east tack, but the wind was so light that we made very little way.
Two more men went into the sick bay that day, and our sailmaker was suddenly attacked by a flux which had every appearance of dysentery; the surgeons could not guess its cause.
Twenty men in the sick bay out of a total of 75, including the scientists and others, could not but considerably reduce the number of men available for working the ship. It was no longer possible for us, and had not been for a long while, either to go about or to wear round without calling all hands on deck, and this too was what forced me to make longer boards than they would have been in other circumstances.
After sunset, the wind having died away completely and the horizon to the south being very murky, I no longer doubted that the winds would come to us from that quarter during the night and would soon enable us to abandon this coast in search of the rest we all needed after nine months spent continuously at sea.
During the night of the 9th to the 10th the winds did not shift to the south, as I had expected from the state of the atmosphere in that quarter. They were extremely variable about the south-west and often calm, so that the ship would not answer her helm.
1802-05-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SW to SSW. At daybreak the port cathead was found carried away and was repaired. Fine weather, the wind falling by degrees. At noon in 40° 53' 36" of latitude observed and in 151° 54' 54" of longitude by account. At 6 a flat calm. At 3.45, 9° 51' 50" of NE variation.

1802-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a light breeze from SW to NW by way of west. At 6.30 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack.
1802-05-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, the winds, or rather the little freshness that made itself felt before daybreak, came to us from north to north-west. We took advantage of it to draw nearer the coast by steering west, and when the breeze freshened a little we steered south-west, with all sail set, to close with it; for I was most impatient to finish the geographical work on this coast, for fear of meeting with some gale that might drive me right away from it, in the season we were in.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 31° 41' 3" (sic). There was no hour angle. The weather, which was gloomy and heavy with vapours and at times rainy, held out no promise of fine days to come; but as the barometer stood at 28 inches two lines, I hoped that it might still clear up.
In the afternoon, the horizon having cleared, the winds shifted to the west, variable variable (sic) to the south-west, which obliged us to beat to windward once more in order to close with the land. The various boards we made during the evening advanced us but little, and we had no sight of the land before nightfall, which we spent, as we had the evening, beating to windward. The weather was fine, dry and even cold. For all that, our sick felt little relief from it and even complained more than ever.
As we had almost no fresh provisions left, and as, luckily for them, I had husbanded the little that had remained to me since my last indisposition, I had them given one of the three pigs I still had, which I had denied myself so that it might serve for anyone who fell ill. They were given enough of it for three meals, and the rest was salted to serve them later on.
Two more men went into the sick bay that day, complaining of severe pains without showing any apparent symptom of illness. Among them was the baker, who was most useful to those already unwell, so that the sick were suddenly deprived of the resource of fresh bread.
1802-05-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from NW to W. At noon in 41° 8' 11" of latitude observed and in 151° 33' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-05-31.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea [one word erased, illegible], a light breeze from NW to W and SW. At 6 p.m. went onto the port tack.
1802-05-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Observed latitude 41° 21' 7" south
By dead reckoning 41° 22' 43"
Estimated longitude 146° 19' east
Rhumb north 62° 49' west
Distance 37.2 miles
Observed variation 8° 6' NE.
C. Baudin.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, the weather remained fine, but the winds held constantly in the west-south-west quarter, which hardly suited us. We stood on the tack from north towards west to try to close with the land, of which we had as yet no sight, although we could not be very far from it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 41° 21' 33", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 146° 39' 30". But we had found that it was losing, so that we were in fact all the further from the coast.
In the afternoon the sky clouded over and became at times gloomy and even rainy. But, judging by the movement of the barometer, this seemed unlikely to last, which is why we sought to close with the coast.
During the night we found a very heavy swell from the south-east. The winds were then in the quarter from east to north-east, very variable and almost calm.
At noon, we had thought we could see the land in the west, and we should certainly have made it out clearly had the horizon been less hazy in that quarter.
In the evening, all hands were turned to clearing the ship for a general cleaning, and not before time, for this had been neglected since our departure from Adventure Bay. When it was done, the ship was fumigated throughout, as was the sick bay.
Most of them complained loudly that I meant to have them die at sea by making no attempt to put in at some place where they might find some relief. So much so that, without regard for the personal privations I imposed on myself in order to give them, in fresh meat, what I might have consumed myself, they looked upon me as the first cause of their illnesses for having kept the sea too long. The officers and the scientists murmured no less, and laid the blame, if not directly on me, at least on the surgeon, telling him at every turn that he was deceiving me about their condition and number, and about the likelihood that we should see them all die.
As I did not see things in the same light as all these gentlemen, I continued to keep the sea, rather than be obliged to return a fourth time to this (coast), which, through their fault, had not been surveyed at the time when, unhappily, I was ill, because they had not taken advantage of so favourable an opportunity as then presented itself, since it had been run over three times from north to south and from south to north.
1802-05-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to south. At 10.15, 12° 16' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 41° 54' 9" of latitude observed and in 151° 16' 36" of longitude by account. At 3.30, 10° 53' 40" of NE variation.

1802-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW to south and SW. At 6 and 9 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks &c.
On the twelfth, we had the winds north-east, a pleasant breeze, but a sky often hazy and rainy. However, when the squalls had passed, the weather was fair enough. We steered for the land with all sail set.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 41° 22' 53", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 145° 46' 9", proof that it had an error to the east, since we still had only a very uncertain sight of the land, owing to the state of the sky and of the horizon, which was not very extensive. However, at two o'clock in the afternoon, the sky having cleared, we saw it distinctly, though still very distant.
During the evening, although the weather was not of the most suitable and we often had squalls and rain, we came within a league and a half of it, or at most that distance, my intention being to spend the night beating to windward in that position so as to be able to continue the survey of the coast from the next day, returning south to reach the point where we had already begun. But during the night the weather became so bad that we had to we had to (sic) make sail to work a little way out to sea. The rain was so heavy and continuous that we were greatly inconvenienced by it. The sky was so black and so dark that, when we had to work the ship, we bumped into one another without seeing each other, and we often mistook one rope for another. Had we been absolutely short of water, it would without question have been a fine opportunity to collect some, and I am persuaded that in less than a quarter of an hour a cask could have been filled. This weather lasted the whole night without the least interruption, and as the barometer did not fall below 28 in. 5 in such foul weather, I remained persuaded that it would not last long and that (we) might have a change in our favour by the next day. During the night we steered south, making as much easting as possible whenever the winds allowed, so as not to find ourselves embayed on the coast should they not turn favourable for us the next day.
1802-06-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 41° 55' 27" of latitude observed and in 150° 44' 36" of longitude by account. At 3.15, 11° 57' 20" of NE variation; a flat calm. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the ENE and we shaped the course S 45° W.

1802-06-02.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SSW, almost calm. At 4 a flat calm. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the ENE; rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail. Shook out all the reefs.
1802-06-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, I was sorely disappointed in my expectation. The weather was infinitely worse than the day before and the rain quite as continuous and heavy. I had had soundings taken several times during the night without finding bottom at 78 and 65 fathoms, which led me to believe that I was at least three leagues from the coast, but that was the most it could be.
As the weather would not allow us to carry much sail, we were obliged successively to furl the mizzen topsail and the fore topsail and to take in every reef in the main topsail, which, with the state of the sea, did not fail to increase our leeway greatly and make our course a rather poor one. For I feared, if there were no change, that we should not be able to weather Schouten Island, and it was hardly possible to go on the other tack with north-easterly winds that were very variable, now towards the east, now towards the north, and never from east towards south.
By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves at noon in 41° 42' 5", and our longitude, likewise estimated, was 146° 15' 7", but very doubtful, given the weather we had had. During the morning we were not spared thunder and hail. I much regretted that our lightning conductors were not in place, but as our topgallant masts were unrigged, they were of no use to us for the moment. This storm lasted lasted (sic) from ten o'clock in the morning until noon, and as it hung for a long time very close to the ship, there was reason to fear that it might cause some damage to our masts, if indeed the consequences were not to be more serious for us.
During the evening the rain was less continuous; the winds held from east to east-north-east, in gusts and strong squalls. This, to my great regret, obliged us to stand constantly on the tack from south towards east, and kept me always in fear of not being able to weather Schouten Island, which juts out a little further to the east than the east coast of Van Diemen's Land.
During the night I carried as much sail as possible to hold my own against the leeway and not be driven onto the coast, which gave me no little anxiety, even though the course I had made before must have taken me some way off the coast. We sounded several times without finding bottom, and I believed myself out of danger.
1802-06-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind freshening by degrees to a strong breeze, a very high sea. At 11.30 the course was given S 33° 45' W. At noon in 42° 29' 9" of latitude by account and in 149° 36' 6" of longitude by account. The wind was from NE to E.

1802-06-03.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from NE to east and ESE. At 8 a.m. took in the studdingsails and lowered the main jib to half mast.
1802-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, at six o'clock in the morning, I again had the lead cast, reckoning myself by dead reckoning to be abreast of Schouten Island, or very nearly so. Having found no bottom at four o'clock at 70 and 80 fathoms, I did not expect to find it, and believed myself far enough out to have nothing more to fear from the bad weather, which still continued without the least sign of a change, so overcast was the horizon on every side. But, contrary to my expectation, we found bottom at 55 fathoms, rocks and large stones. This news was certainly not welcome to me, and yet I had to make little of it so as not to spread consternation through the ship. However, having the bell rung so that everyone should come on deck, I ordered that we wear round at once to go on the other tack. The few hands there were to work the ship made this evolution a long one, and it took more than half an hour. Luckily for us, the winds served us as well as we could wish on this occasion, in that they shifted to east-south-east and made the other tack a fairly good one, despite the leeway, which was three points, although we had set our mainsail to reduce it. As we knew this coast well enough to know that one must be very close to it to find 55 fathoms, I am persuaded that when we had worn we were no more than a league or a league and a quarter from it.
During the morning and all the rest of the day we pressed the ship with sail to try to work out to the east, since there was no longer any doubt that the weather we had had for three days was the beginning of a (gale), and that we must of necessity put ourselves in a position to ride it out without adding to our other fears the most disagreeable of all, which is that of being driven ashore.
At noon our estimated latitude placed us in 42° 21' 41", and according to our dead reckoning we might be four leagues from the coast.
In the evening there was no sign of any change in the weather. On the contrary, the squalls became stronger and more frequent than they had been. We did not shorten sail. Our masts, which we had put to the test more than once, did not, in truth, give us great anxiety. But what was most fortunate for us, despite the bad weather, was to see the winds haul round to the south-east and thereby enable us to stand out to sea so as to be free of fear.
During the night the weather was truly bad, and indeed the roughest we had yet had. The winds shifted to south-south-east without lessening in strength. The sea became extremely high and often troubled us. The thunder had ceased during the evening, and we did not hear it rumble during the night.
1802-06-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from ENE to SE. At noon in 44° 54' 39" of latitude by account and in 146° 14' 54" of longitude by account. At noon shaped the course S 45° W and at 3.30 S 56° 15' W. The 15th [Prairial, 4 June 1802]. Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSW. At 3 a.m. the course was given S 67° 30' W, and at noon S 78° 45' W. At noon in 45° 39' 52" of latitude observed, in 141° 43' 48" of longitude by account and 142° 40' 0" of longitude by the watches. At 3.30, 8° 13' 40" of NE variation. The wind falling away at the close of day.

1802-06-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze, a high sea. At 3.30 shaped our course S 56° 15' W. From SE to SSE.
1802-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, the weather was exactly the same as the day before, and if it was no worse as regards the wind, the gusts and the squalls, the sea at least was very high. A long, hollow, lofty swell seemed to threaten at every moment to engulf us, and I was continually afraid of seeing one of the seas come aboard when they broke against the ship's side. We got off with a fright that day, and lost only our lee bulwark, which was carried away by a sea that came in over the bow. The lashings of our anchors, which had been secured so as to leave nothing to fear in that quarter, were so shaken by it that they very nearly went over, which would have been all the more troublesome to us as the cables were bent to them. We had promptly to set about securing them again, and this with ten men from the two watches, who were all that remained in good health of the rest of the crew.
At noon the observed latitude estimated placed us in 41° 18' 27" and the longitude in 147° 33' 15". There was then no sign of any change in the weather, and the movement of the barometer did not indicate that one was near. We had taken the reefs in the courses to ease our masts. But in hauling down the tack of the foresail, it was torn. In its place we set the fore topsail and the fore staysail. The ship behaved very well under this canvas and the mainsail.
During the night the squalls and gusts were more frequent and even stronger than they had been during the day. But we had the good fortune to have nothing to change in the trim of our sails, for it would have been impossible to manage it, having only four men fit to stay on deck, including the officer of the watch. This decided me to run free and make for Port Jackson, being no longer in a state to keep the sea.
It is much against my will that I was obliged to give up completing the full survey of the east coast of Van Diemen's Land. But it is none the less true that the fault lies solely with the officers who, not knowing that one must not lose a moment at sea, neglected to do it while we were searching for our boat, on the pretext that Citizen Boulanger was engaged on it and that they did not wish to rival him in the matter. None of this would have happened if, at that unhappy time, I had not been very unwell, and we should be in a very different position from the one in which we now find ourselves.

1802-06-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running; the wind, at first a strong breeze, fell away as it hauled from south to SW. At noon the course was set S 78° 45' W.
1802-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, in the morning, we had some hope of a change in the weather. It was announced to us by the barometer, which seemed inclined to rise. It was still blowing a strong breeze, however, and in squalls; but as we were running free, the winds being south, they seemed less violent and more bearable to us.
As soon as it was light we set about changing the foresail, and with the few hands fit to work it was bent at about ten o'clock. A reef was taken in it and it was set. The sea was still high, the swell hollow and deep, but as the ship was making good way we had not much to fear.
During the morning we saw the sun at times, and at noon we were even able to observe the latitude by it, which proved to be 38° 41' 3", whereas that by dead reckoning placed us only in 39° 3' 51". It is true that the observed latitude was a little doubtful, but it cannot differ as much as that given by the dead reckoning of the course run.
In the afternoon the weather continued squally, with gusts, but less strong than usual. The sky also became cloudy and less overcast. We continued to steer north-north-east to weather the eastern point which terminates the land of New Holland and which the English have named Cape Kamhaw.
Towards evening the breeze moderated a good deal, although the squalls were still frequent. We had no doubt of a change in our favour, all the more as the winds were beginning to haul round into the quarter from south towards west.
During the night we weathered the point I have just mentioned and continued on the same course until midnight, when we steered north by east so as not to make too much easting.
The sea, though calmer, was still very high and agitated. And as we had the wind almost astern, the ship rolled a great deal. We consoled ourselves with the certainty we had that the weather would be finer and more manageable the next day. We all needed it, and above all the crew, to dry their clothes, which for six days had been had been (sic) soaked to the point of being of no further use to them.
1802-06-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to W. At 10.30, 9° 20' 10" of NE variation. At noon in 44° 53' 33" of latitude observed and in 140° 26' 54" of longitude by account. At 3 the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts during the night. I had the watch from 8 until midnight; and fearing to draw some rudeness from the captain, I kept the topsails hoisted throughout my watch, at the risk of seeing the topmasts come down at every pitch. The ship laboured a great deal and made 2 inches of water an hour, whereas at Port Jackson she made none. The captain, in spite of all he had been told at Sydney (Governor King said to him as he left, "I hope to see you back here within a month"), was determined to go looking for southerly winds to the south.

1802-06-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from W to SW. At 12.15 wore onto the starboard tack. At 8 blowing hard in gusts. A very high sea.
1802-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, we were not disappointed in our expectation. The weather was fine, though with light squalls and rain from time to time, but it was not heavy and did not last long. As soon as it was light we steered north-west to close with the land, which by my dead reckoning I placed twenty-five leagues off in the latitude where I then was. The sea was now only agitated by the after-effects of the wind that had prevailed, and the swell had gone down a good deal. We were able to shake a reef out of our topsails. And so as not to lose time, we kept those in the courses, for it would have taken the greater part of the day to get our lower yards back into place with the few hands I had; and even then I doubt that it would have been accomplished, at least to judge by the time it took to shake a reef out of the topsails and hoist them.
This day was employed solely in cleaning the inside of the ship, which the great number of sick I had had left in a sorry state.
Those who were well dried part of their clothes, and if the weather continues fine on the day following this one, they will be in a position to use them.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 36° 37' 43", but a little doubtful, in that at the moment of the sun's passage across the meridian a squall hid it from our view. Working from this latitude, an hour angle taken in the evening gave the longitude by the timekeeper as 150° 29' 30". But, according to our later observations, we must be about one degree further east.
During the evening the weather continued fine, still accompanied by a few squalls of little consequence. We held the north-westerly course until eight o'clock, when we steered north for the night.
During the night of the 17th to the 18th we continued to steer north so as to get quickly up to the latitude of Port Jackson, where I expected to find the winds more manageable and less attended by squalls than those we had had for several days.
1802-06-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from SSW to WNW. At 4.15, in wearing ship, the foresail was torn from its bolt-rope. We lay to and bent another foresail. The wind fell and was a fresh breeze at 10; filled and stood on. At noon in 46° 9' 23" of latitude observed and in 140° 12' 48" of longitude by account. In the evening the captain gave orders to serve 6 ounces of boiled wheat for the crew's breakfast and as much for supper, and 6 ounces of beef or 4 ounces of salt pork with half a pound of bread for dinner. On the morning of the 18th at breakfast the crew would not eat the boiled wheat and gave it to the pigs; they asked that bread be made for them instead from the flour and bran, and the captain granted it.

1802-06-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to W and NW. At 8 went about onto the starboard tack. In the forenoon Mabulot, gunner, received 15 lashes with a rope's end for striking the second gunner's mate. On the evening of the 17th the rations were reduced as is known. For breakfast 6 ounces of boiled wheat were served, and for dinner half a pound of bread, 6 ounces of beef and four ounces of salt pork. This measure did not take effect until the morning of the 18th.
1802-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, at daybreak, we left the northerly course to steer more to the west, in order to see the land, of which I flattered myself we should have a good sight before nightfall. The weather, which was fair enough in the morning, with a tolerably clear sky, changed all (of a sudden). The rain, the squalls and the gusts began again worse than ever. Nevertheless we continued to stand in towards the land until five o'clock, when, the weather having every appearance of turning very bad for the night, I changed my mind and stood a little out to sea.
At noon, in a clear spell, we were able to observe the sun's altitude, which proved to place us in 34° 21' 40", so that we had only about ten leagues more to make to the north to be in that of Port Jackson.
A little before sunset the wind became so violent and the squalls so frequent that we were obliged to furl the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail, as well as our mainsail. We also took the third reef in the main topsail.
I was sorry, given the threatening look of the sky, to have stood in so far towards the land during the day, in that it would become very difficult to claw off the coast if the wind continued. Although we were heading north-east, the leeway was so great that, even though the variation was in our favour, our course made good was barely north.
Nevertheless, as at nightfall there was no sight of land, with a horizon estimated at four leagues' range, I believed myself perfectly safe. The barometer, which moreover had not fallen during the day, led me to think that this gale would not last.
During the night of the 18th to the 19th the weather was downright bad and the squalls and gusts very violent. We could hardly have carried our mainsail, even with all (the) reefs in, had we been in a position to use it. In a short time the sea became as high as in the gale we had weathered two days before this fresh blow.
The man Racine, master of the hold, died in the night of the scurvy from which he had long been (suffering). I greatly fear that I shall lose many more of those attacked by this cruel disease in its third stage, if the weather does not change soon.
1802-06-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to N. At 10, 9° 20' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 46° 25' 34" of latitude observed and in 138° 56' 12" of longitude by account. At nightfall the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts. A very high sea; the pitching very hard, and because of the sea and the canvas carried it strained the ship extremely.

1802-06-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea and the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NNW. The wind freshened steadily; by midnight it was blowing hard. The fore staysail halliard parted and the main topsail split.
1802-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, the weather was even less fine than the day before. Squalls, gusts and a strong wind prevailed all day without the least interruption. The sea, which had become very high, caused us so much leeway that, had we been near the coast, it would have been difficult for us to get clear of it; all the more so as neither tack was any good, the winds being east-south-east, variable to east.
All day long we were surrounded by Cape petrels, albatrosses and other birds of ill omen. But as I reckoned myself at least fifteen leagues from the coast, I was free of anxiety. Moreover, as the barometer was falling but little, I hoped that from one moment to the next this gale would cease.
At noon the estimated latitude placed us in 33° 41' 34", and from the last observation of longitude ours was 150° 26' 48". But we set little store by it, knowing that the timekeeper was nearly a degree and a half behind.
During the evening, and especially towards the end of the day, the weather seemed inclined to change and clear up. At several points of the horizon the sky was clear and the view extended tolerably far. We had (no) sight of land at sunset.
The hope of seeing the weather clear up was short-lived. At about seven in the evening the misty squalls, sometimes rainy, and the gusts began again worse than ever and lasted the greater part of the night. At eight o'clock we took the north-north-east tack, with easterly winds which, having veered to east-south, allowed us to head north and even a little to windward.
During this day our sick, and above all those with scurvy, were worse than usual and their pains sharper. And yet the weather (was) less damp than before. Was it the approach of the coast, or the portent of some coming gales, that caused them this greater distress? That is what the surgeons could not decide, and still less understand.
1802-06-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from N to WSW, a high sea. At 4.15 the fore staysail halliard parted and the sail was split; we unbent it. At 10 the main topsail split and was repaired. At noon in 46° 51' 10" of latitude by account and in 135° 29' 10" of longitude by account. In a gust the mainsail tack parted, and for all the speed with which it was clewed up the sail was split and had to be unbent. At 1 the captain assembled the officers to have their opinion on what remained to be done in the situation we were in. There were only 37 days' provisions left aboard, and could we hope, on half rations, to be at Mauritius within 74 days? It was decided to put back to Port Jackson. Accordingly at 2.15 we bore away N 67° 30' E, and at 4, N 56° 15' E. At 6 the weather cleared and the wind fell.

1802-06-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea, from W to WSW and WNW. In the gusts the [one word illegible] of the mainsail parted, and for all the speed with which it was clewed up, the sail was torn from its bolt-rope; we unbent it at once. At 1 the captain held a council on what remained for us to do in the situation we were in: there were only 37 days' provisions left on board, and could we hope to reach Mauritius in 74 days on half rations? It was decided to put back to Port Jackson. After taking the second reef in the main topsail we wore onto the starboard tack and headed N 67° 30' E.
1802-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, the weather, without being finer than on the preceding days, was nevertheless more pleasant and less foul. The winds having shifted to the south-east, the squalls were less frequent and the sky clearer. Although it was blowing a very strong breeze, I had the fore topsail and the mizzen topsail set, steering south-west to close with the land, so that we might find shelter for the winter at the first opportunity that offered.
Throughout the morning it blew hard, but as we were running with the wind free, the gusts seemed less heavy than those we had borne on the preceding days, although they appeared to me much the same, with only this difference, that the sky was infinitely finer. The barometer, which had been falling steadily since the middle of the night, seemed to warn us that the sky would not stay fine for long, and even to be on our guard, since it stood at no more than 28 inches one line, from 28' 4, the height at which it had held in the worst of this last gale.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 49' 47", which placed us roughly in the latitude of Port Jackson, and the timekeeper gave for longitude 149° 33' 12". This result, with the westerly error we attribute to it from our earlier observations, placed us about 25 leagues from the coast.
Throughout the evening we steered west a few degrees south and made good way. The sky was tolerably fine when the squalls had passed, but the sea was singularly agitated and nasty.
During the night of the 20th to the 21st the winds were favourable to us and the sea easy. The gusts, though strong, were less rough than they had been during the day, and the weather seemed likely to be finer the next day.
During the night we held the course from east towards south, so as not to be carried too far north, either by the current or by the leeway that the state of the sea caused the ship.
1802-06-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from WSW to NW. At noon in 45° 55' 28" of latitude by account and in 138° 30' 54" of longitude by account. The mainsail and the fore staysail were bent.

1802-06-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a light breeze from WSW and south. A new mainsail was bent.
1802-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, the hope we had had during the night of seeing the weather clear up soon vanished. At daybreak the sky clouded over once more with dark, thick clouds. The gales and the rain squalls resumed, lasted the greater part of the morning and prevented us from making sail.
Our sick were greatly distressed that day, and two more went into the sick bay, attacked by scurvy. So that our strength for working the ship was diminishing to such a degree that we could no longer do anything without being obliged to call both watches on deck, which did not fail to tire out exceedingly those who still had some strength left.
At noon we had no observed latitude, and that by dead reckoning placed us in 33° 55' 28", so that we needed only one day of fine weather and a fair wind to reach port.
In the afternoon, the weather having cleared a little, we sighted the land. It bore from west-south-west to north-west by north, if indeed it was the land, for we had no firm certainty of it, and it might very well be that what we took for land was nothing but a bank of fog.
Although the weather was gloomy and damp, and the breeze more moderate, the squalls were none the
less frequent and the sea still driven by a heavy swell running from south to south-south-west
The night of the twenty-first to the 22nd passed without incident, except that the squalls became less frequent, with winds from the south variable towards the west. The sky was even fairly clear at times, and we reckoned at last on soon seeing the bad weather end, although the barometer was slow in rising above 28 inches.
We made only two boards in the 24 hours, the weakness of the crew not allowing us to multiply them too much, so as to leave them a few more moments for the rest they so badly needed.
1802-06-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the breeze light from SW to E. At noon in 44° 38' 14" of latitude observed and in 139° 14' of longitude by the watches. At 3.45, 8° 40' 50" of NE variation.

1802-06-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, light rain, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to east and NE. At 8.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.
1802-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 3 h 15' the part of the land that could be made out in the haze bore from W. SW to NW ¼ north.
At noon, the land in sight extended from SW to north-west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, the weather was not as fine as it had looked like becoming on the twenty-first. Nevertheless we held on upon the western tack to come and make the land, our estimated latitude placing us in that of Port Jackson. At daybreak the weather was calm, with light squalls, but it became misty and the horizon limited.
At half past seven we had a good sight of the land and closed with it to about two leagues. The appearance of the shore, on which the sea was breaking heavily, made me realise that we were probably north of the latitude of the port, and this fear was only too well confirmed by the observation of the sun's passage across the meridian, for our latitude proved to be 33° 26' 49", whereas that by our dead reckoning was 34° 0' 4". Some time before the observation we had taken the south-east tack, so as not to have the sun over the land and so be more certain of our true position.
After the observation of the sun at noon we continued to steer south-east, in a very strong breeze from south by west to south-south-west. But we could not make more sail, the wind being too strong and the sea too rough (in another hand: ?). Our learned officers, however, found the breeze pleasant and the sea fine. I think that had they been the masters they would have carried the topgallant sails, to make their skill match the lofty idea they have of their own knowledge. As for me, who went only by mine (in the margin: wondering that he could not gain to windward), I kept the reefs in the courses and all those in the topsails, not even wishing the mainsail to be set, which it would not have been possible to furl by day, and still less by night, had the gales of the past days returned.
In the afternoon we truly had the appearance of seeing the weather clear up. Although there was little variation in the wind, this hope was not confirmed by the barometer, which still stood as it had in the gusts. However, the night having been very fine and the sky clear, everything seemed to tell us that we had come to the end of the bad weather.
1802-06-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather. A breeze from NNE to ESE, and calm. At noon in 44° 43' 44" of latitude by account and in 139° 37' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-06-12.journal_anonyme: The weather, overcast at first, cleared; the sea smooth. A light breeze from ESE to SE.
1802-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five h 15', in a clear spell, the land was seen to the W.S.W.
At noon, it extended from SW ¼ W to NW ¼ N
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, having gone about at midnight, we continued to steer west, with moderate south-south-west winds and a fine sky. We did not see the land at the beginning of the day, but when the sun had dispersed the fog that hid it from us, a great stretch of coast from west-south-west to north-north-west came into view as we approached it. In the course of the morning we recognised our points of the day before, and to all appearances we had gained little to the south, although the dead reckoning told us the contrary.
Throughout the morning the sky was very fine and the breeze moderate, but the winds held constantly south-south-west, dead against the course we had to make to reach the latitude of Port Jackson, for which everyone was longing.
At noon we observed the sun's altitude as 33° 25' 7", and it was not without regret or astonishment that we found ourselves as little advanced as the day before. We had just lost a whole day for nothing, whereas we had not an hour to spare if we were to satisfy everyone and relieve our sick.
The lands north of Port Jackson are very high and can be seen from a great distance in fine, clear weather. The greatest heights do not end in an abrupt, steep slope at the water's edge, as in several other parts of the coast of New Holland. On the contrary, they have land of moderate height along the shore, and the mountains appear to lie a good way inland. To the north of, or at least at a short distance from, Broken Bay, three mountains are to be seen, the most distant of which towers over all the others when they close with one another. This indication alone will show navigators who, like us, may go several days without being able to observe the latitude, that they are north of the port and must work to the south if they seek to put in there.
In the afternoon, the weather being quite fine, we swayed up our lower yards and shook the reefs out of the principal sails. We resumed the course from south towards east, the winds having shifted to the south-west.
During the night the weather remained fine and the sky constantly clear. We steered south as far as the wind allowed, to try to regain the latitude of Port Jackson, from which the winds, the leeway and the currents had carried us away.
1802-06-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to ENE. At 10, 7° 12' 40" of NE variation. At noon in 44° 27' 34" of latitude observed and in 139° 50' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-06-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east. At 5.45 went onto the port tack. At 8.30 a.m. onto the starboard tack.
1802-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the northern extremity of the land in sight bore north 66° west,
the southern extremity south 61° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, at daybreak, after the finest weather in the world during the night of the twenty-third, the atmosphere changed all of a sudden; the sky turned rainy and squally and the winds gusty, so that we were obliged to take a second reef in our topsails. The sea, though still smooth, was driven by a heavy swell from the south, which warned us that we should soon have the winds from that quarter. But as, according to the dead reckoning of the distance run in the twenty-four hours of the day before, I found myself a fair way south of Port Jackson, it was of little consequence to me that they should blow from that direction.
At eight o'clock we took the tack from west towards north to close with the land, of which I flattered myself we should have sight before nightfall. At about ten o'clock the sky, which since morning had taken on so threatening a look, turned (fine) as quickly as it had suddenly changed a few hours before, but it continued to blow a strong breeze.
At noon we observed the latitude as 34° 4' 46", which placed us nowhere near as far south as the dead reckoning of the course we had made. This circumstance, together with previous remarks, leads me to believe that in this season there exists on this coast a rapid current which seems to set towards the north-east.
During the afternoon the weather continued fine. We held the tack from west towards north, the winds being very variable from south-west to south-south-west. Towards evening they moderated somewhat, and we were able to shake out the reef taken in the topsails in the morning. Although we had made a fair distance from eight in the morning until sunset, we had no sight of land; yet it could not have been very far off.
The weather was so fine at sunset that we continued the westerly course without shortening sail, and at ten o'clock we had a perfect sight of it, finding ourselves, according to our reckoning, about three leagues from it. The winds, which then shifted to west-south-west, obliged us to head south, which pleased me very well for the moment, being quite persuaded, from the course we had just made, that we must once again be north of Port Jackson
1802-06-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ENE to SE. At noon in 44° 47' 10" of latitude observed and in 140° 1' 0" of longitude by the watches.

1802-06-14.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SE. At 8.30 p.m. and at 2 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the weather was very fine, but the winds almost always contrary to the direct course we should have had to make to reach Port Jackson. So many setbacks, in constant opposition to the wish we all had to arrive quickly, put everyone out of humour, and the often boisterous gaiety that usually prevailed gave way to an excess of gloom, which was not pleasant for those who know how to bear their troubles patiently and accept events as they come.
As we had sighted the land during the night, we went about at daybreak to close with the coast, from which we found ourselves seven or eight leagues distant at sunrise.
The lands we had in sight during the morning are generally high, and at that distance the mountains offer few recognisable landmarks. Nevertheless we clearly recognised that these lands were new to us and bore no resemblance to those we had seen further north.
At noon the latitude (was) observed to be 33° 48' 22", which still placed us north of Port Jackson, although the dead reckoning of the courses run placed us south of it. Until noon there had been a light breeze from south-west to south-south-west, and sometimes from south-west to west-south-west. But a calm having succeeded it, the ship would no longer answer her helm and we lay broadside to the sea for the rest of the evening and even the greater part of the night, although the sky was very cloudy and the whole of the horizon from south-east to south-west very overcast.
During the night we sounded twice. At midnight we had bottom at 75 fathoms and at two o'clock at 70, proof that the current and the the (sic) sea were carrying us towards the land, since the depth was decreasing.
At three o'clock a squall, or rather a violent thunderstorm, gave us a quantity of rain, very large hail, lightning so dazzling that we could not see, and thunder to our heart's content. This storm lasted an hour and a half without ceasing; it was more intolerable for the rain and hail than for the wind, which nevertheless gave strong enough gusts to oblige us to lower our topsails right down. As it went almost the whole way round the horizon, it obliged us to make various manoeuvres, always slow in such circumstances and far from pleasant when one lacks the hands to carry them out. The worst of the squall having passed, we took the reefs in the topsails, the sky having a very threatening look.
1802-06-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to NE, with rain. At noon in 44° 18' 9" of latitude observed and in 140° 37' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-06-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from east to SE. In the forenoon it freshened and blew in gusts.
1802-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 4 hours 45" (sic),
the land extended from north 17° west to south 59° west.
At noon,
