Broken Bay bore north 20° west
The north point of Botany Bay south 65° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, after the storm we had experienced towards the end of the night had passed, the thunder continued to be heard in the distance, but the whole of the horizon lying between south and north-west by way of west became clear and promised us fine weather for the day. And so indeed it proved, but the winds were so light, so inconstant and so variable that, whenever they had strength enough to make the ship move, the sails had to be worked continually to shift them from one side to the other.
From the survey we made of the land at daybreak, we could easily perceive that, if we had not lost ground to the north-east, we had at least gained very little of it to the south-west, which was confirmed by the observation of the sun at noon, which gave us a difference of only 0' from that of this day, which proved to be 33° 45' 53". At that time our distance from the coast was six to seven leagues, and it was not without regret that we saw ourselves so near the port without being able to enter it.
During the evening the calm continued until half past seven. Various quarters of the horizon became laden with dark, stormy clouds. Thunder was heard in the distance and at eight o'clock one of these storms broke upon us. It was much less violent than the one we had received the day before and lasted only half an hour. As it came to us from the south-west, a second reef was taken in the topsails and we went about to stand out to sea, so that it should not throw us too far towards the land, from which we were three leagues distant (in another hand: ?) and in 75 fathoms of water, hard bottom.
During the night the sky cleared again and the storms disappeared. The thunder was often heard rumbling, but in the direction of the coast, and although what little breeze there was blew from between south-west and west-south-west, the storms dispersed without reaching us. The various tacks which the changeable winds obliged us to make served only to carry us away from the land, which not only did we no longer see during the night, although the horizon was fine, but also from soundings, for we found no bottom at a hundred fathoms.
1802-06-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 43° 31' 52" of latitude observed and in 142° 22' 6" of longitude by account.

1802-06-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At 6 p.m. and at 6 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the winds shifted to the south-west, somewhat variable towards the west, and there was a good breeze throughout the morning, which we spent beating to windward.
It was not without astonishment that, when the day was far enough advanced to make out the land, we saw that the currents had carried us six to seven leagues to the north-east, which was all the more disagreeable to us since the winds had shifted to the south-west and we were obliged once more to run south-south-east to regain our latitude.
So many setbacks, and so unremitting, served only to deepen the gloom that reigned on board, and everyone, not bearing his ills with patience, was preparing fresh torments for himself through vexation at not being able to be set ashore as he wished.
At noon the observed latitude was 33° 30' 42", which confirmed the Remarks made on sighting the land in the morning. Until then we had been standing in on the landward tack, which brought us almost to the entrance of Broken Bay (the two words Broken Bay written in another hand)
After the observation of the sun, we took the offshore tack to stand south again, and I resolved to hold it as long as possible so as to see, since there was no sign of any change in the wind, whether I should be more fortunate in closing with the coast afterwards from the south.
During the evening and part of the night the breeze was light. Nevertheless we found the sea rough and even swelling. About seven o'clock we had a storm which brought us a little rain and little wind. It did not last long.
As soon as it had passed, the winds became variable from south-west to west-south-west, which made them favourable for the course we had to make to the south, but altogether contrary for closing with the coast. We had fine weather all night, and a fresh breeze.
1802-06-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 43° 47' 10" of latitude observed and in 142° 52' 24" of longitude by account. At 4 the land was sighted to the east.

1802-06-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SSE to south. At 4 sighted Van Diemen's Land in the east. At 4.45 p.m. and at 4.30 a.m. changed tacks.
1802-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the breeze, still variable from west-south-west to south-west, became so strong that we had to furl our mainsail and take a second reef in the topsails. While this was being done, we sighted a sail ahead of us. As soon as the reefs were taken in, we went about to meet her. As we drew nearer, we thought we recognised M. Flinders's ship, and she did indeed have the look of her. But when we were only a short distance off, I judged her, from the number of boats about her, to be a vessel newly out of port and going whaling.
As this vessel was on the opposite tack, we soon came together. She hoisted English colours and we answered with ours. When she passed under our stern, her master told me that he came from Port Jackson and was going whaling. I asked him for news of M. Flinders, who, he told me, had arrived in port. He also informed me that the Naturaliste had put in there. As he said he had something to tell me, and was about to lower his boat, we broke off the conversation until he should arrive.
1802-06-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to S, with light rain at intervals. At noon in 44° 2' 51" of latitude observed and in 142° 44' 0" of longitude by account.

1802-06-18.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SE. At 5 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same.
1802-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
[Day missing from the Soviche edition, transcribed by eye from the typescript copy in the BnF (SG MS4-33), view 501. The narrative of the manuscript breaks off on 28 Prairial; the copy notes: "The historical events and remarks cease at this point; however, the astronomical observations etc. continue as follows."]
From 28 to 29 Prairial (18 June 1802).
Course north 27° east. Distance in miles 44 3/10. South latitude by dead reckoning 33° 42' 45", observed 33° 31' 49". East longitude by No. 35, estimated 148° 28' 42". Hygrometer 87°. Barometer 27 inches 0 lines 11. Thermometer 10°.
1802-06-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 44° 12' of latitude observed and in 143° 32' of longitude by the watches. Saw several whales. At 3 the land was sighted from north to N 22° E, about 24 miles off. At 8 shaped the course SE.

1802-06-19.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a swell running, a light breeze from south, SW and SSE. At 3 Van Diemen's Land was sighted; it stretched from north to N 22° 30' E. At 4.15 p.m. and at 8.30 changed tacks.
1802-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
From 29 to 30 Prairial (19 June 1802).
Course south 35° east. Distance 40 miles. South latitude by dead reckoning 34° 4' 13", observed 33° 52' 33". East longitude by dead reckoning 148° 11' 6". Hygrometer 87°. Barometer 28 inches 1 line. Thermometer 11°.
1802-06-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to W. At 8 the course was given east; at 9.30, N 78° 45' E; and at noon, N 67° 30' E. At noon in 44° 41' 33" of latitude observed and in 144° 43' of longitude by account. At 6 the course was given N 45° E, and at midnight N 22° 30' E.

1802-06-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SW. At noon the course was set N 67° E. At 6.30 land was sighted in various quarters from N 67° 30' W as far as S 67° 30' W. At 8 it stretched from N 64° W to S 85° W. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island N 86° W.
1802-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
From 30 Prairial to 1 Messidor (20 June 1802).
Course south 43° west. Distance in miles 24 6/10. South latitude by dead reckoning 34° 11' 9", observed 33° 54' 53". East longitude by dead reckoning 147° 50' 54". Hygrometer 86°. Barometer 28 inches 3 lines. Thermometer 11°.
1802-06-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 6 the course was given north, and at noon N 11° 15' W. At 6.30 the land was sighted from N 68° W to S 68° W. At noon in 42° 51' 16" of latitude observed and in 146° 56' 24" of longitude by account, the middle of Maria Island bearing from us N 86° W. At 4 it bore S 65° W, and the high land of Schouten Island and Peninsula from S 80° W to N 77° W.

1802-06-21.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth. A fresh breeze from W to WNW. At noon the course was set N 11° 15' W. At 4 took the bearing of the middle of Maria Island S 65° W and the high land of the Schouten islands and peninsulas from S 80° W to N 77° W. At daybreak the land was sighted a long way off from the crosstrees; it stretched from N 34° W to S 22° W. At noon in sight in the west at a very great distance.
1802-06-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW to WSW. At daybreak the land was sighted as far as the eye could reach. At noon in 40° 32' of latitude observed and in 147° 11' 36" of longitude by account. The land in sight to the west as far as the eye could reach. At 3, 11° 4' 10" of NE variation. At 8 the wind freshened and blew hard in gusts.

1802-06-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from W to WSW and SW. At 8 p.m. it freshened and blew in gusts. At 6 a.m. the land in sight in the NW. At 8 it stretched as far as N 15° 15' E. The course was given north and then N 11° 15' E. At noon the land from N 15° W to S 44° W.
1802-06-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SW. At 6.30 the land was sighted in the N 45° W; at 8 it stretched as far as N 11° 15' E. The course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 37° 35' 40" of latitude observed and in 147° 38' 0" of longitude by account. The land from N 15° W to S 44° W, 5 miles off. The wind fell and was a fresh breeze. At 6.30 a fire was seen abeam.

1802-06-23.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW. At 4 the land from N 16° W to S 4° W. At 6.30 saw a fire abeam. At 8 a.m. the land from N 20° W to S 21° W. At noon took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 5° W, the Pigeon House S 86°, and the end of the land S 39° W. Almost calm. The corvette was painted.
1802-06-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WSW to S. At noon in 35° 24' 55" of latitude observed and in 148° 7' 6" of longitude by account. Long Nose Point bore from us N 5° W, the Pigeon House S 68° W, the southernmost end of the land in sight S 39° W. The corvette was painted. At 2 almost calm; the air varied from S to N by way of east, and at 4 settled in the north. It freshened from NNE to NNW. At 4 took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 6° W, the middle of the entrance to Jervis Bay N 18° W, the Pigeon House S 67° W.

1802-06-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3 a light air from the north drew round at once to the east and we wore onto the port tack. At 4 took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 6° W, the middle of Jervis Bay N 18° W, the Pigeon House S 67° W, the southernmost visible end of the land S 27° W. At 2 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack. The wind drew round to the north and freshened. At 9.15 a.m. sighted a ship abeam standing on the opposite tack. The cables were bent. Obs. lat. 34° 59' 27"; est. long. 148° 38' 42".
1802-06-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to N. At daybreak a ship was sighted in the NNW. At 9.15 she was abeam; we showed our colours and she did not answer. At 9.30, 13° 13' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 59' 27" of latitude observed and in 148° 38' 42" of longitude by account. The land from W to N 65° W. The cables were bent and the anchors got ready to let go.

1802-06-25.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from north. At 2 p.m. and at 6.15 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same. At 11 very high land was sighted from N 56° W to W. Obs. lat. 34° 20' 22"; est. long. 148° 16' 36". Var. 13° 13' 20" NE.
1802-06-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NW. At 11 the land was sighted from N 56° W to W. At noon in 34° 20' 22" of latitude observed and in 148° 16' 36" of longitude by account. Continual rain during the night.

1802-06-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from N, NW, SW and south. At 1, at 6 and at 9 changed tacks. At 2 a.m., at 5 and at 9 changed tacks. At 8 the land in sight but very hazy. Est. lat. 34° 1' 28"; est. long. 148° 27' 30".
1802-06-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to SSE. At 8 the land was in sight but very hazy. At noon in 34° 1' 28" of latitude by account and in 148° 27' 30" of longitude by account. At 6 a ship's light was thought to be seen in the S 22° W at a short distance.

1802-06-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 4 and at 8 p.m. changed tacks; at 1.30 the same. At 7 sighted the land from N 45° W to S 45° W. Got the port anchor ready to let go. At 10.15 hove to with the main topsail to the wind, the land at a short distance. Obs. lat. 34° 23' 33"; est. long. 148° 15' 12".
1802-06-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At 7 the land was sighted from N 45° W to S 45° W. At 10.15 we hove to to wait for the noon altitude; our reckoning put us abreast of Port Jackson, which could not be seen. At noon, having found 34° 23' 33" of latitude, we filled and stood on and ran along the coast a mile off. At 4 the captain gave the order for every man to his station to go to the anchorage. We showed our colours and fired a swivel gun. At 5, being off the mouth of Port Jackson and able to run in, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 5.30 the lighthouse of the port bore from us S 85° W, 2 miles off. At 6.30 and at 7 the lighthouse light S 68° W, and at 11 S 74° W. The weather turned overcast and the wind freshened; at 9 went onto the port tack.

1802-06-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south, SE and ESE. At noon filled and stood in to close the land; after coming very near it we ran along it at a mile's distance. At 5 p.m., being off the mouth of Port Jackson, we lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the lighthouse light bearing S 85° W. At 9 went onto the port tack. At 4 a.m. hove to; at 8 filled and stood on. At 9.30 a.m. we shaped our course to run into the port, and at 11.30 we anchored between Middle Head and South Head. Lat. 34° 3' 9"; long. 148° 26' 12". The latitude determined at the observatory was 33° 51' 10" and the longitude 149° 5'. Var. 9° 40' 0" NE. We found the commander there, arrived 10 days before; he had three quarters of his crew in hospital. The captain went aboard the commander and from there ashore, which was his place of residence.
1802-06-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE. At midnight went onto the starboard tack; at 3 back onto the port tack. At 4 hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 7 filled and stood west for the land. At 7.30 hove to again with the port side to the wind. At 8 filled and stood on close-hauled on the port tack and made sail. At 9.30 the entrance to Port Jackson was sighted S 22° W; we shaped our course to run in. At 11.30 we anchored between South Head and Middle Head, North Head bearing N 65° E, South Head S 87° E, Camp Cove S 25° E, Bradleys Head S 25° W and Middle Head N 37° W. As soon as we were anchored the pilot came aboard and wanted to make us get under way to take us to Neutral Bay, but the captain would not. The pilot told us that the Géographe had been at Port Jackson since the 1st Messidor [20 June 1802]; that she had arrived with her crew in their cots, and that Governor King had sent him men and boats to warp her to Neutral Bay. The captain at once sent off the Géographe's boat, with her people and an officer of ours, to inform the commander of our arrival.

1802-11-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Year 11 of the French Republic, etc.
On the twenty-sixth, at daybreak, everyone being on board, all was made ready for getting under way. The winds were then westerly and very light, but, being persuaded that they would freshen as the sun rose above the horizon, we set sail, having moreover the tide in our favour.
To break out our anchor we had to use the great purchase, so deeply was it bedded in the mud. The efforts made to weigh it with the messenger were not only useless but even harmful, for the messenger broke.
During the night before our departure, a general search was made through the ship to make sure that no one was hidden aboard. We had all the more reason to believe that we should find no one there, since in the preceding days nine men and a woman who had taken refuge on board had been put ashore. Nevertheless we found twelve more, who were likewise sent back.
At five o'clock, being under sail and becalmed, we let the ship drift while waiting for the breeze, which did not spring up until about seven in the morning. The winds came first from the north and a few minutes later shifted to the north-east. The Naturaliste, which was ahead of us and to leeward of the reef that lies in the middle of the channel, being unable to weather it, was obliged to let go a bower anchor, which made me decide to do the same, although it would have been easy for me to get out of the port by taking advantage of the position I was in. The Casuarina, which was following us, did not anchor for the moment and amused herself beating about in the neighbourhood of the ship.
The American ship the Fanny, which is sailing in company with us on her way to Batavia by way of Bass Strait, followed our example and came to anchor.
Having no further hope of putting to sea that day, I dispatched the Casuarina to carry the astronomer Bernier to the south point of the entrance of the port so that he might determine its latitude precisely. In the meantime three more men were found hidden in our longboat. I informed the harbour master and the Secretary to the Government of this, who came on board after we had anchored. The former claimed the three men, but I did not think it proper to hand them over to him, confining myself to telling him that I would act towards them as I had done with regard to the twelve whom I had put ashore during the night. He seemed satisfied with this answer and we parted good friends.
About nine in the morning I dispatched my boat to take these three men ashore in the charge of the master gunner. I was very far from believing that any attempt would be made to seize them by force, for had I been able to suspect it, I would have guarded against such an outrage. Nevertheless, just as they were about to be landed, the harbour master's boat came alongside mine, and the men in it, being armed, forced the people in my boat, who were not, to hand over these three men to them, and they took them aboard the American ship the Fanny, where the harbour master then was.
As soon as I learnt of this dishonest proceeding, I at once dispatched an officer to ask the harbour master by what order his men or he himself had just stopped one of my boats. I added that the Governor's orders concerning deserters, if there were any, were as well known to me as to himself, and that consequently I would go myself to complain of his conduct in this affair and demand such satisfaction as I should see fit.
The officer who was sent aboard the American, not having found the harbour master there, was informed
that he was fishing in the cove off which we lay at anchor, and went to speak to him. Having discharged his errand, he returned on board. And the harbour master, accompanied by the Secretary to the Government, having followed him very closely, also arrived. I then pointed out to the harbour master how ill-considered his conduct had been, in view of what had just happened, and assured him most positively that had the Casuarina been at hand, I would have ordered her to chase his boat and even to sink it had it persisted, in spite of my prohibition, in trying to carry off the men who were in mine and whom I was putting ashore.
At this speech the harbour master gave me his word of honour that he had had no part in this affair and had given no order concerning it. He offered me every satisfaction I could wish for, but I would accept none, preferring to have a conversation on the matter with the Governor himself.
The harbour master and the Secretary to the Government having withdrawn, I signalled the Casuarina to pass under our stern and went to Sydney on board that vessel.
In the conversation I had with Governor King about what had happened, he publicly censured the conduct that had been shown on this occasion and, as proof of a considered disapproval, he pardoned for this once all those who had deserted, although their departure and their names had been known before they were taken from my boat. I think that the harbour master, on his return, will receive a lesson that will make him more circumspect in future.
About eleven in the evening, an English young lady named Mary Bickaith presented herself on board dressed as a man. I had known her during my stay at Port Jackson, and more than once she had begged me to obtain leave from Governor King for her to return to England in the service of M. Thomson. I had promised her to take an interest in her case, and indeed I spoke of it to the Governor, who would not have refused me this request had it not been contrary to the general instructions concerning the convicts. But he told me that if she wished to leave, no search would be made for her. She was therefore embarked on board the Naturaliste on the eve of our departure, but as she could not reappear in England without an authentic permission from the Governor, I have taken her on board in order to set her down somewhere in the Moluccas, where her youth and her age will soon have got her noticed and found her a happy lot. This young lady belongs to people of good birth in England and came out to accompany her mother, who was condemned to end her days at Port Jackson for having stolen a piece of muslin from the shop of a merchant where she had made some other purchases. The daughter preferred to accompany her mother in her exile rather than be put in a convent, the only con piton élevé that was offered her to make up for the loss of her mother. She is seventeen years old, and engaging more by her conduct than by her prettiness.

1802-11-18.journal_anonyme: On the 26th Brumaire we lay anchored at the mouth of the port, where we had anchored. At 4.30 we hoisted our topsails and got under way, as did the commander. At 6.30, being outside the heads, the pilot left us and we steered out to sea. The winds south to S by W, a strong breeze. At 12.10 the commander made the signal to change tacks, which we did at once. Lat. 34° 1' 24"; long. 149° 19' 30".
1802-11-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock, having discharged the pilot,
The northern extremity of the land in sight in this quarter bore north 3° west.
The south point of the entrance of Port Jackson north 51° west,
The north point of the entrance of the same port north 15° west,
The north point of the entrance of Botany Bay south 34° west.
Historical events & remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, in the morning, the weather being fine and the winds from the west very light, we nevertheless got under sail in the hope that they would freshen at sunrise and that we might get out of the port. The Naturaliste, the Casuarina and the Fanny, an American ship, did likewise, and all four of us shaped our course to pass north of the reef that lies in the middle of the channel at the entrance of this port. Scarcely had we weathered it when the winds shifted to the south-west and south, blowing a strong breeze, so that we no longer had any hope of fine weather for the rest of the day. For when the winds are from this quarter, they usually blow in hard gusts with squalls, accompanied by rain, mist and claps of thunder.
At eight o'clock, being quite outside, we discharged our pilots and stood close-hauled on the starboard tack. During the morning we unrigged our mizzen topgallant mast as a useless burden to carry in the campaign in which we were engaged.
On this first board we did not form a high opinion of the sailing of the Casuarina, which did not come up to our expectations. It is true that the sea was somewhat rough for so small a craft, but the little sail we were carrying, compared with her, who was carrying all of hers, did not prevent her from dropping far astern. The ship the Fanny, whose sailing had been announced to us as remarkable, could not keep up with the Naturaliste under equal canvas.
At noon the observed latitude was so uncertain that we took no account of it. From then on the sky began to cloud over with a very threatening look, and thunder was heard, though still in the distance.
In the afternoon we took the landward tack so as not to lose sight of the coast. The winds were already blowing very fresh and we all had two reefs in our topsails. On this tack we closed with the Casuarina, which must have been finding the weather very bad. Nevertheless this little vessel behaved very well and shipped little water. The board we ran towards the land lasted only two hours, after which we took the offshore tack again, wearing round. When we changed course, the land in sight appeared to extend from north-north-west to west-south-west.
At four o'clock we were struck by a very violent storm. The flashes of lightning and the claps of thunder followed one another so rapidly that the eyes were wearied by the former and the head stunned by the latter. There is no doubt that the lightning struck very near us, and I count myself very fortunate that none of the ships was hit. This storm lasted nearly two hours, moving from the south-west towards the north-north-east.
At sunset, the rain having ceased and the storm having moved off, it was still heard rumbling for a long time, but we had nothing more to fear from it. During the night the breeze was very uneven, the winds varying from south to south-south-east. The sky remained dark and overcast, with little sign of a fine day on the morrow. The sea was very high and the ship laboured a great deal, being obliged to carry little sail so as not to lose sight of the other ships, which were steering by our stern lantern.
1802-11-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather. At 4 a.m. Captain Hamelin took aboard the Géographe the girl he had brought aboard on the 25th. At 5.30 we got under way with the division. The wind a light breeze from the south. At 6.30, being clear of the port, the pilot left us. At 8 the wind freshened and was a strong breeze from S to SSE, the weather squally, with thunder and rain. At noon in 31° 1' 44" of latitude and 149° 19' 30" of longitude, carrying little sail on account of the Casuarina. In the afternoon, being near the vane, I had a strong electric shock; Brue and Bougainville, who were near me, felt the same shock. At nightfall, seeing no ship of the division, we lay to and showed a light.

1802-11-19.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea and a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 3 changed tacks; at 8 hoisted a light at the gaff which we kept all the watch. At 4.25 and 5.30 changed tacks. We were at first standing in to close the commander; at 7.50, he having gone about, we did the same. The land in sight from W to SW. Obs. lat. 34° 20'; long. 149° 54' 30".
1802-11-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock the land in sight appeared to extend from west-north-west to west-south-west.
Historical events & remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, the weather was hardly finer, or more comfortable, than the day before. The winds, which during (the night) had varied from south to south-south-east, shifted in the morning from south-south-east to south-east, but they were so light that the ship scarcely answered her helm. The sea, which was no less high and swelling for that, tossed us in every direction, and for some time I feared damage to my masts, because the lanyards of our lower shrouds, being new, had stretched a great deal with the first rolling the ship had experienced since our departure. During the morning we stood on the south-by-west tack so as not to draw away from the land.
At noon, the sky being overcast, we had no observation of latitude.
During the evening, the Naturaliste and the Casuarina having closed with us, we spoke both of them. The captain of the Casuarina let us know that he had laboured a great deal the previous night and that his vessel had made as much as five inches of water an hour, but that it came for the most part through the upperworks. At the moment he spoke to us, she was making no more than one inch in the same interval of time. I particularly urged him to keep as close to me as he possibly could, and not to strain his masts by crowding on sail when the weather was not fine, since I would always regulate myself by his sailing.
About four o'clock, the winds having shifted to east-south-east, we hoped to have them shortly in the north-east, followed by fine weather. For during our stay at Port Jackson we had almost always (seen) them bring about this change in the atmosphere. But it did not take place on this occasion, for the sky remained dark and overcast. The sea, however, grew calmer and seemed to herald an approaching change.
During the night, which, without being fine, was not nearly as bad as the previous one, we made various manoeuvres so as not to draw away from the other ships, and steered south whenever the winds allowed us to lay that course.
It was remarked during the day that a strong current seemed to be setting us violently to the south-west, which appeared to us all the more certain since, when we ran the board towards the land, it took us roughly half as long to approach it as it had taken to get away from it.
This remark may be useful to navigators who will frequent this coast, for if, during the night near the land, one made (in the margin: the boards) as long on one tack as on the other, one would run the risk of being ashore much sooner than one would have reckoned.
1802-11-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to E. At 4 a.m. the division was sighted and we filled and stood on. At noon the land from S 45° W to W, being in 34° 20' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 54' 30" of longitude by account. At 3 we passed under the commander's stern; he gave us the course south.

1802-11-20.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the sea less swelly, a fresh breeze from east to NE and north. At 3 passed under the Géographe's stern; she ordered us to steer south. At 4 and at 5 laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the Géographe and the Casuarina. At 6 sighted a sail in the SW; at 7 she was made out to be a schooner. The Géographe hove to and sent a boat aboard her, the distance from the land about six leagues. Obs. lat. 36° 3'; long. 149° 43' 58".
1802-11-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At 6 hours 45 minutes the land in sight extended from SW to NW.
At noon, the land in sight bore from north 15° west to south 45° west.
Historical events & remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, in the morning, the winds seeming inclined to settle in the north towards the east, we steered south-south-west, regulating ourselves by the sailing of the other ships, which at daybreak were all a short distance from us. As the Casuarina sailed the worst of all, she prevented us from profiting as much from the fair wind that was blowing as we would have done in other circumstances. But it was essential to keep this little vessel for the use she will be to us hereafter.
At half past seven, having sighted a schooner ahead of us, we gave chase, and having come up with her, we recognised that she was the same one we had already met at sea when my boat went astray on the coast of Van Diemen's Land. Having hove to, I sent a boat on board to see whether the captain, who had just come back again from sealing, might not have some objects of curiosity to give me. For on his departure from Port Jackson he had promised to bring me everything he could procure.
At about seven o'clock the captain of this schooner came on board and made me a present only of a wombat of extraordinary size. We learnt that the schooner l'Entreprise, commanded by Captain Le Corre, which had put in at Port Jackson, had been lost, and that the captain and five men had had the misfortune to be drowned in this wreck, which took place on the islands called the Two Sisters, situated at the northern point of the Furneaux Islands. One of the partners in this schooner was on his way to Port Jackson to charter a vessel there that could go and gather up the remains they had saved from this wreck. Part of the crew had stayed on the island with provisions and were busy sealing until the return of this partner in the venture, who was probably its originator. According to his report, it seems that this event took place following a gale while they were at anchor in the Mauvaise Baie, which lies to the east of this island. We all regretted the loss of Captain Le Corre, whom we had known at Port Jackson and whose company was most agreeable.
At eight o'clock we parted from this schooner, which continued on her way to Port Jackson, and we on ours to seek the entrance of Bass Strait.
At noon we had only a very doubtful observation, on which it was impossible to rely.
In the afternoon a strong breeze continued to blow from the north-north-east, and at four o'clock we made out perfectly the mountain which the English have named Mount Dromedary, very recognisable by its shape. It then bore north 58° west of us. It is one of the best landmarks that the whole coast can offer, from the Promontory to Port Jackson.
During the evening a good breeze continued to blow, but at sunset it fell off a great deal. The ships were informed that the course for the night would be south. They all passed under our stern when I hove to, to windward, to wait for the Casuarina, which was astern.
During the night the winds were very variable and came back to the south-west, which obliged us to stand close-hauled on a south-south-east course. Although the sky had a very threatening look, we passed the night without any very heavy squalls and received only a few showers of rain, which did not last long.
1802-11-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from E to NNW. At 6 a.m. a ship was sighted in the S 45° W, and at 7 she was made out to be an English schooner; the Géographe communicated with her. At noon the land 18 miles off, in 36° 3' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 43' 54" of longitude by account. Sailing under topsails.

1802-11-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from N to SW. We kept the topsails on the caps to wait for the ships; at 6.50 lay to to wait for the commander. The land ahead of us and the Géographe at a middling distance. Lat. 37° 28' 0", long. 149° 29' 58". From the 30th [Brumaire] to the 1st Frimaire [Year 11, 21-22 November 1802]. Overcast weather, the horizon thick, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SW. At 1.55 changed tacks and hove to under the main topsail; at 3 filled and stood on. At 6 and at 7 changed tacks; the commander in the SW at a good distance. Obs. lat. 38° 24', est. long. 150° 24' 28".
1802-11-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock the land in sight extended from north to south as far as the eye could reach.
Mount Dromedary bore north 58° west.
At two o'clock in the night, we thought we saw land in the west.
Historical events & remarks, etc.
On the thirtieth, the winds having come back to the south-west, very variable, they gave us once more dark, overcast weather, with a rather threatening look for the rest of the day. During the morning we stood close-hauled on the west-by-north tack to come and make out the land, which in this quarter is high and mountainous and can be seen from very far off when the weather is fine and clear.
At noon we had no observation of the meridian altitude, and I even remarked that since our departure from Port Jackson we have only once had a good one. The currents in these waters seem so violent that it would be most essential to have fine weather when one is there, in order to guard against great errors of dead reckoning in the course one believes one has followed.
By dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 37° 27' 54", and our longitude estimated since the last observation by No. 35 put us in 148° 32' 30".
About half past three, finding ourselves fairly close to the coast, we took the south-by-east tack, wearing round. We then had in sight a chain of very high mountains whose two extremities visible to us extended from south 50° west to north 50° west.
At sunset the same stretch of land was seen from south 69° west to north 88° west. The coast was too hazy for us to take an exact view of it. However, we thought we observed that the high mountains we had in sight did not end at the seashore, but lay inland, fronted by other, much lower mountains which ended at the shore.
After sunset we brought to, to wait for the Casuarina and the other ships which were astern. We also took the third reef in our topsails so that they should not be obliged to crowd too much sail for the night. The weather, moreover, had a very threatening look and we had reason to fear some squalls.
The night of the 30th to the 1st of Frimaire, however, had nothing disagreeable about it but a very great dampness followed by very dark weather. Thunder was sometimes heard rumbling, but it did not come near us and kept at a great distance. Nor was the sea comfortable, and the ship was violently tossed by the swell, although a good breeze blew from the south-west, varying towards the west.
During the night we frequently made signals to the ships in company with us, in order to learn their positions and show them ours.
1802-11-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to SSW. At noon the land 13 miles off, in 37° 28' 0" of latitude observed and in 149° 29' 54" of longitude by account.

1802-11-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the extremities of the land, though very hazy, were seen from south 50° west to north 50° west.
At sunset,
they extended from south 60° west to north 80° west.
Historical events & remarks.
On the first of Frimaire, Year 11, etc., the winds remained in the south-west, varying towards the west. They came in gusts and squalls, the sea still very high. During the morning we made various manoeuvres so as not to part company with our ships. Although the weather was not fine, we nevertheless set about setting up our mainmast shrouds, which had stretched so much through their lanyards, which were new, that I was in continual fear of suffering damage. We began first by setting up those to leeward, so as to do the same to the others when we changed tack.
We continued on the southerly course until noon, when, reckoning ourselves in latitude 38° 15 and longitude 148° 54' 52", we went about onto the other tack, having first run large to close with the Casuarina, which was much distressed by the bad weather we had had since our departure.
During the evening we did to our starboard shrouds the same as we had done in the morning to the larboard ones, and by this means our masts were out of danger. The weather we had in the afternoon was hardly suited to this work, for we frequently had rain and strong gusts.
In the evening the weather seemed to change and to be setting fair. The winds shifted to the south about three in the afternoon and moderated a great deal. Little by little the heavy clouds that shrouded the whole horizon dispersed, so that the eye could reach quite far over the space lying between west and south-east by way of south. At sunset we closed with the Casuarina, which I spoke, to urge her to keep as close to us as she possibly could. The captain of this little vessel told us that he had been obliged to send down his fore-topmast, one of the crosstrees across the trestletrees* having broken with the rolling of the ship. For the rest, she was making no more water than usual, and only through the upperworks, which is all the less surprising since the planking in that part, having been used green, must necessarily have made the caulking unsound for the first while.
At sunset the man at the masthead thought he saw land in the west, but I think he was mistaken and that we were too far south for him to see it, all the more so since, in the position in which we (placed) ourselves, the land must be very low, or at least our charts show it so.
During the night the weather was fairly fine and the sea grew smoother. We held the south-by-west tack until midnight, and then took the south-by-east one. At that time the winds had become very variable and almost calm. They remained so for the rest of the night.
1802-11-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to south. At noon in 38° 24' 0" of latitude observed and in 150° 24' 24" of longitude by account. Almost calm since noon.

1802-11-23.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, a high sea, from W to south and SW. At noon and at midnight changed tacks; at 5.30 a.m. wore ship. Obs. lat. 38° 40' 24", long. 148° 58' 12".
1802-11-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At sunset we thought we saw land from the mastheads in the west, but the weather was not clear enough for us to be certain that it was land.
Historical events & remarks.
On the second of Frimaire, in the morning, the weather continued fine, but the breeze was very light, variable and inconstant. The winds were for some time in the south and afterwards veered towards the east. At daybreak we had taken the southerly tack, edging to the west. The sea having become smooth and the sky very clear in the east, we hoped for a fine day and a good breeze. This hope was borne out as to the weather, which was fine, but the breeze was too light for our liking
At noon we had an observation of the latitude which placed us in 38° 39' 7", and our longitude, by the rate of No. 35, proved to be 147° 59' 18". This position, compared with that of our dead reckoning, gave us a difference of 0° 10' 45" in latitude and one of 0° 29' 27" in longitude. The error arising from these two differences was attributed to the currents, although this supposition seems to me false, since, from the direction supposed for them, it ought to have been to the south and west, whereas it proved to be to the north and west, the latitude by dead reckoning being 38° 28' 22" and the longitude 148° 28' 34".
In the afternoon the winds shifted to the east and did (not) freshen. We continued to steer south-west by west to come and make the entrance of the strait north of the Kent Group, my intention being to run into the channel which these islands form with the Promontory and the other islands belonging to it.
At six o'clock, the weather continuing fine and the breeze still light, I had the ship hove to so as to wait for the Casuarina, which was a long way astern. I took advantage of this loss of time to send a boat aboard the Naturaliste, and had Captain Hamelin handed what packets I still had for the Minister of Marine, as well as various letters for my private acquaintances.
The captain of the American ship the Fanny having also come on board, I told him of the loss of the schooner the Fany l'Entreprise, Captain Le Corre, as well as of the misfortune the captain had had of being drowned, and five of his men with him. The American supercargo, M. Cornwell, had had the good fortune to save himself.
At seven o'clock he returned to his ship, and the Casuarina having closed with us, we resumed our course south-west by west.
During the night we continued on the same course, having still a good deal of ground to make to the west before reaching the place where the Kent Group lies, in the middle of the channel that separates the Furneaux Islands from the coast of New Holland. The breeze during the night was no stronger than it had been during the day, and the weather, though very dark and overcast, was tolerably fine, apart from a great dampness which at times troubled the men of the watch.
1802-11-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm and a light breeze from ESE to ENE. The course S 56° 15' W, following the commander's, he having signalled none. At noon in 38° 40' 24" of latitude observed and in 149° 58' 48" of longitude by account. At 5, the commander having hove to, the division did the same; a boat from the Géographe brought us packets for the government and a wombat. She told us of the loss of the Surprise, a French schooner, and of an English sloop on the Sisters. The commander had learnt of it from the English schooner he had communicated with on the 29th [Brumaire, 20 November 1802]. Only 5 men of the Surprise were saved, none of them French. We handed over to the boat our flags and the signal book. At 7 we filled and stood on.

1802-11-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from ESE to ENE and NE. The commander having hove to, we did the same; a boat came from the Géographe bringing us the packets to hand to the captain. At 7 we filled and stood on; the wind having freshened we shortened sail so as not to run past the commander. At noon the course was shaped west. Obs. lat. 39° 23' 42", est. long. 148° 32' 42".
1802-11-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven in the morning, in a clear spell, we thought we saw the high land of the Furneaux Islands to the west-south-west. But the weather was too hazy for this to seem certain.
Historical events & remarks.
On the third, the weather was very dark and overcast, the winds were variable from east to north-east, a light breeze, and we found the sea smooth. We continued on our course south-west by west until noon, when, having observed the latitude to be 39° 33' 42", we altered it to steer west by north-west, so as to go no further south and to allow for the effect of the currents.
About eight o'clock, having signalled the Naturaliste to steer in our wake, we also had the Casuarina pass under our stern, to give her some fresh bread, which her people received with all the more pleasure since for several days they had eaten nothing but biscuit and cheese, having been unable to do any cooking while the sea was high.
According to the dead reckoning of the course run in the twenty-four hours, the latitude by dead reckoning proved to be only 39° 16' 10", which gave, compared with the observation, a difference of 0° 17' 32", by which the currents had carried us to the south. There was no hour angle in the course of the day, and it was only by chance that the sun showed itself at the moment of its passage across the meridian. By our dead reckoning, corrected by the previous day's observation, we placed ourselves in (no figures).
In the afternoon the sky continued dark and overcast, without however having any threatening look. The north-east breeze was a little stronger than in the morning, and the sea perfectly smooth. We saw a great number of birds of the white booby kind and many white and grey gulls. We also had the company of a whale, which followed us for some time. It was of good size, but not of the kind that yields spermaceti, since it spouted the water vertically and not horizontally, as those who engage in this fishery maintain, and who, by their own account, have no other means of recognising it.
After sunset, all the ships having closed up, we took the south-by-east tack, being almost becalmed, with very dark and stormy weather, and hearing the thunder rumble in several quarters of the horizon. From eight o'clock until eleven the calm obliged us to make various manoeuvres. At that time we sounded, and it was not without astonishment that we found ourselves in 28 fathoms, bottom of white sand and rotten shells. As by our dead reckoning we could only be in the neighbourhood of the Furneaux Islands, upon which the currents must have set us, judging by the course we had made since noon, we trimmed close-hauled on the northerly tack with very variable winds from east-north-east. We took care to sound every half hour, and we saw with pleasure that the depth was gradually increasing. In the space of an hour we went from 28 to 31 fathoms, and the bottom was then no longer so clean, being mixed with coral. As the breeze was still very light at that time and the currents might set us onto the coast, I had an anchor cleared for letting go, and the whole crew was on watch, with the exception of the officers, who, according to their custom, spent the night in their beds. None appeared on deck but the one who had the watch, waiting impatiently for it to end so that he might do as the others did.
From midnight to four o'clock we had several shifts of wind which made us manoeuvre a great deal. The winds went from west to south-south-south-west (sic), to south and to east, following the direction of the storms that surrounded us. In the intervals we had a little wind and shook the reefs out of our topsails in order to make use of it. At three o'clock in the night the depth was thirty-four fathoms, and we continued on our course to the north with every sail set, except our topgallant sails, which were not rigged.
The Casuarina kept close to us all night and followed our manoeuvres.
1802-11-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to ESE. At noon in 39° 23' 42" of latitude observed and in 148° 33' 18" of longitude by account. In the afternoon overcast and rainy weather, with squalls; from 8 to 10 lay to.

1802-11-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE, falling away entirely calm. At 9 we went onto the port tack; at midnight back onto the starboard tack. During the night the wind shifted rapidly from NNE to W. The commander not being in sight, we kept a light at the foremast head; at 3.30 we sighted him ahead of us. Est. lat. 38° 52' 12", est. long. 147° 23'.
1802-11-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five in the morning we thought we sighted the Furneaux Islands in the west and west-south-west, but the horizon was not clear enough for us to be sure that we were seeing land. The sounding was then 35 fathoms
Historical events & remarks.
On the fourth, at daybreak, the weather was fairly fine in the W, but the whole horizon between east and north by way of south was so laden with vapours that the eye could not reach two leagues. The thunder, which rumbled continually in the southern quarter, announced to us the approach of some storm. And we were not long in having a very violent one from that quarter. The one we received lasted about two hours and was accompanied by heavy rain. The claps of thunder and the flashes of lightning were very frequent. The lightning struck very near us, although we had not foreseen it, but it produced exactly the effect of the whistling of a cannon ball passing a short distance from a ship. When the worst of this storm had passed, the weather seemed about to set fair, but this appearance did not last long; the squalls began again shortly afterwards, and throughout the rest of the day we had a great many more of them than we should have wished.
As we were then carrying little sail to wait for the ships in company, which were astern of us, they closed with us about nine o'clock. Captain Hamelin hailed me to ask leave to go and make out the land. I asked him what he thought of the weather, observing to him that it seemed to me hardly suitable for running into the strait; but as he pointed out to me that he saw no objection to passing through it and that we were losing a good wind, I told him that he might crowd on ahead and that I would follow him, which we both did at once, and we were followed by the Casuarina and the American ship.
At noon we had no observation of latitude; that of our dead reckoning placed us in 38° 54' 42", and the longitude, also by dead reckoning, was 145° 12' 28".
During the evening the sky had a very threatening look and the thunder rumbled on every side, though at a distance. The winds, which had been in the east, shifted to the north-east and at times varied towards the north. The breeze was uneven and often came in heavy squalls, according to the direction of the showers the wind brought us. We sounded only once in the morning so as not to lose time, and we had 40 fathoms. It was then seven in the morning and we were still steering north. We did not bear away to the west until after speaking Captain Hamelin, and it was then about nine o'clock.
At five in the evening, the weather having cleared a little to the south, we saw the summits of the high mountains of the Furneaux Islands showing above the vapours with which the land was enveloped. I thought I recognised the mountain which the English have named the Patriarchs, from the appearance its peaks present to the eye. We continued to steer west until six o'clock and then closed with the ships. The Naturaliste, which had crowded on ahead to make out the Kent Group, did not see it. I informed her that we would spend the night beating about, running four hours to the north and four hours to the south. At eight o'clock the winds shifted suddenly to the north, varying to north-north-west. The weather was then stormy and threatening rain. At nine o'clock the winds suddenly flew round to south-south-west and blew all at once par si with such violence that the ship was laid over on her side and heeled heavily. As she was for quite a long time without answering her helm, we were obliged to let fly the sheets of the main topsail and the mizzen topsail. The spanker was the sail that hampered us most. However, the ship bore away and righted herself. The topsails and the foresail having been clewed up and then furled, we lay to under the fore-topmast staysail and the mizzen staysail, and so passed the night, sounding every hour and with the means of standing off whenever we should judge it proper.
From the south-west the winds shifted to the west and blew with violence. The sky became clear, and as the wind did nothing but increase, we had no doubt that it would continue so for some time. We lay to all night, seeing from time to time the lights of the ships. The soundings were very regular, from 31 to 34 fathoms. The order was to go about when there should be less than 28.
1802-11-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to NNE; at 3 a.m. it shifted to the west and hauled to the south, then east, and at last N and WNW. At noon in 38° 52' 12" of latitude by account and in 147° 43' 48" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands in the S 11° 15' W. Four English convicts were discovered hidden in the hold. At 9 the wind shifted to the west, blowing hard in gusts; we lay to and lost sight of the division.

1802-11-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from ENE to N, W and WNW. At 4 p.m. 4 convicts were found in the hold, where they had hidden themselves. At 8 the winds, drawing round to north and WNW, came on to blow hard; at midnight wore onto the port tack. At daybreak sighted a ship in the WSW. At 9 went onto the starboard tack, the land NW 5° N. Obs. lat. 38° 42' 55", est. long. 147° 0' 52".
1802-11-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight in the morning, the land we sighted, which I presume to be that of Wilson's Promontory, extended from west to north-west. The sounding was then 35 fathoms
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, the gale which had begun the previous day, during the night, lasted the whole day without the slightest break. The sea soon became very high and we were considerably tormented by the violent motion of the ship. The sky was nevertheless fine, and there was no sign that this weather would last very long.
At daybreak we saw the ship the Fanny, which bore south of us at a great distance. The Naturaliste was seen from the mastheads to the east by south-east, but we saw nothing of the Casuarina, about which I was anxious, fearing she might have suffered some damage to her masts from the suddenness with which the gale had come on. At the same time we also sighted land to the west. But we could not tell whether it was that of the Kent Group or that of the Promontory, the latitude in which we then reckoned ourselves being too uncertain for anything positive to be said on the matter.
During the morning we continued to lie to under the fore-topmast staysail and the mizzen staysail. The wind was so strong that these two sails were enough for the ship to keep her motion from becoming too violent. We sounded every two hours throughout the morning and had a fairly regular bottom between thirty and thirty-four fathoms.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 39° 8' 30", and the longitude by dead reckoning placed us in 145° 4' 28". Although the sky was fine and the horizon wide, the wind was so strong that this observation should not be regarded as very good, since it was extremely difficult to (keep) the instruments in the position that would have suited them best. But in any case I do not think that the error which may have resulted from it exceeds four to five minutes, either to the north or to the south.
The latitude by dead reckoning was 38° 57' and even more doubtful than the one we had observed.
During the evening the winds varied a little from south-west towards north. The sea had become very high and, although there was no sign of a calm, I nevertheless expected one to set in after sunset. We continued all the while to lie to, heading between SW and south, making good about south-east once corrected for leeway. From noon until eight in the evening the soundings kept gradually increasing. At noon we were in 35 fathoms and surrounded by a great number of birds of every kind.
During the evening the winds continued to blow very fresh from the west-north-west, the sea rising all the while. However, about five in the evening they were less violent and seemed inclined to abate, the gusts being then less heavy and shorter than they had been during the day. The horizon, though still hazy, cleared from time to time. We continued on the southerly tack until midnight, when we took the northerly one, having 34 fathoms of water when we went about, and the winds in the west, variable to west-south-west.
In the night the sky was fine and the wind moderated a great deal; we made no change in our canvas except for the storm staysail, which we set. From midnight to eight in the morning the depth increased in the same proportion as it had decreased while we lay to heading south, and we had 45 fathoms when we took the southerly course.
1802-11-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from WNW to WSW. At daybreak a ship of the division was sighted, which was lost sight of shortly afterwards. At 9 the land was sighted in the N 40° W. At noon in 38° 42' 55" of latitude observed and in 147° 43' 0" of longitude by account.

1802-11-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, blowing hard from WNW, W and NW. We had no sight of the ships of the division. At 7 p.m. and at midnight changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 3' 0", est. long. 147° 24' 34".
1802-11-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At sunset we thought we saw land in the NW and land in the S. SW. This report must be regarded as very doubtful
One of the three ships which had been lost sight of was seen in the north
Historical events & Remarks, etc.
On the sixth, the weather was fairly fine throughout the morning. The sea, which had gone down a great deal during the night, became smoother still, and there was nothing to suggest that the weather would again become as bad as we had had it the day before.
About five o'clock, standing on the southerly tack, we sighted the Naturaliste, the Casuarina and the Fanny, which we had lost sight of the day before. None of these ships appeared to us to have suffered in her masts from the sudden change brought about by the violent gale that had come on when it was least expected, in the night of the fourth to the fifth.
At eight o'clock we had closed with these three ships, which were to leeward of us, and we continued in company on the south-by-west tack, having at times the winds from west-north
-west, variable towards the north, a light breeze. The soundings during the morning's run gradually increased, and we had forty fathoms at noon. At the same time the observed latitude was 39° 8' 15", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 146° 6' 11". From these data laid down on the English chart of the strait, it followed that the northern part of the Kent Group bore south 64° west of us, the Two Sisters north of the Furneaux Islands south 25° west, the islands of the Promontory south 86° west and the Promontory south 87 west. As the islets which lie to the south of it
The great difference found between the dead reckoning and the observation, in latitude as well as in longitude, does not seem to me to be attributable entirely to the current, but rather to a faulty reckoning of the ship's course, which had made much more northing and easting than had been thought while we were lying to. However that may be, we (had) a difference in latitude of 0° 26' 37" and in longitude of 0° 35' 31", the dead reckoning placing us in 39° 34' 52" of latitude and 145° 30' 40" of longitude.
During the evening the sky, which had been fairly fine and clear in the morning, became very dark and murky. It remained so until about four in the afternoon, when the winds shifted to the west, freshening in such a way as to make us fear a return of the bad weather. The rain and mist that followed made us furl our mainsail, the spanker and the mizzen topsail. At five o'clock, the wind still increasing, we had to take the third reef in the topsails and wait to see what would come of the threatening look that was gathering. At four o'clock we had no more than thirty-five fathoms, having lost five since noon, when we had been steering south by west, the point of the compass on which the Furneaux Islands should bear from us, and I should have been very glad to sight them before nightfall. At six o'clock, having no more than thirty fathoms of water, we should most certainly have sighted the land had the horizon been less murky. The eye reached at most a league and a half from the ship. I put off going about for some time longer in the hope that the weather would clear a little, which indeed it did about seven o'clock. And we saw perfectly the Two Sisters, islets north of the Furneaux Islands. They bore south 25° west of us. As the noon position had given us, we reckoned ourselves three or four leagues from them. As the Naturaliste was close to us, I told her to wear round and stand on the northerly tack during the night. The other ships followed our manoeuvre. During the night the weather was very unsettled, bad and gusty, the winds variable from west towards south. We furled our fore-topsail and often laid the main topsail to the mast, so as not to draw away from the other ships. We sounded every hour and the depth kept increasing.
1802-11-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to NW. At daybreak the division was sighted and closed; we had filled at 5. At noon in 39° 3' 0" of latitude observed and in 148° 6' 42" of longitude by account. At 6 the Furneaux Islands from S 19° W to S 30° W. At 5 we lay to.

1802-11-28.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather. The commander very close astern of us. The wind a strong breeze from WSW to WNW and SW. At 6 saw the land from S 19° W to S 30° W; at 6.30 changed tacks, and at 8 a.m. the same. Obs. lat. 38° 50' 19", est. long. 147° 44' 4".
1802-11-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock, sighted the land from the deck to the south-south-west.
At seven o'clock, took the bearing of the middle of the Sisters, to the north of the Furneaux Islands, south 20° west, distance twelve miles.
Observations, Historical events & remarks.
On the seventh the weather, without being fine, was (less) foul than we had had it in the night of the sixth, though cloudy and squally. The gusts were less heavy. The sea, however, was still hollow and agitated; we stood on the northern tack until eight o'clock, when we took the southern one. At two o'clock in the night before, we had lost bottom at 45 fathoms, and in the soundings of the morning it was no longer found at 60 or at seventy fathoms, which leads me to believe that the course had carried us a good deal more from west to east than had been reckoned, or that the set of the currents had changed.
All the morning the sky, though tolerably fine, did not fail to give us a few squalls, but in general they were of little consequence and short duration.
At noon we observed the latitude of 38° 57' 48", and the longitude by No. 35 was found to be 146° 21' 19". This, contrary to our expectation, gave us some way made to the east, although we ought to have had none on that point of the compass according to the various courses we had followed. The difference between the dead reckoning and the observation was 0° 11' 20" in latitude and 0° 12' 32" in longitude. The difference by observation was north, and east for the longitude.
In the afternoon we continued to stand on the southern tack in the hope of recovering the bottom we had lost, but to no purpose, for we did not succeed, either during the day or even during the night. Nevertheless, we went back onto the northern tack at midnight so as to find ourselves the next day in much the same latitude as the day before.
During the evening the sky cleared of all the clouds that had muddied it during (the day), which gave us hope of a change in our favour before long. As the quarter from east to south was very clear, it seemed to us that we should not be long in having the winds from that point of the horizon. But this conjecture was not borne out; they held fairly steadily in the west, sometimes veering towards the south, a light breeze. The sea also began to grow smoother.
At eight o'clock we were astonished to see Venus so close to the moon. As it seemed to us that she must be eclipsed before setting, we kept watch to observe her and followed her until ten o'clock. The eclipse did not take place, but Venus passed so close to the dark limb of the moon that she seemed to touch it, so slight was the interval between the one and the other. The weather was fairly fine during the night, in the middle of which we shaped our course to the north under little sail.
1802-11-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SW. At noon in 38° 50' 19" of latitude observed and in 148° 26' 12" of longitude by account.

1802-11-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth enough, a strong breeze from WSW to W. At midnight changed tacks. Obs. lat. 38° 51' 10", long. 147° 54'.
1802-11-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mention)
Historical events & remarks.
On the eighth the weather was very fine and the sea had grown remarkably smooth. But the winds were not favourable, and we had to go on beating to windward, now on one tack, now on the other. In the morning we continued on the northern tack, which we had been standing on since midnight. From early in the morning we took advantage of the fine weather to clear the ship fore and aft and fumigate the decks and between-decks. All our sails were likewise put out to dry.
At noon we observed the latitude of 38° 50' 2", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 146° 34' 19", which gave us thirteen minutes of way made to the east and confirmed to us that the strong winds from west to south that we (had) met with in the preceding days had changed the set of the currents, which all the navigators who have frequented these waters before us assert to run to the south-west.
In the afternoon, the weather being very fine and the sea calm, the Casuarina was signalled to pass under our stern to receive some fresh bread, which we sent across to her by means of a traveller line. Citizen Freycinet informed us that in bad weather she made eight inches of water an hour, but that this came in only through the upper works of his vessel, which needed caulking afresh. She made no more than one inch of water when the sea was smooth.
As the weather had almost always been bad and the sea heavy since our departure from Port Jackson, it had hardly been possible until then to attend to the berthing of the crew, who slept anywhere at all, wherever they first happened upon, and above all in the between-decks, which made it very difficult to find them at night when all hands were needed on deck. To remedy this inconvenience in future, all the hammocks were slung under the gangways according to the ordinary practice, with an express prohibition to anyone whatsoever against changing his place.
At sunset, or at least shortly before, Captain Hamelin passed under our stern and, having hailed me, informed me that the man Claine, formerly master gunner aboard the Géographe, who was being sent to France to be tried, the Council of Justice having declared itself not competent to pronounce on the finding of the jury, that this same man had just struck the officer of the watch. When he asked me what punishment I wished to have inflicted on him, my answer was to have him given fifty strokes of the rope's end, without prejudice to the judgement he would have to undergo on his arrival.
After sunset the breeze freshened a little, but held steadily in the west, somewhat variable towards the south. As clouds were beginning to form from south to south-south-east, we hoped soon to have the winds from that quarter and continued our course to the south under the topsails and foresail, having furled our mainsail, which was of no use to us and had been set only to dry it and give it an airing.
During the night of the eighth to the ninth the winds, though variable, did not change. From time to time we had a few squalls, and after the moon had set the sky became damp and the horizon hazy and thick, with little sign of fine weather for the following day.
1802-11-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WSW to W. At 9 filled and stood on under courses. At noon in 38° 51' 10" of latitude observed and in 148° 35' 42" of longitude by account. At 3 Citizen Moreau, officer of the watch, laid a complaint against Barbier (one of the prisoners for theft) who had struck him. The captain sentenced him to 50 lashes with a rope's end. At 5 we spoke the commander, who, on the captain's complaint against Barbier, also sentenced him to 50 lashes. Despite this order the captain did not have them given, though Citizen Moreau asked for it.

1802-11-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a light breeze from WSW which freshened as it drew round to WNW. At 5 spoke the Géographe. Obs. lat. 39° 35' 0", est. long. 147° 43' 54".
1802-11-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, took the bearing of the northern extremity of the two islands called the Sisters, west 16° south
The middle of the islet to the east of the Patriarchs, south 8° west.
Nota: By two sets of distances of the sun from the moon, the longitude was found to be 146° 10' 36", which gave a difference from the timekeeper of 7' 24" more westerly.
Historical events & remarks.
On the ninth, in the four-to-eight morning watch, the Naturaliste, being very close to us to leeward, tried to pass us to windward; the officer of the watch, wishing to amuse himself by passing ahead of us, very nearly carried away our bowsprit by a manoeuvre as ignorant as it was thoughtless. I was then in my cabin and knew nothing of it. But when I came on deck, the officer of the watch having told me what had nearly happened, I closed with that vessel, which was once more to leeward, and hailed her to learn who was the officer of the watch who had carried out such a manoeuvre. I was informed that it was Citizen Hérisson, and was consequently not surprised, for although he thinks himself a very learned seaman, he barely knows how to trim his sails and not at all how to get himself out of a tight spot once he has got into it. I asked Captain Hamelin to tell him that if such a manoeuvre happened a second time, he would no longer stand a watch. Although he was on watch, his lack of care in having his vessel steered was the reason why she ran aboard us again and struck us on the side, abreast of our main shrouds. Fortunately the sea was smooth and the wind slack, for otherwise we should have done ourselves a great deal of damage. No harm was done except to one of my yawls, which was partly crushed but which nevertheless offered enough resistance to make the ship sheer off, by which means we were promptly separated.
During the morning we had an overcast sky, a few squalls with a little rain and little sign of fine weather.
At ten o'clock we sighted the land, from west by south-west to south. We recognised it as the Furneaux Islands and the Sisters, which we had seen in the preceding days. We continued on the south-westerly tack, with the wind from west-north-west, to close with the land.
At noon, the weather, though squally, having cleared, we observed the latitude of 39° 37' 49", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 146° 17' 58". At the same moment the islands called the Sisters bore west 5° south, and the islet lying to the east, about the middle of the largest of the Furneaux Islands, was south 8° west. This bearing, laid down on the chart and corrected for the variation, gave only three minutes' difference east from the longitude by the timekeeper, which proves that this land is placed in its true position. The sounding at noon was 27 fathoms, soft bottom and good for anchoring. After taking the bearing we went onto the northern tack, seeing no improvement in the weather but on the contrary every sign of some fresh gale.
During the evening, as we steered north-west, the sky cleared a little, but the winds shifted only a little from south-west towards south. At four o'clock the Sisters bore south 51° 30' west.
At sunset the weather seemed inclined to set fair, the horizon having cleared of all the dark clouds that had made it unpleasant to look at and its appearance threatening. The wind also dropped a great deal, though it did not change direction. During the night we continued on the northern tack, which we had taken at noon, and it was only at midnight that (we) took the southern one.
Note: For several days we had constantly been experiencing fairly considerable differences to the north, so that it hardly seems open to doubt that the currents are subject rather to following the direction of the winds, when they blow for a long time from the same quarter, than to a constant direction, as we had been told. On our way to Port Jackson we had already experienced the same effect.
1802-11-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to WSW. At noon in 39° 35' 0" of latitude observed and in 148° 20' 42" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands from S 12° W to S 65° W.

1802-12-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from WSW. At 6 passed under the Géographe's stern and laid the mizzen topsail to the mast. At 6 took the bearing of the northernmost end of the [one word illegible] S 45° W; the south end of the Furneaux Islands S 7° W. Obs. lat. 39° 24' 21", long. 147° 34' 54". From the 10th to the 11th [Frimaire, Year 11, 1-2 December 1802]. Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to WNW. At 4 changed tacks. At 6 took the bearing of the land from S 2° W to S 33° W. The Géographe in the NW by N, very close. At 3.45 a.m. changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 17' 45", est. long. 146° 36' 54".
1802-12-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock, the southern extremity of the Furneaux Islands in sight, south 30° west.
The Sisters, to the north of these same islands, south 51° west and south 59° west
At sunset, the land extended from south 15° west to south 50° west
At daybreak, the land could be seen from south-south-west to south-west
At noon, the land in sight extended from south 5° west to south 69° west, 39 fathoms no bottom.
Longitude by two sets of distances 146° 16' 20".
Historical events & remarks.
On the tenth we had very fine weather all the morning, and a light breeze from west-north-west to west-south-west. At daybreak the land of the Furneaux Islands, from which we were at a good distance, could be seen from south-south-west to south-west. The wind was very slack all day, and as we ardently wished to see it change, we flattered ourselves that the calm the sea foretold would bring what we so greatly desired; nevertheless this did not happen that day.
At noon we observed the latitude of 39° 33' 42", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 146° 25' 18". At the same moment the land in sight bore from south 5° west to south 60° west. We were then steering south with the wind at west-north-west. Bottom was lost at 39 fathoms.
Two English prisoners who had hidden themselves in the ship were found while the between-decks was being stowed. When they were questioned as to the motive that had led them to hide on board, they replied that it was to regain their liberty. I warned them that they would be put ashore on King Island, like the four who were on board the Naturaliste and the three who were found on the Fanny. There is no doubt that these desertions were abetted by men of the crew, for in the fourteen days we had been at sea these deserters had lacked neither water nor victuals.
During the evening the weather continued very fine and the sky extremely clear. We steered for the middle of the Furneaux Islands until four in the afternoon, when we went onto the northern tack.
At sunset the land bore from south 74° west to south 29° west.
The night of the tenth to the eleventh was very fine. We spent it almost in a calm, and none of us doubted that this was a presage of an easterly wind for the next day. When we went onto the northern tack, the sounding was 32 fathoms. At eight o'clock, 32, and at midnight, 37 f.
