Although the greater part of the night had passed in a calm, we nevertheless had from time to time some signs that we should have a good wind the next day, in that the little breath of air that reached us sometimes came from the north-east
1802-12-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from WNW to WSW. At daybreak the Furneaux Islands from S 16° W to S 25° W, 8 miles off. At noon their southernmost end in sight S 8° W and the northernmost of the Sisters S 50° W, being in 39° 24' 21" of latitude observed and in 148° 12' 0" of longitude by account. At 11 a flat calm.

1802-12-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven in the evening, the northernmost of the Sisters bore south 74° west, and the Furneaux Islands could be seen from south 68° 30' west to south 29° west.
At five in the morning, the Furneaux Islands could be seen from south 10° west to south 57° west.
At noon, the Kent Group was south 80° west. An islet farther south, south 36° west
Historical events & remarks.
On the morning of the eleventh we were not disappointed in our expectation. The winds came to us from the north-east, variable towards the east. The breeze was light at first and increased only a little in the course of the morning. As the Naturaliste was close to us, I told her to crowd all sail, and did the same myself. Setting our topgallant sails, we steered west, bearing a little towards the south, so as to make the Kent Group as soon as possible, which our dead reckoning and bearings placed ten leagues to the west of us.
At daybreak the Furneaux Islands, including the Sisters, bore from south 11° west to south 57 west.
During the morning the weather was very fine and the sea calm. The breeze increased but little. Towards eleven o'clock we sighted the islands of the Kent Group. And at noon, having observed the latitude of 39° 28' 40", we took the bearing of this group at south 80 west. A small island, to the south of this group, bore south 36° west. The lead brought up 33 fathoms, soft bottom, though not very good for anchoring.
The longitude by No. 35 put us in 146° 44'.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine. We crowded sail to double the Kent Islands before nightfall and by this means enter the strait. But the breeze was so light that we could not manage it. The Naturaliste and I had left the Casuarina and the Fanny astern, though we nevertheless kept them constantly in sight. My intention was to wait for them once inside the islands, as soon as I had doubled them.
At nine in the evening, having a good sight of the northern point of these islands, which we ranged along at half a league's distance, we steered to double them. But the calm having overtaken us, and the ship at certain intervals barely answering her helm, it was only at midnight that the northern cape of this part bore south of us, in 37 fathoms, at two leagues' distance at most, for the land could be seen perfectly even after the moon had set.
During the night the winds were very variable, from east to south and from south to south-west. We were often in (fear) of being obliged to retrace our steps. At various times the sky was hazy and very overcast, and from time to time we received sudden gusts, after which a flat calm followed. However, the sky set fair again, and what little breath of wind we had was from south to south-south-east, or rather, for the greater part of the night it was calm. We kept our stern lantern constantly lit to serve as a guide to the vessels that were astern of us, and which must have seen it.
1802-12-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm until 4, when the breeze got up from ENE to NE; we ran into Bass Strait. At noon in 39° 17' 45" of latitude observed and in 147° 28' 0" of longitude by account. The northernmost end of the Furneaux Islands in sight S 16° E, the Sisters S 10° W, the Kent Group S 80° W, 24 miles off. The Casuarina and the Fanny out of sight astern. Almost calm during the night.

1802-12-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NE, NNW, north, south and SW. We steered to weather the Kent Group to the north. At 7 a.m. spoke the Géographe. Bearings taken at noon: Wilson's Promontory N 23° W; two islets, one S 27° E, the other N 73° E. Obs. lat. 39° 25' 50", est. long. 145° 30' 54".
1802-12-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land: (in the margin: the distances 4° 2 55)
At four o'clock, the Kent Group extended from south 73° west to south 87° w. The northern extremity of the Sisters, south 70° east. The part of the Furneaux Islands in sight, from south 51° east to s 26° east. The rock, la Brioche, about the middle of the channel between the Furneaux and Kent Islands, south 14° east, and a large islet at the mouth of this same channel, south 22° 30' west.
At midnight, the western extremity of the Kent Islands was south 2° west, and the eastern lands in sight, s 22 east.
At five in the morning, the middle of the Kent Group was east 5° north, an islet lying to the west of it, south 40° east. The islets situated to the west and north of the Kent Group having been taken in bearings in order to fix their geography situation, I do not speak of them here.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, having spent the greater part of the night in a calm, we found ourselves we found ourselves (sic) surrounded by islands and islets. I was all the more surprised at this position because, having already cleared Bass Strait by passing to the north of the Kent Group, I had not seen a single one of them. Although they are not far from it and within one or two minutes in the same latitude, to get ourselves out of this labyrinth we put the ship's head south-south-west, with a very light breeze from the south-east variable to the east. We easily passed the most easterly and northerly of them, and we should likewise have doubled the others with ease had the winds held in the same point of the horizon from which we had had them in the morning. But after sunrise they shifted first to the south and then to south-south-west and south-west by west. As I did not wish to leave the channel, I decided to go through the channels that these islets form among themselves, the passage they presented to the eye appearing good and even convenient. The one we chose proved to be so, since we never had less than thirty fathoms, and often more, at a league from the coast. Although these channels are not wide, I am as good as persuaded that they can be used without danger, judging merely by the height and shape of the rocks that form them.
Mr Flinders's new English chart makes no mention of them at all, although the track he followed seems to indicate that he ought to have seen them. I am the less astonished at this since I did not see them myself, although I must have passed very close to them in doubling the Kent Islands to the north on leaving the strait. As I am having exact bearings taken of them, I shall give their position on a particular chart.
At daybreak we had a clear sight of the Casuarina and the Fanny, but they were at the limit of vision to the east. My position not allowing me to wait for them, the Naturaliste and I made sail to get out of the archipelago in which we were entangled, which lies about six leagues to the west of the Kent Group. We passed through the channel formed by the islet that I named the Coin de Mire and the one that bears the name of the Deux Frères. And after doubling them, we continued our course south towards the west as far as the winds allowed us, but with no hope of being able to double the Îlot du Cône, a large and very remarkable rock, of which I give the view and the position on my chart from the Promontory to the port of Bass. As we we we (sic) approached this islet, we sighted a reef awash, which is all the more dangerous when beating to windward in these waters for being of small extent; but as the sea was breaking on it fairly heavily, we were warned of it in good time. The necessary bearings were taken to fix its position for the safety of navigators.
At noon we observed the latitude of 39° 24' 45", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 144° 25' 56". As the weather was fine, we continued on the tack to the west towards the north, following the wind, but at half past one, finding ourselves far enough to windward to double the Coin de Mire to the north, we went onto the tack to the south towards the west. We did in fact double the large rock and the two others that lie to the west of it and a few minutes to the south. The Naturaliste continued on the northern tack. I made her the signal for attention so that, when she came back onto the southern tack, she should take care of the reef I have just mentioned, which we ranged along at three-quarters of a league's distance at most. In the evening we continued on the tack to the south towards the west whenever the winds allowed, and kept to it until midnight, when we trimmed for the northern one. During the night, although the sky was very cloudy and squally with a threatening appearance, we had fairly fine weather and met with only a few small gusts of little consequence. The Naturaliste stood on her tack so far that she did not close with us, although we constantly kept the mizzen topsail set.
1802-12-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from N to W by way of E and south. At 8 the promontory N 36° W, islet A west, islet D S 75° W, islet B S 70° W, the Kent Group S 80° E, islet P N 80° W. The Casuarina out of sight, as was the Fanny. At noon in 39° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 146° 8' 0" of longitude by account, and in 144° 42' 43" of longitude from the bearing of the promontory N 23° W and the observed latitude. At 1.45 the jib boom broke; it was not blowing, and we learnt that it had been sprung for several days. At 12.45 a breaker was seen west of islet P which is not marked on the chart and which we had not seen in Germinal and Floréal of Year 10; it lies in [blank] of latitude and [blank] of longitude. At 6 the promontory N 22° W, islet A N 45° E, islet D N 56° E and islet B N 68° E. During the night the Géographe out of sight.

1802-12-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from W to WSW, freshening. At 1.55 the jib boom broke and was rigged in at once. At 12.45 took the bearing of a breaker not marked on the chart, W 22° S, estimated distance 6 miles. At 10 p.m., at 1 a.m. and at 4 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 39° 49' 27", est. long. 145° 23' 12".
1802-12-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock the middle of the lands of the Promontory bore north 15° 15' west.
At six o'clock the same lands bore north 16° west.
At eight in the morning they were seen in the same direction, extending a little to the east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth the weather was not fine; nevertheless, at daybreak, we sighted the Naturaliste well to windward of us. The American vessel the Fanny was also seen standing on the northern tack, but the Casuarina was not seen, and I do not know why, for she sailed as well as the Fanny. The sky had a very threatening appearance all the morning, and the breeze was unsteady from west-south-west to south-west. As the sea was smooth, we readily persuaded ourselves that this wind would not last long. We continued on the northern tack until five o'clock, at which time we took the southern one, the winds being then at west-south-west; they shifted to the west in the course of the morning.
At noon we observed the latitude of 39° 47' 51", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 144° 15' 16". We then had no more dangers to fear, at least of those that are known. The lands of the Promontory, which we had still had in sight to the west at six in the morning, disappeared from our view, the horizon not being clear.
In the afternoon the clouds that had made it unpleasant for us in the morning dispersed, and everything seemed to promise us a fine day for the morrow. The wind died away as the sun sank towards the horizon, and we remained persuaded that if it fell entirely calm during the night, we should have winds from the east and north-east the next day.
The American vessel crowded sail all day to close with us. And at sunset she was no more than about a league and a half from us, and to windward.
During the night the weather was fine. We made no change in our sail, and I gave orders that, if the winds did not change, we should go about at midnight to take the northern tack. This order was carried out, but towards three in the morning, the breeze having died away entirely, the winds shifted to the south-east and we steered west, setting all sail.
1802-12-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to WSW. At daybreak the commander was sighted and closed. At noon in 39° 49' 27" of latitude observed and in 144° 44' 43" of longitude from the bearing of islet A N 5° E, islets D and B in line N 12° E. A new jib boom was rigged. At 10 the Fanny closed us and passed under our stern.

1802-12-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze from W to SSW, varying to SSE and NE. Rigged a new jib boom. At 8 and at 8.45 changed tacks; at 1 a.m. wore ship. The commander a short distance ahead of us. Obs. lat. 40° 9' 10", est. long. 144° 40' 0".
1802-12-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
(no mentions)
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth the winds, which had gone round to the south-east, were at first very light, but after sunrise, having come to the north and then to east-north-east, they gathered strength, and during the morning we had a pleasant breeze. We steered west under all sail to go in search of King Island, whose position in latitude as well as in longitude is still very doubtful and uncertain, given the diversity of opinion among the English fishermen who have frequented these waters. The chart of it given by Mr Mercy when he commanded the Lady Nelson is, I think, the best that is known of this part up to now, the more so as he seems to have stayed there a fairly long time, though he did not sail round it.
As the breeze blew pleasantly during the morning, the American vessel could not keep up with the Naturaliste, which was carrying all the sail she could set. But I did not think fit to wait for her, since she would have time enough to close with us during the night, as I intended to spend it beating to windward under little sail.
At noon the latitude was observed as 40° 10' 42' and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 143° 38' 0". This position, compared with what we knew of King Island, placed us about twenty leagues to the west of it, a few degrees north.
As this longitude and the observed latitude ought to bring some of the Hunter Islands into sight, I continued the course to the west, persuaded that I should be able to sight them at sunset if the weather continued fine.
In the evening the breeze was fresher than we had had it in the morning, and we made good progress to the west. Someone having come to complain that a watch had been missing from his belongings for three days, a general search was made of all the chests and bags. It did not serve to recover the watch, but it contributed to the recovery of various articles of trade that had been purloined and hidden in different parts of the ship. The perpetrators of these thefts could not be discovered, which is very fortunate for them, for they would have been punished in such a way as to prevent anything of the kind happening in future.
At sunset the weather was still fine, but the horizon became laden with so great a quantity of vapour that its extent was much reduced, which was probably the reason why we saw land neither to the west nor to the south. Captain Hamelin, having closed with me, asked whether I wished to dispatch him, but I pointed out to him that, the navigation of the strait not being well known, it seemed to me prudent to have a good sight of the land before bidding each other farewell. After sunset we continued the course to the west until nine o'clock, but then we came close-hauled on the tack to the north towards the east. The sky at that time was overcast with a threatening appearance. The sounding, which at nine in the evening was 35 fathoms, was no more than 29 at midnight, and at one o'clock it was 25, which decided me to bear up on a course towards the east. The sky grew more and more muddied, and the weather turned squally, with strong gusts and rain for the rest of the night. While standing on the southern tack, the soundings kept increasing, and at five in the morning we again had 35 fathoms.
1802-12-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to SSE, calm, and a strong breeze from NE to E. The Fanny left us and shaped her course for Batavia. At noon in 40° 9' 10" of latitude observed and in 144° 1' 30" of longitude by account. At 9 the commander having hauled close to the wind, we followed his movement.

1802-12-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from ENE to east. The commander very close. At 4.25 a.m. changed tacks. At 7 a.m. the commander hoisted the national flag, clewed up his foresail and lowered his topsails on the caps; at 7.30 he gave orders to make sail. At 9 the winds having shifted to the SW, from which they blew very strong, we at once went onto the starboard tack. At 10 sighted an island to the south and went about at once. At 11 we took the bearing of King Island, 10 miles off, from NW by W to north. Obs. lat. 40° 15' 22", est. long. 143° 0' 0".
1802-12-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon, the lookouts having sighted King Island during the morning, the land in sight bore from west to north-west by west, at a distance of four to five leagues.
At two o'clock, the point forming the southern entrance of the place the English have named Seal Bay was taken in bearing at w. nw, three leagues.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the morning of the fifteenth we had the wind at east, accompanied by rain and very strong gusts. We were then standing on the southern tack, and I meant to keep it for some time to get a little offing, so as to ride out more safely the heavy weather it looked as though we were going to have. The Naturaliste being well to leeward of us, I bore down to close with her, and when I had come near enough, I hoisted the national flag so that she should make sail for France; but whether the haze did not allow her to make out the colours of this flag, or she did not understand the signal, she hove to, thinking I wished to speak to her. This manoeuvre obliged me to close with her, and I then asked her to continue on her way, so as to take advantage, if not of fine weather, for it was very bad at the time, at least of not losing the fair wind to run to the west. After this explanation we wished each other a good voyage and good health, and she bore away. This moment of parting pained me extremely, and I felt such a tightening of the heart over it that I went back into my cabin. I truly loved Captain Hamelin for his personal qualities, and when one has run the same dangers in company for two years, it was natural to feel the impression that the moment of his departure made on me.
The breeze was very strong when Captain Hamelin left, and to keep him longer in sight, I went onto the tack to the north towards the west. But no sooner had we each trimmed our sails than the winds shifted to west-south-west, varying towards south-west, which made him take the southern tack while I was on the north-westerly one, so that we quickly drew away from each other.
Towards ten o'clock we had a sudden shift of wind, which brought it round to the south-west. The sky then became clear and seemed inclined to set fair. So it was that at eleven o'clock we had a good sight of King Island, which bore from west to north-west by west at noon, when the latitude was observed as 40° 10'. We continued close-hauled to close with it and reach the anchorage of the Baie des Éléphants [Sea Elephant Bay] in the evening, if possible. The breeze was very strong and we had the reefs in the topsails. We also had a heavy, swelling sea, but also the hope of finding it smooth as we approached the land.
Towards two o'clock we were astonished to see the Naturaliste again, standing like us on the tack towards the land. When she had closed with us, I made her the signal to rejoin, since, the winds not being suitable for making her way, it was better for her to stay at the anchorage, the more so as I still had letters to give her.
When we had closed with the land, we skirted round it to reach the anchorage, and having made out the Baie des Éléphants, which is, properly speaking, only a cove open to all winds from south-south-west to north-north-west by way of the east, we let go a bower anchor there in 14 fathoms, sandy bottom, having no shelter except from winds from south-west to north-west by way of the west.
Shortly afterwards the Casuarina, which we had lost sight of for several days, appeared and came to anchor beside us. In the evening Captain Hamelin came on board and we talked together about his forthcoming departure. I asked him to stay the next day if the winds were not good, and undertook to have the water he had used since his departure replaced, if it could easily be procured the next day. The night was fine and (the) wind fell entirely calm after sunset.
Stay at King Island
1802-12-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to SW by way of NW. At 7.30 the commander having hove to, we ran alongside him and hove to. He wished us a good voyage and ordered the captain to make sail; we at once filled and stood west, crowding sail. At 9, the wind hauling to the west, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and shifted the mainsail. At 10, having sighted an island to the south 4 miles off, we went onto the port tack. At 11.30 another island was sighted to the west 6 miles off, and King Island from north to N 56° W. At noon in 40° 15' 22" of latitude observed and in 142° 21' 30" of longitude by account. At 12.15 we bore away north to round King Island, which bore from us as far as N 11° 15' W. At 1.30 the Géographe was sighted to the north, holding her wind to close the land. When we had come a little nearer her she made us a signal which we could not understand, having no signal book left; she then made the signal to close and fired a gun, and we closed her. The commander ordered us to follow him to the anchorage. At 4.30 we anchored under the coast near the Géographe, King Island bearing from S 19° W to N 44° W. Shortly afterwards the Casuarina was sighted under the land and came and anchored near us. Five English convicts were sent aboard the Géographe, and we gave her our large boat.

1802-12-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a strong breeze from SW to south and SSE. We bent a new mainsail. King Island was in sight as far as N by NW; we then hauled to the wind to round it. The Géographe, which was to leeward and close-hauled, was closed; she made us a signal we did not understand, then fired a gun and hoisted the signal to close, and we came to the anchorage north of King Island, as did she. The large boat put aboard her the five convicts found on board during the passage; we gave our large boat to the commander. Obs. lat. 39° 53' 0", long. 142° 54' 48".
1802-12-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Sixteenth (7 December 1802) On the morning of the sixteenth we put our boats in the water. I dispatched Citizen Freycinet, commanding the Casuarina, to (proceed) to the Hunter Islands, on the western side of the northern point of Van Diemen's Land, in order to determine their latitude exactly, make plans of the harbours that may be found among the islands and fix their respective positions. This knowledge is all the more necessary for the safety of navigators in that they form the entrance of the strait to the south of King Island. Citizens Freycinet and Boulanger were each entrusted with the following instructions:
The Commander &c. to Citizen Freycinet:
"As soon as Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, has come on board, you will get under sail to proceed to the Hunter Islands, whose geography the French Government wishes to have made with all the exactness of which such work is capable.
"To achieve this as completely as possible, you will facilitate the work of Citizen Boulanger by every means at your disposal, taking care, nevertheless, not to compromise the safety of the vessel you command among these islands, should there be too much risk in venturing among them.
"You will spend as little time on this work as you possibly can, and will contrive to be back at this same place within fifteen days. As the position of the Géographe is not too secure at this anchorage with winds from north to south by way of the east, this need not prevent you from waiting for me here, should you not find me here at the time of your return, for I shall come back again to join you if the winds should oblige me to leave during your absence.
"The English who live ashore will let you know where I have taken the ship, if, in the exploration about to be made of the island, a harbour should be found there where the ship might be in safety.
Greetings, N. B.
The Commander &c. to Citizen Boulanger:
"The benefit to be gained, for the perfection of geography and the safety of navigators, from a sound knowledge of the position of the Hunter Islands, which form the entrance of Bass Strait to the south of King Island, has decided me to invite you to take charge of this work. And in order to enable you to carry it out in a manner that leaves you nothing to wish for, I have decided that the Casuarina, commanded by Citizen Freycinet, shall carry you to the places you have to survey.
"This officer will afford you every means at his disposal for the execution of the work with which you are charged. So it only remains for me to urge you to do it as promptly as possible, so as not to delay too much our departure for other labours no less interesting. As I am persuaded that fifteen days will be more than enough for you, I shall expect you at that time, and even before, at this place, or, should I be absent from it, you will be informed on your return of how we are to rejoin each other. Greetings, N. B.
After dispatching Citizens Freycinet and Boulanger, I had my longboat made ready, the command of which I entrusted to Midshipman First Class Baudin, and I charged Citizen Faure, formerly geographer aboard the Naturaliste and now with me, with making the complete circuit of King Island, beginning with the north. Ten days' victuals were put aboard the boat, and everything that
was necessary for the geography of this coast.
Instructions given to Midshipman Baudin:
"I entrust you, citizen, with the command of my longboat, to carry Citizen Faure, geographer, round King Island, beginning with the north. You will take care to stop at all the points that Citizen Faure judges to deserve particular attention.
"When you are in the southern part of King Island, you must navigate with caution, since it is said that several reefs and rocks awash are met with there, which it is prudent to pass with caution. You will spend as little time as possible on this expedition and will come and join me at the same place from which you set out. Should I not be there, bad weather having forced me to put to sea, I shall not fail to return to this place, and as soon as you sight the ship you will come on board." Greetings, N. B.
To Citizen Faure, geographer:
"Citizen Boulanger having been sent on a mission to survey the Hunter Islands, I have reserved for you, citizen, the entire work on King Island, and you are personally charged with it.
"To give you every facility for doing it, I place at your disposal my longboat, the command of which I entrust to Midshipman 1st Class Baudin. He has orders to carry you round the island and to set you down at the places where you wish to land. I cannot recommend to you too strongly the greatest exactness in the work with which you are charged. You will yourself feel its full importance for the safety of navigators, since this island forms, to the west, the entrance of Bass and of Banks, which are known to you." Greetings. N. B.
Immediately after this boat had left, I sent Citizen Ronsard in another to examine, at some distance to the north of us, a place that seemed to me more convenient for the safety of the ship, in that an islet lying about a league off the land appears likely to give shelter when the winds are in the south.
For the rest of the day the weather was (fine), and the wind, almost calm, was from the south, variable to south-south-west. Captain Hamelin came to dine on board, and we agreed that if my launch, which had gone to look for a suitable watering place, came back loaded, I would send it to him.
During this day we found that the currents were very strong, but that they were only those of a regular tide, since they changed every six hours. On this first day we measured their speed at various times, during the flood as during the ebb, and found by means of the log that its greatest speed was one mile and three-quarters.
It would be hard to say why the name of bay has been given to the place we occupy, for it is positively nothing but a shallow cove that could have led anyone to call it so. The two others, to the north and south of this one, are no better, although the southern one also bears the name of bay.
During the night the wind was calm; the boats returned on board, but the launch brought back no water, the places it visited on this first expedition not being suitable for watering. The sea ashore was found to be very heavy and landing difficult.
Stay at King Island
1802-12-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to south. At daybreak the midshipmen went to walk about on King Island in the small boat, manned by themselves. The dinghy, with the petty officers, went fishing. The commander sent a zoological case and a wombat. At nightfall the small boat came back from King Island. We began setting up the rigging and worked at it all night. At the anchorage, in 39° 50' 17" of latitude and 142° 16' 18" of longitude by account, the currents set N and S at a rate of 1.7 knots (maximum). The Casuarina got under way for the Hunter Islands; a boat of the Géographe went round King Island.

1802-12-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a strong breeze from the south falling away at nightfall. The tide, which until 2 had set south at 1.7 knots, began at 3 to set north.
1802-12-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
The Seventeenth of Frimaire (8 December 1802). On the morning of the seventeenth, having learned of the return of my launch and of one of my boats, which I had sent both to take in water and to communicate with the English who were ashore, engaged in hunting the seal and a species of phoca which they have named the sea elephant, I was informed by the officers who were in these two boats that water was very difficult to obtain at the place where they had landed, but that the people living in the country had pointed out to them another spot that was more convenient, promising to go there the next day and light a fire to show it to us. In accordance with this arrangement, we watched constantly all day for the signal that was to be made to us, and yet we saw nothing.
In the morning the weather was fine and the breeze light from south to south-south-west, as it had been the day before. The Naturaliste being due to leave the next day, I went aboard her with Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, to examine the state of the plants. We found them all in good health, as well as the quadrupeds and living birds. Only we had had the misfortune to lose the last kangaroo we had left. Its death followed an injury it had suffered to its thigh. But I have no doubt that all that remains will arrive safe and sound.
After dinner I took leave of Captain Hamelin and wished him a good voyage. I think it proper to observe that I had the pleasure of seeing only one of his officers, and even then I believe he would not have appeared had Captain Hamelin not invited him to dine with us. On leaving, I had them thanked for their politeness, sending word to them that I was very glad not to have any farewells to make to them.
In the evening we sighted a schooner making for the anchorage, which came, to all appearances, from Port Jackson. She anchored towards eight o'clock, astern of the Naturaliste. As soon as I was back on board, I sent Citizen Depuche two sheep, twelve hens and a pig from my own stores, to help, together with what Captain Hamelin could provide, to ensure that he had fresh provisions for as long as possible during the passage, his health being impaired.
I saw with infinite regret that the officers of that vessel had preferred to spend on frivolous and useless expenses the money I had given them to keep their table, having no other provisions than twelve pigs, which they had had salted even before departure. Had I been able to foresee such an abuse, I should have done with regard to them what I have done with those who are with me and who wished to imitate them; but it was too late when I was informed of part of the conduct of part of those of the Naturaliste.
Towards nine o'clock, the winds having shifted to the south towards the east, Captain Hamelin got under sail and shaped his course to pass to the north of King Island. The weather being very fine, I hope he will have cleared the strait early and will be favoured in making his way to the longitude of the lands of Leeuwin.
1802-12-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. We finished setting up the rigging. The dinghy came back and brought few fish but many penguins, which were distributed to the crew. The commander came to dine aboard. On leaving he said to the captain: "I am spared taking leave of your officers; they have not had the civility to come and salute me." At 6 p.m. a sail was sighted in the east, which was made out to be an English schooner. At 7.30 she anchored near us and her captain came aboard. She was the Cumberland and had left Port Jackson 4 days after us. She was coming to King Island to take off the convicts we had, and was then to go and examine Frederick Hendrik Bay and the North River, where the English intended to form a settlement. She told us that the day after our departure from Port Jackson the Lady Nelson had arrived there, having left the Investigator in 20° of south latitude after bad weather in which he had lost 3 anchors and she all of hers (she had made one of wood). At 8.30 we got under way and shaped our course N 22° 30' E; at midnight the course was given north. An immense fire could be seen on the island at Elephant Bay. Since Port Jackson a wombat, both kangaroos and some birds had died; one of the dogs was injured.

1802-12-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SSE. The rigging was set up and the dinghy hoisted in; the topsails were stopped with rope yarns. The commander came to dine aboard and left at 6. At the same hour a sail was sighted in the east: it was a schooner which had left Port Jackson four days after us. At eight in the evening we got under way and shaped our course. We set about stowing the anchors. At 3 a.m., in sight of the northern coast of the anchorage, we took the bearing of the visible part of King Island, which stretched from S by SE to SSW. King Island at noon SE; the mainland NNW, distant 24 miles. Obs. lat. 39° 19' 55", long. 142° 18' 42".
1802-12-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighteenth of Frimaire (9 December 1802). On the morning of the eighteenth I had my boat put ashore eight men who had hidden themselves, some aboard the Géographe and some on the Naturaliste, when we were on the point of leaving Port Jackson. They were given a bag of bread and some clothing. They were landed with the other Englishmen who are on the island, and who were very ill pleased at their arrival, fearing that they would behave badly towards them. On leaving the ship, they came to beg me to give each of them a knife, but, fearing that they might
make bad use of them, I would not grant their request, on which they insisted a great deal.
Towards nine o'clock a boat came alongside from the schooner that had arrived the day before. At the moment those in it came aboard the Géographe, I was at work in my cabin, and it was not without pain surprise that I saw ushered in an officer of the English Navy, accompanied by a geographer whom I had known at Port Jackson. After we had exchanged compliments on our meeting, I proposed that they breakfast with us, which they accepted. It was then that Mr Roben, who commanded this schooner, handed me a letter from Mr King, Governor of Port Jackson, and, shortly afterwards, his instructions as to what he was to do. After reading Mr King's letter, I read his instructions, which, in all likelihood, are not entirely known to me, for he will not have shown me everything. But the contents of Mr King's letter gave me enough enlightenment to see the motive of his voyage, which had no other object than to watch us. I append here the translation of Governor King's letter:
"To the Commander of the Expedition &c.:
"You will no doubt be surprised to see a vessel so close to you. You knew my intentions of making a settlement to the south, but this has been hastened by the information communicated to me immediately after your departure. This information is that the French intend to make a settlement in the neighbourhood of Storm Bay or in the part called Frederick Henry Bay. It is added that these are the orders you have from the French Republic. This is what Colonel Paterson informed me of after your departure, having himself been told of it by a person from your ship.
"You will readily understand that, had such information been known to me before your departure, I would have asked you for an explanation. But I knew nothing of it, and at present I do not even believe it, and think it a remark lightly hazarded, of which, however, I have thought it proper to inform you in case the Cumberland should happen to meet you. The commander of that vessel is provided with my orders and is enjoined to communicate them to you.
"My family and I wish you everything you can desire and shall long remember the pleasure we have had in your company. We beg you to remember us to all your officers and to Captain Hamelin."
Signed Governor King.
If this letter is not transcribed word for word, it is very nearly what it contains. As I intend to reply to Governor King on this subject in very few words, I was very reserved with these gentlemen who were on board, and contented myself with saying that I fully expected that, after our departure, a good many tales would be told which our presence prevented.
The claim of the English to Van Diemen's Land was strongly asserted in the instructions of the captain of the schooner, but it was founded only on the taking of possession by Captain Phillips, whose limits are set out in what we know from the very beginning of the present settlement. It therefore seems to me beyond doubt that Governor King feared, from what he may have been told, that I might go and put someone on that land to occupy it first, and that it was security
Stay at King Island
that led him to dispatch a vessel to watch us. I was only sorry that the Naturaliste was still found here, because she was handed fresh packets for the English Government, in which no doubt an account is given of the step just taken, as well as of what they believe they have learned. The Naturaliste having left before the Governor's letter reached me, I have been unable to send it in the original to the French Government.
After we had parted, these gentlemen went ashore to see how the work of their countrymen was progressing and to acquaint themselves with the country. I let them know that we dined every day at four o'clock and that they would be welcome whenever they cared to come and share it. They were also informed that I had put ashore eight deserters, in accordance with the promise I had made to Governor King not to carry them off should any be found on board.
The rest of the evening passed without incident. We were busy setting up the tent for the observatory on the Îlot des Éléphants, and preparations were made to carry all the naturalists ashore the next day. During the night the winds were southerly and light.
Of the Eighteenth of Frimaire. (9 December 1802) On the eighteenth, the boats that had come back from shore the day before having found a suitable watering place, the launch was sent there with her complement of empty casks. The longboat also left to carry the savants, their science and their baggage, for these gentlemen go nowhere without pomp and magnificence. The cooks and their utensils, the pots, the saucepans and the cauldrons so encumbered the boat that they could not all be stowed in it and part of them had to be put in the launch. All this paraphernalia put me in such a temper that I went back into my cabin, much displeased that they had not all left on the Naturaliste.
At nine o'clock I sent a boat with an officer aboard the Cumberland to return the visit these gentlemen had paid me. On his return I was informed that during the night they had lost an anchor, their cable having been cut, no doubt, by some coral. Their intention, so I was told, was to ask me for another, but I have none that would suit her. And even if I had, it would not be prudent for me to strip myself of it, for the Casuarina may need one at any moment.
At three in the afternoon the Cumberland's boat came alongside with the captain and Mr Greens, engineer geographer, who was with him. We dined together. The conversation turned on nothing of note, and there was no question at all of the motive of their voyage. But they pointed out to me that, having been dispatched in the greatest haste, they lacked many things, and that someone had even forgotten to give them a little gunpowder. They had, moreover, only one suit of sails, all worn out, and no canvas to mend them if need be, and consequently neither thread nor needles. As they then asked me for several other articles, I invited them to make the request in writing, promising to give them all I could spare without inconvenience. They told me they would not fail to send me this request for the next day. At seven o'clock we parted, and I had them taken back aboard their vessel in one of my boats. The weather was fine all day and during the night, with winds from south to south-east.
1802-12-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ESE to SSW. At 3.30, being abreast of the northern part of King Island, the course was given N 45° W; at 8 it was given S 78° 45' W. King Island bore from us S 11° E to S 22° W. At noon in 39° 19' 55" of latitude observed and in 141° 42' 24" of longitude by account. King Island S 45° E and the mainland N 22° W, 24 miles off; at 6 N 22° E, as far as the eye could reach.

1802-12-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south to SW. At 6 the land of New Holland could still be seen in the NNE as far as the eye could reach. Obs. lat. 39° 1' 5", long. 140° 30' 48".
1802-12-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Nineteenth of Frimaire (10 December 1802). On the nineteenth we went on with the work of replenishing our water. The tents and all the naturalists' great paraphernalia had been landed the day before, so that I found myself rid of them until the moment of re-embarkation. Only M. Bailly, the mineralogist, remains on board, and I hardly know why. I had intended to go ashore in the morning and return in the evening. But at about eight o'clock, the wind having increased, I changed my mind, fearing I might be obliged to get under sail. Although the breeze was fresh and the weather looked as though it would turn bad, it nevertheless cleared up again during the day. When the flood tide was over, the winds fell calm, and the sea, which had been rather rough from the run of the tide, went down likewise.
During the day the schooner the Cumberland got under sail and moved in closer to the coast. I might well have done the same, for the greater convenience of our boats, but I preferred to stay where I was, being better placed for getting under way with winds from the east or south-east.
At nightfall the longboat returned on board with her load of water, that is to say having filled about sixteen casks which served us as butts for the ship's stores.
The night passed without incident, and the breeze died away at about nine o'clock, as it had done ever since we have been at this anchorage.
1802-12-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to SSE. At noon in 39° 3' of latitude by account and in 139° 54' of longitude by account. At 6 an island was sighted in the N 3° E. At 8 the course was given S 67° 30' W. At 9.30 we sounded without finding bottom at 120 fathoms.

1802-12-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds variable from SW, SSE and east. At 6 took the bearing of an island N 3° E. At 9.30 p.m. sounded without finding bottom. Obs. lat. 38° 39' 56", est. long. 137° 31'.
1802-12-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Twentieth of Frimaire (11 December 1802). On the twentieth, the wind being almost calm and the weather very fine, we weighed our anchor, convinced that it must be foul from the turns the ship had made at every change of tide. When we were hove short, the larboard anchor was let go and we weighed the other. As the cable came in on board, it was found to be badly chafed at about twenty fathoms from the clinch. We were all the more vexed at this because it was a new cable going into the water for the first time. When our anchor was awash, we found it not only foul, as we had suspected, but we saw also that the stock was broken, which surprised us greatly. We set about at once getting it inboard to replace the stock, little expecting that it would prove useless to us once it had been placed in the proper position for that work. Only then did we perceive that the palm fitted over the bill of the anchor had come entirely unwelded and was no longer held by anything. This discovery obliged us to condemn it and to bring up another from the hold.
There seems no doubt that the bottom, which the lead everywhere shows to be fine sand, is mixed with patches of coral. And our cable would undoubtedly have been cut had we not examined it in time. Orders were given to worm it for about thirty fathoms from the clinch, so that no such accident should befall it in future. The work I have just described kept our people busy for almost the whole day.
In the morning the Cumberland sent a boat on board to me with a note of what she stood most in need of. Her request was met in full and the following articles were sent to her: a sounding lead, a line of sixty fathoms, a bolt of canvas of one hundred and eight English yards, one pound of sail twine, six needles, and six hasps for padlocks with their staples. The captain also begged me to have an anchor stock made for him. His own being broken, he asked me for a boat to go and sweep for the anchor he had lost. The weather not being suitable for this last task, it was put off to another time, as was his anchor stock, since he had sent no dimensions.
He was also given thirty twelve pounds of powder, as he had not enough on board to fire a musket. During the night the sky was overcast, the weather rainy and the breeze very unsteady from the eastward. The longboat brought her load of water back on board.
1802-12-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to E. At 4 the course given west. At noon in 38° 40' of latitude observed and in 138° 17' of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze.

1802-12-12.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sea getting up a little as the easterly breeze held; the pump sucked at 15 inches. Est. lat. 38° 26' 33", est. long. 134° 14' 0".
1802-12-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind very unsteady from E to N. At noon in 38° 12' of latitude by account and in 135° 23' of longitude by account.

1802-12-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind very unsteady and very variable from east to N and NW. From midnight to 4 a very thick fog. Obs. lat. 38° 41' 17", est. long. 132° 32'.
1802-12-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight in the evening the rock, or rather the islet, which the English have named the Elephants, lay
west-north-west, at an estimated distance of two leagues.
The land was too hazy for us to make out the northern and southern extremities of King Island in sight.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, in the morning, we took on board the water our longboat had brought during the night. My intention was to send her off again at once for a third trip, but the weather had so bad a look that, fearing it might turn seriously foul, I preferred to have her hoisted in, so that she would be safer should I be obliged to get under sail. I took the same precaution with our three other boats which were alongside.
In the course of the morning we set about worming our spare cable, a job which could not be done the day before.
During the evening the sea began to get up and I was inclined to get under sail, but as we had observed that, ever since our arrival on this coast, the wind had always died away after sunset, I thought the same would happen the coming night, and I kept my position.
The schooner the Cumberland had got under sail to move farther into the head of the cove and take in water and wood.
At about half past three I was told that we were dragging, the ship having swung broadside on. But we soon perceived that we were being carried along by the current, our cable having parted. We got under way at once, casting to larboard, and stood on the southerly tack towards the east with winds from the east, which afterwards shifted to east by north-east. As we had a good buoy on our anchor, I was not at all uneasy about it, being quite sure that I should find it as soon as the weather allowed me to return to the anchorage. What had just happened only confirmed me in the view that the spot where we lay at anchor, though clean by the indication of the lead, is by no means so, and that there is a great deal of coral or rock there, thinly covered with very fine sand.
At five o'clock, being a fair distance off the coast, we went about to stand on the northerly tack, and at eight o'clock we were roughly abreast of the rock, or large islet, which the English have named the Elephant. We took its bearing as west-north-west, two leagues distant according to our dead reckoning, which may be in error, since the haze that covered the land did not allow us to do better. After this bearing we held on the northerly tack towards the east as far as the winds allowed. The depth was then eleven fathoms, and I was much astonished that it was not greater at so great a distance from the coast. We nevertheless kept on the same course, sounding often. This course brought us into a tide rip where the sea was very rough and choppy. I had the lead cast at once and we found only six and a half fathoms. We kept on the same course, sounding continually. We then found eight, nine and fifteen, without having run a distance that would suggest the depth should increase so quickly.
For several days I had observed that to the north-east of our anchorage a heavy swell rose from time to time and at times seemed to me to break. On the day I dined on board the Naturaliste, which lay farther to the east than we did, I saw it still better and pointed it out to Captain Hamelin; men were sent aloft to look out, and after watching for a long while they said they could see nothing. But I remained no less convinced that there must be little water in that place, and I
urged him to pay all the more attention to it when he got under sail, since the danger, if danger it is, lay on the course he had to steer.
I therefore remain convinced, from what I have observed of our anchorage and from the little water we found in passing through those parts, that it is prudent to beware of them, and I believe there is even less water to the east of the spot where we found only six and a half fathoms. I fully intend to send a boat to examine this spot as soon as the weather allows, to learn exactly how matters stand.
From fifteen fathoms we passed to 18 and to 22, and at two o'clock in the night we were in fifty.
The night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second was one of the worst we have spent since our departure. The rain was heavy and almost continuous. The winds went several times right round the horizon and obliged us to be continually working our sails. The lightning and thunderclaps were so frequent that it may be said that for more than four hours on end they had no interruption, until the following day. As I spent the night on deck, my sight was so affected by it that towards the end I could make out no object at all.
On the Twenty-second (13 December 1802), at daybreak, the weather was scarcely finer than the day before. We went about at four in the morning to stand on the southerly tack towards the east, so as to keep in the latitude of the island while being far enough to the east to ride out a gale should one come on, as the look of the sky and the behaviour of the barometer, which was below 27 (sic) inches, seemed to foretell. However, as the sea had gone down a good deal, we flattered ourselves that we should get off with a fright, and that in the course of the day the sky would clear. Such sudden changes had already happened several times. What we had foreseen, or rather wished for, came about, for at about eight o'clock the wind began to fall and, having shifted to the north, it dispersed both the clouds and the haze that ringed our horizon.
At eleven o'clock, steering south 87° west, we sighted the land, which then lay from west to west-south-west of us.
At noon we observed 39° 50' 27" south latitude. As the astronomer and the timekeepers were ashore, we had no hour angle for the longitude.
In the afternoon we continued to stand in towards the land. We soon made the islet on which our astronomer Bernier was, and shortly afterwards we saw the schooner the Cumberland at anchor, which astonished us greatly, for the weather of the day before gave no reason to believe she could have remained at her anchorage. So that one may well say that the captain who commands her was more lucky than prudent. Perhaps, too, he could not get under way with easterly winds without running the risk of going ashore, lying as he did right at the head of the cove and about a mile from the land. Be that as it may, his position decided me to approach closer to the coast in the hope that the bottom would be better there, so that I came to anchor in ten fathoms of water, still however on a sandy bottom which could not be good holding ground. But I thought the rocks at the bottom must be covered there by a thicker layer than in 14 fathoms, which had been our first anchorage.
As soon as the ship was moored and our sails furled, the boats were put in the water and I at once sent off the officers Bonnefoy and Ransonnet, the one in my longboat and the other in my large boat, to go and look for the buoy of the anchor whose cable had been cut by the bottom. As we had good bearings of it, it could not be lost.
Each of them was given a signal flag so that they could let us know when they had found it. Immediately after their departure I had our sheet anchor cleared away for letting go and the cable intended for it wormed, in case of need.
For the rest of the evening the weather was very fine and the sea calm, which went a long way towards helping us recover our anchor, which I should have been very sorry to lose.
At seven o'clock we sighted the boat I had sent off under the orders of M. Faure. As she was returning from the south, there was no doubt that she had gone right round the island.
Half an hour later we saw our longboat furl her sails, which led us to conjecture that she was made fast to our buoy, as she signalled to us shortly afterwards.
On the arrival of M. Faure and of the midshipman who commanded the boat, I was informed of the expedition they had just made, but as each of them is to give me a written report of it, I shall speak of it on another occasion.
At midnight our longboat returned on board, but without having been able to weigh our anchor. The same officers who had been charged with this duty were ordered to set out again the next day at first light and not to return on board without bringing it back. During the night the weather was fine and the winds moderate from the north-west.
1802-12-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to SSW by way of west. At noon in 38° 41' of latitude observed and in 133° 59' of longitude by account.

1802-12-14.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a fresh breeze from WSW, SSE and ESE by way of south. At 8 changed tacks; we worked at setting up the main yard slings. Est. lat. 38° 53' 6", long. 131° 46'.
1802-12-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings at the anchorage:
The southern point of the cove south 22° east
The north point north 23 west
The islet north 8° east
The Naturaliste's tents south 18° west
The English fishermen's establishment north 46° west
The schooner the Cumberland abeam of us at one mile. The distance of the ship from the coast: 3 miles.
(continued from page 279) He dined with our scientists, what he had just done not having struck me as an act of courtesy. I do not know whether these were his orders, but it confirmed me in the belief that he had been sent to watch us rather than to hand me the insignificant letter that Governor King addressed to me by this opportunity.
After my return on board, our longboat and the two boats brought back our anchor, which they had had a good deal of trouble in weighing. The precaution had been taken of slipping a shackle down before trying to break it out of the ground, and this was a very prudent measure, for the buoy rope parted twice. As soon as the anchor was on board, it was stowed in its place and bent to the cable at once.
At four o'clock the English schooner got under sail and again sent a boat on board to ask me for the iron hoops I had promised him for his anchor, if they were ready. M. Robbins sent word to me by this opportunity that he was going to look for the anchorage to the north-west of the island, from what he had heard of it from our scientists, to whom the boat's crew had spoken. His four hoops were handed over to him and he went on his way. The winds were then very light from the east, but as the flood tide was in his favour he got away from the coast before nightfall. At sunset the wind continued to freshen, but as the sea had little motion I thought it was only a passing breeze which would not fail to die away at the beginning of the night, as had happened every day since we had been on this coast. Nevertheless, so as not to be hampered should we have to get under way, I had three of my boats hoisted in, leaving out only my longboat, which I meant to make fast to our cable if we had to get under sail.
From eight o'clock to ten the sky was very dark and the winds still from the east but moderate. From time to time a stronger gust passed, which ceased as soon as the cloud that had caused it had gone by the ship. The rain, however, was continuous, but without lightning or thunder, and the sea remained calm.
In spite of so little appearance of bad weather, the wind increased at about ten o'clock, and there began to be fairly strong gusts following one another continually. From that moment I began to fear that we should not be able to remain at anchor. As we could not rely on the bottom, the bell was rung at once to bring all hands on deck and be ready to slip our cable should the ship begin to drag. In spite of this (precaution),
the crew were extremely slow to appear, and more than once men had to be sent below to make them come up. I had already given orders for our longboat to be made fast to the anchor buoy, but it was so long before this was carried out that the ship went adrift before it could be done.
As the current was against us, it was setting us rapidly towards the shore, and we had no more than seven fathoms of water when we had sheeted home our topsails. Happily for us, the winds shifted to the north-east, for otherwise we should have had difficulty in getting clear of the bad position in which we found ourselves.
It is certain that the crew behaved very badly on this occasion, and whether from fear of the rain, which was heavy, or because they did not know the danger we were in, they were very slow in coming up on deck. Once the ship was out of danger, which was soon the case once the sails were set, we turned our attention to our longboat, which there was no longer any means of getting on board, as much because the sea had already become rough as for want of room to stow her, the other boats having been put in the place she should have occupied. We were therefore obliged to veer her astern and tow her by a stout hawser made fast to the crosspiece. As she seemed safe in this position, we kept on our course to stand a little out to sea.
During the rest of the night the weather was very bad. And to have it as we had met with it the day before, only the thunder and lightning were wanting, which did not occur this time.
At about two o'clock, reckoning ourselves far enough out to have nothing to fear, we took the third reef in the topsails, but as we were sounding every half hour, we were very much astonished to find only ten fathoms of water, whereas I expected at least twenty-five from the distance I reckoned we had run to the east-south-east. From then on we sounded continually, and in less than half an hour we passed to eight and seven, which decided me to bear away at once to the south-east, convinced that the flood tide had carried us to the north-east and brought us close to the shoal I have already mentioned. On the south-east course the depth increased markedly; we passed from seven to fifteen. We then hauled our wind again, and shortly afterwards found no more than twelve and then eleven. But as I reckoned myself at the eastern extremity of the shoal and no longer believed myself to be to the west of it, we kept on the same course, sounding all the while so as not to be taken by surprise should the depth go on decreasing. From twelve we came back to fifteen and almost at once to twenty. When we were in twenty-five, having nothing more to fear, I gave orders to continue on the same tack, sounding only every two hours. I then withdrew to my cabin to change, being wet to the bone. The rain continued for the rest of the night and the wind blew very fresh with strong gusts. As the winds were hauling round to the northward, we hoped that fine weather would not be long in coming.
Of the 23rd of Frimaire (14 December 1802). On the twenty-third the longboat and the large boat set off at four in the morning, as had been ordered the day before. At five o'clock both were at the buoy, and we saw from the ship that they were busy weighing it. At seven o'clock a second boat was sent to the island where our observatory was, to bring back four men I had put there to cut hay. She returned on board at ten o'clock, and I sent her off at once to reinforce the men who had gone to weigh my anchor, which we then knew to be up. But as the wind and tide were against them, the longboat could not return.
At about nine o'clock the captain of the English schooner the Cumberland, M. Robben, came on board to ask me to have four iron hoops made for one of his anchors, for which he had the stock. His own having been broken, I gave orders for them to be prepared for him, and he then went ashore. As the weather was very fine in the morning, I decided to go ashore. It was the first time I had left the ship since our arrival on this coast, but I was very glad to see on what and in what manner our scientists, who had been there for several days, were employing their time. I reached the shore at about noon. I found the captain of the English schooner there, which did not surprise me, since he had told me he was going there. But on the other hand I was rather astonished to see an English flag precisely on the spot where our tents were pitched. I thought at first, from the way it was placed, that it was a flag hung out to dry. But having caught sight of a soldier in a red coat with a bayonet in his hand, I inquired what this might mean. Our scientists then told me that about an hour earlier M. Robbins, who had come ashore to dine with them, had placed it in the way I saw it, and that they did not know what it meant, unless it was to let us know that the island belonged to him. I did not think I ought to enter into any explanation on this subject, since it is certain that it was their fishermen who discovered and frequented this island before us. But if the ownership belongs to whoever first went round it, it is beyond question that it is the French.
At two o'clock, the weather not looking good although it was calm, I returned on board and left M. Robbins and his flag quite undisturbed. (continued on page 280)
1802-12-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather with rain, the wind a light breeze from SSW to NE. At 4 the course given N 67° 30' W; a sail was sighted in the S 34° E. At noon in 38° 49' of latitude by account and in 133° 12' of longitude by account. At 2 the wind freshened and was a strong breeze from S to SW.

1802-12-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, continual rain during the watch. The wind light until 2, then a strong breeze from south to SW. Obs. lat. 37° 40' 42", long. 129° 27'.
1802-12-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, as day began to break, it was noticed that our longboat, which we had had in tow all night, was on the point of sinking. I was informed and at once ordered the officer of the watch to heave to and haul her alongside, so as to get her on the tackles and then on board, no matter where. While this manoeuvre was being carried out, which however did not take long, she filled and capsized almost at once. I thought we should get off with the loss of the things that were in her. But it was not to be, for when we tried to haul her alongside, the crosspiece to which the hawser was made fast came away from the longboat, and there is reason to believe that the whole of her bow was smashed. As she was floating on the water, I gave orders to go about so as to close with her and not lose sight of her. But this was of no use, for at that very moment the sheaves that supported and guided the tiller ropes gave way, and the ship could not complete her turn in wearing round and came back again on the larboard tack. A most violent squall followed upon all these mishaps, so that we were obliged to lie to and furl our foresail and topsails as fast as we could, to lie under the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. We at once set about repairing the damage to the tiller, which we were soon able to use again.
After sunrise the wind increased to such a degree that we were very glad to have hove to early, for we should infallibly have lost some sails in furling them. The force of the wind tore so much spray from the crests of the waves that it seemed to be raining continually round the ship, although the sky was fairly clear. This blow lasted without much interruption until noon, when the winds, having varied from north-north-west to west, eased a little and allowed us to set the foresail and the fore topsail, standing on the northerly tack towards the west, having no further hope of meeting with of meeting with (sic) our longboat except by a lucky chance.
In the afternoon the winds varied from west to south-west and were very unsteady, accompanied at times by rain, squalls and strong gusts. The sky nevertheless seemed inclined to clear, and we had it fairly fine at sunset.
During the night the weather was scarcely different from what it had been in the evening; the winds varied little from west by south-west, but they were no less often accompanied by blasts, rain and gusts. Nothing was changed in the sail, and at midnight, being in 39 fathoms, we stood on the southerly tack, which was held until daybreak.
1802-12-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW, with squalls; struck the topgallant masts. At noon in 37° 41' of latitude observed and in 131° 51' of longitude by account.

1802-12-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the wind falling away from SW, W, NW and WSW. At 4 it freshened and the sky clouded over, with a high sea. Obs. lat. 37° 17' 33", long. 128° 45'.
1802-12-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, in the morning, the weather continued squally with strong gusts. However, it appeared from the state of the atmosphere that we should soon have a change in our favour. The sea, though still very heavy and rough, was beginning to go down, and the blasts grew less heavy each time one came upon us. The winds, which had blown steadily from west by south-west, shifted to west by north-north-west at about eleven o'clock and the sky cleared, although the barometer was still low, that is to say below 27 inches.
At noon the latitude was observed as 39° 28' 12", and I was surprised to find myself so far north. From the dead reckoning of the various courses we had steered, we reckoned ourselves to be only in 39° 39' 34", so that we found a difference of 0° 11' 24" farther north than we had reckoned. This error since our departure was attributed to the currents, which we knew to be very strong and very irregular in their directions.
During the evening, the weather being fine, we stood on the southerly tack to regain the latitude of the island. The wind having fallen a good deal, we shook out a reef in the topsails and made more sail.
At noon the lead gave 40 fathoms. At four o'clock it was only (no figures) and at eight, (no figures). We then stood again on the northerly tack, which was held until midnight, and afterwards we returned to the southerly one.
At sunset we did not see the land, to the east of which we doubtless were farther than the dead reckoning showed. The whole horizon to the westward was very heavy and gave warning of some fresh blow for the night. In order to ride it out quietly and without strain, I had the third reef taken in the topsails as a precaution and the other sails that we had set in the course of the evening furled. The precaution I took was not altogether useless, for during the night the weather turned bad and rainy, and there were strong gusts following one another fairly rapidly. The sea, however, did not become very heavy, which led me to believe that we were abreast of the island and not too far out. Had it been otherwise it would have been, as on the preceding days, very rough, heavy and swelling.
1802-12-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather with frequent squalls, the wind a strong breeze from NW to N. At noon in 37° 18' of latitude observed and in 131° 18' of longitude by account. At 1, in a squall, the fore staysail was torn from its stay; it was shifted. At 2 we took the lower reef in the topsails, and at 6 lay to.

1802-12-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather with frequent squalls, a strong breeze from SW. Took all the reefs in the topsails.
1802-12-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth it rained without cease the whole morning, with very violent squalls and strong gusts. We were obliged to furl our mizzen topsail and take the third reef in our topsails. The sea was no less disagreeable than the weather, and several times we shipped seas on board.
At noon we reckoned ourselves by dead reckoning in 39° 50' 6" latitude, but I think we were farther south. Our longitude likewise put us in 142° 29' 6", doubtless farther west than we really are, since we must have drifted a good deal to the east with the wind and sea we have had constantly ever since we left the anchorage. The barometer, which stood at 27° 6 l, gave no sign of any very early change.
In the morning, during a clear spell, the lookouts at the mastheads thought they saw land to the south-west by south. It is possible, but I doubt it. At ten o'clock, having had clear weather and a fairly wide horizon for an hour, we did not see the land to the south-west by south that had been reported to us in the morning, but we made out perfectly, to the south-east by south, two islands and an isolated rock which appeared to lie farther to the west. I have no doubt that these were the islands which belong to King Island and which the Naturaliste had sighted. I was preparing to go and examine them, so as not to waste our time uselessly in beating to windward, but the rain and haze having set in again and the gusts being still more violent, I could not carry out this plan. We were even obliged to furl our fore topsail, so heavy and so thoroughly vicious were the blasts we continually met with.
The depth was then 33 fathoms and we were standing on the northerly tack.
In the afternoon, seeing no sign of any change in the weather, we made ready for the night, which presented a very unpromising aspect. The horizon in every quarter was loaded with thick, stormy vapours that foretold nothing but bad weather for the approaching night, which the darkness of the sky made longer than usual. For by half past seven one could no longer see. However, although the weather was very bad and the blasts in the squalls violent, we got through it better than I had expected. Although the whole horizon was ablaze with continual lightning, not a single thunderclap was heard, and all the clouds dissolved in rain. Several of them gave us fairly thick hail, which was no pleasant thing to receive. Nevertheless we counted ourselves fortunate not to have been more roughly handled.
1802-12-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to WSW. At 9 we filled and stood on, the wind less strong. At noon in 35° 54' of latitude by account and in 131° 0' of longitude by account.

1802-12-18.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the wind a fresh breeze; the wind less fresh at 5.30 and at 9 p.m. Changed tacks. The main topgallant sail and main topsail were repaired, and we took the opportunity to set up the main topmast stay. Obs. lat. 35° 45' 24", long. 128° 23' 6".
1802-12-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh the weather, without being as bad as the day before, was hardly any finer. The winds, which had shifted to west-north-west, varied little and blew hard and in blasts in the squalls, which often gave us hail, though much smaller in size than that of the night before. At midnight we had stood on the southerly tack, which was held until eight in the morning, when we came round to the northerly one, wearing round.
In the morning the sky became fairly fine, but one squall followed immediately upon another. Nevertheless at noon we were able to observe the altitude of the sun, which gave 39° 17' 30". By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 39° 26' 12", which gave us an error of 0° 8' 42" farther north than we had reckoned. The longitude by our dead reckoning was 142° 47' 26".
During the evening the weather, which had been fairly clear in the morning, clouded over again with cloud and haze. At noon we had stood on the southerly tack, and at about three o'clock we sighted a two-masted vessel to the east by north-east. As it might be the Casuarina returning from the Hunter Islands, I gave orders to go and identify her. We accordingly bore down on her and soon came up with her. We then saw that it was not the Casuarina, but the English schooner the Cumberland, which had left the anchorage the same day. When we had identified her at a mile's distance, we stood again on the southerly tack. This vessel was lying to under her mainsail with all reefs in; she hoisted her colours when we had passed her and we answered without stopping. At five o'clock we lost sight of her.
During the night of the 27th to the 28th the weather was as we had had it for four days, that is to say bad, rainy and squally, with thoroughly vicious blasts. Nevertheless the sea seemed to us less bad. At eight o'clock we stood on the northerly tack, which was held until four in the morning, when we trimmed our sails on the southerly one, without the weather having grown any finer or showing any sign of change. Only the barometer stood steadily between 27 7 and 27 8, and although the thermometer was fairly high, this did not prevent our often having hail in the squalls.
1802-12-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 6 we shook out the reefs and rigged the topgallant masts. At noon in 35° 45' of latitude observed and in 130° 55' of longitude by account.

1802-12-19.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea. A fresh breeze from WSW to SW. The main topsail and main topgallant sail being repaired and the backstays and stay set up, we set both sails. At 11 changed tacks. Est. lat. 36° 12' 10", long. 128° 54' 54".
1802-12-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, the sky was very dark and hazy and several squalls gave us plenty of rain, but as the gusts were much less strong than those of the night before, we believed that the bad weather was about to end and that we should have a change in our favour during the day. The sea, which was also beginning to be less heavy, helped to make us believe in this change, which each of us longed for, for we had been tossed about and tormented by the bad weather for a long enough time.
During the morning the sky did indeed clear and the horizon became clear and wide, although the winds were still from the westward; this did not, however, prevent us from meeting from time to time with some fairly smart gusts mixed with rain and hail, but it was a very small matter compared with what had gone before.
At noon the latitude was observed as 39° 42' 51" and we reckoned ourselves in 143° 1' 4" longitude. We were then standing on the southerly tack, and after the observation we changed it for the northerly one. Hardly had we trimmed our sails when a large islet was sighted to the north-east. This sight astonished us at first, as we did not believe we had any land in our neighbourhood. We held on the northerly tack to find out what it was and, as the wind was then much less strong, we shook out a reef in the topsails and set the mizzen topsail. As we advanced to the northward we made out a second islet, and shortly afterwards the coast of New Holland. We could then no longer doubt that the leeway, the currents and the strong wind had thrown us much farther to the west the east than our dead reckoning made it, and we made quite certain, on closing with the coast, that the lands we had in sight were those of Wilson's Promontory, the first islet being the Îlot du Cône and the second the one we had named the Coin de Mire.
