Having made sure of our position, we continued on the northerly course towards the west, the winds having varied to west-south-west. We also sighted the English schooner the Cumberland, which was still farther to the east than we were and was running on the southerly tack.
The weather was fairly fine until about three in the afternoon, but at that time it turned bad again. The sky became loaded with thick clouds, which gave us strong gusts and violent squalls mixed with rain and hail. Although the weather looked very bad, we changed nothing in our sail, so as to get to windward of the land and the islets, in order that the southerly tack, which I intended to take during the night, should be the better for it. At seven in the evening, having had a clear spell, we took a last bearing of the Îlot du Cône, which then lay north 56° east of us, at an estimated distance of seven or eight leagues.
From seven o'clock until ten at night we continued to steer north, edging to the west as much as possible when the winds allowed, but in spite of that the course made good was hardly better than north, so strong was the wind and so bad the sea. We were even obliged to take the third reef in the topsails before going about to the south.
All night the weather was very bad and the squalls violent, always accompanied by rain and hail.
1802-12-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW. At noon in 36° 54' of latitude observed and in 131° 32' of longitude by account. Fine weather and the wind a fresh breeze in the afternoon.

1802-12-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky clear, the horizon thick, a swell running, a fresh breeze from SW. Est. lat. 36° 7' 10", long. 127° 34' 54".
1802-12-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At two in the afternoon,
we sighted the lands of the Promontory, the southernmost of which in sight lay north 28° east
The Îlot du Cône was north 40° east
And Coin de Mire north 73° east
At five o'clock,
The same Îlot du Cône was north 45° east
At six o'clock,
It was north 40° east
And the lands of the Promontory north 20° east
At seven o'clock,
The Îlot du Cône was seen again north 56° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth we had the same weather as the day before, and the squalls were still more frequent. Rain and hail followed each other with such rapidity that I believe the worst winter's day in Europe is finer than this one was. The sea, which had become very heavy, troubled us greatly, and we then shipped a few seas. One of the seamen was knocked over by one and had a fall which may perhaps oblige him to remain a long time in his cot.
As we had a few clear spells between the squalls, we got an observation of the sun at noon, and although it is doubtful, it is surely worth more than what our dead reckoning would have given us. This observation placed us in 40° 27' 5", and according to the bearing of the lands seen the day before, our estimated longitude placed us in 144° 12' instead of the 142° 58' 38" we had reckoned since our departure from King Island.
In the afternoon the weather continued squally, with strong gusts and rain. At times we received some so vigorous that they obliged us to furl our mizzen topsail, for fear of losing the sail or springing the mast. The winds having, towards evening, drawn more southerly in shifting to south-west, we continued on the north-westerly tack, which I intended to hold until midnight if they kept in the same quarter. At sunset, the horizon from south to north being very wide, we saw no land anywhere in the neighbourhood.
During the night the squalls and rain continued without interruption. When they had passed the sky was fairly fine, but the interval between them was so short that one hardly had time to notice it. Only at times they brought the wind round as far as south-south-west, so that I did not take the southerly tack as I had intended, had they not allowed us to lie up to windward of north-west. For the rest, we sounded several times during the night without finding bottom at forty and forty-five fathoms, proof that we were a fair distance from the coast and that the course we had made since noon had carried us a fair way somewhat to the west, in spite of the heavy swell, the leeway and the current.
1802-12-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SW to W. At noon in 36° 7' of latitude by account and in 130° 14' of longitude by account. At 3 a flat calm; at 7 the breeze got up from the NE and drew round to NNE, a fresh breeze. The course was given S 67° 30' W.

1802-12-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm until 7, when the wind made; at 9 it blew a fresh breeze after drawing round to NNE. At 6 a.m. the wind, falling away more and more, drew round to WNW. Est. lat. 34° 54' 4", long. 125° 48' 24".
1802-12-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six in the morning,
The Îlot du Cône lay north 82° east.
At noon,
The lands of the southern extremity of Wilson's Promontory were seen north 85° east
And the northernmost lands in sight extended as far as north 22° 15' west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, in the morning, the weather seemed at last inclined to turn fine, although we still had a few squalls with rain from time to time. They were not to be compared with those we had had during the night, and still less with those of the preceding days. As we had held the north-westerly tack all night, we expected to see the land at daybreak, and indeed we should have made it out had the horizon to the north and east not been very heavy. But at six o'clock, the clouds that hid it from our view having partly dispersed, we sighted the Îlot du Cône, which then lay north 82° east of us, eight or ten leagues distant according to our dead reckoning.
At about seven o'clock, the wind having fallen a good deal, we set the mizzen topsail. Shortly afterwards the mainsail was set, and at about ten o'clock we shook out a reef in our topsails.
During the rest of the morning the sky became quite fine. The clouds and squalls disappeared entirely and everything seemed to herald the return of fine weather, although the winds changed little. The barometer, whose behaviour seldom deceived us, was rising rapidly, which it had not done for a long time.
At noon the latitude was observed as 39° 4' 28". We then had a good view of the west coast of the Promontory, and according to the bearing we took of it, our longitude proved to be 143° 31' 0", not far from Bass's port.
In the afternoon we continued on the north-westerly tack with very variable winds from south-west to west-south-west and the sky still fine, running along the coast at seven or eight leagues' distance. We held this same course until four o'clock, when we stood on the southerly tack.
At sunset the sky, which for the greater part of the day had been fine and clear, clouded over again, but the clouds had not the look of those that bring blasts and hail with them, and so the sky was merely dark and hazy and the wind almost calm until the following day, when we had north-easterly winds. During the night we sounded several times without finding bottom at 45 fathoms.
1802-12-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE; it fell away at 6 and drew round to WNW at 7. Almost calm with continual rain; at 8 the breeze freshened and drew round to NNE, a fresh breeze. At noon in 36° 50' of latitude by account and in 128° 28' of longitude by account. At 2 the wind fell and drew round to the west and then to SSW, a strong breeze; the weather overcast and squally.

1802-12-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather; at 3 squally weather, the wind from W to SSW, a fresh breeze. Obs. lat. 36° 19' 43", est. long. 124° 7' 24".
1802-12-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four in the afternoon,
The lands of the Promontory were seen south 78° east
And the (most) westerly lands north 16° west.
At four in the morning,
the Îlot du Cône was seen north 88° east, and the lands of the mainland north 24° east.
At six o'clock,
the Cône lay to the east at 7 or 8 leagues' distance.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Nivôse, in the morning, the winds having shifted to the north-east, a light breeze, we steered south-west to go in search of King Island and recover the anchor and cable we had left there. I also expected to meet the Casuarina there, as she should have returned from her cruise by the time I had set for her.
Throughout the morning we had a hazy sky and an almost continuous light rain. At daybreak, when the sky was less dark, we had sighted the lands of the Promontory. And at six o'clock, in a momentary clear spell, we took the bearing of the Îlot du Cône, which then lay to the east of us, at 7 or 8 leagues' distance. We attributed our sighting that morning of lands which our dead reckoning placed out of sight to the currents, which during the calm of the previous night must have carried us to the east.
At noon we had no observation of latitude. By our dead reckoning it should have been 39° 31' 34", according to the reduction of the various courses we had steered, and the longitude 142° 59'. But according to the bearing of the land we could only be in 38° 58' latitude and 143° 48' 36" longitude, which was very different from our dead reckoning.
In the afternoon the weather was the same as in the morning, but a pleasant breeze blew from north-east to east-north-east and we made good way until six o'clock, when we sighted the land of King Island, which lay to the west of us. We were astonished to come upon this island so soon, since we reckoned ourselves still ten or twelve leagues from it, a distance to which our horizon could not extend, owing to the state of the atmosphere. But the land was too recognisable to be mistaken. Nevertheless several persons maintained that what we saw could only be the lands of the mainland or some new islands lying to the north-west of King Island. Ridiculous as this assertion was, several remained convinced of it. Be that as it may, I continued to run along the coast of King Island until eight in the evening, and then stood on the northerly tack, which was held for the greater part of the night, that is to say until four in the morning, although it was believed that we were running into the Great Bay in which Port Phillip lies.
During the night the weather was fairly fine and the winds very unsteady from east to east-south-east; we sounded every hour and had almost regularly a depth of 27 fathoms without the slightest change.
1802-12-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 36° 20' of latitude by account and in 126° 48' of longitude by account.

1802-12-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea with a little swell, a fresh breeze from south to SE which drew round to NE. Obs. lat. 36° 39' 52", est. long. 123° 12' 20".
1802-12-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At five in the afternoon,
we sighted King Island lying to the W. SW,
At eight in the morning,
its two extremities in sight lay from south 50° west to south 85° west.
At noon, being at anchor, the bearings of the anchorage were taken as follows:
The islet of Elephant Rock north 8° east.
The land at the watering place south 36° west.
The fishermen's establishment north 12° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second, in the morning, the weather being fine and the horizon very wide, we saw King Island again, lying west-south-west of us at an estimated distance of eight to nine leagues. As the winds were from east-south-east to south-east, I had no wish to go to the anchorage, in spite of my desire and need to recover my anchor and cable. However, I decided to go there in order to make sure at least whether the Casuarina, which according to her instructions should have returned, was not there waiting for me. Our scientists, whom I had left ashore, were also short of bodily sustenance, for one does not live on molluscs, nor even on seals, which are there in great numbers. All these reasons therefore made me once more run the chance of seeing the weather change or of having to put to sea again. I therefore gave orders to steer for our former anchorage, so as to be better placed to recover our anchor with the ship, having no longboat left to go and fetch it.
At noon precisely, having reached the bearings that were to serve us as marks, we anchored in eight and a half fathoms, a very short distance from our buoy. But as the anchor did not bring the ship up at once, the current made us drift about half a league to the south. As soon as our sails were furled, our three boats were put in the water. One was intended to fetch the astronomer from the islet where our observatory had been set up; the second was sent ashore to make our scientists strike camp immediately and bring them on board without the slightest delay; the third, finally, went to make fast to our buoy, which she did not find until shortly before sunset. As soon as she was on it, we got under way with the ship and went and anchored in such a way as to weigh it with the ship. In the meantime the boats returned from their errands, and our astronomer, his baggage, his instruments and his person were taken on board. The boat sent for the other scientists was not so fortunate and came back without having been able to land, so heavy was the swell and so high the surf on the bar. I shall have occasion elsewhere to speak of the difficulties this cove presents for landing, even when the weather is fine and the winds are in the westerly quarter, and so I shall say nothing of them for the moment.
The rest of the day and the greater part of the night were spent on our anchor, which we at last succeeded in breaking out of the ground, together with our cable, which proved to be only slightly damaged. It was half past two in the morning when everything was on board. This long delay was caused by the difficulty of getting a shackle on, owing to the strength of the current. For the rest, the night was very fine and the breeze from the south moderate, although at times fairly strong gusts passed.
I was very sorry not to find the Casuarina at this anchorage, and I was not without anxiety about the accidents that might have befallen her if she was among the islands at the time the gale began.
1802-12-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SE to NW by way of east. At noon in 36° 40' of latitude observed and in 125° 54' of longitude by account. From 9 to 10.30 we passed through immense shoals of fish spawn.

1802-12-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the wind almost calm and very variable. At 8 p.m. it freshened. From 9 p.m. until 10.30 we were surrounded by a great quantity of fish spawn. Obs. lat. 37° 25' 29", est. long. 121° 54' 20".
1802-12-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
At anchor. King Island.
On the third, the wind being almost calm and the sky very fine, I sent off a boat at first light to fetch our savants with their baggage and their collections. I was persuaded that the fine weather of the night must have calmed the surf and that it would be easy to embark them. Nor was I disappointed in my expectation. They all arrived at about nine o'clock, with the exception of M. Péron who, seeing nothing but molluscs at every step he takes, had amused himself by missing the first boat, doubtless counting on returning in the second, which I had sent off with the carpenters and the engineer Ronsard to cut timber fit for building the new longboat that I intended to have built partly on board, so that it would only need to be put together when we should have a favourable opportunity.
In the course of the morning, the master who presides over the establishment of the English sealers in this cove came on board to be repaid for the provisions he had supplied to our savants during my absence, and in this way I learned that they had suffered no more from hunger than we had, which gave me great pleasure. I gave this sealer, whose name is Cooper, fifty pounds of biscuit, a demijohn of rum, twenty pounds of sugar, three pounds of tea and six bottles of red wine. I also bought from these people a few emus or ducks, a male kangaroo, highly prized, and three wombats. They spent part of the morning on board.
In the afternoon, the winds having varied from south-south-west to south-south-east, the breeze freshened considerably, and the sealers told me that I must expect a strong breeze for the night. I had certainly no intention of passing it at anchor, but what they told me made me hasten my departure. I at once recalled my boat by a gun and had the topsails hoisted when the English sealers left us. I handed M. Cooper my reply to M. King, Governor at Port Jackson, to the letter he sent me by the Cumberland. As soon as my boat arrived, we hoisted it in and got under sail; it was then six o'clock in the evening.
During the night the weather was not fine, but we had a very moderate breeze from the south-south-east. I shaped my course so as to make the Hunter Islands in the course of the following day, where I hoped to meet the Casuarina in the channel that separates them from King Island, being unable to conceive how, in spite of my orders both verbal and written, she had not returned, since I had fixed the time by which she was to do so and she had had fair winds for three days past.
1802-12-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 37° 25' of latitude observed and in 124° 34' of longitude by account.

1802-12-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, the wind a light breeze. In the forenoon set up the main topgallant mast. Saw weed. Obs. lat. 38° 24' 36", est. long. 120° 52' 20".
1802-12-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock in the evening,
The northern extremity of King Island lay north 10° west,
the islet north 32° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, in the morning, the winds, which had gone round in the night to east-north-east, brought us a very thick fog that lasted, without much interruption, the whole day. Although the breeze was very moderate, we nevertheless found the sea very heavy and driven by a swell from the south-west, which seemed to announce that we should soon have the wind from that quarter.
At noon there was no observation of latitude; that by dead reckoning placed us in 40° 12' 32", and we reckoned 142° 46' 42" of longitude.
This day work was begun on the frames of our new longboat, which I intend to have continued without interruption so that it need only be put together at the first suitable place that may present itself. The carpenters charged with this work were excused from standing the night watch on condition that they worked all day.
In the afternoon the weather continued very foggy; the winds went round to the east and were very variable, now towards the north, now towards the south. We were often becalmed, with light cat's-paws from time to time. We were standing close-hauled on the larboard tack. At half past five, the fog having lifted for a moment, we sighted a small island of little extent but high. This land was taken in bearing at six o'clock from south 20° west to south 40° west. As the current was setting us strongly to the southward and eastward, we passed very close to it. At seven o'clock we sighted from the deck a fairly extensive line of breakers, which lay south 42° east of us. These breakers served to identify the island for us as the one the English have named Albatross Island. As our position was not very pleasant, since it was almost calm and the ship scarcely answered her helm, an anchor was got ready to let go in case of need. The breeze then coming from north-north-east to east-north-east, we went about and saw Albatross Island a second time, being at most two leagues from it in 31 fathoms of water, bottom of coarse reddish sand. While the calm lasted, which it did until ten o'clock in the evening, we sounded every hour to make sure whether the current was setting us towards the land or out to sea, but we saw with pleasure that the depth was increasing.
At ten o'clock, the winds having come to the west, variable to west-south-west, we stood on the northern tack, which we held until four o'clock in the morning. During the night there was little wind; we had fog constantly and great dampness, with little wind.
1802-12-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NW to SW. At noon in 38° 25' of latitude observed and in 123° 32' of longitude by account. At 8 a flat calm; at midnight it freshened from the north.

1802-12-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather. At 1.15 changed tacks. At 4 a.m. overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze. Saw kelp pass alongside. Obs. lat. 38° 38' 17", long. 119° 35' 26".
1802-12-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At half past five,
having sighted land through the fog, it was taken in bearing,
at six o'clock, from south 28° west to south 40° west.
We also sighted the reef awash on which the sea was breaking heavily, lying SE ¼ E.
The land in sight was the Albatross Island of the English and the reef that lies to the east of it.
At daybreak we sighted Three Hummock Island, which we came to examine.
Historical events & remarks.
On the fifth, at daybreak, we went about to go in search of the Hunter Islands and cruise about in their neighbourhood, to see whether we might not sight the Casuarina, whose delay surprised me more and more. Steering south-south-east, we made the land early and saw clearly that it was not that of the day before, even though, by the dead reckoning of our course, we could not have been far from it. As we approached it, we recognised that it must be Three Hummock Island, which was afterwards confirmed.
During the morning we had the finest weather in the world and a pleasant breeze from the south-west. It was, beyond dispute, the finest day we had had since our departure from Port Jackson.
At noon the latitude was observed as 40° 18' 52", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 143° 0' 31". This longitude proved to be the same as that given on the English chart, or at least the difference is so slight that it deserves no remark. At about ten o'clock in the morning we had sighted the lands of Van Diemen, and no doubt those which bear the name of Circular Head, which must have been given it from the shape it presents to the eye. As I wished to make sure whether the Casuarina was not inside this island, at the anchorage indicated by Mr Flinders, we continued to run along the coast of Three Hummock Island at a short distance, and we were on the point of doubling its eastern point when the winds headed us, which obliged us to stand on the north-west tack.
In the afternoon, the winds having gone round from south-west, variable, to south-south-west, I expected to be able to range along the land fairly easily in order to make the islands to the west of this one, which we had in sight; but the flood tide that set in carried us so fast to the northward that we saw them only from very far off, and could scarcely make them out from the deck. From the mastheads, however, Albatross Island could be seen very well, together with the reef marked on the plan.
At five o'clock, being about midway across the channel that lies between King Island and Three Hummock Island, we sighted the former, which could be seen distinctly. We continued to steer close to the wind, approaching King Island, and at seven o'clock we saw on the horizon to windward a large hummock-shaped islet, which was taken in bearing south 6° west.
It would appear that this islet is one of those lying to the south of King Island which Captain Hamelin had sighted. As I have sent the Casuarina to examine them, and as night was moreover coming on, I continued to stand towards King Island until nine o'clock in the evening, when I went about to stand for a time to the south. During the night the weather was very fine and we spent part of it becalmed.
1802-12-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NW. At midnight the course west. At noon in 38° 39' of latitude observed and in 122° 16' of longitude by account.

1802-12-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy. A strong breeze in gusts and squally. At 1 a.m. wore onto the port tack; at 5 changed tacks. At 11 a.m. we had a squall which forced us to reef the topsails and let the main sheet fly. Est. lat. 39° 13' 41", est. long. 118° 50' 56".
1802-12-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the visible part of the Hunter Islands lay from south 44° east to south 27° east.
At seven o'clock,
the two visible extremities of King Island lay from west 5° south to west 34° north.
An islet could then be seen south 6° west, at an estimated distance of eight leagues.
At noon,
off the middle of the Baie des Eléphants [Sea Elephant Bay], waiting for the Casuarina.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, in the morning, the weather continued fine, and the winds were in the eastern quarter, variable to east-north-east, a light breeze. We steered to close with King Island and come once more to anchor in the Anse aux Eléphants. My intention was, if I did not find the Casuarina there, to leave for her two or three casks of biscuit, which she might need, and to continue at once on my way to Kangaroo Island, informing her of the place where she would find me on that coast.
As the breeze was very light throughout the morning, we made slow progress, and it was nearly eleven o'clock when we were at the entrance of this cove. Shortly afterwards there appeared, at the northern extremity of the cove, a small vessel under sail, which we soon recognised as the Casuarina.
As soon as we were sure it was she, the signal to close was made to her, which she answered. But as the current was against her, she was carried rapidly to the southward, which greatly delayed our meeting, and this could not take place until about four o'clock in the afternoon. As soon as we were alongside each other, I had a boat lowered to go and fetch our geographer, who was on board her, and addressed the following letter to Citizen Freycinet:
The Commander, etc. … to Citizen Freycinet on board the Casuarina,
"We are going to make for Kangaroo Island, situated, in its eastern part, in 35° 39' 50" of "south latitude and 142° 13' 3" 135° 58' of east longitude. This island is easy to recognise by its "extent from east to west, which is about 30 leagues, and the latitude I give you is that of its "north-eastern part. There are a few islets to the east of this island which must be guarded against in approaching it. But "as they are high, they are always seen in time enough to avoid them. It is on the eastern coast that "I intend to look for an anchorage, and there I appoint you a rendezvous in case of separation during the short "passage we have to make to get there.
"The mainland in this part is high and very clear of dangers, and it is to be approached in "preference to the islets, although these are equally very steep-to. It is from the north-eastern part of this "island that the two gulfs begin of which you have heard, and which are found on the mainland".
Your fellow citizen, N. B.
On the return of the boat that carried this letter and brought back Citizen Boulanger, I was informed that M. Freycinet was in need of water, having been obliged to empty his casks to get afloat in the two groundings he suffered while visiting the Hunter Islands and a large bay of Van Diemen's Land, in trying to make sure whether or not there existed a river of which he believed he had seen signs. A little water was sent to him at once, and we continued on our course to pass to the south of King Island. As several lands were seen to the south of that island at nightfall, I would not enter the channel, so as to identify them the following day. We accordingly spent the night beating about, with very variable winds from the eastern quarter, now north-east and now south-east. The breeze was fresh during the night and the sky very hazy. At eleven o'clock we lost sight of the Casuarina, in spite of all our care to keep her in view.
1802-12-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from WNW to WSW, with rain and hail. At noon in 39° 9' of latitude by account and in 120° 49' of longitude by account. At 1.30 struck the topgallant masts and lay to.

1802-12-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the horizon thick, with light hail at intervals. The sea rather high. The lee sheet of the main topsail being about to give way, we clewed the sail up. At 1.30 a.m. furled the topsails and hoisted the mizzen staysail; the weather overcast and squally with hail at intervals. At 4 wore ship; at 6 filled and stood on, taking two reefs in each topsail. The weather having cleared, we set the mizzen and the main jib and shook out one reef in each topsail. Obs. lat. 39° 18' 30", obs. long. 119° 20' 0".
1802-12-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At noon,
off the Anse aux Eléphants [Sea Elephant Bay], waiting for the Casuarina.
At seven o'clock,
the south-eastern lands of King Island lay north 18° west.
A small islet could be seen south 5° west.
From the mastheads other lands could be made out to the S. SE.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, in the morning, the sky was so foggy that our horizon scarcely extended half a league. It blew very fresh. We did not sight the Casuarina, and unless she had been very close to us it would hardly have been possible to see her. At six o'clock, seeing no sign of any change in the weather and wishing to profit by the fair wind to proceed to Kangaroo Island, I had the ship steered west, and we entered the strait, passing to the south of King Island and also, according to my reckoning, to the south of the islands that lie in that channel. At half past nine, the fog being still very thick and so dense that one could see nothing, I had the ship hove to in order to sound, so as to learn by this means whether we were well advanced in the channel or in the neighbourhood of some land unknown to us. The sounding was thirty-six fathoms, and I was surprised not to find it greater. When we got under way again, I had her steered west-south-west so as not to go further to the north, being persuaded that in our position there was nothing to fear in giving my course some southing. At ten o'clock we saw, not without astonishment, the sky suddenly clear and turn fine. We at once sighted King Island, which lay from north to north 40° west of us, at a distance of seven or eight leagues. We then resumed our north-westerly course, edging to the north, and made good way. From the mastheads no land was seen from south-east to south-west.
In the course of the morning, Citizen Boulanger, who had been sent to the Hunter Islands, gave me an account of what he had done in the mission with which I had charged him; but as he and Citizen Freycinet are to make me a detailed written report of it, I shall speak of it on another occasion. He also informed me that they had arrived at the Anse aux Eléphants the day before, and that the Casuarina had lost an anchor there, having no line on her buoy on her anchor. He assured me that the Casuarina had in no way suffered in the two groundings she had had, but that this vessel made a great deal of water through her upperworks when the sea was heavy.
In the afternoon the weather became overcast again and did not look fine for the rest of the day. The fair wind we had had all morning veered by degrees to the north and ended by going round to the west, which made us stand on the southern tack. At noon the latitude of 40° 14' 31" had been observed, and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 141° 38' 27". We had recognised before this time that King Island was placed much too far to the east west in the position the English give it. Its shape is also very different from what they show.
While standing on the southern tack, we sighted the Casuarina to the north-east. We went about to close with her, and the winds having gone round to the south-west, once we had joined her, we steered on the north-west tack.
At sunset it began to blow a fresh breeze. We took two reefs in the topsails and, during the night, which was tolerably fine, did everything necessary to keep that vessel in sight. We found the sea running so high that the ship laboured a great deal in it. We sounded at eight o'clock and at midnight without finding bottom at 70 fathoms.
1802-12-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At 6 filled and stood on. The weather cleared and the wind fell. At noon in 39° 20' of latitude observed, 119° 20' of longitude observed and 121° 31' of longitude by account.

1802-12-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, a swell running. Bent the storm staysail and the repaired main staysail. At 7 p.m. went onto the starboard tack. Saw kelp pass alongside. Obs. lat. 39° 23' 42", obs. long. 118° 15' 0".
1802-12-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock in the morning, the lands of the western part of King Island could be seen to the north-east at a great distance.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighth (written in another hand: nivôse), at four o'clock in the morning, we stood once more on the tack towards the north by west, because at midnight, the Casuarina not answering our signals, we judged her to be astern and making very little way on account of the heavy swell then running, which we had all that day. We did indeed close with her on this course. In the morning the winds went round from west-south-west to south-south-west and became favourable to us (sic) course. We made the most of them that we could, but we advanced little, the breeze being very light.
In the course of the morning I was in a very bad temper on learning that five of the men I had put ashore on King Island had come back on board. As this caused me extraordinary consumption of provisions, I ordered that they should be fed at the expense of the boatmen who had been sent ashore on the ship's service, being persuaded that it was they who had furnished them with the means of returning on board by taking them into their boats. This order was revoked that same day, when I had proof to the contrary and was assured that they had been brought back by the boats of the sealers, who came on board several times on the pretext of selling us emus, wombats and kangaroos, which I did indeed buy from them.
At noon the latitude was observed as 39° 59' 52", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 141° 7' 29". At daybreak it was thought that King Island had been sighted to the north-east, which is very doubtful, although the horizon was very extensive and the thing possible.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the sea still extremely heavy, which showed that some gale from the south-west had lately passed over it. The winds varied to the south, and towards evening they went round to the south-east.
During the night the breeze was fresh and we made good way, steering since noon north 67° 30' west, a course we held until the following day. As this course brought us little nearer the land, no soundings were taken during the night.
1802-12-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NNW. At noon in 39° 24' of latitude observed and in 118° 15' of longitude observed.

1802-12-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze. At 5 a.m. continual rain and the look of squalls. Est. lat. 39° 52' 30", est. long. 115° 50' 38".
1802-12-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and we had a pleasant breeze from the south-east, which we turned to account to advance to the north and west. The slow sailing of the Casuarina compared with ours made us lose a great deal of time and distance in waiting for her; but this little vessel was too necessary to me for the survey of the two gulfs, which I did not wish to leave incomplete, for me not to wait for her. All day long we again had a very heavy swell from the south-west, which tried us greatly, and more than once I feared damage to my masts, so violent and so frequent were the motions of the ship.
At noon we observed the latitude of 38° 51' 1", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 137° 55' 29". This position, laid down on the English chart, put us at a short distance from the land. To make sure of it before nightfall, I had the ship steered north, but we did not sight it, and I am persuaded that the plan they have drawn of the part of the coast along which we were running is as defective in its latitudes as in its longitudes. We were already certain of the second of these errors from their position of King Island, which is 30 minutes further west than it ought to be. And we (are) now equally convinced that the latitude they have given for the island I named Île des Alouettes lies eleven minutes further south than it should. The latitude we observed on that island in very fine weather cannot be doubtful, since we had it to the east of us, at a distance of one league at most, when we observed 38° 27' 32". It is probable that their chart was drawn from the dead reckoning of the courses they sailed rather than from astronomical observations or from continuous bearings taken at a short distance from the coast.
From four o'clock to eight o'clock, having steered north to make the land, we nevertheless did not see it, and had the English chart been accurate we should certainly have sighted it. At the same time, that is to say at eight o'clock, I had the lead cast, and we found bottom in fifty fathoms. Although the wind was very fair for making way during the night, I would not advance any further to the west, and still less to the north; I therefore preferred to stand on the south-south-west tack under little sail, putting off closing with the land until the next day, should the winds continue fair for us. The Casuarina was signalled to follow our manoeuvre, and we kept her in sight all night. At ten o'clock and at midnight we no longer had bottom at 70 fathoms.
1802-12-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind from N to WNW. At noon in 39° 39' of latitude by account and in 116° 8' of longitude by account.

1802-12-31.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth enough, a fresh breeze; about 9 it freshened. At 4 blowing hard; from 4.30 until 5 clewed up the main topsail by degrees to take the second reef and sheeted home again at once. Obs. lat. 41° 16' 35", est. long. 114° 43' 44".
1802-12-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, in the morning, we had a very overcast sky and great dampness. Nevertheless, the winds varied but little and held fairly steadily in the south-eastern quarter, shifting now towards the east and now towards the south. The breeze was light during the morning and we advanced little.
At daybreak we steered north-north-west to close with the land. At about eight o'clock the weather turned fine and we then had a fairly extensive horizon, without sighting it.
At noon the latitude was observed as 37° 47' 10", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 137° 47' 2". Shortly afterwards the land was seen from the mastheads to the north-east, and it was not long before we saw from the deck the sand dunes that form this part of the coast, which made us steer a little more towards the west, as we considered it useless to run once more into deep bays that offer neither interest nor any remarkable feature. Nevertheless, several columns of smoke were seen rising abeam of us, which announced the presence of some inhabitants.
In the afternoon the lookouts at the mastheads announced land to the west by south. We were greatly surprised at this report, having seen none on that point of the compass when we visited this coast for the first time. The sky was not fine at the time and the horizon was laden with vapours. When the direction of the reported land had been pointed out, everyone thought they recognised it, and I was deceived like the rest, for I was persuaded, and even longer than the others, that it was land. I accordingly had the ship steered west at once and crowded all sail to get a good view of it before nightfall, so as to be able to examine it the next day, since the capes, the points and various other features of this land could be seen very well, and were covered from time to time with mist only to show themselves again in the same form in which they had first appeared. At length night came on, with us still steering west and keeping the hope of discovering by means of the lead, during the night, the land we were persuaded we had seen. This hope vanished, for after steering west until midnight without finding bottom, I was undeceived of the error I had been in, and remain persuaded that it was only a bank of fog that we had seen fixed for a long time on the horizon, and not land, which we should certainly have sighted on our first visit to this coast.
During the night the winds, which at about eight o'clock in the evening had come to south-south-west, went round to south-south-east, very light; we continued, as I have said, on a westerly course until midnight, when, having lost all hope, we steered north-west, which course was held until daybreak. The sky was very overcast and damp and the sea calm.
1802-12-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from NNW to W. At 7 lay to. The port anchor was stowed and its cable unbent. At noon in 41° 17' of latitude observed and in 114° 47' of longitude by account. At 1.30 filled and stood on.

1803-01-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, a high sea, a strong breeze in gusts. At 1.35 wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 39° 47' 50", obs. long. 113° 50' 0".
1803-01-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At four o'clock,
the land in sight extended from north 13° east to south 88° east.
At seven o'clock,
it could be seen from north 10° east to north 67° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, the sky, though dull and overcast, was tolerably fine. We had the winds from the south, variable towards the east, very light. In the course of the morning we steered north to make the coast of New Holland, so as then to run along it and come at Kangaroo Island by its eastern part. The weather turned fine during the morning and the clouds dispersed. At that time it was thought that land could be seen from the mastheads, but we did not sight it from the deck.
At noon the latitude was observed as 36° 49' 16", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 136° 39' 15". We found a considerable difference between the latitude by dead reckoning and the observed one, which we attributed to the speed and direction of the currents, which had carried us to the northward far beyond our reckoning.
In the afternoon the breeze was light and the winds still variable in the southern quarter towards the east. We continued on a northerly course until about eight o'clock in the evening without sighting any land, from which, however, we could not have been very far off.
At ten o'clock at night, the officer of the watch, who had orders to sound every hour because we were steering north by west, found bottom in 33 fathoms, which made me trim the sails close-hauled on the tack towards the south by west, knowing that in this part one is very (close) to the coast with such a depth of water. This officer, who thinks himself more experienced than the others, did not warn me that we were in soundings; but as I was not asleep, I had heard the report made to him by the chief helmsman, who had taken the sounding. As the order was to inform me in such a circumstance, I had him called and asked him for what reason he had not warned me that we were in soundings, and in 33 fathoms. His answer was that he intended to report to me on his watch at midnight. Had you continued on the same course, I answered him, you would surely have announced to me that the ship was ashore, for your knowledge does not yet go so far as to remind you that, in the place where we are, the soundings do not extend far out to sea. He then wished to enter into some details to prove to me that he was right, but I ended the conversation by ordering him to go about on the southern tack at once, and not to fail a second time to carry out the orders he received.
The rest of the night passed without incident, except that we had a damp sky and a narrow horizon.
1803-01-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At noon in 39° 48' of latitude observed and in 113° 22' of longitude observed.

1803-01-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running and the wind a fresh breeze. The weather having cleared, we made more sail. In the forenoon unbent the starboard anchor and stowed it. Obs. lat. 38° 29' 52", obs. long. 112° 45' 54".
1803-01-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak, Kangaroo Island was made out, lying to (the) N. NW.
At noon, the extremities of this island in sight extended from north 68° east to south 50° west
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, in the morning, we had an exact view of the mainland of New Holland, as well as of the south-eastern part of Kangaroo Island. At daybreak we found ourselves about three leagues from land, with a perfect view of the channel, of Cap l'Etoile and of the point inside which I had anchored during our first survey of this coast.
As I had lost my longboat in the manner I described at the time that accident befell me, and as the one being built on board was as yet but little advanced, I decided to carry out the geography of the southern part of this island with the ship. I accordingly gave orders to M. Freycinet, who commands the Casuarina, to follow us, keeping as close to the land as he could, and to visit every inlet that might seem likely to offer anything of interest. In accordance with these arrangements, we ourselves closed with the south-eastern point of Kangaroo Island and began our bearings at (no figures) o'clock in the morning, starting from that point.
During the morning the weather was fine and the breeze moderate, but the winds were in the southern quarter, which could not much advance the work of this day if, as we had reason to believe, the coast ran in that direction.
During the morning, the lands along which we ran are tolerably high and end at the sea in a slope that is not extremely steep. The whole ground is sandy and bare of trees. Only here and there are a few tufts of low heath to be seen, which are the sole ornament of these parts. It falls far short of the pleasant aspect of the shore that faces it to the north.
At noon the latitude was observed as 35° 52' 6", and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 135° 41' 42".
During the afternoon we entered a large bay which, at first, by its direction, had seemed to promise us a happy discovery and shelter from the winds from S. W. to north; but we found nothing but a low sandy coast in this part, devoid of all vegetation. To lengthen our board, we ranged along the coast at two miles and often less. It is clear and presents no danger except close inshore, where landing did not appear practicable with the southerly winds then prevailing. The current seemed to us very strong all along this coast, setting to the north-east. I think we were then at the time of the flood.
At two o'clock we made a short board out to sea to get an offing from the coast, from which we were no more than a mile and a half at most. At half past three, having gone back on the inshore tack, we closed with the eastern shore of this large bay, whose south point or cape the direction of the wind did not allow us to weather.
The night was spent beating about with winds from the same quarter and fine weather. We covered about ten leagues of coast this day without meeting anything of interest on it, except that one of the highest hills in this part presents to the eye a summit made entirely of sand, on which a few clumps of greenery are seen here and there. It is a very good landmark for those whom chance may bring to this coast.
1803-01-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from W to WNW. The starboard anchor was stowed and its cable unbent. At noon in 38° 30' of latitude observed and in 112° 46' of longitude observed. A flat calm at 10.

1803-01-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock, the lands of Kangaroo Island in sight extended from SW ¼ W to north 70° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, we resumed the geographical work on the southern exit of Kangaroo Island that we had begun the day before. After exactly identifying our last bearings, we ran along the coast to double a projecting point that hid the other lands to the west from us. When we had doubled it, we sighted the rock lying offshore, about a league and a half from the coast, on which the sea was breaking in an extraordinary manner. Not knowing whether there was a passage between this islet and the main coast, I hauled my wind to pass to the south of it, but was obliged to make a board out to sea, having been unable to weather it.
The channel separating it from the main coast appears fine and convenient, to judge by appearances. As the Casuarina passed inside, she will be able to (tell) us what the depth of water may be, if indeed she sounded, which is very doubtful.
Having doubled this rock to the south, we closed with the coast once more and continued our work. During the morning the weather was fine and at times a pleasant breeze blew. To profit by it, we rigged our topgallant sails and at once set them.
At noon the latitude was observed as 36° 5' 53", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 135° 14' 50". From the latitude observed this day and the one we already knew for the northern part of this island, it was not difficult for us to judge that it was of little breadth from north to south, and was, so to speak, no more than a very narrow tongue of land compared with its length.
In the afternoon we found the sea very heavy and tossed about in several directions, which made our progress slow. Nevertheless we made tolerably good way to the west, in the hope of rounding this island at its western end before nightfall.
At about three o'clock the lookouts at the mastheads announced that they could see two fairly large islets ahead of us and (a) large reef to windward, on which the sea was breaking as violently as on the one we had doubled in the morning. We soon sighted the reef and the islets from the deck. We were astonished to find such a danger so far offshore and so isolated, which led me to believe that it might well be joined by a chain of underwater rocks to the two islets we had in sight, with which it seemed to lie in the same line. I judged it proper to pass to the south of it; we accordingly trimmed close-hauled. On approaching this danger we recognised that it was a cluster of rocks awash, whose extent east and west may be a mile and a half in length. We passed very close to it in doubling it. The channel with the islets looks good, but I do not advise entering it, for supposing the water there to be deep, one would be in great difficulty if caught by a calm.
The two islets I have just spoken of lie precisely at the western end of this island, which from this point at once takes a north-westerly direction, as will be seen from the plan.
At sunset the lookouts at the mastheads announced land to the west and several islets to the south-west, but I doubt the existence of both the one and the other, because the horizon was then laden with a great deal of vapour. However, to make sure of it, I made way during the night towards the points of the compass indicated, persuaded that the lead would announce this land to me if it existed. At eight o'clock we were at most one league from the north-west coast of Kangaroo Island and we
(In the left margin, written vertically) stood on the south-west tack, having 52 fathoms of water. At nine o'clock we no longer found bottom at seventy, nor at midnight at a hundred fathoms, which confirmed me in the belief that there was no land in the quarter reported. However, as several people declare they saw it clearly, I shall come back to look for it when the work on the gulfs is finished. The rest of the night passed without incident.
1803-01-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW; at 11 a flat calm. Saw porpoises. At noon in 38° 3' of latitude observed and in 112° 33' of longitude observed. The mainsail and the mizzen topsail were shifted and the topgallant masts rigged. At 7 the breeze got up from the ENE; the course was given N 67° 30' W.

1803-01-04.journal_anonyme: A flat calm, fine weather, a swell running. The mainsail and mizzen topsail were shifted and the storm staysail repaired. At ten the breeze got up and we made all sail. At 2 a.m. Obs. lat. 38° 7' 5", obs. long. 111° 48' 20".
1803-01-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At sunset, land was thought to have been sighted to the west, and two or three islets to the south-west.
At noon, the visible extremities of Kangaroo Island lay from SW ¼ W to E ¼ SE.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, early, we had finished our geographical work on the whole of Kangaroo Island, so that if the English have the advantage over us of having arrived there a few days earlier, we too have the advantage over them of having sailed right round it and of having determined its geographical position in a manner that leaves nothing to be desired for the safety of navigation.
All the land on the south of this island consists of nothing but sand, dunes and rocky tablelands. Its aspect is dreary and disagreeable to the eye. Two fairly deep bays and an infinite number of coves, larger or smaller, all of sand or rock, are all (that) was offered to our view. But we did not find a single place where a landing seemed practicable, so heavily did the sea break all along the beach. It is true that the winds were then in the southern quarter and that the swell was very considerable. This island did not let us see the smallest tall tree, only heath or other very low plants. It is possible that the far side of the heights is furnished with them, but that is something we cannot affirm. The coast is high in some parts and tolerably low in others.
At noon we observed the latitude of 35° 39' 55", and the longitude by timekeeper was 134° 27' 17". We were then ranging very close along the coast, my intention being to come to anchor in a large bay to the north which I had noticed the first time we explored this coast, and at the head of which there may be some good anchoring ground, to judge by the different ways in which the points closed upon one another.
During the evening we sighted the islets that lie to the south of the western extremity of the first gulf we had entered, and we left them to larboard, having sighted at sunset the mainland of this part, which, as I observed at the time, is low.
In the evening we lost sight of the Casuarina, but I took little account of it, persuaded that she would join us during the night or while beating along the coast to work up it with south-easterly winds.
After sunset the breeze grew strong and the sky looked very threatening. But as the wind came to us over the land, we found the sea smooth. So as not to make too much way, and to make it easier for the Casuarina to rejoin us, we took two reefs in the topsails and spent the night, which had strong gusts, steering east, in order to reach the place where I proposed to anchor the next day if the weather was fine.
As soundings were taken every hour during the night, the depth, which was 25 fathoms at eight o'clock, decreased gradually until midnight, when we had no more than eighteen. We kept this depth for the rest of the night, so that we did not change course. At times we had a hazy and very damp sky, with little sign of fine weather for the next day.
1803-01-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNE to WSW. At noon in 38° 7' of latitude observed and in 111° 48' of longitude observed. At 9 the weather overcast, the wind freshened. The 15th [Nivôse, 5 January 1803]. Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SSW; the main topmast and topgallant mast were set up. At noon in 37° 8' of latitude observed and in 110° 36' of longitude observed. At 7 the course given N 56° 15' W.

1803-01-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth. At 10 p.m. wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 37° 8' 5", obs. long. 110° 30' 50".
1803-01-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven o'clock,
The visible western extremity of Kangaroo Island lay south 53° west and extended to south 74° east.
An islet north 66° west.
The mainland in sight from north 56° west to north 10° east
At noon,
part of Kangaroo Island from south 25° east to south 55° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, we sighted part of the lands that form the western shore of the first gulf, which did not fail to surprise us, since by our course we ought not to have sighted them, all the more as these lands are generally low and level. We saw from this that the currents had carried us much further north than our reckoning, a thing that had happened to us the first time we visited this gulf. The land in sight extended from N. NW to N. NE.
We did not see the Casuarina, which it was thought had been glimpsed during the night, and for which a light was shown in answer to the one we thought we had seen from her.
During the morning the weather was fairly fine, but we had the winds in the south-eastern quarter, ill suited to the course we had to make, which obliged us, once we had closed with the land, to make short boards in order to examine it again; but we saw only the same things as the first time.
At noon the latitude was observed as 35° 26' 48", and the longitude by timekeeper placed us in 135° 30' 47".
In the afternoon we continued to beat about, tack upon tack, with a pleasant breeze from south-south-east, variable to south. The weather, though fine, was a little hazy, so that our horizon was of small extent.
After the setting the setting (sic) of the sun, we stood on the tack towards the south by east, to pass the night at a short distance from the coast. As the weather was very fine and the haze cleared, we had a good view, in the middle of the night, of the mainland that forms the eastern entrance of the first gulf.
During the day we had not sighted the Casuarina at all, and I was very surprised not to see her come up, all the more as we had made little way, the boards we had run having not been very advantageous and having been thwarted by the currents, which seemed to set us strongly to the north-west.
The soundings during the twenty-four hours were between eighteen and 15 fathoms, the bottom varying, now of pure sand, now of sand and broken shells, and at other times of sand mixed with a little mud and weed. These various bottoms seemed to us suitable for anchoring in case of need, but sheltered only from winds from south-east to south-south-west, by way of south.

1803-01-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze, a high sea. The storm staysail, gnawed by rats, was put out to dry and unbent for repair. Obs. lat. 35° 9', obs. long. 108° 46' 56".
1803-01-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Latitude of the anchorage 35° 45' 16"
Longitude by No. 35 135° 39' 39".
STAY AT KANGAROO ISLAND
On the sixteenth, in the morning, we stood on the larboard tack to close with the coast, my intention being to anchor in the first bay, which lies opposite the entrance of the second gulf. The first time I visited this coast, this bay, and even the one following it, had seemed to me likely to offer some good shelter from north-east to west by way of south. But the weather at the time did not allow me to examine it carefully, any more than the one to the west of it, which is much deeper but where there is little water at the entrance, for a fairly great distance from land, as I found only five to six fathoms, sandy bottom.
Having entered the first bay I have just spoken of, we anchored inside it in 8 fathoms of water, bottom of sand and weed, which led me to believe that we should find good holding ground there. We at once moored with a small kedge anchor, so that the current should not make us override our cable as had happened to us several times.
As soon as the ship was moored, the boats were hoisted out and I sent them to examine the coast in order to learn its outline and, above all, to see whether fresh water might not be found in various ravines that we had in sight and which seemed to run down to the sea. Citizens Bonnefoy and Ransonnet each had the
command of a boat for this exploration, with orders to begin, the one on the western side of the bay and the other on the eastern side, so as to meet in the inlet it formed to the south. Citizen Ransonnet, who went to the western part, had orders to light a large fire on a projecting point to show the Casuarina that we were in this bay, should she happen to appear there during the night.
A third boat set off at about eleven o'clock with the carpenters, to cut timber fit for building our longboat, for which we had taken most of the patterns since our departure from King Island.
At sunset, all the boats being back on board, I was informed that at the head of the bay a small harbour had been found, which at first seemed convenient because the boats had entered it at high water. But when the tide went out, it uncovered a considerable number of sandbanks, separated from one another only by very narrow channels, in which no more than two or three fathoms of water remained. The channel through which one must pass had three or four at high tide, but was nonetheless obstructed by banks. The short time the boats had had to examine this place not allowing them to give exact details of it, I put off sending it to be examined again until the next day. The carpenters and those who had been assigned to search for water did not find a drop of it, and the former could not even find timber in the proportions we needed. More than fifty trees that were felled all proved to be rotten at the heart. They also reported having seen such a great number of kangaroos of the large species that they compared them to flocks of sheep, and no wilder.
1803-01-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and the wind a light breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 35° 11' of latitude observed and in 108° 47' of longitude observed.

1803-01-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze. Lowered the gaff to take off an eyebolt and make a new span, the old one having parted in the morning; it was in place at 6 p.m. Obs. lat. 34° 40' 10", est. long. 107° 40' 26".
1803-01-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventeenth (7 January 1803). On the seventeenth, early in the morning, I dispatched my large boat under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy, and had it accompanied by the engineer-geographer Faure, with orders to make an exact examination of the harbour discovered the day before and to draw up its plan. This boat was supplied with two for three days' provisions, with orders to come back on board for more if the details of this harbour required more time than I had fixed.
At about nine o'clock we sighted the Casuarina, which was making for the anchorage we occupied. As soon as she had sighted us, the captain of that vessel came on board shortly afterwards to hand me a statement of her needs, which amounted to no small matter. Before examining his request, I had him given an anchor, a hawser and a warp so that he might moor at once. The caulkers were also sent on board her to cover over her upperworks, which were making her take in a great deal of water.
In the morning we had a strong breeze from the north-west which, having made the sea somewhat rough and choppy, did not allow any work to be done on board that vessel. As the boat that had been sent ashore the day before in search of some stream of fresh water had brought back a kangaroo of the large species, the greater part of it was distributed to the crews.
In the afternoon we were entirely taken up with working for the Casuarina. The forge above all had a great deal to do in repairing one of her
anchors, whose iron stock was broken. It was likewise necessary to make her new hoops for her topmasts, to change their crosstrees, and an infinity of other jobs which the convenience of having us at hand led M. Freycinet to ask of us. This vessel was also short of water, having emptied her casks when she ran aground in the bay she wished to survey on the coast of Van Diemen's Land, to the south of the Hunter Islands. I had four casks of water delivered to her, assuring him firmly that I would give him no more, as I could not expose myself to running short of it myself for the pleasure of giving it to him.
At nightfall the sky looked threatening, which decided me to veer out as much as eighty fathoms of cable for greater safety. This precaution was not useless, for we met with fairly strong squalls and were often on the point of letting go a second anchor. Nevertheless the ship held fast, which confirmed me in the view that the holding ground was not bad, although a small mooring anchor had not held with a hundred and twenty fathoms of cable.
1803-01-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to ENE. At noon in 34° 40' of latitude observed and in 107° 40' of longitude by account. The course given N 33° 45' W.

1803-01-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At 6 a.m. the mizzen topsail tie parted at the collar and was at once refitted. At 8 clewed up and furled the mizzen topsail and rove the top rope to lower the mast and refit the masthead rigging. Est. lat. 33° 30' 35", est. long. 106° 27' 50".
1803-01-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighteenth (8 January 1803). On the eighteenth, the weather was scarcely better than the day before, which led me to send down our topgallant masts. In the course of the morning the boat I had dispatched to examine and survey the harbour at the head of the bay returned on board. The officer in command of her and Citizen Faure told me that the work was finished, which surprised me greatly, the more so since, according to the first reports I had been given, the task was to be a long and even a difficult one. I let these gentlemen know my misgivings about the haste and forced diligence they appeared to have used, but they assured me none the less that they had seen and examined everything, and that this inlet was less a harbour than a mass of sandbanks and shoals, most of which were uncovered at low water. For all their searching they found no fresh water, only several creeks of sea water that lost themselves in the marshes.
As Citizen Faure is to give me a detailed plan of the place, I shall say no more of it until I have received it.
During the day work continued on the Casuarina, to put her in a condition to carry out the mission with which I intended to charge her.
In the evening the weather continued squally, with rain and fairly strong gusts, and the winds varied from south-west to west-south-west; but during the night it was not so unpleasant as we had had it during the day.
1803-01-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from ESE to SSE. The mizzen topmast head rigging was refitted. At noon in 33° 29' of latitude by account and in 106° 28' of longitude by account.

1803-01-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea very smooth. Swayed up and set up the mizzen topgallant mast; at 4 p.m. the sail was set. Est. lat. 32° 5' 5", est. long. 104° 59' 20".
1803-01-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 19th (9 January 1803). On the nineteenth I again dispatched one of my boats, under the command of Citizen Ransonnet, to go and examine a second bay, to the west of the one in which we lie and a good deal deeper. He was ordered to go right round it and to examine its whole extent with care, so as to make sure whether it did not contain some stream of fresh water and some trees fit for shipbuilding. The boat was supplied with three days' provisions and with everything needed to chart the geography of this bay. I put no geographer aboard her, being persuaded that Citizen Ransonnet would acquit himself of the task as well as those who are on board.
Having dispatched this boat, I went ashore to examine a ravine in the neighbourhood of our anchorage, in which I expected to find water, judging by the freshness of the plants on that part of the coast. My intention was also to dig a well in the ground if I found no running water. For that reason
I took men with me and everything necessary for the work. As soon as we had landed I went to examine the spot I have just mentioned, and found nothing in that ravine but the utmost dryness. We dug five large holes in the ground, which were of no use whatever, for at less than two feet down we struck the rock which doubtless forms the core of this island.
The botanist Leschenault and the gardener's boy, who had gone ashore with me, as had Citizen Péron, busied themselves with their own departments; and when they had rejoined us, with little success from their rambles, we thought of returning on board, having for our whole fortune only one live kangaroo, which our dog caught shortly before we left. On leaving I put two Englishmen ashore to kill kangaroos for us by lying in wait for them at night, as they are accustomed to do.
During the night of the nineteenth to the twentieth the weather was fairly (bad), with winds from the south-west. During the day we had moored ourselves securely with two bower anchors, one to the north-east and the other to the south-west.
1803-01-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SSE to SE. Saw flying fish. At noon in 32° 4' of latitude by account and in 104° 59' of longitude by account.

1803-01-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze. A swell from the SW. Made all sail. Obs. lat. 30° 35' 32", est. long. 103° 40' 50".
1803-01-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
"The Commander, etc., to Citizen Freycinet, on board the Casuarina,
"As soon as your vessel has been repaired, you will get under sail and steer directly to examine the west coast of the first gulf, opposite which we are at anchor and whose eastern side is formed by the high land you have in sight to the east-north-east. We penetrated into this gulf as far as the latitude of 34° 38', and we then had a perfect view of the land from north to north-north-west; but we then found the water so shallow that it was not possible for me to approach the coast closely enough to examine it properly.
"The small draught of your vessel will make it all the easier for Citizen Boulanger, our geographer, who accompanies you, to carry out the work that remains to be done in that quarter, which is inconsiderable and will not require much time, since you are in no way to concern yourself with the east coast, which has been well explored with the ship.
"On leaving, therefore, you will steer directly north, so as to reach the head of this gulf as soon as possible, and will then come down it, coasting along the western shore. You will not stand in toward the land in less than two fathoms of water. This order is imperative, and you will be personally answerable to the Government for any mishaps that may befall you if you disregard it. The west coast of this first gulf appeared to us generally low and made up in several places of sand dunes. You must examine it with caution and sound often, to avoid running aground on the banks that may lie there, for I am certain that there are several shoals.
"At the southern extremity of this first gulf the coast forms a projecting cape, and the entrance of a second gulf opens up. You will then have sight of several islands and islets to the south and west. They offer various channels which are navigable with prudence. You will leave these islets to the south, without wasting time examining them, their respective positions having been determined by us. When you are in the second gulf you will do as for the first, that is to say you will at once
"work up to the north to reach its head, without concerning yourself with the east coast, which is known to us. In running up the east coast we were only able to reach the latitude of 34° 11'. I think that it extends further to the north, and that is what you must ascertain. The point at which we stopped, and from which we should have resumed had the bad weather not prevented us, is easy to recognise, being remarkable for a reef awash, not far from the coast, on which the sea breaks heavily. According to the dead reckoning of the course we made from noon until three in the afternoon, and the bearing then taken of this danger, its latitude would be thirty-four degrees eight minutes. It appeared to us to be the top of a sandbank which dries and breaks heavily at low tide. We had eight fathoms of water, sandy bottom, at a distance of about a league.
"The east coast of this second gulf is low and formed of sand dunes of greater or lesser height; but in the bight to the north-north-east, into which we did not penetrate, high land can be seen which I suspect to be mountain peaks in the interior of the country. When you are at the head of this gulf, provided always that you can reach it without danger and without having less than two fathoms of water, you will begin to coast the west side, coming back to the south, having taken bearings of the eastern side starting from the reef I have mentioned to you. The land on the west appeared to us very high, and perhaps you will find something of interest there. On approaching the southern extremity of this same coast there should be a small harbour in which Mr Flinders stayed for a good while. You will examine this harbour and Mr Boulanger will draw up a plan of it.
"If you have an opportunity of replenishing your water, you will not fail to do so, taking care, however, not to spend more time over it than is needed. Fifteen or eighteen days, allowing for the hindrances of the season, are more than enough for the work you have to do. I shall wait for you here until that time, but I give you notice that if you are not back within twenty at the latest, counting from your departure, I shall get under sail and make for the islands of St Peter and St Francis, where I have a great deal to do. The impossibility of replenishing my water does not allow me to wait for you any longer. As the Government has not asked me for the topography of some thankless and barren parts of New Holland, but only for a knowledge of the coast, you will land only at a place where you are certain of being able to take in water with ease. If you come upon any large openings, you will retrace your steps before examining them, so that I may take the ship there. The same will apply if what we judged to be gulfs should prove to be two islands.
"The route I have laid down for you in the present instruction is doubtless the shortest; nevertheless you must modify or change it according to the winds you find, for I suppose them to be equally good for going north as for returning south. You may therefore take whichever route best suits the winds you meet, whether you begin with the first or the second of these two gulfs.
"As I am resolved to get under sail if you are not back by the time I have fixed, you will return here to ascertain whether I have left before steering for the islands of St Peter and St Francis, where I intend to go. This group of islands lies in the latitude of 32° 31' south and the longitude of 131° 25'. I shall make every effort to sight the mainland to the north, which I was unable to reach the first time I visited the southern part of these islands. They are not inhabited. If you see any smoke there, it will certainly be ourselves who have lit a fire to show you that we are in the neighbourhood or
"that we have passed that way. If, as I fear, I should be unable to take in water on that part of the coast, I should go to King George Sound, of which you have a plan in the atlas of Vancouver's voyage. From King George Sound I shall steer for the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], on the Leeuwin coast.
"If you do not find us here, you will leave at once for the islands of St Peter and St Francis, steering west along this same latitude if the winds allow, so as to get quickly clear of all the islets, rocks and reefs that lie on a route which would take too much northing, and which we know, as we do the mainland coast. You will not take my small boat; that craft would undoubtedly be lost if I left her with you. Besides, she is of no use whatever to you. She would only slow your progress or endanger your vessel, which will get under sail tonight or tomorrow morning at the latest. On your return you will give me a written report of your work and of your remarks."
Your fellow citizen. Signed N. B.
"The Commander, etc., to Citizen Boulanger, engineer-geographer,
"I request you, as soon as the Casuarina has been repaired, to go on board that vessel to chart the geography of the two west coasts of the gulfs in whose neighbourhood we now find ourselves. When we explored the eastern part of these same gulfs, the want of water for a ship of our size, and other circumstances no less unfavourable, did not allow us to undertake this work, which is too important for the knowledge of the coast to be abandoned; and it is for that reason that I urge you to carry it out with the greatest exactness possible.
"Citizen Freycinet is ordered to steer directly north to ascertain the exact depth of the first, although I am persuaded that we saw it ourselves when in 34° 38' of latitude, coasting at a short distance along the east coast, at which you will not stop. But it is not the same with the western shores, which you must survey in their entirety. The land in that quarter is generally low, and the water, even at a considerable distance off, is of little depth.
"The work in this first gulf being finished, you will pass into the second, continuing to coast the mainland without stopping at the islets and rocks that will lie to the south and west of you, their respective positions being known to us. When you are in this second gulf, Citizen Freycinet is ordered to do as for the first, that is to say he will work up to the north to find out its depth, and will then examine the west coast, which, quite unlike the one opposite, is high and mountainous, unless indeed the ranges of mountains we sighted lie in the interior of the country. We penetrated into this gulf as far as the latitude of 34° 11', but we were not yet in its deepest recess, and the bad weather that came upon us at that time did not allow us to return there.
"By every probability, and even allowing for the hindrances of the season, fifteen or eighteen days are more than enough for the work you have to do, since you are in no way to concern yourself with the east coast of these two gulfs, which we have examined ourselves sufficiently for the perfection of the geography.
