"The islands and islets to the south and west of the entrance of the second gulf
"must not detain you either; but Citizen Freycinet is enjoined to look for a harbour which should lie at the western extremity of the second gulf, and in which Mr Flinders is said to have stayed. You will draw up a plan of it if possible, this port of call needing to be known. According to the information I have been given, there should be an island opposite the entrance of this harbour which protects it from winds from south-east to north-east.
"I am informing Citizen Freycinet of the date fixed for my departure from here, and as the time I intend to stay is longer than you will need, I have no doubt that you will be back before the date I have fixed. Should it be otherwise, however, I am ordering him to come and join me at the islands of St Peter and St Francis, in latitude 32° 31' and longitude 131° 25'. These islands are easy to recognise and of easy access. I shall make every effort to sight the mainland to the north of this group of islands, which I was unable to see when I was in those waters. If I should be unable to take in water on that part of the coast, I should go to King George Sound for the supplies I need. As he has a plan of that harbour in the atlas of Vancouver's voyage, he will find it easily. I would only point out to you that its latitude is said to be 10 minutes further south. Moreover, in ranging along the coast in that quarter, he will no doubt sight it.
"Although I have laid down for Citizen Freycinet the route he is to follow, since I believe it the best, he must nevertheless conform to whatever route the winds he may meet require him to take, whether he begins with the first or the second of these gulfs. My only wish is to shorten his absence as much as possible, the situation in which we find ourselves not allowing us to waste time needlessly. He is likewise ordered, should he come upon any large openings at the head of the gulfs, or should what we took for gulfs prove to be islands, to retrace his steps without going round them, so that I may take the ship there. He is expressly enjoined not to land and never to go into less than two fathoms of water, so as not to endanger again, as has already happened to him, either his vessel or the safety of those who accompany him. The Government has not asked me for the topography of some thankless and barren parts of New Holland, but only for a knowledge of the coast or of the large openings it might offer. I hope that you will be good enough to keep within these same limits and to finish as soon as possible the work with which you are charged, which would be a matter of only four or five days if the winds were favourable to you." "Your fellow citizen. Signed N. B."
During the day of the twentieth we went on getting the Casuarina ready to leave. The ship's carpenters were employed in going to cut timber for the building of our longboat, which was being constructed on board, and a second boat in examining several small coves to the east of our anchorage, to see whether some streams of fresh water might not be found there.
At sunset, the Casuarina being (ready), Mr Boulanger went on board her, and the vessel got under sail at about ten at night in very fine weather, with a pleasant breeze from the south, varying at times toward the east.
1803-01-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. At noon in 30° 36' of latitude observed and in 103° 41' of longitude by account.

1803-01-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and sky, the sea smooth, almost calm. At 4.30 the topman on his rounds reported that the main topsail tie was about to part; we at once secured the topsail and shifted the main topsail tie, which was doubled. Obs. lat. 29° 50' 19", long. 102° 50' 50".
1803-01-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 21st (11 January 1803). On the twenty-first the weather continued fine, and all day we had a pleasant breeze from the south-east. In the course of the morning we overhauled our cables, and the crew was employed on various other tasks connected with the ship. During the day a fairly large quantity of middling-sized mackerel was taken
with the line. The small boat, which had been sent fishing off a point to the east of our anchorage, was less fortunate than we were. She brought back only some fifty fish, all of the same species and known by the name of parrot fish. Those who went kangaroo hunting did not fare badly; they brought in five of the large species, whose total weight might have been from two hundred and fifty to three hundred pounds.
At about four in the afternoon Citizen Ransonnet returned from the mission with which he had been charged, without having found anything of much interest, and not a single drop of water. On this excursion he saw a great many cassowaries and kangaroos; two of the latter were taken alive, but it was thought better to cut their throats than to bring them on board. As he is drawing up the plan of the bay he surveyed, I shall give the details of it when his work is handed to me.
During the night the weather was fine and the winds south-east.
1803-01-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 29° 50' of latitude observed and in 102° 58' of longitude by account. At 7 a flat calm.

1803-01-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds very light. At 5 the topman on his rounds at the mainmast reported that the main topsail sheet was chafed where it bears on the yardarm block. Obs. lat. 29° 56' 10", est. long. 102° 37' 30".
1803-01-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 22nd (12 January 1803. On the twenty-second, at daybreak, two boats were sent off to fish with the seine. Citizens Leschenault and Péron were of the party. That same day the astronomical circle was landed, but I would not have a tent set up ashore, because the gear that goes with it is so considerable that it usually takes a whole day to bring everything back on board, which is ill suited to an anchorage like the one we occupy, where one must always be ready to leave, and often by cutting or slipping one's cables.
It was agreed that the astronomer Bernier should go ashore in the morning at eight o'clock and come back between three and four in the afternoon. Our timekeepers, whose rate had been well determined at King Island, ought not to need much correction.
At noon one of the fishing boats returned, bringing back nothing at all. According to the report, the cause was put down (to) the great number of seals on the beach where she had been.
The small boat, which had stayed behind to bring back Messrs Leschenault and Péron, did not get on board until four in the afternoon. The former had not been fortunate in his ramble and brought back only two or three plants that he did not know; but Citizen Péron was delighted at having collected three or four molluscs, two small lizards and half a dozen sea-ears, such as the sailors have filled their chests with. During the evening the breeze was light, and the winds were in the south-east quarter, in cat's-paws. The night (passed) without incident, except that it was very damp, though under a very fine sky.
1803-01-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a flat calm until 9, when the breeze got up from NW to N. At noon in 29° 56' of latitude observed and in 102° 45' of longitude by account.

1803-01-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth. Freshened the nip of the main topsail sheet to starboard. At 2.15 the winds having shifted to the SW, we went onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 29° 32' 5", est. long. 101° 17' 32".
1803-01-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 23rd (13 January 1803). On the twenty-third, first thing in the morning, I sent off a boat under the command of Midshipman Baudin to go and examine the cove in which we had anchored the first time we sighted this island, and in which we did not stay because our anchor would not hold. As this cove lies in the eastern part of the island, he spent the day away, and on his return I was informed that a little water might be obtained there by digging wells. The boat's crew had got some in this way, having found, inside the beach, a muddy ground in which they had obtained water of passably good quality. I put off until the next day making more certain of how matters stood.
Another boat was employed during the day in cutting wood,
and brought us two loads of it. A third craft was given to the boatswain to go and gather oysters in the Port des Pélicans.
At sunset, the boats being back on board, the one that had been sent for water returned with only two tierces, which were the produce of the first well; then two more were dug beside this first one, and I hope that the three together will supply our consumption during our stay here. It is only a pity that one has to go so far to fetch it.
The boatswain's boat came back laden with oysters, which were shared out among the whole crew. She also brought a fairly large quantity of pelicans' eggs and some thirty of those birds, taken on their nests.
During the night the weather was fine, the sky damp as usual, and the winds dead calm.
1803-01-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather. At 2.15 the breeze from WNW shifted to SW; shaped the course N 56° 15' W. The breeze freshened as it hauled to the south and was a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 29° 35' of latitude observed and in 101° 25' of longitude by account. The course given N 33° 45' W.

1803-01-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze; set the studdingsails to starboard. Obs. lat. 27° 39' 11", obs. long. 98° 34'.
1803-01-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the 24th (14 January 1803) we laid our longboat on the stocks on board the ship herself. The keel was set up, the stem and sternpost placed, and during the rest of the day all the frames that had been got out beforehand were put in place.
The boats were sent, as usual, to take in water and wood, and in the first of them I sent off one of our hunters to procure us some particular birds which had been described to us as having a red tail and a grey body, being the size of the cockatoo, which it was said to resemble in its beak. The weather was fine all day. We had only a light breeze from the south, varying to south-south-west.
At nightfall the boats returned on board with little water and still fewer objects of curiosity. The red-tailed birds that had been announced to us turned out to be nothing other than black cockatoos with red markings in the tail feathers, exactly like those we had procured at Port Jackson. The best of it was two golden-winged pigeons, which were in very good condition.
The night passed without incident and was fine, though very damp.
1803-01-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 27° 39' of latitude observed, 98° 34' of longitude observed and 99° 43' of longitude by account. At 6 the course given N 45° W.

1803-01-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze. The sea smooth enough. Obs. lat. 26° 22' 40", est. long. 97° 54' 14".
1803-01-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 26° 23' of latitude observed and in 96° 53' of longitude by account.

1803-01-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. Took in the studdingsails and set the staysails. Obs. lat. 25° 20' 46", est. long. 96° 26' 14".
1803-01-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 26th (16 January 1803). On the twenty-sixth our work was the same as the day before, and the boats had the same destinations. On board, we attended to the part of the rigging that needed repair; our lower shrouds as well as our topmast shrouds were set up, and the ship was put in a condition to go to sea whenever we wished.
In the afternoon the sky, which had been very fine in the morning, became dark and stormy, with an appearance of bad weather during the night. The barometer had also fallen a great deal, which warned us to be on our guard. At sunset the thunder began to rumble, and we had some fairly loud claps of it. Nevertheless, little by little the weather set fair, and we got off with a fright. During the night the winds were very variable and in gusts from north round to east.
(no 25 Nivôse; we shall continue with the days given by Nicolas Baudin).
1803-01-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 25° 21' of latitude observed and in 95° 25' of longitude by account.

1803-01-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth, a light breeze. One of the fore topsail tie blocks having broken, we secured the yard to repair the damage. At noon the course NW by W. Obs. lat. 23° 59' 23", obs. long. 94° 24' 38".
1803-01-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 27th (17 January 1803), on the twentieth (sic), we had all day a strong breeze from west to south-west, which made the sea high and swelling; nevertheless our large boat was sent to take ashore the carpenters, who had compass timbers to cut for the fore part of our longboat. She made two trips during the day, although the weather was
hardly suited to a task such as the one she had in hand. The boat detailed for watering did not return on board because of the strength of the wind. For the greater part of the day we had lightning in various quarters of the horizon, but we did not hear the thunder rumble. Towards evening the weather set fair, and the breeze died away entirely during the night, which was fine.
1803-01-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 23° 59' of latitude observed and in 94° 25' of longitude observed. The course given N 56° 15' W. Saw tropic birds. At 10 crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the sixth time.

1803-01-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze. Saw many flying fish. At 10 p.m. on the 27th crossed the Tropic of Capricorn. Obs. lat. 22° 49' 34", obs. long. 90° 1' 0".
1803-01-18.journal_baudin_autographe: Of the 28th (18 January 1803). On the twenty-eighth the winds were south-south-east and moderate. We carried on with the usual work, that is to say we took in water and wood, both for burning and for the building of our longboat, whose gunwales were put in place. The night passed without incident. The wind was almost calm and the sky fine.
1803-01-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. Saw flying fish, bonito and tropic birds. At noon in 22° 50' of latitude observed and in 90° 1' of longitude observed.

1803-01-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. In the forenoon put the small boat on the gratings to repair her. Obs. lat. 21° 24' 21", est. long. 90° 19' 56".
1803-01-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 29th (19 January 1803). On the twenty-ninth the weather continued fine, which gave me all the more pleasure because, the Casuarina having been constantly favoured by the winds, I expected to see her arrive at any moment, provided always that she has conformed to the instruction I gave her, which in my opinion is very doubtful, since officers always believe themselves more learned than those under whose orders they serve.
Little water was taken in that day, the wells filling only very slowly. The other boat was employed in carrying firewood on board. During the night, fine weather and a pleasant breeze from the north-east.
1803-01-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a good breeze from SE to ESE. At 6 the course given N 45° W. At noon in 21° 24' of latitude observed and in 87° 57' of longitude by account. At 3 the course given N 67° 30' W, and at 6 N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze. At 3 shaped the course WNW. The main topgallant halliard having [given way], it was refitted at once. Est. lat. 20° 48' 9", est. long. 87° 31' 56".
1803-01-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the morning of the thirtieth, the weather being fine, I had a cock and two hens put ashore at the place where we water. I also left on this beach a boar and a sow, so that they might multiply there and in time become useful to navigators who will frequent the waters (of) this island in summer, providing good refreshments for ships that wish to stop there. And the anchorage seems to me good enough to be safe in, provided the winds do not blow hard from north-east round to north-west by the north. For then the sea there is very high and rough, but one has the resource of being able to weigh easily and to come back when the bad weather is over.
The hunters who were ashore took during the day, with the help of our dogs, twelve giant kangaroos of various sizes. Seven of them were taken alive and put in pens on board to be kept. Among those we hope to carry to our country are three females with young, which may perhaps thrive. Before leaving I shall try to make up a score of live ones, so as to have a better hope of keeping some of them through the passage.
During the night the weather was overcast, and at times we had violent gusts from the east-north-east quarter.
1803-01-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from ESE to E. At noon in 20° 47' of latitude by account and in 85° 9' of longitude by account. In the 24 hours the main topsail tie, the main topgallant halliard and two studdingsail halliards parted.

1803-01-21.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, a good breeze. The topmast studdingsail halliard having parted, the sail was [recovered] and set again a moment later. At 9.45 the main topsail tie and the port topmast halliard parted; we at once took in the studdingsails, furled the main topgallant sail and clewed up the main topsail. At 1.30 we swayed and hoisted the main topsail and main topgallant sail. Obs. lat. 20° 32', est. long. 84° 51' 56".
1803-01-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the First of Pluviôse (21 January 1803). On the first of Pluviôse the winds were north-west and blustering in the morning. The sky too had an ugly look, being very dark and heavy with clouds, but it all cleared away in the afternoon, when the winds shifted to south-south-west.
The large boat, which I had sent off the day before with two days' provisions under the command of Citizen Bonnefoy, to cut us some spars fit
for masting our boats, returned on board at about seven in the morning, bringing us a few round poles that were barely fit (for) making grating battens. As this was the second time that Citizen Bonnefoy had acquitted himself very badly of the errands with which he had been charged, not liking to leave the ship, where, much to his taste, he has nothing to do, I resolved not to employ him any more. I had also had Citizen Le Sueur embarked in this boat to procure us some live emus, since there are many of them in the neighbourhood of the place where the boat had gone; but they would not give him the time needed to hunt them with the dogs he had taken aboard expressly for the purpose.
The rest of the day was spent on the work of our longboat and on various other jobs on board. During the night the weather was fine and the winds south and moderate, though from time to time some strong puffs came through.
1803-01-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from E. At noon in 20° 32' of latitude observed and in 82° 29' of longitude by account.

1803-01-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fine breeze. At 7 furled the fore topgallant sail and took in the studdingsails. Obs. lat. 20° 15' 50", est. long. 84° 51' 56".
1803-01-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Second (22 January 1803). On the second, at six in the morning, I went ashore with the carpenters to try to cut timber fit for making us planking, of which we were beginning to stand in need to carry on with our longboat, which by then had her wales in place and one strake below them.
Until that moment we had been unable to find straight timber fit for the purpose along the shore, the casuarina wood, which could have taken the place of eucalyptus, being invariably rotten at the heart. More than sixty trees of the latter kind were felled without our being able to find a single one fit for use. All that this laborious excursion procured us was some twenty pieces of compass timber, knees and a few breasthooks, but we brought back only two pieces of straight timber, (one) of which is very doubtful.
As I kept constantly beside the carpenters to hurry the work on, I came within a very little of being crushed by the fall of a tree which, coming down in a direction different from the one we had judged it would take, knocked me over in its fall, and I was so entangled in the branches that it took a long while to get me out. I got off with a few wounds to the head and other parts of the body. This fall made me spend the night ashore, where I rested perfectly well, though very uncomfortably. During the day we had very fine weather and, in the night, a light breeze from the east which made the air very dry and even cold.
1803-01-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to ESE. At noon in 20° 16' of latitude observed and in 79° 26' of longitude by account. The course given N 84° 22' 30" W (west half north).

1803-01-23.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze. The dinghy was got up on deck and, being judged past repair by the master carpenter, was thrown overboard. Obs. lat. 20° 5' 39", est. long. 78° 16' 26".
1803-01-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Third of Pluviôse (23 January 1803). On the third, in the morning, I came back on board with the timber that could not all be carried off the day before. I also brought three live kangaroos, which were put in pens like the others and of which I take the greatest care. There were one female and two males. These three animals were caught by our dogs without being hurt. One of them thought to escape by throwing itself into the water, but it fell into our hands after putting up a fine resistance.
For the rest of the day we were occupied with work on board, and all the carpenters went back to that on the longboat, putting off until the next day going to look for timber in another place where perhaps we shall be more fortunate. During the night the sky was very dark and heavy, and the winds south-east and very light.
Of the Third of Pluviôse (23 January 1803). On the third, at sunrise, the carpenters were again sent ashore to look for timber fit for making planking. A second boat left in the morning to go and observe the latitude at the entrance of the Port des Pélicans, which lies at the head of the bay off which we are lying. It was the chief quartermaster (in another hand: !) who was charged with this task, most of the officers on board having no instruments, and those who have them regarding it as beneath their dignity.
I sent off a third boat, when she had returned from watering, to help carry the timber the carpenters were to cut. Two of our hunters went to spend the day ashore to try to procure us some new birds which I was told they had seen.
During the day these two boats could make only one trip, and our hunters sent us three live kangaroos which, like the others, were put in the pens of two cabins that were taken down to house them. All (day) we had a pleasant breeze from the east-south-east. In the night the winds held in the east, almost calm.
1803-01-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Dark weather, the wind a strong breeze from ESE to E. The dinghy, having been judged unfit for service, was broken up and thrown overboard. The jib boom was rigged in and the topmasts and topgallant masts set up. At noon in 20° 6' of latitude observed and in 75° 53' of longitude by account. The course given west.

1803-01-24.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and a strong breeze, a high sea. We set up the topmast backstays and the topgallant shrouds and backstays. Est. lat. 20° 16' 9", est. long. 74° 28' 26".
1803-01-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fourth of Pluviôse (24 January 1803). On the fourth the work on board was the same as the day before. We went on cutting timber for the planking, and set up our saws on board to rip it to thickness. We had no one who had ever followed that trade, which made the work no easy matter for those who undertook it. As in such a circumstance an example had to be set, I sawed part of the first piece myself with the purser's clerk, Boivin. Citizen Ronsard took my place, but the other officers took good care not to show themselves. Although not one of them knows the first piece of timber that goes into a ship, there is not one of them who has come near the longboat since she has been on the stocks. Such work, they say, is made for the rabble; an officer of the Navy need only know how to have his ship's sails trimmed and to rest when his watch is over.
In the evening the carpenters came back on board, and our hunters too, having had no luck in their rambles. The night passed without incident; the sky was overcast and the horizon hazy, with easterly winds in strong puffs.
1803-01-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from E. The fore topgallant mast was struck; the main topsail tie and a studdingsail halliard parted. At noon in 20° 16' of latitude by account and in 72° 5' of longitude by account.

1803-01-25.journal_anonyme: Dark, overcast weather, with light rain almost throughout. At 9 the main topsail tie having parted, took in the studdingsails and lowered the main topsail on the cap. Obs. lat. 20° 41' 36", est. long. 70° 16' 56".
1803-01-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fifth of Pluviôse (25 January 1803). On the fifth, seeing no sign of the Casuarina's return, she having been absent a fortnight, I began to fear either that she had not carried out the orders I had given her on leaving, or that some unfortunate accident had befallen her. However, the continual fine weather she has had since the time of her departure makes this last conjecture much less likely than the first.
Be that as it may, I shall wait until the date I have fixed; but if she does not appear within the four days still wanting to complete it, I shall continue on my way without troubling myself further about her.
During this day we finished shipping the timber for our longboat, which pleased me greatly. On board, work continued on making planks of it, and those who took charge of this task carried it out much better than the day before. We took in, as usual, our day's consumption of water. We had calm weather by day and by night, and very great heat at both times.
1803-01-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast, rainy and squally weather. The wind blowing hard from E in gusts, the sea extremely high, the ship labouring a great deal. At noon the course given N 78° 45' W, in 20° 42' of latitude observed and in 67° 54' of longitude by account. On taking the watch at noon the captain ordered me to take in nothing until something carried away. We were under the foresail, topsails hoisted, main topgallant sail and studdingsails to starboard and port, forward and aft. The mainmast was labouring a great deal. At 2, in a squall, the main topgallant sheet and the studdingsail halliards or tacks having parted, I had the topgallant sail furled and the studdingsails taken in. We took the lower reef in the main topsail and the second in the fore, struck the main topgallant mast and the gaff, and set up the main topmast and topgallant mast. From 6 until midnight the wind blew very hard in gusts and the sea was higher than at any other time of the voyage, and would have forced us to run before it had it not been our course. We ran 12.5 knots, which is the greatest speed the ship has yet made. The rolling was very heavy; several people were hurt. I was thrown from starboard to port against the gunwale and lay stunned; I had a bad bruise on the right knee, where an abscess formed which kept me from walking — though it did not keep me from standing my watch.

1803-01-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts. Shortened sail and lowered the gaff. Obs. lat. 21° 8' 59", obs. long. 68° 10'.
1803-01-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 6th of Pluviôse (26 January 1803). On the sixth we had a very cloudy sky and the winds north-east, a pleasant breeze. Our occupations for the day were, as usual, replacing the water we had consumed and working on our longboat, which was beginning to come along and to take good shape.
I sent men kangaroo hunting, but we had no luck. Only a single one was taken alive and brought on board, along with three others strangled by the dogs.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind calm.
1803-01-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from ENE to NNE. We shook out the reefs of the topsails, rigged the topgallant masts and the gaff and ran out the jib boom. At noon in 20° 9' of latitude observed, 68° 10' of longitude observed and 64° 2' of longitude by account. The course given N 67° 30' W. Saw a frigate bird. During the night overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts with frequent lulls.

1803-01-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze, a swell running. Crowded sail, hoisted the gaff and ran out the boom. Saw a frigate bird wheeling above our masts. Overcast weather, a strong breeze and continual rain. Obs. lat. 20° 20' 34", est. long. 67° 2' 0".
1803-01-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 7th (27 January 1803). On the seventh the weather was much the same as the day before, and the sky had an ugly enough look as to as to (sic) make us fear some squall, the horizon being heavy with storms in several quarters. But the breeze from the north-east, varying toward the north, which sprang up during the morning, dispersed the clouds that were piling up one upon another, and the weather set fair again.
Work on the longboat continued, and those who had the task of making us planks for the planking acquitted themselves very well.
During the night the sky clouded over again and became stormy. From time to time we had some gusts from the south quarter and occasionally rain.
1803-01-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a good breeze from N to ENE. At noon in 20° 20' of latitude observed and in 66° 40' of longitude observed. The course given N 78° 45' W. The cables were bent. At midnight the course given N 84° 22' 30" W (west half north).

1803-01-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth. Saw tropic birds. In the afternoon bent our cables. Obs. lat. 20° 28' 8", est. long. 63° 49' 0".
1803-01-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
As I intended to get under sail as soon as the time I had allowed the Casuarina for her return should have expired, I began to have branches of the white casuarina taken on board as food for our kangaroos, which were in very good health. We already had fifteen of them; two had died, having been too badly hurt by the dogs to recover.
In the night the wind was calm and the sky fine.
1803-01-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, with rain at intervals. A good breeze from E to N. Saw tropic birds. At noon in 20° 28' of latitude observed and in 63° 11' of longitude by account. The course given N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, rain at intervals, a fresh breeze. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 20° 26' 42", est. long. 60° 58'.
1803-01-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daybreak we laid our longboat on her side to paint her bottom, a job that could not easily be done at sea, because of our other boats, which would have hampered us too much. In the course of the day there was time to put on four strakes, which was enough for the larboard side, which was the first to be planked. The caulkers worked the greater part of the night by torchlight to caulk the part that had (been) planked during the day.
In the evening the boats, returning on board, brought us another live kangaroo, which was put with the others. Citizen Bernier was also sent ashore to go on taking distances.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind almost calm.
1803-01-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to E. At 8 the course given N 67° 3' W. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds. At noon in 20° 27' of latitude observed and in 60° 20' of longitude by account. At 4 the course given N 78° 45' W.

1803-01-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 20° 23' 19", obs. long. 58° 37' 0".
1803-01-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 10th of Pluviôse (30 January 1803). On the tenth, in the morning, we turned our longboat over onto her other side, and during the day she underwent the same operation as the day before. The work was pushed on as fast as possible, and in the evening we set her on her permanent chocks, the caulkers having also finished theirs.
During the day we had very fine weather and a pleasant breeze from the south-south-east. I entirely gave up hope of seeing the Casuarina arrive, and could not conceive any better for what reason she had made so long an absence.
Be that as it may, being resolved to leave, we made the ship ready for it. Our topgallant masts, which had been sent down, were put back in place and the yards crossed.
A little before sunset, a band of several kangaroos having appeared at the water's edge abreast of the ship, I at once sent men to give chase in the hope of taking some of them alive. Nor was I disappointed in my expectation, for at nine o'clock the boat returned, bringing us three fine ones, though one of them was badly hurt.
During the night fire broke out on board above the galley and burned through the deck. It was noticed in time to be put out at once. The officer of the watch was placed under arrest for not having warned me of this accident, which fortunately had no consequences.
1803-01-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from E to ENE. At 8 the course given N 67° 30' W. At noon in 20° 23' of latitude observed and in 58° 37' of longitude observed. At 6 the course given N 78° 45' W. Saw many tropic birds and tropic gulls.

1803-01-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze. Saw many tropic birds and tropic gulls. Obs. lat. 20° 14' 4", est. long. 55° 54'. Departure from Mauritius.
1803-01-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 11th (31 January 1803). On the eleventh I ought to have got under sail, the twenty days I had laid down to the Casuarina as the longest term having expired. However, I spent one more day at anchor in the hope of seeing her arrive, but it was to no purpose that I lost the twenty-four hours.
The weather was very fine during the morning, and we had a pleasant breeze from south-south-east to south-south-west, of which I much regretted not having taken advantage.
The boat charged with supplying our consumption of water brought us on her return two fine live emus, which the men caught with the help of the dogs. For all our attempts we had until then been unable to get near them, although the places they frequent were known to us. This happy capture made me regret less the loss of the day I had just spent waiting for the Casuarina.
During the night the weather was fine and the wind calm.
1803-01-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to ESE. At 8 the course given N 67° 30' E. At noon in 20° 14' of latitude observed and in 55° 53' of longitude by account. During the night we lay close-hauled and hove to.

1803-02-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth of Pluviôse, from four in the morning, we made our preparations to get under sail as soon as the breeze should spring up, as we had usually had it for most of the time we stayed at this anchorage. We began by hoisting in our three boats, and then we weighed our small bower with the ship and hove short on the other. The crew was then sent to breakfast. After which, having hoisted our topsails to the mastheads, we tripped the anchor and got under way, abandoning the Casuarina to her own fortune, as it had pleased her to abandon us to ours.
My intention being to go and examine a land which the look-outs (sic) had reported to us in the western part of Île Borda [Kangaroo Island], I steered west and south. Once I was outside the bay in which we had anchored, I ranged for the third time the whole north coast of this island, recognising again all the points that served us in drawing up the chart of it, which seems to me to leave nothing to be desired.
In the afternoon the winds were south, varying to south-south-east, but the breeze blew so hard that we were obliged that we were obliged (sic) to take two reefs in the topsails and to hand all our staysails. Although the wind came to us over the land, the sea was nevertheless high and rough.
At two o'clock we sighted the Casuarina standing on the eastward tack. I expected that as soon as she caught sight of me she would come about onto the same tack as ourselves and follow us. Accordingly, when we were no more than a cannon shot from each other, I had the mainsail clewed up and furled so that she might have less trouble in following us. But this troubled her very little, and she went on running to the east, so much so that at half past three we lost sight of her. It is doubtless difficult to explain this manoeuvre on the part of Citizen Freycinet, and no doubt he will acquaint us with it at our first meeting.
As I wished to get outside the islands and rocks lying to the north of Île Borda, I held on my course, preferring to wait for the Casuarina at the end of the island rather than lose time chasing after her by working back to the east. For it was not to be supposed that she would keep long on that tack, if indeed her intention was to rejoin us, which I am very far from believing.
At eight o'clock, being off the western part of the island, I carried little sail during the night and kept always in sight of the coast, with the stern lantern lit so that the Casuarina might see us, should it please her not to go to the anchorage or to any other place.
During the night the sky was dark and damp; at times we had a few rain squalls, but they were of little consequence and short duration. The breeze died away entirely and the winds varied from south-south-east to north-east.
1803-02-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from ENE to NE. At daybreak we shaped our course and sighted Mauritius. During the night we stood off and on.

1803-02-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At eight o'clock the western point of Île Borda [Kangaroo Island] bore south 22° west, at a distance of two miles.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, at daybreak, having no sight of the Casuarina, I decided to run a little to the east in the hope of meeting her. But at eight o'clock, not wishing to go inside the western point of Île Borda for the fourth time, I decided to steer south to try to fall in with the land that had been reported to us when we ran up this part of the coast coming from the south. During the morning, and indeed all day, the weather was ill suited to this search, being dark, hazy and often rainy. But as there were a few clear spells from time to time, we had at moments a fairly extensive horizon, without perceiving anything that could make us suspect that there was any land in the neighbourhood.
At noon we had no observed latitude. That by dead reckoning placed us in 36° 5' 7", and the longitude was 134° 21' 10".
In the afternoon the wind fell away considerably, and the haze was almost continuous, with a few intervals. We went on steering south, making a little westing, until nightfall, without any sign of the approach of land. As at that time I gave up hope of meeting with any, and we were well to the south of the spot where it had been said to lie and of which a note was made at the time, I had the course brought more to the west during the night.
If indeed there is any land to the west of Île Borda, it can only be a few inconsiderable islets, which leave a very clear channel between them and the west coast of Île Borda. My opinion is that none exists, although several people claim to have seen it.
During the night the weather was very damp from the haze and the fine rain we had at intervals. The winds, for their part, were extremely variable and often calm; (they) went round various points of the compass. We sounded several times as a precaution, without finding bottom at ninety fathoms. Besides, we had a heavy swell from south to south-west, which told us plainly enough that we had no land to fear in that quarter.
1803-02-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 4 a.m. we shaped our course for the North West Port; at 9.30 doubled Coin de Mire. At 1.30 p.m. we anchored inside the Deux Frères and warped in under Île aux Tonneliers, where we made fast with four moorings.

1803-02-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth the sky remained as hazy as on the preceding days, and the rain, though not heavy, nevertheless troubled us a good deal. We continued to steer west without making much northing, as I wished to make sure that there was no land (in) this latitude that might endanger the navigators who will frequent these waters hereafter, this being the shortest route they have to take to return to Europe. During the morning the breeze was light, and we had the winds south, varying to south-south-east.
At noon we had no observation of latitude, and by our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 36° 21' 27" and 133° 26' 47" of longitude. The barometer, which kept always below 27 28°, gave us no promise of an early end to the disagreeable weather we had had since our departure from Île Borda [Kangaroo Island].
In the afternoon we brought our course a little to the north, and held it so until the middle of the night, when the winds having when the winds having (sic) shifted to the south-west, varying to west-south-west, obliged us to stand close-hauled on (the) course the north-north-west.
As we had for a long while been experiencing a fairly heavy swell from the south-west, we had reason to fear that the winds would settle in that quarter for some time, or even bring us some squalls.
During the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth the weather was far from fine. The winds from the west-south-west blew at times in strong gusts, bringing us very cold rain. In the middle of the night they obliged us to take two reefs in our topsails.
As work had gone on without cease on our longboat since our departure from Île Borda, I flattered myself that she might be fit to serve us at the islands of St Peter and St Francis, where I shall surely have occasion to anchor, being persuaded that among the islands there must be some good shelter and perhaps also a port of call useful to the navigators who will come after us.
1803-02-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the morning I went to the hospital for the abscess on my knee. The port's caulkers worked on the ship. We watered.

1803-02-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather seemed inclined to set fair, and the barometer, within a very short interval, rose from 27 in. 10 l. to 28 in. 2 l., which we took as a good omen. The winds varied from south-south-west to south and at times even to south-south-east. We nevertheless still had a very high swell from the south-west, although the sea was otherwise smooth.
At daybreak we found two of our kangaroos dead in their pens. I had no doubt that it was the bad weather that had cost us them, for they were soaked through by the rain and (the) continual mist we had had for three days, although the greatest care had been taken to cover their pens well with good tarpaulins. This mishap decided me to keep them no longer on the gangways where they had been housed. But to find them another convenient place, two people had to be made discontented, or at least one, for he let me know it in no uncertain manner, reproaching me that if he was on board it was entirely my fault, since I had refused to let him leave in the Naturaliste, in accordance with the written request he had made to me at Port Jackson, etc. "You are right," I said by way of sole reply, "but I should have taken good care not to urge you not to dishonour yourself, had I been able to foresee that you were capable of preferring your ease and a few passing comforts to the greater success of the expedition and to what may be of service to our country." I none the less took the cabin of M. Leschenault, our botanist, and that of M. Ransonnet, which I needed to house the seven kangaroos that were exposed to every inclemency of the weather on our gangways.
At noon the latitude by observation, which we had been without for three days, placed us in 34° 55' 27", and the longitude by the timekeeper was found to be 131° 27' 50". So as to go no further west, I had the ship steered north-north-west in order to close with the mainland a little to the east of the point where I had lost sight of it, having in that quarter a landmark that could not be mistaken, since there lies an islet of peculiar shape which is the last one meets when coming from the east in search of the Isles of St Peter. That is why, on the first occasion, I gave it the name of the Postillon.
During the rest of the day the sky, though very cloudy, was tolerably fine and the winds very variable from south-south-west to south; but as the barometer kept rising, we remained convinced that we should very shortly have fine weather, although the sea was still running very high from the south-west.
At eight in the evening we hauled close to the wind on the tack heading south towards the west, which we held until midnight, and then and at that time (sic) the south-east tack until daylight, so as not to close with the land, from which I did not reckon myself at any great distance, and also for (fear that) the islets lying on our course might extend further south than those whose positions we had already established.

1803-02-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At daybreak,
the islets seen the day before bore east by north, two leagues distant.
At eight o'clock,
we sighted the mainland to the east by south; it could be seen only from the mastheads.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the sixteenth, at daylight, we steered north to close with the land during the day. The weather was fine and the sea smooth, but the swell was so heavy that we were obliged to keep the reefs in our topsails, so greatly were our masts strained by the quick and continual rolling it caused the ship.
Towards six o'clock the lookouts reported that they could see several islets to the east by north. We were not long in making them out from the deck, and at eight o'clock we recognised them beyond doubt as the same ones we had already sighted and whose position we had fixed. During the morning we continued to stand to the north to close with the land at the Postillon islet, from which point I must do my utmost never again to lose sight of the mainland until I have rounded the Isles of St Peter and St Francis to the north.
At noon we observed the latitude of 36° 33' 33° 36' 33", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 131° 36' 13".
During the evening the weather continued fine, and at sunset the breeze freshened greatly. At six o'clock the islets seen in the morning bore from north-east to east-north-east, at a considerable distance. We continued to stand to the north until eight o'clock, when we went on the tack heading south towards the west, which we held until the following day, under little sail.
The weather was fine during (the evening); the winds varied from south-east to south-south-east and fell calm shortly after moonrise.
At eight o'clock we were in 40 fathoms of water, and we kept this depth until daylight, when it was found to be 45 fathoms.
One of the islets we had in sight almost the whole day is easy to recognise by its shape, having the appearance of a haystack at a distance of eight or ten leagues; but on approaching nearer one sees a lower piece of land joining it which gives it the appearance of a saddle. The other islets are much lower and can be seen only when the Meulot de Foin islet presents itself in the form of a saddle. Those lying further to the north-east cannot be seen, or can be seen only, once one has rounded the one I have just described.

1803-02-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At six o'clock,
we sighted three islets to the north-east, which at sunset we recognised,
as being the same ones we had seen during our first run along the coast, having passed to the east of them in order to follow the mainland.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, in the morning, we closed with the mainland, steering north-east. It seemed to us that the currents had carried us a good deal to the east during the night, for at daylight we found ourselves no more than three leagues from the islets seen the day before. The sky, which was then overcast, cleared again, and all morning we had a pleasant breeze from south-east to south-south-east and made good way. The heavy swell, which had not left us since our departure from Île Borda [Kangaroo Island], became much less and we found the sea smooth.
At noon the latitude was observed as 32° 43' 35", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 131° 43' 47".
As we had by then closed with the mainland and clearly recognised our Île du Postillon, we began from this point a fresh series of bearings of the coast, intending to continue them, if possible, as far as the 128th degree of longitude, which, together with what General d'Entrecasteaux accomplished, will give an exact knowledge of the whole southern coast of New Holland.
After rounding the Postillon islet to the north, we followed the coast closely, tracing its various windings. The breeze was very strong in the afternoon, and we made fairly rapid progress until five o'clock in the evening, when, finding ourselves abreast of the Isles of St Peter, we went about and stood off so as not (sic) to become entangled during the night among islands whose position and number are uncertain, the more so as we counted three of them whereas the chart mentions only two.
To the north-west as well as to the south-east of the Île du Postillon, the shores are reefs which run out in these two directions nearly a mile to seaward and on which the sea breaks heavily. The channel they form with the mainland nevertheless appears navigable, but it is more prudent to pass to the south of them in closing with the coast.
The night of the seventeenth to the eighteenth was spent beating to windward, with all reefs taken in the topsails, within sight of the Isles of St Peter. The breeze blew very hard, and the sky, though cloudy, was nevertheless fine. The lead never gave less than 34 fathoms, and at midnight, when we went about onto the tack heading east towards the north, it gave 37, sand and broken shells.
The land we saw in the afternoon is of moderate height and often divided into lower portions that can be distinguished only on approaching. It offers little that is pleasing to the eye, appears to be very thinly wooded, and has no tall timber.

1803-02-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At seven in the evening,
the eastern part of the Isles of St Peter bore north 50° west,
an islet could be seen at north 25° west.
The easternmost point of the mainland bore north 87° east.
On the 18th at 7 in the morning we found ourselves we found ourselves (sic) about a league and a half from the shore of the easternmost of the Isles of St Peter.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, being two leagues from the easternmost of the Isles of St Peter, we closed with the point of the mainland where our bearings of the day before had ended. The coast here forms a great indentation in the shape of a wide bay extending to the north-east by north. We stood into it to learn its depth and to see whether there might not be some harbour in it where ships could lie in safety. As the weather was fine and the breeze fresh, we advanced fairly rapidly, with the lead constantly going. When we found no more than eleven fathoms, we fell in less than a quarter of an hour to six, which obliged us to bear away and even to change tacks in order to reach the other headland, which forms the entrance of this bay on the west. We were still nearly two leagues from the north-eastern bight, but it could be seen perfectly well that it offered neither breaks nor openings that might lead one to believe it contained anything of interest.
This want of water having obliged us to stand a little way out to sea, we sighted a long reef awash, on which the sea rose to a great height and which appeared to us to be more than a league in extent. We then had fifteen fathoms, and being unable to pass between it and the mainland, we were compelled to close with the eastern part of the Isles of St Peter and to pass between these islands and the reef, skirting at a mile and a half at most the third island, of which the chart makes no mention. The channel between this island and the reef is a good league wide, with a depth of 15 to 18 fathoms, sand mixed with broken shells.
After rounding it, we saw several other islands to the west and to the east which we judged must form part of the Isles of St Francis. In the channels separating the islands from one another there are several reefs awash on which the sea breaks heavily, but which may be passed fairly close without any danger, the water being deep. We were often obliged to luff for some and to bear away for others. At length, standing north towards the east to close with the land, we rounded two islands which lie very close to the mainland, and when we were to the north of the first we came in view of a large bay, even deeper than the one passed in the morning. It seemed to me that we should find good shelter there, and I resolved to seek an anchorage in it by going round the western sides of these islands. This conjecture proved correct, for when we had them to the south-east we found the sea very calm there. We then shortened sail and, continuing to stand north in eleven and twelve fathoms, advanced as far as six fathoms, where I anchored a league and a half from the shore on a bottom of grey sand mixed with broken shells and weed. The land at the head of the bay still lay more than two leagues off to the east-south-east, but before venturing in with the ship it was necessary to make sure whether there was (water enough) to go in as well as to come out.
As soon as our sails were furled, two boats were sent off at once to sound around the ship and in various directions.
I learnt on their return that the head of this bay was not at all navigable, even for a small vessel. About a mile from the ship there were no more than five fathoms of water; half a mile further on, four, and almost at once three and two. Further in, nothing could be seen but shoals and an unbroken succession of sandbanks which partly dry at low water.
The boat that had been ordered to head north-west gave us a moment of joy and satisfaction by telling us that it had discovered a fine harbour into which four rivers ran, and that in the one it had entered there were four fathoms of water, and three further in; that the water there was indeed salt, but that in all likelihood it would become fresh further up. This was (sic) all the more welcome to us as it made up for our regret at having found nothing, until that moment, on this coast that might repay our pains and be of use to navigators.
The small boat, which I had likewise sent to the island opposite which we lay at anchor, and in which Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, embarked to explore the country and its productions, did not return until during the night, having been left aground at low water more than two miles from the shore.
According to the gardener's report, this island consists of nothing but sand, on which grow various low shrubs. From this excursion he brought back only a few plants in seed, having found none in flower. Among them is one which has exactly the habit of the olive tree, and whose fruit resembles the olive in miniature, although the seed it contains is quite different. A great fire was lit on this island to serve as a signal to the Casuarina, should she happen to pass in these waters.
As it blew a strong breeze all day all day (sic), and we had only thirty fathoms of cable out, we veered twenty more, and despite the violent gusts from the south-south-east we rode firm at our anchor, proof that the bottom was not bad and the holding good.
1803-02-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: General Magallon came to visit the ship.

1803-02-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
19 Pluviôse (8 February 1803). On the nineteenth, at daybreak, having no hope of being able to go any further into the bay, I sent off two boats to go right round it. As we had the sun to the north as well as to the south, and consequently little facility for observing the latitude on board, Citizen Bernier embarked in the one that began its course by the east, the command of which I gave to Citizen Bonnefoy with the instructions attached:
"To Citizen Bonnefoy, enseigne de vaisseau, etc.,
"Tomorrow at daybreak you will take command of the large bastringue boat and "you will put Citizen Bernier ashore in the deepest recess of the bay within "which we lie at anchor and which bears from you east and east by south by compass.
"To get there, you will first steer for the point which bears east and east by "south by compass from our anchorage, in order to ascertain whether, as is claimed, the land we "have to the south-east is an island. When you have made certain what it is, you will continue "on your way
"to reach the recess of which I have spoken to you.
"Immediately after Citizen Bernier has completed his observation, you will follow the coast and "pay the closest attention to recognising and taking bearings of its outline. Should you meet with any "openings, you will examine them, and if they are too deep you will make a note of them and of their direction "before retracing your steps. As it is probable that the stretch of coast you are to explore is "frequented by the natives, since we have several times seen smoke there, you will carefully avoid "any quarrel with them and will try, on the contrary, by gestures of "friendship or by showing the presents I intend for them, to make them understand how peaceful your intentions are.
"In all likelihood you will be away one or two days before completing the "circuit of the bay in which we lie, so you will take the greatest care not to "let your boat run aground.
"You will note the time of the turn of the tides and their greatest height, by "observing along the shore the lines of demarcation that may reveal it to you.
"I hope that the wish to return on board will not make you too hasty in carrying out "the mission with which you are charged, and that you will acquit yourself of it in such a way as to leave no doubt "about the places you are going to visit. Your boat will be provided with three days' provisions, and in all "circumstances you will refrain from using against the natives the arms that are embarked for the "safety of all those who accompany you." Signed N. B.
In the second boat, which I sent to go round by the north and of which Citizen Ransonnet had command, I embarked Citizen Faure, geographical engineer, to examine in detail the harbour that had been reported to us and to draw a plan of it.
Copy of the instructions given to Citizen Ransonnet.
"Tomorrow, 19 Pluviôse, at daybreak, you will take command of one of our large "boats and proceed to the place that Martin, second quartermaster, will point out to you.
"From the imperfect account he has given me of the harbour he came upon, this place appears "to deserve closer examination, and that is why Citizen Faure accompanies you, in order to draw its "plan as exactly as possible. As this place appears to be frequented by the natives, you must "visit it with prudence and not put yourself at risk by letting your boat run aground. You "will avoid any kind of engagement with them. Should they come to meet you, so as not to be obliged "to use the arms I place at your disposal, you will try, on the contrary, to induce them to "approach you, by showing them the presents I intend for them, and will use all the gestures "of friendship customary on such occasions to make them understand how peaceful "and friendly your intentions are.
"I hope that the wish to carry out your mission well will lead you to devote the necessary time to it and that "you will return on board only when the work is finished. You will provide yourself with provisions for three "days." Signed N. B.
When the two boats had been sent off, I sent the small one to dredge, which brought us back nothing curious or of interest.
It appears that the ground on which we lie has few fish, for not a single one was taken on the line. The small number of sea birds frequenting this bay showed us, moreover, that they are not common here.
Throughout the day it blew a strong breeze from south-south-east to south, and during the night it was even fresher than during the day. The ship nevertheless rode firm at her anchor, though it is true that she had no strain to bear from the sea. The direction of the current, as observed on board, came from the south on the flood and from the east-north-east on the ebb. Its speed was about one mile an hour at two-thirds tide.
1803-02-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: We were ready to put to sea. Two men deserted, two were left in hospital, and we took 10 from La Cayenne, of whom 3 were unfit for service. Citizen Depuche, mineralogist, stayed at Mauritius, being unable to bear the passage to France. Citizens Le Bas, frigate captain (whom we had left wounded at Timor) and Lucas, ensign, came aboard as passengers. We took 120 pots of brandy in place of the same quantity lost on the passage from Port Jackson; 300 lb of rice, 150 lb of beans, 65 lb of coffee, 3 lb of tea and 25 sacks of maize for the voyage to France.

1803-02-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
20 Pluviôse (9 February 1803). On the twentieth the weather continued fine and the winds still southerly, varying to south-south-east, a strong breeze. On board we busied ourselves with finishing the work on our longboat, which was completed that day, together with her masts, sails and rigging. We were thus in a position to use her at the first opportunity that should arise, and I hope that the fate of this third one will be happier than that of the other two.
In the morning I sent the small boat ashore to get us some grass for our kangaroos, which are all in very good condition and have a good appetite. But what was brought back did not suit them at all, and not one would eat it. As they are beginning to grow used to maize, I hope soon to be able to wean them entirely from that food.
In the afternoon we sighted our two boats returning. Citizen Bonnefoy's arrived first. According to the verbal report he made to me, the head of this bay offers no resources, being short of water everywhere and scarcely usable even by small craft. They could not approach the land nearer than a mile, and to put Citizen Bernier ashore the boat had to be run aground. According to his observation, the latitude of the place where he landed would be 32° 24' and the longitude 131° 27' 45". But he regards these observations as very doubtful, owing to the great altitude of the sun relative to an artificial horizon which he was obliged to use. For the rest, in the whole circuit of the bay no opening was met with that might suggest there was any river or stream flowing into the sea. It even appears that in the rainy season the water is absorbed by the sand before it can take any course. The whole interior of the country appeared to them sandy and covered with a kind of low heath, without any tall timber. They brought back a branch of a shrub whose fruits had a pleasant taste, on which the boat's crew feasted thoroughly. Perhaps the written report I am awaiting from Citizen Bonnefoy will tell me something of greater interest.
On the arrival of Citizen Freycinet and M. Faure, the harbour that had been reported to us was found indeed to exist, but the want of water makes it impracticable for a ship of our size, and even for one much smaller, there being at high water among the banks that lie in it only three
fathoms of water. The rivers, moreover, are nothing but arms of the sea which lose themselves in marshes. The isthmus that forms the entrance of this harbour on the south is no more than ninety to a hundred paces wide and is nothing but a heap of sand covered with low shrubs. In this harbour a few fish of the carangue kind were caught, on which the sailors feasted, as well as on the same fruits that the other boat had come upon.
From the isthmus a fire was seen in the interior of the country, and someone even claimed to have seen natives on the beach, but at a great distance. I am awaiting the written report of Citizen Ransonnet and the detailed plan of M. Faure.
M. Bonnefoy's boat also saw some smoke in the interior of the country but did not sight any natives, though some traces of them were thought to have been noticed.
During the night the weather was very cloudy and the breeze still strong. I should have liked to get under sail the next day, but as I had been told that a kind of kangaroo of a colour quite different from that we knew them to have, and some very remarkable birds, had been seen on the island, I decided to stay one day longer, for the sake of the natural history of the country, which it is proper to know.
1803-02-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: The ship swung. I left the hospital and came back aboard in the evening. On reaching Mauritius the only animals left alive were 3 cassowaries, 3 wombats, 2 swans, the goose from Bass Strait, the 2 dogs and a few birds. We took aboard 2 Bengal does, 2 guinea fowl and 1 four-horned sheep.

1803-02-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
21 Pluviôse (10 February 1803). On the twenty-first, in the morning, the weather being as on the preceding days, I sent off the large boat and all our huntsmen with the dogs to try to bring us something new. As it was a pleasure party, all the naturalists, who until then had stayed quietly on board for fear of not being comfortable in a boat that might be one or two nights ashore, asked to go. They were taken there. I hope they enjoy themselves and come back pleased with their outing, if they are not pleased with what may be found.
Citizen Péron is the only one who embarked in the boat commanded by M. Bonnefoy, but the short time he spent ashore did not make his pains very useful (added after the line, in another hand: "I had embarked in spite of you. The objects I collected on the excursion in question were very interesting and numerous. Read my zoological commentaries" by Péron?)
During the morning we hoisted in two of our boats, and everything was made ready to sail tomorrow if the winds are favourable.
The breeze was very strong during the day, and I was astonished to see the ship ride so firmly at her anchor. It is true that we then had seventy fathoms of cable out.
At sunset the boat that had taken the naturalists and our huntsmen ashore returned on board. The former brought back several new plants, and the latter some birds we had not yet seen, two short-tailed opossums alive, three dead, and two kangaroo rats which seemed to us different from those we knew, at least in the colour of their fur.
The boat was hoisted in at once and the ship made ready to get under sail the next day.
Departure from the Baie des Saints
1803-02-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 10 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course to pass north of Réunion, which was sighted during the night.

1803-02-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, smooth sea. At 4 took the bearing of Morne Brabant south 30° east, estimated distance 19 miles. We rounded Réunion by the north, which brought us calms. Longitude and latitude from the bearing: 21° 8'; long. 52° 35' 0".
1803-02-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
(end of page 359) until the moment when the ship, which was making six knots, was about to run upon it. We were lucky enough to avoid it by trimming the sails as smartly as possible close to the wind; I do not think we passed it at half a musket-shot. And from the western end of the reef I have just mentioned, at a mile and a half at most.
At these islands we ended our bearings of the south and south-west coast of New Holland, and I have no doubt that the chart we shall give of it, together with the one published from d'Entrecasteaux's voyage, will provide an exact knowledge of the whole of this region so long unknown to Europeans.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, in the morning, the wind being south-east by east, a strong breeze, we made our preparations for getting under way. As we had seventy fathoms of cable out, we had a good deal of trouble heaving short, at which point I expected to drag, if indeed that did not happen sooner. But I was mistaken in my expectation, for it was a long time before we could break out the anchor.
As soon as it was stowed, we set the topsails, with two reefs in, and the foresail. I had counted on being able to skirt the west shore of the bay we were leaving without difficulty, but we had hardly run a mile and a half to approach it when the depth, which had been eight fathoms, suddenly fell to five, which obliged us to stand a little out to sea until we were outside the points forming its entrance. Then, finding no bottom at ten fathoms, we followed the mainland closely, tracing all its windings. The land in this quarter is all sandy and made up of dunes, most often without the least vegetation. Those parts that had a little shade were covered only with a few low shrubs.
Coasting along, we left to the south the northern part of the Isles of St Francis and the rocky banks lying off their ends or in the channels separating them from one another.
At noon the observed latitude was 32° 2' 56", and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 130° 21' 13". This latitude placed us (no figures) minutes north of our anchorage in the Baie des Saints.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze, and we took advantage of it to push our bearings as far as possible, so as to complete the 129th degree of longitude before nightfall if we could. While running along the mainland coast, which in this last stretch is tolerably high on the second range of mountains visible in the interior of the country, we sighted several islands lying fairly close to the coast which are nothing but rocks, detached from one another, on which the sea breaks heavily. Off the end of every point or cape we rounded, the sea was so hollow and the swell so high that it made the ship fall off 20 to 25 degrees. And I believe it would be very difficult to claw off this coast if one had to beat to windward with winds from south-west to south-east. We attributed the effect of this heavy swell to the currents, having no bottom at 25 fathoms.
At five o'clock we sighted four islets and a large reef lying in the line of our course. We continued to steer for them in order to identify them, and we soon saw that (in the margin: they were those) we had already sighted when, before this last occasion, we sought to reconnoitre the mainland to the north of the Isles of St Peter and St Francis, coming from the west. The four islets and the reef lying a short way to the west of them are not good to frequent, although we passed very close to them. The sun, so beneficent and so useful to navigation, very nearly became the cause of our ruin, since it hid from our view a small flat rock awash, which we did not sight (continued on the previous page 358)

1803-02-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm, a swell running. Clewed up the courses and lay under topsails. At noon went onto the port tack. Est. lat. 22° 1' 42", long. 51° 33' 24".
1803-02-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, having stood to the south-west during the night to draw away from the coast, my intention being to reach King George Sound as soon as possible without reconnoitring the islands of the Espérance archipelago. During the morning we continued to steer south 32° 30' west until noon, when we took a south-westerly course. It seemed to me that this course was useful for the safety of navigation, since it should enable us to make sure whether there were not some islets or reefs among those reconnoitred by General d'Entrecasteaux.
All day we had a good breeze from the east and fine weather, but we found the sea running high and rough. All morning a very great number of birds of the petrel and albatross kinds were seen. They disappeared in the evening.
At noon the latitude was observed as 33° 52' 12", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 128° 37' 5".
During the evening the weather continued fine and the winds varied from east-south-east to south-east. When I consider the winds we have met with since our departure from King Island, I truly find it hard to understand how the English could have persuaded themselves that on the route I had to take one met with nothing but strong westerly and south-westerly winds. This opinion, which I was far from sharing, I could not draw them out of the error in which they are, even by citing to them the winds I had met with the year before, and I do not know on what authority, since none of their ships which, leaving Port Jackson for Europe, will for a long time yet prefer the route by Cape Horn to that by Bass Strait, which is beyond dispute the best in this season.
During the night the weather continued fine, and we had a pleasant breeze from east-south-east, with the help of which we made good progress to the west, edging a little to the south.

1803-02-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, the winds from SE to east, a fresh breeze. Shifted the mizzen topsail tie. Est. lat. 24° 12' 54", est. long. 49° 39' 24".
1803-02-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth the winds continued very favourable to us, and we made the most of them. As on the previous day we had a good breeze from east to east-south-east, and the sea still running high. In the morning we passed through a fairly considerable tide-rip, which came to us from the south-west and lasted nearly half an hour. The noise the waves made as they dashed against one another was exactly like the noise waves make when they roll upon a sandy beach.
In the morning the work on our boats, whose gunwales had to be replaced, was completed.
At noon the latitude was observed as 34° 9' 31", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 134° 58' 23" (124° 58' 5" on the page of astronomical observations, which agree better with the course followed to the west.)
The weather continued fine in the evening and we made our course less southerly, but at sunset the sky took on a very threatening look. The whole horizon was covered with thick clouds and the barometer fell a great deal. There was every sign of bad weather for the night; nevertheless we did not shorten sail, so as to make the most of the fair wind while it lasted.
After sunset the sky was very dark and the night extremely black. We saw several thunderstorms gathering in the north-east, from which came a great deal of lightning, but the sound of the thunder did not reach us. There were only occasional squalls of little duration or consequence. The winds, which towards the end of the day had settled in the east, varied little from it, and we had nothing worse than unpleasant weather, for which we were amply compensated by the good run we made, which brought us rapidly nearer to the islands of the Recherche Archipelago.
In the course of this day we lost one of the kangaroos taken on the Île des Opossum in the Baie des Saints. Its death was the result of the wounds it had received from the dogs, besides a charge of small shot. This species, as I have already observed, is about the same size as those of Shark Bay and differs only in the colour of its fur, which is redder.

1803-02-14.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from NE to ENE. Shifted the [one word illegible] of the main brace, and one of the fore topsail tie blocks. Obs. lat. 26° 11' 46", est. long. 47° 51' 24".
1803-02-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, we (sic) in the morning, we had the winds in the east, varying towards the north, and the breeze fell off a little. The sky was constantly overcast, dark and misty, so that we did not see the sun all day. We steered west to reach the longitude of King George Sound as soon as possible, so as to turn the south-westerly winds to our advantage should they set in, as the state of the atmosphere and the behaviour of the barometer suggested they would.
By our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves at noon in latitude 35° 47' 55", and our longitude was 121° 41' 5".
During the evening the weather was the same as we had had in the morning, but the winds came round again from the east towards the south and were extremely variable. We continued to steer west until eight in the evening, when we steered west by south for the night, so as to make no way to the north.
As I reckoned myself in the neighbourhood of the Recherche Archipelago, I had a sounding taken at midnight to learn whether the bottom extended far to the south of these islands. We found none at 120 fathoms, straight up and down. No change was made in the sail, and we held our course all night, which had a very threatening look without, however, bringing any change in the weather, but a great deal of inconstancy in the winds, which did nothing but shift about from east towards south. During the night we saw several thunderstorms gathering in the north-east, which gave us a great deal of lightning, and only twice was thunder heard rumbling in the distance. The few squalls we had brought us more rain than wind and were not of long duration. The mist alone stayed with us constantly.

1803-02-15.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, continual rain. At 2 the fore topgallant sheet having parted, the sail was furled. Est. lat. 28° 25' 46", est. long. 44° 56' 24".
1803-02-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, in the morning, despite little sign of fine weather for the day, we sought to draw nearer the coast, steering west-north-west with winds from east-south-east which in the course of the morning varied as far as south-south-west, a pleasant breeze. The heavy swell that had accompanied us for so long had begun to subside, and the sea had become smooth.
In the morning, the wind having fallen off a good deal and gone round to south-south-west, we feared we should soon have it from that quarter, accompanied by some squalls, the barometer having fallen below 28 inches.
By our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves at noon in 35° 58' 0" south latitude, and the estimated longitude placed us in 119° 8' 5". As this position, laid down on the chart, put us about sixty leagues west-north-west of King George Sound, we steered north-west by west in the afternoon and held this course until eight in the evening, when, seeing no sign of a change in the weather, we took a course of west by south for the night, although we had found no bottom at eight o'clock at 120 fathoms.
