During the day a fairly large number of brown albatrosses were seen, and several kinds of petrel, among which were several of those that seamen have named storm birds. But as the barometer was beginning to rise again, their appearance was no ill omen for us.
The night passed without incident, save for a thick and continual mist which, however, began to clear after moonrise. The sky nevertheless remained very overcast, and our horizon was no more than half a league across. We sounded twice during the night without finding bottom at 120 fathoms.
From various observations I made during the day of the surface of the sea, which was smooth, I thought I could perceive that the current was setting to the south, inasmuch as the ripples forming on the surface of the waves constantly came from the north, a direction quite opposite to the winds we had during the day.

1803-02-16.journal_anonyme: Rainy and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE which shifted to WSW. Went onto the starboard tack; at 3.30 a.m. it shifted to NW. Obs. lat. 29° 39' 4", est. long. 44° 19' 36".
1803-02-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh we continued to steer west, edging to the north, to close with the coast to windward of the anchorage of King George Sound. That day we had the same weather as on the days before, that is to say a pleasant breeze from the south, varying at times towards the east. The sea, still driven by a heavy swell from south to south-west, warned us that we should not be long in having winds from that quarter, which made us wish to reach the anchorage I intended to occupy as soon as possible.
At noon we had no observation of latitude, and that by dead reckoning, on which we had long been obliged to rely, placed us in (no figures), and the longitude was (no figures).
It had seldom happened to us to go so long without being able to observe the sun's passage across the meridian, and we much regretted that this annoyance should befall us at a time when we most needed it.
However that may be, we continued on our course, and at two o'clock we came in sight of a very high coast on which various mountain summits could be made out which, at the distance we were from them, seemed to form several islands. After closing with the coast so as to see it clearly, we recognised that the land nearest to us, which then bore north (in the margin, in N. B.'s hand: 5° east), was the island General d'Entrecasteaux named Île Pelée [Bald Island]. Vancouver's Mount Gardner bore north 56° west. As it was then too late to enter the harbour before nightfall, we hauled close to the wind on the tack heading south towards the west, but the inconstancy of the winds soon obliged us to take the eastward tack.
During the night the winds were light and variable, and often we even had calm with mist and rain, without any sign of bad weather, although the barometer had fallen a great deal and did not seem inclined to rise. So as not to be carried too far to the east, we lay to for some time with the main topsail to the mast.

1803-02-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a little rain. Lowered the main topsail on the cap to refit its sheet, which had parted. Est. lat. 29° 48' 34", est. long. 43° 37' 36".
1803-02-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Bearings of the land:
At two o'clock,
we sighted the land, and at sunset, after closing with it, Mount Gardner bore north 56° west
And Île Pelée [Bald Island] north by east
On the 28th at noon the entrance of the harbour bore north 85 west
And we anchored there in the bay in 17 fathoms of water, sand and mud bottom.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, in the morning, we found we had been further east than our dead reckoning made us, which obliged us to close with the land again, and we then coasted along it at a short distance. After rounding the western part of Île Pelée and clearly reconnoitring the channel that separates it from the mainland, we saw, in the space between it and Mount Gardner, several inlets which seemed to indicate that some good shelter might be found there. I did not go to examine them with the ship, but I resolved to have them examined in detail by one of my boats as soon as we should be in a safe place. I also pointed out to the officer for whom I intend this duty the spots that seemed to me to deserve it in preference to the others. And we continued on our course.
During the morning the breeze was at times very light, and despite our short distance from the anchorage we feared more than once that we should not reach it before nightfall. However, the wind having freshened a little at sunset, we got there, passing between Seal Island and the mainland so as to anchor abreast of the cove in which lies the watering place Vancouver speaks of. At eight o'clock, reckoning ourselves opposite it, we let go a bower anchor in seventeen fathoms, muddy sand bottom, and moored at once, the weather not looking promising. We also sent down the topgallant sails for the night, and everything was arranged for the greatest safety of the ship.
During the night we had calm, and the sky very overcast and misty.
Stay in King George Sound.

1803-02-18.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SW to south. The sea rather high. The weather overcast. On the morning of the 29th the mizzen shrouds were set up.
1803-02-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth (18 February 1803), at daybreak, we hoisted out our boats. One went at once to reconnoitre the watering place, and the other was employed in setting up our observatory, which was placed on a tolerably pleasant island bearing north-west by north from the ship.
When the watering boat returned, I was informed that the watering place was very good and the water easy to obtain. Ten casks were found there belonging to the Casuarina, which we knew must be in one of the two harbours and which had let us know that she had arrived before us by a flag set up on the summit of Seal Island. Our arrival had been announced to her the evening before by a gun fired during the night, to which she had replied with several rockets, which had told us that she was in Princess Charlotte Harbour.
Towards eight o'clock we sighted that vessel's boat, and shortly afterwards Citizen Freycinet, who commands her, arrived. When I asked him why he had not closed with me at the time of our meeting off Île Borda [Kangaroo Island], he replied that he had not been able to join me and that, besides, I ought to have waited for him. I then pointed out to him the bad seamanship he had shown, of which seamen will be able to judge, but he remained none the less convinced that his manoeuvre had been better than ours and that it was ours alone that had brought about the separation I complained of. As I had named the Isles of St Peter and St Francis to him,
as the first rendezvous, I asked him again whether it was my fault that he had not gone there; he answered likewise that it was, inasmuch as they did not lie in the latitude and longitude I had given him. Although we had come to look for them in precisely the same place, he objected moreover that, having very little water, he had thought it more prudent to make for this harbour than to go on searching for me, being uncertain whether he would find me. Finally he ended by telling me that, his vessel being in need of several repairs, he required caulkers and carpenters, and that he had run her aground on the sand to make this work easier.
The explanations M. Freycinet had just given me were not such as to excuse his conduct, and to show him how little satisfied I was with it, I said to him by way of sole reply that I would send a caulker and a carpenter on board his vessel and that he might employ them as he saw fit. Immediately afterwards I got into my boat and went in person to look at the watering place, to make sure it was as easy and convenient as had been reported. Having examined it, I did indeed find it so, and at once had our tents pitched there, one of them intended for the sick, of whom we then had four, and the other for the naturalists.
I also had a large reservoir made for washing the linen and hammocks of the crew, wishing to take this opportunity to have them washed.
Towards noon we had a violent gust from the west to west-south-west which obliged us to veer on our mooring cable. Nevertheless we were twice set adrift by the force of the wind, and were obliged, as a precaution for the night, to make ready our sheet anchor, which was put in readiness for letting go. The sky looked so threatening and the mountains were so heavily laden with vapour that there was every appearance of our being in for some squalls. The barometer, which was below 28, foretold them too. And they were not long in coming, for during the night rain, hail and wind harassed us in every way. At eight in the evening the sheet anchor was let go, and the ship held fast at her berth. We had also struck the topgallant masts.

1803-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running and a fresh breeze. At 3.30 the fore topgallant brace having parted at the masthead, we took in the studdingsail and clewed up the topgallant sail to repair the damage. Est. lat. 30° 14' 28", est. long. 38° 34' 42".
1803-02-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth (19 February 1803) the weather was less bad than the day before, without the sky having cleared on that account. The winds varied from west-south-west to west and north-west. As the boats could come and go, our empty casks, which were to be used for watering, were taken ashore. We contrived a kind of aqueduct which, by means of our hold hoses, was to carry the water right into our casks in the longboat without the trouble of landing them, which would have been very convenient for us. But the hoses proved so unsuitable that we had to go back to the usual method, since they lost all the water before it reached the longboat. We made only one trip that day, which yielded no more than twenty-eight casks.
In the morning the anchor held ready, which had been let go at the beginning of the night of the 29th to the 30th, was got up weighed, and it was made ready to be let go again in case of need. As the fluke that had taken the ground was found to be loaded with a great quantity of
muddy sand, we could clearly tell the nature of the bottom, which in our opinion proved too soft for the holding to be very good, although the anchors were bound to sink into it deeply enough to make it secure.
In the afternoon the weather seemed inclined to set fair, and although strong gusts often passed over, the heavy dark clouds had gone.
The night passed without incident; it was a mixture of wind, squalls and calm.

1803-02-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from the east; at noon almost calm. Obs. lat. 31° 22' 57", est. long. 36° 2' 12".
1803-02-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the First of Ventôse (20 February 1803). On the first of Ventôse I sent off two boats, one for an absence of six days and the other for ten. The one whose command I gave to Citizen Ransonnet, with ten days' provisions, was to examine the stretch of coast lying between Vancouver's Mount Gardner and d'Entrecasteaux's Île Pelée. Citizen Ransonnet carried the order and instructions that follow:
"I entrust to you, Citizen, the command of my longboat, to explore the part of the coast lying between Vancouver's Mount Gardner and d'Entrecasteaux's Île Pelée. It seemed to me all the more useful to know it in detail since it shows to the eye various windings which may offer resources, or a shelter from bad weather, to navigators who may hereafter frequent these waters.
"General d'Entrecasteaux and Vancouver saw only from afar the coast which you are going to visit close at hand and with scrupulous attention. You will enter every inlet to be found there and examine each of them in detail. If, as I am inclined to believe, you meet with some harbour there, you will make a plan of it, take the soundings, and determine as exactly as you are able the points that form its entrances.
"As you have only eight or ten leagues of coast to explore, eight or ten days ought to be more than enough for this work. That is why you must be back by that time. You will not proceed east of the eastern point of Île Pelée, and you will confine yourself to the survey of the inlet that lies to the north of it.
"Take the greatest care for the preservation of your boat and prudently avoid every occasion that might endanger its safety." Greetings. Signed N. B.
In the second boat, in which I placed Midshipman Baudin, I gave him the following instruction:
"You are to take, Citizen, the command of the large bastringue boat, in which the geographer Faure is to embark. You will go right round the bay and the two harbours in which we find ourselves, beginning with the one to the north-west of our anchorage, as far as Mount Gardner. Citizen Faure being charged with making plans of them, you will take him to the places he points out to you or which may seem to deserve particular attention. You will not forget to take soundings at every place you pass, and above all at the entrance of each harbour. In the one that bears the name of Oyster Harbour there should be a bar with only three fathoms of water over it; you will verify whether this information is correct or not.
"Take the greatest care for the preservation of your boat and carefully avoid anything that might endanger its safety. You will not linger on board the Casuarina, aground in Princess Charlotte Harbour [Princess Royal Harbour], so as not to waste your time in needless visits. Your boat will be supplied with six days' provisions, but you will return, if possible, before you have consumed them, for I do not think that Citizen Faure's work should require so much time."
After sending off the two boats of which I have just spoken, half the crew were ordered to send their linen and hammocks ashore to be washed in the tanks I have had made for that purpose. Four men of the crew were specially charged with this work. In the evening we began shipping our water and put 25 casks of it on board. The small boat, which was sent fishing at Vancouver's Seal Island, brought back only eight or ten fish, of the parrot-fish kind in shape, but very good to eat. No seals were found there, which leads me to believe that they have a particular season of the year during which they frequent these waters.
During the night the weather was tolerably fine and the breeze light and variable from south-west to east.

1803-02-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the breeze light from ENE. Obs. lat. 31° 59' 20", est. long. 33° 40' 54".
1803-02-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 2nd of Ventôse (21 February 1803). On the second, the weather being fine, I left the ship at half past five in the morning in order to see for myself Princess Charlotte Harbour [Princess Royal Harbour] and Oyster Harbour. For this visit I used my own boat, which can hold only five men including the one who steers, which (allowed) me to be its coxswain myself.
On leaving the ship, I ordered the officer of the watch to weigh our north-west anchor, which had dragged in the gust we had had the day after our arrival, and to carry it out again again (sic) on that same bearing.
I went first to the island on which our observatory is placed and visited Citizen Bernier. This island bears no name on Vancouver's plan, although it is pleasant and better wooded than the others. After spending two hours with Citizen Bernier, I made for Princess Charlotte Harbour, following the shore. The entrance of this harbour, which may be a mile wide, is convenient and easy, but for a vessel such as ours one would need the wind free, beating to windward being scarcely practicable in the passage. One should preferably keep to the larboard side of the entrance, the starboard side having much less water.
Inside this harbour I caught sight of the Casuarina aground at its head, and I went on board. This vessel was in complete disorder and remarkably dirty. The captain who commands her answered me that this was the necessary consequence of the situation in which he found himself. Most of the seamen were out hunting or fishing. I remained only half an hour on board this vessel and ordered Citizen Freycinet to come to the anchorage I occupied in two days' time, so that I might have the water and (the) wood he needed put on board him.
Princess Charlotte Harbour seemed to me convenient, and to offer a good place
of shelter for vessels which, battered by storms, might need urgent repairs; but the water, though there is no lack of it, is less good and less easy to take in than at the place where we are. Nor are there, all round the harbour, more than two or three places with a few clumps of trees fit to be used for vessels of any size. Carrying them off is made difficult by the extent of the bank that runs round the bay and dries at spring tides for nearly a mile and a half offshore. The Casuarina, at that distance, had no more than a foot of water at low tide.
Having examined this harbour, I went on to Oyster Harbour, continuing to follow the coast, which on the outside is of a far more pleasant aspect than any I had seen until then. The long sandy beach that closes the head of the bay is formed by low, sandy land. But inland the mountains are high and well wooded with tall trees, to judge them by eye. Arrived at the entrance of the harbour, formed on the north by a projecting sandy point and on the south by fairly high land, we steered into the middle of the channel to sound it and found the bottom at between twelve and thirteen feet at low water, so that I do not think there can be more than fourteen or fifteen there at high water.
The harbour appears to the eye a convenient and well-enclosed place, but we were not long in perceiving that it has no lack of banks, and that to use it one must know them well. After running aground two or three times and getting afloat again, we came ashore at the place where our longboat was, and with it Citizen Faure, whom I had charged with a more detailed survey than the one I was making myself.
As it was beginning to grow late when I arrived, we spent the rest of the day and the night at that spot, taking care only to keep our boats afloat during the night so as to be able, the next day, to go round the harbour and visit every part of it. The longboat, which had visited the island that Vancouver named Green Island, were much astonished to find there none of the seeds he had left there, and only two or three green shrubs. The rest of the island, which is of very small extent, was covered with a kind of very fine grass of a yellowish colour. It seems likely that this quantity of grass trees will have hindered the growth of the seeds he left there, or, more probably still, that the great quantity of ants found there will have destroyed them as fast as they came up.
Before sunset we climbed a fairly high mountain, from which we had a perfect view of the interior of the country and of all the lakes in it. Their their (sic) positions will be placed on the particular plan that we shall give of this harbour.
A little before sunset we saw, at two different times, some of the natives, who, the moment they caught sight of us, though at a great distance, took flight and (made) off into the woods. From the mountains where we were, very thick smoke had been seen, but at too great a distance for us to think of going there.

1803-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. From midnight to 4 stormy and squally weather, the sky overcast in the west with much lightning in the NW. The winds at 5 having shifted to NW, we trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack and made all sail. At 9.30 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Est. lat. 32° 36' 2", est. long. 31° 16' 54".
1803-02-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 3rd of Ventôse (22 February 1803). On the third, from five o'clock in the morning, we made our arrangements to go and visit the head of the harbour and examine the oyster banks of which Vancouver speaks. As the tide was low and we were in the tides of the new moon, we saw all the banks with which this harbour is filled, and which (lead) me to say to say (sic) that it is ill suited even to vessels of middling size. The main channel carries six to seven fathoms of water, but it is of very small extent, and if the force of the winds, which sometimes blow in violent gusts, above all when they are between south-west and north-west, were to make a vessel drag her anchors, she would plainly go aground on the tail of the banks that form it. It is true that she would (sic) come to no harm there, the bottom being sand and weed. But the hull of the vessel would be no less strained for it, since she would take the ground only in part. The other channels that divide the banks have only the water needed for a boat, and even then a boat often grounds, as happened several times to our longboat, and to mine, which drew half as much water.
At last we reached the head of the harbour and lay at the edge of a bank, where we took a fair number of oysters lying on a weedy bottom in a foot and a half to two feet of water. They proved to be of good flavour and very large. While the seamen were busy with this fishing, which lasted three quarters of an hour, Citizens Faure and Bailly were put ashore to visit two lagoons that we had made out from the height we had climbed the day before. And we made our way towards an opening which had every appearance of a river, and for which we long sought the passage among the banks. Before finding it, the longboat grounded several times, which gave me a considerable lead over her, and after many turnings I succeeded in coming upon a channel where I found at first two fathoms of water and then eight feet. This channel led me to a salt-water river, or rather to an arm of the sea that runs deep into the country with countless windings in different directions.
At the first point that forms its entrance I met Citizens Faure and Bailly, whom I took on board despite the little room I had in my boat. And together we went up the arm of the sea in which we found ourselves. The lagoons they had visited contain only salt water, which the high tide brings in through various small gullies running down to the sea. At one o'clock in the afternoon, having gone about a league and a half by water into the interior of the country, we stopped to dine opposite a small stream which ran into the river and in which we judged there must be fresh water. Having landed, we went to look at it and did indeed find a small quantity, which, though unpleasant to the taste, seemed to us very good, since we were in want of it.
In looking about the neighbourhood of the stream I have just mentioned, we found two rather singular and interesting monuments raised by the natives of the country, if one (could) but know their purpose. The first was placed seven or eight feet from the stream, in a spot bare of grass, three feet in circumference, and surrounded by spears, well sharpened and painted red
towards the point. There were eleven of them in all. Parallel to this trophy, on the other side of the stream, there was a similar group, alike in form and in the number of spears, but these seemed to guard the passage from the left bank to the right, as those on the left seemed to guard it against those on the right. Several persons having thought that these spears had been painted red with blood, we took one to examine it more closely, and we found that this colour had been given them with the resin of the eucalyptus.
Each of us tried to guess what these monuments might be, and we reasoned about them in (various) ways. For my part, I think they are two tombs in which lie two warriors of different tribes, who were laid there either after a single combat between them or as the result of a more general action, and who seem still to defy one another after death. I would not allow these tombs to be disturbed nor the spears that adorn them to be carried away, so that if any European comes to these places he may draw from them whatever conclusions his imagination suggests to him; but I placed two medals and a few glass beads on each of them. Maize and some other garden seeds were also sown round about.
Immediately after our dinner we re-embarked to continue up the river, into which I intended to push far enough to find fresh water. But we had scarcely gone a mile farther when we found little water and the passage closed by weirs built like sluices by the natives of the country. These weirs were closed, at the sides of the river, in the middle of which there was an island, by natural rocks belonging to each bank. But in the places where there were none, and which had been scoured out by the currents, the natives had put in stones which, laid with art and symmetry one beside another, prove that they are not without intelligence. Up to that point we had not found less than six feet of water, and it was with great regret that we saw ourselves stopped in the middle of our course. Citizens Faure and Bailly, having been put ashore to observe the further course of the river, reported that it appeared to be obstructed only at the place where we were, and that beyond the two weirs we had in sight it seemed quite as deep and navigable as we had found it until then. Meanwhile the longboat arrived, which, after getting afloat, had followed us at a distance. With this reinforcement I decided to have my boat carried over the weirs, and this operation was done much more easily than I had thought. When it was across, we re-embarked once more and went up another three quarters of a mile, until six more weirs, each standing higher above the water than the last, closed the passages to us entirely and obliged us to turn back. The water was still salt and the current ran at half a knot. A party went ashore to explore as the first time, and again saw nothing closing the river on the other side of these weirs, but as its windings are very numerous, the view did not reach far.
We noticed that the last ones were made with still more intelligence than the first. Among them one could make out several whose widest opening was on the side of the flood tide, while that on the side of the ebb was so narrowed that it seemed rather difficult for the fish, which the sea had easily been able to carry in, to get out (one word illegible)
Obliged to turn back, we carried our boat once more to the other side of the weirs over which we had made it pass, and thought of our return, night beginning to approach.
The banks of the stretch of river we went over are very pleasant to the eye. The land there is high and well furnished with tall trees. I gathered there various kinds of seeds and some plants in flower which are unknown to me. Everywhere we saw traces of fires and signs that the natives frequent these parts from time to time. But in the places where they had gathered, easy to recognise by the spots where they had made their fires, we did not find the slightest sign of what might have served them for food.
We picked up several of their spears, which were found leaning against the trees as though they had been put by in reserve. These weapons of war were roughly made and much less well proportioned than at Port Jackson. At the foot of a high chain of mountains running north and south in the interior of the country we saw a great many columns of smoke, separate from one another, which made us think that the natives were at that moment in the neighbourhood; but they were too far from us for us to try to reach them by crossing an unknown country and without provisions. We gave up the idea of visiting them.
At sunset, after coming down the river by the same way we had come as far as the point to which we had been able to penetrate. We came to spend the night inside the harbour, which we could reach only at about ten o'clock in the evening, after grounding several times. The longboat, to which the same thing happened, did not join us until the middle of the night, and with great difficulty.
From what I saw in the excursion I have just made, I think I may say that Oyster Harbour can hardly be used except by small vessels. It is not nearly as good as Princess Charlotte Harbour [Princess Royal Harbour], though far more pleasant to look upon. In the lagoons and at the head of the harbour we saw only a few ducks, teal, cormorants and gulls, but all these birds were so wild that they could be approached only at very great distances. We did not see a single black swan.
During our stay the boats took fish in abundance, and very good. So we made the most of it. The dogfish, which are plentiful, made us lose many lines and hooks. Land birds are scarce. I shot only one teal of a new species and one golden-winged pigeon.
The sandbanks of Oyster Bay that uncover are full of worm tubes, which must be very harmful to vessels that are not sheathed with copper. Whole shells are very rare there, although many broken ones are found on the shore. We likewise picked up very few, of the clam kind.
No. 5
From the Fourth of Ventôse, Year Ten, to the
Seventeenth of Thermidor of the same year
(reproduce the first page of the volume)
Continuation of our call in King George Sound.

1803-02-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A strong breeze. At 4.30 the main jib halliard block having broken, the sail was hauled down; set up the fore topgallant stay, shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 32° 54' 33", est. long. 29° 3' 24".
1803-02-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth of Ventôse, at daybreak, I made my arrangements to return on board, and left to Citizen Faure the entire survey of the harbour and of the coast that ends at Mount Gardner. From five o'clock in the morning I set out on on (sic) my way. As I intended to stop at the observatory to learn the results of the eclipse of the sun which took place, for us, on the third a little before sunrise, I was greatly astonished to find Citizen Bernier no longer established at the spot where I had had his tent pitched. But having caught sight of him on the mainland opposite the island where he had been at first, I went there and was told that, fire having broken out round about, he had been obliged to move out in haste, and that he thought himself very fortunate that the instruments and the tent had not been touched by it, since in less than a quarter of an hour the greater part of the island had been ablaze. This fire was caused by the cooking fire that was being kept nearby.
The end of the eclipse of the sun was not visible to us, the sun not having shown itself until about eight o'clock in the morning.
Citizen Bernier informed me of the arrival of the American brig in the roadstead. On the very day I had left the ship I had indeed sighted this vessel, but I thought it was the Casuarina and paid it no great attention.
I spent part of the day with Citizen Bernier and went about the neighbourhood, where I came upon some rather pretty plants.
In the afternoon the American captain, having been told by his people that I was at this tent, came to see me. He informed me that he had left New York towards the end of the month of September last, and that he was fitted out for the fur-seal fishery, which until then had not been fortunate for him, since in the various places where he had touched he had been able to procure only three or four hundred skins, and he had twenty thousand to collect before thinking of proceeding to China. He had decided to come to this harbour on the information given by Vancouver, who, in the season when he was here, saw a great many of them. As this vessel came from the east, he told me he had spoken the boat commanded by M. Ransonnet, whom, as I have already said, I had sent to survey the part of the coast between Mount Gardner and Île Pelée.
I invited the captain to dinner for the next day, and after we had parted I returned on board.
Nothing out of the ordinary had happened during my absence; the watering was finished, so that I now awaited only the return
of the Casuarina and of Citizen Ransonnet to fix the day of my departure
The weather, though squally, with a few gusts during the night, had been generally fine, without the ship having dragged.
According to the surgeon's report, the sick who had been put ashore, four in number, were much better.

1803-02-24.journal_anonyme: Obs. lat. 34° 6' 48", est. long. 25°. Fine weather, a light breeze, the sea smooth, the sky cloudy. At daybreak sighted land stretching from N 33° W to N 22° E. Noon bearings: the easternmost end of the land NE by N; the westernmost end WNW 5° W; the nearest land N by NW, distant 12 miles.
1803-02-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Fifth (24 February 1803). On the fifth the Casuarina at last came out of Princess Charlotte Harbour [Princess Royal Harbour] and anchored opposite the watering place where we are taking in her water and ours. I sent a boat on board her to learn whether she was ready (to) receive her water, and Citizen Freycinet, having come on board in that same boat, told me told me (sic) that he was also short of wood and had taken none in Queen Charlotte Harbour, although he had been there nearly a fortnight strolling about and doing nothing. But it is more likely that he did not know the quantity that had been cut for him, since, according to the report of the carpenter I had sent to work on board him, his hold, in which there were only three or four casks, was so full that, to make room where the crew could sleep at night, a fairly large quantity of it had to be brought up on deck.
However that may be, we agreed that I would have some cut for him ashore opposite the watering place, though he claimed he had none. But as I had seen for myself, I knew what to think.
This officer obligingly remained on board until eight o'clock in the evening, when one of my boats had to be (hoisted out) to take him on board and come back.
The American captain whom I had invited to dinner came on board at about two o'clock in the afternoon. Before we sat down to table, he begged me to give him, if possible, a chart of the coast of New Holland, having no information that might guide him in the courses he was about to make in search of the places frequented by fur seals, nor for the trend of the coast or the dangers that lie along it. I gave him two of Citizen Beautemps-Beaupré's charts and one of Bass Strait and Banks Strait by Mr Flinders, as well as particular observations on the entrance of Port Phillip and of Port Bass, and on the position of King Island. I most particularly recommended him, if he put in at Île Borda [Kangaroo Island], to prevent his people from shooting the pigs and the pigs (sic) and the fowls I have left on that island for the future benefit of the navigators who will frequent it. He promised me that no (harm) would be done to them if he touched at that part, for which I pointed out to him the best anchorage, as well as the place where he might find a fair number of fur seals. After dinner he withdrew to his ship to make ready for his departure as soon as his boats, which were out fishing, returned.
During the night of the fifth to the sixth the weather was very bad. The wind varied from west to south-west with very strong and almost continual gusts, accompanied by a great deal of rain. Only towards the end of the night did the squalls cease, which would surely have set us adrift had they lasted longer.
1803-02-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak the land of Natal was sighted to the north; it was in sight all day.

1803-02-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from the east, the course west. Obs. lat. 35° 46' 22", est. long. 21° 5' 30".
1803-02-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Sixth of Pluviôse (sic) (25 February 1803). On the sixth, the weather being tolerably fine, I had the launch manned to carry on board the Casuarina the water and the wood I had had cut the day before. To speed up this work I went in the launch myself, and did a drudging task that would have greatly displeased my officers had I charged them with it.
The wind having freshened considerably when we were off the ship, we were set adrift. The launch not having enough ballast, we came near to filling two or three times, and we were obliged to make for the shore a long way to leeward to bail out the water and unstep our mast, so as to reach the watering place under oars. We could not get there before one o'clock in the afternoon, although we had set off at seven in the morning.
As Citizen Freycinet had been told by me, the day before, of the work he had to do during this day, I had supposed that he would be ashore to hurry it on, the more so as I had seen his boat go there several times; but I was informed that he could not come, having that day a grand dinner and a large company. This conduct put me out of humour, and I remained all day charged with the drudgery and with watching over the launch's men. Seven men from the Casuarina, who had been put ashore in the morning with no one to lead them, had made off into the mountains or gone fishing, so that they did not appear until nightfall, and the launch could not finish, in the evening, the work there was to do, everyone having to be employed in going to cut fetch, at the foot of the hill, the wood that had been cut there. I bore all these annoyances, not without grumbling, and returned on board at nightfall in my boat, having ordered the launch's men to sleep ashore so as to be the better prepared to do what remained for the next day.
On my arrival at the tents I found no one there but Citizen Guichenot, still busy with his plants and his collections. I was told that Citizen Leschenault, the botanist, had gone to pay a visit to M. Bernier, and that the second surgeon and M. Péron, the Observer of Man, had gone to dine on board the Casuarina. Towards evening they all came back, but Citizen Freycinet did not appear, and he did very well, for I was disposed to give him a good dressing-down to teach him his duty, and not to waste his time in pleasure when there is pressing work to be done.
According to the gardener's report, he had gathered during his stay
ashore more than a hundred and fifty different species of plants, and filled sixty-eight pots with living ones. That was work and not wit.
I expect that Citizens Péron and Leschenault will have composed sixty pages of writing, which, for the opposite reason, will be wit and no work.
On my return on board, which came very opportunely, the south-west winds set in again and brought us squalls and rain that lasted all night.

1803-02-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds falling away gradually. At 2 the winds shifted to NW; trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 2 went about onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 35° 30' 59", est. long. 19° 50' 48".
1803-02-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventh (26 February 1803). On the seventh, from first light, the boats were employed in carrying, both to the observatory and to the scientists' tents, the provisions they had been short of for two days, according to the reports they made to me. On board I was assured of the contrary, so that it is difficult to know who is right or wrong. However that may be, as I had seen for myself that they lacked everything, I had them given what was necessary.
At about ten o'clock Lieutenant Freycinet came to ask me for a boat to go ashore. I gave it to him, and also to the surgeon Laridon, who was of the party. But I was much astonished to see it make for the Casuarina, where it stayed until noon, and, having taken off her captain, it went ashore. I learned afterwards that the shore was that day returning the feast of the day before, and without knowing it beforehand I had myself contributed to making it brilliant with a few delicacies I had sent to the scientists in the boat that left in the morning.
The launch, which had taken in the wood and the water for the Casuarina, brought back from her only two empty casks for the replacement provisions that had been asked of me, so that it will be necessary to lose one more day in going to fetch the others, supposing, however, that they have not been thrown overboard or used up in some other way, which would be most vexing, as we have on board neither cask nor case that could stand in their stead.
A boat that was sent fishing off Black Head point came back at sunset with some very fine fish, and in sufficient quantity for two meals for the whole crew. There were many sénapres, one of which, among others, had so peculiar a head that I am having it destined (no continuation). This fish weighed 15 pounds. Another, resembling the tunny without being of that species, weighed 37 pounds and will no doubt be good to eat. Several perch and bream were taken, which will be no less good.
While the boat was busy fishing, three natives armed with spears passed over the mountains; they watched our people for some time and then went on their way, which lay to the south-west.
The night passed without incident. The winds were from south-east to east, almost calm.

1803-02-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds variable from W to SW and WNW. At 7.30 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Sighted two ships standing on the opposite tack. Est. lat. 35° 21' 41", est. long. 19° 42' 48".
1803-02-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighth of Ventôse (27 February 1803). On the eighth, in the morning, the weather being fine and the wind east-south-east, a pleasant breeze, Citizens Boulanger, Faure and Bailly asked me for a boat to go ashore, intending to take various angles from the tops of some mountains for the construction of the plan of the harbour, of which Citizen Faure had taken the bearings. I had the longboat placed at their disposal, in which they are to return at sunset.
The launch was likewise sent to fetch from the shore the wood I had had cut for the Casuarina, which, as had been foreseen, could not take it on board, and which I took for myself, not wishing to have had the trouble of cutting it for nothing, although I had no need of it. The small boat was sent fishing at the same place where it had been the day before.
At about eight o'clock the American vessel, the Union, Captain Penelton of New York, got under sail and beat to windward with rather little success all morning among the islands that form the entrance.
At nine o'clock, seeing no sign of the captain of the Casuarina coming, I put one of the punts in the water and sent him the following letter:
"To Citizen Freycinet, on board the Casuarina,
"Citizen, had it pleased you yesterday to remain on board the Casuarina to attend to the fitting out of that vessel, or had you, as was your duty, come ashore the day before yesterday to share with me the drudgery that I did entirely for you, I should not be obliged to reproach you for conduct so ill considered on your part, for the slowness it brings into your work, for the loss of time that results from it, and finally for the state of drunkenness in which the launch's men were found on returning from your ship.
"On another side, your pleasures, which always take precedence over your duties, have not allowed you to give serious attention to your replacement provisions, for your statement of requirements makes no mention whatever of what remains to you on board, which must greatly reduce it, given what you have already received.
"For your own greater convenience, you have no doubt imagined that I was supplied with the casks, kegs or cases you will need for whatever I might give you. And that is doubtless why you sent me only two empty casks. But you will learn today that I have none, nor even any cases, at my disposal. So, if you have burnt your own or thrown them overboard, you will make whatever other arrangements you please. You will therefore be so good, on receipt of this letter, as to send me a general statement, not of what you wish to have, but of what remains to you on board, for I shall give you only what I can spare." Your fellow citizen. N. B.
Shortly afterwards Citizen Freycinet, having come on board, handed me himself the note I had had requested of him. He received on this visit a reprimand which I hope he will remember, as much for the good of the service as for his own sake.
At about three o'clock in the afternoon we sighted M. Ransonnet's boat on its way back to the ship, where it arrived at about six o'clock in the evening. According to the verbal report he made me, he has discovered three harbours very convenient for vessels of middling size, since there are only three and a half and four fathoms of water in them at most. He also had occasion to communicate with the natives of the country, who showed themselves not at all wild and were the first to give proof of their good disposition, for they began by laying their weapons aside before approaching the boat's people, who did the same and then mingled with them. They made themselves understood as best they could by signs, and the greater part of the day was spent with them on very good terms. Only, they would not allow anyone to go towards the side to which they had sent their women, three in number. On their side they were five. They made no difficulty about drinking and eating everything that was offered them, and regaled themselves amply on the seamen's cooking. As the presents I usually intended for the natives, when communication with them was possible, had been forgotten and not put in the boat, they received from our people only the buttons of their jackets, which they prized highly, some handkerchiefs and a few worn-out smocks which did not please them so much. I refer to the written report M. Ransonnet is to make me for further details.
After sunset Citizens Boulanger, Faure and Bailly returned on board, and I had word sent to the naturalists' tents that they should hold themselves ready to come back on board the next day.
During the night the wind varied from east to north-east and the breeze was moderate, though under a very cloudy sky.

1803-02-28.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from W to WSW. Two three-masters in sight to leeward. At 9.30 a.m. wore ship. Obs. lat. 35° 55' 29", est. long. 20° 16' 56". From the 9th to the 10th [Ventôse, Year 11, 28 February - 1 March 1803]. Fine weather, a light breeze from SW. The ship in sight steering for us. At 5 hoisted our colours to make ourselves known. At 5.30, being abeam, we hove to, as did she, and her captain came aboard. At 6 filled and stood on. Obs. lat. 35° 35' 19", est. long. 19° 46' 56".
1803-02-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the 9th of Ventôse (28 February 1803). On the ninth, from early morning, the launch and the longboat were sent to strike the tents and bring everyone back on board, together with everything that was ashore. On board, our bower anchor was put back in its place and the ship made ready to receive our boats.
The longboat arrived at nine o'clock and the launch at half past ten. The four sick men who had spent this call ashore came back, in my view, much worse than when they were taken there, but in the surgeon's view in much better health, despite the continual damp which had never left them and the little watch kept over their conduct and their regimen, which was certainly not a diet.
As soon as the launch arrived, the living plants gathered by Citizen Guichenot, our gardener, were shipped, to the number of seventy species.
They were placed in various parts of the ship and in my cabin, so as to put off for some (time) longer the lamentations I shall have to hear when it becomes absolutely necessary to take the cabins of those who still occupy them, to stow the other natural history objects we may collect during the rest of the voyage.
As I was resolved to get under sail the next day, whether the winds were fair or foul, I prepared the following instruction for the captain of the Casuarina. He came on board himself on the pretext of asking for it, but I answered him that, as I did not wish everyone to know what I had to say to him, I would send it to him when (I) judged it necessary, and that, moreover, he was to be ready to weigh the next day, etc.
"To Citizen Freycinet, commanding the schooner the Casuarina,
"Citizen, you have already been informed, by the last instruction I gave you at Île Borda [Kangaroo Island], that on leaving King George Sound I shall proceed to Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay] to finish what remains to be done in geography on that part of the coast.
"Before entering that bay, I intend to put in for one day only at Île St Aloüarn [St Alouarn Island] to determine precisely its latitude and longitude, which I believe very doubtful from those assigned to it by the French and English charts.
"If the winds are favourable to me and the weather fine, I may perhaps stay three or four days at Rottnest Island, and proceed from there to the Dirk Hartog roadstead to take a few turtles before going farther north. I would observe to you, nevertheless, that these last two calls are more probable than certain.
"Whether they take place or not, I shall stop for some time at the north-west point of New Holland in order to make positively sure whether the place the Dutch named Willem's River is not an island, as I suspect. Should we happen to be separated at sea on the passage there, that point will be a place of rendezvous, and the only one I can give you.
"The east and north-east winds that I expect to meet on going up to the north will make the course I still have to run on the north coast too uncertain for me to be able to appoint any other rendezvous. Besides, as I do not wish to put in at any place frequented by Europeans, it is only too probable that if we have not rejoined each other off the north-west point, we shall not meet again. Accordingly, after cruising ten full days between the north-west point and Willem's River, you will steer directly for the Isle of France [Mauritius]. This point is, according to the observations we made there, in 21° 36' south latitude and 110° 35' east longitude. It is surrounded on the north by breakers that extend a good way offshore, and to the north of these breakers one
begins to see some of the islets that belong to it.
"As the entrance of Willem's River lies to the south of the latitude I have just given you, you will not go north of that meridian in the cruise you will make should we be separated. But when the time I have fixed has expired, you will, as I have already directed, steer for the Isle of France, keeping within the region of the general south-east winds and in accordance with the instructions of M. D'après.
"On your arrival in port you will hand over your vessel to the Administrators of the Government, to be employed in the service of the colony if they judge it necessary. I think you will keep the command of her until my return, so as to employ your time usefully. But if that does not suit you, you are at liberty to return to France by the first opportunity you please (to) take.
"You will be so good as to deliver to the Administrators of the colony of the Isle of France the letter I hand you for them, and to communicate to them the article of this instruction that concerns the employment of your vessel.
"It will therefore henceforth depend on you alone whether you accompany me or not. I have never neglected to do all that was necessary to prevent the two separations that have already occurred, and which you could easily have avoided, whether by handling your vessel or in carrying out the orders I have given you. You will therefore be personally answerable to the Government for the expenses incurred in fitting out your vessel, since they will have become burdensome to the State and useless to the expedition."
"Your fellow citizen." NB.
"To the Administrators General of the Isles of France and Réunion,
"Citizens,
"The schooner of the Republic, the Casuarina, which I had built at Port Jackson to replace the Naturaliste, sent back to France, being fully laden with the natural history objects we collected during our stay on the coast of New Holland, and having, moreover, been separated from me on the passage from King George Sound to Willem's River, I have ordered Citizen Freycinet, Lieutenant, who commands her, to proceed to the Isle of France and to hand this vessel over to you, to be employed in the service of the colony if you think fit. I think this officer will be very glad to keep the command of her until the time of my return. That is why I beg you to be so good as to allow him to keep it. As I intend to proceed as soon as possible to the Gulf of Carpentaria to carry out in full
the instructions of the Government, I cannot assure you of the precise time of my arrival at the Isle of France; however, I think it will take place in eight or ten months at the latest.
"I shall not for the moment go into the details of what we have done and discovered. But I hope that the Government will be content and the public satisfied.
"Greetings & respects." N. B.
These two letters were sealed separately and sent by a midshipman to M. Freycinet. On the envelope enclosing them was written, by way of address: Citizen Freycinet, Captain of the Casuarina, is expressly forbidden to open this packet before the vessels are outside King George Sound.
In the afternoon we hoisted in the launch and two of our boats, the third being kept back to fetch the astronomical instruments, the tent and Citizen Bernier, who had sent to ask me not to send for him until about three o'clock in the afternoon. He arrived on board at sunset, just as we were weighing one of our anchors.
During this call I made up five months' provisions on board the Casuarina. So that if that vessel should be separated from me in such a way as not to be able to rejoin me at the rendezvous I have appointed her, she will still be furnished with everything she may need to reach the Isle of France with ease.
All day we had a very strong breeze from the east, which was no happy omen for the morrow. But as it usually died away in the night, we hoped that, by setting about getting under sail early, we should have time to get out of the bay with the light land breeze which ordinarily blew from four o'clock in the morning until sunrise, when the winds went round to north-east and then to east, blowing fresh.
This call was very pleasant for the crew, and yet harmful to some of them, who made bad use of it by eating fresh fish to excess. Every day such a quantity of mackerel was taken on the line alongside that, apart from the enormous quantities eaten, it was so considerable that several casks of it were salted. A no less great quantity was dried, and, to put it better, everyone laid in an ample store of it for the sea. In this we were much more fortunate than Vancouver, who, by his account, met with very few in the season when (he) surveyed this harbour.
No attempt was made to fish with the seine, since it would have been a waste of time. The bottom, too steep, did not seem to suit the fish, the more so as it is of a very white sand bare of weed. However,
the people who were ashore took a ray there with pointed sticks, after the manner of the natives of the country.
The botanists were very pleased with the collections they made. According to what Citizen Leschenault told me, he seems to have gathered about two hundred new species of plants that were unknown to him, and as many varieties within the species. The gardener Guichenot is no less less (sic) satisfied, and richer still.
I think that Citizen Péron will also have a volume on the worms and molluscs, and one or two cases of broken shells. For in several places on the beach they can be gathered up with a shovel. This is to serve him, so he claims, to prove the epoch at which New Holland must have risen from the bottom of the sea.
As for me, I observed there that the tides are very irregular. Several times the sea was twice high and low in six hours, which I had never yet seen anywhere. The day tides were generally slight and the night tides very great. By day it did not seem to me to rise more than three feet, whereas at night it rose more than once to seven and eight. It is true that we were then at the change of the moon.
The winds during our stay were very variable. We had them from every point of the compass. But it appears that those from east and west are the prevailing and even the strongest, since we always had them violent from these two quarters of the horizon. Those from west round to south-west are usually accompanied by rain and mist. Those from east to south-east are, on the contrary, clear with a fine sky, but they bring into the bay a very heavy swell which does nothing for the safety of vessels.
Observations made ashore:
Latitude of the site of the observatory: (no figures given)
Longitude of the same place: ( " " " )
Variation of the needle: ( " " " )
Dip of the needle: ( " " " )
1803-02-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: We communicated with an American bound for the whale fishery in Delagoa Bay.

1803-03-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
At nine in the morning,
the Eclipse Islands bore south 80° west,
Cape Howe north 75° west,
Blad Head north 15° west
and Mount Gardner north 5° east.
At noon,
Blad Head bore north 35° 25° west
and the Eclipse Islands north 55° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
Departure from King George Sound
On the tenth (1 March 1803), at about half past four, the weather looking fine and the land breeze having announced itself by a light cool air from the north, variable to the north-west, we made ready to get under way and hove short. The topsails were then hoisted and we weighed, with every sail set, going out to the south of Seal Island. We had come in to the anchorage by the same channel, which nevertheless appeared to us much more convenient to the north of this island, in that it is far easier and allows an easy beat should the winds prove contrary. We passed about (one) half mile from this island, which is clear of dangers and round which the water is deep. We got bottom only once, in nine fathoms, and lost it almost at once in fourteen and fifteen. The course we steered to get out was east-north-east and east by south.
At eight o'clock we were far enough out to have no further fear of the easterly and south-easterly winds, should they spring up, as I expected they would.
In rounding Black Head we sighted the reef shown on Vancouver's particular plan, but it seemed to me that he places it much closer to the coast than it really is.
The winds, which we had had in the north-west, went round by degrees to the south-west. And the promise of a fine day given by the sunrise and a clear sky vanished all at once. A thick haze hid the land from us almost entirely, although we were very close to it. The direction of the wind having obliged us to steer south by east, we held that course until noon, when, the sky having cleared, we went about towards the land.
At nine o'clock, the Eclipse Islands bearing south 80° west, Bald Head north 75° west and Mount Gardner north 5° east, we took our departure from this bearing.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 35° 21' 58" and our longitude, reckoned from the bearing, was by dead reckoning 115° 58' 24".
The board to the north by west that we had taken at noon was held until five o'clock, when, being unable to weather the Eclipse Islands, we took the board to the south by west again, the wind having gone round to the west. A very high swell coming to us from that quarter of the horizon did not promise a fair wind, and the state of the atmosphere foretold bad weather. In the evening several columns of smoke were seen, which proved to us that this part of the coast was fairly well inhabited at that season. At eight o'clock we stood to the south.
During the night the winds were variable from west to west-south-west and the weather squally, with strong gusts and rain, especially after the moon had set. We held on the board to the south by west.
1803-03-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: We sounded and had 102 fathoms, sandy bottom. Two sharks were taken.

1803-03-02.journal_anonyme: A flat calm. At 2 a light breeze got up from the east. At daybreak sighted five ships ahead of us and to windward. At 11 a.m. the lookout thought he saw land in the WNW. Obs. lat. 35° 31' 7", est. long. 18° 15' 26".
1803-03-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six in the evening,
Mount Gardner bore north 17° east,
Bald Head north 10° west,
the Eclipse Islands north 38° west
and the westernmost land of the mainland in sight north 56° west.
At daybreak,
the land was seen from north to north-north-west.
At noon,
Mount Gardner bore north 62° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, in the morning, the weather was fairly fine. At daybreak we closed with the Casuarina, which had been lost sight of during the night. And, having joined her, we trimmed our sails for a course west by north, the winds being variable from south-west to south.
In the course of the morning the sky clouded over and looked very threatening. A very heavy swell from the south-west seemed to announce some squalls from that quarter, although on the other hand the barometer had begun to rise. The land could be seen from north to north-north-west, but too indistinctly for us to make out its points properly.
At noon the observed latitude was 35° 31' 34", and as there was no hour angle, we reckoned ourselves by dead reckoning in longitude 115° 54' 41". At that time, the sky having cleared, we sighted Mount Gardner, which bore north 62° east.
In the afternoon we held on the board to the west by north so as to draw nearer the land. The sky no longer had the threatening look of the morning, and our fears of bad weather to come were dispelled. Nevertheless the sea was still running a heavy swell, although there was little wind.
At sunset the bearings of the land were taken as set down at the end of the log table, and we took the board to the south for the night.
The coast that we had in sight during the morning, and indeed all day, is generally of good height and can easily be seen ten and twelve leagues out to sea when the weather is fine. The shores appear high and steep-to, showing here and there a few islets of little consequence lying not far from the beach. The mountain-like heights seen along the shore most often look like islands, because at four and five leagues' distance the low land joining them one to another cannot be seen.
During the night, and especially after the moon had set, the winds were very variable and unsteady. The sky was sometimes clear and sometimes dark, but we had neither squalls nor gusts as on the previous night.
1803-03-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak five ships were sighted shaping their course to double the Cape. At 11.30 land was thought to be seen in the N 68° W. The ship makes 4 inches of water an hour.

1803-03-03.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW. At 5 a.m. went about. The main topmast backstay having parted near the trestletrees, new masthead rigging was made up on the masthead with the same rope. Obs. lat. 36° 12' 20", est. long. 17° 51' 32".
1803-03-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
Mount Gardner bore north 52° east,
Bald Head north 44° east,
the Eclipse Islands north 21° east,
the most prominent points of the mainland to the west north 61° west.
At sunset,
Bald Head bore north 72° east,
the Eclipse Islands north 85° east,
Cape Howe north 42° west,
the mainland in sight north 52° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth the wind continued from west to south-west, which was ill suited to the course we had to make and was beginning to vex us greatly, for fear that it would not change until the new moon, which was due on the seventeenth. At sea, when a fair wind sets in and the ship is making good way, one readily persuades oneself, and even with pleasure, that it will last as long as it is needed. But if it changes sooner than was supposed, one sees nothing in it but a particular and determined contrariness. This was exactly our situation since leaving King George Sound, for most of us thought that the winds from west to south by way of south-west would not leave us until we had reached the region of the south-east winds in 28° south latitude. It would be hard to say what could have given rise to such reasoning, for those who held it could found it only on their own notions and not on experience, since all of them were on their first voyage.
However that may be, it is no less true that we were in fact thwarted, and that since leaving our last port of call the winds had kept steadily in the quarter our prophets had foretold.
During the morning we had a fairly fine sky and the coast could be made out perfectly, although we were a good way off it.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 35° 27' 30", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 31 put us in 115° 36' 30", which gave us very little progress to the west, even though, according to our dead reckoning, the currents appeared to have set us to the north-west at a rate of 18 miles in 24 hours. This observation is entirely contrary to what Vancouver says, who found currents that set him constantly to the south-east. But I attribute this to the seasons in which he frequented this coast, which in my view are precisely those of the winds from south-west to north-west by way of west, whereas we were in the season of the winds from south-east to north-east by way of east, as is easily seen from those we have met with.
This day having passed like the preceding ones in beating to work as far to the west as possible, we found ourselves in the evening within sight of land, and as we always stood off for the night, the bearings were taken at sunset: Bald Head north 72° east, the middle of the Eclipse Islands north 85° east and Cape Howe north 42° west; the most prominent points of the mainland to the west extended to north 52° west.
During the night, the night, the sky was very cloudy and the sea swelling. Since ten in the morning we had had a long swell from the south-west which made the sea high and hollow. Nevertheless the night was not a bad one, although the sky was constantly heavy with vapours and damp.

1803-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light air, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from WSW. At 2 the winds having shifted to NW, went onto the starboard tack. Obs. lat. 36° 8' 21", est. long. 17° 57' 6".
1803-03-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daybreak the Eclipse Islands were seen to the north 65° east.
The most prominent land to the west north 50° west.
Historical events & Remarks &c.
On the thirteenth, in the morning, the winds varied from south-west to south and from south towards the east, but the breeze was so light that we made little progress to the west. The sky, still overcast and hazy, was hardly more favourable to us; we were, however, still near enough the land to be able to know where we were.
At sunrise, or rather when the day was somewhat advanced, the Eclipse Islands were seen again, the middle of them bearing north 65° east. All morning we steered as far to the west as possible, following the shifts of the wind.
At noon, the sun having appeared, the latitude was observed to be 35° 14' 0", and by dead reckoning the longitude was 115° 9' 54".
The sea, though a little less heavy than the day before, was still hollow, with a very long swell that seemed to come from far off.
In the afternoon we had a few squalls and some rain, but they were neither long nor violent. The wind went round again to the south-west, which gave our prophets such credit that people often went to consult them to learn whether it would last much longer. Their opinion on that score is not known to me.
At eight in the evening we took, as usual, the board to the south, which came a little towards the east. During the night it was almost calm. We sounded, sounded (sic), twice only. The first cast of the lead brought up 57 fathoms and the second 55. We went about at eleven o'clock, the wind being almost calm.
During the day we saw along the whole coast so great a number of fires that there is every appearance this part was fairly well inhabited. Seventeen were counted, all some distance from one another, and in no way resembling those great conflagrations we had often noticed; they seemed on the contrary to be individual fires, which did not last long and all disappeared before the end of the day.
The appearance of the coast was much the same as it had been since our departure from King George Sound, that is to say divided into stretches of high and low land which seemed to us fairly well wooded.

1803-03-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from NW. At 9 p.m. wore onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 36° 3' 17", est. long. 16° 12' 14".
1803-03-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six in the evening,
the two extremities of the mainland in sight were taken, one bearing north 85° east and the other north 61° west.
At noon the next day
it was seen from east by north to west-north-west.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the fourteenth the weather was hardly finer than on the preceding days. However, the winds, which though very light had gone round from south-south-east to north-east, seemed to promise a change in our favour, although the sky was very overcast and often hazy. The change did in fact come in the course of the morning, for, the haze and clouds clearing little by little, we had from time to time a fine sky which allowed us to make out the coast clearly. The part abreast of which we lay was extremely broken and showed various openings which seemed to promise some good places of shelter for ships. This appearance, plain to see, was confirmed by the lookouts at the mastheads, who claimed to see large openings through which the water ran inland beyond the reach of their sight.
Given how closely General d'Entrecasteaux, Vancouver and, more recently still, Mr Flinders had examined this coast, I had grounds for believing that the water seen inland was lagoons with no communication with the sea, since none of these navigators left any break in the coast, of which, judging by the track of their course, they were much nearer than we. Nevertheless, I much regretted being becalmed and unable to approach it.
At noon we had no observation of latitude. That of our dead reckoning put us in 35° 15' 45", and the longitude, also by dead reckoning, was 114° 45' 0".
From noon to four o'clock the weather became altogether fine. And at about two o'clock a light breeze sprang up from the south-west, by means of which we were able to give the ship steerage way. Unable to resist my wish to make sure whether this part of the coast did not, as it appeared, offer some harbours that might be a resource for navigators and had escaped the notice of those who had frequented it before us, I made the signal to the Casuarina to pass under our stern and ordered her to go and examine the openings abreast of us, informing her that I would await her return, standing off and on within sight of the coast. She was enjoined not to stop in these openings if the weather held fine, but only to observe the entrances they might form and to come back at once to report to me. I agreed with the captain of this schooner that if the weather turned bad and I was obliged to leave the coast, I would wait for him at the anchorage of Rottnest Island, which I named to him as a rendezvous in that case only. The stretch of coast Citizen Freycinet had to examine was at most four or five leagues and ought not to take much time. He set off at once and headed for the point at which I had told him to begin, which I believe to be the western part of Cape Nuyts.
During the night the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate. We spent it beating about so as to close the land ourselves the next day, if the wind allowed us to stand off from it in case of need.

1803-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW, south and SSE. Worked at getting the bower anchors to the fore hatchway. Obs. lat. 34° 58' 10", est. long. 14° 45' 20".
1803-03-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset,
the mainland in sight extended from north 75° east to north 60° west.
At noon,
the point lying between Cape Nuyts and Cape Leeuwin bore north 68° west, as did the islet belonging to it.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, in the morning, the weather continued fine and we had a very pleasant breeze from south-east to north. We closed the land to a league and a half and stood off and on steadily all morning and a great part of the afternoon, in the hope of meeting the Casuarina. The course we had held the night before having put us three or four leagues to windward of her, I was in a position all the more advantageous since she could not run along the coast, however close to it she might be, without our sighting her. All the more so as the boards were never longer than two hours on either tack until four in the afternoon. We did not see her, however, which leads me to think that she will have found some convenient and good place to serve as a refuge for ships that accidents might oblige to seek shelter on this part of the coast.
At noon we observed the latitude as 35° 9' 47", and the longitude by our timekeeper put us in 114° 51' 3", which hardly agreed with the one Citizen Beautemps-Beaupré's chart gives to Cape or Point Nuyts.
In the afternoon the sky continued fine and we still had the coast in sight at a short distance. But at about two o'clock so thick a fog came up all at once that we lost sight of it. Nevertheless, convinced that the weather, which did not look bad, would clear at moonrise, we continued to stand on the same boards as in the morning. At sunset, seeing no sign of a change, we took a reef in each topsail and stood out to sea for fear of bad weather, the barometer falling fast. The board to the south by east that we had taken was held until ten in the evening, when we took the one to the north, the wind being in the east, a pleasant breeze, variable to east-north-east.
During the night the weather was fairly fine, but we saw nothing of the land, although the horizon seemed to us fairly wide. We sounded every two hours without getting bottom at 50 and 60 fathoms. The sea was a little rough all night, which we attributed to the currents rather than to the strength of the wind, which was moderate.
1803-03-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: The anchors (all but one) were struck below; and on the 18th [Ventôse, 9 March 1803] the jib boom and spritsail yard were rigged in to ease the ship forward.

1803-03-07.journal_anonyme: The sea smooth, the weather very fine and the winds variable from SE, south, SSW and south. Obs. lat. 33° 30' 20", est. long. 13° 1' 20".
1803-03-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset,
the land could barely be seen, although we were no more than three leagues from it, so hazy was it.
At daybreak the land was made out to the north, the horizon very hazy.
At noon it was likewise seen through the haze, distance estimated three leagues.
Of the 16th. Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, at daybreak, standing in on the inshore board, we expected to see the land, see it (sic), and even fairly close to us, but the horizon was so hazy that we barely made it out, at a distance I estimated at about three leagues. As the day came on, the breeze grew weaker and weaker, and the greater part of the morning was spent in a calm.
In various passing clear spells we saw the land from time to time and believed we recognised the point where the Casuarina was to have begun the survey I had ordered her to make. As we had seen nothing of that vessel during the day, nor the day before, and the weather had been fine, I had no doubt that she had made some good discoveries, but that, instead of coming to inform us of them as I had expressly ordered, she had stopped there, caring very little whether I was waiting for her or not.
These reflections, which I was not making for the first time, put me out of humour, and I was entirely convinced, after all I had already said to this captain, that he set very little store by the orders I gave him. Being persuaded, moreover, that he was only seeking an occasion to part company so as to make for the Isle of France [Mauritius], I resolved to put a stop to it at our first meeting. For this reason I (decided) to cruise off this coast until the weather allowed me to examine the coast myself with the ship.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 35° 18' 56", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 114° 53' 41". So that we found (ourselves) a little further south and a little further west than the day before.
During the morning the haze cleared only in very short intervals, which did not even leave us time to make out the land properly. And in the evening the sky grew so dark that we lost hope of seeing it clear. The barometer, which had fallen nearly four lines in twenty-four hours, did not announce the change I wished for either. Nevertheless, as the sea gave no sign of bad weather, I continued to keep my ground, standing off and on, making each board four hours long.
During the day the lead gave from 48 to 45 fathoms, and at eight o'clock it was 65.
The night passed without incident and was even more pleasant than we had any reason to expect from the look of things at the close of day. The winds were variable from east to east-north-east and the breeze unsteady. We worked the ship as during the day so as not to leave the coast, hoping that the Casuarina might perhaps appear the next day.

1803-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SSW to SW. In the forenoon shifted the foresail. Obs. lat. 30° 56' 7", est. long. 10° 53' 26".
1803-03-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
the mainland was seen from north-north-west to east-north.
The part of the coast the Casuarina had gone to examine (bore) from east-north-east to north-east by north.
At noon,
we had Point Nuyts north 78° east
and the two rocks marked on the chart of the survey made by d'Entrecasteaux north 45° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth the wind went round from south-south-east to south, a strong breeze. We closed the land at the very place where I had sent the Casuarina. But, seeing nothing of her, I decided to continue on my way. It was quite enough to have wasted two days waiting for her over a survey that was a matter of three hours, having expressly ordered her to come and report to me whether the gaps I had pointed out were not the entrances of some harbours, and having forbidden her to stop there if the weather was fine.
This officer, insubordinate on principle, has not so far been able to carry out a commission, nor even to submit to the orders I have given him. That is also why, if he rejoins me at Rottnest Island, which I named to him as a rendezvous, it is very likely that I shall take this command from him, to see whether another will carry out better the orders that circumstances will lead me to give him.
At nine o'clock, therefore, we shaped our course north 70° west and ran along the coast at a short distance, with a very good wind but a disagreeable sky.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 35° 4' 40", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 114° 3' 58". Point Nuyts then bore north 78° east, and the two rocks mentioned on Citizen Beautemps-Beaupré's chart north 45° east.
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze from south-south-east to south-east. We found the sea heavy and swelling. We ran along the coast at about a league and a half to two leagues' distance.
