The land inland is, as I have already observed, of good height, and the shore is formed for the most part of sand dunes, in front of which there are sometimes a few rocks lying close in to the land.
At sunset Cape Leeuwin bore north 30° west. We did not sight Île St Aloüarn [St Alouarn Islands].
During the night, which was dark and damp, we held the board to the south until one o'clock, when we went about so as to be off Cape Leeuwin at daybreak the next day. Although the sky was fine during the night, we passed it quietly with two reefs in our topsails only; we found the sea a little heavy and very swelling.

1803-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south and SE. The course NNW. In the forenoon rigged in the jib boom and spritsail yard. Obs. lat. 29° 20' 44", long. 9° 11' 23".
1803-03-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock Cape Leeuwin bore north 30° west,
At eight in the evening it bore north 5° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, in the morning, we made out Cape Leeuwin, and when day broke we sighted Île St Aloüarn [St Alouarn Islands], which we had searched for in vain when we visited this coast for the first time. From which we concluded that the point we had taken for Cape Leeuwin was not the one to which that name belongs, at least according to the chart of the geographer Beautemps-Beaupré.
During the morning we began a new survey of this whole coast, the one made previously having been judged bad.
As I owe the Government an account of this loss of time, I must tell it that all our men of science were so little versed in the branch that concerned each of them in particular that they could only make themselves useful towards the end of the voyage, supposing they were willing to work to acquire the necessary knowledge and above all the practice of such work, which, with all the theory in the world, will always be incomplete when it is done for the first time and one has not trained one's eye to judge either the distance of a coast or the depth of a cove. This was precisely the case of our geographers, present and to come. At one league, 3 & 4 leagues from the land, the whole coast seemed to them straight and on a single plane. As practice must since then have taught them to judge better, it is likely that the work they are now doing will have merit and that their plans will be well made.
After rounding Île St Aloüarn, we coasted along the shore, running north at a league's distance at most. We were then sailing in the greatest security, and yet we were very near our destruction. At 30 minutes past seven, having cast my eyes to leeward of us, I saw a reef awash on which the sea was breaking heavily, and we (had) barely time to avoid it by luffing up suddenly. The ship was then running 7 to eight miles, so that she answered her helm promptly. Happily for us, this reef was very steep-to, otherwise the voyage was over. In coming up to the wind, the stern of the ship did not pass half a pistol-shot from the rock. No one had noticed this reef, which nothing, however, would have hidden from our view long before had anyone paid attention.
Those who were on lookout were docked for three days and the rest of the crew severely reprimanded. No doubt a very mild punishment in comparison with the grievous consequences of which we came so near to being the victims.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 33° 48' 24", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 112° 50' 49". From the bearings taken in the morning of Cape Leeuwin and of Île St Alouärn, it would follow that this island lies in 34° 27' 18" and in longitude 113° 1' 54", and Cape Leeuwin in 34° 25' 51" and 112° 58' 0", which differs considerably from the position in which this island and this point are placed on the chart of the Dépôt.
In the evening the weather was (a blank) and we worked up as far as the southern point which forms the entrance of the great Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], into which we were to enter the next day for the third time. During the night the weather was fine and the breeze moderate; we carried sail until midnight and lay to until daybreak.

1803-03-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from SSE to south. Stowed the jib boom and spritsail yard among the spare spars. Obs. lat. 27° 51' 20", est. long. 7° 1' 53".
1803-03-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
At 22 minutes past noon, the southern point of the entrance of the bay bore south 46° west
and the easternmost land in sight north 67 east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, in the morning, steering north 34° east, we were much astonished to see to leeward of us a fairly extensive chain of breakers on which the sea was breaking violently. At six o'clock three of them could be made out, which seemed to form a triangle lying north and south. This danger was about two miles from us and bore from north-west to north-west by west. As we had sounded every hour during the night, and at five in the morning the bottom was still at 25 fathoms, we were very far from thinking ourselves so near a reef of which we had had no knowledge the year before (In the margin and in a different hand: "it is the Naturaliste's reef, seen in the year 9"), even though bad weather had then obliged us to beat about in every direction at the mouth of this bay. However that may be, we continued to keep close-hauled on the board to the north by east, to work to windward, and then went about to come and begin our survey at the southern point which forms the entrance of this bay.
When we first made this bay, the winds obliged us, as on this occasion, to stand to the north. The Naturaliste, after running for about two hours, signalled to us that the course she was steering did not seem a good one to follow, according to the report of the lookouts, who claimed to see breakers; but as her captain went up himself to the topgallant crosstrees and saw nothing, he had doubts but no certainty. Today it is proved that the lookouts did indeed see this breaker, which he would have done well to go and examine at the time. Its position will be well determined on our chart of this part of the coast by all the bearings we have taken of it.
In the afternoon we passed near our first anchorage on this coast. We saw many more fires there than the first time (in the margin and in another hand: "unfortunate Vasse"), as well as on the part of the coast lying to the south of this point of the bay. We coasted along it until evening at a short distance, but the weather was so dirty and hazy that it was difficult to make out properly the various points being taken, which were often wrapped in haze just when they needed to be seen. Nevertheless we were able to take enough recognisable ones for the construction of the chart.
At seven o'clock, although the sky was very murky, it did not look fine, we let go a bower anchor in nine fathoms, sand and weed. We spent the night there very quietly, and during it the weather cleared after the moon rose.
During the night the men of the crew caught some very fine fish, some of which weighed as much as twenty-five pounds. They were very good to eat; none of us knows to what species to assign them; however, Citizen Péron believes they belong to that of (a blank).

1803-03-11.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sea smooth, a pleasant breeze from south, SSW and SE. Bent the old foresail, repaired. Obs. lat. 26° 32' 3", est. long. 5° 9' 35".
1803-03-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
At 45 minutes past six,
the point forming the southern entrance of the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay] bore west 10° north, a doubtful bearing because of the haze.
Bearings at the anchorage.
The apparent point of the entrance of the bay of a small bay that I was sending to be examined, south 9° east.
The southern extremity of the land to the west, south 24 heures° west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, at daybreak, we got under way with a light breeze from the south, variable to south-south-east. My intention was to stop in the Anse des Maladroits in order to learn what had become of the gear of our lost longboat and whether the natives had taken possession of it. But as the hazy weather of the previous evening had not allowed us to make out the coast well enough to know how far off we might be, I could not guess that chance had led us to anchor in the very same place. We therefore weighed to go and look for it further to the north-east. And it was only after we had run about three leagues on that point of the compass that we recognised perfectly the anchorage from which we had set out to search for our men; but it was then too late to retrace our steps, with the wind blowing from the very quarter of the horizon towards which we would have had to steer. Rather than lose a day beating about, and perhaps to no purpose, I preferred to continue on my way and take advantage of the fair wind we had to reach the head of the bay to the east, which I did not think very far off. We therefore stood on, following all the windings of the coast, which is made up only of shallow coves without the least shelter from winds from north to south-east by way of west.
At a quarter to twelve, being abreast of an opening which seemed to promise the entrance of a harbour, I had the anchor let go in order to send a boat to examine it. Citizen Bonnefoy was put in charge of this expedition, with orders to see what it might be. He left the ship at half past twelve, being due back before sunset.
At noon the latitude of our anchorage was observed to be 33° 15' 20", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 113° 26' 33". This gave us a difference of longitude of 0° 30' 6" since the previous noon's observation. Judging by the point of the compass on which the land bore, the visible extremity of which was taken at (no figure), there is every appearance that we were right in the deepest part of this bay, to the east. The whole coast is nothing but a succession of sand dunes, behind which a range of mountains can be seen inland, running from north-west to south-east, and fairly high.
At five o'clock, the boat having returned on board, I was informed by Citizen Bonnefoy that the place which had looked like a harbour was indeed one, but that it could suit only small vessels drawing no more than eight or nine feet of water, and even then the channel would have to be well known. He also discovered several salt-water lagoons, which he did not think he should examine, in order to comply with the orders I had given him to be back by sunset. For further details I refer to the plan he has drawn of this place and to his report.
In the evening the wind went round to the south-west and the sea rose. But as the weather was fine, I thought the breeze would drop at sunset. That is why I remained at anchor. Some new plants were brought to us from the shore
(vertically in the margin) and branches of casuarina for our kangaroos.
During the night the weather became altogether fine and the strong breeze we had had in the evening began to die down. The winds, which in their progress had come round as far as west, went back little by little to south-east by way of south. A few fish were caught, but fewer than the night before.

1803-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from south, SSE, SE and east. Overcast and damp weather. Obs. lat. 25° 36' 3", est. long. 3° 33' 30".
1803-03-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock, the entrance into which the boat had gone bore south 15° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, at sunrise, we were under sail, steering to range along the coast and to finish surveying it, if possible, in the course of the day, as regards the bight the land makes here to the east, since at noon our longitude was 113° 25' 53" and our latitude 32° 48' 0". This put us, in that position, 0° 27' 53" to the east of the southern point forming the entrance of the Baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay]. But as on the previous courses we had been 0° 5' 2" further east, it follows that the deepest bight the land makes to the east must be placed at 113° 3' and in the latitude of (no figures).
This easterly longitude, compared with that given on the chart of the Dépôt for Rottnest Island, placed in 112° 8' 0", therefore gave us 35 minutes to run to the west to be clear of the land and entirely out of the bay.
During the morning we ran along the coast at a very short distance so as to take exact bearings. From the moment we got under way until eleven o'clock, the bottom was constantly between nine and ten fathoms, sand and weed. But then it began to shoal and became uneven, between seven and eight. We stood a little out to sea, but not enough to avoid a bank over the end of which we passed in four fathoms of water, the bottom having risen all at once. As the sea was smooth, it could be seen perfectly. We first luffed up, but finding no deeper water and the sea looking whiter than to leeward, we bore away again and steered by eye along a line that seemed to promise more water. In this way we avoided grounding on the western point of this bank, where the whitest water we had noticed lay. And when we had passed it, we luffed up again. The depth then increased markedly, and in less than half an hour we went from 4 to 15. As we were on this bank at noon, its latitude is 32° 48' 0" and our longitude 113° 25' 52".
After passing the bank we closed the land again to continue our bearings, and we were obliged a second time to stand out to sea, having gone all at once from 11 to 12, to 7, which put us a fair way off. Nevertheless the windings of the coast and its points could be made out well. Several inlets were seen, but as they did not seem to me to offer anything of interest, I did not go to examine them particularly. The breeze, moreover, had become very fresh with south-westerly winds, and it strengthened so much towards four o'clock that we had to take a reef in the topsails.
As we were advancing rapidly northward without seeing on the coast any sign that might lead us to suspect it extended to the west, and as we were drawing ever nearer the latitude of Rottnest Island, I began to mistrust the position our chart gave it, and not without reason, for at sunset we sighted it perfectly and were convinced that its longitude had been wrongly determined.
Night coming on,
vertically in the margin: it was put off to verify whether our reasoning was right or not. During the night the sea was very heavy until about two in the morning, when the wind, having gone round to the south-east, dropped. We made two boards only and kept three leagues from the coast, not standing in to less than 30 fathoms.

1803-03-13.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, the winds very light, from ESE to south by way of north and west. Obs. lat. 24° 41' 57", est. long. 2° 15' 0".
1803-03-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
we made out Rottnest Island, the visible extremities of which bore, one north 22° east and the other north 65° east.
The next day, at eight o'clock,
the western point of this island bore south 12° west, and the easternmost land in sight south 27 east.
A rock or small islet very close to the island was seen south 30° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, at daybreak, we found ourselves about three leagues from the coast and were confirmed that it was indeed Rottnest Island. As the weather was very fine and the sea smooth, being to the north of the island, I steered for the anchorage in order to await the Casuarina there, as I had named it to her as a rendezvous should bad weather come on while she was away examining the part of the coast I had pointed out to her, and on which there was reason to believe she had stopped. But at about seven o'clock we sighted that vessel, which was at anchor and which, having seen us, got under way. This unexpected meeting made me decide to pass by this place, which had moreover been visited by the Naturaliste and was not worth my stopping there. All that can be said of it, from the report of Captain Hamelin and his officers, who stayed there a fairly long time, is that the anchorage is very bad and poor holding. The winds from south-west to north-west blow straight in, and in those circumstances the sea there is very heavy. The Swan River, which was ascended for eighteen or twenty leagues, offers no resource. Fresh water is sometimes found in the streams that run into it, but they are of little consequence.
Having hove to to wait for the Casuarina, I had a boat lowered and sent to fetch Citizen Freycinet. In my conversation with him I did not tell him of the resolution I had taken to deprive him of the command of this schooner, and confined myself to asking him why he had once again so badly executed the orders I had given him, his disobedience having caused a fresh separation and the loss of two days that I spent waiting for him. Citizen Freycinet replied that he had himself been much astonished at this fresh separation, since he had spent only five hours examining the coast I had designated to him, and had at once made sail to rejoin me, but that the separation was to be attributed solely to the fog that came on in the afternoon and to the weather of the following day, which seemed to me fair enough.
However that may be, I ordered him to follow me, and we steered north until noon and then north-north-west until nightfall.
At noon the observed latitude had been 31° 35' 12", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 113° 16' 15".
All day we had very fine weather and a pleasant breeze from south-south-east to south-south-west, but we could make little use of it, for, to keep pace with the Casuarina, we had to carry only our topsails, lowered on the cap, with two reefs in each.
At eight in the evening, being in only 27 fathoms of water, bottom of sand, rock and coral, we steered north-west for the night, during which it continued to blow a pleasant breeze.

1803-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky overcast, a light breeze from SE, SSE and ESE. Obs. lat. 23° 34' 12", est. long. 0° 40' east.
1803-03-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset, the land of Eendracht in sight extended from north by compass to east-south-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, in the morning, we resumed our course north-north-west in the hope of passing the latitude of the Abrolhos during the day, and perhaps even of sighting them, although the course we were steering put them a good distance to the west of us. But as the position given to this reef differs from chart to chart, I think that Captain Hamelin, who sighted it on his way from Rottnest Island to Shark Bay, will have determined its position with certainty. That is why it was a matter of indifference to me whether I sighted it or not.
During the morning it blew a pleasant breeze, and we made no more use of it than the day before, in order to keep pace with the Casuarina, which I did not wish to lose sight of.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 29° 51' 34", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 111° 44' 44". We were astonished not to have made more way to the north and no longer had any hope of passing the Abrolhos before nightfall, since according to the Dutch chart, which places them in 28° 58' 0" of latitude, we still had 0° 23' 54" to make directly northward on that point of the compass.
In the evening the weather became very cloudy, but the breeze was none the less good. We nevertheless found the sea heavier and more agitated than on the preceding days, which we attributed to the approach of this danger, whose extent from north to south is fairly considerable.
During the day a tropicbird was seen, which seemed to us rather extraordinary in the latitude we were in, this kind of bird not being in the habit of straying far from the tropics. The others, which we saw in fairly large numbers, were shearwaters, petrels and gulls like those met with everywhere.
At eight o'clock, reckoning ourselves roughly in the latitude of the southernmost point of the Abrolhos, we hove to in order to sound and remained so for three quarters of an hour, to give the Casuarina time to close with us. Having got no bottom at 90 fathoms, we resumed our course north-north-west. At midnight we sounded a second time, without bottom at 60, proof that we were far enough to the west of this danger to have nothing to fear from it. We continued north-north-west until daybreak the next day, when we had the ship steer north by east to close the land, intending to enter Shark Bay by the passage Dampier took, in order to catch some turtles there as fresh provisions for my crew.
1803-03-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: We crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the 8th time. From noon this day the crew had no more liquor.

1803-03-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from east to south and SE. Variation NW 18° 27' 47". Obs. lat. 22° 41' 34", est. long. W 0° 29' 30".
1803-03-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, in the morning, reckoning ourselves to the north of the Abrolhos, we resumed our course north by east so as not to stray too far from the coast. During the day we had a pleasant breeze from south-south-east to east-south-east, of which we made no more use than on the preceding days, being obliged to carry very little sail to wait for the Casuarina.
During the morning we saw several tropicbirds and many other seabirds. We also saw a few flying fish, which had not happened to us for a long time. A bonito of middling size was caught, the only fish of this kind we (had) seen since the beginning of the voyage.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 28° 1' 33", and the longitude by timekeeper put us in 111° 6' 45".
In the afternoon the winds varied from south-east to south, a strong breeze. And although we had our topsails lowered on the cap, with two reefs taken in, we were at times making between seven and eight knots, so that the Casuarina could not keep up with us under all sail.
At four in the afternoon we sighted the land from the mastheads. It then bore, however, from east to north-east as far as the eye could reach. We held our course north by east until eight in the evening, when, being in 62 fathoms, we took for the night the one to the north by west. During the night it blew a strong breeze, and we found the sea heavy as well as very agitated. The lead during the night gave between sixty-two and eighty-five fathoms.
During the day one of our kangaroos and one of the emus died. This was the second time such a misfortune had befallen us. And we attributed the cause of it to the violent motion of the ship, of the ship (sic), which, carrying little sail so as to keep the Casuarina in company, was tossed about in every way by the action of a sea that was neither easy nor smooth. These animals were stuffed so as to preserve their skins.

1803-03-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NE to NW, W and WNW. Obs. lat. 22° 9' 14", obs. long. W 4° 0'.
1803-03-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
At five in the evening,
the land was seen from the mastheads, extending from north-east to east.
At daybreak,
it was seen from north by east to south-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, at daybreak, we had a perfect view of the land, although we had steered all night north 22° 30' west. This led us to suspect that we had made more way than our dead reckoning had so far given us. This conjecture was soon borne out, for, having had some easting put into our course to close the land, we recognised at about ten o'clock that we had passed the middle of Dirk Hartog Island.
We continued to range along this coast, and at noon, being at the opening that separates it from the Îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands], we entered the channel, keeping fairly close to Dirk Hartog Island so as to pass to the east of the bank mentioned on the charts, which was discovered by Dampier.
At noon we observed 25° 34' 21" of south latitude, and timekeeper No. 35 put us in 110° 39' 56" of longitude. This latitude, laid down on the Dutch chart, agreed poorly with the one it gives for the northern point of this island, which it places in 25° 22'. But we took little account of this, having been convinced on other occasions that it puts the whole coast further north than it should be. The difference of 0° 15' 21", including our distance from the coast, which we reckoned at four miles, was much the same, the same (sic), as the one we had found for the northernmost of the Îles Stériles when we set up our observatory there.
At one o'clock, steering east by south to enter the bay, we sighted the bank Dampier speaks of, on which the sea breaks from time to time. We rounded this bank at a distance of about four miles without finding bottom at 18 and 20 fathoms.
From the bearing I had taken of it at a quarter past two in the after(noon), it follows that when the point of the first of the Îles Stériles, that is to say the southernmost, bears true north and the northern point of Dirk Hartog south-west by west true, or corrected for variation, the bank or breaker bears north-north-east at a distance of about four miles.
When we (had) entirely rounded Dirk Hartog Island, steering east by south, we began to find bottom, first in eighteen fathoms and shortly afterwards in 15; then it became very irregular and shoaled from 15 to seven, coming back afterwards to ten and eleven, and from this last figure to 8 and 7. We stood on, still steering south-east under easy sail and sounding continually. And a little before sunset we sighted the northern point of the land that Dampier named the Île du Milieu, but which we now know to be a peninsula, from the plan the Naturaliste made of this part of the bay, which she had ample time to examine during her long stay there.
After sunset, not judging it prudent to go further, I anchored for the night in 7 fathoms, fine clean sand, where we held fast although the breeze was fairly strong; but there was no sea running.

1803-03-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze variable from WSW to SSE and SE by S. Obs. lat. 20° 33' 18", est. long. 5° 42'.
1803-03-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, at daybreak, I had two boats hoisted out and gave the command of them to the first and second quartermasters, with orders to go and sound ahead of the ship, keeping one to port and the other to starboard. When they had set off and were about half a league to windward and to leeward, we made sail to draw nearer to the island where I intend to remain five or six days, as much to take a few turtles there as to have it examined whether the way out of the bay by the north is practicable, something the navigators who preceded us did not seek to learn. As we found ourselves in an unfavourable position when I first approached the north-west part of this peninsula, it was not possible for me to attempt it on leaving, as I had intended, by the southern part of the îles de Dore [Bernier and Dorre Islands], since I had come in by the north.
On the course we steered to close the land, the bottom held for a good while between 6 and seven fathoms of water. But as we drew nearer it fell to five fathoms, and we were still about two leagues from the coast. Fearing to see it shoal further if we went any farther ahead, I came to anchor and made the signal to the Casuarina to do likewise. On the return of the boats, which had run various boards in every direction, I was assured that at a league from the land there were 6 and seven fathoms everywhere, sand and weed bottom, and that the spot where we lay, which was no more than a musket-shot across, was the only one with no more than five fathoms. Nevertheless I kept the anchorage and gave no thought to changing it until our departure.
At nine o'clock two boats were dispatched to go turtle fishing. I gave the command of them to Ensign Ransonnet, with the following instructions:
"To Citizen Ransonnet, &c.:
"You will take, citizen, the command of the two large boats and proceed to the Île aux Tortues [Faure Island] in order to procure as many turtles there as you possibly can, my call in this bay having no other object than that.
"As soon as the boat has its load, you will return on board at once. Although it is provisioned for six days, you will make every effort to be back before those provisions are consumed.
"If the turtles prove difficult to take, you will not permit any of them to be killed on shore for the use of the boats' crews, and will reserve them all for general consumption on board.
"You will complete the loading of the large bastringue boat as soon as it arrives, so that it may come back at once without waiting for you. You will take care to have collected any objects of curiosity or of natural history that chance may lead you to come upon, and you will
"hand them all over to me on your arrival on board.
"As the coxswain of your boat, Lefevre, knows the place where the turtles are to be found, and has already been employed in this fishery in the time of the Naturaliste, he will take you to the place where there is the best hope of finding them." N. B.
After these boats had left, I dispatched two others to fish with lines and to look for an easy landing place. Four men were embarked in one and three in the other, with orders to be back on board after sunset.
During the day we busied ourselves in shifting some of our sails, which were in need of fairly extensive repair.
On the return of the boats I was much astonished to learn that they had been unable to land, because a band of natives, whose number was put at more than a hundred, had opposed their landing and appeared firmly resolved not to allow it. All were armed with spears, clubs and shields. As long as they were in sight of our people, who prudently kept out of range of their weapons, they were in continual agitation, running hither and thither and brandishing their spears.
It is likely that the fright they gave our people so disturbed them that they could not properly judge their number, which some put as high as two hundred and the least frightened at thirty or forty; but all agreed in saying that (they were) very tall, strong and vigorous men, wearing long black beards that came down upon their chests.
As I did not believe this part of the coast to be inhabited, the punt and the small boat had not been provided with arms for their personal safety. This news, and these details, which I had hardly expected, led me to resolve to make the acquaintance of this tribe if it were possible. And to that end I gave orders that the longboat be made ready for the next day and put in the water at daybreak.
During the day I sent for Citizen Freycinet, commanding the Casuarina, and ordered him to get under way the next morning, directing him to steer due north as far as twenty-four degrees of latitude and then to beat back, tack upon tack, to the anchorage where we lay. By this means I wished to make sure whether the route out of the bay to the north, to gain the open sea, was practicable, or whether the banks which I suspect to exist between the southernmost of the îles de Dore and the northern point of the peninsula where we are leave a channel that can be passed through without danger.
During the night we had a pretty fair breeze from the south-south-west and a smooth sea. The sky was very damp and the horizon laden with haze, although the stars were very bright.

1803-03-18.journal_anonyme: The sky overcast, the horizon thick, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 17° 58' 50", est. long. 6° 56' 36". Var. 17° 29' 20" NW.
1803-03-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, at daybreak, the Casuarina got under way to carry out the mission I had given her the day before, which was, as I have already said, to go and ascertain whether there was a practicable passage between the northern point of the presqu'île de Dampier and the îles de Dore [Bernier and Dorre Islands].
For our part, we put our longboat in the water to go and make a landing on shore, and I gave the command of it to Citizen Ronsard, with the following instructions:
"To Citizen Ronsard, Lieutenant,
"You will take, citizen, the command of the longboat and the small boat, and you will go and land on shore at the place that Second Master Le Beau will point out to you.
"According to the details he has given me, it appears that the extremity of this peninsula is fairly well inhabited and that several families of natives are settled there. The object of your mission is to make their acquaintance, employing every means that may contribute to it, whether by the gestures customary in such cases or by the sight of the presents you are bringing them.
"If one were to rely on all that the men I had sent fishing have told us, not only would the natives they saw be extraordinary men, but also little disposed to let you land. You must therefore conduct yourself with prudence and be continually on your guard.
"Take particular care to make use of your arms only after having tried to make your landing without resorting to that means, for you must be persuaded that a few musket shots fired with powder alone will scatter them in such a way that you will have no further opportunity of meeting them.
"You will leave armed men to guard the longboat, and you will not advance too far into the interior of the country with those who accompany you, so as to be better able to protect it should circumstances require, or should you be obliged to re-embark in order to avoid coming to extremities that would be unfortunate for the natives.
"You will return on board this evening, as will all those who accompany you, 15 persons in number, not counting those in the small boat." Signed N. B.
When our longboat approached the coast, we followed her with our eyes, watching all her movements. She was seen to let go her grapnel and furl her sails, and all those in her went on shore without appearing to us to meet the least difficulty. As several of those who had landed could be seen walking along the shore at a
fair distance from one another, it was conjectured that the natives, having seen that we were many in number, might have withdrawn, and that perhaps they would not even be met with.
Be that as it may, I was most impatient to see my longboat return, which was not due back until evening, and waiting for her made that day a very long one for me, although I spent it entirely on geographical work for the construction of our charts.
At last, at six o'clock, she arrived, together with all those who had accompanied Citizen Ronsard. According to that officer's report, no one was met with, although a fairly large extent of ground had been covered. Twelve or fifteen huts, much better made, however, than those found up to then, made up the village where this tribe dwelt. In some of them fire was found still burning, but no household utensils, proof that the natives had abandoned them until after our departure. Among these huts, those that might belong to the heads of the family were thought to be clearly recognisable, in that they were much larger and built with far more symmetry. As I intend to send someone to make a drawing of them, I shall defer describing their shape until I know it better than from the report that has been made to me. No water was found in the neighbourhood of this village, which seemed to me very surprising.
This part of the peninsula is entirely devoid of large trees. Nothing is found there but sparse bushes, and the soil is sandy in places and, in others, of a red ochreous earth that appears ill suited to vegetation.
Our botanists brought back from this excursion no more than three or four new plants; Citizen Péron, a basket full of broken shells; and the hunters, four species of birds that were in no way remarkable.
Our small boat, which had spent its time fishing, was more fortunate than all the others, having having (sic) a full load of good, fine fish, most of which were of the kind the sailors call gros dos, of which I have had a drawing made.
As the party rested for a good while in the natives' huts, a few presents were left there on leaving, consisting of glass beads, metal buttons, a small mirror and a snuffbox bearing the portrait of a Negro. Perhaps, if any of them who watched us during the day comes to see what has been done in their dwelling, the sight of these presents may induce them to place more confidence in us.
During the night the weather was very fine and the breeze moderate from south-south-west to south-east. Towards two o'clock it went round to the east, almost calm.

1803-03-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from ESE to SE. At daybreak sighted Saint Helena bearing NE by compass. Obs. lat. 15° 46' 25", est. long. 8° 13' 36". Var. 14° 19' 40" NW.
1803-03-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth I again sent my longboat ashore, under the command of Ensign Bonnefoy. The object of this second trip was not only to try to make the acquaintance of the natives but also to employ the crew in making salt by boiling sea water in large coppers that had been prepared expressly for the purpose. As the fishing was plentiful, I wished to salt the fish it yielded, which would not keep for twenty-four hours on account of the great heat. As our supply of salt was beginning to run very low, we had to resort to this expedient, the more so as there remained on board only enough for the ship's consumption for four to five months.
The longboat was ordered to spend the night ashore and not to return until the following evening.
I took this opportunity to send the draughtsman to make a drawing of the natives' village and of the shape of their huts. The gardener Guichenot was also of the party, in order to gather plants for us. Of the naturalists, Citizen Péron was the only one who went ashore, the others not finding that the country deserved to be examined with more care than they had given it in the small extent they had been able to see or cover.
In the morning the winds, which had gone round to the east, came back as usual to the south-south-west, and the breeze was very moderate.
In the afternoon the small boat was ordered to go fishing and to spend the night at it, so as to be back on board the next day before the heat set in, for the preservation of whatever fish it might take. On board we busied ourselves with various tasks relating to the ship, awaiting only the return of the Casuarina and of the two boats that were out turtle fishing in order to get under way.
During the night nothing new occurred. We had the fire around which our people were gathered constantly in view, and no movement was seen on their part that could give cause for uneasiness. The south-south-west breeze lasted all night and was fairly fresh, but we had a great deal of damp, although there was not a single cloud in the whole sky.
1803-03-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak Saint Helena was sighted in the N 45° E; at noon it bore from us S 43° E to S 58° E. The day after our departure from Mauritius a man was found who had hidden himself aboard at sailing.

1803-03-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, and squally at the end of the watch. At noon the course was shaped NNW. Obs. lat. 13° 50' 21", est. long. 10° 9'.
1803-03-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth our small boat returned from fishing, as had been agreed, and brought back so great a quantity of fish that, after a liberal distribution to the whole crew, we did not know what to do with the rest. A large quantity was prepared, sprinkled with salt and laid out in the sun to dry.
One of the punts, which had set out early in the morning to gather crabs, shells and oysters, came back at noon with a second load of fish, so plentiful were they. But it found neither crabs nor shellfish, only a few cockscomb oysters. We decided to have the fish it brought cooked, so as to be able to keep it for the following day.
During the day the weather was very fine and the winds from the south to south-west by south, a light breeze.
At sunset I was surprised to see that no preparations were being made in the longboat to come on board; but as the officer I had put in her had express orders to be back before nightfall, I supposed that, not everyone having yet come in, he had been delayed by the absence of one of them, among whom was undoubtedly Citizen Péron.
Be that as it may, at eight o'clock in the evening, again seeing the same fires that had been kept up the night before, I gave orders for a gun to be fired to recall that boat on board. At ten o'clock in the evening, not seeing her return, a second was fired, with no more success. So I lost hope of making, the next day, the excursion I had intended to carry out myself in the south-west part of this peninsula. As the absence of my longboat was a formal disobedience of the orders the officer commanding her had received from me, I have had 30 francs entered against his account for the two blank rounds he obliged me to expend in recalling him.
The rest of the night passed without incident; there was little wind, or rather it passed in calm, with a very damp and often hazy sky.

1803-03-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 12° 5' 52", est. long. 11° 29' 0".
1803-03-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, in the morning, when the day was far enough advanced to make out and distinguish objects on shore, the longboat was at last seen under sail; but as there was little wind, she had fallen far to leeward, carried by the ebb, which was setting her to the north-west.
The weather was very fine until eight o'clock, but then a fog suddenly arose, so thick that we lost sight of both the land and the longboat. This fog lasted until eleven o'clock, after which the weather cleared again.
At half past one, the longboat having returned and made fast alongside, the officer commanding her informed me that he had brought back six hundred pounds of very fine salt, which had been gathered from a salt-water pond that was at present almost dry. After enquiring into what he had had to do on shore, I asked him why he had not complied with the orders I had given him to return the next day at sunset. He then told (me) that he had found himself in a very awkward position through the absence of Citizens Péron, Guichenot and Petit,
who, having left him in the morning without saying anything to him of their plans, did not appear in the afternoon; but that, as they had set out without water or provisions, he had presumed they could not be far from the place of rendezvous, unless they had lost their way. He added that at four o'clock, not seeing them come, he at once sent off four armed men, who searched for them in various directions until nightfall and came back without having found them. Citizen Bonnefoy, fearing my reproaches if he did not bring everyone back, and well knowing that he would be blamed for not having returned, preferred to spend the night waiting still longer. And at last, towards nine o'clock in the evening, the three absent men reappeared, worn out with fatigue and exhausted by hunger and thirst. Two of them lay down twelve or fifteen paces from the tent, and they had to be carried there to reach it.
From fuller details I learned that Citizen Péron, the most thoughtless and improvident of all those on board, had persuaded the other two to cross the island from east to west, assuring them that it was at most a league wide, that he had made sure of this by inspecting the chart, and that consequently they had far more time than they needed for the excursion he proposed. To decide them still further, he promised Citizen Guichenot an ample collection of new plants that they could not fail to meet with, and Citizen Petit a great variety of amusements, which was very agreeable to him. At length, all having followed Citizen Péron and adopted his plan, they set off. They began by climbing a fairly high rise from which the ship could be seen distinctly. This same height, on which stood a fairly tall tree, was taken as a landmark, and they were to come back to it on their return. It was from this point, then, that they took their bearings to cover the league of road that made up the width they had to cross.
After walking for about four hours on end without the least pause, and in the blazing sun, the gardener Guichenot said to Citizen Péron: "But the league you promised us is becoming very long, and I think it is time to think of going back, for we must have as much ground to cover to rejoin the longboat as we have covered since we set out." Citizen Péron fully felt the justice of this reasoning, but he got out of it by saying: "We did not bear enough to the left; that is (what) will have lengthened our walk. Let us now take that direction and we shall very soon reach our goal." They followed him as they would an experienced guide, and while they were advancing, several natives appeared, armed with spears. At first they were afraid of them, having for their only defence a wretched musket they had borrowed from the steward's clerk, and which was unfit to fire, as they found by trying it. As the natives kept pursuing them, they conceived that it was better to overawe them with a confident bearing than to flee before them, and
from then on they decided to go to meet them.
The natives in their turn halted, but seeing that our people kept advancing, they did on their side what ours had done on theirs. Their pace, however, was less hurried, and our people came near enough to them for each side to see the other clearly. They began by signing to our three faint-hearts to follow them, which they took good care not to attempt. As the two parties stood halted facing one another, all the natives but one withdrew to one side. It was thought that this one was the chief. That would no doubt have been the moment to approach him too, but as no move was made to do so, the apparent chief advanced a few paces, made great gestures, signing to them to go away and speaking very loudly. He was exactly obeyed, for our wandering travellers, not finding themselves in sufficient strength, left them and resumed the route that was to take them to the seashore on the other side of the island, where they at last arrived at one o'clock in the afternoon.
In this circumstance the finest opportunity that had yet offered of having some communication with the natives was missed. And the draughtsman, whom I had sent expressly to draw any natives who could be approached, did nothing but a view of the village where those we had met at our first landing on the island dwelt.
After leaving the natives, they set about searching for shells, and brought back several exactly like those that the Naturaliste found and brought back in abundance. This reflection alone should have been enough to make them think of returning. But the leader of the party, the citizen who until now has caused us nothing but trouble and anxiety whenever he has been put ashore with no one to watch over and guide him, preferred to waste the time he had left roaming the seashore rather than go back. So that they did not set out to return until it was certain that they could not arrive before the time fixed for departure, even supposing they took the most direct route. Be that as it may, our travellers thought of returning somewhat late, to tell the truth, having neither water nor provisions. The night that came on increased their difficulty, so much so that they lost their way and went completely astray. Chance alone served them better in this circumstance than their bearings had done, for they found themselves on the opposite shore at the very moment when their dead reckoning of the distance they had covered still put them three leagues from it.
Citizen Péron, having come to announce his return to me, said that he was in no condition to give me an account and begged me to grant him, before making his report, the long rest of which he no doubt stood in great need, since he could scarcely speak or stand.
The rest of the day passed without incident. The gardener Guichenot did not find a single plant and was ill with fatigue,
from having obligingly carried, the whole way, a load of twenty-five to thirty pounds of worthless shells, gathered with as much pleasure as care by Citizen Péron, who himself had to be carried to be got to the tent.
This is the third escapade of this kind that this learned naturalist has led us, but it will also be the last, for he will go ashore no more except when I am myself in the boat that takes him, and the limits I shall set for his excursions will not be wide enough to delay the boat's departure, nor for him to stray very far.
During the night the weather was fine and nothing out of the ordinary occurred. We had the winds from the south-south-west and a fine sky, though more clouded than usual.

1803-03-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. Est. lat. 10° 46' 22", est. long. 12° 34'. Var. 14° 1' 30" NW.
1803-03-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first of Germinal, at daybreak, I sent off my longboat to fetch plants for our kangaroos, as she had not brought me back the day before the load I had ordered, most of the men intended for that work having been employed in searching for Citizen Péron and his company.
The small boat was likewise dispatched to fish.
At ten o'clock we were pleased to see Citizen Ransonnet returning from his mission, and if he brings us back a good number of turtles we shall have no cause to regret the six days I had sacrificed in advance for this call, even though it has procured us few objects of natural history.
At one o'clock in the afternoon the boats were back on board, but we were disappointed in our expectations, for they had only six turtles each, among which only three weighed about two hundred and fifty to three hundred pounds; the nine others were from 25 to forty pounds.
According to Citizen Ransonnet's report, they were very difficult to take. And to procure them, the boats' crews were obliged to catch them in the water and to wade out onto the banks where they lay, in as much as four feet of water, which made the fishing very difficult and even dangerous, since a man named Lefevre was attacked by a large shark, against which he only succeeded in defending himself after stunning it and stabbing it with a harpoon. These turtles, at least the smaller ones, were put in tubs made of cut-down casks, with orders to take good care of them until such time as we should need them for our use.
Little in the way of natural history was brought back from this excursion, only a few common shells; and although we already had many of them, they were nevertheless well paid for by our naturalists and savants, who bought them from the
the sailors in payment of rum, so that in the evening sixteen men were brawling in every part of the ship and I myself was obliged to strike several of them to restore quiet. This was not the first time such disorder had occurred. I had thought to remedy it by forbidding anything to be paid for with rum, but all prohibitions are void for savants such as ours, who believe themselves independent. I gave a particular order to the steward's clerk not to issue a single drop of rum henceforth without an order signed by me, on pain of suspension from his duties.
In the afternoon the breeze blew so hard from the south-west that I gave up hope of seeing my longboat arrive before nightfall. The Casuarina, which we had sighted as early as ten o'clock in the morning, had likewise fallen so far to leeward that we did not see (her) again until about four o'clock in the afternoon, and she did not reach the anchorage until about five.
As my intention was to weigh early the next day, I was greatly vexed in this circumstance, being unable to take on board the four boats I had out before the longboat had been stowed.
According to M. Freycinet's report, it appears that the way out of Shark Bay by the north, passing between the îles de (sic) Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands] and the peninsula which Dampier did not know, is rather difficult, and that one must be continually on one's guard or else know well the channel that lies between the banks running out in different directions from these two lands. The Casuarina often happened to fall suddenly from eight fathoms to four, and from four to two or three, without well knowing whether she should look for deeper water on a southerly or a northerly course. As I had not foreseen all these difficulties, although I had myself got in among some of these banks when coming to seek the peninsula, which, like Dampier, I took for an island, I had not given him the time to examine them properly and fix their position, which would require long labour and small boats to cross them in every direction.
Citizen Freycinet's report decided me to leave the bay by the same way I had entered it, and I ordered him to get under way as soon as he saw us making our preparations to weigh. I also most strongly urged him to keep close to us during the night, on the new course we were about to steer, as the only means of avoiding a separation.
During the night the breeze was very strong; however, we had no need to veer out cable, although we had only forty fathoms out. At half past eleven the longboat arrived, but as a great part of her crew was drunk, thanks be to the officers and naturalists, I put off hoisting her in until the next morning.
Particular remarks on the extent of coast
lying between Cape Leeuwin and
the entrance of Shark Bay discovered by Dampier.
The survey we have just made of the whole stretch of coast called Leeuwin's Land, being far more satisfactory than the one made the first time we visited these waters, leaves nothing further to be desired; the trend and the various windings of the land will henceforth be well known, as will the two dangers which navigators who may frequent it will have to avoid, and which at the outset had escaped our notice.
It follows, then, from our latest observations, made with all the more care as the weather and the winds have on the whole served us well, that from Point Leeuwin to Rottnest Island there is no place that can offer secure shelter against winds from north-east to south-west by way of west, in the whole extent of that bight. And indeed, one can anchor only in the place we have named baie du Géographe [Geographe Bay], where the bottom is clean and good for anchoring. But this bay is good only in the fine season and when the breezes from north-east to south-east are moderate there. Even then, landing is not always easy. For the rest, the coast is clear and can be hugged closely along its whole length. It presents no dangers other than those marked on our charts, whose well-determined position makes it easy to guard against them.
Although I did not anchor at Rottnest Island, that place, according to Captain Hamelin's report and what I saw of it myself, seems to me no better suited to shelter a ship from bad weather than those I have just spoken of, and all these places offer only a temporary, fair-weather retreat in the fine season.
One thing that greatly surprised us in the latter period during which we explored this coast was that we did not meet with a single living whale there, and only three dead ones, whereas the first time we visited it they were there in such numbers that we were often inconvenienced by them. This difference no doubt arises from the season, which in all likelihood does not suit them. For it is a fact that we did not see a single one. Besides, a longer series of observations on this subject would be needed to say exactly how matters stand. But it seems to me beyond doubt that ships bound for this fishery which arrived at the same season in which we first came there would quickly complete their cargo, and with great success. We never saw a single seal there.
On leaving Rottnest Island, where a few seals are to be found, we did not follow the coast to reach Shark Bay, since it has been well seen and represented by the Dutch, whose chart needs only the corrections called for by the imperfections of the instruments still in use when they surveyed it. It was only after having rounded the Abrolhos that we closed with it again.
My first entry into Shark Bay was made by the north, since I judged it easier to penetrate to the head of it by means of the westerly and south-westerly winds, which seemed to have prevailed and predominated until then. But the shallowness of the water (at low tide) and the various sandbanks not having allowed me to pass to the north or to the west of the land that seems to form an island in the middle of the channel, and which I did in fact believe to be one, from the reports of the Dutch and of Dampier, I was obliged to retrace my course and go out by the same way I had come in. This last time, having entered by the same passage as Dampier, I came to anchor in the northern part of this peninsula. And having had the channel that separates it from the southernmost of the îles Stériles examined, I have made sure that it is practicable and that one can leave by steering north; but that the passage between the sandbanks lying there is not practicable for a large ship unless it becomes better known. The bank lying between Dirk Hartog Island and the southernmost of the îles Stériles is all the less dangerous in that the sea breaks heavily on it and it can be seen at more than a league. It is only after rounding this bank, heading up towards the east, that the bottom shoals quickly; from 13 to nine fathoms are found over two-thirds of the way to the northern point of the peninsula, and the course is south-east with the ebb, so as to counter the effect of the current, which sets to the north-west. With the flood, I think that by steering east one would get there directly. At about two-thirds of the way along the channel the soundings are very irregular, between eight, seven, six and five fathoms, and we had them so on our way to the anchorage, at this last sounding about two leagues from the land nearest the ship, which bore east. But had we advanced a quarter of a league farther, we should have had five and a half, six and even seven fathoms closer inshore.
This anchorage seemed to us the safest and most convenient of all those we have made on the coast of New Holland. We had a constantly smooth sea there, and yet fairly strong breezes from south-south-west to south-west, without the ship ever dragging, although we had only forty fathoms of cable out. We found the fishing very plentiful in this spot and the natives unsociable, for it was not possible to approach them despite all our attempts to
succeed in it. They even abandoned the village in which they were gathered on our arrival, and if those who were met with since on the eastern part of the island are not the same, there is every reason to believe that we never saw them again.
In the inlet that Shark Bay makes to the south-east there are an an (sic) infinity of places offering shelter as secure as it is convenient for merchant ships of moderate size drawing no more than twelve feet of water. They would there be so sheltered from every wind that they would have nothing to fear. This place might perhaps deserve to be settled if it were regarded as a suitable place for whale fishing, the only trade on this coast that could offer an advantage not to be neglected. I am persuaded that it is from policy that the Dutch have not given us a more correct plan of it than the one shown on their charts.
As Captain Hamelin had this whole part thoroughly surveyed, and as it was done with care, judging by the details of the plan he has given of it, I did not stop there, the more so as it would have required too long a stay to have it examined anew. I had entered this bay only to procure turtles, and in that I was not very fortunate, since, as I have already observed, we took only twelve, owing to the unfavourable season, which was not the laying time, and those that were brought back had to be caught in the water on the eastern banks. But they are none the less plentiful there for that, and in more favourable times they may be turned to good account for trade. I do not know whether the shell is fit for trade, but that can be judged from the samples I am taking to Europe.
Although no fresh water was found in the brief searches that were made, it is not to be presumed that this part of the bay contains none, and even a considerable quantity, if one looks at the signs that announce there must be some.
I had always regarded as most extraordinary, and I would even say improbable, a fact reported by Dampier, who says he found part of the head of a hippopotamus in the stomach of the shark; but from the dead animal found on the Île aux Tortues [Faure Island] by the men of the boat who had gone there turtle fishing, there seems little doubt that the teeth they brought back and handed to me belonged to a similar species. According to the information given me, this animal may have been six feet long. It was dead and half rotten. Its head, by their estimate, may have been a third of the size of its body; its tail was about two feet long. Its large, wide-open mouth was furnished with teeth like those of which I give the specimen, but they did not count their number. As the animal lay at the edge of the sea, half buried in sand, they saw neither feet nor fins, for they took it for a fish. Its skin was a
dark grey, thick and rough to the touch, with some traces of hair of the same colour, but in small quantity. As the smell it gave off was not very pleasant, they did not try to turn it over to find out how it was made and whether it had feet or fins.
However imperfect the description given me of this animal, I thought I recognised a perfect resemblance to the hippopotamus, which I know well, having killed several in the Quitangone river near Querimbe on the coast of Africa. The arrangement of its teeth in particular seemed to me exactly the same, and the savants of Europe will judge, after seeing them, whether this conjecture is true or false.
The presence of a fine animal in these waters seems to indicate that there must be, in the neighbourhood of the places they frequent, some fresh-water lagoons where it goes to drink, for everyone knows that it does so and that, although amphibious, it comes ashore every night, and sometimes even by day, to graze and drink.
The men in the fishing boats swam across two or three arms of the sea that run into the Île aux Tortues, which they went right round, but which, judging by the distance they say they covered, would appear to be larger than it is made on the chart given of it by Citizen Faure, who was sent expressly to examine it and saw nothing of it.
As I also do not know whether the shell of the turtle that can be taken in this bay is fit for trade, I have particularly ordered that the plates be kept, so that the Government may have it examined. If it is good, it would be one more resource for navigators who might undertake the whale-fishing trade in these waters and in the baie du Géographe. And if not, it would still be a resource for the refreshment of their crews.
Astronomical Observations
Latitude of the ship's anchorage 25° 30' 50"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 31 111° 27' 26"
Longitude by timekeeper No. 35 111° 12' 24" mean 111° 29' 59" (sic)
(In reality 111° 19' 59)
Longitude corrected for the error of the timekeepers 111° 0' 0"
Latitude of the northern point of the peninsula, observed on shore: 25° 29' 45", longitude 111° 7' 35"
Variation of the compass 5° 33' 59", mean of 11 observations.
Note: during our stay at the anchorage and on shore it was observed that the tides were very irregular, and that their strength and duration depended far more on the winds and their direction than on the general laws of the ebb and flow of the sea. When the winds were south-west, they rose very high and fell little; with easterly winds it was quite the reverse.

1803-03-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A pleasant breeze from SSE and ESE. Obs. lat. 9° 16' 30", est. long. 13° 44' 48".
1803-03-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
the northern point of Dirk Hartog Island bore south 44° west.
The middle of the breaker lying in the channel, north 44° east.
The western point of the île de Dore [Dorre Island], north 20° east.
At the same time a reef was seen, on which the sea was breaking heavily, off the eastern coast of Dirk Hartog Island, bearing south 3° east.
Historical events & Remarks &c.
On the second, 23 March, about an hour before dawn, we made our preparations to hoist in our longboat and the four other boats we had to take on board. The work could not be finished until seven o'clock. Immediately afterwards the topsails were set for getting under way and we hove up our anchor, which was stowed at half past seven. On leaving the anchorage of the presqu'île de Dampier, we steered roughly the same course to leave the bay as we had steered to enter it. As we sounded continually on this course, as had been done on the other, we found, with little difference, the same bottom. However, I thought I noticed that the soundings were more regular than we had found them on the way in. The bottom, in the offing, half a league from our anchorage, was 7, 8, 9, 8, 7, 9, until we came in sight of the reef that lies in the middle of the channel between the northern point of Dirk Hartog Island and the southern point of the first of the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands]. From the sight of this danger, which then bore north-north-west and on which the sea breaks heavily, making it less to be feared, the bottom begins to deepen, and one passes rapidly from 9 fathoms to 10, 11, 12 & 15, after which no more bottom is found with the hand lead if the ship is going ahead at four knots.
We passed the reef I have just spoken of at about the same distance as we had passed it on the way in, that is to say, three or four miles at most.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 25° 25' 53", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35, reduced to the same time, put us in 110° 34' 42".
After rounding the reef, we gradually brought our course more to the north until, having rounded the southern point of the first of the îles Stériles, we were able to steer due north to run along its western coast.
However, as we had nothing to do on that coast and I feared the calm of the night, I kept to the offing and, so as not to be delayed, I shaped my course to make the north-west point as quickly as I could.
During the evening the weather continued fine, with a good breeze from south by west to south. During the evening we carried little sail so as to keep pace with the Casuarina.
In the night we had a much less fine sky than usual. The atmosphere grew laden with haze and we had a great deal of damp. The lead, which at eight o'clock had given forty-five fathoms, gave ninety at midnight and eighty-five at four in the morning, bottom of fine gravel.

1803-03-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE. Obs. lat. 7° 57' 31", est. long. 14° 42' 18". Var. 12° 26' NW.
1803-03-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock in the afternoon the îles Stériles [Bernier and Dorre Islands] could be seen from
south-east to north-east by east.
At six o'clock we thought we took a bearing of the point of the northernmost of them, north-north-east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the third, 24 March 1803, we steered north 22° 30' east, which is the direction the coast takes after rounding the point that forms the northern entrance of Shark Bay, to the north of the second of the îles Stériles. We did not see the land during the day, which perhaps arises from the current having carried us farther to the west than our dead reckoning of the course we had run made it. This conjecture seems (to be) confirmed by the result given by the timekeeper at noon, since it gave us 29 minutes 57 seconds of distance made to the west, whereas the dead reckoning gave only 20' 27". Besides, as the land is very low in this part and the water deep at a short distance from the shore, we were not surprised not to see it and to have a great depth of water.
During the morning the weather, though fine, was not as pleasant as we had had it on the preceding days. Many clouds in the sky often veiled the sun, without the heat being any less for it, since the thermometer rose as high as 24° at noon. We had not had it at so high a reading for a long time.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 23° 20' 50", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 110° 4' 45".
In the evening we continued on a north-north-east course, which carried us along the coast, of which, however, we had no sight. All day long we saw many tropic birds and white gulls with red bills and feet. An eagle also came and perched on our topgallant crosstrees, and we should have taken it alive if the man who went to catch it had not taken fright as he tried to seize it.
At eight o'clock, having found no (bottom) at a hundred fathoms, we continued on a north-north-east course. We sounded at midnight and at four o'clock with no better success, which made me fear that we were farther off the coast than I thought.
During the night the sky continued very cloudy and damp, but the breeze was moderate and the sea less agitated than during the day. We carried little sail on account of the Casuarina, for which, nevertheless, we often had to wait.

1803-03-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SSE. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 6° 11' 59", est. long. 15° 48' 18".
1803-03-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth, 25 March 1803, in the morning, persuaded that we could not be far from the coast and that we should easily close with it before noon, in the neighbourhood of Willem's River, I had our course brought much more to the east than I had done until then. But in spite of that, having sighted no land, I clearly perceived that there was an error in the course I had held, but I did not know to what to attribute it.
At noon the latitude having been observed to be 21° 16' 50", and the longitude by No. 35, which I had always used, putting us in 111° 20' 18", I was as much astonished to find myself north of the north point as to have passed it in longitude without noticing. From this the error was evident, and as it only remained to find it, I accordingly asked Citizen Bernier to come to me and enquired of him how it was that he had placed the longitude of the north-west point of New Holland in 110° 16' 40".
Citizen Bernier then rightly pointed out to me that the longitude I had taken was the one the timekeeper had given at that time, but he added: "If you had taken what the correction of that timekeeper produced, (it) is very different, since it puts it in 111° 50' 40"." I had nothing to reply to his observation and acknowledged my error. But as I wished to sight that point a second time before standing farther to the north and to the west east, I had the yards braced up close-hauled, on a course south towards the east, which was held until ten o'clock at night; and then I stood off on a board to seaward, not thinking it prudent to advance any farther in the darkness, although at that time the lead had found no bottom at eighty fathoms.
During the night the breeze was strong and we took a second reef in the topsails to ease the Casuarina, which was cracking on sail to follow us. The sky, which had looked rather threatening during the day, grew clearer and almost all the clouds disappeared. But the breeze was none the less strong for that, and only began to die down towards two o'clock in the morning, at which time we went back on the inshore board, which was held until daylight. We sounded at four o'clock without getting bottom; we could not, however, have been very far from the coast at that time.

1803-03-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SSE. Saw many birds. Obs. lat. 4° 8' 16", est. long. 16° 41' 6".
1803-03-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
At noon,
the north-west point of New Holland bore south 3° east.
The mainland could then be seen as far as south 12° west.
To the south-east several islets could be made out from the mastheads, and between them and the north-west point breakers were visible.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifth, 26 March 1803, at daybreak, we sighted the land, which extended from south-south-west to south-east by south, and by my reckoning we might have been six or seven leagues from it. It is doubtless in error that the officer who had the watch at that time judged its height to be in no way remarkable, for had he known the height of the lands neighbouring this part he would have spoken of it very differently. I shall say, then, knowing it as I do, that it is very remarkable, and may even serve as a landmark in case of need, for a coast that can be made out six or seven leagues out at sea cannot be considered, (in the neighbourhood of) New Holland and in the part where we are, as low land deserving little attention.
In the course of the morning we continued close-hauled on an easterly course, making a little southing, so as to get a good view of the north-west point, which we sighted towards ten o'clock in the morning.
At noon the observed latitude was 21° 31' 3" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us in 111° 51' 37". This result, compared with the dead reckoning of the course we had run in the twenty-four hours, gave a difference of 24 minutes 41 seconds from the reckoning, placing us farther east: proof either that the course was badly estimated or that the currents set us to the west-north-west, since there were also five minutes' difference in the observed latitude.
After doubling the north-west point we ran along the coast at a fair distance. Of the islets marked on the Dutch chart, six were counted within sight during the morning. But a little before sunset we saw a seventh, of which that chart makes no mention and which bore east 11° 30' north.
As my intention was to steer east, making only as much northing as might be needed to range along the coast, which I had resolved to examine in this part, I made no way during the night and spent it beating to windward. At six o'clock we had 24 fathoms, and at half past seven (we tried to come ?) to anchor, but the weather did not allow it, the wind having blown hard from south-south-west to south.
On the tack to the westward and northward we soon lost bottom, but on the south-easterly tack we found it in 65 and 53 fathoms.

1803-03-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from SSE, the course north. The sea very phosphorescent. Est. lat. 1° 53' 46", est. long. 17° 9' 12".
1803-03-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
At sunset, the islets seen in the evening bore from east 11° south to south-east.
At eight o'clock in the morning, the land in sight extended from north-east by north to south-east by east.
At noon, the same land could be seen from north 67° 30' east to south 5° east.
We then had a chain of islands and islets extending from south 5° east to south 22° 30' east. The islets and islands seemed to be joined to one another by reefs.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixth, 27 March 1803, at daybreak, we sighted the land, but only from the mastheads, and it was not until eight o'clock that we could take its bearing from the deck. It then lay from north-east by north to south-east by east, at a distance of about three leagues from the ship. We were then steering east, inclining to the south, so as to examine, if we could, the part of the coast lying farthest to windward, and afterwards bear away to range along the part that lay from east towards north of us. But at six o'clock the colour of the water, which was quite white, warned us that we were running onto a bank. The lead was cast at that very moment and gave twenty-two fathoms (in an inset: no bottom, see the officers' log); I meant to hold on, when the lookouts warned me that, from the agitation of the sea about half a league ahead of us, it seemed to them unlikely that there was any water there, and that if we held on we should not fail to be aground before long. I saw for myself the agitation they spoke of, and I confess that it alarmed me. I ordered the ship brought round to starboard at once, the sea appearing calmer on that side, and we passed without sounding, for it was no longer time to have recourse to that means within musket-shot of this spot, which I think it very prudent to avoid, although I saw there no apparent danger beyond what one may infer from an extraordinary agitation of the sea, visible only in that part. Having passed this danger, which I believe truly to be one, we bore away as far as north 22° 30' east, to range at a good distance along the coast, which appeared by no means safe to approach too closely. We then sighted several banks to the north-east and to the north, and counted ourselves very fortunate not to have become entangled among them. We passed one of these banks at about half a league at most.
In the course of the morning we ran along part of the mainland coast, which we closed with once we were out of danger. The land in sight was of moderate height, but so uniform that it offered few remarkable points. After we had followed it for about three leagues, the course we were steering, which was from north 34° east to north 44° east, brought us onto a second bank of great extent, upon which we ran, although the change in the colour of the water had warned us of it long before we reached it. But as the land in sight in that part formed a great bight, at the head of which none could be seen, I wished to make certain whether these were not the two ends of two islands, or whether the opening we saw did not lead into some inlet that might offer a good harbour. The lead gave 19 fathoms at the edge of this bank. We were still advancing over it when we sighted a reef on which the sea broke heavily and which was not more than a league from us. Disappointed in our expectation, we made haste to get away
from this place. But to do so we had to steer from north 30° west to north 60° west. Several people believed the ship was touching the bottom, because where she passed the sand seemed to mingle with the water, but I am not of that opinion; and as we had to get out on the course we were steering, having no better one to take, I would not allow the lead to be cast, lest too unsatisfactory a decrease in depth should dishearten the crew.
Once clear of this second danger we began to bear away, and at noon we could without fear put her head to the north.
At the same time, the observed latitude was 20° 31' 52" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put
us in 112° 57' 28". The land we then had in sight, at a great distance, extended from north 67° 30' east to south 5° east.
In the afternoon we tried to close with the coast, having no bottom at 25 fathoms, but the masthead lookouts soon warned us that we were running upon yet another danger, for they saw, ahead of us and even to leeward of our course, a long line of reefs on which the sea broke heavily. Before thinking of altering course I sent the chief quartermaster up to the crosstrees to ascertain what it might be. His report having confirmed the lookouts' warning, we had perforce to alter course, and to double this reef at a league and a half at most, we were obliged to keep her head north-west for a good while.
