At two o'clock it was plainly seen from the deck, and at three o'clock its northernmost part bore east 15° north.
We did for this last danger what we had done for the others, that is to say, we gradually hauled our course from north towards east as we brought the reef round from east towards south. At four o'clock it could scarcely be seen.
If one is to trust what the lookouts say and the opinion of those who went to examine these breakers, they think it is a sandbank which must be covered at high water and which has a very great extent from north to south, and someone asserted that he had made out the tops of rocks above water in the middle of the bank. But although I examined this reef as I did the others, I saw nothing of the kind. I saw only that it does not break uniformly along its whole length, and that there are places where the water appears deeper, as I saw there neither swell nor breakers. Moreover, even should the reef offer some passage between itself and the coast, from which it lies more than three leagues off, it would be better to try to coast along the shore leaving the reef to port than to seek to close with the coast through the gaps that might perhaps be found in it.
From half past four until eight o'clock we tried to close with the land; the depth being then 28 fathoms, we first steered north-north-east and went from 28 to 35 fathoms, sand and fine gravel. We then put her head north-east and the depth increased by another five fathoms. As night was coming on, we steered only north-east by east until eight in the evening, and then we trimmed close-hauled on the port tack to spend the night beating to windward.
During the day there had been a pleasant breeze from south to south-south-west, and it was much less strong than it had been for three days. The sea, however, had a fair swell, which led us to believe that the strong breezes we had met with had prevailed for a long time, but that they were perhaps about to cease.
All day we saw a considerable number of seabirds of every kind, especially over the banks we passed. A few dolphins were also seen, and a single sea snake with a broad, flat tail. It was the first we had seen on this second visit to the north-west coast of New Holland.
During the night the weather was fine and the breeze very moderate. We stood on the tack to the westward and northward until six o'clock at night, and then took the south-easterly one, with winds from south-south-south-west (sic). As the order was to sound every two hours, on the offshore tack, which was fixed at four leagues, we went from 42 fathoms to sixty-five, and on the inshore tack from 65 to 45. The depth increased and decreased in the same progression on the one course as on the other.

1803-03-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky overcast, the sea smooth, the winds SSE, a fresh breeze. Obs. lat. 0° 3' 55" north, long. W 17° 32' 42".
1803-03-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
At a quarter to three,
the northern end of the reef was abeam of us, visible from the deck.
At four o'clock it bore south 65° east.
At noon,
the most prominent land, north-south, could be seen from south 70° east to south 66° west.
In the morning the reef of the day before had been seen from the mastheads to the south-west.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventh, 28 March 1803, at daybreak, we sighted the land, which bore south-south-east at a great distance. It has the appearance of an island some four to five leagues or more in extent. It has its two ends than in the middle ( ?), which made the lookouts believe they were seeing lines of dunes. I rather thought it must be some land of the continent higher than the coast generally is, and that we should see the coast only by advancing to the south-east. We then had forty-two fathoms. We also saw, in the quarter from south towards west, the reef we had coasted the day before. At seven o'clock the land sighted at daybreak was visible from the deck, and in appearance as in shape it looked exactly like an island standing apart from all other land.
Throughout the morning we held on the south-easterly tack, believing that at any moment we should see the land, and yet not discovering it ahead of us, having in sight only what lay abeam. Until ten o'clock the depth was regular, between 42 and 40 fathoms, but at noon it was no more than 32. So great a depth of water at four leagues at most from the land in sight would seem to confirm that it was an island, for on the mainland coast one does not usually find such depths.
At noon the observed latitude was 20° 16' 55" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 113° 16' 16". We continued to steer south-east until two o'clock, when, the wind having drawn more to the westward, we made her head as far south as possible. In spite of this, at sunset we had no land in sight.
From noon to four o'clock the lead went from 32 fathoms to 24, and from seven to eight o'clock from 24 to 16. A decrease so sudden and so out of proportion to the distance we had run in that time decided me to stand out to sea at once, and we took the tack to the westward and northward until ten o'clock, when we steered north-north-east. The depth then increased rapidly, and (we) went successively from 16 fathoms to 36. And without our altering course, it decreased in the same way.
Throughout the day we had very fine weather and a pleasant (breeze) which veered as far as west-south-west. During the night the weather was no less fine, but the breeze was fresher; since we had been east of the north-west point, we had always had much stronger winds at night than by day. Yet when we visited this coast for the first time we had found quite the opposite; perhaps the cause might be ascribed to the season, which was not the same.
1803-03-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 11.30 a.m. we crossed the Line in 17° 32' of longitude.

1803-03-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A fresh breeze from south to SSE. Est. lat. 1° 23' 31" north, est. long. 17° 55' 24".
1803-03-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
At daybreak,
the land was seen from south by east to south-east
and at seven o'clock,
we began charting the coast, which was nothing but a chain of islands and islets, larger or smaller, fronted by several rocks,
the land seen in the distance was presumed to be that of the mainland.
Historical events and Remarks.
On the eighth, 29 March 1803, the weather continued fine. At sunrise we saw the land from the mastheads, extending from south by east to south-east. We steered close-hauled to close with it. And at seven o'clock it could be seen distinctly from the deck. It presented itself to us in an extremely strange shape, so full of gaps that we could not tell whether this land was a barrier of islands lying off the mainland or the mainland itself (presenting) a a (sic) form so peculiar. However, when we were no more than two leagues off, we could no longer doubt that the land we were ranging along was a great number of islands interlocked one among another and forming between them all the gaps we had noticed. These islands formed three planes, one behind another, and behind them all could be seen a coast very even in outline, which we judged to be the mainland. The depth of water two leagues from the coast was considerable, and until noon we had from 30 to 28 fathoms.
At the same time, the observed latitude was 20° 25' 2" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 114° 7' 46".
During the evening we continued to range along the land at the same distance as in the morning, and we passed abeam of a fairly large expanse of islands and islets. The largest of them all did not appear to us to be more than three leagues from east to west. Off these islands and islets lay several detached rocks and banks, which often obliged us to alter course to avoid them. The banks, which ran a fair way out to sea, were easily made out by the colour of the water, which was quite white. Some of the channels we saw between these islets are perhaps navigable, and in that case good shelter must be found in them, provided the bottom is fit for anchoring.
It is hard to conceive why the geographers of every nation who have given us the plan of this part of the coast make no mention whatever of them, and have represented the mainland there without offering any difficulty in making it out. What we have done seen proves only too well that they worked from false recollections, or that, being unable to give the details, they found it easier to suppress all the islands and make a mainland of them. But the fact is that off the coast there must be a great number of islands, lying in every direction. We took on board as many bearings as possible of this whole part of the coast, but as these islands merged so much one with another, I still believe (them) imperfect, although every possible care was taken over them. If what Dampier tells us in speaking of his Rosemary Islands (is true), I shall not hesitate to believe that the place where we are is the one where he anchored within one of the channels formed by these islands, which are generally high and such as he describes them. In the position he was in, he must indeed have seen nothing but islands, and we ourselves, without having passed through them to the south, saw nothing but islands all day.
(written vertically in the margin) However, the latitude of 20° 26' cannot suit them, since they are evidently farther south. After sunset, not wishing to draw away from the coast, I anchored in 18 fathoms, bottom of sand and coarse gravel. We veered 70 fathoms of cable and the ship rode firm to her anchor, although the breeze was very fresh. The current ran at one knot, but the fall of the water, neither on the ebb nor on the flood, was perceptible to us.

1803-03-30.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, calm; lay under topsails. At 5 trimmed on the starboard tack. Calm all night; at 7 a.m. a light breeze got up from the west. We at once went onto the port tack and made all sail. Est. lat. 1° 49' 25", obs. long. 19° 47' W.
1803-03-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
At four o'clock,
the western point of the largest island bore south 85° west,
And at six o'clock,
an archipelago of islands and islets was observed from north 78° west to south 22° east
At eight o'clock in the morning,
the continuation of the same land could be seen from north 77° west to south 7° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the ninth, 30 March 1803, as soon as day began to break we made ready to get under sail, and at sunrise we weighed. We first steered east, making some southing, but we soon shoaled rapidly. From 18 fathoms we went in half an hour to 15; a quarter of an hour later we had no more than 12, then eight, and finally six and a half, which obliged us to stand a little out to sea.
During the morning the breeze was very light and the winds variable about south-south-west; the depth varied between eight and eleven fathoms, and we passed several of the islands abreast of which we had spent the night at anchor. As we advanced to the east we discovered others, but lying farther apart from one another. To the south of these islands, the land, which could be seen only from the mastheads, seemed to form a great bay or bight to the south-south (sic), but its entrance was barred by shoals, over which we advanced only as far as 6 and a half fathoms. It was judged that the land seen to the south-south-east must be part of the mainland, since no break was seen in it marked enough to make one believe that this land too was islands. At eleven o'clock we were becalmed. But an hour later we had a light breeze from the north, with which we were able to make a little way to the east.
At noon we observed the latitude 20° 28' 40" and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 114° 58' 45". It follows therefore that the island abeam of us was the one to which, on the previous voyage, we had given the name of Île des Amiraux. This island is, moreover, very remarkable for its shape and height, and seems to bring to an end on the east the great number of islands we had been coasting for two days.
A little to the east of Île des Amiraux there are still some high lands and fairly lofty peaks, which seem to form another row of islands farther south than Île des Amiraux. But we know that these peaks belong to the mainland and join lower lands that keep diminishing in height, so that the coast, which I suppose to be that of the continent, becomes so low that it can scarcely be seen at three leagues.
After sunset we came to anchor; but as we then had only 7 to eight fathoms, about two leagues from land, I would not do so until I had a depth of ten fathoms. To reach it quickly I had her steered north-east, but contrary to my expectation we went through 8 and 7. We then put her head north-east. We sailed for more than half an hour in 6 fathoms. At seven o'clock the two ends of the points forming the northern extremities of the bank we were passing over were clearly made out. The depth in that part was five and a half fathoms for a moment, but then we found 7, 8, 9, 10 and anchored. During the night we had the wind westerly, a pleasant breeze, and the sky was fine.

1803-03-31.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to W. At 3 trimmed close-hauled on the port tack. Obs. lat. 2° 38' 27", est. long. 19° 56'.
1803-03-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
At six o'clock,
Île des Amiraux, seen in Thermidor of the year nine, bore from south 47° west to south 41° west.
The eastern end of the most prominent land, north 58° east.
At the moment of weighing,
a sandbank lying dry was seen bearing south 6° east.
A smoke observed ashore at eight o'clock bearing south 45° east
bore at noon south 20° east.
Historical events & Remarks.
On the tenth, 31 March 1803, in the morning, we got under sail at sunrise. At the same hour, those I had sent aloft as lookouts reported that the land could be seen from south-east by east to south, but they added that about three miles to the south of us they could see an uncovered sandbank. It was doubtless the one over which we had passed, and whose two points, forming its northern end, had seemed to us to have very little water on them, the sea there being quite white.
The winds, which at the moment of weighing were south-south-west, went round after sunrise to south-east, and in the course of the morning varied to east-south-east. The breeze was fairly strong until about eleven o'clock, after which it died away by degrees, drawing more towards the north. The depth increased as we advanced on our course to the eastward and northward, and at noon it was already 20 fathoms.
At the same time, the observed latitude was 20° 4' 22" and the longitude by No. 35 was 115° 40' 35". All through the morning several smokes were seen rising at points of the horizon lying between east and south-east. But we did not on that account see the land, which, as I have already observed several times, is visible in this part only in eight and ten fathoms.
Towards two in the afternoon, the winds, which seemed inclined to box the compass by way of the north, made us go about onto the south-easterly course, and we followed the direction they took, drawing closer to the east. At four o'clock we sighted the land, but as night was drawing on and there was no likelihood of our being near enough to it before sunset to examine it properly, we bore up to close with the Casuarina, and at seven o'clock, being in no more than eight fathoms, we anchored on a very good bottom of sand and mud.
As there had been several disputes during the day between the officers, who on going off watch did not pass on to one another the orders I had given them, I resolved, to prevent this happening again in future, to prescribe to them in writing what each of them was to do when the ship was at anchor during the night and under sail during the day. What I enjoined upon them in this matter is copied into the rough log.
During the night the breeze was light and more often calm. The winds kept between west-north-west and west-south-west until about seven four o'clock in the morning, when they went round to south and south-east. At seven o'clock they were south-east, a good breeze.
The observations made to determine the rise or fall of the water gave one fathom of difference on the flood. The current was scarcely perceptible. During the night a few sharks were caught, and some small perch whose colouring was very pretty to see.
1803-03-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: At daybreak a ship was sighted in the N 45° E. At 6.30 p.m. another was sighted to the east.

1803-04-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm until 11 p.m. Saw several ships. At 6 a light breeze from SSW; at 2 it drew round to NW. Est. lat. 2° 49' 9", est. long. 19° 55'.
1803-04-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eleventh, 1 April 1803, the winds, having gone round to the south-east shortly after we got under sail, did not allow us to examine very well the land we had in sight, the more so as it was very low and even, offering no points more remarkable than others. From the mastheads this land could be seen extending from east to south-west. At six o'clock we lost sight of it entirely and saw only various smokes rising in different directions. As we lost sight of the land the depth increased rapidly, and at noon we had eighteen fathoms, bottom of small red gravel.
I much regretted that the winds had carried us so far from the land during the morning, for I feared I should not see it again before sunset, the breeze from west to north-west being usually light and slow to set in during the evening.
At noon we observed the latitude 19° 51' and the longitude by No. 35 was 115° 58' 13".
In the afternoon the breeze from west to south-west or north-west did not come as we had had it on the preceding days, so that we entirely lost hope of seeing the land before sunset, or even at that time. The winds having nevertheless varied from east to north-east and north-north-east, we steered south, making some easting, but the breeze was so light that we made very little way. As there was every appearance of a dead calm for the night, we anchored at nine in the evening in 15 fathoms, sand and broken shells. The winds at that same time had gone round to the west, and they were fairly fresh for the rest of the night.
The velocity of the current during the night appeared to be eight tenths of a mile, setting to the west. Neither the fall nor the rise of the water was perceptible.
As the heat was extremely great during the day, I had given orders that a kind of drink should be made up for the men of the crew, and a ration of it served out to each of them at ten o'clock in the morning and at two in the afternoon. This drink was made of lemon juice and syrup mixed in water. It caused me a greater consumption of water than usual, but I felt for myself how much they needed it.
The boat that had been sounding round the ship having passed near the Casuarina, two men who were sick were sent aboard to me, one suffering from the onset of dysentery and the other injured by a fall.
1803-04-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Saw tide rips running E and W. At 5 p.m. saw a sail in the S 68° W.

1803-04-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to west. At 10, the breeze having freshened from the NE, went onto the starboard tack. Est. lat. 3° 20' 21", long. 20° 18' 48".
1803-04-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twelfth, 2 April 1803, at sunrise, we got under sail, and I was rather surprised not to sight the land, from which I believed myself to be at no great distance. We steered south 68° east until eight o'clock, and then it was reported to us, bearing east 11° south and visible at that time only from the mastheads.
At nine o'clock this same land that had been reported to us, together with a long chain of reefs lying to the west and north of it, was visible from the deck, and we soon perceived that this land was known to us, having seen it the first time we approached this coast. I did not then think it was an island, and had persuaded myself that it was only a projecting point of the mainland, whose lands could be seen to the south-east. But the Casuarina having passed through the channel that lies between it and the mainland, this error has been corrected. This island is no more than two leagues in extent from south-east to north-west, and has nothing remarkable about it but a great uniformity along its length, ending in a low point at each extremity. Its breadth is small, and in ranging close along the island on its eastern side one finds fairly regularly nine and eight fathoms of water. It may lie four to five leagues from the mainland, which is of little height in this part.
In doubling this island we passed a good league from the reef that lies to the north of it, which is very extensive. It appears to be formed by a sandbank on which one sees, at intervals, fairly high rocks of various shapes. The sea does not break equally throughout the whole extent of this bank, but in certain places it rises so high that it can easily be seen at about two leagues. The depth was no more than (no figure) fathoms as we ran along it, and we had sight of part of the mainland, presenting the same aspect as the land we had passed before.
At noon the observed latitude was 19° 49' 13" and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 116° 23' 48".
In the afternoon the winds were very light, and we had them variable from west-south-west to north-north-west until sunset. In trying to close with the land after passing the long reef I have just spoken of, we sighted a second danger on which the sea broke, but it was of small extent and we doubled it easily. It is likely that the whole of this part of the coast is difficult of approach and that the bottom there is extremely uneven. In the watch from noon to four o'clock we sailed in between ten and fifteen fathoms, but at that time we suddenly dropped to five ½, which did not last long. After that the lead gave 9 and 10 fathoms, but not for long, and we went again to 8, 7, 6, 5. I counted on getting off the bank we were on by steering north, but it was quite the contrary, for after increasing a little the depth decreased again and we went from eight to 4 and to 3 almost at the same moment. I then had all sails laid aback and we went about making sternway,
which quickly brought us back into four and five fathoms. We held on for some time on the south-south-west tack, always with the lead going and a sharp lookout kept, and in less than half an hour we had eleven fathoms. I counted on being able to anchor in that depth, but the bottom was only rock and coarse coral. We had to give it up and look for a better spot. We therefore continued on the south-south-west tack, since the water had kept increasing, although on this course, which could not be held long, we were running towards the land. After running about half a mile from the last cast, which had been eleven fathoms, the depth went from eleven to eight and from eight to seven, still rock and coral. We then went about to work up to the north, without finding any increase; on the contrary, the water kept decreasing. The winds being from west to north-west, it was not possible for us to get out of the dangers among which we found ourselves by the way that had led us into them. So I tried to extricate myself by steering progressively more to the east whenever the depth decreased as we went north. On the various courses we steered, we increased to nine fathoms and dropped again to three. We then bore away from east to south-east and to south and again to south-south-south-west, which put us back into 9 and 10 fathoms for some time. On the south-south-west course we sighted the land, from which we had to draw off by coming round, and, to try every means of getting out of our difficult position, we steered north-east by east as long as we had 9 and 10 fathoms. At last the lead, which until then had always brought up rock and coral, brought up fine sand, fit for (anchoring). But in the space of one or two minutes we went from nine to six, which decided me to anchor with all sail set, the breeze having but little strength. It was then about ten o'clock.
The position in which we found ourselves was such that no proper account could be kept of the various courses we steered on this bank, nor of the duration of each, and the track we have deduced from them is rather the fruit of reflection after the danger was past than of observation at moments when we expected to see the ship aground.
However that may be, between seven and ten o'clock we were twice carried into three fathoms of water, and had we not anchored as hastily as we did, we should have fallen into it a third time, as will be seen from the soundings taken by the boats about a cable and a half from the ship.
As the Casuarina was near us on this occasion, I ordered her to steer east-north-east for about a league and a half, sounding continually, to make sure whether we still had a way out on that point of the compass, and to signal it to us by a light in the most conspicuous place on her vessel. When she had gone, I
had a boat lowered and gave command of it to the chief quartermaster, with orders to sound at two cables' length from the ship and to go round her at that distance, bidding him above all to see, at musket-shot from the ship, what a certain spot might be which, by the light of the moon, seemed to me to have much less water than we had at the anchorage, judging by the height to which the sea appeared to rise there.
On his return I was informed that this place indeed had only three fathoms of water, but that it was of very small extent and that one passed suddenly from three to four and to five. To the east of the ship he found no more than five to six fathoms, to the north four to five, to the west 6 to 7, and to the south 4 for a fair distance. The north-east quarter seemed to him the clearest of all, as far as he had gone, the depth there being more regular, between five and six fathoms. The bottom was everywhere of fine sand.
At one o'clock, the Casuarina having returned, she informed me that she had not found the end of this bank on the east-north-east course I had prescribed, but that she had never found less than five fathoms. She observed to me that she had several times passed from five to eleven fathoms and from twelve fathoms to five, and that one must expect to find these same irregularities in trying to get out by that way. Unsatisfactory as this report was, I was at least glad to know that there was water enough for the ship and that the bottom was not bad.
On the strength of the information I had just received, I decided to spend the night at anchor, at the risk of seeing the ship take the ground if the tide were very strong; I knew at least that no harm would come to her and that the rising tide would float her off, whereas by changing position I might take up a much worse one.
During the night the weather was fine. We had the wind north-west, varying to west-north-west, and the breeze did not oblige us to veer cable, although we had only 25 fathoms out. At midnight the winds went round to the south and the weather remained very fine. We sounded regularly every hour without perceiving any decrease in the depth of the water. The current too was very weak, as we found it running at only 4 tenths of a knot. In this way we were much more fortunate than I had dared to hope.

1803-04-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from N and NNE. At 7 a.m. a light breeze from NNW. Obs. lat. 3° 29' 2", est. long. 20° 22' 30".
1803-04-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirteenth, 3 April 1803, in the morning, we waited for sunrise before getting under sail, so as to judge by the colour of the water which was the best course for us to take to get clear of the banks among which we were entangled. For, from what had happened to us the day before, we supposed there were two of them, one to the north of the ship and the other to the east.
At first light we sighted the land, which lay from south-south-west to south by east, at an estimated distance of three leagues. But at sunrise we made out a portion of the bank over which we had sailed the previous night, which was dry and which at its farthest was not reckoned to be two miles from the ship. No rock was seen on this uncovered portion, only a reddish sand almost at the level of the sea.
We then weighed, and as soon as we were under sail we steered north 67° west. But at that time, when we had run about a mile and a quarter, M. Freycinet, who had been aloft as lookout, reported to me that he had clearly made out the direction of the bank and that it made a great sweep, running from south towards east-north-east as far as the eye could reach. This warning made us haul a little more to the north, and on this new course we ran about two miles, finding from 7 to 11 fathoms of water. We then steered north-east to follow its direction, which we thought we could make out from the deck, but we went rapidly from eleven to 7 and from 7 to 5. As another portion of this bank lay to leeward of us to the north, we bore away only a point and a half and ran and ran (sic) about two miles more on that course. After that, the water having gradually increased to 10 fathoms, we believed ourselves entirely clear of it, so that we brought our course more to the east as we went ahead.
From eight o'clock to noon we steered east to close with the land, from which the morning's course had taken us far enough to lose sight of it; the depth held between 12 and 14 fathoms.
At noon the observed latitude was 19° 41' 28" and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us in 117° 3' 26", which gave us a difference of 12' more to the east than our dead reckoning. The land could still be seen from the mastheads. At that time, it is true, the wind was so light during those four hours that we made more way with the help of the current than with our sails. All through the morning we saw passing alongside a great quantity of sea plants of every sort, many black and white snakes, and others striped with white and yellow. Some had a flat tail three to four fingers broad, and the others a quite round one. Those of the latter kind were much smaller than the others and no more than two feet long, whereas the others were at least three and a half, and were as
thick as one's arm.
From noon until three o'clock we were almost in a flat calm, the ship scarcely answering her helm. In that interval the depth varied from 14 to 12 fathoms. We then had a light air from west-north-west and steered east. The depth having decreased from 12 to 10, although we were well out to sea and almost out of sight of land, since it could scarcely be seen from the mastheads, this made me somewhat uneasy, and I gave orders to steer more to the north. On this course we went from eight fathoms to seven, so that there was every appearance that we were running onto some new dangers, of which, however, no perceptible sign was apparent on the surface of the water, which was as smooth as a basin. We had scarcely run a mile and a half on the course north 68° east when we saw the sea quite white ahead of us. We at once trimmed close-hauled to come to windward of the line indicated by the colour of the water, and in the short time the ship took to luff up, the depth increased decreased to four fathoms and could be seen perfectly alongside; it was sand and weed, with no sign of rock. As we had only a short distance to run to reach this line, we held on our course, but from four fathoms we went to three. The lookouts having claimed that there was more water to starboard than to port, we bore away a little, but only for a moment, for, finding only 14 feet of water, we at once luffed up again and went to four fathoms, five minutes later to six, and all at once to ten, having crossed the line along which the bank was perfectly outlined, and which chance led us to cross at its narrowest part. Its direction appeared to us to be from north 80° east to west-south-west.
By unexpected good fortune we did not scrape on this bank in 14 feet, but had there been the slightest swell, there is no doubt that we should have struck, and perhaps in such a way as to cause damage to our masts.
Everything that had happened to us since we came to this part of the coast, and all that we have seen of it for ourselves, leads me to say that the geographers who have undertaken to trace the direction of the coasts, and even their details, would have done much better to suppress their work than to lead navigators into error or expose them to certain loss, if they place in those plans a confidence that the plans are very far from deserving. All they have done is faulty and purely speculative. The latitudes as well as the longitudes are faulty in them, and I believe it was for their own convenience that they altered them, for they cannot possibly be the results of any observations by navigators who have frequented these waters. For such navigators would not have failed to meet with one or other of the many dangers that lie there.
Having passed the new bank I have just spoken of, we soon went from three fathoms to fifteen and from fifteen to twenty. In this depth of water we brought our course more to the east and continued to carry sail until eight in the evening, when, being in 25 fathoms and on good ground, I anchored, my intention being to try to see the land next morning, from which I could not be very far.
As soon as the Casuarina had anchored beside us, I sent a boat aboard her to ask Citizen Freycinet to come and speak with me. When he had arrived, I asked him whether he had seen the bank over which we had passed. His answer was that he had, and that he too had crossed it, but that he had never found less than six fathoms of water, and that it was for this reason that he had not signalled it to us.
From what Citizen Freycinet, who was about a league to windward of us, told us, it appears that we happened to cross this bank at its shoalest part, and we were very fortunate to find enough water there to get across.
During the night the weather was as fine as we could have wished, and the winds variable from south to south-south-west. The current, however, appeared to be fairly strong, since we could not hold with 60 fathoms of cable out and had to veer 70 to bring the ship up. Perhaps too this came from the nature of the bottom, which, being hard, did not allow our anchor to bed itself in the sand.
By the observations made during the night, the velocity of the current was 4 tenths of a mile and its direction west-south-west, but no fall or rise of the water was noticed, the depth being too great.

1803-04-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and calm, squally, with lightning and thunder; calm from ten in the morning until noon. Obs. lat. 3° 38' 24", est. long. 20° 18' 48".
1803-04-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourteenth, 4 April 1803, we got under sail with the intention of examining some portion of the coast in this part, so as to fix its direction approximately, not having been able to sight it on our first voyage in Thermidor of Year 9. The winds, which were then south-south-west variable to south, gave us hope of arriving there quickly if they held on that point of the compass. But we were disappointed in our expectation, for shortly after sunrise they went round to south-south-east and drew more and more towards the east as the sun rose above the horizon. Nevertheless, the breeze was very light and the distance we made on our course to the eastward and northward was small. This did not prevent the depth from increasing rapidly and putting us in 28 fathoms at noon.
The latitude observed that day fixed the ship's position at 19° 21' 9" and the longitude by No. 35 was 117° 30' 20". As our horizon extended at least six leagues and no land could be seen, it may reasonably be advanced that the coast here forms a fairly deep bight to the south, and that its direction cannot be from east towards north as the charts show it. For the rest, this is only a conjecture, of which the reader may make what he will.
In the afternoon the winds went round, as usual, to north-west, west and south-west, but they were so light until sunset that we could make little use of them. We steered east-south-east to close with the land, and the depth, having by then decreased by six fathoms since noon, told us that we were beginning to approach it. From six o'clock until half past eight we held the east-south-east course with a pleasant breeze from the south-west that gave us four knots and that we much regretted not having had during the day. The depth still holding above 20 fathoms, I held the same course, but at half past eight, having suddenly gone from 21 to 17, I anchored on a bottom of fine sand and small broken shells, very good for anchoring. The Casuarina did the same, and we again spent this night very quietly at anchor, the sky being constantly fine and the breeze moderate.
From the night's observations we were surprised to find the current running as fast as it did, for at the time we anchored its velocity was 2 miles 2 tenths. Thus we could not bring the ship up with 60 fathoms of cable and were obliged to veer 70. Its direction appeared to us to be due east. From ten o'clock until five in the morning it kept decreasing, and by that last hour it was running no more than one mile. The depth in that interval had decreased by 3 fathoms, for having anchored in 17 fathoms we had only 14 at the moment we got under sail, the ship having swung to the same point of the compass as when we anchored.

1803-04-05.journal_anonyme: A flat calm, the weather dark and misty. Wore onto the starboard tack. The winds, which had drawn round to the west during the manoeuvre, came back to the ENE. Obs. lat. 3° 55' 15", est. long. 20° 40' 19".
1803-04-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fifteenth, 5 April 1803, in the morning, being under sail at sunrise, we steered east to close with the land, of which we had had a good sight at daybreak, though only from the mastheads. According to the report of the lookouts, we had one sandbank uncovered on our beam at no great distance, and a second further to the east on which there appeared to be very little water. As I did not see these banks with my own eyes, I can say nothing of them; but I am the more inclined to believe in their existence that I strongly urge the navigators who come after us to search for them with caution. Another reason which may equally lead one to believe in the existence of these banks is that the depth decreased rapidly when we steered east, and at seven o'clock, having no more than nine fathoms without seeing the land from the deck, we hauled further to the north to find more water.
During the morning the weather was very fine and the breeze fairly fresh from the south by east to south-east quarter; but as the sun drew near the meridian it died away by degrees, and at noon the ship would scarcely answer her helm.
The observed latitude was 19° 27' 0", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 118° 3' 38"; the depth was then 18 fathoms.
From noon until three o'clock we were almost in a flat calm, but then a light breeze came up from the north, varying to north-north-west, which allowed us to make a little way.
We steered east, edging a little to the north, to run along a bank which lay from east-north-east to west-north-west of us. We judged it to be one by the colour of the water, which was a very pale green, and by the various irregularities of the soundings, which varied from 18 fathoms to ten, from ten to fifteen, and which at length seemed steady for two hours together, between ten and eleven.
At sunset the men I had sent aloft as lookouts reported to us that we could not doubt the existence of this bank, that they had clearly made it out, and that we would not weather it by steering east-north-east. This advice led me to haul a little more to the north, and I held this course until seven o'clock. Seeing that the depth was still decreasing and that the bottom was very uneven, between twelve and eight fathoms, I had the anchor let go, the more so as the breeze was light and a strong current was visibly setting us to the north-east. The bottom in which we anchored was white sand, in twelve fathoms.
The speed of the current, measured at the moment we anchored, was two and three-tenths miles, and it was then setting to the east. During the night it kept on slackening and took its direction to the W. NW. The shoaling of the water was not very marked, the depth decreasing by only two fathoms, a change in which the swinging of the ship may have had as much share as the current itself on so irregular a bottom.

1803-04-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from SSE to SSW and WNW. In the 24 hours changed tacks twice. Est. lat. 4° 11' 51", est. long. 20° 50' 36".
1803-04-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the sixteenth, 6 April 1803, after getting under sail, we steered north-east to run along the land, which we had in plain sight and which bore from south to south-south-east, three leagues off. As the course we were making was bound to make us lose sight of the land before long, we could keep it in view only until about ten in the morning, when it could no longer be seen, even from the mastheads. The number of tide-rips among which we had been since the moment we got under sail announced to us obliged us to make various courses to avoid them. And, all the soundings decreasing to ten fathoms, I was taking the course, for fear of being carried for the third time onto some shoals from which we might not perhaps have got clear as easily as on the first two occasions when we happened to be caught on them.
During the morning the breeze was very light. The depth, which was only ten fathoms at eight o'clock, was 14 at eleven.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 19° 4' 45", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 118° 29' 16".
From noon until two o'clock we were in a flat calm, as had happened to us every day for some time past, and then the winds shifted to north-north-west. By means of this light breeze, which freshened a little towards evening, we steered east-north-east to close with the land, on which several columns of smoke were beginning to be made out. Nevertheless, at sunset we could not see the land even from the mastheads. As it could not be very far off, we held on our course until half past seven, when, having 13 fathoms of water, a bottom of white sand and good holding ground, we anchored. The wind was then almost calm, and the current seemed to us to set south-south-east at the rate of a mile and a half.
Throughout the day a great number of snakes of the two kinds I have already mentioned had been seen passing alongside, two or three turtles and a great number of porpoises.
During the night what little breeze there was came from the north-west quarter, but in the east the sky looked stormy and a great deal of lightning came from that direction. The sound of thunder, however, was not heard. Nor was any decrease or increase noticed in the depth of water, which remained just as it had been at the moment we anchored. The strength of the current gradually decreased to seven-tenths of a mile, and at eleven o'clock the tide seemed to be slack. At two o'clock its speed was one and three-tenths miles and its apparent direction NW.

1803-04-07.journal_anonyme: Almost continual rain and a flat calm. At 1.30 a.m. a fresh breeze from ESE; at 11 went onto the port tack. Est. lat. 4° 30' 3", long. 21° 8' 6".
1803-04-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the seventeenth, 7 April 1803, at sunrise, we saw the land, which lay from south by west to east-north-east of us. After getting under sail, we steered north-east by east to run along the coast, which appeared to us higher in this part than in any of the other places we had just passed. On this course we passed through several violent tide-rips which set us to the east towards the south, but we did not alter our course on that account, although they brought us very close in to the coast, the bottom appearing clean between thirteen and eleven fathoms.
Throughout the morning the breeze was very light from the south-south-east quarter, and we made little progress until one o'clock, when we were entirely becalmed; which seemed to announce that the breeze from the west or north-west would come to us earlier that day than it usually did.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 18° 51' 31", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us, by No. 35, in 119 4' 36". The land, taken in bearings at the same moment, extended from SE ¼ E to east ¼ north-east. The nearest part of the coast was no more than four or five miles off at most, and the Casuarina was between us and the land.
The winds having then gone round to the west, we held on our north-east course. The lookouts reported land on that point of the compass. Although we were at no great distance from the coast, the soundings were between 13 and 14 fathoms, coarse sand.
From noon until four o'clock we ran along the coast at a short distance, the depth allowing us to follow its outline, which forms several coves, though of no great depth. I was surprised to see that the land ran in quite a different direction from the one I had supposed. In truth, according to the trend given it by our charts, on which I knew from experience that no reliance could be placed, for we were obliged constantly to bear away towards the north to weather the points as each one opened ahead of us.
At four o'clock a shoal was sighted, running out from a point which then bore north-east of us. To weather it at a good distance we put the ship's head to the north, but as the depth kept decreasing we were obliged to keep close-hauled. This shoal appeared to run from south by east to north by west. It seems that on the course we made we passed over its northern end, on which we found (sic) no more than eight and nine fathoms of water. At five o'clock this reef the shoal was visible from the deck, and the sea was breaking heavily on it. The Casuarina, which was closer inshore than we were, signalled to us that there was no water, and went about to stand out to sea so as to be able to weather it. After we had passed this bank the depth increased rapidly from nine to 18 fathoms, and we gradually resumed our north-east course so as to reach an anchorage for the night; at half past seven we anchored in 15 fathoms, two leagues from the coast, on a bottom of sand mixed with broken shells. Although the sky was fine in the west, it was not so in the east, and we often heard the thunder rumbling.
(vertically in the margin) Strong gusts sometimes came from the south-west without our being able to bring the ship head to wind; the speed of the current nevertheless seemed to us less than on the preceding days, and (we) found it to be only (no figures) miles when we anchored.

1803-04-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, continual rain, the wind variable in force and direction from SW, SSE, WNW and SSW. At 3.30 went onto the starboard tack; at 10.30 onto the port tack. Obs. lat. 4° 55' 52", est. long. 21° 7' 23".
1803-04-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the eighteenth, 8 April 1803, in the morning, we resumed our north-east course to run along the coast, from which we were not very far off. This course was held until noon, the bottom being fairly regular between 13 & 14 fathoms.
Throughout the morning we saw a considerable number of birds, several schools of porpoises and a few sharks. One of the latter was caught, and our savants in that branch say that it is a new species, not yet described.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 18° 19' 33", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 117° 35' 20". Since eleven o'clock the winds had gone round to the south-west and the breeze was beginning to gather strength. But in the eastern quarter the sky became very stormy and the thunder was often heard rumbling. The course we were obliged to make in the evening lay much more to the north than that of the morning, since we had the land directly to the north.
All the coast we ran along is moderately high, even, and of a rather pleasant appearance. At about four o'clock we found ourselves abreast of a fairly deep inlet, the two extremities of the land bearing north-east and south-east. I think there may be a bay in this part whose low lands are visible only from very close in, which is why I do not share the opinion of those who think that there are two islands there with the mainland behind them. Besides, as the depth of water was beginning to decrease rapidly, I did not judge it advisable to go and examine it, especially at the close of day.
A little before sunset, the storm which had gathered in the east brought us winds from that quarter, but we had no more than a passing puff of them, and at seven o'clock we were almost becalmed. We then anchored in 10 fathoms, a bottom of grey sand mixed with shells, and spent the rest of the night there.
From the observations made during the night to ascertain the speed of the current, it was found at its greatest strength to be 1 mile 3 tenths; its direction was at first north-north-east, and at four o'clock it was found to be north-west.
The differences found in the soundings should be attributed to the irregularities of the bottom rather than to the fall or rise of the water; at least that is my opinion, founded on the fact that our anchor was let go in ten fathoms and, when the scope of 50 fathoms of cable was paid out, there were twelve abreast of the ship. From midnight to four o'clock the breeze was fresh, but the ship held fast.

1803-04-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from N to NNE. The stay of the middle staysail having parted, it was refitted. Est. lat. 5° 15' 40", est. long. 22° 18' 44".
1803-04-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the nineteenth, 9 April 1803, we steered north towards the east to follow the trend of the coast. We had hopes of a fine day's run, as it blew a pleasant breeze at sunrise, but it did not hold through the morning, for at eleven o'clock we were almost becalmed, while waiting for the winds from the west or north-west which had hitherto been wont to follow the south-east or east winds.
During the morning it seemed to us that the current was setting us rapidly to the east, for we drew very close in to the land, which obliged us to steer north towards the west. The soundings varied constantly between eleven and fifteen fathoms, on a sandy bottom very good for anchoring.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 17° 39' 27", and the longitude by No. 25 (sic) put us in 119° 35' 20".
At one o'clock, the breeze from west to west-north-west having gathered a little strength, we made a little way, but the current served us better than the wind, as we could easily judge from the way (in which) we passed the various points on shore that had been taken in bearings.
The whole stretch of coast along which we ran at a very short distance that day, without being very high, is of a good height and pleasing to the eye. It appeared, from the freshness of the trees, whose foliage was a fine green and very thick, that we had come at the moment of their greatest beauty, which the dry season, now about to begin, will no doubt gradually dim. The places by the sea that appeared covered with grass were not pleasing and seemed to promise a good soil. The edge of the shore, formed now by dunes of very white sand and now by earth of a dark red colour, was not without charm either. In front of the dunes, as in front of the other parts of the coast which were not of the same kind, a long sandy beach could be seen, scattered here and there with a few rocks of a very dark colour. We had already seen this part of the coast on our first voyage, but at a greater distance than we then were.
At six o'clock, finding myself too near the land, I went about to stand off a little from the coast, my intention, if the weather was fine at eight o'clock, being to anchor as I had done every night. Until that moment, after sunset, the breeze fell off greatly and the change of course carried us only a little away from the coast. The fear of being carried closer to it by the current made me anchor at a quarter to eight in 12 fathoms, good bottom of sand and shells, and we passed a very quiet night there.
The speed of the current, at the time of anchoring and during the night, was one and three-tenths miles on the flood as on the ebb. It set to the south-south-east until eleven o'clock; from eleven o'clock until one o'clock it set to the north-west. The lead brought up various kinds of bottom, of which I think it needless to speak.

1803-04-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the breeze light from NNW to north. At 3.15 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 18' 33", est. long. 21° 43'.
1803-04-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twentieth, 10 April 1803, we continued to run along the coast, which still presented a very pleasant appearance, well wooded and fairly high. The depth was very variable, between eight, nine and fifteen fathoms, and we passed from one to the other in turn, taking care only to haul a little further out whenever it decreased too rapidly, so as to try to keep between ten and fifteen. The various views that were taken of the coast will make it very easy to recognise for those who may frequent it after us.
During the morning we had the winds from south to south-east, a light breeze and a fine sky.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 17° 16' 45", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 put us in 119° 39' 48". The first time we crossed these waters we sighted the land we were now coasting, but we were further to the west of it and saw it less well than on this last occasion; the geography of this part will be well done, and we have only to regret that it is not more extensive.
In the afternoon the winds followed their usual course and came to us from the south-west quarter, but they drew nearer to the south than they had done until then. We continued to run along the coast at a distance convenient for the work of the geography, and at half past seven we anchored in twelve fathoms, a clean sandy bottom.
For two or three days past, storms had always gathered in the east towards the end of the evening; they followed the land, lasted an hour and a half or two hours, and then cleared away. During that time the lightning was continual and the thunder could be heard rumbling fairly loudly, but none of them came as far as us. It seemed to us that it must have rained heavily in the places over which they passed, and it was to this cause that we attributed the freshness of the trees and the beauty of the verdure, which we could make out perfectly.
During the night the winds came back to the south-east, a pleasant breeze, and the sky was fine throughout, though very damp. The current having prevented the Casuarina from closing with us, she anchored at a considerable distance from us, so that we did not sight her until the following morning.
At the moment we anchored, the current had more speed than we had found in it until then, being two and a half miles. At ten o'clock it was no more than one and four, and until four in the morning it seemed to us to set to the north-east and north-east by north. At that time it took its course to the south-west. The soundings were from 12 ½ to 14 ½ fathoms, but I do (not) know whether this should be attributed to the rise of the water or to the irregularity of the bottom, for the reasons I have already given.

1803-04-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NNE to north. At noon went onto the starboard tack; at 2 onto the port, and at 9 onto the starboard. Obs. lat. 5° 39', est. long. 21° 49' 0".
1803-04-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-first, 11 April 1803, as soon as we had got under sail, I had the ship steered north 31° west so as not to pass over a large bank which I knew to be not far from our anchorage of the day before, and on which I had found myself rather deeply embayed the first time I visited this coast, in the month of Thermidor of the Year Nine. From the moment we got under sail until eight o'clock the depth varied between 15 and 17 fathoms, which led me to believe that I was far enough out to round it at my ease. So I altered course a little and steered north 22° west. But not for long, for at eight forty the soundings went from 14 to 11, and five minutes later to six and to five. We very quickly trimmed the sails close-hauled, and as the winds were south-south-west, varying to south, we were able to steer west, which made the depth increase as promptly as its decrease had been rapid. When we were back in 14, 15 & 16, we again hauled a little further to the north, without, however, going beyond north-west; but as this course led us into too rapid a shoaling, and we had no more than 10 and 11 fathoms at eleven o'clock, we came back close-hauled and steered west until noon, with a very light breeze and the ship making little headway. On this course the bottom was fairly regular, between eleven and twelve fathoms, sand and coral mixed with fragments of shells.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 16° 43' 8" and the longitude 119° 39' 28". All land was out of sight, even the islands which had been seen in the morning until nine o'clock. The stretch of sea over which we sailed all morning was of so white a colour that only the result of the soundings could persuade one that there was enough water for the ship to pass.
At sunrise, great flocks of seabirds set out set out (sic) from the lands on our starboard hand and directed their course to the west and west-north. Their number was so great that it was this which drew our attention to them. It looked like a complete migration, as though they were changing country.
From noon to one o'clock, although we were almost becalmed, the depth went from 12 to 18 fathoms; from one o'clock to half past one, in the same interval, from 18 to 23; and (from) half past two to three o'clock, to 27. As there was no longer any doubt that we were entirely clear of the banks which we had now crossed and now skirted during the morning, we tried to close with the land, steering by degrees as far round as east, but the depth, instead of decreasing, kept on increasing, and we had thirty fathoms at half past seven, when I anchored on a bottom of coarse sand and broken shells.
According to a remark which is perhaps not without likelihood, even though it rests on rather uncertain grounds, it is that in the afternoon of this day the same countless flights of seabirds in flocks, which had set out from the mainland in the morning,
heading west or west-north-west, and which I believed to be migrating to another country, began from three o'clock until sunset to come back to the mainland. This seemed to me so singular that I tried to guess the cause of it, for it appeared to me that the course they had followed was too extraordinary not to depend on some circumstances unknown to us.
Reflecting, then, on what had happened to us in the morning, and on the banks we had met with off the coast, I am inclined to believe that there are still others lying even further out from it than those over which we passed. I believe, too, that these banks, whose position is not known to us, dry at low water, and that they then provide abundant food for the birds that frequent them. Putting various circumstances together, we saw that by our reckoning the tide must have been low from six in the morning until noon, and that after noon, the banks, if they exist, being covered as the tide rose, the birds abandoned these waters until it uncovered them again.
If these remarks are mistaken, so much the better for navigators, in that they will have one danger the less to fear in these waters. But until they are better known, I think they will do well to be on their guard and to sail, whether by day or by night, with the greatest caution and always with the lead in hand. The change in the colour of the water is not sufficient in several places to tell the approach of a danger, any more than its depth, since in an instant one may pass from 25 to 12, and from 12 to infinitely less, as has happened to us several times.
As in the course of the morning we also saw a fair number of little turtles no bigger than a six-franc écu, we were bound to conclude that they were newly hatched and could not have come from very far away. It would not therefore be absurd to believe that some sandy islets, not entirely covered by the sea, lie in the neighbourhood of the place where we saw them, the one that saw them hatch.
Such is the remark that a particular circumstance led me to make, and of which I should certainly not have spoken on another occasion, in that we are no longer in the days when the flight of birds can indicate whether or not there are lands in the direction they take. Yet everyone knows that the Portuguese, and even the Spaniards, often made important discoveries by this means.
I have already observed that throughout the day we sailed over very white water, and that had the lead not told us there was a good depth, I should have thought myself at every moment on the point of touching. Nevertheless, it is no less true that this water, white as it was, showed from time to time patches that looked yellow, which gave the same
(effect) as if the ship had been ploughing the bottom. Although the sun must have had a part in this phenomenon, and the sky was very cloudy, I should think that the cause of it ought chiefly to be attributed to the strength of the currents and tide-races we met with in these waters, and above all at the steep edges of the banks, which, being of sand, must carry off a great deal of it and bear it in different directions.
When we anchored at eight in the evening, the current then had a speed of only six-tenths of a mile, and its direction was south-west and west-south-west. From nine o'clock until midnight it increased to one mile and took a south-easterly direction until one o'clock, when the tide turned and set to the north-west. At daybreak the greatest speed of the current was a mile and a half.
Little difference was found in the soundings given by the lead, which were constantly between 29 and 30.
The Casuarina, which had anchored too close to us, fell athwart our larboard cathead as she tried to shift her berth; but as it was calm she was quickly shoved off, and no harm was done.
1803-04-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: We passed through tide rips running NE and SW. The crew, who since Mauritius had had rice or beans for supper, had no more; the rice and beans were used up, so that we are now reduced to half a pound of beef or 6 ounces of salt pork and 18 ounces of biscuit a day, with water to drink. We have three meals of fresh bread every ten days.

1803-04-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NNE. Obs. lat. 5° 45' 14", est. long. 22° 37' 56". Var. 8° 29' 15" NW.
1803-04-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-second, 12 April 1803, in the morning, having no land in sight, I steered east-south-east so as to try to sight it during the day, if possible. But as we met with only passing decreases in the depth of the water, it was easy to judge that we were still a good distance from it. But as I wished to ascertain the trend of the coast in this part, not having seen it on my first voyage in this latitude, I held the same course as long as the winds allowed me.
In the morning the breeze was light and we made little way. The latitude observed at noon was found to be 16° 27' 20", and the longitude by our No. 35 put us in 119° 46' 41". We then had 34 fathoms of water, sandy bottom.
During the evening the sky became very cloudy and stormy, especially in the southern quarter. The lightning was continual and the thunder made a great deal of noise. This state of the atmosphere made the breeze very light, and we made little way, at least to all appearances. We held on our course east towards the south until half past seven, when we anchored in 21 fathoms, without having had any sight of land at sunset.
At about ten o'clock at night a storm, passing over the ship, gave us a gust strong enough to make our anchor drag, but it was of short duration. Nevertheless, as the sky did not look promising, cable was veered out for the rest of the night. This measure, taken as a precaution, proved needless, for once the squall we had just received had passed, the wind died away entirely, though under a very stormy sky.
At eight o'clock the speed of the current was found to be one and two-tenths miles and its direction south-south-west. From ten to eleven o'clock it was a mile and a half to the east-south-east and south-east. It then shifted to the east and east-north-east, and from there to the north-west, with a speed more or less the same, having gradually decreased to half a mile.
The lead gave no less than 20 fathoms nor more than 23 ½, which would lead one to believe that the flood was perceptible to us at this anchorage.
For several days past, my health having been steadily failing, I saw myself on the eve of a third illness. Until then I had made little of the pains and discomfort I felt, but that day I was so exhausted that, being scarcely able to stand on my legs, I had to have recourse to medicine. Apart from a general weariness in all my limbs, I suffered a great deal in my chest, and a dry and almost continual cough decided me to try to rid myself of it by the remedies usual in such cases.
1803-04-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: We passed through tide rips running N and south.

1803-04-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NE to N, NNW and north. At 4 and at 8 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 42' 32", est. long. 22° 44' 50".
1803-04-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-third, 13 April 1803, we got under sail at sunrise, and at the same instant we sighted one or, to put it better, several separate lands, which bore south of us and which I have no doubt must be the islets off whose extremity lie the banks over which we passed on the twenty-first, and which obliged us to shape our course to the west to get clear of them.
During the morning the breeze was very light and variable. As the ship was kept as far to the east as possible, we soon made out the land to the south-east by east and south-south-east. But we could not get near enough to it to see it from the deck before noon. The winds, which had moreover gone round to north-east by east, carried us away from it again.
As the sky had been very cloudy and stormy since the morning, we had no observations at noon, but the dead reckoning of the distance run in the 24 hours put us in 16° 22' 45" and 120° 4' 47".
The greater part of the evening having passed in calm, with very light winds varying from east to south and from south to south-south-west, we made little progress. At sunset, however, the land was made out from the mastheads, and it bore east-south-east, five leagues off by dead reckoning. As the land is extremely low in this part, that is assuredly the greatest distance at which it can be seen.
After sunset we held on our course until eight o'clock, when, having fallen calm again, we anchored in 27 fathoms, good sandy bottom.
During the night it was a flat calm, but we were not without lightning, which hurt the eyes and came from different points of the horizon. The sky was very cloudy and the air so full of damp vapours that the men who were not on watch could not sleep on deck, as they usually did.
At this anchorage we found the current less strong than it had been, and its speed was not above 7 tenths of a mile. Its direction was very changeable. It was at first to the south, for about an hour, and from the south to the south-east and to the east. At midnight it took an east-north-east direction, and at three o'clock north-east by east, at which time the sea seemed to be slack. At five o'clock its speed was five-tenths of a mile to the north-west. The shallowest sounding was 25 fathoms, with the ship swung head to the east, and the deepest 28, head to the north-west. The anchor had been let go in 27, head to the south-east.
1803-04-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: At noon a Spanish ship was sighted in the N 45° W, steering S 22° E.

1803-04-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNE to north and NE. At 9 sighted a Spanish ship in the NW. At 3 a.m. and at 6 changed tacks. Obs. lat. 5° 59' 22", obs. long. 23° 22'.
1803-04-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fourth, 14 April 1803, we had no land in sight on getting under sail. But at seven o'clock it was sighted from the mastheads, bearing in the east-south-east quarter, four or five leagues off. As we had the winds in the southern quarter, varying now towards the west and now towards the east, we steered east, edging a little to the south, to close with the coast, which in this place appears to form a fairly deep cove. But the winds having gone round to the south-east as the sun rose above the horizon, we could not approach it as closely as we might have wished. At noon, however, we were not far from it, and it could be made out perfectly from the deck. By the bearing then taken of it, the point nearest the ship bore east, and the two extremities belonging to it bore, the one south 58° east, and the other east-north-east.
At noon we observed the latitude 16° 17' 17", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 120° 21' 47". At noon the depth was 21 and a half fathoms.
In the afternoon the sky, which had been very cloudy and threatening storms at different points of the horizon, seemed inclined to clear, and the south-east quarter was the only one that underwent no change.
At about two in the afternoon we sighted the uncovered sandbank, on the edge of which the sea was breaking a little; but as we had 33 fathoms of water, we bore away only one point to weather this bank, until the lead, which was kept going continually, should warn us to bear away further; this did not happen, for as the depth kept increasing we went from 33 to 35. After weathering this bank we tried to close with the land so as to reach a less considerable depth of water, steering further to the east. The depth then decreased progressively, and at sunset we had no more than 29 fathoms, a bottom of sand and gravel. The same course was held until seven in the evening, when, having no more than 27, and reckoning ourselves only two leagues from the coast, which at sunset bore east ¼ north, we anchored to wait for daylight. The bottom on which we anchored seemed to us very clean, and we had no anxiety for the safety of our cable.
Throughout the night the sky was very stormy and the breeze light, but at the moment we anchored we found the current fairly strong, its speed being two and two-tenths miles, to the west-north-west. It then decreased to one and seven-tenths miles and changed no more. At midnight the sea seemed to be slack, and the current turned, setting to the east, without reaching a speed above one and seven-tenths miles. The soundings, with the ship swung to the west-north-west, were 27 and a half, and swung to the east, 26, which showed little difference from the moment we anchored.
From midnight until 2 o'clock the wind was very light, but at that time a storm came to us from the south-east which made us break loose and set the ship adrift for some time. 20 fathoms of cable were veered out and the ship held fast. When the height of the storm had passed, the sky turned to rain, which fell heavily until the next day. The wind then died away entirely, and we had the thunder constantly for company.

1803-04-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from NE. Obs. lat. 6° 46', obs. long. 24° 26' 0".
1803-04-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-fifth, 15 April 1803, in the morning, the rain began to let up a little before daybreak and we prepared to get under sail. We began by hoisting the topsails, and I gave orders to heave in half the cable and to remain at long stay until the breeze should settle, for we were then in a flat calm, with the ship swung head to the current. As a light breeze sprang up from the south-east, we went on heaving short so as to get under sail at once. And it was not without astonishment that, after heaving with some force, we saw it suddenly slacken and come in with the greatest ease. From the moment we were up and down, we again had to heave hard to break out our anchor, which was soon weighed. But it seems that our cable had been badly damaged, either by its own anchor, round which it had twisted in different directions during the storm, or by some rock on the bottom, for a sudden jerk was felt which told us that the weight of the anchor alone had parted it. This fear was soon confirmed, for shortly afterwards we got in the end of our cable, and our anchor remained on the bottom. As the Casuarina, which was anchored close beside us, suffered no damage of this kind, it is therefore very probable that our cable was cut by our anchor and not by some rocks on the bottom. I regretted the loss of this anchor all the more as we had no more than three (of them) left, including the sheet anchor, which was of little use to us in the circumstances in which we found ourselves.
After setting our topsails we steered we steered (sic) north-east by east to coast along the land, which we could see perfectly, although the horizon was of small extent. This course brought us to the edge of a great uncovered sandbank, in the middle of which a considerable number of rocks could be seen which, at a distance of a league, seemed to form so many small detached islets. The direction of this bank, which appeared to extend from north-north-west east to south-south-east west, made us bear away by degrees to weather it, and we passed a good league to the west of it without having less than 37 fathoms of water. At ten o'clock, its northern end bearing south-east of us, we came up to the wind by degrees, and at eleven we lost sight of it.
At noon there was no observation, the sky being too dark and cloudy. In the morning the last anchor we had left on board was got ready and put in place for letting go, and it is very much in our interest to preserve it as long as we possibly can so as not to be obliged to retrace our steps. I cannot refrain from mentioning here what took place on this subject, and it will be seen from the satisfaction shown by some of those who accompany me how pleasant they find the voyage and how much interest they take in it. I have no doubt that, were it up to them, they would have the others thrown into the sea, or at least would let them go among the rocks in the hope of seeing them stay on the bottom, and by that means bring the campaign to an end.
However that may be, in the afternoon we continued to run along a very low stretch of coast, seeing the land from the deck from time to time, and at other times able to make it out only from the mastheads, so little is it raised above the level of the sea. We nevertheless had a great depth of water throughout, but the winds did not allow us to hug it more closely. At sunset the land nearest to us looked exactly like an island, and I am even convinced that it was one, in that other lands could be seen to the east, lying much further back.
My intention was to anchor for the night, as I had done until then, the bottom being good, or at least appearing so from what the lead brought up; but as the depth of water was very considerable and it seemed to me likely to decrease as we advanced north towards the east, I put it off until we should have no more than 25 to 30 fathoms. We accordingly held on our course, but at eight o'clock, having gone from 32 to 45, there was no longer any thought of it, and I set the course north by east until midnight, at which time I intended to lie to until daylight, now on one tack, now on the other;
At nine o'clock a dark patch was sighted awash, which was at first thought might be a bank. The lead was cast at once and gave 35 fathoms, against the 45 we had had at eight o'clock. At half past nine we had no more than 29 fathoms, and we then steered north-west. The depth increased so rapidly that at ten we were in 40. Orders were given to hold the north-west course until midnight and then to take that of north-north-east. But the wind did not allow it, and the officer of the watch, not having warned me of this, continued on the north-west course, which could not fail to carry us well out to sea.
For the rest, during the night the weather was fairly fine and the breeze light, but whether the current was setting us to the north-west or otherwise, the depth kept on increasing, and during this last watch we went from 40 to 53 fathoms.

1803-04-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NE to ENE. Saw many fish. Obs. lat. 7° 11' 8", est. long. 25° 19' 36". Var. 9° 59' 0" NW.
1803-04-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the twenty-sixth, 16 April 1803, in the morning, the weather the weather (sic) was fine but the breeze so slack that we made very little progress. The winds, which were were (sic) moreover from the eastern quarter, were ill suited to the course we had to make to approach the land, of which, however, we had lost sight since the day before.
In the morning, as we sailed close-hauled in the hope that during the evening we should have the breeze from north-west to south-west, as had been the case ever since we began coasting, we saw a great number of birds flying off to the north-west, as if there had been had been (sic) on that point of the compass some banks drawing them to that quarter. On our course we met with several schools of fish, without having the skill to catch any, except, however, for a porpoise which was clumsy enough not to dodge the harpoon thrown at it. These schools of fish made no difference to the course the birds were taking, which seemed to show that they must find easier means of subsistence in the places towards which they were heading.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 7' 10", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 120° 21' 6".
In the afternoon the breeze held up a little until about 6 in the evening, and then it began to die away, the winds having remained all along in the eastern quarter, varying to east-north-east. We were obliged to keep on the northward tack, which hardly suited our wish to close with the land. Throughout the day we were in a great depth of water, never having less than 45 fathoms and often more. The night passed in a dead calm, without our being able to make the ship answer her helm. At six o'clock we had gone about to close with the Casuarina, which was a long way to the south of us, and we came up with her at about nine in the evening. As the lead was cast every hour although the wind was calm, it was thought that the current was setting to the north-west at a speed of about half a mile.
