We had a great deal of lightning at different points of the horizon during the night, but the calm was no less constant and the sky fine, apart from a great dampness which much inconvenienced those who were on deck.

1803-04-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a pleasant breeze from NNE to NE. The course NW by [W]. Saw many fish of various kinds. Obs. lat. 7° 28' 8", est. long. 26° 16'. Var. 12° 25' 0" NW.
1803-04-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-seventh, 17 April 1803, the calm continued all morning, apart from a few light breezes which came to us from the northern quarter but seldom had strength enough to give the ship steerage way and allow us to lay her head to the east. The depth varied so little that we were constantly between 55 and 56 fathoms of water
At noon the latitude was observed to be 14° 56' 16", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 120° 16' 12", which seemed to confirm the observation made by the quartermasters on the direction of the currents, for the officers of the watch paid no attention to it, as may easily be seen from the report of their watches in the log-book. Yet it was in order to know it that I had given orders for soundings to be taken every hour. But this practice, which they regarded as troublesome to themselves and useless in its results, meant that they carried it out only under constraint and not with any thought.
At about three in the afternoon we had a light breeze from the south-west which allowed us to lay the ship's head east-south-east. It lasted until eight o'clock and began to slacken, although the winds remained in the same quarter. My intention was to let go a kedge anchor for the night if I found good ground and a depth of between twenty-five and thirty fathoms. But as the water remained very deep, I stayed under sail. Moreover, as we had not yet reached the bottom of grey marl which I expected to meet with the next day, I knew that the bottom over which we were then sailing was not very clean.
At sunset land was thought to be seen to the south-south-east, trending to the east, but several of us believe that this was a mistake, and that what was taken for land was a bank of cloud on the horizon, which nevertheless showed itself to us until nightfall in the same form and without any alteration whatever.
During the night I steered, with all sail set, from east-south-east to south-east by east, to come and examine the islands and islets which lay roughly on that point of the compass, but from which I reckoned myself still more than 25 leagues distant.
During the night the weather was fine and the breeze rather light; yet it was noticed from the log that the ship was making fair way, which bears out the first remark we had made on finding that in these waters the current set strongly to the east.

1803-04-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from NE to SE. At 8 p.m. it fell calm; at 10 trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack. Obs. lat. 7° 54' 19", est. long. 27° 3' 48". Var. 11° 4' 0" NW.
1803-04-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-eighth, 18 April 1803, we had no sight of land at sunrise, nor even during the morning. I was the less surprised at this since, this part of the coast having been well determined on our first run, we were not yet due to see it. We therefore held on the same course, fully persuaded that we should see it during the day if only the breeze, which was nevertheless light, should hold.
At noon the latitude was observed to be 15° 10' 38", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 121° 29' 18". We had then come onto the marl bottom I have spoken of, which we knew was bound to begin a little to the west of this longitude.
In the afternoon, at about two o'clock, the land began to be sighted from the mastheads, but we did not see it clearly from the deck until sunset. According to the bearing then taken of it, it extended from south 30° east to south 70° east. As it was much broken up in this part, I had no doubt that this was the beginning of the islands and islets we had examined on our first voyage, and that the lands seen lying further back in the same direction were those of the mainland. My intention was to spend the night at anchor, the ground being very firm, but the sky was so stormy at different points of the horizon that at about eight o'clock, seeing no sign of fine weather for the night, I chose (to) remain under sail and stand out to sea, so as to get a little further from the coast, onto which a strong current setting to the south-east was making us drift.
From eight until ten o'clock the thunder made a great noise and the lightning flashed again and again with unequalled brilliance. Great black clouds, rising little by little above the horizon, soon spread out. The storm began to make itself felt with heavy rain and the wind entirely calm, but as the rain lessened we had the wind in gusts and squalls strong enough to make us lower our topsails right down and clew up our mizzen topsail. This storm lasted about two hours at its greatest strength and went several times round the horizon, obliging us to carry out various manoeuvres. The rest of the night, from one (o'clock) until daylight, was hardly any finer. The thunder, though distant, rumbled continually, and the lightning greatly troubled my eyes.
This storm was the first we had met with since we began coasting along the north coast of New Holland.

1803-04-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NNE to NE. Obs. lat. 8° 21' 33", est. long. 27° 56' 36". Est. var. 11° 30' NW.
1803-04-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the twenty-ninth, 19 April 1803, in the morning, having lain to an hour before daybreak in 35 fathoms, we made sail to close with the land which the look-outs had sighted at sunrise, although the horizon was not very clear, at least over several points of its bearing, which ran from east-south-east to south by east.
All the morning the sky was very cloudy and the air thick, and I feared some serious squalls, such as one sometimes meets in the first months of the change of the monsoons. Towards the middle of the day, however, the clouds gradually dispersed and the air grew less heavy. The barometer, which had several times fallen to 28 inches one line, began to rise again, and I flattered myself that fine weather was returning. For the rest, we spent the morning becalmed, making no other way than that into which we were carried by the current, which seemed fairly strong and to set to the east, to judge by the weed and (the) sea-grapes drifting past the ship.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 58' 11" and the longitude by the timekeeper was 121° 42' 58". We then had a light breeze from the west-south-west, with the help of which we steered east to draw nearer the land, which at four o'clock bore, from the deck, from south to east by south.
In the afternoon the weather became quite fine and the clouds vanished. Before the mainland, which could now be made out, lay several islets of moderate height.
After sunset it continued to blow a pleasant breeze, and I stood on all night, steering north 67° east. As these waters were known to me, I had no fear of meeting anything on that course which might put me in danger. Nevertheless we sounded every hour, and the bottom was very regular, between 40 and 35 fathoms.
At eight o'clock, a great glow having been seen on the horizon, I sent a man aloft to look, and it was found to be a large fire ashore; it bore south 15° east of us.
During the night the weather was fine but very damp. The winds varied little from the west-south-west, but they were very light. My health, which for several days had been rather poor, was beginning to recover, and this allowed me to resume my ordinary occupations.

1803-04-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from NE. Obs. lat. 9° 22' 5", est. long. 29° 16'. Var. 10° 20' NW.
1803-04-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the thirtieth, 20 April 1803, at first light, we sighted the land to the south-east by east at a distance of about two leagues, and at sunrise we saw it stretching away to the north-east by east. We were not long in recognising that this was the archipelago of islands, islets and rocks which we had wished to examine in greater detail in Germin Fructidor of the Year Nine, but into which the want of water had not allowed us to penetrate. We therefore confined ourselves to coasting along this chain of islands as we had done the first time, and to checking whether the positions we had assigned to them were correct, according to the correction applied to the longitudes given by our timekeepers. We were pleased to find so little difference that we altered nothing.
As the breeze was very light in the morning, we made little progress. The current, however, served us well, and we passed this first archipelago, in which the number of islets is probably greater than the chart shows. But they are so numerous, and lie in directions so ill suited to their all being taken with the same accuracy, that I have confined myself to the most conspicuous of them, and to those lying farthest out to sea, for the safety of navigation.
At noon we observed the latitude 14° 37' 24", and the longitude was 122° 24' 12".
Having doubled this first archipelago, we began to make out the second, which lies some five or six leagues from it. Though it has fewer islands, islets and rocks than the first, it is more remarkable, not only for their strange shapes but also for a very extensive reef lying off these islands, along about half their length. This reef appeared to us to be a long sandbank on which stand several rocks awash, over which the sea breaks heavily. Its middle is formed by a small sandy islet which the tide seems not to cover even at high water. Its whole length is about two leagues from north-east to south-west, as far as could be judged. Having doubled this reef, we drew near two rather flat and even islands, and at eight o'clock, the weather being very fine and the breeze light, we anchored in 37 fathoms, marl bottom, and passed the night there very quietly. I took this opportunity to send on board the Casuarina some fresh bread, a turtle, and those of his sick who had recovered. In return for my presents he sent me back two more sick men, with the news that he had lost one of his anchors on the same day as I, so that of the five he had had, only one remained to him, together with a cable in poor condition. He also let me know that in the last storm we had met, his compasses had entirely lost their magnetic virtue and he could no longer use them.

1803-04-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from NE by E to NE by N. Obs. lat. 10° 47', est. long. 30° 40'. Var. 11° 24' 30" NW.
1803-04-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the first of Floréal, 21 April 1803, as soon as we were under sail, the winds being very light from the south-west quarter, we met a strong current which, setting to the south and east, was drifting us down upon some of the islands on our starboard hand, so that by about eight o'clock we were no more than five miles from them. The bottom, however, was still 37 fathoms and very good for anchoring, so that if in the course of the morning the wind did not come to our aid, we always had the resource of letting go an anchor.
The wind did not increase during the morning, but at about ten o'clock the current changed its direction and carried us to the north and west, so that we passed some of the islands much faster than the log showed. We then fell into 40 fathoms, a very clear proof that the current was carrying us briskly to the north-west.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 20' 2", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 122° 37' 6" by No. 35.
In the afternoon the breeze continued very light, and we coasted at a short distance along the islands in sight, steering north-east, for fear that some too sudden change in the current might carry us back upon the coast, from which we were then about two and a half leagues distant. As I meant to anchor at about eight o'clock, the dangers on this coast being too numerous to remain under sail at night, I had her steered north-east by north after sunset. The breeze had then freshened a little, and we were making two miles an hour, not counting whatever the current might be doing for us in any direction, which we could not judge because of the darkness of the night.
While running along the islands, islets and rocks I have just mentioned, we never lost sight of the mainland, which could be seen farther off behind the islands, without any break marked enough to lead us to think that what we still saw was other islands. The smoke which we saw rising here and there confirmed us, moreover, in this opinion, though it is not free from objection, since the islands may just as well be inhabited as the mainland itself.
After anchoring, I sent for the Captain of the Casuarina, who confirmed what he had (told) me the day before about his situation. I had two compasses given him to replace his own, and promised to send him the next day, when we should be at anchor, a 6-inch cable and a grapnel of ninety pounds, the only one I had left for my longboat.
During the night the weather was fine and the breeze almost dead calm. As we were anchored in too great a depth of water for (its) rise or fall to be perceptible to us, we contented ourselves with observing the speed of the current, which at its greatest strength (was) one mile and seven tenths. It set first to the south, then to the north-east and north, slackening as it went.

1803-04-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. At 1.30 shaped the course NNW. Est. lat. 12° 6' 12", est. long. 31° 59' 24". Var. 9° 4' NW.
1803-04-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the second of Floréal, 22 April 1803, we were no better favoured by the wind than on the preceding days, and it blew so little all day that we made way only by the help of the current, whose changes of direction during the day were often against us and carried us farther offshore than we should have wished, while at other times it brought us much too close to the coast. The islands in sight when we weighed extended from south 67° east to south. Among them could be seen several detached rocks, and behind them the mainland, or at least land which we supposed to form part of it.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 6' 33", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 123° 0' 46" by No. 35.
In the afternoon we lay in a flat calm, and were often on the point of anchoring so as not to come too close to the islands abeam of us. But we persevered in keeping under sail, and at four o'clock a light breeze sprang up from the north-north-west, by means of which we were able to stand a little off and come to a good anchorage for the night. What little air we had lasted until about eight o'clock, and then, the calm setting in again, we anchored in 30 fathoms on a good bottom of mud.
As on my first voyage I gave an exact account of the land we saw on this coast, and as I have besides drawings in colour of all its views, I do not repeat here what I have already said of it, since this second account would be superfluous.
During the night the weather was very fine and the winds calm. The speed of the current was one knot and three tenths when we anchored, and it was then setting to the south. From eleven o'clock until midnight it was only six tenths, setting south-south-east. It then took its direction towards the (no indication), at first with little speed, and afterwards to the north-west, running one knot and one knot and three tenths at its greatest strength for us.
My health, which was still very shaky and uncertain, suffered various changes. At times I felt no more than a very bearable discomfort, and at others I was tormented by rather sharp pains, and above all by a dry cough which left me no rest at night.
The Casuarina having anchored too far from us, I could not send her the grapnel and the hawser I had had got ready for her.

1803-04-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a good breeze from ENE. At daybreak set up the main and fore topgallant shrouds. Obs. lat. 13° 57', est. long. 33° 2' 24". Var. 8° 37' NW.
1803-04-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events and Remarks.
On the third of Floréal, 23 April 1803, the same contrariness of the winds as on the preceding days. And it was only at about half past seven that, with the help of a light air from between south and south-south-east, we were able to get under sail, shaping our course north-east by north.
I flattered myself that in the course of the day I might reach the two islands which lie at the northern extremity of the land in this part, and which we could already see from the deck. But the breeze was so light that it was doubtful whether we should reach them even by nightfall.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 58' 58", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 123° 8' 0". This longitude leads me to believe that the timekeeper is fast, and I base this on one great fact which seems beyond doubt, and which is as follows.
When, on our first voyage, we determined the position of this island, it lay in (no figures) of south latitude, and its longitude, according to the correction applied to the timekeeper at Timor, was (no figures).
The longitude given by today's reckoning being 3 minutes farther east, and our distance from the coast being greater than it was then, I think myself justified in believing that the timekeeper is fast and that a great part of our second track lies farther east than it should. Our first port of call will show us whether this reasoning is sound or not.
In the afternoon, although it was almost a flat calm, the current favoured us so well that it drifted us abreast of the two islands I have just mentioned, which we clearly recognised to be those that terminate the land to the north in this part. At four o'clock the middle of the first island bore east by north of us, about two leagues off. Then, as on the day before, a light breeze sprang up from the south-south-west, variable, very variable, which we used to work up a little to the north and east, so as to make out the next morning the banks and reefs which we know to lie to the north and east of these islands.
At eight o'clock we anchored as usual in 33 fathoms, mud bottom, and passed the night very quietly. The current appeared slack when we anchored, or rather, the officer of the watch neglected to have its strength and direction observed.
At midnight its speed was one mile, setting to the north-east, until two o'clock, after which it did nothing until it was found to be nine tenths of a mile to the north-west.
After our sails were furled, the grapnel and hawser I had promised were carried on board the Casuarina.

1803-04-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from ENE, freshening a great deal. At noon shaped the course north. Obs. lat. 15° 48' 18", est. long. 33° 50' 0".
1803-04-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
Historical events & Remarks.
On the fourth of Floréal, 24 April 1803, in the morning, we did not have at sunrise the light breeze from between south and south-south-east which we had had on all the preceding days, and this obliged us to remain hove short on our anchor until it should set in, which did not happen until about nine o'clock. We then got under sail at once. But the current, being much stronger than the wind, was carrying us briskly to the south, so that, unable to stem it and unwilling to lose more ground, we anchored again on the same bottom as before, without furling our sails, in the hope that the breeze might come to us. But it never came all day, and the rest of the day passed in a flat calm.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 52' 0", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 123° 13' 32".
In the afternoon, seeing no prospect of getting away, I had my large boat hoisted out to go and examine the island off which we lay at anchor. I gave the command of it to the coxswain alone, being well persuaded that he would carry out my orders much better than any officer, since such duties are extremely distasteful to them.
He was therefore ordered to go ashore, but also to return on board at once if he had not reached it before nightfall. I had two rockets given him so that he might let me know when he had landed, which he did not fail to do after sunset.
I sent in this boat the gardener Guichenot and Citizen Barbe, the one to bring back the plants of the country, the other to shoot a few birds, should there be any.
During the night the wind was a dead calm and the sea as smooth as glass. Nothing out of the ordinary occurred, except that we observed the current to be stronger than usual and the (sea) to rise and fall for us by about four fathoms. This remark seems to confirm what Dampier says, that for several days after the new or full moon the tides are stronger than at their intermediate changes.
The greatest speed of the current, however, was no more than a mile and a half, setting sometimes south-south-west and sometimes between south and south-east on the ebb, and between north-north-west and north-east on the flood.

1803-04-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to ENE. Obs. lat. 17° 30' 35", est. long. 34° 32' 6".
1803-04-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, in the morning, we sighted our boat trying to make her way back to the ship. As no fire had been seen ashore during the night, I thought they had not been able to land, although the signal agreed upon to let me know they had reached the shore had been made.
At about seven o'clock, the wind being a dead calm, I was surprised to see my boat change course altogether and, instead of returning on board, she she (sic) was running into a kind of bay formed by two islands and some rocks. I supposed they were looking for an anchorage to wait for the turn of the tide, and I was not uneasy, the coxswain in command being an intelligent man, and willing to do his duty well.
On board, the morning passed in a complete calm, without the least breath of air from any point of the horizon.
At noon we again sighted our boat coming back out of the inlet she had entered, and at two o'clock she was alongside.
The news she brought us was most extraordinary. They had sighted four large canoes which made sail at sunrise and headed for the third island we had in sight. They put off from a sandy cove about two hundred paces from where the boat lay at anchor. As soon as the boat saw them, she made sail to give chase and try to come up with them, but as they sailed much better than the boat, they quickly drew away by means of their paddles. On opening the point of the cove from which they had set out, two more were seen, one getting under sail and the other still at anchor. The boat then altered course to come up with one of these last two. The one that had made sail escaped, but the third was at length stopped by a show of firing a musket at her if she went on paddling. The canoe and the boat being side by side, our men were quite astonished to see that the five men who manned her were all of Malay origin, dressed exactly in the manner of the Timorese and armed in the same way. Their clothing consisted of a piece of cloth girded about the loins and passing between the thighs, tucked up behind. Their headdress was a handkerchief wound round the head. All were armed with a dagger, or a kind of kris after the Malay fashion. Their canoe was long, raised at both ends and very neatly kept, as well as newly painted black and white. At the end of the canoe, in the after part, hung bows about four or five feet long and several wooden cases holding arrows.
The Malays were at first greatly afraid of our men, but they soon grew more familiar when they saw when they saw that our people wanted only to speak with them and were doing them no harm. Some of our men got into their canoe, while one of them came across into our boat.
The unlikelihood of such an encounter meant that we had no presents to give them, and our men merely exchanged biscuit with them for turtle eggs. They made it understood that they wanted rum, but were told that they could get it only on board, where they would on no account go. They offered the boat's crew water, which they kept in jars of a kind like those we had
bought at Timor, and such as are made in most of the islands north of New Holland. They also made signs to our men to persuade them to follow. But as our men were poorly armed and almost defenceless, and as I could not imagine that this island might be frequented, they did not think they ought to trust their guide, preferring to come back on board to report to me what had just happened to them.
Some of the Malays in the canoe gave our gardener Guichenot some tobacco, cut very fine in the same way as they usually prepare it for their daily use. To this present they added a leaf of betel, though it was quite dried up, together with an areca nut.
The five men of this canoe were tall, well made and of a reddish colour, with very black teeth, as all Malays generally have from the use of betel and areca. Four musket ramrods were seen in their canoe, but no firearms. The last two canoes were much smaller than the other four. A very fine fish was also found with them, gutted and very neatly wrapped in a mat, which they seemed to be keeping for someone at the place to which they were withdrawing.
So unexpected a piece of news having at once made me determine to find out how there came to be Malays in these parts, I resolved to learn whether they were settled here permanently or visited only at a certain season of the year for the turtle fishery; our men told me they had seen turtles in quantity at the edge of the banks which surround the island, leaving a few small openings through which one can reach the coves.
I therefore had the boat manned at once and gave the command of her to Fortin, the chief quartermaster, with orders to go and examine the place to which the canoes had withdrawn, which the coxswain knew, charging him above all not to compromise himself in any way. For greater safety, I ordered the Casuarina to follow him, to be continually on her guard, and always ready to protect the boat in all circumstances. Both were told that I would myself get under sail the next day to follow them, if the breeze had enough strength for the ship to answer her helm.
At four o'clock the boat and the Casuarina made sail, but Citizen Freycinet handled his vessel so badly that the current, which was then setting to the north-east, drifted him to leeward of the island, which the boat reached that same evening, leaving her thus to her own resources; this would not have happened had Citizen Freycinet stood on the southerly tack with what little wind there was, since in that way the current would have set him across and brought him up with the first island.
The night passed without incident, and the calm was as deep as it had been during the day. The direction of the current was the same as that observed the day before, and the tide was no stronger than had been noted.

1803-04-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 19° 20' 0", est. long. 33° 50'.
1803-04-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Sixth of Floréal, 26 April 1803. The day of the sixth passed in a flat calm, like the preceding days, and had nothing remarkable. The strength and direction of the current had no doubt prevented the Casuarina from following my boat, which she had orders to protect should the Malay craft in these waters come to trouble her. But being separated from her for the moment, she could be of no use to her. If the case required it, this vessel being at anchor to the south-east by east of us, about a league and a half off. After sunrise she got under sail, and in the course of the morning we lost sight of her, little wind though there was.
Towards evening, a little before sunset, several Malay praus were reported in sight. Some were under sail and the others at anchor. At sunset we clearly made out four of them under sail, which appeared off the eastern point of the island abreast of which we lay at anchor. But we saw nothing of either our boat or the Casuarina.
During the night the sky remained fine and the breeze still calm. I waited impatiently for the next day, when the Casuarina and my boat were due back on board.
The direction of the current observed during the night was the same as on the preceding days, and the tide rose and fell about two and a half fathoms.

1803-04-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from ENE to E by N. Obs. lat. 20° 40' 36", est. long. 34° 27' 18".
1803-04-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Seventh of Floréal, 27 April 1803. On the seventh of Floréal, at sunrise, we had the pleasure of seeing the Casuarina and the boat under sail off the eastern point of the island where we had seen the Malay praus the day before. I did not doubt that they had communicated with each other and that we should soon receive some interesting news from them.
As the large boat had orders to bring us branches of leaves for our kangaroos, she parted from the Casuarina to put in to the shore, and that vessel came to join us at the anchorage. When she had anchored, I sent for the Captain, and on coming on board he let me know that he had not been able to communicate with the praus, but that my boat had spent half a day with them and had received from them various pieces of information which seemed to prove that they visit this coast only at certain seasons for the fishery and have no settlement here.
I shall set out in more detail, from the report to be made to me by the chief quartermaster, what draws the Macassarese to these parts, the kind of fishery they carry on here, and the time they spend at it.
My boat having returned, we got under sail at once with the help of a light air from the south-south-west, which held in that quarter until about four o'clock, when the calm set in again. The land we had left in the morning could be seen at sunset from east-south-east to east by north.
As usual, we passed the night very quietly at anchor, lying in 34 fathoms, mud bottom.

1803-04-28.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the wind from NE to east and ENE, variable in force and direction. Obs. lat. 22° 28' 4", est. long. 35° 9' 12".
1803-04-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
Of the Eighth of Floréal, 28 April 1803. On the eighth, in the morning, we got under sail, steering north-east by north to run along the great bank part of which we had coasted the evening before. Several parts of this bank had been seen uncovered, and we had known of its existence since our first voyage, having coasted it along its whole length. And more than once we had even found ourselves entangled on it.
At eight o'clock, the line of this bank stretching ahead of us, we put her head to the north, with very light winds from the south, varying to south-south-west.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 33' 22", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 123° 23' 20".
In the morning, a little after sunrise, No. 31 stopped, or at least it was noticed then. On being taken out of its box to be examined, it started going again, but at noon it was found that it must have been stopped for about half an hour. The cause of this accident is entirely unknown to Citizen Bernier, who has charge of the timekeepers.
At noon the bank, or line of breakers, which we had been coasting since yesterday stretched from east-north-east to east-south-east as far as the eye could reach.
(blank)
Particular remarks on the longitude
of the bay of Kupang and on the placing, on old and even
modern charts, of the south-west point of Timor, as of the islands
of Semau, Roti and Savu
From a long series of observations made during our stay at the settlement the Dutch have in the bay of Kupang, on the island of Timor, it follows that the longitude of Fort Concordia is 121° 30" by the rate of our timekeepers, corrected for the errors they have made since our departure from Paris.
By the lunar distances taken from the sun, both to the east and to the west, the results were exactly the same, so it must follow that the determination we have given for the situation of this settlement comes very close to its true position.
Its latitude 10° 9' 55".
Supposing, as there is reason to believe, that our observations are good, it follows that the longitude given by the Connaissance des Temps for the south-west point of Timor is faulty, since it places it in 121° 39' 0". This would put that point to the east of Kupang, whereas we are quite certain it lies to the west of it, since in going there by the Semau Strait our course was north-east, and after doubling the southern point that forms the bay in question one must steer east and southerly to reach the anchorage.
On leaving Timor on 14 Prairial Year 11 (3 June 1803), I decided to resume the survey of the north coast of New Holland, standing to the south of the island of Roti, persuaded that once I had reached between the 13th and 14th degrees of latitude I should find winds from between south and south-east, and perhaps even south-west, which would allow me easily to work up the coast. Although several seamen whom I had consulted were convinced that it would be impossible for me to make easting against the south-east monsoon, I nonetheless persisted in my plan, and preferred to follow the route I had proposed to myself rather than the one more generally taken, which passes north of the Equator.
It was not, however, out of obstinacy in holding an opinion contrary to everyone else's that I took this course, but because, having twice worked up this coast, I have always found favourable winds there, and the land and sea breezes seemed to me very regular. And we have gone few days without them. So I am very far from believing that the coast of New Holland, in the north as in the south, is subject to the winds which usually prevail out at sea.
When we left Port Jackson, the English were persuaded that it was impossible to work up through the straits and along the south coast of New Holl
without exposing oneself to all kinds of dangers and inconveniences. This prejudice, which has no foundation whatever, has led all their returning ships to go round Cape Horn. I hope that the two voyages I have just made there will change their opinion, and that they will see that in the favourable season this route is to be preferred to any other.
In coasting the island of Roti at a short distance, we made sure that its trend is more westerly than that given it by our charts, and it is likewise certain that this island does not extend as far south as it is marked. Unless it has an extension of coast to the south-east of which the charts make no mention.
Three islands and several reefs lying off its south-west part are shown on Robertson's chart, but wrongly placed. We sighted the two small islands which lie to the south.
It is probable that the island of Savu is also wrongly placed, and that the channel separating it from Roti is much wider than it is marked, since we saw nothing of it. This land is, however, very high and can easily be seen at ten or twelve leagues and even more.
Following the course we steered, we should not have passed out of sight of it, especially as the sky was fine and the horizon wide.
Departure from Timor. 2nd port of call in the bay
of Kupang.
1803-04-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: We crossed the Tropic of Cancer. From the 8th to the 15th we saw a great deal of gulfweed lying E and W.

1803-04-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 24° 19', obs. long. 39° 9'.

1803-04-30.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather with a little rain, a good breeze from ENE. Obs. lat. 25° 57' 36", est. long. 40° 16' 0". Obs. var. 6° 50' NW.

1803-05-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a good breeze from NE to ENE and east, variable in force and direction. Obs. lat. 27° 47' 33", est. long. 41° 20' 0". Var. 11° 29' NW.

1803-05-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze. Saw a great deal of gulfweed. The breeze at ENE. Obs. lat. 29° 36' 51", est. long. 42° 9' 18". Var. 9° 20' NW.

1803-05-03.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sea smooth. A pleasant breeze in puffs from ESE to NE, east and E by S. Set up the main topmast shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 31° 41' 49", est. long. 42° 18' 36".
1803-05-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: The fore topgallant mast was struck.

1803-05-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from ESE to east. Obs. lat. 33° 43', est. long. 42° 29'. Var. 10° 59' NW.

1803-05-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from ESE to east and ENE. Struck the main topgallant mast to shift the sail. Obs. lat. 35° 43' 55", est. long. 42° 53' 24". Var. 10° 11' NW.

1803-05-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze variable from ESE to ENE and SE. Obs. lat. 37° 26' 50", est. long. 42° 37'.

1803-05-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. Shifted the mizzen topsail. Obs. lat. 39° 4' 58", est. long. 41° 26' 30". Var. 1° 30' NW.

1803-05-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, a pleasant breeze from SE to ESE. Saw an American ship to windward of us; we hove to to wait for her, and our small boat went aboard. Obs. lat. 40° 23' 8", est. long. 40° 22'. Est. var. 7° 0' NW.
1803-05-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: We communicated with the American ship Thomas of Charleston, from Liverpool bound for Philadelphia with a cargo of salt; she had English passengers of distinction. We asked her for 6 casks of wine or 2 of rum; she could give us nothing.

1803-05-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze in puffs from SE to ESE. Repaired the main staysail, which had split where it bears on the fore braces. Obs. lat. 42° 6' 24", est. long. 39° 32' 30". Est. var. 7° NW.
1803-05-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Two Spanish ships were sighted standing S 22° E. At 4 p.m. the sea changed colour completely; we sounded at 9.30 without finding bottom at 180 fathoms — though from the way the captain sounded, we should have found no bottom even at 50 fathoms.

1803-05-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a pleasant breeze from E by S to ESE and SE. Saw several ships. Obs. lat. 43° 50' 52", est. long. 38° 36'. Est. var. 9° NW.
1803-05-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the morning the sea had recovered its natural colour. At 4 p.m. we communicated with an English brig from Dartmouth bound for Newfoundland in ballast; we asked her for wine or rum, which she had not, and she offered us a little salt pork, which we refused. At 6.30 we spoke an English sloop from Jersey bound for Newfoundland in ballast. The ship was painted.

1803-05-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a pleasant breeze from SE to south and S by E. Several ships in sight. On the morning of the 21st set up the main topmast shrouds and backstays. Obs. lat. 45° 16', est. long. 37° 22'. Var. 10° NW.

1803-05-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south, SE and SSE. Saw several ships. Shifted the main and fore topsails. Obs. lat. 46° 6' 27", est. long. 36° 10' 26".
1803-05-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: New sails were bent. At 7 p.m. we communicated with the Danish corvette Frederikssteen of 26 guns and 32-pounder carronades, whose captain gave us 1 barrel of 21 pots of brandy and 600 lb of biscuit; he sent 27 bottles of rum or wine for the captain and the officers. The corvette was from Saint Croix (in the Virgin Islands) bound for Copenhagen. Captain Hamelin forbade the officer who went aboard her to say that we had called at Mauritius, and told him to say that we came from the coasts of New Holland. We have 4 men sick.

1803-05-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from south to S by E. Several ships in sight; we spoke one which gave us biscuit and brandy. Obs. lat. 47° 2', est. long. 34° 27' 26". Est. var. 20° NW.
1803-05-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Several ships were in sight, one of them the Danish corvette. The coffee shipped for the crew at Mauritius being used up, the second sailmaker Auvray, who had a bale of it weighing 85½ lb, let the captain have it for the crew, payable at Le Havre at the current price.

1803-05-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south, SSE and SSW. Five ships in sight. Hove to and sent our small boat aboard to fetch the captain. Obs. lat. 48° 11' 50", est. long. 32° 19' 26". Est. var. 20° NW.
1803-05-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: We saw 5 ships and communicated with one of them, the Concorde of Le Havre, 58 days out from Saint-Domingue and bound for Le Havre; she could give us nothing. The salt pork shipped at Port Jackson is used up; we have nothing left but beef.

1803-05-15.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a good breeze from SSE. At 1.30 the main topmast backstay having parted, it was repaired at once. Struck the main topgallant mast to shift its sail. Est. lat. 49° 39' 26", obs. long. 36° 25'. Var. 20° NW.

1803-05-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a pleasant breeze from SE to SSE. During the night the weather turned overcast, the wind variable and unsteady. Four ships in sight. Est. lat. 51° 2' 38", est. long. 33° 58' 2". Var. 20° NW.
1803-05-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: The same brig, made out to be French, and three other ships in sight.

1803-05-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from SSE, SSW and south, in gusts; the sea rather high. Saw birds and porpoises. Est. lat. 51° 59' 38", est. long. 31° 49' 30". Var. 30° NW.

1803-05-18.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze and variable from SSW to SW, in gusts. The sea smooth enough. Obs. lat. 52° 34' 12", est. long. 29° 5' 30". Est. var. 30° NW.
1803-05-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 6 p.m., after a squall, the mainmast — long since sprung, and which the captain would not spare — cracked abaft between the masthead rigging and the trestletrees. The officer of the watch at once had the main topsail and the staysails taken in, with which the captain was not pleased; the staysails (according to him) having never carried away a mast, because they did not strain it. The main topgallant mast was struck. In the afternoon two ships were in sight.

1803-05-19.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from SSW, SW and WSW in gusts. At 6, in a squall, the mainmast cracked below the masthead rigging; lowered the main topsail on the cap and took 2 reefs in it and 1 in the fore. Struck the main topgallant mast and got it down. At daybreak sighted a ship to windward of us. We set about rigging preventer backstays and unbending the main topsail. Obs. lat. 52° 14' 13", est. long. 25° 29' 12". Obs. var. 34° 46' NW.
1803-05-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: The damage to the mainmast was made good. Two preventer backstays were set up to starboard and two to port abaft to support the masthead. The main topmast was lowered about 9 feet; it rested on a stout woolding passed over the cap (the turns of the woolding could not be passed over the trestletrees, the port one being broken). Two fishes were put on the masthead; good woolding was passed round the mast, the fishes, the heel of the topmast and its woolding; wedges were driven between these wooldings and the mast, and a preventer woolding passed. The main topsail and the staysails were unbent. A ship was in sight during the day.

1803-05-20.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind falling away from SW, SSW and WSW. Lowered the main topmast about 9 feet and refitted the lashings of the [one word illegible] shrouds and backstays; meanwhile two fishes for the mainmast were got out of the spare spars. From 5 to 8 went on passing the wooldings on the mainmast fish. From 8 until midnight set up the main topmast rigging, and at 11.45 set the main staysail and bent the main topsail; by midnight it was set. At daybreak worked on the main topmast woolding and on woolding the mainmast. Est. lat. 51° 29', est. long. 22° 31'.
1803-05-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: The main topsail was bent with the three reefs taken in, the middle staysail in place of the main staysail, and the topgallant staysail in place of the middle staysail. The eyebolts to which the mainmast preventer backstays and the main topmast backstays were secured being neither strong nor sound enough, they were brought inboard through the after ports. A ship was in sight during the day.

1803-05-21.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather with rain at intervals, the sea smooth, a strong breeze from WSW to SW. We were busy setting up the mainmast shrouds, finishing the wooldings and refitting the preventer backstays, the eyebolts they had been secured to not being strong enough. At 5.30 all was ready. A ship in sight. We got up our main topgallant mast, swayed it up and rigged it; the shrouds and backstays of that mast were set up. Est. lat. 50° 48' 49", est. long. 19° 59' 42". Est. var. 34° NW. [No more follows.]
1803-05-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: A fore topgallant mast was rigged as a main topgallant mast, and a small staysail set to serve as a topgallant staysail. A reef was added to the main topsail. At 3.30 p.m. we sounded without finding bottom at 160 fathoms. Two ships were in sight during the day.

1803-06-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the Fourteenth of Prairial, 3 June 1803, of the Year Eleven of the French Republic, seeing no further prospect of recovering the deserters I was missing, I decided to get under sail, and at nine o'clock we stood out of the bay of Kupang, passing passing between the small island of Sem des Tortues and to the north of the one which we ranged at three quarters of a league.
My intention on leaving Kupang was to go through the Semau Strait, so as to keep farther to the east and not be carried to leeward of the island of Roti, or even of Savu. But the breeze was so light that it was not possible to attempt this passage, which, though easy with a good wind, is dangerous in a calm. The anchorage being everywhere very deep and foul, one is often exposed either to losing one's anchor or at the very least to badly damaging one's cables, as had already happened to us.
Having doubled the northern part of Semau, I went round it by the west, and at nightfall found myself off the middle of its western side, hoping to enter the next day the channel that separates it from Roti. But as the currents were drifting us strongly to the south-south-west, we had to look for another passage out, and this decided me to take the one which the charts show between Roti and Savu.
During the night the wind was very light and the weather fine. We kept close-hauled on the southerly course as far as possible, and ran along the western coast of this last island within sight of it.
The Casuarina, no doubt overladen and encumbered, sailed so badly that we carried only our topsails with one reef in, and even so we had from time to time to back the mizzen topsail.

1803-06-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, 4 June 1803, we continued to run along the coast of the island of Roti at a short distance, and the course we steered to follow its outline enabled us to judge that its shape is badly drawn on our sea charts. I think the one given it by Arrowsmith, in his large chart of the South Seas, is the best.
At noon we observed the latitude 10° 44' 49", and the longitude by our timekeeper No. 35 put us in 120° 44' 56". At the same time we found ourselves at the entrance of a channel formed by several islands lying to the west of the coast of Roti. This channel appears wide, but it is obstructed by reefs which must make its navigation difficult, the more so as breakers could be plainly seen in several places. Robertson's chart mentions these islands, which are three in number,
but it places them much farther south than they should be.
From the report the surgeon made me, I learned that many of the crew were suffering from venereal disease. Citizen Bernier, who had had a fever for four days, seemed likely to have a serious illness, as did the draughtsman Petit. Both had kept in good health throughout our stay in port, and it was only two or three days before our departure that they began to feel slightly unwell. Each of them, however, had a rather violent bout of fever, which appeared to have no consequences according to the report made to me at the time.
When I visited Citizen Bernier during the morning, I found him much worse than the day before, and began to fear he might have a really serious illness, so dejected and wasted did he look, whereas the day before we (had) chatted and talked together for more than an hour and he had been perfectly well.
In the afternoon the winds, after going round the compass, settled, passing from south-east to east-south-east, and it blew a good breeze. Several rain clouds broke over the land and did not reach us. We doubled in succession the three islands I have mentioned, and a reef, on which the sea rose very high, lying off the southern point of the last of them. Having passed it, we saw the land of the island of Roti at a considerable distance, and at sunset the land of the large island extended from north 43° east to south 72° east.
I am very far from believing that the island of Roti extends as far south as our charts place it. Or, if it does, its shape must be very different from the one given it, and it must run far out to the south-east.
During the evening the physician came to warn me that Citizen Bernier had just shown the most alarming signs, portending an early end. He had been seized by a violent hiccup, and the violent and irregular agitation of his pulse gave cause to fear for his life. He judged it proper to apply blisters. I went at once to see him. But I found him unconscious, and every symptom of death was painted on his face. Unable to bear such a sight, I withdrew. He was, besides, unconscious. I was so struck by so sudden a change that I felt throughout my body a malaise which obliged me to go to bed much earlier than usual, but I did not find there, for all that, the rest I needed. During the night I was seized with a spitting of blood like those I had already had on two different occasions, and the sputum I brought up was so thick that one would have said some parts of the lungs were coming away from my body.
The weather was fine and clear during the night. I had soundings taken several times without finding bottom at 100 fathoms. At times we met very violent tide-rips, which made as much noise as if the sea were breaking on reefs.

1803-06-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, 5 June 1803, at about five in the morning, I was told that Citizen Bernier was no more. This death, which may almost be regarded as a sudden death, made such an impression on me that it would be hard to express all (that) I suffered. The loss of Citizen Bernier is an unfortunate event not only for us but also for the Government, for there is no doubt that he would have become a learned astronomer, useful to his country. For this science, which was both his occupation and his pleasure, he had natural gifts which he turned to account by diligent and unremitting work. His labours, up to the day before his death, will no doubt be found in good order, and I am as good as certain that the Government will be satisfied with them.
This young man, who had moreover excellent qualities of heart, was of a gentle and honest character, and if at times he departed from it, it was only when carried away by example or worn down by bad advice; but as soon as the first moments of ill humour had passed, he was not ashamed to own his faults and to be the first to condemn his conduct. For my own part I sincerely regret him, and I do not hesitate to say that of all the savants who were given me, he is the one who worked hardest, whether to acquire new knowledge or to fulfil the intentions of the Government. It is unfortunate that he was of a very delicate constitution, ill suited to bearing the fatigues of a long voyage, during which one often lacks the things necessary to a constitution such as his.
I will do him the justice of saying, to his praise and to his zeal for his calling, that although he was ill at several ports of call, he never showed the least wish to remain ashore, conduct very different from that of several of his colleagues.
At ten o'clock the officers and the naturalists paid him their last (respects) and his body was committed to the sea.
In the morning the weather was fine and the wind east-north-east, a light breeze. At noon we observed 11° 34' 32" of latitude, and the longitude by our timekeeper No. 35 put us in 120° 33' 16".
During the evening the breeze, which in the morning had been easterly, drawing towards the north, went round to the east and even to east-south-east, which gave me hope that as we advanced southward the winds would take that direction. The breeze was very light all evening and we made little progress during the night. We had the wind at east.
Before sunset we saw great flights of birds, of the black and white booby kind, and of gulls, coming from the west and heading south-east. It may be that they came from some banks or islets lying in that direction, and were withdrawing for the night to the coast of New Holland.

1803-06-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
It is by an error of date that I have entered the death of Citizen Bernier, our astronomer, on the day of the sixteenth; it was on the 17th, at half past four in the morning, that it took place, and as I was myself very unwell that day with a spitting of blood, these two days of my journal were not in order.
In the morning of this day we had the wind at east by south, varying to east-south-east, and the breeze light. We held on the southerly tack, keeping to the pace of the Casuarina, which, sailing very badly, caused us considerable leeway, our ship not carrying enough sail to avoid (being) carried along by the current. We found, nevertheless, that the tide-rips which passed from time to time were beginning to be less long and less strong than we had found them until then.
At noon the observed latitude was 12° 24' 0" and the longitude 120° 34' 6". If we had gained nothing to the east in these 24 hours, at least we had lost nothing, and that was already a great deal.
As on the day before, we saw many of the birds I spoke of yesterday, which, coming from the south-east, were going off to the west. The latitude observed at noon put us very nearly in that which Captain Nacht gives for the sandbank he sighted; I had soundings taken in these waters without finding bottom at 100 fathoms.
During the evening and all night the winds varied little, and we held on our course to the south, hugging the wind as closely as possible.

1803-06-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, 7 June 1803, the weather was much as on the day before, and the breeze still very light. We held on the same course. In the morning we did not see the same number of birds as we had seen the day before.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 2' 46", and the longitude by the timekeeper put us in 120° 38' 18", which gave a fairly large difference from the dead reckoning.
In the evening the winds varied from east towards south, but I did not change course until midnight, when, believing them settled at south-south-east, I went onto the easterly tack in the hope of having them the next day at south and perhaps south-west.
During the day an inventory was made of Citizen Bernier's effects, and all his papers were collected and placed in a separate chest, to be handed over to the Government on our arrival.
Of the Nineteenth of Prairial.

1803-06-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, 8 June 1803, in the morning, the winds went round from south-south-east to south-east and we were able to keep on our easterly course, but the breeze was light and we made little progress during the morning.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 17' 5", and the longitude by No. 35 put us in 120° 58' 48".
In the afternoon the winds continued variable between south and south-south-east and the breeze still light. But at nightfall they went round to south-south-west and then to south-west, freshening a little, so that I no longer doubted that we should henceforth have favourable winds for making our easting, and perhaps even for following the north coast of New (Holland). During the night we held on our easterly course, keeping to the pace of the Casuarina, which was making us waste very fine weather.
As we (were) in the neighbourhood of the sandbank seen by Captain Natch, I had a sounding taken at midnight, but we found no bottom with eighty fathoms up and down.

1803-06-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, 9 June 1803, in the morning, the weather continued fine and the winds varied from south-west to south-south-west. They even went round to south by way of east, but only for a short time. The breeze was very light in the morning, or rather, we spent the greater part of it in a calm.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 1' 16", and the longitude, according to the rate of our timekeeper, was 121° 35' 43".
During the evening the breeze increased a little and we steered east by south, having noticed from the difference in latitude over these 24 hours that the currents were setting to the north.
The night passed passed (sic) without incident; a pleasant breeze blew from between south and south-south-west, which was just what we wished for; we sounded at eight o'clock and at midnight without finding bottom at 80 fathoms up and down.

1803-06-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, 10 June 1803, the winds continued favourable to us, and there was a fair breeze from the south-south-west. We made as much use of it as we could, having regard to the Casuarina.
As the colour of the water changed a great deal in the morning, and to all appearances we were on soundings, I had the lead cast at 11 o'clock, and we found ourselves in 45 fathoms, grey sand, rather coarse. At noon the observed latitude was 13° 1' 17" and our longitude was 121° 23' 14", which put us very nearly in the position we were in when I shaped course for Timor.
During the evening the breeze was less strong than it had been in the morning, and there was every appearance of a calm for the night. We sounded at two in the afternoon; the depth was the same as at eleven in the morning, that is to say 45 fathoms, grey sand bottom.
After sunset, being in 43 fathoms of water, we held on our course, but at ten o'clock, having no more than 31 fathoms, we hove to on the larboard tack and lay on that same tack for the rest of the night. The soundings then gradually increased, and at four in the morning we had 50 fathoms. The currents and the leeway were carrying us to the north-east.

1803-06-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, 11 June 1803, as soon as day began to break, we filled and steered east until sunrise, when we took a course of south-east by south. It blew a good breeze in the morning, and we used it to regain to the southward the ground which lying to during the past night must have lost us by carrying us to the north. I had determined on this course for fear that, by sailing on during the night, we might be carried onto one of the banks and reefs which we knew to lie to the east of the westernmost northern point of this part of the coast.
During the morning we crossed several rather considerable tide-rips, whose direction was north-north-east and south-south-west.
At noon the observed latitude was 12° 54' 32", and the longitude by our timekeeper No. 35 put us in 124° 22' 54". The result of several series of distances of the sun from the moon gave 124° 38' 22".
In the after(noon) the breeze continued favourable, the winds varying from south-west towards south, but as the sun sank towards the horizon it kept almost steadily dropping, so that at sunset we found ourselves almost becalmed; this happily did not last long, for at seven o'clock it came to us again and was stronger than usual, and so it lasted until the middle of the night, when the winds came to us again from the west-south-west quarter, a pleasant breeze. During the night we steered south-east under little sail to wait for the Casuarina, which was far astern, but of which, nevertheless, we saw nothing. For the rest, the night was very fine and clear, but damp.

1803-06-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-third, 12 June 1803, the weather continued fine, but we had the regret of seeing the breeze fall away a great deal. At sunrise we steered south to close with the land, which we might possibly sight in the course of the day, judging by the soundings, which were 55 fathoms, grey mud bottom. At eleven o'clock it was thought to have been made from the mastheads, though without certainty. But at one (o'clock) in the afternoon it was seen perfectly from the topgallant crosstrees. At that distance it showed itself as fairly high and regular in outline.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 26' 6" and our longitude by the timekeeper 125° 8' 47". That by lunar distances placed us in (no figures).
In the afternoon we continued to steer south and at one o'clock we plainly made out the land from the mastheads. The breeze gradually died away until sunset, with every appearance of a calm for the night. At sunset the two extremities of the most prominent land extended from south 85° west to south 35° east. In this position we were steering south 52° east, and we had abeam of us, at about two leagues' distance, a small sandy island which was at first taken for a bank left uncovered by the sea. But as we drew nearer to it, we recognised
that it was indeed a small (island), with some verdure on its highest part and a fairly long reef off the ends of its south-east and north-west points, along the length of which rocky heads could be seen above water here and there. There were also, to the south-west of the ship's position at that time, two other pieces of land which had the look of islands, but we could not properly make out whether they were further projecting points of the mainland or islands.
The part of the coast where we made our landfall is of good height and falls sheer to the sea in the form of a cliff. The water was accordingly deep, for having anchored at seven o'clock, we lay in 45 fathoms on a good mud bottom and at a league and a half at most from the small island I have just spoken of.
The uniformity of the coast in this part offers few landmarks, and the interior of the country presents nothing pleasing to the eye. The lands nearest the sea are thinly wooded. But in the distance, where they rise higher, tall timber trees could be seen in fairly large numbers. In the evening we also saw a few columns of smoke rising far inland.
The greater part (of the night) passed in calm; nevertheless the Casuarina, which had fallen well astern, joined us between eleven o'clock and midnight. By the observations made during the night on the strength and direction of the current, its speed was 6 to 7 tenths of a mile and its direction south-south-east until midnight, when the tide turned and they set to the west. Until two o'clock the speed was 8 tenths of a mile, and from three o'clock to five, one mile. I was surprised not to find them stronger, after what I had already experienced, read or heard said.

1803-06-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-fourth, 13 June 1803, at six in the morning, we got under sail to run along the coast, the survey of which was then begun. We had at that time light winds from the south-west, but the tide, which must have turned at the very moment we weighed, ought to have been in our favour, or at least I hoped so. In running along the coast we found that the two pieces of land which the day before I had suspected to be two islands and not projecting points of the mainland did indeed form two islands quite distinct from each other. During the morning the winds varied from south-west to north-west and the breeze was so light that we made very little progress. The coast had much the same appearance as the day before, still sheer and formed of cliffs, in which there are several coves of greater or lesser size, but which do not seem to offer good places of shelter in case of need.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 51' 41", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 125° 17' 35". The soundings were very regular between 55 & 45 fathoms, still a mud bottom.
In the afternoon the winds shifted from north-west to north-east and the breeze freshened a little. And as we were steering south-east, the wind was fair for us. Nevertheless we made very little way. The ship's progress was held back by a strong current which prevented her from going ahead. The colour of the water changed so markedly during the evening that I was astonished at it. And indeed, within two hours, we went from 45 fathoms to 20, although we had made little way. And the nature of the bottom, which until then had been mud, turned out to be rock, which made me fear that we might be in the neighbourhood of some breakers, although nothing with the appearance of any could be seen from the mastheads. We continued to steer south-east until six in the evening, during which time (the bottom) was from 20 to 23 fathoms; but then it began to shoal, and within half an hour we went from 20 to 12, coarse gravel mixed with mud. On the strength of these soundings we at once steered north-east, and even north as far as the winds allowed us to head, and the bottom deepened from 12 to 15 fathoms. The calm that followed decided me to let go a kedge and to remain in that spot if the breeze during the night was not too strong.
As soon as the ship had brought up and the sails were furled, a boat was lowered and I sent it to sound round the ship, particularly to the east and north-east, the directions in which I supposed the bank must lie if, as I believed, there was one in our vicinity. On the boat's return I was informed that all round the ship, at two cables' length, they had found 15 fathoms everywhere and the same bottom as that on which we were anchored, but that on proceeding at that distance between east and north-east the bottom shoaled, and they had gone as far as 13 fathoms. The report would seem to confirm my opinion.
The night passed without incident, and we spent it almost becalmed, with a light air from north-west to west.
From eight o'clock until eleven the greatest speed of the current was one mile 8 tenths to the south-east, and from ten o'clock to 3 in the morning, one mile two tenths to the north-west and north-west by west. The soundings showed us that the sea had risen two fathoms and fallen one.

1803-06-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-fifth, 14 June 1803, having got under sail, we steered north-east, sounding as we went. The day before, I had ordered the Casuarina to get under sail as soon as day began to break and to steer on that point of the compass, from which she was not to depart and haul round to the south until she was in twenty fathoms. We continued on a course between north-east and east until about eight o'clock, sounding continually. During the first hour the bottom held between 15 and 16 fathoms; then it deepened to 17 and to 22. At nine o'clock it was thirty, and at ten 35, all mud, as we had found it on our arrival on the coast. I therefore remain convinced that there is a shoal in the quarter between south-east and east-north-east of our anchorage, but perhaps there is enough water over it
to allow it to be crossed. At least we saw nothing that indicated the contrary. The wind, moreover, was so light and the sea so calm that we could not judge of it any better.
During the morning the winds varied from south-south-west to south by east, almost calm. We ran along the coast as close as possible, taking bearings of its principal points.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 5' 18", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 125° 38' 6".
The breeze remained very light in the afternoon, and the winds, having shifted from south-south-east to east, then came round from east to north-west; but by then it was beginning to be too late to profit by them, as I did not wish to make way during the night, lest we be carried by the currents in a direction contrary to our dead reckoning. The night passed without incident. The breeze was very moderate, with variable winds from west to north-west.
The depth in which we lay at anchor being too great, no observation was made of the rise or fall of the water, since it would not have been perceptible at that depth. But the speed of the current was found, from eight o'clock until one in the morning, to be (no figures) to the (no direction), and from one o'clock until five, (no figures) to the (no direction).

1803-06-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-sixth, 15 June 1803, the winds were SSE in the morning, which obliged us to steer east after getting under sail. The breeze was light at first, but it then became fairly strong and we were even forced to take two reefs in our topsails. The eastward tack which we had to hold made us lose sight of the land, and at noon it could be seen only from the mastheads. Wind and current made the sea very rough. From the moment we weighed until noon the soundings had been very regular, between 35 and 36 fathoms, and we were much surprised to find only 25 at the last cast. I had given orders to go about at noon in order to close with the land, but wishing to make sure that there was no shoal ahead of us to the east, I held the same course for half an hour to see whether the bottom would deepen or shoal. Having then found it 37, we went about and passed for the second time over the ground where we had found only 25 fathoms, which lasted no more than another half hour, after which we had 32 fathoms. At 3 o'clock the bottom was still 32. It appears that there is at this spot a fairly considerable rise in the bottom, but one of small extent.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 59' 25", and the longitude by timekeeper No. 35 placed us in 125° 58' 46".
In the afternoon it continued to blow a fresh breeze until about two o'clock, but from that time on they kept decreasing and the sea went down in proportion. After sunset, the winds holding up enough to stem the current, which then seemed to us to be setting to the north-west, we did not
(anchor) but continued on the southward tack towards the west until nine o'clock, when, reckoning ourselves not far from the land, we took the eastward tack towards the north and held it until three o'clock. When we went about the first time, the sounding was 24 fathoms, mud bottom, as we had almost always had it until then.
During the night the weather was fine, though hazy on the horizon, and the breeze moderate.

1803-06-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-seventh, 16 June 1803, we expected to see as strong a breeze as the day before, since the sun had set very red the evening before and had looked the same at its rising; but we learned on this occasion that the Remarks of the old navigators are not always to be relied on, for all day long we had a pleasant and very moderate breeze. We had only to complain of the quarter of the winds, which varied little from south-east, either towards east or towards south.
In the morning the Casuarina asked to pass under our stern, which was granted. Her commander then begged me to send him a boat and to receive on board a man of his crew whom he considered very ill and even in danger. I sent for him at once and he was put in the sick bay, which was growing from day to day without our knowing to what to attribute the cause.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 20' 30" and our longitude was 125° 47' 5", so that we had lost to the westward what we had gained to the southward. We went about at the same time and took the eastward tack towards the north, waiting for the winds to allow us a more direct course.
During the evening the winds were exactly the same as in the morning, but lighter, which made us hope that we should have them from the west or south-west towards the end of the day and during the night, but nothing of the kind happened. About six o'clock they did indeed shift to east-north-east and made us change tacks, but they were so light that, as the current was carrying us swiftly to the north-west, we were obliged to let go a kedge in 22 fathoms, mud bottom.
During the night it was calm. The current seemed to us to have a steady direction from south-south-east to south-east. The ship scarcely changed her heading, or at least very little, and her greatest speed was, according to the log, one knot two tenths; the soundings varied between 22 and 24 fathoms.

1803-06-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-eighth, 17 June 1803, at about three in the morning, we had a light air from west-south-west to south-west. We got under sail at five o'clock, steering south towards the east, but the wind did not long allow us to hold that course. Shortly after sunrise they shifted to south and then to south-east by east, which obliged us to steer east towards the north until noon, when we took the southward tack again. During the morning the breeze was moderate, but very strong tide-rips were felt so often that the ship would scarcely answer her helm.
At noon we observed the latitude 14° 8' 40", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 126° 4' 21", so that we had gained to the eastward that day very nearly what we had lost to the southward.
In the afternoon we did not have, as we had expected, the breeze from the west or south-west. The winds held constantly in the quarter from south-east by east to east-south-east, which obliged us to keep the offshore tack, all the more so as the bottom was shoaling rapidly and we were already in 15 fathoms, although very far from the land, which we could nevertheless still see clearly.
At sunset the land in sight extended from south 85° west to south 5° east. From the mastheads an island could be seen, with a rock near it, to the south-south-east.
At about half past eight, being in a dead calm and seeing that the current was carrying us briskly to the north-west, we anchored on a bottom of mud mixed with small pebbles. At midnight the winds shifted to south-south-east, a fresh breeze, and made us drag our anchor. The bell was rung at once and we got under way. No officer appeared on deck, and the only ones present were the two midshipmen Baudin and Debrévedent. For the rest of the night it blew a fresh breeze and the winds varied from south-south-east to south-east by east. We kept between 16 and 24 fathoms of water on a very uneven bottom.

1803-06-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twenty-ninth, 18 June 1803, the winds shifted to east-south-east, a strong breeze. We took the southward tack again. At sunrise the land in sight bore from south 75° west to south 11° east. The breeze held all morning, with no sign of a wind from the westward for the afternoon. The bottom was still uneven, between 24 and 18 fathoms.
At noon the observed latitude was 14° 23' 49" and our longitude was 126° 8' 25". The winds varied little in the afternoon and the bottom was even more irregular than we had had it in the morning. We went about after the observation of the sun, our head being towards a bank awash, on which the sea did not break, but from its very yellow colour it was easy to see that there was very little water over it. The bottom was then 15 fathoms and mud.
At sunset a piece of land which seemed to me to be an island, and which had been reported as such on the preceding days, bore from me east 80° south.
For the night we took the offshore tack. The wind was moderate and often light until midnight, but then so strong a breeze came up from east to east-south-east that we were obliged to take a second reef in our topsails, keeping close-hauled on the northward tack towards the east. The sky, though fine, was very hazy all round the horizon. The bottom during the night was between 18 and 22 fathoms, almost always mud and good for anchoring.

1803-06-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
The thirtieth, 19 June 1803, in the morning, the winds being still the same with no sign of change, I continued on the eastward tack towards the north. During the morning it went on blowing a strong breeze, but it fell away as the sun gained strength, which was quite contrary to my expectation, for I expected to see it increase and perhaps to be obliged to lie to. The sea had
already become very rough and the ship was labouring in it.
At noon we observed the latitude 13° 52' 29" and our longitude was 126° 32' 0".
The winds being still at south-east and varying only as far as east-south-east, almost calm in the afternoon, I did not change course, in order to try to work up as far to the east as possible so as to improve the south-south-west tack when the wind should allow us to take it. But the breeze was so slight in the morning that the current carried us violently to the north, as we could easily judge by the lead and the ship's drift.
What we had experienced until then of the violence of the currents and of the constancy of the winds in the quarter from south-east to east-south-east, since we had been deep in the bend that the coast makes here, showed me that it (is) impossible, or at least very difficult, to get into it coming from the west. And accordingly I continued to work up to the north, and above all to the east, as far as I could, preferring to retrace my steps once I should have reached the coast between 13 and 12 degrees of latitude.
At sunset the ship would scarcely answer her helm, although we were making two knots, and went only sideways. From eight o'clock until midnight the breeze was fairly steady, but then it came on to blow hard and we again had to take a second reef in the topsails; it continued so for the rest of the night. The bottom over which we sailed was between 24 and 29 fathoms, mud less soft than that of the preceding days.

1803-06-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
The first, 20 June 1803, Messidor, in the morning, the winds followed the pattern they had taken for the last two days; that is to say, they began at night between ten o'clock and midnight and kept increasing until about eleven o'clock the next morning. After that they died away gradually, so that at sunset it was almost calm.
I was much surprised to see them follow this pattern, and I am still convinced that it is merely accidental, since it is so contrary to the one they follow in every other country and in the same latitudes. Time will show whether it is a constant rule, which I should much regret. The breezes in the middle of the night, which everywhere else passes in calm, were so fresh that they obliged us to take two reefs in the topsails. And since in places where the water is not deep the sea rises quickly, this, together with the sail we had to carry in order to keep the Casuarina with us, contributed not a little to giving us a great deal of leeway, increased still further by the currents. And so we had every day very large differences between the dead reckoning and the distance actually run.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 9' 38", and the longitude by No. 35 placed us in 127° 2' 54".
