In the afternoon the weather was fine and the wind almost calm. As they were from the eastward, we were forced to keep the northward tack, which we held until nine in the evening, then taking the southward tack with very variable winds at east-north-east. The bottom had deepened considerably and we were in 40 fathoms. During the night, which was fine and almost calm, it shoaled to 34. We did not have the strong breezes of the previous days, and I hope ( ! ) that the new moon will bring us back, with the fine weather, the south-west and west winds that we should be glad to see return.
(() an exclamation mark has been inserted at this point, with the words "and I hope" underlined.)

1803-06-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
The second, 21 June 1803, the breeze was very moderate and did not freshen either at sunrise or when the sun had gained strength. The winds being at east, variable to east-north-east, we continued on our southerly course, making what easting we could, or as much as the winds allowed.
At eight o'clock we were still in 30 fathoms of water, but at ten there were no more than twenty-two, and at noon 21. I was astonished ! () at so sudden a shoaling and attributed the cause to some rise in the bottom, such as we had already met with several times. According to my charts I still reckoned myself at a fair distance from the land, and so believed that we were still far off it.
At noon the observed latitude was 13° 35' 29", and our longitude was only 127° 5' 13", which gave very little progress to the eastward when compared with that of the day before.
In the afternoon the winds gained a little strength and drew round imperceptibly towards the north. We steered east. At three o'clock the lookouts reported (land) ahead of us, which did not fail to surprise me; for granting that the chart of the Dépôt had placed the northern extremity of the land in the same way as that of the point lying to the south of Timor, which we had found to be placed more than two degrees too far west, it followed that this other part of the coast must be affected by the same difference, which in all likelihood will not be the case, since we now have the land in sight.
At four o'clock we clearly made out the coast from the deck, and at five we were no more than two leagues from it at most. It presents a very uniform appearance, lower than that seen on the previous days and without any landmark, except for the fires which could be seen in various places and which were fairly large. The bottom was then between fifteen and sixteen fathoms, very fine grey sand mixed with a little mud.
As night was coming on, we bore up to east-north-east; the bottom not deepening, we headed north-east. The winds were then at south-west, very light. As it was not my intention to anchor, at seven o'clock I had the ship steered north, the direction the coast should take !**. We were proceeding under all sail, sounding as we went, over a fairly regular bottom between 15 and 16 fathoms.
But at a quarter to nine, the wind having failed us entirely, we let go a kedge in 14 fathoms, bottom of very fine, muddy sand. As several fires could be seen on the coast, it was easy to perceive that the current was carrying us to the north-west.
During the night it was calm until about two (o'clock), when a light air came up from the eastward. According to the observations made, the strength of the current, with the ship swung head to south-east, was one mile 1 tenth, and with her swung head to NE, 1 mile 3 tenths. The level of the sea fell by one fathom and rose by only the same amount.
(* followed by an exclamation mark, ** another exclamation mark added in a different manner)

1803-06-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
The third of Messidor, 22 June 1803, in the morning, the winds being from east to south-east, we got under sail at five o'clock and steered close-hauled. About nine o'clock they shifted to east-north-east and obliged us to make more northing than we should have wished. The sounding, which had been 14 fathoms when we weighed, deepened by degrees to eighteen. The land, which in the morning bore from SE to E. NE, was lost to sight on this course, and we did not see it again until the afternoon.
At that time the observed latitude was 13° 27' 48", and the longitude by our timekeeper was 127° 18' 28". All morning we had had a hazy sky and a limited horizon.
The calm, which began at about eleven in the morning, lasted until two in the afternoon. We then had a light air from the north-east which did not last long. At six o'clock they shifted to the north and were no less calm than they had been at north-east. Nevertheless, with the help of the current, we closed with the land, which at sunset bore east-south-east, at about six leagues' distance. All the part of the coast we had seen until then is low and very even, without any particular point that might serve as a landmark.
According to the lookouts' report, they had sighted a sandbank above water, bearing south-east of us, which they assured us they could see quite distinctly and from which, by their estimate, we were no more than two leagues off. As I was very ill that day, I could not see for myself how matters stood. I gave orders to the officer who is to replace me in the event of my death to anchor at eight o'clock if the wind was calm or did not allow us to steer north, the reported bank bearing north-east according to the report made to me. At seven o'clock, the wind being calm, we anchored in 18 fathoms, on a sandy bottom like the one we had had on the preceding days.
The rest of the night passed without incident. The strength of the current was much the same as the day before and its direction from north to north-west. There was little variation in the rise and fall of the water.

1803-06-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fourth, 23 June 1803, we got under sail at four in the morning, steering north-north-east while waiting for daylight, with only fifteen fathoms of water. At sunrise we sighted the coast, which bore from north 33° east to south 32 east. This stretch of coast seemed to us to form several coves, some of which appeared deep. In the northern part of the land we saw a second one, which we judged to be an island from its distance from the mainland; or, if it is joined to it, the land between must be so low that it cannot be made out from the mastheads. Although we were fairly close to it, this whole coast is, moreover, extremely low and can scarcely be seen at three leagues' distance and in 14 fathoms of water.
The sky was finer that day than usual and the sun hot, which we had not felt for several days.
At noon the observed latitude was 16° 23' 15". No hour angle was taken, hazy clouds having hidden the horizon and the sun from us all the evening, whereas the sky had been very fine in the morning. At the close of day the land in sight extended from south to east 28° north.
At eight o'clock, the wind having fallen to a dead calm and the current making us drift to (the) north-west with some violence, to judge by the log, we anchored in 15 fathoms, bottom of coarse gravel and broken shells mixed with a little mud.
During the night the calm continued until three in the morning, when a light breeze came up from the east-south-east. The weather remained overcast and hazy, and yet the sea became somewhat swelly, an effect no doubt produced by some current or other.
During the night, according to the observations made, the current had little speed and did not rise above 6 tenths of a knot to the north-west and north-north-west. The tide having turned at about three in the morning, they set to the south-south-east. The height of the water was much the same.

1803-06-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
The fifth, 24 June 1803, Messidor, we weighed at five in the morning, with the winds from south-south-east to south-east, a pleasant breeze. We stood north-north-east until eleven o'clock, with the land in sight to the north-east by north and stretching, as far as we could see, to the south-east by south. This land, like that of the day before, was low and could scarcely be seen at three leagues' distance, although we were in between fifteen and eighteen fathoms of water.
During the morning the sky was fine and cloudless, though hazy on the horizon. At noon the observed latitude was 12° 44' 56", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 127° 43' 8".
From eleven o'clock we had made our course a little more easterly so as not to lose sight of the land, but in the evening the winds, coming round to east by north and then to north-east, obliged us to stand away from it. As it was calm for the greater part of the evening, we made little way, and at
sunset, the currents carrying us to the north-west, we lost sight of it, and at six o'clock could see nothing but a bright, brilliant fire, which bore south 30° west.
As the weather had become overcast and there was an appearance of wind for the night, I remained under sail until ten o'clock, when the calm obliged me to anchor, the bottom continuing to deepen. We then had nineteen fathoms, mud bottom, which must must (sic), according to our previous remarks, have placed us a fair distance from the coast.
During the night, if the wind was not entirely calm, it was at least very light, from the quarter between south-south-west and west. The currents were so little perceptible by the log during the night that it was not thought worth taking account of them. The soundings, however, decreased by two fathoms, which was attributed to unevenness of the bottom rather than to the tide. The sky during the night was constantly damp and hazy.

1803-06-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
The sixth, 25 June 1803, having got under sail, we steered north-east to close with the land we had lost sight of the evening before, and from which, however, we could not be very far off, judging by the fires we had seen at the beginning of the night. Nevertheless we did not see it at daybreak, nor even about ten o'clock, although the bottom was only 15 fathoms.
At noon it was reported by the lookouts, who sighted it from the mastheads, and by our dead reckoning we could be three or four leagues from it at most. At the same moment the observed latitude was 12° 25' 44", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 127° 52' 37". The weather was then fine and the wind almost calm from the south-east.
In the afternoon they shifted to the north and varied as far as west-south-west without gaining much strength, so that we made little way.
At four o'clock the land extended, as far as we could see, from east-south-east to south-east by south. Like that of the previous days, it was very low and, (moreover), not easy to make out. We remained under sail during the night to take advantage of the wind if it should set in, as appearances seemed to promise. It did in fact blow a little, and we held the northward tack towards the west with north-east winds, the bottom continuing to deepen. The sky during the night was, as usual, hazy and covered with clouds, but the breeze freshened a little in the night.

1803-06-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
The seventh, 26 June 1803, at four o'clock in the morning, the winds having shifted to north-north-east, we went about onto the northward tack. It blew a pleasant breeze in the morning, compared with that of the previous days. We were much surprised at sunrise to hear the lookouts report land to the north-north-west, especially in view of the course we had made during the night. I thought at first that they were mistaken and that what had been taken for land was some cloud
on the horizon that looked like it. But having had it examined more attentively, I found the report confirmed.
At eight o'clock we (sighted) the land perfectly from the deck. It presented itself to us as much higher than that seen on the previous days. And in several places elevated points could be made out which, in case of need, may serve as landmarks.
The sky, though tolerably fine, was overcast and laden with hazy clouds which often hid the coast from us, although we were not then more than three leagues from it.
We had no observed latitude that day, the sky being too overcast, and at noon we took bearings of the land, the northernmost part of which bore north 20° west and the southernmost north 70° east. In the part of the coast in sight several points could be made out, forming between them coves of greater or lesser depth.
In the afternoon the winds were extremely variable. From east-north-east they shifted to north and north-west, accompanied by rain and fairly strong gusts. The sky, which had not looked well since the morning, became dark and laden with very black clouds, which towards the middle of the evening brought us the wind at south-west. We took advantage of it to run along the coast, and after (rounding) the point which, relative to our position, trended from north towards west, we resumed our course north by east to examine other land which then bore north-east of us; but the sky became so overcast, dark and heavy that at the close of day we could make out nothing.
The appearance of bad weather for the night made me take a second reef in the topsails, and even if it had not come on, I should have been forced to do so in order not to lose the Casuarina, which was far astern.
At the beginning of the night the weather was squally, the sky overcast and threatening rain. We were steering west towards the south to stand off from the land, and I intended to hold that direction until midnight and then take one to the north towards the east. The bottom on this course was between twenty-seven and 30 fathoms until ten o'clock, when we found no more than twenty. The course was then made more southerly and the bottom deepened to thirty-two fathoms. But at midnight it was no more than twenty. Not knowing what such uneven and disproportionate soundings within so short a time could signify. With our head north towards the east, the soundings taken every hour varied no less, but they were deep, that is to say over twenty fathoms. We continued on this tack until four in the morning, at which time we took the one to the south towards the east, on which they were equally irregular. We held it until daylight. Although the bottom was almost continually shoaling, which did not fail to weary and trouble me, having spent the greater part of the night on deck and being in poor health, attacked once again by a spitting of blood, which had now recurred for the third time since our departure from Port Jackson.

1803-06-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
The eighth, 27 June 1803, at six in the morning, I expected all the more to sight the land as the lead now brought up only 18 and 19 fathoms of water. We then steered north towards the east while waiting for sunrise. The weather was not fine and even looked rather threatening. Nevertheless, at sunrise we did not sight the land, although our horizon was reasonably extensive. On this course, the bottom continuing to deepen, and even very rapidly, we stood on, hugging the wind as closely as possible.
During the morning the weather cleared, and we were surprised to see it change so quickly. At noon the observed latitude was 11° 20' 32", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 127° 29' 19". This longitude confirmed our remarks of the previous night on the direction of the currents, which, judging by the tide-rips we met with, must have been carrying us violently to the south-west.
In the afternoon the weather continued fine, but the winds shifted to the east. We had to steer more to the north than I should have wished. At two o'clock, although we had still not sighted the coast from the mastheads, we nevertheless saw very distinctly from the deck two columns of smoke rising from the land. One bore south-east and the other south-east by east. During the evening we continued to steer north, making what easting the winds allowed. The lead during the evening always gave a great depth and seemed, by that alone, to indicate to us that we were leaving the land far behind.
At the beginning of the night the weather became very cloudy and the winds fell light. The sea, which until then had been tolerably smooth, became swelly, which led me to believe that we had rounded the northern point of the western shore of the Bay of Van Diemen.
At midnight the sky, which had been clouding over since sunset, turned to rain and squalls. At first they brought us little wind but rain in abundance, as heavy as that which falls in great downpours. About two o'clock the squalls were not only rainy but also accompanied by winds which obliged us to lower our topsails. The first ones came to us with winds from the east, but the next gave us winds winds (sic) from south-south-east to south-east and allowed us to steer east-north-east. As we were sounding every hour, between three and four o'clock we went from forty fathoms to eighteen. So quick and rapid a shoaling made me fear the neighbourhood of some reef or shoal, such as those Arrowsmith lays down on his chart, although we had passed well beyond the latitude he assigns to them; I at once had the ship steered north-west, and within an hour the bottom went from 18 to 36 fathoms. We then came round by degrees to a northerly course, and the bottom kept deepening, so that at six o'clock we were in 48 fathoms.
These irregularities of the bottom, on a coast to which almost every sea chart gives a different position, are very disquieting for navigators, and those who come after us will no doubt experience them likewise, until these waters are better known and determined. Which, in all likelihood, we shall be unable to do if the weather and the winds do not favour us more.

1803-06-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
The ninth, 28 June 1803, in the morning, being in forty-six fathoms of water (at) sunrise, and having (no mention), we resumed our course east-north-east with a pleasant breeze from south-south-east, variable to south-east. The bottom kept deepening until seven o'clock, when it was sixty-four fathoms. At eight o'clock, as the ship was making good way, we found no bottom at 30 and consequently continued on our course. But at nine o'clock we found ourselves, to our astonishment, in 18 fathoms. And the sea being smooth, although it was blowing a good breeze, we bore away two points. Nevertheless we shoaled by another fathom. We bore away again and it deepened in proportion as we advanced northward. What had just happened to us leads me to believe that we were following the edge of the bank which the Dutch have marked on the chart they have given of this part of the coast, and which the others have suppressed. As that chart also places the northern coast of the western land of the Bay of Van Diemen further north than any other sea chart known to us, my opinion would be that it (is) more correctly placed. The extent the Dutch chart gives to the bank along which we have been coasting does not allow the coast to be seen, since one must stand too far off it in order to round it, and it may be presumed that the other navigators who came after Tasman took some other point for the northern one of this part. Otherwise they must have come upon this bank.
However that may be, the weather was not fine in the morning and looked no better for the afternoon. It blew a good breeze and we took two reefs in the topsails, which did not prevent us from losing sight of the Casuarina, for whom we then had to wait, lying to for two hours.
At noon the observed latitude was 27° 10° 25' 5", and the longitude by the timekeeper placed us in 127° 30' 35".
In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze from the south-east, and as we had rounded the northern point of the bank laid down on Valentin's chart, we once more resumed our course east-north-east, the bottom then being fifty-five fathoms, fine sand and mud. This course was was (sic) held until the next day.
The weather was fairly bad during the night, which was dark with strong gusts.

1803-06-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
The tenth, 29 June 1803, in the morning, the weather was even worse than the day before. The winds varied from south-east to south-south-east, a strong breeze, and the sea became heavy, but the squalls were less frequent than during the night. We sounded several times in the morning without finding bottom at 60 and 50 fathoms.
At noon we had no sight of the sun, which did not show itself at all the whole day. By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in 9° 45' 57" of latitude, 128° 13' 44" of longitude. We then took the southward tack towards the west, so as to keep between the ninth and tenth degrees of latitude until the weather should turn fine, which did not seem very near, judging by the state of the atmosphere and of the sea. The barometer, however, varied little.
During the night the weather continued bad and the sea heavy. We held the southward tack until midnight, when we took the northward one.

1803-06-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
The eleventh, 30 June 1803, brought us no change in the weather, whose state resembled what it presents to the eye on the worst winter's day in Europe. Continually laden with fog and with great clouds, dark, black and thick, it seemed all but certain that we were going to have some gale. And I decided to wait in the waters where I then was until it had passed, before pushing further to the east. At ten o'clock we took the southward tack, which I held until nightfall, when we resumed the northward one.
During the morning the topgallant sails were unrigged and we made our preparations for the bad weather, which seemed to me inevitable and which indeed did not fail to come on during the night, obliging us to spend it lying to. The wind was not, however, very violent, and we could easily have carried our four courses and topsails, with all reefs in the topsails, had we not had to wait for the Casuarina, who could not carry hers without straining her vessel too much. There were, nevertheless, some heavy but short-lived gusts. Towards the end of the night, the weather having turned to rain, the wind was less strong, but the sea was no less rough.
As we did not see the sun at noon, our estimated latitude was 9° 41' 33" and the longitude 128° 18' 44". However, from two altitudes of the sun taken in the afternoon, at moments when the sun showed itself very indistinctly, the latitude deduced from them for the moment of noon was found to be 9° 43' 23" and the longitude 128° 17' 12". These results seem to me too doubtful to place much confidence in them.

1803-07-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
The twelfth, 1 July 1803, in the morning, the weather was even worse than on the preceding days; the rain was almost continuous, and the gusts began again and lasted without interruption until about ten o'clock, when they became less frequent. From half past six we had been lying to on the southward tack so as not to be carried too far north of the latitude in which I wished to keep until the bad weather had passed. The main topsail was also set, close-reefed, (so that) the ship's falling off should be less considerable. At eleven o'clock, the wind seeming inclined to drop, we set the mainsail and foresail. The main topsail was furled a second time, as with that sail we were leaving the Casuarina too far behind.
At noon, the sun having appeared between the clouds, we took it at about noon, and the result placed us in (no figures). This latitude, though doubtful, must differ little from the one we should have had if the weather had been fine.
By our dead reckoning we placed ourselves in (no figures) and in (no figures) of longitude.
In the evening the weather was less thick and the clouds began to grow lighter. Those which, being dark and gloomy, gave us a fine drizzle
when the winds drove them across our track. We continued on the southward tack towards the west until six o'clock, when we took the eastward one towards the north for the night. During the twenty-four hours we sounded several times on either tack without finding bottom at 50 and 60 fathoms. The drift was too great to veer out more line.
During the night the weather, which had cleared a little towards the close of day, again became dark and rainy, accompanied by squalls and gales with only very brief intermissions.

1803-07-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
The thirteenth, 2 July 1803, the sky, though still laden with clouds and overcast, took on a better appearance in the morning, and it seemed that we were about to have a change in our favour. We needed it all the more because the weather we had had for four days was causing the ship such violent motion that all our livestock, which I so much desired to preserve for the benefit of France, were greatly distressed by it, and particularly the emus, which had to be force-fed so that they should not die of hunger. The loss of these animals will certainly not be made good by the little geographical knowledge that it appears we shall be able to gain of the part of the coast that remains for us to visit, and I am resolved, if the weather does not turn fine after the full moon, to make sail for the Isle of France [Mauritius] rather than lose them altogether.
The sun having appeared for a few moments in the morning, a very doubtful hour angle was taken, and the same was true of the latitude at noon. Nevertheless the result of these observations, preferable to the dead reckoning, placed us in 9° 53' 40" of latitude and 127° 47' 53" of longitude. By dead reckoning we were in 9° 44' 54" and 128° 18' 6" of longitude.
During the evening the sky again became covered with clouds and haze. It blew a strong breeze, but unevenly and in gusts. The winds were variable from east-south-east to south-east, which made us keep the southward tack towards the west. At seven in the evening we went about, and during the night the course was made a little more easterly, the winds having drawn round towards the south. The breeze was much less strong than during the day, but the sea did not cease to be rough and swelly.

1803-07-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, 3 July 1803, the weather was finer than usual. The sky, although cloudy, had taken on a good appearance, and I still counted upon a change in our favour at the full moon. When the sun had gained a little strength, the winds shifted to the south-east, variable towards the east. During the morning we stood on the southern tack towards the west, keeping as close to the wind as possible.
The sea sea (sic), having become calmer, nevertheless remained swelling, and a ground swell which showed little at the surface of the water made the ship labour very violently, although it was blowing a good breeze and she was well steadied by her sails, with two reefs in each topsail.
Having had good observations in the morning and an exact latitude at noon, we found ourselves in 9° 59' 18" and 128° 9' 52" of longitude, so that in six days we had gained almost nothing to the east, and it seemed useless to persist any longer in trying to work up in that direction unless the winds changed. This seemed likely enough, from the course they had followed since we had been north of the land and, as it were, in the middle of the channel which separates New Holland from the other lands lying to the north of it, between the eighth and ninth degrees of latitude. It is probably to this trend of the coast in that quarter that one must attribute the different course the winds follow south of the tenth degree, where we never lacked breezes from south to south-west and even from the west.
During the morning it blew a good breeze, but it was less strong in the afternoon. The winds varied little, from south-east to east-south-east, until sunset, when they drew nearer to the south. After closing with the Casuarina, we took the eastern tack towards the north. That vessel contributed not a little to our heavy leeway, not only through the little sail we had to carry in order to wait for her, but also through the distance we were obliged to run to the west every evening to close with her, which I estimate at two leagues a day. In spite of all these inconveniences, which did not fail to put me in a very ill humour, I could not bring myself to abandon her and order her to make for the Isle of France [Mauritius], foreseeing that I should have an essential need of her if I afterwards succeeded in reaching the Gulf of Carpentaria.
During the night, misty and damp clouds made themselves felt and seemed to announce that the sky would not be very fine the next day.

1803-07-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, 4 July 1803, the sky was fairly clear though cloudy, but our horizon was laden with thick, misty vapours which greatly limited its extent. At six o'clock, the breeze then being light, we found bottom in 70 fathoms. I think we should have found it at much the same depth in the soundings of the past days had the heavy leeway of the ship, the high sea and the wind allowed us to veer out as much line.
At sunrise the breeze freshened, but it did not follow the same course as on the past days. The winds, which between seven and eight in the morning drew round towards the east, remained south-east, variable to south-east by east, until the middle of the day, when they came more from the south.
At noon the latitude was observed as 9° 43' 21", and our longitude proved to be 128° 41' 19", so that this time we had advanced a little to the east.
In the afternoon the winds continued variable from south-south-east to south, and the sea remained high and swelling, which gave us no promise of an early end to the strong breezes we had been experiencing for several days.
The night passed without incident; we held on the eastern tack towards the north, taking the precaution of sounding every two hours, without finding bottom at 60 or 45 fathoms. The sky remained damp and misty, but the winds were less strong than during the day.

1803-07-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, 5 July 1803, the winds having allowed us to come closer to an easterly course, we took advantage of it and regained heart, in the hope that they would end by becoming, if not entirely favourable, at least fair enough for us not to lose on one tack what we gained on the other.
Although the state of the atmosphere remained the same, the sea was less rough and the gusts more bearable than on the preceding days.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 55' 40", and our longitude was 129° 44' 44", which gave us a large difference from our dead reckoning by the courses run. But we were far from complaining of it, since we found we had advanced nearly a degree to the east, which had not happened to us for a long time.
During the evening we held on the northern tack towards the east until six o'clock, when, not wishing to go further north in our longitude, I had the ship put on the southern tack towards the west. The winds being moderate from the south-east, we held on it through the night, and we found no bottom at 50 or 70 fathoms. For the rest, the weather was fairly fine though cloudy and very damp.

1803-07-06.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, 6 July 1803, as soon as it was light we resumed the tack to the north of east, and the winds served us a little in the morning, in that they sometimes came round as far as south. But this was only fleeting. At sunrise the sky had a very bad appearance, being laden with dark, thick clouds at every point of the horizon. I expected we should have some squalls in the morning, but I was mistaken, for as the sun gained strength the clouds dispersed and the weather became fine.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 58' 49", and our longitude proved to be 130° 2' 23". So we had gained very little to the east in the 24 hours, and it appears that the night's course had carried us more to the west than the dead reckoning indicated, or that the currents which had favoured us the day before had turned contrary, or against us, when we took the southern tack.
In the afternoon the weather remained fine, but the south-south-east breeze having increased, the sea quickly rose. Towards evening the sky clouded over, and there was little likelihood of the weather staying fine during the night. We held on the eastern tack towards the north until midnight until midnight, when the winds allowed us to stand for some time east towards the south. The breeze was moderate and the weather was not bad in spite of appearances; only the sea was high and rough, which caused us a great deal of leeway.

1803-07-07.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighteenth, 7 July 1803, in the morning, although the sky was dark and overcast, the weather was not at all unpleasant; nevertheless we had from time to time some fairly strong gusts from the south-south-east, the point to which the winds had returned.
[5V p. 172 During the morning I was informed that several of our quadrupeds and emus were very ill. We could attribute this only to the violent and repeated motion of the heavy sea, which did not leave them a moment's rest. This news was all the more disagreeable to me as I saw myself on the point of losing them after a care that should have earned them a happier fate. As the emus refused to eat, we made them take food by force, opening their beaks and introducing balls of rice paste into their stomachs. They were given wine and sugar, as were the kangaroos that were unwell, and although I was very short of these same things for myself, I should be very glad to have gone without them for their sake, if they can help to restore them to health.
I suffered that day a spitting of blood more considerable than those which had already occurred. I did not know to what to attribute it, for this complaint had left me some eight days before and I believed myself rid of it for some time. Whether as a consequence of this illness or from some other cause, this spitting of blood was accompanied by such weakness in all my limbs that I was forced to take to my bed, and I did not find much relief there.
At noon the latitude was observed as 8° 26' 33", and the longitude was 131° 11' 14". These observations are very doubtful, for the weather was little suited to obtaining good ones.
In the afternoon, the winds having shifted to the south-east, we went about to take the south-south-west tack. This course was held until eight o'clock, when we hove to in order to wait for the Casuarina, which did not rejoin us until ten. As it was necessary either to send her away if I persisted in trying to reach the entrance of the Gulf of Carpentaria, or to give up reaching it if I kept her, I decided to take the route for the Isle of France [Mauritius], and ordered her to steer south-west by west, which I took myself. It was not without sorrow that I resolved upon this course. A thousand reasons ought even to have made me take it sooner. But without going into them all, I shall confine myself to saying that we had only a month's biscuit left at six ounces a man, and two months' water, allowing for what our birds and quadrupeds consumed. Twenty men were in their cots, several suffering from dysentery and the others unfit for duty from serious venereal diseases caught at Timor, and there was no one to replace me. The Casuarina, which I have never been able to make keep ahead, whatever way I went about it, and which is the sole cause of my not having reached that gulf long ago &c. &c. &c.
This resolution taken, I steered to pass through the channel which separates Roti from Timor, so as not to be thwarted, in passing south of the former island, by the west and north-west winds which I was almost certain of meeting there, having in my favour the experience of two voyages in these waters.
I leave it to be imagined what effect this change of course had, for no one expected it, since no one had ever known either where I was going or what I meant to do (). Throughout the whole voyage several of those who spent the entire night on deck were often at the compass, for fear of being deceived in what they had been told, and this night was the one when there were the most people on deck, although the weather was not fine.
() added, again in the same foreign hand: "nor what I was doing"

1803-07-08.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the nineteenth, 8 July 1803, we continued on the south-west by west course, and the Casuarina was no less troublesome to us with the wind free than she had been a burden to us close-hauled. In order not to abandon her, we had to keep two reefs in the topsails, haul up the foresail and constantly carry the mizzen topsail. Yet she had all her sails set, except for one reef she carried in her main topsail. The breeze was strong and the sea high.
At noon the latitude was observed as 9° 10' 44", and the longitude was 129° 37' 52", quite as doubtful as those of the preceding days.
By the observed latitude, we continued on the same course until eight o'clock in the evening, when I took a westerly one, which was followed during the night. Being then hove to in order to wait for the Casuarina, I had a sounding taken, and we found bottom in 85 fathoms. The night passed without incident. The sky was very cloudy, damp and dark.
As it had been noticed the day before that the sugared wine given to our sick animals had done them good and that they had regained a little strength, they continued to be given the same quantity twice a day.

1803-07-09.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twentieth, 9 July 1803, we had a strong breeze from east-south-east to east, which quickly made the sea high and swelling, and during the morning we met with heavy squalls accompanied by violent gusts and rain.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures), and the longitude by our timekeepers was, for No. 35, (no figure).
In the afternoon the weather was finer than it had been in the morning, but the sea continued high, swelling and rough; the winds varied little, from east to east-south-east.
The night passed without incident and the breeze died down. We continued on the course south 78° west, keeping to the pace of the Casuarina.

1803-07-10.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-first, 10 July 1803, the sky was fine and clear and the sea became smooth, although the winds were much the same in strength as the day before; but the breeze, which had freshened at daybreak, was steady and not in gusts as on most of the preceding days.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figure), and by our longitude we reckoned ourselves in (no figure).
In the afternoon we took the course south 84° 30' west, which we followed until the next day. At sunset the horizon became laden with clouds and damp vapours; nevertheless the night was fine and was troublesome only for the great dampness that made itself felt. At midnight we sounded without finding bottom at a hundred fathoms.

1803-07-11.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-second, 11 July 1803, the weather remained fine and the winds varied from east to south-east, a pleasant breeze. We crowded sail to make the land, from which we could not be be (sic) far, according to the rate of our timekeepers.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures), and our longitude was (no figures) for No. 35 and (no figures) for No. 31.
In the afternoon the weather remained fine, and at about half past five in the evening, the horizon, which had been laden with clouds in the south-east quarter, having cleared, we had a good sight of the land of Timor, whose most prominent points extended from north 71 west to north 66 west. The other parts of the coast were too hazy to be made out clearly. We continued to stand in for the land until eight in the evening, when we trimmed our sails close-hauled on the southern tack, which was held until midnight, when we took the northern tack towards the east to wait for daylight. During the night the sky, though cloudy, was fine, and the dampness less than the day before.

1803-07-12.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-third, 12 July 1803, we closed with the south coast of Timor, which we ran along during the morning at a short distance, with very light winds from the east-south-east quarter, variable to east.
At noon, by a later observation of the sun, our latitude was (no figures), and the longitude of the timekeepers placed us, by No. 35, in (no figures) and, by No. 31, in (no figures). But it seemed to us, from the sight of the land we thought we recognised, that the rate of No. 35 placed us further west than we really were, since we had not yet sighted the island of Roti, which we should have seen had its rate been regular.
During the morning evening, we steered along the direction of the coast relative to the position of the ship. And at sunset part of the island of Roti was seen from the mastheads.
As my intention was not to enter the channel during the night, we ran along the coast only until half past seven in the evening, and then hauled close to the wind to beat about at the entrance of the channel during the night, which was fine, with the wind in brief puffs.

1803-07-13.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fourth, 13 July 1803, before daylight, we closed with the coast of Timor in order to enter the channel early, but at daybreak we found ourselves two or three leagues further from it than our dead reckoning placed me. It appears that the turn of the tide, or a more regular current, had carried us to the east on the two boards made during the night. Nevertheless, we had a perfect view of the island of Roti and shaped our course to pass through the middle of the channel, which we crossed between ten and eleven o'clock.
At noon we found we had rounded the small island that lies off the southern point of Semau, and at the same moment the latitude was observed as (no figures), and the longitude indicated by our timekeepers was, for No. 35, (no figures) and, for No. 31, (no figures).
This longitude, referred to that of Kupang, fixed by our observations at (no figures), gave a difference in longitude of (no figures) for No. 35 and of (no figures) for No. 31. So it appears that since our last departure from Timor this timekeeper had gained on its ordinary rate by (no figures), a change to which I do not know what cause to attribute, unless perhaps to the difference in the manner of winding them each noon, which in the long run may have affected its movement, this being done more or less quickly by the person now in charge of them than it was when they were in the charge of Citizen Bernier.
However that may be, when we had rounded the small island I have just spoken of, everyone expected that I was going to steer to put in at Timor a third time. For no one could conceive why I had come to seek this channel on my way to the Isle of France [Mauritius]. This route, in the opinion of all, was a very bad one, since it only prolonged our stay at sea, whereas we had many good reasons for shortening it as much as possible.
It was not to me that all these remarks were addressed, but they were the subject of the confidential conversation of our learned naval officers. I was sorry to have been informed of it, in that it convinced me more than ever that they had drawn no instruction or profit from the navigation they had already made at three different times, which ought to have taught them that south of the third degree of latitude one is certain of meeting very variable winds from north-west to south-south-west, since at the three different seasons of the year when we visited these waters we always found them in that direction, whereas north of the 12th degree they are constantly from south-east to east.
I mention this incident only to warn seamen who may later find themselves later in the same case that the route which seems the shortest is not always the one to be preferred, and that it is better to rely on experience than on the idle and ill-considered talk of young men who see only superficially or according to their scant judgment.
After rounding the small island south of Semau, we ran along the coast of the island of Roti, my intention being to pass during the night through the channel which separates it from Savu. We crowded sail in the afternoon in order to make, before nightfall, the islands lying off the western point of Roti, which we saw at sunset. Although the Casuarina was astern, I did not shorten sail to wait for her, and stood on until midnight, when, reckoning myself in the middle of the channel and abreast of Savu, I hove to to give her time to rejoin me. We spent the rest of the night there, making signals to her with lights and rockets, to which she made no reply.

1803-07-14.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-fifth, 14 July 1803, having spent half the night hove to waiting for the Casuarina, we still had no sight of her at daylight, which persuaded me that she had not continued the course she was steering at sunset, when she was in our wake at a league's distance. For had she followed it, she could not have passed us without seeing our signals, nor we without seeing her. I therefore made up my mind and, no longer counting on meeting her, we resumed our west-south-west course.
At daylight we had in sight the small island of Savu, which bore from north-west by west to north-north-west, at a distance of 4 to 5 leagues. In the course of the morning we saw the islet lying west by north of it, which I mentioned when we passed north of Savu on our first departure from Timor.
At noon the latitude was observed as 11° 6' 31", and the longitude was, by No. 35, 118° 46' 40" and, by No. 31, 119° 14' 53". The land of Savu was then seen from north 15° east to north 45° east.
During the evening the weather remained fine, and at about four in the afternoon the lookouts reported a sail ahead of us. We had no doubt that it was the Casuarina, and we crowded sail to come up with her before nightfall, without succeeding. As that vessel seemed to be heading more to the south than we were, we steered her course in the hope of joining her, but we saw nothing of her during the night, although it was fine and the view fairly wide.

1803-07-15.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-sixth, 15 July 1803, in the morning, we again sighted the vessel seen the evening before, but she was abeam of us to starboard at about two leagues' distance. Having recognised her as the Casuarina, we closed with her, and I made the signal for her to keep ahead of us from now on and to crowd sail.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 0' 58", and the longitude by No. 35 was 116° 32' 28" and by No. 31, 117° 1' 32".
Although I had ordered the Casuarina to keep ahead of us, she again dropped so far astern, even though we were carrying hardly any sail, that I was led to believe she really wished to part company, and I was confirmed in this opinion on learning that her intention was to put in at Batavia. This warning made me watch her so closely that I forbade anyone, under any pretext whatever, to lose sight of her during the night, and ordered that the course I had given should not even be followed if she departed from it to steer another, and that I should be informed, taking particular care not to pass ahead of her
Throughout the whole day we had a heavy swell from the south-west, which told us that the winds were blowing fresh in that quarter further south. The sky was very overcast during the night, and from time to time we had squalls, which were not of long duration.

1803-07-16.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-seventh, 16 July 1803, the weather turned fine again and we had a pleasant breeze from east to east-south-east, of which we made little use, having our topsails lowered on the cap most of the time in order to wait for the Casuarina.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 33' 32", and the longitude by No. 35 was 114° 31' 48" and by No. 31, 115° 2' 0". Not wishing to go further south, so as not to meet the south-west winds, I signalled a westerly course, but a mistake was made in the signal, for instead of hoisting the pendant above, it was hoisted below; this error was not noticed until about four o'clock, the Casuarina (not) steering west as we were. A fresh signal was made to her, accompanied by a shot from a swivel gun, because she had shortened sail, I know not why.
During the evening the sky was fairly fine, and we continued our course under little sail so as to keep the Casuarina always ahead and in sight. The manoeuvres of the night were the same.

1803-07-17.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-eighth, 17 July 1803, the fine weather continued and the sea was smooth; we continued to steer west. The crew, very discontented at having such fine weather without making use of it, said that as a punishment we should not fail soon to meet with some squalls, and that we would have no cause to complain of them, since it was for mere pleasure that they were being kept at sea, reduced to 6 ounces of bread a day. They were perhaps not altogether wrong to complain, but I did not wish to leave the Casuarina behind unless forced to it by some particular circumstance.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 19' 45", and the longitude by No. 35 was 112° 20' 13", that by No. 31, 112° 50' 45".
The rest of the day passed without incident, as did the night.

1803-07-18.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twenty-ninth, 18 July 1803, the weather was less fine than usual; during the morning we sometimes had squalls with rain, which were of little consequence but made the state of the sky unpleasant to look upon. Our course during these twenty-four hours was the same as on the preceding days, except for the times we had to bear away to close with the Casuarina, which rarely steered the course indicated.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 27' 40", and the longitude by No. 35 was 110° 4' 22" and for No. 31, 110° 36' 3".
In the evening the sky took on a stormy look and kept it for part of the night, without, however, giving us lightning or thunder, but only a heavy, damp and unhealthy air, which lasted until the middle of the night, when the clouds dispersed.

1803-07-19.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirtieth, 19 July 1803, the sky, without being fine, had a better appearance than the day before. Nevertheless, a thick haze encircling the whole horizon made it very narrow for us. This state of the atmosphere lasted until about ten o'clock, when the easterly breeze, having increased, widened it by dispersing for the most part the fog that had formed there.
We had the misfortune to lose one of our emus that day, dead without any sign of illness. This loss was all the greater because, on skinning it to stuff it, it was found to be a female, and among the three that remain to us there is perhaps not one.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 30' 19", and the longitude by No. 35 was 107° 28' 29", that by No. 31, 108° 1' 14".
In the evening the sky cleared entirely and we began to feel no more of the heavy south-west swell we had had for several days. The night passed without incident.

1803-07-20.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the first, 20 July 1803, we had very fine weather and a pleasant easterly breeze. We continued the westerly course, which I had decided to follow between twelve and thirteen degrees of latitude until abreast of the western point of the island of Java.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 38' 6", and the longitude of our timekeepers placed us, by No. 35, in 105° "3' 12" and, by No. 31, in 105° 36' 46".
In the afternoon the sky, which had been fine in the morning, clouded over a little before sunset, and during the night it was very cloudy, with occasional light squalls accompanied by a little rain which did not last long. But we found the sea very swelling, and a heavy south-west sea made us roll very frequently and very sharply. For the rest, nothing happened that deserves particular Remarks.

1803-07-21.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the second, 21 July 1803, the winds were very variable and unsteady in the quarter from east towards south-east. The sky was overcast for the greater part of the morning, and it was only at about eleven o'clock that the clouds began to part.
At noon the latitude was observed as 12° 44' 2", and the longitude of our timekeepers was, for No. 35, 102° 35' 0" and, for No. 31, 103° 9' 0".
At sunset After the observation of the sun, I signalled the course west by south. During the evening the sky again clouded over and had no fine appearance at several points of the horizon. As the obser officers of the watch paid little attention to carrying out what I had prescribed for keeping the Casuarina with us, they were warned that whoever that whoever, in the watch from six to eight o'clock, failed to keep her in sight, would continue that watch until he had brought her back into the prescribed position. The sky remained dark during the night and we had the breeze at east by south, blowing fresh.

1803-07-22.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the third, 22 July 1803, the sky was no finer than on the preceding days, and I was surprised to see it keep for so long a very bad appearance and a stormy disposition at several points of the horizon. The sea, still heavily swelling and raised by a great south-west sea, led one to presume that some gale must have passed from that quarter in a latitude further south than ours.
At noon we observed the latitude as 13° 13' 1", and the longitude of our timekeepers was, for No. 35,
99° 54' 45" and, for No. 31, 100° 31' 4".
In the afternoon and during the night the sky was the same as in the morning, without any sign of wishing to turn fine.

1803-07-23.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourth, 23 July 1803, there was no change in the state of the atmosphere, and I was truly astonished to see the sky in these waters so long overcast and laden with stormy and unhealthy vapours, which did nothing for the recovery of our sick, who then numbered twenty.
At noon the latitude was observed as 13° 44' 43", and the longitude of our timekeepers was, for No. 35, 97° 51' 44" and, for No. 31, 98° 29' 36".
In the afternoon the weather was fairly fine, though dark and overcast, until sunset. But then the whole circle of the horizon became wrapped in thick mist, which until eight in the evening brought us much damp and at times rain, but little wind. It was not so during the rest of the night. From nine o'clock the lightning announced the approach of thunder, and the squalls began to make themselves felt. At first there was little to fear from the strength of their wind, but they brought such quantities of rain that we were drenched on every side. Between eleven and midnight a squall passed over which were (sic) making the winds vary as far as north-north-west; it forced us to lower our topsails right down and run before the wind while it was at its most violent.
The rest of the night passed in continual rain, but the wind died away entirely, and the winds came round by degrees to the east.

1803-07-24.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifth, 24 July 1803, the sky was no finer than on the preceding days, and we were almost continually surrounded by mist or drenched with rain. As what I had been observing for several days in the state of the atmosphere reminded me of the form in which the hurricanes commonly felt at the Isle of France [Mauritius] and Bourbon [Réunion] declare themselves, I began to fear that the sky would not clear before we had met with some squalls, and I took my precautions accordingly.
At about eight o'clock, the Casuarina having asked to pass under our stern, we closed with her, and after we had spoken her, Citizen Freycinet informed me
that he had no more firewood. He also told me that, the jaws of his boom having broken the night before in the squall we had had, he could no longer use his mainsail. I was surprised to hear him speak thus, for what he told me served only to show me how few resources he has in himself, not to know how to repair damage so slight and of that kind.
However that may be, I had one of the boats put in the water and the carpenter went to mend his boom. He was also sent a cord of wood and even more, and I pointed out to him that he must be sparing with it, as I would give him no more; that vessel had taken on board enough for more than four months on leaving Timor.
When this task was finished, we hoisted our boat in again and continued on our course.
At noon, the sky being very overcast and heavy, we had no sight of the sun, nor during the rest of the day. On the contrary, the weather promised to be very bad during the night. Towards the end of the day I closed with the Casuarina and, to let her know that I feared bad weather in the night, I had a second reef taken in the topsails, and she furled hers. As the weather was very dark and it rained continually, I expressly enjoined the officers of the watch not to pass her during the night, telling them it was better to let her go ahead than to have her astern. Accordingly, we carried very little sail. During the night the wind often came in gusts and blasts within the squalls, which obliged us to furl our fore topsail and take a third reef in the main. As the sea was beginning to rise, the main topsail was furled at ten o'clock and we ran under the foresail and the mizzen staysail. As a light was kept burning all night and we saw nothing of the Casuarina's, I began to fear losing her, the more so as she will no doubt have run large to ride out the squalls more easily.
This night was, for us, one of the worst we have spent since our departure from Europe. The wind, though violent, had neither the character nor the variability of those experienced in a hurricane, and we had more to suffer from the rain and the heavy sea than from all the rest.

1803-07-25.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixth, 25 July 1803, in the morning, the weather was the same as during the night. The squalls and gusts came with little interval between them, and the sea was very high and heavy. We saw nothing of the Casuarina, but as we had carried little sail during the night, I presumed she was ahead of us and that I should find her again during the day, provided, however, that she had followed the course signalled to her, which, to tell the truth, I much doubted.
During the morning, though the weather was still squally and rainy, the sun showed itself at times, and at noon we had the latitude of 14° 8', very doubtful, which placed us in 94° 31' 17" of longitude by No. 35 and in 95° 12' 12" by No. 31.
In the afternoon and during the night the weather was still squally, with strong gusts, but we were able to carry both topsails with all reefs in. As we saw nothing of the Casuarina in the course of the day, it is to be presumed that we shall not meet her again until we put in at the Isle of France [Mauritius].
The squalls during the night were less frequent than they had been during the day, and the rain less heavy, but the sea being very high and swelling, the ship laboured a little and made water through her upper works.

1803-07-26.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventh, 26 July 1803, the sky, though still dark and laden with vapours, had a better appearance than on the preceding days, and we thought we had reached the end of the bad weather, which I likewise supposed must change at the first quarter of the moon. During the morning we shook a reef out of our topsails and set the mizzen topsail. The sea was also becoming calmer, and the winds, which had been south-south-east for a long time, were less violent.
At noon we observed the latitude as 14° 33' 8", and our longitude was found to be 91° 27' 28" for No. 35 and 92° 9' 57" for No. 31.
In the afternoon it blew a good breeze and the squalls began again, but the rain which came with them was not as disagreeable to receive as that of the past days. We kept the same sail and followed our course, steering west 11° 15' south
The night passed without incident, except that it was less dark than usual and gave us hope that the weather would soon turn fine again.

1803-07-27.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eighth, 27 July 1803, the sky did not have a fine appearance in the morning, but it became fairly clear during the day, and the return of fine weather seemed to us settled. It blew a good breeze during the day, but the sea was still too rough for us to increase our sail.
At noon the latitude was observed as 15° 3' 16", and our longitude was 87° 47' 45" for No. 35 and 88° 31' 43" for No. 31.
In spite of the appearance we had had in the morning of seeing the weather turn fine, it clouded over again with dark, thick clouds in the evening. The breeze wind, which had shifted to the south-east, had grown stronger, and the sea had lost little of its height and swell. Nevertheless, we had no bad weather during the night, which was merely very dark and during which we had occasional brief showers of rain.

1803-07-28.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the ninth, 28 July 1803, the sea was less high than usual and the wind steadier, without squalls or strong gusts, which allowed us to set our mainsail, but the sky was still dark and of bad appearance.
At noon we observed the latitude as 15° 40' 59", and the longitude indicated by No. 35 was 84° 13' 0" and for No. 31, 84° 58' 41".
During the evening, the clouds having dispersed again, we shook a reef out of our topsails and even set our staysails. During the night, the weather having turned entirely fine, no change was made to the sail and we followed the same course, heading west 11° 15' south.

1803-07-29.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the tenth, 29 July 1803, the sky continued fine, and although it was very cloudy, the clouds (no longer) had the gloomy and disagreeable aspect of those that had accompanied us for so long.
During the morning all hands were turned up for a general clear-out, and everyone was ordered to bring his clothes up on deck to dry them. The decks and between-decks were also fumigated.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 18' 0", and our longitude was, for No. 35, 80° 37' 30" and 81° 25' 55" for No. 31. As the sea was becoming fairly smooth, the topgallant sails were rigged and set as soon as they were aloft.
The night passed without incident. Only a few gusts passed, which made us furl our topgallant sails. The winds varied to east-south-east and were moderate though gusty.

1803-07-30.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the eleventh, 30 July 1803, the sky, though cloudy and fine, was not as pleasant to look upon as the day before, and at various points of the horizon rain clouds could be seen, which foretold a further change in the weather.
At the morning inspection the carpenters reported to me that our main topmast, having laboured in the squalls we had weathered, was somewhat damaged in the mortise through which the fid passes, and that it was to be feared that there might happen (to us) what we had already experienced with our fore topmast on the passage from France to the Isle of France [Mauritius]. The fid had eaten into the mortise by more than an inch, in spite of the iron stirrup that prevents it from bearing on the wood. This defect was remedied by passing a lashing under the heel of the mast, which was then packed with wedges driven home with a maul.
During the morning I addressed the following letter to the staff officers, the geographer and the naturalists:
Citizen,
"In accordance with the imperative orders of the Government, you are advised that you are to collect "all the journals, memoirs and notes which each of you individually must have written from the "beginning of the voyage up to this time. These works being the property of the Government, I "am expressly ordered to claim them.
"You will therefore be so good as to hand me all these papers when we have
"reached the longitude of the island of Rodrigues. They will be placed, in your presence, in a "chest which will be sealed and addressed to the Minister of Marine.
"Each of you, in reply to this letter, will declare on his word of honour that he has kept back "no journal or writing relating to the expedition".
Greetings. N. B.
This letter will be transcribed into the log as soon as it has been read out by the officer of the guard.
At noon the latitude was observed as 16° 59' 29", and our longitude by our timekeepers was 77° 26' 47" for No. 35 and 78° 16' 53" for No. 31.
In the afternoon the sky was fairly fine, but the sea, still heavily swelling, in no way resembled that usually met with in these waters. At the beginning of the night (the sky,) which had seemed about to turn fine, clouded over again, giving us continual though light rain and at times a few squalls. The wind having greatly increased, the studding sails and topgallant sails had to be taken in.

1803-07-31.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the twelfth, 31 July 1803, in the morning, the sky remained overcast and rainy, but the winds were less strong than during the night. We steadily followed the west by south course under easy sail, so as not to strain our masts too much, nor the hull of the ship, which the continual agitation of the heavy sea greatly distressed.
Our sick, who numbered twenty, obtained little relief from the remedies administered to them, which was attributed to the damp and unhealthy air that had surrounded us for so long.
Our quadrupeds were no less wearied than all of us by the bad weather and the motion of the ship, and I much fear losing several of them if it continues any longer without at least some intervals that allow them to regain strength.
At noon we had no sight of the sun, and by our dead reckoning we reckoned ourselves in 18° 1' 38" of latitude and 75° 21' 17" of longitude. As for several days we had always found differences to the north in the latitude of 15 to 18 minutes, it is to be presumed that the estimated latitude of 18° 1' 38" is greater than the one we should have found had the sun shown itself.
In the afternoon it blew a strong breeze with rain and squalls, and the sky took on so bad an appearance for the night that at the end of the day we took a second reef in our topsails. This precaution was not useless, for the night was bad, and we had squalls, rain and strong gusts more continually, which made us make good way on the point of the compass we were following.

1803-08-01.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the thirteenth, 1 August 1803, the rain, squalls and gusts continued as the day before and with the same force. Nevertheless, during the morning, the sky cleared a little. And at noon we were able to observe the latitude, which was 18° 32' 24", and our longitude 71° 27' 55" for No. 31 and 70° 34' 21" for No. 35. These results, compared with the estimated course over 48 hours, gave a difference of 30 minutes to the north, which agreed fairly well with that we had found on the preceding days. The greater part of the cause of these differences must, in my opinion, be attributed to the heavy sea raised by the bad weather rather than to a particular current setting us to the north. Perhaps too these two causes are combined.
In the afternoon the sky, though cloudy, was fairly fine and, although the sea remained very rough, we shook a reef out of our topsails at the end of the day. And during part of the night we were able to carry the topgallant sails, but not for long, for the rain and squalls soon began again once the moon had passed its meridian.

1803-08-02.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fourteenth, 2 August 1803, the winds, though blowing fresh, were unsteady and variable, now from east towards north and now from east towards south. The rain did not cease until about nine o'clock, but then the sky became clear, so as to promise us fine weather at least for the rest of the day.
At noon the latitude was observed as 19° 26' 47", and our longitudes were 67° 13' 29" for No. 35 and 68° 8' 26" for No. 31. These twenty-four hours, contrary to the usual, gave only 3 minutes to the north of the dead reckoning.
During the evening the weather remained fine and the sea seemed to have gone down a little. We lost that day one of our emus, which was stuffed for the Muséum. It was the second to have fallen victim since the heavy weather had been with us. In spite of this misfortune, I should think myself very fortunate if I succeed in preserving the two of this species that remain to me.
At sunset, the sky being decidedly fine, we set our studding sails and topgallant sails, which we kept all night, steering west 5° south, the point of the compass on which we had begun to steer at noon. The sky was very pleasant all night and the sea fairly smooth, though still swelling and rough.

1803-08-03.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the fifteenth, 3 August 1803, in the morning, the weather remained fine, and although the sea was still swelling and rough, we crowded sail to get as far west as possible while the sky had a fine appearance.
At noon the latitude was observed as 20° 7' 51", and our longitude was 64° 24' 19" for No. 35 and 65° 20' 11" for No. 31. We did not experience,
in the twenty-four hours, the differences of the preceding days, and as the sea was hardly less high or swelling than that we had passed through, it seems probable that the differences of 15 to 18 minutes to the north which we had for five or six days running must be attributed to a current setting us in that direction.
During the rest of the day the weather remained fine. It blew a pleasant breeze and we made no change to our sail during the night. At noon the course had been set west by north.

1803-08-04.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the sixteenth, 4 August 1803, the sky, though very cloudy, was fairly fine, and the sea, which we had found swelling, high and rough for so long, became calmer. We continued the same course with all sail set.
At noon the latitude was observed as 20° 3' 1", and our longitude was, for No. 35, 61° 36' 47" and 62° 33' 30" for No. 31. There was only two minutes' difference between the dead reckoning and the altitude.
As, according to our No. 35, which had always given good results, we should sight the island of Rodrigues before nightfall at the rate we were going, we continued to crowd sail, and at five o'clock we sighted that island, which then bore north-north-west of us at a distance of eight or nine leagues. At eight o'clock it bore north, and we took this last bearing as our point of departure for the landfall at the Isle of France [Mauritius].
During the night it blew a strong breeze and we often had squalls which obliged us to furl our topgallant sails. The sea soon became high and the ship was considerably tossed by it.
Towards the end of the night, having sighted two vessels on our starboard side which seemed to be sailing in company, we shortened sail until daylight in order to make them out.

1803-08-05.journal_baudin_autographe:
On the seventeenth, 5 August 1803, in the morning, the vessels seen during the night were found to be astern, sailing less well than we, who had only our topsails lowered on the cap, although they carried their courses. The nearer to us was a three-master and the other a small brig. Both seemed to me to be American vessels, from their rig and their build. At seven o'clock, seeing that they were not gaining on us although they had set their topgallant sails, we made sail and left them behind.
During the morning the sky was fine, but the sea very rough and swelling, the ship rolling a great deal.
At noon the latitude was observed as (no figures), and our longitude was, for No. 35, (no figures) and, for No. 31, (no figures).
